1. Step 1 — Verify Reason (R): Two non-zero vectors make an obtuse angle $\theta \in \left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \pi\right)$ if and only if $\cos\theta \in (-1, 0)$, which is equivalent to $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} < 0$ and the vectors not being anti-parallel ($\theta \ne \pi$). Hence Reason (R) is true.
  2. Step 2 — Compute $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} < 0$ for all $t \in \mathbb{R}$: We have $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} = (\alpha t)(t) + (6)(-2) + (-3)(-2\alpha t) = \alpha t^2 + 6\alpha t - 12 < 0$. If $\alpha = 0$, this reduces to $-12 < 0$, which holds for all $t \in \mathbb{R}$. If $\alpha \ne 0$, the quadratic is negative for all $t \in \mathbb{R}$ iff $\alpha < 0$ and its discriminant $D = 36\alpha^2 + 48\alpha < 0 \implies 12\alpha(3\alpha + 4) < 0 \implies -\dfrac{4}{3} < \alpha < 0$. Combining both cases gives $\alpha \in \left(-\dfrac{4}{3}, 0\right]$.
  3. Step 3 — Check the anti-parallel exclusion: If $\vec{a} = k\vec{b}$ for some $k < 0$, comparing $\hat{j}$-components gives $6 = -2k \implies k = -3$. Comparing $\hat{i}$-components gives $\alpha t = -3t$, and $\hat{k}$-components give $-3 = 6\alpha t \implies \alpha t = -\dfrac{1}{2} \implies t = \dfrac{1}{6}$ and $\alpha = -3$, which lies outside $\left(-\dfrac{4}{3}, 0\right]$.
  4. Step 4 — Conclude: For every $\alpha \in \left(-\dfrac{4}{3}, 0\right]$, $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} < 0$ and $\vec{a}, \vec{b}$ are never anti-parallel for any $t \in \mathbb{R}$. Thus both (A) and (R) are true and (R) correctly explains (A), confirming option (a).
Q17.stepsLatex:
\begin{align*}
  \vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} &= \alpha t^2 + 6\alpha t - 12 < 0 \quad \forall t \in \mathbb{R} \\
  \text{Case 1 ($\alpha=0$): } \vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} &= -12 < 0,\; \vec{a}=(0,6,-3),\; \vec{b}=(t,-2,0) \text{ (never anti-parallel)} \\
  \text{Case 2 ($\alpha\ne 0$): } \alpha < 0 &\text{ and } D = 36\alpha^2 + 48\alpha < 0 \implies 12\alpha(3\alpha+4) < 0 \implies \alpha \in \left(-\frac{4}{3}, 0\right) \\
  \text{Anti-parallel check: } \vec{a}=k\vec{b} &\implies k = -3 \implies \alpha t = -3t \implies \alpha = -3 \notin \left(-\frac{4}{3}, 0\right].
\end{align*}
Combining both cases gives $\alpha \in (-\frac{4}{3}, 0]$. Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) explains (A).
Q17.trapHtml: Always test the boundary case $\alpha=0$ separately; forgetting it yields the open interval $(-4/3, 0)$.
Q17.finalAnsHtml: Correct Option: (a) — Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).

Q18.questionRecapHtml: Match List I [(P) $|\vec{a}\times\vec{b}|$; (Q) parallelogram area from diagonals; (R) scalar projection; (S) $|\vec{a}+\vec{b}|$ for unit vectors] with List II [(I) $5\sqrt{3}$, (II) $1$, (III) $16$, (IV) $\frac{8}{3}$]. Options: (a) P–III,Q–IV,R–I,S–II (b) P–I,Q–III,R–IV,S–II (c) P–III,Q–I,R–II,S–IV (d) P–III,Q–I,R–IV,S–II.
Q18.conceptHtml: Apply Lagrange's identity, $\text{Area}=\frac{1}{2}|\vec{d}_1\times\vec{d}_2|$, projection $\frac{\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}}{|\vec{b}|}$, and parallelogram law.
Q18.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate (P): Using $|\vec{a}\times\vec{b}| = \sqrt{|\vec{a}|^2|\vec{b}|^2 - (\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b})^2} = \sqrt{5^2\cdot 4^2 - 12^2} = \sqrt{400 - 144} = \sqrt{256} = 16$, we get P–III.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate (Q): Computing the cross product of the diagonals, $\vec{d}_1\times\vec{d}_2 = \begin{vmatrix}\hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k}\\ 3 & 1 & -2\\ 1 & -3 & 4\end{vmatrix} = -2\hat{i} - 14\hat{j} - 10\hat{k}$. The area of the parallelogram is $\dfrac{1}{2}|\vec{d}_1\times\vec{d}_2| = \dfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{4 + 196 + 100} = \dfrac{\sqrt{300}}{2} = 5\sqrt{3}$, giving Q–I.
  3. Step 3 — Evaluate (R): The scalar projection of $\vec{a}$ on $\vec{b}$ is $\dfrac{\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}}{|\vec{b}|} = \dfrac{(2)(1) + (-3)(2) + (6)(2)}{\sqrt{1^2 + 2^2 + 2^2}} = \dfrac{2 - 6 + 12}{3} = \dfrac{8}{3}$, giving R–IV.
  4. Step 4 — Evaluate (S) and match: By the parallelogram law, $|\vec{a}+\vec{b}|^2 + |\vec{a}-\vec{b}|^2 = 2(|\vec{a}|^2 + |\vec{b}|^2) = 2(1 + 1) = 4$. With $|\vec{a}-\vec{b}|^2 = 3$, we get $|\vec{a}+\vec{b}|^2 = 1 \implies |\vec{a}+\vec{b}| = 1$, giving S–II. Thus P–III, Q–I, R–IV, S–II, confirming option (d).
Q18.trapHtml: Do not miss the $\frac{1}{2}$ factor in (Q): when diagonals $\vec{d}_1,\vec{d}_2$ are given, area is $\frac{1}{2}|\vec{d}_1\times\vec{d}_2|$, not $|\vec{d}_1\times\vec{d}_2|$.
Q18.finalAnsHtml: Correct Option: (d) — P–III, Q–I, R–IV, S–II

Q19.questionRecapHtml: Count how many of the four statements (I)–(IV) are ALWAYS true for non-zero $\vec{a},\vec{b},\vec{c}\in\mathbb{R}^3$. Options: (a) $1$   (b) $3$   (c) $2$   (d) $4$.
Q19.conceptHtml: Test cancellation laws, orthogonality, Lagrange's identity, and $\ell_\infty$–$\ell_2$ norm bounds.
Q19.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Check Statements 1 and 2: Squaring $|\vec{a}+\vec{b}| = |\vec{a}-\vec{b}|$ yields $|\vec{a}|^2 + |\vec{b}|^2 + 2\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} = |\vec{a}|^2 + |\vec{b}|^2 - 2\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} \implies 4\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} = 0$, so $\vec{a}\perp\vec{b}$ (Statement 1 is true). For Statement 2, $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} = \vec{a}\cdot\vec{c} \implies \vec{a}\cdot(\vec{b}-\vec{c}) = 0$, which allows $\vec{b} \ne \vec{c}$ whenever $\vec{b}-\vec{c}\perp\vec{a}$—for instance $\vec{a}=\hat{i}$, $\vec{b}=\hat{j}$, $\vec{c}=\hat{k}$ (Statement 2 is false).
  2. Step 2 — Check Statement 3: $|\vec{a}\times\vec{b}|^2 + (\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b})^2 = |\vec{a}|^2|\vec{b}|^2(\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta) = |\vec{a}|^2|\vec{b}|^2$, which is Lagrange's identity and holds universally (Statement 3 is true).
  3. Step 3 — Check Statement 4: Let $M = \max\{|a_1|, |a_2|, |a_3|\}$. Since each $a_i^2 \ge 0$ and $a_i^2 \le M^2$, we have $M^2 \le a_1^2 + a_2^2 + a_3^2 \le 3M^2$. Taking square roots gives $M \le |\vec{a}| \le \sqrt{3}M$ (Statement 4 is true).
  4. Step 4 — Count the true statements: Exactly $3$ of the $4$ statements (1, 3, and 4) are always true, confirming option (b).
Q19.stepsLatex:
\begin{align*}
  \text{(I)} \quad |\vec{a}+\vec{b}|^2 = |\vec{a}-\vec{b}|^2 &\iff 4\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} = 0 \iff \vec{a}\perp\vec{b} \quad (\text{TRUE}) \\
  \text{(II)} \quad \vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} = \vec{a}\cdot\vec{c} &\iff \vec{a}\cdot(\vec{b}-\vec{c}) = 0 \not\Rightarrow \vec{b}=\vec{c} \quad (\text{FALSE}) \\
  \text{(III)} \quad |\vec{a}\times\vec{b}|^2 + (\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b})^2 &= |\vec{a}|^2|\vec{b}|^2(\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta) = |\vec{a}|^2|\vec{b}|^2 \quad (\text{TRUE}) \\
  \text{(IV)} \quad M = \max\{|a_1|,|a_2|,|a_3|\} &\implies M^2 \le a_1^2+a_2^2+a_3^2 \le 3M^2 \implies M \le |\vec{a}| \le \sqrt{3}M \quad (\text{TRUE}).
\end{align*}
Exactly $3$ statements (I, III, IV) are always true.
Q19.trapHtml: Vector dot product does NOT obey cancellation: $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}=\vec{a}\cdot\vec{c}$ only implies $\vec{b}-\vec{c} \perp \vec{a}$.

Q20.questionRecapHtml: Tetrahedron $ABCD$ has mutually $\perp$ edges $AB,AC,AD$; areas of $\triangle ABC, \triangle ACD, \triangle ADB$ are $5,6,7$. Find $\text{Area}(\triangle BCD)$. Options: (a) $\sqrt{110}$   (b) $12$   (c) $7\sqrt{3}$   (d) $\sqrt{340}$.
Q20.conceptHtml: Set $A(0,0,0)$, $B(p,0,0)$, $C(0,q,0)$, $D(0,0,r)$ and compute $\text{Area}(\triangle BCD) = \frac{1}{2}|\vec{BC}\times\vec{BD}|$.
Q20.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Place the mutually perpendicular edges along coordinate axes: Choose $A = (0,0,0)$, $B = (a,0,0)$, $C = (0,b,0)$, and $D = (0,0,c)$ with $a, b, c > 0$.
  2. Step 2 — Express the given face areas: Since the three faces meeting at $A$ are right-angled triangles, $\text{Area}(\triangle ABC) = \dfrac{1}{2}ab = 5$, $\text{Area}(\triangle ACD) = \dfrac{1}{2}bc = 6$, and $\text{Area}(\triangle ADB) = \dfrac{1}{2}ca = 7$.
  3. Step 3 — Find $\text{Area}(\triangle BCD)$ using the cross product: With $\overrightarrow{BC} = -a\hat{i} + b\hat{j}$ and $\overrightarrow{BD} = -a\hat{i} + c\hat{k}$, we compute $\overrightarrow{BC}\times\overrightarrow{BD} = \begin{vmatrix}\hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k}\\ -a & b & 0\\ -a & 0 & c\end{vmatrix} = bc\hat{i} + ac\hat{j} + ab\hat{k}$.
  4. Step 4 — Apply de Gua's theorem to compute the value: $\text{Area}(\triangle BCD) = \dfrac{1}{2}|\overrightarrow{BC}\times\overrightarrow{BD}| = \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{bc}{2}\right)^2 + \left(\dfrac{ac}{2}\right)^2 + \left(\dfrac{ab}{2}\right)^2} = \sqrt{6^2 + 7^2 + 5^2} = \sqrt{36 + 49 + 25} = \sqrt{110}$ sq. units, confirming option (a).
Q20.trapHtml: De Gua's theorem (3D Pythagoras for areas) gives $\Delta_{BCD}=\sqrt{\Delta_1^2+\Delta_2^2+\Delta_3^2}$ in 5 seconds.

Q21.questionRecapHtml: $\vec{a}=2\hat{i}-\hat{j}+3\hat{k}$, $\vec{b}=3\hat{i}-5\hat{j}+\hat{k}$, $\vec{a}\times\vec{c}=\vec{c}\times\vec{b}$, $(\vec{a}+\vec{c})\cdot(\vec{b}+\vec{c})=168$. Find max $|\vec{c}|^2$. Options: (a) $77$   (b) $154$   (c) $308$   (d) $462$.
Q21.conceptHtml: $\vec{a}\times\vec{c}=\vec{c}\times\vec{b} \iff (\vec{a}+\vec{b})\times\vec{c}=\vec{0} \implies \vec{c}=\lambda(\vec{a}+\vec{b})$.
Q21.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Express $\vec{c}$ from the cross-product condition: Rearranging $\vec{a}\times\vec{c} = \vec{c}\times\vec{b} = -\vec{b}\times\vec{c}$ gives $(\vec{a} + \vec{b})\times\vec{c} = \vec{0}$. Therefore, $\vec{c} = \lambda(\vec{a} + \vec{b})$ for some scalar $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$.
  2. Step 2 — Compute $\vec{a} + \vec{b}$, $|\vec{a}+\vec{b}|^2$, and $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}$: $\vec{a} + \vec{b} = 5\hat{i} - 6\hat{j} + 4\hat{k}$, so $|\vec{a}+\vec{b}|^2 = 5^2 + (-6)^2 + 4^2 = 77$, and $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} = (2)(3) + (-1)(-5) + (3)(1) = 14$.
  3. Step 3 — Substitute into the dot-product equation: Expanding $(\vec{a}+\vec{c})\cdot(\vec{b}+\vec{c}) = 168$ gives $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} + \vec{c}\cdot(\vec{a}+\vec{b}) + |\vec{c}|^2 = 168$. Using $\vec{c} = \lambda(\vec{a}+\vec{b})$, this becomes $14 + 77\lambda + 77\lambda^2 = 168 \implies 77(\lambda^2 + \lambda) = 154 \implies \lambda^2 + \lambda - 2 = 0$.
  4. Step 4 — Solve for $\lambda$ and maximize $|\vec{c}|^2$: Factoring gives $(\lambda + 2)(\lambda - 1) = 0$, so $\lambda = 1$ or $\lambda = -2$. Since $|\vec{c}|^2 = 77\lambda^2$, its maximum value is $77(-2)^2 = 77 \times 4 = 308$, confirming option (c).
Q21.stepsLatex:
\begin{align*}
  \vec{a}\times\vec{c} + \vec{b}\times\vec{c} = \vec{0} &\implies \vec{c} = \lambda(\vec{a}+\vec{b}), \quad \vec{a}+\vec{b} = 5\hat{i}-6\hat{j}+4\hat{k} \\
  |\vec{a}+\vec{b}|^2 &= 25 + 36 + 16 = 77, \qquad \vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} = 6 + 5 + 3 = 14 \\
  (\vec{a}+\vec{c})\cdot(\vec{b}+\vec{c}) &= \vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} + (\vec{a}+\vec{b})\cdot\vec{c} + |\vec{c}|^2 = 14 + 77\lambda + 77\lambda^2 = 168 \\
  77(\lambda^2 + \lambda - 2) &= 0 \implies (\lambda+2)(\lambda-1) = 0 \implies \lambda \in \{-2, 1\} \\
  \max |\vec{c}|^2 &= \max\{\lambda^2\}\cdot 77 = (-2)^2\cdot 77 = 308.
\end{align*}
Q21.trapHtml: Watch the order in $\vec{a}\times\vec{c} = \vec{c}\times\vec{b} = -\vec{b}\times\vec{c}$, which gives $\vec{a}+\vec{b}$, NOT $\vec{a}-\vec{b}$.

Q22.questionRecapHtml: $|\vec{a}|=2$, $|\vec{b}|=3$, $\vec{a}=\vec{b}\times\vec{c}$, angle $\alpha\in(0,\frac{\pi}{3}]$ between $\vec{b},\vec{c}$. Find min $27|\vec{c}-\vec{a}|^2$. Options: (a) $105$   (b) $110$   (c) $121$   (d) $124$.
Q22.conceptHtml: $\vec{a}=\vec{b}\times\vec{c} \implies \vec{a}\cdot\vec{c}=0$ and $|\vec{a}| = |\vec{b}||\vec{c}|\sin\alpha$.
Q22.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Express $|\vec{c}|$ in terms of $\alpha$: Taking the magnitude of $\vec{a} = \vec{b}\times\vec{c}$ gives $|\vec{a}| = |\vec{b}|\,|\vec{c}|\sin\alpha$. Substituting $|\vec{a}| = 2$ and $|\vec{b}| = 3$ yields $2 = 3|\vec{c}|\sin\alpha \implies |\vec{c}| = \dfrac{2}{3\sin\alpha}$.
  2. Step 2 — Expand $|\vec{c} - \vec{a}|^2$: Since $\vec{a} = \vec{b}\times\vec{c}$ is perpendicular to $\vec{c}$, we have $\vec{c}\cdot\vec{a} = 0$. Thus $|\vec{c} - \vec{a}|^2 = |\vec{c}|^2 + |\vec{a}|^2 - 2(\vec{c}\cdot\vec{a}) = \dfrac{4}{9\sin^2\alpha} + 4$.
  3. Step 3 — Multiply by $27$ and minimize over $\alpha \in \left(0, \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right]$: We get $27|\vec{c} - \vec{a}|^2 = \dfrac{12}{\sin^2\alpha} + 108$. Because $\sin\alpha$ is strictly increasing on $\left(0, \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right]$, $\dfrac{12}{\sin^2\alpha}$ is minimized when $\sin\alpha$ is largest, i.e., at $\alpha = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$ where $\sin^2\alpha = \dfrac{3}{4}$.
  4. Step 4 — Compute the minimum value: Substituting $\sin^2\alpha = \dfrac{3}{4}$ gives $\dfrac{12}{3/4} + 108 = 16 + 108 = 124$, confirming option (d).
Q22.trapHtml: Recognize $\vec{a}\perp\vec{c}$ immediately from $\vec{a}=\vec{b}\times\vec{c}$ so the $-2\vec{a}\cdot\vec{c}$ term drops out.

Q23.subtopic: Section Formula with Dot & Cross Products
Q23.questionRecapHtml: $A$ divides $P(-1,-1,2)$ and $Q(5,5,10)$ internally in ratio $r:1$ ($r>0$). Given $(\vec{OQ}\cdot\vec{OA}) - \frac{1}{5}|\vec{OP}\times\vec{OA}|^2 = 10$, find $r$. Options: (a) $3$   (b) $7$   (c) $\sqrt{7}$   (d) $14$.
Q23.conceptHtml: Write $\vec{OA} = \dfrac{r\vec{q}+\vec{p}}{r+1}$ and use $\vec{p}\times\vec{p}=\vec{0}$ to simplify $\vec{OP}\times\vec{OA} = \dfrac{r}{r+1}(\vec{p}\times\vec{q})$.
Q23.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Write $\vec{OA}$ using the internal section formula: Since $A$ divides $PQ$ internally in the ratio $r:1$, $\vec{OA} = \dfrac{r\vec{OQ} + \vec{OP}}{r + 1}$, where $\vec{OP} = -\hat{i}-\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$ and $\vec{OQ} = 5\hat{i}+5\hat{j}+10\hat{k}$.
  2. Step 2 — Compute $\vec{OQ}\cdot\vec{OA}$: We have $|\vec{OQ}|^2 = 5^2 + 5^2 + 10^2 = 150$ and $\vec{OP}\cdot\vec{OQ} = -5 - 5 + 20 = 10$, so $\vec{OQ}\cdot\vec{OA} = \dfrac{150r + 10}{r + 1}$.
  3. Step 3 — Compute $|\vec{OP}\times\vec{OA}|^2$: Using $\vec{OP}\times\vec{OP} = \vec{0}$, we get $\vec{OP}\times\vec{OA} = \dfrac{r}{r+1}(\vec{OP}\times\vec{OQ})$. Here $\vec{OP}\times\vec{OQ} = \begin{vmatrix}\hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k}\\ -1 & -1 & 2\\ 5 & 5 & 10\end{vmatrix} = -20\hat{i} + 20\hat{j}$, so $|\vec{OP}\times\vec{OQ}|^2 = 800$ and $\dfrac{1}{5}|\vec{OP}\times\vec{OA}|^2 = \dfrac{160r^2}{(r+1)^2}$.
  4. Step 4 — Solve the given equation for $r > 0$: $\dfrac{150r + 10}{r + 1} - \dfrac{160r^2}{(r+1)^2} = 10$. Multiplying by $(r+1)^2$ gives $(150r+10)(r+1) - 160r^2 = 10(r^2 + 2r + 1) \implies -10r^2 + 160r + 10 = 10r^2 + 20r + 10 \implies 20r^2 = 140r \implies r = 7$, confirming option (b).
Q23.stepsLatex:
\begin{align*}
  \vec{p} &= (-1,-1,2),\quad \vec{q} = (5,5,10) \implies |\vec{q}|^2 = 150,\quad \vec{p}\cdot\vec{q} = 10 \\
  \vec{p}\times\vec{q} &= \begin{vmatrix}\hat{i}&\hat{j}&\hat{k}\\-1&-1&2\\5&5&10\end{vmatrix} = -20\hat{i}+20\hat{j} \implies |\vec{p}\times\vec{q}|^2 = 800 \\
  \vec{OQ}\cdot\vec{OA} &= \frac{150r+10}{r+1}, \qquad \frac{1}{5}|\vec{OP}\times\vec{OA}|^2 = \frac{160r^2}{(r+1)^2} \\
  \frac{150r+10}{r+1} - \frac{160r^2}{(r+1)^2} &= 10 \implies (150r+10)(r+1) - 160r^2 = 10(r+1)^2 \\
  -10r^2 + 160r + 10 &= 10r^2 + 20r + 10 \implies 20r^2 = 140r \implies r = 7\;(r>0).
\end{align*}
Q23.trapHtml: Keep $\vec{OA}$ symbolically as $\frac{r\vec{q}+\vec{p}}{r+1}$ instead of expanding coordinates in $\vec{OP}\times\vec{OA}$.

Q24.questionRecapHtml: Least positive integer $\alpha$ for which the angle between $\alpha\hat{i}-2\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$ and $\alpha\hat{i}+2\alpha\hat{j}-2\hat{k}$ is acute.
Q24.conceptHtml: Acute angle between non-parallel non-zero vectors $\iff \vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} > 0$.
Q24.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Apply the condition for an acute angle: Two non-zero vectors $\vec{u}$ and $\vec{v}$ form an acute angle if and only if $\vec{u}\cdot\vec{v} > 0$ (and they are not parallel).
  2. Step 2 — Compute the dot product: $(\alpha\hat{i} - 2\hat{j} + 2\hat{k})\cdot(\alpha\hat{i} + 2\alpha\hat{j} - 2\hat{k}) = \alpha^2 - 4\alpha - 4 > 0$.
  3. Step 3 — Solve the quadratic inequality: The roots of $\alpha^2 - 4\alpha - 4 = 0$ are $\alpha = \dfrac{4 \pm \sqrt{16 + 16}}{2} = 2 \pm 2\sqrt{2}$. For $\alpha > 0$, we need $\alpha > 2 + 2\sqrt{2} \approx 4.828$.
  4. Step 4 — Identify the least positive integer: The smallest positive integer greater than $4.828$ is $\alpha = 5$ (at $\alpha = 5$, the vectors $(5,-2,2)$ and $(5,10,-2)$ are clearly non-parallel). Thus the required value is 5.
Q24.trapHtml: Check $\alpha=4$: $16-16-4 = -4 < 0$ (obtuse); the first positive value is $\alpha=5$.

Q25.questionRecapHtml: Sides of $\triangle ABC$ are $2\hat{i}-\hat{j}+\hat{k}$, $\hat{i}-3\hat{j}-5\hat{k}$, and $3\hat{i}-4\hat{j}-4\hat{k}$; $G$ is centroid. Find $6(|AG|^2+|BG|^2+|CG|^2)$.
Q25.conceptHtml: For any triangle with side lengths $a,b,c$ and centroid $G$: $|AG|^2+|BG|^2+|CG|^2 = \dfrac{1}{3}(a^2+b^2+c^2)$.
Q25.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Compute the squared lengths of the three sides: Note that $(2\hat{i}-\hat{j}+\hat{k}) + (\hat{i}-3\hat{j}-5\hat{k}) = 3\hat{i}-4\hat{j}-4\hat{k}$, confirming these vectors form a closed triangle with side lengths $a^2 = 2^2 + (-1)^2 + 1^2 = 6$, $b^2 = 1^2 + (-3)^2 + (-5)^2 = 35$, and $c^2 = 3^2 + (-4)^2 + (-4)^2 = 41$.
  2. Step 2 — Relate centroid distances to side lengths: By Apollonius's theorem, the medians satisfy $m_a^2 = \dfrac{2b^2 + 2c^2 - a^2}{4}$, and similarly for $m_b^2$ and $m_c^2$. Since the centroid divides each median in the ratio $2:1$, $|AG|^2 = \dfrac{4}{9}m_a^2 = \dfrac{2b^2 + 2c^2 - a^2}{9}$.
  3. Step 3 — Sum over all three vertices: Adding the cyclic expressions gives $|AG|^2 + |BG|^2 + |CG|^2 = \dfrac{3(a^2 + b^2 + c^2)}{9} = \dfrac{a^2 + b^2 + c^2}{3}$.
  4. Step 4 — Compute the final value: $6\bigl(|AG|^2 + |BG|^2 + |CG|^2\bigr) = 2(a^2 + b^2 + c^2) = 2(6 + 35 + 41) = 2(82) = 164$, confirming the answer 164.
Q25.trapHtml: Using the $\frac{1}{3}(a^2+b^2+c^2)$ identity avoids finding individual vertex coordinates or medians.

Q26.questionRecapHtml: $\vec{c}$ is projection vector of $\vec{b}=\lambda\hat{i}+4\hat{k}$ ($\lambda>0$) on $\vec{a}=\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$. If $|\vec{a}+\vec{c}|=7$, find area of parallelogram formed by $\vec{b}$ and $\vec{c}$.
Q26.conceptHtml: Vector projection $\vec{c} = \left(\dfrac{\vec{b}\cdot\vec{a}}{|\vec{a}|^2}\right)\vec{a}$; parallelogram area $= |\vec{b}\times\vec{c}|$.
Q26.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Write the projection vector $\vec{c}$: With $\vec{a} = \hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + 2\hat{k}$ ($|\vec{a}| = 3$) and $\vec{b} = \lambda\hat{i} + 4\hat{k}$, the projection vector of $\vec{b}$ onto $\vec{a}$ is $\vec{c} = \dfrac{\vec{b}\cdot\vec{a}}{|\vec{a}|^2}\vec{a} = \dfrac{\lambda + 8}{9}\vec{a}$.
  2. Step 2 — Find $\lambda > 0$ from $|\vec{a} + \vec{c}| = 7$: We have $\vec{a} + \vec{c} = \left(1 + \dfrac{\lambda + 8}{9}\right)\vec{a} = \dfrac{\lambda + 17}{9}\vec{a}$. Taking magnitudes with $\lambda > 0$ gives $\dfrac{\lambda + 17}{9}\cdot 3 = 7 \implies \lambda + 17 = 21 \implies \lambda = 4$.
  3. Step 3 — Express $\vec{b}$ and $\vec{c}$ explicitly: Substituting $\lambda = 4$ gives $\vec{b} = 4\hat{i} + 4\hat{k}$ and $\vec{c} = \dfrac{12}{9}\vec{a} = \dfrac{4}{3}\vec{a}$.
  4. Step 4 — Compute the area of the parallelogram: $\text{Area} = |\vec{b}\times\vec{c}| = \dfrac{4}{3}|\vec{b}\times\vec{a}|$. Computing $\vec{b}\times\vec{a} = \begin{vmatrix}\hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k}\\ 4 & 0 & 4\\ 1 & 2 & 2\end{vmatrix} = -8\hat{i} - 4\hat{j} + 8\hat{k}$ gives $|\vec{b}\times\vec{a}| = \sqrt{64 + 16 + 64} = 12$. Hence the area is $\dfrac{4}{3}\times 12 = 16$, confirming the answer 16.
Q26.stepsLatex:
\begin{align*}
  |\vec{a}| &= \sqrt{1+4+4} = 3, \qquad \vec{c} = \frac{\lambda+8}{9}\vec{a} \\
  \vec{a} + \vec{c} &= \left(1 + \frac{\lambda+8}{9}\right)\vec{a} = \frac{\lambda+17}{9}\vec{a} \\
  |\vec{a}+\vec{c}| &= \frac{\lambda+17}{9}\cdot 3 = 7 \implies \lambda + 17 = 21 \implies \lambda = 4\;(\lambda>0) \\
  \vec{b} &= 4\hat{i}+4\hat{k}, \qquad \vec{c} = \frac{4}{3}(\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+2\hat{k}) \\
  \vec{b}\times\vec{c} &= \frac{16}{3}\begin{vmatrix}\hat{i}&\hat{j}&\hat{k}\\1&0&1\\1&2&2\end{vmatrix} = \frac{16}{3}(-2\hat{i}-\hat{j}+2\hat{k}) \implies |\vec{b}\times\vec{c}| = \frac{16}{3}\cdot 3 = 16.
\end{align*}
Q26.trapHtml: Factor scalars out of the determinant: $\frac{16}{3}$ pulls clean outside, leaving a tiny $3\times 3$ cross product of length $3$.

Q27.questionRecapHtml: $|\vec{a}|=1$, $|\vec{b}|=4$, $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}=2$, $\vec{c}=(2\vec{a}\times\vec{b})-3\vec{b}$. If angle between $\vec{b}$ and $\vec{c}$ is $\alpha$, find $192\sin^2\alpha$.
Q27.conceptHtml: Since $(\vec{a}\times\vec{b})\perp\vec{b}$, $|\vec{c}|^2 = 4|\vec{a}\times\vec{b}|^2 + 9|\vec{b}|^2$ and $\vec{b}\cdot\vec{c} = -3|\vec{b}|^2$.
Q27.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Compute $|\vec{a}\times\vec{b}|^2$: Using Lagrange's identity, $|\vec{a}\times\vec{b}|^2 = |\vec{a}|^2|\vec{b}|^2 - (\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b})^2 = (1)^2(4)^2 - 2^2 = 16 - 4 = 12$.
  2. Step 2 — Find $|\vec{c}|^2$ using orthogonality: In $\vec{c} = 2(\vec{a}\times\vec{b}) - 3\vec{b}$, the two terms are mutually perpendicular because $(\vec{a}\times\vec{b})\cdot\vec{b} = 0$. By Pythagoras's theorem, $|\vec{c}|^2 = 4|\vec{a}\times\vec{b}|^2 + 9|\vec{b}|^2 = 4(12) + 9(16) = 48 + 144 = 192$.
  3. Step 3 — Find $\sin^2\alpha$: Taking the cross product of $\vec{b}$ with $\vec{c}$ gives $\vec{b}\times\vec{c} = 2\,\vec{b}\times(\vec{a}\times\vec{b})$. Since $\vec{b} \perp (\vec{a}\times\vec{b})$, $|\vec{b}\times\vec{c}| = 2|\vec{b}|\,|\vec{a}\times\vec{b}|$. Therefore, $\sin\alpha = \dfrac{|\vec{b}\times\vec{c}|}{|\vec{b}|\,|\vec{c}|} = \dfrac{2|\vec{a}\times\vec{b}|}{|\vec{c}|} \implies \sin^2\alpha = \dfrac{4|\vec{a}\times\vec{b}|^2}{|\vec{c}|^2} = \dfrac{48}{192}$.
  4. Step 4 — Evaluate $192\sin^2\alpha$: Multiplying both sides by $192$ gives $192\sin^2\alpha = 48$, confirming the answer 48.
Q27.stepsLatex:
\begin{align*}
  |\vec{a}\times\vec{b}|^2 &= |\vec{a}|^2|\vec{b}|^2 - (\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b})^2 = 1(16) - 4 = 12 \\
  |\vec{c}|^2 &= 4(12) + 9(16) = 48 + 144 = 192 \\
  \vec{b}\cdot\vec{c} &= 2\vec{b}\cdot(\vec{a}\times\vec{b}) - 3|\vec{b}|^2 = 0 - 48 = -48 \\
  \cos^2\alpha &= \frac{(\vec{b}\cdot\vec{c})^2}{|\vec{b}|^2|\vec{c}|^2} = \frac{48^2}{16\times 192} = \frac{3}{4} \implies \sin^2\alpha = \frac{1}{4} \\
  192\sin^2\alpha &= 192 \times \frac{1}{4} = 48.
\end{align*}
Q27.trapHtml: Even though $\vec{b}\cdot(\vec{a}\times\vec{b})=0$, the $4|\vec{a}\times\vec{b}|^2$ term still contributes $48$ to $|\vec{c}|^2$; never drop it.

Q28.questionRecapHtml: $\text{Area}(\triangle ABC)=15\sqrt{2}$, $\vec{AB}=\hat{i}+2\hat{j}-7\hat{k}$, $\vec{AC}=6\hat{i}+d\hat{j}-2\hat{k}$ ($d>0$). Find square of largest side of $\triangle ABC$.
Q28.conceptHtml: $\text{Area}(\triangle ABC) = \dfrac{1}{2}|\vec{AB}\times\vec{AC}|$ and $\vec{BC} = \vec{AC} - \vec{AB}$.
Q28.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Compute $\overrightarrow{AB}\times\overrightarrow{AC}$: With $\overrightarrow{AB} = \hat{i} + 2\hat{j} - 7\hat{k}$ and $\overrightarrow{AC} = 6\hat{i} + d\hat{j} - 2\hat{k}$, we have $\overrightarrow{AB}\times\overrightarrow{AC} = \begin{vmatrix}\hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k}\\ 1 & 2 & -7\\ 6 & d & -2\end{vmatrix} = (7d - 4)\hat{i} - 40\hat{j} + (d - 12)\hat{k}$.
  2. Step 2 — Use the triangle area to solve for $d > 0$: Since $\dfrac{1}{2}|\overrightarrow{AB}\times\overrightarrow{AC}| = 15\sqrt{2}$, squaring gives $|\overrightarrow{AB}\times\overrightarrow{AC}|^2 = 1800$, i.e., $(7d - 4)^2 + 1600 + (d - 12)^2 = 1800$. Expanding yields $50d^2 - 80d + 160 = 200 \implies 5d^2 - 8d - 4 = 0 \implies (5d + 2)(d - 2) = 0$. Since $d > 0$, we get $d = 2$.
  3. Step 3 — Find the squared lengths of all three sides: $|\overrightarrow{AB}|^2 = 1^2 + 2^2 + (-7)^2 = 54$; $|\overrightarrow{AC}|^2 = 6^2 + 2^2 + (-2)^2 = 44$; and $\overrightarrow{BC} = \overrightarrow{AC} - \overrightarrow{AB} = 5\hat{i} + 5\hat{k}$, so $|\overrightarrow{BC}|^2 = 5^2 + 0^2 + 5^2 = 50$.
  4. Step 4 — Pick the largest side squared: Comparing $54$, $44$, and $50$, the square of the length of the largest side is 54.
Q28.stepsLatex:
\begin{align*}
  \vec{AB}\times\vec{AC} &= \begin{vmatrix}\hat{i}&\hat{j}&\hat{k}\\1&2&-7\\6&d&-2\end{vmatrix} = (7d-4)\hat{i} - 40\hat{j} + (d-12)\hat{k} \\
  \frac{1}{2}|\vec{AB}\times\vec{AC}| = 15\sqrt{2} &\implies (7d-4)^2 + 1600 + (d-12)^2 = 1800 \\
  50d^2 - 80d + 160 &= 200 \implies 5d^2 - 8d - 4 = 0 \implies (5d+2)(d-2) = 0 \implies d = 2 \\
  |\vec{AB}|^2 &= 1+4+49 = 54, \qquad |\vec{AC}|^2 = 36+4+4 = 44 \\
  \vec{BC} &= \vec{AC}-\vec{AB} = 5\hat{i}+5\hat{k} \implies |\vec{BC}|^2 = 50.
\end{align*}
Largest side squared is $\max\{54, 44, 50\} = 54$.
Q28.trapHtml: Always compute all three sides $|\vec{AB}|^2, |\vec{AC}|^2, |\vec{BC}|^2$; do not assume the side containing $d$ is the largest.

Q29.questionRecapHtml: $\vec{a}=\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+\hat{k}$, $\vec{b}=3\hat{i}-3\hat{j}+3\hat{k}$, $\vec{c}=2\hat{i}-\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$, $\vec{b}\times\vec{d}=\vec{c}\times\vec{d}$, $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{d}=4$. Find $|\vec{a}\times\vec{d}|^2$.
Q29.conceptHtml: $\vec{b}\times\vec{d}=\vec{c}\times\vec{d} \implies (\vec{b}-\vec{c})\times\vec{d}=\vec{0} \implies \vec{d}=\lambda(\vec{b}-\vec{c})$.
Q29.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Express $\vec{d}$ from the cross-product equality: Rearranging $\vec{b}\times\vec{d} = \vec{c}\times\vec{d}$ gives $(\vec{b} - \vec{c})\times\vec{d} = \vec{0}$, so $\vec{d} = \lambda(\vec{b} - \vec{c})$ for some scalar $\lambda$. Here $\vec{b} - \vec{c} = (3-2)\hat{i} + (-3+1)\hat{j} + (3-2)\hat{k} = \hat{i} - 2\hat{j} + \hat{k}$.
  2. Step 2 — Determine $\lambda$ using $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{d} = 4$: Computing $\vec{a}\cdot(\vec{b}-\vec{c}) = (1)(1) + (2)(-2) + (1)(1) = -2$, we get $-2\lambda = 4 \implies \lambda = -2$. Thus $\vec{d} = -2\hat{i} + 4\hat{j} - 2\hat{k}$.
  3. Step 3 — Compute $|\vec{a}\times\vec{d}|^2$ via Lagrange's identity: We have $|\vec{a}|^2 = 1^2 + 2^2 + 1^2 = 6$ and $|\vec{d}|^2 = (-2)^2 + 4^2 + (-2)^2 = 24$. Therefore, $|\vec{a}\times\vec{d}|^2 = |\vec{a}|^2|\vec{d}|^2 - (\vec{a}\cdot\vec{d})^2 = (6)(24) - 4^2 = 144 - 16 = 128$, confirming the answer 128.
Q29.trapHtml: Check Lagrange shortcut: $|\vec{a}|^2=6$, $|\vec{d}|^2=24$, $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{d}=4 \implies |\vec{a}\times\vec{d}|^2 = 6(24)-16 = 128$.

Q30.questionRecapHtml: $\vec{a}=9\hat{i}-13\hat{j}+25\hat{k}$, $\vec{b}=3\hat{i}+7\hat{j}-13\hat{k}$, $\vec{c}=17\hat{i}-2\hat{j}+\hat{k}$, $\vec{r}\times\vec{a}=(\vec{b}+\vec{c})\times\vec{a}$, $\vec{r}\cdot(\vec{b}-\vec{c})=0$. Find $\frac{|593\vec{r}+67\vec{a}|^2}{(593)^2}$.
Q30.conceptHtml: $\vec{r}\times\vec{a}=(\vec{b}+\vec{c})\times\vec{a} \implies \vec{r} = \vec{b}+\vec{c}+\lambda\vec{a}$; avoid computing $\vec{r}$ explicitly!
Q30.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Solve the cross-product equation for $\vec{r}$: Rearranging $\vec{r}\times\vec{a} = (\vec{b}+\vec{c})\times\vec{a}$ gives $\bigl(\vec{r} - (\vec{b}+\vec{c})\bigr)\times\vec{a} = \vec{0}$, so $\vec{r} = (\vec{b}+\vec{c}) + \lambda\vec{a}$ for some scalar $\lambda$.
  2. Step 2 — Compute $\vec{b} + \vec{c}$ and $\vec{b} - \vec{c}$: Adding and subtracting the given vectors gives $\vec{b} + \vec{c} = 20\hat{i} + 5\hat{j} - 12\hat{k}$ and $\vec{b} - \vec{c} = -14\hat{i} + 9\hat{j} - 14\hat{k}$.
  3. Step 3 — Find $\lambda$ using $\vec{r}\cdot(\vec{b}-\vec{c}) = 0$: Dotting $\vec{r} = (\vec{b}+\vec{c}) + \lambda\vec{a}$ with $\vec{b}-\vec{c}$ gives $(\vec{b}+\vec{c})\cdot(\vec{b}-\vec{c}) + \lambda\,\vec{a}\cdot(\vec{b}-\vec{c}) = 0$. Here $(\vec{b}+\vec{c})\cdot(\vec{b}-\vec{c}) = (20)(-14) + (5)(9) + (-12)(-14) = -280 + 45 + 168 = -67$, and $\vec{a}\cdot(\vec{b}-\vec{c}) = (9)(-14) + (-13)(9) + (25)(-14) = -126 - 117 - 350 = -593$. Hence $-67 - 593\lambda = 0 \implies \lambda = -\dfrac{67}{593}$.
  4. Step 4 — Evaluate the target expression: Since $\vec{r} = (\vec{b}+\vec{c}) - \dfrac{67}{593}\vec{a}$, we immediately obtain $\vec{r} + \dfrac{67}{593}\vec{a} = \vec{b} + \vec{c}$. Thus $\dfrac{|593\vec{r} + 67\vec{a}|^2}{(593)^2} = \left|\vec{r} + \dfrac{67}{593}\vec{a}\right|^2 = |\vec{b}+\vec{c}|^2 = 20^2 + 5^2 + (-12)^2 = 400 + 25 + 144 = 569$, confirming the answer 569.
Q30.trapHtml: Spot the exact numbers $593$ and $67$ in the prompt: they cancel $\lambda\vec{a}$ cleanly to leave $|\vec{b}+\vec{c}|^2$.

Q31.conceptHtml: Write $\vec{c} = (x, y, z)$ and solve the linear system formed by $\vec{a} \times \vec{c} = \vec{b}$ together with the scalar dot-product constraint.
Q31.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Take the cross product with $\vec{a}$ on the left: From $\vec{a}\times\vec{c} = \vec{b}$, we get $\vec{a}\times(\vec{a}\times\vec{c}) = \vec{a}\times\vec{b}$. Using the vector triple product identity, $(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{c})\vec{a} - |\vec{a}|^2\vec{c} = \vec{a}\times\vec{b}$.
  2. Step 2 — Compute $|\vec{a}|^2$ and $\vec{a}\times\vec{b}$: $|\vec{a}|^2 = (-1)^2 + 2^2 + 2^2 = 9$, and $\vec{a}\times\vec{b} = \begin{vmatrix}\hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k}\\ -1 & 2 & 2\\ 8 & 7 & -3\end{vmatrix} = -20\hat{i} + 13\hat{j} - 23\hat{k}$. Setting $\lambda = \vec{a}\cdot\vec{c}$, we obtain $9\vec{c} = \lambda(-\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+2\hat{k}) + (20\hat{i} - 13\hat{j} + 23\hat{k})$.
  3. Step 3 — Find $\lambda$ using $\vec{c}\cdot(\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k}) = 4$: Dotting both sides with $\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k}$ gives $9(4) = \lambda(-1 + 2 + 2) + (20 - 13 + 23) \implies 36 = 3\lambda + 30 \implies \lambda = 2$.
  4. Step 4 — Compute $\vec{c}$ and $|\vec{a} + \vec{c}|^2$: Plugging in $\lambda = 2$ gives $9\vec{c} = 18\hat{i} - 9\hat{j} + 27\hat{k} \implies \vec{c} = 2\hat{i} - \hat{j} + 3\hat{k}$. Then $\vec{a} + \vec{c} = \hat{i} + \hat{j} + 5\hat{k}$, so $|\vec{a} + \vec{c}|^2 = 1^2 + 1^2 + 5^2 = 27$, confirming option (d).
Q31.trapHtml: Always verify $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} = -8 + 14 - 6 = 0$ (consistency check) and remember the middle determinant component has a minus sign: $-( (-1)z - 2x) = 2x + z$.

Q32.questionRecapHtml: In $\triangle ABC$, $\vec{p} = \overrightarrow{BC}$, $\vec{q} = \overrightarrow{CA}$, $\vec{r} = \overrightarrow{BA}$ with $|\vec{p}| = 2\sqrt{3}$, $|\vec{q}| = 2$, $\cos\theta = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$. Find $|\vec{p} \times (\vec{q} - 3\vec{r})|^2 + 3|\vec{r}|^2$.
Q32.conceptHtml: By triangle addition, $\overrightarrow{BC} + \overrightarrow{CA} = \overrightarrow{BA}$, so $\vec{r} = \vec{p} + \vec{q}$ (NOT $-\vec{p} - \vec{q}$!). Then use $\vec{p} \times \vec{p} = \vec{0}$ and Lagrange's identity.
Q32.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Relate $\vec{r}$ to $\vec{p}$ and $\vec{q}$ in $\triangle ABC$: By the triangle law of vector addition, $\overrightarrow{BC} + \overrightarrow{CA} = \overrightarrow{BA}$, so $\vec{r} = \vec{p} + \vec{q}$.
  2. Step 2 — Compute $|\vec{r}|^2$: Given $|\vec{p}| = 2\sqrt{3}$, $|\vec{q}| = 2$, and $\cos\theta = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$, we have $\vec{p}\cdot\vec{q} = (2\sqrt{3})(2)\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} = 4$. Thus $|\vec{r}|^2 = |\vec{p}+\vec{q}|^2 = |\vec{p}|^2 + |\vec{q}|^2 + 2(\vec{p}\cdot\vec{q}) = 12 + 4 + 8 = 24$.
  3. Step 3 — Simplify $|\vec{p}\times(\vec{q} - 3\vec{r})|^2$: Substituting $\vec{r} = \vec{p} + \vec{q}$ gives $\vec{q} - 3\vec{r} = -3\vec{p} - 2\vec{q}$. Since $\vec{p}\times\vec{p} = \vec{0}$, $\vec{p}\times(\vec{q} - 3\vec{r}) = -2(\vec{p}\times\vec{q})$. With $\sin^2\theta = 1 - \dfrac{1}{3} = \dfrac{2}{3}$, we obtain $|\vec{p}\times(\vec{q} - 3\vec{r})|^2 = 4|\vec{p}|^2|\vec{q}|^2\sin^2\theta = 4(12)(4)\left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right) = 128$.
  4. Step 4 — Add the two terms: $|\vec{p}\times(\vec{q} - 3\vec{r})|^2 + 3|\vec{r}|^2 = 128 + 3(24) = 128 + 72 = 200$, confirming option (b).
Q32.trapHtml: Watch the arrow direction! $\vec{r} = \overrightarrow{BA}$ (not $\overrightarrow{AB}$), so $\vec{r} = \vec{p} + \vec{q}$; flipping the sign gives the wrong $|\vec{r}|^2 = 8$.

Q33.subtopic: Cross Product & Max Dot Product in Coordinate Plane
Q33.questionRecapHtml: $\vec{a} = (2, -1, 1)$, $\vec{b} = (0, \lambda, 2)$ ($\lambda \in \mathbb{Z}$), $\vec{c} = \vec{a} \times \vec{b}$ with $|\vec{c}| = \sqrt{53}$. For $|\vec{d}| = 2$ in the $yz$-plane, find $\max(\vec{c}\cdot\vec{d})^2$.
Q33.conceptHtml: Solve $|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}|^2 = 53$ for the integer $\lambda$, then apply Cauchy–Schwarz in the $yz$-plane: $\max(\vec{c}\cdot\vec{d})^2 = |\vec{d}|^2(c_y^2 + c_z^2)$.
Q33.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Compute $\vec{c} = \vec{a}\times\vec{b}$: $\vec{c} = \begin{vmatrix}\hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k}\\ 2 & -1 & 1\\ 0 & \lambda & 2\end{vmatrix} = (-2 - \lambda)\hat{i} - 4\hat{j} + 2\lambda\hat{k}$.
  2. Step 2 — Find the integer $\lambda$ from $|\vec{c}| = \sqrt{53}$: Squaring the magnitude gives $(\lambda + 2)^2 + (-4)^2 + (2\lambda)^2 = 53 \implies 5\lambda^2 + 4\lambda - 33 = 0 \implies (5\lambda - 11)(\lambda + 3) = 0$. Since $\lambda \in \mathbb{Z}$, we must have $\lambda = -3$, which gives $\vec{c} = \hat{i} - 4\hat{j} - 6\hat{k}$.
  3. Step 3 — Maximize $(\vec{c}\cdot\vec{d})^2$ in the $yz$-plane: Because $\vec{d}$ lies in the $yz$-plane, write $\vec{d} = y\hat{j} + z\hat{k}$ with $y^2 + z^2 = |\vec{d}|^2 = 4$. Then $\vec{c}\cdot\vec{d} = -4y - 6z = (-4\hat{j} - 6\hat{k})\cdot\vec{d}$.
  4. Step 4 — Apply Cauchy–Schwarz: The maximum value of $(\vec{c}\cdot\vec{d})^2$ occurs when $\vec{d}$ is parallel to $-4\hat{j} - 6\hat{k}$, giving $\bigl((-4)^2 + (-6)^2\bigr)|\vec{d}|^2 = (16 + 36)(4) = 52 \times 4 = 208$, confirming option (c).
Q33.trapHtml: Because $\vec{d}$ lies in the $yz$-plane, $d_x = 0$: do NOT include $c_x^2 = 1$ in the Cauchy–Schwarz bound!

Q34.questionRecapHtml: $\vec{a} = (2, -5, 5)$, $\vec{b} = (1, -1, 3)$, $2(\vec{a} \times \vec{c}) + 3(\vec{b} \times \vec{c}) = \vec{0}$, and $(\vec{a} - \vec{b})\cdot\vec{c} = -97$. Find $|\vec{c} \times \hat{k}|^2$.
Q34.conceptHtml: Factor out $\times\vec{c}$ to get $(2\vec{a} + 3\vec{b}) \times \vec{c} = \vec{0} \implies \vec{c} = t(2\vec{a} + 3\vec{b})$, and note $|\vec{c} \times \hat{k}|^2 = c_x^2 + c_y^2$.
Q34.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Express $\vec{c}$ as a scalar multiple of $2\vec{a} + 3\vec{b}$: Factoring $2(\vec{a}\times\vec{c}) + 3(\vec{b}\times\vec{c}) = \vec{0}$ gives $(2\vec{a} + 3\vec{b})\times\vec{c} = \vec{0}$, so $\vec{c} = \lambda(2\vec{a} + 3\vec{b})$. Computing $2\vec{a} + 3\vec{b} = 2(2\hat{i}-5\hat{j}+5\hat{k}) + 3(\hat{i}-\hat{j}+3\hat{k}) = 7\hat{i} - 13\hat{j} + 19\hat{k}$.
  2. Step 2 — Determine $\lambda$ using $(\vec{a} - \vec{b})\cdot\vec{c} = -97$: Here $\vec{a} - \vec{b} = \hat{i} - 4\hat{j} + 2\hat{k}$, so $(\vec{a} - \vec{b})\cdot(2\vec{a} + 3\vec{b}) = (1)(7) + (-4)(-13) + (2)(19) = 7 + 52 + 38 = 97$. Thus $97\lambda = -97 \implies \lambda = -1$, giving $\vec{c} = -7\hat{i} + 13\hat{j} - 19\hat{k}$.
  3. Step 3 — Compute $|\vec{c}\times\hat{k}|^2$: Since $\hat{i}\times\hat{k} = -\hat{j}$, $\hat{j}\times\hat{k} = \hat{i}$, and $\hat{k}\times\hat{k} = \vec{0}$, we get $\vec{c}\times\hat{k} = 13\hat{i} + 7\hat{j}$. Therefore, $|\vec{c}\times\hat{k}|^2 = 13^2 + 7^2 = 169 + 49 = 218$, confirming option (a).
Q34.trapHtml: Remember $|\vec{c} \times \hat{k}|^2 = c_x^2 + c_y^2$ (drops the $z$-component, NOT $|\vec{c}|^2$).

Q35.questionRecapHtml: Unit vectors $\vec{a}, \vec{b}, \vec{c}$ satisfy $|\vec{a}-\vec{b}|^2 + |\vec{b}-\vec{c}|^2 + |\vec{c}-\vec{a}|^2 = 9$ and $|2\vec{a} + k\vec{b} + k\vec{c}| = 3$. Find $k > 0$.
Q35.conceptHtml: Use the identity $|\vec{a}+\vec{b}+\vec{c}|^2 + |\vec{a}-\vec{b}|^2 + |\vec{b}-\vec{c}|^2 + |\vec{c}-\vec{a}|^2 = 3(|\vec{a}|^2 + |\vec{b}|^2 + |\vec{c}|^2) = 9$.
Q35.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Expand the sum of squared differences: Since $|\vec{a}| = |\vec{b}| = |\vec{c}| = 1$, expanding $|\vec{a}-\vec{b}|^2 + |\vec{b}-\vec{c}|^2 + |\vec{c}-\vec{a}|^2 = 9$ gives $2(|\vec{a}|^2 + |\vec{b}|^2 + |\vec{c}|^2) - 2(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} + \vec{b}\cdot\vec{c} + \vec{c}\cdot\vec{a}) = 9 \implies 6 - 2(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} + \vec{b}\cdot\vec{c} + \vec{c}\cdot\vec{a}) = 9 \implies \vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} + \vec{b}\cdot\vec{c} + \vec{c}\cdot\vec{a} = -\dfrac{3}{2}$.
  2. Step 2 — Show that $\vec{a} + \vec{b} + \vec{c} = \vec{0}$: Computing $|\vec{a} + \vec{b} + \vec{c}|^2 = |\vec{a}|^2 + |\vec{b}|^2 + |\vec{c}|^2 + 2(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} + \vec{b}\cdot\vec{c} + \vec{c}\cdot\vec{a}) = 3 + 2\left(-\dfrac{3}{2}\right) = 0$. Hence $\vec{a} + \vec{b} + \vec{c} = \vec{0}$, so $\vec{b} + \vec{c} = -\vec{a}$.
  3. Step 3 — Substitute into $|2\vec{a} + k\vec{b} + k\vec{c}| = 3$: Replacing $\vec{b} + \vec{c}$ by $-\vec{a}$ gives $|2\vec{a} - k\vec{a}| = |2 - k|\,|\vec{a}| = |2 - k| = 3$.
  4. Step 4 — Solve for the positive value of $k$: $2 - k = \pm 3 \implies k = -1$ or $k = 5$. The positive value is $k = 5$, confirming option (c).
Q35.trapHtml: Never drop the absolute value on $|2 - k| = 3$: both $k = -1$ and $k = 5$ solve it, and the problem specifically asks for the positive value.

Q36.subtopic: Angle Between Parallelogram Sides & Trig Identity
Q36.questionRecapHtml: $\overrightarrow{PQ} = \hat{j}+\hat{k}$ and $\overrightarrow{PS} = \hat{i}-\hat{j}$. Rotate $PS$ by acute angle $\alpha$ in the plane to become $\perp PQ$. Find $\sin^2\frac{5\alpha}{2} - \sin^2\frac{\alpha}{2}$.
Q36.conceptHtml: Find the angle $\phi$ between $\overrightarrow{PQ}$ and $\overrightarrow{PS}$ via dot product, get $\alpha = |\phi - \frac{\pi}{2}|$, and use $\sin^2 A - \sin^2 B = \sin(A+B)\sin(A-B)$.
Q36.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Find the initial angle $\theta$ between $\overrightarrow{PQ}$ and $\overrightarrow{PS}$: With $\overrightarrow{PQ} = \hat{j} + \hat{k}$ ($|\overrightarrow{PQ}| = \sqrt{2}$) and $\overrightarrow{PS} = \hat{i} - \hat{j}$ ($|\overrightarrow{PS}| = \sqrt{2}$), we have $\cos\theta = \dfrac{\overrightarrow{PQ}\cdot\overrightarrow{PS}}{|\overrightarrow{PQ}|\,|\overrightarrow{PS}|} = \dfrac{-1}{\sqrt{2}\cdot\sqrt{2}} = -\dfrac{1}{2}$, so $\theta = \dfrac{2\pi}{3}$.
  2. Step 2 — Determine the acute rotation angle $\alpha$: Rotating $PS$ in the plane of the parallelogram until it is perpendicular to $PQ$ (angle $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$) requires an acute rotation of $\alpha = \dfrac{2\pi}{3} - \dfrac{\pi}{2} = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$.
  3. Step 3 — Simplify the trigonometric expression: Using the identity $\sin^2 A - \sin^2 B = \sin(A + B)\sin(A - B)$, we get $\sin^2\!\left(\dfrac{5\alpha}{2}\right) - \sin^2\!\left(\dfrac{\alpha}{2}\right) = \sin(3\alpha)\sin(2\alpha)$.
  4. Step 4 — Substitute $\alpha = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$: $\sin\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\sin\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = 1\cdot\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$, confirming option (b).
Q36.trapHtml: Do not take $\alpha = 60^\circ$ by taking $|\cos\phi| = \frac{1}{2}$! The negative dot product gives $\phi = 120^\circ$, whose acute rotation to $90^\circ$ is $30^\circ$.

Q37.questionRecapHtml: $\vec{a} = (-1, 1, 3)$, $\vec{b} = (1, 3, 1)$, $\vec{c} = \lambda\vec{a} + \mu\vec{b}$ with $\vec{c}\cdot(3, -6, 2) = 10$ and $\vec{c}\cdot(1, 1, 1) = -2$. Find $|\vec{c}|^2$.
Q37.conceptHtml: Take dot products directly with $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ to get a $2\times 2$ linear system in $(\lambda, \mu)$, then evaluate $\vec{c}$ and $|\vec{c}|^2$.
Q37.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Compute the dot products with $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$: Let $\vec{u} = 3\hat{i} - 6\hat{j} + 2\hat{k}$ and $\vec{v} = \hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k}$. Then $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{u} = -3 - 6 + 6 = -3$, $\vec{b}\cdot\vec{u} = 3 - 18 + 2 = -13$, $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{v} = -1 + 1 + 3 = 3$, and $\vec{b}\cdot\vec{v} = 1 + 3 + 1 = 5$.
  2. Step 2 — Form and solve the linear system for $\lambda$ and $\mu$: Substituting $\vec{c} = \lambda\vec{a} + \mu\vec{b}$ into the two dot-product conditions yields $-3\lambda - 13\mu = 10$ and $3\lambda + 5\mu = -2$. Adding the two equations gives $-8\mu = 8 \implies \mu = -1$, and substituting back gives $3\lambda - 5 = -2 \implies \lambda = 1$.
  3. Step 3 — Find $\vec{c}$ and its squared magnitude: $\vec{c} = \vec{a} - \vec{b} = (-1-1)\hat{i} + (1-3)\hat{j} + (3-1)\hat{k} = -2\hat{i} - 2\hat{j} + 2\hat{k}$. Therefore, $|\vec{c}|^2 = (-2)^2 + (-2)^2 + 2^2 = 4 + 4 + 4 = 12$, confirming option (a).
Q37.trapHtml: Always verify both dot-product equations with your final $\vec{c} = (-2, -2, 2)$ before squaring: $-6 + 12 + 4 = 10$ and $-2 - 2 + 2 = -2$.

Q38.questionRecapHtml: $\vec{a} = (\sqrt{2}, -1, \lambda)$ ($\lambda > 0$) makes an obtuse angle with $\vec{b} = (-\lambda^2, 4\sqrt{2}, 4\sqrt{2})$ and angle $\theta \in (\frac{\pi}{6}, \frac{\pi}{2})$ with $+z$-axis. If $\lambda \in (\alpha, \beta) - \{\gamma\}$, find $\alpha + \beta + \gamma$.
Q38.conceptHtml: Obtuse angle requires $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} < 0$ (strictly negative!), and $\theta \in (\frac{\pi}{6}, \frac{\pi}{2})$ requires $0 < \cos\theta < \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$.
Q38.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Apply the obtuse-angle condition between $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$: We require $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} < 0$. Computing $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} = (\sqrt{2})(-\lambda^2) + (-1)(4\sqrt{2}) + (\lambda)(4\sqrt{2}) = -\sqrt{2}(\lambda^2 - 4\lambda + 4) = -\sqrt{2}(\lambda - 2)^2$. This is strictly negative for all $\lambda \ne 2$ (and since $\lambda > 0$, $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ can never be anti-parallel because $\dfrac{-1}{4\sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{\lambda}{4\sqrt{2}}$ would require $\lambda = -1$).
  2. Step 2 — Apply the $z$-axis angle condition: The angle $\theta$ between $\vec{a}$ and $\hat{k}$ satisfies $\cos\theta = \dfrac{\vec{a}\cdot\hat{k}}{|\vec{a}|} = \dfrac{\lambda}{\sqrt{3 + \lambda^2}}$. Since $\theta \in \left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$, we need $0 < \cos\theta < \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$.
  3. Step 3 — Solve the inequality for $\lambda > 0$: $\cos\theta > 0$ holds automatically for $\lambda > 0$, and $\dfrac{\lambda}{\sqrt{3 + \lambda^2}} < \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \implies 4\lambda^2 < 3(3 + \lambda^2) \implies \lambda^2 < 9 \implies 0 < \lambda < 3$.
  4. Step 4 — Combine conditions and find $\alpha + \beta + \gamma$: Combining $0 < \lambda < 3$ with $\lambda \ne 2$ gives $\lambda \in (0, 3) - \{2\}$. Thus $\alpha = 0$, $\beta = 3$, and $\gamma = 2$, so $\alpha + \beta + \gamma = 0 + 3 + 2 = 5$, confirming the answer 5.
Q38.trapHtml: At $\lambda = 2$, $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} = 0$ (a right angle, NOT obtuse!), so $\lambda = 2$ must be excluded as the single point $\gamma = 2$.

Q39.questionRecapHtml: In $\triangle PQR$, $\overrightarrow{PQ} = (-2, -1, 2)$, $\overrightarrow{PR} = (a, b, -4)$ ($a, b \in \mathbb{Z}$) with $|\overrightarrow{PR}| = 9$. $S$ on $QR$ is equidistant from $PQ, PR$ and $\overrightarrow{PS} = (1, -7, 2)$. Find $3a - 4b$.
Q39.conceptHtml: A point $S$ on side $QR$ equidistant from $PQ$ and $PR$ lies on the internal angle bisector of $\angle QPR$, so $\overrightarrow{PS}$ is parallel to $\widehat{PQ} + \widehat{PR}$.
Q39.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Use the angle-bisector direction property: Since $S$ is equidistant from lines $PQ$ and $PR$, the vector $\overrightarrow{PS}$ lies along an angle bisector of $\overrightarrow{PQ}$ and $\overrightarrow{PR}$, so $\overrightarrow{PS} = \lambda\bigl(\widehat{PQ} \pm \widehat{PR}\bigr)$ for some scalar $\lambda$.
  2. Step 2 — Compute the unit vectors $\widehat{PQ}$ and $\widehat{PR}$: Here $|\overrightarrow{PQ}| = \sqrt{(-2)^2 + (-1)^2 + 2^2} = 3$ and $|\overrightarrow{PR}| = 9$, so $\widehat{PQ} = \dfrac{-2\hat{i} - \hat{j} + 2\hat{k}}{3} = \dfrac{-6\hat{i} - 3\hat{j} + 6\hat{k}}{9}$ and $\widehat{PR} = \dfrac{a\hat{i} + b\hat{j} - 4\hat{k}}{9}$.
  3. Step 3 — Solve for $a$ and $b$ from the internal bisector: For $\overrightarrow{PS} = \lambda(\widehat{PQ} + \widehat{PR}) = \dfrac{\lambda}{9}\bigl[(a-6)\hat{i} + (b-3)\hat{j} + 2\hat{k}\bigr] = \hat{i} - 7\hat{j} + 2\hat{k}$, equating $\hat{k}$-components gives $\dfrac{2\lambda}{9} = 2 \implies \lambda = 9$. Then $a - 6 = 1 \implies a = 7$ and $b - 3 = -7 \implies b = -4$. Checking the magnitude: $\sqrt{7^2 + (-4)^2 + (-4)^2} = \sqrt{81} = 9$ (whereas the external bisector $\widehat{PQ} - \widehat{PR}$ gives $a = -11$, which violates $|\overrightarrow{PR}| = 9$).
  4. Step 4 — Evaluate $3a - 4b$: $3(7) - 4(-4) = 21 + 16 = 37$, confirming the answer 37.
Q39.trapHtml: Always normalize BOTH vectors ($\frac{\overrightarrow{PQ}}{3} + \frac{\overrightarrow{PR}}{9}$) before adding; adding unnormalized $\overrightarrow{PQ} + \overrightarrow{PR}$ only works for isosceles triangles.

Q40.questionRecapHtml: $\vec{a}_k = (\tan\theta_k)\hat{i} + \hat{j}$, $\vec{b}_k = \hat{i} - (\cot\theta_k)\hat{j}$ with $\theta_k = \frac{(2k-1)\pi}{2n+1}$ ($n > 5$). Find $\frac{\sum_{k=1}^n |\vec{a}_k|^2}{\sum_{k=1}^n |\vec{b}_k|^2}$.
Q40.conceptHtml: Note $|\vec{a}_k|^2 = \sec^2\theta_k = 1 + \tan^2\theta_k$ and $|\vec{b}_k|^2 = \csc^2\theta_k = 1 + \cot^2\theta_k$; apply Vieta's formulas to $\sin\bigl((2n+1)\theta\bigr) = 0$.
Q40.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Simplify $|\vec{a}_k|^2$ and $|\vec{b}_k|^2$: Using basic trigonometric identities, $|\vec{a}_k|^2 = \tan^2\theta_k + 1 = \sec^2\theta_k$ and $|\vec{b}_k|^2 = 1 + \cot^2\theta_k = \csc^2\theta_k$.
  2. Step 2 — Map the odd-multiple angles to $\dfrac{j\pi}{2n+1}$: For $k = 1, 2, \dots, n$, the angles $\theta_k = \dfrac{(2k-1)\pi}{2n+1}$ satisfy $\pi - \theta_k = \dfrac{2(n+1-k)\pi}{2n+1}$. Because $\tan^2(\pi - \theta) = \tan^2\theta$ and $\cot^2(\pi - \theta) = \cot^2\theta$, the sets $\{\tan^2\theta_k\}_{k=1}^n$ and $\{\cot^2\theta_k\}_{k=1}^n$ coincide with $\left\{\tan^2\dfrac{j\pi}{2n+1}\right\}_{j=1}^n$ and $\left\{\cot^2\dfrac{j\pi}{2n+1}\right\}_{j=1}^n$.
  3. Step 3 — Evaluate both sums using Vieta's formulas on $\sin\bigl((2n+1)\theta\bigr) = 0$: From De Moivre's expansion, $\binom{2n+1}{1}\cot^{2n}\theta - \binom{2n+1}{3}\cot^{2n-2}\theta + \dots = 0$ has roots $x_j = \cot^2\dfrac{j\pi}{2n+1}$, so $\sum_{j=1}^n \cot^2\dfrac{j\pi}{2n+1} = \dfrac{\binom{2n+1}{3}}{\binom{2n+1}{1}} = \dfrac{n(2n-1)}{3}$, giving $\sum_{k=1}^n \csc^2\theta_k = n + \dfrac{n(2n-1)}{3} = \dfrac{2n(n+1)}{3}$. Similarly, $\tan^{2n}\theta - \binom{2n+1}{2n-1}\tan^{2n-2}\theta + \dots = 0$ gives $\sum_{j=1}^n \tan^2\dfrac{j\pi}{2n+1} = \binom{2n+1}{2} = n(2n+1)$, so $\sum_{k=1}^n \sec^2\theta_k = n + n(2n+1) = 2n(n+1)$.
  4. Step 4 — Compute the ratio: $\dfrac{\sum_{k=1}^n |\vec{a}_k|^2}{\sum_{k=1}^n |\vec{b}_k|^2} = \dfrac{2n(n+1)}{\dfrac{2n(n+1)}{3}} = 3$, confirming the answer 3.
Q40.trapHtml: Remember to add $n$ (from the $+1$ in $\sec^2\theta = 1 + \tan^2\theta$ and $\csc^2\theta = 1 + \cot^2\theta$) to both Vieta sums before dividing!

trapCards.title: 1. Calculation & Sign Traps
trapCards.html:
• Cross-Product Order: $\vec{a}\times\vec{c} = \vec{c}\times\vec{b}$ rewrites as $(\vec{a}+\vec{b})\times\vec{c}=\vec{0}$, NOT $(\vec{a}-\vec{b})\times\vec{c}=\vec{0}$ (anti-commutativity flips the sign).
  • Determinant Middle-Term Minus: In $\vec{a}\times\vec{b}$, the $\hat{j}$-component is $-(a_1b_3 - a_3b_1) = a_3b_1 - a_1b_3$. Double-check it via $(\vec{a}\times\vec{b})\cdot\vec{a}=0$.
  • Section Formula Cross-Multiplication: If $C$ divides $AB$ in ratio $m:n$, then $\vec{OC} = \dfrac{m\vec{OB}+n\vec{OA}}{m+n}$ — the weight $m$ multiplies the far endpoint $B$.
  • Diagonal vs. Side Area: Parallelogram area is $|\vec{a}\times\vec{b}|$ for adjacent sides, but $\dfrac{1}{2}|\vec{d}_1\times\vec{d}_2|$ for diagonals. Missing the $\frac{1}{2}$ doubles the answer.
  • Euler Line Weights: Always $\vec{H} + 2\vec{O} = 3\vec{G}$ ($G$ divides $HO$ in ratio $2:1$); swapping $H$ and $O$ is a classic error.

trapCards.title: 2. Unit-Vector, Angle & Edge-Case Pitfalls
trapCards.html:
• Direction of Vectors at a Vertex: For $\angle QPR$, use $\vec{PQ}$ and $\vec{PR}$ (both tails at $P$). Using $\vec{QP}$ and $\vec{PR}$ gives the supplementary angle $\pi - \angle QPR$.
  • Acute / Obtuse vs. Parallel / Anti-Parallel:
    • $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} > 0$ includes $\theta=0$ (parallel); exclude parallel cases for acute.
    • $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} < 0$ includes $\theta=\pi$ (anti-parallel); exclude anti-parallel cases for obtuse.
  • Boundary Parameter Values: When forcing $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} = pt^2+qt+r < 0\;\forall t\in\mathbb{R}$, ALWAYS test $p=0$ separately (as in Q17 where $\alpha=0$ is valid).
  • Dual Sign of Unit Vectors: A unit vector perpendicular to $\vec{a},\vec{b}$ has TWO valid orientations: $\pm\dfrac{\vec{a}\times\vec{b}}{|\vec{a}\times\vec{b}|}$. Check all four options for either sign.
  • Direction Angle Domain: Angles with positive coordinate axes lie in $[0,\pi]$, so $\cos\alpha = -1$ ($\alpha=\pi$) is valid.

trapCards.title: 3. Formula Applicability Boundaries
trapCards.html:
• NTA 2024–2025 Syllabus Boundary: Scalar Triple Product ($[\vec{a}\;\vec{b}\;\vec{c}]$) and Vector Triple Product ($\vec{a}\times(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})$) are DELETED. Solve every coplanar/perpendicular vector problem via $\vec{c}=\lambda\vec{a}+\mu\vec{b}$ and dot products.
  • No Cancellation in Dot or Cross Products:
    • $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}=\vec{a}\cdot\vec{c} \implies \vec{a}\perp(\vec{b}-\vec{c})$, NOT $\vec{b}=\vec{c}$.
    • $\vec{a}\times\vec{b}=\vec{a}\times\vec{c} \implies \vec{b}-\vec{c} = \lambda\vec{a}$, NOT $\vec{b}=\vec{c}$.
  • Scalar vs. Vector Projection: “Projection of $\vec{a}$ on $\vec{b}$” (scalar) is $\dfrac{\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}}{|\vec{b}|}$ (can be negative); “length of projection” is $\dfrac{|\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}|}{|\vec{b}|}$; “projection vector” is $\dfrac{\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}}{|\vec{b}|^2}\vec{b}$.
  • De Gua's Area Theorem: $\Delta_{BCD}^2 = \Delta_{ABC}^2+\Delta_{ACD}^2+\Delta_{ADB}^2$ applies ONLY when $AB,AC,AD$ are mutually perpendicular.

trapCards.title: 4. NTA Statement / A–R Wordings to Watch
trapCards.html:
• “Projection” vs. “Component”: When NTA gives components along and perpendicular to $\vec{b}$, their sum is immediately $\vec{a}$ (Q02).
  • “All Real $t$” Traps: Phrases like “for all $t \in \mathbb{R}$” signal a quadratic sign condition ($a<0, D<0$) PLUS a separate linear/constant check ($a=0$).
  • “Number of Values in $[p,q]$”: Always verify whether solved roots actually fall inside the stated interval (Q06 has $2$ real roots, but $0$ inside $[-1,3]$).
  • “Largest Side Squared” / “$k\sin^2\alpha$”: Re-read the exact target expression before bubbling — NTA routinely multiplies by $6, 14^2, 27, 192$ to turn fractions into integers.
  • Assertion–Reason Verification: Check (A) and (R) independently first; only select “correct explanation” if (R) mathematically implies (A) without missing edge cases.

subject: Maths
title: 3D Geometry
constantsHtml:
Core 3D Geometry Pillars (Strictly NTA 2024–2025 Syllabus — Planes Excluded):
  • Direction Cosine Identity: $l^2 + m^2 + n^2 = 1 \iff \cos^2\alpha + \cos^2\beta + \cos^2\gamma = 1 \iff \sin^2\alpha + \sin^2\beta + \sin^2\gamma = 2$.
  • Standard Line Equations: Vector: $\vec{r} = \vec{a} + \lambda\vec{b}$;   Cartesian: $\dfrac{x - x_1}{a} = \dfrac{y - y_1}{b} = \dfrac{z - z_1}{c} = \lambda$.
  • Shortest Distance (Skew Lines): $d = \dfrac{\left|(\vec{a}_2 - \vec{a}_1) \cdot (\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2)\right|}{|\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2|}$;   Parallel Lines: $d = \dfrac{\left|(\vec{a}_2 - \vec{a}_1) \times \vec{b}\right|}{|\vec{b}|}$.

formulaCards.title: 1. 3D Coordinates, Distance & Section Formula
formulaCards.html:
• Distance between $P(x_1,y_1,z_1)$ and $Q(x_2,y_2,z_2)$: $PQ = \sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2 + (y_2-y_1)^2 + (z_2-z_1)^2}$.
  • Distance from Coordinate Axes: From $x$-axis: $\sqrt{y^2+z^2}$;   $y$-axis: $\sqrt{x^2+z^2}$;   $z$-axis: $\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$.
  • Distance from Coordinate Planes: From $xy$-plane: $|z|$;   $yz$-plane: $|x|$;   $zx$-plane: $|y|$.
  • Section Formula ($m:n$): $R = \left(\dfrac{mx_2 \pm nx_1}{m \pm n},\; \dfrac{my_2 \pm ny_1}{m \pm n},\; \dfrac{mz_2 \pm nz_1}{m \pm n}\right)$ ($+$ internal, $-$ external).
  • Ratio by Coordinate Planes: $yz$-plane divides $AB$ in ratio $-x_1: x_2$;   $zx$-plane: $-y_1: y_2$;   $xy$-plane: $-z_1: z_2$.
  • Centroid of $\triangle ABC$: $G = \left(\dfrac{\sum x_i}{3}, \dfrac{\sum y_i}{3}, \dfrac{\sum z_i}{3}\right)$.

formulaCards.title: 2. Direction Cosines (D.C.s) & Direction Ratios (D.R.s)
formulaCards.html:
• — D.C.s from D.R.s $(a,b,c)$: $l = \pm\dfrac{a}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2+c^2}},\; m = \pm\dfrac{b}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2+c^2}},\; n = \pm\dfrac{c}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2+c^2}}$.
  • D.R.s of Segment $AB$: $(x_2 - x_1,\; y_2 - y_1,\; z_2 - z_1)$.
  • Angle Identities: $\cos 2\alpha + \cos 2\beta + \cos 2\gamma = -1$;   $\sin^2\alpha + \sin^2\beta + \sin^2\gamma = 2$.
  • Line Equally Inclined to Axes: D.C.s are $\left(\pm\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}, \pm\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}, \pm\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right)$ ($4$ distinct lines through origin).
  • Angle Between Diagonals of a Cube: $\theta = \cos^{-1}\!\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)$.
  • Projection of Segment $AB$ on Line with D.C.s $(l,m,n)$: $\text{Proj} = |l(x_2-x_1) + m(y_2-y_1) + n(z_2-z_1)| = \left|\overrightarrow{AB}\cdot\hat{u}\right|$.

formulaCards.title: 3. Equations of a Line in Space
formulaCards.html:
• — Point-Direction Form: Vector: $\vec{r} = \vec{a} + \lambda\vec{b}$;   Cartesian: $\dfrac{x-x_1}{a} = \dfrac{y-y_1}{b} = \dfrac{z-z_1}{c} = \lambda$.
  • General Point on Line: $P(\lambda) = (x_1 + a\lambda,\; y_1 + b\lambda,\; z_1 + c\lambda)$.
  • Two-Point Form ($A, B$): $\vec{r} = \vec{a} + \lambda(\vec{b}-\vec{a})$;   $\dfrac{x-x_1}{x_2-x_1} = \dfrac{y-y_1}{y_2-y_1} = \dfrac{z-z_1}{z_2-z_1}$.
  • Distance Parameter Form: Point at distance $r$ from $(x_1,y_1,z_1)$ along D.C.s $(l,m,n)$: $(x_1 \pm rl,\; y_1 \pm rm,\; z_1 \pm rn)$.
  • Zero Denominator Convention: $\dfrac{x-x_1}{0} = \dfrac{y-y_1}{b} = \dfrac{z-z_1}{c} \implies x = x_1$ and $\dfrac{y-y_1}{b} = \dfrac{z-z_1}{c}$.

formulaCards.title: 4. Angle, Perpendicularity & Collinearity
formulaCards.html:
• — Acute Angle Between Two Lines: $\cos\theta = \dfrac{|\vec{b}_1 \cdot \vec{b}_2|}{|\vec{b}_1||\vec{b}_2|} = \dfrac{|a_1a_2 + b_1b_2 + c_1c_2|}{\sqrt{a_1^2+b_1^2+c_1^2}\sqrt{a_2^2+b_2^2+c_2^2}}$.
  • Perpendicularity ($L_1 \perp L_2$): $\vec{b}_1 \cdot \vec{b}_2 = 0 \iff a_1a_2 + b_1b_2 + c_1c_2 = 0 \iff l_1l_2 + m_1m_2 + n_1n_2 = 0$.
  • Parallelism ($L_1 \parallel L_2$): $\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2 = \vec{0} \iff \dfrac{a_1}{a_2} = \dfrac{b_1}{b_2} = \dfrac{c_1}{c_2}$.
  • Line Perpendicular to Both $L_1$ and $L_2$: Direction vector is $\vec{b} = \vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2$.
  • Collinearity of $A, B, C$: $\overrightarrow{AB} \times \overrightarrow{AC} = \vec{0}$ (proportional D.R.s).

formulaCards.title: 5. Foot of Perpendicular, Distance & Image in a Line
formulaCards.html:
• — Foot of Perpendicular $M$ from $P$ to $L: \vec{r}=\vec{a}+\lambda\vec{b}$: Let $M = \vec{a} + \lambda\vec{b}$. Enforce $\overrightarrow{PM} \cdot \vec{b} = 0$: $\lambda = \dfrac{(\vec{p} - \vec{a}) \cdot \vec{b}}{|\vec{b}|^2}$.
  • — Image $Q(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$ of $P(x_0,y_0,z_0)$ in $L$: $M$ is midpoint of $PQ \implies \vec{q} = 2\vec{m} - \vec{p}$, i.e., $\alpha = 2x_M - x_0,\; \beta = 2y_M - y_0,\; \gamma = 2z_M - z_0$.
  • — Perpendicular Distance of $P$ from $L$: $d = |\overrightarrow{PM}| = \dfrac{|(\vec{p} - \vec{a}) \times \vec{b}|}{|\vec{b}|} = \sqrt{|\vec{p}-\vec{a}|^2 - \left(\dfrac{(\vec{p}-\vec{a})\cdot\vec{b}}{|\vec{b}|}\right)^2}$.
  • Area of $\triangle PAB$ ($A,B \in L$): $\Delta = \dfrac{1}{2}|\overrightarrow{AB} \times \overrightarrow{AP}| = \dfrac{1}{2}|AB|\cdot d$.

formulaCards.title: 6. Skew Lines, Coplanarity & Line of Shortest Distance
formulaCards.html:
• — Shortest Distance (Skew Lines): $d = \dfrac{\left|(\vec{a}_2 - \vec{a}_1) \cdot (\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2)\right|}{|\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2|} = \dfrac{\left|\det\begin{pmatrix} x_2-x_1 & y_2-y_1 & z_2-z_1 \\ a_1 & b_1 & c_1 \\ a_2 & b_2 & c_2 \end{pmatrix}\right|}{\sqrt{\sum (b_1c_2 - b_2c_1)^2}}$.
  • — Coplanarity Condition: $\left[\vec{a}_2-\vec{a}_1 \;\; \vec{b}_1 \;\; \vec{b}_2\right] = 0$. (If $\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2 \neq \vec{0}$: Intersecting; if $\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2 = \vec{0}$: Parallel/Coincident.)
  • — Parallel Lines Distance ($\vec{b}_1 \parallel \vec{b}_2 \parallel \vec{b}$): $d = \dfrac{\left|(\vec{a}_2 - \vec{a}_1) \times \vec{b}\right|}{|\vec{b}|}$.
  • — Line of Shortest Distance ($MN$): Take $M(\lambda) \in L_1$ and $N(\mu) \in L_2$. Solve the $2\times 2$ linear system $\overrightarrow{MN}\cdot\vec{b}_1 = 0$ and $\overrightarrow{MN}\cdot\vec{b}_2 = 0$ for $(\lambda, \mu)$ to get exact endpoints $M, N$ and line $MN$.
  • Transversal Through $A$ Intersecting Skew Lines $L_1, L_2$: Take $P(\lambda) \in L_1$, $Q(\mu) \in L_2$ and enforce $\overrightarrow{AP} \parallel \overrightarrow{AQ}$ (i.e., $\overrightarrow{AP} \times \overrightarrow{AQ} = \vec{0}$).
