Q01.questionRecapHtml: Area bounded by $y = |x - 1| + |x - 2|$ and $y = 3$. Options: (a) $3$, (b) $4$, (c) $5$, (d) $6$.
Q01.conceptHtml: Piecewise splitting of $|x - 1| + |x - 2|$ yields a trapezium with area $\frac{1}{2}(b_1 + b_2)h$.
Q01.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Rewrite the modulus curve piecewise: Split $y = |x - 1| + |x - 2|$ at its corner points $x = 1$ and $x = 2$: for $x < 1$, $y = (1 - x) + (2 - x) = 3 - 2x$; for $1 \le x \le 2$, $y = (x - 1) + (2 - x) = 1$; and for $x > 2$, $y = (x - 1) + (x - 2) = 2x - 3$.
  2. Step 2 — Find intersection points with $y = 3$: On the left branch, $3 - 2x = 3 \implies x = 0$. On the right branch, $2x - 3 = 3 \implies x = 3$. Thus the bounded region sits between $x = 0$ and $x = 3$, with the flat bottom segment on $y = 1$ from $x = 1$ to $x = 2$.
  3. Step 3 — Compute the area of the trapezium: The region is a trapezium with parallel sides along $y = 3$ (length $3 - 0 = 3$) and $y = 1$ (length $2 - 1 = 1$), separated by height $h = 3 - 1 = 2$. Hence, $\text{Area} = \dfrac{1}{2}(3 + 1) \times 2 = 4\text{ sq. units}$.
  4. Step 4 — Match the verified answer: The enclosed area is $4\text{ sq. units}$, which corresponds to option (b).
Q01.trapHtml: Never integrate piecewise linear modulus bounds when a 5-second trapezium formula applies.

Q02.conceptHtml: Horizontal strip $A = \int_{\alpha}^{\beta} (x_R - x_L)\,dy$ and quadratic shortcut $\frac{|k|(\beta - \alpha)^3}{6}$.
Q02.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Express both curves as $x$ in terms of $y$: From the parabola $y^2 + 4x = 4$, we get $x = 1 - \dfrac{y^2}{4}$. From the line $y - 2x = 2$, we get $x = \dfrac{y - 2}{2}$.
  2. Step 2 — Find the points of intersection: Equating the two expressions for $x$ gives $1 - \dfrac{y^2}{4} = \dfrac{y - 2}{2} \implies 4 - y^2 = 2y - 4 \implies y^2 + 2y - 8 = 0$. Factoring yields $(y + 4)(y - 2) = 0$, so $y = -4$ and $y = 2$.
  3. Step 3 — Integrate along the $y$-axis: Between $y = -4$ and $y = 2$, the parabola lies to the right of the line (check at $y = 0$: $x_{\text{parabola}} = 1 > x_{\text{line}} = -1$). Therefore, $\text{Area} = \displaystyle\int_{-4}^{2} \left[\left(1 - \dfrac{y^2}{4}\right) - \left(\dfrac{y - 2}{2}\right)\right] dy = \dfrac{1}{4}\int_{-4}^{2} (8 - 2y - y^2)\,dy$.
  4. Step 4 — Evaluate and confirm: $\text{Area} = \dfrac{1}{4}\left[8y - y^2 - \dfrac{y^3}{3}\right]_{-4}^{2} = \dfrac{1}{4}\left[\left(16 - 4 - \dfrac{8}{3}\right) - \left(-32 - 16 + \dfrac{64}{3}\right)\right] = \dfrac{1}{4}\left(\dfrac{28}{3} + \dfrac{80}{3}\right) = \dfrac{1}{4}(36) = 9\text{ sq. units}$. This matches option (c).
Q02.trapHtml: Using $dx$ strips here forces splitting at $x = 0$; $dy$ strips solve it in one line.

Q03.questionRecapHtml: Shaded area between $y = 4x - x^2$ and $3y = (x - 4)^2$. Options: (a) $6$, (b) $32/9$, (c) $14/3$, (d) $8$.
Q03.conceptHtml: Area between two quadratics: $A = \dfrac{|a_1 - a_2|(\beta - \alpha)^3}{6}$.
Q03.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the upper and lower curves: We have the downward parabola $y_1 = 4x - x^2$ and the upward parabola $y_2 = \dfrac{(x - 4)^2}{3}$.
  2. Step 2 — Find the intersection points: Set $4x - x^2 = \dfrac{(x - 4)^2}{3} \implies 12x - 3x^2 = x^2 - 8x + 16 \implies 4x^2 - 20x + 16 = 0 \implies x^2 - 5x + 4 = 0$. Factoring gives $(x - 1)(x - 4) = 0$, so the curves meet at $x = 1$ and $x = 4$.
  3. Step 3 — Set up the definite integral: On $[1, 4]$, the downward parabola lies above the upward parabola, so $\text{Area} = \displaystyle\int_{1}^{4} \left[(4x - x^2) - \dfrac{(x - 4)^2}{3}\right] dx = \dfrac{4}{3}\int_{1}^{4} (-x^2 + 5x - 4)\,dx$.
  4. Step 4 — Evaluate using the parabola chord formula: For a quadratic $a(\beta - x)(x - \alpha)$ integrated from $\alpha$ to $\beta$, the integral equals $\dfrac{a}{6}(\beta - \alpha)^3$. Here $a = \dfrac{4}{3}$, $\alpha = 1$, and $\beta = 4$, giving $\text{Area} = \dfrac{4}{3} \cdot \dfrac{(4 - 1)^3}{6} = \dfrac{4}{3} \cdot \dfrac{27}{6} = 6\text{ sq. units}$. This confirms option (a).
Q03.trapHtml: Remember to include the leading coefficient difference $|a_1 - a_2| = 4/3$, not $1$.

Q04.questionRecapHtml: Area enclosed between $y = x|x|$ and $y = x - |x|$. Options: (a) $8/3$, (b) $2$, (c) $2/3$, (d) $4/3$.
Q04.conceptHtml: Split at $x = 0$: for $x \ge 0$ no bounded loop forms; integrate strictly on $[-2, 0]$.
Q04.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Break both curves into $x \ge 0$ and $x < 0$ cases: For $x \ge 0$, $y = x|x| = x^2$ and $y = x - |x| = 0$; these meet only at $x = 0$ and never enclose a bounded region for $x > 0$. For $x \le 0$, $y = x|x| = -x^2$ and $y = x - |x| = 2x$.
  2. Step 2 — Find the intersection points for $x \le 0$: Setting $-x^2 = 2x$ gives $x^2 + 2x = 0 \implies x(x + 2) = 0$, so the curves intersect at $x = -2$ and $x = 0$.
  3. Step 3 — Integrate between the curves on $[-2, 0]$: At $x = -1$, $-x^2 = -1$ is above $2x = -2$, so $\text{Area} = \displaystyle\int_{-2}^{0} (-x^2 - 2x)\,dx = \left[-\dfrac{x^3}{3} - x^2\right]_{-2}^{0}$.
  4. Step 4 — Evaluate and confirm: Substituting the limits gives $0 - \left(\dfrac{8}{3} - 4\right) = 4 - \dfrac{8}{3} = \dfrac{4}{3}\text{ sq. units}$, which corresponds to option (d).
Q04.trapHtml: Do not assume symmetry about the $y$-axis; $y = x - |x|$ is $0$ for $x \ge 0$ and $2x$ for $x < 0$.

Q05.questionRecapHtml: Area enclosed by $y = e^x$, $y = |e^x - 1|$ and $y$-axis. Options: (a) $\log_e 2$, (b) $1 - \log_e 2$, (c) $2\log_e 2 - 1$, (d) $1 + \log_e 2$.
Q05.conceptHtml: For $x < 0$, $e^x < 1 \implies |e^x - 1| = 1 - e^x$; intersect with $y = e^x$ to get limits.
Q05.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Analyze $|e^x - 1|$ on both sides of the $y$-axis: For $x \ge 0$, $e^x \ge 1$ so $|e^x - 1| = e^x - 1$, which is always $1$ unit below $y = e^x$ and never intersects it. For $x < 0$, $0 < e^x < 1$, so $|e^x - 1| = 1 - e^x$.
  2. Step 2 — Find the intersection point: Equating $e^x = 1 - e^x$ gives $2e^x = 1 \implies e^x = \dfrac{1}{2} \implies x = -\log_e 2$. Thus the bounded region lies between $x = -\log_e 2$ and the $y$-axis ($x = 0$).
  3. Step 3 — Set up and evaluate the integral: On $[-\log_e 2, 0]$, $e^x \ge 1 - e^x$, so $\text{Area} = \displaystyle\int_{-\log_e 2}^{0} \left[e^x - (1 - e^x)\right] dx = \int_{-\log_e 2}^{0} (2e^x - 1)\,dx = \left[2e^x - x\right]_{-\log_e 2}^{0}$.
  4. Step 4 — Simplify and confirm: Evaluating the limits gives $(2e^0 - 0) - \left(2 \cdot \dfrac{1}{2} - (-\log_e 2)\right) = 2 - (1 + \log_e 2) = 1 - \log_e 2\text{ sq. units}$. This matches option (b).
Q05.trapHtml: Watch the lower limit sign: $-x\big|_{-\log_e 2} = +\log_e 2$, subtracted at the lower bound gives $-\log_e 2$.

Q06.conceptHtml: Direct $dx$-integration using $\int \frac{1}{x}\,dx = \log_e x$ and $\int x^{-2}\,dx = -x^{-1}$.
Q06.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Verify the upper and lower boundaries: Since $0 < a < 1$ and $1 \le x \le 2$, we have $\dfrac{a}{x^2} < \dfrac{1}{x^2} \le \dfrac{1}{x}$ throughout $[1, 2]$. Thus $y = \dfrac{1}{x}$ is always the upper curve and $y = \dfrac{a}{x^2}$ is the lower curve.
  2. Step 2 — Compute the area in terms of $a$: $\text{Area} = \displaystyle\int_{1}^{2} \left(\dfrac{1}{x} - \dfrac{a}{x^2}\right) dx = \left[\log_e x + \dfrac{a}{x}\right]_{1}^{2} = \left(\log_e 2 + \dfrac{a}{2}\right) - (0 + a) = \log_e 2 - \dfrac{a}{2}$.
  3. Step 3 — Solve for $a$: Equating this to the given area $\log_e 2 - \dfrac{1}{7}$ yields $\dfrac{a}{2} = \dfrac{1}{7} \implies a = \dfrac{2}{7}$.
  4. Step 4 — Find $7a - 3$ and confirm: Substituting $a = \dfrac{2}{7}$ gives $7a - 3 = 7\left(\dfrac{2}{7}\right) - 3 = 2 - 3 = -1$, which matches option (c).
Q06.trapHtml: Check the final expression asked ($7a - 3$), not just $a = 2/7$.

Q07.conceptHtml: Shift $u = x + 2$ to center both curves at $u = 0$, then exploit even symmetry.
Q07.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Shift the origin to simplify the algebra: Rewrite $x^2 + 4x + 2 = (x + 2)^2 - 2$. Substituting $t = x + 2$ shifts the region horizontally without changing its area, transforming it into $t^2 - 2 \le y \le |t|$.
  2. Step 2 — Use symmetry and find intersection points: Both $y = t^2 - 2$ and $y = |t|$ are even functions of $t$, so the region is symmetric about $t = 0$. For $t \ge 0$, setting $t^2 - 2 = t \implies t^2 - t - 2 = 0 \implies (t - 2)(t + 1) = 0$ gives $t = 2$.
  3. Step 3 — Integrate over $[0, 2]$ and double: $\text{Area} = 2\displaystyle\int_{0}^{2} \left(t - (t^2 - 2)\right) dt = 2\left[\dfrac{t^2}{2} - \dfrac{t^3}{3} + 2t\right]_{0}^{2}$.
  4. Step 4 — Evaluate and confirm: $\text{Area} = 2\left(2 - \dfrac{8}{3} + 4\right) = 2\left(6 - \dfrac{8}{3}\right) = 2\left(\dfrac{10}{3}\right) = \dfrac{20}{3}\text{ sq. units}$. This corresponds to option (a).
Q07.stepsLatex:
\begin{align*}
  u &= x + 2 \implies x^2 + 4x + 2 = u^2 - 2. \\
  \text{Region: } & u^2 - 2 \le y \le |u| \quad (\text{even in } u). \\
  u \ge 0 &: \quad u^2 - 2 = u \implies u^2 - u - 2 = 0 \implies u = 2. \\
  A &= 2\int_{0}^{2} (u - u^2 + 2)\,du = 2\left[\frac{u^2}{2} - \frac{u^3}{3} + 2u\right]_{0}^{2} \\
    &= 2\left(2 - \frac{8}{3} + 4\right) = \frac{20}{3}.
\end{align*}
Q07.trapHtml: Completing the square to $u = x + 2$ avoids splitting into two asymmetric intervals $[-4, -2]$ and $[-2, 0]$.

Q08.questionRecapHtml: Area enclosed by $xy + 4y = 16$ and $x + y = 6$. Options: (a) $28-30\log_e 2$, (b) $30-28\log_e 2$, (c) $32-30\log_e 2$, (d) $30-32\log_e 2$.
Q08.conceptHtml: Solve $y = \frac{16}{x+4} = 6 - x$ and integrate $(y_{\text{line}} - y_{\text{hyp}})\,dx$.
Q08.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Isolate $y$ for both curves: From $xy + 4y = 16$, we get $y = \dfrac{16}{x + 4}$. From the line $x + y = 6$, we get $y = 6 - x$.
  2. Step 2 — Find the points of intersection: Equating the two gives $\dfrac{16}{x + 4} = 6 - x \implies 16 = (6 - x)(x + 4) = 24 + 2x - x^2 \implies x^2 - 2x - 8 = 0$. Factoring yields $(x - 4)(x + 2) = 0$, so $x = -2$ and $x = 4$.
  3. Step 3 — Set up the definite integral: Checking at $x = 0$, the line gives $y = 6$ while the hyperbola gives $y = 4$, so the line is above the hyperbola on $[-2, 4]$. Hence, $\text{Area} = \displaystyle\int_{-2}^{4} \left(6 - x - \dfrac{16}{x + 4}\right) dx = \left[6x - \dfrac{x^2}{2} - 16\log_e|x + 4|\right]_{-2}^{4}$.
  4. Step 4 — Evaluate and confirm: Substituting the limits gives $(24 - 8 - 16\log_e 8) - (-12 - 2 - 16\log_e 2) = (16 - 48\log_e 2) - (-14 - 16\log_e 2) = 30 - 32\log_e 2\text{ sq. units}$, matching option (d).
Q08.trapHtml: Simplify $\log_e 8 - \log_e 2 = \log_e 4 = 2\log_e 2$; losing the factor of $2$ gives the wrong coefficient.

Q09.questionRecapHtml: Area inside $(x - 2\sqrt{3})^2 + y^2 = 12$ and outside $y^2 = 2\sqrt{3}x$. Options: (a) $6\pi - 8$, (b) $6\pi - 16$, (c) $3\pi - 8$, (d) $3\pi + 8$.
Q09.conceptHtml: Intersections occur on the vertical diameter $x = 2\sqrt{3}$; the right semicircle lies completely inside the parabola.
Q09.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the circle and find its intersections with the parabola: The circle $(x - 2\sqrt{3})^2 + y^2 = 12$ has center $C(2\sqrt{3}, 0)$ and radius $r = 2\sqrt{3}$. Substituting $y^2 = 2\sqrt{3}x$ gives $(x - 2\sqrt{3})^2 + 2\sqrt{3}x = 12 \implies x^2 - 2\sqrt{3}x = 0$, so $x = 0$ and $x = 2\sqrt{3}$.
  2. Step 2 — Observe the geometry relative to the vertical diameter: The line $x = 2\sqrt{3}$ is the vertical diameter of the circle. For $x \in [2\sqrt{3}, 4\sqrt{3}]$, the entire right semicircle lies inside the parabola $y^2 = 2\sqrt{3}x$. Thus, the required region (inside the circle and outside the parabola) lies entirely within the left semicircle ($0 \le x \le 2\sqrt{3}$).
  3. Step 3 — Compute the area of the left semicircle minus the parabolic region: The left semicircle has area $\dfrac{1}{2}\pi r^2 = \dfrac{1}{2}\pi(12) = 6\pi$. The area inside the parabola for $0 \le x \le 2\sqrt{3}$ is $2\displaystyle\int_{0}^{2\sqrt{3}} \sqrt{2\sqrt{3}x}\,dx = 2\sqrt{2\sqrt{3}} \cdot \dfrac{2}{3}\left[x^{3/2}\right]_{0}^{2\sqrt{3}} = \dfrac{4}{3}(2\sqrt{3})^2 = 16$.
  4. Step 4 — Subtract and confirm: The required area is $6\pi - 16\text{ sq. units}$, which matches option (b).
Q09.trapHtml: Always check whether the right half of the circle lies inside or outside the parabola; here $2\sqrt{3}x > 12$ for $x > 2\sqrt{3}$, so it is inside.

Q10.questionRecapHtml: First-quadrant area inside $x^2 + y^2 = 8$ and outside $y^2 = 2x$. Options: (a) $\pi - 4/3$, (b) $\pi/2 - 2/3$, (c) $\pi - 2/3$, (d) $\pi/2 - 1/3$.
Q10.conceptHtml: Use horizontal strips ($dy$) on $[0, 2]$ and $[2, 2\sqrt{2}]$ so $x$ runs from $0$ to the right boundary.
Q10.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Find the first-quadrant intersection point: Substitute $y^2 = 2x$ into $x^2 + y^2 = 8$ to get $x^2 + 2x - 8 = 0 \implies (x + 4)(x - 2) = 0$. In the first quadrant ($x \ge 0, y \ge 0$), this gives $x = 2$ and $y = 2$.
  2. Step 2 — Find the area inside both curves in the first quadrant: Split at $x = 2$ (circle radius is $2\sqrt{2}$). For $0 \le x \le 2$, the region is bounded above by the parabola $y = \sqrt{2x}$; for $2 \le x \le 2\sqrt{2}$, it is bounded above by the circle $y = \sqrt{8 - x^2}$.
  3. Step 3 — Evaluate both integrals: First, $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{2} \sqrt{2x}\,dx = \sqrt{2}\cdot\dfrac{2}{3}\left[x^{3/2}\right]_{0}^{2} = \dfrac{8}{3}$. Second, $\displaystyle\int_{2}^{2\sqrt{2}} \sqrt{8 - x^2}\,dx = \left[\dfrac{x}{2}\sqrt{8 - x^2} + 4\sin^{-1}\!\left(\dfrac{x}{2\sqrt{2}}\right)\right]_{2}^{2\sqrt{2}} = (0 + 2\pi) - (2 + \pi) = \pi - 2$. Thus the overlap area in the first quadrant is $\dfrac{8}{3} + \pi - 2 = \pi + \dfrac{2}{3}$.
  4. Step 4 — Subtract from the quarter-circle area: The first-quadrant quarter-circle has area $\dfrac{1}{4}\pi(8) = 2\pi$. Hence, the required area outside the parabola is $2\pi - \left(\pi + \dfrac{2}{3}\right) = \pi - \dfrac{2}{3}\text{ sq. units}$, confirming option (c).
Q10.trapHtml: “Outside the parabola $y^2 = 2x$” means $y^2 > 2x$ (above the parabola, left of $x = y^2/2$), not below it.

Q11.conceptHtml: Find the corner where the two upper lines switch ($x + 7 = 11 - 3x \implies x = 1$) and split the integral there.
Q11.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Find the switching point of the upper boundary: The two lines $y = x + 7$ and $y = 11 - 3x$ intersect when $x + 7 = 11 - 3x \implies 4x = 4 \implies x = 1$ (where $y = 8$). Thus $\min\{x + 7, 11 - 3x\}$ equals $x + 7$ for $x \le 1$ and $11 - 3x$ for $x \ge 1$.
  2. Step 2 — Find the intersections with the parabola $y = 1 + x^2$: For $x \le 1$, $1 + x^2 = x + 7 \implies x^2 - x - 6 = 0 \implies (x - 3)(x + 2) = 0 \implies x = -2$. For $x \ge 1$, $1 + x^2 = 11 - 3x \implies x^2 + 3x - 10 = 0 \implies (x + 5)(x - 2) = 0 \implies x = 2$.
  3. Step 3 — Split the area integral at $x = 1$: $A = \displaystyle\int_{-2}^{1} \left[(x + 7) - (1 + x^2)\right] dx + \int_{1}^{2} \left[(11 - 3x) - (1 + x^2)\right] dx = \int_{-2}^{1} (6 + x - x^2)\,dx + \int_{1}^{2} (10 - 3x - x^2)\,dx$.
  4. Step 4 — Evaluate both pieces and compute $3A$: The first integral is $\left[6x + \dfrac{x^2}{2} - \dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_{-2}^{1} = \dfrac{37}{6} - \left(-\dfrac{22}{3}\right) = \dfrac{81}{6}$. The second integral is $\left[10x - \dfrac{3x^2}{2} - \dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_{1}^{2} = \dfrac{34}{3} - \dfrac{49}{6} = \dfrac{19}{6}$. Adding them gives $A = \dfrac{100}{6} = \dfrac{50}{3}$, so $3A = 50$, matching option (a).
Q11.stepsLatex:
\begin{align*}
  x + 7 = 11 - 3x &\implies x = 1. \\
  x \le 1 &: \quad 1 + x^2 = x + 7 \implies x^2 - x - 6 = 0 \implies x = -2. \\
  x \ge 1 &: \quad 1 + x^2 = 11 - 3x \implies x^2 + 3x - 10 = 0 \implies x = 2. \\
  A &= \int_{-2}^{1} (6 + x - x^2)\,dx + \int_{1}^{2} (10 - 3x - x^2)\,dx \\
    &= \left[6x + \frac{x^2}{2} - \frac{x^3}{3}\right]_{-2}^{1} + \left[10x - \frac{3x^2}{2} - \frac{x^3}{3}\right]_{1}^{2} \\
    &= \frac{27}{2} + \frac{19}{6} = \frac{50}{3} \implies 3A = 50.
\end{align*}
Q11.trapHtml: Verify that the corner $(1, 8)$ lies above the parabola $y(1) = 2$; otherwise the two lines would not both form the roof.

Q12.conceptHtml: Upper boundary switches from $y = x^2$ to $y = 8/x$ at $x^3 = 8 \implies x = 2$; floor is $y = 1$ on $[1, 8]$.
Q12.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the bounding curves in the first quadrant: The inequalities $xy \le 8$, $1 \le y \le x^2$, and $x \ge 0$ give the lower boundary $y = 1$ and upper boundary $y = \min\!\left\{x^2, \dfrac{8}{x}\right\}$.
  2. Step 2 — Find the three corner intersections: The parabola $y = x^2$ meets $y = 1$ at $x = 1$ (since $x \ge 0$). The parabola meets $y = \dfrac{8}{x}$ when $x^3 = 8 \implies x = 2$. Finally, $y = \dfrac{8}{x}$ meets $y = 1$ at $x = 8$.
  3. Step 3 — Split the integral at $x = 2$: $\text{Area} = \displaystyle\int_{1}^{2} (x^2 - 1)\,dx + \int_{2}^{8} \left(\dfrac{8}{x} - 1\right) dx$.
  4. Step 4 — Evaluate and confirm: The first integral is $\left[\dfrac{x^3}{3} - x\right]_{1}^{2} = \left(\dfrac{8}{3} - 2\right) - \left(\dfrac{1}{3} - 1\right) = \dfrac{4}{3}$. The second integral is $\left[8\log_e x - x\right]_{2}^{8} = (8\log_e 8 - 8) - (8\log_e 2 - 2) = 16\log_e 2 - 6$. Summing gives $16\log_e 2 - 6 + \dfrac{4}{3} = 16\log_e 2 - \dfrac{14}{3}\text{ sq. units}$, which matches option (d).
Q12.trapHtml: Subtracting the floor $y = 1$ across the full width $[1,8]$ is simply $-7$: $7/3 + 16\log_e 2 - 7 = 16\log_e 2 - 14/3$.

Q13.questionRecapHtml: Area enclosed by $f(x) = \max\{\sin x, \cos x\}$, $-\pi \le x \le \pi$, and $x$-axis. Options: (a) $2\sqrt{2}$, (b) $4$, (c) $2(\sqrt{2}+1)$, (d) $2\sqrt{2}-1$.
Q13.conceptHtml: Split at both curve crossings ($-3\pi/4, \pi/4$) and $x$-axis zeros ($-\pi/2$) so $|f(x)|$ is integrated.
Q13.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Locate where $\sin x$ and $\cos x$ switch on $[-\pi, \pi]$: We have $\sin x = \cos x$ at $x = -\dfrac{3\pi}{4}$ and $x = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$. Therefore, $f(x) = \max\{\sin x, \cos x\}$ equals $\sin x$ on $\left[-\pi, -\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\right]$, $\cos x$ on $\left[-\dfrac{3\pi}{4}, \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right]$, and $\sin x$ on $\left[\dfrac{\pi}{4}, \pi\right]$.
  2. Step 2 — Track the sign of $f(x)$ for geometric area: Note that $f(x) \le 0$ on $\left[-\pi, -\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$ and $f(x) \ge 0$ on $\left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \pi\right]$. So we integrate $|f(x)|$ across four sub-intervals split at $-\dfrac{3\pi}{4}$, $-\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, and $\dfrac{\pi}{4}$.
  3. Step 3 — Evaluate each of the four pieces: On $\left[-\pi, -\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\right]$: $\displaystyle\int_{-\pi}^{-3\pi/4} (-\sin x)\,dx = [\cos x]_{-\pi}^{-3\pi/4} = 1 - \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$. On $\left[-\dfrac{3\pi}{4}, -\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$: $\displaystyle\int_{-3\pi/4}^{-\pi/2} (-\cos x)\,dx = [-\sin x]_{-3\pi/4}^{-\pi/2} = 1 - \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$. On $\left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right]$: $\displaystyle\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/4} \cos x\,dx = [\sin x]_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/4} = 1 + \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$. On $\left[\dfrac{\pi}{4}, \pi\right]$: $\displaystyle\int_{\pi/4}^{\pi} \sin x\,dx = [-\cos x]_{\pi/4}^{\pi} = 1 + \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$.
  4. Step 4 — Sum all four parts and confirm: $\text{Area} = 2\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right) + 2\left(1 + \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right) = 4\text{ sq. units}$, which corresponds to option (b).
Q13.trapHtml: Forgetting that $\max\{\sin x, \cos x\} < 0$ on $(-\pi, -\pi/2)$ causes catastrophic sign cancellation.

Q14.questionRecapHtml: Shaded region $S = \{(x,y) : x^2+y^2 \ge 2y,\; x^2 \le 2y,\; x \ge y\}$ has area $\frac{n+2}{n+1} - \frac{\pi}{n-1}$; find $n$. Options: (a) $3$, (b) $4$, (c) $5$, (d) $6$.
Q14.conceptHtml: $A(S) = (\text{Area between } y=x \text{ and } y=x^2/2) - (\text{circular segment below } y=x)$.
Q14.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Interpret the three inequalities geometrically: $x^2 + y^2 \ge 2y \iff x^2 + (y - 1)^2 \ge 1$ (outside the circle of center $(0,1)$ and radius $1$); $x^2 \le 2y \iff y \ge \dfrac{x^2}{2}$ (above the parabola); and $x \ge y \iff y \le x$ (below the line $y = x$).
  2. Step 2 — Check relative positions and intersections: The line $y = x$ intersects the parabola $y = \dfrac{x^2}{2}$ at $(0,0)$ and $(2,2)$, and intersects the circle at $(0,0)$ and $(1,1)$. For $x \in [0, 1]$, the lower arc of the circle $y = 1 - \sqrt{1 - x^2}$ satisfies $1 - \sqrt{1 - x^2} \ge \dfrac{x^2}{2}$, so the entire circular segment below $y = x$ lies inside the parabola-line region.
  3. Step 3 — Compute the area as (parabola-line region) minus (circular segment): The area between $y = x$ and $y = \dfrac{x^2}{2}$ on $[0, 2]$ is $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{2} \left(x - \dfrac{x^2}{2}\right) dx = \left[\dfrac{x^2}{2} - \dfrac{x^3}{6}\right]_{0}^{2} = 2 - \dfrac{4}{3} = \dfrac{2}{3}$. Since the chord from $(0,0)$ to $(1,1)$ subtends a $90^\circ$ angle at the circle's center $(0,1)$, the circular segment has area $\dfrac{1}{4}\pi(1)^2 - \dfrac{1}{2}(1)(1) = \dfrac{\pi}{4} - \dfrac{1}{2}$.
  4. Step 4 — Subtract and solve for $n$: $\text{Area}(S) = \dfrac{2}{3} - \left(\dfrac{\pi}{4} - \dfrac{1}{2}\right) = \dfrac{7}{6} - \dfrac{\pi}{4}$. Comparing with $\dfrac{n + 2}{n + 1} - \dfrac{\pi}{n - 1}$ gives $n = 5$, which matches option (c).
Q14.trapHtml: Verify that the lower circular arc $1 - \sqrt{1-x^2}$ lies strictly above $x^2/2$ on $(0,1)$, so the entire segment is subtracted.

Q15.questionRecapHtml: Area between $y = (f \circ g)(x)$ (with $f(x)=\max\{x,0\}$, $g(x)=x^2$ for $x\ge 0$, $x$ for $x<0$) and $2y - x = 15$. Options: (a) $72$, (b) $68$, (c) $76$, (d) $64$.
Q15.conceptHtml: Simplify $(f \circ g)(x)$ piecewise first: it is $0$ for $x < 0$ and $x^2$ for $x \ge 0$.
Q15.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Determine the composite function $y = (f \circ g)(x)$: Since $f(t) = \max\{t, 0\}$, for $x \ge 0$ we have $g(x) = x^2 \ge 0 \implies f(g(x)) = x^2$. For $x < 0$, $g(x) = x < 0 \implies f(g(x)) = 0$.
  2. Step 2 — Find intersections with the line $y = \dfrac{x + 15}{2}$: For $x < 0$, setting $\dfrac{x + 15}{2} = 0$ gives $x = -15$. For $x \ge 0$, setting $x^2 = \dfrac{x + 15}{2} \implies 2x^2 - x - 15 = 0 \implies (2x + 5)(x - 3) = 0$ gives $x = 3$.
  3. Step 3 — Split the area at $x = 0$: For $x \in [-15, 0]$, the region is a right triangle bounded by $y = 0$ and $y = \dfrac{x + 15}{2}$ with base $15$ and height $\dfrac{15}{2}$, giving area $\dfrac{1}{2}(15)\left(\dfrac{15}{2}\right) = \dfrac{225}{4}$. For $x \in [0, 3]$, the area is $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{3} \left(\dfrac{x + 15}{2} - x^2\right) dx = \left[\dfrac{x^2}{4} + \dfrac{15x}{2} - \dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_{0}^{3} = \dfrac{9}{4} + \dfrac{45}{2} - 9 = \dfrac{63}{4}$.
  4. Step 4 — Add both regions and confirm: $\text{Total Area} = \dfrac{225}{4} + \dfrac{63}{4} = \dfrac{288}{4} = 72\text{ sq. units}$, which corresponds to option (a).
Q15.trapHtml: Do not discard the negative-$x$ triangle on $[-15, 0]$; $(f\circ g)(x) = 0$ forms the bottom boundary there.

Q16.questionRecapHtml: Area enclosed by $(y - 2)^2 = x - 1$, $x - 2y + 4 = 0$, and positive coordinate axes. Options: (a) $14/3$, (b) $16/3$, (c) $6$, (d) $5$.
Q16.conceptHtml: Integrate with $dy$ strips: left bound is $x = 0$ on $[0, 2]$ and $x = 2y - 4$ on $[2, 3]$.
Q16.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Express the curves as $x$ in terms of $y$: The parabola is $x = 1 + (y - 2)^2$ (vertex at $(1, 2)$, meeting the positive $x$-axis at $(5, 0)$). The line is $x = 2y - 4$ (meeting the positive $y$-axis at $(0, 2)$).
  2. Step 2 — Find the intersection of the line and parabola: Equating $1 + (y - 2)^2 = 2y - 4$ gives $y^2 - 4y + 5 = 2y - 4 \implies y^2 - 6y + 9 = 0 \implies (y - 3)^2 = 0$, so $y = 3$ and $x = 2$ (the line is tangent to the parabola at $(2, 3)$).
  3. Step 3 — Integrate along the $y$-axis from $y = 0$ to $y = 3$: For $0 \le y \le 2$, the left boundary is the $y$-axis ($x = 0$) and the right boundary is the parabola. For $2 \le y \le 3$, the left boundary is the line $x = 2y - 4$ and the right boundary is the parabola. Thus, $\text{Area} = \displaystyle\int_{0}^{2} \left(1 + (y - 2)^2\right) dy + \int_{2}^{3} \left[1 + (y - 2)^2 - (2y - 4)\right] dy$.
  4. Step 4 — Evaluate and confirm: The first integral is $\left[y + \dfrac{(y - 2)^3}{3}\right]_{0}^{2} = 2 - \left(-\dfrac{8}{3}\right) = \dfrac{14}{3}$. In the second integral, the integrand simplifies to $(y - 3)^2$, so $\displaystyle\int_{2}^{3} (y - 3)^2\,dy = \left[\dfrac{(y - 3)^3}{3}\right]_{2}^{3} = \dfrac{1}{3}$. Summing gives $\dfrac{14}{3} + \dfrac{1}{3} = 5\text{ sq. units}$, matching option (d).
Q16.trapHtml: Notice $1 + (y-2)^2 - (2y-4) = (y-3)^2$ immediately because the line is tangent at $y = 3$.

Q17.subtopic: Area Ratio / Division by a Line
Q17.questionRecapHtml: Line $x = -1$ divides $\{(x,y) : 1 + x^2 \le y \le 3 - x\}$ in ratio $m : n$ ($\gcd=1$); find $m + n$. Options: (a) $25$, (b) $27$, (c) $29$, (d) $31$.
Q17.conceptHtml: Compute total area via $\frac{(\beta - \alpha)^3}{6}$ and integrate only one sub-interval $[-2, -1]$.
Q17.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Find the intersection points of the parabola and the line: Setting $1 + x^2 = 3 - x$ gives $x^2 + x - 2 = 0 \implies (x + 2)(x - 1) = 0$, so the region spans from $x = -2$ to $x = 1$.
  2. Step 2 — Compute the total area of the region: On $[-2, 1]$, the line $3 - x$ lies above the parabola $1 + x^2$, so $A_{\text{total}} = \displaystyle\int_{-2}^{1} (2 - x - x^2)\,dx = \dfrac{1}{6}(1 - (-2))^3 = \dfrac{27}{6}$.
  3. Step 3 — Compute the area to the left of $x = -1$: $A_{\text{left}} = \displaystyle\int_{-2}^{-1} (2 - x - x^2)\,dx = \left[2x - \dfrac{x^2}{2} - \dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_{-2}^{-1} = \left(-2 - \dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{1}{3}\right) - \left(-4 - 2 + \dfrac{8}{3}\right) = -\dfrac{13}{6} + \dfrac{20}{6} = \dfrac{7}{6}$.
  4. Step 4 — Find the ratio $m : n$ and $m + n$: The right area is $A_{\text{right}} = \dfrac{27}{6} - \dfrac{7}{6} = \dfrac{20}{6}$. Hence $m : n = 7 : 20$ with $\gcd(7, 20) = 1$, giving $m + n = 7 + 20 = 27$. This matches option (b).
Q17.trapHtml: Computing $A_{\text{total}}$ with the cubic shortcut saves half the arithmetic and acts as a built-in error check.

Q18.questionRecapHtml: Area inside $x^2 + 4y^2 = 4$ and outside $y = |x| - 1$, $y = 1 - |x|$. Options: (a) $2\pi - 1$, (b) $3(\pi - 1)$, (c) $2(\pi - 1)$, (d) $\pi - 2$.
Q18.conceptHtml: Verify containment, then subtract the diamond area $\frac{1}{2}d_1 d_2$ from the ellipse area $\pi ab$.
Q18.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Find the area of the ellipse: Rewriting $x^2 + 4y^2 = 4$ in standard form gives $\dfrac{x^2}{4} + \dfrac{y^2}{1} = 1$, so semi-axes are $a = 2$ and $b = 1$. Its total area is $\pi ab = 2\pi\text{ sq. units}$.
  2. Step 2 — Identify the inner region: The inequalities $y \ge |x| - 1$ and $y \le 1 - |x|$ combine to $|x| + |y| \le 1$, which is a square (rhombus) with vertices $(\pm 1, 0)$ and $(0, \pm 1)$.
  3. Step 3 — Verify containment and compute the rhombus area: All four vertices lie inside or on the ellipse (since $\dfrac{1^2}{4} + 0 < 1$ and $0 + \dfrac{1^2}{1} = 1$). The rhombus has diagonals $d_1 = 2$ and $d_2 = 2$, so its area is $\dfrac{1}{2} d_1 d_2 = \dfrac{1}{2}(2)(2) = 2\text{ sq. units}$.
  4. Step 4 — Subtract and confirm: The required area inside the ellipse and outside the rhombus is $2\pi - 2 = 2(\pi - 1)\text{ sq. units}$, matching option (c).
Q18.trapHtml: Always confirm all vertices of the inner polygon satisfy $\frac{x^2}{a^2} + \frac{y^2}{b^2} \le 1$ before subtracting.

Q19.questionRecapHtml: (A) Geometric area of $y = x^3 - x$ with $x$-axis on $[-1,1]$ is $1/2$. (R) For any odd function, geometric area on $[-a,a]$ equals $\int_{-a}^{a} f(x)\,dx = 0$. Options: (a) Both true, R explains A; (b) Both true, R does not explain A; (c) A false, R true; (d) A true, R false.
Q19.conceptHtml: For an odd function, signed integral is $0$, while geometric area is $2\int_{0}^{a} |f(x)|\,dx$.
Q19.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Check Assertion (A): The curve $y = x^3 - x = x(x - 1)(x + 1)$ crosses the $x$-axis at $x = -1, 0, 1$. It is non-negative on $[-1, 0]$ and non-positive on $[0, 1]$, and it is an odd function, so both lobes have equal geometric area.
  2. Step 2 — Compute the geometric area for (A): $\text{Area} = \displaystyle\int_{-1}^{1} |x^3 - x|\,dx = 2\int_{0}^{1} (x - x^3)\,dx = 2\left[\dfrac{x^2}{2} - \dfrac{x^4}{4}\right]_{0}^{1} = 2\left(\dfrac{1}{2} - \dfrac{1}{4}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}\text{ sq. unit}$. Thus Assertion (A) is true.
  3. Step 3 — Check Reason (R): For an odd function on $[-a, a]$, the signed definite integral $\displaystyle\int_{-a}^{a} f(x)\,dx$ is indeed $0$, but the geometric area is $\displaystyle\int_{-a}^{a} |f(x)|\,dx = 2\int_{0}^{a} |f(x)|\,dx$, which is strictly positive unless $f \equiv 0$. Thus Reason (R) is false.
  4. Step 4 — Match the verified answer: Since (A) is true and (R) is false, the correct choice is option (d).
Q19.trapHtml: NTA frequently tests the confusion between $\int_{-a}^{a} f(x)\,dx$ (signed) and $\int_{-a}^{a} |f(x)|\,dx$ (geometric area).
Q19.finalAnsHtml: Correct Option: (d) — (A) is true but (R) is false.

Q20.questionRecapHtml: Statement I: Area between $y^2 = 4ax$ and $x^2 = 4by$ ($a,b>0$) is $16ab/3$. Statement II: $\int_a^b f(x)\,dx + \int_c^d f^{-1}(y)\,dy = bd - ac$ for strictly increasing continuous $f$. Options: (a) Both true; (b) Both false; (c) I true, II false; (d) I false, II true.
Q20.conceptHtml: Standard two-parabola area and geometric rectangle decomposition for inverse functions.
Q20.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Verify Statement I: The parabolas $y^2 = 4ax$ and $x^2 = 4by$ ($a, b > 0$) intersect at $(0, 0)$ and $(4a^{1/3}b^{2/3},\, 4a^{2/3}b^{1/3})$. Letting $x_0 = 4a^{1/3}b^{2/3}$, the enclosed area is $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{x_0} \left(2\sqrt{ax} - \dfrac{x^2}{4b}\right) dx = \dfrac{4\sqrt{a}}{3}x_0^{3/2} - \dfrac{x_0^3}{12b} = \dfrac{32ab}{3} - \dfrac{16ab}{3} = \dfrac{16ab}{3}$. Thus Statement I is true.
  2. Step 2 — Verify Statement II: Let $y = f(x)$, so $x = f^{-1}(y)$ with $f(a) = c$ and $f(b) = d$. Using integration by parts (or substitution $y = f(x)$), $\displaystyle\int_{c}^{d} f^{-1}(y)\,dy = \int_{a}^{b} x\,f'(x)\,dx = \Big[x f(x)\Big]_{a}^{b} - \int_{a}^{b} f(x)\,dx = bd - ac - \int_{a}^{b} f(x)\,dx$.
  3. Step 3 — Rearrange to confirm Statement II: Moving the integral to the left side gives $\displaystyle\int_{a}^{b} f(x)\,dx + \int_{c}^{d} f^{-1}(y)\,dy = bd - ac$. Thus Statement II is also true.
  4. Step 4 — Match the verified answer: Both Statement I and Statement II are true, corresponding to option (a).
Q20.trapHtml: Statement II holds for any strictly increasing continuous $f$ without requiring $a, c \ge 0$, via $y = f(x) \implies \int f^{-1}(y)\,dy = [xf(x)]_a^b - \int f(x)\,dx$.
Q20.finalAnsHtml: Correct Option: (a) — Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

Q21.questionRecapHtml: Count correct statements among (I) $y^2=4x, y=2x \to 1/3$; (II) $\sin x, \cos x, y$-axis on $[0,\pi/4] \to \sqrt{2}-1$; (III) $|x|+|y|=2 \to 4$; (IV) $e^x, e^{-x}, x=1 \to e+e^{-1}-2$. Options: (a) $2$, (b) $3$, (c) $4$, (d) $1$.
Q21.conceptHtml: Test each region independently using standard shortcuts and direct integration.
Q21.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Check Statements 1 and 2: For Statement 1, $y^2 = 4x$ and $y = 2x$ intersect at $x = 0, 1$; the area is $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1} (2\sqrt{x} - 2x)\,dx = \left[\dfrac{4}{3}x^{3/2} - x^2\right]_{0}^{1} = \dfrac{1}{3}$ (Correct). For Statement 2, on $[0, \pi/4]$ we have $\cos x \ge \sin x$, so $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi/4} (\cos x - \sin x)\,dx = [\sin x + \cos x]_{0}^{\pi/4} = \sqrt{2} - 1$ (Correct).
  2. Step 2 — Check Statement 3: The curve $|x| + |y| = 2$ is a square with vertices $(\pm 2, 0)$ and $(0, \pm 2)$, so its diagonals have length $4$ each. Its area is $\dfrac{1}{2} \times 4 \times 4 = 8\text{ sq. units} \ne 4$ (Incorrect).
  3. Step 3 — Check Statement 4: On $[0, 1]$, $e^x \ge e^{-x}$, so the area is $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1} (e^x - e^{-x})\,dx = [e^x + e^{-x}]_{0}^{1} = (e + e^{-1}) - (1 + 1) = e + e^{-1} - 2$ (Correct).
  4. Step 4 — Count correct statements and confirm: Exactly $3$ of the $4$ statements (1, 2, and 4) are correct, which matches option (b).
Q21.trapHtml: For $|x| + |y| = c$, the area is $2c^2$, not $c^2$; setting $c = 2$ gives $8$, not $4$.

Q22.questionRecapHtml: Match List I: (A) $y=x^2, y=x$; (B) $x^2/9+y^2/4=1$; (C) $y^2=4x, x^2=4y$; (D) $y=|x|, y=2$ with List II: (I) $16/3$, (II) $1/6$, (III) $4$, (IV) $6\pi$. Options: (a) I,IV,II,III; (b) II,III,I,IV; (c) II,IV,I,III; (d) III,IV,I,II.
Q22.conceptHtml: Apply the 4 core enclosed-area formulas directly.
Q22.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Match (A) and (B): For (A), $y = x^2$ and $y = x$ intersect at $x = 0, 1$, giving $\text{Area} = \displaystyle\int_{0}^{1} (x - x^2)\,dx = \dfrac{1}{2} - \dfrac{1}{3} = \dfrac{1}{6}$, so (A)–(II). For (B), the ellipse $\dfrac{x^2}{9} + \dfrac{y^2}{4} = 1$ has $a = 3, b = 2$, giving $\text{Area} = \pi ab = 6\pi$, so (B)–(IV).
  2. Step 2 — Match (C) and (D): For (C), $y^2 = 4x$ and $x^2 = 4y$ have $a = b = 1$, so by the standard formula $\dfrac{16ab}{3}$, $\text{Area} = \dfrac{16}{3}$, giving (C)–(I). For (D), $y = |x|$ and $y = 2$ form a triangle of base $4$ (from $x = -2$ to $2$) and height $2$, so $\text{Area} = \dfrac{1}{2}(4)(2) = 4$, giving (D)–(III).
  3. Step 3 — Combine all four matches: The complete matching is (A)–(II), (B)–(IV), (C)–(I), (D)–(III).
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the option: This exact pairing corresponds to option (c).
Q22.trapHtml: Match the fastest two entries (B)$\to$(IV) and (A)$\to$(II) first to eliminate distractors immediately.

Q23.conceptHtml: Differentiable solution of $f(x+y)=f(x)f(y)$ with $f'(0)=k$ is $f(x) = e^{kx}$.
Q23.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Find the form of $f(x)$ from the functional equation: A differentiable non-zero function satisfying $f(x + y) = f(x)f(y)$ has the exponential form $f(x) = e^{kx}$. Differentiating gives $f'(x) = ke^{kx}$, so $f'(0) = k = 4a$, which gives $f(x) = e^{4ax}$.
  2. Step 2 — Determine $a$ using the differential equation: Substitute $f'(x) = 4a f(x)$ and $f''(x) = 16a^2 f(x)$ into $f''(x) - 3af'(x) - f(x) = 0$: we get $(16a^2 - 12a^2 - 1)f(x) = 0 \implies 4a^2 - 1 = 0$. Since $a > 0$, we obtain $a = \dfrac{1}{2}$.
  3. Step 3 — Find $f(ax)$ and integrate over $[0, 2]$: With $a = \dfrac{1}{2}$, we have $f(ax) = e^{4a^2 x} = e^{4(1/4)x} = e^x$. Therefore, the area of $R$ is $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{2} e^x\,dx = \left[e^x\right]_{0}^{2} = e^2 - 1$.
  4. Step 4 — Match the verified answer: The enclosed area is $e^2 - 1\text{ sq. units}$, which corresponds to option (a).
Q23.trapHtml: Do not integrate $f(x) = e^{2x}$ by mistake; the region specifies $y \le f(ax) = e^x$.

Q24.questionRecapHtml: Area enclosed by $y = x^2 - 5x$ and $y = 7x - x^2$.
Q24.conceptHtml: Use the quadratic-difference shortcut $A = \dfrac{|a_1 - a_2|(\beta - \alpha)^3}{6}$.
Q24.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Find the intersection points of the two parabolas: Equating $x^2 - 5x = 7x - x^2$ gives $2x^2 - 12x = 0 \implies 2x(x - 6) = 0$, so the parabolas intersect at $x = 0$ and $x = 6$.
  2. Step 2 — Identify the upper and lower curves: Testing at $x = 1$, $7x - x^2 = 6$ lies above $x^2 - 5x = -4$. Thus the enclosed area is $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{6} \left[(7x - x^2) - (x^2 - 5x)\right] dx = \int_{0}^{6} (12x - 2x^2)\,dx$.
  3. Step 3 — Evaluate the definite integral: $\text{Area} = \left[6x^2 - \dfrac{2x^3}{3}\right]_{0}^{6} = 6(36) - \dfrac{2(216)}{3} = 216 - 144 = 72$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the numerical answer: The area enclosed by the parabolas is 72 sq. units.
Q24.trapHtml: Both parabolas have $|a| = 1$, so their difference has leading coefficient $2$, not $1$.

Q25.questionRecapHtml: Area $A$ of $\{(x,y) : 0 \le y \le \min\{2x,\; 6x - x^2\}\}$; find $12A$.
Q25.conceptHtml: Switch from $y = 2x$ to $y = 6x - x^2$ at their non-zero intersection $x = 4$, and stop at $x = 6$.
Q25.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Determine the domain and switching point: For $y \ge 0$, both $2x \ge 0$ and $6x - x^2 \ge 0$ require $0 \le x \le 6$. The line and parabola intersect when $2x = 6x - x^2 \implies x^2 - 4x = 0 \implies x = 0$ or $x = 4$.
  2. Step 2 — Identify $\min\{2x, 6x - x^2\}$ on each sub-interval: On $[0, 4]$, $6x - x^2 - 2x = x(4 - x) \ge 0$, so the minimum is $2x$. On $[4, 6]$, $6x - x^2 \le 2x$, so the minimum is $6x - x^2$.
  3. Step 3 — Compute the area $A$: $A = \displaystyle\int_{0}^{4} 2x\,dx + \int_{4}^{6} (6x - x^2)\,dx = \left[x^2\right]_{0}^{4} + \left[3x^2 - \dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_{4}^{6} = 16 + \left[(108 - 72) - \left(48 - \dfrac{64}{3}\right)\right] = 16 + 36 - \dfrac{80}{3} = \dfrac{76}{3}$.
  4. Step 4 — Compute $12A$ and confirm: Multiplying by $12$ gives $12A = 12 \times \dfrac{76}{3} = 4 \times 76 = 304$. Thus the final numerical answer is 304.
Q25.trapHtml: Do not stop at $x = 4$; the parabola remains positive up to $x = 6$, forming the right tail of the region.

Q26.questionRecapHtml: Area $A$ of $\{(x,y) : |x - 5| \le y \le 4\sqrt{x}\}$; find $3A$.
Q26.conceptHtml: Solve $|x - 5| = 4\sqrt{x}$ as quadratics in $\sqrt{x}$, then subtract two right triangles from $\int_1^{25} 4\sqrt{x}\,dx$.
Q26.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Find the intersection points of $y = |x - 5|$ and $y = 4\sqrt{x}$: Let $t = \sqrt{x} \ge 0$, so $x = t^2$. For $x \le 5$, $5 - t^2 = 4t \implies t^2 + 4t - 5 = 0 \implies (t + 5)(t - 1) = 0 \implies t = 1$, so $x = 1$. For $x \ge 5$, $t^2 - 5 = 4t \implies t^2 - 4t - 5 = 0 \implies (t - 5)(t + 1) = 0 \implies t = 5$, so $x = 25$.
  2. Step 2 — Set up the area as upper integral minus two triangles: $A = \displaystyle\int_{1}^{25} 4\sqrt{x}\,dx - \int_{1}^{5} (5 - x)\,dx - \int_{5}^{25} (x - 5)\,dx$.
  3. Step 3 — Evaluate each term: $\displaystyle\int_{1}^{25} 4\sqrt{x}\,dx = \dfrac{8}{3}\left[x^{3/2}\right]_{1}^{25} = \dfrac{8}{3}(125 - 1) = \dfrac{992}{3}$. The two triangles below $y = |x - 5|$ have areas $\dfrac{1}{2}(4)(4) = 8$ and $\dfrac{1}{2}(20)(20) = 200$, totaling $208$.
  4. Step 4 — Compute $A$ and $3A$: $A = \dfrac{992}{3} - 208 = \dfrac{992 - 624}{3} = \dfrac{368}{3}$, so $3A = 368$. Thus the verified numerical answer is 368.
Q26.stepsLatex:
\begin{align*}
  x < 5 &: \quad 5 - x = 4\sqrt{x} \implies (\sqrt{x} + 5)(\sqrt{x} - 1) = 0 \implies x = 1. \\
  x \ge 5 &: \quad x - 5 = 4\sqrt{x} \implies (\sqrt{x} - 5)(\sqrt{x} + 1) = 0 \implies x = 25. \\
  A &= \int_{1}^{25} 4\sqrt{x}\,dx - \frac{1}{2}(4)(4) - \frac{1}{2}(20)(20) \\
    &= \frac{8}{3}\bigl[x^{3/2}\bigr]_{1}^{25} - 208 = \frac{8(125 - 1)}{3} - 208 = \frac{992 - 624}{3} = \frac{368}{3} \\
    &\implies 3A = 368.
\end{align*}
Q26.trapHtml: Treat the lower V-shape $|x - 5|$ on $[1,5]$ and $[5,25]$ as two triangles of areas $8$ and $200$ to avoid sign mistakes.

Q27.questionRecapHtml: Area $A$ enclosed by $y = \min\{\sin x, \cos x\}$ and $x$-axis on $[-\pi, \pi]$; find $A^2$.
Q27.conceptHtml: Split at curve crossings ($-3\pi/4, \pi/4$) and $x$-axis zeros ($0, \pi/2$), taking absolute value on each piece.
Q27.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the switching points of $y = \min\{\sin x, \cos x\}$ on $[-\pi, \pi]$: Since $\sin x = \cos x$ at $x = -\dfrac{3\pi}{4}$ and $x = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$, the minimum curve is $\cos x$ on $\left[-\pi, -\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\right]$, $\sin x$ on $\left[-\dfrac{3\pi}{4}, \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right]$, and $\cos x$ on $\left[\dfrac{\pi}{4}, \pi\right]$.
  2. Step 2 — Split at zeros to integrate $|y|$ for geometric area: The zeros where the active curve crosses the $x$-axis are $x = 0$ (for $\sin x$) and $x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$ (for $\cos x$). Notice $y \le 0$ on $[-\pi, 0]$ and $[\pi/2, \pi]$, while $y \ge 0$ on $[0, \pi/2]$.
  3. Step 3 — Evaluate the five sub-integrals: On $\left[-\pi, -\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\right]$: $\displaystyle\int_{-\pi}^{-3\pi/4} (-\cos x)\,dx = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$. On $\left[-\dfrac{3\pi}{4}, 0\right]$: $\displaystyle\int_{-3\pi/4}^{0} (-\sin x)\,dx = 1 + \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$. On $\left[0, \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right]$: $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi/4} \sin x\,dx = 1 - \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$. On $\left[\dfrac{\pi}{4}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$: $\displaystyle\int_{\pi/4}^{\pi/2} \cos x\,dx = 1 - \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$. On $\left[\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \pi\right]$: $\displaystyle\int_{\pi/2}^{\pi} (-\cos x)\,dx = 1$.
  4. Step 4 — Sum to find $A$ and $A^2$: Adding all five values cancels the $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$ terms, giving $A = 4$. Therefore, $A^2 = 16$, confirming the numerical answer 16.
Q27.trapHtml: Every $1/\sqrt{2}$ cancels cleanly; if your sum retains $\sqrt{2}$, recheck the sign on $[\pi/2, \pi]$ or $[-3\pi/4, 0]$.

Q28.conceptHtml: Exploit symmetry about $x = 1/2$: integrate on $[1/3, 1/2]$ and double.
Q28.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Exploit symmetry about $x = \dfrac{1}{2}$: Replacing $x$ by $1 - x$ swaps $x^2$ with $(1 - x)^2$ and leaves $2x(1 - x)$ unchanged. Hence the region is symmetric about the vertical line $x = \dfrac{1}{2}$.
  2. Step 2 — Find the boundary on the left half $x \le \dfrac{1}{2}$: For $x \le \dfrac{1}{2}$, $(1 - x)^2 \ge x^2$, so the lower boundary is $y = (1 - x)^2$. Intersecting it with the upper boundary $y = 2x(1 - x)$ gives $(1 - x)^2 = 2x(1 - x) \implies (1 - x)(1 - 3x) = 0$, so $x = \dfrac{1}{3}$.
  3. Step 3 — Integrate on $\left[\dfrac{1}{3}, \dfrac{1}{2}\right]$ and double: $A = 2\displaystyle\int_{1/3}^{1/2} \left[2x(1 - x) - (1 - x)^2\right] dx = 2\int_{1/3}^{1/2} (-3x^2 + 4x - 1)\,dx = 2\left[-x^3 + 2x^2 - x\right]_{1/3}^{1/2}$.
  4. Step 4 — Evaluate and compute $540A$: At $x = \dfrac{1}{2}$, $-x^3 + 2x^2 - x = -\dfrac{1}{8}$. At $x = \dfrac{1}{3}$, it equals $-\dfrac{1}{27} + \dfrac{2}{9} - \dfrac{1}{3} = -\dfrac{4}{27}$. Thus $A = 2\left(\dfrac{4}{27} - \dfrac{1}{8}\right) = 2\left(\dfrac{5}{216}\right) = \dfrac{5}{108}$, so $540A = 540 \times \dfrac{5}{108} = 25$. The verified answer is 25.
Q28.stepsLatex:
\begin{align*}
  \text{For } x \le \frac{1}{2} &: \quad (1 - x)^2 \ge x^2 \implies \text{floor is } y = (1 - x)^2. \\
  (1 - x)^2 &= 2x(1 - x) \implies (1 - x)(1 - 3x) = 0 \implies x = \frac{1}{3}. \\
  A &= 2\int_{1/3}^{1/2} \bigl[2x(1 - x) - (1 - x)^2\bigr]\,dx = 2\int_{1/3}^{1/2} (-3x^2 + 4x - 1)\,dx \\
    &= 2\bigl[-x^3 + 2x^2 - x\bigr]_{1/3}^{1/2} = 2\left(-\frac{1}{8} + \frac{4}{27}\right) = \frac{5}{108} \\
    &\implies 540A = 540 \times \frac{5}{108} = 25.
\end{align*}
Q28.trapHtml: Using symmetry about $x = 1/2$ cuts the calculation in half and prevents mixing up $x^2$ and $(1-x)^2$.

Q29.questionRecapHtml: Sum of squares of all $k$ maximizing the area bounded by $2y^2 = kx$ and $ky^2 = 2(y - x)$.
Q29.conceptHtml: Integrate in $y$ to get $A(k) = \dfrac{2k^2}{3(k^2+4)^2}$, then maximize via AM–GM.
Q29.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Express $x$ in terms of $y$ for both parabolas: Clearly $k \ne 0$ for a bounded region. The curves rewrite as $x = \dfrac{2}{k}y^2$ and $x = y - \dfrac{k}{2}y^2$.
  2. Step 2 — Find the intersection points: Setting $\dfrac{2}{k}y^2 = y - \dfrac{k}{2}y^2$ gives $\left(\dfrac{k^2 + 4}{2k}\right)y^2 = y$, so $y = 0$ and $y = \dfrac{2k}{k^2 + 4}$.
  3. Step 3 — Express the enclosed area $A(k)$ as a function of $k$: Using the quadratic chord formula $\dfrac{|a|}{6}(\beta - \alpha)^3$ with $|a| = \dfrac{k^2 + 4}{2|k|}$ and $|\beta - \alpha| = \dfrac{2|k|}{k^2 + 4}$, we get $A(k) = \dfrac{1}{6}\cdot\dfrac{k^2 + 4}{2|k|}\cdot\dfrac{8|k|^3}{(k^2 + 4)^3} = \dfrac{2k^2}{3(k^2 + 4)^2} = \dfrac{2}{3\left(|k| + \dfrac{4}{|k|}\right)^2}$.
  4. Step 4 — Maximize $A(k)$ using AM-GM: By AM-GM, $|k| + \dfrac{4}{|k|} \ge 2\sqrt{4} = 4$, with equality when $|k| = \dfrac{4}{|k|} \implies k^2 = 4 \implies k = 2$ or $k = -2$. The sum of squares of all possible values of $k$ is $2^2 + (-2)^2 = 8$, confirming the answer 8.
Q29.stepsLatex:
\begin{align*}
  x_1 &= \frac{2y^2}{k}, \qquad x_2 = y - \frac{k}{2}y^2. \\
  \frac{2y^2}{k} &= y - \frac{k}{2}y^2 \implies y = 0,\quad y = \frac{2k}{k^2 + 4} = \alpha. \\
  A(k) &= \left|\int_{0}^{\alpha} \left(y - \frac{y^2}{\alpha}\right)dy\right| = \frac{\alpha^2}{6} = \frac{2}{3}\cdot\frac{k^2}{(k^2 + 4)^2} = \frac{2}{3\left(|k| + \frac{4}{|k|}\right)^2}. \\
  \text{AM--GM: } & |k| + \frac{4}{|k|} \ge 4 \text{ with equality at } |k| = 2 \implies k = \pm 2. \\
  \sum k^2 &= 2^2 + (-2)^2 = 8.
\end{align*}
Q29.trapHtml: Do not drop $k = -2$; the area formula depends on $k^2$, so both $+2$ and $-2$ achieve the maximum.

Q30.questionRecapHtml: Area of $\{(x,y) : x - 2y + 4 \ge 0,\; x + 2y^2 \ge 0,\; x + 4y^2 \le 8,\; y \ge 0\}$ is $m/n$ ($\gcd=1$); find $m + n$.
Q30.conceptHtml: Write every bound as $x = g(y)$ and split at $y = 1$ where the two left boundaries cross.
Q30.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Rewrite all inequalities for $x$ in terms of $y$ ($y \ge 0$): We have $x \ge 2y - 4$, $x \ge -2y^2$, and $x \le 8 - 4y^2$. Thus the right boundary is $x = 8 - 4y^2$, and the left boundary is $x = \max\{2y - 4, -2y^2\}$.
  2. Step 2 — Find the switching point on the left boundary and upper $y$-limit: Equating $2y - 4 = -2y^2$ gives $y^2 + y - 2 = 0 \implies y = 1$ (since $y \ge 0$). For $0 \le y \le 1$, $-2y^2 \ge 2y - 4$; for $y \ge 1$, $2y - 4 \ge -2y^2$. The upper limit occurs where $2y - 4 = 8 - 4y^2 \implies 2y^2 + y - 6 = 0 \implies (2y - 3)(y + 2) = 0 \implies y = \dfrac{3}{2}$.
  3. Step 3 — Split and evaluate the area integral along $y$: $\text{Area} = \displaystyle\int_{0}^{1} \left[(8 - 4y^2) - (-2y^2)\right] dy + \int_{1}^{3/2} \left[(8 - 4y^2) - (2y - 4)\right] dy = \int_{0}^{1} (8 - 2y^2)\,dy + \int_{1}^{3/2} (12 - 2y - 4y^2)\,dy$.
  4. Step 4 — Compute $\dfrac{m}{n}$ and $m + n$: The first integral is $\left[8y - \dfrac{2y^3}{3}\right]_{0}^{1} = \dfrac{22}{3}$. The second is $\left[12y - y^2 - \dfrac{4y^3}{3}\right]_{1}^{3/2} = \left(18 - \dfrac{9}{4} - \dfrac{9}{2}\right) - \left(12 - 1 - \dfrac{4}{3}\right) = \dfrac{45}{4} - \dfrac{29}{3} = \dfrac{19}{12}$. Adding gives $\dfrac{22}{3} + \dfrac{19}{12} = \dfrac{107}{12}$. Since $\gcd(107, 12) = 1$, $m + n = 107 + 12 = 119$, confirming the answer 119.
Q30.stepsLatex:
\begin{align*}
  \text{Left bounds: } & x = -2y^2 \text{ and } x = 2y - 4 \text{ meet at } y^2 + y - 2 = 0 \implies y = 1 \; (y \ge 0). \\
  \text{Top corner: } & 2y - 4 = 8 - 4y^2 \implies 2y^2 + y - 6 = 0 \implies y = \frac{3}{2}. \\
  A &= \int_{0}^{1} \bigl[(8 - 4y^2) - (-2y^2)\bigr]\,dy + \int_{1}^{3/2} \bigl[(8 - 4y^2) - (2y - 4)\bigr]\,dy \\
    &= \left[8y - \frac{2y^3}{3}\right]_{0}^{1} + \left[12y - y^2 - \frac{4y^3}{3}\right]_{1}^{3/2} \\
    &= \frac{22}{3} + \left(\frac{45}{4} - \frac{29}{3}\right) = \frac{22}{3} + \frac{19}{12} = \frac{107}{12} \implies m + n = 107 + 12 = 119.
\end{align*}
Q30.trapHtml: At $y = 0$, $-2y^2 = 0 > 2y - 4 = -4$, so $x = -2y^2$ is the tighter left bound on $[0,1]$, switching to $2y - 4$ on $[1, 3/2]$.

Q31.conceptHtml: For $a(x-\alpha)(x-\beta) \le 0$, the enclosed area is $\dfrac{|a|(\beta - \alpha)^3}{6}$.
Q31.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Find the intersection points: Equating $x^2 - 8x = -x$ gives $x^2 - 7x = 0 \implies x(x - 7) = 0$, so the curves intersect at $x = 0$ and $x = 7$.
  2. Step 2 — Set up the area integral: On $[0, 7]$, the line $y = -x$ lies above the parabola $y = x^2 - 8x$, so $\text{Area} = \displaystyle\int_{0}^{7} \left[(-x) - (x^2 - 8x)\right] dx = \int_{0}^{7} (7x - x^2)\,dx$.
  3. Step 3 — Evaluate the integral: $\text{Area} = \left[\dfrac{7x^2}{2} - \dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_{0}^{7} = \dfrac{343}{2} - \dfrac{343}{3} = \dfrac{343}{6}\text{ sq. units}$.
  4. Step 4 — Match the verified answer: The required area is $\dfrac{343}{6}\text{ sq. units}$, which corresponds to option (a).
Q31.trapHtml: Always verify upper minus lower: at $x = 1$, $-1 > -7$, so the line $y = -x$ is indeed above $y = x^2 - 8x$.

Q32.questionRecapHtml: Area bounded by $x + 3y^2 = 0$ and $x + 4y^2 = 1$. (a) $\frac{2}{3}$   (b) $\frac{4}{3}$   (c) $\frac{5}{3}$   (d) $2$
Q32.conceptHtml: Express both curves as $x = f(y)$ and integrate $(x_{\text{right}} - x_{\text{left}})\,dy$ between intersections.
Q32.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Rewrite both parabolas as $x$ in terms of $y$: We get $x = -3y^2$ and $x = 1 - 4y^2$.
  2. Step 2 — Find the points of intersection: Equating $-3y^2 = 1 - 4y^2$ gives $y^2 = 1 \implies y = -1$ and $y = 1$.
  3. Step 3 — Integrate along the $y$-axis: Between $y = -1$ and $y = 1$, $1 - 4y^2 \ge -3y^2$ (at $y = 0$, $1 > 0$). By symmetry about the $x$-axis, $\text{Area} = \displaystyle\int_{-1}^{1} \left[(1 - 4y^2) - (-3y^2)\right] dy = 2\int_{0}^{1} (1 - y^2)\,dy$.
  4. Step 4 — Evaluate and confirm: $\text{Area} = 2\left[y - \dfrac{y^3}{3}\right]_{0}^{1} = 2\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{3}\right) = \dfrac{4}{3}\text{ sq. units}$, matching option (b).
Q32.trapHtml: Integrating with respect to $x$ forces splitting at $x = 0$; horizontal strips ($dy$) solve it in a single clean integral.

Q33.conceptHtml: Use symmetry about the $x$-axis and integrate from $x_{\text{left}} = y^2/4$ to $x_{\text{right}} = \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{8 - y^2}$ over $y \in [-2, 2]$.
Q33.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Find the intersection points and note symmetry: Both $4x^2 + y^2 \le 8$ (ellipse with right vertex at $x = \sqrt{2}$) and $y^2 \le 4x$ (parabola with $x \ge 0$) are symmetric about the $x$-axis. Substituting $y^2 = 4x$ into $4x^2 + y^2 = 8$ gives $4x^2 + 4x - 8 = 0 \implies x^2 + x - 2 = 0 \implies x = 1$ (since $x \ge 0$), where $y = \pm 2$.
  2. Step 2 — Split the upper-half area at $x = 1$: By symmetry, $\text{Area} = 2\left(\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1} 2\sqrt{x}\,dx + \int_{1}^{\sqrt{2}} \sqrt{8 - 4x^2}\,dx\right) = 4\int_{0}^{1} \sqrt{x}\,dx + 4\int_{1}^{\sqrt{2}} \sqrt{2 - x^2}\,dx$.
  3. Step 3 — Evaluate both integrals: First, $4\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1} \sqrt{x}\,dx = 4\left[\dfrac{2}{3}x^{3/2}\right]_{0}^{1} = \dfrac{8}{3}$. Second, $4\displaystyle\int_{1}^{\sqrt{2}} \sqrt{2 - x^2}\,dx = 4\left[\dfrac{x}{2}\sqrt{2 - x^2} + \sin^{-1}\!\left(\dfrac{x}{\sqrt{2}}\right)\right]_{1}^{\sqrt{2}} = 4\left[\left(0 + \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) - \left(\dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)\right] = \pi - 2$.
  4. Step 4 — Add and confirm: $\text{Total Area} = \dfrac{8}{3} + \pi - 2 = \pi + \dfrac{2}{3}\text{ sq. units}$, which corresponds to option (c).
Q33.trapHtml: Be careful with the factor of $1/2$ in $x = \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{8-y^2}$; doubling for $[-2,2]$ symmetry cleanly cancels that $1/2$.

Q34.questionRecapHtml: Area inside $x^2 + 4y^2 = 4$ and outside $y = |x|-1$, $y = 1-|x|$. (a) $2\pi-1$   (b) $\pi-2$   (c) $2\pi-4$   (d) $2(\pi-1)$
Q34.conceptHtml: Area of ellipse $\frac{x^2}{a^2}+\frac{y^2}{b^2}=1$ is $\pi ab$; the region $|x|+|y| \le 1$ is a rhombus with diagonals $d_1 = d_2 = 2$.
Q34.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Compute the area of the ellipse: Dividing $x^2 + 4y^2 = 4$ by $4$ gives $\dfrac{x^2}{4} + \dfrac{y^2}{1} = 1$, with semi-axes $a = 2$ and $b = 1$. Its total area is $\pi ab = 2\pi\text{ sq. units}$.
  2. Step 2 — Identify the inner bounded region: The curves $y = |x| - 1$ and $y = 1 - |x|$ enclose the diamond $|x| + |y| \le 1$, with vertices $(\pm 1, 0)$ and $(0, \pm 1)$ lying completely inside the ellipse.
  3. Step 3 — Compute the area of the diamond: Its diagonals along the coordinate axes have lengths $d_1 = 2$ and $d_2 = 2$, so its area is $\dfrac{1}{2} d_1 d_2 = \dfrac{1}{2}(2)(2) = 2\text{ sq. units}$.
  4. Step 4 — Subtract and confirm: The required area is $2\pi - 2 = 2(\pi - 1)\text{ sq. units}$, matching option (d).
Q34.trapHtml: Always verify the rhombus lies completely inside the ellipse: at $(\pm 1, 0)$, $1/4 < 1$; at $(0, \pm 1)$, $1 = 1$ (touches smoothly).

Q35.conceptHtml: Find all three boundary intersections to split the upper curve at $x = 3$: $y = x^2$ on $[1,3]$ and $y = 27/x$ on $[3,27]$.
Q35.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the bounding curves: In the first quadrant ($x \ge 0$), the region satisfies $1 \le y \le \min\!\left\{x^2, \dfrac{27}{x}\right\}$.
  2. Step 2 — Find the three intersection $x$-coordinates: $y = x^2$ meets $y = 1$ at $x = 1$; $y = x^2$ meets $y = \dfrac{27}{x}$ when $x^3 = 27 \implies x = 3$; and $y = \dfrac{27}{x}$ meets $y = 1$ at $x = 27$.
  3. Step 3 — Split the area integral at $x = 3$: $\text{Area} = \displaystyle\int_{1}^{3} (x^2 - 1)\,dx + \int_{3}^{27} \left(\dfrac{27}{x} - 1\right) dx$.
  4. Step 4 — Evaluate and confirm: The first integral is $\left[\dfrac{x^3}{3} - x\right]_{1}^{3} = (9 - 3) - \left(\dfrac{1}{3} - 1\right) = \dfrac{20}{3}$. The second integral is $\left[27\log_e x - x\right]_{3}^{27} = (27\log_e 27 - 27) - (27\log_e 3 - 3) = 54\log_e 3 - 24$. Summing gives $54\log_e 3 - 24 + \dfrac{20}{3} = 54\log_e 3 - \dfrac{52}{3}\text{ sq. units}$, matching option (b).
Q35.trapHtml: Do not forget to subtract the lower floor $y = 1$ across the ENTIRE span $[1, 27]$, and simplify $27\log_e 9 = 54\log_e 3$.

Q36.questionRecapHtml: Area enclosed between $x^2 + y^2 = 4$ and $x^2 + (y-2)^2 = 4$. (a) $\frac{4\pi}{3}-\sqrt{3}$   (b) $\frac{8\pi}{3}-\sqrt{3}$   (c) $\frac{8\pi}{3}-2\sqrt{3}$   (d) $\frac{4\pi}{3}-2\sqrt{3}$
Q36.conceptHtml: Each circle of radius $r = 2$ passes through the other's centre (distance $d = 2$), so each subtends central angle $\theta = \frac{2\pi}{3}$ at the common chord.
Q36.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the two circles and their intersections: Circle $C_1: x^2 + y^2 = 4$ has center $(0, 0)$ and radius $r = 2$; Circle $C_2: x^2 + (y - 2)^2 = 4$ has center $(0, 2)$ and radius $r = 2$. Subtracting the two equations gives $y^2 - (y - 2)^2 = 0 \implies 4y - 4 = 0 \implies y = 1$, and $x = \pm\sqrt{3}$.
  2. Step 2 — Find the central angle of each circular segment: Since each circle passes through the other's center, the distance between centers equals $r = 2$. At $(0, 0)$, the chord connecting $(-\sqrt{3}, 1)$ and $(\sqrt{3}, 1)$ subtends angle $\theta = 2\cos^{-1}\!\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = \dfrac{2\pi}{3}$.
  3. Step 3 — Compute the area of one circular segment: $\text{Area}_{\text{segment}} = \dfrac{1}{2}r^2(\theta - \sin\theta) = \dfrac{1}{2}(4)\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{3} - \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) = \dfrac{4\pi}{3} - \sqrt{3}$.
  4. Step 4 — Double for the full lens and confirm: The overlap region consists of two identical circular segments, so $\text{Total Area} = 2\left(\dfrac{4\pi}{3} - \sqrt{3}\right) = \dfrac{8\pi}{3} - 2\sqrt{3}\text{ sq. units}$. This matches option (c).
Q36.trapHtml: Remember to double the single-segment area $\frac{4\pi}{3} - \sqrt{3}$ because the lens consists of TWO identical circular segments.

Q37.questionRecapHtml: Area of $\{(x,y): 1-2x \le y \le 4-x^2,\; x\ge 0,\; y\ge 0\}$ is $\alpha/\beta$ ($\gcd=1$). Find $\alpha+\beta$. (a) $67$   (b) $69$   (c) $71$   (d) $73$
Q37.conceptHtml: Notice $1 - 2x \le 4 - x^2$ everywhere on $[0, 2]$, so the required region is simply the Q1 parabolic cap minus the corner right triangle under $y = 1 - 2x$.
Q37.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Sketch the boundaries in the first quadrant: The parabola $y = 4 - x^2$ meets the $y$-axis at $(0, 4)$ and the positive $x$-axis at $(2, 0)$. The line $y = 1 - 2x$ meets the $y$-axis at $(0, 1)$ and the positive $x$-axis at $\left(\dfrac{1}{2}, 0\right)$, staying completely below the parabola for $x \ge 0$.
  2. Step 2 — Express the region as (parabola area) minus (corner triangle): In the first quadrant, the region $1 - 2x \le y \le 4 - x^2$ is the entire area under $y = 4 - x^2$ from $x = 0$ to $x = 2$, minus the right triangle below $y = 1 - 2x$ from $x = 0$ to $x = \dfrac{1}{2}$.
  3. Step 3 — Compute both areas: Under the parabola, $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{2} (4 - x^2)\,dx = \left[4x - \dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_{0}^{2} = 8 - \dfrac{8}{3} = \dfrac{16}{3}$. The right triangle has base $\dfrac{1}{2}$ and height $1$, so its area is $\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)(1) = \dfrac{1}{4}$.
  4. Step 4 — Subtract and find $\alpha + \beta$: $\text{Area} = \dfrac{16}{3} - \dfrac{1}{4} = \dfrac{64 - 3}{12} = \dfrac{61}{12}$. Since $\gcd(61, 12) = 1$, $\alpha = 61$ and $\beta = 12$, giving $\alpha + \beta = 73$. This confirms option (d).
Q37.trapHtml: Do not integrate $1 - 2x$ past $x = 1/2$ because $y \ge 0$ clips the lower boundary to the $x$-axis for $x \in [1/2, 2]$.

Q38.questionRecapHtml: Area $A$ bounded by $16x^2 - 9y^2 = 144$ and $8x - 3y = 24$. Find $3(A + 6\log_e 3)$.
Q38.conceptHtml: Solve for intersections, identify the upper branch $y = \frac{4}{3}\sqrt{x^2 - 9}$ vs the line $y = \frac{8x-24}{3}$, and apply $\int \sqrt{x^2 - a^2}\,dx$.
Q38.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Find the intersection points of the hyperbola and line: From $8x - 3y = 24$, we have $3y = 8x - 24$. Substituting into $16x^2 - (3y)^2 = 144$ gives $16x^2 - (8x - 24)^2 = 144 \implies -48x^2 + 384x - 720 = 0 \implies x^2 - 8x + 15 = 0 \implies (x - 3)(x - 5) = 0$. Thus the intersections are $(3, 0)$ and $\left(5, \dfrac{16}{3}\right)$.
  2. Step 2 — Set up the area integral on $[3, 5]$: On $[3, 5]$, the upper branch of the hyperbola $y = \dfrac{4}{3}\sqrt{x^2 - 9}$ lies above the line $y = \dfrac{8}{3}(x - 3)$. Hence $A = \displaystyle\int_{3}^{5} \dfrac{4}{3}\sqrt{x^2 - 9}\,dx - \int_{3}^{5} \dfrac{8}{3}(x - 3)\,dx$.
  3. Step 3 — Evaluate both integrals: The line integral is a triangle of base $2$ and height $\dfrac{16}{3}$, giving area $\dfrac{16}{3}$. For the hyperbola, $\dfrac{4}{3}\left[\dfrac{x}{2}\sqrt{x^2 - 9} - \dfrac{9}{2}\log_e\!\left|x + \sqrt{x^2 - 9}\right|\right]_{3}^{5} = \dfrac{4}{3}\left[\left(10 - \dfrac{9}{2}\log_e 9\right) - \left(0 - \dfrac{9}{2}\log_e 3\right)\right] = \dfrac{4}{3}\left(10 - \dfrac{9}{2}\log_e 3\right) = \dfrac{40}{3} - 6\log_e 3$.
  4. Step 4 — Compute $A$ and the target expression: Subtracting gives $A = \left(\dfrac{40}{3} - 6\log_e 3\right) - \dfrac{16}{3} = 8 - 6\log_e 3$. Therefore, $3(A + 6\log_e 3) = 3(8) = 24$, confirming the numerical answer 24.
Q38.stepsLatex:
\begin{align*}
16x^2 - (8x - 24)^2 = 144 &\implies -48x^2 + 384x - 720 = 0 \implies x^2 - 8x + 15 = 0 \implies x = 3,\; 5 \\
A &= \int_{3}^{5} \left(\frac{4}{3}\sqrt{x^2 - 9} - \frac{8x - 24}{3}\right)dx \\
&= \frac{4}{3}\left[\frac{x}{2}\sqrt{x^2 - 9} - \frac{9}{2}\log_e\!\left|x + \sqrt{x^2 - 9}\right|\right]_{3}^{5} - \frac{1}{3}\bigl[4x^2 - 24x\bigr]_{3}^{5} \\
&= \frac{4}{3}\left(10 - \frac{9}{2}\log_e\!\left(\frac{9}{3}\right)\right) - \frac{16}{3} = \frac{40 - 16}{3} - 6\log_e 3 = 8 - 6\log_e 3 \\
3(A + 6\log_e 3) &= 3 \times 8 = 24
\end{align*}
Q38.trapHtml: At $x = 3$, $\log_e(3 + 0) = \log_e 3$ does NOT vanish; subtracting the lower limit gives $\log_e(9) - \log_e(3) = \log_e 3$.

Q39.subtopic: Area Division Ratio by Vertical Line
Q39.questionRecapHtml: $x = -1$ divides the area of $\{(x,y) : 1 + x^2 \le y \le 3 - x\}$ in ratio $m:n$ ($\gcd=1$). Find $m+n$.
Q39.conceptHtml: Find the endpoints of $1+x^2 = 3-x$, then evaluate the two sub-integrals on $[-2, -1]$ and $[-1, 1]$ separately.
Q39.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Find the intersection points of the bounding curves: Equating $1 + x^2 = 3 - x$ gives $x^2 + x - 2 = 0 \implies (x + 2)(x - 1) = 0$, so the bounded region extends from $x = -2$ to $x = 1$.
  2. Step 2 — Compute the total area of the region: Since $3 - x \ge 1 + x^2$ on $[-2, 1]$, $A_{\text{total}} = \displaystyle\int_{-2}^{1} (2 - x - x^2)\,dx = \dfrac{1}{6}(1 - (-2))^3 = \dfrac{27}{6}$.
  3. Step 3 — Compute the two sub-areas split by $x = -1$: To the left of $x = -1$, $A_1 = \displaystyle\int_{-2}^{-1} (2 - x - x^2)\,dx = \left[2x - \dfrac{x^2}{2} - \dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_{-2}^{-1} = \left(-2 - \dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{1}{3}\right) - \left(-4 - 2 + \dfrac{8}{3}\right) = \dfrac{7}{6}$. To the right of $x = -1$, $A_2 = \dfrac{27}{6} - \dfrac{7}{6} = \dfrac{20}{6}$.
  4. Step 4 — Find $m + n$ and confirm: The ratio is $m : n = A_1 : A_2 = 7 : 20$ with $\gcd(7, 20) = 1$, so $m + n = 7 + 20 = 27$. The verified numerical answer is 27.
Q39.trapHtml: Cross-check $A_1 + A_2 = \frac{27}{6} = \frac{9}{2}$ against the shortcut $\frac{(1 - (-2))^3}{6} = \frac{27}{6}$ to guarantee zero arithmetic errors.

Q40.questionRecapHtml: Area bounded by $y = \max\{\sin x, \cos x\}$, $x = 0$, $x = \frac{3\pi}{2}$, and the $x$-axis.
Q40.conceptHtml: Split $[0, 3\pi/2]$ at BOTH curve switch points ($x = \pi/4, 5\pi/4$) AND the $x$-axis crossing ($x = \pi$), integrating $|y|$ on each sub-interval.
Q40.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Find where $\sin x$ and $\cos x$ cross on $\left[0, \dfrac{3\pi}{2}\right]$: The two curves intersect at $x = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$ and $x = \dfrac{5\pi}{4}$. Thus $y = \max\{\sin x, \cos x\}$ equals $\cos x$ on $\left[0, \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right]$, $\sin x$ on $\left[\dfrac{\pi}{4}, \dfrac{5\pi}{4}\right]$, and $\cos x$ on $\left[\dfrac{5\pi}{4}, \dfrac{3\pi}{2}\right]$.
  2. Step 2 — Identify where $y$ is positive or negative: On $[0, \pi]$, $y \ge 0$. On $\left[\pi, \dfrac{3\pi}{2}\right]$, both $\sin x \le 0$ and $\cos x \le 0$, so $y \le 0$ and we integrate $-y$ for geometric area.
  3. Step 3 — Evaluate the four sub-integrals: On $\left[0, \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right]$: $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi/4} \cos x\,dx = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$. On $\left[\dfrac{\pi}{4}, \pi\right]$: $\displaystyle\int_{\pi/4}^{\pi} \sin x\,dx = [-\cos x]_{\pi/4}^{\pi} = 1 + \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$. On $\left[\pi, \dfrac{5\pi}{4}\right]$: $\displaystyle\int_{\pi}^{5\pi/4} (-\sin x)\,dx = [\cos x]_{\pi}^{5\pi/4} = 1 - \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$. On $\left[\dfrac{5\pi}{4}, \dfrac{3\pi}{2}\right]$: $\displaystyle\int_{5\pi/4}^{3\pi/2} (-\cos x)\,dx = [-\sin x]_{5\pi/4}^{3\pi/2} = 1 - \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$.
  4. Step 4 — Sum all four parts and confirm: $\text{Total Area} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} + \left(1 + \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right) + \left(1 - \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right) + \left(1 - \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right) = 3\text{ sq. units}$. This confirms the verified numerical answer 3.
Q40.stepsLatex:
\begin{align*}
\text{On } [0, \pi/4] &: y = \cos x \ge 0 \implies I_1 = \int_{0}^{\pi/4} \cos x\,dx = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\
\text{On } [\pi/4, \pi] &: y = \sin x \ge 0 \implies I_2 = \int_{\pi/4}^{\pi} \sin x\,dx = 1 + \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\
\text{On } [\pi, 5\pi/4] &: y = \sin x \le 0 \implies I_3 = \int_{\pi}^{5\pi/4} (-\sin x)\,dx = 1 - \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\
\text{On } [5\pi/4, 3\pi/2] &: y = \cos x \le 0 \implies I_4 = \int_{5\pi/4}^{3\pi/2} (-\cos x)\,dx = 1 - \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\
\text{Total Area} &= I_1 + I_2 + I_3 + I_4 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} + 1 + \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} + 1 - \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} + 1 - \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} = 3
\end{align*}
Q40.trapHtml: Forgetting that $\max\{\sin x, \cos x\}$ dips BELOW the $x$-axis on $(\pi, 3\pi/2)$ gives signed integral $2\sqrt{2} - 1$ instead of true geometric area $3$.

trapCards.title: 1. Signed-Integral vs Geometric-Area Traps
trapCards.html:
• Zero-crossing cancellation: $\int_{a}^{b} f(x)\,dx$ subtracts area below the $x$-axis. Always locate every zero of $f(x)$ in $(a,b)$ and integrate $|f(x)|$.
  • Odd-function fallacy: On $[-a, a]$, $\int_{-a}^{a} f(x)\,dx = 0$ for odd $f$, but geometric area is $2\int_{0}^{a} |f(x)|\,dx > 0$ (e.g., $y = x^3 - x$ on $[-1,1]$ has area $1/2$, not $0$).
  • Trig envelopes below zero: Functions like $\max\{\sin x, \cos x\}$ and $\min\{\sin x, \cos x\}$ dip below $y = 0$ on $[-\pi, \pi]$; split at both intersections and $x$-axis zeros.

trapCards.title: 2. Upper/Lower Curve Swap, Modulus & Symmetry Pitfalls
trapCards.html:
• Missed interior crossing: If $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ intersect at $c \in (a,b)$, integrating $(f - g)$ straight from $a$ to $b$ cancels the two lobes.
  • Unbroken modulus: Never integrate $|x - c|$ or $|e^x - 1|$ as a single expression; split at the critical point where the inside equals $0$.
  • False symmetry assumption: Check both curves before doubling $[0, a]$. For example, $y = x|x|$ and $y = x - |x|$ enclose a region only for $x \le 0$.
  • Negative parameter drop: In area-optimization problems (e.g., $A(k) \propto k^2/(k^2+4)^2$), check whether $-k$ also yields a valid enclosed region.

trapCards.title: 3. Formula Applicability Boundaries ($dx$ vs $dy$ Strip Choice)
trapCards.html:
• Wrong strip orientation: Using $dx$ strips on $y^2 = 4ax$ or multi-inequality bounds in $y$ forces messy square roots and unnecessary splits; switch to $dy$ strips whenever boundaries are clean functions $x = g(y)$.
  • Quadratic shortcut coefficient: In $A = \frac{|a_1 - a_2|(\beta - \alpha)^3}{6}$, never omit $|a_1 - a_2|$ when the leading coefficients are not $1$ and $0$.
  • Containment check: Before writing $A_{\text{outer}} - A_{\text{inner}}$ (circle vs parabola or ellipse vs diamond), verify that the inner curve does not protrude outside the outer curve.
  • Diamond area slip: $|x| + |y| = c$ has diagonals $2c$ and $2c$, giving area $2c^2$ (not $c^2$).

trapCards.title: 4. NTA Statement / A–R Wordings to Watch
trapCards.html:
• “Inside $C_1$ and outside $C_2$”: Verify which side of a parabola $y^2 = 4ax$ is “inside” ($y^2 < 4ax$) vs “outside” ($y^2 > 4ax$) by testing a point like the focus $(a,0)$.
  • Scaled final answer: NTA numericals routinely ask for $3A$, $12A$, $540A$, $A^2$, or $m + n$ (with $\gcd(m,n)=1$), not $A$ itself. Re-read the last 8 words before bubbling.
  • Composite/scaled argument: Watch for $y \le f(ax)$ instead of $y \le f(x)$ in ODE/functional-equation hybrids.
  • A–R trap: A true numerical value in (A) paired with a false theoretical shortcut in (R) makes (d) correct — always verify (R) independently.

subject: Maths
title: Trigonometry
constantsHtml:
Standard Non-Elementary Angles, ASTC Quadrant Signs & Transformation Quick-Ref
  • Key Angles: $\sin 15^\circ = \cos 75^\circ = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}-1}{2\sqrt{2}}$,   $\cos 15^\circ = \sin 75^\circ = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}+1}{2\sqrt{2}}$,   $\tan 15^\circ = \cot 75^\circ = 2-\sqrt{3}$,   $\tan 75^\circ = \cot 15^\circ = 2+\sqrt{3}$.
  • Golden-Ratio & Half Angles: $\sin 18^\circ = \cos 72^\circ = \dfrac{\sqrt{5}-1}{4}$,   $\cos 36^\circ = \sin 54^\circ = \dfrac{\sqrt{5}+1}{4}$,   $\sin 36^\circ = \dfrac{\sqrt{10-2\sqrt{5}}}{4}$,   $\cos 18^\circ = \dfrac{\sqrt{10+2\sqrt{5}}}{4}$,   $\tan 22.5^\circ = \sqrt{2}-1$,   $\cot 22.5^\circ = \sqrt{2}+1$.
  • ASTC Sign Rule: QI $(0, \pi/2)$: All $+$;   QII $(\pi/2, \pi)$: Sin, $\csc$ $+$;   QIII $(\pi, 3\pi/2)$: Tan, $\cot$ $+$;   QIV $(3\pi/2, 2\pi)$: Cos, $\sec$ $+$.
  • Product-to-Sum / Sum-to-Product: $2\sin A\cos B = \sin(A+B)+\sin(A-B)$;   $2\cos A\cos B = \cos(A+B)+\cos(A-B)$;   $2\sin A\sin B = \cos(A-B)-\cos(A+B)$;   $\sin C \pm \sin D = 2\sin\dfrac{C\pm D}{2}\cos\dfrac{C\mp D}{2}$;   $\cos C + \cos D = 2\cos\dfrac{C+D}{2}\cos\dfrac{C-D}{2}$;   $\cos C - \cos D = -2\sin\dfrac{C+D}{2}\sin\dfrac{C-D}{2}$.

formulaCards.title: 1. Fundamental Identities & Allied Angles
formulaCards.html:
• $\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1$;   $1+\tan^2\theta = \sec^2\theta$;   $1+\cot^2\theta = \csc^2\theta$.
  • $\sec\theta \pm \tan\theta = \dfrac{1}{\sec\theta \mp \tan\theta}$;   $\csc\theta \pm \cot\theta = \dfrac{1}{\csc\theta \mp \cot\theta}$.
  • $\sin^4\theta + \cos^4\theta = 1 - 2\sin^2\theta\cos^2\theta$;   $\sin^6\theta + \cos^6\theta = 1 - 3\sin^2\theta\cos^2\theta$.
  • Allied Reduction: For $n\pi \pm \theta$, ratio stays same; for $(2n+1)\frac{\pi}{2} \pm \theta$, ratio co-switches ($\sin \leftrightarrow \cos$, $\tan \leftrightarrow \cot$, $\sec \leftrightarrow \csc$). Attach sign from original quadrant (ASTC).
  • Parity: $\cos(-\theta)=\cos\theta$, $\sec(-\theta)=\sec\theta$ (even); $\sin, \tan, \cot, \csc$ are odd.

formulaCards.title: 2. Compound Angles ($A \pm B$)
formulaCards.html:
• $\sin(A\pm B) = \sin A\cos B \pm \cos A\sin B$.
  • $\cos(A\pm B) = \cos A\cos B \mp \sin A\sin B$.
  • $\tan(A\pm B) = \dfrac{\tan A \pm \tan B}{1 \mp \tan A\tan B}$;   $\cot(A\pm B) = \dfrac{\cot A\cot B \mp 1}{\cot B \pm \cot A}$.
  • $\sin(A+B)\sin(A-B) = \sin^2 A - \sin^2 B = \cos^2 B - \cos^2 A$.
  • $\cos(A+B)\cos(A-B) = \cos^2 A - \sin^2 B = \cos^2 B - \sin^2 A$.
  • Conditional ($A+B = 45^\circ$ or $225^\circ$): $(1+\tan A)(1+\tan B) = 2$.

formulaCards.title: 3. Multiple & Sub-Multiple Angles
formulaCards.html:
• $\sin 2\theta = 2\sin\theta\cos\theta = \dfrac{2\tan\theta}{1+\tan^2\theta}$.
  • $\cos 2\theta = \cos^2\theta-\sin^2\theta = 2\cos^2\theta-1 = 1-2\sin^2\theta = \dfrac{1-\tan^2\theta}{1+\tan^2\theta}$.
  • $\tan 2\theta = \dfrac{2\tan\theta}{1-\tan^2\theta}$;   $1+\cos 2\theta = 2\cos^2\theta$;   $1-\cos 2\theta = 2\sin^2\theta$.
  • $\sin 3\theta = 3\sin\theta - 4\sin^3\theta$;   $\cos 3\theta = 4\cos^3\theta - 3\cos\theta$.
  • $\tan 3\theta = \dfrac{3\tan\theta - \tan^3\theta}{1-3\tan^2\theta}$.
  • (Triple Products): $\sin\theta\sin(60^\circ-\theta)\sin(60^\circ+\theta) = \dfrac{1}{4}\sin 3\theta$;   $\cos\theta\cos(60^\circ-\theta)\cos(60^\circ+\theta) = \dfrac{1}{4}\cos 3\theta$;   $\tan\theta\tan(60^\circ-\theta)\tan(60^\circ+\theta) = \tan 3\theta$.

formulaCards.title: 4. Trigonometric Series & Bounds
formulaCards.html:
• (Cosine Product): $\displaystyle\prod_{k=0}^{n-1}\cos(2^k\theta) = \dfrac{\sin(2^n\theta)}{2^n\sin\theta}$ ($\sin\theta \neq 0$).
  • Sine / Cosine AP Sums: $\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\sin(\alpha+k\beta) = \dfrac{\sin(n\beta/2)}{\sin(\beta/2)}\sin\!\left(\alpha+\dfrac{(n-1)\beta}{2}\right)$;   $\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\cos(\alpha+k\beta) = \dfrac{\sin(n\beta/2)}{\sin(\beta/2)}\cos\!\left(\alpha+\dfrac{(n-1)\beta}{2}\right)$.
  • (Linear Extrema): $a\sin\theta + b\cos\theta \in \left[-\sqrt{a^2+b^2},\; \sqrt{a^2+b^2}\right]$.
  • Auxiliary Angle: $a\cos\theta + b\sin\theta = R\cos(\theta-\phi)$ with $R=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$, $\tan\phi = b/a$.
  • Periods: $\sin(kx), \cos(kx), \sec(kx), \csc(kx) \to \frac{2\pi}{|k|}$;   $\tan(kx), \cot(kx) \to \frac{\pi}{|k|}$.

formulaCards.title: 5. ITF: Domains & Principal Value Branches
formulaCards.html:
• Func.DomainRange (PVB)
    $\sin^{-1}x$$[-1,1]$$[-\pi/2,\pi/2]$
    $\cos^{-1}x$$[-1,1]$$[0,\pi]$
    $\tan^{-1}x$$\mathbb{R}$$(-\pi/2,\pi/2)$
    $\cot^{-1}x$$\mathbb{R}$$(0,\pi)$
    $\sec^{-1}x$$|x|\ge 1$$[0,\pi]\setminus\{\pi/2\}$
    $\csc^{-1}x$$|x|\ge 1$$[-\pi/2,\pi/2]\setminus\{0\}$
    }
  • Negative Arguments: $\sin^{-1}(-x)=-\sin^{-1}x$, $\tan^{-1}(-x)=-\tan^{-1}x$, $\csc^{-1}(-x)=-\csc^{-1}x$;   $\cos^{-1}(-x)=\pi-\cos^{-1}x$, $\cot^{-1}(-x)=\pi-\cot^{-1}x$, $\sec^{-1}(-x)=\pi-\sec^{-1}x$.

formulaCards.title: 6. ITF: Core Properties & Identities
formulaCards.html:
• (Complementary): $\sin^{-1}x + \cos^{-1}x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$ ($|x|\le 1$);   $\tan^{-1}x + \cot^{-1}x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$ ($x\in\mathbb{R}$);   $\sec^{-1}x + \csc^{-1}x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$ ($|x|\ge 1$).
  • Reciprocal: $\sin^{-1}(1/x)=\csc^{-1}x$ ($|x|\ge 1$); $\cos^{-1}(1/x)=\sec^{-1}x$ ($|x|\ge 1$); $\tan^{-1}(1/x)=\cot^{-1}x$ ($x>0$), $= -\pi+\cot^{-1}x$ ($x<0$).
  • ($\tan^{-1}$ Addition, $x,y>0$): $\tan^{-1}x + \tan^{-1}y = \begin{cases} \tan^{-1}\!\left(\dfrac{x+y}{1-xy}\right), & xy < 1 \\ \dfrac{\pi}{2}, & xy = 1 \\ \pi + \tan^{-1}\!\left(\dfrac{x+y}{1-xy}\right), & xy > 1 \end{cases}$
  • $\tan^{-1}$ Difference ($xy > -1$): $\tan^{-1}x - \tan^{-1}y = \tan^{-1}\!\left(\dfrac{x-y}{1+xy}\right)$.
  • Double-Angle ITF: $2\tan^{-1}x = \sin^{-1}\!\left(\dfrac{2x}{1+x^2}\right)$ ($|x|\le 1$) $= \cos^{-1}\!\left(\dfrac{1-x^2}{1+x^2}\right)$ ($x\ge 0$) $= \tan^{-1}\!\left(\dfrac{2x}{1-x^2}\right)$ ($|x|<1$).
  • Composition: $f(f^{-1}(x)) = x$ on domain of $f^{-1}$;   $f^{-1}(f(\theta)) = \theta$ only when $\theta \in \text{PVB}$ (otherwise fold using period/symmetry).
