Q01.questionRecapHtml: Evaluate five statements (A–E) from the given piecewise-linear $x$-$t$ graph over 0–9 s.
Q01.conceptHtml: Instantaneous velocity $=$ local slope; average velocity $=\Delta x/\Delta t$.
Q01.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Given & Concept: We are given a displacement-time ($x$-$t$) graph and need to verify five statements. Remember two core graphical rules: average velocity over an interval is the total displacement divided by total time ($v_{\text{avg}} = \frac{\Delta x}{\Delta t}$), whereas instantaneous velocity at a point is the local slope of the $x$-$t$ graph ($\frac{dx}{dt}$) at that exact instant.
  2. Step 2 — Check Statements (A), (B), and (C): From the graph, at $t = 0\text{ s}$, $x = 0\text{ m}$, and at $t = 3\text{ s}$, $x = 5\text{ m}$. Thus, $v_{\text{avg}}(0\text{ to }3\text{ s}) = \frac{5 - 0}{3 - 0} = \frac{5}{3}\text{ m/s} \neq 10\text{ m/s}$, so (A) is false. From $t = 3\text{ s}$ to $t = 5\text{ s}$, the graph is a horizontal line at $x = 5\text{ m}$, meaning $\Delta x = 0$ and $v_{\text{avg}} = 0\text{ m/s}$, so (B) is true. At $t = 2\text{ s}$, the point lies on the straight segment connecting $(1\text{ s}, -5\text{ m})$ to $(3\text{ s}, 5\text{ m})$, whose slope is $\frac{5 - (-5)}{3 - 1} = \frac{10}{2} = 5\text{ m/s}$, so (C) is true.
  3. Step 3 — Check Statements (D) and (E): From $t = 5\text{ s}$ to $t = 7\text{ s}$, the particle starts at $x = 5\text{ m}$ and ends at $x = 0\text{ m}$, giving $v_{\text{avg}} = \frac{0 - 5}{7 - 5} = -2.5\text{ m/s}$. However, at $t = 6.5\text{ s}$, the particle is on the steep downward segment from $(6\text{ s}, 10\text{ m})$ to $(7\text{ s}, 0\text{ m})$, whose slope is $\frac{0 - 10}{7 - 6} = -10\text{ m/s}$. Since $-2.5 \neq -10$, (D) is false. From $t = 0\text{ s}$ to $t = 9\text{ s}$, both $x(0) = 0$ and $x(9) = 0$, so $\Delta x = 0$ and $v_{\text{avg}} = 0$, making (E) true.
  4. Final Answer: Statements (B), (C), and (E) are correct, which matches option (d).
Q01.stepsLatex:
1. (A) 0 to 3 s: $x(0)=0,x(3)=5 \implies v_{avg}= \frac{5}{^3=}$ m/s $̸=10$ m/s (False). 2. (B) 3 to 5 s: horizontal segment at $x=5$ m $\Rightarrow v_{avg}$ (True).
3. (C) At $t=2$ s (on line from $(1,-5)$ to (3,5)): slope $= \frac{=5-0(-5)}{.53-1} =5$ m/s (True).
4. (D) 5 to 7 s: $v_{avg}= \frac{0-5}{0^2} =-2.5$ m/s, whereas at $t=6$ s (segment $(6,10)\to (7,0)$), slope $=-10$ m/s (False). 5. (E) 0 to 9 s: $x(0)=$ and $x(9)=0 \implies v_{avg}=0$ (True).
Q01.trapHtml: Check endpoints carefully: between 5 s and 7 s the graph peaks at $t=6$ s, so slope is NOT constant across [5,7].

Q02.questionRecapHtml: Given $x=c_0(t^2-2)+c(t-2)^2$, identify the true statement about acceleration or initial velocity.
Q02.conceptHtml: Differentiate twice with respect to $t$: $v=dx/dt$ and $a=dv/dt$.
Q02.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Given & Concept: The displacement as a function of time is $x(t) = c_0(t^2 - 2) + c(t - 2)^2$. To find velocity and acceleration from a position-time equation, we differentiate with respect to time once for velocity ($v = \frac{dx}{dt}$) and a second time for acceleration ($a = \frac{dv}{dt}$).
  2. Step 2 — Find Velocity & Initial Velocity: Differentiating $x(t)$ with respect to $t$ using the power and chain rules gives $v(t) = \frac{dx}{dt} = 2c_0 t + 2c(t - 2)$. Substituting $t = 0$ gives the initial velocity $v(0) = 2c_0(0) + 2c(-2) = -4c$. Because of the minus sign, option (d) stating $+4c$ is incorrect.
  3. Step 3 — Find Acceleration: Differentiating $v(t)$ with respect to $t$ gives $a = \frac{dv}{dt} = 2c_0 + 2c = 2(c + c_0)$, which is a constant acceleration.
  4. Final Answer: The acceleration is $2(c + c_0)$, which matches option (a).
Q02.stepsLatex: 1. Expand or differentiate directly: $v= \frac{dx}{dt} =2c_0t+2c(t-2)$. 2. Initial velocity at $t 0$: $v(0)=-4c$ (so option D is false due to missing minus sign). 3. Acceleration: $a= \frac{d=v}{dt} =2c_0+2c=2(c+c_0)$.
Q02.trapHtml: Watch the sign in $v(0)=-4c$; option (D) omits the negative sign as a trap.

Q03.questionRecapHtml: Identify which of curves A (Phase-$t$), B ($v$-$x$ circle), C ($v$-$t$ circle), and D (Distance-$t$) can represent 1D motion.
Q03.conceptHtml: Time cannot have two values of velocity simultaneously; phase-space ($v$-$x$) loops are valid (e.g. SHM); total distance is non- decreasing.
Q03.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Given & Concept: We must identify which of the four graphs (A, B, C, D) can physically represent one-dimensional motion. Two fundamental rules apply: a particle cannot have two different velocities at the exact same instant of time $t$, and total distance travelled can never decrease with time.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Curves (A) and (B): Curve (A) shows phase increasing linearly with time ($\phi = \omega t + \phi_0$), which accurately describes 1D simple harmonic motion (SHM) — valid. Curve (B) shows a closed loop (circle/ellipse) on a velocity-displacement ($v$-$x$) graph. In 1D SHM, $v^2 + \omega^2 x^2 = \text{constant}$ forms an ellipse, because a particle can pass the same position $x$ with $+v$ going forward and $-v$ coming back — valid.
  3. Step 3 — Evaluate Curves (C) and (D): Curve (C) shows a closed circle on a velocity-time ($v$-$t$) graph. Drawing a vertical line at a fixed time $t$ cuts the circle twice, implying two different velocities at the same instant, which is physically impossible — invalid. Curve (D) shows total distance increasing monotonically from zero without ever dropping, which is always true for any moving particle — valid.
  4. Final Answer: Curves A, B, and D can represent 1D motion, which matches option (c).
Q03.stepsLatex:
1. (A) Phase vs. Time: Linear increase $\phi =\omega t+\phi _0$ represents 1D SHM (Valid). 2. (B) Velocity vs. Displacement: Circle/ellipse $v^2+\omega ^2x^2=$ const represents 1D SHM (Valid).
3. (C) Velocity vs. Time: Closed circle gives two velocities at the same instant $t$ (Impossible). 4. (D) Total Distance vs. Time: Monotonically non-decreasing curve starting from 0 (Valid).
Q03.trapHtml: Never confuse a $v$-$x$ circle (completely valid for SHM!) with a $v$-$t$ circle (impossible because $v(t)$ must be single-valued).

Q04.questionRecapHtml: Sportsman traverses path $ABAB$ on a circular track of radius $r$ ($A,B$ diametrically opposite).
Q04.conceptHtml: Each semicircle $A\to B$ or $B\to A$ has arc length $\pi r$; net displacement depends only on start ($A$) and finish ($B$).
Q04.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Given & Concept: A runner moves along a circular track of radius $r$ along the path $A \to B \to A \to B$, where $A$ and $B$ are diametrically opposite points. Distance is the total actual path length covered, while displacement is simply the straight-line vector from the starting point to the final point.
  2. Step 2 — Calculate Total Distance: One semicircle from $A$ to $B$ (or $B$ to $A$) has arc length $\pi r$. Carefully counting the transitions in $A \to B \to A \to B$, there are exactly $3$ semicircular arcs (not $4$). Therefore, $\text{Distance} = 3 \times \pi r = 3\pi r$.
  3. Step 3 — Calculate Net Displacement: The runner starts at point $A$ and finishes at point $B$. The shortest straight-line distance between two diametrically opposite points on a circle of radius $r$ is its diameter, so $\text{Displacement} = AB = 2r$.
  4. Final Answer: The distance travelled is $3\pi r$ and the displacement is $2r$, which matches option (c).
Q04.stepsLatex: 1. Path $A\to B\to A\to B$ consists of 3 semicircular arcs: Distance $=3\times (\pi r)=3\pi r$. 2. Start is $A$ and final position is $B$: Displacement $=$ diameter $AB=2r$.
Q04.trapHtml: Count segments carefully: $ABAB$ has 3 transitions ($A\to B$, $B\to A$, $A\to B$), not 4!

Q05.questionRecapHtml: Find distance covered between $t=0$ and $t=4$ s from the $v$-$t$ graph (ramp $0\to 10$ in 0–2 s, flat 10 in 2–4 s).
Q05.conceptHtml: Since $v\ge 0$ throughout [0,4 s], distance equals the trapezium area under $v(t)$.
Q05.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Given & Concept: We are given a velocity-time ($v$-$t$) graph and asked for the distance covered between $t = 0\text{ s}$ and $t = 4\text{ s}$. Because the velocity stays positive ($v \ge 0$) throughout this interval, the object never reverses direction, so the distance equals the total area under the $v$-$t$ curve from $t = 0$ to $t = 4\text{ s}$.
  2. Step 2 — Split the Area into Simple Shapes: Break the region from $t = 0$ to $t = 4\text{ s}$ into two easy geometric shapes (ignoring any part of the graph after $t = 4\text{ s}$): a right triangle from $t = 0$ to $t = 2\text{ s}$ reaching $v = 10\text{ m/s}$, and a rectangle from $t = 2\text{ s}$ to $t = 4\text{ s}$ at constant $v = 10\text{ m/s}$.
  3. Step 3 — Calculate Each Area & Sum: Area of triangle ($0\text{ to }2\text{ s}$): $A_1 = \frac{1}{2} \times \text{base} \times \text{height} = \frac{1}{2} \times 2 \times 10 = 10\text{ m}$. Area of rectangle ($2\text{ to }4\text{ s}$): $A_2 = \text{width} \times \text{height} = (4 - 2) \times 10 = 20\text{ m}$. Total distance $= A_1 + A_2 = 10 + 20 = 30\text{ m}$.
  4. Final Answer: The distance covered is $30\text{ m}$, which matches option (b).
Q05.stepsLatex: 1. Triangle (0 to 2 s): $A_1= \frac{1}{=^2} \times 2\times 10=10$ m. 2. Rectangle (2 to 4 s): $A_2 (4-2)\times 10=20$ m. 3. Total distance $=10+20=30$ m.
Q05.trapHtml: Stop at $t=4$ s as asked—do NOT include the descending tail after $t=4$ s!

Q06.questionRecapHtml: Airplane $v$-$t$ graph rises linearly from 200 m/s at $t=0$ to 400 m/s at $t=2$ s, then stays at 400 m/s. Find distance in 30.5 s (in km).
Q06.conceptHtml: Compute area under $v$-$t$ graph from $t=0$ to $t=30.5$ s as trapezium + rectangle.
Q06.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Given & Concept: From the velocity-time ($v$-$t$) graph of the airplane, the velocity starts at $200\text{ m/s}$ at $t = 0$, increases linearly to $400\text{ m/s}$ at $t = 2\text{ s}$, and then stays constant at $400\text{ m/s}$ up to $t = 30.5\text{ s}$. Since $v > 0$ throughout, the distance covered equals the area under the $v$-$t$ graph.
  2. Step 2 — Area from $t = 0$ to $t = 2\text{ s}$ (Trapezium): Because the graph starts at $200\text{ m/s}$ (not $0$), this region is a trapezium with parallel sides $200\text{ m/s}$ and $400\text{ m/s}$ and width $2\text{ s}$: $s_1 = \frac{1}{2}(200 + 400) \times 2 = 600\text{ m}$.
  3. Step 3 — Area from $t = 2\text{ s}$ to $t = 30.5\text{ s}$ (Rectangle): Here the speed is constant at $400\text{ m/s}$ for a duration of $30.5 - 2 = 28.5\text{ s}$: $s_2 = 400 \times 28.5 = 11400\text{ m}$.
  4. Step 4 — Total Distance in Kilometres: Adding both parts gives $s = 600 + 11400 = 12000\text{ m}$. Converting to kilometres by dividing by $1000$ gives $s = 12\text{ km}$.
  5. Final Answer: The airplane covers $12\text{ km}$, which matches option (a).
Q06.trapHtml: Check the $y$-axis intercept at $t=0$: it starts at 200 m/s, not 0!

Q07.questionRecapHtml: Two cars approach at 20 m/s each from 300 m apart and retard at 2 m/$s^2$. Find final separation.
Q07.conceptHtml: Each car travels stopping distance $s=u^2/(2a)$ before halting.
Q07.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Given & Concept: Two cars are initially $300\text{ m}$ apart and move towards each other with initial speed $u = 20\text{ m/s}$ each. Both decelerate uniformly at $a = -2\text{ m/s}^2$ until they stop ($v = 0$). We can find how far each car travels before stopping and subtract both distances from $300\text{ m}$.
  2. Step 2 — Stopping Distance of One Car: Using the third kinematic equation $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$ (which relates speed and distance without needing time): $0^2 = 20^2 + 2(-2)s_1 \implies 4s_1 = 400 \implies s_1 = 100\text{ m}$.
  3. Step 3 — Remaining Separation: Since both cars have identical initial speeds and retardations, the second car also travels $s_2 = 100\text{ m}$ towards the first car. Together they close a gap of $s_1 + s_2 = 100 + 100 = 200\text{ m}$. The remaining distance between them is $d = 300 - 200 = 100\text{ m}$.
  4. Final Answer: The distance between the cars when they come to rest is $100\text{ m}$, which matches option (b).
Q07.stepsLatex: 1. Stopping distance of one car: $s_1= \frac{u2}{2sa} = \frac{202}{2s(2)=} =100$ m. 2. Total distance covered by both cars:$_1+_2 100+100=200$ m. 3. Remaining separation: $d=300-200=100$ m.
Q07.trapHtml: Double the single-car stopping distance since both cars move towards each other.

Q08.questionRecapHtml: First half of distance at 6 m/s; second half in two equal time intervals at 9 m/s and 15 m/s.
Q08.conceptHtml: Compute the arithmetic mean for the equal-time second half, then apply the harmonic mean across the two equal-distance halves.
Q08.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Given & Concept: The particle covers the first half of the total distance at $v_1 = 6\text{ m/s}$, and the second half in two equal time intervals at $9\text{ m/s}$ and $15\text{ m/s}$. Two quick rules make this effortless: for equal time intervals, average speed is the arithmetic mean; for equal distances, average speed is the harmonic mean.
  2. Step 2 — Average Speed of the Second Half: Because the second half is split into two equal time intervals, its effective speed is the arithmetic mean: $v_2 = \frac{9 + 15}{2} = 12\text{ m/s}$.
  3. Step 3 — Overall Average Speed: Now the motion consists of two equal halves of distance covered at $v_1 = 6\text{ m/s}$ and $v_2 = 12\text{ m/s}$. Applying the harmonic mean formula: $v_{\text{avg}} = \frac{2v_1 v_2}{v_1 + v_2} = \frac{2 \times 6 \times 12}{6 + 12} = \frac{144}{18} = 8\text{ m/s}$.
  4. Final Answer: The average speed for the entire motion is $8\text{ m/s}$, which matches option (d).
Q08.stepsLatex:
1. Average speed of second half (equal times): $v_2= \frac{9+15}{^2v} =12$ m/s. 2. Overall average speed (equal distances at $v_1=6$ an$d_2=12$):
$v_{av}= \frac{2v_1v_2}{v_1+v_2} = \frac{2(6)(12)}{6+12} = \frac{144}{18} =8$ m/s
Q08.trapHtml: Two-step shortcut (AM for equal time $\to$ HM for equal distance) solves this in 10 seconds without defining variables.

Q09.questionRecapHtml: Upward throw from tower takes $t_1$, downward throw (same speed) takes $t_2$. Find free-fall drop time $t$.
Q09.conceptHtml: Write displacement equations for upward ($-H=ut_1- \frac{1}{2} gt^2_1$) and downward ($-H=-ut_2- \frac{1}{2} gt^2_2$) throws and eliminate $u$.
Q09.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Given & Concept: A body thrown upward with speed $u$ from a tower of height $H$ reaches the ground in time $t_1$; thrown downward with the same speed $u$, it takes time $t_2$. Taking downward as the positive direction, the net displacement from the tower top to the ground is $+H$ and acceleration is $+g$.
  2. Step 2 — Set Up Displacement Equations: Using $s = ut + \frac{1}{2}gt^2$ with downward positive: For the upward throw (initial velocity $-u$): $H = -ut_1 + \frac{1}{2}gt_1^2 \quad \text{--- (1)}$ For the downward throw (initial velocity $+u$): $H = +ut_2 + \frac{1}{2}gt_2^2 \quad \text{--- (2)}$
  3. Step 3 — Eliminate $u$ to Find $H$: Multiply equation (1) by $t_2$ and equation (2) by $t_1$, then add them so the $u$ terms cancel cleanly: $H(t_2 + t_1) = \frac{1}{2}gt_1^2 t_2 + \frac{1}{2}gt_2^2 t_1 = \frac{1}{2}gt_1 t_2(t_1 + t_2)$. Dividing both sides by $(t_1 + t_2)$ gives $H = \frac{1}{2}gt_1 t_2$.
  4. Step 4 — Compare with Free Fall from Rest: If dropped from rest ($u = 0$), the body takes time $t$ satisfying $H = \frac{1}{2}gt^2$. Equating the two expressions for $H$ gives $\frac{1}{2}gt^2 = \frac{1}{2}gt_1 t_2 \implies t^2 = t_1 t_2 \implies t = \sqrt{t_1 t_2}$.
  5. Final Answer: The time taken when dropped from rest is $\sqrt{t_1 t_2}$, which matches option (b).
Q09.stepsLatex:
1. Multiply upward equation by $t_2$ and downward equation by $t_1$, then add:
$H(t_1+t_2)= \frac{1}{2} gt_1t_2(t_1+t_2) \implies H= \frac{1}{2} gt_1t_2$
$2\sqrt{2}$ 2. For free fall from rest: $H= \frac{1}{2} gt \implies t =t_1t_2 \implies t= t_1t_2$.
Q09.trapHtml: Memorize $t= t_1t_2$ as a direct NTA formula—it recurs frequently in JEE Main!

Q10.questionRecapHtml: Train accelerates uniformly from 0 to 80 km/h in time $t$, then cruises at 80 km/h for $3t$.
Q10.conceptHtml: Use $s=(\frac{u+v}{2})t$ for the accelerated phase and $s=vt$ for the constant-speed phase.
Q10.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Given & Concept: The train starts from rest ($u = 0$), accelerates uniformly to $v = 80\text{ km/h}$ in time $t$, and then cruises at $80\text{ km/h}$ for time $3t$. Average speed is $\frac{\text{Total Distance}}{\text{Total Time}}$. Since $t$ cancels out and the answer is needed in $\text{km/h}$, no unit conversion is required.
  2. Step 2 — Distance in Each Phase: In phase 1 (uniform acceleration from $0$ to $80\text{ km/h}$), distance equals average speed times time: $s_1 = \left(\frac{u + v}{2}\right)t = \left(\frac{0 + 80}{2}\right)t = 40t$. In phase 2 (constant speed $80\text{ km/h}$ for $3t$), distance is $s_2 = 80 \times 3t = 240t$.
  3. Step 3 — Compute Overall Average Speed: Total distance is $s_1 + s_2 = 40t + 240t = 280t$, and total time is $t + 3t = 4t$. Therefore: $v_{\text{avg}} = \frac{280t}{4t} = 70\text{ km/h}$.
  4. Final Answer: The average speed of the train is $70\text{ km/h}$, which matches option (a).
Q10.stepsLatex: 1. Distance in phase 1 (time $t$): $s_1= \frac{0+80}{8^20(3} t=40t$. 2. Distance in phase 2 (time $3t$): $s_2= t$. 3. Average speed over total time $4t$: $v_{av}= \frac{4t0)t+=24204t0}{4t} = \frac{280}{4} =70$ km/h.
Q10.trapHtml: No unit conversion needed since $t$ cancels out and the answer is requested in km/h.

Q11.questionRecapHtml: Body covers 102.5 m in $n^{th}$ second and 115.0 m in $(n+2)^{th}$ second. Find $a$.
Q11.conceptHtml: In uniformly accelerated motion, $S_{n+k}-S_n=ka$.
Q11.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Given & Concept: For a uniformly accelerated body, the distance covered in the $n^{\text{th}}$ second is $S_n = u + \frac{a}{2}(2n - 1)$. We are given $S_n = 102.5\text{ m}$ and $S_{n+2} = 115.0\text{ m}$. Notice that each successive second adds an extra distance $a$ to the distance travelled in the previous second.
  2. Step 2 — Set Up the Difference Equation: Writing $S_{n+2}$ and subtracting $S_n$ eliminates both $u$ and $n$ immediately: $S_{n+2} - S_n = \left[u + \frac{a}{2}(2(n+2) - 1)\right] - \left[u + \frac{a}{2}(2n - 1)\right] = \frac{a}{2}(4) = 2a$.
  3. Step 3 — Solve for Acceleration $a$: Substituting the given values: $115.0 - 102.5 = 2a \implies 12.5 = 2a \implies a = 6.25\text{ m/s}^2$.
  4. Final Answer: The acceleration of the body is $6.25\text{ m/s}^2$, which matches option (a).
Q11.stepsLatex: 1. Here $k=2$: $S_{n+2}-S_n=2a$. 2. Substitute values: $115.0-102.5=2a \implies 12.5=2a \implies a=6.25$ m/$s^2$.
Q11.trapHtml: You don’t need $u$ or $n$! Remembering $S_{n+k}-S_n=ka$ avoids messy algebra.

Q12.questionRecapHtml: Train $A$: 72 km/h North; Train $B$: 108 km/h South. Find $v_{B/A}$ and $v_{ground/B}$ in m/s.
Q12.conceptHtml: Take North as $+$; $v_{B/A}=v_B-v_A$ and $v_{G/B}=v_G-v_B=-v_B$.
Q12.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Given & Concept: Take North as the positive ($+$) direction and South as negative ($-$). First convert both speeds from $\text{km/h}$ to $\text{m/s}$ by multiplying by $\frac{5}{18}$, then use the relative velocity definition $v_{X/Y} = v_X - v_Y$.
  2. Step 2 — Convert Velocities to $\text{m/s}$: Train $A$ (North): $v_A = +72 \times \frac{5}{18} = +20\text{ m/s}$. Train $B$ (South): $v_B = -108 \times \frac{5}{18} = -30\text{ m/s}$. Ground is stationary: $v_G = 0\text{ m/s}$.
  3. Step 3 — Compute Required Relative Velocities: Velocity of $B$ with respect to $A$: $v_{B/A} = v_B - v_A = -30 - (+20) = -50\text{ m/s}$. Velocity of ground with respect to $B$: $v_{G/B} = v_G - v_B = 0 - (-30) = +30\text{ m/s}$ (the ground appears to move North relative to southbound train $B$).
  4. Final Answer: The velocities are $-50\text{ m/s}$ and $30\text{ m/s}$, which matches option (b).
Q12.trapHtml: Ground appears to move opposite to train $B$’s motion, so $v_{G/B}=-v_B=+30$ m/s (North).

Q13.questionRecapHtml: Given $t=\alpha x^2+\beta x$, express acceleration $a$ in terms of velocity $v$.
Q13.conceptHtml: Differentiate $t(x)$ with respect to $x$ to get $1/v$, then differentiate again w.r.t. $t$.
Q13.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Given & Concept: Time is given as a function of position: $t = \alpha x^2 + \beta x$. Instead of solving this quadratic for $x(t)$, it is much cleaner to differentiate implicitly to get $\frac{dt}{dx} = \frac{1}{v}$, and then differentiate once more with respect to $t$ to get acceleration $a = \frac{dv}{dt}$.
  2. Step 2 — Differentiate with Respect to $x$: Taking $\frac{d}{dx}$ on both sides: $\frac{dt}{dx} = 2\alpha x + \beta \implies \frac{1}{v} = 2\alpha x + \beta$.
  3. Step 3 — Differentiate with Respect to $t$: Now take $\frac{d}{dt}$ on both sides (remembering $\frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{1}{v}\right) = -\frac{1}{v^2}\frac{dv}{dt}$ and $\frac{dx}{dt} = v$): $-\frac{1}{v^2}\frac{dv}{dt} = 2\alpha \frac{dx}{dt} + 0 = 2\alpha v$.
  4. Step 4 — Solve for Acceleration $a$: Multiply both sides by $-v^2$: $a = \frac{dv}{dt} = -2\alpha v^3$.
  5. Final Answer: The relation is $a = -2\alpha v^3$, which matches option (c).

1. Differentiate w.r.t. $x$: $\frac{dt}{-^d} \alpha x+ \implies \frac{1}{^vv} =2\alpha x+\beta$. 2. Differentiate w.r.t. $t$: $\frac{x1}{-^v2^2} \frac{=_{dv}2}{\alpha dvt3} =2\alpha \frac{d\beta x}{dt} =2\alpha$ .
3. Rearrange: $a= \frac{dv}{dt} =$ .
Q13.trapHtml: Classic NCERT/JEE standard result: $t=\alpha x^2+\beta x ⇐\Rightarrow a=-2\alpha v^3$ (independent of $\beta$!).

Q14.questionRecapHtml: Position $x=t^3-6t^2+20t+15$ m. Find velocity when $a=0$.
Q14.conceptHtml: Differentiate $x(t)$ to get $v(t)$ and $a(t)$; solve $a(t)=0$ and substitute back into $v(t)$.
Q14.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Given & Concept: The position is $x(t) = t^3 - 6t^2 + 20t + 15\text{ m}$. We need the velocity at the exact instant when acceleration becomes zero. So we find $v(t) = \frac{dx}{dt}$, then $a(t) = \frac{dv}{dt}$, solve $a(t) = 0$ for $t$, and plug that $t$ back into $v(t)$.
  2. Step 2 — Differentiate to Get $v(t)$ and $a(t)$: $v(t) = \frac{dx}{dt} = 3t^2 - 12t + 20$. $a(t) = \frac{dv}{dt} = 6t - 12$.
  3. Step 3 — Find When $a(t) = 0$ and Evaluate $v$: Setting $6t - 12 = 0$ gives $t = 2\text{ s}$. Substituting $t = 2\text{ s}$ into $v(t)$: $v(2) = 3(2)^2 - 12(2) + 20 = 12 - 24 + 20 = 8\text{ m/s}$.
  4. Final Answer: The velocity when acceleration is zero is $8\text{ m/s}$, which matches option (c).
Q14.trapHtml: Double-check arithmetic: $12-24+20=8$ (minimum velocity since $da/dt=6>0$).

Q15.questionRecapHtml: Starting from rest with constant $a$, body covers $S_1$ in $(p-1)$ s and $S_2$ in $p$ s. Find time for $S_1+S_2$.
Q15.conceptHtml: From rest, $S= \frac{1}{2} at^2 \implies S\propto t^2$.
Q15.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Given & Concept: Starting from rest ($u = 0$) with constant acceleration $a$, displacement is given by $S = \frac{1}{2}at^2$. This means displacement is directly proportional to the square of time ($S \propto t^2$).
  2. Step 2 — Express $S_1$, $S_2$, and $S_1 + S_2$: In the first $(p - 1)$ seconds: $S_1 = \frac{1}{2}a(p - 1)^2$. In the first $p$ seconds: $S_2 = \frac{1}{2}ap^2$. Let $T$ be the time required to cover displacement $S_1 + S_2$ starting from rest, so $S_1 + S_2 = \frac{1}{2}aT^2$.
  3. Step 3 — Solve for $T$: Equating the two expressions for $S_1 + S_2$ and cancelling $\frac{1}{2}a$: $T^2 = (p - 1)^2 + p^2 = (p^2 - 2p + 1) + p^2 = 2p^2 - 2p + 1$. Taking the square root gives $T = \sqrt{2p^2 - 2p + 1}\text{ s}$.
  4. Final Answer: The required time is $\sqrt{2p^2 - 2p + 1}\text{ s}$, which matches option (d).

Q15.trapHtml: Don’t forget to take the square root at the end—option (C) is $T^2$ without the radical!

Q16.questionRecapHtml: Given $x=(5t^2-4t+5)$ m, find $|v|$ at $t=2$ s.
Q16.conceptHtml: Instantaneous velocity is $v=dx/dt$.
Q16.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Given & Concept: The position of the particle is $x(t) = 5t^2 - 4t + 5\text{ m}$. Instantaneous velocity at any time $t$ is the first derivative of position with respect to time, $v(t) = \frac{dx}{dt}$ (not $\frac{x}{t}$, which would give an average value).
  2. Step 2 — Differentiate $x(t)$: Applying the power rule term by term: $v(t) = \frac{d}{dt}(5t^2 - 4t + 5) = 10t - 4$.
  3. Step 3 — Evaluate at $t = 2\text{ s}$: Substituting $t = 2$: $v(2) = 10(2) - 4 = 20 - 4 = 16\text{ m/s}$.
  4. Final Answer: The magnitude of velocity at $t = 2\text{ s}$ is $16\text{ m/s}$, which matches option (b).
Q16.stepsLatex: 1. Differentiate: $v(t)= \frac{dx}{(^d2^t)} =10t-4$. 2. At $t=2$ s: $v(2)=10 -4=16$ m/s.
Q16.trapHtml: Never compute $x(2)/2$ (that gives average velocity from $x=0$, not instantaneous velocity!).

Q17.questionRecapHtml: Distance $s=2.5t^2$. Find instantaneous speed at $t=5$ s.
Q17.conceptHtml: Instantaneous speed is $v=ds/dt$.
Q17.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Given & Concept: The distance travelled is $s(t) = 2.5t^2$. Instantaneous speed is the rate of change of distance with respect to time, $v(t) = \frac{ds}{dt}$.
  2. Step 2 — Differentiate $s(t)$: Using the power rule: $v(t) = \frac{d}{dt}(2.5t^2) = 2.5 \times 2t = 5t$.
  3. Step 3 — Evaluate at $t = 5\text{ s}$: Substituting $t = 5$: $v(5) = 5 \times 5 = 25\text{ m/s}$.
  4. Final Answer: The instantaneous speed at $t = 5\text{ s}$ is $25\text{ m/s}$, which matches option (d).
Q17.stepsLatex: 1. Differentiate: $v(t)= \frac{ds}{5^d)^t} =2(2.5)t=5t$. 2. At $t=5$ s: $v(5)=5( =25$ m/s.
Q17.trapHtml: Alternatively, compare with $s= \frac{1}{2} at^2 \implies a=5$ m/$s^2$, so $v=at=25$ m/s.

Q18.questionRecapHtml: Passenger in train $A$ (90 km/h) sees train $B$ (54 km/h, opposite direction) pass in 8 s. Find $L_B$.
Q18.conceptHtml: A point observer (passenger) sees only the length of the other train: $L_B=v_{rel}\times t$.
Q18.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Given & Concept: A passenger in train $A$ ($90\text{ km/h}$) watches train $B$ ($54\text{ km/h}$) pass in the opposite direction for $t = 8\text{ s}$. Because the passenger is a point observer, the length of train $A$ does not matter — train $B$ simply moves past the passenger by its own length $L_B = v_{\text{rel}} \times t$.
  2. Step 2 — Convert Speeds to $\text{m/s}$ and Find Relative Speed: $v_A = 90 \times \frac{5}{18} = 25\text{ m/s}$, and $v_B = 54 \times \frac{5}{18} = 15\text{ m/s}$. Since the trains move in opposite directions, their speeds add: $v_{\text{rel}} = 25 + 15 = 40\text{ m/s}$.
  3. Step 3 — Calculate Length of Train $B$: $L_B = v_{\text{rel}} \times t = 40 \times 8 = 320\text{ m}$.
  4. Final Answer: The length of train $B$ is $320\text{ m}$, which matches option (d).

Q18.trapHtml: Because the observer is a passenger (point object), the length of train $A$ is irrelevant.

Q20.questionRecapHtml: Ball thrown up at 150 m/s; ratio of velocity at $t=3$ s to $t=5$ s is $\frac{x+1}{x}$. Find $x$.
Q20.conceptHtml: Apply $v=u-gt$ at $t=3$ s and $t=5$ s.
Q20.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Given & Concept: A ball is thrown vertically upward with initial velocity $u = 150\text{ m/s}$ under downward gravitational acceleration $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$. Its upward velocity at any time $t$ is given by $v(t) = u - gt$.
  2. Step 2 — Compute Velocities at $t = 3\text{ s}$ and $t = 5\text{ s}$: At $t = 3\text{ s}$: $v(3) = 150 - 10(3) = 120\text{ m/s}$. At $t = 5\text{ s}$: $v(5) = 150 - 10(5) = 100\text{ m/s}$.
  3. Step 3 — Equate the Ratio to Find $x$: $\frac{v(3)}{v(5)} = \frac{120}{100} = \frac{6}{5}$. Comparing $\frac{6}{5} = \frac{x + 1}{x}$ gives $6x = 5x + 5 \implies x = 5$.
  4. Final Answer: The value of $x$ is $5$, which matches option (c).
Q20.trapHtml: Quick check: $\frac{5+1}{5} = \frac{6}{5}$ matches immediately.

Q21.questionRecapHtml: From the piecewise $v$-$t$ graph over 0–25 s, find the ratio Distance$/$Displacement.
Q21.conceptHtml: Split the graph into positive area (0–20 s) and negative area (20–25 s).
Q21.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Given & Concept: From the $v$-$t$ graph over $0$ to $25\text{ s}$, we need the ratio $\frac{\text{Total Distance}}{\text{Net Displacement}}$. Remember that displacement is the signed area under the $v$-$t$ curve (positive above the axis, negative below), while total distance adds the absolute magnitudes of all areas.
  2. Step 2 — Calculate Positive Area ($0$ to $20\text{ s}$): Break the region above the time axis into four simple pieces: $0\text{–}5\text{ s}$ (triangle): $\frac{1}{2}(5)(10) = 25\text{ m}$; $5\text{–}10\text{ s}$ (rectangle): $5 \times 10 = 50\text{ m}$; $10\text{–}15\text{ s}$ (trapezium from $10$ to $20\text{ m/s}$): $\frac{1}{2}(10 + 20)(5) = 75\text{ m}$; $15\text{–}20\text{ s}$ (triangle): $\frac{1}{2}(5)(20) = 50\text{ m}$. Total positive area $A_+ = 25 + 50 + 75 + 50 = 200\text{ m}$.
  3. Step 3 — Calculate Negative Area ($20$ to $25\text{ s}$) & Ratio: From $20$ to $25\text{ s}$, the triangle lies below the time axis down to $-20\text{ m/s}$, so $A_- = -\frac{1}{2}(5)(20) = -50\text{ m}$. Total distance $= |A_+| + |A_-| = 200 + 50 = 250\text{ m}$. Net displacement $= A_+ + A_- = 200 - 50 = 150\text{ m}$. Ratio $= \frac{250}{150} = \frac{5}{3}$.
  4. Final Answer: The ratio of total distance to net displacement is $\frac{5}{3}$, which matches option (d).

Q21.trapHtml: Check which quantity is in the numerator: Distance/Displacement $\ge 1$, eliminating options (B) and (C) immediately!

Q22.questionRecapHtml: Person covers two equal distances $x$ in the same direction at $v_1$ and $v_2$. Relate average velocity $V$ to $v_1,v_2$.
Q22.conceptHtml: Total displacement is $2x$ and total time is $t_1+t_2= \frac{x}{v1} + \frac{x}{v2}$.
Q22.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Given & Concept: The person travels two equal distances $x$ in the same direction at speeds $v_1$ and $v_2$. Average velocity is defined as $V = \frac{\text{Total Displacement}}{\text{Total Time}}$.
  2. Step 2 — Express Total Displacement and Total Time: Total displacement $= x + x = 2x$. Time for the first segment is $t_1 = \frac{x}{v_1}$, and for the second segment is $t_2 = \frac{x}{v_2}$, so total time $= \frac{x}{v_1} + \frac{x}{v_2} = x\left(\frac{1}{v_1} + \frac{1}{v_2}\right)$.
  3. Step 3 — Rearrange to Match the Reciprocal Form: $V = \frac{2x}{x\left(\frac{1}{v_1} + \frac{1}{v_2}\right)} = \frac{2}{\frac{1}{v_1} + \frac{1}{v_2}}$. Cross-multiplying gives the clean harmonic-mean form: $\frac{2}{V} = \frac{1}{v_1} + \frac{1}{v_2}$.
  4. Final Answer: The correct relation is $\frac{2}{V} = \frac{1}{v_1} + \frac{1}{v_2}$, which matches option (d).
Q22.stepsLatex:
1. $V = \frac{x2}{v1} + \frac{xx}{v2} = \frac{2}{+} \frac{1}{v1} \frac{1}{v2}$ .
2. Rearranging directly gives $\frac{2}{V} = \frac{1}{v_1} + \frac{1}{v_2}$ .
Q22.trapHtml: Harmonic mean form $\frac{2}{V} = \frac{1}{v1} + \frac{1}{v2}$ is the reciprocal-average version of $V = \frac{2v1v2}{v1+v2}$.

Q23.questionRecapHtml: Compare two students $A$ and $B$ returning home from school using their $x$-$t$ graphs ending at the same time.
Q23.conceptHtml: Height on $x$-axis = distance from school; slope of $x$-$t$ line = speed; horizontal span = travel time.
Q23.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Given & Concept: We are given straight-line position-time ($x$-$t$) graphs for students $A$ and $B$ returning home from school ($x = 0$) and reaching home at the same final instant. On an $x$-$t$ graph: the vertical height gives distance from school, the horizontal span gives travel time, and the slope gives speed.
  2. Step 2 — Check Distance & Travel Time (A, B, C): Since the final vertical coordinate satisfies $x_A < x_B$, $A$ lives closer to the school — so (A) is true and (B) is false. Looking at the $t$-axis, $A$ starts at $t = 0$ whereas $B$ starts later ($t > 0$), yet both reach home at the same final instant. Thus $B$ takes less time than $A$, so (C) is false.
  3. Step 3 — Compare Speeds (D, E): Because line $B$ is steeper than line $A$ (greater slope $\frac{\Delta x}{\Delta t}$), $B$ travels faster than $A$ — so (E) is true and (D) is false.
  4. Final Answer: Only statements (A) and (E) are correct, which matches option (b).
Q23.stepsLatex: 1. Final position: $x_A \lt x_B \implies$ (A) $A$ lives closer to the school is true; (B) is false. 2. $A$ starts at $t=0$ while $B$ starts later ($t>0$), and both finish at the same instant $\implies B$ takes less time, so (C) is false. 3. Slope of line $B$ is steeper than line $A \implies$ (E) $B$ travels faster than $A$ is true; (D) is false.
Q23.trapHtml: Check the starting point on the $t$-axis carefully: $B$ starts later than $A$ and finishes at the same instant!

Q24.questionRecapHtml: Evaluate Statement I (area under $v$-$t$ gives distance) and Statement II (area under $a$-$t$ gives change in velocity).
Q24.conceptHtml: Signed area under $v$-$t$ gives displacement (NOT always distance if $v$ reverses sign); signed area under $a$-$t$ always equals $\Delta v$.
Q24.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Given & Concept: We need to test two fundamental calculus statements about kinematic graphs: the area under a $v$-$t$ graph and the area under an $a$-$t$ graph.
  2. Step 2 — Check Statement I: Mathematically, the signed area under a velocity-time graph is $\int v\,dt = \Delta x$, which gives displacement, not distance. If the particle reverses direction ($v$ becomes negative), distance is $\int |v|\,dt$, which differs from the signed area. Therefore, Statement I is incorrect.
  3. Step 3 — Check Statement II: Since acceleration is $a = \frac{dv}{dt}$, the area under the acceleration-time graph is $\int a\,dt = \int dv = \Delta v$, which is always equal to the change in velocity over that time interval. Therefore, Statement II is true.
  4. Final Answer: Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is true, which matches option (c).
Q24.stepsLatex: 1. Statement I: $vdt=\Delta$ (displacement), whereas distance is $|v|dt$. Thus Statement I is incorrect. 2. Statement II: $adt= \frac{xdv}{dt} dt=\Delta v$ (change in velocity). Thus Statement II is true.
Q24.trapHtml: This is a classic NTA conceptual trap: always distinguish displacement ( $vdt$) from distance ( $|v|dt$).

Q25.questionRecapHtml: Particle accelerates uniformly from 10.0 m/s to 60.0 m/s at 2.0 m/$s^2$. Find time taken.
Q25.conceptHtml: Apply $v=u+at$.
Q25.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Given & Concept: A particle has initial velocity $u = 10.0\text{ m/s}$, constant acceleration $a = 2.0\text{ m/s}^2$, and final velocity $v = 60.0\text{ m/s}$. Since acceleration is uniform, we directly use the first equation of motion, $v = u + at$.
  2. Step 2 — Rearrange & Substitute: Solving for time $t$: $t = \frac{v - u}{a} = \frac{60.0 - 10.0}{2.0} = \frac{50.0}{2.0} = 25\text{ s}$.
  3. Step 3 — Quick Sanity Check: Starting at $10\text{ m/s}$ and gaining $2\text{ m/s}$ every second for $25\text{ s}$ adds $50\text{ m/s}$, reaching exactly $60\text{ m/s}$.
  4. Final Answer: The time taken is $25\text{ s}$, which matches option (d).
Q25.trapHtml: Straightforward plug-in—avoid dividing $60/2=30$ s by forgetting $u=10$ m/s!

Q26.questionRecapHtml: Object covers $AB$, $BC$, $CD$ at speeds $v_1,v_2,v_3$ where $AB=BC$ and $AD=3AB$. Find average speed.
Q26.conceptHtml: Since $AB=BC$ and $AD=3AB$, all three segments have equal length $x$.
Q26.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Given & Concept: An object moves along collinear segments $AB$, $BC$, and $CD$ with speeds $v_1$, $v_2$, and $v_3$. Since $AB = BC$ and total length $AD = 3AB$, the remaining segment $CD$ must also equal $AB$. Let each of the three equal segments have length $x$.
  2. Step 2 — Compute Total Distance & Total Time: Total distance $= x + x + x = 3x$. Total time $= t_1 + t_2 + t_3 = \frac{x}{v_1} + \frac{x}{v_2} + \frac{x}{v_3} = x\left(\frac{v_2 v_3 + v_1 v_3 + v_1 v_2}{v_1 v_2 v_3}\right)$.
  3. Step 3 — Compute Average Speed: Dividing total distance by total time cancels $x$: $v_{\text{avg}} = \frac{3x}{x\left(\frac{v_1 v_2 + v_2 v_3 + v_3 v_1}{v_1 v_2 v_3}\right)} = \frac{3v_1 v_2 v_3}{v_1 v_2 + v_2 v_3 + v_3 v_1}$.
  4. Final Answer: The average speed is $\frac{3v_1 v_2 v_3}{v_1 v_2 + v_2 v_3 + v_3 v_1}$, which matches option (d).
Q26.stepsLatex:
1. Total distance $=3x$; total time $= \frac{x}{vv31} + \frac{x}{v2} + \frac{x}{v3} =x \frac{v1v2+v2v3+v3v1}{v1v2v3}$ .
2. Average speed: $v_{av}= \frac{3v_1v_2}{v_1v_2+v_2v_3+v_3v_1}$ .
Q26.trapHtml: Harmonic mean of three speeds—check dimensions ([L/T$]^3/[$L/T$]^2=[$L/T]) to eliminate (A) and (C) instantly!

Q27.questionRecapHtml:
Vehicle travels 4 km at 3 km/h and another 4 km at 5 km/h. Find average speed.
$2v_1v_2$
Q27.conceptHtml: Equal distances $\implies v_{av}=$. $v_1+v_2$
Q27.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Given & Concept: The vehicle covers two equal distances of $4\text{ km}$ each, first at $v_1 = 3\text{ km/h}$ and then at $v_2 = 5\text{ km/h}$. For two equal distances, the average speed is the harmonic mean $v_{\text{avg}} = \frac{2v_1 v_2}{v_1 + v_2}$.
  2. Step 2 — Substitute & Calculate: $v_{\text{avg}} = \frac{2 \times 3 \times 5}{3 + 5} = \frac{30}{8} = 3.75\text{ km/h}$.
  3. Step 3 — Quick Check: Since the vehicle spends more time moving at the slower speed ($3\text{ km/h}$), the average speed must be strictly less than the simple average $4.00\text{ km/h}$, confirming $3.75\text{ km/h}$.
  4. Final Answer: The average speed is $3.75\text{ km/h}$, which matches option (a).

$v_{av}= \frac{2(3)(5)}{3+5} = \frac{30}{8} =3.75$ km/h
Q27.trapHtml: Harmonic mean is always strictly less than the arithmetic mean (4.00 km/h), ruling out (B) and (D).

Q28.questionRecapHtml: Match four $x$-$t$ graphs (A–D) in Column-I with their corresponding $v$-$t$ graphs (I–IV) in Column-II.
Q28.conceptHtml: The $v$-$t$ graph is the derivative (slope) of the $x$-$t$ graph at every instant.
Q28.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Given & Concept: We need to match each position-time ($x$-$t$) graph in Column-I with its corresponding velocity-time ($v$-$t$) graph in Column-II. The key rule is that the value of $v$ at any time $t$ equals the slope ($\frac{dx}{dt}$) of the $x$-$t$ graph at that instant.
  2. Step 2 — Match Graphs A and B: Graph A is an upward-opening parabola ($x \propto t^2$): its slope starts at $0$ and increases linearly with time, giving a straight line through the origin in the first quadrant $\Rightarrow$ A–II. Graph B is an exponential decay curve ($x = x_0 e^{-kt}$): since $x$ decreases, the slope is negative everywhere and gradually approaches $0$ from below $\Rightarrow$ B–IV.
  3. Step 3 — Match Graphs C and D: Graph C is a symmetric triangular peak: first it rises with a constant positive slope, then falls with a constant negative slope, producing a positive horizontal step followed by a negative horizontal step $\Rightarrow$ C–III. Graph D is a straight line with constant positive slope, which means constant positive velocity $\Rightarrow$ D–I.
  4. Final Answer: The correct matching is A–II, B–IV, C–III, D–I, which matches option (b).
Q28.stepsLatex:
1. A (upward-curving parabola): Slope starts at 0 and increases linearly $\implies$ II. 2. B (exponential decay $x_0e^{-kt}$): Slope is negative and approaches 0 from below ($-v_0\to 0$) $\implies$ IV.
3. C (symmetric triangle): Constant positive slope then constant negative slope $\implies$ III. 4. D (straight line with constant positive slope): Constant positive velocity $\implies$ I.
Q28.trapHtml: Check graph B carefully: $x$ decreases, so $v<0$ throughout, matching IV (below the $t$-axis).

Q29.questionRecapHtml: Given $x=4t^2$, find the velocity at $t=5$ s.
Q29.conceptHtml: Differentiate $x(t)$ w.r.t. $t$: $v=dx/dt$.
Q29.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Given & Concept: Distance is given as $x(t) = 4t^2$. Instantaneous velocity is the time derivative of position, $v(t) = \frac{dx}{dt}$.
  2. Step 2 — Differentiate $x(t)$: Using the power rule $\frac{d}{dt}(t^2) = 2t$: $v(t) = \frac{d}{dt}(4t^2) = 4(2t) = 8t$.
  3. Step 3 — Substitute $t = 5\text{ s}$: $v(5) = 8 \times 5 = 40\text{ m/s}$.
  4. Final Answer: The velocity of the particle at $t = 5\text{ s}$ is $40\text{ m/s}$, which matches option (d).
Q29.stepsLatex:
1. $v(t)= \frac{d}{5dt} (4t^2)=8t$.
2. At $t=$ s: $v(5)=8\times 5=40$ m/s.
Q29.trapHtml: Don’t forget the factor of 2 from differentiating $t^2$ (otherwise you get distractor B: 20 m/s).

Q30.questionRecapHtml: Car covers distance $x$ at speed $v_1$ and another $x$ at speed $v_2$ in the same direction. Find average speed.
Q30.conceptHtml: Apply $v_{av}=$ Total Distance$/$Total Time.
Q30.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Given & Concept: The car covers two equal distances $x$ at speeds $v_1$ and $v_2$. Average speed is $\frac{\text{Total Distance}}{\text{Total Time}}$.
  2. Step 2 — Write Total Distance and Total Time: Total distance $= x + x = 2x$. Total time $= \frac{x}{v_1} + \frac{x}{v_2} = x\left(\frac{v_1 + v_2}{v_1 v_2}\right)$.
  3. Step 3 — Simplify the Ratio: Dividing total distance by total time cancels $x$: $v_{\text{avg}} = \frac{2x}{x\left(\frac{v_1 + v_2}{v_1 v_2}\right)} = \frac{2v_1 v_2}{v_1 + v_2}$.
  4. Final Answer: The average speed is $\frac{2v_1 v_2}{v_1 + v_2}$, which matches option (b).
Q30.stepsLatex: 1. $v_{av}= \frac{+}{+} = \frac{2v_1v_2}{v_1+v_2}$ . $\frac{_xx}{v1} \frac{x_x}{v2}$
Q30.trapHtml: Direct NCERT/NTA staple formula—takes 3 seconds!

Q31.questionRecapHtml: Find ratio of displacement to distance over 0–10 s from the rectangular-step $v$-$t$ graph.
Q31.conceptHtml: Sum signed rectangular areas for displacement and absolute areas for total distance.
Q31.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Given & Concept: From the step-like $v$-$t$ graph between $t = 0$ and $t = 10\text{ s}$, we want the ratio $\frac{\text{Net Displacement}}{\text{Total Distance}}$. Each constant-velocity segment forms a rectangle: we keep the $+$ or $-$ sign for displacement, and take absolute values for distance.
  2. Step 2 — Compute Signed Area of Each Rectangle: $0\text{–}2\text{ s}$: $A_1 = 2 \times (+8) = +16\text{ m}$; $2\text{–}4\text{ s}$: $A_2 = 2 \times (-4) = -8\text{ m}$; $4\text{–}8\text{ s}$: $A_3 = 4 \times (+4) = +16\text{ m}$; $8\text{–}10\text{ s}$: $A_4 = 2 \times (-4) = -8\text{ m}$.
  3. Step 3 — Find Displacement, Distance, and Ratio: Net displacement $= 16 - 8 + 16 - 8 = 16\text{ m}$. Total distance $= |16| + |-8| + |16| + |-8| = 16 + 8 + 16 + 8 = 48\text{ m}$. Ratio $= \frac{\text{Net Displacement}}{\text{Total Distance}} = \frac{16}{48} = \frac{1}{3}$ (or $1:3$).
  4. Final Answer: The ratio is $1:3$, which matches option (b).
Q31.stepsLatex:
1. Segment areas:
• 0–2 s: $2\times (+8)=+16$ m; 2–4 s: $2\times (-4)=-8$ m. • 4–8 s: $4\times (+4)=+16$ m; 8–10 s: $2\times (-4)=-8$ m.
2. Net displacement $=16-8+16-8=16$ m. 3. Total distance $=16+8+16+8=48$ m.
4. Ratio $= \frac{16}{48} =1:3$.
Q31.trapHtml: Note the order asked: Displacement to Distance ($\le 1$), NOT Distance to Displacement!

Q32.questionRecapHtml: Person travels $x$ at $v_1=5$ m/s and $\frac{3}{2} x$ at $v_2$; overall average velocity is $\frac{50}{7}$ m/s. Find $v_2$.
Q32.conceptHtml: Apply $v_{avg}=$ Total Displacement$/$Total Time and cancel $x$.
Q32.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Given & Concept: The person covers distance $x$ at $v_1 = 5\text{ m/s}$ and the next distance $\frac{3}{2}x$ at unknown speed $v_2$, with overall average velocity $v_{\text{avg}} = \frac{50}{7}\text{ m/s}$. Using $v_{\text{avg}} = \frac{\text{Total Displacement}}{\text{Total Time}}$, the unknown distance $x$ will cancel out.
  2. Step 2 — Write Total Displacement and Total Time: Total displacement $= x + \frac{3}{2}x = \frac{5}{2}x$. Total time $= \frac{x}{5} + \frac{3x/2}{v_2} = x\left(\frac{1}{5} + \frac{3}{2v_2}\right)$.
  3. Step 3 — Equate and Solve for $v_2$: $\frac{\frac{5}{2}x}{x\left(\frac{1}{5} + \frac{3}{2v_2}\right)} = \frac{50}{7} \implies \frac{5/2}{50/7} = \frac{1}{5} + \frac{3}{2v_2} \implies \frac{7}{20} = \frac{1}{5} + \frac{3}{2v_2}$. Subtracting $\frac{1}{5} = \frac{4}{20}$ from both sides: $\frac{3}{2v_2} = \frac{7}{20} - \frac{4}{20} = \frac{3}{20} \implies 2v_2 = 20 \implies v_2 = 10\text{ m/s}$.
  4. Final Answer: $10$

1. Total distance $=x+ \frac{3}{2} x= \frac{5}{2} x$; total time $= \frac{x}{5} + \frac{3x}{2v2}$ .
2. $\frac{5/}{+} = \frac{50}{7} \implies \frac{1}{5} + \frac{3}{2v_2} = \frac{7}{20}$ . $\frac{1}{^53} \frac{2_3}{2v2}$
3. $= \frac{7}{20} - \frac{4}{20} = \frac{3}{20} \implies v_2=10$ m/s. $2v_2$
Q32.trapHtml: Keep fractions exact ( $\frac{7}{20} - \frac{4}{20} = \frac{3}{20}$ ) so 3 cancels cleanly.

Q33.questionRecapHtml: Car $P$ has linearly increasing acceleration; car $Q$ has constant acceleration. Both cross at $t=0$. Find maximum possible crossings.
Q33.conceptHtml: Write relative displacement $\Delta x(t)=x_P(t)-x_Q(t)$ and count the maximum number of non-negative real roots.
Q33.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Given & Concept: Car $P$ has linearly increasing acceleration ($a_P = kt + a_{P0}$ with $k > 0$), while car $Q$ has constant acceleration ($a_Q$). Both cars cross each other when their relative displacement $\Delta x(t) = x_P(t) - x_Q(t) = 0$. The maximum number of crossings is the maximum number of non-negative real roots ($t \ge 0$) of $\Delta x(t) = 0$.
  2. Step 2 — Form the Relative Displacement Polynomial: Relative acceleration is $a_{\text{rel}}(t) = kt + (a_{P0} - a_Q)$. Integrating twice with respect to time gives a cubic polynomial: $\Delta x(t) = \frac{k}{6}t^3 + \frac{a_{P0} - a_Q}{2}t^2 + (u_P - u_Q)t + 0$, where the constant term is $0$ because they already cross at $t = 0$.
  3. Step 3 — Count Maximum Non-Negative Roots: Factoring out $t$ gives $t(At^2 + Bt + C) = 0$, where $A = \frac{k}{6} > 0$. One root is $t = 0$, and the quadratic factor $At^2 + Bt + C = 0$ can have at most $2$ distinct positive real roots (which occurs whenever $B < 0$, $C > 0$, and $B^2 - 4AC > 0$).
  4. Step 4 — Total Crossings: Adding the initial crossing at $t = 0$ and the maximum $2$ subsequent crossings gives $1 + 2 = 3$ crossings in total.
  5. Final Answer: $3$
Q33.stepsLatex:
1. Since $a_P(t)=kt+a_{P0}$ ($k>0$) and $a_Q=$ const, integrating twice gives:
$x (t)-x (t)= \frac{k}{6} t^3+ \frac{a_{P0}-a_Q}{2} t^2+(u -u )t=t(At^2+Bt+C) P Q P Q$
(constant term is 0 because they cross at $t=0$). 2. The quadratic $At^2+Bt+C=0$ can have at most 2 distinct positive roots (when $B<0$ and $C>0$).
3. Including $t=0$, the maximum possible number of crossings is $1+2=3$.
Q33.trapHtml: A degree-3 polynomial with $t=0$ as a root can have at most 3 crossings total.

Q34.questionRecapHtml: Given $x^2=1+t^2$, acceleration is $x^{-n}$. Find $n$.
Q34.conceptHtml: Differentiate implicitly twice with respect to $t$ and use $x^2-t^2=1$.
Q34.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Given & Concept: The particle's position satisfies $x^2 = 1 + t^2$, and we are told its acceleration has the form $a = x^{-n}$. Instead of taking square roots and using the messy quotient rule, implicit differentiation with respect to $t$ keeps the algebra clean and fast.
  2. Step 2 — First Implicit Derivative (Velocity): Differentiating $x^2 = 1 + t^2$ with respect to $t$: $2x\frac{dx}{dt} = 2t \implies xv = t \implies v = \frac{t}{x}$.
  3. Step 3 — Second Implicit Derivative (Acceleration): Differentiate $xv = t$ with respect to $t$ using the product rule: $x\frac{dv}{dt} + v\frac{dx}{dt} = 1 \implies xa + v^2 = 1$.
  4. Step 4 — Substitute $v = \frac{t}{x}$ and Use $x^2 - t^2 = 1$: $xa = 1 - v^2 = 1 - \frac{t^2}{x^2} = \frac{x^2 - t^2}{x^2}$. From the given equation, $x^2 - t^2 = 1$, so $xa = \frac{1}{x^2} \implies a = \frac{1}{x^3} = x^{-3}$. Comparing with $x^{-n}$ gives $n = 3$.
  5. Final Answer: $3$
Q34.stepsLatex: 1. First derivative: $2x \frac{dx}{x^d} =2t \implies xv=t \implies v= \frac{t}{2x}$ . 2. Second derivative: $\frac{tdv}{=dt} +v^2=1 \implies xa=1- \frac{t}{x2} = \frac{x2-t2}{x2} = \frac{1}{x2}$ . 3. Divide by $x$: $a= \frac{1}{x3} x^{-3} \implies n=3$.
Q34.trapHtml: Implicit differentiation ($xv=t \implies xa+v^2=1$) is much faster and less error-prone than quotient rule!

Q35.questionRecapHtml: From rest with constant $a$, $\frac{n-1}{Sn} =1- \frac{2}{x}$ for $n=10$. Find $x$.
Q35.conceptHtml: From rest, $Sn= \frac{a}{2} (2n-1)$ and $S_{n-1}= \frac{a}{2} (2n-3)$.
Q35.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Given & Concept: A body starts from rest ($u = 0$) with constant acceleration $a$. The distance travelled in the $n^{\text{th}}$ second (between $t = n - 1$ and $t = n$) is $S_n = \frac{a}{2}(2n - 1)$, and in the $(n - 1)^{\text{th}}$ second is $S_{n-1} = \frac{a}{2}(2n - 3)$.
  2. Step 2 — Compute the Ratio $\frac{S_{n-1}}{S_n}$: The common factor $\frac{a}{2}$ cancels cleanly: $\frac{S_{n-1}}{S_n} = \frac{2n - 3}{2n - 1} = \frac{(2n - 1) - 2}{2n - 1} = 1 - \frac{2}{2n - 1}$.
  3. Step 3 — Substitute $n = 10$ and Find $x$: Comparing $1 - \frac{2}{2n - 1}$ with $1 - \frac{2}{x}$ gives $x = 2n - 1$. For $n = 10$: $x = 2(10) - 1 = 19$.
  4. Final Answer: $19$
Q35.trapHtml: For $n=10$, odd numbers are 17 and 19: $\frac{17}{19} =1- \frac{2}{19} \implies x=19$ in 5 seconds!

Q36.questionRecapHtml: Bus moving at 72 km/h halts uniformly in 4 s. Find stopping distance (in m).
Q36.conceptHtml: Convert $u$ to m/s and apply $s=(\frac{u+v}{2})t$.
Q36.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Given & Concept: The bus has initial speed $u = 72\text{ km/h}$, comes to rest ($v = 0$) in time $t = 4\text{ s}$ under uniform retardation. For uniform acceleration/retardation, distance equals average velocity times time: $s = \left(\frac{u + v}{2}\right)t$, which saves us from even needing to calculate $a$.
  2. Step 2 — Convert Initial Speed to $\text{m/s}$: $u = 72 \times \frac{5}{18} = 20\text{ m/s}$.
  3. Step 3 — Calculate Stopping Distance: $s = \left(\frac{20 + 0}{2}\right) \times 4 = 10 \times 4 = 40\text{ m}$.
  4. Final Answer: $40$
Q36.stepsLatex: 1. Initial speed: $u=72\times \frac{5}{1280}$ 20 m/s; final speed $v=0$. 2. Stopping distance: $s= \frac{+=0}{2} \times 4=40$ m.
Q36.trapHtml: Using $s= \frac{u+v}{2} t$ skips computing $a$ altogether!

Q37.questionRecapHtml: Particle starts at $x=0$ with $v=4 x$ m/s. Find acceleration $a$.
Q37.conceptHtml: Use $a=v \frac{dv}{dx}$ or square both sides to match $v^2=u^2+2ax$.
Q37.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Given & Concept: The particle starts from rest at $x = 0$ with velocity varying as $v = 4\sqrt{x}\text{ m/s}$. When velocity is given as a function of position $x$, we can either use $a = v\frac{dv}{dx}$ or simply square both sides to match the standard kinematic equation $v^2 = u^2 + 2ax$.
  2. Step 2 — Square Both Sides & Compare: Squaring $v = 4\sqrt{x}$ gives $v^2 = 16x$. Comparing this directly with $v^2 = 0 + 2ax$ tells us immediately that the acceleration is constant and satisfies $2a = 16$.
  3. Step 3 — Solve for $a$: $a = \frac{16}{2} = 8\text{ m/s}^2$.
  4. Final Answer: $8$
Q37.stepsLatex: 1. Square both sides: $v^2=16x$. 2. Compare with $v^2=2ax$ (since $u=0$): $2a=16 \implies a=8$ m/$s^2$.
Q37.trapHtml: Whenever $v=k x$, acceleration is constant and equals $a=k^2/2$.

Q38.questionRecapHtml: Position $x=-3t^3+18t^2+16t$. Find velocity when $a=0$.
Q38.conceptHtml: Differentiate twice to solve $a(t)=0$, then substitute into $v(t)$.
Q38.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Given & Concept: The position is $x(t) = -3t^3 + 18t^2 + 16t$ (note that any constant initial offset differentiates to zero and does not affect velocity or acceleration). We differentiate once for $v(t)$, once more for $a(t)$, find when $a(t) = 0$, and substitute that time into $v(t)$.
  2. Step 2 — Find $v(t)$ and $a(t)$: $v(t) = \frac{dx}{dt} = -9t^2 + 36t + 16$. $a(t) = \frac{dv}{dt} = -18t + 36$.
  3. Step 3 — Solve $a(t) = 0$ and Find Velocity: $-18t + 36 = 0 \implies t = 2\text{ s}$. At $t = 2\text{ s}$: $v(2) = -9(2)^2 + 36(2) + 16 = -36 + 72 + 16 = 52\text{ m/s}$.
  4. Final Answer: $52$
Q38.trapHtml: Note: the stated initial offset "16 m right of origin" does not alter $v=dx/dt$ (constant term differentiates to 0).

Q39.questionRecapHtml:
Body falls from height $H$, bounces elastically off an incline at height $h$ so velocity becomes horizontal. Maximize total fall time to find $H/h$.
$\sqrt{2(H-h)} $
Q39.conceptHtml: Vertical velocity resets to 0 after impact, so total time is $T(h)=_g + \frac{2h}{g}$.
Q39.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Given & Concept: A body drops from height $H$ and hits an incline at height $h$ above the ground, bouncing off with purely horizontal velocity. Because horizontal velocity has zero vertical component ($v_{y0} = 0$), the body starts a fresh vertical free fall from height $h$ after the bounce!
  2. Step 2 — Write Total Time $T(h)$: Time to fall distance $(H - h)$ from rest: $t_1 = \sqrt{\frac{2(H - h)}{g}}$. Time to fall the remaining height $h$ with zero initial vertical velocity: $t_2 = \sqrt{\frac{2h}{g}}$. Total time: $T(h) = \sqrt{\frac{2}{g}}\left(\sqrt{H - h} + \sqrt{h}\right)$.
  3. Step 3 — Maximize $T(h)$ Using Calculus: To maximize $T(h)$ with respect to $h$, set $\frac{dT}{dh} = 0$: $\frac{d}{dh}\left(\sqrt{H - h} + \sqrt{h}\right) = \frac{-1}{2\sqrt{H - h}} + \frac{1}{2\sqrt{h}} = 0$. Rearranging gives $\sqrt{H - h} = \sqrt{h} \implies H - h = h \implies H = 2h \implies \frac{H}{h} = 2$.
  4. Final Answer: $2$
Q39.stepsLatex:
$\sqrt{2(H-h)} $ 1. Fall time to incline: $t_1=$ . After elastic deflection to horizontal, $v_{y0}=0$, so remaining fall time is $t_2= \frac{2h}{g}$ . $\sqrt{( } \frac{g}{H-h} )$ 2. Total time $T(h)= \frac{2}{g} + h$ . Set $\frac{dT}{dh} =0$:
$\sqrt{\sqrt}{} \sqrt{\frac{-1}{H-h}} + \frac{1}{2 h} =0 \implies H-h= h \implies H=2h \implies \frac{H}{h} =2$ 2
Q39.trapHtml: Horizontal velocity after bounce does NOT affect vertical fall time $t_2= 2h/g$!

Q40.questionRecapHtml: In the 1 s interval $t\to (t+1)$ s, displacement is 125 m and $\Delta v=50$ m/s. Find distance in $(t+2)^{th}$ second.
Q40.conceptHtml: Constant acceleration $a=\Delta v/\Delta t$; consecutive-second displacement increases by $a$: $S_{n+1}=S_n+a$.
Q40.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Given & Concept: During the $1\text{ s}$ interval from $t$ to $(t + 1)\text{ s}$ — which is the $(t + 1)^{\text{th}}$ second — the velocity increases by $\Delta v = 50\text{ m/s}$ and displacement is $S_{t+1} = 125\text{ m}$. Under uniform acceleration, the displacement in each consecutive $1\text{ s}$ interval increases by exactly $a$ ($S_{n+1} = S_n + a$).
  2. Step 2 — Find Acceleration $a$: Since velocity increases by $50\text{ m/s}$ in $\Delta t = 1\text{ s}$: $a = \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t} = \frac{50}{1} = 50\text{ m/s}^2$.
  3. Step 3 — Find Distance in the $(t + 2)^{\text{th}}$ Second: Since the $(t + 2)^{\text{th}}$ second immediately follows the $(t + 1)^{\text{th}}$ second: $S_{t+2} = S_{t+1} + a = 125 + 50 = 175\text{ m}$.
  4. Final Answer: $175$
Q40.stepsLatex:
1. Acceleration: $a= \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t} = \frac{50}{(t^1+} =50$ m/$s^2$.
2. Interval $t$ to $t+1$ is the $1)^{th}$ second ($S_{t+1}=125$ m). 3. Displacement in the very next, $(t+2)^{th}$, second: $S_{t+2}=S_{t+1}+a=125+50=175$ m.
Q40.trapHtml: No need to solve for $u$ or $t$—using $S_{n+1}-S_n=a$ makes this a 1-line mental calculation!

Q41.questionRecapHtml: Freely falling body covers 80 m between points $A$ and $B$ in 2 s. Find distance of $A$ below start ($g=10$ m/$s^2$).
Q41.conceptHtml: Find velocity $v_A$ at point $A$ using $s=v_At+ \frac{1}{2} gt^2$, then get $h_A=v^2/(2g)$. $A$
Q41.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Given & Concept: A body falls freely from rest ($u = 0$, $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$) and covers the vertical gap $AB = 80\text{ m}$ in $t = 2\text{ s}$. First find its downward speed $v_A$ as it passes the upper point $A$, then use $v_A^2 = 2gh_A$ to find how far below the starting point $A$ lies.
  2. Step 2 — Find Velocity $v_A$ at Point $A$: Applying $s = v_A t + \frac{1}{2}gt^2$ to segment $AB$: $80 = v_A(2) + \frac{1}{2}(10)(2)^2 \implies 80 = 2v_A + 20 \implies 2v_A = 60 \implies v_A = 30\text{ m/s}$.
  3. Step 3 — Find Distance of $A$ from the Starting Point: Using $v_A^2 = u^2 + 2gh_A$ with $u = 0$: $30^2 = 2(10)h_A \implies 900 = 20h_A \implies h_A = 45\text{ m}$.
  4. Final Answer: $45$
Q41.stepsLatex:
1. For segment $AB$ ($s=80$ m$,t=2$ s): $80=2v_A+ \frac{1}{v22} (10)(2)^2 \implies 2v_A=60 \implies v_A=30$ m/s.
2. Distance of $A$ from starting point ($u=0$): $h_A= \frac{A}{2g} = \frac{302}{2(10)} =45$ m.
Q41.trapHtml: Shortcut: average speed in $AB$ is $80/2=40$ m/s, reached at midpoint ($t_A+1$ s), so $v_A=40-10(1)=30$ m/s.

Q42.questionRecapHtml: Train at 20 m/s needs 500 m to stop. If brakes are applied at 250 m, it crosses station at $x$ m/s. Find $x$.
Q42.conceptHtml: Use $v^2=u^2-2as$ for full stopping distance $s_0=500$ m and half distance $s_0/2$.
Q42.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Given & Concept: A train moving at $u = 20\text{ m/s}$ stops completely ($v = 0$) in distance $s_0 = 500\text{ m}$ under constant retardation $a$. If brakes are applied at half the distance ($s = \frac{s_0}{2} = 250\text{ m}$), it crosses the station with speed $\sqrt{x}\text{ m/s}$. We use $v^2 = u^2 - 2as$.
  2. Step 2 — Relate $2as_0$ to $u^2$: From the full stopping condition: $0 = u^2 - 2as_0 \implies 2as_0 = u^2 = 20^2 = 400$.
  3. Step 3 — Find Speed at Half Distance ($s = \frac{s_0}{2}$): $v^2 = u^2 - 2a\left(\frac{s_0}{2}\right) = u^2 - \frac{2as_0}{2} = u^2 - \frac{u^2}{2} = \frac{u^2}{2} = \frac{400}{2} = 200$. Thus $v = \sqrt{200}\text{ m/s}$, which gives $x = 200$.
  4. Final Answer: $200$
Q42.stepsLatex:
1. Full stop: $0=u^2-2as_0 \implies 2as_0=u^2= 00$.
2. At half distance ($s=s /2$): $v^2=u^2-2a( \frac{s40}{2} )=u^2- \frac{u2}{2} = \frac{u2}{2} = \frac{400}{2} =200$. 0 3. Thus $v= 200$ m/s $\implies x=200$.
Q42.trapHtml: Universal shortcut: at half the stopping distance, speed is always $u/ 2$ (regardless of $s_0$)!

Q43.questionRecapHtml: First half of distance at 5 m/s; second half at 10 m/s and 15 m/s for equal times. Mean speed is $x/7$ m/s.
Q43.conceptHtml: Apply AM to the equal-time second half, then HM to the two equal-distance halves.
Q43.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Given & Concept: The rider covers the first half of the total distance at $v_1 = 5\text{ m/s}$, and the remaining half in two equal time intervals at $10\text{ m/s}$ and $15\text{ m/s}$. We apply the arithmetic mean to the equal-time second half, then the harmonic mean across the two equal-distance halves.
  2. Step 2 — Average Speed of the Second Half: Since the two speeds ($10\text{ m/s}$ and $15\text{ m/s}$) are maintained for equal durations: $v_2 = \frac{10 + 15}{2} = 12.5\text{ m/s} = \frac{25}{2}\text{ m/s}$.
  3. Step 3 — Overall Average Speed & Value of $x$: Combining the two equal halves of distance using the harmonic mean: $v_{\text{avg}} = \frac{2v_1 v_2}{v_1 + v_2} = \frac{2(5)(12.5)}{5 + 12.5} = \frac{125}{17.5} = \frac{250}{35} = \frac{50}{7}\text{ m/s}$. Comparing with $\frac{x}{7}\text{ m/s}$ gives $x = 50$.
  4. Final Answer: $50$
Q43.stepsLatex:
1. Average speed of second half: $v_2= \frac{10+15}{2} =12.5$ m/s $= \frac{25}{2}$ m/s.
2. Overall average speed: $v_{av}= \frac{2(5)(12.5)}{5+12.5} = \frac{125}{17.5} = \frac{250}{35} = \frac{50}{7}$ m/s $\implies x=50$.
Q43.trapHtml: Notice this is the exact same template as Q15—NTA repeats this AM$\to$HM hybrid pattern across years!

Q44.questionRecapHtml: Ball dropped from 9.8 m rebounds to 5.0 m after 0.2 s floor contact. Find average acceleration ($g=10$ m/$s^2$).
Q44.conceptHtml: Velocity reverses direction on rebound, so $|\Delta v|=v_{up}+v_{down}$ (vector subtraction!).
Q44.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Given & Concept: A ball is dropped from $h_1 = 9.8\text{ m}$, rebounds to $h_2 = 5.0\text{ m}$, and stays in contact with the floor for $\Delta t = 0.2\text{ s}$. Take upward as positive ($+$). Because velocity reverses direction during the bounce, we must use vector subtraction $\Delta v = v_f - v_i$ so the two speeds add in magnitude.
  2. Step 2 — Find Velocity Just Before and Just After Impact: Speed just before hitting the floor (downward, so negative): $v_i = -\sqrt{2gh_1} = -\sqrt{2(10)(9.8)} = -\sqrt{196} = -14\text{ m/s}$. Speed just after leaving the floor (upward, so positive): $v_f = +\sqrt{2gh_2} = +\sqrt{2(10)(5.0)} = +\sqrt{100} = +10\text{ m/s}$.
  3. Step 3 — Calculate Magnitude of Average Acceleration: $a_{\text{avg}} = \frac{v_f - v_i}{\Delta t} = \frac{10 - (-14)}{0.2} = \frac{24}{0.2} = 120\text{ m/s}^2$.
  4. Final Answer: $120$

3. Average acceleration: $a_{avg}= \frac{v_f-v_i}{\Delta t} = \frac{10-(-14)}{0.2} = \frac{24}{0.2} =120$ m/$s^2$.

Q45.questionRecapHtml: Balloon rises at 10 m/s; stone dropped at $h_0=75$ m. Find balloon height when stone hits ground.
Q45.conceptHtml: A dropped stone inherits the balloon’s upward velocity ($u=+10$ m/s) while accelerating downwards at $a=-g=-10$ m/$s^2$.
Q45.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Given & Concept: When the stone is dropped from the rising balloon at height $75\text{ m}$, it does not start from rest — by inertia, it inherits the balloon's upward velocity $u = +10\text{ m/s}$ while accelerating downward at $a = -g = -10\text{ m/s}^2$. Take upward as positive with the release point as $y = 0$, so the ground is at $y = -75\text{ m}$.
  2. Step 2 — Find Time for the Stone to Hit the Ground: Applying $y = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^2$: $-75 = 10t - \frac{1}{2}(10)t^2 \implies 5t^2 - 10t - 75 = 0 \implies t^2 - 2t - 15 = 0$. Factoring gives $(t - 5)(t + 3) = 0$. Rejecting negative time, the stone hits the ground at $t = 5\text{ s}$.
  3. Step 3 — Find the Balloon's Height at $t = 5\text{ s}$: During those $5\text{ s}$, the balloon keeps rising at a constant $10\text{ m/s}$: $H = 75 + 10(5) = 75 + 50 = 125\text{ m}$.
  4. Final Answer: The height of the balloon is $125\text{ m}$, which matches option (d).
Q45.stepsLatex:
1. Taking upward as positive from release point ($y_0=0$), ground is at $y=-75$ m:
$-75=10t- \frac{1}{2} (10)t^2 \implies 5t^2-10t-75=0 \implies t^2-2t-15=0$
2. Factoring: $(t-5)(t+3)=0 \implies t=5$ s (rejecting $t<0$). 3. Balloon height at $t=5$ s: $H=75+v_bt=75+10(5)=125$ m.
Q45.trapHtml: Forgetting that the stone starts with $u=+10$ m/s (not 0) gives $t= 15\approx 3.87$ s and a wrong height.

Q46.questionRecapHtml:
Triangular $v$-$t$ graph: $+5$ m/s peak over 0–20 s and $-5$ m/s trough over 20–40 s.
$\sum$
Q46.conceptHtml: Distance $= |$Area$|$; Displacement $= ($Signed Area); $v_{avg}=\Delta x/\Delta t$.
Q46.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Given & Concept: The $v$-$t$ graph over $40\text{ s}$ consists of two identical triangles: one above the time axis ($0\text{–}20\text{ s}$, peak $+5\text{ m/s}$) and one below the time axis ($20\text{–}40\text{ s}$, trough $-5\text{ m/s}$). Total distance sums the magnitudes of both areas, while net displacement sums the signed areas.
  2. Step 2 — Calculate Areas of Both Triangles: Positive triangle ($0$ to $20\text{ s}$): $A_1 = \frac{1}{2}(20)(+5) = +50\text{ m}$. Negative triangle ($20$ to $40\text{ s}$): $A_2 = \frac{1}{2}(20)(-5) = -50\text{ m}$.
  3. Step 3 — Find Total Distance & Average Velocity: Total distance $= |A_1| + |A_2| = 50 + 50 = 100\text{ m}$. Net displacement $= A_1 + A_2 = +50 - 50 = 0\text{ m}$, so $v_{\text{avg}} = \frac{0}{40} = 0$.
  4. Final Answer: The total distance is $100\text{ m}$ and the average velocity is zero, which matches option (c).

Q46.trapHtml: Symmetric positive and negative loops immediately signal zero net displacement and zero average velocity.

Q47.questionRecapHtml: Car $A$ at 100 km/h ahead of car $B$ at 80 km/h; stone thrown from $B$ at speed $v$ hits $A$ at 5 m/s.
Q47.conceptHtml: Stone speed in ground frame is $v_s=v_B+v$; its impact speed relative to $A$ is $v_{s/A}=v_s-v_A$.
Q47.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Given & Concept: Car $A$ ($100\text{ km/h}$) is ahead of car $B$ ($80\text{ km/h}$), both moving in the same direction. A stone thrown forward from car $B$ at speed $v$ relative to $B$ has ground-frame speed $v_s = v_B + v$. Its impact speed relative to car $A$ is $v_{s/A} = v_s - v_A = 5\text{ m/s}$.
  2. Step 2 — Convert Impact Speed to $\text{km/h}$: To keep all speeds in $\text{km/h}$, multiply by $\frac{18}{5}$: $v_{s/A} = 5 \times \frac{18}{5} = 18\text{ km/h}$.
  3. Step 3 — Solve for $v$: Substituting into $(v_B + v) - v_A = v_{s/A}$: $(80 + v) - 100 = 18 \implies v - 20 = 18 \implies v = 38\text{ km/h}$.
  4. Final Answer: The throwing speed $v$ is $38\text{ km/h}$, which matches option (c).
Q47.stepsLatex:
1. Convert impact speed to km/h: $v_{s/A}=5\times \frac{18}{^51} =18$ km/h. 2. Relative velocity equation: $(v_B+v)-v_A= 8 \implies (80+v)-100=18$. 3. Solve: $v=18+20=38$ km/h.
18
Q47.trapHtml: Always convert m/s $\to$ km/h via $\times _5$ before combining speeds!

Q48.questionRecapHtml: Given $x(t)=4t^3-3t$ for $t\ge 0$, identify the correct statements among A–E.
Q48.conceptHtml: Set $x=0$ for return to origin, $v=dx/dt=0$ for turning point, and inspect $a=d^2x/dt^2$.
Q48.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Given & Concept: The position for $t \ge 0$ is $x(t) = 4t^3 - 3t$. To test all five statements, we check when $x(t) = 0$ (return to origin), when $v(t) = \frac{dx}{dt} = 0$ (turning point), and the sign of $a(t) = \frac{dv}{dt}$.
  2. Step 2 — Check Return to Origin (Statement A): Setting $x(t) = t(4t^2 - 3) = 0$ gives $t = 0$ (start) and $t = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \approx 0.866$ units. Thus, the particle returns to the origin $0.866$ units later — A is true.
  3. Step 3 — Check Turning Point (Statements B, D, E): Differentiating gives $v(t) = 12t^2 - 3$. Setting $v(t) = 0$ gives $t^2 = \frac{1}{4} \implies t = 0.5$ (so the particle does turn back, making E false). At $t = 0.5$, the position is $x(0.5) = 4(0.125) - 3(0.5) = 0.5 - 1.5 = -1$, which is $1$ unit away from the origin — so B is true and D is false.
  4. Step 4 — Check Acceleration (Statement C): Differentiating $v(t)$ gives $a(t) = 24t$. Since $t \ge 0$, $a(t) \ge 0$ always (it can still turn around because initial velocity $v(0) = -3$ is negative) — C is true.
  5. Final Answer: Statements A, B, and C are correct, which matches option (b).
Q48.stepsLatex:
1. Origin return: $x(t)=t(4t^2-3)=0 \implies t= \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \approx 0.866$ units (A is true). 2. Velocity: $v=12t^2-3=0 \implies t=0.5$ (turning point exists, so E is false).
3. Position at turning point: $x(0.5)=4(0.125)-3(0.5)=-1 \implies |x|=1$ unit (B is true, D is false). 4. Acceleration: $a= \frac{dv}{dt} =24t\ge 0$ for all $t\ge 0$ (C is true).
Q48.trapHtml: Non-negative acceleration does NOT prevent a turning point if initial velocity is negative ($v(0)=-3$).

Q49.questionRecapHtml: Water drops fall from 5 m high tap; 1st strikes floor when 6th begins to fall. Find height of 4th drop.
Q49.conceptHtml: For $N=6$ drops at interval $\tau$, 1st falls for $5\tau$ and 4th falls for $(6-4)\tau =2\tau$.
Q49.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Given & Concept: Drops fall at equal time intervals $\tau$ from a tap at height $H = 5\text{ m}$. When the $6^{\text{th}}$ drop just starts falling, there are $(6 - 1) = 5$ intervals separating it from the $1^{\text{st}}$ drop (which hits the ground), so the $1^{\text{st}}$ drop has fallen for $5\tau$, and the $4^{\text{th}}$ drop has fallen for $(6 - 4)\tau = 2\tau$.
  2. Step 2 — Find the Time Interval $\tau$: Total fall time of the $1^{\text{st}}$ drop from $H = 5\text{ m}$ ($g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$): $T = \sqrt{\frac{2H}{g}} = \sqrt{\frac{2 \times 5}{10}} = 1\text{ s}$. Since $T = 5\tau$, each interval is $\tau = \frac{1}{5} = 0.2\text{ s}$.
  3. Step 3 — Find Distance Fallen by the $4^{\text{th}}$ Drop & Its Height: The $4^{\text{th}}$ drop has been falling for $t_4 = 2\tau = 0.4\text{ s}$, so the distance it has fallen below the tap is: $y_4 = \frac{1}{2}gt_4^2 = \frac{1}{2}(10)(0.4)^2 = 5 \times 0.16 = 0.8\text{ m}$. Therefore, its height above the ground is $h_4 = 5 - 0.8 = 4.2\text{ m}$.
  4. Final Answer: The height of the fourth drop above the ground is $4.2\text{ m}$, which matches option (c).
Q49.stepsLatex:
1. Total fall time of 1st drop: $T = \frac{2H}{g} = \frac{2(5)}{10} =1$ s $=5\tau \implies \tau =0.2$ s.
2. Distance fallen by 4th drop in $2\tau =0.4$ s: $y_4= \frac{1}{2} (10)(0.4)^2=0.8$ m (or $5\times \frac{22}{52} =0.8$ m).
3. Height above ground: $h_4=5-0.8=4.2$ m.
Q49.trapHtml: There are $(6-1)=5$ intervals between 1st and 6th drops, not 6! Also subtract $y_4$ from 5 m for height from ground.

Q50.questionRecapHtml:
Given a straight-line $v$-$x$ graph with negative slope and positive $v$-intercept, find the $a$-$x$ graph.
$dv$
Q50.conceptHtml: Use $a=v$ directly on the linear equation $v=-mx+c$ ($m,c>0$). $dx$
Q50.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Given & Concept: The given velocity-distance ($v$-$x$) graph is a downward-sloping straight line with a positive $v$-intercept. Because $v$ is given as a function of $x$ (not $t$), we find acceleration using the chain-rule identity $a = v\frac{dv}{dx}$.
  2. Step 2 — Write the Equation of the $v$-$x$ Line: Since the line slopes downward with constant negative slope $-m$ (where $m > 0$) and positive intercept $c > 0$: $v = -mx + c$, which immediately gives $\frac{dv}{dx} = -m$.
  3. Step 3 — Derive the $a$-$x$ Relation: Substitute both expressions into $a = v\frac{dv}{dx}$: $a = (-mx + c)(-m) = m^2 x - mc$. This is a straight line on an $a$-$x$ graph with a positive slope ($+m^2$) and a negative $a$-intercept ($-mc$), crossing $a = 0$ at $x = \frac{c}{m}$.
  4. Final Answer: The linear graph starting at a negative $a$-intercept with positive slope is option (d).
Q50.stepsLatex: 1. From the graph: $v mx+c$, where slope $\frac{dv}{dmx} =-m$ (negative constant) and $c>0$. 2. Acceleration: $a=v \frac{=_{dv}-}{dx} =(-mx+c)(-m)=^2x-mc$. 3. This is a straight line with positive slope ($+m^2$) and negative $a$-intercept ($-mc$), crossing $a=0$ at $x=c/m$.
Q50.trapHtml: Do not confuse $v$-$x$ with $v$-$t$: in $v$-$x$, a straight line does NOT give constant $a$, it gives linear $a(x)$!

Q51.questionRecapHtml: Paratrooper falls freely for 2 s, then decelerates at 3 m/$s^2$, reaching 5 m/s at 10 m height.
Q51.conceptHtml: Split total height into three segments: $H=h_1$ (free fall) $+h_2$ (parachute) $+10$ m.
Q51.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Given & Concept: The paratrooper's descent has three parts: free fall for $2\text{ s}$ (distance $h_1$), parachute deceleration at $a = -3\text{ m/s}^2$ down to speed $5\text{ m/s}$ (distance $h_2$), and a remaining $10\text{ m}$ above the ground. Total initial height is $H = h_1 + h_2 + 10\text{ m}$.
  2. Step 2 — Free-Fall Phase ($t = 2\text{ s}$, $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$): Distance fallen: $h_1 = \frac{1}{2}gt^2 = \frac{1}{2}(10)(2)^2 = 20\text{ m}$. Downward speed when the parachute opens: $u_2 = gt = 10 \times 2 = 20\text{ m/s}$.
  3. Step 3 — Parachute Deceleration Phase: Slowing from $u_2 = 20\text{ m/s}$ to $v = 5\text{ m/s}$ with deceleration $3\text{ m/s}^2$ using $v^2 = u_2^2 - 2ah_2$: $5^2 = 20^2 - 2(3)h_2 \implies 25 = 400 - 6h_2 \implies 6h_2 = 375 \implies h_2 = 62.5\text{ m}$.
  4. Step 4 — Total Initial Height: Don't forget the final $10\text{ m}$ still below the paratrooper: $H = 20 + 62.5 + 10 = 92.5\text{ m}$.
  5. Final Answer: The initial height of the aeroplane is $92.5\text{ m}$, which matches option (a).
Q51.stepsLatex:
1. Free fall (2 s): $h_1= \frac{1}{2} (10)(2)^2=20$ m; speed at opening $u_2=gt=20$ m/s. 2. Parachute deceleration ($a=-3$ m/$s^2$, $v=5$ m/s): $5^2=20^2-2(3)h_2 \implies h_2= \frac{375}{6} =62.5$ m.
3. Total initial height: $H=20+62.5+10=92.5$ m.
Q51.trapHtml: Remember to add the final 10 m height above the ground ($20+62.5=82.5$ is the classic distractor D).

Q52.questionRecapHtml: Masses 3.4 kg ($u_1=5$ m/s, $S_{5,1}=104$ m) and 2.5 kg ($u_2=12$ m/s, $S_{5,2}=129$ m). Ratio of momenta at 10 s is $x/8$.
Q52.conceptHtml: Extract $a_1,a_2$ from $S_n=u+ \frac{a}{2} (2n-1)$ with $n=5$, then compute $p=m(u+at)$ at $t=10$ s.
Q52.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Given & Concept: Two masses ($m_1 = 3.4\text{ kg}$, $u_1 = 5\text{ m/s}$ and $m_2 = 2.5\text{ kg}$, $u_2 = 12\text{ m/s}$) travel $104\text{ m}$ and $129\text{ m}$ in the $5^{\text{th}}$ second. We extract each acceleration using $S_n = u + \frac{a}{2}(2n - 1)$ with $n = 5$, find their velocities at $t = 10\text{ s}$ via $v = u + at$, and take the ratio of momenta $p = mv$.
  2. Step 2 — Find Accelerations $a_1$ and $a_2$ (for $n = 5$, $2n - 1 = 9$): Mass 1: $104 = 5 + \frac{9}{2}a_1 \implies 99 = 4.5a_1 \implies a_1 = 22\text{ m/s}^2$. Mass 2: $129 = 12 + \frac{9}{2}a_2 \implies 117 = 4.5a_2 \implies a_2 = 26\text{ m/s}^2$.
  3. Step 3 — Velocities at $t = 10\text{ s}$: $v_1 = 5 + 22(10) = 225\text{ m/s}$. $v_2 = 12 + 26(10) = 272\text{ m/s}$.
  4. Step 4 — Ratio of Momenta: $\frac{p_1}{p_2} = \frac{m_1 v_1}{m_2 v_2} = \frac{3.4 \times 225}{2.5 \times 272} = \frac{765}{680} = \frac{9}{8}$. Comparing with $\frac{x}{8}$ gives $x = 9$.
  5. Final Answer: $9$
Q52.stepsLatex:
1. Mass 1: $104=5+ \frac{9}{+^2} _1 \implies 99=4.5a_1 \implies a_1=22$ m/$s^2$. At 10 s, $v_1=5+220=225$ m/s. 2. Mass 2: $129=12 \frac{_9a}{12} a_2 \implies 117=4.5a_2 \implies a_2=26$ m/$s^2$. At 10 s, $v_2=12+260=272$ m/s.
3. Momentum ratio: $\frac{p}{p_2} = \frac{3.4\times 225}{2.5\times 272} = \frac{765}{680} = \frac{9}{8} \implies x=9$.
Q52.trapHtml: Notice $3.4/272=1/80$ and $225/2.5=90$, so $\frac{p1}{p2} = \frac{90}{80} = \frac{9}{8}$ without big multiplication!

Q53.questionRecapHtml: Ball dropped from 18 m. Find height above ground where $|v|=g$ (numerically, $v=10$ m/s).
Q53.conceptHtml: Use $v^2=2gy$ to find distance fallen $y$, then subtract from 18 m.
Q53.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Given & Concept: A ball is dropped from rest ($u = 0$) from a height of $18\text{ m}$ with $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$. We want the height above the ground where its speed numerically equals $g$, i.e., $v = 10\text{ m/s}$. First find the distance fallen $y$ from the top using $v^2 = 2gy$, then subtract $y$ from $18\text{ m}$.
  2. Step 2 — Find Distance Fallen $y$: $10^2 = 2(10)y \implies 100 = 20y \implies y = 5\text{ m}$.
  3. Step 3 — Find Height Above the Ground: $h = 18 - 5 = 13\text{ m}$.
  4. Final Answer: $13$
Q53.stepsLatex:
1. Set $v=10$ m/s: $10^2=2(10)y \implies y= \frac{100}{1^23^0} =5$ m.
2. Height above the ground: $h=18-5=$ m.
Q53.trapHtml: Always read whether the question asks for distance fallen (5 m) or height above ground (13 m).

trapCards.title: 1. Distance vs Displacement & $n^{\text{th}}$ Second Traps
trapCards.html:
• Turning Point inside $n^{\text{th}}$ Second: If velocity reverses inside $(n-1, n)$, $S_n$ gives displacement, NOT distance! Find $t_{\text{stop}}$ first.
  • Last Second of Fall: Check whether total time $T$ is an integer before using $S_n$.

trapCards.title: 2. Sign Reversal & Free Fall Traps
trapCards.html:
• Balloon / Lift Release: A stone dropped from a rising balloon starts with $u = +v_{\text{balloon}}$, NOT $0$!
  • Consistent Sign Convention: Fix $+y$ upward ($a = -g$) or downward ($a = +g$) and stick to it for $s, u, v, a$.

trapCards.title: 3. Graph Axes Confusion
trapCards.html: • Non-Standard Axes: Always check if the graph is $v$–$x$, $v^2$–$x$, $1/v$–$x$, or $x$–$t$ before taking slope or area!

trapCards.title: 4. Unit Conversions & Average Speed Traps
trapCards.html:
• km/h to m/s: Multiply by $\frac{5}{18}$, never $\frac{18}{5}$.
  • Harmonic vs Arithmetic Mean: Use $\frac{2v_1v_2}{v_1+v_2}$ ONLY for equal distances, and $\frac{v_1+v_2}{2}$ ONLY for equal times.

subject: Physics
title: Motion in a Plane
constantsHtml:
• Independence of Perpendicular Axes: Horizontal ($x$) and vertical ($y$) motions in a projectile are completely independent and share only time $t$.
  • Standard Values: $\sin 15^\circ = \dfrac{\sqrt{6}-\sqrt{2}}{4}$, $\sin 75^\circ = \dfrac{\sqrt{6}+\sqrt{2}}{4}$, $\sin(2\theta)$ max at $\theta = 45^\circ$.

formulaCards.title: 1. 2D Vector Kinematics
formulaCards.html:
• Position, Velocity & Acceleration: $\vec{r}(t) = x(t)\hat{i} + y(t)\hat{j}$, $\vec{v} = \dfrac{d\vec{r}}{dt} = v_x\hat{i} + v_y\hat{j}$, $\vec{a} = \dfrac{d\vec{v}}{dt} = a_x\hat{i} + a_y\hat{j}$.
  • Constant Acceleration 2D: $\vec{v} = \vec{u} + \vec{a}t$, $\vec{r} = \vec{r}_0 + \vec{u}t + \dfrac{1}{2}\vec{a}t^2$.
  • Tangential & Normal Acceleration: $a_t = \dfrac{d|\vec{v}|}{dt} = \vec{a}\cdot\hat{v}$; $a_n = \dfrac{v^2}{R} = \sqrt{a^2 - a_t^2}$.

formulaCards.title: 2. Ground-to-Ground Projectile
formulaCards.html:
• Time of Flight, Height & Range: Launch speed $u$ at angle $\theta$ with horizontal: $T = \dfrac{2u\sin\theta}{g}$, $H = \dfrac{u^2\sin^2\theta}{2g}$, $R = \dfrac{u^2\sin 2\theta}{g}$.
  • Range–Height Relations: $\dfrac{H}{R} = \dfrac{\tan\theta}{4}$, $R_{\max} = \dfrac{u^2}{g}$ (at $\theta = 45^\circ$, where $H = R_{\max}/4$).
  • Velocity at Time $t$: $v_x = u\cos\theta$ (constant), $v_y = u\sin\theta - gt$; at apex $v = u\cos\theta$.

formulaCards.title: 3. Complementary Angles & Equation of Trajectory
formulaCards.html:
• Complementary Angles ($\theta_1 + \theta_2 = 90^\circ$, same $u$): $R_1 = R_2 = R$; $T_1 T_2 = \dfrac{2R}{g}$; $H_1 H_2 = \dfrac{R^2}{16}$; $H_1 + H_2 = \dfrac{u^2}{2g}$.
  • Equation of Trajectory: $y = x\tan\theta - \dfrac{gx^2}{2u^2\cos^2\theta} = x\tan\theta\left(1 - \dfrac{x}{R}\right)$.

formulaCards.title: 4. Horizontal, Tower & Inclined Projectile
formulaCards.html:
• Horizontal Throw from Height $h$ ($u_y = 0$): $T = \sqrt{\dfrac{2h}{g}}$, $R = u\sqrt{\dfrac{2h}{g}}$, $v_{\text{hit}} = \sqrt{u^2 + 2gh}$.
  • Inclined Plane (Incline $\beta$, launch $\alpha$ above incline): $T = \dfrac{2u\sin\alpha}{g\cos\beta}$, $R = \dfrac{u^2}{g\cos^2\beta}[\sin(2\alpha + \beta) - \sin\beta]$ (up incline; replace $+\beta \to -\beta$ for down incline).
  • Max Range on Incline: $R_{\max,\text{up}} = \dfrac{u^2}{g(1+\sin\beta)}$; $R_{\max,\text{down}} = \dfrac{u^2}{g(1-\sin\beta)}$.

formulaCards.title: 5. Relative Velocity in 2D (River–Boat & Rain–Man)
formulaCards.html:
• River–Boat Problem (width $d$, boat speed $v_b$, river speed $v_r$): Minimum time to cross: $t_{\min} = \dfrac{d}{v_b}$ (steer $\perp$ bank; drift $= v_r t_{\min}$).
  • Shortest Path / Zero Drift ($v_b > v_r$): Steer upstream at $\sin\theta = \dfrac{v_r}{v_b}$ from normal; crossing speed $= \sqrt{v_b^2 - v_r^2}$, $t = \dfrac{d}{\sqrt{v_b^2 - v_r^2}}$.
  • Rain–Man Problem: $\vec{v}_{\text{rain,man}} = \vec{v}_{\text{rain}} - \vec{v}_{\text{man}}$ (hold umbrella opposite to $\vec{v}_{\text{rain,man}}$).
