Q70.questionRecapHtml:
Horizontal variable-area tube; find $\Delta P$ from $A_A,A_B,v_A,\rho$.
1
Q70.conceptHtml: Apply continuity ($A_Av_A=A_Bv_B$) and horizontal Bernoulli’s equation ($P_A-P_B= \rho (v^2 -v^2)$). $2 B A$
Q70.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Find the liquid speed at point B using continuity: Given $A_A = 1.0\text{ cm}^2 = 100\text{ mm}^2$, $A_B = 20\text{ mm}^2$, and $v_A = 10\text{ cm/s} = 0.1\text{ m/s}$. By continuity ($A_A v_A = A_B v_B$), we get $v_B = v_A \frac{A_A}{A_B} = 0.1 \times \frac{100}{20} = 0.5\text{ m/s}$.
  2. Step 2 — Apply Bernoulli's equation in the horizontal plane: Since $A$ and $B$ are at the same height, $P_A - P_B = \frac{1}{2}\rho(v_B^2 - v_A^2)$.
  3. Step 3 — Compute the pressure difference: With $\rho = 600\text{ kg/m}^3$, $P_A - P_B = \frac{1}{2}(600)(0.5^2 - 0.1^2) = 300(0.25 - 0.01) = 300 \times 0.24 = 72\text{ Pa}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: This matches option d ($72$ Pa).
Q70.trapHtml: Convert both areas to the same unit (1 c$m^2=100$ m$m^2$) and $v_A$ to m/s before substituting into Bernoulli’s equation.

Q71.questionRecapHtml: Drop splits into 64 identical droplets; find ratio of terminal speeds $v_1/v_2$.
Q71.conceptHtml: Volume conservation gives $R=n^{1/3}r$, and terminal velocity scales as $v_t\propto r^2$.
Q71.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Find the radius ratio via volume conservation: When a drop of radius $R$ breaks into 64 identical droplets of radius $r$, $\frac{4}{3}\pi R^3 = 64 \times \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3 \implies R = 64^{1/3}r = 4r$.
  2. Step 2 — Relate terminal velocity to radius: From Stokes' law, $v_T = \frac{2r^2(\rho - \sigma)g}{9\eta}$, so for the same liquid and gas, $v_T \propto r^2$.
  3. Step 3 — Compute the ratio of terminal velocities: Therefore, $\frac{v_1}{v_2} = \left(\frac{R}{r}\right)^2 = 4^2 = 16$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: This corresponds to option d ($16$).
Q71.stepsLatex:
$\frac{4}{3} \pi R^3=64\cdot \frac{4}{)3} \pi r^3 \implies \frac{R}{r} =64^{1/3}=4$
$( 2 \frac{v_1}{v_2} = \frac{R}{r} =4^2=16$
Q71.trapHtml: Remember the direct scaling shortcut: $v_{big}/v_{small}=n^{2/3}$, not $n^{1/3}$.

Q72.questionRecapHtml: Tank on block of equal height $H$; find initial efflux range from hole 70 cm below top.
Q72.conceptHtml: Find vessel height $H$ from $V =\pi R^2H$, then use $R_{horiz}=2 hH_{fall}$ where $H_{fall}=2H-h$.
Q72.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Find the height of the cylindrical vessel: The vessel has radius $r = 40\text{ cm}$ and volume $V = 528\text{ dm}^3 = 528000\text{ cm}^3$. Using $V = \pi r^2 H$ with $\pi = \frac{22}{7}$, we get $H = \frac{528000}{(22/7) \times 40^2} = \frac{528000 \times 7}{22 \times 1600} = 105\text{ cm}$.
  2. Step 2 — Determine the hole's depth and height above the ground: Since the vessel rests on a solid block of the same height $H = 105\text{ cm}$, the top water surface is at $2H = 210\text{ cm}$ above the ground. The hole is punched at depth $h = 70\text{ cm}$ below the water surface, so its height above the ground is $y = 210 - 70 = 140\text{ cm}$.
  3. Step 3 — Calculate the horizontal range using Torricelli's theorem: The efflux speed is $v = \sqrt{2gh}$ and the time of fall is $t = \sqrt{\frac{2y}{g}}$. Hence the horizontal range is $R = v t = 2\sqrt{h y} = 2\sqrt{70 \times 140} = 2\sqrt{70^2 \times 2} = 140\sqrt{2}\text{ cm}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: This matches option b ($140\sqrt{2}$ cm).
Q72.stepsLatex:
$R=40$ cm $=4$ dm$, V =\pi R^2H \implies \frac{22}{7} (16)H=528 \implies H=10.5$ dm $=105$ cm
Height of hole above ground: $H_{fall}=2H 210 0$ cm $\sqrt{\frac{-h=}{hH}} \sqrt{\frac{-70=14}{70\times 140}} \sqrt{\sqrt}{} R_{horiz}=2_{fall}=2 =2\times 70 2=140 2$ cm
Q72.trapHtml: Do not forget the solid block of height $H$ beneath the vessel—the fall height is $2H-h$, not $H-h$.

Q73.questionRecapHtml: 8 identical drops of radius $r$ coalesce; find released surface energy.
Q73.conceptHtml: Conserve volume ($R=n^{1/3}r$) and compute $\Delta U=S(n\cdot 4\pi r^2-4\pi R^2)$.
Q73.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Find the radius of the bigger drop: By volume conservation, $\frac{4}{3}\pi R^3 = 8 \times \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3 \implies R = 2r$.
  2. Step 2 — Calculate the change in total surface area: Initial surface area of 8 drops: $A_i = 8 \times 4\pi r^2 = 32\pi r^2$. Final surface area of the single big drop: $A_f = 4\pi R^2 = 4\pi(2r)^2 = 16\pi r^2$. Decrease in area: $\Delta A = 32\pi r^2 - 16\pi r^2 = 16\pi r^2$.
  3. Step 3 — Compute the surface energy released: Energy released is $\Delta E = S \cdot \Delta A = 16\pi r^2 S$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: This corresponds to option b ($16\pi r^2 S$).
Q73.trapHtml: Use $4\pi r^2$ (single surface) for liquid drops; factor $8\pi r^2$ is only for soap bubbles.

Q74.questionRecapHtml: Hose (30 c$m^2$, 50 cm/s) feeds 10 nozzles (15 m$m^2$ each); find exit speed.
Q74.conceptHtml: Equation of continuity for multiple outlets: $A_1v_1=NA_2v_2$.
Q74.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Convert areas to consistent units: Hose cross-sectional area $A_1 = 30\text{ cm}^2 = 3000\text{ mm}^2$ and flow speed $v_1 = 50\text{ cm/s} = 0.5\text{ m/s}$. Total area of the 10 perforations is $A_2 = 10 \times 15\text{ mm}^2 = 150\text{ mm}^2$.
  2. Step 2 — Apply the equation of continuity: Since water is incompressible, $A_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2$.
  3. Step 3 — Solve for the exit speed: $v_2 = v_1 \frac{A_1}{A_2} = 0.5 \times \frac{3000}{150} = 0.5 \times 20 = 10\text{ m/s}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: This matches option b ($10$ m/s).
Q74.trapHtml: Watch mixed units: 1 c$m^2=10^{-4} m^2$ while 1 m$m^2=10^{-6} m^2$, and remember to multiply $A_2$ by $N=10$.

Q75.subtopic: Work Done in Blowing a Soap Bubble
Q75.questionRecapHtml: Soap bubble diameter expands from 2 cm to 6 cm; find $\alpha$ in $W=\alpha \pi \times 10^{-4}$ J.
Q75.conceptHtml: A soap bubble has two free surfaces: $W =2S\Delta A=8\pi S(r_2^2-r_1^2)$.
Q75.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the radii and surface tension: Initial diameter is $2\text{ cm} \implies r_1 = 1\text{ cm} = 10^{-2}\text{ m}$. Final diameter is $6\text{ cm} \implies r_2 = 3\text{ cm} = 3\times 10^{-2}\text{ m}$. Surface tension $T = 0.03\text{ N/m}$.
  2. Step 2 — Write the work done formula for a soap bubble: A soap bubble has two free surfaces, so $W = 2 \cdot T \cdot 4\pi(r_2^2 - r_1^2) = 8\pi T(r_2^2 - r_1^2)$.
  3. Step 3 — Substitute and simplify: $W = 8\pi (0.03)\left[(3\times 10^{-2})^2 - (1\times 10^{-2})^2\right] = 0.24\pi (9 - 1)\times 10^{-4} = 1.92\pi \times 10^{-4}\text{ J}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Comparing with $\alpha\pi \times 10^{-4}\text{ J}$ gives $\alpha = 1.92$, which is option c.
Q75.trapHtml: Halve the given diameters to get radii! Using diameters directly inflates the answer by $4\times$ to the distractor 7.68.

Q76.questionRecapHtml:
Air bubble ($d=2$ mm) rises steadily at 0.5 cm/s; find viscosity in Poise.
$2r2\rho g$
Q76.conceptHtml: Neglecting air density, $v_t=_{9\eta}$, and 1 Pa $\cdot$ s $=10$ Poise.
Q76.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Convert all quantities to SI units: Bubble diameter is $2\text{ mm} \implies r = 1\text{ mm} = 10^{-3}\text{ m}$. Liquid density $\rho = 2000\text{ kg/m}^3$, steady rising speed $v_T = 0.5\text{ cm/s} = 5\times 10^{-3}\text{ m/s}$, and $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$.
  2. Step 2 — Use Stokes' law to find viscosity in SI units: Neglecting air density, $v_T = \frac{2r^2 \rho g}{9\eta} \implies \eta = \frac{2r^2 \rho g}{9 v_T} = \frac{2 \times (10^{-3})^2 \times 2000 \times 10}{9 \times 5\times 10^{-3}} = \frac{4\times 10^{-2}}{4.5\times 10^{-2}} = \frac{8}{9} \approx 0.888\text{ Pa}\cdot\text{s}$.
  3. Step 3 — Convert viscosity from SI units to Poise: Since $1\text{ Pa}\cdot\text{s} = 10\text{ Poise}$, we get $\eta \approx 0.888 \times 10 = 8.88\text{ Poise} \approx 8.8\text{ Poise}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: This matches option b ($8.8$ Poise).
Q76.trapHtml: Always convert SI viscosity (Pa $\cdot$ s) to CGS (Poise) by multiplying by 10; forgetting this gives distractor 0.88.

Q77.questionRecapHtml: Drop ($d=2$ mm) breaks into 512 droplets; find $\alpha$ in $\Delta U=\alpha \times 10^{-6}$ J.
Q77.conceptHtml: When one drop of radius $R$ splits into $n$ droplets, $\Delta U=4\pi R^2T(n^{1/3}-1)$.
Q77.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the parameters and number of droplets: Original drop diameter is $2\text{ mm} \implies R = 1\text{ mm} = 10^{-3}\text{ m}$. It breaks into $n = 512$ identical droplets, so $n^{1/3} = 8$. Surface tension $T = 0.08\text{ N/m}$.
  2. Step 2 — Use the standard formula for change in surface energy: When a drop of radius $R$ splits into $n$ identical droplets, the increase in surface energy is $\Delta U = 4\pi R^2 T (n^{1/3} - 1)$.
  3. Step 3 — Substitute and evaluate: $\Delta U = 4 \times 3.14 \times (10^{-3})^2 \times 0.08 \times (8 - 1) = 4 \times 3.14 \times 0.56 \times 10^{-6} \approx 7.03 \times 10^{-6}\text{ J} \approx 7 \times 10^{-6}\text{ J}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Comparing with $\alpha \times 10^{-6}\text{ J}$ gives $\alpha = 7$, which is option b.
Q77.trapHtml: Use radius $R=d/2=1$ mm and remember $(n^{1/3}-1)=7$, not $n^{1/3}=8$.

Q78.questionRecapHtml: Cube ($H=8$ cm, $\rho _b=600$) floats in liquid ($\rho _l=900$); find submerged height.
Q78.conceptHtml: For a floating uniform prism, fraction submerged equals density ratio: $h_{sub}/H=\rho _b/\rho _l$.
Q78.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Apply the principle of flotation: For a floating block of height $H$ and cross-sectional area $A$, its weight equals the buoyant force: $\rho_b (A H) g = \rho_l (A h_{\text{sub}}) g$.
  2. Step 2 — Solve for the submerged height: Cancelling $A$ and $g$ gives $h_{\text{sub}} = H \frac{\rho_b}{\rho_l}$.
  3. Step 3 — Substitute the given values: With $H = 8.0\text{ cm}$, $\rho_b = 600\text{ kg/m}^3$, and $\rho_l = 900\text{ kg/m}^3$, we get $h_{\text{sub}} = 8.0 \times \frac{600}{900} = \frac{16}{3} \approx 5.33\text{ cm} \approx 5.3\text{ cm}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: This matches option d ($5.3$ cm).
Q78.stepsLatex: $\rho _bAHg=\rho _lAh_{sub}g \implies h_{sub}= \frac{\rho _b}{\rho _l} H= \frac{600}{900} \times 8.0= \frac{16}{3} \approx 5.33$ cm
Q78.trapHtml: Read carefully whether the question asks for the submerged height (5.3 cm) or the exposed height above liquid (2.7 cm).

Q79.questionRecapHtml:
Sphere ($d=2$ mm, $\rho =10.5$) falls in glycerine ($\sigma =1.5$, $\eta =10$ P); find $v_t$ in cm/s.
$2r2(\rho -\sigma)g$
Q79.conceptHtml: Stokes’ terminal velocity in CGS units: $v_t=_{9\eta}$.
Q79.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Convert all values to SI units: Sphere diameter is $2\text{ mm} \implies r = 1\text{ mm} = 10^{-3}\text{ m}$. Sphere density $\rho_s = 10.5\text{ g/cm}^3 = 10500\text{ kg/m}^3$, glycerine density $\rho_l = 1.5\text{ g/cm}^3 = 1500\text{ kg/m}^3$, viscosity $\eta = 10\text{ Poise} = 1\text{ Pa}\cdot\text{s}$, and $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$.
  2. Step 2 — Apply Stokes' formula for terminal velocity: $v_T = \frac{2r^2(\rho_s - \rho_l)g}{9\eta}$.
  3. Step 3 — Compute the terminal velocity: $v_T = \frac{2 \times (10^{-3})^2 \times (10500 - 1500) \times 10}{9 \times 1} = \frac{2 \times 10^{-6} \times 9000 \times 10}{9} = 0.02\text{ m/s} = 2.0\text{ cm/s}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: This corresponds to option d ($2.0$ cm/s).
Q79.trapHtml: Work purely in CGS when $\rho ,\eta ,v_t$ are in CGS, and remember $g=1000$ cm/s (not 10).

Q80.questionRecapHtml: Air bubble rises from 5 m depth ($17^{^\circ}$C) to surface ($27^{^\circ}$C); find final volume.
Q80.conceptHtml: Apply combined gas law $\frac{P1V1}{T1} = \frac{P2V2}{T2}$ with $P_1=P_0+\rho gh$ and Kelvin temperatures.
Q80.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Find pressures and absolute temperatures at bottom and surface: At the surface (state 2): $P_2 = P_0 = 10^5\text{ Pa}$ and $T_2 = 27 + 273 = 300\text{ K}$. At the bottom (state 1, depth $h = 5\text{ m}$): $P_1 = P_0 + \rho g h = 10^5 + (10^3)(10)(5) = 1.5\times 10^5\text{ Pa}$ and $T_1 = 17 + 273 = 290\text{ K}$, with $V_1 = 2.9\text{ cm}^3$.
  2. Step 2 — Apply the combined ideal gas law: Since the amount of air in the bubble is constant, $\frac{P_1 V_1}{T_1} = \frac{P_2 V_2}{T_2}$.
  3. Step 3 — Solve for the surface volume: $V_2 = V_1 \left(\frac{P_1}{P_2}\right)\left(\frac{T_2}{T_1}\right) = 2.9 \times \left(\frac{1.5\times 10^5}{10^5}\right) \times \left(\frac{300}{290}\right) = 2.9 \times 1.5 \times \frac{30}{29} = 4.5\text{ cm}^3$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: This matches option d ($4.5$ cm$^3$).
Q80.trapHtml: Always convert Celsius to Kelvin (290 K and 300 K); notice how $2.9/290=0.01$ cancels cleanly.

Q81.questionRecapHtml:
In capillary rise $h= \frac{2Tcos\theta}{r\rho g}$, $r,\rho ,T$ each decrease by $1%$; find $%\Delta h$.
$\Delta h \Delta T \Delta r \Delta \rho$
Q81.conceptHtml: Use small-change differentiation (keeping signs):$_h =_T -_r -_{\rho}$.
Q81.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Write the capillary rise formula: The height of liquid in a vertical capillary tube is $h = \frac{2T\cos\theta}{\rho g r}$, where $T$ is surface tension, $\rho$ is density, and $r$ is the inner radius.
  2. Step 2 — Apply small-percentage change (differential) approximation: Taking logarithms and differentiating gives $\frac{\Delta h}{h} = \frac{\Delta T}{T} - \frac{\Delta \rho}{\rho} - \frac{\Delta r}{r}$.
  3. Step 3 — Substitute the given percentage changes: Each of $T$, $\rho$, and $r$ decreases by $1\%$, so $\frac{\Delta T}{T} = \frac{\Delta \rho}{\rho} = \frac{\Delta r}{r} = -1\%$. Hence $\frac{\Delta h}{h} = (-1\%) - (-1\%) - (-1\%) = +1\%$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The height changes by $+1\%$, which is option b.
Q81.stepsLatex:
$h= \frac{2Tcos\theta}{r\rho g}$
$\frac{\Delta h}{h} = \frac{\Delta T}{T} - \frac{\Delta r}{r} - \frac{\Delta \rho}{\rho} =(-1%)-(-1%)-(-1%)=+1%$
Q81.trapHtml: Do not confuse maximum error (all positive) with directional percentage change (preserve minus signs!).

Q82.questionRecapHtml: Evaluate two conceptual statements on hydrostatic pressure and origin of surface tension.
Q82.conceptHtml: Fluid pressure is a scalar field existing at every point inside a static fluid; surface tension arises from excess surface potential energy.
Q82.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement I: Hydrostatic pressure exists at every point inside a static fluid and acts equally in all directions (Pascal's law), not merely at solid boundaries. Therefore, Statement I is false.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement II: Molecules at the free surface of a liquid experience a net inward cohesive pull compared to bulk molecules, giving them excess potential energy per unit area. This excess surface energy is directly responsible for surface tension. Therefore, Statement II is true.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the final answer: Statement I is false and Statement II is true, which matches option a.
Q82.stepsLatex: Statement I: False. Static fluid pressure $P =P_0+\rho gh$ acts at every interior point in all directions. Statement II: True. Surface molecules experience net inward cohesive pull, hence carry excess potential energy.
Q82.trapHtml: Pressure is defined everywhere inside a fluid continuum, not merely at solid boundaries.

Q83.questionRecapHtml: Capillary tubes with $r_1>r_2$; compare heights $h_1,h_2$ and surface tensions $T_1,T_2$.
Q83.conceptHtml: Jurin’s law gives $h= \frac{2Tcos\theta}{r\rho g} \propto \frac{1}{r}$, while surface tension $T$ is an intrinsic property independent of tube radius.
Q83.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Compare surface tensions T1 and T2: Surface tension is an intrinsic property of a liquid at a given temperature and does not depend on the radius of the capillary tube. For the same liquid-glass pair, $T_1 = T_2$.
  2. Step 2 — Compare capillary rise heights h1 and h2: From Jurin's law, $h = \frac{2T\cos\theta}{\rho g r}$. Since $T$, $\theta$, $\rho$, and $g$ are identical, $h \propto \frac{1}{r}$.
  3. Step 3 — Apply the given radius inequality: Because $r_1 > r_2$, the narrower tube produces a higher rise, giving $h_1 < h_2$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Thus $h_1 < h_2$ and $T_1 = T_2$, which is option b.
Q83.stepsLatex:
$T_1=T_2($independent of tube radius $r)$
$h\propto \frac{1}{r}$ and $r_1>r_2 \implies h_1 \lt h_2$
Q83.trapHtml: Wider tube ($r_1>r_2$) always produces a smaller capillary rise ($h_1 \lt h_2$).

Q84.questionRecapHtml:
Horizontal venturimeter ($A_A=6$ c$m^2,A_B=3$ c$m^2,\Delta h=5$ cm); find flow rate $Q$.
$\sqrt{2gh}$
Q84.conceptHtml: Venturimeter discharge formula: $Q=A_1A_2_{A2-A2}$. $1 2$
Q84.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Write the Venturimeter flow-rate formula: For a horizontal tube with cross-sectional areas $A_1$ and $A_2$ and pressure-head difference $\Delta h$, combining Bernoulli's theorem and continuity gives the volume flow rate $Q = A_1 A_2 \sqrt{\frac{2g\Delta h}{A_1^2 - A_2^2}}$.
  2. Step 2 — Substitute the given values in CGS units: Here $A_1 = 6\text{ cm}^2$, $A_2 = 3\text{ cm}^2$, $\Delta h = 5\text{ cm}$, and $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2 = 1000\text{ cm/s}^2$.
  3. Step 3 — Compute the volume flow rate: $Q = (6)(3)\sqrt{\frac{2 \times 1000 \times 5}{6^2 - 3^2}} = 18\sqrt{\frac{10000}{27}} = 18 \times \frac{100}{3\sqrt{3}} = \frac{600}{\sqrt{3}} = 200\sqrt{3}\text{ cm}^3/\text{s}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: This corresponds to option d ($200\sqrt{3}$ cm$^3$/s).
Q84.trapHtml: Keep $g=1000$ cm/$s^2$ when areas are in c$m^2$ and $h$ is in cm.

Q85.subtopic: Work Done in Expanding Soap Bubble
Q85.questionRecapHtml: Soap bubble radius grows from 1 cm to 2 cm ($T=3.5\times 10^{-2}$); find $\alpha$ in $W=\alpha \times 10^{-6}$ J.
Q85.conceptHtml: For a soap bubble (two surfaces), $W =8\pi T(r_2^2-r_1^2)$.
Q85.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the work done to expand a soap bubble: Since a soap bubble has two free surfaces, $W = 8\pi T(r_2^2 - r_1^2)$.
  2. Step 2 — Convert the given parameters to SI units: $T = 3.5\times 10^{-2}\text{ N/m}$, $r_1 = 1\text{ cm} = 10^{-2}\text{ m}$, $r_2 = 2\text{ cm} = 2\times 10^{-2}\text{ m}$, and $\pi = \frac{22}{7}$.
  3. Step 3 — Evaluate the work done: $W = 8 \times \frac{22}{7} \times (3.5\times 10^{-2}) \times (4 - 1)\times 10^{-4} = 8 \times 22 \times 0.5\times 10^{-2} \times 3\times 10^{-4} = 264\times 10^{-6}\text{ J}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Comparing with $\alpha \times 10^{-6}\text{ J}$, we obtain $\alpha =$ 264.
Q85.trapHtml: Use $8\pi T$ (not $4\pi T$) because a soap bubble has both inner and outer surfaces.

Q86.questionRecapHtml: Coin placed on floating 10 cm cube increases immersion by 3.87 cm; find coin mass in grams.
Q86.conceptHtml: Added weight equals extra buoyant force: $m_{coin}g=\rho _w(A\Delta h)g$.
Q86.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Check that the cube remains floating: The wooden cube has side $a = 10\text{ cm}$ and density $0.4\text{ g/cm}^3$, so initially it is submerged to $0.4 \times 10 = 4\text{ cm}$. With an extra immersion of $\Delta h = 3.87\text{ cm}$, total depth is $7.87\text{ cm} < 10\text{ cm}$, so it stays afloat.
  2. Step 2 — Equate the coin's weight to the extra buoyant force: By Archimedes' principle, the weight of the metal coin equals the weight of the additional water displaced: $m_{\text{coin}} g = \rho_{\text{water}} (A \cdot \Delta h) g$.
  3. Step 3 — Compute the mass of the coin: With base area $A = 10 \times 10 = 100\text{ cm}^2$, $\rho_{\text{water}} = 1\text{ g/cm}^3$, and $\Delta h = 3.87\text{ cm}$, we get $m_{\text{coin}} = 1 \times 100 \times 3.87 = 387\text{ g}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The mass of the metal coin is 387 gram.
Q86.stepsLatex: $m =\rho _wA\Delta h=(1$ g/c$m^3)(10\times 10$ c$m^2)(3.87$ cm$)=387$ g coin
Q86.trapHtml: Wood density (0.4 g/c$m^3$) is extra information (only confirms the cube does not sink since $4+3.87=7.87<10$ cm).

Q87.subtopic: Work Done in Blowing Soap Bubble
Q87.questionRecapHtml: Soap bubble diameter expands 7 cm $\to 14$ cm ($T=0.04$); find $x$ if $W=(15000-x)\mu$J.
Q87.conceptHtml: Convert diameters to radii ($r_1=3.5$ cm$,r_2=7$ cm) and compute $W =8\pi T(r_2^2-r_1^2)$.
Q87.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the radii and surface tension: Initial diameter is $7\text{ cm} \implies r_1 = 3.5\text{ cm} = 0.035\text{ m}$. Final diameter is $14\text{ cm} \implies r_2 = 7\text{ cm} = 0.07\text{ m}$. Surface tension $T = 0.04\text{ N/m}$ and $\pi = \frac{22}{7}$.
  2. Step 2 — Compute the work done to blow the soap bubble further: For a soap bubble (two surfaces), $W = 8\pi T(r_2^2 - r_1^2) = 8 \times \frac{22}{7} \times 0.04 \times (7^2 - 3.5^2)\times 10^{-4} = 8 \times \frac{22}{7} \times 0.04 \times 36.75\times 10^{-4}$.
  3. Step 3 — Simplify and convert to microjoules: Since $\frac{36.75}{7} = 5.25$, we get $W = 176 \times 0.04 \times 5.25\times 10^{-4} = 36.96\times 10^{-4}\text{ J} = 3696\text{ }\mu\text{J}$.
  4. Step 4 — Solve for x and confirm the final answer: Setting $15000 - x = 3696$ gives $x = 15000 - 3696 =$ 11304.
Q87.trapHtml: Halve diameters to radii first, and remember to subtract $W$ from 15000 to find $x$.

Q88.questionRecapHtml: 64 drops falling at 10 cm/s coalesce; find new terminal speed in cm/s.
Q88.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Find the radius of the bigger drop: By volume conservation for 64 drops of radius $r$ forming one drop of radius $R$, $\frac{4}{3}\pi R^3 = 64 \times \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3 \implies R = 64^{1/3}r = 4r$.
  2. Step 2 — Relate terminal velocity to radius: From Stokes' law, terminal velocity scales as $v_T \propto r^2$ when fluid and drop properties remain unchanged.
  3. Step 3 — Calculate the new terminal velocity: $v_2 = v_1 \left(\frac{R}{r}\right)^2 = 10 \times 4^2 = 10 \times 16 = 160\text{ cm/s}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The terminal velocity of the bigger drop is 160 cm/s.
Q88.trapHtml: The initial radius 1 mm is unused because the scaling depends solely on $n=64$.

Q89.questionRecapHtml: Same-material ball radius halved (6 mm $\to 3$ mm); find new terminal velocity.
Q89.conceptHtml: For identical material and fluid, $v_t\propto r^2$.
Q89.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Relate terminal velocity to ball radius: For metallic balls of the same material falling in the same viscous fluid, Stokes' law gives $v_T = \frac{2r^2(\rho - \sigma)g}{9\eta}$, so $v_T \propto r^2$.
  2. Step 2 — Set up the ratio for the two balls: Given $r_1 = 6\text{ mm}$, $v_1 = 20\text{ cm/s}$, and $r_2 = 3\text{ mm}$, we have $\frac{v_2}{v_1} = \left(\frac{r_2}{r_1}\right)^2$.
  3. Step 3 — Compute the terminal velocity of the smaller ball: $v_2 = 20 \times \left(\frac{3}{6}\right)^2 = 20 \times \frac{1}{4} = 5\text{ cm/s}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The terminal velocity of the second ball is 5 cm/s.
Q89.trapHtml: Halving radius quarters the terminal velocity ($1/4$), not halves it.

trapCards.title: 1. One vs Two Surfaces (Drop vs Soap Bubble)
trapCards.html: • Soap Bubble Factor of 2: A soap bubble in air has TWO free surfaces ($\Delta P = 4T/R$, $W = 8\pi r^2 T$), whereas a drop or air bubble in liquid has ONE ($\Delta P = 2T/R$, $W = 4\pi r^2 T$).

trapCards.title: 2. Stokes' Law & Terminal Velocity Traps
trapCards.html: • Air Bubble Rising in Water: Since $\rho_{\text{air}} < \sigma_{\text{water}}$, net upward buoyancy drives it up ($v_T$ upward); $v_T \propto r^2$.

trapCards.title: 3. Bernoulli Geometry & Wing Count
trapCards.html: • Airplane Wings: Lift $= \frac{1}{2}\rho(v_{\text{top}}^2 - v_{\text{bot}}^2)A_{\text{total}}$; check if area $A$ is per wing (multiply by 2) or total!

trapCards.title: 4. Buoyancy, Capillarity & Ice Melting
trapCards.html: • Floating Ice Melting: Pure ice in pure water: level UNCHANGED; ice in denser liquid (saltwater): level RISES; ice with embedded denser stone: level FALLS.

subject: Physics
title: Thermal Properties of Matter
constantsHtml: • Water / Ice Constants: $c_{\text{water}} = 1\text{ cal/g}\cdot^\circ\text{C} = 4200\text{ J/kg}\cdot\text{K}$; $c_{\text{ice}} = 0.5\text{ cal/g}\cdot^\circ\text{C}$; $L_f = 80\text{ cal/g}$; $L_v = 540\text{ cal/g}$; $1\text{ cal} = 4.186\text{ J}$.

formulaCards.title: 1. Thermometry & Temperature Scales
formulaCards.html:
• Linear Scale Conversion: $\dfrac{X - X_{\text{LFP}}}{X_{\text{UFP}} - X_{\text{LFP}}} = \dfrac{C - 0}{100} = \dfrac{F - 32}{180} = \dfrac{K - 273.15}{100}$.
  • Temperature Intervals: $\Delta C = \Delta K = \dfrac{5}{9}\Delta F$ (for changes, do NOT add $273.15$ or $32$!).

formulaCards.title: 2. Thermal Expansion of Solids & Liquids
formulaCards.html:
• Linear, Areal & Volume Expansion: $\Delta L = L_0\alpha\Delta T$, $\Delta A = A_0\beta\Delta T$, $\Delta V = V_0\gamma\Delta T$; for isotropic solids $\alpha: \beta: \gamma = 1: 2: 3$.
  • Apparent Liquid Expansion: $\gamma_{\text{app}} = \gamma_{\text{liquid}} - \gamma_{\text{vessel}}$ ($\gamma_{\text{vessel}} = 3\alpha$).
  • Pendulum Clock Error: $\dfrac{\Delta T}{T} = \dfrac{1}{2}\alpha\Delta\theta$; seconds lost/gained per day $= \frac{1}{2}\alpha\Delta\theta \times 86400\text{ s}$.

formulaCards.title: 3. Calorimetry & Phase Transitions
formulaCards.html:
• Sensible & Latent Heat: $Q_{\text{sensible}} = mc\Delta T = C\Delta T$, $Q_{\text{latent}} = mL$; Water equivalent $W = ms$.
  • Principle of Calorimetry: Heat Lost $=$ Heat Gained (check phase boundaries at $0^\circ\text{C}$ and $100^\circ\text{C}$ first!).

formulaCards.title: 4. Heat Conduction & Thermal Circuits
formulaCards.html:
• Fourier's Law & Thermal Resistance: $H = \dfrac{dQ}{dt} = \dfrac{kA(T_1 - T_2)}{L} = \dfrac{\Delta T}{R_{\text{th}}}$, where $R_{\text{th}} = \dfrac{L}{kA}$.
  • Series & Parallel Rods: Series ($R_{\text{eq}} = R_1 + R_2$, same $H$): $k_{\text{eq}} = \dfrac{L_1 + L_2}{L_1/k_1 + L_2/k_2}$. Parallel ($1/R_{\text{eq}} = 1/R_1 + 1/R_2$, same $\Delta T$): $k_{\text{eq}} = \dfrac{k_1 A_1 + k_2 A_2}{A_1 + A_2}$.

formulaCards.title: 5. Thermal Radiation, Stefan's & Wien's Laws
formulaCards.html:
• Stefan–Boltzmann Law ($T$ strictly in K!): $P = \dfrac{dQ}{dt} = e\sigma A T^4$; Net emission $P_{\text{net}} = e\sigma A(T^4 - T_0^4)$.
  • Wien's Displacement Law: $\lambda_m T = b = 2.898 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m}\cdot\text{K}$.

formulaCards.title: 6. Newton's Law of Cooling
formulaCards.html:
• Average Form (JEE Main Favorite): $\dfrac{T_1 - T_2}{t} = K\left(\dfrac{T_1 + T_2}{2} - T_0\right)$ (valid when $T - T_0$ is small).
  • Exact Exponential Form: $\dfrac{dT}{dt} = -K(T - T_0) \implies \dfrac{T_2 - T_0}{T_1 - T_0} = e^{-Kt}$, where $K = \dfrac{4e\sigma A T_0^3}{mc}$.

Q01.questionRecapHtml: Calculate temperature rise of water falling from $h=200$ m with zero heat loss.
Q01.conceptHtml: Gravitational potential energy converts completely into thermal energy of water: $mgh=mc\Delta T$.
Q01.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the energy conversion: When water falls from a height $h = 200\text{ m}$ with no heat dissipation, its entire gravitational potential energy converts into thermal energy: $mgh = mc\Delta T$.
  2. Step 2 — Simplify the formula: Canceling mass $m$ from both sides gives the rise in temperature as $\Delta T = \frac{gh}{c}$.
  3. Step 3 — Substitute the given values: Using $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$, $h = 200\text{ m}$, and $c = 4200\text{ J/(kg}\cdot\text{K)}$, we get $\Delta T = \frac{10 \times 200}{4200} = \frac{2000}{4200} = \frac{10}{21}\text{ K} \approx 0.476\text{ K}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Rounding to two decimal places gives $0.48\text{ K}$, which matches option (c).
Q01.stepsLatex:
Step 1: Equate potential energy loss to thermal energy gain:
$mgh=mc\Delta T \implies \Delta T = \frac{gh}{c}$ .
Step 2: Substitute $g=10$ m/$s^2$, $h=200$ m, $c=4200$ J/(kg $\cdot$ K):
$\Delta T = \frac{10\times 200}{4200} = \frac{20}{42} = \frac{10}{21} \approx 0.476$ K $\approx 0.48$ K.
Q01.trapHtml: Mass $m$ cancels out! Memorize the quick benchmark: a 420 m waterfall raises water temperature by 1 K, so 200 m gives $\approx 0.48$ K.

Q02.questionRecapHtml: Find change in area of a 9 cm $\times 4$ cm sheet ($m=0.1$ kg) when 810 J heat is supplied.
Q02.conceptHtml: Combine $Q=mC_v\Delta T$ with areal expansion $\Delta A=A\beta \Delta T =2A\alpha \Delta T$.
Q02.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Find the temperature rise: Using $Q = mC\Delta T$ with $Q = 8.1 \times 10^2\text{ J}$, $m = 0.1\text{ kg}$, and $C = 900\text{ J kg}^{-1}\text{ K}^{-1}$, we get $\Delta T = \frac{810}{0.1 \times 900} = \frac{810}{90} = 9\text{ K}$.
  2. Step 2 — Calculate initial area and areal expansion coefficient: The initial area is $A = l \times d = 9\text{ cm} \times 4\text{ cm} = 36\text{ cm}^2 = 36 \times 10^{-4}\text{ m}^2$. For an isotropic solid, the coefficient of areal expansion is $\beta = 2\alpha = 2 \times 3.1 \times 10^{-5} = 6.2 \times 10^{-5}\text{ K}^{-1}$.
  3. Step 3 — Compute the change in area: Using $\Delta A = A\beta\Delta T$, we obtain $\Delta A = (36 \times 10^{-4})(6.2 \times 10^{-5})(9) = 2008.8 \times 10^{-9}\text{ m}^2 \approx 2.0 \times 10^{-6}\text{ m}^2$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The change in area is $2.0 \times 10^{-6}\text{ m}^2$, which corresponds to option (a).

Step 1: Find temperature rise $\Delta T$:
$\Delta T = \frac{Q}{mC_v} = \frac{8.1\times 10^2}{0.1\times 900} = \frac{810}{90} =9$ K.
Step 2: Initial area $A=9$ cm $\times 4$ cm $=36$ c$m^2=36\times 10^{-4} m^2$, and $\beta =2\alpha =6.2\times 10^{-5} K^{-1}$. Step 3: Change in area:
$\Delta A=A\beta \Delta T =(36\times 10^{-4})(6.2\times 10^{-5})(9)=2008.8\times 10^{-9} m^2\approx 2.0\times 10^{-6} m^2.$
Q02.trapHtml: Do not forget the factor of 2 in $\beta =2\alpha$ and convert c$m^2\to 10^{-4} m^2$ before multiplying!

Q03.questionRecapHtml:
Match Heat capacity, Specific heat capacity, Latent heat, and Thermal conductivity with their SI units.
$QL$
Q03.conceptHtml: Derive SI units directly from defining formulas: $C=Q/\Delta T$, $c=Q/(m\Delta T)$, $L=Q/m$, and $k=_{At\Delta T}$.
Q03.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Match heat capacity and specific heat capacity: Heat capacity is defined as $C = \frac{\Delta Q}{\Delta T}$, so its SI unit is $\text{J K}^{-1}$, giving (A)-(II). Specific heat capacity is $c = \frac{\Delta Q}{m\Delta T}$, so its SI unit is $\text{J kg}^{-1}\text{ K}^{-1}$, giving (B)-(III).
  2. Step 2 — Match latent heat: Latent heat is heat required per unit mass for a phase change, $L = \frac{\Delta Q}{m}$, whose SI unit is $\text{J kg}^{-1}$, giving (C)-(I).
  3. Step 3 — Match thermal conductivity: From Fourier’s law $\frac{\Delta Q}{\Delta t} = \frac{K A \Delta T}{L}$, we have $K = \frac{\Delta Q \cdot L}{A \Delta T \Delta t}$, which has the SI unit $\text{J m}^{-1}\text{ K}^{-1}\text{ s}^{-1}$, giving (D)-(IV).
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The complete matching is (A)-(II), (B)-(III), (C)-(I), (D)-(IV), which is option (d).

Step 1: Match each quantity to its SI unit:
• (A) Heat capacity: $C= \frac{Q}{\Delta T} \implies$ J $K^{-1}$ (II).
• (B) Specific heat capacity: $c= \frac{Q}{m\Delta T} \implies$ J k$g^{-1} K^{-1}$ (III).
• (C) Latent heat: $L= \frac{Q}{m} \implies$ J k$g^{-1}$ (I).
• (D) Thermal conductivity: $k= \frac{QL}{At\Delta T} \implies$ J $m^{-1} K^{-1} s^{-1}$ (IV).
Step 2: Combining gives (A)-(II), (B)-(III), (C)-(I), (D)-(IV).
Q03.trapHtml: Only Option (D) pairs (A) with (II) — one check solves this question in under 10 seconds!

Q04.questionRecapHtml:
Identify the ideal thermal and electrical conductivity for harvesting heat into electricity via $\Delta T$.
$S^2\sigma T$
Q04.conceptHtml: A thermoelectric generator’s efficiency depends on the dimensionless figure of merit $ZT =$. $k$
Q04.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Understand thermoelectric energy harvesting: Converting a temperature difference into electrical energy (the Seebeck effect) requires maintaining a steady temperature gradient across the material while extracting electric current efficiently.
  2. Step 2 — Requirement on thermal conductivity: The material must have low thermal conductivity ($\kappa$) so that heat does not rapidly conduct from the hot end to the cold end, which would otherwise destroy the temperature difference.
  3. Step 3 — Requirement on electrical conductivity: The material must have high electrical conductivity ($\sigma$) so that the generated electric current flows with minimal internal resistance and Joule heating loss ($I^2 R$). This maximizes the thermoelectric figure of merit $ZT = \frac{S^2 \sigma T}{\kappa}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Hence, the material should have low thermal conductivity and high electrical conductivity, matching option (a).
Q04.stepsLatex: Step 1: To sustain the temperature difference $\Delta T$ across the material (so heat does not short-circuit across without doing work), the material needs low thermal conductivity ($k$). Step 2: To allow the generated electric current to flow with minimal $I^2R$ Joule heating loss, the material needs high electrical conductivity ($\sigma$).
Q04.trapHtml: Remember the golden rule of thermoelectrics (“phonon-glass, electron-crystal”): low $k$, high $\sigma$.

Q05.questionRecapHtml:
Coffee cools $90^{^\circ}$C $\to 80^{^\circ}$C in $t$ min at $20^{^\circ}$C room temp; find time from $80^{^\circ}$C $\to 60^{^\circ}$C.
$T_1-T_2 (T_1+T_2)$
Q05.conceptHtml: Use the average form of Newton’s Law of Cooling: $=K -T_0$. $t 2$
Q05.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — State Newton’s law of cooling (average form): For a body cooling from $T_1$ to $T_2$ in time $\Delta t$ with surrounding temperature $T_0 = 20^\circ\text{C}$, we use $\frac{T_1 - T_2}{\Delta t} = K\left(\frac{T_1 + T_2}{2} - T_0\right)$.
  2. Step 2 — Apply to the first cooling interval ($90^\circ\text{C} \to 80^\circ\text{C}$): Substituting $T_1 = 90^\circ\text{C}$, $T_2 = 80^\circ\text{C}$, and $\Delta t = t$ gives $\frac{90 - 80}{t} = K\left(\frac{90 + 80}{2} - 20\right) \implies \frac{10}{t} = 65K$.
  3. Step 3 — Apply to the second cooling interval ($80^\circ\text{C} \to 60^\circ\text{C}$): Let the required time be $t^\prime$. Then $\frac{80 - 60}{t^\prime} = K\left(\frac{80 + 60}{2} - 20\right) \implies \frac{20}{t^\prime} = 50K$.
  4. Step 4 — Divide the two equations to find $t^\prime$: Dividing the first equation by the second yields $\frac{10/t}{20/t^\prime} = \frac{65K}{50K} \implies \frac{t^\prime}{2t} = \frac{13}{10} \implies t^\prime = \frac{13}{5}t$, which matches option (a).

$( ) \frac{90-80}{t} =K \frac{90+80}{2} -20 \implies \frac{10}{t} =65K.$ (1)
Step 2: Second interval ($80^{^\circ}$C $\to 60^{^\circ}$C in time $t^'$):
$( ) \frac{80-60}{t'} =K \frac{80+60}{2} -20 \implies \frac{20}{t'} =50K.$ (2)
Step 3: Divide (1) by (2): $\frac{10/t}{20/t'} = \frac{65}{50} \implies \frac{t^'}{2t} = \frac{13}{10} \implies t^'= \frac{13}{5} t.$
Q05.trapHtml: Sanity check: cooling slows down as the body approaches room temperature, so dropping $20^{^\circ}$C from $80^{^\circ}$C MUST take $>2t$; only $\frac{13}{5} t=2.6t$ satisfies $t^'>2t$!

Q06.questionRecapHtml: Body cools $40^{^\circ}$C $\to 24^{^\circ}$C in 4 min ($T_0=16^{^\circ}$C); find temperature after next 4 min.
Q06.conceptHtml: Apply Newton’s Law of Cooling for two consecutive equal time intervals ($t=4$ min).
Q06.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Write Newton’s law of cooling in average form: With surrounding air temperature $T_0 = 16^\circ\text{C}$, the cooling relation is $\frac{T_1 - T_2}{\Delta t} = K\left(\frac{T_1 + T_2}{2} - T_0\right)$.
  2. Step 2 — Find the cooling constant $K$ from the first 4 minutes: As the body cools from $40^\circ\text{C}$ to $24^\circ\text{C}$ in $4\text{ min}$, we have $\frac{40 - 24}{4} = K\left(\frac{40 + 24}{2} - 16\right) \implies 4 = K(32 - 16) = 16K \implies K = \frac{1}{4}\text{ min}^{-1}$.
  3. Step 3 — Set up the equation for the next 4 minutes: Let the temperature after the next $4\text{ min}$ be $T$. Then $\frac{24 - T}{4} = \frac{1}{4}\left(\frac{24 + T}{2} - 16\right)$.
  4. Step 4 — Solve for $T$ and confirm the answer: Multiplying both sides by $4$ gives $24 - T = 12 + \frac{T}{2} - 16 = \frac{T}{2} - 4 \implies 28 = \frac{3T}{2} \implies T = \frac{56}{3}^\circ\text{C}$, which corresponds to option (b).

Q07.questionRecapHtml: Identify the straight-line graph of Celsius ($C$, vertical) vs. Fahrenheit ($F$, horizontal).
Q07.conceptHtml: Rewrite the scale conversion in slope-intercept form $y=mx+c$ with $y=C$ and $x=F$.
Q07.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the Celsius–Fahrenheit conversion formula: The two temperature scales are linearly related by $T_F = \frac{9}{5}T_C + 32$, or equivalently $T_C = \frac{5}{9}T_F - \frac{160}{9}$.
  2. Step 2 — Identify the slope of the graph: Since both $\frac{9}{5}$ and $\frac{5}{9}$ are positive constants, the graph between $T_C$ and $T_F$ must be a straight line with a positive slope (rising from left to right).
  3. Step 3 — Check the axis intercepts: At $T_C = 0^\circ\text{C}$, we get $T_F = +32^\circ\text{F}$ (a positive intercept on the Fahrenheit axis). At $T_F = 0^\circ\text{F}$, we get $T_C = -\frac{160}{9}^\circ\text{C} \approx -17.8^\circ\text{C}$ (a negative intercept on the Celsius axis).
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The only straight-line plot showing a positive slope with a negative Celsius intercept and positive Fahrenheit intercept is option (d).
Q07.stepsLatex:
Step 1: Express $C$ as a linear function of $F$:
$\frac{C}{100} = \frac{F-32}{180} \implies C= \frac{5}{9} F- \frac{160}{9}$ .
Step 2: Check graph features:
• Slope $m=+ \frac{5}{9} >0$ (line rises left to right) $\implies$ eliminates (B) and (C).
• $C$-intercept (at $F =0$) is $- \frac{160}{9} <0$, and $F$-intercept (at $C=0$) is $+32>0 \implies$ eliminates (A), which passes through (0,0).
Only graph (D) has positive slope, negative $C$-intercept, and positive $F$-intercept.
Q07.trapHtml: Always check which axis is $C$ and which is $F$! If $F$ were on the vertical axis, the intercept would be $+32$ (positive).

Q08.questionRecapHtml: Find mass of a lead bullet heated from 300 K to 600 K and melted using 625 J.
Q08.conceptHtml: Total heat equals sensible heat to reach melting point plus latent heat of fusion: $Q=m(c\Delta T+L_f)$.
Q08.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Break down the total heat required: To heat the lead bullet from $T_i = 300\text{ K}$ to its melting point $T_m = 600\text{ K}$ ($\Delta T = 300\text{ K}$) and then melt it completely, the total heat is $Q = mc\Delta T + mL_f = m(c\Delta T + L_f)$.
  2. Step 2 — Compute the heat required per kilogram: Substituting $c = 125\text{ J kg}^{-1}\text{ K}^{-1}$, $\Delta T = 300\text{ K}$, and $L_f = 2.5 \times 10^4\text{ J kg}^{-1}$ gives $c\Delta T + L_f = (125 \times 300) + 25000 = 37500 + 25000 = 62500\text{ J/kg}$.
  3. Step 3 — Solve for the mass $m$: Given $Q = 625\text{ J}$, we obtain $m = \frac{625}{62500} = 0.01\text{ kg} = 10\text{ g}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The mass of the lead bullet is $10\text{ g}$, which matches option (d).
Q08.stepsLatex:
Step 1: Temperature rise $\Delta T =600-300=300$ K. Step 2: Apply $Q=m(c\Delta T+L_f)$: $625=m(125\times 300+2.5\times 10^4)=m(37500+25000)=62500m.$
Step 3: Solve for $m$ in grams: $m= \frac{625}{62500} =0.01$ kg $=10$ g.
Q08.trapHtml: Always factor out $m$ first: $c\Delta T+L_f =62500$ J/kg divides 625 J cleanly to $10^{-2}$ kg $=10$ g.

Q09.questionRecapHtml: Compare radiated energy from two spheres of radii 0.2 m,0.8 m at 800 K,400 K.
Q09.conceptHtml: For spheres of the same material (same $e$) with negligible surrounding effect, $E\propto AT^4\propto r^2T^4$.
Q09.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Apply the Stefan–Boltzmann law: Neglecting surrounding temperature, the thermal energy radiated per unit time by a sphere of radius $R$ and absolute temperature $T$ is $E = e\sigma A T^4 = e\sigma (4\pi R^2) T^4$.
  2. Step 2 — Form the ratio for identical materials: Since both spheres are made of the same material, emissivity $e$ is identical, so $E \propto R^2 T^4$. Thus, $\frac{E_2}{E_1} = \left(\frac{R_2}{R_1}\right)^2 \left(\frac{T_2}{T_1}\right)^4$.
  3. Step 3 — Substitute the given radii and temperatures: With $R_1 = 0.2\text{ m}$, $T_1 = 800\text{ K}$ and $R_2 = 0.8\text{ m}$, $T_2 = 400\text{ K}$, we get $\frac{E_2}{E} = \left(\frac{0.8}{0.2}\right)^2 \left(\frac{400}{800}\right)^4 = 4^2 \times \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^4 = 16 \times \frac{1}{16} = 1$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Therefore, $E_2 = E$, which corresponds to option (c).

$( )4 \frac{E}{E} ^{big} =(4)^2 \frac{1}{2} =16\times \frac{1}{16} =1 \implies E =E.$ big

Q10.questionRecapHtml: Compute total heat/work needed to convert $10^{-3}$ kg ice at $-10^{^\circ}$C to steam at $110^{^\circ}$C.
Q10.conceptHtml: Sum all 5 sequential energy stages: warm ice $\to$ melt ice $\to$ warm water $\to$ boil water $\to$ warm steam.
Q10.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — List the five heating and phase-change stages: For $m = 10^{-3}\text{ kg}$ going from ice at $-10^\circ\text{C}$ to steam at $110^\circ\text{C}$, the total heat (equivalent work) is $Q = Q_1 + Q_2 + Q_3 + Q_4 + Q_5$.
  2. Step 2 — Calculate heat for warming and melting ice: Warming ice ($-10^\circ\text{C} \to 0^\circ\text{C}$): $Q_1 = 10^{-3} \times 2100 \times 10 = 21\text{ J}$. Melting ice at $0^\circ\text{C}$: $Q_2 = 10^{-3} \times 3.35 \times 10^5 = 335\text{ J}$.
  3. Step 3 — Calculate heat for warming water, boiling, and warming steam: Warming water ($0^\circ\text{C} \to 100^\circ\text{C}$): $Q_3 = 10^{-3} \times 4180 \times 100 = 418\text{ J}$. Vaporizing water at $100^\circ\text{C}$: $Q_4 = 10^{-3} \times 2.25 \times 10^6 = 2250\text{ J}$. Warming steam ($100^\circ\text{C} \to 110^\circ\text{C}$): $Q_5 = 10^{-3} \times 1920 \times 10 = 19.2\text{ J}$.
  4. Step 4 — Sum all stages and confirm the answer: Adding all contributions gives $Q = 21 + 335 + 418 + 2250 + 19.2 = 3043.2\text{ J} \approx 3043\text{ J}$, which matches option (b).

Q11.questionRecapHtml:
Find platinum wire resistance at $400^{^\circ}$C given $R_0=8\Omega$ and $R_{100}=10\Omega$.
$R -R$
Q11.conceptHtml: Resistance varies linearly with temperature: $T = \frac{T 0}{R100-R0} \times 100^{^\circ}$C.
Q11.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Use the linear resistance thermometer relation: Temperature on a platinum resistance thermometer is given by $T = \frac{R_T - R_0}{R_{100} - R_0} \times 100^\circ\text{C}$, where $R_0 = 8\ \Omega$ (ice point) and $R_{100} = 10\ \Omega$ (steam point).
  2. Step 2 — Substitute the bath temperature: For $T = 400^\circ\text{C}$, we write $400 = \frac{R_T - 8}{10 - 8} \times 100$.
  3. Step 3 — Solve for $R_T$: Simplifying gives $4 = \frac{R_T - 8}{2} \implies R_T - 8 = 8 \implies R_T = 16\ \Omega$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The resistance of the platinum wire at $400^\circ\text{C}$ is $16\ \Omega$, which matches option (b).

Q12.questionRecapHtml:
Convert a temperature increase of $40^{^\circ}$C to the Fahrenheit scale.
9
Q12.conceptHtml: For temperature differences (not absolute readings), the $+32$ offset drops out: $\Delta T_F = \Delta T_C$. 5
Q12.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Relate temperature intervals on Celsius and Fahrenheit scales: Between the ice point and steam point, there are $100$ divisions on the Celsius scale and $180$ divisions on the Fahrenheit scale, so $\frac{\Delta T_C}{100} = \frac{\Delta T_F}{180}$.
  2. Step 2 — Rearrange for $\Delta T_F$: Simplifying the fraction gives $\Delta T_F = \frac{180}{100}\Delta T_C = \frac{9}{5}\Delta T_C$. Note that the $+32$ offset cancels out for a temperature change.
  3. Step 3 — Substitute $\Delta T_C = 40^\circ\text{C}$: We get $\Delta T_F = \frac{9}{5} \times 40 = 9 \times 8 = 72^\circ\text{F}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The increase in temperature on the Fahrenheit scale is $72^\circ\text{F}$, matching option (c).

Q13.subtopic: Calorimetry (Heating Curve: Ice to Steam at $100^{^\circ}$C)
Q13.questionRecapHtml: Select the qualitative $T$ vs. Heat curve for heating ice at $-10^{^\circ}$C to steam at $100^{^\circ}$C.
Q13.conceptHtml: Converting ice at $-10^{^\circ}$C to steam at $100^{^\circ}$C involves 4 stages and ends on the second horizontal plateau (no superheating above $100^{^\circ}$C).
Q13.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Trace the warming of ice ($-10^\circ\text{C} \to 0^\circ\text{C}$): As heat is supplied slowly, the temperature of solid ice rises linearly from $-10^\circ\text{C}$ to $0^\circ\text{C}$.
  2. Step 2 — Identify the first horizontal plateau at $0^\circ\text{C}$: At $0^\circ\text{C}$, the supplied heat goes into breaking the solid lattice (latent heat of fusion $L_f$), so the temperature remains constant until all ice melts into water.
  3. Step 3 — Trace the warming of liquid water and boiling at $100^\circ\text{C}$: After melting, water heats linearly from $0^\circ\text{C}$ to $100^\circ\text{C}$ (with a gentler slope than ice because $c_{\text{water}} > c_{\text{ice}}$). At $100^\circ\text{C}$, a second horizontal plateau occurs as water vaporizes into steam (longer than the melting plateau since $L_v \gg L_f$).
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The heating curve starting at $-10^\circ\text{C}$ with two flat phase-change plateaus at $0^\circ\text{C}$ and $100^\circ\text{C}$ is accurately represented by option (a).

At $0^{^\circ}$C: horizontal plateau (melting). 3. $0^{^\circ}$C $\to 100^{^\circ}$C: inclined rising segment (water heats up). 4. At $100^{^\circ}$C: horizontal plateau (boiling to steam at $100^{^\circ}$C; heating stops here).
Step 2: Only graph (A) shows inclined $\to$ flat $\to$ inclined $\to$ flat without vertical jumps or extra rising steam segments.

Q14.questionRecapHtml:
Convert $-95^{^\circ}$X to Fahrenheit given LF$P_X=-15^{^\circ}$X and UF$P_X=65^{^\circ}$X.
$X-$ LF$P_X F-32$
Q14.conceptHtml: Equate normalized scale readings: $=$. UF$P_X-$ LF$P_X 212-32$
Q14.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Set up the linear scale conversion equation: For any two linear temperature scales, $\frac{T_X - \text{LFP}_X}{\text{UFP}_X - \text{LFP}_X} = \frac{T_F - \text{LFP}_F}{\text{UFP}_F - \text{LFP}_F}$.
  2. Step 2 — Identify the fixed points: On scale X, $\text{LFP}_X = -15^\circ\text{X}$ and $\text{UFP}_X = 65^\circ\text{X}$ (span $= 80$). On the Fahrenheit scale, $\text{LFP}_F = 32^\circ\text{F}$ and $\text{UFP}_F = 212^\circ\text{F}$ (span $= 180$).
  3. Step 3 — Substitute $T_X = -95^\circ\text{X}$ and solve for $T_F$: $\frac{-95 - (-15)}{65 - (-15)} = \frac{T_F - 32}{180} \implies \frac{-80}{80} = \frac{T_F - 32}{180} \implies -1 = \frac{T_F - 32}{180}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Solving gives $T_F - 32 = -180 \implies T_F = -148^\circ\text{F}$, which corresponds to option (a).

$\frac{-95-(-15)}{65-(-15)} = \frac{F-32}{180} \implies \frac{-80}{80} = \frac{F-32}{180}$ .
Step 2: Solve for $F$: $-1= \frac{F-32}{180} \implies F =32-180=-148^{^\circ}$F.

Q15.questionRecapHtml: Determine final temperature and ice–water mass ratio when 184 kJ is given to 600 g ice at $-12^{^\circ}$C.
Q15.conceptHtml: Step through thermal thresholds: first warm ice to $0^{^\circ}$C, then check how much of the remaining heat melts ice at $0^{^\circ}$C.
Q15.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Find the heat needed to warm ice to $0^\circ\text{C}$: For $m = 600\text{ g} = 0.6\text{ kg}$ of ice warmed from $-12^\circ\text{C}$ to $0^\circ\text{C}$, $Q_1 = m c_{\text{ice}} \Delta T = 0.6 \times 2222.3 \times 12 \approx 16000.56\text{ J} \approx 16\text{ kJ}$.
  2. Step 2 — Determine remaining heat and compare with complete melting: Out of $184\text{ kJ}$ supplied, the heat left for melting is $Q_{\text{rem}} = 184 - 16 = 168\text{ kJ}$. Complete melting would require $Q_{\text{all}} = 0.6 \times 336 = 201.6\text{ kJ}$. Since $Q_{\text{rem}} < Q_{\text{all}}$, only part of the ice melts and the final temperature stays at $0^\circ\text{C}$ (so statement A is correct).
  3. Step 3 — Compute the ice-to-water mass ratio: The mass of ice that melts into water is $m_{\text{water}} = \frac{Q_{\text{rem}}}{L_f} = \frac{168}{336} = 0.5\text{ kg} = 500\text{ g}$. The remaining unmelted ice is $m_{\text{ice}} = 600 - 500 = 100\text{ g}$. Thus, $\frac{m_{\text{ice}}}{m_{\text{water}}} = \frac{100}{500} = 1:5$ (so statement D is correct).
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Both statements A and D are correct, matching option (d).

Step 2: Remaining heat available for melting:
$Q_{rem}=184$ kJ $-16$ kJ $=168$ kJ.

$m = \frac{Q}{L_f}$ rem $= \frac{168}{336} =0.5$ kg $=500$ g $\implies m =600-500=100$ g. water ice
Thus $m_{ice}:m_{water}=100:500=1:5$ (Statement D is true).
Q15.trapHtml: Check the ratio order! “ice and water” is $100:500=1:5$ (Statement D), not 5:1 (Statement C).

Q16.questionRecapHtml:
Find the conversion relation between scales P and Q from the given $t_P$ vs. $t_Q$ graph.
$t_Q-$ LF$P_Q t_P-$ LF$P_P$
Q16.conceptHtml: Read LFP and UFP directly from the graph intercepts and spans, then equate $=$. $\Delta t_Q \Delta t_P$
Q16.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Read the fixed points from the graph: Along the horizontal axis ($^\circ\text{Q}$), the interval between the lower and upper fixed points spans from $t_Q = 0$ to $t_Q = 100$ ($\Delta t_Q = 100^\circ$). Along the vertical axis ($^\circ\text{P}$), the upper fixed point is at $180^\circ\text{P}$ with $\Delta t_P = 150^\circ$.
  2. Step 2 — Determine the lower fixed point of scale P: Subtracting the span from the upper fixed point gives $\text{LFP}_P = 180 - 150 = 30^\circ\text{P}$, while $\text{LFP}_Q = 0^\circ\text{Q}$.
  3. Step 3 — Write the conversion relation between scales P and Q: Using the general linear scale relation $\frac{t_P - \text{LFP}_P}{\Delta t_P} = \frac{t_Q - \text{LFP}_Q}{\Delta t_Q}$, we obtain $\frac{t_P - 30}{150} = \frac{t_Q}{100}$ (equivalently $\frac{t_Q}{100} = \frac{t_P - 30}{150}$).
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Matching the scale ratio $\frac{t_Q}{100} = \frac{t_P - 30}{150}$ with the given key confirms option (d).

Step 2: Write the linear conversion formula:
$\frac{t_Q-0}{100} = \frac{t_P -30}{150} \implies \frac{t_Q}{100} = \frac{t_P -30}{150}$ .

Q17.questionRecapHtml:
Find interface temperature of two cylindrical rods in series given ratios of $L$, $r$, and $K$.
$T_A-T T-T_B L$
Q17.conceptHtml: In steady state, heat current is equal in both rods: $=$, where $R=_2$. $R_A R_B K\pi r$
Q17.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Apply steady-state heat flow in series: Since rods A and B are joined end-to-end, the steady-state heat current is the same through both: $\frac{K_A A_A (400 - T)}{L_A} = \frac{K_B A_B (T - 200)}{L_B}$, where $T$ is the interface temperature.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate the ratio of thermal conductances: Because area $A = \pi r^2$, we have $\frac{A_A}{A_B} = \left(\frac{r_A}{r_B}\right)^2 = 2^2 = 4$. Combining all given ratios: $\frac{K_A A_A / L_A}{K_B A_B / L_B} = \left(\frac{K_A}{K_B}\right)\left(\frac{A_A}{A_B}\right)\left(\frac{L_B}{L_A}\right) = \frac{1}{2} \times 4 \times 2 = 4$.
  3. Step 3 — Solve for the interface temperature $T$: Substituting the ratio $4$ into the heat balance gives $4(400 - T) = T - 200 \implies 1600 - 4T = T - 200 \implies 5T = 1800 \implies T = 360\text{ K}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The equilibrium temperature of the interface is 360 K.

$( )( )( )2 ( ) ( )2 \frac{R_A}{R_B} = \frac{L_A}{L_B} \frac{K_B}{K_A} \frac{r_B}{r_A} = \frac{1}{2}$ (2) $\frac{1}{2} = \frac{1}{4}$ .
Step 2: Apply steady-state heat current continuity ($T_A=400$ K, $T_B=200$ K):
$\frac{400-T}{R_A} = \frac{T-200}{R_B} \implies 4(400-T)=T-200.$
Step 3: Solve for $T$: $1600-4T =T-200 \implies 5T =1800 \implies T =360$ K.
$r A R$

Q18.questionRecapHtml: Find $x$ where emissivity $e=x/8$ for a bulb wire ($l=10$ cm$,d=0.5$ mm) at $1727^{^\circ}$C radiating 94.2 W.
Q18.conceptHtml: Use Stefan–Boltzmann law $P =e\sigma AT^4$ with cylindrical lateral area $A=\pi dl$ and temperature in Kelvin.
Q18.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Convert all quantities to SI units: Length $L = 10\text{ cm} = 0.1\text{ m}$, diameter $d = 0.5\text{ mm} = 5 \times 10^{-4}\text{ m}$, and absolute temperature $T = 1727 + 273 = 2000\text{ K}$.
  2. Step 2 — Calculate the radiating surface area of the wire: The curved surface area of the cylindrical wire is $A = \pi d L = 3.14 \times (5 \times 10^{-4}) \times 0.1 = 1.57 \times 10^{-4}\text{ m}^2$.
  3. Step 3 — Use the Stefan–Boltzmann law to find emissivity $e$: From $P = e\sigma A T^4$, substitute $P = 94.2\text{ W}$, $\sigma = 6.0 \times 10^{-8}\text{ W m}^{-2}\text{ K}^{-4}$, and $T^4 = (2 \times 10^3)^4 = 16 \times 10^{12}\text{ K}^4$: $94.2 = e \times (6.0 \times 10^{-8}) \times (1.57 \times 10^{-4}) \times (16 \times 10^{12}) = e \times 9.42 \times 16$.
  4. Step 4 — Solve for $x$ and confirm the answer: We get $e = \frac{94.2}{9.42 \times 16} = \frac{10}{16} = \frac{5}{8}$. Comparing with $e = \frac{x}{8}$ gives $x =$ 5.

Step 2: Lateral surface area of wire:
$A=\pi dl=3.14\times (5\times 10^{-4})\times 0.1=1.57\times 10^{-4} m^2.$
Step 3: Substitute into $P =e\sigma AT^4$:
$94.2=e\times (6.0\times 10^{-8})\times (1.57\times 10^{-4})\times (2\times 10^3)^4$
$94.2=e\times 6.0\times 1.57\times 16\times 10^0=e\times 150.72 \implies e= \frac{94.2}{150.72} = \frac{60}{96} = \frac{5}{8}$ .
Comparing with $e= \frac{x}{8}$ gives $x=5$.
Q18.trapHtml: Notice $94.2/1.57=60$ exactly! Spotting multiples of $\pi =3.14$ turns messy decimals into clean integer division.

Q19.questionRecapHtml: Find steady-state junction temperature $\theta$ for parallel blocks ($k_1,k_2$, area $A$ each) in series with block 3 ($k_3$, area $2A$).
Q19.conceptHtml: In steady state, total heat current entering the junction through conductors 1 and 2 equals the heat current leaving through conductor 3.
Q19.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the conductor arrangement from the diagram: Conductors 1 ($k_1 = 60$, area $A$) and 2 ($k_2 = 120$, area $A$) are connected in parallel between $100^\circ\text{C}$ and the junction at $\theta^\circ\text{C}$. Conductor 3 ($k_3 = 135$, area $2A$) is in series between $\theta^\circ\text{C}$ and $0^\circ\text{C}$. All three have the same length $L$.
  2. Step 2 — Write the steady-state heat current balance at the junction: Total heat entering from conductors 1 and 2 equals the heat leaving through conductor 3: $\frac{k_1 A (100 - \theta)}{L} + \frac{k_2 A (100 - \theta)}{L} = \frac{k_3 (2A) (\theta - 0)}{L}$.
  3. Step 3 — Simplify and substitute thermal conductivities: Canceling $\frac{A}{L}$ gives $(k_1 + k_2)(100 - \theta) = 2k_3 \theta \implies (60 + 120)(100 - \theta) = 2(135)\theta \implies 180(100 - \theta) = 270\theta$.
  4. Step 4 — Solve for $\theta$ and confirm the answer: Dividing both sides by $90$ yields $2(100 - \theta) = 3\theta \implies 200 = 5\theta \implies \theta = 40^\circ\text{C}$. Thus, the numerical answer is 40.

Step 1: Equate incoming and outgoing heat currents (all lengths $=L$):
$H_1+H_2=H_3 \implies \frac{k_1A(100-\theta )}{L} + \frac{k_2A(100-\theta )}{L} = \frac{k_3(2A)(\theta -0)}{L}$ .
Step 2: Cancel $\frac{A}{L}$ and substitute $k_1=60$, $k_2=120$, $k_3=135$:
$(60+120)(100-\theta )=2(135)\theta \implies 180(100-\theta )=270\theta .$
Step 3: Divide by 90: $2(100-\theta )=3\theta \implies 200=5\theta \implies \theta =40^{^\circ}$C.
Q19.trapHtml: Equivalent conductivity of parallel blocks 1 and 2 (area $2A$ total) is simply $k_{eff}= \frac{k1+k2}{2} =90$, so $\theta = \frac{90(100)+135(0)}{90+135} =40^{^\circ}$C.

Q20.questionRecapHtml: Find contact-surface temperature of two identical-geometry plates ($k_A=84$, $k_B=126$) between $100^{^\circ}$C and $0^{^\circ}$C.
Q20.conceptHtml: For two slabs of equal thickness and area in series, the interface temperature is the conductivity-weighted average $T = \frac{k_AT_1+k_BT_2}{k_A+k_B}$.
Q20.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Set up steady-state heat flow across the two plates: Since plates A and B have identical cross-sectional area $A$ and thickness $L$ and are placed in series, the heat current through both is equal: $\frac{K_A A (100 - T)}{L} = \frac{K_B A (T - 0)}{L}$.
  2. Step 2 — Substitute the thermal conductivities: Canceling $\frac{A}{L}$ and plugging in $K_A = 84\text{ W m}^{-1}\text{ K}^{-1}$ and $K_B = 126\text{ W m}^{-1}\text{ K}^{-1}$ gives $84(100 - T) = 126T$.
  3. Step 3 — Solve for the contact temperature $T$: Dividing both sides by $42$ simplifies the equation to $2(100 - T) = 3T \implies 200 - 2T = 3T \implies 5T = 200 \implies T = 40^\circ\text{C}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The steady-state temperature of the surface of contact is 40 $^\circ\text{C}$.

Step 1: Apply the direct series-slab junction formula:
$T = \frac{k_AT_1+k_BT_2}{k_A+k_B} = \frac{84(100)+126(0)}{84+126}$ .
Step 2: Simplify: $T = \frac{8400}{210} =40^{^\circ}$C.
Q20.trapHtml: Notice $84:126=2:3$, so the $100^{^\circ}$C temperature drop splits inversely as 3:2 ($60^{^\circ}$C across A, $40^{^\circ}$C across B) $\implies T =40^{^\circ}$C in 5 seconds!

Q21.questionRecapHtml: Find time to heat 2 kg water from $10^{^\circ}$C to $60^{^\circ}$C using a 2000 W heater at $70%$ efficiency.
Q21.conceptHtml: Useful electrical energy delivered in time $t$ equals heat gained by water: $\eta Pt=mc\Delta T$.
Q21.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Calculate the effective heating power: With rated power $P = 2000\text{ W}$ and efficiency $\eta = 70\%$, the useful power delivered to the water is $P_{\text{eff}} = 0.70 \times 2000 = 1400\text{ W}$.
  2. Step 2 — Find the total heat required by the water: Heating $m = 2\text{ kg}$ of water from $10^\circ\text{C}$ to $60^\circ\text{C}$ ($\Delta T = 50\text{ K}$) requires $Q = mc\Delta T = 2 \times 4200 \times 50 = 420000\text{ J}$.
  3. Step 3 — Compute the time required: Using $t = \frac{Q}{P_{\text{eff}}}$, we obtain $t = \frac{420000}{1400} = 300\text{ s}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The time required is 300 s.

Step 1: Compute useful heating power: $P_{eff}=\eta P =0.70\times 2000=1400$ W. Step 2: Heat required by water ($\Delta T =60-10=50^{^\circ}$C):
$Q=mc\Delta T =2\times 4200\times 50=420000$ J.
Step 3: Time required: $t= \frac{Q}{P} = \frac{420000}{1400} =300$ s. eff
Q21.trapHtml: Always multiply $P$ by $\eta$ (not divide by $\eta$): lower efficiency means longer heating time (300 s vs. 210 s at $100%$).

Q22.questionRecapHtml: Find true temperature in Kelvin when a faulty thermometer (LFP $=5^{^\circ}$C,UFP $=95^{^\circ}$C) reads $41^{^\circ}$C.
Q22.conceptHtml: Use the universal linear scale formula to get $T_C$ first, then convert to absolute scale via $T_K=T_C+273$.
Q22.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Relate the faulty thermometer to the true Celsius scale: Using the linear scale formula $\frac{T_C - 0}{100 - 0} = \frac{X - \text{LFP}}{\text{UFP} - \text{LFP}}$, where $\text{LFP} = 5^\circ\text{C}$ (melting ice) and $\text{UFP} = 95^\circ\text{C}$ (steam).
  2. Step 2 — Find the true Celsius temperature: For the faulty reading $X = 41^\circ\text{C}$, we have $\frac{T_C}{100} = \frac{41 - 5}{95 - 5} = \frac{36}{90} = 0.4 \implies T_C = 40^\circ\text{C}$.
  3. Step 3 — Convert to the absolute (Kelvin) scale: Adding $273$ gives $T = 40 + 273 = 313\text{ K}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The correct temperature on the absolute scale is 313 K.

Step 1: Convert faulty reading ($41^{^\circ}$C) to true Celsius temperature $T_C$:
$\frac{T_C-0}{100} = \frac{41-5}{95-5} = \frac{36}{90} =0.4 \implies T_C=40^{^\circ}$C.
Step 2: Convert to Kelvin (absolute scale): $T_K=40+273=313$ K.
Q22.trapHtml: Never stop at 40! Read the unit before the blank carefully — “absolute scale” means Kelvin ($+273$).

Q23.questionRecapHtml: Find $d$ where diameter change of a 5 cm hole heated from $27^{^\circ}$C to $177^{^\circ}$C is $d\times 10^{-3}$ cm.
Q23.conceptHtml: A cavity or hole in a heated solid expands outward at the same linear rate $\alpha$ as the solid itself: $\Delta D=D\alpha \Delta T$.
Q23.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Apply thermal expansion to a cavity/hole: When a metal sheet is heated uniformly, a hole in the sheet expands just like a solid piece of the same metal would, so $\Delta D = D\alpha\Delta T$.
  2. Step 2 — Compute the temperature change: The sheet is heated from $27^\circ\text{C}$ to $177^\circ\text{C}$, giving $\Delta T = 177 - 27 = 150^\circ\text{C}$.
  3. Step 3 — Calculate $\Delta D$: Substituting $D = 5\text{ cm}$, $\alpha = 1.6 \times 10^{-5}\ /^\circ\text{C}$, and $\Delta T = 150^\circ\text{C}$ gives $\Delta D = 5 \times (1.6 \times 10^{-5}) \times 150 = 1200 \times 10^{-5}\text{ cm} = 12 \times 10^{-3}\text{ cm}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Comparing with $d \times 10^{-3}\text{ cm}$ yields $d =$ 12.

Step 1: Temperature rise $\Delta T =177-27=150^{^\circ}$C. Step 2: Compute change in hole diameter:
$\Delta D=D\alpha \Delta T =5\times (1.6\times 10^{-5})\times 150=1200\times 10^{-5}$ cm $=12\times 10^{-3}$ cm.
Step 3: Comparing with $d\times 10^{-3}$ cm gives $d=12$.
Q23.trapHtml: Photographic enlargement rule: heating a metal sheet zooms every linear dimension (outer edge, hole diameter, distance between holes) by the exact same factor $(1+\alpha \Delta T)$.

Q24.questionRecapHtml: Find second elongation $\Delta L_2$ for equal successive temperature steps $T_1\to T_2\to T_3$.
Q24.conceptHtml: Linear expansion uses the length at the start of each heating step: $\Delta L=L_{initial}\alpha \Delta T$.
Q24.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Find the second temperature interval: Given $T_3 + T_1 = 2T_2$, rearranging gives $T_3 - T_2 = T_2 - T_1 = \Delta T$. Thus, both heating steps have the same temperature rise $\Delta T$.
  2. Step 2 — Express the first expansion $\Delta L_1$ and new length $L_2$: Let the initial length at $T_1$ be $L_0$. Heating from $T_1$ to $T_2$ gives $\Delta L_1 = L_0\alpha\Delta T$, and the length at $T_2$ becomes $L_2 = L_0(1 + \alpha\Delta T)$.
  3. Step 3 — Compute the second expansion $\Delta L_2$: Heating from $T_2$ to $T_3$ starts from length $L_2$, so $\Delta L_2 = L_2\alpha\Delta T = L_0(1 + \alpha\Delta T)\alpha\Delta T = (L_0\alpha\Delta T)(1 + \alpha\Delta T)$.
  4. Step 4 — Substitute $\Delta L_1$ and confirm the answer: Replacing $L_0\alpha\Delta T$ with $\Delta L_1$ gives $\Delta L_2 = \Delta L_1[1 + \alpha\Delta T]$, which matches option (d).
Q24.stepsLatex:
Step 1: From $T_3+T_1=2T_2$, the two temperature increments are equal:
$T_3-T_2=T_2-T_1=\Delta T.$
Step 2: First heating ($T_1\to T_2$): $\Delta L_1=L_1\alpha \Delta T \implies L_2=L_1+\Delta L_1=L_1(1+\alpha \Delta T).$ Step 3: Second heating ($T_2\to T_3$) starts from length $L_2$:
$\Delta L_2=L_2\alpha (T_3-T_2)=L_1(1+\alpha \Delta T)\alpha \Delta T =\Delta L_1[1+\alpha \Delta T].$
Q24.trapHtml: Do not carelessly assume $\Delta L_2=\Delta L_1$; when exact compounding is asked in options, update the base length to $L_2=L_1(1+\alpha \Delta T)$.

Q25.questionRecapHtml: Identify the $T$ vs. Heat supplied graph for water from $-20^{^\circ}$C to $120^{^\circ}$C.
Q25.conceptHtml: During sensible heating, $T$ rises linearly with slope $\frac{1}{mc}$; during phase change ($0^{^\circ}$C melting and $100^{^\circ}$C boiling), $T$ stays constant (horizontal plateau).
Q25.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Analyze the sloped segments (sensible heating): For a temperature vs. heat supplied ($T$–$Q$) graph, the slope is $\frac{dT}{dQ} = \frac{1}{mc}$. Because $c_{\text{water}} \approx 4200\text{ J/(kg}\cdot\text{K)}$ is roughly double $c_{\text{ice}}$ and $c_{\text{steam}}$, the rising line from $0^\circ\text{C}$ to $100^\circ\text{C}$ has a gentler slope than the ice ($-20^\circ\text{C}$ to $0^\circ\text{C}$) and steam ($100^\circ\text{C}$ to $120^\circ\text{C}$) segments.
  2. Step 2 — Analyze the horizontal plateaus (phase transitions): Temperature stays constant during melting at $0^\circ\text{C}$ and boiling at $100^\circ\text{C}$, producing two flat horizontal segments.
  3. Step 3 — Compare the lengths of the two plateaus: Since the latent heat of vaporization ($L_v \approx 2260\text{ kJ/kg}$) is much larger than the latent heat of fusion ($L_f \approx 336\text{ kJ/kg}$), the flat plateau at $100^\circ\text{C}$ must be significantly wider than the plateau at $0^\circ\text{C}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The curve displaying all three sloped segments and two plateaus with the $100^\circ\text{C}$ plateau much longer than the $0^\circ\text{C}$ plateau is option (c).
Q25.stepsLatex:
Step 1: Track the five stages from $-20^{^\circ}$C to $120^{^\circ}$C:
1. $-20^{^\circ}$C $\to 0^{^\circ}$C: Ice warms up (positive slope). 2. At $0^{^\circ}$C: Ice melts to water (first horizontal plateau). 3. $0^{^\circ}$C $\to 100^{^\circ}$C: Liquid water warms up (positive slope). 4. At $100^{^\circ}$C: Water boils to steam (second horizontal plateau). 5. $100^{^\circ}$C $\to 120^{^\circ}$C: Steam warms up (positive slope, steeper than liquid water since $c_{steam} \lt c_{water}$).
Step 2: Option (A) has three plateaus, (B) misses the $0^{^\circ}$C plateau, and (D) has no plateaus. Only graph (C) shows exactly two plateaus at $0^{^\circ}$C and $100^{^\circ}$C with rising segments before, between, and after.
Q25.trapHtml: Count the phase-change plateaus first! Two phase changes (solid$\to$liquid, liquid$\to$gas) = exactly 2 horizontal flat segments.

Q26.questionRecapHtml: Find the drop in temperature of 100 kg water at $25^{^\circ}$C when 10 kg ice at $-10^{^\circ}$C is added.
Q26.conceptHtml: Check whether all ice melts first ($Q_{ice\to 0^\circCwater}$ vs. $Q_{water\to 0^\circC}$), then apply Heat Gained $=$ Heat Lost.
Q26.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Check if all the ice melts: Heat needed to warm $10\text{ kg}$ of ice from $-10^\circ\text{C}$ to $0^\circ\text{C}$ and melt it completely is $Q_{\text{ice}} = m_i c_i \Delta T_i + m_i L_f = (10)(2100)(10) + (10)(3.36 \times 10^5) = 2.1 \times 10^5 + 33.6 \times 10^5 = 35.7 \times 10^5\text{ J}$. Maximum heat $100\text{ kg}$ of water can release cooling to $0^\circ\text{C}$ is $100 \times 4200 \times 25 = 105 \times 10^5\text{ J} > Q_{\text{ice}}$, so all ice melts and the final temperature $T > 0^\circ\text{C}$.
  2. Step 2 — Apply the principle of calorimetry: Heat gained by ice (and melted water) equals heat lost by warm water: $35.7 \times 10^5 + (10)(4200)(T - 0) = (100)(4200)(25 - T)$.
  3. Step 3 — Solve for the final equilibrium temperature $T$: Dividing every term by $42000$ gives $85 + T = 10(25 - T) = 250 - 10T \implies 11T = 165 \implies T = 15^\circ\text{C}$.
  4. Step 4 — Find the temperature decrement and confirm the answer: The water cools from $25^\circ\text{C}$ to $15^\circ\text{C}$, so the decrement in temperature is $25 - 15 = 10^\circ\text{C}$, matching option (b).

$Q =m_ic_i(10)+m_iL_f =10(2100)(10)+10(3.36\times 10^5)=2.1\times 10^5+33.6\times 10^5=35.7\times 10^5$ J. ice Step 2: Max heat 100 kg water can release down to $0^{^\circ}$C:
$Q_{w,max}=100(4200)(25)=105\times 10^5$ J $>35.7\times 10^5$ J $\implies$ all ice melts, $T_f >0^{^\circ}$C.
Step 3: Energy balance for final temperature $T_f$:
$35.7\times 10^5+10(4200)(T_f-0)=100(4200)(25-T_f)$
$35.7+0.42T_f =105-4.2T_f \implies 4.62T_f =69.3 \implies T_f =15^{^\circ}$C.
Step 4: Decrement in temperature of water: $\Delta T =25^{^\circ}$C $-15^{^\circ}$C $=10^{^\circ}$C.
Q26.trapHtml: Classic NTA trap: Option (A) is $15^{^\circ}$C (the final temperature), whereas the question asks for the decrement ($25-15=10^{^\circ}$C)!

Q27.questionRecapHtml: Find junction temperatures $T_B$ and $T_E$ in a series–parallel network of rods $x$ and $y$ ($k_x=3k_y$).
Q27.conceptHtml: Replace each rod with its thermal resistance $R= \frac{L}{kA}$; equal dimensions with $k_x=3k_y$ give $R_x=R$ and $R_y=3R$.
Q27.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Assign thermal resistances to rods $x$ and $y$: Thermal resistance is $R = \frac{L}{KA}$. Since both rods have equal dimensions and $K_x = 3K_y$, let $R_x = R$; then $R_y = 3R$.
  2. Step 2 — Simplify the thermal circuit from the diagram: Segment $AB$ has resistance $R_{AB} = R_x = R$, and segment $EF$ has resistance $R_{EF} = R_y = 3R$. Between $B$ and $E$, the upper path $BCE$ (two $y$ rods in series) has resistance $2R_y = 6R$, and the lower path $BDE$ (two $x$ rods in series) has resistance $2R_x = 2R$. Their parallel combination is $R_{BE} = \frac{6R \times 2R}{6R + 2R} = 1.5R$.
  3. Step 3 — Find the total steady-state heat current: Total resistance is $R_{\text{eq}} = R + 1.5R + 3R = 5.5R$. Thus, the heat current is $H = \frac{T_A - T_F}{R_{\text{eq}}} = \frac{100 - 40}{5.5R} = \frac{120}{11R}$.
  4. Step 4 — Compute $T_B$ and $T_E$ and confirm the answer: At junction $B$, $T_B = T_A - H R_{AB} = 100 - \frac{120}{11} \approx 89.1^\circ\text{C} \approx 89^\circ\text{C}$. At junction $E$, $T_E = T_F + H R_{EF} = 40 + \frac{120}{11R}(3R) = 40 + \frac{360}{11} \approx 72.7^\circ\text{C} \approx 73^\circ\text{C}$. This matches option (c).

Q27.trapHtml: Always set the higher-conductivity rod as $R_x=R$ and lower-conductivity rod as $R_y=3R$ to avoid messy fractions in parallel branches.

Q28.questionRecapHtml: Find final length of a 120 cm composite Al–steel rod heated from $30^{^\circ}$C to $100^{^\circ}$C.
Q28.conceptHtml: Total expansion of rods joined end-to-end is the sum of individual elongations: $\Delta L=L_1\alpha _1\Delta T+L_2\alpha _2\Delta T$.
Q28.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify individual lengths and temperature rise: Since the aluminium and steel rods have equal lengths summing to $120\text{ cm}$, each has initial length $L_1 = L_2 = 60\text{ cm}$. The temperature rise is $\Delta T = 100 - 30 = 70^\circ\text{C}$.
  2. Step 2 — Write the total linear expansion: Total increase in length is the sum of both expansions: $\Delta L = L_1\alpha_{\text{Al}}\Delta T + L_2\alpha_{\text{steel}}\Delta T = 60(\alpha_{\text{Al}} + \alpha_{\text{steel}})\Delta T$.
  3. Step 3 — Substitute the expansion coefficients: With $\alpha_{\text{Al}} = 24 \times 10^{-6}\ /^\circ\text{C}$ and $\alpha_{\text{steel}} = 1.2 \times 10^{-5} = 12 \times 10^{-6}\ /^\circ\text{C}$, we get $\Delta L = 60 \times (24 + 12) \times 10^{-6} \times 70 = 60 \times 36 \times 70 \times 10^{-6} = 0.1512\text{ cm}$.
  4. Step 4 — Find the new composite length and confirm the answer: The final length is $L^\prime = 120 + 0.1512 \approx 120.15\text{ cm}$, which corresponds to option (c).
Q28.stepsLatex:
Step 1: Both rods have equal initial length: $L_1=L_2= \frac{120}{/_{^\circ}2} =60$ cm, and $\Delta T =100-30=70^{^\circ}$C. Step 2: Given $\alpha _1=24\times 10^{-6}/^{^\circ}$C and $\alpha _2=1.2\times 10^{-5}$ C $=12\times 10^{-6}/^{^\circ}$C:
$\Delta L=60\times (24+12)\times 10^{-6}\times 70=60\times 36\times 70\times 10^{-6}=151200\times 10^{-6}=0.1512$ cm.
Step 3: New total length: $L^'=120+0.1512\approx 120.15$ cm.
Q28.trapHtml: Shortcut for equal-length rods in series: $\alpha _{eff}= \frac{\alpha 1+\alpha 2}{2} =18\times 10^{-6}/^{^\circ}$C, then $\Delta L=120\times 18\times 10^{-6}\times 70=0.1512$ cm.

Q29.questionRecapHtml: Find gas consumption rate (g/s) to heat water flowing at 5.0 L/min from $27^{^\circ}$C to $87^{^\circ}$C.
Q29.conceptHtml: Power supplied by burning fuel equals rate of heat absorbed by flowing water: $m˙_{gas}H_c=m˙_wc_w\Delta T$.
Q29.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Convert the water flow rate to $\text{kg/s}$: Since $1\text{ L}$ of water has mass $1\text{ kg}$, a flow rate of $5.0\text{ L/min}$ corresponds to $\frac{dm_w}{dt} = \frac{5.0\text{ kg}}{60\text{ s}} = \frac{1}{12}\text{ kg/s}$.
  2. Step 2 — Calculate the rate of heat absorbed by water: With $\Delta T = 87 - 27 = 60^\circ\text{C}$ and $c = 4200\text{ J/(kg}\cdot^\circ\text{C)}$, the heat power required is $\frac{dQ}{dt} = \left(\frac{dm_w}{dt}\right) c \Delta T = \frac{1}{12} \times 4200 \times 60 = 21000\text{ J/s}$.
  3. Step 3 — Compute the gas consumption rate: Using the heat of combustion $H_c = 5.0 \times 10^4\text{ J/g}$, the rate of gas consumption is $\frac{dm_g}{dt} = \frac{dQ/dt}{H_c} = \frac{21000}{5.0 \times 10^4} = 0.42\text{ g/s}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The rate of consumption of gas is $0.42\text{ g/s}$, which matches option (d).
Q29.stepsLatex:
Step 1: Convert water flow rate to kg/s (1 L water $=1$ kg):
$\frac{5.0}{60}$ kg $\frac{1}{12} m˙_w= =$ kg/s. s Step 2: Heat absorbed by water per second ($\Delta T =87-27=60^{^\circ}$C):
$P =m˙_wc_w\Delta T = \frac{1}{12} \times 4200\times 60=21000$ J/s.
Step 3: Rate of gas consumption ($H_c=5.0\times 10^4$ J/g):
$m˙_{gas}= \frac{P}{H_c} = \frac{21000}{5.0\times 104} =0.42$ g/s.
Q29.trapHtml: Watch the units carefully: $H_c$ is given in J/g (not J/kg), which directly yields $m˙_{gas}$ in g/s without an extra $10^3$ factor!

Q30.questionRecapHtml: Find $x$ (g) of water cooled $50^{^\circ}$C $\to 0^{^\circ}$C whose extracted heat evaporates $(1000-x)$ g water initially at $50^{^\circ}$C.
Q30.conceptHtml: To evaporate water initially at $50^{^\circ}$C, it must first be heated to $100^{^\circ}$C and then vaporized at $100^{^\circ}$C.
Q30.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Express the heat extracted from $x$ grams of water: Cooling $x\text{ g}$ of water from $50^\circ\text{C}$ to $0^\circ\text{C}$ (using $c = 4200\text{ J/(kg}\cdot\text{K)} = 4.2\text{ J/(g}\cdot\text{K)}$) extracts $Q_{\text{extracted}} = x \times 4.2 \times (50 - 0) = 210x\text{ J}$.
  2. Step 2 — Express the heat needed to evaporate $(1000 - x)$ grams of water: Since this water starts at $50^\circ\text{C}$, it must first be heated to $100^\circ\text{C}$ and then vaporized (using $L_v = 2256\text{ kJ/kg} = 2256\text{ J/g}$): $Q_{\text{needed}} = (1000 - x)\left[4.2 \times (100 - 50) + 2256\right] = (1000 - x)(210 + 2256) = 2466(1000 - x)\text{ J}$.
  3. Step 3 — Equate the two heats and solve for $x$: Setting $210x = 2466(1000 - x)$ gives $(210 + 2466)x = 2466000 \implies 2676x = 2466000 \implies x = \frac{2466000}{2676} \approx 921.52$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Rounding to the closest integer gives $x =$ 922.
Q30.stepsLatex:
Step 1: Heat extracted from $x$ g water cooling from $50^{^\circ}$C to $0^{^\circ}$C:
$Q_{ext}=x\times 10^{-3}\times c_w\times 50=x\times 10^{-3}\times 4200\times 50=210x$ J.
Step 2: Heat required to heat $(1000-x)$ g water from $50^{^\circ}$C to $100^{^\circ}$C and vaporize it ($L_v=2256\times 10^3$ J/kg):
$Q =(1000-x)\times 10^{-3}4200(50)+2256\times 10^3=(1000-x)(210+2256)=2466(1000-x)$ J. req
Step 3: Equate $Q_{ext}=Q_{req}$:
$210x=2466(1000-x) \implies 2676x=2466000 \implies x= \frac{2466000}{2676} \approx 921.52\approx 922.$
Q30.trapHtml: Do not forget the sensible heating term $mc(100-50)$ for the evaporating water! Omitting it yields 915 instead of the official answer 922.

trapCards.title: 1. Celsius vs Kelvin Trap
trapCards.html: • $T^4$ Must Be in Kelvin: In Stefan's law and Wien's law, ALWAYS convert $^\circ\text{C} \to \text{K}$ ($T + 273$). For $\Delta T$ in conduction/expansion, $^\circ\text{C}$ and $\text{K}$ are identical.

trapCards.title: 2. Partial Melting & Missing Heating Stages
trapCards.html: • Ice + Steam / Water Mixing: Always calculate max heat available to melt ice ($m_{\text{ice}}L_f$) vs heat available from hot water cooling to $0^\circ\text{C}$ — if insufficient, final temperature is $0^\circ\text{C}$ with partial ice remaining!

trapCards.title: 3. Cavity Expansion Myths
trapCards.html: • Holes Expand Too: On heating a metal plate with a circular hole, the hole diameter INCREASES with the exact same $\alpha$ as the solid!

trapCards.title: 4. Thermal Circuits & Graph Traps
trapCards.html: • Series Conduction Junction Temp: Set $H_1 = H_2 \implies \dfrac{k_1 A_1(T_1 - T_j)}{L_1} = \dfrac{k_2 A_2(T_j - T_2)}{L_2}$.

subject: Physics
title: Thermodynamics
constantsHtml:
• Universal Gas Constant: $R = 8.314\text{ J/mol}\cdot\text{K} \approx 2\text{ cal/mol}\cdot\text{K}$; $1\text{ atm}\cdot\text{L} = 101.3\text{ J}$.
  • Physics Sign Convention: $\Delta Q > 0$ (heat absorbed by gas), $W > 0$ (work done BY gas), $\Delta U > 0$ (internal energy increases).

formulaCards.title: 1. Zeroth & First Law of Thermodynamics
formulaCards.html:
• Zeroth Law: Defines thermal equilibrium and temperature ($T$).
  • First Law (Energy Conservation): $\Delta Q = \Delta U + W$ (differential: $dQ = dU + P\,dV$).
  • Internal Energy (Ideal Gas): Depends ONLY on $T$: $\Delta U = n C_V \Delta T = \dfrac{f}{2}nR\Delta T = \dfrac{f}{2}(P_2V_2 - P_1V_1)$ (valid for ALL processes!).
  • Work Done by Gas: $W = \int_{V_1}^{V_2} P\,dV =$ signed area under $P$–$V$ curve.

formulaCards.title: 2. Specific Heats & Mayer's Relation
formulaCards.html:
• Mayer's Relation: $C_P - C_V = R$ (ideal gas); $C_V = \dfrac{f}{2}R$, $C_P = \left(\dfrac{f}{2} + 1\right)R$.
  • Adiabatic Index: $\gamma = \dfrac{C_P}{C_V} = 1 + \dfrac{2}{f}$ ($5/3$ monatomic, $7/5$ diatomic rigid, $4/3$ polyatomic).

formulaCards.title: 3. Standard Thermodynamic Processes
formulaCards.html:
• Isochoric ($V = \text{const}$): $P \propto T$, $W = 0$, $\Delta Q = \Delta U = nC_V\Delta T$.
  • Isobaric ($P = \text{const}$): $V \propto T$, $W = P\Delta V = nR\Delta T$, $\Delta Q = nC_P\Delta T$, $\dfrac{W}{\Delta Q} = 1 - \dfrac{1}{\gamma}$ ($2/5$ for monatomic, $2/7$ for diatomic).
  • Isothermal ($T = \text{const}$): $PV = \text{const}$, $\Delta U = 0$, $\Delta Q = W = nRT\ln\left(\dfrac{V_2}{V_1}\right) = nRT\ln\left(\dfrac{P_1}{P_2}\right)$.
  • Adiabatic ($\Delta Q = 0$): $PV^\gamma = \text{const}$, $TV^{\gamma-1} = \text{const}$, $P^{1-\gamma}T^\gamma = \text{const}$; $W = -\Delta U = \dfrac{P_1V_1 - P_2V_2}{\gamma - 1} = \dfrac{nR(T_1 - T_2)}{\gamma - 1}$.

formulaCards.title: 4. Polytropic Process, Cyclic Work & Carnot Engine
formulaCards.html:
• Polytropic ($PV^x = \text{const}$): $W = \dfrac{P_1V_1 - P_2V_2}{x - 1} = \dfrac{nR(T_1 - T_2)}{x - 1}$; Molar heat capacity $C = C_V + \dfrac{R}{1 - x}$.
  • Cyclic Process: $\Delta U_{\text{cycle}} = 0 \implies Q_{\text{net}} = W_{\text{cycle}} =$ enclosed area on $P$–$V$ ($+$ clockwise, $-$ anticlockwise).
  • Heat Engine & Carnot Efficiency: $\eta = \dfrac{W}{Q_{\text{in}}} = 1 - \dfrac{Q_{\text{out}}}{Q_{\text{in}}}$; Carnot $\eta = 1 - \dfrac{T_L}{T_H}$ ($T$ in K). Refrigerator COP $\beta = \dfrac{Q_L}{W} = \dfrac{T_L}{T_H - T_L}$.
