Q64.questionRecapHtml:
Gas in closed cylinder at 3.23 kPa and $50^{^\circ}$C is heated to double its temperature; find final pressure in Pa.
$T_2$
Q64.conceptHtml: At constant volume, $P \propto T_{Kelvin}$, so $P_2=P_1$. Note the wording ambiguity between doubling Celsius vs. Kelvin temperature. $T_1$
Q64.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the initial state at constant volume: In a closed cylinder ($V$ constant), $P \propto T$. Initial pressure is $P_1 = 3.23\text{ kPa} = 3230\text{ Pa}$ and initial temperature is $T_1 = 50 + 273 = 323\text{ K}$.
  2. Step 2 — Case 1 (doubling the Celsius temperature): If $50^{\circ}\text{C}$ is doubled to $100^{\circ}\text{C}$, then $T_2 = 100 + 273 = 373\text{ K}$, giving $P_2 = P_1 \frac{T_2}{T_1} = 3230 \times \frac{373}{323} = 3730\text{ Pa}$.
  3. Step 3 — Case 2 (doubling the absolute Kelvin temperature): If the absolute temperature is doubled ($T_2 = 2 T_1 = 646\text{ K}$), then $P_2 = 2 P_1 = 2 \times 3230 = 6460\text{ Pa}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Due to the phrasing ambiguity, both values are accepted, confirming the verified answer 3730 / 6460.

$P_2=3230\times \frac{373}{323} =3730$ Pa.
Step 3 (Interpretation 2 – Doubling Kelvin $T_2=2T_1$):

Q65.questionRecapHtml:
Gas at 60 c$m^3,27^{^\circ}$C,2 atm compressed to 20 c$m^3$ at $77^{^\circ}$C; find final $P$ in atm.
$P_1V_1 P_2V_2$
Q65.conceptHtml: For a fixed mass of ideal gas, $=$ with $T$ in Kelvin. $T_1 T_2$
Q65.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Convert temperatures to Kelvin and list states: Initial state: $P_1 = 2\text{ atm}$, $V_1 = 60\text{ cm}^3$, $T_1 = 27 + 273 = 300\text{ K}$. Final state: $V_2 = 20\text{ cm}^3$, $T_2 = 77 + 273 = 350\text{ K}$.
  2. Step 2 — Apply the combined ideal gas law: Since the mass of gas is fixed, $\frac{P_1 V_1}{T_1} = \frac{P_2 V_2}{T_2}$.
  3. Step 3 — Solve for $P_2$: $P_2 = P_1 \left(\frac{V_1}{V_2}\right) \left(\frac{T_2}{T_1}\right) = 2 \times \frac{60}{20} \times \frac{350}{300} = 2 \times 3 \times \frac{7}{6} = 7\text{ atm}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The final pressure is 7 atmospheric pressure.

trapCards.title: 1. Celsius vs Kelvin & Molar Mass Units
trapCards.html: • Molar Mass in kg/mol: In $v_{\text{rms}} = \sqrt{3RT/M}$, $M$ MUST be in $\text{kg/mol}$ (e.g., $O_2 = 0.032\text{ kg/mol}$, NOT $32$)!

trapCards.title: 2. Translational vs Total KE
trapCards.html: • Translational vs Total: Average translational KE is ALWAYS $\frac{3}{2}k_BT$ for ANY ideal gas (even diatomic/polyatomic), whereas total KE is $\frac{f}{2}k_BT$.

trapCards.title: 3. Vibrational Modes & $\gamma_{\text{mix}}$ Shortcut
trapCards.html: • Never Average $\gamma$ Directly: $\gamma_{\text{mix}} \ne \frac{n_1\gamma_1 + n_2\gamma_2}{n_1+n_2}$; always average $C_V$ (or $f$) first!

trapCards.title: 4. Mean Free Path & Graph Axes
trapCards.html: • Constant $V$ vs Constant $P$: At constant volume ($n$ fixed), $\lambda$ is independent of $T$; at constant pressure, $\lambda \propto T$.

subject: Physics
title: Simple Harmonic Motion
constantsHtml: • Phase-Circle Key Times: $0 \to A/2$: $T/12$; $A/2 \to A$: $T/6$; $0 \to A/\sqrt{2}$: $T/8$; $0 \to \sqrt{3}A/2$: $T/6$; $0 \to A$: $T/4$.

formulaCards.title: 1. Equation & Kinematics of SHM
formulaCards.html:
• Restoring Force & Diff. Eq.: $F = -kx$, $a = \dfrac{d^2x}{dt^2} = -\omega^2 x$, $\omega = \sqrt{\dfrac{k}{m}} = \dfrac{2\pi}{T} = 2\pi f$.
  • Displacement, Velocity & Acceleration: $x(t) = A\sin(\omega t + \phi)$, $v = \omega\sqrt{A^2 - x^2}$ ($v_{\max} = \omega A$ at $x=0$), $a = -\omega^2 x$ ($a_{\max} = \omega^2 A$ at $x = \pm A$).
  • Amplitude from $(x, v)$: $A = \sqrt{x^2 + \dfrac{v^2}{\omega^2}}$; from two positions: $\omega = \sqrt{\dfrac{v_1^2 - v_2^2}{x_2^2 - x_1^2}}$.

formulaCards.title: 2. Energy in SHM & Frequency Doubling
formulaCards.html:
• Potential & Kinetic Energy: $U = \dfrac{1}{2}kx^2 = E\sin^2(\omega t + \phi)$, $K = \dfrac{1}{2}k(A^2 - x^2) = E\cos^2(\omega t + \phi)$, Total $E = \dfrac{1}{2}kA^2 = \dfrac{1}{2}m\omega^2 A^2$.
  • Frequency Doubling: $K$ and $U$ oscillate with frequency $2f$ (period $T/2$); $\langle K \rangle = \langle U \rangle = \dfrac{E}{2}$ over one full cycle. $K = U$ at $x = \pm\dfrac{A}{\sqrt{2}}$.

formulaCards.title: 3. Spring–Block Systems & Combinations
formulaCards.html:
• Spring–Mass Period: $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{m}{k}}$ (same on horizontal, vertical, or smooth incline — gravity only shifts equilibrium!).
  • Cutting a Spring: $kl = \text{const} \implies$ cutting into $n$ equal parts gives $k' = nk$ and $f' = \sqrt{n}f$ per part.
  • Series & Parallel: Parallel: $k_{\text{eq}} = k_1 + k_2$; Series: $\dfrac{1}{k_{\text{eq}}} = \dfrac{1}{k_1} + \dfrac{1}{k_2}$. Two-body spring ($m_1, m_2$): $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{\mu}{k}}$ where $\mu = \dfrac{m_1m_2}{m_1+m_2}$.

formulaCards.title: 4. Simple, Physical & Floating Pendulums
formulaCards.html:
• Simple Pendulum: $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{L}{g_{\text{eff}}}}$ ($\vec{g}_{\text{eff}} = \vec{g} - \vec{a}_{\text{frame}} + \frac{q\vec{E}}{m}$).
  • Long Pendulum ($L \sim R_E$): $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{1}{g(1/L + 1/R_E)}}$ (for $L \to \infty$, $T \to 84.6\text{ min}$).
  • Physical & Torsional Pendulums: $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{I}{mgd}}$ ($d =$ pivot to CM); Torsional: $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{I}{C}}$.

formulaCards.title: 5. Phase-Circle Timing & Superposition
formulaCards.html:
• Phase-Circle Intervals: $x = 0 \to A/2$: $t = T/12$; $x = A/2 \to A$: $t = T/6$; $x = 0 \to A/\sqrt{2}$: $t = T/8$.
  • Collinear Superposition: $x_1 = A_1\sin(\omega t)$, $x_2 = A_2\sin(\omega t + \delta) \implies A_{\text{net}} = \sqrt{A_1^2 + A_2^2 + 2A_1A_2\cos\delta}$.
  • Perpendicular Superposition: $\delta = 0$: straight line; $\delta = \pi/2, A_1 = A_2$: circle; $\delta = \pi/2, A_1 \ne A_2$: ellipse.

formulaCards.title: 6. Periodic vs SHM & Damped SHM
formulaCards.html:
• SHM Condition: Must reduce to $x = c + A\sin(\omega' t + \phi)$ with a single frequency $\omega'$. $\sin^2(\omega t) = \frac{1}{2}(1 - \cos 2\omega t)$ IS SHM (with $\omega' = 2\omega$); $\sin(\omega t) + \cos(2\omega t)$ is periodic but NOT SHM.
  • Damped SHM: $A(t) = A_0 e^{-bt/(2m)}$, $E(t) = E_0 e^{-bt/m}$.

Q01.subtopic: Equal Angular Accelerations of Two Pendulums
Q01.questionRecapHtml: Two simple pendulums of lengths $l_1,l_2$ have small angular displacements $\theta _1,\theta _2$ and equal angular accelerations. Relate $\theta$ and $l$.
Q01.conceptHtml: For small oscillations of a simple pendulum, angular acceleration magnitude is $\alpha = \frac{g}{l} \theta$.
Q01.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall angular acceleration in a simple pendulum: For a simple pendulum of length $l$ undergoing small angular displacement $\theta$, the restoring torque gives angular acceleration $\alpha = -\frac{g}{l}\theta$, so its magnitude is $|\alpha| = \frac{g\theta}{l}$.
  2. Step 2 — Equate the angular accelerations of both pendulums: Since both pendulums experience equal angular accelerations at displacements $\theta_1$ and $\theta_2$, we have $\frac{g\theta_1}{l_1} = \frac{g\theta_2}{l_2}$.
  3. Step 3 — Simplify the relation: Cancelling $g$ from both sides gives $\frac{\theta_1}{l_1} = \frac{\theta_2}{l_2}$, and cross-multiplying yields $\theta_1 l_2 = \theta_2 l_1$.
  4. Step 4 — Match with the options: This matches Option (a) ($\theta_1 l_2 = \theta_2 l_1$).
Q01.stepsLatex: $\alpha _1=\alpha _2 \implies \frac{g}{l_1} \theta _1= \frac{g}{l_2} \theta _2 \implies \theta _1l_2=\theta _2l_1$
Q01.trapHtml: Cross-multiply carefully: $\theta _1/l_1=\theta _2/l_2 \implies \theta _1l_2=\theta _2l_1$ (not $\theta _1l_1=\theta _2l_2$).

Q02.questionRecapHtml: Block $m$ sits on block $M$ (friction $\mu$) attached to spring $k$ on a smooth table. Verify five statements about $T$, $a$, friction, and max amplitude.
Q02.conceptHtml: Without slipping, both blocks move as mass $(M+m)$ with $a=- \frac{kx}{M+m}$; static friction supplies $f_s=m|a|\le \mu mg$.
Q02.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Analyze the combined two-block oscillation (Statements A and B): When the upper block ($m$) does not slip over the lower block ($M$), both move together as a single mass $(M+m)$ attached to the spring of constant $k$. Hence, the time period is $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{m+M}{k}}$ (A is correct) and the restoring force $-kx$ gives acceleration $a = -\frac{kx}{M+m}$ (B is correct).
  2. Step 2 — Find the friction force on the upper block (Statements C and E): Static friction is the only horizontal force accelerating the upper block, so $f = m|a| = \frac{mk|x|}{M+m}$, not $\frac{m\mu|x|}{M+m}$ (so C is incorrect). The maximum static friction between the two blocks depends only on the normal force from the upper block, $f_{\max} = \mu mg$, not $\mu(M+m)g$ (so E is incorrect).
  3. Step 3 — Determine the maximum non-slipping amplitude (Statement D): At maximum displacement $x = A_{\max}$, friction reaches its limit $f_{\max} = \mu mg$: $\frac{mkA_{\max}}{M+m} = \mu mg \implies A_{\max} = \frac{\mu(M+m)g}{k}$ (D is correct).
  4. Step 4 — Final selection: Only statements A, B, and D are correct, which corresponds to Option (c).
Q02.stepsLatex:
A: $T =2\pi \frac{m+M}{k}$ (True), B: $a=- \frac{kx}{M+m}$ (True)
C: $f_s=m|a|= \frac{mk|x|}{M+m} ̸= \frac{m\mu |x|}{M+m}$ (False) Only A, B, and D are correct.
D: $f_{s,max}=\mu mg \implies \frac{mkA_{max}}{M+m} =\mu mg \implies A_{max}= \frac{\mu (M+m)g}{k}$ (True)
E: $f_{s,max}=\mu mg̸=\mu (M+m)g ($False)
Q02.trapHtml: Notice the subtle typo in statement C ($\mu$ instead of $k$); always check dimensions ($[m\mu x/(M+m)]=$ m, not Newtons!).

Q03.subtopic: Superposition of Two Collinear SHM s
Q03.questionRecapHtml: Particle undergoes $x_1= 7sin5t$ cm and $x_2=2 7\sin(5t+\pi /3)$ cm. If $a_{max}=x\times 10^{-2}$ m/$s^2$, find $x$.
Q03.conceptHtml: Use phasor addition for same-frequency SHMs: $A_{net}= A^2_1+A^2_2+2A_1A_2\cos\phi$, then $a_{max}=\omega ^2A_{net}$.
Q03.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify amplitudes, angular frequency, and phase difference: The two collinear SHMs are $x_1 = \sqrt{7}\sin(5t)\text{ cm}$ and $x_2 = 2\sqrt{7}\sin\left(5t + \frac{\pi}{3}\right)\text{ cm}$. Thus $A_1 = \sqrt{7}\text{ cm}$, $A_2 = 2\sqrt{7}\text{ cm}$, $\omega = 5\text{ rad/s}$, and phase difference $\phi = \frac{\pi}{3}$.
  2. Step 2 — Compute the resultant amplitude using vector addition: $A = \sqrt{A_1^2 + A_2^2 + 2A_1 A_2 \cos\phi} = \sqrt{7 + 28 + 2(\sqrt{7})(2\sqrt{7})\cos\frac{\pi}{3}} = \sqrt{35 + 28 \times \frac{1}{2}} = \sqrt{49} = 7\text{ cm}$.
  3. Step 3 — Calculate the maximum acceleration: $a_{\max} = \omega^2 A = 5^2 \times 7\text{ cm/s}^2 = 175\text{ cm/s}^2 = 175 \times 10^{-2}\text{ m/s}^2$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: Comparing with $x \times 10^{-2}\text{ m/s}^2$ gives $x = 175$, matching Option (d).
Q03.stepsLatex:
$\sqrt{\sqrt{\sqrt}{} \sqrt{\sqrt}{}} A_{net}= 2 2+2( 7)(2 7)cos \frac{\pi}{3}$
$\sqrt{\frac{( 7) +(2 7)}{7+28+28\cdot}} = \frac{1}{2} = 49=7$ cm $=7\times 10^{-2}$ m
$a_{max}=\omega ^2A_{net}=5^2\times 7\times 10^{-2}=175\times 10^{-2}$ m/$s^2 \implies x=175$
Q03.trapHtml: Keep track of cm vs. m: $A_{net}=7$ cm cleanly matches the $10^{-2}$ m/$s^2$ factor in the prompt.

Q04.subtopic: Ratio of Maximum Velocities of Two Springs
Q04.questionRecapHtml: Equal masses on springs $k_1$ and $k_2$ oscillate vertically with equal amplitudes. Find $v_{max,A}/v_{max,B}$.
Q04.conceptHtml: Maximum speed is $v_{max}=\omega A=A k/m$; for equal $m$ and $A$, $v_{max}\propto k$.
Q04.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Write the maximum speed formula in SHM: For a mass $m$ oscillating on a spring of stiffness $k$ with amplitude $A$, the angular frequency is $\omega = \sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}$ and the maximum speed is $v_{\max} = \omega A = A\sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}$.
  2. Step 2 — Take the ratio for bodies $A$ and $B$: Since both bodies have equal mass $m$ and identical amplitude $A$, we get $\frac{v_{\max,A}}{v_{\max,B}} = \frac{A\sqrt{k_1/m}}{A\sqrt{k_2/m}} = \sqrt{\frac{k_1}{k_2}}$.
  3. Step 3 — Match with the options: The ratio $\sqrt{\frac{k_1}{k_2}}$ corresponds to Option (b).
Q04.stepsLatex:
$\sqrt{\frac{vmax,A}{vmax,B}} = \frac{A}{A} \sqrt{\frac{k_1/m}{k_2/m}} = \frac{k_1}{k_2}$
$1\sqrt{1}$
Q04.trapHtml: Energy conservation gives the same result instantly: $mv_m^2_{ax}= kA^2 \implies v_{max}\propto k$. $2$

Q05.questionRecapHtml: (A): Pendulum period is longer at mountain top than base. (R): Period decreases with increasing $g$ and vice versa.
Q05.conceptHtml: Since $g(h)=g_0/(1+h/R)^2 \lt g_0$ at altitude $h$, $T =2\pi L/g$ increases as $g$ decreases.
Q05.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the time period of a simple pendulum: The period is given by $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{l}{g}}$, which shows $T \propto \frac{1}{\sqrt{g}}$. Thus, as $g$ increases, $T$ decreases, and as $g$ decreases, $T$ increases. Therefore, Reason (R) is true.
  2. Step 2 — Compare gravity at a mountain peak and base: Acceleration due to gravity decreases with altitude above Earth's surface ($g_h = \frac{g}{(1+h/R)^2}$), so $g_{\text{peak}} < g_{\text{base}}$.
  3. Step 3 — Link Reason to Assertion: Because $g$ is smaller at the mountain peak and $T \propto \frac{1}{\sqrt{g}}$, the pendulum has a longer time period at the peak than at the base. Thus Assertion (A) is true and (R) directly explains (A).
  4. Step 4 — Final choice: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A), which is Option (c).
Q05.stepsLatex: At a mountain top, altitude $h>0 \implies g_{top} \lt g_{base}$. Because $T \propto 1/ g$ (Reason R is true), a smaller $g$ directly causes a longer time period $T$ (Assertion A is true and R correctly explains A).
Q05.trapHtml: Watch option ordering in NTA Assertion–Reason questions: "Both true and correct explanation" is option (C) here, not (A)!

Q06.questionRecapHtml: (A): Knowing $x_0$ and $p_0$ with given $\omega$ determines $x(t)$ and $p(t)$ for all $t$. (R): Amplitude and phase are expressible in terms of $x_0,p_0$.
Q06.conceptHtml: For $x(t)=Asin(\omega t+\phi)$ and $p(t)=m\omega Acos(\omega t+\phi)$, the two constants $A$ and $\phi$ are uniquely fixed by $x_0,p_0$.
Q06.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Write general SHM equations: Position is $x(t) = A\sin(\omega t + \phi)$ and momentum is $p(t) = mv(t) = m\omega A\cos(\omega t + \phi)$.
  2. Step 2 — Express $A$ and $\phi$ using initial values $x_0$ and $p_0$: At $t = 0$, $x_0 = A\sin\phi$ and $\frac{p_0}{m\omega} = A\cos\phi$. Squaring and adding gives $A = \sqrt{x_0^2 + \left(\frac{p_0}{m\omega}\right)^2}$, and dividing gives $\tan\phi = \frac{m\omega x_0}{p_0}$ (with quadrant fixed by the signs of $x_0$ and $p_0$). Thus Reason (R) is true.
  3. Step 3 — Check uniqueness of motion: Since $\omega$ is known and both $A$ and $\phi$ are uniquely determined from $x_0$ and $p_0$, $x(t)$ and $p(t)$ are uniquely fixed for all $t$. Thus Assertion (A) is true and (R) correctly explains (A).
  4. Step 4 — Final choice: This matches Option (d).
Q06.stepsLatex: $x_0=A \frac{p_0}{m} =\omega Acos\phi \sqrt{\frac{sin\phi , v_0=}{x2_0+( )^2,}}$ Thus both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) directly explains (A). $A= \frac{p_0}{m\omega} tan\phi = \frac{m\omega x_0}{p_0}$
Q06.trapHtml: A second-order ODE ($x¨+\omega ^2x=0$) always has a unique solution once two initial values ($x_0,p_0$) are specified.

Q07.questionRecapHtml: SHM has period $T=2$ s and amplitude $A=1$ cm. Find the ratio $D/d$ of distance to displacement in $t=12.5$ s.
Q07.conceptHtml: Decompose $t=12.5$ s into full cycles plus a quarter-cycle: $12.5=6T+T/4$.
Q07.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Find the number of oscillations in $12.5\text{ s}$: Given period $T = 2\text{ s}$ and amplitude $A = 1\text{ cm}$, the number of cycles is $N = \frac{t}{T} = \frac{12.5}{2} = 6.25 = 6 + \frac{1}{4}$ oscillations.
  2. Step 2 — Compute total distance $D$: In each full oscillation, the particle travels $4A$, and in an extra quarter-period ($T/4$) starting from the mean (or extreme) position, it travels $A$. Thus $D = 6(4A) + A = 25A = 25\text{ cm}$.
  3. Step 3 — Compute net displacement $d$: After $6$ complete oscillations, the particle returns to its starting point (zero net displacement). In the remaining $T/4$, it moves from mean to extreme (or extreme to mean), giving net displacement $d = A = 1\text{ cm}$.
  4. Step 4 — Find the ratio: $\frac{D}{d} = \frac{25A}{A} = 25$, which matches Option (c).
Q07.stepsLatex:
$t=12.5$ s $=6(2$ s$)+0.5$ s $=6T+ \frac{T}{4}$
$D=6(4A)+A=25A=25$ cm $d=0+A=1$ cm (starting from mean or extreme)
$\frac{D}{d} = \frac{25}{1} =25$
Q07.trapHtml: Over every full period $T$, displacement is 0 and distance is $4A$. Only the leftover $T/4$ contributes to net displacement $d=A$.

Q08.subtopic: Oscillation Period of a Floating Hollow Cube
Q08.questionRecapHtml: Hollow cube of edge 10 cm and mass 10 g floats in water ($\rho =10^3$ kg/$m^3$, $g=10$ m/$s^2$). Period is $y\pi \times 10^{-2}$ s; find $y$.
Q08.conceptHtml: Use the floating-prism formula $T =2\pi M/(\rho Ag)$ with base area $A=L^2$.
Q08.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Convert given values to SI units: Edge length $a = 10\text{ cm} = 0.1\text{ m}$, base area $A = a^2 = 0.01\text{ m}^2$, mass $m = 10\text{ g} = 0.01\text{ kg}$, water density $\rho = 10^3\text{ kg/m}^3$, and $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$.
  2. Step 2 — Find the effective spring constant from buoyancy: When the cube is pushed down by a small distance $x$, the extra upward buoyant force is $F = -\rho A g x$. Comparing with $F = -k_{\text{eff}} x$ gives $k_{\text{eff}} = \rho A g = 10^3 \times 0.01 \times 10 = 100\text{ N/m}$.
  3. Step 3 — Calculate the time period: $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{m}{k_{\text{eff}}}} = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{0.01}{100}} = 2\pi\sqrt{10^{-4}} = 2\pi \times 10^{-2}\text{ s}$.
  4. Step 4 — Identify $y$: Comparing with $y\pi \times 10^{-2}\text{ s}$ gives $y = 2$, matching Option (a).
Q08.stepsLatex: $M =10$ g $=10^{-2}$ kg$, A=(0.1$ m$)^2=10^{-2} m^2 \sqrt{\sqrt}{ }$ Comparing with $y\pi \times 10^{-2}$ s gives $y=2$. $T =2\pi \frac{M}{\rho Ag} =2\pi \frac{10-2}{103\times 10-2\times 10} =2\pi 10-4=2\pi \times 10^{-2}$ s
Q08.trapHtml: Convert both 10 g and 10 cm cleanly to SI units; notice $M=10^{-2}$ kg and $A=10^{-2} m^2$ cancel immediately!

Q09.questionRecapHtml: (A): Pendulum period is unchanged on a planet with $M^'=4M_E,R^'=2R_E$. (R): Bob mass is unchanged on both planets.
Q09.conceptHtml: Compute $g^'=GM^'/R^{'2}$ and recall $T =2\pi L/g$ is completely independent of bob mass $m$.
Q09.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Check gravity on the other planet: Acceleration due to gravity is $g = \frac{GM}{R^2}$. With $M' = 4M$ and $R' = 2R$, we get $g' = \frac{G(4M)}{(2R)^2} = \frac{4GM}{4R^2} = g$.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Assertion (A): Since $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{l}{g}}$ and $g' = g$, the simple pendulum has the exact same time period on the planet as on Earth. So Assertion (A) is true.
  3. Step 3 — Evaluate Reason (R) and its link to (A): Mass is an intrinsic property of matter, so the bob's mass is indeed identical on both planets (Reason (R) is true). However, a simple pendulum's time period does not depend on the bob's mass—it depends on $g$. Therefore, (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
  4. Step 4 — Final choice: This corresponds to Option (d).
Q09.stepsLatex:
$\sqrt{g^}'= \frac{G(4M_E)}{(2R_E)2} = \frac{4GM_E}{4R_{E2}} =g_E \implies T^'=2\pi \frac{L}{g'} =T_E$ Assertion (A) is true because $g^'=g_E$. Reason (R) is factually true (mass
is invariant), but $T$ does not depend on bob mass, so (R) does NOT explain (A).
Q09.trapHtml: Classic NTA trap: a true Reason statement that is physically irrelevant to the Assertion means "Both true, NOT the correct explanation."

Q10.subtopic: Kinetic Energy vs. Position Graph for $x=x_0sin^2(t/2)$
Q10.questionRecapHtml: Particle moves as $x(t)=x_0\sin^2(t/2)$ with $x_0=1$ m. Identify the graph of kinetic energy $K$ vs. $x$.
Q10.conceptHtml: Rewrite $x(t)= \frac{x0}{2} (1-cost)$: this is SHM with mean position $x= \frac{1}{2}$ m and amplitude $A= \frac{1}{2}$ m between $x=0$ and $x=1$.
Q10.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Rewrite $x(t)$ in standard SHM form: Using $\sin^2\theta = \frac{1 - \cos 2\theta}{2}$, we get $x(t) = x_0\sin^2\left(\frac{t}{2}\right) = \frac{x_0}{2}(1 - \cos t) = 0.5 - 0.5\cos t$ (since $x_0 = 1\text{ m}$).
  2. Step 2 — Identify mean position and extreme positions: The particle performs SHM with angular frequency $\omega = 1\text{ rad/s}$, amplitude $A = 0.5\text{ m}$, and mean position at $x = 0.5\text{ m}$. Its extreme positions are $x = 0$ and $x = 1\text{ m}$.
  3. Step 3 — Determine the shape of $K(x)$: Kinetic energy is $K(x) = \frac{1}{2}m\omega^2\left[A^2 - (x - 0.5)^2\right]$, which is a downward-opening parabola that equals zero at the extremes $x = 0$ and $x = 1\text{ m}$ and reaches its maximum at the mean position $x = 0.5\text{ m}$.
  4. Step 4 — Match the graph: The downward parabola spanning $x = 0$ to $x = 1\text{ m}$ with its peak at $x = 0.5\text{ m}$ is shown in Option (d).
Q10.stepsLatex:
$x(t)= \frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{2} cost \implies v= \frac{1}{2} sint sin^2t=1-cos^2t=1-(1-2x)^2=4x(1-x)$ This is a downward-opening parabola with zeros at $x=0,1$ and maximum at $x=1/2$,
$K(x)= \frac{1}{2} mv^2= \frac{1}{8} msin^2t= \frac{1}{2} mx(1-x)$
matching graph (D).
Q10.trapHtml: Don’t mistake the mean position for $x=0$! Because $\sin^2(t/2)\in [0,1]$, the oscillator swings between 0 and 1 with centre at $x=1/2$.

Q11.subtopic: Simple Pendulum Period at Heights $R$ and $2R$
Q11.questionRecapHtml:
Pendulum has period $T_1=4$ s at height $R$ and $T_2$ at height $2R$ above Earth’s surface. Relate $T_1$ and $T_2$.
$GM \sqrt{L}$
Q11.conceptHtml: Since $g(h)=_{(R+h)2}$, we have $T(h)=2\pi _{g(h)} \propto (R+h)$.
Q11.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Relate time period to distance from Earth's centre: At distance $r = R + h$ from Earth's centre, $g(r) = \frac{GM}{r^2}$, so $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{l}{g(r)}} \propto \frac{1}{\sqrt{1/r^2}} = r$.
  2. Step 2 — Find $r_1$ and $r_2$ for the two altitudes: At altitude $h_1 = R$, $r_1 = R + R = 2R$. At altitude $h_2 = 2R$, $r_2 = R + 2R = 3R$.
  3. Step 3 — Take the ratio of time periods: $\frac{T_1}{T_2} = \frac{r_1}{r_2} = \frac{2R}{3R} = \frac{2}{3} \implies 3T_1 = 2T_2$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: This matches Option (a) ($3T_1 = 2T_2$).
Q11.stepsLatex: $\frac{T_1}{T_2} = \frac{R+R}{R+2R} = \frac{2R}{3R} = \frac{2}{3} \implies 3T_1=2T_2$
Q11.trapHtml: At height $h$ above Earth’s surface, distance from Earth’s centre is $r=R+h$, so $T \propto (R+h)$ linearly!

Q12.subtopic: Total Mechanical Energy vs. Mass at Fixed Amplitude
Q12.questionRecapHtml: Spring-mass system has total energy $E$. If mass $m$ is doubled while keeping amplitude $A$ unchanged, find the new energy.
Q12.conceptHtml: Total energy of a spring-mass oscillator is $E= \frac{1}{2} kA^2$, which depends only on $k$ and $A$, not on mass $m$.
Q12.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Write total mechanical energy of a spring-mass oscillator: For a spring of force constant $k$ oscillating with amplitude $A$, the total mechanical energy of SHM (measured relative to equilibrium) is $E = \frac{1}{2}kA^2$.
  2. Step 2 — Check dependence on mass: Notice that $E = \frac{1}{2}kA^2$ depends only on the spring constant $k$ and the amplitude $A$, and is completely independent of the oscillating mass $m$.
  3. Step 3 — Apply the given change: Doubling the mass of particle $P$ while keeping $k$ and amplitude $A$ unchanged leaves the total mechanical energy unchanged at $E$.
  4. Step 4 — Final choice: The new mechanical energy is $E$, matching Option (d).
Q12.stepsLatex:
$E= \frac{1}{21} kA^2 ($independent of $m)$
$E^'= kA^2=E$ 2
Q12.trapHtml: Writing $E= \frac{1}{2} m\omega ^2A^2$ can mislead you into thinking $E\propto m$, forgetting that $\omega ^2=k/m$ cancels $m$!

Q13.questionRecapHtml: Identify the graph of total energy minus potential energy ($E-U$) versus displacement $x\in [-A,+A]$.
Q13.conceptHtml: By conservation of mechanical energy, $E-U=K= \frac{1}{2} k(A^2-x^2)$, a downward-opening parabola.
Q13.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the quantity $E - U$: In SHM, total mechanical energy is $E = K + U$, so $E - U = K$ (the kinetic energy of the particle).
  2. Step 2 — Write $K$ as a function of displacement $x$: $K(x) = \frac{1}{2}k(A^2 - x^2)$, where $A$ is the amplitude and $x = 0$ is the mean position.
  3. Step 3 — Analyze the graph shape: $K(x)$ is a symmetric downward-opening parabola centered at $x = 0$, reaching its maximum value $E = \frac{1}{2}kA^2$ at $x = 0$ and dropping to zero at the extreme positions $x = \pm A$.
  4. Step 4 — Match with the options: This downward-opening parabolic graph peaking at $x = 0$ is Option (a).
Q13.stepsLatex: $E-U =K(x)= \frac{1}{2} k(A^2-x^2)$ At $x=0$, $K=E$ (maximum); at $x=\pm A$, $K=0$. This downward parabola is graph (A).
Q13.trapHtml: Notice the disguised wording: "difference between total energy and potential energy" simply means kinetic energy $K(x)$!

Q14.questionRecapHtml: Identify the true statements among (A) $F\propto x$, (B)$a$ opposite $x$, (C) $v_{max}$ at mean, (D) $a_{min}$ at extremes.
Q14.conceptHtml: In SHM, $F =-kx$, $a=-\omega ^2x$ (max magnitude at extremes, zero at mean), and $v=\pm \omega A2-x2$ (max at $x=0$).
Q14.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Check Statements (A) and (B): In linear SHM, $F = -kx$ and $a = -\omega^2 x$. Thus the restoring force magnitude is directly proportional to displacement (A is true), and the minus sign shows acceleration and displacement are oppositely directed (B is true).
  2. Step 2 — Check Statements (C) and (D): Velocity is $v = \omega\sqrt{A^2 - x^2}$, which is maximum ($v_{\max} = \omega A$) at the mean position $x = 0$ (C is true). Acceleration magnitude is $|a| = \omega^2 |x|$, which is maximum (not minimum) at the extreme positions $x = \pm A$ (so D is false).
  3. Step 3 — Select the correct combination: Statements (A), (B), and (C) only are correct, matching Option (c).
Q14.stepsLatex: Statements (A), (B), and (C) are true. Statement (D) is false because acceleration magnitude $|a|=\omega ^2|x|$ is maximum at the extreme positions ($x=\pm A$) and minimum (0) at the mean position.
Q14.trapHtml: Read statement (D) carefully: velocity is zero at extremes, while acceleration is maximum there.

Q15.subtopic: Position Where Kinetic Energy Equals Potential Energy
Q15.questionRecapHtml: Particle executes SHM with amplitude $A$. Find the distance from mean position where $K=U$.
Q15.conceptHtml: Equate $U= \frac{1}{2} kx^2$ to half of total energy $E= \frac{1}{2} kA^2$.
Q15.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Write formulas for kinetic and potential energy: At displacement $x$ from the mean position, $K = \frac{1}{2}k(A^2 - x^2)$ and $U = \frac{1}{2}kx^2$.
  2. Step 2 — Equate $K$ and $U$: Setting $\frac{1}{2}k(A^2 - x^2) = \frac{1}{2}kx^2$ gives $A^2 - x^2 = x^2 \implies 2x^2 = A^2$.
  3. Step 3 — Solve for distance $|x|$: Taking the square root gives $|x| = \frac{A}{\sqrt{2}}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: The distance $\frac{A}{\sqrt{2}}$ matches Option (a).
Q15.stepsLatex:
$( ) K=U \implies U = \frac{E}{2} \implies \frac{1}{2} kx^2= \frac{1}{2} \frac{1}{2} kA^2$
$x^2= \frac{A^2}{2} \implies |x|= \sqrt{\frac{A}{2}}$
Q15.trapHtml: A must-know JEE benchmark: $K=U$ at $x=\pm A/ 2$ (and at phase $45^{^\circ}$, $t=T/8$).

Q16.subtopic: Ratio of Potential Energy to Kinetic Energy at $x=A/2$
Q16.questionRecapHtml: Find $U:K$ for a particle in SHM when its displacement is half the amplitude ($x=A/2$).
Q16.conceptHtml: Use the direct energy ratio $\frac{U}{K} = \frac{x2}{A2-x2}$.
Q16.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Substitute $x = \frac{A}{2}$ into the energy formulas: Potential energy is $U = \frac{1}{2}kx^2 = \frac{1}{2}k\left(\frac{A}{2}\right)^2 = \frac{1}{4}\left(\frac{1}{2}kA^2\right) = \frac{E}{4}$.
  2. Step 2 — Find kinetic energy: Since total energy $E = K + U$, kinetic energy is $K = E - U = E - \frac{E}{4} = \frac{3E}{4}$.
  3. Step 3 — Compute the ratio $U : K$: $\frac{U}{K} = \frac{E/4}{3E/4} = \frac{1}{3}$, i.e., $1:3$.
  4. Step 4 — Match with the options: The ratio $1:3$ corresponds to Option (d).
Q16.trapHtml: At $x=A/2$, $U=E/4$ and $K=3E/4$, so $U:K=1:3$ (always check whether the question asks $U:K$ or $K:U$).

Q17.subtopic: Kinetic Energy vs. Displacement Graph on $[0,A]$
Q17.questionRecapHtml: Identify the graph of KE versus $x$ from mean position ($x=0$) to extreme position ($x=A$).
Q17.conceptHtml: KE$(x)= \frac{1}{2} k(A^2-x^2)$ starts at its maximum at $x=0$ and curves downward parabolically to 0 at $x=A$.
Q17.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Write kinetic energy as a function of $x$: For an SHM particle, $K(x) = \frac{1}{2}k(A^2 - x^2)$.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate endpoints on $0 \le x \le A$: At the mean position $x = 0$, $K = K_{\max} = \frac{1}{2}kA^2$ (with horizontal tangent $\frac{dK}{dx} = -kx = 0$). As $x$ increases toward $A$, $K$ decreases parabolically (concave downward) and reaches $0$ at $x = A$.
  3. Step 3 — Match the graph: The concave-down parabolic curve decreasing from $K_{\max}$ at $x = 0$ to $0$ at $x = A$ is Option (c).
Q17.stepsLatex: At $x=0$, KE $= \frac{1}{2} kA^2$ with zero slope ( $\frac{dK}{dx} =-kx=0$); at $x=A$, KE $=0$. This concave-down parabolic arc matches graph (C).
Q17.trapHtml: Distinguish concave-down parabola (C) from straight line or concave-up curve (D, which represents $U$ vs. $x$).

Q18.questionRecapHtml: Find the amplitude of the periodic motion $y=\sin\omega t+\cos\omega t$.
Q18.conceptHtml: Combine $asin\omega t+bcos\omega t= a2+b2\sin(\omega t+\phi)$.
Q18.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall superposition of sine and cosine of the same frequency: Any expression of the form $y = a\sin(\omega t) + b\cos(\omega t)$ can be rewritten as $y = A\sin(\omega t + \phi)$ with amplitude $A = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$.
  2. Step 2 — Substitute the coefficients: Here $y = 1\cdot\sin(\omega t) + 1\cdot\cos(\omega t)$, so $a = 1$ and $b = 1$.
  3. Step 3 — Calculate the amplitude: $A = \sqrt{1^2 + 1^2} = \sqrt{2}$.
  4. Step 4 — Final choice: Amplitude $\sqrt{2}$ corresponds to Option (b).
Q18.stepsLatex: $\sqrt{( ) } y=si \omega t+cos\omega t= 12+12sin \omega t+ \frac{\pi}{4} = 2sin \omega t+ \frac{\pi}{4} \sqrt{\frac{n}{2}} A=$
Q18.trapHtml: Two orthogonal unit-amplitude SHMs ($\phi =\pi /2$) always combine to amplitude $12+12= 2$.

Q19.subtopic: Initial Phase from Position and Direction
Q19.questionRecapHtml: SHM $x=Asin(\omega t+\delta)$ starts at $t=0$ from $x=A/2$ moving along $+x$. Find $\delta$.
Q19.conceptHtml: Substitute $t=0$ into both $x(0)=Asin\delta =A/2$ and $v(0)=\omega Acos\delta >0$.
Q19.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Apply the initial position condition at $t = 0$: Given $x = A\sin(\omega t + \delta)$ and $x(0) = \frac{A}{2}$, we have $A\sin\delta = \frac{A}{2} \implies \sin\delta = \frac{1}{2}$. This gives two possibilities in $[0, 2\pi)$: $\delta = \frac{\pi}{6}$ or $\delta = \frac{5\pi}{6}$.
  2. Step 2 — Use the velocity direction to pick the right quadrant: Velocity is $v(t) = \frac{dx}{dt} = A\omega\cos(\omega t + \delta)$. At $t = 0$, the particle moves in the $+x$ direction, so $v(0) = A\omega\cos\delta > 0 \implies \cos\delta > 0$.
  3. Step 3 — Select $\delta$: Between $\frac{\pi}{6}$ (where $\cos\frac{\pi}{6} = +\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} > 0$) and $\frac{5\pi}{6}$ (where $\cos\frac{5\pi}{6} < 0$), only $\delta = \frac{\pi}{6}$ satisfies $v(0) > 0$.
  4. Step 4 — Match with the options: $\delta = \frac{\pi}{6}$ corresponds to Option (d).
Q19.stepsLatex:
$sin\delta = \frac{1}{2} \implies \delta = \frac{\pi}{6}$ or $\frac{5\pi}{6}$
$v(0)=\omega Acos\delta >0 \implies cos\delta >0 \implies \delta = \frac{\pi}{6}$
Q19.trapHtml: Always check the velocity sign! Moving toward $+x$ picks the first-quadrant angle $\pi /6$, whereas moving toward $-x$ would pick $5\pi /6$.

Q20.subtopic: SHM as Projection of Uniform Circular Motion
Q20.questionRecapHtml: Particle $P$ revolves counter-clockwise around $O$ with radius $r$, angular velocity $\omega$, starting at $30^{^\circ}$ above $+x$. Find $x(t)$.
Q20.conceptHtml: Counter-clockwise angle from $+x$-axis at time $t$ is $\theta (t)=\omega t+\theta _0=\omega t+ \frac{\pi}{6}$; projection on $x$-axis is $rcos\theta (t)$.
Q20.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Read the initial angle and rotation direction from the figure: At $t = 0$, the radius vector $OP$ makes an angle $\theta_0 = 30^\circ = \frac{\pi}{6}$ above the $+x$-axis, and the arrow shows anticlockwise rotation at angular velocity $\omega$.
  2. Step 2 — Find the angular position at time $t$: Since the particle rotates anticlockwise, its angle with the $+x$-axis increases linearly with time: $\theta(t) = \omega t + \frac{\pi}{6}$.
  3. Step 3 — Project $OP$ onto the $x$-axis: The $x$-coordinate of $P$ is $x(t) = r\cos\theta(t) = r\cos\left(\omega t + \frac{\pi}{6}\right)$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: This matches Option (c).
Q20.stepsLatex:
$\theta (t)=\omega t+30^{^\circ}=\omega t+ \frac{\pi}{(6}$
) $x(t)=rcos\theta (t)=rcos \omega t+ \frac{\pi}{6}$
$\pi$
Q20.trapHtml: Option (A) is dimensionally invalid ($_6\omega$ is not dimensionless); $x$-projection always takes $\cos\theta (t)$ when $\theta$ is measured from $+x$.

Q21.questionRecapHtml: Mass $m$ on a smooth surface is connected between two springs $K_1$ and $K_2$ attached to opposite walls. Find $T$.
Q21.conceptHtml: Displacing $m$ by $x$ compresses one spring by $x$ and stretches the other by $x$; both push back in the same direction, so $K_{eq}=K_1+K_2$.
Q21.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Analyze the restoring force for a small displacement $x$: When the block is displaced by $x$ to the right, one spring stretches by $x$ (pulling left with $K_1 x$) and the other compresses by $x$ (pushing left with $K_2 x$).
  2. Step 2 — Find the equivalent spring constant: Both forces act in the same restoring direction, so $F_{\text{net}} = -(K_1 + K_2)x$. The springs act in parallel with $K_{\text{eq}} = K_1 + K_2$.
  3. Step 3 — Write the oscillation period: $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{m}{K_{\text{eq}}}} = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{m}{K_1 + K_2}}$.
  4. Step 4 — Match with the options: This matches Option (a).
Q21.stepsLatex: $F_{net}=-K_1x-K_2x=-(K_1+K_2)x \implies K_{eq}=K_1+K_2 \sqrt{T} =2\pi \frac{m}{K_1+K_2}$
Q21.trapHtml: Even though the springs sit on opposite sides visually, they act in parallel ($K_{eq}=K_1+K_2$), never in series!

Q22.subtopic: Graph of $T^2$ vs. Length $L$ for Simple Pendulum
Q22.questionRecapHtml:
Identify the correct graph of $T^2$ versus length $L$ for a simple pendulum.
$\sqrt{( 2)}$
Q22.conceptHtml: Squaring $T =2\pi L/g$ gives $T^2= \frac{4\pi}{g} L$, a straight line through the origin with positive slope.
Q22.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Square the simple pendulum period formula: Starting from $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{L}{g}}$, squaring both sides yields $T^2 = \left(\frac{4\pi^2}{g}\right)L$.
  2. Step 2 — Identify the graph shape: This has the linear form $y = mx$ with positive constant slope $m = \frac{4\pi^2}{g}$ and zero $y$-intercept, so the plot of $T^2$ versus $L$ is a straight line passing through the origin.
  3. Step 3 — Match with the options: The straight line through the origin with positive slope is shown in Option (d).
Q22.stepsLatex:
Since $T^2\propto L$ with zero intercept and slope $4\pi ^2/g>0$, the graph is a straight line passing through the origin in the first quadrant,
matching (D).
Q22.trapHtml: Compare Q11 ($1/T^2$ vs. $L$: hyperbola) with Q34 ($T^2$ vs. $L$: straight line through origin).

Q23.subtopic: Kinetic Energy at $x=A/2$ from Maximum Potential Energy
Q23.questionRecapHtml:
Maximum potential energy of an SHM block is 25 J. Find its kinetic energy at displacement $x=A/2$.
$( 2)$
Q23.conceptHtml: Maximum PE equals total energy $E=25$ J; kinetic energy at $x$ is $K=E 1- \frac{x}{A2}$.
Q23.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Relate maximum potential energy to total energy: In SHM, maximum potential energy occurs at the extreme position ($K = 0$), so total mechanical energy is $E = U_{\max} = \frac{1}{2}kA^2 = 25\text{ J}$.
  2. Step 2 — Find potential energy at $x = A/2$: $U = \frac{1}{2}k\left(\frac{A}{2}\right)^2 = \frac{1}{4}\left(\frac{1}{2}kA^2\right) = \frac{25}{4} = 6.25\text{ J}$.
  3. Step 3 — Calculate kinetic energy: $K = E - U = 25 - 6.25 = 18.75\text{ J}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: $K = 18.75\text{ J}$ matches Option (c).
Q23.trapHtml: At half-amplitude, $25%$ of total energy is potential (6.25 J) and $75%$ is kinetic (18.75 J).

Q24.subtopic: Angular Frequency Ratio for Two Block Masses
Q24.questionRecapHtml: Horizontal spring-mass system has angular frequency $\omega _1$ for 1 kg and $\omega _2$ for 2 kg. Find $\omega _2/\omega _1$.
Q24.conceptHtml: Angular frequency $\omega = k/m\propto 1/ m$ for the same spring constant $k$.
Q24.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall angular frequency of a spring-block oscillator: $\omega = \sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}$, so for the same spring ($k$ constant), $\omega \propto \frac{1}{\sqrt{m}}$.
  2. Step 2 — Compute the ratio $\omega_2 / \omega_1$: With $m_1 = 1\text{ kg}$ and $m_2 = 2\text{ kg}$, $\frac{\omega_2}{\omega_1} = \sqrt{\frac{m_1}{m_2}} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{2}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$.
  3. Step 3 — Match with the options: $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$ corresponds to Option (a).
Q24.stepsLatex: $\sqrt{\sqrt}{\frac{\omega _2}{\omega _1}} = \frac{m_1}{m_2} = \frac{1}{2} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{2}}$
Q24.trapHtml: Double-check the ratio order: $\omega _2/\omega _1$ (heavier mass on top $\implies$ smaller $\omega _2 \implies$ ratio $<1$).

Q25.questionRecapHtml: In SHM between $-A$ and $+A$, time from 0 to $A/2$ is 2 s. Find time from $A/2$ to $A$.
Q25.conceptHtml: From the phase circle, $0\to A/2$ takes $T/12$ while $A/2\to A$ takes $T/6$ (twice as long because the particle slows down near $A$).
Q25.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Use the phase relation for $x = 0 \to x = A/2$: Starting from the mean position, $x = A\sin(\omega t)$. At $x = \frac{A}{2}$, $\sin(\omega t_1) = \frac{1}{2} \implies \omega t_1 = \frac{\pi}{6}$, which means $t_1 = \frac{T}{12}$.
  2. Step 2 — Find the total time period $T$: Given $t_1 = 2\text{ s}$, we get $\frac{T}{12} = 2\text{ s} \implies T = 24\text{ s}$.
  3. Step 3 — Find the time from $x = A/2$ to $x = A$: Reaching $x = A$ from $x = 0$ takes $\frac{T}{4} = 6\text{ s}$. Therefore, moving from $x = \frac{A}{2}$ to $x = A$ takes $t_2 = \frac{T}{4} - \frac{T}{12} = \frac{T}{6} = \frac{24}{6} = 4\text{ s}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: $4\text{ s}$ matches Option (a).
Q25.stepsLatex:
$T t_{0\to A/2}= =2$ s $\implies T =24$ s
$tA/2\to A= \frac{1T2}{4} - \frac{T}{12} = \frac{T}{6} = \frac{24}{6} =4$ s
Q25.trapHtml: Never assume constant speed! The outer half ($A/2\to A$) always takes twice as long as the inner half ($0\to A/2$).

Q26.questionRecapHtml:
Pendulum period $T$ on Earth’s surface becomes $xT$ at height $R$ above the surface. Find $x$.
$( )$
Q26.conceptHtml: Using $T(h)=T 1+ \frac{h}{R}$ for $h=R$ gives $T(R)=2T$.
Q26.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Compare gravity at the surface and at altitude $h = R$: On Earth's surface ($r_1 = R$), $g_1 = \frac{GM}{R^2}$. At altitude $R$ ($r_2 = 2R$), $g_2 = \frac{GM}{(2R)^2} = \frac{g_1}{4}$.
  2. Step 2 — Calculate the new time period: Since $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{l}{g}}$, the period at altitude $R$ is $T' = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{l}{g_1/4}} = 2\left(2\pi\sqrt{\frac{l}{g_1}}\right) = 2T$.
  3. Step 3 — Identify $x$: Comparing $T' = xT$ with $2T$ gives $x = 2$, which matches Option (c).
Q26.stepsLatex:
$g^'= \frac{g}{(1+R/R)2} = \frac{g}{4}$
$T^'=2\pi \frac{L}{g/4} =2T \implies x=2$
Q26.trapHtml: A 10-second mental formula: $T(h)=T_0(1+h/R)$. At $h=R$, $x=1+1=2$.

Q27.subtopic: Time Period from Linear Restoring Force
Q27.questionRecapHtml: Mass 0.50 kg moves under $F=-50x$ N. Time period is $x/35$ s ($\pi =22/7$); find $x$.
Q27.conceptHtml: Identify $k=50$ N/m from $F =-kx$ and compute $T =2\pi m/k$.
Q27.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Extract mass and spring constant: From $F = -50x$, the force constant is $k = 50\text{ N/m}$, and the particle's mass is $m = 0.50\text{ kg}$.
  2. Step 2 — Compute the time period: $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{m}{k}} = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{0.50}{50}} = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{1}{100}} = \frac{2\pi}{10} = \frac{\pi}{5}\text{ s}$.
  3. Step 3 — Substitute $\pi = \frac{22}{7}$: $T = \frac{1}{5} \times \frac{22}{7} = \frac{22}{35}\text{ s}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the numerical answer: Comparing with $\frac{x}{35}\text{ s}$ gives $x = \mathbf{22}$.
Q27.stepsLatex: $\sqrt{\sqrt}{} \sqrt{T} =2\pi \frac{m}{k} =2\times \frac{22}{7} \frac{0.5}{50} = \frac{44}{7} \frac{1}{100} = \frac{44}{70} = \frac{22}{35}$ s Hence $x=22$.
Q27.trapHtml: Reduce the fraction $\frac{44}{70} = \frac{22}{35}$ cleanly to match the denominator 35.

Q28.questionRecapHtml: At an instant in SHM, $|x|=4$ m, $|v|=2$ m/s, $|a|=16$ m/$s^2$. Amplitude is $x$ m; find $x$.
Q28.conceptHtml: Extract $\omega ^2=|a|/|x|$ first, then plug into $v^2=\omega ^2(A^2-x^2)$.
Q28.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Find $\omega^2$ from acceleration and displacement: In SHM, $|a| = \omega^2 |x|$. Given $|a| = 16\text{ m/s}^2$ and $|x| = 4\text{ m}$, we get $\omega^2 = \frac{16}{4} = 4\text{ rad}^2/\text{s}^2$.
  2. Step 2 — Use the velocity-displacement relation to find $A^2$: $v^2 = \omega^2(A^2 - x^2)$. Substituting $v = 2\text{ m/s}$, $\omega^2 = 4$, and $x = 4\text{ m}$ gives $2^2 = 4(A^2 - 4^2) \implies 4 = 4(A^2 - 16)$.
  3. Step 3 — Solve for amplitude $A$: $1 = A^2 - 16 \implies A^2 = 17 \implies A = \sqrt{17}\text{ m}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the numerical answer: Comparing with $A = \sqrt{x}\text{ m}$ gives $x = \mathbf{17}$.
Q28.stepsLatex:
$\omega ^2= \frac{|a|}{|x|} = \frac{16}{4} =4 s^{-2}$
Thus $x=17$. $2 2 2 \sqrt{A} =x + \frac{v^2}{\omega 2} =4 + \frac{2^2}{4} =16+1=17 \implies A= 17$ m
$v2x 4\times 4$
Q28.trapHtml: Clean two-line formula: $A^2=x^2+ =16+ =17$. $|a| 16$

Q29.subtopic: Amplitude from Instantaneous KE, PE and Frequency
Q29.questionRecapHtml: Mass 0.2 kg oscillates at $f=(25/\pi)$ Hz. At $x=0.04$ m, $K=0.5$ J and $U=0.4$ J. Find amplitude in cm.
Q29.conceptHtml: Total energy $E=K+U= \frac{1}{2} m\omega ^2A^2$ with $\omega =2\pi f$.
Q29.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Compute angular frequency $\omega$: Given frequency $f = \frac{25}{\pi}\text{ Hz}$, $\omega = 2\pi f = 2\pi \times \frac{25}{\pi} = 50\text{ rad/s}$.
  2. Step 2 — Find total mechanical energy $E$: At $x = 0.04\text{ m}$, $K = 0.5\text{ J}$ and $U = 0.4\text{ J}$, so total energy is $E = K + U = 0.5 + 0.4 = 0.9\text{ J}$.
  3. Step 3 — Solve for amplitude $A$: Using $E = \frac{1}{2}m\omega^2 A^2$ with $m = 0.2\text{ kg}$: $0.9 = \frac{1}{2}(0.2)(50^2)A^2 = 250 A^2 \implies A^2 = \frac{0.9}{250} = \frac{9}{2500}$.
  4. Step 4 — Convert to centimetres and confirm: Taking the square root gives $A = \frac{3}{50}\text{ m} = 0.06\text{ m} = 6\text{ cm}$. The numerical answer is 6.
Q29.trapHtml: Note that $x=0.04$ m is redundant data (and self-consistent since $U= \frac{1}{2} (500)(0.04)^2=0.4$ J)! Remember to convert to cm.

Q30.subtopic: Maximum Velocity from Amplitude and Period
Q30.questionRecapHtml: SHM has $A=0.06$ m and $T=3.14$ s. Find $v_{max}$ in cm/s.
Q30.conceptHtml: $vmax=\omega A= \frac{2\pi}{T} A$, noting $T =3.14\approx \pi$.
Q30.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Convert amplitude to centimetres and find $\omega$: $A = 0.06\text{ m} = 6\text{ cm}$, and $T = 3.14\text{ s} \approx \pi\text{ s}$, so $\omega = \frac{2\pi}{T} = \frac{2\pi}{\pi} = 2\text{ rad/s}$.
  2. Step 2 — Calculate maximum speed: $v_{\max} = \omega A = 2 \times 6 = 12\text{ cm/s}$.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the numerical answer: The maximum speed is 12 cm/s.
Q30.stepsLatex:
$\omega = \frac{2\pi}{3.14} \approx 2$ rad/s
$v_{max}=\omega A=2\times 0.06$ m/s $=0.12$ m/s $=12$ cm/s
Q30.trapHtml: Watch the requested output unit (cm/s, not m/s): 0.12 m/s $=12$ cm/s.

Q31.questionRecapHtml: For $x=10\sin(\omega t+\pi /3)$ m with $T=3.14$ s, find velocity at $t=0$ in m/s.
Q31.conceptHtml: Differentiate $x(t)$ to get $v(t)=10\omega \cos(\omega t+\pi /3)$ and substitute $t=0$, $\omega =2\pi /T \approx 2$ rad/s.
Q31.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Differentiate displacement to get velocity: Given $x = 10\sin\left(\omega t + \frac{\pi}{3}\right)\text{ m}$, velocity is $v(t) = \frac{dx}{dt} = 10\omega\cos\left(\omega t + \frac{\pi}{3}\right)\text{ m/s}$.
  2. Step 2 — Find $\omega$ from the time period: With $T = 3.14\text{ s} \approx \pi\text{ s}$, $\omega = \frac{2\pi}{T} = \frac{2\pi}{\pi} = 2\text{ rad/s}$.
  3. Step 3 — Evaluate velocity at $t = 0$: $v(0) = 10(2)\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{3}\right) = 20 \times \frac{1}{2} = 10\text{ m/s}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the numerical answer: The velocity at $t = 0$ is 10 m/s.
Q31.stepsLatex: $\omega = \frac{2\pi}{3.14} \approx 2$ rad/s $( ) v(0)=10\omega cos \frac{\pi}{3} =10(2) \frac{1}{2} =10$ m/s
Q31.trapHtml: Whenever NTA gives $T =3.14$ s, immediately set $\omega =2\pi /\pi =2$ rad/s!

Q32.subtopic: Frequency Ratio for Two Masses on Same Spring
Q32.questionRecapHtml:
Mass $m$ oscillates at $f_1$ and mass $9m$ oscillates at $f_2$ on the same spring. Find $f_1/f_2$.
1
Q32.conceptHtml: Since $f=_{2\pi} k/m\propto 1/ m$, we get $f_1/f_2= m_2/m_1$.
Q32.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall frequency dependence on mass: For a spring-mass system, $f = \frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}$, so for the same spring ($k$ fixed), $f \propto \frac{1}{\sqrt{m}}$.
  2. Step 2 — Compute the ratio $f_1 / f_2$: With $m_1 = m$ and $m_2 = 9m$, we get $\frac{f_1}{f_2} = \sqrt{\frac{m_2}{m_1}} = \sqrt{\frac{9m}{m}} = \sqrt{9} = 3$.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the numerical answer: The ratio $\frac{f_1}{f_2}$ is 3.
Q32.stepsLatex: $ \frac{f_1}{f_2} = \frac{9m}{m} = 9=3$
Q32.trapHtml: Heavier mass oscillates slower, so $f_1>f_2 \implies f_1/f_2=3$.

Q33.questionRecapHtml: Four identical springs $k$ support mass $M$ (one full-length spring in parallel with a branch of two parallel springs in series with a fourth). Period is $\pi \sqrt{\alpha M/(5k); find \alpha.}$
Q33.conceptHtml: Reduce the right branch first (two parallel $k$’s $\to 2k$, in series with $k\to 2k/3$), then add in parallel with the left spring $k$.
Q33.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Simplify the right-hand spring branch: From the figure, the two upper springs on the right (each of stiffness $k$) are in parallel, giving $k_p = k + k = 2k$. This parallel pair is in series with the lower spring of stiffness $k$, giving $k_{\text{right}} = \frac{(2k)(k)}{2k + k} = \frac{2k}{3}$.
  2. Step 2 — Combine left and right branches in parallel: The single left spring (stiffness $k$) and the right branch ($k_{\text{right}} = \frac{2k}{3}$) both connect the ceiling directly to mass $M$, so they act in parallel: $k_{\text{eq}} = k + \frac{2k}{3} = \frac{5k}{3}$.
  3. Step 3 — Compute the time period: $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{M}{k_{\text{eq}}}} = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{3M}{5k}} = \pi\sqrt{\frac{4 \times 3M}{5k}} = \pi\sqrt{\frac{12M}{5k}}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the numerical answer: Comparing with $\pi\sqrt{\frac{\alpha M}{5k}}$ gives $\alpha = \mathbf{12}$.

$k_{eq}=k+k_{right}=k+ \frac{2k}{3} = \frac{5k}{3} \sqrt{\sqrt}{} \sqrt{T} =2\pi \frac{M}{k} =2\pi \frac{3M}{5k} =\pi \frac{12M}{5k} \implies \alpha =12$ eq
Q33.trapHtml: Remember to pull the factor 2 inside the square root as 4: $2 3/5= 12/5$, so $\alpha =12$ (not 3)!

Q34.subtopic: New Amplitude After Instantaneous Speed Change
Q34.questionRecapHtml: SHM of amplitude $A$ has its speed tripled at $x=2A/3$. New amplitude is $nA/3$; find $n$.
Q34.conceptHtml: An instantaneous velocity kick does not change $\omega$; apply $v^{'2}=\omega ^2(A^{'2}-x^2)$ with $v^'=3v$.
Q34.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Find the initial speed at $x = \frac{2A}{3}$: Using $v = \omega\sqrt{A^2 - x^2}$, we get $v = \omega\sqrt{A^2 - \frac{4A^2}{9}} = \omega\sqrt{\frac{5A^2}{9}} = \frac{\sqrt{5}}{3}\omega A$.
  2. Step 2 — Triple the speed at the same position: The new speed at $x = \frac{2A}{3}$ is $v' = 3v = \sqrt{5}\,\omega A$. Since the restoring system is unchanged, $\omega$ remains the same.
  3. Step 3 — Solve for the new amplitude $A'$: Applying $v'^2 = \omega^2(A'^2 - x^2)$ gives $5\omega^2 A^2 = \omega^2\left(A'^2 - \frac{4A^2}{9}\right) \implies A'^2 = \left(5 + \frac{4}{9}\right)A^2 = \frac{49}{9}A^2 \implies A' = \frac{7A}{3}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the numerical answer: Comparing with $\frac{nA}{3}$ gives $n = \mathbf{7}$.
Q34.stepsLatex:
$( ) v^2=\omega ^2 A^2- \frac{4A^2}{9} = \frac{5}{(9} \omega ^2A^2$
) $v^{'2}=9v^2=5\omega ^2A^2=\omega ^2 A^{'2}- \frac{4A^2}{9}$
$A^{'2}=5A^2+ \frac{4A^2}{9} = \frac{49A^2}{9} \implies A^'= \frac{7A}{3} \implies n=7$
Q34.trapHtml: Using $v^2/\omega ^2=A^2-x^2$ keeps $\omega$ completely cancelled out and yields a clean square $49/9$.

Q35.questionRecapHtml: SHM has amplitude $A$ and period $6\pi$ s. Time from $x=A$ to $x= \frac{3}{2} A$ is $\pi /x$ s; find $x$.
Q35.conceptHtml: Measuring from extreme position, $x=Acos(\omega t)$ gives $\cos(\omega t)= 3/2 \implies \omega t=\pi /6 \implies t=T/12$.
Q35.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Find the angular frequency $\omega$: Given time period $T = 6\pi\text{ s}$, $\omega = \frac{2\pi}{T} = \frac{2\pi}{6\pi} = \frac{1}{3}\text{ rad/s}$.
  2. Step 2 — Measure time from the extreme position $x = A$: Using $x = A\cos(\omega t)$ (where $t = 0$ corresponds to $x = A$), set $x = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}A$: $\cos(\omega t) = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \implies \omega t = \frac{\pi}{6}$.
  3. Step 3 — Solve for $t$: $t = \frac{\pi}{6\omega} = \frac{\pi}{6 \times (1/3)} = \frac{\pi}{2}\text{ s}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the numerical answer: Comparing with $\frac{\pi}{x}\text{ s}$ gives $x = \mathbf{2}$.
Q35.stepsLatex:

$t= \frac{T2}{12} = \frac{6\pi}{12} = \frac{\pi}{2}$ s $\implies x=2$
Q35.trapHtml: Even though the oscillator started at mean position initially, the time between $A$ and $\frac{3}{2} A$ is always $T/12$.

Q36.subtopic: Ratio of Total Energy to Kinetic Energy at $x=A/3$
Q36.questionRecapHtml:
At displacement $x=A/3$, the ratio $E/K=x/8$. Find $x$.
2
Q36.conceptHtml: Use $\frac{E}{K} = \frac{A}{A2-x2}$.
Q36.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Write total energy and kinetic energy: $E = \frac{1}{2}kA^2$ and $K = \frac{1}{2}k(A^2 - x^2)$.
  2. Step 2 — Substitute $x = \frac{A}{3}$: $K = \frac{1}{2}k\left(A^2 - \frac{A^2}{9}\right) = \frac{8}{9}\left(\frac{1}{2}kA^2\right) = \frac{8}{9}E$.
  3. Step 3 — Compute the ratio $E / K$: $\frac{E}{K} = \frac{E}{\frac{8}{9}E} = \frac{9}{8}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the numerical answer: Comparing with $\frac{x}{8}$ gives $x = \mathbf{9}$.
Q36.stepsLatex: $\frac{E}{K} = \frac{A^2}{A2-(A/3)2} = \frac{1}{1-1/9} = \frac{9}{8} \implies x=9$
Q36.trapHtml: Check that total energy is strictly larger than kinetic energy ($E/K>1$), confirming $9/8$.

Q37.subtopic: Displacement from Mean-Position Speed and Current Speed
Q37.questionRecapHtml: SHM has $A=4$ cm and $v_{max}=10$ cm/s. Distance from mean when $v=5$ cm/s is $\alpha$ cm; find $\alpha$.
Q37.conceptHtml: Divide $v=\omega A2-x2$ by $v_{max}=\omega A$ to eliminate $\omega$: $(v/v_{max})^2+(x/A)^2=1$.
Q37.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Find $\omega$ from mean-position speed: At the mean position, $v_{\max} = \omega A$. Given $v_{\max} = 10\text{ cm/s}$ and $A = 4\text{ cm}$, we get $\omega = \frac{10}{4} = 2.5\text{ rad/s}$.
  2. Step 2 — Use the velocity-displacement equation: $v^2 = \omega^2(A^2 - x^2)$. Notice that $v = 5\text{ cm/s} = \frac{v_{\max}}{2}$, so $\frac{v^2}{v_{\max}^2} = \frac{1}{4} = 1 - \frac{x^2}{A^2}$.
  3. Step 3 — Solve for $x$: $\frac{x^2}{A^2} = \frac{3}{4} \implies x^2 = \frac{3}{4}(4^2) = 12 \implies x = \sqrt{12}\text{ cm}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the numerical answer: Comparing with $\sqrt{\alpha}\text{ cm}$ gives $\alpha = \mathbf{12}$.
Q37.stepsLatex: $( )2 ( )2 ( )2 ( )2 \frac{v}{vmax} + \frac{x}{A} =1 \implies \frac{5}{10} + \frac{x}{4} =1$ Thus $\alpha =12$. $_2 \sqrt{\frac{x^2}{16}} =1- \frac{1}{4} = \frac{3}{4} \implies x =12 \implies x= 12$ cm
Q37.trapHtml: The ellipse identity $(v/v_{max})^2+(x/A)^2=1$ avoids calculating $\omega$ altogether!

Q38.subtopic: Force Constant from Kinetic Energy at $y=Acos30^{^\circ}$
Q38.questionRecapHtml: At $y=Acos30^{^\circ}$ with $A=40$ cm, kinetic energy is 200 J. Force constant is $1.0\times 10^x$ N/m; find $x$.
Q38.conceptHtml: Use $K= \frac{1}{2} k(A^2-y^2)= \frac{1}{2} kA^2\sin^230^{^\circ}$ and convert $A=0.4$ m.
Q38.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Express kinetic energy at $y = A\cos 30^\circ$: $K = \frac{1}{2}k(A^2 - y^2) = \frac{1}{2}kA^2(1 - \cos^2 30^\circ) = \frac{1}{2}kA^2\sin^2 30^\circ$.
  2. Step 2 — Substitute given values in SI units: With $A = 40\text{ cm} = 0.4\text{ m}$, $\sin 30^\circ = \frac{1}{2}$, and $K = 200\text{ J}$, we get $200 = \frac{1}{2}k(0.4)^2\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^2 = \frac{1}{2}k(0.16)(0.25) = 0.02k$.
  3. Step 3 — Solve for spring constant $k$: $k = \frac{200}{0.02} = 10000 = 1.0 \times 10^4\text{ N/m}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the numerical answer: Comparing with $1.0 \times 10^x\text{ N/m}$ gives $x = \mathbf{4}$.
Q38.trapHtml: Watch units: $A=40$ cm $=0.4$ m; forgetting to convert cm to m would give $x=0$ instead of 4.

Q39.subtopic: Maximum Spring Force from Mass, Amplitude and Period
Q39.questionRecapHtml: A 5 kg block on a spring executes SHM with $A=1$ m and $T=3.14$ s. Find $F_{max}$ in N.
Q39.conceptHtml: Maximum restoring force is $F_{max}=ma_{max}=m\omega ^2A$, with $\omega =2\pi /T \approx 2$ rad/s.
Q39.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Find angular frequency $\omega$: With period $T = 3.14\text{ s} \approx \pi\text{ s}$, $\omega = \frac{2\pi}{T} = \frac{2\pi}{\pi} = 2\text{ rad/s}$.
  2. Step 2 — Calculate maximum restoring force: The maximum force exerted by the spring occurs at the extreme position: $F_{\max} = m a_{\max} = m\omega^2 A$.
  3. Step 3 — Substitute values: With $m = 5\text{ kg}$, $\omega = 2\text{ rad/s}$, and $A = 1\text{ m}$, $F_{\max} = 5 \times 2^2 \times 1 = 20\text{ N}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the numerical answer: The maximum spring force is 20 N.
Q39.stepsLatex: $\omega = \frac{2\pi}{3.14_2} \approx 2$ rad/s $F_{max}=m\omega A=5\times 2^2\times 1=20$ N
Q39.trapHtml: Recognize $T =3.14$ s $\implies \omega =2$ rad/s immediately to finish in 10 seconds.

Q40.subtopic: Maximum Tension in a Simple Pendulum String
Q40.questionRecapHtml:
Simple pendulum ($L=100$ cm, $m=250$ g, $A=10$ cm, $g=10$ m/$s^2$) has max string tension $x/40$ N. Find $x$.
$mv2$
Q40.conceptHtml: Maximum tension occurs at the lowest (mean) position: $T_{max}=mg+ \frac{max}{L} =mg(1+\theta _0^2)$ for small $\theta _0=A/L$.
Q40.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the parameters in SI units: For a simple pendulum of length $L = 100\text{ cm} = 1\text{ m}$, bob mass $m = 250\text{ g} = 0.25\text{ kg}$, amplitude $A = 10\text{ cm} = 0.1\text{ m}$, and $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$, the small angular amplitude is $\theta_0 = \frac{A}{L} = 0.1\text{ rad}$.
  2. Step 2 — Write maximum string tension at the lowest point: At the mean position, speed is maximum ($v_{\max} = \omega A = \sqrt{\frac{g}{L}}A$), so $T_{\max} = mg + \frac{mv_{\max}^2}{L} = mg\left(1 + \frac{A^2}{L^2}\right) = mg(1 + \theta_0^2)$.
  3. Step 3 — Compute $T_{\max}$: $mg = 0.25 \times 10 = 2.5\text{ N} = \frac{100}{40}\text{ N}$, and $1 + \theta_0^2 = 1 + (0.1)^2 = 1.01 = \frac{101}{100}$. Therefore, $T_{\max} = \frac{100}{40} \times \frac{101}{100} = \frac{101}{40}\text{ N}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the numerical answer: Comparing with $\frac{x}{40}\text{ N}$ gives $x = \mathbf{101}$.
Q40.trapHtml: Using energy conservation $v_m^2_{ax}=2gL(1-\cos\theta _0)\approx gL\theta _0^2$ gives $T_{max}=mg(1+\theta _0^2)$ directly!

Q41.subtopic: Displacement Where KE Exceeds PE by $25%$
Q41.questionRecapHtml:
SHM has amplitude $A=3$ cm. Find displacement $x$ (in cm) where kinetic energy is $25%$ more than potential energy.
5
Q41.conceptHtml: "$25%$ more than PE" means $K=1.25U=_4U$; substitute into $K+U=E$.
Q41.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Translate the energy condition into an equation: Kinetic energy exceeds potential energy by $25\%$, meaning $K = U + 0.25U = 1.25U = \frac{5}{4}U$.
  2. Step 2 — Relate $U$ to total energy $E$: Since $E = K + U = \frac{5}{4}U + U = \frac{9}{4}U$, we have $\frac{U}{E} = \frac{4}{9}$.
  3. Step 3 — Solve for displacement $x$: Because $\frac{U}{E} = \frac{\frac{1}{2}kx^2}{\frac{1}{2}kA^2} = \frac{x^2}{A^2}$, we get $\frac{x^2}{A^2} = \frac{4}{9} \implies x = \frac{2}{3}A$. With $A = 3\text{ cm}$, $x = \frac{2}{3}(3) = 2\text{ cm}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the numerical answer: The displacement is 2 cm.
Q41.stepsLatex: $K= \frac{5}{14} U \implies U+ \frac{5}{4} U =E \implies \frac{9}{4} U =E ( ) \frac{9}{4} \frac{1}{2} kx^2 = kA^2 \implies x^2= \frac{4}{9} A^2 \implies x= \frac{2}{3} A= \frac{2}{3} (3)=2$ cm 2
Q41.trapHtml: Read "$25%$ more than PE" carefully: $K=1.25U$ (NOT $K=0.25U$).

Q42.subtopic: Oscillation Count for Block Between Two Springs
Q42.questionRecapHtml: Block $M=490$ g sits between two springs ($K=2$ N/m each) on a smooth table. Find number of oscillations in $14\pi$ s.
Q42.conceptHtml: Opposing springs act in parallel ($K_{eq}=2K=4$ N/m); compute $T =2\pi M/K_{eq}$ and $N=t/T$.
Q42.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Find equivalent spring constant from the diagram: The block is between two horizontal springs of stiffness $K = 2\text{ N/m}$ fixed to opposite walls. Displacing the block stretches one spring and compresses the other, so they act in parallel: $k_{\text{eq}} = K + K = 4\text{ N/m}$.
  2. Step 2 — Calculate the time period $T$: With $M = 490\text{ g} = 0.49\text{ kg}$, $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{M}{k_{\text{eq}}}} = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{0.49}{4}} = 2\pi \times \frac{0.7}{2} = 0.7\pi\text{ s}$.
  3. Step 3 — Find the number of complete oscillations in $14\pi\text{ s}$: $N = \frac{t}{T} = \frac{14\pi}{0.7\pi} = 20$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the numerical answer: The block executes 20 complete oscillations.
Q42.trapHtml: Remember $M=490$ g $=0.49$ kg whose square root is 0.7 cleanly; using series $K_{eq}=K/2$ would halve $N$ to 10.

Q43.questionRecapHtml: Velocity and displacement satisfy $4v^2=50-x^2$. Period is $x/7$ s ($\pi =22/7$); find $x$.
Q43.conceptHtml: Divide by 4 to match $v^2=\omega ^2(A^2-x^2)$ and extract $\omega$.
Q43.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Rewrite the velocity equation in standard SHM form: Dividing $4v^2 = 50 - x^2$ by $4$ gives $v^2 = \frac{1}{4}(50 - x^2)$.
  2. Step 2 — Identify $\omega$: Comparing with $v^2 = \omega^2(A^2 - x^2)$ yields $\omega^2 = \frac{1}{4} \implies \omega = \frac{1}{2}\text{ rad/s}$.
  3. Step 3 — Calculate the time period: $T = \frac{2\pi}{\omega} = \frac{2\pi}{1/2} = 4\pi$. Substituting $\pi = \frac{22}{7}$ gives $T = 4 \times \frac{22}{7} = \frac{88}{7}\text{ s}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the numerical answer: Comparing with $\frac{x}{7}\text{ s}$ gives $x = \mathbf{88}$.
Q43.stepsLatex:
$v^2= \frac{1}{24} (50-x^2) \implies \omega ^2= \frac{1}{848} \implies \omega = \frac{1}{2}$ rad/s
$T = \frac{\pi}{\omega} =4\pi =4\times \frac{22}{7} =$ s $\implies x=88$ 7
Q43.trapHtml: Compare directly with Q39 ($v^2=50-x^2 \implies T =44/7$ s): the factor of 4 on $v^2$ halves $\omega$ and doubles $T$!

Q44.subtopic: Maximum Slope of Potential Energy vs. Time Curve
Q44.questionRecapHtml: For $x=Asin\omega t$ (period $T$), slope of $U(t)$ vs. $t$ is maximum at $t=T/\beta$. Find $\beta$.
Q44.conceptHtml: Differentiate $U(t)= \frac{1}{2} kA^2\sin^2(\omega t)$ to find $\frac{dU}{dt} = \frac{1}{2} kA^2\omega \sin(2\omega t)$, maximized at $2\omega t=\pi /2$.
Q44.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Express potential energy as a function of time: Given $x = A\sin(\omega t)$, potential energy is $U(t) = \frac{1}{2}kx^2 = \frac{1}{2}kA^2\sin^2(\omega t)$.
  2. Step 2 — Differentiate $U(t)$ to find the slope: $\frac{dU}{dt} = \frac{1}{2}kA^2(2\sin\omega t\cos\omega t)\omega = \frac{1}{2}kA^2\omega\sin(2\omega t)$.
  3. Step 3 — Maximize the slope: $\frac{dU}{dt}$ is maximum when $\sin(2\omega t) = 1$, which first occurs at $2\omega t = \frac{\pi}{2} \implies t = \frac{\pi}{4\omega}$. Substituting $\omega = \frac{2\pi}{T}$ gives $t = \frac{\pi}{4(2\pi/T)} = \frac{T}{8}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the numerical answer: Comparing with $t = \frac{T}{\beta}$ gives $\beta = \mathbf{8}$.
Q44.stepsLatex:
$U(t)= \frac{1}{2} kA^2sin^2(\omega t)$
$\frac{dU}{dt} =kA^2\omega sin(\omega t)cos(\omega t)= \frac{1}{\pi 2} kA^2\omega sin(2\omega t)$ Hence $\beta =8$.
$sin(2\omega t)=1 \implies 2\omega t= \frac{\pi}{2} \implies \frac{4}{T} t= \frac{\pi}{2} \implies t= \frac{T}{8}$
Q44.trapHtml: Notice the distinction: $U$ itself is max at $t=T/4$ (Q40), whereas the rate of change $dU/dt$ is max at $t=T/8$ (when $U=K=E/2$).

Q45.subtopic: Amplitude from Restoring Force and Maximum Speed
Q45.questionRecapHtml: A 250 g particle under $F=-25x$ N reaches $v_{max}=4$ m/s. Find amplitude in cm.
Q45.conceptHtml: Compute $\omega = k/m$ from $k=25$ N/m and $m=0.25$ kg, then use $A=v_{max}/\omega$.
Q45.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Find $\omega$ from mass and force constant: From $F = -25x$, we have $k = 25\text{ N/m}$, and mass is $m = 250\text{ g} = 0.25\text{ kg}$. Thus $\omega = \sqrt{\frac{k}{m}} = \sqrt{\frac{25}{0.25}} = \sqrt{100} = 10\text{ rad/s}$.
  2. Step 2 — Calculate amplitude from maximum speed: Using $v_{\max} = \omega A$ with $v_{\max} = 4\text{ m/s}$, we get $A = \frac{v_{\max}}{\omega} = \frac{4}{10} = 0.4\text{ m}$.
  3. Step 3 — Convert to centimetres and confirm: $A = 0.4\text{ m} = 40\text{ cm}$, so the numerical answer is 40.
Q45.stepsLatex:
$\sqrt{\sqrt}{ } \omega = \frac{k}{m} = \frac{25}{0.25} = 100=10$ rad/s
$A= \frac{vmax}{\omega} = \frac{4}{10} =0.4$ m $=40$ cm
Q45.trapHtml: Convert 250 g $=0.25$ kg at the start and 0.4 m $=40$ cm at the end.

Q46.subtopic: Finding Unknown Mass from Period Increase
Q46.questionRecapHtml: Mass $m$ on a spring has $T_1=1$ s; adding 3 kg increases period by 1 s ($T_2=2$ s). Find $m$ in kg.
Q46.conceptHtml: Since $T \propto m$, write $\frac{T2}{T1} = \frac{m+3}{m}$ and square both sides.
Q46.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Relate time period to hanging mass: For a spring-mass oscillator, $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{m}{k}}$, so $T \propto \sqrt{m}$ or $\frac{T_2}{T_1} = \sqrt{\frac{m_2}{m_1}}$.
  2. Step 2 — Substitute the two states: Initially $m_1 = m$ and $T_1 = 1\text{ s}$. Adding $3\text{ kg}$ gives $m_2 = m + 3$ and $T_2 = 1 + 1 = 2\text{ s}$.
  3. Step 3 — Solve for $m$: $\frac{2}{1} = \sqrt{\frac{m + 3}{m}} \implies 4 = \frac{m + 3}{m} \implies 4m = m + 3 \implies 3m = 3 \implies m = 1\text{ kg}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the numerical answer: The initial mass is 1 kg.
Q46.stepsLatex: $\sqrt{\frac{2}{1}} = \frac{m+3}{m} \implies 4= \frac{m+3}{m} \implies 4m=m+3 \implies m=1$ kg
Q46.trapHtml: Read "increases by one second" carefully: $T_2=1+1=2$ s (so $m+3=4m \implies m=1$ kg).

Q47.subtopic: Time Period of 2 kg Block Between Two Springs
Q47.questionRecapHtml: Block of mass 2 kg sits between two identical 20 N/m springs on a smooth surface. Period is $\pi / x$ s; find $x$.
Q47.conceptHtml: Opposing wall-mounted springs act in parallel: $k_{eq}=20+20=40$ N/m.
Q47.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Find the equivalent spring constant: The $2\text{ kg}$ block sits between two identical springs ($k = 20\text{ N/m}$ each) fixed to opposite walls, so they act in parallel: $k_{\text{eq}} = k + k = 40\text{ N/m}$.
  2. Step 2 — Calculate the time period: $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{m}{k_{\text{eq}}}} = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{2}{40}} = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{1}{20}} = \frac{2\pi}{2\sqrt{5}} = \frac{\pi}{\sqrt{5}}\text{ s}$.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the numerical answer: Comparing with $\frac{\pi}{\sqrt{x}}\text{ s}$ gives $x = \mathbf{5}$.
Q47.stepsLatex: $k_{eq}=20+20=40$ N/m Hence $x=5$. $T =2\pi \frac{m}{k} =2\pi \frac{2}{40} =2\pi \frac{1}{20} = \frac{2}{2} \sqrt{\frac{\pi}{5}} = \sqrt{\frac{\pi}{5}}$ s eq
Q47.trapHtml: Cancel the 2 cleanly using $20=2 5$ so the numerator is $\pi$ and $x=5$.

5
