Q05.subtopic: Torque on Dipole Between Capacitor Plates
Q05.questionRecapHtml: Dipole (2 µC, 0.5 µm) rotated 30 in capacitor (V = 5 V, d = 0.5 mm); find torque.
Q05.conceptHtml: τ = pE sin θ with p = qℓ and E = V /d.
Q05.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Calculate the dipole moment: Each charge has magnitude $q = 2\,\mu\text{C} = 2 \times 10^{-6}\text{ C}$ and separation $d = 0.5\,\mu\text{m} = 0.5 \times 10^{-6}\text{ m}$, so $p = qd = (2 \times 10^{-6})(0.5 \times 10^{-6}) = 10^{-12}\text{ C}\cdot\text{m}$.
  2. Step 2 — Find the electric field between the capacitor plates: For potential difference $V = 5\text{ V}$ and plate separation $D = 0.5\text{ mm} = 0.5 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m}$, the uniform field is $E = \frac{V}{D} = \frac{5}{0.5 \times 10^{-3}} = 10^4\text{ V/m}$.
  3. Step 3 — Apply the torque formula: When rotated by $\theta = 30^\circ$ from the field direction, the restoring torque magnitude is $\tau = pE\sin\theta = (10^{-12})(10^4)\sin 30^\circ$.
  4. Step 4 — Simplify and confirm: Since $\sin 30^\circ = 0.5$, we get $\tau = 10^{-8} \times 0.5 = 5 \times 10^{-9}\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$. Therefore, the correct answer is Option (d).
Q05.trapHtml: Watch micro vs milli prefixes: 0.5 µm = 5 × 10<sup>−7</sup> m and 0.5 mm = 5 × 10<sup>−4</sup> m.

  3. Step 3 — Link (R) to (A): The protection of passengers occurs directly because the enclosed metallic cavity maintains zero internal electric field, so (R) is the correct explanation of (A).

Q09.questionRecapHtml: Two identical +σ sheets and a +ρ sphere between them; compare fields at A, B, C, D.

Q10.questionRecapHtml: Dipole (±2 µC, 20 cm) at 30 near non-conducting sheet (σ = 100 µC/m ); find torque.
Q10.conceptHtml: Field of infinite non-conducting sheet is E = 2ε ; torque is τ = pE sin θ. 0
Q10.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Calculate the dipole moment of the rod: The charges are $\pm 2\,\mu\text{C} = \pm 2 \times 10^{-6}\text{ C}$ separated by $l = 20\text{ cm} = 0.2\text{ m}$, giving $p = ql = (2 \times 10^{-6})(0.2) = 4 \times 10^{-7}\text{ C}\cdot\text{m}$.
  2. Step 2 — Find the electric field of the non-conducting sheet: For $\sigma = 100\,\mu\text{C/m}^2 = 10^{-4}\text{ C/m}^2$, the uniform field is $E = \frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0} = \frac{10^{-4}}{2 \times 8.85 \times 10^{-12}} = \frac{10^8}{17.7}\text{ N/C}$.
  3. Step 3 — Compute the net torque: The rod makes an angle $\theta = 30^\circ$ with $\vec{E}$, so $\tau = pE\sin 30^\circ = (4 \times 10^{-7})\left(\frac{10^8}{17.7}\right)\left(\frac{1}{2}\right) = \frac{20}{17.7}\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$.
  4. Step 4 — Evaluate and confirm: $\tau \approx 1.13\text{ N}\cdot\text{m} \approx 1.12\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$, which matches Option (a).

Q11.questionRecapHtml: Shell (R = 10 cm) has Vsurface = 120 V; find V at r = 0, 5 cm, 15 cm.
Q11.conceptHtml: Inside (r ≤ R), V = V0 = const; outside (r > R), V (r) = V0 R r.
Q11.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Potential inside a uniformly charged spherical shell: For any point on or inside a uniformly charged spherical shell ($r \le R$), the electric field is zero, so the potential remains constant and equal to the surface potential: $V(r) = V_{\text{surface}} = 120\text{ V}$.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate at $r = 0$ and $r = 5\text{ cm}$: Since both $r = 0$ (centre) and $r = 5\text{ cm}$ are less than $R = 10\text{ cm}$, we immediately have $V(0) = 120\text{ V}$ and $V(5\text{ cm}) = 120\text{ V}$.
  3. Step 3 — Evaluate outside the shell at $r = 15\text{ cm}$: For $r > R$, the shell behaves like a point charge at its centre, so $V(r) = V_{\text{surface}} \frac{R}{r} = 120 \times \frac{10}{15} = 80\text{ V}$.
  4. Step 4 — Final confirmation: The three potentials are $120\text{ V}, 120\text{ V}, 80\text{ V}$, confirming Option (b).

Q12.questionRecapHtml: Assertion (A) claims polar dielectric has non-zero net dipole moment in zero field; Reason (R) says dipoles are randomly oriented.
Q12.conceptHtml: Although each polar molecule has a permanent dipole moment, thermal agitation orients them randomly so net dipole moment is zero in zero field.

1. Step 1 — Evaluate Reason (R): Molecules of a polar dielectric possess permanent electric dipole moments. When no external electric field is applied, thermal agitation orients these permanent dipoles in completely random directions. Thus, Reason (R) is correct.

Q17.subtopic: Equilibrium of Pendulum Near Charged Sheet
Q17.questionRecapHtml: Bob (m = 100 mg, q = 10 µC) hangs at 45 near non-conducting sheet +σ ; find σ .
Q17.conceptHtml: At equilibrium, tan θ = mg = 2ε mg. 0
Q17.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Write equilibrium equations for the bob: The bob experiences downward gravity $mg$, horizontal electrostatic repulsion $F_e = qE$ away from the sheet, and string tension $T$ at $45^\circ$ to the vertical. Balancing forces gives $T\cos 45^\circ = mg$ and $T\sin 45^\circ = qE$.
  2. Step 2 — Relate $\sigma$ to the angle: Dividing the two equations gives $\tan 45^\circ = \frac{qE}{mg} = 1 \implies qE = mg$. For an infinite non-conducting sheet, $E = \frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}$, so $\frac{q\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0} = mg \implies \sigma = \frac{2\varepsilon_0 mg}{q}$.
  3. Step 3 — Substitute SI values: With $m = 100\text{ mg} = 10^{-4}\text{ kg}$, $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$, $q = 10\,\mu\text{C} = 10^{-5}\text{ C}$, and $\varepsilon_0 = 8.85 \times 10^{-12}\text{ F/m}$, we get $\sigma = \frac{2 \times 8.85 \times 10^{-12} \times 10^{-4} \times 10}{10^{-5}} = 17.7 \times 10^{-10}\text{ C/m}^2$.
  4. Step 4 — Convert to $\text{nC/m}^2$ and confirm: $\sigma = 1.77 \times 10^{-9}\text{ C/m}^2 = 1.77\text{ nC/m}^2$, which matches Option (a).
Q17.trapHtml: Convert 100 mg = 10<sup>−4</sup> kg carefully, and remember E = σ/(2ε<sub>0</sub> ) for a non-conducting sheet.

Q18.questionRecapHtml: Flux -2 × 10 Nm C through 8 cm sphere; find enclosed point charge.
Q18.conceptHtml: Gauss's law: q = ε<sub>0</sub> Φ (independent of sphere radius).
Q18.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Apply Gauss's law: The electric flux through a closed Gaussian surface depends only on the enclosed charge $q$ (and not on the radius $8.0\text{ cm}$): $\Phi = \frac{q}{\varepsilon_0} \implies q = \varepsilon_0 \Phi$.
  2. Step 2 — Substitute the given values: Using $\varepsilon_0 = 8.85 \times 10^{-12}\text{ C}^2\text{N}^{-1}\text{m}^{-2}$ and $\Phi = -2 \times 10^4\text{ Nm}^2\text{C}^{-1}$, we compute $q = (8.85 \times 10^{-12})(-2 \times 10^4)$.
  3. Step 3 — Simplify and confirm: $q = -17.7 \times 10^{-8}\text{ C}$. The negative sign reflects inward electric flux, confirming Option (b).
Q18.trapHtml: Negative (inward) flux means a NEGATIVE enclosed charge; radius 8.0 cm is distractor information.

Q19.questionRecapHtml: Dipole (-q nearer, +q farther) placed near infinite +σ<sub>0</sub> sheet; identify force, torque, and PE.
Q19.conceptHtml: Field of infinite sheet is UNIFORM and directed away from sheet, so p
Q19.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the directions of $\vec{E}$ and $\vec{p}$: An infinite plane sheet with positive charge density $+\sigma_0$ creates a uniform electric field $\vec{E} = \frac{\sigma_0}{2\varepsilon_0}\hat{i}$ pointing away from the sheet (to the right). From the figure, $-q$ is on the left and $+q$ is on the right, so the dipole moment $\vec{p}$ (directed from $-q$ to $+q$) also points to the right.
  2. Step 2 — Check net force and torque: Because the electric field of an infinite sheet is uniform, the net force on the dipole is $\vec{F}_{\text{net}} = q\vec{E} - q\vec{E} = 0$. Since the angle between $\vec{p}$ and $\vec{E}$ is $\theta = 0^\circ$, the torque is $\tau = pE\sin 0^\circ = 0$.
  3. Step 3 — Evaluate potential energy: The dipole's potential energy is $U = -pE\cos\theta = -pE\cos 0^\circ = -pE$, which is its minimum possible value (stable equilibrium).
  4. Step 4 — Final confirmation: Potential energy is minimum and torque is zero, confirming Option (b).

  2. Step 2 — Find the moment of inertia $I$: For the dipole modeled as two point masses $m$ at the ends of length $l$ (each at distance $l/2$ from the centre), the moment of inertia about the centre is $I = m\left(\frac{l}{2}\right)^2 + m\left(\frac{l}{2}\right)^2 = \frac{ml^2}{2}$.

Q22.subtopic: Equipotential Surface of Three Line Charges
Q22.questionRecapHtml: Three infinite wires of density λ along x, y, z axes; find equation of equipotential surface.
Q22.conceptHtml: Potential of an infinite wire at perpendicular distance r⊥ is V = - 2πε ln r⊥ + C. 0
Q22.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the potential of an infinite line charge: At a perpendicular distance $r$ from an infinitely long wire with linear charge density $\lambda$, the electric field is $E = \frac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 r}$, so the potential is $V(r) = -\frac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0}\ln r + C = -\frac{\lambda}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\ln(r^2) + C$.
  2. Step 2 — Write perpendicular distances to the three coordinate axes: For a general point $(x, y, z)$, the squared perpendicular distances to the $x$-, $y$-, and $z$-axes are $(y^2 + z^2)$, $(z^2 + x^2)$, and $(x^2 + y^2)$, respectively.
  3. Step 3 — Sum the potentials by superposition: $V(x,y,z) = -\frac{\lambda}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\left[\ln(y^2+z^2) + \ln(z^2+x^2) + \ln(x^2+y^2)\right] + C_{\text{tot}} = -\frac{\lambda}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\ln\left[(x^2+y^2)(y^2+z^2)(z^2+x^2)\right] + C_{\text{tot}}$.
  4. Step 4 — Condition for an equipotential surface: Setting $V(x,y,z) = \text{constant}$ requires $(x^2+y^2)(y^2+z^2)(z^2+x^2) = \text{constant}$, confirming Option (a).

Q24.questionRecapHtml: Uncharged sphere touches identical sphere with 4 × 10 C, then repels with 9 × 10 N; find separation.
Q24.conceptHtml: Identical spheres split total charge equally (q ′ = q/2), then F = kq ′2 /r 2.
Q24.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Find the charge on each sphere after contact: When an uncharged conducting sphere touches an identical sphere carrying $Q = 4 \times 10^{-8}\text{ C}$, the total charge splits equally between them: $q_1 = q_2 = \frac{Q}{2} = 2 \times 10^{-8}\text{ C}$.
  2. Step 2 — Apply Coulomb's law: The repulsive force is $F = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{q_1 q_2}{r^2}$, so $r^2 = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{q_1 q_2}{F}$.
  3. Step 3 — Substitute the given values: $r^2 = \frac{(9 \times 10^9)(2 \times 10^{-8})^2}{9 \times 10^{-3}} = \frac{9 \times 10^9 \times 4 \times 10^{-16}}{9 \times 10^{-3}} = 4 \times 10^{-4}\text{ m}^2$.
  4. Step 4 — Solve for $r$ and confirm: $r = \sqrt{4 \times 10^{-4}} = 2 \times 10^{-2}\text{ m} = 2\text{ cm}$, confirming Option (b).
Q24.trapHtml: Halve the charge BEFORE squaring: (q/2)2 = 4 × 10<sup>−16</sup> .

Q26.questionRecapHtml: Dipole (±4 µC at x = ∓9 cm) rotated 180 from equilibrium in E = 10 N/C; find W.
Q26.conceptHtml: Work from stable (0° ) to unstable (180° ) equilibrium: W = pE(1 - cos 180° ) = 2pE.
Q26.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Find the dipole moment: The charges $\pm 4\,\mu\text{C} = \pm 4 \times 10^{-6}\text{ C}$ are located at $(-9, 0, 0)\text{ cm}$ and $(9, 0, 0)\text{ cm}$, so their separation is $2a = 18\text{ cm} = 0.18\text{ m}$. Hence $p = q(2a) = (4 \times 10^{-6})(0.18) = 7.2 \times 10^{-7}\text{ C}\cdot\text{m}$.
  2. Step 2 — Use the work formula for dipole rotation: The external work done in rotating a dipole from stable equilibrium ($\theta_1 = 0^\circ$) through $180^\circ$ ($\theta_2 = 180^\circ$) is $W = pE(\cos\theta_1 - \cos\theta_2) = pE(1 - (-1)) = 2pE$.
  3. Step 3 — Substitute values and evaluate: With $E = 10^4\text{ N/C}$, $W = 2(7.2 \times 10^{-7})(10^4) = 14.4 \times 10^{-3}\text{ J} = 14.4\text{ mJ}$.
  4. Step 4 — Final confirmation: This matches Option (d).

Q27.subtopic: Potential Energy of Two Point Charges
Q27.questionRecapHtml: Charges 7 µC and -4 µC at (∓7 cm, 0, 0); find electrostatic PE.
Q27.conceptHtml: U = r with separation r = 14 cm = 0.14 m.
Q27.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Find the separation between the two charges: The charges $q_1 = 7\,\mu\text{C} = 7 \times 10^{-6}\text{ C}$ and $q_2 = -4\,\mu\text{C} = -4 \times 10^{-6}\text{ C}$ are at $x_1 = -7\text{ cm}$ and $x_2 = +7\text{ cm}$, so their separation is $r = 14\text{ cm} = 0.14\text{ m}$.
  2. Step 2 — Write the electrostatic potential energy formula: $U = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{q_1 q_2}{r}$, where $\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^9\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}^2\text{C}^{-2}$.
  3. Step 3 — Substitute and calculate: $U = \frac{(9 \times 10^9)(7 \times 10^{-6})(-4 \times 10^{-6})}{0.14} = \frac{-252 \times 10^{-3}}{0.14} = -1.8\text{ J}$.
  4. Step 4 — Final confirmation: The electrostatic potential energy is $-1.8\text{ J}$, confirming Option (d).
Q27.trapHtml: Distance between -7 cm and +7 cm is 14 cm, and opposite charges give NEGATIVE PE.

Q28.questionRecapHtml: Charge Q at P feels zero net force from axial Dipole 1 and equatorial Dipole 2 (both at distance r, length 2a); find a/r.

Q47.questionRecapHtml: Assertion (A) on zero work on equipotential surface and Reason (R) on field lines being perpendicular to equipotentials.

1. Step 1 — Evaluate Assertion (A): By definition, every point on an equipotential surface has the same electric potential ($\Delta V = 0$). Therefore, the work done by the electric field in moving a charge $q$ along it is $W = -q\Delta V = 0$, so Assertion (A) is correct.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Reason (R): For any infinitesimal displacement $d\vec{r}$ along the equipotential surface, $dW = q\vec{E}\cdot d\vec{r} = 0$. Since $q \ne 0$ and $d\vec{r} \ne 0$, the electric field $\vec{E}$ must always be perpendicular to $d\vec{r}$, meaning electric field lines are perpendicular to equipotential surfaces. Thus Reason (R) is correct.
  3. Step 3 — Check the logical link: Because the electric force $q\vec{E}$ is everywhere perpendicular to any displacement along the equipotential surface, the dot product $\vec{F}\cdot d\vec{r}$ vanishes, directly explaining why the work done is always zero.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A), matching option (a).

Q55.conceptHtml: Inside (r < R): E = 3ε ∝ r (straight line from origin); outside (r > R): E = kQ r2 ∝ 1/r2. 0
Q55.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Electric field inside the solid insulating sphere ($r < R$): By Gauss's Law, the enclosed charge is $q_{\text{in}} = Q\frac{r^3}{R^3}$, so $E_{\text{in}} = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{Qr}{R^3}$. Thus $E$ increases linearly with $r$ ($E \propto r$) from $0$ at the center to a maximum at $r = R$.
  2. Step 2 — Electric field outside the sphere ($r > R$): The entire charge $Q$ behaves as if concentrated at the center, giving $E_{\text{out}} = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{Q}{r^2}$. Thus $E$ decreases as $\frac{1}{r^2}$ for $r > R$.
  3. Step 3 — Match the curve shape: The correct graph starts at the origin, rises in a straight line up to $r = R$, and then falls hyperbolically as $\frac{1}{r^2}$ beyond $R$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: This matches Graph (D), which corresponds to option (d).

Q56.questionRecapHtml: Dipole (±q, length l) has masses m and 2m; find angular frequency ω of small oscillations in E.
Q56.conceptHtml: A free dipole oscillates about its centre of mass, with ICOM = µl2 where reduced mass µ = m 1+m<sup>2</sup> . 1 2
Q56.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the masses and reduced mass: The positive charge $+q$ has mass $m_1 = m$, and since $m$ is half the mass of the negative charge, the negative charge $-q$ has mass $m_2 = 2m$. Because the dipole is free to oscillate about its center of mass, its reduced mass is $\mu = \frac{m_1 m_2}{m_1 + m_2} = \frac{m(2m)}{m + 2m} = \frac{2m}{3}$.
  2. Step 2 — Find the moment of inertia about the center of mass: For two point masses separated by distance $l$, $I = \mu l^2 = \frac{2}{3}ml^2$.
  3. Step 3 — Compute the angular frequency of small oscillations: For a small angular displacement $\theta$, the restoring torque is $\tau = -pE\theta = -qlE\theta$, giving angular frequency $\omega = \sqrt{\frac{pE}{I}} = \sqrt{\frac{qlE}{\frac{2}{3}ml^2}} = \sqrt{\frac{3qE}{2ml}}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The angular frequency of small oscillations is $\sqrt{\frac{3qE}{2ml}}$, matching option (a).

Q57.subtopic: Potential Graph of Thin Spherical Shell
Q57.questionRecapHtml: Identify V vs r graph for a uniformly charged thin spherical shell of radius R.
Q57.conceptHtml: V = R = const for r ≤ R, and V = r ∝ r1 (hyperbolic decay) for r > R.
Q57.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Potential inside and on the spherical shell ($r \le R$): Inside a uniformly charged thin spherical shell, the electric field is zero ($E = 0$), which means the electric potential remains constant everywhere inside and equals the surface value: $V = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{Q}{R}$.
  2. Step 2 — Potential outside the spherical shell ($r > R$): Outside the shell, the potential behaves like that of a point charge at the center: $V = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{Q}{r} \propto \frac{1}{r}$ (hyperbolic decay).
  3. Step 3 — Match with the given graphs: The graph must be a horizontal flat line from $r = 0$ to $r = R$, followed by a smooth $\frac{1}{r}$ curve decreasing toward zero for $r > R$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: This matches Graph (A), corresponding to option (a).

Q58.subtopic: Electric Field of Two Identical Sheets
Q58.questionRecapHtml: Two infinite thin sheets each with +σ ; find E ⃗ II, E
Q58.conceptHtml: Each sheet gives 2ε directed away from it: they cancel in region II and add in regions I and III. 0
Q58.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the field of a single infinite sheet: Each positively charged infinite thin sheet of density $+\sigma$ produces a uniform electric field of magnitude $\frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}$ pointing perpendicularly away from the sheet on both sides. Let $\hat{n}$ be the unit vector pointing to the right.
  2. Step 2 — Find the net field in Region I (left of both sheets): Both sheets push electric field lines to the left ($-\hat{n}$), so $\vec{E}_{\text{I}} = -\frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}\hat{n} - \frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}\hat{n} = -\frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}\hat{n}$.
  3. Step 3 — Find the net field in Region II (between the sheets): The left sheet pushes to the right ($+\hat{n}$) while the right sheet pushes to the left ($-\hat{n}$), so they cancel: $\vec{E}_{\text{II}} = \frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}\hat{n} - \frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}\hat{n} = \vec{0}$.
  4. Step 4 — Find the net field in Region III (right of both sheets) and confirm: Both sheets push to the right ($+\hat{n}$), giving $\vec{E}_{\text{III}} = \frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}\hat{n} + \frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}\hat{n} = \frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}\hat{n}$. This matches option (c).

Q59.subtopic: Potential vs Field of Positive Charges
Q59.questionRecapHtml: For a group of positive charges, can net V or net E
Q59.conceptHtml: Every positive charge contributes Vi > 0 (scalar sum cannot be zero), whereas field vectors can cancel.
Q59.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Analyze the net electric potential: Electric potential is a scalar quantity given by $V = \sum_i \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{q_i}{r_i}$. Since every charge in the group is positive ($q_i > 0$) and every distance is positive ($r_i > 0$), each term is strictly positive, so the net potential can never be zero at any finite point.
  2. Step 2 — Analyze the net electric field: Electric field $\vec{E} = \sum_i \vec{E}_i$ is a vector quantity. Fields from different positive charges can point in opposite directions and cancel out (for example, at the midpoint between two equal positive charges, $\vec{E}_{\text{net}} = \vec{0}$).
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the final answer: Therefore, the net potential cannot be zero at a point, whereas the net electric field can be zero at that point, matching option (a).

Q61.questionRecapHtml: Charge Q at centre of conducting shell (a < r < b); determine if E is zero or non-zero in regions I, II, III.
Q61.conceptHtml: Electrostatic equilibrium forces EII = 0 inside the conducting wall; Gauss's law gives EI = EIII = r2 ̸= 0.
Q61.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Determine the induced charges on the conducting shell: Placing a point charge $+Q$ at the center induces a charge $-Q$ uniformly on the inner surface ($r = a$) and $+Q$ uniformly on the outer surface ($r = b$) of the neutral conducting shell.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate the field in Region I ($r < a$): A spherical Gaussian surface of radius $r < a$ encloses $q_{ ext{in}} = +Q$, so $E_{ ext{I}} = rac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} rac{Q}{r^2} e 0$.
  3. Step 3 — Evaluate the field in Region II ($a < r < b$): Inside the bulk of a conductor in electrostatic equilibrium, $q_{ ext{in}} = Q + (-Q) = 0$, so $E_{ ext{II}} = 0$.
  4. Step 4 — Evaluate Region III ($r > b$) and confirm: Outside the shell, $q_{ ext{in}} = Q - Q + Q = +Q$, giving $E_{ ext{III}} = rac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} rac{Q}{r^2} e 0$. Hence $E_{ ext{I}} e 0$, $E_{ ext{II}} = 0$, $E_{ ext{III}} e 0$, matching option (c).

Q62.conceptHtml: Dimensional homogeneity: [A] = [E][x2 ] and [B] = [E][y 3 ] with [E] = N C<sup>−1</sup> .
Q62.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Apply the principle of dimensional homogeneity: In the electric field expression $\vec{E} = \frac{A}{x^2}\hat{i} + \frac{B}{y^3}\hat{j}$, each term must have the SI unit of electric field, which is $\text{N C}^{-1}$.
  2. Step 2 — Find the SI unit of $A$: Since $\left[\frac{A}{x^2}\right] = \text{N C}^{-1}$ and $[x^2] = \text{m}^2$, we get $[A] = \text{N C}^{-1} \cdot \text{m}^2 = \text{N m}^2\text{C}^{-1}$.
  3. Step 3 — Find the SI unit of $B$: Since $\left[\frac{B}{y^3}\right] = \text{N C}^{-1}$ and $[y^3] = \text{m}^3$, we get $[B] = \text{N C}^{-1} \cdot \text{m}^3 = \text{N m}^3\text{C}^{-1}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The SI units of $A$ and $B$ are $\text{N m}^2\text{C}^{-1}$ and $\text{N m}^3\text{C}^{-1}$ respectively, matching option (d).

Q63.questionRecapHtml: Spheres of radii R, 2R initially have equal σ , then connected by wire; find σ /σ for bigger sphere.
Q63.conceptHtml: Total charge Q = σ(4πR2 + 4π(2R)2 ) redistributes in ratio R: 2R (1: 2) at equal potential.
Q63.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Calculate initial charges and total charge: Both spheres initially have surface charge density $\sigma$. For the smaller sphere ($R$), $q_1 = \sigma(4\pi R^2)$; for the bigger sphere ($2R$), $q_2 = \sigma(4\pi(2R)^2) = 4\sigma(4\pi R^2)$. Total charge is $Q_{\text{tot}} = q_1 + q_2 = 5\sigma(4\pi R^2)$.
  2. Step 2 — Redistribute charge at common potential: When connected by a thin conducting wire, charge flows until both spheres reach the same potential: $\frac{kq_1'}{R} = \frac{kq_2'}{2R} \Rightarrow q_2' = 2q_1'$. Since $q_1' + q_2' = Q_{\text{tot}}$, the bigger sphere gets $q_2' = \frac{2}{3}Q_{\text{tot}} = \frac{10}{3}\sigma(4\pi R^2)$.
  3. Step 3 — Find the new surface charge density $\sigma'$: Dividing $q_2'$ by the bigger sphere's surface area $4\pi(2R)^2 = 4(4\pi R^2)$ gives $\sigma' = \frac{\frac{10}{3}\sigma(4\pi R^2)}{4(4\pi R^2)} = \frac{10}{12}\sigma = \frac{5}{6}\sigma$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The ratio $\frac{\sigma'}{\sigma} = \frac{5}{6}$, matching option (b).

Q64.subtopic: Work Done by Uniform Electric Field
Q64.questionRecapHtml: Move q = 2 × 10 C from P (1, 2, 0) to S(0, 0, 0) in E
Q64.conceptHtml: Wfield = q E rS - ⃗ rP ).
Q64.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Find the displacement vector: Moving from $P(1, 2, 0)\text{ m}$ to $S(0, 0, 0)\text{ m}$ gives $\Delta\vec{r} = \vec{r}_S - \vec{r}_P = (0-1)\hat{i} + (0-2)\hat{j} + (0-0)\hat{k} = (-\hat{i} - 2\hat{j})\text{ m}$.
  2. Step 2 — Write the electric force vector: Given $q = 2 \times 10^{-2}\text{ C}$ and $\vec{E} = 30\hat{i}\text{ N C}^{-1}$, the electric force is $\vec{F} = q\vec{E} = (2 \times 10^{-2})(30\hat{i}) = 0.6\hat{i}\text{ N}$.
  3. Step 3 — Compute the work done by the electric field: $W = \vec{F}\cdot\Delta\vec{r} = (0.6\hat{i})\cdot(-\hat{i} - 2\hat{j}) = -0.6\text{ J} = -600\text{ mJ}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The work done by the electric field is $-600\text{ mJ}$, matching option (d).
Q64.trapHtml: Check whether the question asks for work done BY THE ELECTRIC FIELD (-600 mJ) or by an external agent (+600 mJ).

Q65.questionRecapHtml: Cuboid 2L × 2L × L has charge q at centre of 2L × 2L face S; find flux through opposite face.
Q65.conceptHtml: Attach an identical cuboid across face S to form a 2L × 2L × 2L CUBE with q at its exact centre!
Q65.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Use symmetry to form a complete cube: The cuboid has dimensions $2L \times 2L \times L$, and the charge $q$ sits at the center of the $2L \times 2L$ face $S$. Attach an identical second cuboid against face $S$ so the two cuboids together form a symmetric cube of side $2L \times 2L \times 2L$ with $q$ at its exact geometric center.
  2. Step 2 — Apply Gauss's Law to the full cube: The total electric flux emerging from the cube is $\Phi_{\text{total}} = \frac{q}{\varepsilon_0}$.
  3. Step 3 — Divide equally among the 6 identical faces: By symmetry, each of the 6 square faces of the $2L \times 2L \times 2L$ cube receives $\frac{1}{6}$ of the total flux. The face opposite to $S$ is one full face of this cube, so $\Phi = \frac{q}{6\varepsilon_0}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The flux through the face opposite to $S$ is $\frac{q}{6\varepsilon_0}$, matching option (d).

Q66.questionRecapHtml: 10 µC at origin; where should 40 µC be placed so E = 0 at x = 2 cm?
Q66.conceptHtml: For like charges, null point lies between them: 210 40 2 = (x-2)2.
Q66.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Locate the null-field region: Both charges $q_1 = 10\text{ }\mu\text{C}$ (at $x = 0$) and $q_2 = 40\text{ }\mu\text{C}$ (at $x = d$) are positive, so the electric field can cancel only at a point lying between them. Since the null point is at $x = 2\text{ cm}$, we must have $d > 2\text{ cm}$.
  2. Step 2 — Equate the field magnitudes at $x = 2\text{ cm}$: $\frac{kq_1}{(2)^2} = \frac{kq_2}{(d - 2)^2} \Rightarrow \frac{10}{4} = \frac{40}{(d - 2)^2}$.
  3. Step 3 — Solve for $d$: $(d - 2)^2 = \frac{40 \times 4}{10} = 16 \Rightarrow d - 2 = 4$ (taking the positive root since $d > 2$), so $d = 6\text{ cm}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The $40\text{ }\mu\text{C}$ charge should be placed at $x = 6\text{ cm}$, matching option (a).
Q66.trapHtml: Only x > 2 cm places x = 2 cm BETWEEN the two positive charges (choosing x - 2 = -4 =⇒ x = -2 cm makes fields add, not cancel!).

Q67.questionRecapHtml: Two concentric half rings of radii R1, R2 with same linear density λ; find V at centre O.
Q67.conceptHtml: For a half ring of radius R, V = R = 4ελ (independent of R!). 0
Q67.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Find the potential due to one semicircular ring: For a half-ring of radius $R$ and uniform linear charge density $\lambda$, the total charge is $Q = \lambda(\pi R)$. Because every charge element $dq$ lies at the same distance $R$ from the center $O$, its potential at $O$ is $V_{\text{half}} = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{Q}{R} = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{\lambda \pi R}{R} = \frac{\lambda}{4\varepsilon_0}$.
  2. Step 2 — Notice the radius independence: The potential at the center of a uniformly charged semicircular arc depends only on $\lambda$, not on $R$. Hence both half-rings (radii $R_1$ and $R_2$) contribute $\frac{\lambda}{4\varepsilon_0}$ each.
  3. Step 3 — Superpose the scalar potentials: $V_{\text{net}} = V_1 + V_2 = \frac{\lambda}{4\varepsilon_0} + \frac{\lambda}{4\varepsilon_0} = \frac{\lambda}{2\varepsilon_0}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The net electric potential at the center is $\frac{\lambda}{2\varepsilon_0}$, matching option (a).

Q68.questionRecapHtml: Charges separated by d in dielectric K; find equivalent air separation for same force.
Q68.conceptHtml: Equate Kd 2 = . d2 air
Q68.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Write the Coulomb force in the dielectric medium: For charges $q_1$ and $q_2$ separated by distance $d$ in a medium of dielectric constant $K$, $F_{\text{med}} = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 K}\frac{q_1 q_2}{d^2}$.
  2. Step 2 — Write the Coulomb force in air at equivalent distance $d_{\text{eq}}$: In air ($K = 1$), $F_{\text{air}} = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{q_1 q_2}{d_{\text{eq}}^2}$.

Q69.conceptHtml: Area vector of an x-z surface points along ĵ, so Φ = Ey A.
Q69.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the electric field component normal to the surface: From the complete JEE Main problem statement (partially truncated in the printed text), the electric field is $\vec{E} = \left(\frac{3}{5}E_0\hat{i} + \frac{4}{5}E_0\hat{j}\right)$ with $E_0 = 5 \times 10^3\text{ N/C}$. Since the surface is parallel to the $x$-$z$ plane, its area vector is $\vec{A} = A\hat{j}$, so only the $y$-component $E_y = \frac{4}{5}(5 \times 10^3) = 4 \times 10^3\text{ N/C}$ contributes to the flux.
  2. Step 2 — Relate flux to surface area: Using $\Phi = \vec{E}\cdot\vec{A} = E_y A$ with $\Phi = 6.0\text{ N m}^2\text{C}^{-1}$, we solve for $A$: $A = \frac{\Phi}{E_y} = \frac{6.0}{4 \times 10^3} = 1.5 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m}^2$.
  3. Step 3 — Convert area to $\text{cm}^2$: Since $1\text{ m}^2 = 10^4\text{ cm}^2$, $A = 1.5 \times 10^{-3} \times 10^4\text{ cm}^2 = 15\text{ cm}^2$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The area of the surface is 15 $\text{cm}^2$, confirming the numerical answer 15.

Q70.questionRecapHtml: Dipole (p = 6 × 10<sup>−6</sup> Cm) rotated from parallel to antiparallel in E = 106 V/m; find W.
Q70.conceptHtml: W = pE(cos 0° - cos 180° ) = 2pE.
Q70.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the work done in rotating an electric dipole: The external work required to rotate a dipole of moment $p$ in a uniform electric field $E$ from angle $\theta_1$ to $\theta_2$ is $W = U_f - U_i = pE(\cos\theta_1 - \cos\theta_2)$.
  2. Step 2 — Substitute the initial and final orientations: Initially parallel ($\theta_1 = 0^\circ \Rightarrow \cos 0^\circ = 1$) and finally opposite/antiparallel ($\theta_2 = 180^\circ \Rightarrow \cos 180^\circ = -1$), so $W = pE[1 - (-1)] = 2pE$.
  3. Step 3 — Compute the numerical value: With $p = 6 \times 10^{-6}\text{ C}\cdot\text{m}$ and $E = 10^6\text{ V/m}$, $W = 2 \times (6 \times 10^{-6}) \times 10^6 = 12\text{ J}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The work required is 12 J, confirming the numerical answer 12.
Q70.trapHtml: Don't forget the factor of 2 for 0° → 180° rotation (using pE gives 6). Correct

Q71.subtopic: Gauss’s Law & Partial Square Face Flux
Q71.questionRecapHtml: Charge q = 1 C at a/2 in front of square of side a; flux through shaded 5/8 region is pε ; find p.
Q71.conceptHtml: Flux through the full square face of a cube of side a is 6ε ; by symmetry, the shaded region covers 5 of the 8 congruent right 0 triangles.
Q71.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Find the flux through the entire square face: The point charge $q = 1\text{ C}$ is placed normally at distance $\frac{a}{2}$ from the center of a square of side $a$. Imagining a cube of side $a$ centered at $q$, this square is one of its 6 identical faces, so the flux through the whole square is $\Phi_{\text{square}} = \frac{q}{6\varepsilon_0}$.
  2. Step 2 — Divide the square into symmetric sub-regions: The two midlines split the square into 4 identical quadrants (each receiving $\frac{1}{4}$ of $\Phi_{\text{square}}$). The diagonal from the center to the top-left corner splits the top-left quadrant into two symmetric halves (each receiving $\frac{1}{8}$ of $\Phi_{\text{square}}$).
  3. Step 3 — Sum the shaded fraction: From the diagram, the shaded area covers 2 full bottom quadrants ($\frac{2}{4} = \frac{4}{8}$) plus 1 half of the top-left quadrant ($\frac{1}{8}$), totaling $\frac{5}{8}$ of the square's flux: $\Phi_{\text{shaded}} = \frac{5}{8} \times \frac{q}{6\varepsilon_0} = \frac{5}{48} \times \frac{1}{\varepsilon_0}$ (for $q = 1\text{ C}$).
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Comparing $\frac{5}{48}\times\frac{1}{\varepsilon_0}$ with $\frac{5}{p}\times\frac{1}{\varepsilon_0}$ gives $p = 48$, confirming the numerical answer 48.

Q72.conceptHtml: F = Gm1 m<sup>2</sup> (distance r cancels out). g 1 2
Q72.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Write the ratio of electrostatic to gravitational force: Both forces obey an inverse-square law, so $r^2$ cancels out: $\frac{F_e}{F_g} = \frac{kq_A q_B}{G m_A m_B}$.
  2. Step 2 — Substitute the given values: $\frac{F_e}{F_g} = \frac{(9 \times 10^9)(6.67 \times 10^{-19})(9.6 \times 10^{-10})}{(6.67 \times 10^{-11})(19.2 \times 10^{-27})(9 \times 10^{-27})}$.
  3. Step 3 — Simplify the factors and powers of 10: The factors $9$ and $6.67$ cancel directly, leaving $\frac{9.6}{19.2} \times \frac{10^{9 - 19 - 10}}{10^{-11 - 27 - 27}} = 0.5 \times \frac{10^{-20}}{10^{-65}} = 0.5 \times 10^{45} = 5 \times 10^{44}$.
  4. Step 4 — Identify the official exam misprint: The problem asks to express this huge ratio as $P \times 10^{-13}$ (a printing error in the exponent of $10$ and/or $q_B$), which does not yield a valid integer $P$. Consequently, NTA declared this question a Bonus.

Q73.subtopic: Flux of Non-Uniform Field Through Cube
Q73.conceptHtml: Only the left (x = 2) and right (x = 4) faces of area A = 4 m<sup>2</sup> have non-zero flux: Φ = (ER - EL )A.
Q73.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the faces with non-zero flux: The electric field $\vec{E} = 2x\hat{i}\text{ N C}^{-1}$ is purely along the $x$-axis. Therefore, the 4 faces parallel to the $x$-axis have $\vec{E} \perp \vec{A}$ (zero flux), and only the left face ($x = 2\text{ m}$) and right face ($x = 4\text{ m}$) contribute.
  2. Step 2 — Calculate the area of each face: The cube has side length $a = 2\text{ m}$, so each face has area $A = a^2 = 4\text{ m}^2$.
  3. Step 3 — Compute flux through the left and right faces: At the left face ($x = 2\text{ m}$, outward normal $-\hat{i}$), $\Phi_L = (2 \times 2)(-4) = -16\text{ N m}^2\text{C}^{-1}$. At the right face ($x = 4\text{ m}$, outward normal $+\hat{i}$), $\Phi_R = (2 \times 4)(+4) = +32\text{ N m}^2\text{C}^{-1}$.
  4. Step 4 — Sum for the net flux and confirm: $\Phi_{\text{net}} = \Phi_L + \Phi_R = -16 + 32 = 16\text{ N m}^2\text{C}^{-1}$, confirming the numerical answer 16.
Q73.trapHtml: Faster check via Divergence Theorem: ∇ · E Correct

Q74.subtopic: Potential at Centre of Half Ring
Q74.questionRecapHtml: Half ring (R = 10 cm, λ = 4 nC/m); potential at centre is xπ V; find x.
Q74.conceptHtml: V = R = kπλ (independent of R).
Q74.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Express the total charge on the half-ring: For a semicircular ring of radius $R$ and linear charge density $\lambda = 4\text{ nC m}^{-1} = 4 \times 10^{-9}\text{ C m}^{-1}$, the arc length is $\pi R$, so total charge is $Q = \lambda \pi R$.
  2. Step 2 — Compute the potential at the center: Every element of the half-ring is at the same distance $R$ from the center, so $V = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{Q}{R} = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{\lambda \pi R}{R} = \left(\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\right)\lambda\pi$.
  3. Step 3 — Substitute the numerical values: $V = (9 \times 10^9)(4 \times 10^{-9})\pi = 36\pi\text{ V}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Comparing $36\pi\text{ V}$ with $x\pi\text{ V}$ gives $x = 36$, confirming the numerical answer 36.
Q74.trapHtml: Radius R = 10 cm cancels out completely in V = kλ(πR)/R = kπλ. Correct

Q75.questionRecapHtml: +q2 at (-2, 0) cm, -q3 at (3, 0) cm, P at (0, 4) cm; Ey = 0 at P; find x in |q2 /q3 | = 5√ x
Q75.conceptHtml: Equate upward y-component from +q2 to downward y-component from -q3: 2 sin θ<sub>2</sub> = 2 sin θ<sub>3</sub> . r2 r3
Q75.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Find the distances from both charges to point $P$: From the diagram, $+q_2$ is at $2\text{ cm}$ to the left of the perpendicular foot, $-q_3$ is at $3\text{ cm}$ to the right, and $P$ is at height $y = 4\text{ cm}$. Thus $r_2 = \sqrt{2^2 + 4^2} = \sqrt{20} = 2\sqrt{5}\text{ cm}$ and $r_3 = \sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = \sqrt{25} = 5\text{ cm}$.
  2. Step 2 — Write the $y$-components of both electric fields at $P$: The field due to $+q_2$ points away from it, giving an upward component $E_{2y} = \frac{kq_2}{r_2^2}\cdot\frac{y}{r_2} = \frac{4kq_2}{r_2^3}$. The field due to $-q_3$ points toward it, giving a downward component $E_{3y} = \frac{kq_3}{r_3^2}\cdot\frac{y}{r_3} = \frac{4kq_3}{r_3^3}$.
  3. Step 3 — Set the net $y$-component to zero: $E_{2y} = E_{3y} \Rightarrow \frac{q_2}{r_2^3} = \frac{q_3}{r_3^3} \Rightarrow \frac{q_2}{q_3} = \left(\frac{r_2}{r_3}\right)^3 = \frac{(2\sqrt{5})^3}{5^3} = \frac{8 \times 5\sqrt{5}}{125} = \frac{8\sqrt{5}}{25} = \frac{8}{5\sqrt{5}}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Comparing $\frac{8}{5\sqrt{5}}$ with $\frac{8}{5\sqrt{x}}$ gives $x = 5$, confirming the numerical answer 5.
Q75.trapHtml: Since sin θ = y/r, the y-component scales as qy/r 3, so |q2 /q3 | = (r2 /r3 )3 directly! Correct

Q76.questionRecapHtml: E √ , A = 4 m<sup>2</sup> , n̂ = √ ; find flux.
Q76.conceptHtml: Φ = E
Q76.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Write down the field and area vectors: The electric field is $\vec{E} = \frac{2\hat{i} + 6\hat{j} + 8\hat{k}}{\sqrt{6}}\text{ V/m}$, and the surface area vector is $\vec{A} = A\hat{n} = 4\left(\frac{2\hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k}}{\sqrt{6}}\right)\text{ m}^2$.
  2. Step 2 — Apply the flux formula $\Phi = \vec{E}\cdot\vec{A}$: $\Phi = \frac{4}{(\sqrt{6})(\sqrt{6})}\left[(2)(2) + (6)(1) + (8)(1)\right]$.
  3. Step 3 — Evaluate the arithmetic: $\Phi = \frac{4}{6}(4 + 6 + 8) = \frac{4}{6}(18) = 4 \times 3 = 12\text{ V}\cdot\text{m}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The electric flux through the surface is 12 $\text{V}\cdot\text{m}$, confirming the numerical answer 12.
Q76.trapHtml: Notice 6× 6 = 6 in the denominator cancels 4 + 6 + 8 = 18 cleanly. Correct

Q77.subtopic: Field of Three Infinite Charged Sheets
Q77.questionRecapHtml: Sheets +σ at x = -a, -2σ at x = a, +σ at x = 3a; point P between a and 3a; find x in E = xσ/ε<sub>0</sub> .
Q77.conceptHtml: Superpose fields of all three sheets at P (a < x < 3a), keeping track of sign (+î vs -î).
Q77.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Read the positions and densities from the diagram: Three infinite thin sheets lie perpendicular to the $x$-axis: Sheet 1 ($-\sigma$) at $x = -a$, Sheet 2 ($-2\sigma$) at $x = a$, and Sheet 3 ($+\sigma$) at $x = 3a$. Point $P$ lies between $x = a$ and $x = 3a$.
  2. Step 2 — Find the direction and magnitude of each sheet's field at $P$: Recall that a negative sheet pulls field lines toward itself and a positive sheet pushes them away, with magnitude $\frac{|\sigma_{\text{sheet}}|}{2\varepsilon_0}$. At $P$: Sheet 1 (to the left, $-\sigma$) gives $\frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}$ along $-\hat{i}$; Sheet 2 (to the left, $-2\sigma$) gives $\frac{2\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}$ along $-\hat{i}$; Sheet 3 (to the right, $+\sigma$) gives $\frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}$ along $-\hat{i}$.
  3. Step 3 — Superpose all three fields: Since all three point along $-\hat{i}$, their magnitudes add directly: $E_P = \frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0} + \frac{2\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0} + \frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0} = \frac{4\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0} = \frac{2\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Comparing $\frac{2\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}$ with $\frac{x\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}$ gives $x = 2$, confirming the numerical answer 2.

Q78.questionRecapHtml: Field at axial point P (distance r ) is E; field at equatorial point R (distance 2r ) is E/x; find x.
Q78.conceptHtml: EP = r3 and ER = (2r)3 = 8r3 = 16.

  2. Step 2 — Write the electric field at equatorial point $R$: Point $R$ lies on the equatorial line at distance $2r$ from $O$. Using $E_{\text{eq}} = \frac{kp}{d^3}$ with $d = 2r$, we get $E_R = \frac{kp}{(2r)^3} = \frac{kp}{8r^3}$.
  3. Step 3 — Express $E_R$ in terms of $E$: Since $\frac{kp}{r^3} = \frac{E}{2}$, we obtain $E_R = \frac{1}{8}\left(\frac{E}{2}\right) = \frac{E}{16}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Comparing $\frac{E}{16}$ with $\frac{E}{x}$ gives $x = 16$, confirming the numerical answer 16.

Q79.subtopic: Sheet vs Line Charge Electric Field Ratio
Q79.questionRecapHtml: Sheet +σs on xy -plane, line +λe at z = 4 m (|σs | = 2|λe |); find n in Esheet /Eline = π n at (0, 0, 2).
Q79.conceptHtml: Esheet = 2ε and Eline = 2πε r with r = 4 - 2 = 2 m. 0 0
Q79.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Electric field due to the infinite sheet: The sheet lies in the $x$-$y$ plane ($z = 0$) with density $+\sigma_s$, so at $(0,0,2)$ its electric field magnitude is $E_{\text{sheet}} = \frac{|\sigma_s|}{2\varepsilon_0}$.
  2. Step 2 — Electric field due to the infinite line charge: The line charge lies at $z = 4\text{ m}$ parallel to the $y$-axis (along $x = 0, z = 4\text{ m}$). Its perpendicular distance from $(0,0,2)$ is $r = |4 - 2| = 2\text{ m}$, giving $E_{\text{line}} = \frac{|\lambda_e|}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 r} = \frac{|\lambda_e|}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}$.
  3. Step 3 — Compute the ratio of magnitudes: $\frac{E_{\text{sheet}}}{E_{\text{line}}} = \frac{|\sigma_s|/(2\varepsilon_0)}{|\lambda_e|/(4\pi\varepsilon_0)} = 2\pi\frac{|\sigma_s|}{|\lambda_e|}$. Substituting $|\sigma_s| = 2|\lambda_e|$ yields $\frac{E_{\text{sheet}}}{E_{\text{line}}} = 4\pi = \pi\sqrt{16}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Comparing $\pi\sqrt{16} : 1$ with $\pi\sqrt{n} : 1$ gives $n = 16$, confirming the numerical answer 16.

Q80.questionRecapHtml: Bob (2 g) on 20 cm thread stays 10 cm from wall with E = 2 × 10 N/C; find x in q = √1x µC.
Q80.conceptHtml: Geometry gives sin θ = 10/20 = 1/2 =⇒ θ = 30° , and equilibrium gives qE = mg tan θ.

1. Step 1 — Find the angle of the thread with the vertical wall: The thread has length $L = 20\text{ cm}$ and the particle stays at horizontal distance $d = 10\text{ cm}$ from the wall. Thus $\sin\theta = \frac{d}{L} = \frac{10}{20} = \frac{1}{2} \Rightarrow \theta = 30^\circ$, so $\tan 30^\circ = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$.
  2. Step 2 — Apply static equilibrium equations: Balancing horizontal and vertical forces gives $T\sin\theta = qE$ and $T\cos\theta = mg$. Dividing the two equations yields $qE = mg\tan\theta$.
  3. Step 3 — Solve for charge $q$: With $m = 2\text{ g} = 2 \times 10^{-3}\text{ kg}$, $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$, and $E = 2 \times 10^4\text{ N/C}$, we get $q = \frac{(2 \times 10^{-3})(10)(1/\sqrt{3})}{2 \times 10^4} = \frac{10^{-6}}{\sqrt{3}}\text{ C} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\text{ }\mu\text{C}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Comparing $\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\text{ }\mu\text{C}$ with $\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\text{ }\mu\text{C}$ gives $x = 3$, confirming the numerical answer 3.

Q81.questionRecapHtml: Charged spheres (ρ = 1.5 g/cc) keep same angle in air and water (ρw = 1 g/cc); find K.
Q81.conceptHtml: Equal angle requires mg = mg(1-ρ /ρ) =⇒ K = ρ-ρ . l l
Q81.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Write the equilibrium condition in air: Each sphere is in equilibrium under tension $T$, weight $mg$, and electrostatic repulsion $F_e$, giving $\tan\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right) = \frac{F_e}{mg}$.
  2. Step 2 — Write the equilibrium condition in water: In water (dielectric constant $K$, density $\rho_l = 1\text{ g/cc}$), the electrostatic force reduces to $F_e' = \frac{F_e}{K}$ and buoyancy reduces the effective weight to $W_{\text{eff}} = mg\left(1 - \frac{\rho_l}{\rho_s}\right)$.
  3. Step 3 — Equate the tangent of the unchanged angle: $\frac{F_e}{mg} = \frac{F_e / K}{mg(1 - \rho_l/\rho_s)} \Rightarrow K = \frac{1}{1 - \rho_l/\rho_s} = \frac{\rho_s}{\rho_s - \rho_l}$. Substituting $\rho_s = 1.5\text{ g/cc}$ and $\rho_l = 1\text{ g/cc}$ gives $K = \frac{1.5}{1.5 - 1.0} = 3$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The dielectric constant of water is 3, confirming the numerical answer 3.

Q83.questionRecapHtml: Charged spheres (ρ = 1.4 g/cm ) keep 37 angle in liquid (0.7 g/cm ); find K.
Q83.conceptHtml: Same-angle immersion shortcut: K = ρ-σ (independent of θ = 37° ).
Q83.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the unchanged-angle condition in a dielectric liquid: When suspended charged spheres maintain the same separation angle in air and in a liquid of density $\rho_l$ and dielectric constant $K$, the reduction in Coulomb force by factor $K$ matches the reduction in effective weight due to buoyancy: $\frac{F_e}{mg} = \frac{F_e / K}{mg(1 - \rho_l/\rho_s)}$.
  2. Step 2 — Solve for the dielectric constant $K$: Canceling $\frac{F_e}{mg}$ gives $K = \frac{\rho_s}{\rho_s - \rho_l}$ (note that the result is independent of the specific angle $37^\circ$).
  3. Step 3 — Substitute the given densities: With $\rho_s = 1.4\text{ g/cm}^3$ and $\rho_l = 0.7\text{ g/cm}^3$, $K = \frac{1.4}{1.4 - 0.7} = \frac{1.4}{0.7} = 2$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The dielectric constant of the liquid is 2, confirming the numerical answer 2.
Q83.trapHtml: The angle 37° and tan 37° = 3/4 are pure distractors—they cancel out completely! Correct

Q84.subtopic: Kinematics of Electron Near Charged Sheet
Q84.questionRecapHtml: Electron at 1 m from +σ sheet moves at 1 m/s and strikes at t = 1 s; find max σ coefficient α.
Q84.conceptHtml: To maximize σ (acceleration a = 2mε toward sheet), launch electron AWAY from sheet (u = -1 m/s toward sheet) so 0 s = ut + 21 at2 = 1.
Q84.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Find the electron's acceleration toward the sheet: An infinite sheet with $+\sigma$ creates a uniform field $E = \frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}$ pointing away from it. The negatively charged electron (charge $-e$, mass $m$) is pulled toward the sheet with constant acceleration $a = \frac{eE}{m} = \frac{e\sigma}{2m\varepsilon_0}$.
  2. Step 2 — Choose the velocity direction that maximizes $\sigma$: To require the maximum possible acceleration (and hence maximum $\sigma$) while still striking the sheet at $t = 1\text{ s}$, the electron must be initially launched straight away from the sheet ($u = -1\text{ m/s}$ measured toward the sheet) from $s = 1\text{ m}$.
  3. Step 3 — Apply kinematics to find $a$ and $\sigma$: Using $s = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^2$ with $s = 1\text{ m}$, $u = -1\text{ m/s}$, and $t = 1\text{ s}$: $1 = (-1)(1) + \frac{1}{2}a(1)^2 \Rightarrow \frac{1}{2}a = 2 \Rightarrow a = 4\text{ m/s}^2$. Setting $\frac{e\sigma}{2m\varepsilon_0} = 4$ gives $\sigma = \frac{8m\varepsilon_0}{e}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Comparing with $\alpha\frac{m\varepsilon_0}{e}$ gives $\alpha = 8$, confirming the numerical answer 8.

Q85.questionRecapHtml: Charges -4 µC at A(1, 0, 4) and +4 µC at B(2, -1, 5) in E
Q85.conceptHtml: p rB - ⃗ ⃗ = q(⃗ rA ) and ⃗ ⃗ ⃗ × E. τ =p
Q85.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Find the dipole moment vector $\vec{p}$: The displacement vector from the negative charge at $A(1,0,4)\text{ m}$ to the positive charge at $B(2,-1,5)\text{ m}$ is $\vec{d} = \vec{r}_B - \vec{r}_A = (2-1)\hat{i} + (-1-0)\hat{j} + (5-4)\hat{k} = (\hat{i} - \hat{j} + \hat{k})\text{ m}$. Thus $\vec{p} = q\vec{d} = 4 \times 10^{-6}(\hat{i} - \hat{j} + \hat{k})\text{ C}\cdot\text{m}$.
  2. Step 2 — Convert the electric field to SI units: $\vec{E} = 0.20\hat{i}\text{ V/cm} = 0.20 \times 100\hat{i}\text{ V/m} = 20\hat{i}\text{ N/C}$.
  3. Step 3 — Compute the torque vector $\vec{\tau} = \vec{p} \times \vec{E}$: $\vec{\tau} = (4 \times 10^{-6})(\hat{i} - \hat{j} + \hat{k}) \times (20\hat{i}) = 80 \times 10^{-6}(0 + \hat{k} + \hat{j}) = 8 \times 10^{-5}(\hat{j} + \hat{k})\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$.
  4. Step 4 — Find the magnitude and confirm: $|\vec{\tau}| = 8 \times 10^{-5}\sqrt{1^2 + 1^2} = 8\sqrt{2} \times 10^{-5}\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$. Comparing with $8\sqrt{\alpha} \times 10^{-5}\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$ gives $\alpha = 2$, confirming the numerical answer 2.

Q86.subtopic: Potential at Surface of Atomic Nucleus
Q86.questionRecapHtml: Find potential at surface of nucleus (Z = 50, R = 9 × 10 cm) in 10 V.
Q86.conceptHtml: V = R with R converted to metres (9 × 10<sup>−15</sup> m).
Q86.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Calculate the total nuclear charge: For atomic number $Z = 50$, the charge of the nucleus is $q = Ze = 50 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C} = 8 \times 10^{-18}\text{ C}$.
  2. Step 2 — Convert the nuclear radius to meters: $R = 9 \times 10^{-13}\text{ cm} = 9 \times 10^{-15}\text{ m}$.
  3. Step 3 — Compute the surface electric potential: Treating the spherical nucleus as a point charge at its center for the surface potential, $V = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{q}{R} = \frac{(9 \times 10^9)(8 \times 10^{-18})}{9 \times 10^{-15}} = 8 \times 10^6\text{ V}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The surface potential is $8 \times 10^6\text{ V}$, confirming the numerical answer 8.
Q86.trapHtml: Notice 9 × 10<sup>−13</sup> cm = 9 × 10<sup>−15</sup> m cancels the 9 in k = 9 × 10<sup>9</sup> cleanly. Correct

Q87.subtopic: Tension in Charged Ring with Central Charge
Q87.questionRecapHtml: Ring (R = 30 cm, Q = 2π C) with q = 30 pC at centre; find ring tension T in N.
Q87.conceptHtml: Radial outward force on element dθ balances 2T sin(dθ/2) = T dθ: T = 2πR2.
Q87.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the given quantities: The metallic ring has radius $R = 30\text{ cm} = 0.3\text{ m}$ and carries a uniform charge $Q = 2\pi\text{ C}$. A central point charge $q = 30\text{ pC} = 30 \times 10^{-12}\text{ C}$ is placed at its center, and $k = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^9\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{C}^2$.
  2. Step 2 — Relate tension to the radial electrostatic force on a small arc: Consider a tiny arc element of the ring subtending angle $d\theta$ at the center. Its charge is $dQ = \frac{Q}{2\pi}\,d\theta$, so the outward radial repulsive force from the central charge is $dF = \frac{kq\,dQ}{R^2} = \frac{kqQ}{2\pi R^2}\,d\theta$.
  3. Step 3 — Apply radial equilibrium for the arc element: The inward component of the ring tension $T$ at the two ends of the arc balances $dF$: $2T\sin\!\left(\frac{d\theta}{2}\right) \approx T\,d\theta = dF$, which gives $T = \frac{kqQ}{2\pi R^2}$.

Q90.questionRecapHtml: 64 identical drops at 10 mV combine into 1 big drop; find big drop potential.
Q90.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Relate the radius of the bigger drop to the small drops: When $N = 64$ identical drops of radius $r$ merge into one bigger drop of radius $R$, volume conservation gives $\frac{4}{3}\pi R^3 = N \cdot \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3$, so $R = N^{1/3}r = 64^{1/3}r = 4r$.
  2. Step 2 — Apply conservation of charge: If each small drop carries charge $q$, the total charge on the bigger drop is $Q = Nq = 64q$.
  3. Step 3 — Compute the new potential: The potential of one small drop is $V = \frac{kq}{r} = 10\text{ mV}$. The potential of the bigger drop is $V_{\text{big}} = \frac{kQ}{R} = \frac{k(Nq)}{N^{1/3}r} = N^{2/3}V$.
  4. Step 4 — Substitute values and confirm the answer: $V_{\text{big}} = (64)^{2/3} \times 10\text{ mV} = 16 \times 10\text{ mV} = 160\text{ mV}$. Hence, the verified numerical answer is 160.

Q91.questionRecapHtml: Two equal charges (q0 = 2 µC, m = 20 g) in equilibrium on 30 smooth incline; find x in h = x × 10 m.
Q91.conceptHtml: Along the incline, electrostatic repulsion balances mg sin 30° : d20 = mg sin 30° , with h = d sin 30° .
Q91.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Express the separation along the incline: From the diagram, the smooth inclined plane makes an angle $\theta = 30^\circ$ with the horizontal, and the upper charge $q_0$ is at vertical height $h$ above the lower charge. Hence, the separation between the two charges along the incline is $d = \frac{h}{\sin 30^\circ} = 2h$.
  2. Step 2 — Set up the equilibrium condition along the incline: For the upper charge of mass $m = 20\text{ g} = 0.02\text{ kg}$ to remain at rest without friction, the upward electrostatic repulsion must balance the downward component of gravity: $\frac{kq_0^2}{d^2} = mg\sin 30^\circ$.
  3. Step 3 — Solve for $h$: Substituting $d = 2h$, $q_0 = 2 \times 10^{-6}\text{ C}$, $k = 9 \times 10^9\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{C}^2$, and $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$: $\frac{9 \times 10^9 \times (2 \times 10^{-6})^2}{4h^2} = (0.02)(10)(0.5) = 0.1$. This simplifies to $4h^2 = \frac{36 \times 10^{-3}}{0.1} = 0.36 \implies h^2 = 0.09 \implies h = 0.3\text{ m}$.
  4. Step 4 — Express in the required form: $h = 0.3\text{ m} = 300 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m}$, so $x = 300$. Thus, the verified numerical answer is 300.

Q92.questionRecapHtml: Electron orbits infinite wire (λ = 2 × 10 C/m); find speed in 10 m/s.
Q92.conceptHtml: mv r = eE = 2kλe r =⇒ v = 2kλe m (independent of r).
Q92.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Write the electric field of an infinite line charge: At radial distance $r$ from an infinite cylindrical wire with linear charge density $\lambda = 2 \times 10^{-8}\text{ C/m}$, the electric field magnitude is $E = \frac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 r} = \frac{2k\lambda}{r}$.
  2. Step 2 — Equate centripetal force to the electrostatic attraction: For the electron (charge $e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}$, mass $m = 9 \times 10^{-31}\text{ kg}$) moving in a circle of radius $r$, $\frac{mv^2}{r} = eE = \frac{2ke\lambda}{r}$.
  3. Step 3 — Notice that $r$ cancels out and solve for $v$: $v^2 = \frac{2ke\lambda}{m} = \frac{2(9 \times 10^9)(1.6 \times 10^{-19})(2 \times 10^{-8})}{9 \times 10^{-31}} = 6.4 \times 10^{13} = 64 \times 10^{12}\text{ m}^2/\text{s}^2$.
  4. Step 4 — Take the square root and confirm the answer: $v = \sqrt{64 \times 10^{12}} = 8 \times 10^6\text{ m/s}$. Hence, the verified numerical answer is 8.

Q93.questionRecapHtml: Three concentric shells (a = 2, b = 3, c cm) have σ, -σ, +σ and VX = VZ; find c.
Q93.conceptHtml: VX = εσ (a - b + c) and VZ = εσ a -bc +c; equate VX = VZ. 0 0
Q93.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Write the charges on the three concentric shells: The shells $X, Y, Z$ have radii $a, b, c$ ($a < b < c$) and surface charge densities $+\sigma, -\sigma, +\sigma$. Their charges are $q_X = 4\pi a^2\sigma$, $q_Y = -4\pi b^2\sigma$, and $q_Z = 4\pi c^2\sigma$.
  2. Step 2 — Find the potential of shell $X$: Since $X$ lies inside both $Y$ and $Z$, its potential is $V_X = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\left(\frac{q_X}{a} + \frac{q_Y}{b} + \frac{q_Z}{c}\right) = \frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}(a - b + c)$.
  3. Step 3 — Find the potential of shell $Z$: Since $Z$ is the outermost shell, all three charges act as if concentrated at the center: $V_Z = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\left(\frac{q_X + q_Y + q_Z}{c}\right) = \frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}\left(\frac{a^2 - b^2 + c^2}{c}\right)$.
  4. Step 4 — Equate $V_X = V_Z$ and solve for $c$: $a - b + c = \frac{a^2 - b^2}{c} + c \implies a - b = \frac{(a - b)(a + b)}{c}$. Since $a \neq b$, we divide by $(a - b)$ to get $c = a + b = 2\text{ cm} + 3\text{ cm} = 5\text{ cm}$. Thus, the verified numerical answer is 5.

Q94.subtopic: Work Done Rotating Dipole by 180 Degrees
Q94.questionRecapHtml: Dipole (6 × 10<sup>−6</sup> Cm) in E = 1.5 × 10<sup>3</sup> N/C rotated 180° from alignment; find W in mJ.
Q94.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the work done in rotating an electric dipole: The external work required to rotate a dipole of moment $p$ in a uniform electric field $E$ from angle $\theta_1$ to $\theta_2$ is $W = pE(\cos\theta_1 - \cos\theta_2)$.
  2. Step 2 — Substitute the initial and final angles: Initially the dipole is aligned with the field ($\theta_1 = 0^\circ$), and it is rotated by $180^\circ$ ($\theta_2 = 180^\circ$). Thus, $W = pE(\cos 0^\circ - \cos 180^\circ) = pE(1 - (-1)) = 2pE$.
  3. Step 3 — Calculate the numerical value: Given $p = 6.0 \times 10^{-6}\text{ C}\cdot\text{m}$ and $E = 1.5 \times 10^3\text{ N/C}$, $W = 2(6.0 \times 10^{-6})(1.5 \times 10^3) = 18 \times 10^{-3}\text{ J} = 18\text{ mJ}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The work done is $18\text{ mJ}$, so the verified numerical answer is 18.
Q94.trapHtml: Direct W = 2pE; watch the unit mJ (10<sup>−3</sup> J). Correct

At $x = 0$, $E = 0$, so $\Phi_{\text{left}} = 0$. At $x = a$, $E = E_0 a$, so $\Phi_{\text{right}} = (E_0 a)(a^2) = E_0 a^3$.

Q103.conceptHtml: Vector Coulomb's law: F |⃗ r -⃗ r -⃗ (⃗ r |3 2 r1 ). 2 1
Q103.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Find the displacement vector from $q_1$ to $q_2$: Given $\vec{r}_1 = 2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} + 3\hat{k}$ and $\vec{r}_2 = \hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k}$, the vector from $q_1$ to $q_2$ is $\vec{r}_{21} = \vec{r}_2 - \vec{r}_1 = -\hat{i} - 2\hat{j} - 2\hat{k}\text{ m}$.
  2. Step 2 — Compute the distance $|\vec{r}_{21}|$: $|\vec{r}_{21}| = \sqrt{(-1)^2 + (-2)^2 + (-2)^2} = \sqrt{1 + 4 + 4} = 3\text{ m}$.
  3. Step 3 — Apply Coulomb's Law in vector form: $\vec{F}_{21} = \frac{kq_1 q_2}{|\vec{r}_{21}|^3}\vec{r}_{21} = \frac{(9 \times 10^9)(3 \times 10^{-6})(-4 \times 10^{-6})}{3^3}(-\hat{i} - 2\hat{j} - 2\hat{k})$.
  4. Step 4 — Simplify and match the option: $\frac{9 \times (-12) \times 10^{-3}}{27} = -4 \times 10^{-3}\text{ N}$, so $\vec{F}_{21} = (-4 \times 10^{-3})(-\hat{i} - 2\hat{j} - 2\hat{k}) = (4\hat{i} + 8\hat{j} + 8\hat{k}) \times 10^{-3}\text{ N}$. This matches option b.
Q103.trapHtml: Always substitute the SIGNED values of q1, q2 and use ⃗ rsource; reversing the subtraction flips the sign to distractor (D).

Q104.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the relation between electric field and potential: The electric field is the negative gradient of potential: $\vec{E} = -\frac{\partial V}{\partial x}\hat{i} - \frac{\partial V}{\partial y}\hat{j}$.
  2. Step 2 — Compute the partial derivatives of $V = 5(x^2 - y^2)$: $\frac{\partial V}{\partial x} = 10x$ and $\frac{\partial V}{\partial y} = -10y$.
  3. Step 3 — Substitute into $\vec{E}$ and evaluate at $(2, 3)$: $\vec{E} = -10x\hat{i} + 10y\hat{j}$. At $x = 2\text{ m}$ and $y = 3\text{ m}$, $\vec{E} = -10(2)\hat{i} + 10(3)\hat{j} = (-20\hat{i} + 30\hat{j})\text{ V/m}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the correct option: The electric field is $(-20\hat{i} + 30\hat{j})\text{ V/m}$, which corresponds to option a.

Q105.subtopic: Electric Field of Charged Half Ring
Q105.questionRecapHtml: Half ring (R = 35 cm) produces E = 100 V/m at centre; find total charge Q in nC.
Q105.conceptHtml: Field at centre of uniformly charged semicircular ring: E = 2kλ R = 2π<sub>2</sub> ε R2. 0
Q105.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Write the electric field at the center of a uniformly charged semicircular ring: For a thin half ring of radius $R$ and linear charge density $\lambda = \frac{Q}{\pi R}$, the electric field at the center is $E = \frac{2k\lambda}{R} = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\cdot\frac{2Q}{\pi R^2} = \frac{Q}{2\pi^2\varepsilon_0 R^2}$.
  2. Step 2 — Rearrange to solve for total charge $Q$: $Q = 2\pi^2\varepsilon_0 R^2 E$.
  3. Step 3 — Substitute the given values: With $\pi = 3.14$, $\varepsilon_0 = 8.85 \times 10^{-12}\text{ C}^2/(\text{N}\cdot\text{m}^2)$, $R = 0.35\text{ m}$, and $E = 100\text{ V/m}$, we have $Q = 2(3.14)^2(8.85 \times 10^{-12})(0.35)^2(100) \approx 2(9.86)(8.85 \times 10^{-12})(12.25) \approx 2.14 \times 10^{-9}\text{ C} = 2.14\text{ nC}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the correct option: The total charge is $2.14\text{ nC}$, matching option a.
Q105.trapHtml: Since λ = Q/(πR), the formula in terms of total charge Q has π 2 in the denominator: E = Q/(2π 2 ε<sub>0</sub> R2 ).

Q106.conceptHtml: Small-oscillation frequency of a dipole: f = 2π I ∝ E.
Q106.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the oscillation frequency of a dipole in a uniform field: For small-angle SHM of a rigid dipole of moment $p$ and moment of inertia $I$ in field $E$, the frequency is $f = \frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{\frac{pE}{I}}$, so $f \propto \sqrt{E}$.
  2. Step 2 — Find the initial and final electric field magnitudes: Initially, $\vec{E}_1 = E_0\hat{x}$, so $E_{\text{initial}} = E_0$. After introducing $\vec{E}_2 = 2E_0(\hat{y} + \hat{z})$, the resultant field is $\vec{E}_{\text{final}} = E_0\hat{x} + 2E_0\hat{y} + 2E_0\hat{z}$, whose magnitude is $E_{\text{final}} = \sqrt{1^2 + 2^2 + 2^2}\,E_0 = 3E_0$.
  3. Step 3 — Compute the percentage change in frequency: $\frac{f_{\text{final}}}{f_{\text{initial}}} = \sqrt{\frac{E_{\text{final}}}{E_{\text{initial}}}} = \sqrt{3} \approx 1.732$. Thus, the percentage increase is $\left(\frac{f_{\text{final}} - f_{\text{initial}}}{f_{\text{initial}}}\right) \times 100\% \approx (1.732 - 1) \times 100\% = 73.2\% \approx 73\%$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the correct option: The approximate percentage change is $73\%$, matching option a.

Q107.questionRecapHtml: Evaluate Assertion A (no net charge inside conductor) and Reason R (free charges drift inside vacuum capacitor).
Q107.conceptHtml: Inside a conductor in electrostatic equilibrium, E ⃗ = q E. plates experience F ⃗
Q107.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Assertion A: Under electrostatic conditions, the electric field inside the bulk of a conductor is zero ($\vec{E} = \vec{0}$). By Gauss's Law, any Gaussian surface inside the conductor encloses zero net charge, so all excess charge resides on the outer surface. Thus, Assertion A is true.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Reason R: Between the plates of a charged capacitor (with no dielectric), there exists a uniform electric field $\vec{E}$. Any free charge carrier placed in this region experiences an electrostatic force $\vec{F} = q\vec{E}$ and drifts accordingly. Thus, Reason R is also true.
  3. Step 3 — Check whether R explains A: Reason R describes the motion of free charges in the electric field between capacitor plates, which does not explain why the electrostatic field and net interior charge inside a conductor are zero.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the correct option: Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A, matching option b.

Q108.questionRecapHtml: Oil droplet (r = 1 mm, ρ = 1.5 g/cm<sup>3</sup> , q = 5 nC) floats between horizontal plates d = 12
Q108.conceptHtml: Upward electric force balances gravity: q d = 34 πr3 ρg (with bottom plate B at higher potential for +q).

Step 1 — Balance gravitational and electrostatic forces on each droplet: For positively charged droplets ($q = 5\text{ nC} = 5 \times 10^{-9}\text{ C}$) not to descend, the electric field $\vec{E}$ between top plate $A$ and bottom plate $B$ must point vertically upward, requiring $V_B > V_A$ and $qE = mg$.

Q109.questionRecapHtml: Charges 8 µC at x = 2 cm and -2 µC at x = 4 cm; find flux ratio through spheres of radii 3 cm and 5 cm.
Q109.conceptHtml: By Gauss's law, Φ = qenc /ε<sub>0</sub> depends only on charges strictly inside the sphere.

1. Step 1 — Determine the charge enclosed by the first sphere ($R_1 = 3\text{ cm}$): The charge $8\,\mu\text{C}$ is at $x = 2\text{ cm}$ (inside the $3\text{ cm}$ sphere), whereas $-2\,\mu\text{C}$ is at $x = 4\text{ cm}$ (outside). So $q_{\text{in},1} = 8\,\mu\text{C}$.

  4. Step 4 — Confirm the correct option: The flux ratio is $4 : 3$, which matches option c.

Q112.questionRecapHtml: Identify correct statements among A-E regarding field lines, Gauss's law, conservative work, and central force motion.
Q112.conceptHtml: Electrostatic field is conservative (never forms closed loops), radial outward for q > 0, central (planar motion), and Gauss's law requires 1/r2.
Q112.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Check Statements A and B: Statement A is false because electrostatic fields are conservative ($\oint \vec{E}\cdot d\vec{l} = 0$), so electrostatic field lines can never form closed loops. Statement B is true because field lines originate on positive charges and point radially outward.
  2. Step 2 — Check Statements C and D: Statement C is true because Gauss's Law holds precisely due to the inverse-square ($1/r^2$) dependence of Coulomb's force cancelling the $r^2$ surface area factor. Statement D is true because the electrostatic force is conservative, making closed-loop work zero.
  3. Step 3 — Check Statement E: Statement E is true because Coulomb's force is a central force ($\vec{\tau} = \vec{0}$), which conserves angular momentum $\vec{L}$ and restricts the particle's trajectory to a single plane.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the correct option: Statements B, C, D, and E only are correct, matching option c.

Q113.questionRecapHtml: Bring 3 nC from ∞ to third corner of equilateral triangle (a = 3 cm) with 1 nC, 2 nC at other corners.

1. Step 1 — Find the electric potential at the third corner: The two existing charges $q_1 = 1\text{ nC}$ and $q_2 = 2\text{ nC}$ are each at distance $a = 3\text{ cm} = 0.03\text{ m}$ from the third corner. Thus, $V = \frac{k(q_1 + q_2)}{a} = \frac{(9 \times 10^9)(3 \times 10^{-9})}{0.03} = 900\text{ V}$.
  2. Step 2 — Calculate the work done in bringing $q_3 = 3\text{ nC}$ from infinity: Since $V_\infty = 0$, the external work done is $W = q_3 V = (3 \times 10^{-9}\text{ C})(900\text{ V}) = 2.7 \times 10^{-6}\text{ J}$.
  3. Step 3 — Convert to microjoules and confirm the option: $W = 2.7\,\mu\text{J}$, which corresponds to option c.

Q116.questionRecapHtml: Find resultant dipole moment about origin for +2q at (0, -3a), +3q at (2a, 0), -4q at (-2a, 0).
Q116.conceptHtml: General definition about origin: p ⃗= ri. qi ⃗
Q116.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the definition of dipole moment about the origin: For a system of point charges $q_i$ at position vectors $\vec{r}_i$, the resultant dipole moment about the origin is $\vec{p} = \sum_i q_i \vec{r}_i$.
  2. Step 2 — Substitute each charge and its position vector: $\vec{p} = (+2q)(-3a\hat{j}) + (+3q)(2a\hat{i}) + (-4q)(-2a\hat{i})$.
  3. Step 3 — Simplify the components: $\vec{p} = -6qa\hat{j} + 6qa\hat{i} + 8qa\hat{i} = 14qa\hat{i} - 6qa\hat{j} = 2qa(7\hat{i} - 3\hat{j})$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the correct option: The resultant dipole moment is $2qa(7\hat{i} - 3\hat{j})$, which matches option a.

1. Step 1 — Calculate the dipole moments and distance to $P$: For dipole $A$, $p_A = (2 \times 10^{-6}\text{ C})(0.01\text{ m}) = 2 \times 10^{-8}\text{ C}\cdot\text{m}$. Q118.questionRecapHtml: Charges 7 µC, -2 µC at (∓9, 0, 0) cm in E = A2 r̂ (A = 9 × 10<sup>5</sup> ); find total energy.

1. Step 1 — Find the external electrostatic potential $V(r)$: Given $\vec{E} = \frac{A}{r^2}\hat{r}$ with $V(\infty) = 0$, integrating gives $V(r) = -\int_\infty^r \frac{A}{r'^2}\,dr' = \frac{A}{r}$. Both charges are at distance $r = 9\text{ cm} = 0.09\text{ m}$ from the origin, so $V(0.09) = \frac{9 \times 10^5}{0.09} = 10^7\text{ V}$.

  3. Step 3 — Compute the mutual interaction energy between $q_1$ and $q_2$: Their separation is $r_{12} = 18\text{ cm} = 0.18\text{ m}$, so $U_{12} = \frac{kq_1 q_2}{r_{12}} = \frac{(9 \times 10^9)(7 \times 10^{-6})(-2 \times 10^{-6})}{0.18} = -0.7\text{ J}$.

Q119.questionRecapHtml: Charges 2q at vertex A and q at centre of face CDEF of a cube; find flux through cube.
Q119.conceptHtml: A vertex charge is shared by 8 cubes (q/8) and a face-centre charge by 2 cubes (q/2).
Q119.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Find the fraction of the vertex charge inside the cube: A charge $2q$ placed at corner vertex $A$ is shared equally by $8$ identical cubes meeting at that vertex. Hence, its effective enclosed contribution to our cube is $\frac{2q}{8} = \frac{q}{4}$.
  2. Step 2 — Find the fraction of the face-center charge inside the cube: A charge $q$ placed at the center of face $CDEF$ is shared equally by $2$ adjacent cubes. Hence, its effective enclosed contribution is $\frac{q}{2}$.
  3. Step 3 — Apply Gauss's Law for total flux: $q_{\text{eff}} = \frac{q}{4} + \frac{q}{2} = \frac{3q}{4}$, so the electric flux through the cube is $\Phi = \frac{q_{\text{eff}}}{\varepsilon_0} = \frac{3q}{4\varepsilon_0}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the correct option: The electric flux is $\frac{3q}{4\varepsilon_0}$, matching option b.

Q121.questionRecapHtml: Three identical charged bubbles coalesce; find ratio Vsmall: Vbig.
Q121.conceptHtml: Volume conservation gives R = n1/3 r and Q = nq, so Vbig = n2/3 Vsmall.
Q121.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Apply volume conservation to relate the radii: When $N = 3$ identical water bubbles of radius $r$ coalesce into one bigger bubble of radius $R$, $\frac{4}{3}\pi R^3 = 3 \cdot \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3 \implies R = 3^{1/3}r$.
  2. Step 2 — Express the potential of the bigger bubble: By charge conservation, the total charge is $Q = 3q$. Thus, $V_{\text{big}} = \frac{kQ}{R} = \frac{k(3q)}{3^{1/3}r} = 3^{2/3}\left(\frac{kq}{r}\right) = 3^{2/3}V_{\text{initial}}$.
  3. Step 3 — Take the required ratio and confirm the option: $\frac{V_{\text{initial}}}{V_{\text{big}}} = \frac{1}{3^{2/3}}$, i.e., $1 : 3^{2/3}$, which matches option a.

Q123.conceptHtml: At equilibrium, tension balances the vector sum of perpendicular forces mg (vertical) and qE (horizontal).

Q124.questionRecapHtml: Five +Q and one -Q placed 60 apart on circle of radius R; find net E
Q124.conceptHtml: Opposite identical +Q pairs cancel; only the -Q (at 150° ) and its opposite +Q (at -30° ) contribute additively.
Q124.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Cancel diametrically opposite equal charges: From the diagram, the two $+Q$ charges at $90^\circ$ and $270^\circ$ cancel each other's fields at the center. Similarly, the two $+Q$ charges at $30^\circ$ and $210^\circ$ are diametrically opposite and cancel each other.
  2. Step 2 — Add the fields of the remaining opposite pair: Only $+Q$ at $-30^\circ$ (fourth quadrant) and $-Q$ at $150^\circ$ (second quadrant) remain. Both produce electric fields pointing toward $150^\circ$, each of magnitude $E_0 = \frac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 R^2}$.
  3. Step 3 — Resolve the resultant field into $\hat{i}$ and $\hat{j}$ components: The unit vector along $150^\circ$ is $(-\cos 30^\circ\,\hat{i} + \sin 30^\circ\,\hat{j}) = \left(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\hat{i} + \frac{1}{2}\hat{j}\right)$. Therefore, $\vec{E}_{\text{net}} = 2E_0\left(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\hat{i} + \frac{1}{2}\hat{j}\right) = -\frac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 R^2}(\sqrt{3}\hat{i} - \hat{j})$.

Q125.questionRecapHtml: Two spheres (R, Q, m) at 4R move toward each other at speed u; find minimum u to just touch.
Q125.conceptHtml: By momentum conservation, both come to rest when touching (rf = 2R); conserve total mechanical energy (kinetic + electrostatic + gravitational).

1. Step 1 — Identify the initial and final center separations: Initially, the two identical spheres of radius $R$ are separated by center-to-center distance $r_i = 4R$, each moving toward the other with speed $u$. When they just touch, they come instantaneously to rest at center-to-center separation $r_f = 2R$.
  2. Step 2 — Apply conservation of mechanical energy: Including both electrostatic repulsion ($+\frac{kQ^2}{r}$) and gravitational attraction ($-\frac{Gm^2}{r}$), we have $2\left(\frac{1}{2}mu^2\right) + \frac{kQ^2 - Gm^2}{4R} = 0 + \frac{kQ^2 - Gm^2}{2R}$.

Q126.subtopic: Work Done in Point Charge Field
Q126.questionRecapHtml: Q = 10 C at origin; find work done moving q = 2 µC from A(4, 4, 2) to B(2, 2, 1).
Q126.conceptHtml: W = q(VB - VA ) = kQq rB - r1. A
Q126.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Calculate the distances of points $A$ and $B$ from the origin: For $A(4, 4, 2)\text{ m}$, $r_A = \sqrt{4^2 + 4^2 + 2^2} = \sqrt{36} = 6\text{ m}$. For $B(2, 2, 1)\text{ m}$, $r_B = \sqrt{2^2 + 2^2 + 1^2} = \sqrt{9} = 3\text{ m}$.
  2. Step 2 — Write the work done in moving $q = 2\,\mu\text{C}$ from $A$ to $B$: Since the electrostatic force is conservative, $W = q(V_B - V_A) = kQq\left(\frac{1}{r_B} - \frac{1}{r_A}\right)$.
  3. Step 3 — Substitute the given values: With $Q = 10^{-8}\text{ C}$, $q = 2 \times 10^{-6}\text{ C}$, and $k = 9 \times 10^9\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{C}^2$, we get $W = (9 \times 10^9)(10^{-8})(2 \times 10^{-6})\left(\frac{1}{3} - \frac{1}{6}\right) = (180 \times 10^{-6})\left(\frac{1}{6}\right) = 30 \times 10^{-6}\text{ J}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the correct option: The work done is $30 \times 10^{-6}\text{ J}$, which matches option a.
Q126.trapHtml: Potential of a point charge depends only on radial distance r = x2 + y 2 + z 2; here rA = 6 m and rB = 3 m are exact integers.

Q127.questionRecapHtml: q = 3 C moves from (0, -2, -5) to (5, 1, 2) in E
Q127.conceptHtml: W = q E r=q 0 2x dx + -2 3y dy + -5 4 dz.
Q127.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Set up the work integral for the charge: For a charge $q = 3\text{ C}$ moving in $\vec{E} = 2x\hat{i} + 3y^2\hat{j} + 4\hat{k}\text{ N/C}$, the work done by the electric field is $W = q\int \vec{E}\cdot d\vec{r} = q\left(\int_0^5 2x\,dx + \int_{-2}^1 3y^2\,dy + \int_{-5}^2 4\,dz\right)$.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate each component integral separately: $\int_0^5 2x\,dx = [x^2]_0^5 = 25$; $\int_{-2}^1 3y^2\,dy = [y^3]_{-2}^1 = 1 - (-8) = 9$; and $\int_{-5}^2 4\,dz = [4z]_{-5}^2 = 8 - (-20) = 28$.
  3. Step 3 — Multiply the sum by $q = 3\text{ C}$: $W = 3(25 + 9 + 28) = 3(62) = 186\text{ J}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The work done is $186\text{ J}$, so the verified numerical answer is 186.
Q127.trapHtml: Watch negative lower limits: (-2)3 = -8, so 1 - (-8) = +9, and 8 - (-20) = +28. Correct

Q128.subtopic: Force Between Point Charge & Finite Rod
Q128.questionRecapHtml: Charge q = 1 µC at d = 2 cm from end of rod (L = 10 cm, Q = 24 µC); find force.
Q128.conceptHtml: Standard result for point charge on axis of uniform rod: F = d(d+L).
Q128.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Set up the force integral along the collinear rod: Place the point charge $q = 1\,\mu\text{C}$ at the origin; the uniformly charged rod of length $L = 10\text{ cm} = 0.10\text{ m}$ and charge $Q = 24\,\mu\text{C}$ extends from $x = d = 0.02\text{ m}$ to $x = d + L = 0.12\text{ m}$. A small element $dx$ carries charge $dQ = \frac{Q}{L}\,dx$.
  2. Step 2 — Integrate to obtain the standard formula: $F = \int_d^{d+L} \frac{kq(Q/L)}{x^2}\,dx = \frac{kQq}{L}\left[-\frac{1}{x}\right]_d^{d+L} = \frac{kQq}{L}\left(\frac{1}{d} - \frac{1}{d+L}\right) = \frac{kQq}{d(d+L)}$.
  3. Step 3 — Substitute the numerical values: $F = \frac{(9 \times 10^9)(24 \times 10^{-6})(1 \times 10^{-6})}{(0.02)(0.12)} = \frac{216 \times 10^{-3}}{2.4 \times 10^{-3}} = 90\text{ N}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The electrostatic force between $q$ and the wire is $90\text{ N}$, so the verified numerical answer is 90.
Q128.trapHtml: Memorize F = r r (geometric mean distance r1 r2 ) instead of wasting time integrating on exam day! 1 2 Correct

constantsHtml:
• Coulomb Constant: $k = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} = 8.99 \times 10^9 \approx 9 \times 10^9\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{C}^2$.
  • Permittivity of Free Space: $\varepsilon_0 = 8.854 \times 10^{-12}\text{ C}^2/(\text{N}\cdot\text{m}^2)$, $[\varepsilon_0] = [M^{-1}L^{-3}T^4A^2]$.
  • Elementary Charge: $e = 1.602 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}$; $1\text{ eV} = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\text{ J}$.
  • Relative Permittivity: $\varepsilon = K\varepsilon_0 = \varepsilon_r\varepsilon_0$ ($K \ge 1$; $K = \infty$ for ideal conductors).
  • Electron & Proton Mass: $m_e = 9.1 \times 10^{-31}\text{ kg}$, $m_p = 1.67 \times 10^{-27}\text{ kg}$.

formulaCards.title: 1. Coulomb’s Law & Superposition
formulaCards.html:
• Scalar & Vector Form: $F = \frac{kq_1 q_2}{r^2}$ (vacuum), $F_{\text{med}} = \frac{F_{\text{vac}}}{K}$; $\vec{F}_{21} = \frac{kq_1 q_2}{|\vec{r}_2 - \vec{r}_1|^3}(\vec{r}_2 - \vec{r}_1)$.
  • Equilibrium of Three Charges: Null point lies closer to the smaller-magnitude charge: $\frac{x}{d - x} = \sqrt{\frac{|q_1|}{|q_2|}}$ (same sign: between charges; opposite sign: outside, near smaller $|q|$).
  • Two-Ball Pendulum Equilibrium: $T\sin\theta = F_e$, $T\cos\theta = mg \implies \tan\theta = \frac{F_e}{mg}$.

formulaCards.title: 2. Electric Field & Continuous Distributions
formulaCards.html:
• Point Charge & Ring: $E = \frac{kq}{r^2}$; on axis of ring of radius $R$: $E = \frac{kQx}{(R^2+x^2)^{3/2}}$ (max at $x = \pm\frac{R}{\sqrt{2}}$).
  • Arc & Infinite Line: Arc of angle $\theta$: $E = \frac{2k\lambda}{R}\sin\frac{\theta}{2}$ (half-ring: $\frac{2k\lambda}{R} = \frac{Q}{\pi^2\varepsilon_0 R^2}$); infinite line: $E = \frac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 r}$.
  • Sheets & Disc: Infinite non-conducting sheet: $E = \frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}$; conducting surface: $E = \frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}$; disc on axis: $E = \frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}\left(1 - \frac{x}{\sqrt{R^2+x^2}}\right)$.
  • Solid Non-Conducting Sphere ($Q, R$): $E_{\text{in}} = \frac{kQr}{R^3} = \frac{\rho r}{3\varepsilon_0}$ ($r \le R$); $E_{\text{out}} = \frac{kQ}{r^2}$ ($r \ge R$).
  • Spherical Cavity (off-center $\vec{a}$): Uniform field inside cavity: $\vec{E}_{\text{cav}} = \frac{\rho\vec{a}}{3\varepsilon_0}$.

formulaCards.title: 3. Gauss’s Law & Symmetry Flux
formulaCards.html:
• Gauss’s Law: $\Phi = \oint \vec{E}\cdot d\vec{A} = \frac{q_{\text{in}}}{\varepsilon_0}$ (depends only on algebraic sum of enclosed charges).
  • Cube Symmetry: Charge $q$ at center: $\Phi_{\text{face}} = \frac{q}{6\varepsilon_0}$; at corner: $\Phi_{\text{cube}} = \frac{q}{8\varepsilon_0}$, each of 3 non-adjacent faces gets $\frac{q}{24\varepsilon_0}$ (0 through 3 touching faces).
  • Cone / Disc Flux: Point charge $q$ at distance $h$ from disc of radius $R$: $\Phi = \frac{q}{2\varepsilon_0}(1 - \cos\theta)$ where $\cos\theta = \frac{h}{\sqrt{R^2+h^2}}$.

formulaCards.title: 4. Electric Potential, Potential Energy & Work
formulaCards.html:
• Field–Potential Relation: $\vec{E} = -\nabla V = -\left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial x}\hat{i} + \frac{\partial V}{\partial y}\hat{j} + \frac{\partial V}{\partial z}\hat{k}\right)$; $\Delta V = -\int \vec{E}\cdot d\vec{r}$.
  • Solid Non-Conducting Sphere Potential: $V_{\text{in}} = \frac{kQ}{2R}\left(3 - \frac{r^2}{R^2}\right)$, so $V_{\text{center}} = 1.5\,V_{\text{surface}}$.
  • Electrostatic Potential Energy: $U = \sum_{i
  • Work Done: $W_{\text{ext}} = +\Delta U = q\Delta V$, $W_{\text{field}} = -\Delta U = -q\Delta V$.

formulaCards.title: 5. Electric Dipole & Conductors
formulaCards.html:
• Dipole Field & Potential: $E_{\text{axial}} = \frac{2kp}{r^3}$, $E_{\text{eq}} = \frac{kp}{r^3}$; general $(r,\theta)$: $E = \frac{kp}{r^3}\sqrt{1+3\cos^2\theta}$, $\tan\alpha = \frac{1}{2}\tan\theta$; $V = \frac{kp\cos\theta}{r^2}$.
  • Torque, Energy & SHM: $\vec{\tau} = \vec{p}\times\vec{E}$, $U = -\vec{p}\cdot\vec{E}$; SHM time period: $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{I}{pE}}$.
  • Conducting Shells & Charge Sharing: Connected spheres ($r_1, r_2$): $V_1 = V_2 \implies \frac{q_1}{q_2} = \frac{r_1}{r_2}$, $\frac{\sigma_1}{\sigma_2} = \frac{r_2}{r_1}$, $\frac{E_1}{E_2} = \frac{r_2}{r_1}$.
  • Electrostatic Pressure: $P = \frac{\sigma^2}{2\varepsilon_0} = \frac{1}{2}\varepsilon_0 E^2$; energy density $u = \frac{1}{2}\varepsilon_0 E^2$.

trapCards.title: 1. Sign Errors in E = −∇V, Work & Flux
trapCards.html:
• Gradient Minus Sign: Always keep the minus sign in $\vec{E} = -\nabla V$. If $V = ar^3 + b$ ($a > 0$), $E_r = -3ar^2$ points inward, so enclosed charge is negative.
  • Work by Field vs. External Agent: $W_{\text{field}} = -\Delta U$, whereas $W_{\text{ext}} = +\Delta U$. Read which agent is asked before choosing the sign.
  • Algebraic Sum in Gauss’s Law: Sum enclosed charges and face fluxes with signs ($+5q + q - 2q = 4q$).

trapCards.title: 2. Sheet Factors, Shells & Connected Spheres
trapCards.html:
• Non-Conducting vs. Conducting Sheet: Single infinite non-conducting sheet has $E = \frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}$, while a conducting surface or space between opposite sheets has $E = \frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}$.
  • Potential vs. Field Inside Shell: Inside a charged spherical shell, $E = 0$ but $V = \frac{kQ}{R} = \text{const} \ne 0$.
  • Connected Spheres Ratios: At equal potential, $Q \propto R$ while $\sigma \propto \frac{1}{R}$ and $E_{\text{surface}} \propto \frac{1}{R}$.

trapCards.title: 3. Dipole Angle & SHM Traps
trapCards.html:
• Dipole Field Angle $\alpha$: Resultant field makes angle $\alpha$ with $\vec{r}$ where $\tan\alpha = \frac{1}{2}\tan\theta$, NOT with the dipole axis ($\theta + \alpha$ is the angle with the axis).
  • SHM with Combined Fields: When an extra field $\vec{E}_2$ is added, use resultant $|\vec{E}_1 + \vec{E}_2|$ in $\omega = \sqrt{pE_{\text{net}}/I}$.

trapCards.title: 4. Unit Conversions & Cavity Superposition
trapCards.html:
• Micro/Nano Prefixes: Convert $\mu\text{C} = 10^{-6}\text{ C}$, $\text{nC} = 10^{-9}\text{ C}$, and $\text{cm} = 10^{-2}\text{ m}$ before substituting $k = 9 \times 10^9$.
  • Cavity Problems: Treat a cavity as solid sphere ($+\rho$) superposed with cavity sphere ($-\rho$); inside the cavity, $\vec{E} = \frac{\rho\vec{a}}{3\varepsilon_0}$ is uniform.
