cannot be explained by classical wave theory.
Q11.trapHtml: Both photoelectric effect and Compton effect are signature proofs of the quantum/particle nature of light.

1. Step 1 — Write the equation of the $V_0$ versus $ u$ graph: From Einstein's photoelectric equation, $eV_0 = h\nu - \phi_0 \implies V_0 = \left(\frac{h}{e}\right)\nu - \frac{\phi_0}{e}$. This is a straight-line equation of the form $y = mx + c$.

The magnitude of the vertical intercept on the $V_0$-axis is $\frac{\phi_0}{e}$, so $\phi_0 = e \times |V_0\text{-intercept}|$ can be estimated without knowing $h$, making (E) true.

  3. Step 3 — Match the wavelength to the EM spectrum: The visible spectrum spans approximately $400\text{ nm}$ to $700\text{ nm}$, while $10\text{ nm}$ to $400\text{ nm}$ is the ultraviolet region. Thus $\lambda = 330\text{ nm}$ lies in the ultraviolet region.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The radiation belongs to the Ultraviolet region, which matches Option (d).

1. Step 1 — Convert temperature to Kelvin and write the thermal de Broglie formula: $T = 27^\circ\text{C} = 27 + 273 = 300\text{ K}$. Using average kinetic energy $K = \frac{3}{2}k_B T$, the de Broglie wavelength is $\lambda = \frac{h}{\sqrt{3mk_B T}}$.

Step 2 — Evaluate the denominator $\sqrt{3mk_B T}$: $3mk_B T = 3 \times (5.31 \times 10^{-26}) \times (1.38 \times 10^{-23}) \times 300 \approx 6.595 \times 10^{-46}\text{ kg}^2\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{s}^2$. Taking the square root gives $\sqrt{3mk_B T} \approx 2.568 \times 10^{-23}\text{ kg}\cdot\text{m/s}$.

Q79.questionRecapHtml: ϕ = 110 × 10 J, Kmax = 0; find angular frequency ω .

1. Step 1 — Apply the zero kinetic energy (threshold) condition: When emitted photoelectrons have zero kinetic energy, the incident photon energy equals the work function: $h\nu = \phi$. Since angular frequency is $\omega = 2\pi\nu$, we have $\frac{h}{2\pi}\omega = \phi \implies \omega = \frac{2\pi\phi}{h}$.
  2. Step 2 — Substitute the given values: With $\phi = 110 \times 10^{-20}\text{ J}$ and $h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34}\text{ J}\cdot\text{s}$: $\omega = \frac{2 \times 3.14 \times 110 \times 10^{-20}}{6.63 \times 10^{-34}} = \frac{690.8 \times 10^{-20}}{6.63 \times 10^{-34}} \approx 1.04 \times 10^{16}\text{ rad/s}$.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the final answer: The angular frequency of the incident light is $1.04 \times 10^{16}\text{ rad/s}$, which matches Option (d).

Q83.subtopic: Matter Wave Wavelength of Charged Particle
Q83.questionRecapHtml: q = 3 × 10<sup>−19</sup> C, m = 6 × 10<sup>−27</sup> kg, V = 1.21 V; find λ in 10<sup>−12</sup> m.
Q83.conceptHtml: λ = √ . 2mqV
Q83.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Write the de Broglie wavelength for an accelerated charged particle: $\lambda = \frac{h}{\sqrt{2mqV}}$, where $q = 3 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}$, $m = 6 \times 10^{-27}\text{ kg}$, $V = 1.21\text{ V}$, and $h = 6.6 \times 10^{-34}\text{ J}\cdot\text{s}$.
  2. Step 2 — Compute the momentum $\sqrt{2mqV}$: $2mqV = 2 \times (6 \times 10^{-27}) \times (3 \times 10^{-19}) \times 1.21 = 36 \times 1.21 \times 10^{-46}\text{ kg}^2\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{s}^2$. Taking the square root gives $\sqrt{2mqV} = 6 \times 1.1 \times 10^{-23} = 6.6 \times 10^{-23}\text{ kg}\cdot\text{m/s}$.
  3. Step 3 — Calculate the de Broglie wavelength $\lambda$: $\lambda = \frac{6.6 \times 10^{-34}}{6.6 \times 10^{-23}} = 10^{-11}\text{ m} = 10 \times 10^{-12}\text{ m}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the numerical answer: Comparing with $\alpha \times 10^{-12}\text{ m}$, we get $\alpha = \mathbf{10}$.
Q83.trapHtml: Notice 36×1.21 is a perfect square (62 ×1.12 ), giving 6.6 which cancels h = 6.6 cleanly! Watch the exponent: 10<sup>−11</sup> = 10×10<sup>−12</sup> , so α = 10 (not 1). Correct

constantsHtml:
• Planck’s Constant: $h = 6.626 \times 10^{-34}\text{ J}\cdot\text{s}$; $hc = 1240\text{ eV}\cdot\text{nm} = 12400\text{ eV}\cdot\text{\AA}$ (also $1242\text{ eV}\cdot\text{nm}$ if given).
  • Electron Mass & Charge: $m_e = 9.1 \times 10^{-31}\text{ kg}$, $e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}$.

formulaCards.title: 1. Photon Properties & Radiation Force
formulaCards.html:
• Energy & Momentum: $E = h\nu = \frac{hc}{\lambda}$, $p = \frac{h}{\lambda} = \frac{E}{c}$, effective mass $m = \frac{h}{c\lambda}$.
  • Photon Flux: Number of photons/sec from source of power $P$: $N = \frac{P}{E} = \frac{P\lambda}{hc}$.
  • Radiation Force: $F = \frac{P}{c}$ (absorbed), $\frac{2P}{c}$ (reflected), $(1 + r)\frac{P}{c}\cos^2\theta$ (at incidence angle $\theta$).

formulaCards.title: 2. Photoelectric Effect & Einstein’s Equation
formulaCards.html:
• Einstein’s Equation: $K_{\max} = eV_0 = h u - \phi_0 = rac{hc}{\lambda} - rac{hc}{\lambda_0}$.
  • Threshold Frequency & Wavelength: $\phi_0 = h u_0 = rac{hc}{\lambda_0}$ (emission occurs iff $ u \ge u_0$ or $\lambda \le \lambda_0$).
  • Graph Slopes: $V_0$ vs. $ u$ has slope $ rac{h}{e}$ (universal, independent of metal!); $K_{\max}$ vs. $ u$ has slope $h$.
  • Saturation Current vs. Stopping Potential: Saturation current $\propto$ Intensity (at fixed $ u$); stopping potential $V_0$ depends ONLY on $ u$ (and $\phi_0$), independent of intensity.

formulaCards.title: 3. Matter Waves (de Broglie Wavelength)
formulaCards.html:
• General Formula: $\lambda = \frac{h}{p} = \frac{h}{mv} = \frac{h}{\sqrt{2mK}} = \frac{h}{\sqrt{2mqV}}$.
  • Electron Accelerated by $V$ Volts: $\lambda_e = \frac{12.27}{\sqrt{V}}\text{ \AA} \approx \frac{1.227}{\sqrt{V}}\text{ nm}$.
  • Proton, Alpha & Thermal Neutron: $\lambda_p = \frac{0.286}{\sqrt{V}}\text{ \AA}$, $\lambda_\alpha = \frac{0.101}{\sqrt{V}}\text{ \AA}$; thermal particle at $T$: $\lambda = \frac{h}{\sqrt{3mk_B T}}$.

trapCards.title: 1. Intensity vs. Frequency in Photoelectric Effect
trapCards.html:
• No Effect of Intensity on $K_{\max}$: Increasing intensity increases ONLY the number of photoelectrons (saturation current), NEVER $K_{\max}$ or $V_0$ (for monochromatic light).
  • Below Threshold $\lambda > \lambda_0$: Zero photoelectrons are emitted regardless of how high the intensity is.

trapCards.title: 2. Slope & Intercept of $V_0$–$\nu$ Graph
trapCards.html:
• $h/e$ vs. $h$: Slope of $V_0$ vs. $\nu$ is $\frac{h}{e}$ (in $\text{V}\cdot\text{s}$), whereas slope of $K_{\max}$ vs. $\nu$ is $h$.
  • Work Function Intercept: Vertical intercept on $V_0$ axis is $-\frac{\phi_0}{e}$ (in Volts), not $-\phi_0$ (unless in eV).

trapCards.title: 3. de Broglie Comparison Ratios
trapCards.html:
• Same $K$ vs. Same $V$ vs. Same $v$: At same $K$, $\lambda \propto \frac{1}{\sqrt{m}}$; at same $V$, $\lambda \propto \frac{1}{\sqrt{mq}}$; at same $v$, $\lambda \propto \frac{1}{m}$. Read which quantity is equal!
  • Alpha Particle ($q = 2e, m = 4m_p$): $\frac{\lambda_p}{\lambda_\alpha} = \sqrt{\frac{m_\alpha q_\alpha}{m_p q_p}} = \sqrt{8} = 2\sqrt{2}$ for same accelerating potential $V$.

trapCards.title: 4. Unit Shortcut $hc = 1240\text{ eV}\cdot\text{nm}$
trapCards.html: • Watch $1240$ vs. $1242$: Use the exact value of $hc$ (or $h, c$) given in the problem statement; if none is given, $1240\text{ eV}\cdot\text{nm}$ works cleanly.

Q01.questionRecapHtml: Dependence of nuclear mass density on mass number A.
Q01.conceptHtml: ρ = 4Am3u 3mu = 4πR 3 ≈ 2.3 × 10 17 kg/m<sup>3</sup> , independent of A. 3 πR0 A 0
Q01.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall nuclear radius relation: The radius $R$ of a nucleus with mass number $A$ is given by $R = R_0 A^{1/3}$, where $R_0 \approx 1.2 \times 10^{-15}\text{ m}$ is an empirical constant.
  2. Step 2 — Express nuclear mass and volume: Taking $m$ as the average mass of one nucleon, the total mass of the nucleus is $M = A m$, and its spherical volume is $V = \frac{4}{3}\pi R^3 = \frac{4}{3}\pi R_0^3 A$.
  3. Step 3 — Calculate nuclear mass density: Dividing mass by volume gives $\rho = \frac{M}{V} = \frac{A m}{\frac{4}{3}\pi R_0^3 A} = \frac{3m}{4\pi R_0^3}$, where $A$ cancels out completely.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: Since $\rho$ does not depend on $A$, nuclear mass density is independent of $A$, matching option (b).

Q01.trapHtml: Nuclear volume ∝ A and nuclear mass ∝ A, so their ratio is universal across all nuclei.

Q02.questionRecapHtml: Assertion-Reason on nuclear density of Cu vs C and R ∝ A.
Q02.conceptHtml: Because R = R0 A1/3, nuclear density ρ is constant and independent of A.
Q02.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Reason (R): Experimentally, the radius of a nucleus of mass number $A$ follows $R = R_0 A^{1/3}$, so $R \propto A^{1/3}$. Therefore, Reason (R) is correct.
  2. Step 2 — Derive nuclear density from $R \propto A^{1/3}$: Since nuclear volume $V = \frac{4}{3}\pi R^3 \propto A$ and nuclear mass $M \propto A$, the density $\rho = \frac{M}{V}$ is practically constant ($\approx 2.3 \times 10^{17}\text{ kg/m}^3$) for all nuclei, regardless of $A$.
  3. Step 3 — Evaluate Assertion (A): Because nuclear density is independent of mass number, the density of $^{64}_{29}\text{Cu}$ is virtually the same as that of $^{12}_{6}\text{C}$, not greater. Thus, Assertion (A) is not correct.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: (A) is not correct but (R) is correct, which matches option (c).
Q02.stepsLatex:
Reason (R): R = R0 A1/3 is true.
Assertion (A): Since ρ is independent of A, ρ(Cu) = ρ(C), so (A) is false.
Q02.trapHtml: Do not confuse macroscopic density of solid Cu vs C with nuclear density!

Q03.questionRecapHtml: Find Z when E3 - E1 = 108.8 eV.
Q03.conceptHtml: 2nd excited state is n = 3! ∆E = 13.6Z 2 (1 - 1/32 ) = 12.09Z 2 eV.
Q03.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the quantum numbers: The ground state corresponds to $n_1 = 1$, and the 2nd excited state corresponds to $n_2 = 3$ (since $n = 2$ is the 1st excited state).
  2. Step 2 — Write the energy difference formula: For a hydrogen-like ion of atomic number $Z$, $\Delta E = E_3 - E_1 = 13.6 Z^2 \left(\frac{1}{n_1^2} - \frac{1}{n_2^2}\right)\text{ eV}$.
  3. Step 3 — Substitute the given values and solve for $Z$: $108.8 = 13.6 Z^2 \left(\frac{1}{1^2} - \frac{1}{3^2}\right) = 13.6 Z^2 \left(\frac{8}{9}\right)$. Since $13.6 \times 8 = 108.8$, this simplifies to $\frac{Z^2}{9} = 1 \implies Z^2 = 9 \implies Z = 3$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: The atomic number of the ion is $Z = 3$, matching option (c).
Q03.trapHtml: 2nd excited state means n = 3, NOT n = 2! Note 108.8/13.6 = 8 cleanly.

Q04.questionRecapHtml: Ratio λmax,Lyman /λmax,Balmer.
Q04.conceptHtml: Lyman λmax (2 → 1) = 3R; Balmer λmax (3 → 2) = 5R.
Q04.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Relate largest wavelength to energy jump: Since $\lambda = \frac{hc}{\Delta E}$, the largest wavelength in any spectral series corresponds to the smallest energy transition (from the immediately adjacent higher level).
  2. Step 2 — Find largest wavelength in Lyman series ($n=2 \to 1$): Using the Rydberg formula, $\frac{1}{\lambda_L} = R\left(\frac{1}{1^2} - \frac{1}{2^2}\right) = \frac{3R}{4} \implies \lambda_L = \frac{4}{3R}$.
  3. Step 3 — Find largest wavelength in Balmer series ($n=3 \to 2$): Similarly, $\frac{1}{\lambda_B} = R\left(\frac{1}{2^2} - \frac{1}{3^2}\right) = \frac{5R}{36} \implies \lambda_B = \frac{36}{5R}$.
  4. Step 4 — Take the ratio and confirm the answer: $\frac{\lambda_L}{\lambda_B} = \frac{4/(3R)}{36/(5R)} = \frac{4 \times 5}{3 \times 36} = \frac{5}{27}$. This gives $5:27$, matching option (a).

λmax,Balmer 36/(5R) 3 36 27
Q04.trapHtml: Lyman has higher energy transitions than Balmer, so its wavelength must be smaller (ratio < 1, ruling out 27: 5).

Q05.questionRecapHtml: Identify mass vs. time curves for successive decay P → Q → R (stable).
Q05.conceptHtml: P (t) decays exponentially to 0; intermediate Q(t) starts at 0, rises to a maximum, then decays to 0; stable R(t) rises monotonically from 0 to m0.
Q05.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Analyze parent nucleus $P$: Initially all the mass is in $P$. As $P$ decays into $Q$, its mass decreases exponentially with time ($m_P = m_0 e^{-\lambda_1 t}$) toward zero.
  2. Step 2 — Analyze intermediate nucleus $Q$: $Q$ starts at zero mass, builds up as $P$ decays into it, reaches a maximum when its rate of formation equals its rate of decay, and then decays exponentially back toward zero as $P$ gets depleted.
  3. Step 3 — Analyze stable daughter $R$: Since $R$ is non-radioactive, it only accumulates from the decay of $Q$. Its mass starts at zero and rises monotonically, leveling off as all mass eventually converts into $R$.
  4. Step 4 — Match with the given graphs: Graph (B) is the only one where $P$ falls monotonically, $Q$ rises to a peak and then falls, and $R$ rises monotonically to saturation. This matches option (b).
Q05.stepsLatex:
P (t) = P0 e-λ1 t (monotonically decreasing to 0).
Q(t) : starts at 0, peaks when λ1 P = λ2 Q, then decays to 0.
R(t) : stable end-product, increases monotonically and saturates at P0 .
Only Graph (B) matches all three behaviours.
Q05.trapHtml: In Graph (C), the labels Q and R are swapped—always check which curve peaks and which saturates!

Q06.questionRecapHtml: Verify dimensions of h and L, and Bohr's quantization condition.
Q06.conceptHtml: [h] = [L] = [M L2 T -1 ], and Bohr's condition is L = n 2π (not nh).
Q06.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Check Statement I (dimensions): From $E = h\nu$, Planck's constant has dimensions $[h] = \frac{[ML^2T^{-2}]}{[T^{-1}]} = [ML^2T^{-1}]$. Angular momentum $L = mvr$ also has dimensions $[L] = [M][LT^{-1}][L] = [ML^2T^{-1}]$. Hence, Statement I is correct.
  2. Step 2 — Check Statement II (Bohr's quantization): According to Bohr's second postulate, the orbital angular momentum is quantized as $L = n\frac{h}{2\pi}$ ($n = 1, 2, 3, \dots$).
  3. Step 3 — Identify the flaw in Statement II: Angular momentum is an integral multiple of $\frac{h}{2\pi}$ (reduced Planck's constant $\hbar$), not Planck's constant $h$ itself. Hence, Statement II is incorrect.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect, matching option (b).

  3. Step 3 — Compute the ratio of radii: $\frac{r_5(\text{Li}^{2+})}{r_5(\text{He}^{+})} = \frac{5^2 / 3}{5^2 / 2} = \frac{2}{3}$.

Q08.questionRecapHtml: Assertion-Reason on why Bohr's model applies only to single-electron species.
Q08.conceptHtml: Bohr's model assumes a purely central Coulomb attraction between one electron and the nucleus, ignoring electron-electron repulsion.
Q08.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Assertion A: Bohr's atomic model accurately predicts spectra only for single-electron systems such as $\text{H}$, $\text{He}^+$, and $\text{Li}^{2+}$. Therefore, Assertion A is true.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Reason R: In deriving energy levels and radii, Bohr's model only accounts for the Coulomb attraction between the nucleus and a single orbiting electron, omitting electron-electron electrostatic repulsion. Therefore, Reason R is true.
  3. Step 3 — Check causal link: Because multi-electron atoms involve significant inter-electronic repulsion (and shielding), ignoring it is precisely why Bohr's model cannot be applied to them. Thus, R correctly explains A.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A, matching option (b).
Q08.stepsLatex:
Assertion A: True (valid strictly for 1-electron species like H, He+ , Li2+ ).
Reason R: True, and directly explains why multi-electron atoms cannot be treated by Bohr's model.
Q08.trapHtml: Read the causal link: omission of e- - e- repulsion is the exact physical reason for single-electron restriction.

Q09.questionRecapHtml: Match fission, chemical reaction, exothermic fusion, and endothermic fusion.
Q09.conceptHtml: A is 235 U fission (III); B is combustion of H<sub>2</sub> (I); C is standard D-D exothermic fusion (II); D converts tightly bound 3 H (BE ≈ 8.5 MeV) into two loosely bound 2 H (2 × 2.2 = 4.4 MeV), so Q < 0 (IV).
Q09.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Classify reactions A and B: In A, a heavy $^{235}_{92}\text{U}$ nucleus splits into lighter fragments ($^{140}_{54}\text{Xe}$ and $^{94}_{38}\text{Sr}$) after neutron capture, which is Fission (A-III). In B, $2\text{H}_2 + \text{O}_2 \to 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$ involves only electron rearrangement, which is a Chemical reaction (B-I).
  2. Step 2 — Classify reaction C: $^2_1\text{H} + ^2_1\text{H} \to ^3_2\text{He} + ^1_0\text{n}$ combines two deuterons into a more tightly bound $^3_2\text{He}$ nucleus, releasing energy ($\approx 3.27\text{ MeV}$). Thus it is Fusion with positive $Q$-value (C-II).
  3. Step 3 — Classify reaction D: $^1_1\text{H} + ^3_1\text{H} \to ^2_1\text{H} + ^2_1\text{H}$ converts tritium (binding energy $\approx 8.48\text{ MeV}$) into two deuterons (total binding energy $\approx 2 \times 2.22 = 4.44\text{ MeV}$). Since final binding energy is lower, energy must be absorbed, giving Fusion with negative $Q$-value (D-IV).
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: The complete matching is A-III, B-I, C-II, D-IV, matching option (b).
Q09.stepsLatex:
A → III (Fission), B → I (Chemical reaction),
C → II (Q > 0), D → IV (Q ≈ 4.4 - 8.5 = -4.1 MeV < 0).
Q09.trapHtml: To distinguish C vs D, recall that 3 H and 3 He have higher BE/nucleon than 2 H, so making 3 He releases energy while breaking 3 H into 2 H absorbs energy.

Q10.questionRecapHtml: Energy released in 2 2 4
Q10.conceptHtml: Q = BE(4 He) - 2 BE(2 H).
Q10.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Write the fusion reaction: Two deuterons fuse to form one helium nucleus: $^2_1\text{H} + ^2_1\text{H} \to ^4_2\text{He} + Q$.
  2. Step 2 — Find total binding energy of reactants: Each $^2_1\text{H}$ has $2$ nucleons with binding energy $1.1\text{ MeV}$ per nucleon, so $\text{BE}_{\text{reactants}} = 2 \times (2 \times 1.1) = 4.4\text{ MeV}$.
  3. Step 3 — Find total binding energy of product: $^4_2\text{He}$ has $4$ nucleons with binding energy $7.0\text{ MeV}$ per nucleon, so $\text{BE}_{\text{product}} = 4 \times 7.0 = 28.0\text{ MeV}$.
  4. Step 4 — Calculate energy released and confirm: $Q = \text{BE}_{\text{product}} - \text{BE}_{\text{reactants}} = 28.0 - 4.4 = 23.6\text{ MeV}$, matching option (c).
Q10.trapHtml: Direct twin of Q02 with 7.0 MeV instead of 7.2 MeV.

1. Step 1 — Recall Bohr radius for hydrogen-like ions: The radius of the $n$-th orbit is $r_n = \frac{n^2}{Z} a_0$, where $a_0$ is the first Bohr radius of hydrogen.
  2. Step 2 — Substitute $n$ and $Z$ for $\text{Li}^{2+}$: For $\text{Li}^{2+}$, the atomic number is $Z = 3$, and the ground state corresponds to $n = 1$.
  3. Step 3 — Compute $r_1$ and find $X$: $r_1 = \frac{1^2}{3} a_0 = \frac{1}{3} a_0$. Comparing this with $\frac{1}{X} a_0$ gives $X = 3$.

Q12.questionRecapHtml: Compare Bohr energies across H, He, and Li.
Q12.conceptHtml: En = -13.6 Z n2 eV, so states with equal Z/n have identical energy.
Q12.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Use the Bohr energy formula: The energy of an electron in the $n$-th state of a hydrogen-like species is $E_n = -13.6 \frac{Z^2}{n^2}\text{ eV}$. Thus two states have the same energy whenever $\frac{Z}{n}$ is identical.
  2. Step 2 — Check statements (A) and (B): For H in ground state ($Z=1, n=1$), $\frac{Z}{n} = 1$ ($E = -13.6\text{ eV}$). For $\text{He}^+$ in 1st excited state ($Z=2, n=2$), $\frac{Z}{n} = 1$ ($E = -13.6\text{ eV}$). For $\text{Li}^{2+}$ in 2nd excited state ($Z=3, n=3$), $\frac{Z}{n} = 1$ ($E = -13.6\text{ eV}$). So both (A) and (B) are correct.
  3. Step 3 — Check statements (C) and (D): $\text{He}^+$ in ground state ($Z=2, n=1$) has $E = -54.4\text{ eV} \neq -13.6\text{ eV}$, so (C) is false. $\text{Li}^{2+}$ in ground state ($Z=3, n=1$) has $E = -122.4\text{ eV} \neq -13.6\text{ eV}$, so (D) is false.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: Only statements (A) and (B) are correct, matching option (a).

He+ 1st excited (n = 2) : Z/n = 2/2 = 1 =⇒ E = -13.6 eV (A True).
Li2+ 2nd excited (n = 3) : Z/n = 3/3 = 1 =⇒ E = -13.6 eV (B True).
He+ ground (n = 1) : -54.4 eV; Li2+ ground (n = 1) : -122.4 eV (C, D False).
Q12.trapHtml: Quick shortcut: check Z/n! Whenever Z/n = 1, E = -13.6 eV.

Q13.questionRecapHtml: Number of emission lines from n = 4 to ground state.
Q13.conceptHtml: Maximum spectral lines from level n to 1 is N = 2.
Q13.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the spectral line count formula: When a large sample of hydrogen atoms is in the $n$-th energy level, every pair of levels from $1$ to $n$ can produce a distinct downward transition, giving $N = \frac{n(n-1)}{2}$ maximum spectral lines.
  2. Step 2 — Substitute $n = 4$: $N = \frac{4(4-1)}{2} = \frac{4 \times 3}{2} = 6$.
  3. Step 3 — Verify by listing transitions: The 6 possible transitions are $4\to 3$, $4\to 2$, $4\to 1$, $3\to 2$, $3\to 1$, and $2\to 1$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: The maximum number of emitted spectral lines is $6$, matching option (b).

Q14.questionRecapHtml: Dependence of orbital frequency f on n.
Q14.conceptHtml: f = 2πr; since v ∝ Z/n and r ∝ n2 /Z, f ∝ Z 2 /n3.
Q14.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Write orbital frequency in terms of $v$ and $r$: For circular motion in the $n$-th Bohr orbit, the frequency of revolution is $f_n = \frac{v_n}{2\pi r_n}$.
  2. Step 2 — Recall Bohr scaling laws for $v_n$ and $r_n$: In Bohr's model, orbital speed varies as $v_n \propto \frac{1}{n}$ and orbital radius varies as $r_n \propto n^2$.
  3. Step 3 — Combine the dependencies: Substituting these into the frequency formula yields $f_n \propto \frac{1/n}{n^2} = \frac{1}{n^3}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: The frequency of revolution varies as $\frac{1}{n^3}$, matching option (c).

Q15.questionRecapHtml: Identify the correct β -decay equation of a neutron.
Q15.conceptHtml: Conservation of charge (0 = +1 + (-1) + 0) and lepton number (0 = 0 + (+1) + (-1)) gives n → p + e- + ν̄.
Q15.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the process: A free neutron decays into a proton via $ eta^-$ decay, emitting an electron ($e^-$) to conserve electric charge.
  2. Step 2 — Apply charge and baryon number conservation: Charge: $0 o (+1) + (-1) + 0$ (conserved). Baryon number: $1 o 1 + 0 + 0$ (conserved).
  3. Step 3 — Apply lepton number conservation: The initial lepton number is $0$. Since $e^-$ has lepton number $+1$, an electron antineutrino ($ ar{ u}$, lepton number $-1$) must be emitted: $n o p + e^- + ar{ u}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: The correct nuclear process is $n o p + e^- + ar{ u}$, matching option (b).

Q16.questionRecapHtml: Find λAB given λAC = 2000 Å and λBC = 6000 Å.
Q16.conceptHtml: Energy conservation: EAC = EAB + EBC =⇒ λ 1 = λ 1 + λ 1. AC AB BC

1. Step 1 — Apply energy conservation to the transitions: The energy gap between states $A$ and $C$ equals the sum of the gaps from $A$ to $B$ and $B$ to $C$: $\Delta E_{AC} = \Delta E_{AB} + \Delta E_{BC}$.
  2. Step 2 — Convert energy differences to wavelengths: Using $\Delta E = \frac{hc}{\lambda}$, we get $\frac{hc}{\lambda_{AC}} = \frac{hc}{\lambda_{AB}} + \frac{hc}{\lambda_{BC}}$, so $\frac{1}{\lambda_{AB}} = \frac{1}{\lambda_{AC}} - \frac{1}{\lambda_{BC}}$.
  3. Step 3 — Substitute the given wavelengths: $\frac{1}{\lambda_{AB}} = \frac{1}{2000\text{ \AA}} - \frac{1}{6000\text{ \AA}} = \frac{3 - 1}{6000\text{ \AA}} = \frac{2}{6000\text{ \AA}} = \frac{1}{3000\text{ \AA}} \implies \lambda_{AB} = 3000\text{ \AA}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: The wavelength emitted during the transition from $A$ to $B$ is $3000\text{ \AA}$, matching option (d).

Q17.questionRecapHtml: Evaluate BE/nucleon constancy (30 < A < 170) and range of nuclear force.
Q17.conceptHtml: Constancy of BE/nucleon (≈ 8 MeV) for 30 < A < 170 is due to saturation of the short-range nuclear force.
Q17.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Assertion (A): From the binding energy per nucleon curve, $\text{BE}/A$ remains nearly constant ($\approx 8.0\text{–}8.8\text{ MeV}$) for intermediate nuclei with $30 < A < 170$. Thus, Assertion (A) is true.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Reason (R): The strong nuclear force acts only over very tiny distances of the order of a few femtometers ($1\text{–}3\text{ fm}$), which causes saturation (each nucleon interacts only with its immediate neighbors). It is a short-range force, not long-range. Thus, Reason (R) is false.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the answer: (A) is true but (R) is false, matching option (a).

1. Step 1 — Set up the decay equations: Let initial nuclei be $N_0$ for both. Given $\lambda_2 = 3\lambda_1$, at time $t$ we have $N_1 = N_0 e^{-\lambda_1 t}$ and $N_2 = N_0 e^{-\lambda_2 t} = N_0 e^{-3\lambda_1 t}$.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate at one half-life of $n_1$: At $t = T_{1/2,1}$, by definition of half-life, $e^{-\lambda_1 t} = \frac{1}{2}$, so $N_1 = \frac{N_0}{2}$.
  3. Step 3 — Find $N_2$ and the ratio $N_2 / N_1$: Since $e^{-3\lambda_1 t} = (e^{-\lambda_1 t})^3 = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^3 = \frac{1}{8}$, we get $N_2 = \frac{N_0}{8}$. Therefore, $\frac{N_2}{N_1} = \frac{N_0/8}{N_0/2} = \frac{1}{4}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: The required ratio is $1/4$, matching option (a).

Q19.conceptHtml: Initial momentum is zero: m1⃗

Q20.questionRecapHtml: Ratio of energy released by equal masses (2 kg) of H fusion vs U fission.
Q20.conceptHtml: For equal mass m, E = M NA × (energy per atom).
Q20.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Calculate fusion energy $E_H$ from $2\text{ kg}$ of hydrogen: $2\text{ kg} = 2000\text{ g}$ of $^1_1\text{H}$ contains $\frac{2000}{1} N_A = 2000 N_A$ nuclei. Since $4$ protons release $26.7\text{ MeV}$, $E_H = \frac{2000 N_A}{4} \times 26.7 = 13350 N_A\text{ MeV}$.
  2. Step 2 — Calculate fission energy $E_U$ from $2\text{ kg}$ of $^{235}\text{U}$: $2000\text{ g}$ of $^{235}\text{U}$ contains $\frac{2000}{235} N_A$ nuclei. Each fission releases $200\text{ MeV}$, so $E_U = \frac{2000 N_A}{235} \times 200 = \frac{400000}{235} N_A \approx 1702.1 N_A\text{ MeV}$.
  3. Step 3 — Compute the ratio $E_H / E_U$: $\frac{E_H}{E_U} = \frac{13350 \times 235}{400000} \approx 7.84$ (using the exact molar mass $1.008\text{ g/mol}$ for H gives $\approx 7.78$; using the NCERT rounded value $26\text{ MeV}$ per cycle gives $\approx 7.64$).
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: Among the choices, $7.62$ is the closest match, confirming option (a).

Q21.questionRecapHtml: Number of emission lines when ground-state H absorbs 10.2 eV.
Q21.conceptHtml: E2 - E1 = -3.4 - (-13.6) = 10.2 eV, so the electron reaches n = 2.
Q21.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Find the excited state reached: A hydrogen atom in the ground state has energy $E_1 = -13.6\text{ eV}$. After absorbing $10.2\text{ eV}$, its new energy is $E = -13.6 + 10.2 = -3.4\text{ eV}$.
  2. Step 2 — Identify the quantum number $n$: Using $E_n = -\frac{13.6}{n^2}\text{ eV} = -3.4\text{ eV}$, we get $n^2 = \frac{13.6}{3.4} = 4 \implies n = 2$.
  3. Step 3 — Count the emitted spectral lines: From $n = 2$, the electron can only make a single downward transition ($n = 2 \to n = 1$), giving $N = \frac{n(n-1)}{2} = \frac{2(1)}{2} = 1$ spectral line.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: Only $1$ spectral line is emitted, matching option (d).
Q21.trapHtml: From n = 2 only one downward transition (2 → 1) exists.

Q22.questionRecapHtml: Energy equivalent of 1 g in MeV.
Q22.conceptHtml: E = mc2 = 10<sup>−3</sup> × (3 × 10<sup>8</sup> )2 = 9 × 10<sup>13</sup> J; convert via 1 MeV = 1.6 × 10<sup>−13</sup> J.
Q22.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Apply Einstein's mass-energy equivalence: For $m = 1\text{ g} = 10^{-3}\text{ kg}$ and $c = 3 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}$, $E = mc^2 = 10^{-3} \times (3 \times 10^8)^2 = 9 \times 10^{13}\text{ J}$.
  2. Step 2 — Convert Joules to MeV: Since $1\text{ MeV} = 1.6 \times 10^{-13}\text{ J}$, we divide by $1.6 \times 10^{-13}$: $E = \frac{9 \times 10^{13}}{1.6 \times 10^{-13}} = 5.625 \times 10^{26}\text{ MeV}$.
  3. Step 3 — Round and confirm the answer: Rounding to two significant figures gives $5.6 \times 10^{26}\text{ MeV}$, matching option (a).
Q22.trapHtml: Watch the exponent: 1013 /10<sup>−13</sup> = 1026 (not 100 or 1012 ).

Q23.questionRecapHtml: Binding energy expression for 12
Q23.conceptHtml: BE = [ZMp + (A - Z)Mn - M0 ]c2; for 12 5 B, Z = 5 protons and A - Z = 7 neutrons.
Q23.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Count protons and neutrons in $^{12}_{5}\text{B}$: The atomic number is $Z = 5$ (so there are $5$ protons), and the neutron number is $N = A - Z = 12 - 5 = 7$ neutrons.
  2. Step 2 — Write the mass defect $\Delta m$: The mass defect is the total mass of individual nucleons minus the actual nuclear mass $M_0$: $\Delta m = 5M_p + 7M_n - M_0$.
  3. Step 3 — Multiply by $c^2$ for binding energy: $\text{BE} = \Delta m\,c^2 = (5M_p + 7M_n - M_0)c^2$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: This expression matches option (a).

Q23.trapHtml: Constituent nucleons always weigh MORE than the bound nucleus, so ∆m = 5Mp + 7Mn - M0 > 0.

Q24.questionRecapHtml: Identify particle R by conserving A and Z.
Q24.conceptHtml: Conserve mass number A and atomic number Z across the reaction.
Q24.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Write the reaction with unknown particle $^A_Z R$: $^{236}_{92}\text{X} \to ^{141}_{56}\text{Y} + ^{92}_{36}\text{Z} + 3\,^A_Z R$.
  2. Step 2 — Conserve mass number (superscripts): $236 = 141 + 92 + 3A \implies 236 = 233 + 3A \implies 3A = 3 \implies A = 1$.
  3. Step 3 — Conserve atomic number (subscripts): $92 = 56 + 36 + 3Z \implies 92 = 92 + 3Z \implies Z = 0$.
  4. Step 4 — Identify $R$ and confirm: A particle with mass number $A = 1$ and charge $Z = 0$ is a neutron ($^1_0\text{n}$), matching option (b).
Q24.trapHtml: Always check both A and Z: AR = 1, ZR = 0 uniquely identifies a neutron.

Q25.questionRecapHtml: Find mass defect ∆m for BE = 18 × 10<sup>8</sup> J.
Q25.conceptHtml: ∆m = BE/c2.
Q25.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Relate binding energy to mass defect: The difference between the total mass of nucleons and the nuclear mass is the mass defect $\Delta m$, related to binding energy by $\text{BE} = \Delta m\,c^2$.
  2. Step 2 — Solve for $\Delta m$ in kg: $\Delta m = \frac{\text{BE}}{c^2} = \frac{18 \times 10^8}{(3 \times 10^8)^2} = \frac{18 \times 10^8}{9 \times 10^{16}} = 2 \times 10^{-8}\text{ kg}$.
  3. Step 3 — Convert to micrograms ($\mu\text{g}$): Since $1\text{ kg} = 10^9\text{ }\mu\text{g}$, $\Delta m = 2 \times 10^{-8} \times 10^9\text{ }\mu\text{g} = 20\text{ }\mu\text{g}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: The mass difference is $20\text{ }\mu\text{g}$, matching option (a).
Q25.trapHtml: Convert kg to µg carefully: 1 kg = 103 g = 109 µg, so 2 × 10<sup>−8</sup> kg = 20 µg.

Q26.questionRecapHtml: Calculate λmax of Paschen series (n = 4 → 3).
Q26.conceptHtml: Paschen series ends at n1 = 3; longest wavelength is n2 = 4 → n1 = 3.
Q26.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the transition for longest Paschen wavelength: The Paschen series ends at $n_1 = 3$. The longest wavelength (smallest energy jump) comes from the adjacent level $n_2 = 4 \to n_1 = 3$.
  2. Step 2 — Apply the Rydberg formula: $\frac{1}{\lambda} = R_H \left(\frac{1}{3^2} - \frac{1}{4^2}\right) = R_H \left(\frac{1}{9} - \frac{1}{16}\right) = \frac{7 R_H}{144}$.
  3. Step 3 — Compute $\lambda$: $\lambda = \frac{144}{7 \times 1.097 \times 10^7} = \frac{144}{7.679 \times 10^7} \approx 1.875 \times 10^{-6}\text{ m} \approx 1.876 \times 10^{-6}\text{ m}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: The longest wavelength in the Paschen series is $1.876 \times 10^{-6}\text{ m}$, matching option (b).
Q26.trapHtml: Paschen is n1 = 3, NOT n1 = 2 (Balmer) or n1 = 4 (Brackett).

Q27.conceptHtml: Series limit (n2 = ∞): λmin = n21 /R.

Step 2 — Find shortest wavelength of Balmer ($n_1 = 2$) and Lyman ($n_1 = 1$) series: For Balmer, $\frac{1}{\lambda_B} = R\left(\frac{1}{2^2} - 0\right) = \frac{R}{4} \implies \lambda_B = \frac{4}{R}$. For Lyman, $\frac{1}{\lambda_L} = R\left(\frac{1}{1^2} - 0\right) = R \implies \lambda_L = \frac{1}{R}$.
  3. Step 3 — Compute the ratio and confirm: $\frac{\lambda_B}{\lambda_L} = \frac{4/R}{1/R} = \frac{4}{1}$, giving $4:1$ and matching option (d).

Q29.questionRecapHtml: Relation between total energy E and potential energy U in a Coulomb orbit.
Q29.conceptHtml: Virial theorem for 1/r potential: K = -E and U = 2E.
Q29.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Write kinetic and potential energies in a circular orbit: Equating centripetal and electrostatic forces gives $\frac{mv^2}{r} = \frac{kZe^2}{r^2} \implies K = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 = \frac{kZe^2}{2r}$. The electrostatic potential energy is $U = -\frac{kZe^2}{r}$.
  2. Step 2 — Find the total energy $E$: $E = K + U = \frac{kZe^2}{2r} - \frac{kZe^2}{r} = -\frac{kZe^2}{2r}$.
  3. Step 3 — Compare $E$ and $U$ and confirm: Comparing $E = -\frac{kZe^2}{2r}$ with $U = -\frac{kZe^2}{r}$ immediately gives $2E = U$, matching option (c).

Q31.questionRecapHtml: Check A and Z conservation for 1 235
Q31.conceptHtml: Left-hand side has Atotal = 1 + 235 = 236 and Ztotal = 0 + 92 = 92.

1. Step 1 — Determine total initial $A$ and $Z$: The reactants $^1_0 ext{n} + ^{235}_{92} ext{U}$ have total mass number $A_{ ext{total}} = 1 + 235 = 236$ and total atomic number $Z_{ ext{total}} = 0 + 92 = 92$.

Q32.subtopic: Properties of Nuclear Force & Packing Fraction
Q32.questionRecapHtml: Identify true statements about Bohr orbits, nuclear force, and packing fraction.
Q32.conceptHtml: Nuclear forces are non-central (they have a tensor component depending on spin orientation), spin-dependent, charge- independent, and short-range (not 1/r2 ).
Q32.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Check statements (A), (B), and (C): (A) In Bohr's model, $L = n\hbar$ (True). (B) Strong nuclear force is short-range and decays much faster than $1/r^2$, so it does not obey the inverse square law (True). (C) Nuclear force depends on whether nucleon spins are parallel or antiparallel, so it is spin dependent (True).
  2. Step 2 — Check statement (D): Although nuclear forces are charge independent, they contain a tensor component that depends on spin orientation relative to the line joining nucleons, making them non-central. Hence, (D) is False.
  3. Step 3 — Check statement (E): Packing fraction is $f = \frac{M - A}{A}$; a lower (more negative) packing fraction corresponds to higher mass defect per nucleon and greater stability. Thus stability is inversely related to packing fraction (True).
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: Statements (A), (B), (C), and (E) are correct, matching option (c).
Q32.stepsLatex:
(A) True: L = nℏ. (B) True: short-range, not 1/r2 .
(C) True: stronger for parallel spins.
(D) False: nuclear force is NON-central.
(E) True: lower (more negative) packing fraction =⇒ higher stability.
Q32.trapHtml: Statement (D) is the classic trap: nuclear force is charge-independent, but it is non-central!

Q33.subtopic: Minimum Excitation Energy for Balmer Emission
Q33.questionRecapHtml: Minimum energy from n = 1 to produce a Balmer line.
Q33.conceptHtml: To emit a Balmer line (ending at n = 2), the atom must be excited at least to n = 3.
Q33.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the minimum excited state needed for Balmer emission: Balmer lines are emitted when an electron jumps down to $n = 2$ from $n \ge 3$. Thus, the atom must be excited from the ground state ($n = 1$) to at least $n = 3$.
  2. Step 2 — Calculate the excitation energy: Using $E_n = -\frac{13.6}{n^2}\text{ eV}$, we have $E_1 = -13.6\text{ eV}$ and $E_3 = -\frac{13.6}{9} \approx -1.51\text{ eV}$.
  3. Step 3 — Find $\Delta E$ and confirm: $\Delta E = E_3 - E_1 = -1.51 - (-13.6) = 12.09\text{ eV} \approx 12.1\text{ eV}$, matching option (c).
Q33.trapHtml: Exciting to n = 2 (10.2 eV) only produces a Lyman line (2 → 1); Balmer emission requires reaching at least n = 3 (12.1 eV).

Q34.questionRecapHtml: Find A2 when R2 = R1 /2 and A1 = 192.
Q34.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the nuclear radius relation: $R = R_0 A^{1/3}$, which gives the ratio $\frac{R_2}{R_1} = \left(\frac{A_2}{A_1}\right)^{1/3}$.
  2. Step 2 — Substitute the given values: Given $\frac{R_2}{R_1} = \frac{1}{2}$ and $A_1 = 192$, we cube both sides: $\frac{A_2}{192} = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^3 = \frac{1}{8}$.
  3. Step 3 — Solve for $A_2$ and confirm: $A_2 = \frac{192}{8} = 24$, matching option (b).
Q34.trapHtml: Halving the radius reduces mass number by 23 = 8, not by 2.

Q35.questionRecapHtml: Find λ<sub>2</sub> (3 → 1) in terms of λ (2 → 1).
Q35.conceptHtml: First Lyman line: 2 → 1; second Lyman line: 3 → 1.
Q35.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Write Rydberg equation for the first Lyman line ($n = 2 \to 1$): $\frac{1}{\lambda} = R\left(\frac{1}{1^2} - \frac{1}{2^2}\right) = \frac{3R}{4}$.
  2. Step 2 — Write Rydberg equation for the second Lyman line ($n = 3 \to 1$): $\frac{1}{\lambda_2} = R\left(\frac{1}{1^2} - \frac{1}{3^2}\right) = \frac{8R}{9}$.
  3. Step 3 — Divide the two equations to find $\lambda_2$: $\frac{\lambda_2}{\lambda} = \frac{3R/4}{8R/9} = \frac{3}{4} \times \frac{9}{8} = \frac{27}{32} \implies \lambda_2 = \frac{27}{32}\lambda$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: The wavelength of the second member is $\frac{27}{32}\lambda$, matching option (c).

Q36.subtopic: Orbital Magnetic Moment in Bohr Model
Q36.questionRecapHtml: Power x in µn ∝ nx for Bohr orbits.
Q36.conceptHtml: Gyromagnetic relation: µn = 2m Ln = n 4πm = nµB ∝ n1.
Q36.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Express orbital magnetic moment $\mu_n$: An orbiting electron forms a current loop with $I = \frac{e}{T} = \frac{ev}{2\pi r}$ and area $A = \pi r^2$, so $\mu_n = IA = \frac{evr}{2}$.
  2. Step 2 — Relate $\mu_n$ to angular momentum $L$: Since $L = mvr$, we can rewrite $\mu_n = \frac{e}{2m} L$.
  3. Step 3 — Substitute Bohr's quantization $L = \frac{nh}{2\pi}$: $\mu_n = \frac{e}{2m}\left(\frac{nh}{2\pi}\right) = n\left(\frac{eh}{4\pi m}\right)$, which shows $\mu_n \propto n^1$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: Comparing with $\mu_n \propto n^x$ gives $x = 1$, matching option (d).

Q37.questionRecapHtml: Speed of each of three identical daughter nuclei from fission with mass defect ∆M.
Q37.conceptHtml: Total released energy ∆M c2 is shared equally among 3 daughters of mass ≈ M/3 each: 3 × 12 M 3 v 2 = ∆M c2.
Q37.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Relate energy released to mass defect: The total energy released in the fission is $Q = \Delta M\,c^2$, which appears as the total kinetic energy of the three identical daughter nuclei.
  2. Step 2 — Express total kinetic energy of the fragments: Each daughter nucleus has mass $m \approx \frac{M}{3}$ (since $\Delta M \ll M$) and speed $v$. Total kinetic energy is $K_{\text{total}} = 3 \times \frac{1}{2}mv^2 = \frac{1}{2}(3m)v^2 \approx \frac{1}{2}Mv^2$.
  3. Step 3 — Equate and solve for $v$: $\frac{1}{2}Mv^2 = \Delta M\,c^2 \implies v^2 = \frac{2\Delta M}{M}c^2 \implies v = c\sqrt{\frac{2\Delta M}{M}}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: The speed of each daughter nucleus is $c\sqrt{\frac{2\Delta M}{M}}$, matching option (c).

Q38.questionRecapHtml: Find |K|/|U | in the 5 excited state of H.
Q38.conceptHtml: For every bound Bohr orbit (any n or Z), |K|/|U | = 1/2.
Q38.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall energy relations in any Bohr orbit: For an electron in any orbit $n$ (including the 5th excited state, $n = 6$), kinetic energy is $K = \frac{kZe^2}{2r}$ and potential energy is $U = -\frac{kZe^2}{r}$.
  2. Step 2 — Take the ratio of magnitudes: $\frac{|K|}{|U|} = \frac{kZe^2 / (2r)}{kZe^2 / r} = \frac{1}{2}$, which is completely independent of the quantum number $n$.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the answer: The ratio of the magnitude of kinetic energy to potential energy is $\frac{1}{2}$, matching option (c).

Q39.questionRecapHtml: Distinguish Rutherford's nuclear model from Thomson's plum-pudding model.
Q39.conceptHtml: Statement I describes Rutherford's nuclear model; Statement II describes J. J. Thomson's plum-pudding model, which was disproved by Rutherford's experiment.
Q39.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement I: Rutherford's nuclear model established that nearly all of an atom's mass and all its positive charge reside in a tiny central nucleus, with electrons revolving around it. Thus, Statement I is true.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement II: A spherical cloud of positive charge with embedded electrons is J.J. Thomson's plum-pudding model, which Rutherford's $\alpha$-scattering experiment disproved—it is not a special case of Rutherford's model. Thus, Statement II is false.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the answer: Statement I is true but Statement II is false, matching option (b).
Q39.stepsLatex:
Statement I: True (Rutherford's planetary/nuclear model).
Statement II: False (describes Thomson's model, not a special case of Rutherford's).
Q39.trapHtml: Thomson's model and Rutherford's model are fundamentally distinct, not special cases of one another.

Q40.questionRecapHtml: Net energy released by adding the two fusion steps.
Q40.conceptHtml: Add the two equations so 10 n and 31 H cancel: 63 Li + 21 H → 2 42 He + Q.
Q40.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Combine the two chain reactions: Adding $^6_3\text{Li} + ^1_0\text{n} \to ^4_2\text{He} + ^3_1\text{H}$ and $^2_1\text{H} + ^3_1\text{H} \to ^4_2\text{He} + ^1_0\text{n}$ cancels $^1_0\text{n}$ and $^3_1\text{H}$, leaving the net reaction: $^6_3\text{Li} + ^2_1\text{H} \to 2\,^4_2\text{He}$.
  2. Step 2 — Calculate the mass defect $\Delta m$: $\Delta m = M(^6_3\text{Li}) + M(^2_1\text{H}) - 2M(^4_2\text{He}) = 6.01690 + 2.01471 - 2(4.00388) = 8.03161 - 8.00776 = 0.02385\text{ amu}$.
  3. Step 3 — Convert mass defect to energy: $Q = 0.02385 \times 931.5\text{ MeV} = 22.216\text{ MeV} \approx 22.22\text{ MeV}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: The energy released is approximately $22.22\text{ MeV}$, matching option (a).
Q40.trapHtml: Always add the two reactions first—you are not even given M (31 H) or M (n) because they cancel!

Q41.questionRecapHtml: Neutron separation energy of 13 12
Q41.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Write the neutron-removal process: Removing one neutron from $^{13}_6\text{C}$ yields $^{12}_6\text{C}$ and a free neutron: $^{13}_6\text{C} + \text{Energy} \to ^{12}_6\text{C} + ^1_0\text{n}$.
  2. Step 2 — Calculate the mass difference $\Delta m$: $\Delta m = m(^{12}_6\text{C}) + m_n - m(^{13}_6\text{C}) = 12.000000 + 1.008665 - 13.003354 = 0.005311\text{ u}$.
  3. Step 3 — Compute the required energy: $E = \Delta m \times 931.5\text{ MeV/u} = 0.005311 \times 931.5 \approx 4.947\text{ MeV} \approx 4.95\text{ MeV}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: The neutron separation energy is $4.95\text{ MeV}$, matching option (c).
Q41.trapHtml: Watch decimal alignment: 0.005311 × 931.5 ≈ 4.95 MeV (not 49.5 MeV, distractor D).

Q42.questionRecapHtml: Find r4 given r3 = R.
Q42.conceptHtml: rn ∝ n2.
Q42.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall Bohr orbit radius scaling: For a given atom, the radius of the $n$-th stationary orbit is proportional to $n^2$, i.e., $r_n \propto n^2$.
  2. Step 2 — Set up the ratio for $n = 4$ and $n = 3$: $\frac{r_4}{r_3} = \frac{4^2}{3^2} = \frac{16}{9}$.
  3. Step 3 — Substitute $r_3 = R$ and confirm: $r_4 = \frac{16}{9}R$, matching option (b).

Q43.questionRecapHtml: Compute Q-value of U α-decay.
Q43.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Find the mass defect $\Delta m$ in atomic mass units: $\Delta m = m(^{238}_{92}\text{A}) - \left[m(^{234}_{90}\text{B}) + m(^4_2\text{D})\right] = 238.05079 - (234.04363 + 4.00260) = 238.05079 - 238.04623 = 0.00456\text{ u}$.
  2. Step 2 — Multiply by $931.5\text{ MeV/u}$ to get $Q$: $Q = 0.00456 \times 931.5 = 4.24764\text{ MeV} \approx 4.25\text{ MeV}$.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the answer: The approximate energy released is $4.25\text{ MeV}$, matching option (b).
Q43.trapHtml: Keep 5 decimal places when subtracting nuclear masses—rounding early destroys accuracy.

Q44.questionRecapHtml: Emission lines when H is bombarded with 12.5 eV electrons.
Q44.conceptHtml: Electrons can transfer any energy ≤ 12.5 eV. Since E3 - E1 = 12.09 eV < 12.5 eV < 12.75 eV = E4 - E1, maximum level reached is n = 3.
Q44.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Compare electron beam energy with H excitation energies: At room temperature, hydrogen atoms are in the ground state ($n = 1$, $E_1 = -13.6\text{ eV}$). Excitation to $n = 2$ needs $10.2\text{ eV}$, to $n = 3$ needs $12.09\text{ eV}$, and to $n = 4$ needs $12.75\text{ eV}$.
  2. Step 2 — Identify highest accessible level: Since $12.09\text{ eV} < 12.5\text{ eV} < 12.75\text{ eV}$, the $12.5\text{ eV}$ electrons can excite hydrogen atoms up to $n = 3$ (the excess kinetic energy stays with the scattered bombarding electron).
  3. Step 3 — Count total spectral lines from $n = 3$: $N = \frac{n(n-1)}{2} = \frac{3(3-1)}{2} = 3$ lines ($3\to 2$, $3\to 1$, and $2\to 1$).
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: The number of emitted spectral lines is $3$, matching option (c).

Q45.questionRecapHtml: Find E2 of He (Z = 2).
Q45.conceptHtml: En = -13.6 Z n2 eV; first excited state is n = 2.
Q45.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall energy formula for hydrogen-like ions: $E_n = -13.6 \frac{Z^2}{n^2}\text{ eV}$.
  2. Step 2 — Identify $Z$ and $n$: For $\text{He}^+$, $Z = 2$. The first excited state corresponds to $n = 2$.
  3. Step 3 — Compute $E_2$ and confirm: $E_2 = -13.6 \times \frac{2^2}{2^2} = -13.6\text{ eV}$, matching option (a).
Q45.trapHtml: First excited state is n = 2, so Z 2 /n2 = 4/4 = 1.

Q46.questionRecapHtml: Find ∆L = L2 - L1 given L1 = L.
Q46.conceptHtml: Ln = nL1 = nL =⇒ ∆L = L2 - L1 = 2L - L = L.
Q46.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Write Bohr's angular momentum for $n = 1$ and $n = 2$: In the $n$-th orbit, $L_n = n\frac{h}{2\pi}$. Given $L_1 = \frac{h}{2\pi} = L$, in the second orbit ($n = 2$) we have $L_2 = 2\frac{h}{2\pi} = 2L$.
  2. Step 2 — Calculate the change in angular momentum: $\Delta L = L_2 - L_1 = 2L - L = L$.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the answer: The change in angular momentum is $L$, matching option (a).
Q46.trapHtml: Read carefully: it asks for the *change* in angular momentum (2L - L = L), not the new value (2L).

Q47.questionRecapHtml: Evaluate statements on volume, surface, and Coulomb terms of nuclear binding energy.
Q47.conceptHtml: In the semi-empirical mass formula: total volume energy = +av A, total surface energy = -as A2/3 (proportional to surface area Z(Z-1) 4πR2 ∝ A2/3 ), total Coulomb energy = -ac. A1/3
Q47.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Check the semi-empirical mass formula (liquid drop model): Total binding energy is $B = a_v A - a_s A^{2/3} - a_c \frac{Z(Z-1)}{A^{1/3}} + \dots$. Thus the volume energy term is $b_v = a_3 A$ (C is correct).
  2. Step 2 — Check surface and Coulomb terms (A, B, D): Total surface energy is $-a_1 A^{2/3}$, which is proportional to nuclear surface area $4\pi R^2 \propto A^{2/3}$ (D is correct), whereas surface energy per nucleon scales as $A^{-1/3}$, not $A^{2/3}$ (A is incorrect). Total Coulomb energy scales as $\frac{Z(Z-1)}{A^{1/3}}$, not $\frac{Z(Z-1)}{A^{4/3}}$ (B is incorrect).
  3. Step 3 — Check statement E: Surface energy arises specifically because nucleons on the surface have fewer neighbors than interior nucleons, rather than assuming every nucleon interacts with $12$ nucleons (E is incorrect).
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: Only statements C and D are correct, matching option (a).
Q47.stepsLatex:
A: False — surface energy *per nucleon* is - a1 A-1/3 (total is - a1 A2/3 ).
B: False — total Coulomb term has A1/3 in denominator (A4/3 is per nucleon).
C: True — total volume energy bv = a3 A.
D: True — surface deficit ∝ 4πR2 ∝ A2/3 .
E: False — no fixed 12-neighbour assumption is made in standard derivation.
Q47.trapHtml: Watch 'total energy' vs. 'energy per nucleon' in A and B! That single distinction separates C, D only from all distractors.

Q48.questionRecapHtml: Identify the shortest-wavelength emission arrow among A (4 → 3), B (4 → 2), C (3 → 2), D (3 → 1).
Q48.conceptHtml: Shortest wavelength ⇐⇒ largest energy gap ∆E = hc/λ.
Q48.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Relate shortest wavelength to energy gap: Since $\lambda = \frac{hc}{\Delta E}$, the shortest emitted wavelength corresponds to the downward transition with the largest energy release $\Delta E$.
  2. Step 2 — Read the four transitions from the figure: Transition A is $n=4 \to 3$ ($\Delta E = 0.66\text{ eV}$), B is $n=4 \to 2$ ($\Delta E = 2.55\text{ eV}$), C is $n=3 \to 2$ ($\Delta E = 1.89\text{ eV}$), and D is $n=3 \to 1$ ($\Delta E = 12.09\text{ eV}$).
  3. Step 3 — Identify maximum $\Delta E$ and confirm: Transition D ($n=3 \to 1$, Lyman-$\beta$) has by far the largest energy difference ($12.09\text{ eV}$) and therefore emits the shortest wavelength, matching option (d).

A (4 → 3) : ∆E = 0.66 eV, B (4 → 2) : ∆E = 2.55 eV,
C (3 → 2) : ∆E = 1.89 eV, D (3 → 1) : ∆E = 12.09 eV (Maximum).
=⇒ Transition D emits the shortest wavelength.
Q48.trapHtml: Any Lyman transition (ending at n = 1) always has a much larger ∆E than any Balmer or Paschen transition!

Q49.questionRecapHtml: Energy released for n = 4 → 2 in Z = 4 ion.
Q49.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Write the transition energy formula: For a hydrogen-like atom with atomic number $Z$, $\Delta E = Rch\,Z^2 \left(\frac{1}{n_1^2} - \frac{1}{n_2^2}\right)$.
  2. Step 2 — Substitute $Z = 4$, $n_2 = 4$, $n_1 = 2$, and $Rch = 13.6\text{ eV}$: $\Delta E = 13.6 \times 4^2 \left(\frac{1}{2^2} - \frac{1}{4^2}\right) = 13.6 \times 16 \left(\frac{1}{4} - \frac{1}{16}\right)$.
  3. Step 3 — Simplify and confirm: $\Delta E = 13.6 \times 16 \times \frac{3}{16} = 13.6 \times 3 = 40.8\text{ eV}$, matching option (b).
Q49.trapHtml: Notice 42 = 16 cancels the denominator 16 immediately: 13.6 × 3 = 40.8 eV!

Q50.questionRecapHtml: Total binding energy of 4
Q50.conceptHtml: BE = [2mp + 2mn - M (4 He)] × 931.5 MeV.
Q50.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify nucleons in a helium nucleus ($^4_2\text{He}$): It consists of $2$ protons and $2$ neutrons.
  2. Step 2 — Calculate the mass defect $\Delta m$: $\Delta m = 2m_p + 2m_n - M_{\text{He}} = 2(1.0073) + 2(1.0087) - 4.0015 = 2.0146 + 2.0174 - 4.0015 = 0.0305\text{ u}$.
  3. Step 3 — Convert to binding energy in MeV: $\text{BE} = \Delta m \times 931.5\text{ MeV/u} = 0.0305 \times 931.5 \approx 28.41\text{ MeV} \approx 28.4\text{ MeV}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: The binding energy of the helium nucleus is $28.4\text{ MeV}$, matching option (a).
Q50.trapHtml: Do not confuse total BE (28.4 MeV) with BE per nucleon (7.1 MeV, distractor C).

Q51.questionRecapHtml: Find r3 given r2 = R.
Q51.conceptHtml: rn ∝ n2.
Q51.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall Bohr radius dependence on $n$: For a given atom, the orbital radius satisfies $r_n \propto n^2$.
  2. Step 2 — Take the ratio of the 3rd orbit to the 2nd orbit: $\frac{r_3}{r_2} = \frac{3^2}{2^2} = \frac{9}{4} = 2.25$.
  3. Step 3 — Substitute $r_2 = R$ and confirm: $r_3 = 2.25R$, matching option (a).
Q51.trapHtml: Direct n2 ratio: (3/2)2 = 2.25.

Q52.questionRecapHtml: Find v3 given v7 = 3.6 × 10 m/s.
Q52.conceptHtml: vn ∝ 1/n for a given Z.
Q52.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall Bohr speed scaling law: For a hydrogen atom, the orbital speed of the electron is inversely proportional to $n$, i.e., $v_n \propto \frac{1}{n}$.
  2. Step 2 — Set up the ratio between $n = 3$ and $n = 7$: $\frac{v_3}{v_7} = \frac{7}{3}$.
  3. Step 3 — Substitute $v_7 = 3.6 \times 10^6\text{ m/s}$ and compute: $v_3 = \frac{7}{3} \times 3.6 \times 10^6 = 7 \times 1.2 \times 10^6 = 8.4 \times 10^6\text{ m/s}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: The speed in the 3rd orbit is $8.4 \times 10^6\text{ m/s}$, matching option (c).
Q52.trapHtml: Inner orbits are faster (v ∝ 1/n), so v3 > v7.

Q53.questionRecapHtml: Identify the transition emitting a 124.1 nm photon.
Q53.conceptHtml: ∆E = hc λ ≈ 1241 λ (nm).
Q53.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Calculate the energy of the emitted photon in eV: Using $E = \frac{hc}{\lambda}$ with $h = 6.62 \times 10^{-34}\text{ J}\cdot\text{s}$, $c = 3 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}$, and $\lambda = 124.1 \times 10^{-9}\text{ m}$, we get $E = \frac{6.62 \times 10^{-34} \times 3 \times 10^8}{124.1 \times 10^{-9} \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19}} \approx \frac{1241.25}{124.1} \approx 10.0\text{ eV}$.
  2. Step 2 — Compute energy differences for each transition in the figure: A ($0.0 \to -2.2\text{ eV}$): $\Delta E = 2.2\text{ eV}$; B ($0.0 \to -5.2\text{ eV}$): $\Delta E = 5.2\text{ eV}$; C ($-2.2 \to -5.2\text{ eV}$): $\Delta E = 3.0\text{ eV}$; D ($0.0 \to -10.0\text{ eV}$): $\Delta E = 10.0\text{ eV}$.
  3. Step 3 — Match and confirm the answer: Transition D releases exactly $10.0\text{ eV}$, producing a $124.1\text{ nm}$ photon, matching option (d).

Q54.questionRecapHtml: Wavelength of 4 → 1 transition in H using h = 4 × 10 eV s.
Q54.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Find the energy released in the $n = 4 \to n = 1$ transition: $\Delta E = 13.6\left(\frac{1}{1^2} - \frac{1}{4^2}\right) = 13.6 \times \frac{15}{16} = 12.75\text{ eV}$.
  2. Step 2 — Compute $hc$ using the given value of $h$: With $h = 4 \times 10^{-15}\text{ eV}\cdot\text{s}$ and $c = 3 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}$, $hc = 1.2 \times 10^{-6}\text{ eV}\cdot\text{m} = 1200\text{ eV}\cdot\text{nm}$.
  3. Step 3 — Calculate the wavelength $\lambda$: $\lambda = \frac{hc}{\Delta E} = \frac{1200}{12.75} \approx 94.12\text{ nm} \approx 94.1\text{ nm}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: The emitted wavelength is $94.1\text{ nm}$, matching option (b).
Q54.trapHtml: Use the *given* h = 4 × 10<sup>−15</sup> eV s (so hc = 1200 eV nm instead of 1240 eV nm), which yields 94.1 nm cleanly!

Q55.questionRecapHtml: Find final state n when H electron drops from 4 excited state emitting 2.86 eV.
Q55.conceptHtml: Fourth excited state is ni = 5 (E5 = -13.6/25 = -0.544 eV). Final energy En = E5 - 2.86 eV.
Q55.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the initial quantum number and energy: The fourth excited state corresponds to $n_i = 5$. Its energy is $E_5 = -\frac{13.6}{5^2} = -0.544\text{ eV}$.
  2. Step 2 — Find the final state energy $E_n$: Emitting a photon of energy $2.86\text{ eV}$ lowers the atom's energy to $E_n = E_5 - 2.86 = -0.544 - 2.86 = -3.404\text{ eV} \approx -3.4\text{ eV}$.
  3. Step 3 — Solve for the integer $n$: Setting $-\frac{13.6}{n^2} = -3.4$ gives $n^2 = \frac{13.6}{3.4} = 4 \implies n = 2$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: The final energy level is 2.
Q55.trapHtml: 'Fourth excited state' means n = 5, NOT n = 4! Correct

Q56.subtopic: Triple-Alpha Fusion Rate in a Star
Q56.questionRecapHtml: Reaction rate P/Q for 3 He → C at power 5.808 × 10 W.
Q56.conceptHtml: Reaction rate = P/Q, where Q = [3m(4 He) - m(12 C)] × 931.5 MeV.
Q56.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Find the mass defect per triple-alpha reaction: $\Delta m = 3\,m(^4\text{He}) - m(^{12}\text{C}) = 3(4.0026) - 12 = 12.0078 - 12 = 0.0078\text{ u}$.
  2. Step 2 — Calculate energy $Q$ released per reaction in Joules: $Q = 0.0078 \times 931.5\text{ MeV} = 7.2657\text{ MeV} = 7.2657 \times 10^6 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\text{ J} \approx 1.1625 \times 10^{-12}\text{ J}$.
  3. Step 3 — Compute the reaction rate: Given power $P = 5.808 \times 10^{30}\text{ W}$, the number of reactions per second is $R = \frac{P}{Q} = \frac{5.808 \times 10^{30}}{1.1625 \times 10^{-12}} \approx 4.996 \times 10^{42}\text{ s}^{-1} \approx 5 \times 10^{42}\text{ s}^{-1}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: Comparing with $n \times 10^{42}\text{ s}^{-1}$ gives the integer value 5.
Q56.trapHtml: The star's mass (2.0 × 10<sup>32</sup> kg) is extra unused information—do not let it distract you! Correct

Q57.subtopic: Distance of Closest Approach & Alpha Speed
Q57.questionRecapHtml: Find initial (maximum) speed of α-particle given r0 = 4.5 × 10 m and Z = 80.
Q57.conceptHtml: Energy conservation: 21 mα v 2 = 4πϵ r. 0 0
Q57.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Apply conservation of energy at closest approach: All initial kinetic energy of the $\alpha$-particle ($q_\alpha = 2e$) converts into electrostatic potential energy against the target nucleus ($q = Ze$): $\frac{1}{2}m_\alpha v^2 = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{(Ze)(2e)}{r_0}$.
  2. Step 2 — Calculate the potential energy at $r_0 = 4.5 \times 10^{-14}\text{ m}$: $U = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{80 \times 2 \times (1.6 \times 10^{-19})^2}{4.5 \times 10^{-14}} = 2 \times 160 \times 2.56 \times 10^{-15} = 8.192 \times 10^{-13}\text{ J}$.
  3. Step 3 — Solve for the maximum velocity $v$: $v = \sqrt{\frac{2U}{m_\alpha}} = \sqrt{\frac{2 \times 8.192 \times 10^{-13}}{6.72 \times 10^{-27}}} = \sqrt{2.4381 \times 10^{14}} \approx 1.5614 \times 10^7\text{ m/s} = 156.14 \times 10^5\text{ m/s}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: Rounding to the nearest integer gives 156 (in units of $10^5\text{ m/s}$).
Q57.trapHtml: Do not forget the factor of 2 in qα = 2e and another factor of 2 from 12 mv 2 (total factor of 4 in v 2 ). Correct

Q58.questionRecapHtml: Emission wavelength for ∆E = 10.2 eV using hc = 1245 eV nm.
Q58.conceptHtml: λ = ∆E.
Q58.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Relate the Franck-Hertz dip to excitation energy: The first dip at $V = 10.2\text{ V}$ means the bombarding electrons transfer $\Delta E = eV = 10.2\text{ eV}$ of energy to excite hydrogen atoms to the first excited state.
  2. Step 2 — Write the photon wavelength formula: When an excited atom returns to the ground state, it emits a photon of energy $\Delta E = \frac{hc}{\lambda}$, so $\lambda = \frac{hc}{\Delta E}$.
  3. Step 3 — Substitute the given values: Using $hc = 1245\text{ eV}\cdot\text{nm}$ and $\Delta E = 10.2\text{ eV}$, we get $\lambda = \frac{1245}{10.2} \approx 122.06\text{ nm}$.
  4. Step 4 — Round to the nearest integer: Rounding $122.06\text{ nm}$ gives the final numerical answer as 122.

1245 eV nm
λ= = 122.06 nm ≈ 122 nm
10.2 eV
Q58.trapHtml: Use the given hc = 1245 eV nm (which gives 122.06 → 122, whereas 1240 would give 121.6). Correct

Q59.questionRecapHtml: Find x = n when rn = 8.48 Å.
Q59.conceptHtml: rn = n2 a0 and En = E/n2 =⇒ x = n2 = rn /a0.
Q59.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall Bohr orbit radius scaling: For a hydrogen atom ($Z = 1$), the radius of the $n$-th orbit is $r_n = a_0 n^2$, where $a_0 = 0.529\text{ \AA}$.
  2. Step 2 — Find the principal quantum number $n$: Dividing the given radius by $a_0$ gives $n^2 = \frac{r_n}{a_0} = \frac{8.48}{0.529} \approx 16.03 \approx 16$, so $n = 4$.
  3. Step 3 — Express the orbit energy in terms of ground-state energy $E$: Since $E_n = \frac{E}{n^2}$ for hydrogen, substituting $n^2 = 16$ yields $E_4 = \frac{E}{16}$.
  4. Step 4 — Match with the given form: Comparing $E_4 = \frac{E}{16}$ with $\frac{E}{x}$ gives the final numerical answer as 16.

Q61.questionRecapHtml: Energy released in 3 He → C in units of 10 MeV.
Q61.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Write the fusion reaction: Three helium nuclei combine to form one carbon-12 nucleus: $3\,{}^4_2\text{He} \to {}^{12}_6\text{C} + Q$. By definition of the atomic mass unit, the mass of ${}^{12}_6\text{C}$ is exactly $12\text{ u}$.
  2. Step 2 — Calculate the mass defect $\Delta m$: $\Delta m = 3 m({}^4_2\text{He}) - m({}^{12}_6\text{C}) = 3(4.002603) - 12 = 12.007809 - 12 = 0.007809\text{ u}$.
  3. Step 3 — Convert mass defect into energy released: Using $1\text{ u} = 931\text{ MeV}/c^2$, we get $Q = 0.007809 \times 931 \approx 7.2702\text{ MeV}$.
  4. Step 4 — Express in the required format: Writing $7.27\text{ MeV}$ as $727 \times 10^{-2}\text{ MeV}$ confirms the numerical answer is 727.
Q61.trapHtml: Watch the scaling factor ×10<sup>−2</sup> MeV—answer is 727, not 7.27. Correct

Q62.questionRecapHtml: Compute Q for U→ Ce + Zr + n.
Q62.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Sum the masses of the products: For ${}^{235}\text{U} \to {}^{140}\text{Ce} + {}^{94}\text{Zr} + n$, the total product mass is $m_{\text{products}} = 139.9054 + 93.9063 + 1.0086 = 234.8203\text{ u}$.
  2. Step 2 — Find the mass defect $\Delta m$: $\Delta m = m_{\text{reactant}} - m_{\text{products}} = 235.0439 - 234.8203 = 0.2236\text{ u}$.
  3. Step 3 — Calculate the disintegration energy $Q$: Multiplying by $c^2 = 931\text{ MeV/u}$ gives $Q = 0.2236 \times 931 \approx 208.17\text{ MeV}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final integer answer: Rounding to the nearest integer gives 208 MeV.
Q62.trapHtml: Sum the three product masses carefully before subtracting from 235.0439 u. Correct

Q63.questionRecapHtml: Percentage change in emitted wavelength due to recoil in H (n = 3 → 2).
Q63.conceptHtml: Recoil energy Kr = 2M = 2M c2; fractional wavelength shift ∆λ λ ≈ ∆E ∆E = 2M c2.
Q63.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Find the ideal transition energy: For $n = 3 \to n = 2$ in hydrogen, $\Delta E = 13.6\left(\frac{1}{2^2} - \frac{1}{3^2}\right) = 13.6 \times \frac{5}{36} \approx 1.889\text{ eV}$.
  2. Step 2 — Relate recoil kinetic energy to fractional wavelength shift: By momentum conservation, the atom recoils with momentum $p = \frac{\Delta E}{c}$ and kinetic energy $K_r = \frac{p^2}{2M} = \frac{(\Delta E)^2}{2Mc^2}$. Since $K_r \ll \Delta E$, the fractional drop in photon energy equals the fractional increase in wavelength: $\frac{\Delta \lambda}{\lambda} \approx \frac{K_r}{\Delta E} = \frac{\Delta E}{2Mc^2}$.
  3. Step 3 — Compute $Mc^2$ in eV and evaluate $\frac{\Delta \lambda}{\lambda}$: $Mc^2 = \frac{1.6 \times 10^{-27} \times (3 \times 10^8)^2}{1.6 \times 10^{-19}} = 9 \times 10^8\text{ eV}$. Therefore, $\frac{\Delta \lambda}{\lambda} = \frac{1.889}{2 \times 9 \times 10^8} \approx 1.05 \times 10^{-9}$.
  4. Step 4 — Convert to percentage change: Multiplying by $100\%$ gives $\approx 1.05 \times 10^{-7}\% \approx 1 \times 10^{-7}\%$, so $n =$ 7.
Q63.trapHtml: Do not forget ×100% for *percentage* change (10<sup>−9</sup> fractional = 10<sup>−7</sup> %, so n = 7, not 9!). Correct

Q64.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Write the frequency proportionality for a hydrogen-like ion: From Bohr theory, the emitted frequency is $ u = R c Z^2 \left( rac{1}{n_f^2} - rac{1}{n_i^2} ight)$, so for the same ion, $ u \propto \left( rac{1}{n_f^2} - rac{1}{n_i^2} ight)$.
  2. Step 2 — Take the ratio of frequencies for the two transitions: For $n = 2 o 1$, the factor is $1 - rac{1}{4} = rac{3}{4}$. For $n = 3 o 1$, the factor is $1 - rac{1}{9} = rac{8}{9}$.
  3. Step 3 — Solve for $ u_{3 o 1}$: $ rac{ u_{3 o 1}}{ u_{2 o 1}} = rac{8/9}{3/4} = rac{32}{27}$, so $ u_{3 o 1} = rac{32}{27} imes (3 imes 10^{15} ext{ Hz}) = rac{32}{9} imes 10^{15} ext{ Hz}$.
  4. Step 4 — Match with the given expression: Comparing with $ rac{x}{9} imes 10^{15} ext{ Hz}$ confirms the numerical answer is 32.

  2. Step 2 — Substitute the given radii and mass number: With $R_1 = 4.8\text{ fm}$, $A_1 = 64$, and $R_2 = 4\text{ fm}$, we have $\frac{4}{4.8} = \frac{5}{6} = \left(\frac{A_2}{64}\right)^{1/3}$.
  3. Step 3 — Cube both sides to solve for $A_2$: $\frac{A_2}{64} = \left(\frac{5}{6}\right)^3 = \frac{125}{216}$, so $A_2 = \frac{64 \times 125}{216} = \frac{8000}{216} = \frac{1000}{27}$.

Q70.questionRecapHtml: Recoil speed of H atom after 2 → 1 photon emission.
Q70.conceptHtml: Momentum conservation: M v = pphoton = ∆E c.
Q70.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Find the energy of the emitted photon: For the transition $n = 2 \to n = 1$ in hydrogen, $E = 13.6\left(1 - \frac{1}{4}\right) = 10.2\text{ eV} = 10.2 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\text{ J}$.
  2. Step 2 — Apply conservation of linear momentum: Initially at rest, the atom recoils with momentum equal in magnitude to the photon momentum: $mv = \frac{E}{c}$, so $v = \frac{E}{mc}$.
  3. Step 3 — Substitute the numerical values: With $m = 1.6 \times 10^{-27}\text{ kg}$ and $c = 3 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}$, $v = \frac{10.2 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19}}{(1.6 \times 10^{-27})(3 \times 10^8)} = \frac{10.2}{3} = 3.4\text{ m/s}$.
  4. Step 4 — Express as $\frac{x}{5}\text{ m/s}$: Since $3.4 = \frac{17}{5}$, the final numerical answer is 17.

  2. Step 2 — Apply the Rydberg formula: $\frac{1}{\lambda} = R\left(\frac{1}{3^2} - \frac{1}{4^2}\right) = R\left(\frac{1}{9} - \frac{1}{16}\right) = R\left(\frac{16 - 9}{144}\right) = \frac{7R}{144}$.

Q72.questionRecapHtml: Energy released when A = 236 (7.6 MeV/A) splits into two A = 118 (8.6 MeV/A).
Q72.conceptHtml: Q = A × ∆(BE/A).
Q72.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the energy release formula from binding energies: In any nuclear reaction, the energy released is $Q = \text{BE}_{\text{products}} - \text{BE}_{\text{reactants}}$.
  2. Step 2 — Compute total binding energy before and after fission: Initial binding energy is $\text{BE}_{\text{initial}} = 236 \times 7.6\text{ MeV}$. Final binding energy of the two fragments is $\text{BE}_{\text{final}} = 2 \times (118 \times 8.6) = 236 \times 8.6\text{ MeV}$.
  3. Step 3 — Subtract to find $Q$: $Q = 236(8.6 - 7.6) = 236 \times 1.0 = 236\text{ MeV}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The energy released in the fission process is 236 MeV.

Q73.conceptHtml: Centripetal force F = dU dr = mω 2 r = mv r =⇒ v = ωr, combined with mvr = nh 2π .
Q73.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Set up the central force from the harmonic potential: In this standard Bohr-quantization problem, the particle moves in a central potential $U = a r^2$ (or $\frac{1}{2}m\omega^2 r^2$), so the restoring force magnitude is $F = \left|-\frac{dU}{dr}\right| = 2ar$.
  2. Step 2 — Equate central force to centripetal force: For a circular orbit of radius $r$, $\frac{mv^2}{r} = 2ar$, which simplifies to $v = r\sqrt{\frac{2a}{m}}$.
  3. Step 3 — Apply Bohr angular momentum quantization: Using $mvr = \frac{nh}{2\pi}$ and substituting $v$, we get $m r^2 \sqrt{\frac{2a}{m}} = \frac{nh}{2\pi} \implies r^2 = \frac{nh}{2\pi\sqrt{2am}}$.
  4. Step 4 — Determine the scaling with $n$: Taking the square root gives $r_n \propto \sqrt{n}$, which matches Option (A) (verified answer: a).

1. Step 1 — Map the energy levels from the figure: Levels $A$, $B$, and $C$ are the 1st, 2nd, and 3rd excited states of hydrogen, so $n_A = 2$, $n_B = 3$, and $n_C = 4$. From the diagram, $\lambda_1$ is the transition $B \to A$ ($3 \to 2$) and $\lambda_2$ is $C \to B$ ($4 \to 3$).
  2. Step 2 — Write $\frac{1}{\lambda_1}$ and $\frac{1}{\lambda_2}$ using Rydberg formula: $\frac{1}{\lambda_1} = R\left(\frac{1}{2^2} - \frac{1}{3^2}\right) = \frac{5R}{36}$, and $\frac{1}{\lambda_2} = R\left(\frac{1}{3^2} - \frac{1}{4^2}\right) = \frac{7R}{144}$.
  3. Step 3 — Compute the ratio $\frac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_2}$: $\frac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_2} = \frac{1/\lambda_2}{1/\lambda_1} = \frac{7/144}{5/36} = \frac{7}{144} \times \frac{36}{5} = \frac{7}{20}$.

  3. Step 3 — Compute the ratio $\frac{r_2}{r_1}$: $\frac{r_2}{r_1} = \frac{4a_0}{2a_0} = \frac{2}{1}$.

Q81.questionRecapHtml: Total gain in BE when A = 242 (7.6 MeV/A) splits into two A = 121 (8.1 MeV/A).
Q81.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Calculate initial binding energy: For the parent nucleus with $A = 242$ and binding energy per nucleon $7.6\text{ MeV}$, $\text{BE}_{\text{initial}} = 242 \times 7.6\text{ MeV}$.
  2. Step 2 — Calculate final binding energy: For the two fragments each with $A = 121$ and binding energy per nucleon $8.1\text{ MeV}$, $\text{BE}_{\text{final}} = 2 \times (121 \times 8.1) = 242 \times 8.1\text{ MeV}$.
  3. Step 3 — Find the total gain in binding energy: $\Delta \text{BE} = \text{BE}_{\text{final}} - \text{BE}_{\text{initial}} = 242(8.1 - 7.6) = 242 \times 0.5 = 121\text{ MeV}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The total gain in binding energy is 121 MeV.
Q81.trapHtml: Direct arithmetic: 242 × 0.5 = 121 MeV. Correct

Q82.questionRecapHtml: Find x where r = (9/x) × 10 m for binding energy 12.8 eV.
Q82.conceptHtml: Total energy magnitude |E| = 4πϵ 2r. 0
Q82.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Relate binding energy to orbital radius: For an electron in a circular orbit around a proton, the total energy is $E = -\frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{e^2}{2r}$, so the separation (binding) energy is $|E| = \frac{k e^2}{2r}$, where $k = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^9\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{C}^2$.
  2. Step 2 — Solve for the orbital radius $r$: Rearranging gives $r = \frac{k e^2}{2|E|}$.
  3. Step 3 — Substitute the given values: With $|E| = 12.8 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\text{ J}$ and $e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}$, $r = \frac{9 \times 10^9 \times (1.6 \times 10^{-19})^2}{2 \times 12.8 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19}} = \frac{9 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-10}}{25.6} = \frac{9}{16} \times 10^{-10}\text{ m}$.
  4. Step 4 — Match with $\frac{9}{x} \times 10^{-10}\text{ m}$: Comparing directly confirms $x =$ 16.
Q82.trapHtml: Do not omit the factor of 2 in the denominator (|E| = ke2 /(2r), not ke2 /r!). Correct

Q83.questionRecapHtml: Find r5 (Li ) in units of 10 m using a0 = 0.51 Å.
Q83.conceptHtml: rn = a0 nZ with n = 5, Z = 3, 1 Å = 100 × 10<sup>−12</sup> m.
Q83.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Use the Bohr radius formula: For a hydrogen-like ion of atomic number $Z$, $r_n = r_0 \frac{n^2}{Z}$. Here $r_0 = 0.51\text{ \AA}$, $n = 5$, and $Z = 3$ (for $\text{Li}^{2+}$).
  2. Step 2 — Substitute the values: $r_5 = 0.51 \times \frac{5^2}{3} = 0.17 \times 25 = 4.25\text{ \AA}$.
  3. Step 3 — Convert from angstroms to $10^{-12}\text{ m}$: Since $1\text{ \AA} = 10^{-10}\text{ m} = 100 \times 10^{-12}\text{ m}$, we get $r_5 = 4.25 \times 100 \times 10^{-12}\text{ m} = 425 \times 10^{-12}\text{ m}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The required numerical value is 425.
Q83.trapHtml: Note 0.51/3 = 0.17 cleanly, and 1 Å = 10<sup>−10</sup> m = 100 × 10<sup>−12</sup> m. Correct

Q84.conceptHtml: BE = A × (BE/A). For A: N = Z = 17 =⇒ AA = 34; for B: AB = 26.
Q84.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Find the total binding energy of nucleus $A$: Nucleus $A$ has $Z = 17$ protons and an equal number of neutrons ($N = 17$), so $A_A = 17 + 17 = 34$. Thus $\text{BE}_A = 34 \times 1.2 = 40.8\text{ MeV}$.
  2. Step 2 — Find the total binding energy of nucleus $B$: Nucleus $B$ has $A_B = 26$ total nucleons and $1.8\text{ MeV}$ per nucleon, so $\text{BE}_B = 26 \times 1.8 = 46.8\text{ MeV}$.
  3. Step 3 — Take the difference $\text{BE}_B - \text{BE}_A$: $\text{BE}_B - \text{BE}_A = 46.8 - 40.8 = 6\text{ MeV}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The difference in binding energies is 6 MeV.
Q84.stepsLatex:
BEA = 34 × 1.2 = 40.8 MeV
BEB = 26 × 1.8 = 46.8 MeV
BEB - BEA = 46.8 - 40.8 = 6 MeV
Q84.trapHtml: For nucleus A, total nucleons is Z + N = 17 + 17 = 34, not 17! Correct

Q85.questionRecapHtml: Angular momentum after ground-state H absorbs 12.75 eV.
Q85.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Determine the excited state $n$: Absorbing $12.75\text{ eV}$ from the ground state ($-13.6\text{ eV}$) brings the electron to $E_n = -13.6 + 12.75 = -0.85\text{ eV}$. Since $E_n = -\frac{13.6}{n^2}$, we get $n^2 = \frac{13.6}{0.85} = 16 \implies n = 4$.
  2. Step 2 — Write Bohr angular momentum for $n = 4$: $L = \frac{nh}{2\pi} = \frac{4h}{2\pi} = \frac{2h}{\pi}$.
  3. Step 3 — Substitute $h = 4.14 \times 10^{-15}\text{ eV}\cdot\text{s}$: $L = \frac{2 \times 4.14 \times 10^{-15}}{\pi} = \frac{8.28 \times 10^{-15}}{\pi} = \frac{828 \times 10^{-17}}{\pi}\text{ eV}\cdot\text{s}$.
  4. Step 4 — Match with $\frac{x}{\pi} \times 10^{-17}\text{ eV}\cdot\text{s}$: Comparing directly confirms $x =$ 828.

Q86.questionRecapHtml: Ionization energy from 2nd excited state (n = 3) of Li2+ (Z = 3).
Q86.conceptHtml: Ionization energy from level n is |En | = 13.6 Z n2 eV.
Q86.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify $n$ and $Z$: The second excited state corresponds to $n = 3$ (ground state is $n = 1$, first excited is $n = 2$). For $\text{Li}^{2+}$, the atomic number is $Z = 3$.
  2. Step 2 — Calculate the ionization (binding) energy in this state: For a hydrogen-like ion, $|E_n| = 13.6 \frac{Z^2}{n^2}\text{ eV} = 13.6 \times \frac{3^2}{3^2} = 13.6\text{ eV}$.
  3. Step 3 — Express in the form $x \times 10^{-1}\text{ eV}$: Writing $13.6\text{ eV} = 136 \times 10^{-1}\text{ eV}$ gives $x = 136$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The required numerical value is 136.
Q86.trapHtml: 'Second excited state' is n = 3, so Z 2 /n2 = 9/9 = 1, and 13.6 = 136 × 10<sup>−1</sup> . Correct

Q87.questionRecapHtml: Find λ<sub>1</sub> /λ<sub>2</sub> where transition 1 is n = 3 → 1 and transition 2 is n = 2 → 1.
Q87.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Read the transitions from the figure: Transition 1 is from $n = 3$ to $n = 1$ (emitting $\lambda_1$), and transition 2 is from $n = 2$ to $n = 1$ (emitting $\lambda_2$).
  2. Step 2 — Apply the Rydberg formula to each transition: $\frac{1}{\lambda_1} = R\left(\frac{1}{1^2} - \frac{1}{3^2}\right) = \frac{8R}{9}$, and $\frac{1}{\lambda_2} = R\left(\frac{1}{1^2} - \frac{1}{2^2}\right) = \frac{3R}{4}$.
  3. Step 3 — Compute the ratio $\frac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_2}$: $\frac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_2} = \frac{1/\lambda_2}{1/\lambda_1} = \frac{3/4}{8/9} = \frac{3}{4} \times \frac{9}{8} = \frac{27}{32}$.
  4. Step 4 — Match with $\frac{x}{32}$: Comparing both fractions confirms $x =$ 27.
Q87.trapHtml: Read the arrow labels carefully: arrow 1 is the *longer* jump (3 → 1), so λ<sub>1</sub> < λ<sub>2</sub> . Correct

Q88.questionRecapHtml: Find λ(4 → 2) in terms of λ<sub>0</sub> (3 → 2).
Q88.conceptHtml: 2nd excited → 1st excited is 3 → 2 (λ<sub>0</sub> ); 3rd excited → 2nd orbit is 4 → 2 (λ).
Q88.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the first transition ($\lambda_0$): Jumping from the second excited state ($n = 3$) to the first excited state ($n = 2$) gives $\frac{1}{\lambda_0} = R\left(\frac{1}{2^2} - \frac{1}{3^2}\right) = \frac{5R}{36}$.
  2. Step 2 — Identify the second transition ($\lambda$): Jumping from the third excited state ($n = 4$) to the second orbit ($n = 2$) gives $\frac{1}{\lambda} = R\left(\frac{1}{2^2} - \frac{1}{4^2}\right) = \frac{3R}{16}$.
  3. Step 3 — Find $\lambda$ in terms of $\lambda_0$: Taking the ratio $\frac{\lambda}{\lambda_0} = \frac{1/\lambda_0}{1/\lambda} = \frac{5/36}{3/16} = \frac{5}{36} \times \frac{16}{3} = \frac{20}{27}$, so $\lambda = \frac{20}{27}\lambda_0$.
  4. Step 4 — Match with $\frac{20}{x}\lambda_0$: Comparing directly confirms $x =$ 27.
Q88.trapHtml: Watch mixed wording: 'third excited state' = n = 4, while 'second orbit' = n = 2! Correct

Q89.questionRecapHtml: Total fission energy of 120 g of X at 200 MeV/fission.
Q89.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Calculate the number of moles of ${}^{240}\text{X}$: Since molar mass is $240\text{ g/mol}$, the number of moles in $120\text{ g}$ is $n = \frac{120}{240} = 0.5\text{ mol}$.
  2. Step 2 — Find the total number of nuclei: $N = n N_A = 0.5 \times 6 \times 10^{23} = 3 \times 10^{23}$ nuclei.
  3. Step 3 — Multiply by the energy released per fission: $E_{\text{total}} = (3 \times 10^{23}) \times 200\text{ MeV} = 600 \times 10^{23}\text{ MeV} = 6 \times 10^{25}\text{ MeV}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Matching with $\underline{\phantom{x}} \times 10^{25}\text{ MeV}$ gives 6.
Q89.trapHtml: 120 g of A = 240 is exactly 0.5 mole (3 × 10<sup>23</sup> atoms). Correct

Q90.questionRecapHtml: Ratio of α-particle kinetic energies for A = 200 and A = 212 at equal Q.
Q90.conceptHtml: In α-decay of a nucleus at rest with mass number A, momentum conservation gives Kα = A<sup>−4</sup> A Q.
Q90.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the kinetic energy share of an $\alpha$-particle: When a parent nucleus of mass number $A$ decays at rest into a daughter of mass number $A - 4$ and an $\alpha$-particle ($4$), momentum conservation gives $K_\alpha = \frac{A - 4}{A} Q$.
  2. Step 2 — Compute $K_\alpha$ for both nuclei: Since both have the same $Q = 1\text{ MeV}$, we have $K_{\alpha A} = \frac{200 - 4}{200} Q = \frac{196}{200} Q$ and $K_{\alpha B} = \frac{212 - 4}{212} Q = \frac{208}{212} Q$.
  3. Step 3 — Simplify the ratio $\frac{K_{\alpha A}}{K_{\alpha B}}$: $\frac{K_{\alpha A}}{K_{\alpha B}} = \frac{196}{200} \times \frac{212}{208} = \frac{49}{50} \times \frac{53}{52} = \frac{2597}{2600}$.
  4. Step 4 — Match with the options: The ratio $\frac{2597}{2600}$ corresponds to Option (C) (verified answer: c).
Q90.trapHtml: Do not use A instead of A - 4 for the daughter nucleus mass number.

Q91.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Write the fusion reaction: Two deuterons fuse to form one helium-4 nucleus: $2\,{}^2_1\text{H} \to {}^4_2\text{He} + Q$.
  2. Step 2 — Compute total binding energy of reactants and product: Each deuteron has $2$ nucleons, so $\text{BE}_{\text{reactants}} = 2 \times (2 \times 1.1) = 4.4\text{ MeV}$. The helium nucleus has $4$ nucleons, so $\text{BE}_{\text{product}} = 4 \times 7.2 = 28.8\text{ MeV}$.
  3. Step 3 — Find the energy released $Q$: $Q = \text{BE}_{\text{product}} - \text{BE}_{\text{reactants}} = 28.8 - 4.4 = 24.4\text{ MeV}$.
  4. Step 4 — Match with the options: $24.4\text{ MeV}$ corresponds to Option (B) (verified answer: b).
Q91.trapHtml: Always multiply BE per nucleon by the total nucleon count A (here 4).

Q92.questionRecapHtml: Momentum ratio of Hα (3 → 2) and Hβ (4 → 2) photons.
Q92.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Relate photon momentum to transition wavenumber: A photon has momentum $p = \frac{h}{\lambda}$, so $p \propto \frac{1}{\lambda} \propto \left(\frac{1}{n_f^2} - \frac{1}{n_i^2}\right)$.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate the factor for the 1st and 2nd Balmer lines: The 1st line ($3 \to 2$) has factor $\frac{1}{2^2} - \frac{1}{3^2} = \frac{5}{36}$. The 2nd line ($4 \to 2$) has factor $\frac{1}{2^2} - \frac{1}{4^2} = \frac{3}{16}$.
  3. Step 3 — Take the ratio of momenta: $\frac{p_1}{p_2} = \frac{5/36}{3/16} = \frac{5}{36} \times \frac{16}{3} = \frac{20}{27}$.
  4. Step 4 — Match with the options: Thus $\alpha = 20$ and $\beta = 27$, which corresponds to Option (D) (verified answer: d).
Q92.trapHtml: Wavelength ratio λ<sub>1</sub> /λ<sub>2</sub> = 27/20, so momentum ratio p1 /p2 = λ<sub>2</sub> /λ<sub>1</sub> = 20/27.

Q93.conceptHtml: ∆m = Zmp + (A - Z)mn - M, converted via 1 u = 931.5 MeV/c2.
Q93.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Count the nucleons in ${}^{12}_6\text{C}$: A carbon-12 nucleus contains $6$ protons and $6$ neutrons.
  2. Step 2 — Calculate the mass defect $\Delta m$ in atomic mass units: $\Delta m = 6 m_p + 6 m_n - m({}^{12}_6\text{C}) = 6(1.00727 + 1.00866) - 12 = 6(2.01593) - 12 = 0.09558\text{ u}$.
  3. Step 3 — Convert $\Delta m$ to $\text{MeV}/c^2$: Multiplying by $931.5\text{ MeV}/c^2\text{ per u}$ gives $\Delta m = 0.09558 \times 931.5 \approx 89.03\text{ MeV}/c^2$.
  4. Step 4 — Match with the options: $89.03\text{ MeV}/c^2$ corresponds to Option (B) (verified answer: b).
Q93.trapHtml: Use mp = 1.00727 u as given rather than 1.007825 u (which includes electron mass).

Q94.questionRecapHtml: Emitted wavelength when ri: rf = 16: 4 in H-atom.
Q94.conceptHtml: Since rn ∝ n2, ri: rf = 16: 4 =⇒ ni = 4, nf = 2 (Balmer Hβ line).
Q94.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the initial and final orbits from the radius ratio: Since $r \propto n^2$, the given ratio $r_i : r_f = 16 : 4 = 4^2 : 2^2$ corresponds to a transition from $n_i = 4$ to $n_f = 2$ (the $H_\beta$ Balmer line).
  2. Step 2 — Apply the Rydberg formula: $\frac{1}{\lambda} = R\left(\frac{1}{2^2} - \frac{1}{4^2}\right) = R\left(\frac{1}{4} - \frac{1}{16}\right) = \frac{3R}{16}$.
  3. Step 3 — Calculate $\lambda$ in nanometers: $\lambda = \frac{16}{3 \times 1.0973 \times 10^7\text{ m}^{-1}} \approx 4.860 \times 10^{-7}\text{ m} = 486\text{ nm}$.
  4. Step 4 — Match with the options: $486\text{ nm}$ corresponds to Option (C) (verified answer: c).
