  2. Step 2 — Verify Statement I: All $4$ pairs consist of oxides of the same nature, so Statement I is true.
  3. Step 3 — Verify Statement II: Among $\text{Na}_2\text{O}$ (strongly basic alkali metal oxide), $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ (amphoteric), $\text{CO}$ (neutral), and $\text{Cl}_2\text{O}_7$ (strongly acidic non-metal oxide), the most basic oxide is $\text{Na}_2\text{O}$ and the most acidic oxide is $\text{Cl}_2\text{O}_7$. Thus, Statement II is also true.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: Both Statement I and Statement II are true, which matches option (a).
Q03.stepsLatex:
Check each pair in Statement I:
• [Al2O3, Cr2O3]: Both are amphoteric (same nature).
• [Cl2O7, Mn2O7]: Both have +7 oxidation state and are strongly acidic (same nature).
• [Na2O, V2O3]: Na2O is strongly basic; V2O3 (+3 low O.S. metal oxide) is also basic (same nature).
• [CO, N2O]: Both are neutral oxides (same nature).
All 4 pairs have oxides of the same nature =⇒ Statement I is true. In Statement II, Na2O is strongly basic and
Cl2O7 is strongly acidic (whereas Al2O3 is amphoteric and CO is neutral) =⇒ Statement II is also true.
Q03.trapHtml: V<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> (+3) is basic, VO<sub>2</sub> (+4) is amphoteric, and V<sub>2</sub>O<sub>5</sub> (+5) is amphoteric/acidic; Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> is amphoteric while CrO<sub>3</sub> is acidic.
Q03.finalAnsHtml: (a) — Both Statement I and Statement II are true

Q04.conceptHtml: Pauling electronegativity order: F (4.0) > O (3.5) > N (3.0). The more electronegative atom always gets the negative oxidation state.
Q04.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Verify Statement I (Electronegativity trend): Across Period 2 from left to right, atomic size decreases and nuclear attraction for shared electrons increases. On the Pauling scale, $\text{F} (4.0) > \text{O} (3.44) > \text{N} (3.04)$, so Statement I is true.
  2. Step 2 — Find oxidation state of oxygen in $\text{OF}_2$: Since fluorine is more electronegative than oxygen, fluorine always takes $-1$. Let oxygen's oxidation state be $x$: $x + 2(-1) = 0 \implies x = +2$.
  3. Step 3 — Find oxidation state of oxygen in $\text{Na}_2\text{O}$: Sodium is an alkali metal with fixed oxidation state $+1$. Let oxygen's oxidation state be $y$: $2(+1) + y = 0 \implies y = -2$. Thus, Statement II is true.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: Both Statement I and Statement II are true, matching option (a).
Q04.stepsLatex:
• Statement I: Across Period 2, electronegativity increases from N to F: F > O > N. True.
• Statement II: In OF2, F is more electronegative than O (2 × (−1) + x = 0 =⇒ x = +2). In Na2O, O is
more electronegative than Na (2 × (+1) + x = 0 =⇒ x = −2). True.
Q04.trapHtml: OF<sub>2</sub> is the classic exception where oxygen shows a +2 oxidation state because fluorine is the only element more electronegative than oxygen.
Q04.finalAnsHtml: (a) — Both Statement I and Statement II are true

Q05.conceptHtml: All ionization enthalpies (IE<sub>1</sub>, IE<sub>2</sub>, IE<sub>3</sub>, . . . ) are positive (endothermic), and IE<sub>2</sub> > IE<sub>1</sub> because removing an electron from a positively charged cation requires more energy.
Q05.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Check the sign of ionization enthalpy: Removing an electron from a gaseous atom or ion always requires energy input, so every ionization enthalpy is endothermic (positive). This immediately eliminates negative options ($-906$ and $-856\text{ kJ/mol}$).
  2. Step 2 — Compare successive ionization enthalpies ($IE_2$ vs. $IE_1$): After removing the first electron from $\text{Mg}$ ($[\text{Ne}]3s^2$), the remaining $\text{Mg}^+$ ion ($[\text{Ne}]3s^1$) has the same nuclear charge pulling on fewer electrons, so $Z_{\text{eff}}$ is higher and $IE_2$ must always be greater than $IE_1$.
  3. Step 3 — Select the valid estimate: Given $IE_1 = +737\text{ kJ/mol}$, we need a positive value larger than $737\text{ kJ/mol}$. Between $+1450\text{ kJ/mol}$ and $+590\text{ kJ/mol}$, only $+1450\text{ kJ/mol}$ satisfies $IE_2 > IE_1$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: The most probable estimated value of $IE_2(\text{Mg})$ is $+1450\text{ kJ/mol}$, which is option (c).
Q05.stepsLatex:
Since IE1(Mg) = +737 kJ/mol, IE2(Mg) must be positive and significantly greater than
+737 kJ/mol.
• Options (a) and (b) are negative (impossible for IE).
• Option (d) +590 kJ/mol is less than IE1 (impossible).
• Option (c) +1450 kJ/mol is positive and ≈ 2 × IE1 (exact NCERT value for Mg is 1451 kJ/mol).
Q05.trapHtml: Never pick a negative value or a value smaller than IE<sub>1</sub> for IE<sub>2</sub>.

Q06.conceptHtml: Basic: K<sub>2</sub>O, Na<sub>2</sub>O; Acidic: Cl<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub>; Amphoteric: Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>, As<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>; Neutral: CO, NO, N<sub>2</sub>O.
Q06.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the four oxide categories: Metal oxides of Group 1/2 are basic (e.g., $\text{Na}_2\text{O}, \text{K}_2\text{O}$), high-oxidation non-metal oxides are acidic (e.g., $\text{Cl}_2\text{O}_7$), certain metalloid/metal oxides are amphoteric (e.g., $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3, \text{As}_2\text{O}_3$), and $\text{CO}, \text{NO}, \text{N}_2\text{O}$ are neutral.
  2. Step 2 — Inspect the options:
    • Option (a): $\text{Na}_2\text{O}, \text{K}_2\text{O}$ (both basic), $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3, \text{As}_2\text{O}_3$ (both amphoteric) — misses acidic and neutral.
    • Option (b): $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3, \text{As}_2\text{O}_3$ (amphoteric), $\text{CO}, \text{NO}$ (neutral) — misses basic and acidic.
    • Option (d): $\text{Na}_2\text{O}$ (basic), $\text{N}_2\text{O}, \text{CO}$ (neutral), $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ (amphoteric) — misses acidic.
  3. Step 3 — Check option (c): $\text{K}_2\text{O}$ is basic, $\text{Cl}_2\text{O}_7$ is acidic, $\text{As}_2\text{O}_3$ is amphoteric, and $\text{NO}$ is neutral — all four types are present.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: Option (c) is the correct set.
Q06.stepsLatex:
Check each set:
• (a) Na2O (basic), K2O (basic), Al2O3 (amphoteric), As2O3 (amphoteric) — missing acidic and neutral.
• (b) Al2O3, As2O3 (amphoteric), CO, NO (neutral) — missing basic and acidic.
• (c) K2O (basic), Cl2O7 (acidic), As2O3 (amphoteric), NO (neutral) — contains all four!
• (d) Na2O (basic), N2O (neutral), Al2O3 (amphoteric), CO (neutral) — missing acidic.
Q06.trapHtml: As<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> is a metalloid oxide and is amphoteric; N<sub>2</sub>O, NO, CO are neutral.

Q07.conceptHtml: Across Period 3, IE<sub>1</sub> increases left to right (Na < Mg < Cl < Ar). Removing a 3<sup>rd</sup> electron from Ca<sup>2+</sup> disrupts a noble-gas [Ar] core.
Q07.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement I: $\text{Na}, \text{Mg}, \text{Cl}, \text{Ar}$ all belong to Period 3. Moving left to right across a period, atomic radius decreases and $Z_{\text{eff}}$ increases, so $IE_1$ increases: $\text{Na} < \text{Mg} < \text{Cl} < \text{Ar}$. The given decreasing order is reversed, so Statement I is false.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement II using electronic configurations: Calcium has configuration $[\text{Ar}]4s^2$. After losing two electrons to form $\text{Ca}^{2+}$, it attains the very stable noble-gas configuration $[\text{Ar}]$.
  3. Step 3 — Compare third ionization enthalpies ($IE_3$): Removing a third electron from $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ requires breaking into the closed $3p^6$ noble-gas core, causing an enormous jump in $IE_3$ compared to $\text{Al}, \text{Fe}, \text{B}$ (whose 3rd electron is still a valence electron). Thus, Statement II is true.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: Statement I is false and Statement II is true, matching option (d).
Q07.stepsLatex:
• Statement (I): In Period 3, nuclear charge increases from Na to Ar, so IE1 increases: Na < Mg < Cl < Ar.
The given order Na > Mg > Cl > Ar is reversed =⇒ False.
• Statement (II): Ca has configuration [Ar]4s2. After losing 2 electrons, Ca2+ attains the stable noble-gas
configuration [Ar], making IE3 extremely high (4912 kJ mol−1) compared to Al, Fe, and B =⇒ True.
Q07.trapHtml: A massive jump in IE<sub>3</sub> occurs for Group 2 elements (Be, Mg, Ca) because the 3<sup>rd</sup> electron comes from a closed noble-gas shell.
Q07.finalAnsHtml: (d) — Statement I is false but Statement II is true

Q08.conceptHtml: Metallic character increases down a group and decreases from left to right across a period.
Q08.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Locate the elements on the periodic table:
    • Period 2: $\text{N}$ (Group 15), $\text{O}$ (Group 16), $\text{F}$ (Group 17).
    • Period 3: $\text{P}$ (Group 15), $\text{S}$ (Group 16), $\text{Cl}$ (Group 17).
  2. Step 2 — Find the most and least metallic elements: Metallic character increases down a group and decreases from left to right across a period. Therefore, the most metallic element sits at the bottom-left of this block ($\text{P}$), and the least metallic element sits at the top-right ($\text{F}$).
  3. Step 3 — Count their valence electrons: Phosphorus ($\text{P}$, Group 15: $[\text{Ne}]3s^2 3p^3$) has $5$ valence electrons, while Fluorine ($\text{F}$, Group 17: $[\text{He}]2s^2 2p^5$) has $7$ valence electrons.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: The respective numbers of valence electrons are $5$ and $7$, which is option (c).
Q08.stepsLatex:
Among N, P, O, S, Cl, F (all p-block non-metals):
• Most metallic character: P (leftmost in Period 3 among these, Group 15, below N). Group 15 has 5 valence
electrons (3s23p3).
• Least metallic character: F (top-right, most electronegative non-metal, Group 17). Group 17 has 7 valence
electrons (2s22p5).
Q08.trapHtml: Check the order requested: “most and least metallic character... respectively” =⇒ P (5) first, F (7) second.

Q09.conceptHtml: In any period (excluding noble gases), the Group 1 alkali metal has the largest atomic radius and the Group 17 halogen has the smallest covalent radius.
Q09.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the elements of Period 4: Period 4 starts with the alkali metal Potassium ($\text{K}, Z = 19$) and ends with the halogen Bromine ($\text{Br}, Z = 35$) followed by the noble gas Krypton ($\text{Kr}, Z = 36$).
  2. Step 2 — Apply the periodic trend for atomic radius: Across a period from left to right, electrons are added to the same shell while nuclear charge increases, pulling the electron cloud closer. Excluding noble gases (which are measured by van der Waals radius), atomic radius decreases steadily from Group 1 to Group 17.
  3. Step 3 — Pick the highest and lowest radii in Period 4: The largest atomic radius in Period 4 belongs to $\text{K}$, and the smallest belongs to $\text{Br}$. (Note: $\text{Na}, \text{Cl}$ are Period 3, and $\text{Rb}$ is Period 5.)
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: The pair is $\text{K}$ & $\text{Br}$, matching option (c).
Q09.stepsLatex:
Period 4 starts with K (Z = 19, Group 1) and ends (before Kr) with Br (Z = 35, Group 17).
Thus, highest atomic radius = K and lowest = Br.
Q09.trapHtml: Rb is Period 5 and Na, Cl are Period 3 — always verify the period number!

Q10.conceptHtml: For IE<sub>2</sub>, inspect the electronic configuration of the +1 cations (C<sup>+</sup>, N<sup>+</sup>, O<sup>+</sup>, F<sup>+</sup>). O<sup>+</sup> has a half-filled 2p<sup>3</sup> shell.
Q10.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Write the electronic configurations of the $+1$ cations: Second ionization potential ($IE_2$) of an atom equals $IE_1$ of its monopositive ion:
    • $\text{C}^+: 1s^2 2s^2 2p^1$
    • $\text{N}^+: 1s^2 2s^2 2p^2$
    • $\text{O}^+: 1s^2 2s^2 2p^3$ (half-filled $2p$ subshell)
    • $\text{F}^+: 1s^2 2s^2 2p^4$
  2. Step 2 — Apply the general trend across Period 2: Moving from $\text{C}^+$ to $\text{F}^+$, nuclear charge increases, so $IE_2$ generally increases left to right.
  3. Step 3 — Account for the half-filled stability of $\text{O}^+$: Because $\text{O}^+$ has an extra-stable half-filled $2p^3$ configuration, removing an electron from $\text{O}^+$ requires more energy than removing one from $\text{F}^+$ ($2p^4$, where pairing repulsion lowers $IE$). Hence, $IE_2(\text{O}) > IE_2(\text{F})$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: The correct increasing order is $\text{C} < \text{N} < \text{F} < \text{O}$, which corresponds to option (a).
Q10.stepsLatex:
Write the configurations of the singly charged ions:
• C+: 2s22p1 (easy to lose 2p1 to get 2s2)
• N+: 2s22p2
• O+: 2s22p3 (stable half-filled 2p3!)
• F+: 2s22p4
Since O+ has half-filled 2p3, its IE2 exceeds F+. Thus: C < N < F < O.
Q10.trapHtml: For IE<sub>1</sub>, N > O; for IE<sub>2</sub>, the anomaly shifts one step right so O > F!

Q11.subtopic: Metallic Character & Ionic vs Atomic Radius
Q11.conceptHtml: Metallic character increases down a group and decreases across a period. Anions are always larger than their parent neutral atoms.
Q11.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement I (Metallic character): Metallic character increases down a group and decreases left to right across a period. Comparing $\text{K}$ (Group 1, Period 4), $\text{Mg}$ (Group 2, Period 3), $\text{Al}$ (Group 13, Period 3), and $\text{B}$ (Group 13, Period 2, metalloid) gives $\text{K} > \text{Mg} > \text{Al} > \text{B}$. Thus, Statement I is true.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement II (Atomic vs. ionic radius): While a cation is smaller than its parent neutral atom ($r_{\text{cation}} < r_{\text{atom}}$), an anion is always larger than its parent neutral atom ($r_{\text{anion}} > r_{\text{atom}}$, e.g., $r_{\text{Cl}^-} > r_{\text{Cl}}$) due to increased electron-electron repulsion.
  3. Step 3 — Judge Statement II: Because anions have larger radii than their neutral atoms, saying atomic radius is "always greater" than ionic radius is false.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: Statement I is true and Statement II is false, matching option (c).
Q11.stepsLatex:
• Statement I: K (Gr 1, Per 4) > Mg (Gr 2, Per 3) > Al (Gr 13, Per 3) > B (Gr 13, Per 2, non-metal/metalloid).
True.
• Statement II: “Atomic radius is always greater than the ionic radius for any element” is False because anions
(e.g., F− > F, Cl− > Cl) are larger than their parent atoms due to increased e−–e− repulsion and lower Zeff/e−.
Q11.trapHtml: “Always” in Statement II fails for anions: r<sub>cation</sub> < r<sub>atom</sub> < r<sub>anion</sub>.
Q11.finalAnsHtml: (c) — Statement I is true but Statement II is false

Q12.subtopic: IE2 of Na vs Mg & Isoelectronic Radii
Q12.conceptHtml: Na<sup>+</sup> has a noble-gas [Ne] core so its IE<sub>2</sub> is huge; for isoelectronic species, higher nuclear charge Z means smaller radius.
Q12.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement I ($IE_2$ of $\text{Na}$ vs. $\text{Mg}$): Removing the first electron gives $\text{Na}^+ (1s^2 2s^2 2p^6$, stable noble-gas core) and $\text{Mg}^+ ([\text{Ne}]3s^1)$. Removing a second electron from the closed $2p^6$ shell of $\text{Na}^+$ requires far more energy than removing the $3s^1$ electron from $\text{Mg}^+$. Thus, $IE_2(\text{Na}) > IE_2(\text{Mg})$, so Statement I is true.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement II (Ionic radius of $\text{O}^{2-}$ vs. $\text{F}^-$): Both $\text{O}^{2-}$ ($Z = 8$) and $\text{F}^-$ ($Z = 9$) have $10$ electrons, making them isoelectronic species.
  3. Step 3 — Compare nuclear attraction: For isoelectronic species, a smaller nuclear charge $Z$ pulls the $10$ electrons less tightly, resulting in a larger radius. Since $Z(\text{O}) < Z(\text{F})$, we have $r(\text{O}^{2-}) > r(\text{F}^-)$, so Statement II is true.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: Both Statement I and Statement II are true, which is option (c).
Q12.stepsLatex:
• Statement I: Na+ (1s22s22p6) has a stable octet, whereas Mg+ ([Ne]3s1) readily loses its 3s1 electron to
attain [Ne]. Hence IE2(Na) ≫ IE2(Mg). True.
• Statement II: Both O2− (Z = 8) and F− (Z = 9) have 10 electrons. Lower Z gives weaker nuclear pull, so
r(O2−) > r(F−). True.
Q12.trapHtml: Both statements are textbook NCERT facts.
Q12.finalAnsHtml: (c) — Both Statement I and Statement II are true

Q13.conceptHtml: In Group 15 (N, P, As, Sb, Bi), electronegativity drops sharply from N (3.0) to P (2.1), then decreases very gradually (As ≈ 2.0, Sb ≈ 1.9, Bi ≈ 1.9).
Q13.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall Group 15 electronegativity values (Pauling scale): Moving down Group 15: $\text{N} = 3.0$, $\text{P} = 2.1$, $\text{As} = 2.0$, $\text{Sb} = 1.9$, and $\text{Bi} = 1.9$.
  2. Step 2 — Compute differences with Phosphorus ($\text{P} = 2.1$):
    • $|\text{EN}(\text{N}) - \text{EN}(\text{P})| = |3.0 - 2.1| = 0.9$
    • $|\text{EN}(\text{P}) - \text{EN}(\text{As})| = |2.1 - 2.0| = 0.1$
    • $|\text{EN}(\text{P}) - \text{EN}(\text{Sb})| = |2.1 - 1.9| = 0.2$
    • $|\text{EN}(\text{P}) - \text{EN}(\text{Bi})| = |2.1 - 1.9| = 0.2$
  3. Step 3 — Check the condition $|\text{EN}(X) - \text{EN}(\text{P})| > |\text{EN}(\text{P}) - \text{EN}(Y)|$: Nitrogen has by far the sharpest electronegativity difference with $\text{P}$ ($0.9$) compared to $\text{As}$ ($0.1$). Testing the given options, only $X = \text{N}$ and $Y = \text{As}$ satisfies the inequality ($0.9 > 0.1$).
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: $X$ and $Y$ are $\text{N}$ & $\text{As}$ respectively, matching option (c).
Q13.stepsLatex:
Let’s compute |χX − χP| and |χP − χY |:
• χN = 3.0, χP = 2.1, χAs = 2.0, χSb = 1.9, χBi = 1.9.
• |χN − χP| = 0.9, whereas |χP − χAs| = 0.1.
Thus X = N and Y = As gives |χX − χP| > |χP − χY |.
Q13.trapHtml: Because 2<sup>nd</sup>-period elements are much smaller than 3<sup>rd</sup>-period elements, the biggest electronegativity gap in any p-block group is between Period 2 and Period 3.

Q14.conceptHtml: In Period 3, IE<sub>1</sub> increases left to right, except Mg > Al (3s<sup>2</sup> vs 3p<sup>1</sup>) and P > S (half-filled 3p<sup>3</sup> vs 3p<sup>4</sup>).
Q14.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Arrange the Period 3 elements by atomic number: The five given elements in Period 3 are $\text{Al} (13)$, $\text{Si} (14)$, $\text{P} (15)$, $\text{S} (16)$, and $\text{Cl} (17)$.
  2. Step 2 — Apply the general period trend: Across Period 3, $Z_{\text{eff}}$ increases and atomic radius decreases, so $IE_1$ generally increases from $\text{Al}$ to $\text{Cl}$.
  3. Step 3 — Apply the P vs. S half-filled exception: Phosphorus ($[\text{Ne}]3s^2 3p^3$) has a stable half-filled $3p$ subshell, whereas Sulfur ($[\text{Ne}]3s^2 3p^4$) has paired electrons in one $3p$ orbital experiencing repulsion. Therefore, $IE_1(\text{P}) > IE_1(\text{S})$, swapping $\text{S}$ and $\text{P}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: The correct increasing order is $\text{Al} < \text{Si} < \text{S} < \text{P} < \text{Cl}$, which is option (b).
Q14.stepsLatex:
Ordering Al, Si, P, S, Cl:
• Al (577) < Si (786) < S (1000) < P (1012) < Cl (1256 kJ mol−1).
Note that P > S because P has a half-filled 3s23p3 configuration.
Q14.trapHtml: Do not swap Si and S; only adjacent P and S swap!

Q15.conceptHtml: Half-filled 2p<sup>3</sup> gives N > O in IE<sub>1</sub>. In Group 16, oxygen has the smallest |∆<sub>eg</sub>H| due to compact 2p inter-electronic repulsion.
Q15.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement I (Period 2 $IE_1$): Across Period 2, $IE_1$ generally increases as $\text{C} < \text{N} < \text{O} < \text{F}$, except that Nitrogen ($2s^2 2p^3$) has a stable half-filled $2p$ subshell, making $IE_1(\text{N}) > IE_1(\text{O})$. Thus, $\text{C} < \text{O} < \text{N} < \text{F}$ is true.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement II (Group 16 electron gain enthalpy magnitude): Normally, $|\Delta_{eg}H|$ decreases down a group ($\text{S} > \text{Se} > \text{Te} > \text{Po}$). However, Oxygen's $2p$ subshell is very small and compact, creating strong inter-electronic repulsion when an extra electron enters.
  3. Step 3 — Place Oxygen in the Group 16 order: This repulsion reduces Oxygen's $|\Delta_{eg}H|$ ($141\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$) below every other chalcogen, giving $\text{S} > \text{Se} > \text{Te} > \text{Po} > \text{O}$. Thus, Statement II is true.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: Both Statement I and Statement II are true, matching option (d).
Q15.stepsLatex:
• Statement I: C < O < N < F is the exact IE1 order (N beats O). True.
• Statement II: Magnitude of ∆egH in Group 16 (NCERT Table 3.7): S (200) > Se (195) > Te (190) >
Po (174) > O (141 kJ mol−1). True.
Q15.trapHtml: Oxygen is at the bottom of Group 16 in |∆<sub>eg</sub>H|, even below Po!
Q15.finalAnsHtml: (d) — Both Statement I and Statement II are true

Q16.conceptHtml: Across Period 3, r(Mg) > r(Al). For ∆<sub>eg</sub>H magnitude, 3p elements (Cl, S) exceed their 2p congeners (F, O).
Q16.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement I (Atomic/ionic radii): Both $\text{Mg}$ ($Z = 12$) and $\text{Al}$ ($Z = 13$) are in Period 3. Atomic radius decreases from left to right across a period, so $r(\text{Mg}) > r(\text{Al})$, not $\text{Al} > \text{Mg}$. The true order is $\text{Mg} > \text{Al} > \text{Mg}^{2+} > \text{Al}^{3+}$, making Statement I false.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement II (Magnitude of $\Delta_{eg}H$): Compare standard magnitudes of electron gain enthalpy:
    • Halogens (Group 17) release far more energy than chalcogens (Group 16), with $\text{Cl} (349\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}) > \text{Br} (325\text{ kJ mol}^{-1})$.
    • In Group 16, $\text{S} (200\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}) > \text{O} (141\text{ kJ mol}^{-1})$ due to compact $2p$ repulsion in $\text{O}$.
  3. Step 3 — Verify the combined order: Putting them together gives $\text{Cl} > \text{Br} > \text{S} > \text{O}$, so Statement II is true.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: Statement I is false and Statement II is true, which matches option (c).
Q16.stepsLatex:
• Statement I: In Period 3, Mg (160 pm) is larger than Al (143 pm), so Al > Mg is False.
• Statement II: |∆egH| values (kJ mol−1): Cl (349) > Br (325) > S (200) > O (141). True.
Q16.trapHtml: Always check neutral atom size across a period: Na > Mg > Al > Si.
Q16.finalAnsHtml: (c) — Statement I is false but Statement II is true

Q17.conceptHtml: Verify each trend individually: IE<sub>1</sub>, EA, metallic character (Mg > Al), and basicity of oxides.
Q17.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Check trends A and B:
    • A ($IE_1$): $\text{F} (1681) > \text{P} (1012) > \text{S} (1000) > \text{B} (801)\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$ (half-filled $\text{P} > \text{S}$). Correct.
    • B (Electron Affinity): $\text{Cl} (349) > \text{F} (328) > \text{S} (200) > \text{P} (74)\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$ ($\text{Cl} > \text{F}$ due to $2p$ repulsion in $\text{F}$). Correct.
  2. Step 2 — Check trend C (Metallic character): Across Period 3, metallic character decreases from left to right, so $\text{Mg} > \text{Al}$. The listed order $\text{K} > \text{Al} > \text{Mg} > \text{B}$ reverses $\text{Mg}$ and $\text{Al}$, making C incorrect.
  3. Step 3 — Check trend D (Basic character of oxides): Oxide basicity increases with metallic character of the element: $\text{K} > \text{Na} > \text{Mg} > \text{Al}$, giving $\text{K}_2\text{O} > \text{Na}_2\text{O} > \text{MgO} > \text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$. Correct.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: Only A, B, and D are correct, matching option (b).
Q17.stepsLatex:
• A: IE1 (kJ mol−1): F (1681) > P (1012) > S (1000) > B (801). True.
• B: EA (kJ mol−1): Cl (349) > F (328) > S (200) > P (74). True.
• C: Metallic character: K > Mg > Al > B (Mg is more metallic than Al, so Al > Mg is wrong!). False.
• D: Basic character of oxides: K2O > Na2O > MgO > Al2O3 (increases down Gr 1, decreases left to right).
True.
Q17.trapHtml: In Statement C, Al is less metallic than Mg (and Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> is amphoteric while MgO is basic).

Q18.conceptHtml: Alkali metals (Group 1) have the lowest IE<sub>1</sub> in their periods, and IE<sub>1</sub> decreases down the group.
Q18.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify each element from its atomic number:
    • $Z = 32$: $\text{Ge}$ (Group 14, Period 4)
    • $Z = 35$: $\text{Br}$ (Group 17, Period 4)
    • $Z = 19$: $\text{K}$ (Group 1, Period 4)
    • $Z = 87$: $\text{Fr}$ (Group 1, Period 7)
  2. Step 2 — Apply ionization enthalpy trends: First ionization enthalpy decreases down a group (larger atomic size and greater shielding) and increases from left to right across a period.
  3. Step 3 — Find the element with the lowest $IE_1$: Alkali metals (Group 1) have the lowest $IE_1$ in their periods, and moving down Group 1 from $\text{K}$ (Period 4) to $\text{Fr}$ (Period 7) lowers $IE_1$ further because the valence $7s^1$ electron is farthest from the nucleus.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: Atomic number $87$ ($\text{Fr}$) has the lowest $IE_1$, which is option (d).
Q18.stepsLatex:
Identify the elements:
• Z = 32: Ge (Gr 14, Per 4)
• Z = 35: Br (Gr 17, Per 4)
• Z = 19: K (Gr 1, Per 4)
• Z = 87: Fr (Gr 1, Per 7)
Being at the bottom of Group 1, Fr (Z = 87) has the largest radius and lowest IE1.
Q18.trapHtml: Remember magic numbers for Group 1: 3 (Li), 11 (Na), 19 (K), 37 (Rb), 55 (Cs), 87 (Fr).

Q19.conceptHtml: Atomic radius increases down a group and decreases from left to right across a period.
Q19.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Check options (a), (b), and (c):
    • (a) $r_{\text{Rb}} < r_{\text{Cs}}$: Both are in Group 1; atomic radius increases down a group. Correct.
    • (b) $r_{\text{At}} < r_{\text{Cs}}$: Both are in Period 6; radius decreases left to right ($\text{Cs}$ to $\text{At}$). Correct.
    • (c) $r_{\text{Br}} < r_{\text{K}}$: Both are in Period 4; radius decreases left to right ($\text{K}$ to $\text{Br}$). Correct.
  2. Step 2 — Check option (d): Both $\text{Mg}$ ($Z = 12$) and $\text{Al}$ ($Z = 13$) lie in Period 3.
  3. Step 3 — Spot the error: Moving left to right across Period 3 increases $Z_{\text{eff}}$ and shrinks the atom, so $r_{\text{Mg}} > r_{\text{Al}}$. Writing $r_{\text{Mg}} < r_{\text{Al}}$ is incorrect.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: The incorrect trend is option (d).
Q19.stepsLatex:
• (a) rRb < rCs: True (down Group 1).
• (b) rAt < rCs: True (Group 17 < Group 1).
• (c) rBr < rK: True (across Period 4).
• (d) rMg < rAl: Incorrect! Across Period 3, rMg (160 pm) > rAl (143 pm).
Q19.trapHtml: Read carefully for “incorrect trend” — Mg is larger than Al, not smaller.

Q20.conceptHtml: Removing an electron from half-filled Mn<sup>2+</sup> (3d<sup>5</sup>) requires more energy than from Fe<sup>2+</sup> (3d<sup>6</sup>), so IE<sub>3</sub>(Mn) > IE<sub>3</sub>(Fe).
Q20.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Understand what each inequality compares: Comparing the ionization enthalpy of two ions means comparing the energy needed to remove the next electron from each ion.
  2. Step 2 — Check option (a) ($\text{Mn}^{2+}$ vs. $\text{Fe}^{2+}$):
    • $\text{Mn}^{2+}$ has configuration $[\text{Ar}]3d^5$ (extra-stable half-filled $3d$ subshell).
    • $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ has configuration $[\text{Ar}]3d^6$ (removing one electron relieves pairing repulsion and produces the stable $[\text{Ar}]3d^5$ configuration).
    Therefore, $IE(\text{Mn}^{2+}) > IE(\text{Fe}^{2+})$, so writing $\text{Mn}^{2+} < \text{Fe}^{2+}$ is incorrect.
  3. Step 3 — Verify the remaining options are correct:
    • (b) $\text{Mn}^+ < \text{Mn}^{2+}$ and (d) $\text{Fe}^{2+} < \text{Fe}^{3+}$ are true because successive ionization enthalpies of the same element always increase ($IE_2 < IE_3 < IE_4$).
    • (c) $\text{Mn}^+$ ($[\text{Ar}]3d^5 4s^1$) $< \text{Cr}^+$ ($[\text{Ar}]3d^5$) is true because $\text{Cr}^+$ has a half-filled $3d^5$ core.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: The incorrect relationship is option (a).
Q20.stepsLatex:
Check each pair (relating to IE of the species shown):
• (a) Mn2+ < Fe2+: Incorrect! Mn2+ ([Ar]3d5) is half-filled and stable, whereas Fe2+ ([Ar]3d6) attains 3d5
upon losing an electron. Thus IE(Mn2+) > IE(Fe2+).
• (b) Mn+ < Mn2+: True (IE3 > IE2).
• (c) Mn+ < Cr+: True (Cr+ is 3d5 stable, Mn+ is 3d54s1).
• (d) Fe2+ < Fe3+: True (IE4 > IE3).
Q20.trapHtml: Always compare the 3d<sup>n</sup> stability of the ion before and after electron removal.

Q21.conceptHtml: Period 7 p-block elements: Mc (Z = 115, Gr 15), Lv (Z = 116, Gr 16), Ts (Z = 117, Gr 17), Og (Z = 118, Gr 18).
Q21.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the Period 7 $p$-block superheavy elements (Groups 15–18): Starting from atomic number $115$ across to $118$: $\text{Mc}$ ($115$), $\text{Lv}$ ($116$), $\text{Ts}$ ($117$), and $\text{Og}$ ($118$).
  2. Step 2 — Match each element to its periodic family:
    • Group 15 (Pnictogen): Moscovium ($\text{Mc}, Z = 115$) $\rightarrow$ A–IV.
    • Group 16 (Chalcogen): Livermorium ($\text{Lv}, Z = 116$) $\rightarrow$ B–III.
    • Group 17 (Halogen): Tennessine ($\text{Ts}, Z = 117$) $\rightarrow$ C–I.
    • Group 18 (Noble gas): Oganesson ($\text{Og}, Z = 118$) $\rightarrow$ D–II.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the answer: The correct matching is $\text{A–IV, B–III, C–I, D–II}$, which is option (b).
Q21.stepsLatex:
• A. Pnictogen (Group 15) → Mc (Moscovium, Z = 115) → IV
• B. Chalcogen (Group 16) → Lv (Livermorium, Z = 116) → III
• C. Halogen (Group 17) → Ts (Tennessine, Z = 117) → I
• D. Noble gas (Group 18) → Og (Oganesson, Z = 118) → II
Q21.trapHtml: Memorize the Z = 113–118 sequence: Nh, Fl, Mc, Lv, Ts, Og (Groups 13 to 18).

Q22.conceptHtml: Ionization is always endothermic (∆H > 0), whereas electron gain can be exothermic or endothermic (e.g., Be, N, Ne).
Q22.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Check statements A and B:
    • A is false: Adding an electron to a neutral gaseous atom can be endothermic for elements with stable filled or half-filled subshells (e.g., $\text{Be}, \text{Mg}, \text{N}$, and all noble gases).
    • B is true: Removing an electron from an isolated gaseous atom always overcomes nuclear attraction, so it is always endothermic.
  2. Step 2 — Check statement C: $\text{Be}$ ($2s^2$) has a fully filled, more penetrating $2s$ orbital compared to $\text{B}$ ($2s^2 2p^1$), so $IE_1(\text{B}) < IE_1(\text{Be})$. Thus, C is true.
  3. Step 3 — Check statements D and E:
    • D is false: Electronegativity is not a constant property of an atom; it varies with oxidation state and chemical environment (carbon in $\text{CCl}_4$ has a higher effective electronegativity than in $\text{CH}_4$).
    • E is false: Electropositive character increases down Group 1, so $\text{Li}$ is the least electropositive alkali metal, not the most.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: Only statements B and C are correct, matching option (b).
Q22.stepsLatex:
• A: False (∆egH > 0 for Be, Mg, N and noble gases).
• B: True (removing an e− from a neutral atom always requires energy).
• C: True (IE1(B) = 801 < IE1(Be) = 899 kJ mol−1).
• D: False (electronegativity increases with partial positive charge on C in CCl4 vs CH4).
• E: False (Cs/Fr is the most electropositive in Group 1, not Li).
Q22.trapHtml: Statement D is a subtle NCERT concept: electronegativity of an atom is NOT constant and depends on its chemical environment/oxidation state.

Q23.conceptHtml: Across Period 2, Pauling electronegativity increases monotonically from left to right: C (2.5) < N (3.0) < O (3.5) < F (4.0).
Q23.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify each element from its electronic configuration:
    • (A) $1s^2 2s^2 2p^3 \rightarrow \text{N}$ ($Z = 7$)
    • (B) $1s^2 2s^2 2p^4 \rightarrow \text{O}$ ($Z = 8$)
    • (C) $1s^2 2s^2 2p^5 \rightarrow \text{F}$ ($Z = 9$)
    • (D) $1s^2 2s^2 2p^2 \rightarrow \text{C}$ ($Z = 6$)
  2. Step 2 — Apply the Period 2 electronegativity trend: Moving left to right across Period 2, atomic size decreases and $Z_{\text{eff}}$ increases, so Pauling electronegativity increases steadily: $\text{C} (2.5) < \text{N} (3.0) < \text{O} (3.5) < \text{F} (4.0)$.
  3. Step 3 — Map back to letters A–D: Substituting the element labels gives $\text{D} < \text{A} < \text{B} < \text{C}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: The correct increasing order is $\text{D} < \text{A} < \text{B} < \text{C}$, which is option (a).
Q23.stepsLatex:
Identify the elements from their configurations:
• (D) 1s22s22p2 → C (χ = 2.5)
• (A) 1s22s22p3 → N (χ = 3.0)
• (B) 1s22s22p4 → O (χ = 3.5)
• (C) 1s22s22p5 → F (χ = 4.0)
Increasing order: D < A < B < C.
Q23.trapHtml: Unlike IE<sub>1</sub> (where N > O), electronegativity has NO half-filled anomaly between N and O.

Q24.conceptHtml: Due to poor shielding by 3d<sup>10</sup> electrons, metallic/atomic radius of Ga (135 pm) is smaller than Al (143 pm), while ionic radius of Ga<sup>3+</sup> (62 pm) is larger than Al<sup>3+</sup> (53.5 pm).
Q24.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement I (Metallic radius of $\text{Al}$ vs. $\text{Ga}$): Gallium ($Z = 31$) follows the first transition ($3d$) series. Because the ten $3d$ electrons shield the nuclear charge poorly ($d$-block contraction), $\text{Ga}$'s valence electrons are pulled in strongly, making $r_{\text{Ga}} (135\text{ pm}) < r_{\text{Al}} (143\text{ pm})$. Hence, saying $r_{\text{Al}} < r_{\text{Ga}}$ is incorrect.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement II (Ionic radius of $\text{Al}^{3+}$ vs. $\text{Ga}^{3+}$): Once the three valence electrons are removed, $\text{Al}^{3+}$ has only $2$ shells ($1s^2 2s^2 2p^6$, $r \approx 53.5\text{ pm}$), whereas $\text{Ga}^{3+}$ has $3$ full shells ($[\text{Ar}]3d^{10}$, $r \approx 62\text{ pm}$).
  3. Step 3 — Compare ionic radii: The extra shell in $\text{Ga}^{3+}$ makes $r(\text{Al}^{3+}) < r(\text{Ga}^{3+})$, so Statement II is correct.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: Statement I is incorrect and Statement II is correct, matching option (c).
Q24.stepsLatex:
• Statement (I): rmetallic(Al) = 143 pm > rmetallic(Ga) = 135 pm. So “Al is less than Ga” is Incorrect.
• Statement (II): r(Al3+) = 53.5 pm < r(Ga3+) = 62 pm (extra 3rd shell outweighs contraction for +3 ions).
Correct.
Q24.trapHtml: Do not confuse neutral atomic radius (Ga < Al) with +3 ionic radius (Al<sup>3+</sup> < Ga<sup>3+</sup>)!
Q24.finalAnsHtml: (c) — Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

Q25.conceptHtml: Among F, Cl, Br, I, covalent radius, ionic radius, and IE<sub>1</sub> vary regularly down the group; only electron affinity (∆<sub>eg</sub>H) shows an anomaly (Cl > F).
Q25.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the first four elements of Group 17: They are $\text{F}, \text{Cl}, \text{Br}, \text{I}$.
  2. Step 2 — Check properties (A), (C), and (D) for regularity:
    • (A) Covalent radius: Increases smoothly down the group ($\text{F} < \text{Cl} < \text{Br} < \text{I}$).
    • (C) Ionic radius ($\text{X}^-$): Increases smoothly down the group ($\text{F}^- < \text{Cl}^- < \text{Br}^- < \text{I}^-$).
    • (D) First ionization energy: Decreases smoothly down the group ($\text{F} > \text{Cl} > \text{Br} > \text{I}$).
  3. Step 3 — Check property (B) (Electron affinity): Due to Fluorine's very small $2p$ subshell, inter-electronic repulsion lowers its electron affinity below Chlorine's, giving the irregular order $\text{Cl} > \text{F} > \text{Br} > \text{I}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: Only property B shows irregularity, matching option (c).
Q25.stepsLatex:
Down Group 17 (F → Cl → Br → I):
• (A) Covalent radius: increases regularly (F < Cl < Br < I).
• (B) Electron affinity: irregular! Cl > F > Br > I.
• (C) Ionic radius (X−): increases regularly (F− < Cl− < Br− < I−).
• (D) IE1: decreases regularly (F > Cl > Br > I).
Q25.trapHtml: Unlike Group 13 (IE<sub>1</sub> irregular) or Group 14 (IE<sub>1</sub> irregular), Group 17 IE<sub>1</sub> decreases smoothly down the group.

Q26.conceptHtml: Among Li, Na, Be, Mg, B, Al, Boron (B) is furthest right in Period 2 and has the smallest atomic radius, forming B<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> (A<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>).
Q26.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Group the given elements by period:
    • Period 2: $\text{Li}$ (Group 1), $\text{Be}$ (Group 2), $\text{B}$ (Group 13).
    • Period 3: $\text{Na}$ (Group 1), $\text{Mg}$ (Group 2), $\text{Al}$ (Group 13).
  2. Step 2 — Find the element with the least atomic radius: Atomic radius decreases from left to right across a period and increases down a group. Therefore, the smallest atom is at the top-right of this set: Boron ($\text{B}$, Period 2, Group 13).
  3. Step 3 — Determine the oxide formula for Boron: Being in Group 13, Boron exhibits a $+3$ oxidation state in its oxide, forming $\text{B}_2\text{O}_3$, which has the general formula $\text{A}_2\text{O}_3$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: The oxide type is $\text{A}_2\text{O}_3$, matching option (d).
Q26.stepsLatex:
• Period 2 is smaller than Period 3 (Li, Be, B < Na, Mg, Al).
• Across Period 2: r(Li) > r(Be) > r(B).
• Boron (Group 13, valency 3) forms the oxide B2O3 (type A2O3).
Q26.trapHtml: Check both period and group: B (88 pm) is smaller than Be (111 pm) and Al (143 pm).

Q27.conceptHtml: Phosphorus (P) is the main component of the apatite family (Ca<sub>9</sub>(PO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>6</sub> · CaX<sub>2</sub>). IE<sub>1</sub> decreases down Group 15: N (1402) > P (1012) > As (947) > Sb (834 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>).
Q27.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the Group 15 element in the apatite family: Apatite minerals have the general formula $\text{Ca}_9(\text{PO}_4)_6 \cdot \text{CaX}_2$ (where $\text{X} = \text{F}, \text{Cl}, \text{OH}$), so the main Group 15 component is Phosphorus ($\text{P}$).
  2. Step 2 — Rank $IE_1$ of the first four Group 15 elements: Moving down Group 15 ($\text{N} \rightarrow \text{P} \rightarrow \text{As} \rightarrow \text{Sb}$), atomic size increases and $IE_1$ decreases regularly: $\text{N} > \text{P} > \text{As} > \text{Sb}$.
  3. Step 3 — Map the four given values in decreasing order:
    • $\text{N} = 1402\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$
    • $\text{P} = 1012\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$
    • $\text{As} = 947\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$
    • $\text{Sb} = 834\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: The first ionization enthalpy of Phosphorus is $1012\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$, which is option (d).
Q27.stepsLatex:
1. The apatite mineral family consists of calcium phosphates, so the Group 15 element is Phosphorus (P) (2nd
element in Group 15).
2. Arrange the given Group 15 IE1 values in decreasing order: 1402 (N) > 1012 (P) > 947 (As) > 834 (Sb).
Q27.trapHtml: You don’t need to memorize exact IE<sub>1</sub> values — just rank the four options from highest (N) to lowest (Sb) and pick the 2nd highest (P)!

Q28.conceptHtml: Greater the magnitude of negative ∆<sub>eg</sub>H of the non-metal (with the same electropositive metal E), greater is its tendency to form an anion and higher the ionic character of the bond.
Q28.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Relate ionic character to ionization enthalpy and electron gain enthalpy: Ionic bond formation between a low-$IE$ metal $E$ ($IE_1 = 374\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$, like $\text{Cs}$) and a non-metal $X$ is more favorable—and the resulting compound $EX$ has greater ionic character—when $X$ has a more negative electron gain enthalpy (higher tendency to accept an electron).
  2. Step 2 — Rank A, B, C, and D by magnitude of negative $\Delta_{eg}H$:
    • $B: -349\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$ (most negative)
    • $A: -328\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$
    • $C: -325\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$
    • $D: -295\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$ (least negative)
  3. Step 3 — Write the ionic character order: Following the order $B > A > C > D$, the ionic character of the products decreases as $\text{EB} > \text{EA} > \text{EC} > \text{ED}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: The correct order is $\text{EB} > \text{EA} > \text{EC} > \text{ED}$, matching option (a).
Q28.stepsLatex:
Element E has low IE1 (374 kJ mol−1, alkali metal like Cs). Comparing |∆egH| of A, B, C,
D:
B (349) > A (328) > C (325) > D (295) kJ mol−1.
(Note: these are Cl, F, Br, I.) Higher |∆egH| gives more favourable anion formation and greater ionic character (Wait:
note that by electronegativity F > Cl, but this JEE Main question explicitly tests the magnitude of ∆egH!). Thus
EB > EA > EC > ED.
Q28.trapHtml: Rank strictly by the given |∆<sub>eg</sub>H| values (349 > 328 > 325 > 295), giving EB > EA > EC > ED.

Q29.conceptHtml: For 10-electron isoelectronic ions, radius decreases as Z increases (Mg<sup>2+</sup> < Na<sup>+</sup> < F<sup>−</sup> < O<sup>2−</sup>). Halogen |∆<sub>eg</sub>H| follows Cl > F > Br > I.
Q29.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement I (Isoelectronic radii): $\text{Mg}^{2+} (Z = 12)$, $\text{Na}^+ (Z = 11)$, $\text{F}^- (Z = 9)$, and $\text{O}^{2-} (Z = 8)$ all contain $10$ electrons. As nuclear charge $Z$ decreases, the nucleus pulls the $10$ electrons less tightly, so the radius increases: $\text{Mg}^{2+} < \text{Na}^+ < \text{F}^- < \text{O}^{2-}$. Statement I is correct.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement II (Halogen electron gain enthalpy): Down Group 17, $|\Delta_{eg}H|$ normally decreases ($\text{Cl} > \text{Br} > \text{I}$), except Fluorine's compact $2p$ subshell causes strong inter-electronic repulsion, placing $\text{F}$ below $\text{Cl}$.
  3. Step 3 — Verify the halogen order: The resulting decreasing order of magnitude is $\text{Cl} > \text{F} > \text{Br} > \text{I}$, so Statement II is correct.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct, matching option (b).
Q29.stepsLatex:
• Statement (I): Z values: Mg (12) > Na (11) > F (9) > O (8), so radii increase as Mg2+ < Na+ < F− < O2−.
Correct.
• Statement (II): |∆egH| of halogens: Cl (349) > F (328) > Br (325) > I (295). Correct.
Q29.trapHtml: Both statements are core NCERT trends.
Q29.finalAnsHtml: (b) — Both Statement I and Statement II are correct

Q30.conceptHtml: Newlands’ Law of Octaves (1865) and Lothar Meyer’s atomic volume curves (1869) both used atomic weight (atomic mass), NOT atomic number (Moseley, 1913).
Q30.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement I (Newlands' Law of Octaves): In 1865, John Newlands arranged elements in increasing order of their atomic weights (not atomic numbers) and noted that every eighth element had similar properties. Thus, Statement I is false.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement II (Lothar Meyer's curve): Lothar Meyer plotted physical properties such as atomic volume, melting point, and boiling point against atomic weights (not atomic numbers), since atomic number was discovered much later by Moseley in 1913. Thus, Statement II is false.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the answer: Both Statement I and Statement II are false, matching option (a).
Q30.stepsLatex:
• Statement I: Newlands arranged elements in increasing order of atomic weights, not atomic numbers =⇒
False.
• Statement II: Lothar Meyer plotted physical properties (atomic volume, m.p., b.p.) against atomic weights,
not atomic numbers =⇒ False.
Q30.trapHtml: Watch for “atomic number” vs “atomic weight” in historical periodic table statements — only Moseley (1913) used atomic number!
Q30.finalAnsHtml: (a) — Both Statement I and Statement II are false

Q31.conceptHtml: Atomic radius increases down a group (adding a new shell) and decreases across a period.
Q31.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Check options (a), (b), and (c):
    • (a) $\text{Si} > \text{P} > \text{Cl} > \text{F}$: Radius decreases across Period 3 ($\text{Si} > \text{P} > \text{Cl}$) and increases down Group 17 ($\text{Cl} > \text{F}$). Correct.
    • (b) $\text{Mg} > \text{Al} > \text{C} > \text{O}$: Period 3 atoms are larger than Period 2 atoms, and radius decreases left to right in both periods. Correct.
    • (c) $\text{Al} > \text{B} > \text{N} > \text{F}$: $\text{Al}$ (Period 3) $> \text{B}$ (Period 2), and $\text{B} > \text{N} > \text{F}$ across Period 2. Correct.
  2. Step 2 — Check option (d) ($\text{Be} > \text{Mg} > \text{Al} > \text{Si}$): Both $\text{Be}$ (Period 2) and $\text{Mg}$ (Period 3) belong to Group 2.
  3. Step 3 — Spot the error: Atomic radius increases down a group because an extra electron shell is added, so $r_{\text{Mg}} > r_{\text{Be}}$. Writing $\text{Be} > \text{Mg}$ is incorrect.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: The incorrect decreasing order is option (d).
Q31.stepsLatex:
Check each order:
• (a) Si > P > Cl > F: Correct (Period 3 decreases, F in Period 2 is smaller than Cl).
• (b) Mg > Al > C > O: Correct (Period 3 > Period 2, decreasing left to right).
• (c) Al > B > N > F: Correct (Al in Per 3 > B in Per 2 > N > F).
• (d) Be > Mg > Al > Si: Incorrect! Mg (Period 3, 160 pm) is larger than Be (Period 2, 111 pm), so Be < Mg.
Q31.trapHtml: Never put a Period 2 element (Be) above a Period 3 element (Mg) in the same or adjacent group for atomic radius.

Q32.conceptHtml: Among In, Tl, Al, Pb, Sn, Ge: Ge (smallest, Gr 14) has the highest IE<sub>1</sub> (stable O.S. +4), while In has the lowest IE<sub>1</sub> (stable O.S. +3).
Q32.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Compare first ionization enthalpies ($IE_1$) of the six elements:
    • Group 13: $\text{Al} = 577$, $\text{In} = 558$, $\text{Tl} = 589\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$ (note $\text{Tl} > \text{Al} > \text{In}$ due to lanthanoid contraction in $\text{Tl}$).
    • Group 14: $\text{Ge} = 761$, $\text{Sn} = 708$, $\text{Pb} = 715\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$ (Group 14 has higher $Z_{\text{eff}}$ than Group 13).
  2. Step 2 — Identify the elements with highest and lowest $IE_1$:
    • Highest $IE_1$: Germanium ($\text{Ge}$, $761\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$).
    • Lowest $IE_1$: Indium ($\text{In}$, $558\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$).
  3. Step 3 — Determine their most stable oxidation states: For $\text{Ge}$ (Period 4, Group 14), the inert pair effect is weak, so its most stable oxidation state is $+4$. For $\text{In}$ (Period 5, Group 13), $+3$ is still more stable than $+1$ ($+1$ becomes dominant only in $\text{Tl}$).
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: The respective most stable oxidation states are $+4$ and $+3$, matching option (b).
Q32.stepsLatex:
1. Compare IE1 (kJ mol−1):
• Group 14: Ge (762) > Pb (716) > Sn (709).
• Group 13: Tl (589) > Al (577) > In (558).
2. Highest IE1: Ge =⇒ most stable oxidation state is +4.
3. Lowest IE1: In =⇒ inert pair effect is dominant only in Tl (+1); for In, +3 is still more stable than +1 in
aqueous/general compounds (NCERT Group 13).
Q32.trapHtml: Don’t confuse Tl (+1 most stable, IE<sub>1</sub> = 589) with In (+3 most stable, IE<sub>1</sub> = 558 — lowest!).

Q33.conceptHtml: A huge jump between IE<sub>n</sub> and IE<sub>n+1</sub> indicates n valence electrons.
Q33.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Inspect the successive ionization energies:
    • $IE_1 = 800\text{ kJ/mol}$
    • $IE_2 = 2427\text{ kJ/mol}$
    • $IE_3 = 3658\text{ kJ/mol}$
    • $IE_4 = 25024\text{ kJ/mol}$
    • $IE_5 = 32824\text{ kJ/mol}$
  2. Step 2 — Locate the sharpest jump: While $IE_1 \rightarrow IE_2 \rightarrow IE_3$ rises moderately, there is a massive jump (nearly $7\times$) from $IE_3$ ($3658$) to $IE_4$ ($25024\text{ kJ/mol}$).
  3. Step 3 — Deduce the number of valence electrons and group: A huge jump after $IE_3$ means the first $3$ electrons are valence electrons and the 4th electron comes from a stable inner noble-gas core. An element with $3$ valence electrons ($ns^2 np^1$, here Boron) belongs to Group 13.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: The element is in Group 13, which is option (c).
Q33.stepsLatex:
Look at the successive IE values (kJ/mol):
IE1 = 800 → IE2 = 2427 → IE3 = 3658 −m−a−s−si−ve−−∼−7×−−ju−m−→p IE4 = 25024 → IE5 = 32824.
The huge jump occurs after removing 3 electrons (IE3 → IE4), so the element has 3 valence electrons =⇒ Group
13 (in fact, this is Boron!).
Q33.trapHtml: Count the number of electrons removed before the jump (3), and map 3 valence e<sup>−</sup> to Group 13 (not Group 3).

Q34.conceptHtml: In Group 14, IE<sub>1</sub> follows C > Si > Ge > Pb > Sn: Pb > Sn due to lanthanoid contraction (4f<sup>14</sup> poor shielding), while Si > Ge normally.
Q34.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement I ($IE_1$ of $\text{Pb}$ vs. $\text{Sn}$): Lead ($\text{Pb}, Z = 82$) lies after the lanthanoids, so its fourteen $4f$ electrons provide very poor shielding (lanthanoid contraction). This increases $Z_{\text{eff}}$ on the valence $6p$ electrons, giving $IE_1(\text{Pb}) = 715\text{ kJ mol}^{-1} > IE_1(\text{Sn}) = 708\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$. Thus, Statement I is true.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement II ($IE_1$ of $\text{Ge}$ vs. $\text{Si}$): Moving down Group 14 from $\text{Si}$ to $\text{Ge}$, although $3d^{10}$ electrons in $\text{Ge}$ shield poorly, the increase in principal quantum number ($n = 3 \rightarrow 4$) still dominates slightly, so $IE_1(\text{Ge}) = 761\text{ kJ mol}^{-1} < IE_1(\text{Si}) = 786\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$.
  3. Step 3 — Judge Statement II: Since $IE_1(\text{Ge})$ is less than $IE_1(\text{Si})$, Statement II is false.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: Statement I is true and Statement II is false, matching option (d).
Q34.stepsLatex:
• Statement (I): IE1(Pb) = 716 > IE1(Sn) = 709 kJ mol−1 due to lanthanoid contraction. True.
• Statement (II): IE1(Ge) = 762 < IE1(Si) = 786 kJ mol−1. False.
Q34.trapHtml: In Group 14, only Pb > Sn is inverted; Si > Ge is normal (unlike Group 13 where Ga > Al).
Q34.finalAnsHtml: (d) — Statement I is true but Statement II is false

Q35.conceptHtml: Modern periodic law is based on atomic number; elements with similar outer configurations lie in the same group (not period); period length = 2 × (number of orbitals).
Q35.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Check statements A and B: According to the Modern Periodic Law, properties of elements are a periodic function of their atomic numbers (so B is true and A is NOT true).
  2. Step 2 — Check statements C and D: Elements with similar outer electronic configurations are placed in the same group, not the same period (so C is NOT true). Statement D is true because an element's block, period, and group directly reflect the quantum numbers of its last filled orbital.
  3. Step 3 — Check statement E: By Pauli's exclusion principle, each atomic orbital holds up to $2$ electrons. Hence, the number of elements in a period is twice the number of available atomic orbitals being filled, not equal to it (so E is NOT true).
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: The statements that are NOT true are A, C, and E only, matching option (a).
Q35.stepsLatex:
Identify which statements are NOT true:
• A: False (properties are functions of atomic numbers, not weights).
• B: True.
• C: False (similar outer configuration = same group, not period).
• D: True.
• E: False (each orbital holds 2 electrons, so number of elements = 2× number of orbitals, e.g., n = 2 has 4
orbitals → 8 elements).
Thus A, C and E are NOT true.
Q35.trapHtml: Read the negative qualifier “NOT true” carefully, and remember 2 electrons per orbital in Statement E!

Q36.conceptHtml: Group 8–10 triad in 4d (Period 5): Ru, Rh, Pd; in 5d (Period 6): Os, Ir, Pt.
Q36.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the atomic numbers and $d$-series of the four metals:
    • Osmium ($\text{Os}, Z = 76$): $5d$ series, Period 6.
    • Iridium ($\text{Ir}, Z = 77$): $5d$ series, Period 6.
    • Platinum ($\text{Pt}, Z = 78$): $5d$ series, Period 6.
    • Palladium ($\text{Pd}, Z = 46$): $4d$ series, Period 5.
  2. Step 2 — Spot the odd one out: While $\text{Os}, \text{Ir}$, and $\text{Pt}$ all belong to Period 6, Palladium sits directly above Platinum in Group 10 of Period 5.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the answer: Palladium does not belong to the same period as the others, matching option (d).
Q36.stepsLatex:
• Osmium (Os, Z = 76), Iridium (Ir, Z = 77), Platinum (Pt, Z = 78) all belong to Period 6 (5d series).
• Palladium (Pd, Z = 46) belongs to Period 5 (4d series).
Q36.trapHtml: Keep the 4d (Ru, Rh, Pd) and 5d (Os, Ir, Pt) platinum-group triads distinct.

Q37.conceptHtml: Extreme left elements (alkali metals) form basic oxides; extreme right reactive elements (halo- gens/chalcogens) form acidic oxides that yield acids with water.
Q37.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement I: Elements on the extreme left of the periodic table are alkali metals (Group 1), which are strongly electropositive metals. Their oxides (such as $\text{Na}_2\text{O}$ and $\text{K}_2\text{O}$) are strongly basic, not acidic. Thus, Statement I is false.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement II: Reactive elements on the extreme right (halogens, Group 17) are strongly electronegative non-metals. Their oxides are acidic and dissolve in water to form acids—for example, $\text{Cl}_2\text{O}_7 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow 2\text{HClO}_4$. Thus, Statement II is true.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the answer: Statement I is false and Statement II is true, matching option (d).
Q37.stepsLatex:
• Statement (I): Alkali metals (extreme left) form basic oxides (e.g., Na2O), not acidic oxides =⇒ False.
• Statement (II): Reactive non-metals on the extreme right (e.g., Cl2O7) react with water to form acids
(Cl2O7 + H2O → 2HClO4) =⇒ True.
Q37.trapHtml: “Extreme right reactive elements” refers to Group 16/17 non-metals (noble gases are unreactive).
Q37.finalAnsHtml: (d) — Statement I is false but Statement II is true

Q38.conceptHtml: Match each ordered series to the periodic property whose anomalies/rules it obeys.
Q38.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Match (A) and (B):
    • (A) $\text{Al}^{3+} < \text{Mg}^{2+} < \text{Na}^+ < \text{F}^-$: All are $10$-electron isoelectronic ions; radius increases as nuclear charge $Z$ decreases ($13 \rightarrow 12 \rightarrow 11 \rightarrow 9$). Matches (IV) Ionic radii.
    • (B) $\text{B} < \text{C} < \text{O} < \text{N}$: Period 2 first ionization enthalpy with the half-filled $\text{N} (2p^3) > \text{O} (2p^4)$ anomaly. Matches (I) Ionisation Enthalpy.
  2. Step 2 — Match (C) and (D):
    • (C) $\text{B} < \text{Al} < \text{Mg} < \text{K}$: Moving left and down the periodic table increases metallic character. Matches (II) Metallic character.
    • (D) $\text{Si} < \text{P} < \text{S} < \text{Cl}$: Moving left to right across Period 3 increases electronegativity steadily without any exception. Matches (III) Electronegativity.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the answer: The matching is (A)-(IV), (B)-(I), (C)-(II), (D)-(III), which is option (a).
Q38.stepsLatex:
• (A) Al3+ < Mg2+ < Na+ < F−: 10-e− isoelectronic series → Ionic radii (IV).
• (B) B < C < O < N: N exceeds O due to half-filled 2p3 → Ionisation Enthalpy (I).
• (C) B < Al < Mg < K: Increases down group, decreases across period → Metallic character (II).
• (D) Si < P < S < Cl: Smoothly increases across Period 3 → Electronegativity (III).
Q38.trapHtml: Notice (B) has O < N (IE anomaly) while (D) has P < S (EN has no half-filled anomaly).

Q39.conceptHtml: Electronegativity increases across a period and decreases down a group: Al (1.5) > Mg (1.2), so Al < Mg is wrong.
Q39.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall electronegativity trends: Electronegativity increases from left to right across a period and decreases down a group.
  2. Step 2 — Check options (a), (b), and (d):
    • (a) $\text{S} (2.58) < \text{Cl} (3.16) < \text{O} (3.44) < \text{F} (3.98)$ — correct.
    • (b) $\text{Al} (1.61) < \text{Si} (1.90) < \text{C} (2.55) < \text{N} (3.04)$ — correct.
    • (d) $\text{Mg} (1.31) < \text{Be} (1.57) < \text{B} (2.04) < \text{N} (3.04)$ — correct.
  3. Step 3 — Check option (c) ($\text{Al} < \text{Mg} < \text{B} < \text{N}$): Both $\text{Mg}$ ($Z = 12$) and $\text{Al}$ ($Z = 13$) are in Period 3. Since electronegativity increases across a period, $\text{Mg} (1.31) < \text{Al} (1.61)$, so writing $\text{Al} < \text{Mg}$ is incorrect.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: The incorrect electronegativity order is option (c).
Q39.stepsLatex:
Check Pauling electronegativities:
• (a) S (2.5) < Cl (3.0) < O (3.5) < F (4.0): Correct.
• (b) Al (1.5) < Si (1.8) < C (2.5) < N (3.0): Correct.
• (c) Al (1.5) < Mg (1.2) < B (2.0) < N (3.0): Incorrect! Mg (1.2) is less electronegative than Al (1.5).
• (d) Mg (1.2) < Be (1.5) < B (2.0) < N (3.0): Correct.
Q39.trapHtml: Across Period 3, electronegativity increases smoothly (Na < Mg < Al < Si < P < S < Cl).

Q40.conceptHtml: Period number = highest n; group number (p-block) = 12 + (number of np electrons).
Q40.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Write electronic configurations of N and S: Nitrogen has atomic number $Z = 7$, so its configuration is $[\text{He}]2s^2 2p^3$, which matches III. Sulfur has atomic number $Z = 16$, so its configuration is $[\text{Ne}]3s^2 3p^4$, which matches II.
  2. Step 2 — Write electronic configurations of Br and Kr: Bromine ($Z = 35$) lies in Period 4, Group 17, giving $[\text{Ar}]3d^{10}4s^2 4p^5$, which matches I. Krypton ($Z = 36$) is the next element (Period 4 noble gas), giving $[\text{Ar}]3d^{10}4s^2 4p^6$, which matches IV.
  3. Step 3 — Combine the matches: Putting all four pairs together gives A–III, B–II, C–I, D–IV.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: This combination corresponds to option (c).
Q40.stepsLatex:
• A. N (Z = 7, Gr 15, Per 2): [He]2s22p3 → III.
• B. S (Z = 16, Gr 16, Per 3): [Ne]3s23p4 → II.
• C. Br (Z = 35, Gr 17, Per 4): [Ar]3d104s24p5 → I.
• D. Kr (Z = 36, Gr 18, Per 4): [Ar]3d104s24p6 → IV.
Q40.trapHtml: Count valence ns + np electrons to immediately pin down the group.

Q41.conceptHtml: Oxidation state is defined using electronegativity (not electron gain enthalpy). Second-period elements form strong pπ–pπ bonds due to small size.
Q41.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement I: The oxidation state of an element in a compound is defined as the hypothetical charge acquired by its atom based on electronegativity differences with other bonded atoms, not electron gain enthalpy. Therefore, Statement I is incorrect.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement II: Second-period elements (such as $\text{C}$, $\text{N}$, and $\text{O}$) have small atomic radii and compact $2p$ orbitals, allowing strong sideways overlap to form stable $p\pi\text{–}p\pi$ multiple bonds. Larger elements from higher periods have diffuse $3p$/$4p$ orbitals with weaker sideways overlap. Therefore, Statement II is correct.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the final answer: Since Statement I is incorrect and Statement II is correct, the right choice is option (c).
Q41.stepsLatex:
• Statement (I): Per NCERT, oxidation state of an element in a compound is the charge acquired by its atom
on the basis of electronegativity consideration from other atoms in the molecule (not electron gain enthalpy)
=⇒ Incorrect.
• Statement (II): Small 2p orbitals of C, N, O overlap effectively laterally, making pπ–pπ multiple bonding
much more prevalent in Period 2 than in heavier periods =⇒ Correct.
Q41.trapHtml: Statement I swaps “electronegativity” with “electron gain enthalpy” — classic NCERT line-by-line trap!
Q41.finalAnsHtml: (c) — Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

Q42.conceptHtml: Match iconic element pairs to their signature periodic extremes: Cl, S (highest |∆<sub>eg</sub>H|), Ge, As (metalloids), Fr, Ra (largest size), F, O (highest EN).
Q42.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Match A (Cl, S) and D (F, O): In Group 17 and Group 16, $\text{Cl}$ and $\text{S}$ have the most negative electron gain enthalpies in their respective groups (because $\text{F}$ and $\text{O}$ suffer from strong inter-electronic repulsion in compact $2p$ orbitals), so A–IV. Meanwhile, $\text{F}$ and $\text{O}$ are the smallest and most electronegative elements in their respective groups, so D–I.
  2. Step 2 — Match B (Ge, As) and C (Fr, Ra): Germanium ($\text{Ge}$) and Arsenic ($\text{As}$) are classic metalloids exhibiting properties of both metals and non-metals, so B–III. Francium ($\text{Fr}$) and Radium ($\text{Ra}$) sit at the bottom of Groups 1 and 2 (Period 7), giving them the largest atomic sizes in their respective groups, so C–II.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the final answer: The complete matching A–IV, B–III, C–II, D–I matches option (d).
Q42.stepsLatex:
• A. Cl, S: Highest negative electron gain enthalpy in Gr 17 & 16 → IV.
• B. Ge, As: Metalloids (both metal & non-metal properties) → III.
• C. Fr, Ra: Bottom-left of periodic table, largest atomic size → II.
• D. F, O: Top two most electronegative elements (4.0, 3.5) → I.
Q42.trapHtml: Distinguish highest electronegativity (F, O) from highest negative electron gain enthalpy (Cl, S).

Q43.conceptHtml: Note the sign convention: EA = −∆<sub>eg</sub>H. Negative EA means ∆<sub>eg</sub>H > 0 (endothermic electron addition).
Q43.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Relate electron affinity to electron gain enthalpy: Electron affinity ($EA$) and electron gain enthalpy ($\Delta_{eg}H$) have opposite signs ($EA \approx -\Delta_{eg}H$). An electron affinity is negative when adding an electron is endothermic ($\Delta_{eg}H > 0$), meaning energy must be supplied.
  2. Step 2 — Check processes A, B, and C: For A ($\text{Be} \to \text{Be}^-$), $\text{Be}$ has a filled $2s^2$ subshell, so the incoming electron must enter the higher-energy $2p$ orbital ($\Delta_{eg}H > 0 \Rightarrow EA < 0$). For B ($\text{N} \to \text{N}^-$), $\text{N}$ has an extra-stable half-filled $2p^3$ subshell, making electron addition endothermic ($EA < 0$). For C ($\text{O} \to \text{O}^{2-}$), adding the second electron to $\text{O}^-$ overcomes strong electrostatic repulsion, making the overall process strongly endothermic ($EA < 0$).
  3. Step 3 — Check processes D and E: Both $\text{Na} \to \text{Na}^-$ (completing $3s^2$) and $\text{Al} \to \text{Al}^-$ release energy ($\Delta_{eg}H < 0$), so their electron affinity values are positive.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Negative electron affinity holds for A, B, and C only, which corresponds to option (d).
Q43.stepsLatex:
Check each process:
• A. Be → Be−: Be has a full 2s2 subshell =⇒ ∆egH > 0 =⇒ EA < 0.
• B. N → N−: N has a stable half-filled 2p3 subshell =⇒ ∆egH > 0 =⇒ EA < 0.
• C. O → O2−: Adding the 2nd electron to O− faces strong electrostatic repulsion, making the overall process
endothermic (∆egHtotal = −141 + 780 = +639 kJ mol−1) =⇒ EA < 0.
• D. Na → Na− & E. Al → Al−: Both are exothermic (∆egH < 0 =⇒ EA > 0).
Q43.trapHtml: “Negative electron affinity” means ∆<sub>eg</sub>H > 0 (endothermic). Both N (2p<sup>3</sup>) and O → O<sup>2−</sup> are endother- mic!

Q44.subtopic: Metallic vs Ionic Radius of Sodium
Q44.conceptHtml: Cations are smaller than their parent atoms, whereas anions are larger than their parent atoms.
Q44.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement I: Neutral $\text{Na}$ ($1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^1$) has a metallic radius of $1.86\ \text{\AA}$. When it loses its single $3s$ valence electron to form $\text{Na}^+$ ($1s^2 2s^2 2p^6$), it loses an entire principal shell and the remaining 10 electrons are pulled more tightly by 11 protons, reducing its ionic radius to $\approx 0.95\ \text{\AA} < 1.86\ \text{\AA}$. Thus, Statement I is correct.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement II: While cations are always smaller than their parent atoms, anions are always larger than their parent atoms because extra electrons increase inter-electronic repulsion and lower the effective nuclear charge per electron (e.g., $r(\text{Cl}^-) > r(\text{Cl})$). Thus, Statement II is false.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the final answer: Statement I is correct and Statement II is false, matching option (d).
Q44.stepsLatex:
• Statement I: Metallic radius of Na is 1.86 Å (NCERT), and Na+ (cation, 1.02 Å) is smaller than 1.86 Å.
Correct.
• Statement II: “Ions are always smaller in size than the corresponding elements” is False because anions
(Cl− > Cl, F− > F) are larger than their parent atoms.
Q44.trapHtml: “Ions” includes both cations and anions — only cations are always smaller than the parent atom.
Q44.finalAnsHtml: (d) — Statement I is correct but Statement II is false

Q45.conceptHtml: Isoelectronic species have the same number of electrons but different nuclear charges (Z); radius ∝ <sub>Z</sub><sup>1</sup> .
Q45.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Count electrons and protons for each species: For $\text{O}^{2-}$: $Z = 8$, electrons $= 10$; for $\text{F}^-$: $Z = 9$, electrons $= 10$; for $\text{Na}^+$: $Z = 11$, electrons $= 10$; for $\text{Mg}^{2+}$: $Z = 12$, electrons $= 10$.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate statements (A) and (B): All four species have the exact same number of electrons ($10$), so they are isoelectronic — statement (A) is correct. However, their nuclear charges ($Z = 8, 9, 11, 12$) are different — statement (B) is incorrect.
  3. Step 3 — Compare ionic radii for (C) and (D): For isoelectronic species, a higher nuclear charge pulls the electron cloud closer, so ionic radius $\propto \frac{1}{Z}$. This gives $\text{Mg}^{2+} < \text{Na}^+ < \text{F}^- < \text{O}^{2-}$. Hence $\text{O}^{2-}$ is the largest ((C) is correct) and $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ is the smallest ((D) is correct).
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Statements (A), (C), and (D) are correct, which corresponds to option (b).
Q45.stepsLatex:
For O2− (Z = 8), F− (Z = 9), Na+ (Z = 11), Mg2+ (Z = 12):
• (A) All have 10 electrons =⇒ isoelectronic. True.
• (B) Nuclear charges are 8, 9, 11, 12 (different!). False.
• (C) O2− has the lowest Z = 8 =⇒ largest ionic radius. True.
• (D) Mg2+ has the highest Z = 12 =⇒ smallest ionic radius. True.
Q45.trapHtml: Isoelectronic = same electron count, NEVER same nuclear charge.

Q46.conceptHtml: Group 13 IE<sub>1</sub> order is B > Tl > Ga > Al > In due to poor shielding by 3d<sup>10</sup> in Ga and 4f<sup>14</sup>5d<sup>10</sup> in Tl.
Q46.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the Group 13 first ionization enthalpy trend: Unlike a simple downward decrease, Group 13 shows notable anomalies due to poor shielding by inner $d$ and $f$ electrons. The experimental $IE_1$ order is $\text{B} > \text{Tl} > \text{Ga} > \text{Al} > \text{In}$.
  2. Step 2 — Explain the Ga and Tl anomalies: In $\text{Ga}$ ($[\text{Ar}]3d^{10}4s^2 4p^1$), poorly shielding $3d^{10}$ electrons increase $Z_{\text{eff}}$, making $IE_1(\text{Ga}) = 579\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ slightly greater than $IE_1(\text{Al}) = 577\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$. In $\text{Tl}$ ($[\text{Xe}]4f^{14}5d^{10}6s^2 6p^1$), very poor shielding by $4f^{14}$ electrons (lanthanoid contraction) raises $Z_{\text{eff}}$ even further, making $IE_1(\text{Tl}) = 589\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ higher than both $\text{Ga}$ and $\text{Al}$.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the final answer: Thus $\text{Tl} > \text{Ga} > \text{Al}$ is the correct order, matching option (b).
Q46.stepsLatex:
Exact IE1 values (kJ mol−1): B (801) > Tl (589) > Ga (579) > Al (577) > In (558). Checking
the subset {Al, Ga, Tl}:
Tl > Ga > Al.
Q46.trapHtml: Group 13 IE<sub>1</sub> is one of the most tested anomalies in JEE Main: remember the W-shaped order B > Tl > Ga > Al > In.

Q47.subtopic: IE1 & ∆egH of Li, Na, F, Cl
Q47.conceptHtml: Halogens have much higher IE<sub>1</sub> and |∆<sub>eg</sub>H| than alkali metals; Cl has higher |∆<sub>eg</sub>H| than F.
Q47.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement I (First ionization enthalpy): $IE_1$ decreases down a group and increases sharply across a period from alkali metals (Group 1) to halogens (Group 17). Comparing the values: $\text{Na}\ (496) < \text{Li}\ (520) < \text{Cl}\ (1256) < \text{F}\ (1681)\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$. Therefore, Statement I is true.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement II (Negative electron gain enthalpy): Alkali metals have small negative $\Delta_{eg}H$ values ($\text{Na}: -53$, $\text{Li}: -60\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$), while halogens have large negative values. Between $\text{F}$ ($-328\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$) and $\text{Cl}$ ($-349\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$), $\text{Cl}$ has a more negative value because $\text{F}$ has strong inter-electronic repulsion in its compact $2p$ shell. Thus, in order of increasing magnitude of negative $\Delta_{eg}H$: $\text{Na} < \text{Li} < \text{F} < \text{Cl}$. Statement II is true.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the final answer: Since both Statement I and Statement II are true, the correct choice is option (d).
Q47.stepsLatex:
• Statement I: IE1 (kJ mol−1): Na (496) < Li (520) < Cl (1256) < F (1681). True.
• Statement II: Negative ∆egH (kJ mol−1): Na (53) < Li (60) < F (328) < Cl (349). True.
Q47.trapHtml: In Group 1, Li has both higher IE<sub>1</sub> and slightly higher |∆<sub>eg</sub>H| than Na.
Q47.finalAnsHtml: (d) — Both Statement I and Statement II are true

Q48.conceptHtml: Period 2 IE<sub>1</sub>: Li < B < Be < C < O < N < F < Ne (Be > B and N > O).
Q48.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the elements and their period: All five elements belong to Period 2: $\text{Be (C)}$, $\text{B (E)}$, $\text{N (B)}$, $\text{O (A)}$, and $\text{F (D)}$. Generally, first ionization enthalpy ($IE_1$) increases from left to right across a period.
  2. Step 2 — Apply the two Period 2 anomalies: First, $\text{Be}$ ($2s^2$) has a higher $IE_1$ than $\text{B}$ ($2s^2 2p^1$) because removing an electron from a fully filled, more penetrating $2s$ orbital is harder than from a $2p$ orbital, so $\text{B} < \text{Be}$. Second, $\text{N}$ ($2p^3$) has a higher $IE_1$ than $\text{O}$ ($2p^4$) because $\text{N}$ has an extra-stable half-filled $2p$ subshell while $\text{O}$ has spin-pairing repulsion, so $\text{O} < \text{N}$.
  3. Step 3 — Write the full increasing order: Combining these gives $\text{B} < \text{Be} < \text{O} < \text{N} < \text{F}$, which in terms of the labels is $\text{E} < \text{C} < \text{A} < \text{B} < \text{D}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The sequence $\text{E} < \text{C} < \text{A} < \text{B} < \text{D}$ matches option (c).
Q48.stepsLatex:
Map letters to elements: (A) O, (B) N, (C) Be, (D) F, (E) B. Correct increasing order:
B (E) < Be (C) < O (A) < N (B) < F (D).
Q48.trapHtml: Double-check the letter mapping: (E) is B, (C) is Be, (A) is O, (B) is N, (D) is F.

Q49.conceptHtml: Period 2 elements (N, O, F) lack vacant d-orbitals and have a maximum covalency of 4 (or 1 for F), so they cannot attain their group valencies (5, 6, 7).
Q49.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Understand group valency vs. maximum covalency: For $p$-block elements, the group valency equals the number of valence electrons ($3, 4, 5, 6, 7$ for Groups 13–17). Second-period elements have only four valence orbitals ($2s$ and three $2p$) and lack vacant $d$-orbitals, so their maximum covalency is strictly limited to $4$.
  2. Step 2 — Check each of the 9 given elements: Elements that can show their group valency: $\text{B}$ (Group 13, valency 3), $\text{Al}$ (Group 13, valency 3), $\text{C}$ (Group 14, valency 4), $\text{Si}$ (Group 14, valency 4), $\text{P}$ (Group 15, expands octet using $3d$ to show valency 5, e.g., $\text{PCl}_5$), and $\text{S}$ (Group 16, shows valency 6, e.g., $\text{SF}_6$).
  3. Step 3 — Identify elements that CANNOT match their group valency: $\text{N}$ (Group 15, cannot show covalency 5), $\text{O}$ (Group 16, cannot show covalency 6), and $\text{F}$ (Group 17, cannot show covalency 7) all lack $d$-orbitals and cannot expand their octet. That gives $3$ elements.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The count is $3$, which corresponds to option (b).
Q49.stepsLatex:
Check each of the 9 elements against its group valency (= group number − 10):
• B (Gr 13, valency 3): forms BF3 (matches).
• C (Gr 14, valency 4) & Si (Gr 14, valency 4): form CH4, SiCl4 (match).
• Al (Gr 13, valency 3): forms AlCl3 (matches).
• P (Gr 15, valency 5) & S (Gr 16, valency 6): form PCl5, SF6 (match).
• N (Gr 15, max covalency 4 ≠ 5), O (Gr 16, max covalency 4 ≠ 6), F (Gr 17, max covalency 1 ≠ 7): 3 elements
cannot match group valency.
Q49.trapHtml: Period 2 elements B and C CAN match their group valencies (3 and 4) within 4 orbitals, but N, O, F CANNOT (5, 6, 7 > 4).

Q50.conceptHtml: Among V, Cr, Mn, Fe, Mn<sup>2+</sup> has a half-filled 3d<sup>5</sup> configuration, giving Mn the highest IE<sub>3</sub>.
Q50.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Write the $M^{2+} \to M^{3+} + e^-$ configurations: The 3rd ionization enthalpy ($IE_3$) is the energy needed to remove an electron from the $M^{2+}$ ion: $\text{V}^{2+}: [\text{Ar}]3d^3 \to 3d^2$; $\text{Cr}^{2+}: [\text{Ar}]3d^4 \to 3d^3$; $\text{Mn}^{2+}: [\text{Ar}]3d^5 \to 3d^4$; $\text{Fe}^{2+}: [\text{Ar}]3d^6 \to 3d^5$.
  2. Step 2 — Compare electronic stability before and after ionization: For $\text{Mn}^{2+}$, removing the 3rd electron breaks the extra-stable, symmetrically half-filled $3d^5$ configuration, requiring a very large amount of energy ($IE_3 \approx 3248\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$). In contrast, $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ loses its 3rd electron relatively easily to attain the stable $3d^5$ configuration ($IE_3 \approx 2957\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$).
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the final answer: Therefore, $\text{Mn}$ has the highest 3rd ionization enthalpy, matching option (a).
Q50.stepsLatex:
Compare the +2 ions before the 3rd electron is removed:
• Mn2+: [Ar]3d5 (extra-stable half-filled d5 shell =⇒ highest IE3 = 3248 kJ mol−1).
• Fe2+: [Ar]3d6 (loses e− easily to become 3d5, IE3 = 2957 kJ mol−1).
• Cr2+: [Ar]3d4 (IE3 = 2987 kJ mol−1); V2+: [Ar]3d3 (IE3 = 2828 kJ mol−1).
Q50.trapHtml: For IE<sub>2</sub> of 3d metals, Cr and Cu are anomalously high (3d<sup>5</sup>, 3d<sup>10</sup>); for IE<sub>3</sub>, Mn and Zn are anomalously high!

Q51.conceptHtml: The p-block contains metals, non-metals, and metalloids, whereas the d-block consists exclusively of metals.
Q51.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement I: The $p$-block indeed contains metals, metalloids, and non-metals. However, the $d$-block (transition elements) consists exclusively of metals — there are no non-metals in the $d$-block. Therefore, Statement I is false.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement II: Non-metals lie toward the top-right of the periodic table, where atomic size is small and effective nuclear charge is high. Consequently, non-metals hold electrons tightly and have higher ionization enthalpies and higher electronegativities than metals. Therefore, Statement II is true.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the final answer: Statement I is false and Statement II is true, which matches option (c).
Q51.stepsLatex:
• Statement (I): d-block elements are all transition/post-transition metals — there are NO non-metals in the
d-block =⇒ False.
• Statement (II): Non-metals have higher ionisation enthalpy and higher electronegativity than metals =⇒
True.
Q51.trapHtml: Only the p-block contains all three categories (metals, metalloids, non-metals); s- (except H), d-, and f-blocks are all metals.
Q51.finalAnsHtml: (c) — Statement I is false but Statement II is true

Q52.conceptHtml: Isoelectronic species have the same n and same electron count; their size is governed by nuclear charge (Z).
Q52.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Verify the electron count and principal quantum number: $\text{F}^-$, $\text{Ne}$, and $\text{Na}^+$ all have the exact same electronic configuration $1s^2 2s^2 2p^6$ ($10$ electrons and valence shell $n = 2$).
  2. Step 2 — Identify what differs among them: Their atomic numbers (nuclear charges $Z$) are $9$ ($\text{F}^-$), $10$ ($\text{Ne}$), and $11$ ($\text{Na}^+$). As nuclear charge $Z$ increases for the same 10-electron cloud, the nucleus pulls the electrons more strongly, shrinking the size ($\text{Na}^+ < \text{Ne} < \text{F}^-$).
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the final answer: The size of these isoelectronic species is governed by nuclear charge ($Z$), corresponding to option (a).
Q52.stepsLatex:
F− (Z = 9), Ne (Z = 10), and Na+ (Z = 11) all have 10 electrons (1s22s22p6). Higher nuclear
charge Z pulls the electron cloud closer, decreasing radius.
Q52.trapHtml: Principal quantum number n = 2 is identical for all three, so Z is the deciding factor.

Q53.conceptHtml: Moving right across a period decreases atomic/ionic radius and metallic character; moving down a group increases both.
Q53.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Read the periodic positions from the diagram: In the given grid, $A^\prime$ and $B^\prime$ lie in the same period ($A^\prime$ on the left, $B^\prime$ on the right), while $C^\prime$ and $D^\prime$ lie directly below $A^\prime$ and $B^\prime$ in the next lower period ($C^\prime$ on the left, $D^\prime$ on the right).
  2. Step 2 — Check atomic radius (Statements A and C): Atomic radius decreases from left to right across a period ($B^\prime < A^\prime$ and $D^\prime < C^\prime$) and increases down a group ($A^\prime < C^\prime$ and $B^\prime < D^\prime$). Combining these gives $B^\prime < A^\prime < D^\prime < C^\prime$. Thus, A is true and C is false.
  3. Step 3 — Check metallic character (B) and ionic radii (D): Metallic character decreases across a period and increases down a group, following the same order $B^\prime < A^\prime < D^\prime < C^\prime$ (B is true). Similarly, the ionic radii of the corresponding unipositive ions follow the same periodic trend: $B^{\prime+} < A^{\prime+} < D^{\prime+} < C^{\prime+}$ (D is true).
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Statements A, B, and D are true, which corresponds to option (d).
Q53.stepsLatex:
From the diagram: A′, B′ are in the upper period (A′ left, B′ right); C′, D′ are in the lower
period (C′ left, D′ right).
• A (Atomic radii): B′ < A′ < D′ < C′. True.
• B (Metallic character): Decreases left → right, increases down =⇒ B′ < A′ < D′ < C′. True.
• C (Size): D′ < C′ < B′ < A′ puts lower period smaller than upper period =⇒ False.
• D (Ionic radii of +1 cations): B′+ < A′+ < D′+ < C′+. True.
Q53.trapHtml: Remember both atomic radius and metallic character share the exact same directional trend (increase down, decrease right).

Q54.conceptHtml: When ordered with sign (algebraic value, not magnitude), noble gases (∆<sub>eg</sub>H > 0) are highest, and more negative values are lower!
Q54.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the sign convention for electron gain enthalpy ($\Delta_{eg}H$): When comparing $\Delta_{eg}H$ directly (with sign), positive values are greater than negative values, and less negative values are greater than more negative values.
  2. Step 2 — List the $\Delta_{eg}H$ values of the four elements: A ($\text{Ar}$): $+96\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ (noble gas with stable $3s^2 3p^6$ shell, endothermic); D ($\text{S}$): $-200\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ (Group 16); B ($\text{Br}$): $-325\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ (Group 17); C ($\text{F}$): $-328\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ (Group 17, slightly more negative than $\text{Br}$).
  3. Step 3 — Arrange in decreasing algebraic order: $+96 > -200 > -325 > -328$, giving $\text{Ar (A)} > \text{S (D)} > \text{Br (B)} > \text{F (C)}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The sequence $\text{A} > \text{D} > \text{B} > \text{C}$ matches option (b).
Q54.stepsLatex:
List the actual ∆egH values (kJ mol−1, with sign):
• A. Ar = +96 (endothermic, positive)
• D. S = −200
• B. Br = −325
• C. F = −328
Decreasing algebraic order: +96 > −200 > −325 > −328 =⇒ A > D > B > C.
Q54.trapHtml: Notice the prompt asks for “electron gain enthalpy” (not “magnitude of” or “negative”), so +96 > −200 > −325 > −328!

Q55.subtopic: Chemical Reactivity & Oxide Nature Across Period
Q55.conceptHtml: Reactivity is highest at the two extremes (Group 1 and Group 17) and lowest in the middle (and zero at Group 18).
Q55.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement I: Across a period, chemical reactivity is high at the two extremes — Group 1 (easily loses electrons) and Group 17 (easily gains electrons) — is lowest in the middle, and drops to nearly zero at Group 18 (inert noble gases). It does not gradually increase from Group 1 to Group 18. Therefore, Statement I is false.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement II: Group 1 elements are strongly electropositive metals that form basic oxides (e.g., $\text{Na}_2\text{O}$), whereas Group 17 elements are electronegative non-metals that form acidic oxides (e.g., $\text{Cl}_2\text{O}_7$). Therefore, Statement II is true.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the final answer: Statement I is false and Statement II is true, which corresponds to option (a).
Q55.stepsLatex:
• Statement - I: Chemical reactivity does NOT gradually increase from Group 1 to Group 18; it is high at
Group 1, drops in the middle, rises to Group 17, and drops to zero at Group 18 =⇒ False.
• Statement - II: Group 1 forms basic oxides (Na2O), while Group 17 forms acidic oxides (Cl2O7) =⇒ True.
Q55.trapHtml: Noble gases (Group 18) are chemically inert, immediately falsifying any “increases to Group 18” claim.
Q55.finalAnsHtml: (a) — Statement I is False but Statement II is true

Q56.conceptHtml: Both (A) and (R) are true, but the small increase from As to Bi is caused by poor shielding of d and f orbitals, not by the general down-the-group trend.
Q56.stepsHtml:
1.
