Step 1 — Evaluate Assertion (A): In Group 15, moving from $\text{N}$ to $\text{P}$ adds a new shell with good shielding from $s$ and $p$ electrons, causing a large jump in covalent radius ($70\ \text{pm} \to 110\ \text{pm}$). From $\text{As}$ to $\text{Bi}$, completely filled inner $d$ and $f$ orbitals provide poor shielding, so the radius increases only slightly. Thus, Assertion (A) is true.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Reason (R): Generally, covalent and ionic radii in a particular oxidation state increase down a group as the principal quantum number $n$ increases. Thus, Reason (R) is also true.
  3. Step 3 — Check whether (R) explains (A): Reason (R) only states the general downward increase; it does not mention poor shielding of $d$/$f$ orbitals, which is the actual reason for the small increase from $\text{As}$ to $\text{Bi}$. Hence (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A), matching option (c).
Q56.stepsLatex:
• Assertion (A): In Group 15, covalent radius jumps from N (70 pm) to P (110 pm) (+40 pm), but increases
only slightly from As (121 pm) to Bi (148 pm) due to filled d and f orbitals (poor shielding). True.
• Reason (R): Covalent and ionic radii in a particular oxidation state increase down the group. True, but it
does NOT explain why the As → Bi increase is unusually small.
Q56.trapHtml: Both statements are verbatim NCERT Group 15 lines, making it a classic “Both true, R is NOT the correct explanation” case.
Q56.finalAnsHtml: (c) — Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)

Q57.conceptHtml: In both Group 16 and Group 17, the 2<sup>nd</sup>-period element has a smaller |∆<sub>eg</sub>H| than its 3<sup>rd</sup>-period congener: Cl > F and O is lowest in Group 16.
Q57.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement I (Group 17): In Group 17, $\text{Cl}$ ($\Delta_{eg}H = -349\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$) has the most negative electron gain enthalpy, not $\text{F}$ ($-328\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$). The very small $2p$ subshell of $\text{F}$ causes strong inter-electronic repulsion for the incoming electron. Thus, Statement I is false.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement II (Group 16): In Group 16, the same compact $2p$ inter-electronic repulsion lowers the electron gain enthalpy of $\text{O}$ ($\Delta_{eg}H = -141\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$) below all heavier chalcogens ($\text{S}: -200$, $\text{Se}: -195$, $\text{Te}: -190$, $\text{Po}: -174\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$). Thus, $\text{O}$ has the least negative $\Delta_{eg}H$ in Group 16, making Statement II true.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the final answer: Statement I is false and Statement II is true, corresponding to option (c).
Q57.stepsLatex:
• Statement I: Cl (−349 kJ mol−1) has a more negative ∆egH than F (−328 kJ mol−1) =⇒ False.
• Statement II: O (−141 kJ mol−1) has the least negative ∆egH in Group 16 (S > Se > Te > Po > O) =⇒
True.
Q57.trapHtml: Compact 2p repulsion lowers |∆<sub>eg</sub>H| for both F and O, but O drops below Po while F only drops below Cl.
Q57.finalAnsHtml: (c) — Statement I is false but Statement II is true

Q58.conceptHtml: IE<sub>1</sub> increases across a period and decreases down a group.
Q58.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Group the elements by period: $\text{C}$ ($Z=6$) and $\text{N}$ ($Z=7$) belong to Period 2, whereas $\text{Al}$ ($Z=13$) and $\text{Si}$ ($Z=14$) belong to Period 3. Period 2 elements have smaller atomic radii and much higher first ionization enthalpies ($IE_1$) than Period 3 elements.
  2. Step 2 — Compare C and N: Moving from $\text{C}$ ($1s^2 2s^2 2p^2$, $IE_1 = 1086\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$) to $\text{N}$ ($1s^2 2s^2 2p^3$, $IE_1 = 1402\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$), both nuclear charge increases and $\text{N}$ attains an extra-stable half-filled $2p^3$ configuration.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the final answer: Therefore, $\text{N}$ has the highest first ionization enthalpy, matching option (d).
Q58.stepsLatex:
Compare Al (Per 3, Gr 13), Si (Per 3, Gr 14), C (Per 2, Gr 14), N (Per 2, Gr 15):
Al (577) < Si (786) < C (1086) < N (1402 kJ mol−1).
Nitrogen has both Period 2 small size and a half-filled 2p3 subshell.
Q58.trapHtml: Period 2 non-metals (C, N) easily beat Period 3 (Al, Si).

Q59.conceptHtml: Across a period, increasing nuclear charge outweighs shielding, causing IE<sub>1</sub> to increase (not decrease).
Q59.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Assertion A: Across a period from left to right, atomic size decreases and valence electrons are held more tightly, so the first ionization enthalpy generally increases (not decreases). Therefore, Assertion A is false.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Reason R: Across a period, each successive electron is added to the same valence shell, where inner-shell shielding changes very little while nuclear charge ($Z$) increases by $+1$ each step. Thus, increasing nuclear charge outweighs shielding across a period. Reason R is true.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the final answer: A is false but R is true, which corresponds to option (a).
Q59.stepsLatex:
• Assertion A: “The first ionisation enthalpy decreases across a period” is False (it increases).
• Reason R: “The increasing nuclear charge outweighs the shielding across the period” is True.
Q59.trapHtml: Always verify Assertion A independently before checking Reason R.
Q59.finalAnsHtml: (a) — A is false but R is true

Q60.conceptHtml: In Group 14, electronegativity drops from C (2.5) to Si (1.8), then stays nearly constant/slightly rises at Pb (1.9) — it does NOT gradually decrease from Si to Pb.
Q60.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement I (Group 14 electronegativity): According to NCERT Pauling electronegativity data for Group 14: $\text{C} = 2.5$, $\text{Si} = 1.8$, $\text{Ge} = 1.8$, $\text{Sn} = 1.8$, and $\text{Pb} = 1.9$. From $\text{Si}$ to $\text{Pb}$, electronegativity remains almost constant and actually increases slightly at $\text{Pb}$ (due to poor shielding of $d$ and $f$ orbitals), rather than gradually decreasing. Thus, Statement I is false.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement II (Metallic/non-metallic nature): Group 14 spans all three categories: $\text{C}$ is a non-metal, $\text{Si}$ and $\text{Ge}$ are metalloids, and $\text{Sn}$ and $\text{Pb}$ are metals. Thus, Statement II is true.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the final answer: Statement I is false and Statement II is true, matching option (a).
Q60.stepsLatex:
• Statement I: Pauling EN of Group 14: C (2.5), Si (1.8), Ge (1.8), Sn (1.8), Pb (1.9). From Si to Pb it does not
gradually decrease (in fact it is roughly constant and rises at Pb due to lanthanoid contraction) =⇒ False.
• Statement II: Group 14 contains non-metal (C), metalloids (Si, Ge), and metals (Sn, Pb) =⇒ True.
Q60.trapHtml: NCERT explicitly notes that Group 14 electronegativity from Si to Pb is “almost the same” (1.8–1.9), not gradually decreasing.
Q60.finalAnsHtml: (a) — Statement I is false but Statement II is true

Q61.subtopic: Placement of f-Block & Reactivity of s-Block
Q61.conceptHtml: 4f and 5f series are placed separately at the bottom to keep the periodic table compact and preserve group classification; s-block metals are too reactive to occur free in nature.
Q61.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement I: The $4f$ (lanthanoid) and $5f$ (actinoid) series are placed separately at the bottom of the periodic table to keep the table manageable in width and preserve the principle of classification (keeping elements with similar properties aligned in vertical groups). Thus, Statement I is true.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement II: $s$-block elements (Groups 1 and 2) have very low ionization enthalpies and are highly reactive, so they readily react with air and moisture and are never found in pure/native form in nature (they occur only in combined states). Thus, Statement II is false.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the final answer: Statement I is true and Statement II is false, matching option (c).
Q61.stepsLatex:
• Statement (I): True (standard NCERT justification for separating lanthanoids and actinoids).
• Statement (II): False (s-block elements are highly reactive electropositive metals and are never found in
pure/native elemental form in nature).
Q61.trapHtml: Group 1 and 2 metals always occur in combined mineral/salt forms, never in pure native state.
Q61.finalAnsHtml: (c) — Statement I is true but Statement II is false

Q62.conceptHtml: Identify incorrect statements: Cl beats F in |∆<sub>eg</sub>H|; EN depends on bonded atoms; NO is neutral (not amphoteric).
Q62.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Check clearly incorrect statements A and D: A is incorrect because $\Delta_{eg}H(\text{Cl}) = -349\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ is more negative than $\Delta_{eg}H(\text{F}) = -328\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$. D is incorrect because while $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ is amphoteric, $\text{NO}$ is a neutral oxide (along with $\text{N}_2\text{O}$ and $\text{CO}$).
  2. Step 2 — Check clearly correct statement B: B is correct because ionization enthalpy decreases down a group as atomic size increases and valence electrons are farther from the nucleus.
  3. Step 3 — Match against the given options: Since we must select the statements that are not correct, any valid option must include A and D and exclude B. Only option (b) (A, C and D Only) satisfies this — in this question, statement C is treated as incorrect because standard Pauling electronegativity is taken as a tabulated periodic property of an atom itself.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Therefore, the correct choice is option (b).
Q62.stepsLatex:
Check each statement for NOT correct:
• A: Incorrect (∆egH of Cl is more negative than F).
• B: Correct (IE generally decreases down a group).
• C: Incorrect? Wait: in NCERT, “Electronegativity is not a constant; it depends on the element to which it
is bound” — however, NTA officially keyed (b) A, C and D Only (treating EN as a fixed Pauling property
in C, and clearly A and D as wrong since NO is neutral).
• D: Incorrect (Al2O3 is amphoteric, but NO is neutral).
Q62.trapHtml: Per the official NTA Answer Key for this shift, A, C and D are marked incorrect =⇒ Option (b).

Q63.conceptHtml: Period 2 IE<sub>1</sub> order: Li < B < Be < C < O < N < F.
Q63.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Arrange the Period 2 elements left to right: Across Period 2 ($\text{Li}, \text{Be}, \text{B}, \text{C}, \text{N}, \text{O}, \text{F}$), effective nuclear charge increases and atomic radius decreases, so $IE_1$ generally increases from $\text{Li}$ to $\text{F}$.
  2. Step 2 — Apply the two electronic-configuration exceptions: 1) $\text{Be}$ ($2s^2$, fully filled $s$ subshell) has higher $IE_1$ than $\text{B}$ ($2s^2 2p^1$), swapping them to $\text{B} < \text{Be}$. 2) $\text{N}$ ($2p^3$, stable half-filled $p$ subshell) has higher $IE_1$ than $\text{O}$ ($2p^4$), swapping them to $\text{O} < \text{N}$.
  3. Step 3 — Assemble the complete order: This yields $\text{Li} < \text{B} < \text{Be} < \text{C} < \text{O} < \text{N} < \text{F}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: This exact order appears in option (d).
Q63.stepsLatex:
Apply the two Period 2 anomalies (Be > B and N > O):
Li (520) < B (801) < Be (899) < C (1086) < O (1314) < N (1402) < F (1681 kJ mol−1).
Q63.trapHtml: Check both swaps (B < Be and O < N) before selecting the option.
Q63.finalAnsHtml: (d) — Li < B < Be < C < O < N < F

Q64.conceptHtml: Forming Mg<sup>2+</sup> from Mg requires IE<sub>1</sub> +IE<sub>2</sub> (737+1451 = 2188 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>), which is much higher than IE<sub>1</sub> alone because removing an electron from smaller, positively charged Mg<sup>+</sup> (and forming Mg<sup>2+</sup>) is harder.
Q64.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Assertion A: Forming $\text{Mg}^+$ from $\text{Mg}$ requires only $IE_1 = 737\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$, whereas forming $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ from $\text{Mg}$ requires $IE_1 + IE_2 = 737 + 1451 = 2188\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$, which is much higher. Thus, Assertion A is true.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Reason R and its link to A: After removing the first electron, $\text{Mg}^+$ has a higher effective nuclear charge per electron, and removing a second electron against greater electrostatic attraction produces the smaller, doubly charged $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ ion. Thus, Reason R is true and correctly explains why forming $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ demands much more energy than forming $\text{Mg}^+$.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the final answer: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A, matching option (c).
Q64.stepsLatex:
• Assertion A: Energy for Mg → Mg2+ (IE1 + IE2) is ∼ 3× that for Mg → Mg+ (IE1). True.
• Reason R: Mg2+ is smaller and carries more positive charge than Mg+, reflecting the stronger nuclear attrac-
tion on remaining electrons. True and explains why IE2 ≫ IE1.
Q64.trapHtml: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Q64.finalAnsHtml: (c) — Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A

Q65.conceptHtml: Pauling electronegativities: Br (2.8) > C (2.5) > At (2.2) > P (2.1).
Q65.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall Pauling electronegativity values: The standard Pauling electronegativity values are: $\text{Br} \approx 2.8\text{–}3.0$, $\text{C} \approx 2.5$, $\text{At} \approx 2.2$, and $\text{P} \approx 2.1$.
  2. Step 2 — Verify using periodic trends: $\text{Br}$ is a Group 17 halogen (highest here). $\text{C}$ (Period 2, Group 14) is significantly more electronegative than $\text{P}$ (Period 3, Group 15) and $\text{At}$ (Period 6, Group 17). Between $\text{At}$ and $\text{P}$, $\text{At}$ is slightly more electronegative ($2.2 > 2.1$).
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the final answer: The decreasing order is $\text{Br} > \text{C} > \text{At} > \text{P}$, matching option (b).
Q65.stepsLatex:
Comparing the four elements:
• Br (Group 17, Period 4): χ = 2.8
• C (Group 14, Period 2): χ = 2.5
• At (Group 17, Period 6): χ = 2.2
• P (Group 15, Period 3): χ = 2.1
Decreasing order: Br > C > At > P.
Q65.trapHtml: Note that C (2.5) is more electronegative than P (2.1) and At (2.2).

Q66.subtopic: Melting Point of Gallium in Boiling Water
Q66.conceptHtml: Gallium (Ga) has a low melting point of 303 K (29.8<sup>°</sup>C) and a very high boiling point (2676 K), so it remains liquid at 100<sup>°</sup>C (boiling water).
Q66.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — State the condition for remaining liquid in boiling water: Pure boiling water is at $100^\circ\text{C}$ ($373\ \text{K}$). To remain a liquid inside it, the element must have a melting point below $100^\circ\text{C}$, a boiling point above $100^\circ\text{C}$, and must not react violently with water.
  2. Step 2 — Test each option: $\text{Li}$: m.p. $= 180.5^\circ\text{C}$ (solid) and reacts with water. $\text{Br}$: b.p. $= 58.8^\circ\text{C}$ (boils/vaporizes below $100^\circ\text{C}$). $\text{Cs}$: m.p. $= 28.5^\circ\text{C}$, but reacts explosively with water. $\text{Ga}$: m.p. $= 29.8^\circ\text{C}$ ($303\ \text{K}$), b.p. $= 2400^\circ\text{C}$ ($2676\ \text{K}$), and is stable in water.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the final answer: Gallium ($\text{Ga}$) remains a liquid inside boiling water, matching option (d).
Q66.stepsLatex:
Check states at 100◦C (373 K):
• Li: m.p. 180.5◦C (solid).
• Br2: b.p. 58.8◦C (gas/vapour at 100◦C!).
• Cs: m.p. 28.5◦C, reacts violently with water!
• Ga: m.p. 29.8◦C, b.p. 2400◦C, inert to pure water =⇒ remains liquid inside pure boiling water.
Q66.trapHtml: Br<sub>2</sub> boils at 58.8<sup>°</sup>C and Cs reacts explosively with water; only Ga stays liquid in boiling water!

Q67.conceptHtml: Down Group 13, metallic character increases, so oxide character changes from acidic (B<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>) → amphoteric (Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>, Ga<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>) → basic (In<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>, Tl<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>).
Q67.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the acid–base trend of oxides down a group: As we move down Group 13 ($\text{B} \to \text{Al} \to \text{Ga} \to \text{In} \to \text{Tl}$), atomic size increases and ionization enthalpy decreases, so metallic character increases.
  2. Step 2 — Classify the Group 13 $\text{M}_2\text{O}_3$ oxides: $\text{B}_2\text{O}_3$ is acidic; $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ and $\text{Ga}_2\text{O}_3$ are amphoteric; $\text{In}_2\text{O}_3$ and $\text{Tl}_2\text{O}_3$ are basic, with $\text{Tl}_2\text{O}_3$ being the most basic among the choices.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the final answer: Therefore, $\text{Tl}_2\text{O}_3$ is the most basic oxide, matching option (b).
Q67.stepsLatex:
As electropositive/metallic character increases down Group 13 (B < Al < Ga < In < Tl), the
basicity of M2O3 increases down the group. Thus Tl2O3 is the most basic oxide among the options.
Q67.trapHtml: B<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> is acidic, Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> and Ga<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> are amphoteric, and Tl<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> is basic.

Q68.conceptHtml: Choose the pair combining the most positive ∆<sub>eg</sub>H (Ne = +116 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>) with the most negative ∆<sub>eg</sub>H (Cl = −349 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>).
Q68.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall $\Delta_{eg}H$ values of the noble gases and halogens listed: Noble gases have positive $\Delta_{eg}H$: $\text{Ne} = +116\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ (highest positive value among all noble gases) and $\text{Ar} = +96\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$. Halogens have negative $\Delta_{eg}H$: $\text{Cl} = -349\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ (most negative value in the periodic table) and $\text{F} = -328\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$.
  2. Step 2 — Maximize the difference: The maximum difference is obtained by pairing the most positive value ($\text{Ne}$) with the most negative value ($\text{Cl}$): $|+116 - (-349)| = 465\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the final answer: The difference is maximum between $\text{Ne}$ and $\text{Cl}$, matching option (b).
Q68.stepsLatex:
Compute |∆egH1 − ∆egH2|:
• Ar (+96) and Cl (−349): ∆ = 445 kJ mol−1.
• Ne (+116) and Cl (−349): ∆ = 465 kJ mol−1 (maximum!).
• Ne (+116) and F (−328): ∆ = 444 kJ mol−1.
• Ar (+96) and F (−328): ∆ = 424 kJ mol−1.
Q68.trapHtml: In noble gases, Ne has the most positive ∆<sub>eg</sub>H (+116); in halogens, Cl has the most negative (−349).

Q69.conceptHtml: With sign included, more negative ∆<sub>eg</sub>H is algebraically smaller. Compare Group 16 and 17 values.
Q69.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the algebraic meaning of $\Delta_{eg}H(X) < \Delta_{eg}H(Y)$: Since $\Delta_{eg}H$ is negative for these non-metals, a more negative value is algebraically smaller.
  2. Step 2 — Check options (a), (b), and (c) using NCERT values (in $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$): (a) $\Delta_{eg}H(\text{I}) = -295 < \Delta_{eg}H(\text{At}) = -270$ (correct). (b) $\Delta_{eg}H(\text{Te}) = -190 < \Delta_{eg}H(\text{Po}) = -174$ (correct). (c) $\Delta_{eg}H(\text{Cl}) = -349 < \Delta_{eg}H(\text{F}) = -328$ (correct, due to $2p$ repulsion in $\text{F}$).
  3. Step 3 — Check option (d): In Group 16, $\Delta_{eg}H(\text{S}) = -200\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ is more negative than $\Delta_{eg}H(\text{Se}) = -195\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$, so $\Delta_{eg}H(\text{S}) < \Delta_{eg}H(\text{Se})$. Writing $\Delta_{eg}H(\text{Se}) < \Delta_{eg}H(\text{S})$ is incorrect.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The incorrect inequality is in option (d).
Q69.stepsLatex:
Check each inequality (algebraic values in kJ mol−1):
• (a) ∆egH(I) = −295 < ∆egH(At) = −270. True.
• (b) ∆egH(Te) = −190 < ∆egH(Po) = −174. True.
• (c) ∆egH(Cl) = −349 < ∆egH(F) = −328. True.
• (d) ∆egH(Se) = −195 vs ∆egH(S) = −200: −195 > −200, so ∆egH(Se) < ∆egH(S) is Incorrect!
Q69.trapHtml: Be careful with negative signs: S (−200) is more negative (algebraically smaller) than Se (−195).

Q70.subtopic: IE1 of 3d Series vs Group 2 Metals
Q70.conceptHtml: 3d series elements have higher Z<sub>eff</sub> (due to poor shielding by 3d electrons) and smaller radii than Group 2 metals, giving higher IE<sub>1</sub>.
Q70.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Assertion (A): Across Period 4, the first ionization enthalpies of $3d$ transition metals ($\text{Sc}$ to $\text{Zn}$, ranging from $631$ to $906\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$) are higher than that of the Period 4 Group 2 metal $\text{Ca}$ ($590\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$) and generally exceed Group 2 metals. Thus, Assertion (A) is true.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Reason (R) and its link to (A): In the $3d$ series, electrons are successively filled into the inner $3d$ orbitals. Because $d$-orbitals have poor shielding ability, the effective nuclear charge ($Z_{\text{eff}}$) acting on the outer $4s$ electrons increases, making electron removal harder and raising $IE_1$. Thus, Reason (R) is true and correctly explains Assertion (A).
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the final answer: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A), matching option (a).
Q70.stepsLatex:
• Assertion (A): IE1 of 3d metals (Sc (631) to Zn (906 kJ mol−1)) is greater than Group 2 metals (Ca (590),
Sr (549), Ba (503)). True.
• Reason (R): In 3d series, successive filling of 3d orbitals occurs (poor shielding increases Zeff). True and
explains (A).
Q70.trapHtml: Poor shielding of 3d electrons is the root cause of higher IE<sub>1</sub> across the 3d series.
Q70.finalAnsHtml: (a) — Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)

Q71.conceptHtml: For 18-electron isoelectronic ions (S<sup>2−</sup>, Cl<sup>−</sup>, K<sup>+</sup>, Ca<sup>2+</sup>), ionic radius decreases as nuclear charge Z increases.
Q71.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify that the ions are isoelectronic: All four ions have $18$ electrons ($[\text{Ar}]$ configuration): $\text{Ca}^{2+}\ (Z = 20)$, $\text{K}^+\ (Z = 19)$, $\text{Cl}^-\ (Z = 17)$, and $\text{S}^{2-}\ (Z = 16)$.
  2. Step 2 — Apply the isoelectronic size rule: For isoelectronic species, a greater nuclear charge ($Z$) pulls the 18-electron cloud more tightly, so ionic radius $\propto \frac{1}{Z}$. Since $Z$ decreases in the order $20 > 19 > 17 > 16$, the ionic radius increases in the order $\text{Ca}^{2+} < \text{K}^+ < \text{Cl}^- < \text{S}^{2-}$.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the final answer: This exact increasing order is given in option (c).
Q71.stepsLatex:
Nuclear charges: Ca2+ (Z = 20) > K+ (Z = 19) > Cl− (Z = 17) > S2− (Z = 16). Increasing
order of ionic radii:
Ca2+ < K+ < Cl− < S2−.
Q71.trapHtml: Higher positive charge = smaller radius; higher negative charge = larger radius.

Q72.conceptHtml: Use noble-gas anchor atomic numbers: Kr (36), Xe (54), Rn (86).
Q72.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the block for A ($Z = 37$) and C ($Z = 52$): $Z = 37$ is Rubidium ($\text{Rb}$), one atomic number after $\text{Kr}$ ($36$): $[\text{Kr}]5s^1 \Rightarrow$ $s$-block (IV). $Z = 52$ is Tellurium ($\text{Te}$), two before $\text{Xe}$ ($54$): $[\text{Kr}]4d^{10}5s^2 5p^4 \Rightarrow$ $p$-block (I).
  2. Step 2 — Identify the block for B ($Z = 78$) and D ($Z = 65$): $Z = 65$ lies in the lanthanoid range ($Z = 58\text{–}71$, Terbium, $[\text{Xe}]4f^9 6s^2$) $\Rightarrow$ $f$-block (III). $Z = 78$ lies in the $5d$ transition series ($Z = 72\text{–}80$, Platinum, $[\text{Xe}]4f^{14}5d^9 6s^1$) $\Rightarrow$ $d$-block (II).
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the final answer: The complete match A–IV, B–II, C–I, D–III corresponds to option (c).
Q72.stepsLatex:
• A. Z = 37 (Rb): 1 after Kr (36) =⇒ [Kr]5s1 → s-block (IV).
• B. Z = 78 (Pt): [Xe]4f145d96s1 → d-block (II).
• C. Z = 52 (Te): 2 before Xe (54) =⇒ [Kr]4d105s25p4 → p-block (I).
• D. Z = 65 (Tb): between La (57) and Lu (71) =⇒ f-block (III).
Q72.trapHtml: Remember lanthanoids span Z = 58–71 (4f-block) and 5d series starts after 71 (Z = 72–80).
Q72.finalAnsHtml: (c) — A - IV, B - II, C - I, D - III

Q73.subtopic: Group 13 IE1 Drop (B → Al vs Al → Ga)
Q73.conceptHtml: Poor shielding by the completely filled 3d<sup>10</sup> subshell in Ga increases Z<sub>eff</sub>, preventing the expected drop in IE<sub>1</sub> from Al to Ga.
Q73.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement I: In Group 13, $IE_1$ drops sharply from $\text{B}$ ($801\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$) to $\text{Al}$ ($577\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$), a decrease of $224\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ as a new shell is added. From $\text{Al}$ ($577\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$) to $\text{Ga}$ ($579\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$), $IE_1$ barely changes (in fact rises slightly) because of poor $3d$-electron shielding. Hence the decrease from $\text{B}$ to $\text{Al}$ is much larger than from $\text{Al}$ to $\text{Ga}$. Statement I is correct.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement II: Gallium ($Z = 31$) has the ground-state electronic configuration $[\text{Ar}]3d^{10}4s^2 4p^1$, meaning its $3d$ orbitals are completely filled. Thus, Statement II is correct.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the final answer: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct, matching option (c).
Q73.stepsLatex:
• Statement I: IE1 drops sharply from B (801) to Al (577) (∆ = −224 kJ mol−1), whereas from Al (577) to
Ga (579) it does not drop (in fact slightly increases). True.
• Statement II: Ga ([Ar]3d104s24p1) has completely filled 3d orbitals. True.
Q73.trapHtml: Both statements are true and directly explain the Al → Ga d-block contraction.
Q73.finalAnsHtml: (c) — Both the statements I and II are correct

Q74.subtopic: Positive Electron Gain Enthalpy of Noble Gases
Q74.conceptHtml: NCERT Table 3.7 values for noble gases (∆<sub>eg</sub>H in kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>): He (+48), Ne (+116), Ar (+96), Kr (+96), Xe (+77), Rn (+68).
Q74.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall NCERT $\Delta_{eg}H$ values for Group 18 noble gases: Noble gases have completely filled valence shells, so adding an extra electron into the next higher principal shell is endothermic ($\Delta_{eg}H > 0$). The NCERT values (in $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$) are: $\text{He} = +48$, $\text{Ne} = +116$, $\text{Ar} = +96$, $\text{Kr} = +96$, and $\text{Xe} = +77$.
  2. Step 2 — Understand the trend: $\text{Ne}$ has the highest positive $\Delta_{eg}H$ ($+116$) due to strong inter-electronic repulsion in its compact $2p^6$ shell, after which $\Delta_{eg}H$ decreases down the group ($\text{Ne} > \text{Kr} > \text{Xe}$). Meanwhile, $\text{He}$ ($+48$) has the smallest positive value because it has only $1s^2$ electrons and least repulsion.
  3. Step 3 — Arrange the four given elements: $+48 < +77 < +96 < +116$, giving $\text{He} < \text{Xe} < \text{Kr} < \text{Ne}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: This exact order matches option (b).
Q74.stepsLatex:
Comparing He, Xe, Kr, Ne:
He (+48) < Xe (+77) < Kr (+96) < Ne (+116).
He is lowest (+48) and Ne is highest (+116).
Q74.trapHtml: This is a direct NCERT Table 3.7 data question: He < Xe < Kr ≈ Ar < Ne.

Q75.conceptHtml: Total energy to form Li<sup>2+</sup>(g) from Li(g) per mole is IE<sub>1</sub> + IE<sub>2</sub>; multiply by moles n = <sub>M</sub><sup>w</sup> .
Q75.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Find the total ionization enthalpy per mole of Li: Converting $\text{Li}(g) \to \text{Li}^{2+}(g)$ requires both the first and second ionization enthalpies: $\Delta H_{\text{total}} = IE_1 + IE_2 = 520 + 7297 = 7817\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$.
  2. Step 2 — Calculate the number of moles of Li: Mass of $\text{Li} = 3.5\ \text{mg} = 3.5 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{g}$, and molar mass $= 7\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$. Thus, $n = \frac{3.5 \times 10^{-3}}{7} = 0.5 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{mol} = 5 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{mol}$.
  3. Step 3 — Compute the total energy required: $E = n \times \Delta H_{\text{total}} = (5 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{mol}) \times (7817\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}) = 3.9085\ \text{kJ}$.
  4. Step 4 — Round to the nearest integer: Rounding $3.9085\ \text{kJ}$ to the nearest integer gives 4.
Q75.stepsLatex:
1. Moles of Li in 3.5 mg (3.5 × 10−3 g):
3.5 × 10−3 g 3
n = = 0.5 × 10− mol.
7 g mol−1
2. Total molar energy for Li(g) → Li2+(g) + 2e−:
∆H = IE1 + IE2 = 520 + 7297 = 7817 kJ mol−1.
3. Energy for 0.5 × 10−3 mol:
E = 0.5 × 10−3 × 7817 = 3.9085 kJ ≈ 4 kJ.
Q75.trapHtml: Do not forget to add BOTH IE<sub>1</sub> and IE<sub>2</sub>, and convert mg → g!

Q76.conceptHtml: IUPAC roots: un = 1, nil = 0. Elements with Z = 104–118 map to Groups 4–18 (last two digits = group number for Z = 104–118!).
Q76.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Decode the IUPAC systematic name: In IUPAC nomenclature for elements with $Z > 100$, the root "un" stands for the digit $1$. Therefore, "Unununium" corresponds to atomic number $Z = 111$ (Roentgenium, $\text{Rg}$).
  2. Step 2 — Determine its group number: The noble gas at the end of Period 7 is Oganesson ($Z = 118$, Group 18). Counting backward from $Z = 118$: $\text{Group number} = 18 - (118 - 111) = 18 - 7 = 11$. (Equivalently, its valence configuration is $[\text{Rn}]5f^{14}6d^{9}7s^2$ or $6d^{10}7s^1$, giving $d + s = 11$.)
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the final answer: The element belongs to Group 11, so $n = \mathbf{11}$.
Q76.stepsLatex:
1. “Unununium” =⇒ 1-1-1 =⇒ Z = 111 (Rg, Roentgenium).
2. Configuration: [Rn]5f146d107s1 (coinage metal family below Cu, Ag, Au).
3. Group number n = 11.
Q76.trapHtml: Shortcut for Z = 104–118: the group number is simply Z − 100 (e.g., Z = 111 =⇒ Group 11).

Q77.conceptHtml: Non-metal oxides are acidic EXCEPT the three neutral oxides (CO, NO, N<sub>2</sub>O); alkali/alkaline-earth metal oxides are basic.
Q77.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Classify the metal oxides (basic): Metals from Groups 1 and 2 form basic oxides. Thus, $\text{CaO}$ and $\text{Na}_2\text{O}$ are basic oxides ($2$ oxides).
  2. Step 2 — Identify the neutral non-metal oxides: Memorize the three classic NCERT neutral oxides: $\text{N}_2\text{O}$, $\text{NO}$, and $\text{CO}$. All three appear in the list, so these are neutral oxides ($3$ oxides).
  3. Step 3 — Count the remaining acidic non-metal oxides: The remaining oxides are $\text{N}_2\text{O}_3$, $\text{NO}_2$, $\text{Cl}_2\text{O}_7$, and $\text{SO}_2$, all of which are non-metal oxides in higher oxidation states that form acids in water. Counting them gives $4$ acidic oxides.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The total number of acidic oxides is 4.
Q77.stepsLatex:
Classify each of the 9 oxides:
• Acidic (4): N2O3, NO2, Cl2O7, SO2.
• Neutral (3): N2O, CO, NO.
• Basic (2): CaO, Na2O.
Total number of acidic oxides = 4.
Q77.trapHtml: N<sub>2</sub>O and NO are neutral oxides, whereas N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>, NO<sub>2</sub>, N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>5</sub> are acidic!

trapCards.title: 1. Ionization Enthalpy (IE<sub>1</sub>, IE<sub>2</sub>, IE<sub>3</sub>) Traps
trapCards.html:
• Half/full-filled IE1 swaps: In Period 2, Be > B and N > O; in Period 3, Mg > Al and P > S (Q01, Q14, Q48, Q63).
  • IE2 shifts the anomaly one step right: For Period 2 IE2, O+(2p3) > F+(2p4), giving C < N < F < O (Q10).
  • Group 13 & 14 W-trends: Group 13 IE1 is B > Tl > Ga > Al > In (Q46, Q73); Group 14 IE1 is C > Si > Ge > Pb > Sn (Pb > Sn only, Q34).
  • 3d-series IE3 trap: Mn2+ (3d5) has higher IE3 than Fe2+ (3d6) (Q20, Q50); Ca2+ ([Ar]) has massive IE3 (Q07).
  • IE is ALWAYS endothermic: Never pick a negative value for any IE (Q05, Q22).

trapCards.title: 2. Electron Gain Enthalpy (∆<sub>eg</sub>H) & EA Traps
trapCards.html:
• Sign vs Magnitude: “Negative ∆egH” or “magni- tude” compares |∆egH| (Cl > F > Br > I), whereas plain “∆egH” compares algebraic values (Ar > S > Br > F, Q54, Q69).
  • Oxygen is LAST in Group 16: |∆egH| order is S > Se > Te > Po > O (Q15, Q57).
  • Endothermic (∆egH > 0, EA < 0) species: Be, Mg, N, noble gases (He < Xe < Kr < Ne, Q74), and ALL 2nd elec- tron additions (O → O2−, Q43).
  • Largest |∆egH| gap: Ne (+116) to Cl (−349) gives 465 kJ mol−1 (Q68).

trapCards.title: 3. Atomic, Metallic & Ionic Radii Traps
trapCards.html:
• Ga < Al neutral, but Al3+ < Ga3+ ionic: 3d10 con- traction makes metallic Ga (135 pm) < Al (143 pm), while Ga3+ (62 pm) > Al3+ (53.5 pm) (Q24).
  • Mg > Al in Period 3: Atomic radius decreases across Period 3, so Mg > Al (Q16, Q19).
  • Anions are LARGER than parent atoms: Never fall for “ions are always smaller than atoms” (Q11, Q44).
  • Isoelectronic = same e−, NOT same Z: Radius ∝ 1/Z (Ca2+ < K+ < Cl− < S2−, Q45, Q52, Q71).
  • Period 2 vs Period 3 jump: A Period 3 element is larger than Period 2 (Be < Mg, Q31).

trapCards.title: 4. Oxides, EN, Blocks & NTA Wordings
trapCards.html:
• Neutral vs Acidic/Amphoteric oxides: Only CO, NO, N2O are neutral! Al2O3, Cr2O3, As2O3 are am- photeric; V2O3 is basic; N2O3, NO2, Cl2O7, Mn2O7 are acidic (Q03, Q06, Q77).
  • Period 2 max covalency = 4: N, O, F cannot reach group valencies 5, 6, 7 (Q49).
  • Atomic weight vs Atomic number: Newlands & Lothar Meyer used atomic weight; only Moseley used atomic number (Q30).
  • All d-block elements are metals: Non-metals exist ONLY in p-block (+ H) (Q51).
  • Read qualifiers: Check “incorrect” (Q19, Q20, Q31, Q39), “NOT true” (Q35), and “respectively” (Q08, Q09, Q13).

subject: Chemistry
title: Chemical Bonding & Molecular Structure
constantsHtml:
• Chemical Bonding & Molecular Structure
  • High-Yield NTA JEE Main 2023–2026 Exam Intelligence (127 PYQs: 88 MCQs + 39 Numericals)
  • Chemical Bonding is the single highest-ROI chapter in Inorganic Chemistry, delivering 2–3 questions per shift (8–
  • 12 marks). Over 85% of 2023–2026 PYQs cluster into four core zones: (1) VSEPR Shape, Lone Pairs & Hybridization
  • (especially ClF3, SF4, BrF5, XeF2, XeF4, XeO2F2, XeOF4, I−3 , ICl4−), (2) MOT Bond Order, Paramagnetism & s–p
  • Mixing (N2, O2 ions, CO, NO+, C2, B2), (3) Dipole Moment & Bond Angle Trends (NH3 vs NF3, OF2 vs H2O vs
  • Cl2O), and (4) Fajan’s Rules, Octet Exceptions, Formal Charge & H-Bonding.

formulaCards.title: 1. Kossel–Lewis Octet Rule & Formal Charge
formulaCards.html:
• Formal Charge (FC): FC = V − L − 1B, where V = valence e− in free atom, L = non-bonding2(lone pair) e−, B = bonding e−.
  • Octet Exceptions: – Incomplete octet (< 8e−): BeCl2, BeH2, BF3, BCl3, AlCl3, LiCl. – Odd-electron (7e− / unpaired): NO, NO2, ClO2, O−2 . – Expanded octet (> 8e−): PF5, PCl5, SF4, SF6, H2SO4, IF7, XeF2, XeF4, XeO2F2
  • Non-existent Species: OF4, OF6, NCl5, FCl3, He2, Be2 (no d-orbitals in 2nd period; BO = 0 in MOT).

formulaCards.title: 2. Ionic Bonding, Lattice Enthalpy & Fajan’s Rules
formulaCards.html:
• Lattice Enthalpy (U): U ∝ |q+q−| . Higher charge & r+ + r− smaller size =⇒ higher U and higher m.p.
  • Fajan’s Rules (Covalent Character in Ionic Bonds): Covalent character ∝ Polarising power of cation (ϕ = q+ ) × Polarisability of anion (∝ r−, |q−|). r+2 – Small, high-charge cation: Li+ > Na+ > K+; Sn4+ > Sn2+ (SnCl4 > SnCl2). – Large, high-charge anion: I− > Br− > Cl− > F− (CaI2 > CaBr2 > CaCl2 > CaF2). – Pseudo-noble gas (18e−) shell: Cu+, Ag+, Zn2+ polarise much more strongly than 8e− cations (CuCl > NaCl, AgCl < KCl in ionic character).
  • Solvation vs Lattice: Soluble if |∆Hhyd| ≳ |∆Hlattice|.

formulaCards.title: 3. Bond Parameters, Dipole Moment & Resonance
formulaCards.html:
• Dipole Moment (µ): µ = q × d (1 D = 10−18 esu · cm = 3.3356×10−30 C·m). Vector from δ+ to δ− (crossed arrow 7−→ points toward δ−).
  • % Ionic Character: % ionic = µobs × 100. µcalc
  • NH3 vs NF3: µ(NH3) = 1.47 D > µ(NF3) = 0.23 D (in NH3, lone-pair orbital dipole reinforces N − H bond dipoles; in NF3, it opposes N − F dipoles).
  • Zero Dipole (µ = 0): Symmetric linear (CO2, BeCl2, BeH2, XeF2), trigonal planar (BF3), tetra- hedral (CH4, CCl4, SiF4), TBP (PF5), octahedral (SF6), square planar (XeF4), trans-alkenes, p-dichlorobenzene.
  • Bond Length & Energy: BL ∝ 1 ∝ size. Halogen BDE: Cl > Br > F > I (F weakBdOue to lone-pair re- 2 2 2 2 2 pulsion).
  • Resonance: O3 has two equal O − O bonds (BO = 1.5, 128 pm); Resonance Energy = Eactual − Emost stable canonical.

formulaCards.title: 4. VSEPR Theory & Hybridization Master Table
formulaCards.html:
• Steric Number (SN): SN = 1(V + M − C + A) = σ-bonds + lp. 2
  • Repulsion Order: lp–lp > lp–bp > bp–bp.
  • Key Geometries (SN = 2 to 7): – SN = 2 (sp): 2+0 Linear (BeCl2, CO2, NO+2 , C2H2). – SN = 3 (sp2): 3 + 0 Trigonal planar (BF3, NO−3 , CO23−); 2 + 1 Bent/V-shape (SO2, O3, NO−2 ). – SN = 4 (sp3): 4+0 Tetrahedral (CH4, NH+4 , SO24−); 3 + 1 Pyramidal (NH3, H3O+, SO23−, XeO3); 2 + 2 Bent (H2O, OF2, SCl2, ClO−2 ). – SN = 4 (dsp2): Square planar (d8 complexes: [Ni(CN)4]2−, [PtCl4]2−, [Cu(NH3)4]2+). – SN = 5 (sp3d): 5 + 0 TBP (PF5, PCl5); 4 + 1 See-saw (SF4, XeO2F2, IF+4 ); 3 + 2 T-shape (ClF3, BrF3, ICl3); 2 + 3 Linear (XeF2, I−3 , ICl−2 ). – SN = 6 (sp3d2): 6+0 Octahedral (SF6); 5+1 Square pyramidal (BrF5, IF5, ClF5, XeOF4); 4 + 2 Square planar (XeF4, ICl−4 , BrF−4 ). – SN = 7 (sp3d3): 7+0 Pentagonal bipyramidal (IF7); 6 + 1 Distorted octahedral (XeF6).

formulaCards.title: 5. Bent’s Rule, Drago’s Rule & Bond Angles
formulaCards.html:
• Bent’s Rule: More electronegative substituents (e.g., F) prefer orbitals with less s-character (longer, axial bonds in sp3d: PCl3F2 puts F axial; lp prefers equatorial in sp3d!).
  • Drago’s Rule: Central atoms from Period 3+ with EN ≤ 2.5 (PH3, AsH3, H2S, H2Se) use nearly pure p-orbitals (no hybridization; angle ≈ 90◦–93◦).
  • Bond Angle Trends: OF2 (103◦) < H2O (104.5◦) < Cl2O (111◦); ClF3 (87.5◦) < PF3 (97.8◦) < BF3 (120◦); H2O (104.5◦) < NH3 (107.5◦) < CH4 (109.5◦).

formulaCards.title: 6. Molecular Orbital Theory (MOT) & s–p Mixing
formulaCards.html:
• With s–p Mixing (≤ 14e−: B2, C2, N2): σ1s < σ1∗s < σ2s < σ2∗s < (π2px = π2py) < σ2pz < (π2∗p = π2∗p ) < σ∗ . x y 2pz
  • Without s–p Mixing (> 14e−: O2, F2, Ne2): σ2pz drops below π2px = π2py.
  • Bond Order (BO): BO = 1(Nb − Na). BE ∝ BO, 1 2 BL ∝ BO.
  • Isoelectronic 14e− (BO = 3, diamagnetic): N2, CO, NO+, CN−, C22+.
  • O2 Series: O+2 (2.5, 1 e−) > O2 (2.0, 2 e−) > O−2 (1.5, 1 e−) > O22− (1.0, 0 e−).
  • Paramagnetic Traps: B2 (2 e− in π2p), O2, S2 (2 e− in π2∗p), NO, N+2 , N−2 , O+2 , O−2 . (C2 is diamagnetic, both bonds are π!).
  • LCAO Symmetry (z-axis): 2s+2pz forms σ; 2px +2px forms π; 2s + 2px or 2pz + 2px gives zero overlap.

Q01.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Shapes of BrF<sup>+</sup><sub>2</sub> and BrF<sup>−</sup><sub>4</sub>
Q01.conceptHtml: Steric number SN = <sup>1</sup><sub>2</sub>(V + M − C + A) determines hybridization and lone pairs around the central atom.
Q01.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Write the autoionization reaction: Liquid bromine trifluoride autoionizes as $2\,\text{BrF}_3 \rightleftharpoons \text{BrF}_2^+ + \text{BrF}_4^-$.
  2. Step 2 — Find the shape of $\text{BrF}_2^+$: Bromine has $7$ valence electrons. The steric number is $\text{SN} = \frac{1}{2}(7 + 2 - 1) = 4$ ($sp^3$ hybridization), consisting of $2$ bond pairs and $2$ lone pairs, which gives a bent (V-shaped) geometry.
  3. Step 3 — Find the shape of $\text{BrF}_4^-$: The steric number is $\text{SN} = \frac{1}{2}(7 + 4 + 1) = 6$ ($sp^3d^2$ hybridization), consisting of $4$ bond pairs and $2$ lone pairs placed trans to each other, giving a square planar shape.
  4. Step 4 — Match the option: The cation and anion are bent and square planar respectively, confirming option (a).
Q01.stepsLatex:
1. For BrF+2 : SN = 1(7 + 2 − 1) = 4 (sp3, 2 bp + 2 lp) =⇒ Bent (V-shaped).
2
2. For BrF−4 : SN = 1(7 + 4 + 1) = 6 (sp3d2, 4 bp + 2 lp) =⇒ Square planar.
2
Q01.trapHtml: Both ions have 2 lone pairs on Br, but SN = 4 gives bent while SN = 6 gives square planar.

Q02.format: Two-Statement MCQ | Expanded octets and central-atom lone pairs
Q02.conceptHtml: Count valence electrons around the central atom for octet exceptions, and use lp = SN − σ-bonds for lone pairs.
Q02.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement I (octet rule around S): Check the valence electrons around sulphur in each molecule: $\text{H}_2\text{S}$ has $8\,e^-$ (obeys octet), whereas $\text{SO}_2$ ($10\,e^-$ in $\text{O}=\text{S}=\text{O}$), $\text{SO}_3$ ($12\,e^-$ in $\text{S}(=\text{O})_3$), $\text{SF}_4$ ($10\,e^-$), and $\text{SF}_6$ ($12\,e^-$) all have expanded octets.
  2. Step 2 — Check the count for Statement I: There are $4$ compounds ($\text{SO}_2, \text{SO}_3, \text{SF}_4, \text{SF}_6$) where sulphur does not obey the octet rule, not $3$. Hence, Statement I is false.
  3. Step 3 — Evaluate Statement II (lone pairs on central atom): Count lone pairs on the central atom in each set: $[\text{H}_2\text{O}(2), \text{ClF}_3(2), \text{SF}_4(1)]$, $[\text{NH}_3(1), \text{BrF}_5(1), \text{SF}_4(1)]$, $[\text{BrF}_5(1), \text{ClF}_3(2), \text{XeF}_4(2)]$, and $[\text{XeF}_4(2), \text{ClF}_3(2), \text{H}_2\text{O}(2)]$. Only $1$ set ($[\text{NH}_3, \text{BrF}_5, \text{SF}_4]$) has all molecules with $1$ lone pair, so Statement II is true.
  4. Step 4 — Conclusion: Statement I is false and Statement II is true, confirming option (d).

Q03.format: Two-Statement MCQ | F<sub>2</sub>O, H<sub>2</sub>O, Cl<sub>2</sub>O angles and Group 14 tetrahalides
Q03.conceptHtml: Higher terminal electronegativity pulls bonding electron density away, decreasing bp–bp repulsion and bond angle; large steric size of Cl opens the angle.
Q03.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Compare bond angles for Statement I: All three molecules ($\text{F}_2\text{O}, \text{H}_2\text{O}, \text{Cl}_2\text{O}$) have $sp^3$ hybridized oxygen with $2$ bond pairs and $2$ lone pairs. Highly electronegative $\text{F}$ pulls bonding electron pairs away from $\text{O}$, lowering bp–bp repulsion ($\angle \text{F}-\text{O}-\text{F} \approx 103^\circ < \angle \text{H}-\text{O}-\text{H} \approx 104.5^\circ$).
  2. Step 2 — Account for bulky $\text{Cl}$ atoms: In $\text{Cl}_2\text{O}$, steric repulsion between the bulky chlorine atoms (and $p\pi\text{–}d\pi$ back-bonding) opens the angle to $\approx 111^\circ$. Thus $\text{F}_2\text{O} < \text{H}_2\text{O} < \text{Cl}_2\text{O}$ is correct, so Statement I is true.
  3. Step 3 — Evaluate Statement II (nature of tetrafluorides): Among group 14 tetrafluorides, $\text{SnF}_4$ and $\text{PbF}_4$ are ionic solids, whereas $\text{SiF}_4$ is a covalent gas due to the small size and high polarizing power of $\text{Si}^{4+}$. Hence, Statement II is false.
  4. Step 4 — Conclusion: Statement I is true and Statement II is false, confirming option (c).

power, making SnF4/PbF4 polymeric/covalent (especially SiF4 is purely covalent). Statement II is false.
Q03.trapHtml: SiF<sub>4</sub> is a classic covalent tetrahedral gas, immediately falsifying Statement II.
Q03.finalAnsHtml: (c) Statement I is true but Statement II is false

Q04.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Identify pairs with dissimilar Lewis structures
Q04.conceptHtml: Species with the same number of atoms and same total valence electrons generally share similar Lewis dot structures.
Q04.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Check valence electrons and Lewis structures for pairs B, C, and D: Pair B $[\text{O}_2^{2-}, \text{F}_2]$ both have $14$ valence $e^-$ (single bond, $3$ lone pairs on each atom). Pair C $[\text{CN}^-, \text{CO}]$ both have $10$ valence $e^-$ (triple bond, $1$ lone pair on each atom). Pair D $[\text{NH}_3, \text{H}_3\text{O}^+]$ both have $8$ valence $e^-$ ($3$ single bonds, $1$ lone pair on the central atom). All three pairs have similar Lewis structures.
  2. Step 2 — Check pair A $[\text{SO}_3^{2-}, \text{CO}_3^{2-}]$: $\text{SO}_3^{2-}$ has $26$ valence $e^-$ ($1$ lone pair on $\text{S}$, pyramidal), whereas $\text{CO}_3^{2-}$ has $24$ valence $e^-$ ($0$ lone pairs on $\text{C}$, trigonal planar). Their Lewis dot structures are not similar.
  3. Step 3 — Check pair E $[\text{MnO}_4^{2-}, \text{CrO}_4^{2-}]$: $\text{MnO}_4^{2-}$ has $\text{Mn}^{6+}$ ($d^1$, $33$ valence $e^-$, odd-electron paramagnetic ion), whereas $\text{CrO}_4^{2-}$ has $\text{Cr}^{6+}$ ($d^0$, $32$ valence $e^-$, all paired). Their Lewis dot structures are not similar.
  4. Step 4 — Conclusion: Only pairs A and E do not have similar Lewis dot structures, confirming option (b).

• B : O22−, F2 (14e− valence, single bond) =⇒ Similar.
• C : CN−, CO (10e− valence, triple bond) =⇒ Similar.
• D : NH3, H3O+ (8e− valence, pyramidal) =⇒ Similar.

valence e−) =⇒ Dissimilar.

Q05.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Bond length vs total length of diatomic AB
Q05.conceptHtml: Covalent bond length d<sub>A−B</sub> = r<sub>A</sub> + r<sub>B</sub>. For a diatomic AB molecule modeled as touching spheres of radii r<sub>A</sub>, r<sub>B</sub>, total length = 2r<sub>A</sub> + 2r<sub>B</sub> = 2(r<sub>A</sub> + r<sub>B</sub>).
Q05.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the definition of covalent bond length: For a heteronuclear diatomic molecule $\text{AB}$ formed by two atoms with covalent radii $r_A$ and $r_B$, the covalent bond length is the equilibrium internuclear distance between the two nuclei: $d_{A-B} = r_A + r_B$.
  2. Step 2 — Calculate the total length of the $\text{AB}$ molecule: Moving from the outer boundary of atom $\text{A}$ to its nucleus covers $r_A$, from nucleus $\text{A}$ to nucleus $\text{B}$ covers $r_A + r_B$, and from nucleus $\text{B}$ to the outer boundary of atom $\text{B}$ covers $r_B$.
  3. Step 3 — Sum the segments: $\text{Total length} = r_A + (r_A + r_B) + r_B = 2(r_A + r_B)$.
  4. Step 4 — Conclusion: The covalent bond length and total length are $(r_A + r_B)$ and $2(r_A + r_B)$ respectively, confirming option (a).
Q05.stepsLatex:
1. Internuclear distance (covalent bond length) = rA + rB.
2. End-to-end total length of the AB molecule = dA + dB = 2rA + 2rB = 2(rA + rB).
Q05.trapHtml: Do not confuse bond length (r<sub>A</sub> + r<sub>B</sub>) with total molecular span (2r<sub>A</sub> + 2r<sub>B</sub>).

Q06.format: Diagram MCQ | Identify π<sup>∗</sup> MO with z-internuclear axis
Q06.conceptHtml: In a π<sup>∗</sup> antibonding MO, two parallel p-orbitals (p<sub>x</sub> or p<sub>y</sub>) overlap out-of-phase laterally, creating two perpendicular nodal planes (one along the z-axis and one between the nuclei).
Q06.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the orbitals forming a $\pi^*$ MO: With the internuclear axis along the $z$-direction, a $\pi^*$ (antibonding) molecular orbital arises from the out-of-phase (destructive) sideways overlap of two $p_x$ (or two $p_y$) atomic orbitals.
  2. Step 2 — Determine the nodal planes and lobe phases: Destructive sideways overlap creates two nodal planes—one containing the internuclear $z$-axis and one perpendicular to it between the two nuclei. The four lobes bend away from the internuclear region with opposite phases (shaded vs. unshaded) across both nodal planes.
  3. Step 3 — Compare the four diagrams: Diagram (A) represents a $\pi$ bonding orbital; Diagram (B) shows identical phases on the same side (incorrect for antibonding); Diagram (D) shows a $\sigma^*$ orbital along the $z$-axis; Diagram (C) correctly shows four lobes bent away with diagonally matched phases (top-left and bottom-right shaded).
  4. Step 4 — Conclusion: Diagram (C) accurately represents the $\pi^*$ molecular orbital, confirming option (c).
Q06.stepsLatex:
• (A) shows constructive π bonding overlap (continuous lobes above and below z-axis).
• (B) shows in-phase lobes on top and unshaded on bottom (still symmetric, not π∗ out-of-phase).
• (C) shows opposite-phase shading diagonally across the internuclear bisector =⇒ π∗ antibonding MO.
• (D) shows σ∗ antibonding overlap along the z-axis.
Q06.trapHtml: In π<sup>∗</sup>, opposite signs (shaded/unshaded) must face each other both across the z-axis AND across the internuclear midpoint.

Q07.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Identify see-saw (4 bp + 1 lp) species
Q07.conceptHtml: SF<sub>4</sub> has SN = 5 (4 bp + 1 lp, sp<sup>3</sup>d), giving a see-saw geometry.
Q07.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Determine the structure of $\text{SF}_4$: Sulphur has $6$ valence electrons, so $\text{SN} = \frac{1}{2}(6 + 4) = 5$ ($sp^3d$) with $4$ bond pairs and $1$ lone pair, giving a see-saw shape.
  2. Step 2 — Determine the shapes of species A, B, and D: $\text{BrF}_4^-$ has $\text{SN} = 6$ ($4\text{ bp} + 2\text{ lp}$, square planar); $\text{CH}_4$ has $\text{SN} = 4$ ($4\text{ bp} + 0\text{ lp}$, tetrahedral); $\text{XeF}_4$ has $\text{SN} = 6$ ($4\text{ bp} + 2\text{ lp}$, square planar). None of these match $\text{SF}_4$.
  3. Step 3 — Determine the shapes of species C and E: For $\text{IF}_4^+$, $\text{SN} = \frac{1}{2}(7 + 4 - 1) = 5$ ($4\text{ bp} + 1\text{ lp}$, see-saw). For $\text{XeO}_2\text{F}_2$, $\text{Xe}$ forms $4\,\sigma$ bonds ($2$ to $\text{O}$, $2$ to $\text{F}$) and has $1$ lone pair ($\text{SN} = 5$, see-saw).
  4. Step 4 — Conclusion: Only C ($\text{IF}_4^+$) and E ($\text{XeO}_2\text{F}_2$) are isostructural with $\text{SF}_4$, confirming option (b).
Q07.stepsLatex:
• A. BrF−4 : 4 bp + 2 lp → Square planar.
• B. CH4: 4 bp + 0 lp → Tetrahedral.
• C. IF+4 : SN = 1(7 + 4 − 1) = 5 (4 bp + 1 lp) → See-saw.
2
• D. XeF4: 4 bp + 2 lp → Square planar.
• E. XeO2F2: 4 σ-bp + 1 lp (sp3d) → See-saw.
Q07.trapHtml: Double-bonded oxygens in XeO<sub>2</sub>F<sub>2</sub> count as 1 σ-domain each in VSEPR, so XeO<sub>2</sub>F<sub>2</sub> is also see-saw.

Q08.subtopic: MOT — O2 Series Bond Length & Unpaired Electrons
Q08.format: Two-Statement MCQ | Bond length and paramagnetism in O<sup>+</sup><sub>2</sub> , O<sub>2</sub>, O<sup>−</sup><sub>2</sub> , O<sup>2</sup><sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup>
Q08.conceptHtml: Bond length ∝ <sub>B</sub><sup>1</sup><sub>O</sub>. Adding electrons to π<sup>∗</sup> lowers BO and increases bond length.
Q08.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Compute bond orders using MOT: The electron counts and bond orders ($\text{BO} = \frac{N_b - N_a}{2}$) are: $\text{O}_2^+$ ($15\,e^-$, $\text{BO} = 2.5$), $\text{O}_2$ ($16\,e^-$, $\text{BO} = 2.0$), $\text{O}_2^-$ ($17\,e^-$, $\text{BO} = 1.5$), and $\text{O}_2^{2-}$ ($18\,e^-$, $\text{BO} = 1.0$).
  2. Step 2 — Verify Statement I (bond length order): Since bond length is inversely proportional to bond order, $\text{O}_2^+ < \text{O}_2 < \text{O}_2^- < \text{O}_2^{2-}$. Thus, Statement I is true.
  3. Step 3 — Verify Statement II (unpaired electrons): Counting electrons in the $\pi^*_{2p}$ orbitals gives: $\text{O}_2$ ($2$ unpaired), $\text{O}_2^+$ ($1$ unpaired), $\text{O}_2^-$ ($1$ unpaired), and $\text{O}_2^{2-}$ ($0$ unpaired). Because $\text{O}_2^+$ and $\text{O}_2^-$ have the same number of unpaired electrons ($1$ each), the strict inequality $\text{O}_2^+ > \text{O}_2^-$ is incorrect. Thus, Statement II is false.
  4. Step 4 — Conclusion: Statement I is true and Statement II is false, confirming option (c).

1. Bond orders: O+2 (2.5) > O2 (2.0) > O−2 (1.5) > O22− (1.0), so bond length order O+2 < O2 < O−2 < O22− is
true.
2. Unpaired e− in π2∗ : O2 (2), O+2 (1), O−2 (1), O22− (0). Since O+2 and O−2 both have 1 unpaired electron,
+ p
O2 > O−2 in Statement II is false.
Q08.trapHtml: Both O<sup>+</sup><sub>2</sub> (π<sup>∗1</sup>) and O<sup>−</sup><sub>2</sub> (π<sup>∗3</sup>) have exactly 1 unpaired electron.
Q08.finalAnsHtml: (c) Statement I is true but Statement II is false

Q09.subtopic: VSEPR — Shape Matching of Xenon Compounds
Q09.format: Match List-I with List-II | Isostructural pairs
Q09.conceptHtml: Match species having the exact same (bp, lp) count and molecular shape.
Q09.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Match A ($\text{XeO}_3$) and B ($\text{XeF}_2$): $\text{XeO}_3$ has $3\,\sigma$ bonds and $1$ lone pair ($sp^3$, trigonal pyramidal), matching $\text{NH}_3$ (II). $\text{XeF}_2$ has $2\,\sigma$ bonds and $3$ lone pairs ($sp^3d$, linear), matching $[\text{I}_3]^-$ (III).
  2. Step 2 — Match C ($\text{XeO}_2\text{F}_2$) and D ($\text{XeOF}_4$): $\text{XeO}_2\text{F}_2$ has $4\,\sigma$ bonds and $1$ lone pair ($sp^3d$, see-saw), matching $\text{SF}_4$ (IV). $\text{XeOF}_4$ has $5\,\sigma$ bonds and $1$ lone pair ($sp^3d^2$, square pyramidal), matching $\text{BrF}_5$ (I).
  3. Step 3 — Combine the matches: The complete correspondence is A-II, B-III, C-IV, D-I.
  4. Step 4 — Conclusion: This exact match corresponds to option (c).
Q09.stepsLatex:
• A. XeO3 (3 bp + 1 lp, pyramidal) ↔ II. NH3.
• B. XeF2 (2 bp + 3 lp, linear) ↔ III. [I3]−.
• C. XeO2F2 (4 bp + 1 lp, see-saw) ↔ IV. SF4.
• D. XeOF4 (5 bp + 1 lp, square pyramidal) ↔ I. BrF5.
Q09.trapHtml: Always count σ-bonds + lone pairs on Xe (8 valence e<sup>−</sup>); each = O uses 2e<sup>−</sup> and contributes 1 σ-pair.

Q10.subtopic: Bond Length Equivalence & MOT Bond Order
Q10.format: Two-Statement MCQ | Unequal E − F bonds and O<sub>2</sub>/F<sub>2</sub> BO
Q10.conceptHtml: In sp<sup>3</sup>d trigonal bipyramidal geometry, axial bonds are longer than equatorial bonds; symmetric sp<sup>3</sup> and sp<sup>3</sup>d<sup>2</sup> (4 + 2) species have equal bond lengths.
Q10.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Check bond-length equality for Statement I: $\text{BF}_4^-$ (tetrahedral), $\text{SiF}_4$ (tetrahedral), and $\text{XeF}_4$ (square planar) are completely symmetric, so all $\text{E}-\text{F}$ bonds in each are equal. Only $\text{SF}_4$ (see-saw, $sp^3d$) has longer axial bonds than equatorial bonds.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement I: Only one species ($\text{SF}_4$) has unequal $\text{E}-\text{F}$ bond lengths, not two. Hence, Statement I is false.
  3. Step 3 — Evaluate Statement II (bond orders): Calculate bond orders via MOT: $\text{O}_2^-$ ($1.5$), $\text{O}_2^{2-}$ ($1.0$), $\text{F}_2$ ($1.0$), and $\text{O}_2^+$ ($2.5$). The highest bond order belongs to $\text{O}_2^+$ ($2.5$), not $\text{O}_2^-$. Hence, Statement II is false.
  4. Step 4 — Conclusion: Both Statement I and Statement II are false, confirming option (a).
Q10.stepsLatex:
1. Statement I: BF−4 (tetrahedral), SiF4 (tetrahedral), and XeF4 (square planar) all have equal E − F bond
lengths. Only 1 species (SF4, see-saw: axial > equatorial) has unequal E − F bond lengths =⇒ Statement I
is false.
2. Statement II: Bond orders: O−2 (1.5), O22− (1.0), F2 (1.0), O+2 (2.5). Highest BO is O+2 (not O−2 ) =⇒
Statement II is false.
Q10.trapHtml: XeF<sub>4</sub> has 4 equivalent equatorial Xe − F bonds and 2 axial lone pairs, so all four Xe − F bonds are equal!
Q10.finalAnsHtml: (a) Both Statement I and Statement II are false

Q11.subtopic: MOT — Same Bond Order & Paramagnetic Character
Q11.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Identify pair with equal BO and unpaired e<sup>−</sup>
Q11.conceptHtml: Species with the same total electron count (or symmetric around 14e<sup>−</sup>) share the same bond order.
Q11.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall MOT bond orders and unpaired electrons: For $13\,e^-$ ($\text{N}_2^+$): $\text{BO} = 2.5$, $1$ unpaired $e^-$. For $15\,e^-$ ($\text{O}_2^+$ and $\text{N}_2^-$): $\text{BO} = 2.5$, $1$ unpaired $e^-$. For $16\,e^-$ ($\text{N}_2^{2-}$): $\text{BO} = 2.0$, $2$ unpaired $e^-$. For $17\,e^-$ ($\text{O}_2^-$): $\text{BO} = 1.5$, $1$ unpaired $e^-$.
  2. Step 2 — Check each pair: Option (a) $\text{O}_2^-(1.5)$ vs $\text{N}_2^+(2.5)$ — different BO. Option (b) $\text{O}_2^+(2.5)$ vs $\text{N}_2^{2-}(2.0)$ — different BO. Option (c) $\text{O}_2^-(1.5)$ vs $\text{N}_2^-(2.5)$ — different BO.
  3. Step 3 — Verify option (d): Both $\text{O}_2^+$ and $\text{N}_2^-$ are isoelectronic ($15\,e^-$), giving the exact same bond order ($\text{BO} = 2.5$) and $1$ unpaired electron each (both paramagnetic).
  4. Step 4 — Conclusion: The matching pair is $\text{O}_2^+, \text{N}_2^-$, confirming option (d).
Q11.stepsLatex:
• O+2 (15e−): BO = 2.5, 1 unpaired e− (paramagnetic).
• N−2 (15e−): BO = 2.5, 1 unpaired e− in π∗ (paramagnetic).
• Check others: O−2 (17e−, BO = 1.5) vs N+2 (13e−, BO = 2.5); N22− (16e−, BO = 2.0).
Q11.trapHtml: Both O<sup>+</sup><sub>2</sub> and N<sup>−</sup><sub>2</sub> are 15-electron species (BO = 2.5, paramagnetic).

Q12.subtopic: Dipole Moment, MOT, Formal Charge & Octet Rule
Q12.format: Multi-Statement MCQ | Identify all correct statements
Q12.conceptHtml: Evaluate each statement independently using VSEPR, MOT, and formal charge rules.
Q12.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate statements A and B (dipole moments): In $\text{NH}_3$, the lone-pair dipole reinforces the $\text{N}-\text{H}$ bond dipoles ($\mu \approx 1.47\,\text{D}$), whereas in $\text{NF}_3$ it opposes the $\text{N}-\text{F}$ dipoles ($\mu \approx 0.23\,\text{D}$); thus A is false. $\text{BeH}_2$ is linear and symmetric, so its two $\text{Be}-\text{H}$ dipoles cancel ($\mu = 0$); thus B is true.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate statement C (bond order): Both $\text{O}_2^{2-}$ and $\text{F}_2$ have $18$ electrons, giving the same bond order of $1.0$; thus C is true.
  3. Step 3 — Evaluate statements D and E: In ozone ($\text{O}=\text{O}^+-\text{O}^-$), the central oxygen has $1$ lone pair and $3$ bonds, so its formal charge is $6 - 2 - \frac{6}{2} = +1$ (not $-1$), making D false. In $\text{NO}_2$, nitrogen has an odd electron ($7\,e^-$ around $\text{N}$, incomplete octet), so it readily dimerizes to $\text{N}_2\text{O}_4$, making E false.
  4. Step 4 — Conclusion: Only statements B and C are correct, confirming option (a).
Q12.stepsLatex:
• A. False: µ(NH3) = 1.47 D > µ(NF3) = 0.23 D.
• B. True: BeH2 is linear (sp), so µ = 0.
• C. True: Both O22− and F2 have 18e− =⇒ BO = 1.
+ 1
• D. False: Central O in O3 (O = O − O−) has FC = 6 − 2 − (6) = +1 (not −1).
2
• E. False: NO2 is an odd-electron (17e−) molecule; N has 7e−.
Q12.trapHtml: Central O in O<sub>3</sub> carries +1 formal charge, while the singly bonded terminal O carries −1.

Q13.format: Multi-Statement MCQ | Verify shape + hybridization combinations
Q13.conceptHtml: Check SN = <sub>2</sub><sup>1</sup>(V + M − C + A) for each species.
Q13.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Verify A ($\text{IF}_3$) and B ($\text{IF}_5$): For $\text{IF}_3$, $\text{SN} = \frac{1}{2}(7 + 3) = 5$ ($sp^3d$) with $3$ bond pairs and $2$ equatorial lone pairs $\Rightarrow$ T-shaped (A is correct). For $\text{IF}_5$, $\text{SN} = \frac{1}{2}(7 + 5) = 6$ ($sp^3d^2$) with $5$ bond pairs and $1$ lone pair $\Rightarrow$ square pyramidal (B is correct).
  2. Step 2 — Verify C ($\text{IF}_7$): For $\text{IF}_7$, $\text{SN} = \frac{1}{2}(7 + 7) = 7$ ($sp^3d^3$) with $7$ bond pairs and $0$ lone pairs $\Rightarrow$ pentagonal bipyramidal (C is correct).
  3. Step 3 — Verify D ($\text{ClO}_4^-$): In perchlorate ion, chlorine forms $4\,\sigma$ bonds (plus $3\,\pi$ bonds) with $0$ lone pairs, giving $\text{SN} = 4$ ($sp^3$, tetrahedral), not square planar ($sp^2d$). Thus D is incorrect.
  4. Step 4 — Conclusion: Combinations A, B, and C only are correct, confirming option (c).
Q13.stepsLatex:
• A. IF3: 3 bp + 2 lp, sp3d, T-shaped (Correct).
• B. IF5: 5 bp + 1 lp, sp3d2, Square pyramidal (Correct).
• C. IF7: 7 bp + 0 lp, sp3d3, Pentagonal bipyramidal (Correct).
• D. ClO−4 : 4 σ-bonds + 0 lp, sp3, Tetrahedral (NOT square planar sp2d).
Q13.trapHtml: ClO<sup>−</sup><sub>4</sub> is sp<sup>3</sup> tetrahedral, not sp<sup>2</sup>d square planar.

Q14.format: Multi-Statement MCQ | Identify statements that are NOT TRUE
Q14.conceptHtml: In XeO<sub>2</sub>F<sub>2</sub> (sp<sup>3</sup>d, see-saw), F atoms occupy axial positions (Bent’s rule) and = O + lone pair occupy equatorial positions.
Q14.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Determine the structure of $\text{XeO}_2\text{F}_2$: Xenon ($8$ valence $e^-$) forms two $\text{Xe}=\text{O}$ double bonds and two $\text{Xe}-\text{F}$ single bonds, leaving $1$ lone pair. Its steric number is $5$ ($sp^3d$, TBP electron geometry) with $4\,\sigma$ bonds $+ 1$ lone pair, giving a see-saw shape (A is true).
  2. Step 2 — Check bond angles (C and D): By Bent's rule, the more electronegative $\text{F}$ atoms occupy axial positions ($\angle \text{F}-\text{Xe}-\text{F} \approx 174.7^\circ$, close to $180^\circ$, so D is true), while the double-bonded $\text{O}$ atoms and the lone pair occupy equatorial positions ($\angle \text{O}-\text{Xe}-\text{O} \approx 105.7^\circ$, far from $180^\circ$, so C is NOT true).
  3. Step 3 — Count total valence electrons and electron pairs around $\text{Xe}$ (B and E): Around $\text{Xe}$, there are $2$ double bonds ($8\,e^-$), $2$ single bonds ($4\,e^-$), and $1$ lone pair ($2\,e^-$), totaling $14$ valence electrons ($7$ electron pairs). Therefore, claiming $5$ electron pairs (B is NOT true) or $16$ valence electrons (E is NOT true) is incorrect.
  4. Step 4 — Conclusion: The statements that are NOT true are B, C, and E only, confirming option (c).

• A. True: XeO2F2 is see-saw (4 σ + 1 lp).
• B. False: Xe has 5 hybrid/steric domains, but 6 bond pairs (2σ + 2π to O, 2σ to F) +1 lp = 7 electron pairs
(14 valence e−).
• C. False: O = Xe = O are equatorial, so ∠O − Xe − O ≈ 106◦ (not 180◦).
• D. True: Axial F − Xe − F angle is ≈ 175◦ (close to 180◦).
• E. False: Xe has 8 + 2(2) + 2(1) = 14 valence e− (not 16).
Thus B, C, and E are NOT TRUE.

Q15.subtopic: Lewis Structures — Total Lone Pairs & Bond Angle
Q15.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Count total lone pairs in molecule, then find bond angle
Q15.conceptHtml: Count total lone pairs across all atoms in the Lewis dot structure (not just the central atom).
Q15.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Count total lone pairs in each Lewis structure: In $\text{HNO}_3$ ($\text{H}-\text{O}-\text{N}(=\text{O})-\text{O}^-$), the oxygens carry $2 + 2 + 3 = 7$ lone pairs. In $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ ($(\text{HO})_2\text{S}(=\text{O})_2$), the four oxygens carry $2 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 8$ lone pairs.
  2. Step 2 — Count lone pairs in $\text{NF}_3$ and $\text{O}_3$: In $\text{NF}_3$, nitrogen has $1$ lone pair and each of the three fluorines has $3$ lone pairs, giving $1 + 3(3) = 10$ lone pairs. In $\text{O}_3$ ($\text{O}=\text{O}^+-\text{O}^-$), there are $2 + 1 + 3 = 6$ lone pairs.
  3. Step 3 — Identify (X) and its bond angle: Molecule (X) with the maximum lone pairs ($10$) is $\text{NF}_3$. Because $\text{N}$ is $sp^3$ hybridized with $1$ lone pair and highly electronegative $\text{F}$ atoms pull bonding pairs away from $\text{N}$, the $\angle \text{F}-\text{N}-\text{F}$ bond angle compresses to $\approx 102^\circ$.
  4. Step 4 — Conclusion: The bond angle of $\text{NF}_3$ is $102^\circ$, confirming option (b).
Q15.stepsLatex:
1. HNO3: 2 + 2 + 3 = 7 lp.
2. H2SO4: 2(−OH) + 2(= O) = 2(2) + 2(2) = 8 lp.
3. NF3: 1(N) + 3 × 3(F) = 10 lp (maximum!).
4. O3: 1 + 2 + 3 = 6 lp.
5. Therefore X = NF3. In NF3 (sp3, 3 bp+1 lp), high EN of F reduces bp–bp repulsion, compressing ∠F − N − F
to 102◦ (NCERT value).
Q15.trapHtml: Each terminal F carries 3 lone pairs, giving NF<sub>3</sub> 10 total lone pairs; its bond angle is 102<sup>°</sup> (smaller than NH<sub>3</sub>’s 107<sup>°</sup>).

Q16.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Lowest µ among H<sub>2</sub>S, H<sub>2</sub>O, NF<sub>3</sub>, NH<sub>3</sub>, CHCl<sub>3</sub>
Q16.conceptHtml: In NF<sub>3</sub>, the lone-pair orbital dipole opposes the resultant of the three N − F bond dipoles, giving a very small net dipole moment (0.23 D).
Q16.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Compare dipole moments of the given molecules: Their experimental dipole moments are: $\text{NF}_3 \approx 0.23\,\text{D}$, $\text{H}_2\text{S} \approx 0.97\,\text{D}$, $\text{CHCl}_3 \approx 1.04\,\text{D}$, $\text{NH}_3 \approx 1.47\,\text{D}$, and $\text{H}_2\text{O} \approx 1.85\,\text{D}$.
  2. Step 2 — Identify molecule (X): In $\text{NF}_3$, the lone-pair orbital dipole points opposite to the resultant of the three $\text{N}-\text{F}$ bond dipoles, largely cancelling them out. Hence, $\text{NF}_3$ has the lowest dipole moment.
  3. Step 3 — Count lone pairs on the central atom of $\text{NF}_3$: Nitrogen has $5$ valence electrons and uses $3$ to form single bonds with three $\text{F}$ atoms, leaving $2$ non-bonding electrons, i.e., $1$ lone pair on $\text{N}$.
  4. Step 4 — Conclusion: The central atom of $\text{NF}_3$ has $1$ lone pair, confirming option (d).
Q16.stepsLatex:
1. Dipole moments: H2O (1.85 D) > NH3 (1.47 D) > CHCl3 (1.04 D) > H2S (0.95 D) > NF3 (0.23 D).
2. Thus X = NF3, and nitrogen has 1 lone pair of electrons.
Q16.trapHtml: Despite F being the most electronegative element, NF<sub>3</sub> has the lowest dipole moment (0.23 D) due to vector cancellation.

Q17.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Hybridization of XF<sub>3</sub> (Lewis acid) and YF<sub>3</sub> (Lewis base)
Q17.conceptHtml: Group 13 trihalides (BF<sub>3</sub>) are electron-deficient Lewis acids (sp<sup>2</sup>); Group 15 trihalides (NF<sub>3</sub>, PF<sub>3</sub>) have a lone pair and act as Lewis bases (sp<sup>3</sup>).
Q17.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the Lewis acid $\text{XF}_3$: A $p$-block trifluoride acts as a Lewis acid when its central atom is electron-deficient with a vacant $p$-orbital, such as $\text{BF}_3$ (group 13, $3$ valence $e^-$).
  2. Step 2 — Find the hybridization of $\text{X}$ in $\text{XF}_3$: With $3$ bond pairs and $0$ lone pairs, $\text{SN} = 3$, so $\text{X}$ is $sp^2$ hybridized.
  3. Step 3 — Identify the Lewis base $\text{YF}_3$ and its hybridization: A $p$-block trifluoride acts as a Lewis base when its central atom has a donatable lone pair, such as $\text{NF}_3$ or $\text{PF}_3$ (group 15, $5$ valence $e^-$). With $3$ bond pairs and $1$ lone pair, $\text{SN} = 4$, so $\text{Y}$ is $sp^3$ hybridized.
  4. Step 4 — Conclusion: The hybridizations of $\text{XF}_3$ and $\text{YF}_3$ are $sp^2$ and $sp^3$ respectively, confirming option (a).
Q17.stepsLatex:
1. XF3 (Lewis acid, e.g., BF3): 3 bp + 0 lp =⇒ sp2.
2. YF3 (Lewis base, e.g., NF3): 3 bp + 1 lp =⇒ sp3.
Q17.trapHtml: Lewis acidity requires an incomplete octet / vacant orbital (sp<sup>2</sup>); Lewis basicity requires an available lone pair (sp<sup>3</sup>).

Q18.subtopic: Formal Charge in HNO3 Lewis Structure
Q18.format: Diagram MCQ | Compute formal charge on atoms (1) to (4)
Q18.conceptHtml: FC = V − L − 1B. 2
Q18.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the formal charge formula: $\text{FC} = V - N - \frac{B}{2}$, where $V$ is the number of valence electrons, $N$ is the number of non-bonding (lone-pair) electrons, and $B$ is the number of bonding electrons.
  2. Step 2 — Calculate FC for atoms (1) and (2): Atom (1) is the $-\text{OH}$ oxygen ($V=6, N=4, B=4$): $\text{FC}_1 = 6 - 4 - \frac{4}{2} = 0$. Atom (2) is the central nitrogen ($V=5, N=0, B=8$): $\text{FC}_2 = 5 - 0 - \frac{8}{2} = +1$.
  3. Step 3 — Calculate FC for atoms (3) and (4): Atom (3) is the doubly bonded $=\text{O}$ ($V=6, N=4, B=4$): $\text{FC}_3 = 6 - 4 - \frac{4}{2} = 0$. Atom (4) is the singly bonded $-\text{O}$ ($V=6, N=6, B=2$): $\text{FC}_4 = 6 - 6 - \frac{2}{2} = -1$.
  4. Step 4 — Conclusion: The formal charges on atoms (1) to (4) are $0, +1, 0, -1$, confirming option (c).
Q18.trapHtml: Check the numbering order (1) to (4) carefully in the diagram before matching options.

Q19.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Order of C − H, C − O, C = O, C ≡ N
Q19.conceptHtml: Bond length decreases with increasing bond order and decreasing atomic radius (H is much smaller than N, O).
Q19.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Compare atomic size for $\text{C}-\text{H}$ (A): Hydrogen has a much smaller covalent radius ($37\,\text{pm}$) than $\text{N}$ or $\text{O}$, making the $\text{C}-\text{H}$ bond the shortest ($\approx 109\,\text{pm}$).
  2. Step 2 — Compare bond orders for $\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$ (D), $\text{C}=\text{O}$ (C), and $\text{C}-\text{O}$ (B): Higher bond order pulls the bonded atoms closer together, shortening the bond: triple bond $\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$ ($\approx 116\,\text{pm}$) $<$ double bond $\text{C}=\text{O}$ ($\approx 121\,\text{pm}$) $<$ single bond $\text{C}-\text{O}$ ($\approx 143\,\text{pm}$).
  3. Step 3 — Arrange in increasing order of bond length: $\text{C}-\text{H}\,(109\,\text{pm}) < \text{C}\equiv\text{N}\,(116\,\text{pm}) < \text{C}=\text{O}\,(121\,\text{pm}) < \text{C}-\text{O}\,(143\,\text{pm})$, i.e., $\text{A} < \text{D} < \text{C} < \text{B}$.
  4. Step 4 — Conclusion: The increasing order is $\text{A} < \text{D} < \text{C} < \text{B}$, confirming option (d).
Q19.stepsLatex:
• Standard covalent bond lengths: C − H (A) ≈ 109 pm, C ≡ N (D) ≈ 116 pm, C = O (C) ≈ 121 pm, C − O (B)
≈ 143 pm.
• Increasing order: A < D < C < B.
Q19.trapHtml: C − H (109 pm) is shorter than even C ≡ N (116 pm) because hydrogen has only a 1s shell.

Q20.subtopic: Halogen Bond Dissociation Enthalpy & Fajan’s Rules
Q20.format: Two-Statement MCQ | BDE of X<sub>2</sub> and covalent character of halides
Q20.conceptHtml: For F<sub>2</sub>, strong lp–lp repulsion in the small 2p shell lowers BDE below Cl<sub>2</sub> and Br<sub>2</sub>. By Fajan’s rules, higher cation oxidation state gives higher covalent character.
Q20.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement I (halogen bond dissociation enthalpy): Normally bond enthalpy decreases down the group as bond length increases, so $\text{Cl}_2 > \text{Br}_2 > \text{I}_2$. However, $\text{F}_2$ has an anomalously low bond enthalpy due to strong lone pair–lone pair repulsion between the tiny $\text{F}$ atoms, giving $\text{Cl}_2 > \text{Br}_2 > \text{F}_2 > \text{I}_2$. Thus, Statement I is true.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement II using Fajan's rule: Higher positive charge on the cation increases its polarizing power and therefore increases covalent character. Accordingly, $\text{SnCl}_4 > \text{SnCl}_2$ and $\text{PbCl}_4 > \text{PbCl}_2$ are correct.
  3. Step 3 — Spot the error in the uranium halides: By the same rule, $\text{U}^{6+}$ in $\text{UF}_6$ is much more polarizing than $\text{U}^{4+}$ in $\text{UF}_4$, so covalent character follows $\text{UF}_6 > \text{UF}_4$ (not $\text{UF}_4 > \text{UF}_6$). Hence, Statement II is false.
  4. Step 4 — Conclusion: Statement I is true and Statement II is false, confirming option (d).
Q20.stepsLatex:
1. Statement I: Cl2 (242.6) > Br2 (192.8) > F2 (158.8) > I2 (151.1 kJ mol−1) =⇒ True.
2. Statement II: SnCl4 > SnCl2 and PbCl4 > PbCl2 are true, but UF6 > UF4 (not UF4 > UF6) because U6+
has higher polarising power than U4+ =⇒ False.
Q20.trapHtml: Always check all three pairs in Statement II; UF<sub>4</sub> > UF<sub>6</sub> reverses Fajan’s charge rule.
Q20.finalAnsHtml: (d) Statement I is true but Statement II is false

Q21.format: Two-Statement MCQ | Count tetrahedral species and check octet set
Q21.conceptHtml: Distinguish sp<sup>3</sup> tetrahedral (NH<sup>+</sup><sub>4</sub> , weak-field [NiCl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2−</sup>) from dsp<sup>2</sup> square planar ([Ni(CN)<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2−</sup>, [PtCl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2−</sup>) and sp<sup>3</sup>d see-saw (SF<sub>4</sub>, SeF<sub>4</sub>).
Q21.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Determine the geometry of each species in Statement I: $\text{SF}_4$ (see-saw), $\text{NH}_4^+$ (tetrahedral, $sp^3$), $[\text{NiCl}_4]^{2-}$ (tetrahedral, weak-field $\text{Cl}^-$, $sp^3$), $\text{XeF}_4$ (square planar), $[\text{PtCl}_4]^{2-}$ (square planar, $5d$ $dsp^2$), $\text{SeF}_4$ (see-saw), and $[\text{Ni(CN)}_4]^{2-}$ (square planar, strong-field $\text{CN}^-$, $dsp^2$).
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement I: Only $2$ species ($\text{NH}_4^+$ and $[\text{NiCl}_4]^{2-}$) are tetrahedral, not $3$. Hence, Statement I is false.
  3. Step 3 — Evaluate Statement II (incomplete octet): Count valence electrons around the central atom in each molecule: $\text{NO}_2$ has $7\,e^-$ on $\text{N}$, $\text{BeH}_2$ has $4\,e^-$ on $\text{Be}$, $\text{BF}_3$ has $6\,e^-$ on $\text{B}$, and $\text{AlCl}_3$ has $6\,e^-$ on $\text{Al}$. Every molecule in the set has fewer than $8\,e^-$ around its central atom, so Statement II is true.
  4. Step 4 — Conclusion: Statement I is false and Statement II is true, confirming option (c).
Q21.stepsLatex:
1. Statement I: Tetrahedral species are NH+4 and [NiCl4]2− only (2 species, not 3). (SF4, SeF4 are see-saw;
XeF4, [PtCl4]2−, [Ni(CN)4]2− are square planar.) Statement I is false.
2. Statement II: NO2 (7 e− on N), BeH2 (4 e−), BF3 (6 e−), and AlCl3 (6 e−) all have fewer than 8 valence
electrons around the central atom (incomplete octet) =⇒ Statement II is true.
Q21.trapHtml: [PtCl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2−</sup> is 5d<sup>8</sup> square planar even with weak-field Cl<sup>−</sup>, whereas [NiCl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2−</sup> (3d<sup>8</sup>) is tetrahedral.
Q21.finalAnsHtml: (c) Statement I is false but Statement II is true

Q22.conceptHtml: Calculate SN = σ-bonds + lp on the central atom.
Q22.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Find the hybridization of $\text{S}$ in $\text{SO}_2$: Sulphur forms $2\,\sigma$ bonds with oxygen and retains $1$ lone pair ($\text{SN} = 2 + 1 = 3$), so its hybridization is $sp^2$.
  2. Step 2 — Find the hybridization of $\text{N}$ in $\text{NO}_2^-$: Nitrogen forms $2\,\sigma$ bonds with oxygen and retains $1$ lone pair ($\text{SN} = 2 + 1 = 3$), so its hybridization is $sp^2$.
  3. Step 3 — Find the hybridization of central $\text{N}$ in $\text{N}_3^-$: The azide ion ($[\text{N}=\text{N}=\text{N}]^-$) is linear; the central nitrogen forms $2\,\sigma$ bonds and has $0$ lone pairs ($\text{SN} = 2 + 0 = 2$), so its hybridization is $sp$.
  4. Step 4 — Conclusion: The hybridizations are $sp^2$, $sp^2$, and $sp$ respectively, confirming option (d).
Q22.stepsLatex:
• SO2: 2σ + 1 lp = 3 =⇒ sp2.
• NO−2 : 2σ + 1 lp = 3 =⇒ sp2.
• N−3 ([: N¨ = N = N¨ :]−): 2σ + 0 lp = 2 =⇒ sp (linear).
Q22.trapHtml: N<sup>−</sup><sub>3</sub> is isoelectronic with CO<sub>2</sub> (16 valence e<sup>−</sup>) and is sp linear.

Q23.format: Two-Statement Diagram MCQ | Dipole moment and b.p. of cyclobutene dihalides
Q23.conceptHtml: In cis-1,2-dihalocyclobutene, C − Cl has a larger bond dipole than C − Br; trans-isomer has zero/near-zero dipole moment and lower boiling point than polar cis-isomer.
Q23.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement I (cis-dichloro vs cis-dibromo polarity): Because chlorine is more electronegative than bromine, the $\text{C}-\text{Cl}$ bond dipole moment is greater than the $\text{C}-\text{Br}$ bond dipole moment. In the cis configuration, the two bond dipoles add constructively, making the cis-dichloro compound more polar than the cis-dibromo compound. Thus, Statement I is correct.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement II (trans vs cis polarity and boiling point): In the trans-dibromo isomer, the two equal $\text{C}-\text{Br}$ bond dipoles point in exactly opposite directions and cancel out ($\mu = 0$, non-polar), whereas the cis-dibromo isomer has a net dipole moment ($\mu > 0$, polar).
  3. Step 3 — Identify the false claim in Statement II: Because the cis isomer is polar, it has stronger dipole–dipole attractions and a higher boiling point than the trans isomer; however, Statement II wrongly claims that the trans isomer is more polar than the cis isomer. Thus, Statement II is incorrect.
  4. Step 4 — Conclusion: Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect, confirming option (d).
Q23.stepsLatex:
1. Statement (I): Cl is more electronegative than Br, so cis-dichloride has a higher net dipole moment than
cis-dibromide =⇒ Correct.
2. Statement (II): trans-dibromide has lower boiling point than cis-dibromide (true), but the trans-isomer is
less polar (bond dipoles cancel) than the cis-isomer =⇒ Incorrect.
Q23.trapHtml: Polar cis isomers have both higher dipole moment and higher boiling point than symmetric trans isomers.
Q23.finalAnsHtml: (d) Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect

Q24.subtopic: VSEPR — Bond Pair : Lone Pair Ratio
Q24.format: Match List-I with List-II | Match (bp : lp) ratios
Q24.conceptHtml: Count σ-bond pairs and lone pairs on the central atom.
Q24.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Find bond pair: lone pair ratios for (A) $\text{ICl}_2^-$ and (B) $\text{H}_2\text{O}$: In $\text{ICl}_2^-$, iodine ($7 + 1 = 8$ valence $e^-$) forms $2$ single bonds and has $3$ lone pairs $\Rightarrow 2 : 3$ (III). In $\text{H}_2\text{O}$, oxygen ($6$ valence $e^-$) forms $2$ single bonds and has $2$ lone pairs $\Rightarrow 2 : 2$ (IV).
  2. Step 2 — Find bond pair: lone pair ratios for (C) $\text{SO}_2$ and (D) $\text{XeF}_4$: In $\text{SO}_2$ ($\text{O}=\text{S}=\text{O}$), sulphur shares $4$ total bonding electron pairs ($2\,\sigma + 2\,\pi$) and retains $1$ lone pair $\Rightarrow 4 : 1$ (II). In $\text{XeF}_4$, xenon ($8$ valence $e^-$) forms $4$ single bonds and retains $2$ lone pairs $\Rightarrow 4 : 2$ (I).
  3. Step 3 — Combine all pairs: The match is A-III, B-IV, C-II, D-I.
  4. Step 4 — Conclusion: This matches option (d).
Q24.stepsLatex:
• (A) ICl2−: 2 bp : 3 lp → (III).
• (B) H2O: 2 bp : 2 lp → (IV).
• (C) SO2: 4 bond pairs (counting σ + π: 2σ + 2π = 4) : 1 lp → (II).
• (D) XeF4: 4 bp : 2 lp → (I).
Q24.trapHtml: In SO<sub>2</sub>, NTA counts total bond pairs (2 double bonds = 4 bp): 1 lp = 4: 1.

Q25.subtopic: VSEPR — Stability of ClF3 TBP Isomers
Q25.format: Two-Statement Diagram MCQ | Equatorial vs axial lone pairs in sp<sup>3</sup>d
Q25.conceptHtml: In trigonal bipyramidal (sp<sup>3</sup>d) geometry, lone pairs always occupy equatorial positions (120<sup>°</sup> apart) to minimize 90<sup>°</sup> lp–bp repulsions.
Q25.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement I (possible TBP arrangements for $\text{ClF}_3$): $\text{ClF}_3$ has $\text{SN} = \frac{1}{2}(7 + 3) = 5$ ($sp^3d$, trigonal bipyramidal electron geometry) with $3$ bond pairs and $2$ lone pairs. The three possible placements of the $2$ lone pairs—both equatorial (I), one axial and one equatorial (II), and both axial (III)—are all correctly drawn. Thus, Statement I is correct.
  2. Step 2 — Compare $90^\circ$ repulsions in Structures I, II, and III: In a TBP geometry, $90^\circ$ interactions dominate stability. Structure I (both lp equatorial) has zero $90^\circ$ lp–lp repulsions and $4$ $90^\circ$ lp–bp repulsions. Structure II has one $90^\circ$ lp–lp and $3$ $90^\circ$ lp–bp repulsions. Structure III (both lp axial) has six $90^\circ$ lp–bp repulsions ($3$ per axial lone pair).
  3. Step 3 — Evaluate Statement II: Structure I (equatorial lone pairs, T-shaped) has the minimum repulsion and is the most stable, NOT Structure III (axial lone pairs). Hence, Statement II is incorrect.
  4. Step 4 — Conclusion: Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect, confirming option (c).
Q25.stepsLatex:
1. Statement (I): Structures I (both lp equatorial), II (1 eq, 1 ax), and III (both lp axial) represent all three
possible arrangements =⇒ Correct.
2. Statement (II): Structure I (both lp equatorial, only four 90◦ lp–bp repulsions) is most stable, NOT Structure
III (six 90◦ lp–bp repulsions) =⇒ Incorrect.
Q25.trapHtml: Axial positions have three 90<sup>°</sup> neighbours, whereas equatorial positions have only two 90<sup>°</sup> neighbours.
Q25.finalAnsHtml: (c) Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect

Q26.subtopic: Resonance — Dipole Moment & Bond Length in
Q26.conceptHtml: Conjugation between C = C and C = O creates charge-separated resonance (C<sup>+</sup>H − CH = CH − O<sup>−</sup>), increasing µ and giving C<sub>1</sub> − C<sub>2</sub> partial double-bond character.
Q26.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement I (dipole moment comparison): In $\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}=\text{CH}-\text{CH}=\text{O}$ (crotonaldehyde), the $\text{C}=\text{C}$ and $\text{C}=\text{O}$ bonds are conjugated, allowing resonance: $\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}=\text{CH}-\text{CH}=\text{O} \leftrightarrow \text{CH}_3-\overset{+}{\text{C}}\text{H}-\text{CH}=\text{CH}-\text{O}^-$. This charge separation over a longer distance increases the dipole moment compared to saturated butanal ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CHO}$). Hence, Statement I is true.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement II ($\text{C}_1-\text{C}_2$ bond length): Because of the same resonance contributor ($\text{CH}_3-\overset{+}{\text{C}}\text{H}-\text{CH}=\text{CH}-\text{O}^-$), the $\text{C}_1-\text{C}_2$ bond in crotonaldehyde acquires partial double-bond character.
  3. Step 3 — Compare the $\text{C}_1-\text{C}_2$ bond lengths: Partial double-bond character makes the $\text{C}_1-\text{C}_2$ bond in crotonaldehyde shorter (not greater) than the pure $\text{C}_1-\text{C}_2$ single bond in butanal. Hence, Statement II is false.
  4. Step 4 — Conclusion: Statement I is true and Statement II is false, confirming option (b).
Q26.stepsLatex:
1. Statement I: Conjugation increases charge separation =⇒ µ(but-2-enal) > µ(butanal) =⇒ True.
2. Statement II: Because of resonance, C1 − C2 in but-2-enal has partial double-bond character, making it
shorter (not greater) than C1 − C2 in butanal =⇒ False.
Q26.trapHtml: Partial double-bond character from resonance always shortens the single bond between conjugated π-systems.
Q26.finalAnsHtml: (b) Statement I is true but Statement II is false

Q27.conceptHtml: Both O<sub>2</sub> and vapour-phase S<sub>2</sub> have 12 valence electrons (2 unpaired electrons in π<sub>2</sub><sup>∗</sup><sub>p</sub> / π<sub>3</sub><sup>∗</sup><sub>p</sub>) and are paramagnetic.
