Q27.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Apply Molecular Orbital Theory to $\text{O}_2$ (A) and $\text{S}_2$ (D): $\text{O}_2$ ($16\,e^-$) has two unpaired electrons in its degenerate $\pi^*_{2p_x}$ and $\pi^*_{2p_y}$ orbitals, making it paramagnetic. Sulphur lies directly below oxygen in group 16, so vapor-phase $\text{S}_2$ has an analogous valence MO configuration with two unpaired electrons in $\pi^*_{3p}$ orbitals, making $\text{S}_2$ paramagnetic too.
  2. Step 2 — Check $\text{N}_2$ (B), $\text{F}_2$ (C), and $\text{Cl}_2$ (E): $\text{N}_2$ ($14\,e^-$), $\text{F}_2$ ($18\,e^-$), and $\text{Cl}_2$ (valence-isoelectronic with $\text{F}_2$) have all electrons paired in their molecular orbitals, so all three are diamagnetic.
  3. Step 3 — Select the paramagnetic species: Only A ($\text{O}_2$) and D ($\text{S}_2$) exhibit paramagnetic behavior.
  4. Step 4 — Conclusion: A & D only are paramagnetic, confirming option (c).
Q27.stepsLatex:
• O2 (2 unpaired e− in π2∗ ) and S2 (2 unpaired e− in π3∗ ) are paramagnetic.
p p
• N2, F2, Cl2 have all electrons paired (diamagnetic).
Q27.trapHtml: S<sub>2</sub> is the Period 3 analogue of O<sub>2</sub> and is paramagnetic just like O<sub>2</sub>.

Q28.subtopic: Hydrogen Bonding — Cotton vs Nylon Drying
Q28.format: Two-Statement MCQ | Cellulose H-bonding with water
Q28.conceptHtml: Cellulose (cotton) has abundant −OH groups per glucose unit, forming extensive intermolecular H-bonds with water, whereas nylon has fewer polar amide groups.
Q28.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Compare functional groups in cotton vs. nylon: Cotton is made of cellulose, a polysaccharide rich in polar $-\text{OH}$ (hydroxyl) groups on every glucose unit. Nylon is a synthetic polyamide with far fewer H-bonding sites (amide linkages separated by long hydrophobic $-\text{CH}_2-$ chains).
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement I: Because cellulose forms extensive intermolecular hydrogen bonds with water molecules, wet cotton absorbs and retains much more water and takes comparatively longer to dry than nylon clothes. Thus, Statement I is true.
  3. Step 3 — Evaluate Statement II: Statement II claims intermolecular H-bonding with water is greater in nylon than in cotton, which is the exact opposite of the chemical reality. Thus, Statement II is false.
  4. Step 4 — Conclusion: Statement I is true and Statement II is false, confirming option (d).
Q28.stepsLatex:
1. Statement I: Wet cotton takes longer to dry than wet nylon =⇒ True.
2. Statement II: Intermolecular H-bonding with water is more in cotton (cellulose), not in nylon =⇒ False.
Q28.trapHtml: More −OH groups in cotton = stronger water retention = slower drying.
Q28.finalAnsHtml: (d) Statement I is true but Statement II is false

Q29.format: Match List-I with List-II | Match species to hybridization
Q29.conceptHtml: Use VSEPR for main-group compounds and CFT/VBT for coordination complexes.
Q29.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Determine hybridizations of A ($\text{PF}_5$) and B ($\text{SF}_6$): In $\text{PF}_5$, $\text{P}$ forms $5\,\sigma$ bonds with $0$ lone pairs ($\text{SN} = 5 \Rightarrow sp^3d$, II). In $\text{SF}_6$, $\text{S}$ forms $6\,\sigma$ bonds with $0$ lone pairs ($\text{SN} = 6 \Rightarrow sp^3d^2$, III).
  2. Step 2 — Determine hybridizations of C ($\text{Ni(CO)}_4$) and D ($[\text{PtCl}_4]^{2-}$): In $\text{Ni(CO)}_4$, $\text{Ni}^0$ ($3d^8 4s^2$) pairs all electrons into $3d^{10}$ under strong-field $\text{CO}$, leaving vacant $4s$ and $4p$ orbitals $\Rightarrow sp^3$ (IV). In $[\text{PtCl}_4]^{2-}$, $\text{Pt}^{2+}$ is a $5d^8$ ion (large CFSE), so it is low-spin square planar $\Rightarrow dsp^2$ (I).
  3. Step 3 — Combine the matches: A-II, B-III, C-IV, D-I.
  4. Step 4 — Conclusion: This corresponds to option (c).
Q29.stepsLatex:
• A. PF5 (5 bp + 0 lp) → II. sp3d.
• B. SF6 (6 bp + 0 lp) → III. sp3d2.
• C. Ni(CO)4 (Ni0 3d10 with strong-field CO) → IV. sp3 (tetrahedral).
• D. [PtCl4]2− (5d8 square planar) → I. dsp2.
Q29.trapHtml: Ni(CO)<sub>4</sub> is sp<sup>3</sup> tetrahedral (3d<sup>10</sup>), whereas [Ni(CN)<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2−</sup> and [PtCl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2−</sup> (d<sup>8</sup>) are dsp<sup>2</sup> square planar.

Q30.subtopic: VSEPR — sp3d, Unequal Bond Lengths & Lone Pair
Q30.conceptHtml: Among sp<sup>3</sup>d molecules, PF<sub>5</sub> has 0 lp, XeF<sub>2</sub> has equal axial bonds, while SF<sub>4</sub> has 1 equatorial lp and unequal axial vs equatorial S − F bonds.
Q30.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Test condition (a) ($sp^3d$ hybridization): $\text{XeF}_4$ has $\text{SN} = 6$ ($sp^3d^2$), so eliminate (a). $\text{XeF}_2$, $\text{PF}_5$, and $\text{SF}_4$ all have $\text{SN} = 5$ ($sp^3d$).
  2. Step 2 — Test condition (b) (different bond lengths) and condition (c) (lone pair on central atom): In $\text{XeF}_2$ (linear), both $\text{Xe}-\text{F}$ axial bonds are equal in length (fails b). In $\text{PF}_5$ (trigonal bipyramidal), axial bonds are longer than equatorial bonds, but $\text{P}$ has $0$ lone pairs (fails c).
  3. Step 3 — Verify $\text{SF}_4$: Sulphur in $\text{SF}_4$ is $sp^3d$ hybridized (satisfies a), has a see-saw shape with longer axial $\text{S}-\text{F}$ bonds than equatorial $\text{S}-\text{F}$ bonds (satisfies b), and carries $1$ equatorial lone pair (satisfies c).
  4. Step 4 — Conclusion: Only $\text{SF}_4$ satisfies all three conditions, confirming option (d).
Q30.stepsLatex:
• XeF4: sp3d2. XeF2: sp3d, 3 lp, equal Xe − F bonds.
• PF5: sp3d, 0 lp. SF4: sp3d, 1 lp, axial S − F (164 pm) > equatorial S − F (154 pm).
Q30.trapHtml: PF<sub>5</sub> also has unequal axial/equatorial bond lengths, but it has no lone pair on P.

Q31.subtopic: Periodic Identification + VSEPR Shape of AX4Y
Q31.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Identify A = Xe, X = F, Y = O
Q31.conceptHtml: Rarest monoatomic non-radioactive p-block element in Group 18 is Xe; highest EN elements are F (X) and O (Y ).
Q31.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify elements A, X, and Y: The rarest non-radioactive monoatomic $p$-block element (noble gas, excluding radioactive $\text{Rn}$) is xenon ($\text{Xe}$), which also has the lowest ionization enthalpy among the three. The elements with the first and second highest electronegativity are fluorine ($\text{X} = \text{F}$) and oxygen ($\text{Y} = \text{O}$).
  2. Step 2 — Write the molecular formula: Substituting $\text{A}=\text{Xe}$, $\text{X}=\text{F}$, and $\text{Y}=\text{O}$ into $\text{AX}_4\text{Y}$ gives $\text{XeF}_4\text{O}$, commonly written as $\text{XeOF}_4$.
  3. Step 3 — Determine the shape of $\text{XeOF}_4$: Xenon ($8$ valence $e^-$) uses $2\,e^-$ for one $\text{Xe}=\text{O}$ double bond and $4\,e^-$ for four $\text{Xe}-\text{F}$ single bonds, leaving $1$ lone pair. With $5\,\sigma$ bonds $+ 1$ lone pair ($\text{SN} = 6$, $sp^3d^2$), the molecular shape is square pyramidal.
  4. Step 4 — Conclusion: The shape of $\text{XeOF}_4$ is square pyramidal, confirming option (b).
Q31.stepsLatex:
1. A = Xe, X = F, Y = O =⇒ Molecule is XeOF4.
2. XeOF4 has 5 σ-bonds + 1 lp (SN = 6, sp3d2) =⇒ Square pyramidal.
Q31.trapHtml: Second highest electronegativity among all elements is Oxygen (F > O > N ≈ Cl).

Q32.subtopic: Dipole Moment + Max Lone Pairs Hybridization
Q32.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Nonzero µ and highest lp on central atom
Q32.conceptHtml: Filter for µ ̸= 0 first, then pick the species with the maximum central-atom lone pairs.
Q32.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Filter for molecules with non-zero dipole moment ($\mu \neq 0$): Check each molecule: $\text{XeF}_2$ is linear and symmetric, so $\mu = 0$ (eliminate it despite having $3$ lone pairs). The remaining five molecules—$\text{SO}_2$ (bent), $\text{NF}_3$ (pyramidal), $\text{NH}_3$ (pyramidal), $\text{ClF}_3$ (T-shaped), and $\text{SF}_4$ (see-saw)—all have $\mu \neq 0$.
  2. Step 2 — Count lone pairs on the central atom of the polar molecules: $\text{SO}_2$ ($1$ lp), $\text{NF}_3$ ($1$ lp), $\text{NH}_3$ ($1$ lp), $\text{SF}_4$ ($1$ lp), and $\text{ClF}_3$ ($2$ lp).
  3. Step 3 — Find the hybridization of the selected molecule: $\text{ClF}_3$ has the highest number of lone pairs ($2$) among the polar molecules. Its steric number is $\text{SN} = \frac{1}{2}(7 + 3) = 5$, which corresponds to $sp^3d$ hybridization.
  4. Step 4 — Conclusion: The hybridization of $\text{ClF}_3$ is $sp^3d$, confirming option (d).
Q32.stepsLatex:
• XeF2 has 3 lp, but µ = 0 (linear).
• ClF3 has 2 lp and µ ≠ 0 (T-shaped, sp3d).
• SO2, NF3, NH3, SF4 all have 1 lp and µ ≠ 0.
• Hence the required molecule is ClF3 with hybridization sp3d.
Q32.trapHtml: Do not pick XeF<sub>2</sub> (3 lp) because its symmetric linear geometry gives µ = 0.

Q33.format: Multi-Ion MCQ | Match equatorial lp in ClF<sub>3</sub> to d<sup>n</sup> unpaired e<sup>−</sup>
Q33.conceptHtml: In ClF<sub>3</sub> (sp<sup>3</sup>d, T-shaped), both lone pairs sit in equatorial positions, so n = 2.
Q33.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Find the value of $n$ from $\text{ClF}_3$: $\text{ClF}_3$ is $sp^3d$ hybridized ($3\text{ bp} + 2\text{ lp}$). To minimize $90^\circ$ repulsions, both lone pairs occupy equatorial positions in its most stable T-shaped structure. Thus, $n = 2$.
  2. Step 2 — Determine the number of unpaired electrons in each transition metal ion: Write the $3d$ configurations: $\text{V}^{3+}$ ($[\text{Ar}]\,3d^2 \Rightarrow 2$ unpaired), $\text{Ti}^{3+}$ ($[\text{Ar}]\,3d^1 \Rightarrow 1$ unpaired), $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ ($[\text{Ar}]\,3d^9 \Rightarrow 1$ unpaired), $\text{Ni}^{2+}$ ($[\text{Ar}]\,3d^8 \Rightarrow 2$ unpaired), and $\text{Ti}^{2+}$ ($[\text{Ar}]\,3d^2 \Rightarrow 2$ unpaired).
  3. Step 3 — Pick the ions with exactly $n = 2$ unpaired electrons: $\text{V}^{3+}$ (A), $\text{Ni}^{2+}$ (D), and $\text{Ti}^{2+}$ (E) each have $2$ unpaired electrons.
  4. Step 4 — Conclusion: Ions A, D, and E only match $n = 2$, confirming option (b).
Q33.stepsLatex:
1. n = 2 equatorial lone pairs in ClF3.
2. Unpaired e− in 3d ions: V3+ (3d2 → 2), Ti3+ (3d1 → 1), Cu2+ (3d9 → 1), Ni2+ (3d8 → 2), Ti2+ (3d2 → 2).
3. Ions with 2 unpaired electrons: A (V3+), D (Ni2+), E (Ti2+).
Q33.trapHtml: In 3d ions, remove 4s electrons first before removing 3d electrons.

Q34.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Identify molecules with 5 bp + 1 lp
Q34.conceptHtml: Square pyramidal shape corresponds to SN = 6 (5 bp + 1 lp, sp<sup>3</sup>d<sup>2</sup>).
Q34.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the requirement for square pyramidal geometry: A central atom must have $\text{SN} = 6$ ($sp^3d^2$, octahedral electron geometry) with $5$ bond pairs and $1$ lone pair.
  2. Step 2 — Check $\text{PCl}_5$ and $\text{SbF}_5$: Both $\text{P}$ and $\text{Sb}$ belong to group 15 ($5$ valence $e^-$), forming $5\,\sigma$ bonds with $0$ lone pairs ($\text{SN} = 5$, $sp^3d$). Both have trigonal bipyramidal geometry, eliminating options (a), (b), and (d).
  3. Step 3 — Verify $\text{BrF}_5$ and $\text{XeOF}_4$: In $\text{BrF}_5$, $\text{Br}$ ($7$ valence $e^-$) has $5\text{ bp} + 1\text{ lp}$ ($\text{SN} = 6$, square pyramidal). In $\text{XeOF}_4$, $\text{Xe}$ ($8$ valence $e^-$) forms $5\,\sigma$ bonds ($1$ to $\text{O}$, $4$ to $\text{F}$) and has $1\text{ lp}$ ($\text{SN} = 6$, square pyramidal).
  4. Step 4 — Conclusion: Both $\text{BrF}_5$ and $\text{XeOF}_4$ are square pyramidal, confirming option (c).
Q34.stepsLatex:
• BrF5: 5 bp + 1 lp =⇒ Square pyramidal.
• XeOF4: 5 σ-bp + 1 lp =⇒ Square pyramidal.
• PCl5 and SbF5 (5 bp + 0 lp) are trigonal bipyramidal.
Q34.trapHtml: SbF<sub>5</sub> has 5 valence electrons on Sb and 0 lone pairs, so it is TBP, not square pyramidal.

Q35.subtopic: Hybridization Counting in Conjugated Organic Molecule
Q35.format: Diagram MCQ | Count sp and sp<sup>2</sup> carbons
Q35.conceptHtml: Carbon with 1π-bond (C = C or C = O) is sp<sup>2</sup>; carbon with 2π-bonds (C ≡ C or C ≡ N) is sp.
Q35.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Read the skeletal structure from left to right: The molecule shown is $\text{CH}_3-\text{C}(=\text{O})-\text{CH}=\text{CH}-\text{CH}_2-\text{C}\equiv\text{C}-\text{CH}=\text{CH}-\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$.
  2. Step 2 — Count the $sp$ hybridized carbons (triple-bonded carbons): There are $2$ carbons in the internal alkyne group ($-\text{C}\equiv\text{C}-$) and $1$ carbon in the terminal nitrile group ($-\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$), giving a total of $2 + 1 = 3$ $sp$ hybridized carbon atoms.
  3. Step 3 — Count the $sp^2$ hybridized carbons (double-bonded carbons): There is $1$ carbonyl carbon ($\text{C}=\text{O}$), $2$ carbons in the first alkene ($-\text{CH}=\text{CH}-$), and $2$ carbons in the second alkene ($-\text{CH}=\text{CH}-$), giving a total of $1 + 2 + 2 = 5$ $sp^2$ hybridized carbon atoms. (The $-\text{CH}_3$ and $-\text{CH}_2-$ carbons are $sp^3$.)
  4. Step 4 — Conclusion: The number of $sp$ and $sp^2$ hybridized carbons is $3$ and $5$ respectively, confirming option (a).
Q35.stepsLatex:
1. Tracing from left to right: CH3 (sp3), C = O (sp2), CH = CH (2 sp2), CH2 (sp3), C ≡ C (2 sp), CH = CH
(2 sp2), C ≡ N (1 sp).
2. Total sp carbons = 2 + 1 = 3; total sp2 carbons = 1 + 2 + 2 = 5.
Q35.trapHtml: Count the carbonyl carbon (C = O) as sp<sup>2</sup> and the nitrile carbon (−C ≡ N) as sp.

Q36.format: Two-Statement MCQ | Equal O − O bond lengths in O<sub>3</sub>
Q36.conceptHtml: Equal O − O bond lengths (128 pm, BO = 1.5) in O<sub>3</sub> arise from resonance, not lone-pair repulsion.
Q36.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement I (ozone bond length): Due to resonance between $\text{O}=\text{O}^+-\text{O}^-$ and $^-\text{O}-\text{O}^+=\text{O}$, both oxygen–oxygen bonds in $\text{O}_3$ are identical with a bond order of $1.5$ and an experimental bond length of $128\,\text{pm}$. This is greater than an $\text{O}=\text{O}$ double bond ($121\,\text{pm}$) and less than an $\text{O}-\text{O}$ single bond ($148\,\text{pm}$). Thus, Statement I is true.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement II: Statement II is wrong on two counts: first, the equal intermediate bond length is caused by resonance (delocalization of $\pi$ electrons), not lone pair–lone pair repulsion; second, it reverses the bond-length comparison ("smaller than a double bond but more than a single bond"). Thus, Statement II is false.
  3. Step 3 — Conclusion: Statement I is true and Statement II is false, confirming option (c).
Q36.stepsLatex:
1. Statement I: True (O = O = 121 pm < O3 = 128 pm < O − O = 148 pm).
2. Statement II: False (attributed to lp–lp repulsion instead of resonance, and also reverses the inequality).
Q36.trapHtml: Read Statement II’s wording carefully: it fails both on the reason (resonance) and the inequality.
Q36.finalAnsHtml: (c) Statement I is true but Statement II is false

Q37.subtopic: LCAO Symmetry Rules for Molecular Orbitals
Q37.format: Multi-Option MCQ | Allowed orbital combinations along z-axis
Q37.conceptHtml: Atomic orbitals combine only if they have comparable energy and the same symmetry about the internuclear (z) axis.
Q37.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the symmetry condition for LCAO: Along the $z$-internuclear axis, two atomic orbitals can combine to form a molecular orbital only if they have the same symmetry about the $z$-axis (giving a non-zero overlap integral).
  2. Step 2 — Check symmetry mismatches (A, B, C, and E): In A ($2p_z + 2p_x$) and B ($2s + 2p_x$), $2s$ and $2p_z$ are $\sigma$-symmetric while $2p_x$ is $\pi$-symmetric, so positive and negative overlaps cancel to zero. In C ($3d_{xy} + 3d_{x^2-y^2}$), the lobes are rotated by $45^\circ$ relative to each other (zero net overlap). In E ($2p_z + 3d_{x^2-y^2}$), $2p_z$ is $\sigma$-symmetric while $3d_{x^2-y^2}$ is $\delta$-symmetric (zero net overlap).
  3. Step 3 — Verify D ($2s$ and $2p_z$): Both $2s$ and $2p_z$ are cylindrically symmetric ($\sigma$-symmetric) about the $z$-axis, so they overlap effectively to form $\sigma$ bonding and $\sigma^*$ antibonding molecular orbitals (the basis of $s\text{–}p$ mixing).
  4. Step 4 — Conclusion: Only combination D leads to MO formation, confirming option (a).
Q37.stepsLatex:
• D. 2s and 2pz: both have σ-symmetry (cylindrically symmetric about z-axis) =⇒ Forms MO.
• A (2pz, 2px), B (2s, 2px), C (3dxy, 3dx2−y2), E (2pz, 3dx2−y2) have mismatched symmetries =⇒ Zero overlap.
Q37.trapHtml: Along the z-axis, s and p<sub>z</sub> have σ symmetry, while p<sub>x</sub> and p<sub>y</sub> have π symmetry.

Q38.subtopic: VSEPR, Bond Angles, Dipole Moment & Acid-Base of
Q38.format: Multi-Statement MCQ | Evaluate A–E for H<sub>2</sub>O, NH<sub>3</sub>, CH<sub>4</sub>
Q38.conceptHtml: All three are sp<sup>3</sup> hybridized; bond angle and dipole moment trends follow lone-pair count and polarity.
Q38.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Verify statements A and B (hybridization and bond angles): $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ ($2\text{ bp}+2\text{ lp}$), $\text{NH}_3$ ($3\text{ bp}+1\text{ lp}$), and $\text{CH}_4$ ($4\text{ bp}+0\text{ lp}$) all have $\text{SN} = 4$ ($sp^3$, A is true). Because $\text{lp–lp} > \text{lp–bp} > \text{bp–bp}$ repulsion, their bond angles are $104.5^\circ$, $\approx 107^\circ\text{–}107.5^\circ$, and $109.5^\circ$ respectively (B is true).
  2. Step 2 — Verify statement C (dipole moment): $\text{CH}_4$ is symmetric ($\mu = 0$), $\text{NH}_3$ has $\mu \approx 1.47\,\text{D}$, and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ has $\mu \approx 1.85\,\text{D}$, so $\text{CH}_4 < \text{NH}_3 < \text{H}_2\text{O}$ (C is true).
  3. Step 3 — Disprove statements D and E: $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ and $\text{NH}_3$ have lone pairs and act as Lewis bases, whereas $\text{CH}_4$ has no lone pair (D is false). In aqueous ammonia ($\text{NH}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{NH}_4^+ + \text{OH}^-$), $\text{NH}_3$ accepts a proton (Bronsted base) and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ donates a proton (Bronsted acid), so E is false.
  4. Step 4 — Conclusion: Statements A, B, and C only are true, confirming option (c).
Q38.stepsLatex:
• A. True: Central atoms in H2O, NH3, CH4 are sp3.
• B. True: Bond angles are 104.5◦ (H2O), 107.5◦ (NH3), 109.5◦ (CH4).
• C. True: µ: CH4 (0) < NH3 (1.47 D) < H2O (1.85 D).
• D. False: H2O and NH3 are Lewis bases (lone pairs); CH4 is neither.
• E. False: NH3 accepts H+ (Bronsted base) and H2O donates H+ (Bronsted acid).
Q38.trapHtml: Statement E swaps "acid" and "base" for NH<sub>3</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>O!

Q39.format: Match List-I with List-II | Match octet categories
Q39.conceptHtml: Classify by central-atom valence electron count: 8 (obeys), < 8 even (incomplete), odd (odd-electron), > 8 (expanded).
Q39.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Match (A) and (B): $\text{CCl}_4$ and $\text{CO}_2$ have exactly $8$ valence electrons around carbon, so they obey the octet rule $\Rightarrow$ A-IV. $\text{BCl}_3$ and $\text{AlCl}_3$ have only $6$ electrons around $\text{B}$ and $\text{Al}$ (incomplete octet) $\Rightarrow$ B-II.
  2. Step 2 — Match (C) and (D): $\text{NO}$ ($11$ valence $e^-$) and $\text{NO}_2$ ($17$ valence $e^-$) are odd-electron molecules with an incomplete octet on nitrogen $\Rightarrow$ C-I. $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ ($12\,e^-$ on $\text{S}$) and $\text{PCl}_5$ ($10\,e^-$ on $\text{P}$) have expanded octets $\Rightarrow$ D-III.
  3. Step 3 — Assemble the matching: A-IV, B-II, C-I, D-III.
  4. Step 4 — Conclusion: This matches option (c).
Q39.stepsLatex:
• (A) Obeying octet: CCl4, CO2 → (IV).
• (B) Incomplete octet: BCl3, AlCl3 (6e−) → (II).
• (C) Odd electron: NO, NO2 → (I).
• (D) Expanded octet: H2SO4, PCl5 (12e−, 10e−) → (III).
Q39.trapHtml: Directly from NCERT Class 11 Chemical Bonding Section 4.1.5 (Limitations of Octet Rule).

Q40.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Increasing µ of HBr, H<sub>2</sub>S, NF<sub>3</sub>, CHCl<sub>3</sub>
Q40.conceptHtml: Compare NCERT/experimental dipole moments: NF<sub>3</sub> < HBr < H<sub>2</sub>S < CHCl<sub>3</sub>.
Q40.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the lowest dipole moment: In $\text{NF}_3$, the lone-pair dipole opposes the resultant of the three $\text{N}-\text{F}$ bond dipoles, giving a very small net dipole moment ($\mu \approx 0.23\,\text{D}$).
  2. Step 2 — Compare $\text{HBr}$, $\text{H}_2\text{S}$, and $\text{CHCl}_3$: Their standard experimental dipole moments (from NCERT) are: $\text{HBr} \approx 0.79\,\text{D}$, $\text{H}_2\text{S} \approx 0.97\,\text{D}$ (bent geometry with two $\text{H}-\text{S}$ dipoles and two lone pairs reinforcing), and $\text{CHCl}_3 \approx 1.04\,\text{D}$ (three $\text{C}-\text{Cl}$ dipoles and one $\text{C}-\text{H}$ dipole pointing in the same net direction).
  3. Step 3 — Arrange in increasing order: $\text{NF}_3\,(0.23\,\text{D}) < \text{HBr}\,(0.79\,\text{D}) < \text{H}_2\text{S}\,(0.97\,\text{D}) < \text{CHCl}_3\,(1.04\,\text{D})$.
  4. Step 4 — Conclusion: The increasing order is $\text{NF}_3 < \text{HBr} < \text{H}_2\text{S} < \text{CHCl}_3$, confirming option (c).
Q40.stepsLatex: • Experimental dipole moments: NF<sub>3</sub> (0.23 D) < HBr (0.82 D) < H<sub>2</sub>S (0.95 D) < CHCl<sub>3</sub> (1.04 D).
Q40.trapHtml: NF<sub>3</sub> (0.23 D) has the smallest µ due to opposing lone-pair and N − F dipoles.

Q41.subtopic: Bond Angle Comparison: BF3, PF3, ClF3
Q41.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Increasing order of bond angles
Q41.conceptHtml: More lone pairs on the central atom compress the bond angle.
Q41.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Find the hybridization and bond angle of $\text{BF}_3$: $\text{BF}_3$ has $3\text{ bp} + 0\text{ lp}$ ($sp^2$, trigonal planar), giving an exact bond angle of $120^\circ$.
  2. Step 2 — Find the hybridization and bond angle of $\text{PF}_3$: $\text{PF}_3$ has $3\text{ bp} + 1\text{ lp}$ ($sp^3$, trigonal pyramidal). Lone-pair repulsion and electronegative $\text{F}$ atoms compress the angle well below $109.5^\circ$ to $\approx 97.8^\circ$.
  3. Step 3 — Find the hybridization and bond angle of $\text{ClF}_3$: $\text{ClF}_3$ has $3\text{ bp} + 2\text{ lp}$ ($sp^3d$, T-shaped). The two equatorial lone pairs push the axial $\text{Cl}-\text{F}$ bonds slightly inward from $90^\circ$ to $\approx 87.5^\circ$.
  4. Step 4 — Conclusion: Ordering from smallest to largest gives $\text{ClF}_3\,(87.5^\circ) < \text{PF}_3\,(97.8^\circ) < \text{BF}_3\,(120^\circ)$, confirming option (c).
Q41.stepsLatex:
• ClF3 (sp3d, T-shaped, 2 lp): ∠F − Cl − F ≈ 87.5◦.
• PF3 (sp3, pyramidal, 1 lp): ∠F − P − F ≈ 97.8◦.
• BF3 (sp2, trigonal planar, 0 lp): ∠F − B − F = 120◦.
Q41.trapHtml: Increasing order: ClF<sub>3</sub> < PF<sub>3</sub> < BF<sub>3</sub>.

Q42.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Identify pair where both central atoms are sp<sup>2</sup>
Q42.conceptHtml: Check SN = 3 for both species in the pair.
Q42.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Check the hybridization of $\text{BF}_3$ and $\text{NO}_2^-$: In $\text{BF}_3$, boron has $3\text{ bp} + 0\text{ lp}$ ($\text{SN} = 3 \Rightarrow sp^2$). In $\text{NO}_2^-$, nitrogen forms $2\,\sigma$ bonds and has $1$ lone pair ($\text{SN} = 3 \Rightarrow sp^2$).
  2. Step 2 — Eliminate the other pairs: Both $\text{NH}_2^-$ ($2\text{ bp} + 2\text{ lp}$, $\text{SN} = 4$) and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ ($2\text{ bp} + 2\text{ lp}$, $\text{SN} = 4$) are $sp^3$ hybridized, which rules out options (b), (c), and (d).
  3. Step 3 — Conclusion: Both central atoms in $\text{BF}_3$ and $\text{NO}_2^-$ exhibit $sp^2$ hybridization, confirming option (a).
Q42.stepsLatex:
• BF3: 3 bp + 0 lp = 3 =⇒ sp2.
• NO−2 : 2σ + 1 lp = 3 =⇒ sp2.
• (NH−2 and H2O are sp3.)
Q42.trapHtml: NO<sup>−</sup><sub>2</sub> has 1 lone pair (sp<sup>2</sup>), whereas NO<sup>+</sup><sub>2</sub> has 0 lone pairs (sp).

Q43.conceptHtml: A carbocation (CH<sup>+</sup><sub>3</sub> ) has 3 bp + 0 lp (SN = 3, sp<sup>2</sup>).
Q43.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Count valence electrons and electron pairs on the positively charged carbon: A carbocation ($\text{R}_3\text{C}^+$) has $3$ valence electrons on carbon after losing one electron, forming $3\,\sigma$ bonds with $0$ lone pairs and leaving one empty unhybridized $p$-orbital.
  2. Step 2 — Determine hybridization and geometry: With $\text{SN} = 3 + 0 = 3$, the positively charged carbon is $sp^2$ hybridized, placing the three substituents at $120^\circ$ in a single plane.
  3. Step 3 — Conclusion: The shape of a carbocation is trigonal planar, confirming option (d).
Q43.stepsLatex: sp2 hybridization with 0 lone pairs gives a trigonal planar shape (120◦ bond angles).
Q43.trapHtml: Carbanions (R<sub>3</sub>C<sup>−</sup>) are pyramidal (sp<sup>3</sup>), while carbocations (R<sub>3</sub>C<sup>+</sup>) are trigonal planar (sp<sup>2</sup>).

Q44.subtopic: MOT — Wave Function of Antibonding σ∗ MO
Q44.format: Single-Choice MCQ | LCAO expression for σ<sup>∗</sup>
Q44.conceptHtml: Constructive interference (ψ<sub>A</sub> +ψ<sub>B</sub>) gives bonding σ; destructive interference (ψ<sub>A</sub> −ψ<sub>B</sub>) gives antibonding σ<sup>∗</sup>.
Q44.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall LCAO principle: In Molecular Orbital Theory (MOT), atomic orbitals combine linearly (LCAO) in two ways: constructive interference (addition) and destructive interference (subtraction) of their wave functions $\psi_A$ and $\psi_B$.
  2. Step 2 — Distinguish bonding vs. antibonding MOs: Adding the wave functions ($\sigma = \psi_A + \psi_B$) increases electron density between the nuclei to form a bonding molecular orbital ($\sigma$). Subtracting them ($\sigma^* = \psi_A - \psi_B$) creates a nodal plane between the nuclei to form an antibonding molecular orbital ($\sigma^*$).
  3. Step 3 — Match with options: The expression $\psi_A - \psi_B$ directly represents the $\sigma^*$ antibonding molecular orbital, which corresponds to Option (b).
Q44.stepsLatex: By LCAO, ψ<sub>σ∗</sub> = ψ<sub>A</sub> − ψ<sub>B</sub>.
Q44.trapHtml: In-phase addition is σ; out-of-phase subtraction is σ<sup>∗</sup>.

Q45.format: Match List-I with List-II | Shapes of NH<sub>3</sub>, BrF<sub>5</sub>, PCl<sub>5</sub>, CH<sub>4</sub>
Q45.conceptHtml: Determine (bp, lp) for each molecule.
Q45.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Apply VSEPR theory to each molecule: Count bond pairs ($\text{bp}$) and lone pairs ($\text{lp}$) around each central atom using steric number $\text{SN} = \text{bp} + \text{lp}$.
  2. Step 2 — Determine individual shapes: A. $\text{NH}_3$ has $3\text{ bp} + 1\text{ lp}$ ($sp^3$) $\rightarrow$ Trigonal pyramidal (III). B. $\text{BrF}_5$ has $5\text{ bp} + 1\text{ lp}$ ($sp^3d^2$) $\rightarrow$ Square pyramid (I). C. $\text{PCl}_5$ has $5\text{ bp} + 0\text{ lp}$ ($sp^3d$) $\rightarrow$ Trigonal bipyramidal (IV). D. $\text{CH}_4$ has $4\text{ bp} + 0\text{ lp}$ ($sp^3$) $\rightarrow$ Tetrahedral (II).
  3. Step 3 — Combine the matches: The matching sequence is A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II, confirming Option (b).
Q45.stepsLatex:
• A. NH3 (3 + 1) → III. Trigonal pyramidal.
• B. BrF5 (5 + 1) → I. Square pyramid.
• C. PCl5 (5 + 0) → IV. Trigonal bipyramidal.
• D. CH4 (4 + 0) → II. Tetrahedral.
Q45.trapHtml: Note the distinction between trigonal pyramidal (NH<sub>3</sub>) and trigonal bipyramidal (PCl<sub>5</sub>).

Q46.format: Two-Statement MCQ | sp<sup>3</sup>d vs sp<sup>3</sup>d<sup>2</sup> vs d<sup>2</sup>sp<sup>3</sup>
Q46.conceptHtml: BrF<sub>5</sub> has 5 bp + 1 lp = 6 (sp<sup>3</sup>d<sup>2</sup>), while [Co(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup> is a low-spin inner-orbital complex (d<sup>2</sup>sp<sup>3</sup>, NOT sp<sup>3</sup>d<sup>2</sup>).
Q46.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement I: In $\text{PF}_5$, phosphorus has $5\text{ bp} + 0\text{ lp}$ ($\text{SN} = 5$), giving $sp^3d$ hybridisation. In $\text{BrF}_5$, bromine has $5\text{ bp} + 1\text{ lp}$ ($\text{SN} = 6$), giving $sp^3d^2$ hybridisation (not $sp^3d$). Hence, Statement I is false.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement II: $\text{SF}_6$ has $6\text{ bp} + 0\text{ lp}$, so sulfur is $sp^3d^2$ hybridised. However, in $[\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_6]^{3+}$, $\text{Co}^{3+}$ ($3d^6$) pairs its $3d$ electrons under the strong-field ligand $\text{NH}_3$, forming an inner-orbital complex with $d^2sp^3$ hybridisation (not $sp^3d^2$). Hence, Statement II is also false.
  3. Step 3 — Conclude the answer: Since both Statement I and Statement II are false, the correct choice is Option (a).
Q46.stepsLatex:
1. Statement I: PF5 is sp3d, but BrF5 is sp3d2 (5 + 1 = 6) =⇒ False.
2. Statement II: SF6 is sp3d2, but [Co(NH3)6]3+ has strong-field NH3 ligands pairing 3d6 electrons to use inner
3d orbitals (d2sp3) =⇒ False.
Q46.trapHtml: Distinguish inner-orbital d<sup>2</sup>sp<sup>3</sup> ([Co(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup>) from outer-orbital sp<sup>3</sup>d<sup>2</sup> (SF<sub>6</sub>).
Q46.finalAnsHtml: (a) Both Statement I and Statement II are false

Q47.subtopic: VSEPR — Shape Matching (SF4, BrF3, BrO−, NH+)
Q47.format: Match List-I with List-II | Identify shapes
Q47.conceptHtml: Compute SN and lone pairs for each ion/molecule.
Q47.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Find steric number and lone pairs: Use $\text{SN} = \frac{1}{2}(V + M - C + A)$ to identify hybridisation and lone pairs on each central atom.
  2. Step 2 — Assign shape to each species: A. $\text{SF}_4$: $4\text{ bp} + 1\text{ lp}$ ($sp^3d$) $\rightarrow$ See-saw (III). B. $\text{BrF}_3$: $3\text{ bp} + 2\text{ lp}$ ($sp^3d$) $\rightarrow$ Bent T-shape (IV). C. $\text{BrO}_3^-$: $3\text{ bp} + 1\text{ lp}$ ($sp^3$) $\rightarrow$ Pyramidal (II). D. $\text{NH}_4^+$: $4\text{ bp} + 0\text{ lp}$ ($sp^3$) $\rightarrow$ Tetrahedral (I).
  3. Step 3 — Verify the final match: Matching A-III, B-IV, C-II, D-I gives Option (b).
Q47.stepsLatex:
• A. SF4 (4 + 1) → III. See saw.
• B. BrF3 (3 + 2) → IV. Bent T-Shape.
• C. BrO−3 (3σ + 1 lp) → II. Pyramidal.
• D. NH+4 (4 + 0) → I. Tetrahedral.
Q47.trapHtml: BrO<sup>−</sup><sub>3</sub> has 1 lone pair on Br (<sup>7+</sup><sub>2</sub><sup>0+1</sup> = 4 domains), making it pyramidal.

Q48.format: Match List-I with List-II | SO<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>, NO, NO<sup>−</sup><sub>2</sub> , I<sup>−</sup><sub>3</sub>
Q48.conceptHtml: Combine VSEPR shape with odd/even electron magnetic behaviour.
Q48.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Determine shapes of $ ext{SO}_2 ext{Cl}_2$ and $ ext{I}_3^-$: In $\text{SO}_2\text{Cl}_2$, sulfur forms $4\,\sigma$ bonds ($2\,\text{S=O}$ and $2\,\text{S-Cl}$) with $0\text{ lp}$ ($sp^3$) $\rightarrow$ Tetrahedral (III). In $\text{I}_3^-$, the central iodine has $2\text{ bp} + 3\text{ lp}$ ($sp^3d$), with lone pairs in equatorial positions $\rightarrow$ Linear (IV).
  2. Step 2 — Determine magnetic nature of $ ext{NO}$ and $ ext{NO}_2^-$: $\text{NO}$ has $7 + 8 = 15$ electrons (an odd electron in $\pi^*2p$) $\rightarrow$ Paramagnetic (I). $\text{NO}_2^-$ has $7 + 16 + 1 = 24$ electrons, all paired $\rightarrow$ Diamagnetic (II).
  3. Step 3 — Combine the matches: The correct pairing is A-III, B-I, C-II, D-IV, which matches Option (b).
Q48.stepsLatex:
• A. SO2Cl2 (4σ + 0 lp, sp3) → III. Tetrahedral.
• B. NO (15e−, 1 unpaired e−) → I. Paramagnetic.
• C. NO−2 (24e−, all paired) → II. Diamagnetic.
• D. I−3 (2 bp + 3 lp, sp3d) → IV. Linear.
Q48.trapHtml: NO is paramagnetic (15e<sup>−</sup>), while NO<sup>−</sup><sub>2</sub> (24e<sup>−</sup>) is diamagnetic.

Q49.format: Match List-I with List-II | Standard hybridization geometries
Q49.conceptHtml: Match each hybridization to its ideal parent geometry.
Q49.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Relate hybridisation to ideal spatial orientation: Each hybridisation corresponds to a characteristic electron-domain geometry that minimizes repulsion.
  2. Step 2 — Match each hybridisation: A. $sp^3$ (4 domains) $\rightarrow$ Tetrahedral (III). B. $dsp^2$ (4 coplanar domains) $\rightarrow$ Square planar (IV). C. $sp^3d$ (5 domains) $\rightarrow$ Trigonal bipyramidal (I). D. $sp^3d^2$ (6 domains) $\rightarrow$ Octahedral (II).
  3. Step 3 — Verify the correct option: The sequence A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II corresponds to Option (b).
Q49.stepsLatex:
• A. sp3 → III. Tetrahedral; B. dsp2 → IV. Square planar;
• C. sp3d → I. Trigonal bipyramidal; D. sp3d2 → II. Octahedral.
Q49.trapHtml: dsp<sup>2</sup> (d<sub>x2−y2</sub> + s + p<sub>x</sub> + p<sub>y</sub>) is always square planar.

Q50.format: Match List-I with List-II | ICl, ICl<sub>3</sub>, ClF<sub>5</sub>, IF<sub>7</sub>
Q50.conceptHtml: All interhalogens follow VSEPR with 7 valence electrons on the central halogen.
Q50.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify interhalogen types and lone pairs: For interhalogens $\text{XX}'_n$, the central halogen has 7 valence electrons: $\text{lp} = \frac{7 - n}{2}$.
  2. Step 2 — Assign molecular shapes: A. $\text{ICl}$ is diatomic $\rightarrow$ Linear (IV). B. $\text{ICl}_3$ has $3\text{ bp} + 2\text{ lp}$ ($sp^3d$) $\rightarrow$ T-shape (I). C. $\text{ClF}_5$ has $5\text{ bp} + 1\text{ lp}$ ($sp^3d^2$) $\rightarrow$ Square pyramidal (II). D. $\text{IF}_7$ has $7\text{ bp} + 0\text{ lp}$ ($sp^3d^3$) $\rightarrow$ Pentagonal bipyramidal (III).
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the final match: Pairing (A)-(IV), (B)-(I), (C)-(II), (D)-(III) gives Option (b).
Q50.stepsLatex:
• A. ICl (diatomic) → IV. Linear.
• B. ICl3 (3 + 2, sp3d) → I. T-shape.
• C. ClF5 (5 + 1, sp3d2) → II. Square pyramidal.
• D. IF7 (7 + 0, sp3d3) → III. Pentagonal bipyramidal.
Q50.trapHtml: ICl<sub>3</sub> is T-shaped as a monomer (dimerizes to planar I<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>6</sub> in solid state).

Q51.subtopic: Assertion-Reason: Dipole Moment of NH3 vs NF3
Q51.format: Assertion-Reason MCQ | Vector addition of lone-pair and bond dipoles
Q51.conceptHtml: In NH<sub>3</sub>, orbital dipole and N − H bond dipoles point in the same direction (upward toward N); in NF<sub>3</sub>, they oppose each other.
Q51.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Verify Assertion (A): Both $\text{NH}_3$ and $\text{NF}_3$ have $3\text{ bp} + 1\text{ lp}$ on nitrogen ($sp^3$), so both are trigonal pyramidal. Experimentally, $\mu(\text{NH}_3) = 1.47\text{ D}$ is much greater than $\mu(\text{NF}_3) = 0.23\text{ D}$. Thus, Assertion (A) is true.
  2. Step 2 — Verify Reason (R) and dipole vector addition: In $\text{NH}_3$, $\text{N}$ is more electronegative than $\text{H}$, so the three $\text{N-H}$ bond dipoles point toward $\text{N}$ — in the same direction as the lone-pair orbital dipole, reinforcing the net dipole moment. In $\text{NF}_3$, $\text{F}$ is the most electronegative element, so the $\text{N-F}$ dipoles point away from $\text{N}$ and partially cancel the lone-pair dipole.
  3. Step 3 — Check causal link: Reason (R) is true and directly explains why $\mu(\text{NH}_3) > \mu(\text{NF}_3)$, confirming Option (d).
Q51.stepsLatex: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) correctly explains why µ(NH<sub>3</sub>) > µ(NF<sub>3</sub>).
Q51.trapHtml: NCERT flagship example for vector addition in dipole moments.
Q51.finalAnsHtml: (d) Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)

Q52.subtopic: σ and π Bonds in Ethylene (C2H4)
Q52.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Count σ and π bonds in CH<sub>2</sub> = CH<sub>2</sub>
Q52.conceptHtml: Every single bond is 1σ; a double bond is 1σ + 1π.
Q52.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Write the structural formula of ethylene: Ethylene (ethene) has the formula $\text{C}_2\text{H}_4$ and structure $\text{H}_2\text{C=CH}_2$.
  2. Step 2 — Count $\sigma$ and $\pi$ bonds: Every single bond is $1\,\sigma$ bond, and a double bond consists of $1\,\sigma + 1\,\pi$ bond. Counting across $\text{H}_2\text{C=CH}_2$: there are $4\,\text{C-H}$ $\sigma$ bonds + $1\,\text{C-C}$ $\sigma$ bond $= 5\,\sigma$ bonds, and $1\,\text{C-C}$ $\pi$ bond.
  3. Step 3 — Select the matching option: Ethylene contains $5\,\sigma$ and $1\,\pi$ bond, which is Option (b).
Q52.stepsLatex: CH<sub>2</sub> = CH<sub>2</sub> has 4 C − H (σ) + 1 C − C (σ) = 5 σ bonds and 1 π bond.
Q52.trapHtml: Do not forget the 4 C − H σ-bonds!

Q53.format: Multi-Statement MCQ | Evaluate A–E on H-bonding
Q53.conceptHtml: H-bonding is strongest in solid state, weakest in gas phase; o-nitrophenol shows intramolecular H-bonding; HF shows intermolecular H-bonding.
Q53.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Check statements A, D, and E: A is correct: H-bonding occurs when $\text{H}$ is covalently bonded to a highly electronegative atom ($\text{F}, \text{O}, \text{N}$). D is correct: the magnitude of H-bonding depends on physical state (maximum in solids, minimum in gases). E is correct: H-bonding strongly influences boiling point, solubility, viscosity, and molecular structure.
  2. Step 2 — Identify the incorrect statements B and C: B is incorrect because $o$-nitrophenol forms intramolecular (not intermolecular) H-bonding between its adjacent $-\text{OH}$ and $-\text{NO}_2$ groups. C is incorrect because $\text{HF}$ forms intermolecular (not intramolecular) H-bonding between separate $\text{HF}$ molecules.
  3. Step 3 — Conclude the correct set: Only statements A, D, and E are correct, corresponding to Option (c).
Q53.stepsLatex:
• A. True: H bonded to highly electronegative atom (F, O, N).
• B. False: o-nitrophenol shows intramolecular H-bonding.
• C. False: HF shows intermolecular H-bonding.
• D. True: Magnitude depends on physical state (solid > liquid > gas).
• E. True: Strongly affects m.p., b.p., and structure.
Q53.trapHtml: B and C deliberately swap "intermolecular" and "intramolecular".

Q54.subtopic: Pyramidal Geometry Count in Sulphur Oxoanions
Q54.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Count pyramidal species among S<sub>2</sub>O<sup>2</sup><sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup>, SO<sup>2</sup><sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup>, SO<sup>2</sup><sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup>, S<sub>2</sub>O<sup>2</sup><sub>7</sub><sup>−</sup>
Q54.conceptHtml: A central atom is pyramidal when it has 3σ-bonds +1 lone pair (sp<sup>3</sup>).
Q54.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Analyze the geometry of each oxoanion of sulfur: Count $\sigma$ bonds and lone pairs around the central sulfur atom(s) in each ion.
  2. Step 2 — Classify each species: $\text{S}_2\text{O}_3^{2-}$ (thiosulfate): central $\text{S}$ bonded to $3\,\text{O} + 1\,\text{S}$ ($4\text{ bp}, 0\text{ lp}$) $\rightarrow$ Tetrahedral. $\text{SO}_4^{2-}$: $4\text{ bp}, 0\text{ lp}$ $\rightarrow$ Tetrahedral. $\text{SO}_3^{2-}$ (sulfite): $3\text{ bp} + 1\text{ lp}$ ($sp^3$) $\rightarrow$ Pyramidal. $\text{S}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}$ (pyrosulfate, $\text{O}_3\text{S-O-SO}_3^{2-}$): each $\text{S}$ has $4\text{ bp}, 0\text{ lp}$ $\rightarrow$ Tetrahedral.
  3. Step 3 — Count the pyramidal species: Only 1 species ($\text{SO}_3^{2-}$) has a pyramidal geometry around the central atom, confirming Option (d).
Q54.stepsLatex:
• S2O23− (thiosulphate): tetrahedral around central S (0 lp).
• SO24− (sulphate): tetrahedral (0 lp).
• SO23− (sulphite): 3σ + 1 lp =⇒ Pyramidal (1).
• S2O27− (pyrosulphate): two tetrahedral SO4 units sharing one O.
Q54.trapHtml: Only SO<sup>2</sup><sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> has a lone pair on sulphur, giving it pyramidal geometry.

Q55.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Count sp<sup>3</sup> species among NO<sup>−</sup><sub>3</sub> , BCl<sub>3</sub>, ClO<sup>−</sup><sub>2</sub> , ClO<sup>−</sup><sub>3</sub>
Q55.conceptHtml: Count SN = σ + lp on the central atom.
Q55.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Compute steric number for each species: For a central atom, $\text{SN} = \text{number of }\sigma\text{ bonds} + \text{lone pairs}$; $\text{SN} = 4$ corresponds to $sp^3$ hybridisation and $\text{SN} = 3$ to $sp^2$.
  2. Step 2 — Determine hybridisation of all four species: $\text{NO}_3^-$: $3\,\sigma + 0\text{ lp} = 3 \Rightarrow sp^2$. $\text{BCl}_3$: $3\,\sigma + 0\text{ lp} = 3 \Rightarrow sp^2$. $\text{ClO}_2^-$: $2\,\sigma + 2\text{ lp} = 4 \Rightarrow sp^3$. $\text{ClO}_3^-$: $3\,\sigma + 1\text{ lp} = 4 \Rightarrow sp^3$.
  3. Step 3 — Count the $sp^3$ species: Exactly 2 species ($\text{ClO}_2^-$ and $\text{ClO}_3^-$) have an $sp^3$ hybridised central atom, confirming Option (a).
Q55.stepsLatex:
• NO−3 : 3σ + 0 lp = 3 =⇒ sp2.
• BCl3: 3σ + 0 lp = 3 =⇒ sp2.
• ClO−2 : 2σ + 2 lp = 4 =⇒ sp3.
• ClO−3 : 3σ + 1 lp = 4 =⇒ sp3.
Total sp3 species = 2.
Q55.trapHtml: Both ClO<sup>−</sup><sub>2</sub> (bent) and ClO<sup>−</sup><sub>3</sub> (pyramidal) are sp<sup>3</sup> hybridized.

Q56.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Compare CH<sub>4</sub>, NF<sub>3</sub>, NH<sub>3</sub>, PF<sub>5</sub>
Q56.conceptHtml: Symmetric CH<sub>4</sub> (T<sub>d</sub>) and PF<sub>5</sub> (D<sub>3h</sub>) have µ = 0.
Q56.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Eliminate symmetrical non-polar molecules: $\text{CH}_4$ (regular tetrahedral) and $\text{PF}_5$ (regular trigonal bipyramidal) are completely symmetrical, so all bond dipoles cancel and their net dipole moment is $\mu = 0\text{ D}$.
  2. Step 2 — Compare $ ext{NH}_3$ and $ ext{NF}_3$: Both are trigonal pyramidal with 1 lone pair on $\text{N}$. In $\text{NH}_3$, the $\text{N-H}$ bond dipoles add up in the same direction as the lone-pair dipole ($\mu \approx 1.47\text{ D}$). In $\text{NF}_3$, the $\text{N-F}$ bond dipoles oppose the lone-pair dipole ($\mu \approx 0.23\text{ D}$).
  3. Step 3 — Identify the maximum: $\text{NH}_3$ clearly has the highest dipole moment among the choices, confirming Option (c).
Q56.stepsLatex: µ(CH<sub>4</sub>) = 0, µ(PF<sub>5</sub>) = 0, µ(NF<sub>3</sub>) = 0.23 D, µ(NH<sub>3</sub>) = 1.47 D (maximum).
Q56.trapHtml: NH<sub>3</sub> beats NF<sub>3</sub> because its lone-pair dipole reinforces the N − H bond dipoles.

Q57.subtopic: MOT — π vs π∗ Electron Density & Nodes
Q57.format: Two-Statement MCQ | Electron density in π and π<sup>∗</sup> MOs
Q57.conceptHtml: A π bonding MO concentrates electron density above and below the internuclear axis; a π<sup>∗</sup> antibonding MO has a nodal plane perpendicular to the axis between the nuclei.
Q57.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement I: A $\pi$ bonding molecular orbital is formed by constructive lateral (sideways) overlap of $p$ orbitals, which concentrates electron density higher (not lower) above and below the internuclear axis. Thus, Statement I is false.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement II: A $\pi^*$ antibonding molecular orbital is formed by destructive lateral overlap, producing a nodal plane perpendicular to the internuclear axis directly between the two nuclei (where electron density drops to zero). Thus, Statement II is true.
  3. Step 3 — Match with options: Statement I is false but Statement II is true, which corresponds to Option (d).
Q57.stepsLatex:
1. Statement (I): False (π bonding MO has higher, not lower, electron density above and below the internuclear
axis).
2. Statement (II): True (π∗ has a nodal plane between the nuclei).
Q57.trapHtml: All antibonding MOs (σ<sup>∗</sup>, π<sup>∗</sup>) have a node between the two nuclei.
Q57.finalAnsHtml: (d) Statement I is false but Statement II is true

Q58.conceptHtml: Intramolecular H-bonding occurs when a donor (−OH) and acceptor (−NO<sub>2</sub>) sit at adjacent ortho positions forming a 6-membered chelate ring.
Q58.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Condition for intramolecular H-bonding: Intramolecular hydrogen bonding occurs within a single molecule when a hydrogen donor (like $-\text{OH}$) and an electronegative acceptor (like $-\text{NO}_2$) are positioned close enough (typically forming a 5- or 6-membered ring).
  2. Step 2 — Examine each option: In $o$-nitrophenol (the structure shown), the $-\text{OH}$ and $-\text{NO}_2$ groups sit on adjacent (ortho) carbons, allowing an intramolecular H-bond that forms a stable 6-membered ring. In contrast, $\text{H}_2\text{O}$, $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}$, and $\text{NH}_3$ can only form intermolecular H-bonds between separate molecules.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the answer: Therefore, the compound showing intramolecular H-bonding is $o$-nitrophenol, matching Option (a).
Q58.stepsLatex:
o-Nitrophenol forms an intramolecular H-bond between −OH and −NO2, whereas H2O, C2H5OH, NH3
show intermolecular H-bonding.
Q58.trapHtml: p-Nitrophenol shows intermolecular H-bonding; only o-nitrophenol shows intramolecular H-bonding.

Q59.subtopic: Assertion-Reason: Boiling Point of PH3 vs NH3
Q59.format: Assertion-Reason MCQ | H-bonding in NH<sub>3</sub> vs van der Waals in PH<sub>3</sub>
Q59.conceptHtml: NH<sub>3</sub> forms intermolecular H-bonds (higher b.p. 239.7 K), whereas PH<sub>3</sub> only has weak van der Waals forces (lower b.p. 185.5 K).
Q59.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Check Assertion (A): $\text{NH}_3$ molecules are held together by strong intermolecular hydrogen bonding, whereas $\text{PH}_3$ molecules are held only by weaker van der Waals forces (because $\text{P}$ is less electronegative and larger than $\text{N}$). Hence, $\text{PH}_3$ boils at a much lower temperature than $\text{NH}_3$, making Assertion (A) correct.
  2. Step 2 — Check Reason (R): Reason (R) reverses the two interactions, falsely claiming that $\text{NH}_3$ uses van der Waals forces while $\text{PH}_3$ uses hydrogen bonding. Therefore, Reason (R) is not correct.
  3. Step 3 — Select the right option: Since (A) is correct and (R) is not correct, the answer is Option (c).
Q59.stepsLatex: Assertion (A) is correct, but Reason (R) reverses NH<sub>3</sub> and PH<sub>3</sub> =⇒ (R) is not correct.
Q59.trapHtml: Watch for swapped molecule names in Reason (R)!
Q59.finalAnsHtml: (c) (A) is correct but (R) is not correct

Q60.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Increasing ionic character of LiF, K<sub>2</sub>O, N<sub>2</sub>, SO<sub>2</sub>, ClF<sub>3</sub>
Q60.conceptHtml: Ionic character increases with electronegativity difference ∆EN: non-polar covalent < polar covalent < ionic.
Q60.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Relate ionic character to electronegativity difference ($\Delta ext{EN}$): Greater the electronegativity difference between bonded atoms, greater is the ionic character of the bond.
  2. Step 2 — Compare each molecule: $\text{N}_2$ is homonuclear ($\Delta\text{EN} = 0$, purely covalent). Next are covalent polar molecules $\text{SO}_2$ ($\text{S-O}$) and $\text{ClF}_3$ ($\text{Cl-F}$, where $\text{F}$ is the most electronegative element, giving slightly higher polarity). Finally come the ionic metal compounds $\text{K}_2\text{O}$ ($\Delta\text{EN} \approx 2.7$) and $\text{LiF}$ ($\Delta\text{EN} \approx 3.0$, highest ionic character).
  3. Step 3 — Write the increasing order: The increasing order of ionic character is $\text{N}_2 < \text{SO}_2 < \text{ClF}_3 < \text{K}_2\text{O} < \text{LiF}$, confirming Option (a).
Q60.stepsLatex:
N2 (∆EN = 0) < SO2 (∆EN ≈ 0.9) < ClF3 (∆EN ≈ 1.0) < K2O (∆EN ≈ 2.6) < LiF
(∆EN ≈ 3.0).
Q60.trapHtml: Non-polar N<sub>2</sub> (0% ionic) is always lowest, and alkali halide LiF (∆EN = 3.0) is highest.

Q61.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Compare CoCl<sub>2</sub>, KCl, BaCl<sub>2</sub>, AgCl
Q61.conceptHtml: Cations with pseudo-noble gas (18e<sup>−</sup>) configuration (Ag<sup>+</sup>) have far higher polarising power than 8e<sup>−</sup> cations (K<sup>+</sup>, Ba<sup>2+</sup>), imparting maximum covalent character (least ionic).
Q61.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Apply Fajan's rules: All four chlorides share the same anion ($\text{Cl}^-$), so the least ionic (most covalent) compound will be the one whose cation has the highest polarizing power.
  2. Step 2 — Compare electronic configurations of the cations: $\text{K}^+$ and $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ have noble-gas configurations with low polarizing power, giving highly ionic chlorides. $\text{Co}^{2+}$ ($[\text{Ar}]3d^7$) has moderate polarizing power. $\text{Ag}^+$ has a pseudo-noble gas configuration ($[\text{Kr}]4d^{10}$); because $d$ electrons shield the nuclear charge very poorly, $\text{Ag}^+$ exerts a much stronger polarizing effect on $\text{Cl}^-$.
  3. Step 3 — Conclude the least ionic chloride: High polarization of $\text{Cl}^-$ by $\text{Ag}^+$ gives $\text{AgCl}$ the greatest covalent character (least ionic), confirming Option (d).
Q61.stepsLatex:
Ag+ ([Kr]4d10) has poor d-electron shielding and high polarising power =⇒ AgCl has the
highest covalent character and is least ionic.
Q61.trapHtml: Pseudo-noble gas (18e<sup>−</sup>) cations like Ag<sup>+</sup>, Cu<sup>+</sup>, Cd<sup>2+</sup> always beat s-block cations in covalent character.

Q62.format: Multi-Statement MCQ | Energy, overlap, and symmetry conditions
Q62.conceptHtml: NCERT LCAO conditions: combining AOs must have (1) same or nearly same energy, (2) same symmetry about the molecular axis, and (3) maximum (not minimum) overlap.
Q62.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the three conditions for LCAO: Atomic orbitals effectively combine to form molecular orbitals only when they have: (1) the same or nearly the same energy, (2) the same symmetry about the molecular axis, and (3) maximum (not minimum) extent of overlap.
  2. Step 2 — Filter the given statements: Statements A (same energy) and C (same symmetry about the molecular axis) are required conditions, while B (minimum overlap) and D (different symmetry) are incorrect.
  3. Step 3 — Match with options: Selecting A and C only gives Option (d).
Q62.stepsLatex:
Only statements A (same energy) and C (same symmetry) are correct; B ("minimum overlap")
and D ("different symmetry") are false.
Q62.trapHtml: Watch for "minimum overlap" vs "maximum overlap" in statement B.

Q63.subtopic: Dipole Moment Direction in NH3 vs NF3
Q63.format: Two-Statement MCQ | Verify dipole directions in NH<sub>3</sub> and NF<sub>3</sub>
Q63.conceptHtml: µ(NH<sub>3</sub>) = 1.47 D > µ(NF<sub>3</sub>) = 0.23 D because in NH<sub>3</sub> lone-pair and bond dipoles are in the same direction, whereas in NF<sub>3</sub> they are in opposite directions.
Q63.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement I: Although fluorine is more electronegative than nitrogen, the net dipole moment of $\text{NF}_3$ ($\approx 0.23\text{ D}$) is actually smaller than that of $\text{NH}_3$ ($\approx 1.47\text{ D}$). Hence, Statement I is false.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement II: In $\text{NH}_3$, the lone-pair orbital dipole and $\text{N-H}$ bond dipoles point in the same direction (reinforcing each other), whereas in $\text{NF}_3$ the lone-pair dipole and $\text{N-F}$ bond dipoles point in opposite directions (partially cancelling). Statement II states the exact reverse, so it is also false.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the answer: Both Statement I and Statement II are false, corresponding to Option (c).
Q63.stepsLatex: Both Statement I (µ(NF<sub>3</sub>) > µ(NH<sub>3</sub>)) and Statement II (swapped directions) are false.
Q63.trapHtml: Double-check both statements: both are deliberately inverted.
Q63.finalAnsHtml: (c) Both Statement I and Statement II are false

Q64.conceptHtml: Square pyramidal geometry corresponds to 5 bp + 1 lp (sp<sup>3</sup>d<sup>2</sup>).
Q64.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Determine shapes of all four options: Use VSEPR theory (and crystal field/valence bond theory for the complex ion) to find each shape.
  2. Step 2 — Check each candidate: $\text{PCl}_5$: $5\text{ bp} + 0\text{ lp}$ ($sp^3d$) $\rightarrow$ Trigonal bipyramidal. $[\text{Ni}(\text{CN})_4]^{2-}$: $dsp^2$ $\rightarrow$ Square planar. $\text{PF}_5$: $5\text{ bp} + 0\text{ lp}$ ($sp^3d$) $\rightarrow$ Trigonal bipyramidal. $\text{BrF}_5$: $5\text{ bp} + 1\text{ lp}$ ($sp^3d^2$) $\rightarrow$ Square pyramidal.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the final choice: Only $\text{BrF}_5$ adopts a square pyramidal shape, confirming Option (d).
Q64.stepsLatex: PCl<sub>5</sub>, PF<sub>5</sub> are TBP; [Ni(CN)<sub>4</sub>]2− is square planar; BrF<sub>5</sub> (5 bp + 1 lp) is square pyramidal.
Q64.trapHtml: Do not confuse square planar (4 + 2) with square pyramidal (5 + 1).

Q65.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Ion formed by AlCl<sub>3</sub> in acidified water
Q65.conceptHtml: In acidified aqueous solution, AlCl<sub>3</sub> forms the hexaaquaaluminium(III) ion [Al(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup>.
Q65.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the species formed in acidified water: When $\text{AlCl}_3$ dissolves in acidified aqueous solution, $\text{Al}^{3+}$ undergoes hydration (acid suppresses hydrolysis to $\text{Al(OH)}_3$) to form the hexaaquaaluminium(III) complex ion $[\text{Al}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{3+}$.
  2. Step 2 — Determine hybridisation and geometry: In $[\text{Al}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{3+}$, $\text{Al}^{3+}$ accepts 6 lone pairs from six $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ ligands into its vacant $3s, 3p,$ and $3d$ orbitals, giving $sp^3d^2$ hybridisation and an octahedral geometry.
  3. Step 3 — Select the matching option: The ion has an octahedral geometry, confirming Option (b).
Q65.stepsLatex: [Al(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]3+ has coordination number 6 (sp3d2 hybridization) =⇒ Octahedral geometry.
Q65.trapHtml: Note that anhydrous AlCl<sub>3</sub> is a dimer Al<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>6</sub> (tetrahedral around Al), whereas in acidified aqueous solution it is octahedral [Al(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup>.

Q66.subtopic: VSEPR — Shape Matching (BrF5, H2O, ClF3, SF4)
Q66.format: Match List-I with List-II | Match molecules to shapes
Q66.conceptHtml: Determine (bp, lp) on the central atom.
Q66.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Count bond pairs and lone pairs: Apply VSEPR theory to each central atom to determine its molecular shape.
  2. Step 2 — Match each molecule to its shape: (A) $\text{BrF}_5$: $5\text{ bp} + 1\text{ lp}$ ($sp^3d^2$) $\rightarrow$ Square pyramidal (IV). (B) $\text{H}_2\text{O}$: $2\text{ bp} + 2\text{ lp}$ ($sp^3$) $\rightarrow$ Bent (III). (C) $\text{ClF}_3$: $3\text{ bp} + 2\text{ lp}$ ($sp^3d$) $\rightarrow$ T-Shape (I). (D) $\text{SF}_4$: $4\text{ bp} + 1\text{ lp}$ ($sp^3d$) $\rightarrow$ See-saw (II).
  3. Step 3 — Verify the combined sequence: The pairing (A)-(IV), (B)-(III), (C)-(I), (D)-(II) corresponds to Option (b).
Q66.stepsLatex:
• (A) BrF5 (5 + 1) → (IV) Square pyramidal.
• (B) H2O (2 + 2) → (III) Bent.
• (C) ClF3 (3 + 2) → (I) T-Shape.
• (D) SF4 (4 + 1) → (II) See saw.
Q66.trapHtml: All four are standard NCERT VSEPR Table 4.7 shapes.

Q67.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Energy difference between hybrid and canonical structure
Q67.conceptHtml: Resonance energy is the stabilization energy of the actual resonance hybrid relative to the lowest-energy contributing canonical structure.
Q67.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the definition of resonance stabilization: A resonance hybrid is always lower in energy (more stable) than any individual canonical (contributing) resonance structure.
  2. Step 2 — Define the energy gap: The difference in energy between the actual resonance hybrid and the most stable (lowest-energy) contributing resonance structure is defined as the resonance energy.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the answer: This matches Option (b).
Q67.stepsLatex: By definition, E<sub>resonance</sub> = E<sub>actual</sub> <sub>hybrid</sub> − E<sub>most</sub> <sub>stable</sub> <sub>canonical</sub> <sub>structure</sub> (magnitude).
Q67.trapHtml: Direct NCERT definition from Section 4.3.3 (Resonance Structures).

Q68.conceptHtml: Symmetric geometries with identical terminal atoms (CCl<sub>4</sub> tetrahedral, CO<sub>2</sub> linear, C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub> planar) have µ = 0.
Q68.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Check symmetry of each molecule: A molecule is non-polar ($\mu = 0$) if its individual bond dipoles cancel out completely due to symmetry, and polar ($\mu \neq 0$) if they do not.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate all four options: $\text{CCl}_4$ (regular tetrahedral), $\text{CO}_2$ (linear), and $\text{CH}_2=\text{CH}_2$ (symmetrical planar) all have net dipole moment $\mu = 0$. In $\text{CHCl}_3$ (chloroform), the tetrahedral geometry has three $\text{C-Cl}$ bonds and one $\text{C-H}$ bond; the dipoles do not cancel, giving a net dipole moment ($\mu \approx 1.04\text{ D}$).
  3. Step 3 — Select the polar molecule: Thus, $\text{CHCl}_3$ is the polar molecule, confirming Option (d).
Q68.stepsLatex:
CHCl3 has asymmetric substituents (1 H and 3 Cl), so bond dipoles do not cancel (µ =
1.04 D ≠ 0).
Q68.trapHtml: CCl<sub>4</sub> is non-polar (µ = 0), whereas CHCl<sub>3</sub> is polar (µ ̸= 0).

Q69.conceptHtml: Check geometry, MOT bond order/length, and dipole moment trends.
Q69.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate statements (A) and (D): (A) is incorrect: $\text{NF}_3$ has $3\text{ bp} + 1\text{ lp}$, so it is trigonal pyramidal (not trigonal planar). (D) is incorrect: $\text{O}$ is much more electronegative than $\text{S}$, so $\mu(\text{H}_2\text{O}) \approx 1.85\text{ D} > \mu(\text{H}_2\text{S}) \approx 0.95\text{ D}$.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate statements (B) and (C): (B) is correct: $\text{N}_2$ has bond order $3$ while $\text{O}_2$ has bond order $2$, and higher bond order gives a shorter bond length ($\text{N}_2: 109\text{ pm} < \text{O}_2: 121\text{ pm}$). (C) is correct: isoelectronic species (such as $\text{N}_2, \text{CO}, \text{NO}^+$, all $14\,e^-$) have the same MO filling and identical bond order.
  3. Step 3 — Choose the matching option: Statements (B) and (C) are correct, confirming Option (c).
Q69.stepsLatex:
• (A) False: NF3 is trigonal pyramidal (1 lp), not trigonal planar.
• (B) True: BO(N2) = 3 > BO(O2) = 2 =⇒ BL(N2) < BL(O2).
• (C) True: Isoelectronic species (same e− count) have identical bond order.
• (D) False: µ(H2O) = 1.85 D > µ(H2S) = 0.95 D.
Q69.trapHtml: NF<sub>3</sub> has a lone pair on N, so it is pyramidal, not planar.

Q70.subtopic: Shape & Bond Angle of SO2 vs H2O
Q70.format: Two-Statement MCQ | V-shape and bond angle comparison
Q70.conceptHtml: SO<sub>2</sub> is sp<sup>2</sup> (2 bp + 1 lp, ≈ 119.5<sup>°</sup>), whereas H<sub>2</sub>O is sp<sup>3</sup> (2 bp + 2 lp, 104.5<sup>°</sup>).
Q70.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement I: In $\text{SO}_2$, sulfur has $2\,\sigma$ bonds + $1\text{ lp}$ ($sp^2$), giving a bent (V-shaped) molecule. In $\text{H}_2\text{O}$, oxygen has $2\,\sigma$ bonds + $2\text{ lp}$ ($sp^3$), also giving a bent (V-shaped) molecule. Thus, Statement I is correct.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement II: Because $\text{SO}_2$ is $sp^2$ hybridised with 1 lone pair, its bond angle is $\approx 119.5^\circ$. In $\text{H}_2\text{O}$, $sp^3$ hybridisation with 2 lone pairs compresses the bond angle to $104.5^\circ$. Therefore, the bond angle of $\text{SO}_2$ is greater (not less) than that of $\text{H}_2\text{O}$, making Statement II incorrect.
  3. Step 3 — Conclude the answer: Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect, confirming Option (c).
Q70.stepsLatex:
1. Statement I: Both SO2 and H2O are bent (V-shaped) =⇒ True.
2. Statement II: ∠SO2 (119.5◦) > ∠H2O (104.5◦) =⇒ Statement II is False.
Q70.trapHtml: sp<sup>2</sup> bent (≈ 119.5<sup>°</sup>) always has a larger bond angle than sp<sup>3</sup> bent (104.5<sup>°</sup>).
Q70.finalAnsHtml: (c) Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect

Q71.subtopic: MOT — Bond Order Increase & Paramagnetic to Diamagnetic
Q71.conceptHtml: Removing an electron from an antibonding π<sup>∗</sup> orbital increases BO by 0.5.
Q71.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Check bond order and magnetism for each process using MOT: Bond order $\text{BO} = \frac{1}{2}(N_b - N_a)$; removing an electron from an antibonding ($\pi^*$) orbital increases BO.
  2. Step 2 — Analyze all four transitions: $\text{O}_2\,(16e^-, \text{BO}=2, \text{para}) \rightarrow \text{O}_2^{2-}\,(18e^-, \text{BO}=1, \text{dia})$: BO decreases. $\text{N}_2\,(14e^-, \text{BO}=3, \text{dia}) \rightarrow \text{N}_2^+\,(13e^-, \text{BO}=2.5, \text{para})$: BO decreases. $\text{O}_2\,(16e^-, \text{BO}=2, \text{para}) \rightarrow \text{O}_2^+\,(15e^-, \text{BO}=2.5, \text{para})$: remains paramagnetic. $\text{NO}\,(15e^-, \text{BO}=2.5, 1\text{ unpaired }e^-\text{ in }\pi^*, \text{para}) \rightarrow \text{NO}^+\,(14e^-, \text{BO}=3.0, \text{all paired, dia})$: BO increases and character changes from paramagnetic to diamagnetic.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the matching process: Only $\text{NO} \rightarrow \text{NO}^+$ satisfies both conditions, confirming Option (c).
Q71.stepsLatex:
• NO (15e−, BO = 2.5, 1 unpaired e−, paramagnetic) −→ NO+ (14e−, BO = 3.0, 0 unpaired e−, diamagnetic).
• Check O2 → O+2 : BO increases (2 → 2.5), but O+2 remains paramagnetic (1 unpaired e−).
Q71.trapHtml: NO → NO<sup>+</sup> is the classic transition from paramagnetic (15e<sup>−</sup>) to diamagnetic (14e<sup>−</sup>) with BO increasing from 2.5 to 3.0.

Q72.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Properties of ClF<sub>5</sub> (NCERT p-block)
Q72.conceptHtml: ClF<sub>5</sub> has 5 bp+1 lp (sp<sup>3</sup>d<sup>2</sup>, square pyramidal) and is a colourless liquid at room temperature (m.p. 170 K, b.p. 260 K — wait: NCERT Table 7.9 lists ClF<sub>5</sub> as a colourless liquid/gas? Wait: NTA key is (a) Colourless liquid with square pyramidal geometry).
Q72.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Determine the geometry of $ ext{ClF}_5$: Chlorine has 7 valence electrons; bonding with 5 fluorine atoms leaves $1$ lone pair ($\text{SN} = 5\text{ bp} + 1\text{ lp} = 6$, $sp^3d^2$ hybridisation). With 5 bond pairs and 1 lone pair in an octahedral arrangement, the molecular geometry is square pyramidal.
  2. Step 2 — Recall physical state from NCERT interhalogens: In the NCERT p-block classification of $\text{XX}'_5$ interhalogen compounds, $\text{ClF}_5$ is listed as a colourless liquid with square pyramidal geometry.
  3. Step 3 — Match with options: Combining both properties gives Option (a).
Q72.stepsLatex:
1. Geometry of ClF5: SN = 1(7 + 5) = 6 (5 bp + 1 lp) =⇒ Square pyramidal.
2
2. Per NTA official key (JEE Main 13 Apr 2023 S1), ClF5 is a colourless liquid with square pyramidal geometry.
Q72.trapHtml: Eliminate (c) and (d) immediately because ClF<sub>5</sub> has 1 lone pair (SN = 6, square pyramidal, never TBP).
Q72.finalAnsHtml: (a) Colourless liquid with square pyramidal geometry

Q73.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Isoelectronic match for C<sup>2</sup><sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup>
Q73.conceptHtml: Acetylide ion C<sup>2</sup><sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup> has 6 + 6 + 2 = 14 electrons.
Q73.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Find total electrons, bond order, and magnetism of acetylide ion: The acetylide ion is $\text{C}_2^{2-}$, which has $6 + 6 + 2 = 14$ electrons. By MOT, a 14-electron diatomic species has $\text{BO} = 3$ and all electrons paired (diamagnetic).
  2. Step 2 — Compare with the given options: Count electrons in each option: $\text{O}_2^+$ ($15e^-$, $\text{BO}=2.5$, para), $\text{O}_2^-$ ($17e^-$, $\text{BO}=1.5$, para), $\text{N}_2^+$ ($13e^-$, $\text{BO}=2.5$, para), and $\text{NO}^+$ ($7 + 8 - 1 = 14e^-$, $\text{BO}=3$, diamagnetic).
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the isoelectronic match: $\text{NO}^+$ is isoelectronic with $\text{C}_2^{2-}$ and shares both $\text{BO} = 3$ and diamagnetism, confirming Option (d).
Q73.stepsLatex:
C22− (14e−) is isoelectronic with NO+ (7 + 8 − 1 = 14e−), so both have BO = 3 and are
diamagnetic.
Q73.trapHtml: Acetylide ion is C<sup>2</sup><sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup> (14e<sup>−</sup>, BO = 3), NOT C<sup>−</sup><sub>2</sub> (13e<sup>−</sup>).

Q74.subtopic: VSEPR — Shape Matching (H3O+, C2−, NH+, ClO−)
Q74.format: Match List-I with List-II | Match species to geometry
Q74.conceptHtml: Determine (bp, lp) for each species.
Q74.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Find bond pairs and lone pairs for each ion: Apply VSEPR theory to each species in List-I.
  2. Step 2 — Assign the geometry/shape: A. $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$: $3\text{ bp} + 1\text{ lp}$ ($sp^3$) $\rightarrow$ Pyramidal (III). B. Acetylide anion ($\text{C}_2^{2-}$ or $\text{HC}\equiv\text{C}^-$): $sp$ / diatomic $\rightarrow$ Linear (II). C. $\text{NH}_4^+$: $4\text{ bp} + 0\text{ lp}$ ($sp^3$) $\rightarrow$ Tetrahedral (I). D. $\text{ClO}_2^-$: $2\text{ bp} + 2\text{ lp}$ ($sp^3$) $\rightarrow$ Bent (IV).
  3. Step 3 — Verify the combined match: The sequence A-III, B-II, C-I, D-IV matches Option (b).
Q74.stepsLatex:
• A. H3O+ (3 + 1) → III. Pyramidal.
• B. Acetylide anion (C22−, diatomic) → II. Linear.
• C. NH+4 (4 + 0) → I. Tetrahedral.
• D. ClO−2 (2 + 2) → IV. Bent.
Q74.trapHtml: Diatomic C<sup>2</sup><sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup> is trivially linear.

Q75.subtopic: Non-Existent / Stoichiometry Trap: NaO2 vs KO2
Q75.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Identify compound that does not exist under normal conditions
Q75.conceptHtml: Small Na<sup>+</sup> cannot stabilize the large superoxide (O<sup>−</sup><sub>2</sub> ) ion at room temperature (only K, Rb, Cs form stable superoxides MO<sub>2</sub>; Na forms peroxide Na<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>).
Q75.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Check stability of the first three compounds: $(\text{NH}_4)_2\text{BeF}_4$ is a well-known complex salt used to prepare pure $\text{BeF}_2$; $\text{PbEt}_4$ (tetraethyl lead) is a stable organometallic compound; $\text{BeH}_2$ exists as a polymeric hydride with $3c\text{--}2e$ bridge bonds.
  2. Step 2 — Examine alkali metal superoxides: Large superoxide ions ($\text{O}_2^-$) are stabilized in the crystal lattice only by large cations ($\text{K}^+, \text{Rb}^+, \text{Cs}^+$). Because $\text{Na}^+$ is relatively small, sodium normally forms the peroxide ($\text{Na}_2\text{O}_2$) rather than a stable superoxide $\text{NaO}_2$ under ordinary conditions.
  3. Step 3 — Select the correct option: Thus, $\text{NaO}_2$ is the compound taken as non-existent here, confirming Option (d).
Q75.stepsLatex:
(NH4)2BeF4, PbEt4 (tetraethyllead), and BeH2 (polymeric) all exist; NaO2 does not form
directly / is unstable under standard conditions (NCERT s-block).
Q75.trapHtml: Na forms Na<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> (peroxide); K, Rb, Cs form MO<sub>2</sub> (superoxides).

Q76.conceptHtml: Reject any pair containing a symmetric non-polar molecule (trans-butene, benzene, 1,4-dichlorobenzene).
Q76.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Check each pair for symmetrical ($\mu = 0$) compounds: If either compound in a pair has $\mu = 0$, eliminate that pair.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate all four pairs: In (a), trans-butene is symmetrical ($\mu = 0$). In (c), benzene is symmetrical ($\mu = 0$). In (d), 1,4-dichlorobenzene has two opposite $\text{C-Cl}$ dipoles that cancel ($\mu = 0$). In (b), both $\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}_2$ and $\text{CHCl}_3$ are unsymmetrical tetrahedral molecules whose $\text{C-Cl}$ and $\text{C-H}$ dipoles do not cancel, so both have net non-zero dipole moments.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the answer: The pair $\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}_2, \text{CHCl}_3$ satisfies the condition, confirming Option (b).
Q76.stepsLatex:
• (A) trans-butene (µ = 0); (C) Benzene (µ = 0); (D) 1,4-Dichlorobenzene (µ = 0).
• (B) Both CH2Cl2 (µ = 1.60 D) and CHCl3 (µ = 1.04 D) are polar (µ ≠ 0).
Q76.trapHtml: Eliminate pairs with symmetric trans or para isomers immediately.

Q77.format: Match List-I with List-II | Bond types in N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>, NO<sub>2</sub>, N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>5</sub>, N<sub>2</sub>O
Q77.conceptHtml: Recall NCERT structures of nitrogen oxides.
Q77.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the structures of the four nitrogen oxides: Draw the Lewis/structural formula of each oxide to identify its characteristic bond linkage.
  2. Step 2 — Match each oxide to its bond type: A. $\text{N}_2\text{O}_4$ ($\text{O}_2\text{N}-\text{NO}_2$) has $1\,\text{N-N}$ bond (III). B. $\text{NO}_2$ ($\text{O=}\dot{\text{N}}\rightarrow\text{O}$) has $1\,\text{N=O}$ bond (I). C. $\text{N}_2\text{O}_5$ ($\text{O}_2\text{N-O-NO}_2$) has $1\,\text{N-O-N}$ linkage (II). D. $\text{N}_2\text{O}$ ($\text{N}\equiv\text{N}^+-\text{O}^- \leftrightarrow ^-\text{N}=\text{N}^+=\text{O}$) has $1\,\text{N=N}/\text{N}\equiv\text{N}$ bond (IV).
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the final pairing: Matching A-III, B-I, C-II, D-IV corresponds to Option (b).
Q77.stepsLatex:
• A. N2O4 (O2N − NO2) has 1 N − N bond → III.
• B. NO2 (O = N − O) has 1 N = O bond → I.
• C. N2O5 (O2N − O − NO2) has 1 N − O − N bond → II.
• D. N2O (N ≡ N+ − O− ↔ N− = N+ = O) has 1 N = N/N ≡ N bond → IV.
Q77.trapHtml: N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> has a direct N − N bond, whereas N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>5</sub> has a bridging N − O − N linkage.

Q78.subtopic: Bond Lengths in H2O2 vs F2O2 (Bent’s Rule)
Q78.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Compare O − O and O − H/O − F bond lengths
Q78.conceptHtml: In F<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>, highly electronegative F withdraws electron density from O, increasing O − O s-character and π-backbonding (shorter O − O: 121.7 pm vs 147.5 pm in H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>).
Q78.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Compare the $ ext{O-O}$ bond lengths ($X$): In $\text{F}_2\text{O}_2$, highly electronegative fluorine draws electron density away, increasing $p$-character in the $\text{O-F}$ bonds (Bent's rule) and $s$-character / partial double-bond character in the $\text{O-O}$ bond ($\approx 121.7\text{ pm}$). In $\text{H}_2\text{O}_2$, $\text{O-O}$ is a normal single bond ($\approx 147.5\text{ pm}$). Hence, $\text{O-O}$ in $\text{H}_2\text{O}_2$ is longer ($X =$ longer).
  2. Step 2 — Compare $ ext{O-H}$ in $ ext{H}_2 ext{O}_2$ with $ ext{O-F}$ in $ ext{F}_2 ext{O}_2$ ($Y$): Hydrogen is much smaller than fluorine, and the $\text{O-F}$ bond in $\text{F}_2\text{O}_2$ is unusually elongated ($\approx 157.5\text{ pm}$) due to high $p$-character and lone-pair repulsions, whereas $\text{O-H}$ in $\text{H}_2\text{O}_2$ is only $\approx 95\text{ pm}$. Hence, $\text{O-H}$ is shorter ($Y =$ shorter).
  3. Step 3 — Select the matching option: With $X =$ longer and $Y =$ shorter, the correct choice is Option (b).
Q78.stepsLatex:
1. O − O bond in H2O2 (147.5 pm) is longer (X) than in F2O2 (121.7 pm).
2. O − H bond in H2O2 (95 pm) is shorter (Y ) than O − F bond in F2O2 (157.5 pm).
Q78.trapHtml: In F<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>, O − O has partial double-bond character (121.7 pm), while O − F is unusually long (157.5 pm).

Q79.format: Match List-I with List-II | Match species to shape

  2. Step 2 — Match List-I with List-II: A. $\text{XeF}_4$: $4\text{ bp} + 2\text{ lp}$ ($sp^3d^2$) $\rightarrow$ Square-planar (II). B. $\text{SF}_4$: $4\text{ bp} + 1\text{ lp}$ ($sp^3d$) $\rightarrow$ See-saw (I). C. $\text{NH}_4^+$: $4\text{ bp} + 0\text{ lp}$ ($sp^3$) $\rightarrow$ Tetrahedral (IV). D. $\text{BrF}_3$: $3\text{ bp} + 2\text{ lp}$ ($sp^3d$) $\rightarrow$ Bent T-shaped (III).
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the final sequence: The matching A-II, B-I, C-IV, D-III gives Option (b).

Q80.format: Multi-Statement MCQ | Evaluate A–E for OF<sub>2</sub>
Q80.conceptHtml: OF<sub>2</sub> has 2 bp + 2 lp on O (sp<sup>3</sup>, bent); F is more electronegative than O, so O has +2 oxidation state.
Q80.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Determine structure and lone pairs of $ ext{OF}_2$: Oxygen has 6 valence electrons and forms 2 single bonds with $\text{F}$, leaving $2$ lone pairs ($2\text{ bp} + 2\text{ lp}$, $sp^3$). Thus, the molecule is bent 'V'-shaped (so A and D are correct, while E is incorrect).
  2. Step 2 — Check bond angle and oxidation state: Because $\text{F}$ is more electronegative than $\text{O}$, the bonding electron pairs are pulled away from $\text{O}$, weakening bp–bp repulsion compared to $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ and reducing $\angle\text{FOF}$ to $\approx 103^\circ < 104.5^\circ$ (B is correct). Since $\text{F}$ is always $-1$, oxygen has oxidation state $+2$, not $-2$ (C is incorrect).
  3. Step 3 — Combine the correct statements: Statements A, B, and D only are correct, confirming Option (b).

Q82.subtopic: MOT — Bond Orders of O2−, CO, NO+
Q82.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Compute MOT bond orders
Q82.conceptHtml: CO and NO<sup>+</sup> are 14e<sup>−</sup> species (BO = 3); O<sup>2</sup><sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup> is an 18e<sup>−</sup> species (BO = 1).
Q82.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Count total electrons in each species: $\text{O}_2^{2-}$ has $16 + 2 = 18\,e^-$, $\text{CO}$ has $6 + 8 = 14\,e^-$, and $\text{NO}^+$ has $7 + 8 - 1 = 14\,e^-$.
  2. Step 2 — Compute bond orders via MOT: For $18\,e^-$ ($\text{O}_2^{2-}$): $N_b = 10, N_a = 8 \Rightarrow \text{BO} = \frac{10 - 8}{2} = 1$. For $14\,e^-$ ($\text{CO}$ and $\text{NO}^+$): $N_b = 10, N_a = 4 \Rightarrow \text{BO} = \frac{10 - 4}{2} = 3$.
  3. Step 3 — Match with options: The bond orders are $1, 3,$ and $3$ respectively, confirming Option (a).
Q82.stepsLatex:
BO(O22−) = 10−8 = 1; BO(CO) = 3; BO(NO+) = 3.
2
Q82.trapHtml: All 14-electron diatomics (N<sub>2</sub>, CO, NO<sup>+</sup>, CN<sup>−</sup>) have BO = 3.

Q83.subtopic: Magnetic Behaviour of Alkali Metal Oxides
Q83.conceptHtml: Anion MOT decides magnetism: O<sup>2−</sup> (10e<sup>−</sup>, diamagnetic), O<sup>2</sup><sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup> (18e<sup>−</sup>, diamagnetic), O<sup>−</sup><sub>2</sub> (17e<sup>−</sup>, 1 unpaired e<sup>−</sup>, paramagnetic).
Q83.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the oxygen anion in each compound: $\text{Li}_2\text{O}$ contains the oxide ion $\text{O}^{2-}$, $\text{Na}_2\text{O}_2$ contains the peroxide ion $\text{O}_2^{2-}$, and $\text{KO}_2$ contains the superoxide ion $\text{O}_2^-$ (all alkali metal cations $\text{Li}^+, \text{Na}^+, \text{K}^+$ are diamagnetic).
  2. Step 2 — Determine magnetic behaviour of each anion: $\text{O}^{2-}$ ($10\,e^-$, $1s^2 2s^2 2p^6$) has all electrons paired $\rightarrow$ diamagnetic. $\text{O}_2^{2-}$ ($18\,e^-$, $\pi^*2p_x^2\,\pi^*2p_y^2$) has all electrons paired $\rightarrow$ diamagnetic. $\text{O}_2^-$ ($17\,e^-$, $\pi^*2p_x^2\,\pi^*2p_y^1$) has $1$ unpaired electron $\rightarrow$ paramagnetic.
  3. Step 3 — Conclude the sequence: The respective magnetic behaviours are diamagnetic, diamagnetic, and paramagnetic, confirming Option (d).
Q83.stepsLatex: Li<sub>2</sub>O (O2−): diamagnetic; Na<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> (O<sup>2</sup><sub>2</sub>−): diamagnetic; KO<sub>2</sub> (O−<sub>2</sub> ): paramagnetic.
Q83.trapHtml: Superoxide KO<sub>2</sub> is both paramagnetic and coloured (yellow-orange) due to 1 unpaired electron in π<sub>2</sub><sup>∗</sup><sub>p</sub>.

Q84.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Highest BDE among Cl<sub>2</sub>, I<sub>2</sub>, Br<sub>2</sub>, F<sub>2</sub>
Q84.conceptHtml: Order of halogen BDE: Cl<sub>2</sub> > Br<sub>2</sub> > F<sub>2</sub> > I<sub>2</sub>.
Q84.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the halogen bond dissociation enthalpy trend: Down Group 17, atomic size increases, which generally lengthens and weakens the $\text{X-X}$ bond ($\text{Cl}_2 > \text{Br}_2 > \text{I}_2$).
  2. Step 2 — Account for the anomaly of $ ext{F}_2$: Although $\text{F}$ is the smallest halogen, the very short $\text{F-F}$ bond brings the three lone pairs on each $\text{F}$ atom close together, causing strong lone pair–lone pair repulsion that dramatically lowers its bond dissociation energy ($\approx 158\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$ vs. $\approx 242\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$ for $\text{Cl}_2$).
  3. Step 3 — Identify the highest value: Thus, the overall order is $\text{Cl}_2 > \text{Br}_2 > \text{F}_2 > \text{I}_2$, making $\text{Cl}_2$ the highest and confirming Option (a).
Q84.stepsLatex:
Cl2 has the highest bond dissociation enthalpy (242.6 kJ mol−1), as F2 is weakened by strong
inter-electronic lp–lp repulsion in its compact 2p orbitals.
Q84.trapHtml: Do not rank F<sub>2</sub> highest; Cl<sub>2</sub> is highest!

Q85.conceptHtml: In chemistry, the crossed dipole arrow (7−→) has its tail (plus sign) on the positive centre and its head pointing toward the negative centre, showing the shift of electron density.
Q85.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement I: Dipole moment is indeed a vector quantity, but by standard chemistry convention its crossed arrow has the tail (crossed end) on the positive centre ($\delta^+$) and the head pointing towards the negative centre ($\delta^-$). Statement I reverses this, so Statement I is incorrect.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement II: The crossed arrow ($\mapsto$) specifically symbolizes the direction of the shift of electron density (charges) in the molecule from the positive centre to the negative centre. Thus, Statement II is correct.
  3. Step 3 — Select the matching option: Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct, confirming Option (b).
Q85.stepsLatex:
1. Statement I: False (head points toward the negative centre, tail on the positive centre).
2. Statement II: True (crossed arrow symbolizes the direction of shift of charges).
Q85.trapHtml: Remember the "+" on the tail of 7−→ sits on δ<sup>+</sup>.
Q85.finalAnsHtml: (b) Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

Q86.subtopic: MOT — Unpaired Electrons in HOMO of N2, N+, O2, O+
Q86.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Count unpaired e<sup>−</sup> in HOMO
Q86.conceptHtml: Write the valence MO occupancy using s–p mixing for N<sub>2</sub> (≤ 14e<sup>−</sup>) and no mixing for O<sub>2</sub> (> 14e<sup>−</sup>).
Q86.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall MOT Filling Order: For diatomic species with $\le 14$ electrons (like $\text{N}_2$ and $\text{N}_2^+$), $s$-$p$ mixing places $\pi 2p_x = \pi 2p_y$ below $\sigma 2p_z$. For species with $> 14$ electrons (like $\text{O}_2$ and $\text{O}_2^+$), $\sigma 2p_z$ lies below $\pi 2p_x = \pi 2p_y$, followed by degenerate antibonding $\pi^* 2p_x = \pi^* 2p_y$.
  2. Step 2 — Check $\text{N}_2$ and $\text{N}_2^+$: $\text{N}_2$ has $14$ electrons with HOMO $(\sigma 2p_z)^2$, giving $0$ unpaired electrons. Removing one electron gives $\text{N}_2^+$ ($13$ electrons) with HOMO $(\sigma 2p_z)^1$, giving $1$ unpaired electron.
  3. Step 3 — Check $\text{O}_2$ and $\text{O}_2^+$: $\text{O}_2$ has $16$ electrons with HOMO $(\pi^* 2p_x)^1(\pi^* 2p_y)^1$ by Hund's rule, giving $2$ unpaired electrons. Removing one antibonding electron gives $\text{O}_2^+$ ($15$ electrons) with HOMO $(\pi^* 2p_x)^1$, giving $1$ unpaired electron.
  4. Step 4 — Match with Options: The sequence of unpaired electrons in the HOMO is $0, 1, 2, 1$, which corresponds to option (c).

pz
• O2 (16e−): HOMO π2∗1 π2∗1 =⇒ 2 unpaired.
