Q87.subtopic: Hydrogen Bonding Strength in Forms of Water
Q87.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Ice vs Liquid water vs Impure water
Q87.conceptHtml: In solid ice, each H<sub>2</sub>O forms 4 rigid tetrahedral H-bonds; thermal motion breaks some H-bonds in liquid water, and dissolved impurities disrupt H-bonding further.
Q87.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Analyze Ice (B): In solid ice, water molecules lock into a rigid, open tetrahedral cage where every $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ molecule forms the maximum possible four hydrogen bonds with neighbouring molecules.
  2. Step 2 — Compare with Liquid Water (A): When ice melts, increased thermal kinetic energy breaks a fraction of these hydrogen bonds, so liquid water has a lower average extent of hydrogen bonding than ice.
  3. Step 3 — Compare with Impure Water (C): Dissolved solute ions or molecules in impure water get interposed between water molecules and form solute–solvent interactions, disrupting the water–water hydrogen-bond network even further.
  4. Step 4 — State the Decreasing Order: The extent of hydrogen bonding decreases in the order $\text{Ice (B)} > \text{Liquid water (A)} > \text{Impure water (C)}$, confirming option (b).
Q87.stepsLatex: Decreasing order of H-bonding: Ice (B) > Liquid water (A) > Impure water (C).
Q87.trapHtml: Maximum H-bonding occurs in crystalline ice (4 H-bonds per molecule).

Q88.format: Multi-Statement MCQ | Identify correct covalent character orders
Q88.conceptHtml: Covalent character increases with larger anion (I<sup>−</sup> > F<sup>−</sup>), higher cation charge (Sn<sup>4+</sup> > Sn<sup>2+</sup>), smaller cation (Li<sup>+</sup> > K<sup>+</sup>), and pseudo-noble gas 18e<sup>−</sup> shell (Cu<sup>+</sup> > Na<sup>+</sup>).
Q88.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall Fajan's Rules: Greater covalent character in an ionic bond is favoured by a smaller cation, higher cation charge, a pseudo-noble gas ($d^{10}$) cation configuration, and a larger (more polarisable) anion.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Cation and Anion Pairs: Between $\text{KF}$ and $\text{KI}$, $\text{I}^-$ is much larger than $\text{F}^-$, so $\text{KF} < \text{KI}$. Between $\text{LiF}$ and $\text{KF}$, $\text{Li}^+$ is smaller than $\text{K}^+$, so $\text{LiF} > \text{KF}$.
  3. Step 3 — Evaluate Charge and Electronic Configuration Pairs: Between $\text{SnCl}_4$ and $\text{SnCl}_2$, $\text{Sn}^{4+}$ has higher positive charge and smaller radius than $\text{Sn}^{2+}$, so $\text{SnCl}_4 > \text{SnCl}_2$. Between $\text{CuCl}$ and $\text{NaCl}$, $\text{Cu}^+$ ($[\text{Ar}]3d^{10}$) has poorer shielding and higher polarising power than $\text{Na}^+$ ($[\text{Ne}]$), so $\text{CuCl} > \text{NaCl}$.
  4. Step 4 — Identify All Correct Statements: Statements B ($\text{KF} < \text{KI};\ \text{LiF} > \text{KF}$), C ($\text{SnCl}_4 > \text{SnCl}_2;\ \text{CuCl} > \text{NaCl}$), and E ($\text{KF} < \text{KI};\ \text{CuCl} > \text{NaCl}$) are all correct, while A and D are incorrect. Hence the correct answer is option (d).
Q88.stepsLatex:
• B: KF < KI and LiF > KF (Correct).
• C: SnCl4 > SnCl2 and CuCl > NaCl (Correct).
• E: KF < KI and CuCl > NaCl (Correct).
Q88.trapHtml: All three (B, C, E) are true!

Q89.format: Numerical | Count sp<sup>3</sup>d species among 10 candidates
Q89.conceptHtml: sp<sup>3</sup>d hybridization corresponds to Steric Number SN = 5.
Q89.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — State the Condition for $sp^3d$ Hybridisation: A central atom is $sp^3d$ hybridised when its steric number $\text{SN} = (\text{number of } \sigma\text{-bonds}) + (\text{number of lone pairs}) = 5$.
  2. Step 2 — Compute Steric Number for the First Five Species: $\text{BrF}_5$ ($5+1=6,\ sp^3d^2$), $\text{XeF}_5^-$ ($5+2=7,\ sp^3d^3$), $\text{BF}_4^-$ ($4+0=4,\ sp^3$), $\text{ICl}_4^-$ ($4+2=6,\ sp^3d^2$), and $\text{XeF}_4$ ($4+2=6,\ sp^3d^2$). None of these five is $sp^3d$.
  3. Step 3 — Compute Steric Number for the Next Five Species: $\text{SF}_4$ ($4+1=5,\ sp^3d$), $\text{NH}_4^+$ ($4+0=4,\ sp^3$), $\text{ClF}_3$ ($3+2=5,\ sp^3d$), $\text{XeF}_2$ ($2+3=5,\ sp^3d$), and $\text{ICl}_2^-$ ($2+3=5,\ sp^3d$).
  4. Step 4 — Count the $sp^3d$ Species: The species with $sp^3d$ hybridised central atoms are $\text{SF}_4$, $\text{ClF}_3$, $\text{XeF}_2$, and $\text{ICl}_2^-$, giving a total of 4.
Q89.stepsLatex:
• BrF5 (SN = 6), XeF−5 (SN = 7), BF−4 (SN = 4), ICl4− (SN = 6), XeF4 (SN = 6).
• SF4 (4 + 1 = 5), NH+4 (4), ClF3 (3 + 2 = 5), XeF2 (2 + 3 = 5), ICl− (2 + 3 = 5).
2
Total sp3d species = 4.
Q89.trapHtml: XeF<sub>2</sub> and ICl<sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup> are linear in shape (2 bp + 3 lp), so students often miscount their hybridization as sp instead of sp<sup>3</sup>d.

Q90.subtopic: Numerical — σ Bond Pairs + Lone Pairs in XeO4−
Q90.conceptHtml: Xe has 8 valence electrons; in XeO<sup>4</sup><sub>6</sub><sup>−</sup>, Xe forms 6 σ-bonds to six oxygens (4 −O<sup>−</sup> and 2 = O).
Q90.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Count Valence Electrons on Central Xenon: Xenon belongs to Group $18$ and has $8$ valence electrons.
  2. Step 2 — Determine Bonding in $\text{XeO}_6^{4-}$: In the perxenate ion $\text{XeO}_6^{4-}$, the $4-$ charge resides on four singly bonded oxygen atoms ($\text{Xe}-\text{O}^-$), while the remaining two oxygen atoms form double bonds ($\text{Xe}=\text{O}$).
  3. Step 3 — Count $\sigma$ Bond-Pairs and Lone Pairs on Xe: Xenon forms $6$ $\sigma$-bonds (one to each of the $6$ oxygen atoms). Electrons used by Xe in bonding $= 4(1) + 2(2) = 8$, leaving $8 - 8 = 0$ non-bonding electrons ($0$ lone pairs).
  4. Step 4 — Compute the Total: Total $\sigma$ bond-pairs plus lone pairs around central Xe $= 6 + 0 =$ 6.
Q90.stepsLatex:
σ bond pairs = 6; lone pairs on Xe = 1(8 + 4 − 12) = 0 =⇒ 6 + 0 = 6.
2
Q90.trapHtml: XeO<sup>4</sup><sub>6</sub><sup>−</sup> is sp<sup>3</sup>d<sup>2</sup> octahedral with 0 lone pairs on Xe.

Q91.format: Numerical | Total non-bonded (lone-pair) electrons in NO<sup>−</sup><sub>2</sub>
Q91.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Calculate Total Valence Electrons in $\text{NO}_2^-$: Nitrogen contributes $5$, two oxygen atoms contribute $2 \times 6 = 12$, and the $-1$ charge adds $1$, giving $5 + 12 + 1 = 18$ valence electrons.
  2. Step 2 — Draw the Lewis Structure: In the nitrite ion $[\text{O}=\ddot{\text{N}}-\text{O}]^-$, nitrogen forms one double bond ($2$ shared pairs) with one oxygen and one single bond ($1$ shared pair) with the other oxygen.
  3. Step 3 — Subtract Bonding Electrons: The $3$ covalent bonds use $3 \times 2 = 6$ bonding electrons. The remaining electrons are non-bonded: $18 - 6 = 12$ electrons ($1$ lone pair on N, $2$ lone pairs on $=\text{O}$, and $3$ lone pairs on $-\text{O}^-$).
  4. Step 4 — Confirm Final Answer: Thus, the total number of non-bonded electrons in $\text{NO}_2^-$ is 12.
Q91.stepsLatex:
In the Lewis structure [O¨ = N¨ − O¨ :]−:
1. Bonding electrons = 3 bonds × 2 = 6e−.
2. Non-bonded electrons = 18 − 6 = 12 (1 lp on N + 2 lp on = O + 3 lp on −O− = 6 lp = 12e−).
Q91.trapHtml: The question asks for electrons (12), not lone pairs (6), across the entire ion (not just N)!

Q92.conceptHtml: Check unpaired electrons in both diatomic/polyatomic molecules (MOT) and 3d coordination complexes (CFT).
Q92.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Check Simple Molecules and Ions via MOT/Electron Count: $\text{O}_2$ ($16e^-$, two unpaired $e^-$ in $\pi^* 2p$), $\text{O}_2^+$ ($15e^-$, one unpaired $e^-$), $\text{O}_2^-$ ($17e^-$, one unpaired $e^-$), $\text{NO}$ ($15e^-$, one unpaired $e^-$), and $\text{NO}_2$ ($23e^-$, one unpaired $e^-$) are all paramagnetic. $\text{CO}$ ($14e^-$) has all electrons paired and is diamagnetic.
  2. Step 2 — Analyze $\text{K}_2[\text{NiCl}_4]$: Here $\text{Ni}^{2+}$ ($3d^8$) is coordinated to four weak-field $\text{Cl}^-$ ligands in a tetrahedral ($sp^3$) geometry, leaving $2$ unpaired electrons in the $3d$ orbitals; hence it is paramagnetic.
  3. Step 3 — Analyze the Other Two Complexes: In $[\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_6]\text{Cl}_3$, $\text{Co}^{3+}$ ($3d^6$) with strong-field $\text{NH}_3$ forms a low-spin $t_{2g}^6 e_g^0$ complex ($0$ unpaired $e^-$, diamagnetic). In $\text{K}_2[\text{Ni}(\text{CN})_4]$, $\text{Ni}^{2+}$ ($3d^8$) with strong-field $\text{CN}^-$ forms a square planar ($dsp^2$) complex ($0$ unpaired $e^-$, diamagnetic).
  4. Step 4 — Count Paramagnetic Species: The paramagnetic species are $\text{O}_2$, $\text{O}_2^+$, $\text{O}_2^-$, $\text{NO}$, $\text{NO}_2$, and $\text{K}_2[\text{NiCl}_4]$, giving a total of 6.

with weak-field Cl−, 2 unpaired e−).
• Diamagnetic (3): CO (14e−), [Co(NH3)6]Cl3 (Co3+ d6 low-spin t62 ), K2[Ni(CN)4] (Ni2+ d8 square planar).
g
Q92.trapHtml: [NiCl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2−</sup> is tetrahedral paramagnetic, whereas [Ni(CN)<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2−</sup> is square planar diamagnetic.

Q93.format: Numerical | Count linear species among 10 candidates
Q93.conceptHtml: Linear geometry occurs for SN = 2 (sp: 2 + 0) and SN = 5 (sp<sup>3</sup>d: 2 + 3).
Q93.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall Conditions for Linear Geometry: A triatomic species is linear either when its central atom is $sp$ hybridised with $0$ lone pairs ($\text{AB}_2$) or $sp^3d$ hybridised with $3$ equatorial lone pairs ($\text{AB}_2\text{L}_3$).
  2. Step 2 — Identify Linear Species: $\text{BeCl}_2$ ($sp$, $0$ LP), $\text{CO}_2$ ($sp$, $0$ LP), $\text{N}_3^-$ ($sp$, $0$ LP), $\text{NO}_2^+$ ($sp$, $0$ LP), $\text{XeF}_2$ ($sp^3d$, $3$ LP), and $\text{I}_3^-$ ($sp^3d$, $3$ LP) all have a linear shape ($180^\circ$).
  3. Step 3 — Eliminate Non-Linear (Bent) Species: $\text{SO}_2$ ($sp^2$, $1$ LP), $\text{NO}_2$ ($sp^2$, $1$ odd $e^-$), $\text{F}_2\text{O}$ ($sp^3$, $2$ LP), and $\text{O}_3$ ($sp^2$, $1$ LP) are all bent/angular.
  4. Step 4 — Count Total Linear Species: Counting $\text{BeCl}_2, \text{CO}_2, \text{N}_3^-, \text{XeF}_2, \text{NO}_2^+,$ and $\text{I}_3^-$ gives 6.
Q93.stepsLatex:
• Linear (6): BeCl2, CO2, N−3 , XeF2, NO+2 , I−3 .
• Bent (4): SO2, NO2, F2O, O3.
Q93.trapHtml: NO<sup>+</sup><sub>2</sub> (16e<sup>−</sup>, sp) is linear, whereas NO<sub>2</sub> (17e<sup>−</sup>) and NO<sup>−</sup><sub>2</sub> (18e<sup>−</sup>) are bent.

Q94.subtopic: Numerical — Electrons in π∗ MOs of O2, O+, O−
Q94.format: Numerical | Sum of π<sup>∗</sup> electrons across three species
Q94.conceptHtml: In O<sub>2</sub> (16e<sup>−</sup>), the HOMO is π<sub>2</sub><sup>∗</sup><sub>p</sub>.
Q94.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Write Valence MO Configuration of $\text{O}_2$: $\text{O}_2$ has $16$ total electrons. After filling up to $\pi 2p_x^2 = \pi 2p_y^2$ ($14$ electrons), the remaining $2$ electrons enter $\pi^* 2p$: $(\pi^* 2p_x)^1(\pi^* 2p_y)^1$, giving $2$ electrons in $\pi^*$ MOs.
  2. Step 2 — Find $\pi^*$ Electrons in $\text{O}_2^+$: Removing $1$ electron from the HOMO ($\pi^* 2p$) of $\text{O}_2$ leaves $(\pi^* 2p_x)^1(\pi^* 2p_y)^0$, giving $1$ electron in $\pi^*$ MOs.
  3. Step 3 — Find $\pi^*$ Electrons in $\text{O}_2^-$: Adding $1$ electron to the HOMO ($\pi^* 2p$) of $\text{O}_2$ gives $(\pi^* 2p_x)^2(\pi^* 2p_y)^1$, giving $3$ electrons in $\pi^*$ MOs.
  4. Step 4 — Sum Across All Three Species: Total $\pi^*$ electrons $= 2 + 1 + 3 =$ 6.
Q94.stepsLatex: π∗ electron counts: O<sub>2</sub> (2) + O<sup>+</sup><sub>2</sub> (1) + O−<sub>2</sub> (3) = 6.
Q94.trapHtml: Ionizing O<sub>2</sub> → O<sup>+</sup><sub>2</sub> removes 1 e<sup>−</sup> from π<sup>∗</sup>; reducing O<sub>2</sub> → O<sup>−</sup><sub>2</sub> adds 1 e<sup>−</sup> to π<sup>∗</sup>.

Q95.subtopic: Numerical — Species with Exactly One Unpaired Electron
Q95.conceptHtml: Odd-electron diatomics generally have 1 unpaired electron.
Q95.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Rule Out Even-Electron Diamagnetic or 2-Unpaired Species: $\text{N}_2$ ($14e^-$), $\text{O}_2^{2-}$ ($18e^-$), and $\text{CN}^-$ ($14e^-$) have all electrons paired ($0$ unpaired). $\text{O}_2$ ($16e^-$) has $(\pi^* 2p_x)^1(\pi^* 2p_y)^1$, which is $2$ unpaired electrons.
  2. Step 2 — Check Odd-Electron Species: Every diatomic species with an odd total electron count here has a single unpaired electron in its HOMO: $\text{C}_2^-$ ($13e^-$, HOMO $\sigma 2p_z^1$), $\text{O}_2^-$ ($17e^-$, HOMO $\pi^* 2p^3$), $\text{H}_2^+$ ($1e^-$, HOMO $\sigma 1s^1$), and $\text{He}_2^+$ ($3e^-$, HOMO $\sigma^* 1s^1$).
  3. Step 3 — Count Qualifying Species: Exactly four species ($\text{C}_2^-, \text{O}_2^-, \text{H}_2^+, \text{He}_2^+$) possess one unpaired electron.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm Final Answer: The total number of such species is 4.

Q96.conceptHtml: Compute BO = <sup>1</sup><sub>2</sub>(N<sub>b</sub> − N<sub>a</sub>) for each homonuclear diatomic.
Q96.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the Bond Order Formula: $\text{Bond Order (BO)} = \frac{N_b - N_a}{2}$, where $N_b$ and $N_a$ are the numbers of bonding and antibonding electrons.
  2. Step 2 — Calculate Bond Order for Each Molecule: $\text{C}_2$ ($12e^-$): $\text{BO} = \frac{8-4}{2} = 2$; $\text{O}_2$ ($16e^-$): $\text{BO} = \frac{10-6}{2} = 2$; $\text{Be}_2$ ($8e^-$): $\text{BO} = 0$; $\text{Li}_2$ ($6e^-$): $\text{BO} = 1$; $\text{Ne}_2$ ($20e^-$): $\text{BO} = 0$; $\text{N}_2$ ($14e^-$): $\text{BO} = 3$; $\text{He}_2$ ($4e^-$): $\text{BO} = 0$.
  3. Step 3 — Count Molecules with $\text{BO} = 2$: Only $\text{C}_2$ and $\text{O}_2$ have a bond order equal to $2$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm Final Answer: The number of molecules having bond order $2$ is 2.

= 2.

Q97.format: Numerical | Incomplete, odd-electron, and expanded octet
Q97.conceptHtml: Any molecule whose central atom has ̸= 8 valence electrons is an octet exception.
Q97.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the Three Types of Octet Rule Exceptions: Exceptions include electron-deficient (incomplete octet, $<8e^-$), odd-electron molecules, and hypervalent (expanded octet, $>8e^-$) central atoms.
  2. Step 2 — Identify All Exceptions in the List: Incomplete octet: $\text{BF}_3$ ($6e^-$ on B) and $\text{BeF}_2$ ($4e^-$ on Be). Odd-electron molecules: $\text{NO}_2$ ($7e^-$ on N) and $\text{ClO}_2$ (odd electron on Cl). Expanded octet: $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ ($12e^-$ around S) and $\text{PCl}_5$ ($10e^-$ around P).
  3. Step 3 — Verify Molecules Obeying the Octet Rule: $\text{CO}_2, \text{CH}_4, \text{SiF}_4, \text{C}_2\text{H}_6, \text{CHCl}_3,$ and $\text{CBr}_4$ all have exactly $8$ valence electrons around their central carbon or silicon atoms.
  4. Step 4 — Count the Exceptions: The six exceptions are $\text{NO}_2, \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4, \text{BF}_3, \text{ClO}_2, \text{PCl}_5,$ and $\text{BeF}_2$, giving 6.
Q97.stepsLatex:
• Exceptions (6): NO2 (7e−), H2SO4 (12e−), BF3 (6e−), ClO2 (11e−), PCl5 (10e−), BeF2 (4e−).
• Obey octet (6): CO2, CH4, SiF4, C2H6, CHCl3, CBr4.
Q97.trapHtml: Both NO<sub>2</sub> and ClO<sub>2</sub> are odd-electron species and violate the octet rule.

Q98.subtopic: Numerical — Protons Not Involved in H-Bonding in
Q98.conceptHtml: NiS + aqua regia → NiCl<sub>2</sub> (A); with dimethylglyoxime (dmgH<sub>2</sub>) + NH<sub>4</sub>OH, it forms scarlet-red [Ni(dmg)<sub>2</sub>] (B).
Q98.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify Intermediate A: $\text{NiS}$ dissolves in aqua regia ($\text{HNO}_3 + \text{HCl}$) to form nickel(II) chloride, so $\text{A} = \text{NiCl}_2$.
  2. Step 2 — Identify Product B: Treating $\text{NiCl}_2$ with dimethylglyoxime ($\text{dmgH}$) in ammoniacal medium ($\text{NH}_4\text{OH}$) precipitates the classic rosy-red square planar complex $\text{B} = [\text{Ni}(\text{dmg})_2]$.
  3. Step 3 — Count Protons and Hydrogen Bonds in $[\text{Ni}(\text{dmg})_2]$: Each $\text{dmg}^-$ ligand ($\text{CH}_3\text{C}(=\text{NOH})\text{C}(=\text{NO}^-)\text{CH}_3$) contains $2$ methyl groups ($6$ protons) and $1$ oximino $-\text{OH}$ proton. Across two $\text{dmg}^-$ ligands, there are $14$ total protons: the $2$ oximino protons form two strong intramolecular $\text{O}-\text{H}\cdots\text{O}$ hydrogen bonds between the ligands.
  4. Step 4 — Find Protons Not Involved in H-Bonding: The remaining $4$ methyl groups ($4 \times 3 = 12$ protons) do not participate in hydrogen bonding. Hence the answer is 12.

1. Each dmg− ligand has two −CH3 groups (6 H) and one −OH group (1 H).
2. In [Ni(dmg)2], both oxime −OH protons (2 H) form strong intramolecular O − H · · · O hydrogen bonds.
3. The four −CH3 groups contain 4 × 3 = 12 protons that do NOT participate in H-bonding.
Q98.trapHtml: Total protons in [Ni(dmg)<sub>2</sub>] is 14: 2 are H-bonded, 12 (methyl protons) are not.

Q99.subtopic: Numerical — Central Atom Using sp2 Hybrid Orbitals
Q99.format: Numerical | Count sp<sup>2</sup> species among 11 candidates
Q99.conceptHtml: Look for SN = 3 around the central atom(s).
Q99.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — State the Condition for $sp^2$ Hybridisation: A central atom uses $sp^2$ hybrid orbitals when its steric number ($\sigma$-bonds + lone pairs) equals $3$.
  2. Step 2 — Identify $sp^2$ Hybridised Species: $\text{SO}_2$ ($2\sigma + 1\text{ LP} = 3$), $\text{C}_2\text{H}_4$ (each C has $3\sigma + 0\text{ LP} = 3$), $\text{BCl}_3$ ($3\sigma + 0\text{ LP} = 3$), $\text{HCHO}$ (C has $3\sigma + 0\text{ LP} = 3$), $\text{C}_6\text{H}_6$ (each C has $3\sigma + 0\text{ LP} = 3$), and $\text{BF}_3$ ($3\sigma + 0\text{ LP} = 3$).
  3. Step 3 — Check Remaining Species: $\text{NH}_3$ ($sp^3$), $\text{SiO}_2$ (3D covalent network with $sp^3$ Si), $\text{BeCl}_2$ ($sp$), $\text{C}_2\text{H}_2$ ($sp$), and $\text{C}_2\text{H}_4\text{Cl}_2$ ($sp^3$ carbons) do not use $sp^2$ hybridisation.
  4. Step 4 — Count Total $sp^2$ Species: There are $6$ qualifying species ($\text{SO}_2, \text{C}_2\text{H}_4, \text{BCl}_3, \text{HCHO}, \text{C}_6\text{H}_6, \text{BF}_3$), so the answer is 6.
Q99.stepsLatex:
• SO2 (sp2), C2H4 (sp2), BCl3 (sp2), HCHO (sp2), C6H6 (sp2), BF3 (sp2) =⇒ 6 species.
• Others: NH3 (sp3), SiO2 (sp3 3D network), BeCl2 (sp), C2H2 (sp), C2H4Cl2 (sp3).

Q100.conceptHtml: A molecule exhibits H-bonding (inter- or intramolecular) if H is covalently attached to F, O, N.
Q100.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the Condition for Hydrogen Bonding: A molecule can form hydrogen bonds when a hydrogen atom is covalently bonded to a small, highly electronegative atom ($\text{F}, \text{O},$ or $\text{N}$).
  2. Step 2 — Inspect the Seven Molecules Shown: The diagram lists $\text{CH}_3\text{OH}$, $\text{H}_2\text{O}$, $\text{C}_2\text{H}_6$, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_6$, $o$-nitrophenol, $\text{HF}$, and $\text{NH}_3$.
  3. Step 3 — Classify Each Molecule: $\text{CH}_3\text{OH}$, $\text{H}_2\text{O}$, $\text{HF}$, and $\text{NH}_3$ exhibit intermolecular H-bonding, while $o$-nitrophenol exhibits intramolecular H-bonding between its $-\text{OH}$ and $-\text{NO}_2$ groups. $\text{C}_2\text{H}_6$ and $\text{C}_6\text{H}_6$ have only non-polar $\text{C}-\text{H}$ bonds and cannot H-bond.
  4. Step 4 — Count Total Molecules: Five molecules ($\text{CH}_3\text{OH}, \text{H}_2\text{O}, o\text{-nitrophenol}, \text{HF}, \text{NH}_3$) exhibit hydrogen bonding, giving 5.

• C2H6 and C6H6 have only C − H bonds (no H-bonding).

Q101.conceptHtml: Symmetric geometries with identical terminal atoms have µ = 0.
Q101.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall When Dipole Moment Is Zero: A molecule has $\mu = 0$ if it is a homonuclear diatomic or has a perfectly symmetrical geometry with identical surrounding atoms and no lone-pair asymmetry, causing all bond dipoles to cancel.
  2. Step 2 — Identify Zero-Dipole Molecules: $\text{H}_2$ (homonuclear), $\text{CO}_2$ (linear symmetric), $\text{BF}_3$ (trigonal planar symmetric), $\text{CH}_4$ (tetrahedral symmetric), $\text{SiF}_4$ (tetrahedral symmetric), and $\text{BeF}_2$ (linear symmetric) all have $\mu = 0$.
  3. Step 3 — Eliminate Polar Molecules: $\text{HF}$ (heteronuclear), $\text{H}_2\text{S}$ (bent), $\text{NH}_3$ (trigonal pyramidal), $\text{CHCl}_3$ (asymmetric tetrahedral), and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ (bent) all have $\mu \neq 0$.
  4. Step 4 — Count Total Non-Polar Species: Counting $\text{H}_2, \text{CO}_2, \text{BF}_3, \text{CH}_4, \text{SiF}_4,$ and $\text{BeF}_2$ gives 6.
Q101.stepsLatex:
• Zero µ (6): H2 (homonuclear), CO2 (linear), BF3 (trigonal planar), CH4 (Td), SiF4 (Td), BeF2 (linear).
• Non-zero µ (5): HF, H2S, NH3, CHCl3, H2O.
Q101.trapHtml: Don’t forget homonuclear H<sub>2</sub> has µ = 0!

Q102.subtopic: Numerical — Valence Electrons Around N in NO−
Q102.format: Numerical | Lewis dot octet around central N
Q102.conceptHtml: In the Lewis structure [O¨ = N¨ − O¨ :]<sup>−</sup>, nitrogen obeys the octet rule.
Q102.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Draw the Lewis Dot Structure of $\text{NO}_2^-$: In $[\text{O}=\ddot{\text{N}}-\text{O}]^-$, the central nitrogen atom forms one double bond ($\text{N}=\text{O}$) and one single bond ($\text{N}-\text{O}^-$), and retains one lone pair.
  2. Step 2 — Count Shared Electrons Around Nitrogen: The double bond contributes $4$ shared electrons and the single bond contributes $2$ shared electrons, making $4 + 2 = 6$ bonding electrons around N.
  3. Step 3 — Add Non-Bonded Electrons on Nitrogen: Including the $1$ lone pair ($2$ electrons) on nitrogen gives $6 + 2 = 8$ valence electrons (a complete octet).
  4. Step 4 — Confirm Final Answer: The total number of valence electrons around nitrogen in $\text{NO}_2^-$ is 8.
Q102.stepsLatex: Nitrogen has 3 bonding pairs (6e−) +1 lone pair (2e−) = 8 valence electrons around it.
Q102.trapHtml: Note the contrast with Q91: Q91 asked for total non-bonded e<sup>−</sup> in the whole ion (12); Q102 asks for valence e<sup>−</sup> around nitrogen (8).

Q103.conceptHtml: Asymmetric or bent/pyramidal molecules with polar bonds have µ ̸= 0.
Q103.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Separate Symmetrical Non-Polar Species ($\mu = 0$): $\text{BeCl}_2$ (linear), $\text{BCl}_3$ (trigonal planar), $\text{XeF}_4$ (square planar), $\text{CCl}_4$ (tetrahedral), $\text{CO}_2$ (linear), and $\text{H}_2$ (homonuclear diatomic) all have $\mu = 0$.
  2. Step 2 — Identify Polar Species ($\mu \neq 0$): $\text{NF}_3$ (trigonal pyramidal, $1$ LP), $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ (bent, $2$ LP), $\text{H}_2\text{S}$ (bent, $2$ LP), $\text{HBr}$ (heteronuclear diatomic), and $\text{HCl}$ (heteronuclear diatomic) have net non-zero dipole moments.
  3. Step 3 — Count Qualifying Species: There are $5$ species with non-zero dipole moment: $\text{NF}_3, \text{H}_2\text{O}, \text{H}_2\text{S}, \text{HBr},$ and $\text{HCl}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm Final Answer: The total number of species with non-zero dipole moment is 5.
Q103.stepsLatex:
• Non-zero µ (5): NF3, H2O, H2S, HBr, HCl.
• Zero µ (6): BeCl2, BCl3, XeF4, CCl4, CO2, H2.
Q103.trapHtml: XeF<sub>4</sub> is square planar (4 + 2), so its four Xe − F dipoles cancel completely (µ = 0).

Q104.subtopic: Numerical — Species with One Unpaired Electron
Q104.conceptHtml: Count odd-electron species with 1 unpaired electron.

1. Step 1 — Count Total Electrons in Each Species: $\text{O}_2$ ($16e^-$), $\text{O}_2^-$ ($17e^-$), $\text{NO}$ ($15e^-$), $\text{CN}^-$ ($14e^-$), and $\text{O}_2^{2-}$ ($18e^-$).

Step 2 — Determine Unpaired Electrons via MOT: $\text{O}_2$ has $(\pi^* 2p_x)^1(\pi^* 2p_y)^1 \Rightarrow 2$ unpaired $e^-$; $\text{O}_2^-$ has $(\pi^* 2p_x)^2(\pi^* 2p_y)^1 \Rightarrow$ $1$ unpaired $e^-$; $\text{NO}$ has $(\pi^* 2p_x)^1 \Rightarrow$ $1$ unpaired $e^-$; $\text{CN}^-$ ($14e^-$) and $\text{O}_2^{2-}$ ($18e^-$) have $0$ unpaired $e^-$.
  3. Step 3 — Count Species with One Unpaired Electron: Only $\text{O}_2^-$ and $\text{NO}$ have exactly one unpaired electron.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm Final Answer: The required count is 2.

Q105.format: Numerical | Count 5 bp + 0 lp TBP species
Q105.conceptHtml: Trigonal bipyramidal shape requires 5 bond pairs and 0 lone pairs.
Q105.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall Condition for Trigonal Bipyramidal (TBP) Shape: A species has TBP shape when the central atom has $5$ bond pairs and $0$ lone pairs ($sp^3d$ or $dsp^3$ hybridisation).
  2. Step 2 — Identify TBP Species: $\text{PF}_5$ ($5\text{ BP} + 0\text{ LP},\ sp^3d$), $\text{PCl}_5$ ($5\text{ BP} + 0\text{ LP},\ sp^3d$), and $\text{Fe}(\text{CO})_5$ ($5$ CO ligands around $\text{Fe}(0)$, $dsp^3$) all adopt a trigonal bipyramidal shape.
  3. Step 3 — Check Remaining Species: $\text{BrF}_5$ ($5\text{ BP} + 1\text{ LP}$) is square pyramidal, $[\text{PtCl}_4]^{2-}$ ($dsp^2$) is square planar, and $\text{BF}_3$ ($3\text{ BP} + 0\text{ LP}$) is trigonal planar.
  4. Step 4 — Count TBP Species: Counting $\text{PF}_5$, $\text{PCl}_5$, and $\text{Fe}(\text{CO})_5$ gives 3.

Q106.subtopic: Numerical — Valence Electrons from Lowest Oxidation State
Q106.conceptHtml: Minimum oxidation number of a non-metal = Group − 18 = Valence e<sup>−</sup> − 8.
Q106.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the Element with Lowest Oxidation State: In a compound of formula $\text{A}_2\text{B}$, the oxidation state of $\text{B}$ is $-2$ (with $\text{A}$ at $+1$, as in $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ or $\text{Na}_2\text{S}$).
  2. Step 2 — Relate Minimum Oxidation Number to Valence Electrons: For a representative non-metal, the lowest oxidation number corresponds to gaining enough electrons to complete its octet: $\text{Minimum OS} = (\text{Valence electrons}) - 8$.
  3. Step 3 — Solve for Valence Electrons: Setting $(\text{Valence electrons}) - 8 = -2$ gives $\text{Valence electrons} = 8 - 2 = 6$ (Group $16$, oxygen family).
  4. Step 4 — Confirm Final Answer: The number of electrons in its valence shell is 6.
Q106.stepsLatex:
In A2B (e.g., H2O, Na2S), B has oxidation number −2 =⇒ V − 8 = −2 =⇒ V = 6 valence
electrons.
Q106.trapHtml: Lowest oxidation state −2 corresponds to Group 16 (chalcogens, ns<sup>2</sup>np<sup>4</sup>).

Q107.subtopic: Numerical — Dipole Moment Fractional Charge Unit Trap
Q107.format: Numerical | µ = q × d unit conversion
Q107.conceptHtml: µ = q × d =⇒ q = µ. d 1.2 × 10<sup>−18</sup> esu cm <sub>10</sub> <sub>9</sub> <sub>1</sub> <sub>9</sub>

1. Step 1 — Convert Given Quantities to CGS Units: Dipole moment $\mu = 1.2\text{ D} = 1.2 \times 10^{-18}\text{ esu}\cdot\text{cm}$, and bond distance $d = 1\text{ \AA} = 10^{-8}\text{ cm}$.
  2. Step 2 — Calculate Charge $q$ on Each Atom: Using $\mu = q \times d$, we get $q = \frac{\mu}{d} = \frac{1.2 \times 10^{-18}\text{ esu}\cdot\text{cm}}{10^{-8}\text{ cm}} = 1.2 \times 10^{-10}\text{ esu}$.

Step 3 — Express in Terms of the Printed Factor ($\times 10^{-1}\text{ esu}$): Rewriting $1.2 \times 10^{-10}\text{ esu}$ as $1.2 \times 10^{-9} \times 10^{-1}\text{ esu}$ shows that the coefficient before $10^{-1}\text{ esu}$ is $0.0000000012$ (the exam prompt printed $10^{-1}$ instead of $10^{-10}$).
  4. Step 4 — Round to Nearest Integer: Rounding $1.2 \times 10^{-9}$ to the nearest integer gives 0.

Q108.format: Numerical | Count sp<sup>3</sup> species among 8 candidates
Q108.conceptHtml: Check SN = 4 for each species, including network solids.

  2. Step 2 — Identify $sp^3$ Hybridised Species: $\text{NH}_3$ ($3\sigma + 1\text{ LP} = 4$), $\text{SiO}_2$ (3D covalent network where each Si forms $4$ single $\sigma$-bonds to O, $\text{SN} = 4$), $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ ($2\sigma + 2\text{ LP} = 4$), and $\text{CH}_4$ ($4\sigma + 0\text{ LP} = 4$).
  3. Step 3 — Eliminate Non-$sp^3$ Species: $\text{SO}_2$ ($sp^2$), $\text{BeCl}_2$ ($sp$), $\text{CO}_2$ ($sp$), and $\text{BF}_3$ ($sp^2$) have steric numbers $2$ or $3$.
  4. Step 4 — Count Total $sp^3$ Species: Counting $\text{NH}_3$, $\text{SiO}_2$, $\text{H}_2\text{O}$, and $\text{CH}_4$ gives 4.

Q109.subtopic: Numerical — Total MOs from 2s and 2p Atomic Orbitals
Q109.format: Numerical | Conservation of orbital count in MOT
Q109.conceptHtml: Total MOs formed = Total combining AOs from both atoms.
Q109.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Count Atomic Orbitals Contributed by Each Atom: In the $n = 2$ shell, each atom has one $2s$ orbital and three $2p$ orbitals ($2p_x, 2p_y, 2p_z$), giving $1 + 3 = 4$ atomic orbitals per atom.
  2. Step 2 — Apply Conservation of Orbitals (LCAO): The total number of molecular orbitals formed always equals the total number of combining atomic orbitals. For two atoms, total AOs $= 4 + 4 = 8$.
  3. Step 3 — List the Resulting Molecular Orbitals: They consist of $4$ bonding MOs ($\sigma 2s, \sigma 2p_z, \pi 2p_x, \pi 2p_y$) and $4$ antibonding MOs ($\sigma^* 2s, \pi^* 2p_x, \pi^* 2p_y, \sigma^* 2p_z$).
  4. Step 4 — Confirm Final Answer: The total number of molecular orbitals formed is 8.
Q109.stepsLatex:
Each atom contributes one 2s + three 2p = 4 AOs. Across two atoms: 4 + 4 = 8 molecular
orbitals (4 bonding + 4 antibonding).
Q109.trapHtml: Do not include 1s orbitals when the question specifies 2s and 2p only.

Q110.format: Numerical | Count non-polar molecules among 7 candidates
Q110.conceptHtml: Symmetric CH<sub>4</sub>, BF<sub>3</sub>, CO<sub>2</sub> have µ = 0.
Q110.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify Symmetrical Zero-Dipole Molecules: $\text{CH}_4$ (regular tetrahedral), $\text{BF}_3$ (symmetrical trigonal planar), and $\text{CO}_2$ (symmetrical linear) have bond dipoles that cancel completely, giving $\mu = 0$.
  2. Step 2 — Check Remaining Molecules: $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ (bent, $2$ LP), $\text{HF}$ (heteronuclear diatomic), $\text{NH}_3$ (trigonal pyramidal, $1$ LP), and $\text{SO}_2$ (bent, $1$ LP) all possess a net non-zero dipole moment.
  3. Step 3 — Count Qualifying Molecules: Exactly three molecules ($\text{CH}_4, \text{BF}_3, \text{CO}_2$) have zero dipole moment.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm Final Answer: The total number of molecules with $\mu = 0$ is 3.
Q110.stepsLatex: Zero µ (3): CH<sub>4</sub>, BF<sub>3</sub>, CO<sub>2</sub>. (Polar (4): H<sub>2</sub>O, HF, NH<sub>3</sub>, SO<sub>2</sub>.)
Q110.trapHtml: SO<sub>2</sub> is bent (2 bp + 1 lp), so it has µ ̸= 0 (1.62 D).

Q111.format: Numerical | Half of total MOs are antibonding
Q111.conceptHtml: Every pair of combining AOs forms 1 bonding MO and 1 antibonding MO.
Q111.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Count Total Combining Atomic Orbitals: Each atom in a diatomic molecule contributes $4$ valence atomic orbitals ($2s, 2p_x, 2p_y, 2p_z$), giving $4 + 4 = 8$ total molecular orbitals.
  2. Step 2 — Split into Bonding and Antibonding MOs: Every pair of combining atomic orbitals generates one bonding MO and one antibonding MO, so half of the $8$ MOs are antibonding.
  3. Step 3 — Name the Four Antibonding MOs: They are $\sigma^* 2s$, $\pi^* 2p_x$, $\pi^* 2p_y$, and $\sigma^* 2p_z$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm Final Answer: The total number of antibonding molecular orbitals is 4.

Out of 8 total MOs from 2s and 2p (4+4), exactly half are antibonding: σ2∗ , π2∗ , π2∗ , σ2∗ =⇒
s px py pz
4.

Q112.format: Numerical | MOT dual filter: paramagnetic AND BO = 1
Q112.conceptHtml: Compute both BO and unpaired electrons for each species.
Q112.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Filter for Bond Order $= 1$: Computing $\text{BO} = \frac{N_b - N_a}{2}$: $\text{H}_2$ ($2e^-$, $\text{BO}=1$), $\text{He}_2^+$ ($3e^-$, $\text{BO}=0.5$), $\text{O}_2^+$ ($15e^-$, $\text{BO}=2.5$), $\text{N}_2^{2-}$ ($16e^-$, $\text{BO}=2$), $\text{O}_2^{2-}$ ($18e^-$, $\text{BO}=1$), $\text{F}_2$ ($18e^-$, $\text{BO}=1$), $\text{Ne}_2^+$ ($19e^-$, $\text{BO}=0.5$), and $\text{B}_2$ ($10e^-$, $\text{BO}=1$).
  2. Step 2 — Check Magnetism of the $\text{BO} = 1$ Candidates: $\text{H}_2$ ($\sigma 1s^2$), $\text{O}_2^{2-}$ ($\pi^* 2p^4$), and $\text{F}_2$ ($\pi^* 2p^4$) have all electrons paired and are diamagnetic.
  3. Step 3 — Verify $\text{B}_2$: Because of $s$-$p$ mixing, $\text{B}_2$ ($10e^-$) has configuration $(\sigma 1s)^2(\sigma^* 1s)^2(\sigma 2s)^2(\sigma^* 2s)^2(\pi 2p_x)^1(\pi 2p_y)^1$, which gives $\text{BO} = 1$ and $2$ unpaired electrons (paramagnetic).
  4. Step 4 — Confirm Final Answer: Only $\text{B}_2$ satisfies both conditions, so the answer is 1.

Q113.subtopic: Numerical — Compounds with One Lone Pair on Central
Q113.conceptHtml: Calculate lone pairs on the central atom for each.
Q113.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Formula for Lone Pairs on Central Atom: $\text{LP} = \frac{\text{Valence } e^- \text{ of central atom} - \text{Electrons used in bonding}}{2}$.
  2. Step 2 — Check Species with One Lone Pair: $\text{O}_3$ (central O has $6$ valence $e^-$, forms $1$ double bond and $1$ coordinate bond $\Rightarrow 1$ LP), $\text{SF}_4$ ($\frac{6-4}{2} = 1$ LP), $\text{NH}_3$ ($\frac{5-3}{2} = 1$ LP), and $\text{BrF}_5$ ($\frac{7-5}{2} = 1$ LP).
  3. Step 3 — Check Remaining Species: $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ ($\frac{6-2}{2} = 2$ LP), $\text{ClF}_3$ ($\frac{7-3}{2} = 2$ LP), and $\text{XeF}_4$ ($\frac{8-4}{2} = 2$ LP) each have two lone pairs on the central atom.
  4. Step 4 — Count Qualifying Compounds: Four compounds ($\text{O}_3, \text{SF}_4, \text{NH}_3, \text{BrF}_5$) have one lone pair on the central atom, giving 4.
Q113.stepsLatex:
• 1 lone pair (4): O3 (2 + 1), SF4 (4 + 1), NH3 (3 + 1), BrF5 (5 + 1).
• Others: H2O (2), ClF3 (2), XeF4 (2).
Q113.trapHtml: Central O in O<sub>3</sub> has 1 lone pair (2σ + 1 lp).

Q114.format: Numerical | Count µ = 0 molecules among 10 candidates
Q114.conceptHtml: Homonuclear diatomics and symmetric geometries with identical terminal atoms have µ = 0.
Q114.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify Non-Polar Molecules ($\mu = 0$): $\text{H}_2$ (homonuclear diatomic), $\text{CO}_2$ (linear symmetric), $\text{CH}_4$ (tetrahedral symmetric), and $\text{BF}_3$ (trigonal planar symmetric) have zero net dipole moment.
  2. Step 2 — Identify Polar Molecules ($\mu \neq 0$): $\text{HF}$ and $\text{HCl}$ (heteronuclear diatomics), $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ and $\text{SO}_2$ (bent with lone pairs), $\text{NH}_3$ (trigonal pyramidal), and $\text{CHCl}_3$ (unsymmetrical tetrahedral) are all polar.
  3. Step 3 — Count Non-Polar Molecules: Counting $\text{H}_2$, $\text{CO}_2$, $\text{CH}_4$, and $\text{BF}_3$ gives $4$ non-polar molecules.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm Final Answer: The number of non-polar molecules is 4.
Q114.stepsLatex: Non-polar (4): H<sub>2</sub>, CO<sub>2</sub>, CH<sub>4</sub>, BF<sub>3</sub>. (Polar (6): HF, H<sub>2</sub>O, SO<sub>2</sub>, NH<sub>3</sub>, HCl, CHCl<sub>3</sub>.)
Q114.trapHtml: Do not overlook H<sub>2</sub> in the list!

Q115.subtopic: Numerical — Sum of Bond Orders of CO and NO+
Q115.conceptHtml: Both CO and NO<sup>+</sup> have 14 electrons.
Q115.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Count Total Electrons in $\text{CO}$ and $\text{NO}^+$: $\text{CO}$ has $6 + 8 = 14$ electrons, and $\text{NO}^+$ has $7 + 8 - 1 = 14$ electrons. Both species are isoelectronic with $\text{N}_2$.
  2. Step 2 — Determine Bond Order of Each Species: By MOT, any $14$-electron diatomic species has $N_b = 10$ and $N_a = 4$, giving $\text{BO} = \frac{10 - 4}{2} = 3$. Thus $\text{BO}(\text{CO}) = 3$ and $\text{BO}(\text{NO}^+) = 3$.
  3. Step 3 — Add the Bond Orders: $\text{Sum} = 3 + 3 = 6$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm Final Answer: The sum of bond orders of $\text{CO}$ and $\text{NO}^+$ is 6.

Q116.subtopic: Numerical — Maximum Lone Pairs on Central Atom
Q116.format: Numerical | Max lp among ClO<sup>−</sup><sub>3</sub> , XeF<sub>4</sub>, SF<sub>4</sub>, I<sup>−</sup><sub>3</sub>
Q116.conceptHtml: Count central-atom lone pairs for all four species.
Q116.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Find Lone Pairs on Central Atom of Each Species: Use $\text{LP} = \frac{V - \text{bonding } e^- \pm \text{charge}}{2}$ for each central atom.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate All Four Species: In $\text{ClO}_3^-$, Cl uses $5$ valence $e^-$ (two $\text{Cl}=\text{O}$ and one $\text{Cl}-\text{O}^-$), leaving $7 - 5 = 2e^- \Rightarrow 1$ LP. In $\text{XeF}_4$, $\frac{8 - 4}{2} = 2$ LP. In $\text{SF}_4$, $\frac{6 - 4}{2} = 1$ LP. In $\text{I}_3^-$, central I has $7 + 1 = 8$ valence $e^-$ and forms $2$ single bonds, leaving $\frac{8 - 2}{2} = 3$ LP.
  3. Step 3 — Identify the Maximum: Comparing $1, 2, 1,$ and $3$, the maximum number of lone pairs on the central atom is $3$ (in $\text{I}_3^-$).
  4. Step 4 — Confirm Final Answer: The maximum number of lone pairs is 3.
Q116.trapHtml: I<sup>−</sup><sub>3</sub> (2 bp + 3 lp) has 3 equatorial lone pairs.

Q117.subtopic: Numerical — Molecules with Only Two Lone Pairs
Q117.format: Numerical | Total lone pairs in entire molecule = 2
Q117.conceptHtml: Count total lone pairs in the Lewis structure of the whole molecule (not just the central atom).
Q117.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Interpret "Only Two Lone Pairs" for the Entire Molecule: Count the total lone pairs on all atoms in each molecule's Lewis structure.
  2. Step 2 — Identify Molecules with Exactly 2 Lone Pairs: $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ ($2$ LP on O, $0$ on H $\Rightarrow 2$ LP total), $\text{N}_2$ ($:\text{N}\equiv\text{N}:$, $1$ LP on each N $\Rightarrow 2$ LP total), and $\text{CO}$ ($:\text{C}\equiv\text{O}:$, $1$ LP on C and $1$ LP on O $\Rightarrow 2$ LP total).
  3. Step 3 — Check Remaining Molecules: $\text{XeF}_4$ ($2$ on Xe $+ 12$ on four F $= 14$ LP), $\text{NH}_3$ ($1$ LP), $\text{NO}$ ($3$ LP + $1$ unpaired $e^-$), $\text{CO}_2$ ($4$ LP, $2$ on each O), and $\text{F}_2$ ($6$ LP, $3$ on each F).
  4. Step 4 — Confirm Final Answer: Exactly three molecules ($\text{H}_2\text{O}, \text{N}_2, \text{CO}$) contain only two lone pairs of electrons, giving 3.

• H2O: 2 lp on O (total = 2).
• N2: 1 lp on each N (total = 2).
• CO: 1 lp on C +1 lp on O (total = 2).
• Others: XeF4 (2 + 12 = 14), NH3 (1), NO (1 + 2 = 3 + 1e−), CO2 (4), F2 (6).
Total = 3.
Q117.trapHtml: Count lone pairs on ALL atoms in the molecule: H<sub>2</sub>O, N<sub>2</sub>, CO each have 2 total lone pairs.

Q118.format: Numerical | Count bent species among N<sup>−</sup><sub>3</sub> , NO<sup>−</sup><sub>2</sub> , I<sup>−</sup><sub>3</sub> , O<sub>3</sub>, SO<sub>2</sub>
Q118.conceptHtml: Bent shape requires 2σ-bonds with 1 or 2 lone pairs (sp<sup>2</sup> or sp<sup>3</sup>).
Q118.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Determine Hybridisation and Lone Pairs for Each Species: $\text{N}_3^-$ ($sp$, $2\text{ BP} + 0\text{ LP} \Rightarrow$ linear); $\text{NO}_2^-$ ($sp^2$, $2\text{ BP} + 1\text{ LP} \Rightarrow$ bent); $\text{I}_3^-$ ($sp^3d$, $2\text{ BP} + 3\text{ LP} \Rightarrow$ linear); $\text{O}_3$ ($sp^2$, $2\text{ BP} + 1\text{ LP} \Rightarrow$ bent); $\text{SO}_2$ ($sp^2$, $2\text{ BP} + 1\text{ LP} \Rightarrow$ bent).
  2. Step 2 — Group the Bent-Shaped Species: $\text{NO}_2^-$, $\text{O}_3$, and $\text{SO}_2$ are all V-shaped (bent) due to one lone pair on an $sp^2$ central atom.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm Final Answer: The number of bent-shaped molecules/ions is 3.

Q118.trapHtml: N<sup>−</sup><sub>3</sub> (sp, 0 lp) and I<sup>−</sup><sub>3</sub> (sp<sup>3</sup>d, 3 lp) are both linear.

Q119.subtopic: Numerical — Sum of Central Lone Pairs in IF5 and IF7
Q119.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Find Lone Pairs on Iodine in $\text{IF}_5$: Iodine has $7$ valence electrons and forms $5$ single bonds with fluorine, leaving $7 - 5 = 2$ non-bonding electrons, i.e., $1$ lone pair.
  2. Step 2 — Find Lone Pairs on Iodine in $\text{IF}_7$: Iodine uses all $7$ valence electrons to form $7$ single bonds with fluorine, leaving $7 - 7 = 0$ lone pairs.
  3. Step 3 — Sum the Lone Pairs: $\text{Total lone pairs} = 1 + 0 = 1$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm Final Answer: The sum of lone pairs on the central atom of $\text{IF}_5$ and $\text{IF}_7$ is 1.
Q119.stepsLatex: IF<sub>5</sub> has 1 lp; IF<sub>7</sub> has 0 lp =⇒ 1 + 0 = 1.
Q119.trapHtml: IF<sub>7</sub> uses all 7 valence electrons of iodine in bonding (0 lp).

Q120.subtopic: Numerical — Xenon Species with Single Lone Pair
Q120.format: Numerical | Count 1-lp Xe species among 7 candidates
Q120.conceptHtml: Each = O uses 2 valence electrons of Xe; each −F uses 1.
Q120.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Count Lone Pairs on Central Xe ($8$ Valence $e^-$): Each fluorine uses $1$ electron from Xe, each oxygen uses $2$ electrons (double bond), a $+1$ charge removes $1$ electron, and a $-1$ charge adds $1$ electron.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Each Xenon Species: $\text{XeF}_5^+$: $\frac{8 - 1 - 5}{2} = 1$ LP; $\text{XeO}_3$: $\frac{8 - 6}{2} = 1$ LP; $\text{XeO}_2\text{F}_2$: $\frac{8 - 4 - 2}{2} = 1$ LP; $\text{XeF}_5^-$: $\frac{8 + 1 - 5}{2} = 2$ LP; $\text{XeO}_3\text{F}_2$: $\frac{8 - 6 - 2}{2} = 0$ LP; $\text{XeOF}_4$: $\frac{8 - 2 - 4}{2} = 1$ LP; $\text{XeF}_4$: $\frac{8 - 4}{2} = 2$ LP.
  3. Step 3 — Count Species with a Single Lone Pair: The four species with exactly $1$ lone pair on Xe are $\text{XeF}_5^+$, $\text{XeO}_3$, $\text{XeO}_2\text{F}_2$, and $\text{XeOF}_4$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm Final Answer: The total number of such species is 4.

Q121.format: Numerical | Identify factors affecting covalent character
Q121.conceptHtml: By Fajan’s rules, covalent character depends on (A) polarising power of cation, (C) polarisability of anion, and (B) extent of distortion of anion.
Q121.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall Fajan's Rules of Polarisation: Covalent character in an ionic bond arises when the positively charged cation attracts and distorts the electron cloud of the negatively charged anion.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Each Listed Factor: (A) Polarising power of the cation — Yes, directly determines how strongly it distorts the anion. (B) Extent of distortion of the anion — Yes, greater distortion means greater electron sharing (covalent character). (C) Polarisability of the anion — Yes, measures how easily the anion's electron cloud is distorted.
  3. Step 3 — Eliminate Factor (D): (D) Polarising power of the anion — No, because anions are polarised by cations rather than acting as the polarising species.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm Final Answer: Three factors (A, B, and C) affect the percent covalent character, giving 3.
Q121.stepsLatex:
Statements (A), (B), and (C) are valid factors (3 factors); (D) "polarising power of anion" is
incorrect (anions are polarised, cations polarise).
Q121.trapHtml: Cations have polarising power; anions have polarisability.

Q122.format: Numerical | Count 4 bp + 2 lp (sp<sup>3</sup>d<sup>2</sup>) and dsp<sup>2</sup> complexes
Q122.conceptHtml: Square planar occurs in main-group 4 bp + 2 lp (sp<sup>3</sup>d<sup>2</sup>) and d<sup>8</sup>/d<sup>9</sup> dsp<sup>2</sup> complexes.
Q122.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall Conditions for Square Planar Shape: Main-group species are square planar when $\text{SN} = 6$ with $4\text{ BP} + 2\text{ LP}$ ($sp^3d^2$); $d^8/d^9$ coordination complexes are square planar when $dsp^2$ hybridised.
  2. Step 2 — Identify Square Planar Species: $\text{XeF}_4$ ($4\text{ BP} + 2\text{ LP},\ sp^3d^2$), $\text{BrF}_4^-$ ($4\text{ BP} + 2\text{ LP},\ sp^3d^2$), $[\text{Cu}(\text{NH}_3)_4]^{2+}$ ($d^9,\ dsp^2$), and $[\text{PtCl}_4]^{2-}$ ($5d^8,\ dsp^2$) are all square planar.
  3. Step 3 — Eliminate Non-Square-Planar Species: $\text{SF}_4$ is see-saw ($4\text{ BP} + 1\text{ LP}$), while $\text{SiF}_4$, $\text{BF}_4^-$, and $[\text{FeCl}_4]^{2-}$ (weak-field $\text{Cl}^-$, $sp^3$) are tetrahedral.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm Final Answer: Counting $\text{XeF}_4, \text{BrF}_4^-, [\text{Cu}(\text{NH}_3)_4]^{2+},$ and $[\text{PtCl}_4]^{2-}$ gives 4.
Q122.stepsLatex:
• Square planar (4): XeF4 (4 + 2), BrF−4 (4 + 2), [Cu(NH3)4]2+ (dsp2), [PtCl4]2− (dsp2).
• Others: SF4 (see-saw), SiF4, BF−4 , [FeCl4]2− (tetrahedral).
Q122.trapHtml: Both [Cu(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> and [PtCl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2−</sup> are classic dsp<sup>2</sup> square planar complexes.

Q123.subtopic: Numerical — H-Bonds per H2O in Ice
Q123.conceptHtml: In crystalline ice, each oxygen is tetrahedrally surrounded by four other oxygens via H-bonds.
Q123.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Examine the Structure of a Water Molecule: Each $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ molecule has $2$ partially positive hydrogen atoms (H-bond donors) and $2$ lone pairs on the oxygen atom (H-bond acceptors).
  2. Step 2 — Apply to the Ice Crystal Lattice: In hexagonal ice, every water molecule uses both H atoms to form $2$ hydrogen bonds and both lone pairs on O to accept $2$ hydrogen bonds, creating a tetrahedral coordination around each oxygen atom.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm Final Answer: Each water molecule in an ice crystal is hydrogen bonded to 4 neighbouring water molecules.

Each H2O molecule forms 2 H-bonds via its two H atoms and 2 H-bonds via its two lone pairs
on O =⇒ 4 neighbouring molecules.
Q123.trapHtml: Direct NCERT Hydrogen chapter / Chemical Bonding fact: 4 H-bonds per H<sub>2</sub>O in ice.

Q124.conceptHtml: Square pyramidal corresponds to SN = 6 (5 bp + 1 lp).
Q124.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall Condition for Square Pyramidal Structure: A species adopts a square pyramidal shape when its central atom has steric number $6$ ($sp^3d^2$) with $5$ bond pairs and $1$ lone pair ($\text{AB}_5\text{L}$).
  2. Step 2 — Check Each Species: $\text{IF}_5$ ($5\text{ BP} + 1\text{ LP}$), $\text{BrF}_5$ ($5\text{ BP} + 1\text{ LP}$), and $\text{XeOF}_4$ ($5\sigma\text{-BP} + 1\text{ LP}$) are all square pyramidal.
  3. Step 3 — Rule Out Other Geometries: $\text{PF}_5$ ($5\text{ BP} + 0\text{ LP}$) is trigonal bipyramidal, while $\text{BrF}_4^-$ and $\text{ICl}_4^-$ ($4\text{ BP} + 2\text{ LP}$) are square planar.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm Final Answer: There are $3$ square pyramidal species ($\text{IF}_5, \text{BrF}_5, \text{XeOF}_4$), giving 3.
Q124.stepsLatex: Square pyramidal (3): IF<sub>5</sub>, BrF<sub>5</sub>, XeOF<sub>4</sub>. (PF<sub>5</sub> is TBP; BrF−<sub>4</sub> , ICl<sub>4</sub>− are square planar.)
Q124.trapHtml: BrF<sup>−</sup><sub>4</sub> and ICl<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup> have 2 lone pairs (square planar), not 1 lone pair.

Q125.format: Numerical | Count linear species among 8 candidates
Q125.conceptHtml: Linear species have either SN = 2 (sp) or SN = 5 (2 bp + 3 lp).
Q125.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify Linear Species: $\text{XeF}_2$ ($sp^3d,\ 2\text{ BP} + 3\text{ LP}$), $\text{C}_3\text{O}_2$ ($\text{O}=\text{C}=\text{C}=\text{C}=\text{O}$, all three carbons $sp$ hybridised), $\text{I}_3^-$ ($sp^3d,\ 2\text{ BP} + 3\text{ LP}$), $\text{CO}_2$ ($sp,\ 2\text{ BP} + 0\text{ LP}$), and $\text{BeCl}_2$ ($sp,\ 2\text{ BP} + 0\text{ LP}$) are all linear.
  2. Step 2 — Check the Non-Linear Species: $\text{I}_3^+$ ($sp^3,\ 2\text{ BP} + 2\text{ LP}$), $\text{SO}_2$ ($sp^2,\ 2\text{ BP} + 1\text{ LP}$), and $\text{BCl}_2^-$ (B has $3 + 1 = 4$ valence $e^-$, forming $2\text{ BP} + 1\text{ LP} \Rightarrow sp^2$) are all bent/angular.
  3. Step 3 — Count Total Linear Species: Counting $\text{XeF}_2, \text{C}_3\text{O}_2, \text{I}_3^-, \text{CO}_2,$ and $\text{BeCl}_2$ gives $5$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm Final Answer: The number of linear species is 5.
Q125.stepsLatex:
• Linear (5): XeF2 (2 + 3), C3O2 (O = C = C = C = O, all sp), I−3 (2 + 3), CO2 (sp), BeCl2 (sp).
• Bent (3): I+3 (2 + 2), SO2 (2 + 1), BCl2− (2 + 1).
Q125.trapHtml: I<sup>+</sup><sub>3</sub> is bent (2 bp + 2 lp), whereas I<sup>−</sup><sub>3</sub> is linear (2 bp + 3 lp)!

Q126.format: Numerical | Count species that do NOT have odd electrons
Q126.conceptHtml: Sum total valence electrons; even sum =⇒ no odd electron.
Q126.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Count Total Electrons in Each Species: A species does not have an odd number of electrons when its total electron count is even.
  2. Step 2 — Check Odd-Electron Species: (A) $\text{NO}_2$: $7 + 2(8) = 23$ (odd); (D) $\text{ClO}_2$: $17 + 2(8) = 33$ (odd); (F) $\text{NO}$: $7 + 8 = 15$ (odd).
  3. Step 3 — Check Even-Electron Species: (B) $\text{ICl}_4^-$: $53 + 4(17) + 1 = 122$ (even); (C) $\text{BrF}_3$: $35 + 3(9) = 62$ (even); (E) $\text{NO}_2^+$: $7 + 2(8) - 1 = 22$ (even).
  4. Step 4 — Confirm Final Answer: Three species ($\text{ICl}_4^-, \text{BrF}_3, \text{NO}_2^+$) do not have an odd number of electrons, giving 3.
Q126.stepsLatex:
• Even electrons (3): (B) ICl4− (36e−), (C) BrF3 (28e−), (E) NO+2 (16e−).
• Odd electrons (3): (A) NO2 (17e−), (D) ClO2 (19e−), (F) NO (11e− valence).
Q126.trapHtml: Check the negation: "do not have odd number of electrons".

Q127.subtopic: Numerical — Total Lone Pairs on Oxygen Atoms of Ozone
Q127.format: Numerical | Sum of lone pairs in O<sub>3</sub>
Q127.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Calculate Total Valence Electrons in Ozone ($\text{O}_3$): Each oxygen atom has $6$ valence electrons, so $\text{O}_3$ has $3 \times 6 = 18$ valence electrons.
  2. Step 2 — Draw the Lewis Structure: Ozone is represented as $\ddot{\text{O}}=\ddot{\text{O}}^+-\ddot{\text{O}}^-:$ (resonance hybrid of two equivalent forms), which contains $3$ covalent bonds ($1$ double bond and $1$ single bond), accounting for $3 \times 2 = 6$ bonding electrons.
  3. Step 3 — Count Lone Pairs Across All Three Oxygen Atoms: Non-bonded electrons $= 18 - 6 = 12$, corresponding to $\frac{12}{2} = 6$ lone pairs ($2$ on the double-bonded terminal O, $1$ on the central O, and $3$ on the single-bonded terminal O).
  4. Step 4 — Confirm Final Answer: The total number of lone pairs on oxygen atoms of ozone is 6.
Q127.stepsLatex:
In O¨ = O¨ − O¨ :: 3 bonding pairs (6e−) leave 12 non-bonding electrons = 6 lone pairs (2 on
= O, 1 on central O, 3 on −O−).
Q127.trapHtml: Count lone pairs across all three oxygen atoms (2 + 1 + 3 = 6), not just the central atom (1).

trapCards.title: Trap 1: VSEPR Lone-Pair & Steric Number Traps
trapCards.html:
• Linear vs sp Hybridization (Q22, Q89, Q93): XeF2, I−3 , and ICl−2 are linear in shape, but their hybridization is sp3d (2 bp + 3 lp), NOT sp!
  • I+3 vs I−3 (Q125): I+3 has 2 bp + 2 lp (bent), while I−3 has 2 bp + 3 lp (linear).
  • Equatorial Lone Pairs in sp3d (Q25, Q33): Lone pairs in TBP always sit in equatorial positions; ClF3 has 2 equatorial lp, never axial.
  • SiO2 vs CO2 (Q99, Q108): CO2 is sp linear, whereas SiO2 is a 3D covalent network with sp3 tetrahedral silicon.

trapCards.title: Trap 2: MOT s–p Mixing & Unpaired Electrons
trapCards.html:
• The 14e− Crossover (Q27, Q86, Q112): For ≤ 14e− (B2, C2, N2), π2p < σ2pz. Hence B2 (π22p) is paramag- netic (BO = 1) and C2 (π24p) is diamagnetic (BO = 2, two π-bonds!).
  • O+2 vs O−2 Unpaired e− (Q08, Q11): Both O+2 (π∗1) and O−2 (π∗3) have 1 unpaired electron (equal, not O+2 > O−2 ).
  • Orbital Symmetry Along z-Axis (Q06, Q37): 2s + 2pz → σ; 2s + 2px or 2pz + 2px → zero overlap; π∗ has a nodal plane between the nuclei. trapCards.title: Trap 3: Dipole Moment, Bond Angles & Fajan’s Rules
trapCards.html:
• NH3 vs NF3 (Q16, Q51, Q63): µ(NH3) = 1.47 D > µ(NF3) = 0.23 D because lone-pair and bond dipoles re- inforce in NH3 and oppose in NF3.
  • Dipole Arrow Convention (Q85): Tail (+) sits on δ+ and arrowhead points to δ−.
  • Bond Angle Reversals (Q03, Q41, Q70): OF2 (103◦) < H2O (104.5◦) < Cl2O (111◦); SO2 (119.5◦) > H2O (104.5◦).
  • Fajan’s 18e− Shell Rule (Q61, Q88): Cu+, Ag+ po- larise much more strongly than Na+, K+ (CuCl > NaCl covalent; AgCl least ionic).

trapCards.title: Trap 4: Counting Traps (Whole Molecule vs Cen- tral Atom)

title: p-Block Elements
constantsHtml:
• p-Block Elements
  • High-Yield NTA JEE Main 2023–2026 Exam Intelligence (88 PYQs: 64 MCQs + 24 Section B)
  • Under the revised NTA 2024–2026 syllabus, p-Block Elements (Groups 13–18) focuses heavily on general peri-
  • odic trends, anomalous first-member behaviour, inert pair effect, hydride/oxide/halide properties, and
  • structure/oxidation-state logic rather than industrial preparation processes. Across 2023–2026 shifts, this chapter deliv-
  • ers 1–2 questions per paper (4–8 high-accuracy marks). Over 80% of recent questions test: (1) Group 13–14 anomalies
  • (Ga vs Al radius/∆iH1, inert pair Tl+ > Tl3+, Pb2+ > Pb4+, amphoteric oxides), (2) Group 15–16 hydrides & oxides
  • (thermal stability, basicity, reducing power, H2O/HF H-bonding vs S8/O2 atomicity, SO2/TeO2 redox), (3) Group 17–18
  • reactivity (interhalogen geometries, disproportionation of X2, noble gas boiling points), and (4) Oxoacids of P, S, Cl &
  • Borax/Xenon stoichiometry (frequently tested in numericals and legacy 2023 shifts).

formulaCards.title: 1. Group 13 (Boron Family) Trends & Anomalies
formulaCards.html:
• Valence Configuration: ns2np1 (B, Al, Ga, In, Tl).
  • Atomic Radius: B < Ga < Al < In < Tl (d-block con- traction: 3d10 poor shielding makes rGa < rAl).
  • Ionic Radius (M3+): Regular increase down the group: B3+ < Al3+ < Ga3+ < In3+ < Tl3+.
  • First Ionisation Enthalpy (∆iH1): B > Tl > Ga > Al > In (3d10 and 4f14 poor shielding boosts Ga and Tl). Highest: B; Lowest: In.
  • Second IE (∆iH2): B > Ga > Al (removing e− from ns2 vs 3d104s1).
  • Electronegativity (χ): B(2.0) > Tl(1.8) > In(1.7) > Ga(1.6) > Al(1.5) (de- creases B → Al, then increases due to d/f contraction; χGa ≈ χGe? Note: χB = 2.0, χGe ≈ 1.8–2.0, χTl ≈ 1.8).
  • Melting Point: B(2453 K) ≫ Al > Tl > In > Ga(303 K) (Ga is liquid in summer, used in high-T thermometers; B has icosahedral B12 crystal lattice).
  • Density: Increases regularly B < Al < Ga < In < Tl.
  • Inert Pair Effect: Stability of +1 OS: Ga+ < In+ < Tl+; Tl3+ is a strong oxidising agent, while Al3+ is stable. E◦(Tl3+/Tl) > 0 (+1.26 V), E◦(Al3+/Al) < 0 (−1.66 V).
  • Halides & Hydrolysis: BX3 Lewis acidity: BF3 < BCl3 < BBr3 < BI3 (due to pπ–pπ back-bonding in BF3). AlCl3 in acidified water gives octahedral [Al(H2O)6]3+ (sp3d2); Al + NaOH gives [Al(OH)4]−. BCl3 hydrolyses to B(OH)3 / [B(OH)4]− (never [B(H2O)6]3+).

formulaCards.title: 2. Group 14 (Carbon Family) Trends & Oxides
formulaCards.html:
• Covalent Radius: Increases regularly C < Si < Ge < Sn < Pb.
  • First IE (∆iH1): C > Si > Ge > Pb > Sn (4f14 lan- thanoid contraction makes Pb > Sn).
  • Melting Point: C > Si > Ge > Pb > Sn (Sn has the low- est m.p.).
  • C–C vs M–M Bond Enthalpy: C − C > Si − Si > Ge − Ge > Sn − Sn (catenation decreases down the group).
  • Inert Pair Effect: Pb2+ is more stable than Pb4+ (PbO2 is an oxidising agent; PbO2 + Pb → 2PbO has ∆rG◦ < 0); Sn4+ is more stable than Sn2+ (Sn2+ is a reducing agent; SnO2 + Sn → 2SnO has ∆rG◦ > 0).
  • Oxide Nature: – Neutral: CO (sparingly soluble in water). – Acidic: CO2 (most acidic), SiO2, GeO2 (weakly acidic). – Amphoteric: SnO, SnO2, PbO, PbO2 (also Al2O3, Ga2O3 in Gr 13).
  • C Isotopes: 12C,13 C (stable), 14C (radioactive, β− emit- ter).
  • Max Covalency: C is restricted to 4 (no d-orbitals); Si, Ge, Sn, Pb expand to 6 (e.g., [SiF6]2−).

formulaCards.title: 3. Group 15 (Pnictogens) Hydrides, Oxides & Ni- trogen
formulaCards.html:
• Nitrogen Anomalies: Max covalency = 4 (only four va- lence orbitals: 2s, 2px, 2py, 2pz), hence NF5 does not exist. Forms pπ–pπ multiple bonds (N ≡ N). N − N single bond is weaker (and shorter) than P − P due to interelectronic lone-pair repulsion.

formulaCards.title: 4. Group 16 (Chalcogens) Trends, Hydrides & Ox- ides
formulaCards.html:
• Oxygen Anomalies: Small size, high χ, no d-orbitals =⇒ covalency usually 2 (max 4). Exists as O2 (pπ–pπ); S exists as puckered S8 ring (hence large m.p./b.p. jump between O and S due to atomicity).
  • Hydrides (H2E): – Acidic Strength: H2O < H2S < H2Se < H2Te (H– E bond dissociation enthalpy decreases down the group). – Reducing Character: H2S < H2Se < H2Te (H2O is non-reducing). – Boiling Point: H2S < H2Se < H2Te < H2O (inter- molecular H-bonding in H2O).
  • Oxides (EO2, EO3): All acidic; SO2 is reducing (turns acidified K2Cr2O7 paper green: Cr6+ → Cr3+), whereas TeO2 is oxidising (inert pair effect).
  • Oxidation States: O shows −2, −1 (H2O2), +2 (OF2), +1 (O2F2). Down Gr 16, +4 stability increases and +6 stability decreases.
  • Ozone (O3): Bent (116.8◦), 6 lone pairs total (3 on terminal O, 2 on other terminal O, 1 on central O). PbS + 4O3 → PbSO4 + 4O2.

formulaCards.title: 5. Group 17 (Halogens) & Group 18 (Noble Gases)
formulaCards.html:
• Halogen Properties: F2, Cl2 (gases), Br2 (liquid, Z = 35, A = 80), I2 (solid). F shows only −1 OS (no d-orbitals, highest χ).
  • Disproportionation in Alkali: Cl2, Br2, I2 dispropor- tionate in cold/hot NaOH; F2 does NOT disproportionate (gives OF2 or O2).
  • HX Boiling & Melting Points: – Boiling Point: HCl < HBr < HI < HF (H-bonding makes HF highest). – Melting Point: HCl < HBr < HF < HI (HI has highest m.p. due to large molar mass/van der Waals).
  • Interhalogen / Polyhalide Geometries (VSEPR): – ICl−4 : 4 bp + 2 lp (sp3d2) → Square planar. – ClO−3 : 3 bp + 1 lp (sp3) → Pyramidal. – IBr−2 : 2 bp + 3 lp (sp3d) → Linear.
  • Noble Gases (Group 18): Monoatomic gases held by weak London dispersion forces =⇒ very low boiling points (He has lowest b.p. of any known substance, 4.2 K).
  • Xenon Fluorides: – XeF4 + SbF5 → [XeF3]+[SbF6]− (F− donor- acceptor). – Complete hydrolysis: 6XeF4 + 12H2O → 4Xe + 2XeO3 + 24HF + 3O2 (Xe: +4 → 0 and +6).

formulaCards.title: 6. Oxoacids of P, S, Cl & Key Reactions (Section B / Legacy)
formulaCards.html: • Phosphorus Oxoacids: – H3PO2 (1 P–OH, 2 P–H, 1 P=O): monobasic, re- duces AgNO3 → Ag. – H3PO3 (2 P–OH, 1 P–H, 1 P=O): dibasic, reduces AgNO3 → Ag. – H4P2O5 (pyrophosphorous): has two P − H bonds → gives silver mirror with AgNO3. – H4P2O7 (pyrophosphoric): 1 P–O–P, 2 P=O (π = 2), 12 σ bonds. – (HPO3)3 (cyclotrimetaphosphoric): 3 P–O–P; P O : 6 P–O–P.

Q01.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Properties of EH<sub>3</sub> (NH<sub>3</sub> to BiH<sub>3</sub>)
Q01.conceptHtml: Down Group 15 (N → Bi), central atom size increases, E − H bond length increases, and E − H bond dissociation enthalpy decreases.
Q01.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the core periodic trend for Group 15 hydrides ($\text{EH}_3$): As we move down Group 15 from $\text{NH}_3$ to $\text{BiH}_3$, the atomic size of the central element $\text{E}$ increases steadily. This lengthens the $\text{E}-\text{H}$ bond and lowers its bond dissociation enthalpy.
  2. Step 2 — Check stability (C) and reducing nature (A): Because the $\text{E}-\text{H}$ bond becomes progressively weaker down the group, thermal stability decreases from $\text{NH}_3$ to $\text{BiH}_3$ (Statement C is true). A weaker $\text{E}-\text{H}$ bond also releases hydrogen more readily, so reducing character increases from $\text{NH}_3$ to $\text{BiH}_3$ (Statement A is true).
  3. Step 3 — Check basicity (B) and bond angle (D): Down the group, the lone pair on $\text{E}$ is spread over a larger orbital, lowering electron density and making lone-pair donation harder, so basicity decreases from $\text{NH}_3$ to $\text{BiH}_3$ (Statement B is true). Simultaneously, decreasing electronegativity of $\text{E}$ shifts bond pairs away from the central atom, lowering bond-pair–bond-pair repulsion and reducing the $\text{H}-\text{E}-\text{H}$ angle from $107.8^\circ$ in $\text{NH}_3$ to $91.3^\circ$ in $\text{SbH}_3$ (Statement D is true).
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: All four statements A, B, C, and D are correct, which corresponds to option (c).
Q01.stepsLatex:
Step 1: Evaluate each statement:
• A (True): Weaker E − H bond down the group makes H release easier, so reducing nature increases from NH3
to BiH3.
• B (True): Electron density on larger central atoms is more diffused, so Lewis basicity (lone-pair donation)
decreases from NH3 to BiH3.
• C (True): Thermal stability decreases down the group (NH3 > PH3 > AsH3 > SbH3 > BiH3).
• D (True): H − E − H bond angle decreases: NH3(107.8◦) > PH3(93.6◦) > AsH3(91.8◦) > SbH3(91.3◦).
Q01.trapHtml: Only boiling point has a hydrogen-bonding anomaly (PH<sub>3</sub> < AsH<sub>3</sub> < NH<sub>3</sub> < SbH<sub>3</sub> < BiH<sub>3</sub>); stability, basicity, bond angle, and reducing power all vary monotonically.

Q02.subtopic: Brown Ring Test of Nitrate / NO
Q02.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Reaction of gas X with freshly prepared FeSO<sub>4</sub>
Q02.conceptHtml: In the brown ring test, NO gas coordinates to Fe<sup>2+</sup> in aqueous FeSO<sub>4</sub> to form the brown nitrosyl complex [Fe(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>5</sub>(NO)]SO<sub>4</sub> (written concisely as [Fe(NO)]SO<sub>4</sub>).
Q02.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the qualitative test described: The formation of a brown ring when a gas reacts with freshly prepared aqueous ferrous sulphate ($\text{FeSO}_4$) is the classic brown ring test used to detect nitrate ions ($\text{NO}_3^-$).
  2. Step 2 — Identify gas X: During the test, nitrate ions are reduced by $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ in acidic medium to liberate nitric oxide gas, $\text{NO}$ (gas X): $\text{NO}_3^- + 3\text{Fe}^{2+} + 4\text{H}^+ \rightarrow \text{NO} + 3\text{Fe}^{3+} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$.
  3. Step 3 — Identify the brown ring complex Y: The liberated $\text{NO}$ coordinates with the remaining aqueous $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ ions ($[\text{Fe}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+}$) to form the brown nitrosyl complex $[\text{Fe}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_5(\text{NO})]\text{SO}_4$, which is represented in simplified form as $[\text{Fe}(\text{NO})]\text{SO}_4$ (compound Y).
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Thus, X is $\text{NO}$ and Y is $[\text{Fe}(\text{NO})]\text{SO}_4$, matching option (a).
Q02.stepsLatex:
Step 1: Write the reaction of NO with freshly prepared FeSO4:
[Fe(H2O)6]2+ + NO −→ [Fe(H2O)5(NO)]2+ + H2O
Step 2: Thus X = NO and Y = [Fe(NO)]SO4.
Q02.trapHtml: Do not confuse NO with NO<sub>2</sub> or N<sub>2</sub>O; only NO forms the characteristic brown ring complex with FeSO<sub>4</sub>.

Q03.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Two-statement evaluation on B, Al, Tl
Q03.conceptHtml: Standard reduction potentials reflect electropositivity and oxidation-state stability: E<sub>A</sub><sup>°</sup><sub>l3+/Al</sub> = −1.66 V (highly electropositive), whereas E<sub>T</sub><sup>°</sup><sub>l3+/Tl</sub> = +1.26 V (Tl<sup>3+</sup> is unstable/oxidising).
Q03.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement I using standard reduction potentials: For Group 13 metals, $E^\circ_{\text{Al}^{3+}/\text{Al}} = -1.66\text{ V}$ (negative) whereas $E^\circ_{\text{Tl}^{3+}/\text{Tl}} = +1.26\text{ V}$ (positive). A more negative standard reduction potential indicates a much stronger tendency to lose electrons and form cations, so aluminium is indeed more electropositive than thallium. Thus, Statement I is true.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement II using ionization enthalpies: The sum of the first three ionization enthalpies of boron ($\Delta_i H_1 + \Delta_i H_2 + \Delta_i H_3 \approx 6887\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$) is extremely high compared to aluminium ($\approx 5137\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$).
  3. Step 3 — Connect ionization enthalpy to bonding nature: Because removing three electrons from tiny boron requires prohibitive energy, boron cannot form free $\text{B}^{3+}$ ions and forms only covalent compounds; aluminium, having a much lower total ionization enthalpy, readily forms $\text{Al}^{3+}$ ions. Thus, Statement II is true.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Both Statement I and Statement II are true, which corresponds to option (a).

solution. True.
Q03.trapHtml: Both statements come directly from NCERT Group 13 trends on ionisation enthalpies and standard electrode potentials.
Q03.finalAnsHtml: (A) Both Statement I and Statement II are true

Q04.conceptHtml: Al dissolves in aqueous NaOH to form tetrahydroxidoaluminate(III), [Al(OH)<sub>4</sub>]<sup>−</sup> (not [Al(OH)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3−</sup>). In- terhalogen/polyhalide shapes follow VSEPR steric numbers.
Q04.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement I (reaction of Al with NaOH): Aluminium is amphoteric and dissolves in aqueous $\text{NaOH}$ to form the tetrahydroxoaluminate(III) ion, $[\text{Al}(\text{OH})_4]^-$, not $[\text{Al}(\text{OH})_6]^{3-}$: $2\text{Al} + 2\text{NaOH} + 6\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow 2\text{Na}^+[\text{Al}(\text{OH})_4]^- + 3\text{H}_2$. Hence, Statement I is false.
  2. Step 2 — Determine geometries of the three anions in Statement II using VSEPR theory: For $\text{ICl}_4^-$, steric number $= \frac{7 + 4 + 1}{2} = 6$ ($4$ bond pairs $+ 2$ lone pairs, $sp^3d^2$), giving a square planar shape. For $\text{ClO}_3^-$, steric number $= \frac{7 + 0 + 1}{2} = 4$ ($3$ bond pairs $+ 1$ lone pair, $sp^3$), giving a trigonal pyramidal shape.
  3. Step 3 — Determine the geometry of $\text{IBr}_2^-$: For $\text{IBr}_2^-$, steric number $= \frac{7 + 2 + 1}{2} = 5$ ($2$ bond pairs $+ 3$ lone pairs at equatorial positions, $sp^3d$), giving a linear shape. All three shapes match Statement II, so Statement II is true.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Statement I is false and Statement II is true, which corresponds to option (d).

Q04.finalAnsHtml: (D) Statement I is false but Statement II is true

Q05.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Multi-statement selection on Nitrogen
Q05.conceptHtml: Nitrogen has only four valence orbitals (2s, 2p<sub>x</sub>, 2p<sub>y</sub>, 2p<sub>z</sub>), no d-orbitals, high lone-pair repulsion in N − N, and intermediate oxidation states (+1 to +4) that disproportionate in acid.
Q05.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Check Statements A and E (true properties of nitrogen): Nitrogen in intermediate oxidation states ($+1$ to $+4$) disproportionates in acidic solution, for example $3\text{HNO}_2 \rightarrow \text{HNO}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O} + 2\text{NO}$ (Statement A is true). Also, nitrogen lies in Period 2 and has only four valence orbitals ($2s, 2p_x, 2p_y, 2p_z$), restricting its maximum covalency to $4$ (Statement E is true).
  2. Step 2 — Check Statement B ($\pi$-bonding): Because nitrogen has no vacant $d$-orbitals, it forms $p\pi\text{–}p\pi$ multiple bonds—not $d\pi\text{–}p\pi$ bonds—with itself and other small electronegative atoms. Thus, Statement B is false.
  3. Step 3 — Check Statements C and D (bond strength and density): The $\text{N}-\text{N}$ single bond ($\approx 159\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$) is actually weaker than the $\text{P}-\text{P}$ single bond ($\approx 213\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$) due to strong lone-pair–lone-pair repulsion between small N atoms (Statement C is false). Density increases down Group 15, so gaseous $\text{N}_2$ has the lowest—not highest—density (Statement D is false).
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Only statements A and E are correct, which matches option (d).
