Step 1: Check each statement:
• A (True): e.g., 3HNO2 → HNO3 + H2O + 2NO.
• B (False): N forms pπ–pπ bonds, NOT dπ–pπ (no 2d orbitals).
• C (False): N − N single bond (159 kJ mol−1) is weaker than P − P (213 kJ mol−1) due to lone-pair repulsion.
• D (False): N2 is a gas and has the lowest density in Group 15 (Bi is highest).
• E (True): Max covalency of N is 4 (e.g., NH+4 ).
Q05.trapHtml: Watch for “dπ–pπ” vs “pπ–pπ”—a classic NTA word swap.

Q06.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Identifying ‘E’ from Pauling χ match with Ge
Q06.conceptHtml: On the Pauling scale (to 1 decimal place), χ(Ge) = 1.8 (or 2.0 in some tables; in Group 13, Tl has χ = 1.8, matching Ge = 1.8 in NCERT).
Q06.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify Group 13 element E from Pauling electronegativity: On the Pauling scale (NCERT values), germanium ($\text{Ge}$) has an electronegativity of $1.8$. In Group 13 ($\text{B}=2.0$, $\text{Al}=1.5$, $\text{Ga}=1.6$, $\text{In}=1.7$, $\text{Tl}=1.8$), thallium ($\text{Tl}$) also has an electronegativity of $1.8$, so $\text{E} = \text{Tl}$.
  2. Step 2 — Apply the inert pair effect to $\text{Tl}^{3+}$: Due to poor shielding by filled $4f^{14}$ and $5d^{10}$ subshells, the $6s^2$ electrons of thallium are strongly held by the nucleus. Consequently, $\text{Tl}^+$ is much more stable than $\text{Tl}^{3+}$ (Statement C is false).
  3. Step 3 — Determine redox behaviour and $E^\circ$ of $\text{Tl}^{3+}$: Because $\text{Tl}^{3+}$ readily gains electrons to convert into the more stable $\text{Tl}^+$ (or $\text{Tl}$), it acts as a strong oxidising agent (Statement B is true; Statement A is false). Correspondingly, its standard reduction potential $E^\circ_{\text{Tl}^{3+}/\text{Tl}} = +1.26\text{ V}$ is positive (Statement D is true).
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Only statements B and D are correct, which corresponds to option (c).
Q06.stepsLatex:
Step 1: Identify ‘E’: χ(Tl) = 1.8 = χ(Ge) (NCERT Group 13/14 tables: B = 2.0, Al = 1.5, Ga = 1.6, In = 1.7, Tl =
1.8). Thus E = Tl. Step 2: Check statements for Tl3+:
• A (False): Tl3+ is in its highest OS (+3); it cannot be oxidised further.
• B (True): Tl3+ readily accepts 2e− to form stable Tl+, acting as a strong oxidising agent.
• C (False): Due to inert pair effect, Tl+ is more stable than Tl3+.
• D (True): E◦(Tl3+/Tl) = +1.26 V > 0.
Q06.trapHtml: NCERT lists χ<sub>Ge</sub> = 1.8 and χ<sub>Tl</sub> = 1.8; pairing that with statements B and D uniquely confirms E = Tl.

Q07.subtopic: Identifying Group 17 Element from Ion Composition
Q07.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Atomic number, mass number, group, physical state
Q07.conceptHtml: For a monoatomic anion A<sup>−</sup>, Z = n<sub>e−</sub> − 1 and A = Z + n<sub>n</sub>.
Q07.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Find the atomic number ($Z$) of element A: The monoatomic anion $\text{A}^-$ has $36$ electrons, meaning the neutral atom $\text{A}$ gained $1$ electron to reach $36$. Therefore, the number of electrons (and protons) in neutral $\text{A}$ is $Z = 36 - 1 = 35$, which is bromine ($\text{Br}$).
  2. Step 2 — Calculate the atomic mass (mass number): Mass number $= \text{protons} + \text{neutrons} = 35 + 45 = 80$.
  3. Step 3 — Identify group number and room-temperature physical state: With electronic configuration $[\text{Ar}]3d^{10}4s^24p^5$, bromine belongs to Group 17 (halogens) and is the only non-metal that exists as a liquid at room temperature.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The atomic mass, group, and physical state are $80$, $17$, and liquid respectively, matching option (a).
Q07.stepsLatex:
Step 1: A− has 36 electrons =⇒ neutral atom A has Z = 36 − 1 = 35 (Bromine, Br). Step 2: Atomic mass
A = 35 + 45 = 80. Step 3: Bromine (Z = 35) belongs to Group 17 and is a liquid at room temperature.
Q07.trapHtml: Do not forget to subtract 1 from 36 electrons to get Z = 35 (Kr has Z = 36, not Br).

Q08.subtopic: Oxygen Covalency, Oxidation State & Anomalous Behaviour
Q08.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Two-statement evaluation on Oxygen
Q08.conceptHtml: Oxygen typically shows covalency 2, can reach 3 (e.g., H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>) or 4 (e.g., basic beryllium acetate Be<sub>4</sub>O(CH<sub>3</sub>COO)<sub>6</sub>), and shows +2 OS in OF<sub>2</sub> because F is more electronegative than O.
Q08.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement I (covalency and oxidation states of oxygen): Oxygen normally exhibits a covalency of $2$, though in rare cases it can extend up to $4$ using its four valence orbitals ($2s, 2p_x, 2p_y, 2p_z$). In $\text{SO}_2$, oxygen is more electronegative than sulphur, so its oxidation state is $-2$; in $\text{OF}_2$, fluorine is more electronegative than oxygen, so oxygen shows a $+2$ oxidation state. Thus, Statement I is true.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement II (anomalous behaviour of oxygen): Like other first members of $p$-block groups, oxygen shows anomalous properties (such as strong H-bonding, forming $\text{O}_2$ gas, and inability to expand its octet) primarily due to its very small atomic size and high electronegativity (along with absence of $d$-orbitals). Thus, Statement II is true.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the final answer: Both Statement I and Statement II are true, which corresponds to option (a).
Q08.stepsLatex:
Step 1: Statement I: Covalency of O is generally 2 and can exceed up to 4; OS of O in SO2 is −2 and in OF2 is
+2. True. Step 2: Statement II: Anomalous behaviour of O is due to small size and high electronegativity (and
absence of d-orbitals). True.
Q08.trapHtml: In OF<sub>2</sub>, F is −1, so O is +2 (not −2).
Q08.finalAnsHtml: (A) Both Statement I and Statement II are true

Q09.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Two-statement evaluation on ∆<sub>i</sub>H<sub>2</sub> and ∆<sub>i</sub>H<sub>1</sub>
Q09.conceptHtml: For ∆<sub>i</sub>H<sub>2</sub> of Group 13, we remove an electron from M<sup>+</sup> (ns<sup>2</sup>): B<sup>+</sup>(2s<sup>2</sup>) > Ga<sup>+</sup>(3d<sup>10</sup>4s<sup>2</sup>) > Al<sup>+</sup>(3s<sup>2</sup>). For ∆<sub>i</sub>H<sub>1</sub> of Group 14, lanthanoid contraction makes Pb > Sn: C > Si > Ge > Pb > Sn.
Q09.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement I ($\Delta_i H_2$ of B, Al, Ga): Removing the second electron takes an electron from the $ns^2$ subshell of $\text{M}^+$. In $\text{Ga}^+$ ($[\text{Ar}]3d^{10}4s^2$), the poor shielding of $3d^{10}$ electrons increases effective nuclear charge, making $\Delta_i H_2(\text{Ga}) = 1979\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$ higher than $\Delta_i H_2(\text{Al}) = 1816\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$ (while $\text{B} = 2427\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$). The true order is $\text{B} > \text{Ga} > \text{Al}$, so Statement I is false.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement II ($\Delta_i H_1$ of Group 14): Down Group 14, $\Delta_i H_1$ decreases from $\text{Si}$ ($786$) to $\text{Ge}$ ($761$) to $\text{Sn}$ ($708\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$), then slightly rises at $\text{Pb}$ ($715\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$) due to poor shielding by $4f^{14}$ electrons (lanthanoid contraction).
  3. Step 3 — Compare with the given order: The correct increasing order is $\text{Sn} < \text{Pb} < \text{Ge} < \text{Si}$, which is the reverse of the trend stated in Statement II. Hence, Statement II is false.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Both Statement I and Statement II are false, matching option (b).
Q09.stepsLatex:
Step 1: Statement I claims ∆iH2: B > Al > Ga. False! Due to poor shielding of 3d10 electrons in Ga, ∆iH2(Ga) =
1979 kJ mol−1 > ∆iH2(Al) = 1816 kJ mol−1, so the true order is B > Ga > Al. Step 2: Statement II claims
∆iH1: Si < Ge < Pb < Sn. False! Down Group 14, ∆iH1 decreases C > Si > Ge > Sn, with Pb > Sn (Sn = 708,
Pb = 715 kJ mol−1), so Sn < Pb < Ge < Si.
Q09.trapHtml: Remember 3d<sup>10</sup> contraction affects both ∆<sub>i</sub>H<sub>1</sub> and ∆<sub>i</sub>H<sub>2</sub> of Ga relative to Al.
Q09.finalAnsHtml: (B) Both Statement I and Statement II are false

Q10.subtopic: Boiling & Melting Points of Hydrogen Halides (HX)
Q10.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Two-statement evaluation on HX
Q10.conceptHtml: Strong intermolecular H-bonding makes HF have the highest boiling point (HCl < HBr < HI < HF), whereas higher molecular mass/crystal packing puts HI above HF in melting point (HCl < HBr < HF < HI).
Q10.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement I (boiling points of hydrogen halides): Among $\text{HCl}$ ($189\text{ K}$), $\text{HBr}$ ($206\text{ K}$), and $\text{HI}$ ($238\text{ K}$), boiling point rises with increasing molar mass and stronger van der Waals forces. However, $\text{HF}$ ($293\text{ K}$) has the highest boiling point due to strong intermolecular hydrogen bonding. Thus, $\text{HCl} < \text{HBr} < \text{HI} < \text{HF}$, so Statement I is true.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement II (melting points of hydrogen halides): In the solid lattice, melting points are $\text{HCl}$ ($159\text{ K}$) $< \text{HBr}$ ($185\text{ K}$) $< \text{HF}$ ($190\text{ K}$) $< \text{HI}$ ($222\text{ K}$).
  3. Step 3 — Understand why $\text{HI}$ melts higher than $\text{HF}$: In the solid state, the much larger molecular mass and stronger dispersion forces of $\text{HI}$ outweigh the hydrogen-bonding contribution in $\text{HF}$. Thus, Statement II is true.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Both Statement I and Statement II are true, which corresponds to option (d).
Q10.stepsLatex:
Step 1: Statement I: b.p. order HCl(189 K) < HBr(206 K) < HI(238 K) < HF(293 K). True. Step 2: Statement II:
m.p. order HCl(159 K) < HBr(185 K) < HF(190 K) < HI(222 K). True.
Q10.trapHtml: Do not assume HF has the highest melting point too—HI (222 K) exceeds HF (190 K).
Q10.finalAnsHtml: (D) Both Statement I and Statement II are true

Q11.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Stability, basicity, reducing character, boiling point
Q11.conceptHtml: Down Group 15 hydrides (NH<sub>3</sub> → BiH<sub>3</sub>), stability and basicity decrease, reducing charac- ter increases, while boiling point does NOT increase monotonically because NH<sub>3</sub> (238.5 K) has H-bonding (PH<sub>3</sub> < AsH<sub>3</sub> < NH<sub>3</sub> < SbH<sub>3</sub> < BiH<sub>3</sub>).
Q11.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statements A and C (stability and reducing character): Down Group 15 from $\text{NH}_3$ to $\text{SbH}_3$, the $\text{E}-\text{H}$ bond becomes longer and weaker. Therefore, thermal stability decreases down the group (A is true) and reducing power increases down the group (C is true).
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement B (basicity): As the central atom gets larger from N to Sb, the lone pair occupies a more diffuse orbital, reducing electron density and proton affinity. Hence, basicity decreases down the group (B is true).
  3. Step 3 — Evaluate Statement D (boiling point): Boiling point does not increase smoothly down the group because $\text{NH}_3$ ($238.5\text{ K}$) forms intermolecular hydrogen bonds, giving it a higher boiling point than both $\text{PH}_3$ ($185.5\text{ K}$) and $\text{AsH}_3$ ($210.6\text{ K}$). The actual order is $\text{PH}_3 < \text{AsH}_3 < \text{NH}_3 < \text{SbH}_3$, so Statement D is false.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Only statements A, B, and C are correct, matching option (a).
Q11.stepsLatex:
Step 1: Statements A, B, and C are correct. Step 2: Statement D is false because b.p. drops sharply from NH3 to
PH3 (185.5 K) before rising again.
Q11.trapHtml: NH<sub>3</sub> has a higher boiling point than PH<sub>3</sub> and AsH<sub>3</sub>, breaking the monotonic increase.

Q12.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Identify incorrect statement about Carbon
Q12.conceptHtml: Carbon has two stable isotopes (<sup>12</sup>C,<sup>13</sup> C) and one radioactive isotope (<sup>14</sup>C, half-life 5770 yr).
Q12.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Check options (a), (b), and (d): Carbon displays $+4$ (e.g., $\text{CO}_2$), $+2$ (e.g., $\text{CO}$), and negative oxidation states (e.g., $-4$ in $\text{CH}_4$), so (a) is true. Lacking $d$-orbitals, carbon has a maximum covalency of $4$, so (b) is true. Since non-metallic character decreases down Group 14, $\text{CO}_2$ is the most acidic dioxide in the group, so (d) is true.
  2. Step 2 — Check option (c) (isotopes of carbon): Carbon has three naturally occurring isotopes: $^{12}\text{C}$ and $^{13}\text{C}$ are stable isotopes, while $^{14}\text{C}$ is the radioactive isotope (half-life $\approx 5770\text{ years}$).
  3. Step 3 — Identify the incorrect statement: Calling $^{13}\text{C}$ radioactive is factually wrong.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The incorrect statement is option (c).
Q12.stepsLatex:
Step 1: Check options: (A) True (C shows −4 in CH4, +2 in CO, +4 in CO2); (B) True (no d-orbitals =⇒ max
covalency 4); (C) False (14C is radioactive, not 13C); (D) True (CO2 is most acidic among Group 14 dioxides).
Q12.trapHtml: <sup>13</sup>C is a stable isotope used in NMR; <sup>14</sup>C is the radioactive radiocarbon-dating isotope.
Q12.finalAnsHtml: (C) Among the isotopes of carbon, 13C is a radioactive isotope.

Q13.subtopic: Inert Pair Effect Thermodynamics (Pb vs Sn)
Q13.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Sign of ∆<sub>r</sub>G<sup>◦</sup> for MO<sub>2</sub> + M → 2MO
Q13.conceptHtml: A reaction is thermodynamically spontaneous (∆<sub>r</sub>G<sup>°</sup> < 0) when the product oxidation state is more stable than the reactant oxidation states.
Q13.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Connect stability to Gibbs free energy ($\Delta_r G^\circ$): A chemical reaction that converts a less stable oxidation state into a more stable oxidation state is thermodynamically spontaneous and has $\Delta_r G^\circ < 0$, whereas the reverse is non-spontaneous ($\Delta_r G^\circ > 0$).
  2. Step 2 — Analyse Reaction (1) for lead: In $\text{PbO}_2(+4) + \text{Pb}(0) \rightarrow 2\text{PbO}(+2)$, lead moves into its more stable $+2$ state (favoured by the inert pair effect). Therefore, this comproportionation is spontaneous and $\Delta_r G^\circ(1) < 0$.
  3. Step 3 — Analyse Reaction (2) for tin: In $\text{SnO}_2(+4) + \text{Sn}(0) \rightarrow 2\text{SnO}(+2)$, tin is forced from its more stable $+4$ state into the less stable $+2$ state. Therefore, this reaction is non-spontaneous and $\Delta_r G^\circ(2) > 0$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: We get $\Delta_r G^\circ(1) < 0$ and $\Delta_r G^\circ(2) > 0$, matching option (b).
Q13.stepsLatex:
Step 1: For PbO2 + Pb → 2PbO: Pb2+ is more stable than Pb4+, so formation of PbO is spontaneous =⇒
∆rG◦(1) < 0. Step 2: For SnO2 + Sn → 2SnO: Sn4+ is more stable than Sn2+, so formation of SnO is non-
spontaneous =⇒ ∆rG◦(2) > 0.
Q13.trapHtml: Negative ∆<sub>r</sub>G<sup>°</sup> corresponds to the more stable product state.

Q14.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Multi-statement evaluation on Group 13
Q14.conceptHtml: In Group 13, M<sup>3+</sup> ionic radii increase down the group, χ decreases B → Al then increases Al → Tl, B has highest ∆<sub>i</sub>H<sub>1</sub>, and MCl<sub>3</sub>, MI<sub>3</sub> are covalent.
Q14.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Check Statements A and B (false trends): Adding new electron shells down Group 13 causes the ionic radius of $\text{M}^{3+}$ cations to increase regularly ($\text{B}^{3+} < \text{Al}^{3+} < \text{Ga}^{3+} < \text{In}^{3+} < \text{Tl}^{3+}$), so A is false. Electronegativity first decreases from B ($2.0$) to Al ($1.5$) and then increases marginally from Al to Tl ($1.5 \rightarrow 1.6 \rightarrow 1.7 \rightarrow 1.8$), so B is false.
  2. Step 2 — Check Statement C (first ionization enthalpy): Boron has the smallest atomic radius in Group 13 and its valence electron is held tightly by the nucleus, giving it the highest $\Delta_i H_1$ ($801\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$) in the group. Thus, C is true.
  3. Step 3 — Check Statement D (nature of trihalides): By Fajans' rules, the small, highly charged $\text{M}^{3+}$ cations strongly polarize the large $\text{Cl}^-$ and $\text{I}^-$ anions, making the trichlorides and triiodides of Group 13 covalent in nature. Thus, D is true.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Only statements C and D are correct, which corresponds to option (b).
Q14.stepsLatex:
Step 1: Evaluate each statement:
• A (False): Ionic radii of M3+ increase down the group.
• B (False): Electronegativity decreases from B (2.0) to Al (1.5), then increases marginally to Tl (1.8).
• C (True): Boron has the highest ∆iH1 (801 kJ mol−1) in Group 13.
• D (True): Due to high charge density on M3+ (Fajan’s rules), MCl3 and MI3 are covalent.
Q14.trapHtml: Electronegativity in Group 13 does NOT decrease monotonically; it rises from Al (1.5) to Tl (1.8).

Q15.conceptHtml: Among N, P, As, Sb, N is most electronegative (N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> is acidic) and Sb is least electronegative (Sb<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> is amphoteric). BCl<sub>3</sub> hydrolyses to B(OH)<sub>3</sub> and [B(OH)<sub>4</sub>]<sup>−</sup>, never [B(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup>.
Q15.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement I: Electronegativity decreases down Group 15 ($\text{N} > \text{P} > \text{As} > \text{Sb}$), so the most electronegative element is $\text{X} = \text{N}$ and the least electronegative is $\text{Y} = \text{Sb}$. Among $\text{E}_2\text{O}_3$ oxides, $\text{N}_2\text{O}_3$ (non-metal oxide) is acidic while $\text{Sb}_2\text{O}_3$ (metalloid oxide) is amphoteric. Hence, Statement I is true.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement II: $\text{BCl}_3$ is indeed covalent and undergoes hydrolysis in water to form $\text{H}_3\text{BO}_3$ / tetrahedral $[\text{B}(\text{OH})_4]^-$ ions.
  3. Step 3 — Spot the impossibility in Statement II: Because boron belongs to Period 2 and lacks vacant $d$-orbitals, its maximum covalency is $4$; it cannot form the octahedral $[\text{B}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{3+}$ ion (unlike Al, which forms $[\text{Al}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{3+}$). Hence, Statement II is false.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Statement I is true and Statement II is false, matching option (b).
Q15.stepsLatex:
Step 1: Statement I: X = N (N2O3 acidic) and Y = Sb (Sb2O3 amphoteric). True. Step 2: Statement II: Boron
lacks d-orbitals, so its maximum coordination number is 4; it cannot form octahedral [B(H2O)6]3+. False.
Q15.trapHtml: Only AlCl<sub>3</sub> (and heavier Group 13 halides) form [M(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup>; BCl<sub>3</sub> forms tetrahedral [B(OH)<sub>4</sub>]<sup>−</sup> / H<sub>3</sub>BO<sub>3</sub>.
Q15.finalAnsHtml: (B) Statement I is true but Statement II is false

Q16.subtopic: HX Bond Length vs Group 15 Hydride Boiling Point
Q16.conceptHtml: HI has the longest H − X bond because I has the largest covalent radius in Group 17. PH<sub>3</sub> has the lowest b.p. among Group 15 hydrides, and P has max covalency > 4 (e.g., 5 in PCl<sub>5</sub>, 6 in PCl<sub>6</sub><sup>−</sup>).
Q16.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement I: In hydrogen halides ($\text{HX}$), bond length increases down Group 17 as halogen size grows ($\text{HF} < \text{HCl} < \text{HBr} < \text{HI}$). The longest bond is in $\text{HI}$, and iodine has the largest—not smallest—covalent radius among the stable halogens. Thus, Statement I is false.
  2. Step 2 — Identify element E in Statement II: Among Group 15 hydrides, $\text{NH}_3$ ($238.5\text{ K}$) has an elevated boiling point due to hydrogen bonding, so $\text{PH}_3$ ($185.5\text{ K}$) has the lowest boiling point. Therefore, $\text{E} = \text{P}$ (phosphorus).
  3. Step 3 — Check the maximum covalency of phosphorus: Phosphorus lies in Period 3 and possesses vacant $3d$-orbitals, allowing it to expand its octet up to a maximum covalency of $6$ (e.g., $\text{PF}_6^-$), not $4$. Thus, Statement II is false.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Both Statement I and Statement II are false, matching option (d).
Q16.stepsLatex:
Step 1: Statement I: I makes the longest bond in HI, and I has the largest (not smallest) covalent radius in Group
17. False. Step 2: Statement II: The Group 15 hydride with lowest b.p. is PH3, and P has 3d orbitals so its
maximum covalency is 6 (not 4). False.
Q16.trapHtml: Watch out: PH<sub>3</sub> (not NH<sub>3</sub>) has the lowest boiling point in Group 15!
Q16.finalAnsHtml: (D) Both Statement I and Statement II are false

Q17.subtopic: Nessler’s Reagent Test & Period 2 First IE
Q17.conceptHtml: NH<sub>3</sub> reacts with alkaline K<sub>2</sub>HgI<sub>4</sub> (Nessler’s reagent) to give a brown precipitate of basic mercury(II) amido-iodide (H<sub>2</sub>N · HgO · HgI).
Q17.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify element E from Nessler's reagent test: Treatment of $\text{EH}_3$ with alkaline $\text{K}_2\text{HgI}_4$ (Nessler's reagent) producing a brown precipitate of basic mercury(II) amido-iodide ($\text{HgO}\cdot\text{Hg}(\text{NH}_2)\text{I}$) is the confirmatory test for ammonia ($\text{NH}_3$), which also forms the binary cation $\text{NH}_4^+$. Hence, $\text{E} = \text{N}$ (Group 15).
  2. Step 2 — Compare $\Delta_i H_1$ of first elements of Groups 13–16: Across Period 2, ionization enthalpy generally increases with nuclear charge, with an extra jump at nitrogen due to its stable half-filled $2p^3$ subshell: $\text{B} = 801$, $\text{C} = 1086$, $\text{O} = 1312\text{ (or }1314\text{)}$, and $\text{N} = 1402\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$.
  3. Step 3 — Match the value for nitrogen: Nitrogen has the highest first ionization enthalpy among the four given values, namely $1402\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The correct value is $1402\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$, corresponding to option (a).
Q17.stepsLatex:
Step 1: From the Nessler’s test, EH3 = NH3, so E = N (Group 15). Step 2: Among Period 2 elements (B, C, N, O),
nitrogen has a half-filled 2p3 subshell, giving it the highest ∆iH1 (1402 kJ mol−1, vs B = 801, C = 1086, O =
1312 kJ mol−1).
Q17.trapHtml: ∆<sub>i</sub>H<sub>1</sub>(N) = 1402 > ∆<sub>i</sub>H<sub>1</sub>(O) = 1312 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup> due to half-filled 2p<sup>3</sup> stability.

Q18.subtopic: Group 14 Amphoteric Oxides & BF3 Lewis Acidity
Q18.conceptHtml: In Group 14, CO<sub>2</sub>, SiO<sub>2</sub>, GeO<sub>2</sub> are acidic, CO is neutral, while SnO, SnO<sub>2</sub>, PbO, PbO<sub>2</sub> (and GeO is acidic/weakly amphoteric, though GeO<sub>2</sub> is acidic) are amphoteric.
Q18.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Classify the Group 14 oxide pairs in Statement I: According to NCERT, $\text{CO}_2$, $\text{SiO}_2$, $\text{GeO}$, and $\text{GeO}_2$ are acidic, whereas $\text{SnO}$, $\text{SnO}_2$, $\text{PbO}$, and $\text{PbO}_2$ are all amphoteric.
  2. Step 2 — Count pairs with both oxides amphoteric: Out of the four listed pairs, exactly $2$ pairs—$[\text{SnO}, \text{SnO}_2]$ and $[\text{PbO}, \text{PbO}_2]$—contain two amphoteric oxides. Thus, Statement I is true.
  3. Step 3 — Evaluate Statement II (structure and Lewis acidity of $\text{BF}_3$): Boron in $\text{BF}_3$ has only $6$ valence electrons (incomplete octet), making it an electron-deficient Lewis acid that readily accepts a lone pair from $\text{NH}_3$ to form the adduct $\text{F}_3\text{B}\leftarrow\text{NH}_3$. With $3$ bond pairs and $0$ lone pairs ($sp^2$), $\text{BF}_3$ is trigonal planar. Thus, Statement II is true.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Both Statement I and Statement II are true, which corresponds to option (c).
Q18.stepsLatex:
Step 1: Statement I: Among the four pairs, [SnO, SnO2] and [PbO, PbO2] contain oxides that are both amphoteric
=⇒ 2 pairs. True. Step 2: Statement II: BF3 is sp2 trigonal planar, electron-deficient (6e−), acts as a Lewis acid,
and forms the adduct F3B ← NH3. True.
Q18.trapHtml: GeO<sub>2</sub> is distinctly acidic (dissolves in base, not acid), so [GeO, GeO<sub>2</sub>] is not an amphoteric pair.
Q18.finalAnsHtml: (C) Both Statement I and Statement II are true

Q19.subtopic: Acidity & Bond Dissociation Enthalpy of Group 16 Hydrides
Q19.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Comparing H<sub>2</sub>Se and H<sub>2</sub>Te
Q19.conceptHtml: Down Group 16 (H<sub>2</sub>O → H<sub>2</sub>Te), H − E bond dissociation enthalpy decreases, making H<sup>+</sup> release easier and increasing acidic strength.
Q19.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Compare bond dissociation enthalpy of $\text{H}_2\text{Se}$ and $\text{H}_2\text{Te}$: Tellurium ($\text{Te}$) is larger than selenium ($\text{Se}$), so the $\text{Te}-\text{H}$ bond is longer and weaker than the $\text{Se}-\text{H}$ bond. Consequently, $\text{H}_2\text{Se}$ has a higher bond dissociation enthalpy than $\text{H}_2\text{Te}$. Thus, Statement II is true.
  2. Step 2 — Relate bond enthalpy to acidic strength: Acidic strength of Group 16 hydrides depends on how easily $\text{H}^+$ is released in water. Because the $\text{Te}-\text{H}$ bond breaks more easily than the $\text{Se}-\text{H}$ bond, acidic strength follows $\text{H}_2\text{O} < \text{H}_2\text{S} < \text{H}_2\text{Se} < \text{H}_2\text{Te}$.
  3. Step 3 — Evaluate Statement I: Since $\text{H}_2\text{Te}$ is more acidic than $\text{H}_2\text{Se}$, claiming $\text{H}_2\text{Se}$ is more acidic is wrong. Thus, Statement I is false.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Statement I is false and Statement II is true, matching option (d).
Q19.stepsLatex:
Step 1: Statement I: H2Te is more acidic than H2Se (so claiming H2Se is more acidic is false). Step 2: Statement
II: H2Se has a shorter, stronger H − E bond and hence higher bond dissociation enthalpy than H2Te. True.
Q19.trapHtml: Higher bond dissociation enthalpy means weaker acid, not stronger!
Q19.finalAnsHtml: (D) Statement I is false but Statement II is true

Q20.subtopic: Inert Pair Effect in Al vs Tl
Q20.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Multi-statement selection on Al<sup>3+</sup>, Tl<sup>3+</sup>, Tl<sup>+</sup>
Q20.conceptHtml: In Group 13, Al<sup>3+</sup> is highly stable (E<sub>A</sub><sup>°</sup><sub>l3+/Al</sub> = −1.66 V), while Tl<sup>+</sup> is more stable than Tl<sup>3+</sup> due to the inert pair effect, making Tl<sup>3+</sup> a powerful oxidising agent.
Q20.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall oxidation state stability in Group 13: At the top of the group, $\text{Al}^{3+}$ is extremely stable ($E^\circ_{\text{Al}^{3+}/\text{Al}} = -1.66\text{ V}$), so $\text{Al}^{3+}$ does not get reduced easily (Statement B is true). At the bottom of the group, the inert pair effect makes $\text{Tl}^+$ far more stable than $\text{Tl}^{3+}$ (Statements D and E are true).
  2. Step 2 — Check the oxidising power and solution stability of $\text{Tl}^{3+}$: Because $\text{Tl}^{3+}$ strongly prefers to gain two electrons and convert into $\text{Tl}^+$ ($E^\circ_{\text{Tl}^{3+}/\text{Tl}^+} = +1.25\text{ V}$), $\text{Tl}^{3+}$ acts as a powerful oxidising agent (Statement A is true).
  3. Step 3 — Eliminate the incorrect statement: Since $\text{Tl}^{3+}$ is unstable and readily reduced in solution, Statement C ("Both $\text{Al}^{3+}$ and $\text{Tl}^{3+}$ are very stable in solution") is false.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Statements (A), (B), (D), and (E) are correct, matching option (a).
Q20.stepsLatex: Step 1: (A) True; (B) True; (C) False (Tl3+ is unstable in solution and oxidises water/halides); (D) True; (E) True.
Q20.trapHtml: Statement (C) contradicts (A) and (D) directly.

Q21.subtopic: Group 14 ∆iH1 & Redox Nature of Sn2+ and Pb4+
Q21.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Identifying A = Sn and B = Pb
Q21.conceptHtml: In Group 14, the two lowest ∆<sub>i</sub>H<sub>1</sub> values belong to Sn (708 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>) and Pb (715 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>).
Q21.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify Group 14 elements A and B from $\Delta_i H_1$: The first ionization enthalpies of Group 14 are $\text{C} = 1086$, $\text{Si} = 786$, $\text{Ge} = 761$, $\text{Sn} = 708$, and $\text{Pb} = 715\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$ (Pb is slightly higher than Sn due to poor shielding by $4f^{14}$ electrons). Thus, $\text{A} = \text{Sn}$ ($708$) and $\text{B} = \text{Pb}$ ($715$).
  2. Step 2 — Determine the nature of $\text{A}^{2+}$ ($\text{Sn}^{2+}$): For tin, the $+4$ oxidation state is more stable than $+2$, so $\text{Sn}^{2+}$ readily loses two electrons to become $\text{Sn}^{4+}$. Hence, $\text{Sn}^{2+}$ acts as a reducing agent.
  3. Step 3 — Determine the nature of $\text{B}^{4+}$ ($\text{Pb}^{4+}$): For lead, the inert pair effect makes $+2$ much more stable than $+4$, so $\text{Pb}^{4+}$ readily gains two electrons to become $\text{Pb}^{2+}$. Hence, $\text{Pb}^{4+}$ acts as an oxidising agent.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: $\text{A}^{2+}$ and $\text{B}^{4+}$ are reducing and oxidising respectively, matching option (d).
Q21.stepsLatex:
Step 1: A = Sn (708 kJ mol−1) and B = Pb (715 kJ mol−1). Step 2: For Sn, +4 is more stable than +2, so Sn2+
tends to oxidise to Sn4+ =⇒ reducing agent. Step 3: For Pb, +2 is more stable than +4, so Pb4+ tends to reduce
to Pb2+ =⇒ oxidising agent.
Q21.trapHtml: Note that ∆<sub>i</sub>H<sub>1</sub>(Pb) > ∆<sub>i</sub>H<sub>1</sub>(Sn) due to 4f<sup>14</sup> lanthanoid contraction, so A = Sn and B = Pb (not the reverse!).

Q22.subtopic: Group 13 vs Group 14: ∆iH1 and Melting/Boiling Points
Q22.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Comparing Group 13 and Group 14
Q22.conceptHtml: Across a period, nuclear charge increases so ∆<sub>i</sub>H<sub>1</sub>(Gr 14) > ∆<sub>i</sub>H<sub>1</sub>(Gr 13). However, Group 14 elements (especially C, Si, Ge) form strong 3D covalent network lattices, giving them much higher m.p./b.p. than Group 13.
Q22.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement I (first ionization enthalpy): Moving from Group 13 ($ns^2np^1$) to Group 14 ($ns^2np^2$) in the same period, nuclear charge increases and atomic radius decreases. Therefore, removing the first electron requires more energy in Group 14 than in Group 13. Thus, Statement I is correct.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement II (melting and boiling points): Group 14 elements form four strong covalent bonds per atom (creating rigid 3D covalent network structures in C, Si, and Ge), giving them much higher melting and boiling points than the corresponding Group 13 elements.
  3. Step 3 — Compare with Statement II: Statement II claims Group 13 elements have much higher melting and boiling points than Group 14, which is reversed. Thus, Statement II is incorrect.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Statement I is correct and Statement II is incorrect, matching option (a).
Q22.stepsLatex:
Step 1: Statement I: ∆iH1 of Group 14 > Group 13. True. Step 2: Statement II: Melting and boiling points
of Group 14 are much higher than Group 13 (NCERT Group 14: “Melting points and boiling points of group 14
elements are much higher than those of corresponding elements of group 13”). Thus Statement II is false.
Q22.trapHtml: Do not let Boron’s high m.p. (2453 K) fool you—Diamond/C (> 4000 K), Si (1687 K vs Al 933 K), and Ge (1211 K vs Ga 303 K) are all much higher.
Q22.finalAnsHtml: (A) Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect

Q23.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Extremes of ∆<sub>i</sub>H<sub>1</sub> in Group 13
Q23.conceptHtml: The ∆<sub>i</sub>H<sub>1</sub> order in Group 13 is B(801) > Tl(589) > Ga(579) > Al(577) > In(558) kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>.
Q23.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the Group 13 $\Delta_i H_1$ anomaly: Moving down Group 13, $\Delta_i H_1$ does not decrease smoothly because poor shielding by $3d^{10}$ electrons in Ga and $4f^{14}5d^{10}$ electrons in Tl raises effective nuclear charge.
  2. Step 2 — List the NCERT $\Delta_i H_1$ values (in $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$): $\text{B} = 801$, $\text{Tl} = 589$, $\text{Ga} = 579$, $\text{Al} = 577$, and $\text{In} = 558$.
  3. Step 3 — Identify the highest and lowest elements: The decreasing order is $\text{B} > \text{Tl} > \text{Ga} > \text{Al} > \text{In}$, so boron ($\text{B}$) has the highest and indium ($\text{In}$) has the lowest first ionization enthalpy.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The required pair is $\text{B}$ and $\text{In}$, matching option (c).
Q23.stepsLatex: Step 1: Highest ∆<sub>i</sub>H<sub>1</sub>: B (801 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>). Step 2: Lowest ∆<sub>i</sub>H<sub>1</sub>: In (558 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>).
Q23.trapHtml: Many students guess Tl is lowest, forgetting 4f<sup>14</sup> lanthanoid contraction raises Tl above Ga, Al, In.

Q24.subtopic: Nitrogen Oxides vs Halides (+5 Oxidation State)
Q24.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Two-statement evaluation on Nitrogen
Q24.conceptHtml: Nitrogen forms +1 to +5 oxides (e.g., N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>5</sub>) via pπ–pπ bonding with O (covalency stays ≤ 4), but cannot form NX<sub>5</sub> halides because it lacks d-orbitals.
Q24.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement I (oxides of nitrogen): Because both nitrogen and oxygen are small Period 2 atoms with high electronegativity, they undergo effective sideways overlap to form strong $p\pi\text{–}p\pi$ multiple bonds, stabilizing oxides across all oxidation states from $+1$ to $+5$ ($\text{N}_2\text{O}, \text{NO}, \text{N}_2\text{O}_3, \text{NO}_2/\text{N}_2\text{O}_4, \text{N}_2\text{O}_5$). Thus, Statement I is true.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement II (pentahalides of nitrogen): Forming a pentahalide ($\text{NX}_5$, $+5$ oxidation state) requires five single covalent bonds around nitrogen (covalency $= 5$). Since Period 2 nitrogen lacks vacant $d$-orbitals, its maximum covalency is $4$, so $\text{NX}_5$ does not exist. Thus, Statement II is true.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the final answer: Both Statement I and Statement II are true, which corresponds to option (a).
Q24.stepsLatex: Step 1: Both Statement I and Statement II are directly true per NCERT Group 15.
Q24.trapHtml: In N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>5</sub>, N has oxidation state +5 while its covalency is still 4 (one coordinate/double bond).
Q24.finalAnsHtml: (A) Both Statement I and Statement II are true

Q25.subtopic: Group 13 Atomic Radius Anomaly & M3+ Ionic Radius
Q25.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Identifying Al vs Ga anomaly
Q25.conceptHtml: Due to poor shielding of 3d<sup>10</sup> electrons, atomic radius of Ga (135 pm) is smaller than Al (143 pm), whereas M<sup>3+</sup> ionic radius increases regularly: Al<sup>3+</sup>(53.5 pm) < Ga<sup>3+</sup>(62 pm).
Q25.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Check the atomic radius trend in Group 13: Because of poor shielding by the intervening $3d^{10}$ subshell (transition contraction), gallium ($135\text{ pm}$) has a smaller atomic radius than aluminium ($143\text{ pm}$). The true order is $\text{B} < \text{Ga} < \text{Al} < \text{In} < \text{Tl}$.
  2. Step 2 — Identify the incorrect pair: Among the four given pairs, $(\text{Al} < \text{Ga})$ is incorrect because actually $\text{Ga} < \text{Al}$.
  3. Step 3 — Compare $\text{M}^{3+}$ ionic radii in the $(\text{Al}, \text{Ga})$ pair: Unlike neutral atomic radii, the $\text{M}^{3+}$ ionic radius increases smoothly down the group because $\text{Ga}^{3+}$ ($[\text{Ar}]3d^{10}$, $62\text{ pm}$) has an entire extra electron shell compared to $\text{Al}^{3+}$ ($[\text{Ne}]$, $53.5\text{ pm}$). Thus, the element with the larger $\text{M}^{3+}$ radius is $\text{X} = \text{Ga}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The atomic number of gallium ($\text{Ga}$) is $31$, matching option (c).
Q25.stepsLatex:
Step 1: The incorrect pair among (B < Al), (Al < Ga), (Ga < In), (In < Tl) is (Al < Ga) because Ga < Al. Step
2: Between Al (Z = 13, r(Al3+) = 53.5 pm) and Ga (Z = 31, r(Ga3+) = 62 pm), the element with the higher M3+
ionic radius is Ga (Z = 31).
Q25.trapHtml: Atomic radius has the 3d<sup>10</sup> contraction anomaly (r<sub>Ga</sub> < r<sub>Al</sub>), whereas M<sup>3+</sup> ionic radius increases regularly down the group (r<sub>Ga3+</sub> > r<sub>Al3+</sub>).

Q26.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Evaluating four Group 13 orders
Q26.conceptHtml: Group 13 key orders: Radius B < Ga < Al < In < Tl; χ: Al < Ga < In < Tl < B; Density: B < Al < Ga < In < Tl; ∆<sub>i</sub>H<sub>1</sub>: In < Al < Ga < Tl < B.
Q26.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Check Statements A and C (incorrect orders): Due to $3d^{10}$ poor shielding, $\text{Ga}$ is smaller than $\text{Al}$, so atomic radius is $\text{B} < \text{Ga} < \text{Al} < \text{In} < \text{Tl}$ (Statement A is false). Density increases down Group 13 ($\text{B} < \text{Al} < \text{Ga} < \text{In} < \text{Tl}$), opposite to Statement C (Statement C is false).
  2. Step 2 — Check Statement B (electronegativity): Pauling electronegativity values in Group 13 are $\text{Al} = 1.5 < \text{Ga} = 1.6 < \text{In} = 1.7 < \text{Tl} = 1.8 < \text{B} = 2.0$. Thus, Statement B is true.
  3. Step 3 — Check Statement D (1st ionization energy): NCERT $\Delta_i H_1$ values (in $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$) are $\text{In} = 558 < \text{Al} = 577 < \text{Ga} = 579 < \text{Tl} = 589 < \text{B} = 801$. Thus, Statement D is true.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Only statements B and D are correct, matching option (a).
Q26.stepsLatex:
Step 1: Check each order:
• A (False): Ga < Al, so B < Al < Ga is wrong.
• B (True): Al(1.5) < Ga(1.6) < In(1.7) < Tl(1.8) < B(2.0).
• C (False): Density increases down the group (B < Al < Ga < In < Tl), not decreases.
• D (True): ∆iH1: In(558) < Al(577) < Ga(579) < Tl(589) < B(801).
Q26.trapHtml: Memorise the exact ∆<sub>i</sub>H<sub>1</sub> order In < Al < Ga < Tl < B—it appears almost every year.

Q27.subtopic: N − N vs P − P Bond Length & +3 Disproportionation
Q27.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Two-statement evaluation on Group 15
Q27.conceptHtml: N − N single bond (145 pm, 159 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>) is weaker AND shorter than P − P single bond (221 pm, 213 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>). Group 15 +3 compounds (like HNO<sub>2</sub>, H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>3</sub>) readily disproportionate.
Q27.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement I (bond strength vs. bond length): The $\text{N}-\text{N}$ single bond is indeed weaker than the $\text{P}-\text{P}$ single bond due to high interelectronic repulsion between lone pairs on small N atoms. However, because nitrogen is much smaller than phosphorus, the $\text{N}-\text{N}$ bond ($145\text{ pm}$) is shorter—not longer—than the $\text{P}-\text{P}$ bond ($221\text{ pm}$). Thus, Statement I is false.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement II (disproportionation of $+3$ state in Group 15): While $\text{HNO}_2$ and $\text{H}_3\text{PO}_3$ disproportionate, down the group the $+3$ oxidation state becomes progressively more stable due to the inert pair effect (for $\text{Bi}$, $+3$ is the most stable state). Hence, heavier Group 15 compounds in $+3$ state do not readily disproportionate. Thus, Statement II is false.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the final answer: Both Statement I and Statement II are false, matching option (c).
Q27.stepsLatex:
Step 1: Statement I says N − N is “weaker and longer” than P − P—False (N is smaller, so N − N is shorter).
Step 2: Statement II: In Group 15, only nitrogen in +1 to +4 states (e.g., HNO2) and H3PO3 disproportionate; +3
oxidation state compounds of heavier Group 15 elements (As, Sb, Bi) are stable and do NOT readily disproportionate.
False.
Q27.trapHtml: “Weaker and longer” is false for N − N vs P − P (it is shorter), and +3 disproportionation is NOT a general property of all Group 15 elements (Bi<sup>3+</sup> is the most stable state of Bi).
Q27.finalAnsHtml: (C) Both Statement I and Statement II are false

Q28.subtopic: Redox Nature of TeO2 and Acidic Nature of TeH2
Q28.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Group 16 oxide and hydride
Q28.conceptHtml: In Group 16, SO<sub>2</sub> is reducing while TeO<sub>2</sub> is oxidising (stability of +4 increases and +6 decreases down the group). All H<sub>2</sub>E hydrides (H<sub>2</sub>S → H<sub>2</sub>Te) are acidic.
Q28.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Determine the redox nature of $\text{TeO}_2$: For Group 16 dioxides ($\text{EO}_2$), reducing character decreases down the group while oxidising character increases (due to the inert pair effect stabilizing lower states and weaker $\text{E}=\text{O}$ bonding). While $\text{SO}_2$ is a reducing agent, $\text{TeO}_2$ acts as an oxidising agent.
  2. Step 2 — Determine the acid–base nature of $\text{TeH}_2$ ($\text{H}_2\text{Te}$): Down Group 16 hydrides ($\text{H}_2\text{O} < \text{H}_2\text{S} < \text{H}_2\text{Se} < \text{H}_2\text{Te}$), the $\text{E}-\text{H}$ bond weakens, making $\text{H}^+$ donation easier. Hence, $\text{TeH}_2$ is acidic.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the final answer: $\text{TeO}_2$ is oxidising and $\text{TeH}_2$ is acidic, matching option (c).
Q28.stepsLatex: Step 1: TeO<sub>2</sub> is an oxidising agent. Step 2: TeH<sub>2</sub> (H<sub>2</sub>Te) is the strongest acid among Group 16 hydrides.
Q28.trapHtml: NCERT explicitly contrasts SO<sub>2</sub> (reducing) with TeO<sub>2</sub> (oxidising).

Q29.subtopic: Melting/Boiling Point Gap Between Oxygen and Sulphur
Q29.conceptHtml: Oxygen exists as a diatomic molecule (O<sub>2</sub>, atomicity 2) with weak van der Waals forces, whereas sulphur exists as a polyatomic puckered ring (S<sub>8</sub>, atomicity 8) with much stronger intermolecular forces.
Q29.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Compare the molecular forms of oxygen and sulphur: Oxygen forms strong $p\pi\text{–}p\pi$ double bonds and exists as small diatomic molecules ($\text{O}_2$, atomicity $= 2$). Sulphur cannot form effective $p\pi\text{–}p\pi$ bonds and instead catenates via single bonds into puckered eight-membered rings ($\text{S}_8$, atomicity $= 8$).
  2. Step 2 — Connect atomicity to intermolecular forces: Because $\text{S}_8$ has a much larger molecular mass and surface area than $\text{O}_2$, its London dispersion (van der Waals) forces are vastly stronger, making sulphur a solid with much higher melting and boiling points than gaseous oxygen.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the final answer: This large difference is directly explained on the basis of atomicity, matching option (a).
Q29.stepsLatex:
Step 1: The large jump in melting and boiling points from O to S is explained on the basis of atomicity (O2 vs
S8).
Q29.trapHtml: Do not pick atomic size or electronegativity—NCERT directly attributes this to atomicity.

Q30.conceptHtml: Group 14 melting points: C(6) > Si(14) > Ge(32) > Pb(82) > Sn(50).
Q30.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the Group 14 elements from their atomic numbers: $Z = 6$ is carbon ($\text{C}$), $Z = 14$ is silicon ($\text{Si}$), $Z = 50$ is tin ($\text{Sn}$), and $Z = 82$ is lead ($\text{Pb}$).
  2. Step 2 — Compare their melting points (NCERT data): $\text{C} = 4373\text{ K}$, $\text{Si} = 1693\text{ K}$, $\text{Sn} = 505\text{ K}$, and $\text{Pb} = 600\text{ K}$.
  3. Step 3 — Note the Sn vs. Pb anomaly: Although melting point generally falls down Group 14 as covalent network bonding transitions to metallic bonding, tin ($505\text{ K}$) has a lower melting point than lead ($600\text{ K}$) due to its less closely packed, distorted crystal lattice.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The element with the lowest melting point is tin ($Z = 50$), matching option (b).
Q30.stepsLatex:
Step 1: Sn (Z = 50, m.p. 505 K) has a lower melting point than Pb (Z = 82, m.p. 600 K), Si (Z = 14, 1687 K),
and C (Z = 6, > 4000 K).
Q30.trapHtml: Just like Group 13 (Ga lowest) and Group 14 ∆<sub>i</sub>H<sub>1</sub> (Sn < Pb), Sn (Z = 50) has a lower melting point than Pb (Z = 82).

Q31.subtopic: Redox Behaviour of SO2 & Group 15 Properties
Q31.conceptHtml: In SO<sub>2</sub>, sulphur is in the +4 oxidation state (intermediate between −2 and +6), so SO<sub>2</sub> can act as BOTH an oxidising agent and a reducing agent.
Q31.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Verify options (a), (c), and (d): $\text{PH}_3$ is less basic than $\text{NH}_3$ and therefore has lower proton affinity (a is true). $\text{NO}_2$ is an odd-electron radical that easily dimerises to $\text{N}_2\text{O}_4$ (c is true). $\text{PF}_3$ exists, whereas $\text{NF}_5$ does not because nitrogen lacks vacant $d$-orbitals (d is true).
  2. Step 2 — Analyse the redox nature of $\text{SO}_2$ in option (b): In $\text{SO}_2$, sulphur is in the $+4$ oxidation state, which lies between its minimum ($-2$) and maximum ($+6$) oxidation states.
  3. Step 3 — Identify the incorrect statement: Because $+4$ can both increase to $+6$ (e.g., reducing $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ or $\text{MnO}_4^-$) and decrease to $0$ or $-2$ (e.g., oxidising $\text{H}_2\text{S}$ to $\text{S}$), $\text{SO}_2$ acts as both an oxidising agent and a reducing agent. Claiming it cannot act as a reducing agent is false.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The incorrect statement is option (b).
Q31.stepsLatex:
Step 1: (A) True (NH3 is more basic than PH3); (B) False (SO2 acts as both oxidising and reducing agent); (C)
True (2NO2 ⇌ N2O4); (D) True (N lacks d-orbitals).
Q31.trapHtml: Any species in an intermediate oxidation state (like +4 in SO<sub>2</sub>) can both oxidise and reduce.
Q31.finalAnsHtml: (B) SO<sub>2</sub> can act as an oxidizing agent, but not as a reducing agent.

Q32.subtopic: Non-Metallic Group 15 Element with Weakest E − E Bond
Q32.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Identifying Nitrogen and its max covalency
Q32.conceptHtml: Among non-metallic Group 15 elements (N, P, As), N − N has the weakest single bond due to small size and lone-pair repulsion.
Q32.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the non-metallic Group 15 element E: The non-metals in Group 15 are nitrogen ($\text{N}$) and phosphorus ($\text{P}$). Between them, the $\text{N}-\text{N}$ single bond ($\approx 159\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$) is weaker than the $\text{P}-\text{P}$ single bond ($\approx 213\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$) because of high lone-pair–lone-pair repulsion between the small nitrogen atoms. Thus, $\text{E} = \text{N}$.
  2. Step 2 — Determine the maximum covalency of nitrogen: Nitrogen is a Period 2 element ($1s^22s^22p^3$) with only four valence orbitals ($2s, 2p_x, 2p_y, 2p_z$) and no $d$-orbitals.
  3. Step 3 — Conclude the maximum number of covalent bonds: Using all four valence orbitals (as in $\text{NH}_4^+$), nitrogen can achieve a maximum covalency of $4$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The maximum covalency is $4$, corresponding to option (c).
Q32.stepsLatex:
Step 1: Element ‘E’ is Nitrogen (N). Step 2: Since N has only four valence orbitals (2s, 2px, 2py, 2pz), its maximum
covalency is 4.
Q32.trapHtml: Read carefully: it asks for the maximum covalency (4), not the common covalency (3).

Q33.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Match List I with List II for Group 13
Q33.conceptHtml: Match all four Group 13 trends: m.p. B > Al > Tl > In > Ga; M<sup>3+</sup> ionic radius Tl > In > Ga > Al > B; ∆<sub>i</sub>H<sub>1</sub> B > Tl > Al ≈ Ga > In; atomic radius Tl > In > Al > Ga > B.
Q33.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Match A (Melting Point) and B (Ionic Radius $\text{M}^{3+}$): In Group 13, gallium has an unusually low melting point ($303\text{ K}$), giving the melting point order $\text{B} > \text{Al} > \text{Tl} > \text{In} > \text{Ga}$ (A–IV). Ionic radius of $\text{M}^{3+}$ increases smoothly down the group: $\text{Tl} > \text{In} > \text{Ga} > \text{Al} > \text{B}$ (B–I).
  2. Step 2 — Match C ($\Delta_i H_1$) and D (Atomic Radius): Due to $d$- and $f$-electron poor shielding, first ionization enthalpy follows $\text{B} (801) > \text{Tl} (589) > \text{Ga} (579) \approx \text{Al} (577) > \text{In} (558\text{ kJ mol}^{-1})$ (C–II). Atomic radius has the $\text{Ga} < \text{Al}$ anomaly: $\text{Tl} > \text{In} > \text{Al} > \text{Ga} > \text{B}$ (D–III).
  3. Step 3 — Combine all matches: We get A–IV, B–I, C–II, D–III.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: This matches option (a).
Q33.stepsLatex:
Step 1: Match each row:
• A (Melting Point) → IV (B > Al > Tl > In > Ga).
• B (Ionic Radius M3+) → I (Tl > In > Ga > Al > B).
• C (∆iH1) → II (B > Tl > Al ≈ Ga > In).
• D (Atomic Radius) → III (Tl > In > Al > Ga > B).
Q33.trapHtml: Distinguish M<sup>3+</sup> ionic radius (I: Ga > Al) from atomic radius (III: Al > Ga).

Q34.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Assertion–Reason on S<sub>8</sub> vs O<sub>2</sub>
Q34.conceptHtml: Oxygen’s small size and high electronegativity allow strong pπ–pπ bonding (O = O), whereas larger S atoms have poor 3pπ–3pπ overlap and instead form S − S single-bonded S<sub>8</sub> rings.
Q34.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Assertion (A): Both rhombic ($\alpha$-sulphur) and monoclinic ($\beta$-sulphur) allotropes consist of puckered $\text{S}_8$ rings, whereas elemental oxygen exists as diatomic $\text{O}_2$ molecules. Thus, (A) is correct.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Reason (R): Due to its small size and high electronegativity, oxygen forms strong $p\pi\text{–}p\pi$ multiple bonds with itself ($\text{O}=\text{O}$) and with other small atoms like C and N. Larger sulphur atoms have poor sideways $3p\text{–}3p$ overlap and do not form stable $p\pi\text{–}p\pi$ double bonds at room temperature, preferring $\text{S}-\text{S}$ single bonds in $\text{S}_8$ rings. Thus, (R) is correct.
  3. Step 3 — Check the causal link: Because oxygen stabilizes itself via a $p\pi\text{–}p\pi$ double bond ($\text{O}_2$) while sulphur relies on two single bonds per atom ($\text{S}_8$), Reason (R) directly explains Assertion (A).
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A), matching option (d).
Q34.stepsLatex: Step 1: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the exact explanation of (A).
Q34.trapHtml: Both rhombic (α) and monoclinic (β) sulphur consist of S<sub>8</sub> molecules.
Q34.finalAnsHtml: (D) Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)

Q35.subtopic: Reaction of PbS with Dilute HNO3
Q35.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Products of PbS + dil. HNO<sub>3</sub>
Q35.conceptHtml: Dilute HNO<sub>3</sub> oxidises sulphide (S<sup>2−</sup>) to elemental sulphur (S) while itself reducing to nitric oxide (NO), NOT N<sub>2</sub>O.
Q35.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Write the balanced reaction of $\text{PbS}$ with dilute $\text{HNO}_3$: Dilute nitric acid oxidises sulphide ($\text{S}^{2-}$) to elemental sulphur ($\text{S}$) while itself being reduced to nitric oxide ($\text{NO}$): $3\text{PbS} + 8\text{HNO}_3\text{ (dil.)} \rightarrow 3\text{Pb}(\text{NO}_3)_2 + 2\text{NO} + 3\text{S} + 4\text{H}_2\text{O}$.
  2. Step 2 — List all products formed: The reaction produces lead nitrate ($\text{Pb}(\text{NO}_3)_2$), nitric oxide ($\text{NO}$), elemental sulphur ($\text{S}$), and water.

  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The substance not formed is nitrous oxide, corresponding to option (d).

Q36.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Metals vs non-metals in p-block
Q36.conceptHtml: Non-metals have higher electronegativity and higher ionisation enthalpy than metals, form ionic compounds with reactive metals, and form acidic/neutral oxides (while metal oxides are generally basic).
Q36.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Check Statements (A) and (C) (true statements): Non-metals lie on the upper right of the periodic table and have higher electronegativity than metals (A is true). When a highly reactive metal (low ionization enthalpy) reacts with a highly reactive non-metal (high electron affinity), electron transfer occurs to form an ionic compound (C is true).
  2. Step 2 — Check Statements (B), (D), and (E) (false statements): Non-metals have higher—not lower—ionization enthalpies than metals (B is false). Non-metal oxides are generally acidic or neutral, not basic (D is false), while metal oxides are generally basic or amphoteric, not acidic/neutral (E is false).
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the final answer: Only statements (A) and (C) are correct, matching option (d).

Q37.conceptHtml: Down Group 15, due to the inert pair effect, stability of +5 OS decreases and +3 OS increases. Nitrogen’s max covalency is 4, not 6.
Q37.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the correct statements (A, B, and C): Dinitrogen ($\text{N}\equiv\text{N}$) has a very high bond enthalpy ($941.4\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$), making it nearly inert at room temperature (A is correct). Group 15 elements commonly exhibit $-3, +3,$ and $+5$ oxidation states (B is correct), and nitrogen uniquely forms strong $p\pi\text{–}p\pi$ multiple bonds (C is correct).
  2. Step 2 — Identify the incorrect statements (D and E): Due to the inert pair effect, the stability of the $+5$ oxidation state decreases (while $+3$ increases) down Group 15 (D is incorrect). Furthermore, lacking $d$-orbitals, nitrogen has a maximum covalency of $4$—not $6$ (E is incorrect).
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the final answer: The incorrect statements are (D) and (E) only, matching option (b).

Q38.subtopic: Inert Pair Effect in Group 13 (+1 Oxidation State)
Q38.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Assertion–Reason on Ga < In < Tl
Q38.conceptHtml: Poor shielding by intervening d and f electrons pulls ns<sup>2</sup> electrons closer to the nucleus, making them reluctant to bond and stabilising the +1 oxidation state down Group 13.
Q38.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Assertion A: In Group 13, the stability of the $+1$ oxidation state increases progressively down the group: $\text{Ga}^+ < \text{In}^+ < \text{Tl}^+$ (with $\text{Tl}^+$ being more stable than $\text{Tl}^{3+}$). Thus, Assertion A is true.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Reason R: Down the group, intervening $d$- and $f$-electrons shield the nucleus poorly, so the valence $ns^2$ electrons are pulled closer to the nucleus and become reluctant to participate in bonding (the inert pair effect). This stabilizes the lower ($+1$) oxidation state. Thus, Reason R is true.
  3. Step 3 — Verify the explanation link: The inert pair effect directly accounts for why the $+1$ state becomes increasingly stable from $\text{Ga}$ to $\text{Tl}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A, matching option (d).

down the group) is true and is the exact explanation of A.

Q38.finalAnsHtml: (D) Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

Q39.conceptHtml: Disproportionation requires an element to be simultaneously oxidised and reduced. Since fluorine is the most electronegative element, it can only be reduced (0 → −1) and never oxidised to a positive state.
Q39.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the requirement for disproportionation: An element in a disproportionation reaction must simultaneously be oxidised to a higher oxidation state and reduced to a lower oxidation state.
  2. Step 2 — Check fluorine ($\text{F}_2$): Fluorine is the most electronegative element and has no vacant $d$-orbitals; it only shows $-1$ (and $0$) oxidation states and cannot form positive oxidation states. Hence, $\text{F}_2$ never undergoes disproportionation.
  3. Step 3 — Check $\text{Cl}_2, \text{Br}_2,$ and $\text{I}_2$: Chlorine, bromine, and iodine can exhibit both $-1$ and positive ($+1, +3, +5, +7$) oxidation states, so they readily disproportionate (e.g., $\text{X}_2 + 2\text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{X}^- + \text{OX}^- + \text{H}_2\text{O}$).
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: $\text{Cl}_2, \text{Br}_2,$ and $\text{I}_2$ undergo disproportionation, matching option (b).
Q39.stepsLatex:
Step 1: Cl2, Br2, I2 disproportionate in alkali (e.g., X2 + 2OH− → X− + XO− + H2O), whereas F2 does NOT (2F2+
2H2O → 4HF + O2).

Q40.subtopic: Group 14 Trends: Radius, χ, Covalency, π-Bonds & OS
Q40.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Multi-statement evaluation on Group 14
Q40.conceptHtml: In Group 14, covalent radius increases down the group, χ stays nearly constant from Si to Pb (1.8–1.9), C max covalency is 4 (others expand via d-orbitals), heavier elements do not form pπ–pπ bonds, and C shows negative OS (e.g., CH<sub>4</sub>, Al<sub>4</sub>C<sub>3</sub>).
Q40.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Eliminate false statements (A) and (B): Down Group 14 from C to Pb, new electron shells are added, so covalent radius increases—not decreases (A is false). Electronegativity drops from C ($2.5$) to Si ($1.8$), remains nearly constant across Si, Ge, Sn ($1.8$), and rises slightly at Pb ($1.9$), rather than decreasing gradually (B is false).
  2. Step 2 — Verify true statements (C), (D), and (E): Carbon has no $d$-orbitals (max covalency $= 4$), while Si to Pb can expand their covalency to $6$ using vacant $d$-orbitals (C is true). Heavier Group 14 atoms are too large for effective sideways $p$-orbital overlap and do not form $p\pi\text{–}p\pi$ bonds (D is true). Carbon can also show negative oxidation states such as $-4$ in $\text{CH}_4$ (E is true).
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the final answer: Statements (C), (D), and (E) only are correct, matching option (c).

Step 1: (A) False (increases, not decreases); (B) False (χ drops C (2.5) → Si (1.8) then remains ≈ 1.8–1.9 for
Si, Ge, Sn, Pb); (C) True; (D) True; (E) True.
Q40.trapHtml: In Group 14, electronegativity does NOT decrease gradually from Si to Pb (Si = 1.8, Ge = 1.8, Sn = 1.8, Pb = 1.9).

Q41.subtopic: Gallium Thermometers & Freezing Point of Brine
Q41.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Liquid range of Gallium
Q41.conceptHtml: Gallium has an unusually low melting point (303 K = 29.8<sup>°</sup>C) and a very high boiling point (2676 K), making it ideal for high-temperature thermometers—but it freezes below 303 K.
Q41.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement I: Gallium has a very low melting point ($303\text{ K}$) and an exceptionally high boiling point ($2676\text{ K}$), giving it a huge liquid range that makes it ideal for high-temperature thermometers. Thus, Statement I is true.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement II: A liquid thermometer can only operate at temperatures where the thermometric substance remains liquid. At $256\text{ K}$ (the freezing point of brine), gallium is well below its melting point ($303\text{ K}$) and is therefore solid, so it cannot measure $256\text{ K}$. Thus, Statement II is false.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the final answer: Statement I is true and Statement II is false, matching option (b).

Step 1: Statement I: Ga is used in high-temperature thermometers. True. Step 2: Statement II: At 256 K (freezing
point of brine), pure Ga (m.p. 303 K) is a solid, so a gallium thermometer cannot measure 256 K. False.
Q41.trapHtml: Always check the melting point of Ga (303 K) vs the target temperature (256 K).
Q41.finalAnsHtml: (B) Statement I is true but Statement II is false

Q42.subtopic: Group 13 Radii, χ, Passivity in HNO3 & [Al(H2O)6]3+
Q42.conceptHtml: Al becomes passive in conc. HNO<sub>3</sub> due to a protective Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> film, and [Al(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup> is octahedral (sp<sup>3</sup>d<sup>2</sup>).

Step 1 — Eliminate false statements (A), (B), and (D): Atomic radius in Group 13 has the $\text{Ga} < \text{Al}$ anomaly ($\text{Tl} > \text{In} > \text{Al} > \text{Ga} > \text{B}$), so (A) is false. Electronegativity falls from B to Al and then rises from Al to Tl, so (B) is false. Only heavier Group 13 elements (especially Tl) show a highly stable $+1$ state, not all elements, so (D) is false.

Step 2 — Verify Statement (C): Aluminium reacts with dilute $\text{HCl}$ to evolve $\text{H}_2$ gas ($2\text{Al} + 6\text{HCl} \rightarrow 2\text{AlCl}_3 + 3\text{H}_2$), whereas concentrated $\text{HNO}_3$ renders it passive by forming a thin protective $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ oxide film. Thus, (C) is true.
  3. Step 3 — Verify Statement (E): In the octahedral complex $[\text{Al}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{3+}$, aluminium forms $6$ coordinate bonds using its outer $3s, 3p,$ and $3d$ orbitals, corresponding to $sp^3d^2$ hybridisation. Thus, (E) is true.

Q43.subtopic: Group 13 +1 Stability & Ga vs Al Atomic Size
Q43.conceptHtml: Down Group 13, +1 stability increases (Ga < In < Tl) via the inert pair effect, and atomic size of Ga (135 pm) is smaller than Al (143 pm) due to poor 3d<sup>10</sup> shielding.

1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement I: Due to the inert pair effect becoming stronger down Group 13, the valence $ns^2$ electrons become increasingly reluctant to ionize, so the stability of the $+1$ oxidation state increases down the group ($\text{Ga} < \text{In} < \text{Tl}$). Thus, Statement I is correct.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement II: Gallium has $10$ intervening $3d$ electrons that shield the nuclear charge poorly. This pulls the outer electrons inward, making the atomic radius of gallium ($135\text{ pm}$) smaller—not greater—than that of aluminium ($143\text{ pm}$). Thus, Statement II is incorrect.

Q44.subtopic: Boron Isotope Neutrons & Oxidation State in Oxide
Q44.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Calculating x + y for Boron
Q44.conceptHtml: Natural boron consists of <sup>10</sup>B (19%) and <sup>11</sup>B (81%, more abundant). Amorphous boron burns in air to form B<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> (and BN), where B is in +3 OS.
Q44.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Find $x$ (neutrons in the more abundant isotope of boron): Naturally occurring boron ($Z = 5$) consists of $^{10}\text{B}$ ($\approx 19\%$) and $^{11}\text{B}$ ($\approx 81\%$). The more abundant isotope is $^{11}\text{B}$, so the number of neutrons is $x = A - Z = 11 - 5 = 6$.
  2. Step 2 — Find $y$ (oxidation state of boron on heating in air): Heating amorphous boron in air produces boron trioxide and boron nitride: $4\text{B} + 3\text{O}_2 \xrightarrow{\Delta} 2\text{B}_2\text{O}_3$ and $2\text{B} + \text{N}_2 \xrightarrow{\Delta} 2\text{BN}$. In both $\text{B}_2\text{O}_3$ and $\text{BN}$, boron has an oxidation state of $y = +3$.
  3. Step 3 — Compute $x + y$: Adding the two values gives $x + y = 6 + 3 = 9$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The value of $x + y$ is $9$, which corresponds to option (a).

Step 1: More abundant isotope is 151B, so neutrons x = 11 − 5 = 6. Step 2: 4B + 3O2 −∆→ 2B2O3, where oxidation
state of B is y = +3. Step 3: x + y = 6 + 3 = 9.
Q44.trapHtml: <sup>11</sup>B (80–81%) is more abundant than <sup>10</sup>B (19–20%).

Q45.conceptHtml: SiO<sub>2</sub>, GeO<sub>2</sub> are acidic while SnO, PbO are amphoteric. Carbon allotropes arise from catenation and pπ–pπ (NOT pπ–dπ) bonding.
Q45.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement I (Acid-base nature of Group 14 oxides): In Group 14, metallic character increases down the group, so oxide character shifts from acidic to amphoteric. Both $\text{SiO}_2$ and $\text{GeO}_2$ are acidic oxides, whereas $\text{SnO}$ and $\text{PbO}$ react with both acids and bases and are therefore amphoteric. Thus, Statement I is true.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement II (Cause of carbon allotropy): Carbon forms multiple allotropes (diamond, graphite, fullerenes) due to its strong catenation tendency and its ability to form $p\pi\text{–}p\pi$ multiple bonds with itself.
  3. Step 3 — Spot the error in Statement II: Carbon belongs to the second period ($1s^2 2s^2 2p^2$) and has no vacant $d$-orbitals, so it cannot form $p\pi\text{–}d\pi$ bonds. Hence, Statement II is false.
  4. Step 4 — Final Conclusion: Statement I is true but Statement II is false, confirming option (d).

Step 1: Statement I is true. Step 2: Statement II is false because carbon has no d-orbitals and forms pπ–pπ
bonds.
Q45.trapHtml: Catch the pπ–dπ vs pπ–pπ swap for carbon!
Q45.finalAnsHtml: (D) Statement I is true but Statement II is false

Q46.subtopic: Strongest Reducing Agent in Group 15 Hydrides
Q46.conceptHtml: Reducing power of Group 15 hydrides increases down the group as E − H bond strength decreases: NH<sub>3</sub> < PH<sub>3</sub> < AsH<sub>3</sub> < SbH<sub>3</sub> < BiH<sub>3</sub>.
Q46.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the trend for Group 15 hydrides: The given compounds $\text{NH}_3$, $\text{PH}_3$, $\text{SbH}_3$, and $\text{BiH}_3$ are hydrides of Group 15 elements ($\text{E} = \text{N, P, Sb, Bi}$).
  2. Step 2 — Relate bond strength to reducing power: Down the group, the atomic radius of the central atom $\text{E}$ increases, so the $\text{E–H}$ bond length increases and its bond dissociation enthalpy decreases.
  3. Step 3 — Compare reducing character: A weaker $\text{E–H}$ bond releases hydrogen more readily, making the hydride a stronger reducing agent. Therefore, reducing strength increases in the order $\text{NH}_3 < \text{PH}_3 < \text{AsH}_3 < \text{SbH}_3 < \text{BiH}_3$.
  4. Step 4 — Final Conclusion: $\text{BiH}_3$ has the weakest $\text{E–H}$ bond and is the strongest reducing agent, confirming option (c).

Q46.trapHtml: Thermal stability decreases down the group, so reducing power increases down the group.

Q47.conceptHtml: Group 13 trihalides (MX<sub>3</sub>) are covalent and readily hydrolysed in water; AlCl<sub>3</sub> in acidified aqueous medium forms octahedral [Al(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup>.
Q47.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement I (Hydrolysis of Group 13 trihalides): Group 13 trivalent halides ($\text{MX}_3$) are predominantly covalent and electron-deficient (the central atom has an incomplete octet with a vacant $p$-orbital). Because they readily accept a lone pair from water molecules, they undergo easy hydrolysis. Thus, Statement I is true.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement II (Hydrolysis of $\text{AlCl}_3$ in acidified water): When anhydrous $\text{AlCl}_3$ dissolves in acidified aqueous solution, the $\text{Al}^{3+}$ ion coordinates with six $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ ligands using its vacant $3s$, $3p$, and $3d$ orbitals ($sp^3d^2$ hybridisation).
  3. Step 3 — Identify the resulting complex: This forms the octahedral hexaaquaaluminium(III) complex ion $[\text{Al}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{3+}$, making Statement II true.
  4. Step 4 — Final Conclusion: Both Statement I and Statement II are true, confirming option (b).

Q47.trapHtml: Unlike BCl<sub>3</sub> (which forms B(OH)<sub>3</sub>), AlCl<sub>3</sub> in acidified water forms [Al(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup>.
Q47.finalAnsHtml: (B) Both statement I and statement II are true

Q48.subtopic: Group 16 Oxides, Hydrides & Ozone Lone Pairs
Q48.conceptHtml: In Group 16, EO<sub>2</sub> and EO<sub>3</sub> are acidic, SO<sub>2</sub> is reducing while TeO<sub>2</sub> is oxidising, reducing power of H<sub>2</sub>E increases down the group, and O<sub>3</sub> has 6 lone pairs.
Q48.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Check Statements A and B: Group 16 elements ($\text{E} = \text{S, Se, Te, Po}$) form dioxides ($\text{EO}_2$) and trioxides ($\text{EO}_3$), and both oxide types are acidic in nature, so A is correct. Down the group, the stability of the $+6$ oxidation state decreases due to the inert pair effect; hence $\text{SO}_2$ acts as a reducing agent (easily oxidised to $+6$) whereas $\text{TeO}_2$ acts as an oxidising agent, so B is correct.
  2. Step 2 — Check Statement C: Down Group 16, the $\text{E–H}$ bond dissociation enthalpy decreases from $\text{H}_2\text{S}$ to $\text{H}_2\text{Te}$, so reducing character increases (not decreases) from $\text{H}_2\text{S}$ to $\text{H}_2\text{Te}$. Thus, C is incorrect.
  3. Step 3 — Check Statement D: Ozone ($\text{O}_3$) has $3 \times 6 = 18$ valence electrons. Its resonance structure $\text{O}=\text{O}^+\text{–}\text{O}^-$ uses $3$ shared electron pairs ($6$ bonding electrons), leaving $18 - 6 = 12$ non-bonding electrons, which equals $6$ lone pairs (not $5$). Thus, D is incorrect.
  4. Step 4 — Final Conclusion: Only statements A and B are correct, confirming option (a).

• A (True): All Group 16 elements form EO2 and EO3, which are acidic (NCERT Group 16).
• B (True): TeO2 is an oxidising agent and SO2 is a reducing agent.
• C (False): Reducing property increases from H2S to H2Te.
• D (False): O3 has 18 valence e−: 3 bonds (6e−) + 6 lone pairs (12e−), NOT 5 lone pairs.

  2. Step 2 — Classify each listed oxide: $\text{CO}$ is a neutral oxide; $\text{SiO}_2$, $\text{GeO}_2$, and $\text{GeO}$ are acidic oxides.

Q50.subtopic: Boiling Points & Dispersion Forces of Noble Gases
Q50.conceptHtml: Noble gases are monoatomic with only weak London dispersion forces between atoms, so they have very low boiling points and are liquefied only at very low temperatures.
Q50.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Analyze intermolecular forces in noble gases: Noble gases exist as monoatomic species with completely filled valence shells, so the only intermolecular forces between their atoms are weak van der Waals (London dispersion) forces.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement I: Because these dispersion forces are very weak, noble gases require very little thermal energy to boil and therefore have very low boiling points. Thus, Statement I is false.
  3. Step 3 — Evaluate Statement II: Statement II incorrectly claims that noble gases are held together by strong dispersion forces and have very high boiling points. Thus, Statement II is also false.
  4. Step 4 — Final Conclusion: Both Statement I and Statement II are false, confirming option (a).

Step 1: Statement I is false (very low, not high b.p.). Step 2: Statement II is false (weak dispersion forces, not
strong, and very low b.p., not high).

Q50.finalAnsHtml: (A) Both Statement I and Statement II are false.

Q51.subtopic: Group 15 Hydrides: Stability, Reducing Power & Basicity
Q51.conceptHtml: Down Group 15 hydrides (NH<sub>3</sub> → BiH<sub>3</sub>): thermal stability decreases, basicity decreases (NH<sub>3</sub> > PH<sub>3</sub> > AsH<sub>3</sub> > SbH<sub>3</sub> > BiH<sub>3</sub>), and reducing ability increases.
Q51.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Check thermal stability (Statement A): Down Group 15, the $\text{E–H}$ bond length increases and bond dissociation enthalpy decreases, so thermal stability decreases in the order $\text{NH}_3 > \text{PH}_3 > \text{AsH}_3 > \text{SbH}_3 > \text{BiH}_3$. Thus, A is correct.
  2. Step 2 — Check reducing ability (Statements B and C): As $\text{E–H}$ bond strength decreases down the group, hydrogen is donated more easily, so reducing power increases in the order $\text{NH}_3 < \text{PH}_3 < \text{AsH}_3 < \text{SbH}_3 < \text{BiH}_3$ ($\text{NH}_3$ is a mild reducing agent while $\text{BiH}_3$ is the strongest). Thus, B is correct and C is incorrect.
  3. Step 3 — Check basicity (Statement D): As the size of the central atom increases down the group, the lone pair becomes more diffused over a larger volume, reducing electron density and basicity ($\text{NH}_3 > \text{PH}_3 > \text{AsH}_3 > \text{SbH}_3 > \text{BiH}_3$). Thus, D is incorrect.
  4. Step 4 — Final Conclusion: Only statements A and B are correct, confirming option (c).
Q51.stepsLatex:
Step 1: A is true; B is true; C is false (NH3 is mildest, BiH3 is strongest reducing agent); D is false (basicity
decreases down the group).
Q51.trapHtml: Check direction of inequalities in B (<) vs D (<): basicity decreases while reducing ability increases.

Q52.subtopic: Acidic Strength of H2Te vs H2S
Q52.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Assertion–Reason on Group 16 hydrides
Q52.conceptHtml: Acidic character of H<sub>2</sub>E increases down Group 16 (H<sub>2</sub>O < H<sub>2</sub>S < H<sub>2</sub>Se < H<sub>2</sub>Te) because the H − E bond dissociation enthalpy decreases as E gets larger.
Q52.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Assertion (A): Acidic strength of Group 16 hydrides increases down the group ($\text{H}_2\text{O} < \text{H}_2\text{S} < \text{H}_2\text{Se} < \text{H}_2\text{Te}$), so $\text{H}_2\text{Te}$ is indeed more acidic than $\text{H}_2\text{S}$. Thus, A is true.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Reason (R): Because $\text{Te}$ has a much larger atomic radius than $\text{S}$, the $\text{Te–H}$ bond is longer and weaker than the $\text{S–H}$ bond, giving $\text{H}_2\text{Te}$ a lower bond dissociation enthalpy than $\text{H}_2\text{S}$. Thus, R is true.
  3. Step 3 — Check the causal link: A lower $\text{E–H}$ bond dissociation enthalpy allows $\text{H}_2\text{Te}$ to release $\text{H}^+$ ions more readily in aqueous solution than $\text{H}_2\text{S}$, so R correctly explains A.
  4. Step 4 — Final Conclusion: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A, confirming option (a).
Q52.stepsLatex: Step 1: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A.
Q52.trapHtml: Compare with Q19 (same concept, opposite statement).
Q52.finalAnsHtml: (A) Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

Q53.subtopic: Cause of Anomalous Behaviour of Oxygen
Q53.conceptHtml: First members of p-block groups (B, C, N, O, F) show anomalous behaviour due to their small atomic size, high electronegativity, and absence of d-orbitals.
Q53.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall why second-period elements show anomalous behaviour: The first member of each $p$-block group differs significantly from the heavier congeners because of three main factors: exceptionally small atomic size, high electronegativity, and the absence of vacant $d$-orbitals.
  2. Step 2 — Apply to oxygen (Group 16): Oxygen is the smallest and most electronegative element in Group 16, which enables strong hydrogen bonding in $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ and $p\pi\text{–}p\pi$ double bonding in $\text{O}_2$.
  3. Step 3 — Match with the options: Only "small size and high electronegativity" matches these governing factors.
  4. Step 4 — Final Conclusion: The anomalous behaviour of oxygen is due to its small size and high electronegativity, confirming option (b).
Q53.stepsLatex: Step 1: Oxygen’s anomalous behaviour is due to its small size and high electronegativity.
Q53.trapHtml: Same reason applies to N and F.

Q54.subtopic: Important Minerals & Ores of p-Block Elements
Q54.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Identify incorrect mineral formula
Q54.conceptHtml: Fluorspar (fluorite) is calcium fluoride (CaF<sub>2</sub>), NOT BF<sub>3</sub>.
Q54.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Verify the first three mineral formulas: Fluoroapatite is $3\text{Ca}_3(\text{PO}_4)_2 \cdot \text{CaF}_2$ (correct), Carnallite is $\text{KCl} \cdot \text{MgCl}_2 \cdot 6\text{H}_2\text{O}$ (correct), and Cryolite is $\text{Na}_3\text{AlF}_6$ (correct).
  2. Step 2 — Check the formula of Fluorspar: Fluorspar (fluorite) is the naturally occurring mineral form of calcium fluoride, whose chemical formula is $\text{CaF}_2$.
  3. Step 3 — Identify the mismatch: Option (d) pairs Fluorspar with $\text{BF}_3$ (boron trifluoride), which is incorrect.
  4. Step 4 — Final Conclusion: The incorrect pair is Fluorspar – $\text{BF}_3$, confirming option (d).
Q54.stepsLatex:
Step 1: Check pairs: Fluoroapatite 3Ca3(PO4)2 · CaF2 (correct); Carnallite KCl · MgCl2 · 6H2O (correct); Cryolite
Na3AlF6 (correct); Fluorspar BF3 (incorrect, should be CaF2).
Q54.trapHtml: Cryolite (Na<sub>3</sub>AlF<sub>6</sub>) and Fluorspar (CaF<sub>2</sub>) are both used in the Hall–Héroult process.

Q55.subtopic: Oxidation States of Oxygen & Group 16 Stability Trend
Q55.conceptHtml: Oxygen shows −2 (most common), −1 (H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>), +1 (O<sub>2</sub>F<sub>2</sub>), and +2 (OF<sub>2</sub>). Down Group 16, +4 stability increases and +6 stability decreases (inert pair effect).
Q55.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement I (Oxidation states of oxygen): Although $-2$ is the most common oxidation state of oxygen, it also exhibits $-1$ in peroxides (e.g., $\text{H}_2\text{O}_2$), $-1/2$ in superoxides (e.g., $\text{KO}_2$), and positive states $+2$ in $\text{OF}_2$ and $+1$ in $\text{O}_2\text{F}_2$. Therefore, Statement I is incorrect.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement II (Stability of $+4$ vs $+6$ down Group 16): Due to the inert pair effect (reluctance of the $ns^2$ electrons to participate in bonding in heavier elements), the stability of the higher $+6$ oxidation state decreases while the stability of the lower $+4$ oxidation state increases down Group 16.
  3. Step 3 — Compare with Statement II: Statement II states the exact reverse trend, so Statement II is also incorrect.
  4. Step 4 — Final Conclusion: Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect, confirming option (b).
Q55.stepsLatex:
Step 1: Statement I is false (O shows −1, +1, +2 as well). Step 2: Statement II is false (down the group, +4
stability increases and +6 stability decreases).
Q55.trapHtml: Remember: down any p-block group, the lower oxidation state (n − 2) becomes more stable.
Q55.finalAnsHtml: (B) Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect

Q56.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Oxidation state of Fluorine
Q56.conceptHtml: Fluorine has no d-orbitals and is the most electronegative element (χ = 4.0), so it exhibits only −1 oxidation state in its compounds.
Q56.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Examine the valence orbitals of halogens: Chlorine, bromine, and iodine belong to periods $3$, $4$, and $5$ respectively, so they possess vacant $d$-orbitals and can expand their octet to exhibit variable oxidation states ($-1, +1, +3, +5, +7$).
  2. Step 2 — Analyze fluorine: Fluorine ($1s^2 2s^2 2p^5$) is the most electronegative element in the periodic table and lacks vacant $d$-orbitals in its valence shell ($n = 2$).
  3. Step 3 — Determine fluorine's oxidation state: Consequently, fluorine cannot exhibit positive oxidation states and always shows a fixed oxidation state of $-1$ in all its compounds.
  4. Step 4 — Final Conclusion: Fluorine does not show variable oxidation states, confirming option (d).
Q56.stepsLatex: Step 1: Cl, Br, I show −1, +1, +3, +5, +7, while Fluorine shows only −1 (and 0 in F<sub>2</sub>).
Q56.trapHtml: Fluorine never shows a positive oxidation state.

Q57.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Assertion–Reason on Boron’s m.p.
Q57.conceptHtml: Boron has an unusually high melting point (2453 K) in Group 13 because solid crystalline boron consists of tightly bonded B<sub>12</sub> icosahedral units forming a very strong crystalline lattice.
Q57.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Assertion (A): Unlike the other Group 13 elements (which are soft metals with low to moderate melting points), boron is a hard non-metallic solid with an unusually high melting point of $2453\text{ K}$. Thus, (A) is correct.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Reason (R): Solid crystalline boron consists of tightly bonded three-dimensional icosahedral $\text{B}_{12}$ units forming an exceptionally strong covalent crystalline lattice. Thus, (R) is correct.
  3. Step 3 — Verify the explanation: Breaking this strong three-dimensional crystalline lattice requires a very large amount of thermal energy, which directly accounts for boron's unusually high melting point.
  4. Step 4 — Final Conclusion: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A), confirming option (b).
Q57.stepsLatex: Step 1: Both (A) and (R) are correct, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Q57.trapHtml: Contrast Boron (2453 K, covalent icosahedral lattice) with Gallium (303 K, molecular Ga<sub>2</sub> pairs).
Q57.finalAnsHtml: (B) Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)

Q58.subtopic: Counting P − O − P Linkages in Phosphorus
Q58.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Structures of H<sub>4</sub>P<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub>, (HPO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>, P<sub>4</sub>O<sub>10</sub>
Q58.conceptHtml: Count bridging P − O − P bonds from standard structures: pyrophosphoric acid (H<sub>4</sub>P<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub>) is a linear dimer; cyclotrimetaphosphoric acid (HPO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub> is a 6-membered ring; P<sub>4</sub>O<sub>10</sub> is a tetrahedral cage.
Q58.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Count $\text{P–O–P}$ bonds in pyrophosphoric acid ($\text{H}_4\text{P}_2\text{O}_7$): Its structure is $(\text{HO})_2\text{P}(=\text{O})\text{–O–P}(=\text{O})(\text{OH})_2$, where two phosphorus atoms are linked by $1$ bridging $\text{P–O–P}$ bond.
  2. Step 2 — Count $\text{P–O–P}$ bonds in cyclotrimetaphosphoric acid ($(\text{HPO}_3)_3$): It forms a six-membered alternating ring of three $\text{P}$ and three $\text{O}$ atoms, containing $3$ $\text{P–O–P}$ bonds.
  3. Step 3 — Count $\text{P–O–P}$ bonds in phosphorus pentoxide ($\text{P}_4\text{O}_{10}$): The four $\text{P}$ atoms sit at the vertices of a tetrahedron, and each of the $6$ edges has a bridging oxygen atom, giving $6$ $\text{P–O–P}$ bonds (plus $4$ terminal $\text{P}=\text{O}$ bonds).
  4. Step 4 — Final Conclusion: The number of $\text{P–O–P}$ bonds are $1, 3, 6$ respectively, confirming option (a).
