Step 1: H4P2O7: (HO)2P(= O) − O − P(= O)(OH)2 =⇒ 1 P − O − P bond. Step 2: (HPO3)3: cyclic trimer
with 3 P atoms alternating with 3 bridging O atoms =⇒ 3 P − O − P bonds. Step 3: P4O10: 4 P atoms at
tetrahedron vertices, one bridging O along each of the 4 = 6 edges =⇒ 6 P − O − P bonds.
2
Q58.trapHtml: In P<sub>4</sub>O<sub>10</sub>, there are 6 bridging P − O − P linkages (12 P − O single bonds) plus 4 terminal P = O bonds.

Q59.subtopic: Covalency and Oxidation State of Boron in [BF4]−
Q59.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Distinguishing covalency vs OS
Q59.conceptHtml: Covalency is the number of covalent/coordinate bonds formed by an atom; oxidation state is the hypothetical charge assuming ionic cleavage.
Q59.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Determine the covalency of boron in $[\text{BF}_4]^-$: Covalency is the number of covalent bonds formed by the central atom. In $[\text{BF}_4]^-$, boron forms $3$ normal covalent bonds and $1$ coordinate covalent bond with four fluorine atoms (using one $2s$ and three $2p$ orbitals), so its covalency is $4$.
  2. Step 2 — Calculate the oxidation state of boron: Let the oxidation state of $\text{B}$ be $x$. Since each $\text{F}$ has an oxidation state of $-1$ and the overall charge on the ion is $-1$: $x + 4(-1) = -1$.
  3. Step 3 — Solve for $x$: $x - 4 = -1 \implies x = +3$. Thus, the oxidation state of boron is $3$.
  4. Step 4 — Final Conclusion: The covalency and oxidation state of boron in $[\text{BF}_4]^-$ are $4$ and $3$ respectively, confirming option (b).
Q59.stepsLatex:
Step 1: In [BF4]−, boron forms 4 single bonds (3 covalent + 1 coordinate from F−) =⇒ covalency = 4. Step 2:
Let OS of B be x: x + 4(−1) = −1 =⇒ x = +3.
Q59.trapHtml: Notice the order requested: “covalency and oxidation state respectively” → 4 and 3 (not 3 and 4).

Q60.subtopic: Hardness, Lattice Energy & Boiling/Melting Point of Boron
Q60.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Two-statement evaluation on Boron
Q60.conceptHtml: Boron is an extremely hard solid with high lattice energy and the highest melting point (2453 K) and boiling point (3923 K) in Group 13.
Q60.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement I: Crystalline boron is an extremely hard solid (almost as hard as diamond) because its atoms are held together in a rigid three-dimensional covalent network with very high lattice energy. Thus, Statement I is correct.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement II: Due to its small atomic size and exceptionally strong crystalline lattice, boron has the highest melting point ($2453\text{ K}$) and highest boiling point ($3923\text{ K}$) among all Group 13 elements. Thus, Statement II is correct.
  3. Step 3 — Final Conclusion: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct, confirming option (d).
Q60.stepsLatex: Step 1: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Q60.trapHtml: Boron’s boiling point (3923 K) is also highest in Group 13 (Al is 2743 K, Ga is 2676 K).
Q60.finalAnsHtml: (D) Both Statement I and Statement II are correct

Q61.subtopic: Fajan’s Rules (SbCl5 vs SbCl3) & Halogen Oxides
Q61.conceptHtml: By Fajan’s rules, higher cation charge (Sb<sup>5+</sup> vs Sb<sup>3+</sup>) gives greater polarising power and higher covalent character. Per NCERT Group 17, higher oxides of halogens tend to be more stable than lower ones.
Q61.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement I using Fajan's rules: In $\text{SbCl}_5$, antimony is in the $+5$ oxidation state, whereas in $\text{SbCl}_3$ it is in the $+3$ oxidation state. A higher positive charge on the central atom gives greater polarising power, distorting the electron cloud of $\text{Cl}^-$ more strongly; hence $\text{SbCl}_5$ is more covalent than $\text{SbCl}_3$. Statement I is correct.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement II (Halogen oxides stability): Among oxides of a given halogen (such as chlorine or iodine), higher oxides (e.g., $\text{Cl}_2\text{O}_7$, $\text{I}_2\text{O}_5$) generally exhibit greater thermal stability than lower oxides due to stronger halogen–oxygen bonding and more extensive $p\pi\text{–}d\pi$ interactions. Statement II is correct.
  3. Step 3 — Final Conclusion: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct, confirming option (a).
Q61.stepsLatex:
Step 1: Statement I: SbCl5 (+5) is more covalent than SbCl3 (+3). True. Step 2: Statement II: NCERT Group
17 verbatim: “The higher oxides of halogens tend to be more stable than the lower ones.” True.
Q61.trapHtml: Do not confuse halogen oxides (Cl<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> more stable than Cl<sub>2</sub>O) with Group 15/16 +5/ + 6 halides.
Q61.finalAnsHtml: (A) Both Statement I and Statement II are correct

Q62.conceptHtml: Due to the inert pair effect, Ga can exist as Ga<sup>+</sup>, while Al strongly prefers Al<sup>3+</sup>. Thus GaAlCl<sub>4</sub> is the ionic salt Ga<sup>+</sup>[AlCl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>−</sup>.
Q62.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the ionic structure of $\text{GaAlCl}_4$: The compound $\text{GaAlCl}_4$ is an ionic salt consisting of the monovalent gallium cation $\text{Ga}^+$ and the tetrahedral tetrachloroaluminate anion $[\text{AlCl}_4]^-$: $\text{Ga}^+[\text{AlCl}_4]^-$.
  2. Step 2 — Check the oxidation state and coordination: Here, gallium is in the $+1$ oxidation state (stabilised by the inert pair effect) and aluminium is in the $+3$ oxidation state coordinated to all four $\text{Cl}$ atoms, so options (a), (b), and (c) are false.
  3. Step 3 — Compare electronegativity of $\text{Ga}$ and $\text{Al}$: Due to poor shielding by the intervening $3d^{10}$ electrons in gallium, $\text{Ga}$ has a higher effective nuclear charge and is slightly more electronegative ($1.81$) than $\text{Al}$ ($1.61$), yet it forms the cationic part ($\text{Ga}^+$) of the salt.
  4. Step 4 — Final Conclusion: $\text{Ga}$ is more electronegative than $\text{Al}$ and is present as the cationic part of $\text{GaAlCl}_4$, confirming option (d).
Q62.stepsLatex:
Step 1: In Ga+[AlCl4]−, Ga is in +1 OS (cationic part) and Al is in +3 OS (tetrahedral [AlCl4]− anion). Step 2:
Check options: (A) False (Cl is bonded only to Al); (B) False (Ga is +1, not +3); (C) False (Al is coordinated to
Cl); (D) True (χGa = 1.6 > χAl = 1.5, and Ga+ is the cationic part).
Q62.trapHtml: If it were Al<sup>+</sup>[GaCl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>−</sup>, Al<sup>+</sup> would be unstable; Ga<sup>+</sup>[AlCl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>−</sup> is favoured by the inert pair effect and hydration/lattice stability.
Q62.finalAnsHtml: (D) Ga is more electronegative than Al and is present as a cationic part of the salt GaAlCl<sub>4</sub>

Q63.subtopic: E − H Bond Dissociation Energy in Group 16 Hydrides
Q63.format: Single-Choice MCQ | H<sub>2</sub>E bond energy order
Q63.conceptHtml: Down Group 16, atomic size increases, orbital overlap with H 1s weakens, and E − H bond dissociation energy decreases monotonically: O − H > S − H > Se − H > Te − H.
Q63.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the factor controlling $\text{E–H}$ bond dissociation energy: In Group 16 hydrides ($\text{H}_2\text{O}$, $\text{H}_2\text{S}$, $\text{H}_2\text{Se}$, $\text{H}_2\text{Te}$), the strength of the $\text{E–H}$ bond depends primarily on orbital overlap and bond length.
  2. Step 2 — Trace the trend down Group 16: Going from $\text{O} \to \text{S} \to \text{Se} \to \text{Te}$, the atomic radius of $\text{E}$ increases steadily, causing the $\text{E–H}$ bond length to increase and the orbital overlap with hydrogen's $1s$ orbital to weaken.
  3. Step 3 — Write the decreasing order: Therefore, the $\text{E–H}$ bond dissociation energy decreases regularly down the group: $\text{O–H} > \text{S–H} > \text{Se–H} > \text{Te–H}$, which corresponds to $\text{A} > \text{B} > \text{C} > \text{D}$.
  4. Step 4 — Final Conclusion: The correct order is $\text{A} > \text{B} > \text{C} > \text{D}$, confirming option (a).
Q63.stepsLatex: Step 1: Order is A (O) > B (S) > C (Se) > D (Te).
Q63.trapHtml: This monotonic decrease in E − H bond energy directly explains why thermal stability decreases and acidity/reducing power increase down Group 16.

Q64.subtopic: Action of SO2 on Acidified K2Cr2O7 Paper
Q64.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Reducing property of SO<sub>2</sub>
Q64.conceptHtml: Sulphur dioxide reduces orange dichromate (Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sup>2</sup><sub>7</sub><sup>−</sup>, +6) in acidic medium to green chromium(III) (Cr<sup>3+</sup>, +3).
Q64.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the colour change of acidified dichromate: Acidified potassium dichromate ($\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$ in dilute $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$) is orange due to $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}$ ($\text{Cr}$ in $+6$ state) and turns green when reduced to $\text{Cr}^{3+}$ ($\text{Cr}_2(\text{SO}_4)_3$).
  2. Step 2 — Write the redox reaction with $\text{SO}_2$: Sulphur dioxide ($\text{SO}_2$) is a strong reducing gas that cleanly reduces orange $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}$ to green $\text{Cr}^{3+}$ while getting oxidised to $\text{SO}_4^{2-}$: $\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7 + 3\text{SO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \to \text{K}_2\text{SO}_4 + \text{Cr}_2(\text{SO}_4)_3\text{ (green)} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$.
  3. Step 3 — Eliminate the other options: $\text{SO}_3$ and $\text{CO}_2$ have central atoms already in their maximum oxidation states ($+6$ and $+4$) and cannot reduce $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}$; while $\text{H}_2\text{S}$ also reduces dichromate, it deposits yellow colloidal sulphur, whereas the classic clean green-paper confirmatory test is for $\text{SO}_2$.
  4. Step 4 — Final Conclusion: Acidified $\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$ paper turns green when exposed to sulphur dioxide, confirming option (a).
Q64.stepsLatex:
Step 1: Write the balanced redox reaction:
K2Cr2O7 + 3SO2 + H2SO4 −→ K2SO4 + Cr2(SO4)3 (green) + H2O
Step 2: Note: H2S also reduces acidified K2Cr2O7 to green Cr3+ (with yellow S precipitate), whereas SO2 gives a
clear green solution/paper—the classic NCERT test for SO2 (and NTA official key is (A) Sulphur dioxide).
Q64.trapHtml: In NCERT Group 16, turning acidified K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> paper green is the standard confirmatory test for SO<sub>2</sub>.

Q65.conceptHtml: Group 15 elements from Period 3 onwards (P, As, Sb, Bi) have vacant d-orbitals and can form dπ–dπ bonds with transition metals (unlike N).
Q65.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Filter Group 15 elements that form $d\pi\text{–}d\pi$ bonds: To form $d\pi\text{–}d\pi$ bonds with transition metals, the Group 15 element must possess vacant $d$-orbitals. Nitrogen ($n = 2$) lacks $d$-orbitals, so the eligible elements are $\text{P}$, $\text{As}$, $\text{Sb}$, and $\text{Bi}$.
  2. Step 2 — Compare basicity of their hydrides: Down Group 15, the lone pair on the central atom becomes more diffused over a larger atomic volume, so basic strength decreases in the order $\text{PH}_3 > \text{AsH}_3 > \text{SbH}_3 > \text{BiH}_3$.
  3. Step 3 — Identify the element and its atomic number: Among the hydrides of elements that form $d\pi\text{–}d\pi$ bonds, $\text{PH}_3$ is the strongest base. Therefore, the element is Phosphorus ($\text{P}$), which has atomic number $Z = 15$.
  4. Step 4 — Final Conclusion: The atomic number of the element is 15.

Step 1: Among PH3, AsH3, SbH3, BiH3 (the Group 15 members that form dπ–dπ bonds), basicity decreases down
the group: PH3 > AsH3 > SbH3 > BiH3. Step 2: Therefore, the element whose hydride is the strongest base among
dπ–dπ forming members is Phosphorus (P), with atomic number Z = 15.

Q66.format: Numerical | Counting oxygen atoms in H<sub>2</sub>S<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub>
Q66.conceptHtml: Fuming sulphuric acid (oleum / pyrosulphuric acid) is formed by dissolving SO<sub>3</sub> in H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>, giving H<sub>2</sub>S<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub>.
Q66.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify fuming sulphuric acid: Fuming sulphuric acid is commonly known as oleum (pyrosulphuric acid), formed by dissolving $\text{SO}_3$ gas in concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$: $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 + \text{SO}_3 \to \text{H}_2\text{S}_2\text{O}_7$.
  2. Step 2 — Count the oxygen atoms in its formula: In the chemical formula $\text{H}_2\text{S}_2\text{O}_7$, there are $2$ hydrogen atoms, $2$ sulphur atoms, and $7$ oxygen atoms.
  3. Step 3 — Final Conclusion: The number of oxygen atoms in fuming sulphuric acid is 7.

Q67.subtopic: Counting Amphoteric Oxides of p-Block Elements
Q67.format: Numerical | Acidic, neutral & amphoteric p-block oxides
Q67.conceptHtml: Classify each oxide: CO, N<sub>2</sub>O, NO are neutral; Cl<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub>, SiO<sub>2</sub>, N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>5</sub> are acidic; Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>, SnO<sub>2</sub>, PbO<sub>2</sub> are amphoteric.
Q67.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Classify the acidic oxides: Non-metal oxides in high oxidation states are acidic. From the given list, $\text{Cl}_2\text{O}_7$, $\text{SiO}_2$, and $\text{N}_2\text{O}_5$ are acidic oxides.
  2. Step 2 — Classify the neutral oxides: The three classic neutral oxides of $p$-block non-metals present in the list are $\text{CO}$, $\text{N}_2\text{O}$, and $\text{NO}$.
  3. Step 3 — Identify and count the amphoteric oxides: The remaining oxides—$\text{PbO}_2$, $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$, and $\text{SnO}_2$—react with both acids and bases and are therefore amphoteric. Counting them gives $3$ oxides.
  4. Step 4 — Final Conclusion: The number of amphoteric oxides is 3.

• Acidic (3): Cl2O7, SiO2, N2O5

Step 2: Count of amphoteric oxides = 3.

Q68.conceptHtml: Ozone is a powerful oxidising agent that oxidises black lead(II) sulphide (PbS) to white lead(II) sulphate (PbSO<sub>4</sub>), liberating O<sub>2</sub>.
Q68.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Write the reaction of $\text{PbS}$ with ozone: Ozone ($\text{O}_3$) is a powerful oxidising agent that oxidises black lead(II) sulphide ($\text{PbS}$) to white lead(II) sulphate ($\text{PbSO}_4$), releasing dioxygen ($\text{O}_2$).
  2. Step 2 — Balance the chemical equation: Each $\text{O}_3$ molecule supplies one nascent oxygen atom ($\text{O}_3 \to \text{O}_2 + [\text{O}]$), and converting $\text{PbS}$ to $\text{PbSO}_4$ requires $4$ oxygen atoms: $\text{PbS} + 4\text{O}_3 \to \text{PbSO}_4 + 4\text{O}_2$.
  3. Step 3 — Extract $X$ and $Y$ and compute their sum: From the balanced equation, $1\text{ mole}$ of $\text{PbS}$ requires $X = 4\text{ moles}$ of $\text{O}_3$ and produces $Y = 4\text{ moles}$ of $\text{O}_2$. Therefore, $X + Y = 4 + 4 = 8$.
  4. Step 4 — Final Conclusion: The value of $X + Y$ is 8.
Q68.stepsLatex:
Step 1: Write the balanced equation:
PbS(s) + 4O3(g) −→ PbSO4(s) + 4O2(g)

Q69.format: Numerical | Oxidation state of S in 6 species
Q69.conceptHtml: Calculate the oxidation state of S using standard rules (O = −2, H = +1, F = −1, Cl = −1, Ba = +2).
Q69.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Calculate the oxidation state of sulphur in the first three compounds:
    • $\text{SO}_3$: $x + 3(-2) = 0 \implies x = +6$.
    • $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_3$: $2(+1) + x + 3(-2) = 0 \implies x = +4$.
    • $\text{SOCl}_2$: $x + (-2) + 2(-1) = 0 \implies x = +4$.
  2. Step 2 — Calculate the oxidation state of sulphur in the remaining three compounds:
    • $\text{SF}_4$: $x + 4(-1) = 0 \implies x = +4$.
    • $\text{BaSO}_4$: $(+2) + x + 4(-2) = 0 \implies x = +6$.
    • $\text{H}_2\text{S}_2\text{O}_7$: $2(+1) + 2x + 7(-2) = 0 \implies 2x = +12 \implies x = +6$.
  3. Step 3 — Count the compounds with $+4$ oxidation state: The compounds with sulphur in the $+4$ oxidation state are $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_3$, $\text{SOCl}_2$, and $\text{SF}_4$, giving a total of $3$.
  4. Step 4 — Final Conclusion: The number of compounds with $+4$ oxidation state of sulphur is 3.

• SF4: +4; BaSO4: +6; H2S2O7: +6

Q70.format: Numerical | Total oxygen atoms in products X and Y
Q70.conceptHtml: Basic metal oxides hydrolyse to hydroxides (Na<sub>2</sub>O + H<sub>2</sub>O → 2NaOH), while acidic non-metal oxides hy- drolyse to oxoacids (Cl<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O → 2HClO<sub>4</sub>).
Q70.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify product $X$ from the first reaction: $\text{Na}_2\text{O}$ is a basic oxide that reacts with water to form sodium hydroxide: $\text{Na}_2\text{O} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \to 2\text{NaOH}$. Thus, $X = \text{NaOH}$, which contains $1$ oxygen atom.
  2. Step 2 — Identify product $Y$ from the second reaction: $\text{Cl}_2\text{O}_7$ is the acidic anhydride of perchloric acid and reacts with water as: $\text{Cl}_2\text{O}_7 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \to 2\text{HClO}_4$. Thus, $Y = \text{HClO}_4$, which contains $4$ oxygen atoms.
  3. Step 3 — Sum the oxygen atoms in $X$ and $Y$: Total number of oxygen atoms in one formula unit of $X$ and one formula unit of $Y$ is $1 + 4 = 5$.
  4. Step 4 — Final Conclusion: The total number of oxygen atoms in $X$ and $Y$ is 5.

Q71.format: Numerical | Structures of H<sub>2</sub>S<sub>2</sub>O<sub>8</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>S<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub>
Q71.conceptHtml: Both H<sub>2</sub>S<sub>2</sub>O<sub>8</sub> (HO − SO<sub>2</sub> − O − O − SO<sub>2</sub> − OH) and H<sub>2</sub>S<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> (HO − SO<sub>2</sub> − O − SO<sub>2</sub> − OH) have two S atoms, each forming two S = O double bonds.
Q71.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Count $\pi$-bonds in peroxodisulphuric acid ($\text{H}_2\text{S}_2\text{O}_8$, Marshall's acid): Its structure is $\text{HO–S}(=\text{O})_2\text{–O–O–S}(=\text{O})_2\text{–OH}$. Each sulphur atom has two $\text{S}=\text{O}$ double bonds, giving $2 + 2 = 4$ $\pi$-bonds.
  2. Step 2 — Count $\pi$-bonds in pyrosulphuric acid ($\text{H}_2\text{S}_2\text{O}_7$, oleum): Its structure is $\text{HO–S}(=\text{O})_2\text{–O–S}(=\text{O})_2\text{–OH}$. Again, each sulphur atom has two $\text{S}=\text{O}$ double bonds, giving $2 + 2 = 4$ $\pi$-bonds.
  3. Step 3 — Add the $\pi$-bonds from both acids: Total number of $\pi$-bonds $= 4 + 4 = 8$.
  4. Step 4 — Final Conclusion: The sum of $\pi$-bonds present in both acids is 8.

Q73.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Standard reduction potentials of X<sub>2</sub>/X<sup>−</sup> vs O<sub>2</sub>/H<sub>2</sub>O
Q73.conceptHtml: For O<sub>2</sub> (E<sub>O</sub><sup>°</sup> <sub>/H</sub> <sub>O</sub> = +1.23 V) to oxidise X<sup>−</sup> to X<sub>2</sub> in acidic medium, we need E<sub>X</sub><sup>°</sup> <sub>/X−</sub> < +1.23 V. 2 2 2

Q75.subtopic: Reaction of White Phosphorus (P4) with SOCl2
Q75.conceptHtml: White phosphorus reacts with thionyl chloride (SOCl<sub>2</sub>) to form phosphorus trichloride (PCl<sub>3</sub>), sulphur dioxide (SO<sub>2</sub>), and disulphur dichloride (S<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>).
Q75.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the reaction of white phosphorus with thionyl chloride: White phosphorus ($\text{P}_4$) reacts with thionyl chloride ($\text{SOCl}_2$) to produce phosphorus trichloride ($\text{PCl}_3$), sulphur dioxide ($\text{SO}_2$), and disulphur dichloride ($\text{S}_2\text{Cl}_2$).
  2. Step 2 — Write and balance the equation: $\text{P}_4 + 8\text{SOCl}_2 \to 4\text{PCl}_3 + 4\text{SO}_2 + 2\text{S}_2\text{Cl}_2$. Let's verify atom balance: $\text{P}: 4 = 4$, $\text{S}: 8 = 4 + 4$, $\text{O}: 8 = 8$, $\text{Cl}: 16 = 12 + 4$.
  3. Step 3 — Match with $A$, $B$, and $x$: Comparing with $\text{P}_4 + 8\text{SOCl}_2 \to 4A + x\text{SO}_2 + 2B$, we get $A = \text{PCl}_3$, $B = \text{S}_2\text{Cl}_2$, and $x = 4$.
  4. Step 4 — Final Conclusion: $A$, $B$, and $x$ are $\text{PCl}_3$, $\text{S}_2\text{Cl}_2$, and $4$ respectively, confirming option (b).

Q76.subtopic: Group 14 M − M Bond Enthalpy Order
Q76.conceptHtml: As atomic size increases down Group 14 (C → Sn), orbital overlap weakens and M − M single bond enthalpy decreases monotonically.
Q76.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Relate single-bond enthalpy to atomic size in Group 14: As we move down Group 14 from $\text{C}$ to $\text{Sn}$, atomic radius increases, so the $\text{E–E}$ bond length increases and orbital overlap becomes less effective.
  2. Step 2 — Compare standard bond enthalpy values: The $\text{E–E}$ single bond enthalpies (in $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$) are $\text{C–C} = 348$, $\text{Si–Si} = 297$, $\text{Ge–Ge} = 260$, and $\text{Sn–Sn} = 240$.
  3. Step 3 — Arrange in decreasing order: The bond enthalpy strictly decreases down the group: $\text{C–C} > \text{Si–Si} > \text{Ge–Ge} > \text{Sn–Sn}$.
  4. Step 4 — Final Conclusion: The correct order of bond enthalpy is $\text{C–C} > \text{Si–Si} > \text{Ge–Ge} > \text{Sn–Sn}$, confirming option (c).

Q76.finalAnsHtml: (C) C − C > Si − Si > Ge − Ge > Sn − Sn

Q77.conceptHtml: Chlorine forms several oxides (Cl<sub>2</sub>O, ClO<sub>2</sub>, Cl<sub>2</sub>O<sub>6</sub>, Cl<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub>) that are strong oxidising agents and tend to explode. Reactivity of an element is assessed via its reactions with O<sub>2</sub> and X<sub>2</sub>.

These chlorine oxides are highly reactive oxidising agents and have a strong tendency to decompose explosively. Thus, Statement I is true.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement II: According to periodic classification principles, the chemical reactivity of an element is systematically assessed by examining its reactions with oxygen (forming oxides) and halogens (forming halides). Thus, Statement II is true.
  3. Step 3 — Final Conclusion: Both Statements I and II are true, confirming option (d).

Q78.subtopic: Lewis Acid Strength of Boron Trihalides (BX3)
Q78.format: Single-Choice MCQ | pπ–pπ back-bonding in BX<sub>3</sub>
Q78.conceptHtml: In BX<sub>3</sub>, filled np orbitals of halogen donate electron density into boron’s vacant 2p orbital (pπ–pπ back- bonding). Overlap is strongest for 2p–2p (BF<sub>3</sub>) and weakest for 2p–5p (BI<sub>3</sub>).
Q78.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify why electronegativity alone fails here: Based purely on electronegativity, $\text{BF}_3$ would seem most electron-deficient; however, experimentally $\text{BF}_3$ is the weakest Lewis acid among boron trihalides.
  2. Step 2 — Apply $p\pi\text{–}p\pi$ back-bonding: Boron has a vacant $2p$-orbital that accepts a lone pair internally from the filled $p$-orbitals of the halogen atoms. The $2p(\text{F})\text{–}2p(\text{B})$ overlap in $\text{BF}_3$ is strongest because both orbitals have comparable size and energy.
  3. Step 3 — Trace the trend across the halides: Going from $\text{F} \to \text{Cl} \to \text{Br} \to \text{I}$, the halogen valence $p$-orbital ($2p \to 3p \to 4p \to 5p$) grows larger, so back-bonding weakens ($\text{BF}_3 > \text{BCl}_3 > \text{BBr}_3 > \text{BI}_3$). Consequently, boron remains most electron-deficient in $\text{BI}_3$, giving the Lewis acidity order $\text{BI}_3 > \text{BBr}_3 > \text{BCl}_3 > \text{BF}_3$.
  4. Step 4 — Final Conclusion: The Lewis acid strength follows $\text{BI}_3 > \text{BBr}_3 > \text{BCl}_3 > \text{BF}_3$, confirming option (a).
Q78.stepsLatex:
Step 1: Stronger back-bonding reduces electron deficiency on B, lowering Lewis acidity. Step 2: Therefore, Lewis
acid strength order is BI3 > BBr3 > BCl3 > BF3.
Q78.trapHtml: Electronegativity alone would predict BF<sub>3</sub> strongest, which is the exact opposite of the experimental order!

Q79.subtopic: Physical State of Boric Acid vs BF3
Q79.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Intermolecular H-bonding in H<sub>3</sub>BO<sub>3</sub>
Q79.conceptHtml: Boric acid (H<sub>3</sub>BO<sub>3</sub>) forms extensive 2D polymeric sheets held together by strong intermolecular hydrogen bonds, making it a solid, whereas BF<sub>3</sub> is a discrete nonpolar trigonal planar gas.
Q79.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Examine the intermolecular forces in boric acid ($\text{H}_3\text{BO}_3$): Each $\text{B(OH)}_3$ molecule has three $\text{–OH}$ groups that form extensive, strong intermolecular hydrogen bonds, linking the planar trigonal units into two-dimensional polymeric sheets. This strong association makes boric acid a white crystalline solid at room temperature.
  2. Step 2 — Examine the intermolecular forces in $\text{BF}_3$: $\text{BF}_3$ is a symmetric, non-polar trigonal planar monomer ($\mu = 0$) with no hydrogen atoms, so its molecules attract each other only through weak London dispersion forces, making it a gas at room temperature.
  3. Step 3 — Final Conclusion: Boric acid is a solid whereas $\text{BF}_3$ is a gas because of strong hydrogen bonding in boric acid, confirming option (c).

Q79.trapHtml: Boric acid is a weak monobasic Lewis acid (accepts OH<sup>−</sup> from water), not a proton donor.
Q79.finalAnsHtml: (C) Strong hydrogen bond in Boric acid

Q80.subtopic: Ostwald’s Process & Brown Ring Test Identification
Q80.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Identifying A = NO and B = NO<sub>2</sub>
Q80.conceptHtml: In Ostwald’s process: 4NH<sub>3</sub> + 5O<sub>2</sub> <sup>−P</sup><sup>−t</sup><sup>−/R</sup>−→<sup>h</sup> 4NO + 6H<sub>2</sub>O (A = NO), followed by 2NO + O<sub>2</sub> → 2NO<sub>2</sub> (B = NO<sub>2</sub>), and 3NO<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O → 2HNO<sub>3</sub> + NO.
Q80.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Step 1 of Ostwald's process (find $A$): Catalytic air oxidation of ammonia over $\text{Pt/Rh}$ gauze produces nitric oxide ($\text{NO}$): $4\text{NH}_3 + 5\text{O}_2 \xrightarrow{\text{Pt/Rh}, 500\text{ K}} 4\text{NO} + 6\text{H}_2\text{O}$. Hence, $A = \text{NO}$.
  2. Step 2 — Further air oxidation (find $B$): Nitric oxide readily combines with atmospheric oxygen to form nitrogen dioxide: $2\text{NO} + \text{O}_2 \to 2\text{NO}_2$. Hence, $B = \text{NO}_2$.
  3. Step 3 — Verify hydration and brown ring test: Dissolving $\text{NO}_2$ in water gives nitric acid and regenerates $\text{NO}$: $3\text{NO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \to 2\text{HNO}_3 + \text{NO}$. Furthermore, $\text{HNO}_3$ (nitrate ion) gives the brown ring test by producing $\text{NO}$, which forms $[\text{Fe}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_5(\text{NO})]^{2+}$.
  4. Step 4 — Final Conclusion: $A$ and $B$ are $\text{NO}$ and $\text{NO}_2$ respectively, confirming option (d).

Q81.subtopic: Acidic vs Neutral Nature of CO2 and CO

Thus, R is correct.

Q82.subtopic: Reaction of P4 with SOCl2 & Hydrolysis of PCl3
Q82.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Identifying [A] = PCl<sub>3</sub> and [B] = H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>3</sub>
Q82.conceptHtml: White phosphorus reacts with SOCl<sub>2</sub> to give PCl<sub>3</sub> ([A]), which hydrolyses completely to phosphorous acid H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>3</sub> ([B]), a dibasic acid (2 P − OH + 1 P − H).
Q82.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Reaction of white phosphorus with thionyl chloride (find $[A]$): White phosphorus reacts with $\text{SOCl}_2$ to give phosphorus trichloride: $\text{P}_4 + 8\text{SOCl}_2 \to 4\text{PCl}_3 + 4\text{SO}_2 + 2\text{S}_2\text{Cl}_2$. Thus, $[A] = \text{PCl}_3$.
  2. Step 2 — Hydrolysis of $[A]$ (find $[B]$): Phosphorus trichloride undergoes complete hydrolysis with water to form phosphorous acid: $\text{PCl}_3 + 3\text{H}_2\text{O} \to \text{H}_3\text{PO}_3 + 3\text{HCl}$. Thus, $[B] = \text{H}_3\text{PO}_3$.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm basicity of $[B]$: The structure of $\text{H}_3\text{PO}_3$ is $\text{H–P}(=\text{O})(\text{OH})_2$, which has two ionisable $\text{P–OH}$ groups and one non-ionisable $\text{P–H}$ bond, confirming it is a dibasic acid.
  4. Step 4 — Final Conclusion: $[A]$ and $[B]$ are $\text{PCl}_3$ and $\text{H}_3\text{PO}_3$ respectively, confirming option (d).

Q83.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Identifying A, B, C in Solvay cycle
Q83.conceptHtml: In the Solvay ammonia-recovery and carbonation sequence: slaked lime Ca(OH)<sub>2</sub> (A) reacts with NH<sub>4</sub>Cl to regenerate NH<sub>3</sub> (B); NH<sub>3</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O + CO<sub>2</sub> → NH<sub>4</sub>HCO<sub>3</sub> (C); and NH<sub>4</sub>HCO<sub>3</sub> + NaCl → NaHCO<sub>3</sub> ↓ +NH<sub>4</sub>Cl.
Q83.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify $A$ and $B$ (ammonia recovery in Solvay process): Slaked lime, $\text{Ca(OH)}_2$ ($A$), reacts with $\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$ to liberate ammonia gas, $\text{NH}_3$ ($B$): $2\text{NH}_4\text{Cl} + \text{Ca(OH)}_2 \to 2\text{NH}_3 + \text{CaCl}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$.
  2. Step 2 — Identify $C$ (carbonation step): Ammonia ($B$) reacts with water and excess $\text{CO}_2$ to form ammonium hydrogen carbonate, $\text{NH}_4\text{HCO}_3$ ($C$): $\text{NH}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{CO}_2 \to \text{NH}_4\text{HCO}_3$.
  3. Step 3 — Verify precipitation of $\text{NaHCO}_3$: Passing $\text{NH}_4\text{HCO}_3$ through saturated brine ($\text{NaCl}$) precipitates sparingly soluble sodium hydrogen carbonate: $\text{NH}_4\text{HCO}_3 + \text{NaCl} \to \text{NaHCO}_3\downarrow + \text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$.
  4. Step 4 — Final Conclusion: Compounds $A$, $B$, and $C$ are $\text{Ca(OH)}_2$, $\text{NH}_3$, and $\text{NH}_4\text{HCO}_3$ respectively, confirming option (d).
Q83.stepsLatex: Step 1: A = Ca(OH)<sub>2</sub>, B = NH<sub>3</sub>, C = NH<sub>4</sub>HCO<sub>3</sub>.
Q83.trapHtml: CaCl<sub>2</sub> is the by-product of Ca(OH)<sub>2</sub> + 2NH<sub>4</sub>Cl, not the starting reagent A.

Q84.subtopic: Reducing Phosphorus Oxoacids & Silver Mirror Test
Q84.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Presence of P − H bonds
Q84.conceptHtml: Only phosphorus oxoacids containing at least one P − H bond act as reducing agents and reduce AgNO<sub>3</sub> to metallic Ag (silver mirror).
Q84.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the requirement for reducing $\text{AgNO}_3$ to metallic silver: Phosphorus oxoacids act as reducing agents (reducing $\text{Ag}^+$ to $\text{Ag}$, giving a silver mirror) only if they contain at least one directly bonded $\text{P–H}$ bond.
  2. Step 2 — Inspect the structures of all four oxoacids:
    • $\text{H}_4\text{P}_2\text{O}_5$ (pyrophosphorous acid): $\text{H(HO)P(=O)–O–P(=O)(OH)H}$ has $2$ $\text{P–H}$ bonds.
    • $\text{H}_4\text{P}_2\text{O}_7$ (pyrophosphoric acid): $0$ $\text{P–H}$ bonds.
    • $(\text{HPO}_3)_n$ (metaphosphoric acid): $0$ $\text{P–H}$ bonds.
    • $\text{H}_4\text{P}_2\text{O}_6$ (hypophosphoric acid): contains a $\text{P–P}$ bond and $0$ $\text{P–H}$ bonds.
  3. Step 3 — Identify the reducing oxoacid: Only $\text{H}_4\text{P}_2\text{O}_5$ possesses $\text{P–H}$ bonds and can reduce $\text{AgNO}_3$ to a silver mirror.
  4. Step 4 — Final Conclusion: The oxoacid that creates a silver mirror from $\text{AgNO}_3$ is $\text{H}_4\text{P}_2\text{O}_5$, confirming option (a).
Q84.stepsLatex:
Step 1: Check structures:
• H4P2O5 (pyrophosphorous acid): has two P − H bonds (H(HO)P(= O) − O − P(= O)(OH)H) =⇒ reduces
AgNO3.
• H4P2O7, (HPO3)n, H4P2O6: zero P − H bonds (all P in +5 or +4 with P − P).
Q84.trapHtml: H<sub>4</sub>P<sub>2</sub>O<sub>6</sub> (hypophosphoric acid) has a P − P bond and NO P − H bond, so it does not reduce AgNO<sub>3</sub>.

Q85.conceptHtml: Borax (Na<sub>2</sub>B<sub>4</sub>O<sub>7</sub> · 10H<sub>2</sub>O) actually contains the tetranuclear [B<sub>4</sub>O<sub>5</sub>(OH)<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2−</sup> unit with 8 molecules of water of crystallisation.
Q85.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Write the actual structural formula of Borax: Although commonly written as $\text{Na}_2\text{B}_4\text{O}_7 \cdot 10\text{H}_2\text{O}$, borax actually contains the tetranuclear anion $[\text{B}_4\text{O}_5(\text{OH})_4]^{2-}$.
  2. Step 2 — Express borax in the requested hydrated form: Writing it with the complex anion and remaining water of crystallisation gives $\text{Na}_2[\text{B}_4\text{O}_5(\text{OH})_4] \cdot 8\text{H}_2\text{O}$ (notice $4\text{ OH}^-$ account for $2\text{ H}_2\text{O}$, leaving $10 - 2 = 8\text{ H}_2\text{O}$).
  3. Step 3 — Extract $x, y, z$ and compute their sum: Comparing with $\text{Na}_2\text{B}_4\text{O}_x(\text{OH})_y \cdot z\text{H}_2\text{O}$, we obtain $x = 5$, $y = 4$, and $z = 8$. Therefore, $x + y + z = 5 + 4 + 8 = 17$.
  4. Step 4 — Final Conclusion: The value of $x + y + z$ is 17.
Q85.stepsLatex: Step 1: Structural formula: Na<sub>2</sub>B<sub>4</sub>O<sub>5</sub>(OH)<sub>4</sub> · 8H<sub>2</sub>O. Step 2: x = 5, y = 4, z = 8 =⇒ x + y + z = 5 + 4 + 8 = 17.
Q85.trapHtml: Verify total atom balance: O atoms = 5 + 4 + 8 = 17 (same as 7 + 10 = 17 in Na<sub>2</sub>B<sub>4</sub>O<sub>7</sub> · 10H<sub>2</sub>O).

Q86.format: Numerical | Oxidation state change of Xe
Q86.conceptHtml: Complete hydrolysis of XeF<sub>4</sub> is a disproportionation reaction yielding Xe (0) and XeO<sub>3</sub> (+6).
Q86.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Write the complete hydrolysis reaction of $\text{XeF}_4$: Xenon tetrafluoride undergoes disproportionation upon complete hydrolysis: $6\text{XeF}_4 + 12\text{H}_2\text{O} \to 4\text{Xe} + 2\text{XeO}_3 + 24\text{HF} + 3\text{O}_2$.
  2. Step 2 — Determine the oxidation states of $\text{Xe}$:
    • In $\text{XeF}_4$: $x + 4(-1) = 0 \implies x = +4$.
    • In the reduced product $\text{Xe}$: oxidation state $= 0$.
    • In the oxidised product $\text{XeO}_3$: $y + 3(-2) = 0 \implies y = +6$.
  3. Step 3 — Compute the difference: The difference in oxidation state of $\text{Xe}$ between the oxidised product ($\text{XeO}_3$, $+6$) and $\text{XeF}_4$ ($+4$) is $6 - 4 = 2$.
  4. Step 4 — Final Conclusion: The difference in oxidation state is 2.
Q86.stepsLatex:
Step 1: Write the balanced reaction:
6XeF4 + 12H2O −→ 4Xe + 2XeO3 + 24HF + 3O2
Step 2: Oxidation state of Xe in XeF4 = +4; in the oxidised product XeO3 = +6. Step 3: Difference = 6 − 4 = 2.
Q86.trapHtml: Read carefully: “oxidised product of Xe” is XeO<sub>3</sub> (+6), not the reduced product Xe (0).

Q87.subtopic: Ratio of σ and π Bonds in Pyrophosphoric Acid
Q87.conceptHtml: Pyrophosphoric acid (H<sub>4</sub>P<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub>) has the structure (HO)<sub>2</sub>P(= O) − O − P(= O)(OH)<sub>2</sub>.
Q87.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Draw the structure of pyrophosphoric acid ($\text{H}_4\text{P}_2\text{O}_7$): Its structural formula is $(\text{HO})_2\text{P}(=\text{O})\text{–O–P}(=\text{O})(\text{OH})_2$.
  2. Step 2 — Count all $\sigma$-bonds and $\pi$-bonds:
    • Four $\text{O–H}$ single bonds $= 4\sigma$.
    • Four $\text{P–O(H)}$ single bonds $= 4\sigma$.
    • Two bridging $\text{P–O}$ single bonds (in $\text{P–O–P}$) $= 2\sigma$.
    • Two terminal $\text{P}=\text{O}$ double bonds $= 2\sigma + 2\pi$.
    Total $\sigma$-bonds $= 4 + 4 + 2 + 2 = 12$; total $\pi$-bonds $= 2$.
  3. Step 3 — Compute the $\sigma / \pi$ ratio: $\dfrac{\text{Number of }\sigma\text{ bonds}}{\text{Number of }\pi\text{ bonds}} = \dfrac{12}{2} = 6$.
  4. Step 4 — Final Conclusion: The ratio of $\sigma$ to $\pi$ bonds in pyrophosphoric acid is 6.
Q87.stepsLatex:
Step 1: Count σ-bonds: 4 (O − H) + 4 (P − OH) + 2 (P − O − P) + 2 (P = O σ) = 12. Step 2: Count π-bonds:
2 (P = O π) = 2. Step 3: Ratio σ/π = 12/2 = 6.
Q87.trapHtml: Do not forget the 4 O − H σ-bonds when counting total σ-bonds!

Q88.format: Numerical | Adduct formation of XeF<sub>4</sub> with SbF<sub>5</sub>
Q88.conceptHtml: Xenon fluorides act as F<sup>−</sup> donors to strong Lewis acids like SbF<sub>5</sub> or PF<sub>5</sub> to form cationic xenon fluoro- complexes.
Q88.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Write the fluoride-transfer reaction: Xenon fluorides act as fluoride ion ($\text{F}^-$) donors toward strong Lewis acid fluoride acceptors like $\text{SbF}_5$: $\text{XeF}_4 + \text{SbF}_5 \to [\text{XeF}_3]^+[\text{SbF}_6]^-$.
  2. Step 2 — Match the subscripts and charges: Comparing $[\text{XeF}_3]^+[\text{SbF}_6]^-$ with $[\text{XeF}_m]^{n+}[\text{SbF}_y]^{z-}$, we obtain $m = 3$, $n = 1$, $y = 6$, and $z = 1$.
  3. Step 3 — Compute the sum: $m + n + y + z = 3 + 1 + 6 + 1 = 11$.
  4. Step 4 — Final Conclusion: The value of $m + n + y + z$ is 11.
Q88.stepsLatex:
Step 1: Write the reaction:
XeF4 + SbF5 −→ [XeF3]+[SbF6]−
Step 2: Match with [XeFm]n+[SbFy]z−: m = 3, n = 1, y = 6, z = 1. Step 3: m + n + y + z = 3 + 1 + 6 + 1 = 11.
Q88.trapHtml: XeF<sub>2</sub> + PF<sub>5</sub> → [XeF]<sup>+</sup>[PF<sub>6</sub>]<sup>−</sup>, XeF<sub>4</sub> + SbF<sub>5</sub> → [XeF<sub>3</sub>]<sup>+</sup>[SbF<sub>6</sub>]<sup>−</sup>, and XeF<sub>6</sub> + MF<sub>5</sub> → [XeF<sub>5</sub>]<sup>+</sup>[MF<sub>6</sub>]<sup>−</sup>.

trapCards.title: Trap 1: Group 13 & 14 Contraction Anomalies (d10 & f14)
trapCards.html:
• The Mistake: Assuming atomic radius, ∆iH1, and electroneg- ativity change monotonically down Group 13 and Group 14. The Fix:
  • Atomic Radius (Gr 13): rGa (135 pm) < rAl (143 pm), while M3+ ionic radius increases regularly (Al3+ < Ga3+) (Q25, Q33, Q43).
  • ∆iH1 (Gr 13): B > Tl > Ga > Al > In (lowest is In, not Tl; Q23, Q26).
  • ∆iH1 & m.p. (Gr 14): Pb > Sn in both ∆iH1 (715 > 708) and m.p. (600 > 505 K) (Q09, Q21, Q30).
  • Electronegativity (Gr 13): B(2.0) > Tl(1.8) > In(1.7) > Ga(1.6) > Al(1.5) (Q14, Q26).

trapCards.title: Trap 2: Hydride Boiling Points vs Acidic/Basic/Reducing Trends
trapCards.html:
• The Mistake: Applying the H-bonding boiling point order to melting points, basicity, or thermal stability. The Fix:
  • Group 15 b.p.: PH3 < AsH3 < NH3 < SbH3 < BiH3 (PH3 is lowest; Q11, Q16).
  • Group 17 b.p. vs m.p.: b.p. is HCl < HBr < HI < HF, but m.p. is HCl < HBr < HF < HI (HI highest; Q10).
  • Monotonic Trends: Stability and basicity decrease down Group 15; reducing power increases down Group 15 & 16; acidity of H2E increases down Group 16 (H2Te > H2Se > H2S > H2O; Q01, Q19, Q51, Q52).

trapCards.title: Trap 3: Period 2 (pπ–pπ) vs Heavier (d-Orbital) Bonding
trapCards.html:
• The Mistake: Attributing dπ–pπ or dπ–dπ bonding or cova- lency > 4 to B, C, N, O, F, or calling N − N longer than P − P. The Fix:
  • Period 2 elements have only 2s and 2p (4 valence orbitals) =⇒ max covalency = 4 (NF5, [B(H2O)6]3+ do not exist; Q05, Q15, Q24, Q37).
  • C, N, O form pπ–pπ bonds (never pπ–dπ; Q05, Q45).
  • N − N single bond is shorter and weaker than P − P (Q27), whereas C − C > Si − Si > Ge − Ge > Sn − Sn (Q76).
  • Only Period 3+ (P, As, Sb, Bi) form dπ–dπ bonds (Q65).

trapCards.title: Trap 4: Inert Pair Effect, Oxides & Oxoacid Bond Counting
trapCards.html:
• The Mistake: Confusing oxidising vs reducing oxides, missing P − H bonds, or miscounting O/π-bonds in oxoacids. The Fix:
  • Inert Pair Redox: Tl3+, Pb4+, TeO2 are oxidising; Sn2+, SO2 are reducing (Q13, Q20, Q21, Q28, Q31).
  • Amphoteric Oxides: Al2O3, Ga2O3, SnO, SnO2, PbO, PbO2 (CO, NO, N2O are neutral; SiO2, GeO2 are acidic; Q18, Q49, Q67).
  • Oxoacids: H3PO2 (2 P − H), H3PO3 (1 P − H), H4P2O5 (2 P − H) reduce AgNO3; H4P2O7 has 1 P − O − P, 12 σ, 2 π (Q58, Q84, Q87).
  • S Oxoacids: H2S2O7 (7 O, 4 π, no O − O); H2S2O8 (8 O, 4 π, 1 O − O) (Q66, Q71).

formulaCards.title: 2. Electrode Potentials (E<sup>◦</sup>) & Oxidation States
formulaCards.html:
• Highest Oxidation State: Mn shows +7 in Mn2O7 (covalent oil, Mn − O − Mn bridge, tetrahedral Mn) and KMnO4; max fluoride of Mn is MnF4 (+4). Ru and Os show +8 in RuO4, OsO4. Sc shows only +3 OS (other than 0).
  • Stability Down a Group: Unlike p-block, higher OS becomes more stable down a d-group (e.g., Mo(VI) and W(VI) are more stable than Cr(VI); hence CrO3 is a stronger oxidising agent than MoO3).
  • E◦(M2+/M) Trends (3d): All negative except Cu (+0.34 V) (high ∆aH◦ + ∆iH1 + ∆iH2 not compensated by ∆hydH). Thus Cu cannot liberate H2 from dilute acids.
  • Anomalously Negative E◦(M2+/M): Mn (−1.18 V, d5 stability), Zn (−0.76 V, d10), Ni (−0.25 V, high ∆hydH).
  • Hydration Enthalpy (∆hydH): Mn2+ has the least negative ∆hydH among Cr2+, Mn2+, Fe2+, Co2+ (zero CFSE for d5).
  • E◦(M3+/M2+) Trends: – Negative: Cr3+/Cr2+ (−0.41 V) =⇒ Cr2+ (d4 → d3 half-filled t32g) is a strong reducing agent and liberates H2 from dilute acid (along with Ti2+, V2+). – Positive: Mn3+/Mn2+ (+1.57 V), Fe3+/Fe2+ (+0.77 V), Co3+/Co2+ (+1.97 V). Mn3+ (d4 → d5) and Co3+ are strong oxidising agents.
  • Cu+ vs Cu2+ in Water: Cu2+ is more stable than Cu+ in aqueous medium because ∆hydH(Cu2+) is much more negative (greater) than Cu+, compensating ∆iH2. 2Cu+ → Cu2+ + Cu.
  • Oxide Acidity/Basicity: Increases acidity with OS: CrO (basic) < Cr2O3 (amphoteric) < CrO3 (acidic); V2O3 (basic) < V2O4 (less basic/amphoteric) < V2O5 (ampho- teric, mainly acidic; gives VO34− with alkali and VO+2 with acid). Ionic character decreases as OS increases.

formulaCards.title: 4. K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> (Potassium Dichromate)
formulaCards.html:
• Preparation from Chromite Ore (FeCr2O4): 1. 4FeCr2O4 + 8Na2CO3 + 7O2 −∆→ 8Na2CrO4 + 2Fe2O3 ↓ +8CO2 ↑ (Fe2O3 is water-insoluble, M = 160 g mol−1). 2. 2Na2CrO4 + 2H+ → Na2Cr2O7 + 2Na+ + H2O 3. Na2Cr2O7 + 2KCl → K2Cr2O7 ↓ +2NaCl. (Note: Na2Cr2O7 is hygroscopic, so K2Cr2O7 is used as pri- mary volumetric standard!)
  • pH Interconversion: 2CrO24− (yellow, Td) +2H+ ⇌ Cr2O27− (orange, two Td sharing 1 O, ∠Cr − O − Cr = 126◦, 6 terminal O) +H2O.
  • Chromyl Chloride Test: K2Cr2O7 + 4NaCl + 6H2SO4 → 2CrO2Cl2 ↑ (red vapour, Cr(+6), d0) +2KHSO4 + 4NaHSO4 + 3H2O. CrO2Cl2 + 4NaOH → Na2CrO4 + 2NaCl + 2H2O.
  • CrO5 (Blue Peroxide): Cr2O27− + 2H+ + 4H2O2 → 2CrO5 + 5H2O (deep blue in ether/amyl alcohol; butterfly structure, Cr(+6)).
  • Oxidising Action (Acidic, Cr6+ → Cr3+ green, neq = 6): Oxidises I− → I2, S2− → S, Fe2+ → Fe3+, Sn2+ → Sn4+, SO2/SO23− → SO24− (turns K2Cr2O7 pa- per green), C2O24− → CO2.

formulaCards.title: 5. KMnO<sub>4</sub> (Potassium Permanganate)
formulaCards.html:
• Preparation from Pyrolusite (MnO2): 1. Alkaline oxidative fusion (KOH + O2 or KNO3): 2MnO2 + 4KOH + O2 → 2K2MnO4 (dark green, paramagnetic d1, Td) +2H2O. 2. Electrolytic oxidation in alkaline medium (or dispro- portionation in neutral/acidic medium): 3MnO24− + 4H+ → 2MnO−4 + MnO2 + 2H2O.
  • Lab Prep: 2Mn2+ + 5S2O28− + 8H2O → 2MnO−4 + 10SO24− + 16H+.
  • Thermal Decomposition (513 K): 2KMnO4 −5−1−3−K→ K2MnO4 + MnO2 + O2.
  • Oxidising Reactions: – Acidic (MnO−4 → Mn2+, ∆OS = 5): I− → I2, Fe2+ → Fe3+, C2O24− → CO2, S2− → S, SO23− → SO24−, NO−2 → NO−3 . – Neutral / Faintly Alkaline (MnO−4 → MnO2, ∆OS = 3): I− → IO−3 (iodate!), S2O23− → SO24−, Mn2+ → MnO2. 6. f-Block: Lanthanoids (4f) & Actinoids (5f) ⋆ High-ROI
  • Key 4f Configurations ([Xe]4f1–145d0–16s2): La(57) : 5d16s2; Ce(58) : 4f15d16s2; Nd(60) : 4f46s2 (Nd2+ : 4f4); Eu(63) : 4f76s2; Gd(64) : 4f75d16s2; Yb(70) : 4f146s2; Lu(71) : 4f145d16s2.
  • Common OS: +3. Anomalous +2 (Eu2+ : 4f7, Yb2+ : 4f14, Sm2+) are strong reducing agents. Anomalous +4 (Ce4+ : 4f0, Tb4+ : 4f7) are strong oxidising agents.
  • High ∆iH3: Eu (4f7) and Yb (4f14) have very high ∆iH3.
  • Colourless / Diamagnetic Ln3+: 4f0 (La3+, Ce4+, Th4+) and 4f14 (Yb2+, Lu3+, Lr3+).
  • Actinoids (5f): Es(99) : [Rn]5f116d07s2; Cm(96) : 5f76d17s2; Am(95) : 5f77s2 (both Am and Cm have 7 unpaired 5f electrons). Actinoid contraction > Lan- thanoid contraction (poorer shielding of 5f vs 4f). 5f electrons participate in bonding to a greater extent than 4f (less buried, closer energy to 6d/7s).

Q01.subtopic: Colour & Diamagnetism of d- and f-Block Ions
Q01.conceptHtml: Aqueous d-block ions with d<sup>1</sup>–d<sup>9</sup> configurations are coloured (d–d transitions), whereas d<sup>0</sup>/d<sup>10</sup> are colourless. Ions with f<sup>0</sup> or f<sup>14</sup> configurations have zero unpaired electrons and are diamagnetic. Step 1 (Check Statement I): • [Ti4+, V2+]: Ti4+ is 3d0 (colourless), V2+ is 3d3 (violet) =⇒ NOT both coloured. • [V2+, Mn2+]: 3d3 (violet) and 3d5 (pale pink) =⇒ both coloured. • [Mn2+, Fe3+]: 3d5 (pale pink) and 3d5 (yellow) =⇒ both coloured. • [V2+, Cr2+]: 3d3 (violet) and 3d4 (blue) =⇒ both coloured. Total pairs where both are coloured = 3. Hence, Statement I is correct. Step 2 (Check Statement II): • [La3+, Yb2+]: 4f0 and 4f14 =⇒ both diamagnetic. • [Lu3+, Ce4+]: 4f14 and 4f0 =⇒ both diamagnetic. • [Ac3+, Lr3+]: 5f0 and 5f14 =⇒ both diamagnetic. Total diamagnetic pairs = 3. Hence, Statement II is correct.
Q01.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Check colour of ions in Statement I: In aqueous solution, transition metal ions with partially filled $d$-orbitals ($d^1$ to $d^9$) are coloured due to $d\text{--}d$ transitions, while $d^0$ and $d^{10}$ ions are colourless. Checking each ion: $\text{Ti}^{4+}$ ($3d^0$, colourless), $\text{V}^{2+}$ ($3d^3$, violet), $\text{Mn}^{2+}$ ($3d^5$, pale pink), $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ ($3d^5$, yellow), and $\text{Cr}^{2+}$ ($3d^4$, blue).
  2. Step 2 — Count pairs with both ions coloured: In $[\text{Ti}^{4+}, \text{V}^{2+}]$, $\text{Ti}^{4+}$ is colourless, so this pair does not qualify. In the remaining three pairs—$[\text{V}^{2+}, \text{Mn}^{2+}]$, $[\text{Mn}^{2+}, \text{Fe}^{3+}]$, and $[\text{V}^{2+}, \text{Cr}^{2+}]$—both ions have unpaired $d$-electrons and are coloured. Thus, the count is $3$, making Statement I correct.
  3. Step 3 — Check diamagnetism in Statement II: An $f$-block ion is diamagnetic if it has $0$ unpaired electrons ($f^0$ or $f^{14}$). Checking each ion: $\text{La}^{3+}$ ($4f^0$), $\text{Yb}^{2+}$ ($4f^{14}$), $\text{Lu}^{3+}$ ($4f^{14}$), $\text{Ce}^{4+}$ ($4f^0$), $\text{Ac}^{3+}$ ($5f^0$), and $\text{Lr}^{3+}$ ($5f^{14}$). All six ions have zero unpaired electrons.
  4. Step 4 — Verify count and conclude: All $3$ pairs ($[\text{La}^{3+}, \text{Yb}^{2+}]$, $[\text{Lu}^{3+}, \text{Ce}^{4+}]$, and $[\text{Ac}^{3+}, \text{Lr}^{3+}]$) contain only diamagnetic ions, so Statement II is also correct. Therefore, the correct option is (a).

Ions with f<sup>0</sup> or f<sup>14</sup> configurations have zero unpaired electrons and are diamagnetic. Step 1 (Check Statement I): • [Ti4+, V2+]: Ti4+ is 3d0 (colourless), V2+ is 3d3 (violet) =⇒ NOT both coloured. • [V2+, Mn2+]: 3d3 (violet) and 3d5 (pale pink) =⇒ both coloured. • [Mn2+, Fe3+]: 3d5 (pale pink) and 3d5 (yellow) =⇒ both coloured. • [V2+, Cr2+]: 3d3 (violet) and 3d4 (blue) =⇒ both coloured. Total pairs where both are coloured = 3. Hence, Statement I is correct. Step 2 (Check Statement II): • [La3+, Yb2+]: 4f0 and 4f14 =⇒ both diamagnetic. • [Lu3+, Ce4+]: 4f14 and 4f0 =⇒ both diamagnetic. • [Ac3+, Lr3+]: 5f0 and 5f14 =⇒ both diamagnetic. Total diamagnetic pairs = 3. Hence, Statement II is correct.
Q01.trapHtml: Mn<sup>2+</sup> (3d<sup>5</sup>) is very pale pink (spin-forbidden d–d transition), not colourless; NCERT explicitly lists it as coloured in aqueous solution.
Q01.finalAnsHtml: (A) Both Statement I and Statement II are correct

Q02.conceptHtml: Transition metals act as catalysts because they use both (n−1)d and ns electrons to form transient surface bonds with reactants, weakening reactant bonds and lowering activation energy.
Q02.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall how transition metals act as heterogeneous catalysts: Transition metals provide a large surface area where reactant molecules get adsorbed and form weak temporary bonds with surface metal atoms, lowering the activation energy of the reaction.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement I: First-row transition metals use both their $3d$ and $4s$ electrons (not $3d$ electrons only) to form bonds with reactant molecules on the catalyst surface. Hence, Statement I is incorrect.
  3. Step 3 — Evaluate Statement II: Adsorption increases the concentration of reactants on the catalyst surface, which weakens (not strengthens) the existing bonds inside the reacting molecules so they can break and rearrange more easily. Hence, Statement II is incorrect.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Since both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect, the correct option is (b).
Q02.stepsLatex:
Step 1: Statement I claims first-row transition metals utilise only their 3d electrons. In reality, they use both 3d
and 4s electrons for forming surface bonds with reactant molecules. Thus, Statement I is incorrect.
Step 2: Statement II claims higher reactant concentration on the catalyst surface strengthens the bonds in reacting
molecules. Adsorption actually weakens the intramolecular bonds of the reacting molecules, lowering the activation
energy. Thus, Statement II is incorrect.
Q02.trapHtml: Watch for absolute qualifiers like “only” and reversed effects like “strengthens” vs “weakens” in NCERT theory statements.
Q02.finalAnsHtml: (B) Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect

Q03.subtopic: Ionisation Enthalpies of Cr and Mn
Q03.conceptHtml: ∆<sub>i</sub>H<sub>1</sub> depends on removing the outer 4s electron, whereas ∆<sub>i</sub>H<sub>2</sub> of Cr removes an electron from a stable half-filled 3d<sup>5</sup> subshell. Step 1 (∆<sub>i</sub>H<sub>1</sub>): Cr = [Ar]3d54s1 and Mn = [Ar]3d54s2. Removing the first 4s electron is harder from the filled 4s2 subshell and higher Z<sub>eff</sub> of Mn, so ∆<sub>i</sub>H<sub>1</sub>(Mn) > ∆<sub>i</sub>H<sub>1</sub>(Cr) (Statement C is correct, A is false). Step 2 (∆<sub>i</sub>H<sub>2</sub>): Cr+ = [Ar]3d5 (half-filled) while Mn+ = [Ar]3d54s1. Removing the second electron from half- filled 3d5 in Cr+ requires much more energy than removing the 4s1 electron from Mn+, so ∆<sub>i</sub>H<sub>2</sub>(Cr) > ∆<sub>i</sub>H<sub>2</sub>(Mn) (Statement B is correct, D is false).
Q03.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Write the ground-state electronic configurations: For $\text{Cr}$ ($Z = 24$), the configuration is $[\text{Ar}]3d^5 4s^1$. For $\text{Mn}$ ($Z = 25$), the configuration is $[\text{Ar}]3d^5 4s^2$.
  2. Step 2 — Compare first ionisation enthalpies ($\Delta_i H_1$): Removing one electron from $\text{Mn}$ requires breaking a fully filled $4s^2$ subshell under a higher nuclear charge, whereas $\text{Cr}$ easily loses its single $4s^1$ electron to leave a stable half-filled $3d^5$ shell. Therefore, $\Delta_i H_1 : \text{Mn} > \text{Cr}$ (Statement C is correct, and A is incorrect).
  3. Step 3 — Compare second ionisation enthalpies ($\Delta_i H_2$): After losing one electron, $\text{Cr}^+$ has $[\text{Ar}]3d^5$ while $\text{Mn}^+$ has $[\text{Ar}]3d^5 4s^1$. Removing a second electron from $\text{Cr}^+$ disrupts the extra-stable half-filled $3d^5$ configuration, whereas $\text{Mn}^+$ readily loses its remaining $4s^1$ electron to achieve $3d^5$. Therefore, $\Delta_i H_2 : \text{Cr} > \text{Mn}$ (Statement B is correct, and D is incorrect).
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Statements B and C are correct, matching option (b).
Q03.stepsLatex: ∆<sub>i</sub>H<sub>1</sub> depends on removing the outer 4s electron, whereas ∆<sub>i</sub>H<sub>2</sub> of Cr removes an electron from a stable half-filled 3d<sup>5</sup> subshell. Step 1 (∆<sub>i</sub>H<sub>1</sub>): Cr = [Ar]3d54s1 and Mn = [Ar]3d54s2. Removing the first 4s electron is harder from the filled 4s2 subshell and higher Z<sub>eff</sub> of Mn, so ∆<sub>i</sub>H<sub>1</sub>(Mn) > ∆<sub>i</sub>H<sub>1</sub>(Cr) (Statement C is correct, A is false). Step 2 (∆<sub>i</sub>H<sub>2</sub>): Cr+ = [Ar]3d5 (half-filled) while Mn+ = [Ar]3d54s1. Removing the second electron from half- filled 3d5 in Cr+ requires much more energy than removing the 4s1 electron from Mn+, so ∆<sub>i</sub>H<sub>2</sub>(Cr) > ∆<sub>i</sub>H<sub>2</sub>(Mn) (Statement B is correct, D is false).
Q03.trapHtml: Never confuse ∆<sub>i</sub>H<sub>1</sub> (Mn > Cr) with ∆<sub>i</sub>H<sub>2</sub> (Cr > Mn).

Q04.conceptHtml: Know the exact composition and oxidation states of industrial catalysts: Contact process (V<sub>2</sub>O<sub>5</sub>), Ziegler- Natta (TiCl<sub>4</sub> + Al(C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>)<sub>3</sub>), and Wacker process (PdCl<sub>2</sub>).
Q04.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement A: The vanadium oxide used as a catalyst in the Contact Process for manufacturing $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ is $\text{V}_2\text{O}_5$. Because $\text{V}$ is in its highest $+5$ oxidation state, $\text{V}_2\text{O}_5$ is amphoteric (predominantly acidic), not basic. Thus, A is incorrect.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statements B and C (Ziegler–Natta catalyst): The Ziegler–Natta catalyst is a mixture of $\text{TiCl}_4$ and $\text{Al}(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5)_3$. In $\text{TiCl}_4$, titanium is in the $+4$ oxidation state ($\text{Ti}^{4+}$: $3d^0$), giving $n = 0$ unpaired electrons and a spin-only magnetic moment of $\mu = \sqrt{0(0+2)} = 0\text{ BM}$ (not $2.84\text{ BM}$), so B is incorrect. In the $p$-block organometallic compound $\text{Al}(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5)_3$, aluminium is in the $+3$ oxidation state, so C is correct.
  3. Step 3 — Evaluate Statement D (Wacker process): The Wacker process (oxidation of ethene to ethanal) uses $\text{PdCl}_2$ as the transition metal halide catalyst. Neutral $\text{Pd}$ ($Z = 46$) has configuration $[\text{Kr}]4d^{10}5s^0$, so $\text{Pd}^{2+}$ has $[\text{Kr}]4d^8$, which contains $8$ electrons in the outermost $4d$ orbital. Thus, D is correct.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Only statements C and D are correct, which corresponds to option (c).
Q04.stepsLatex:
Step 1: Check Statement A: V2O5 is used in the Contact process (H2SO4 manufacture), and V2O5 is amphoteric
(predominantly acidic), NOT basic. So A is incorrect.
Step 2: Check Statement B: Ziegler-Natta catalyst uses TiCl4 (Ti4+ is 3d0, n = 0 unpaired e− =⇒ µ = 0 BM, not
2.84 BM). So B is incorrect.
Step 3: Check Statement C: The p-block metal compound in Ziegler-Natta is Al(C2H5)3 (triethylaluminium), where
Al is in +3 oxidation state. So C is correct.
Step 4: Check Statement D: Wacker process uses PdCl2, where Pd2+ (Z = 46: [Kr]4d105s0) has 4d8 configuration
=⇒ 8 electrons in the outermost d-orbital. So D is correct.
Q04.trapHtml: Even though TiCl<sub>3</sub> is sometimes formed in situ, NCERT/JEE treats Ziegler-Natta as TiCl<sub>4</sub> + Al(C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>)<sub>3</sub> (Ti<sup>4+</sup>, d<sup>0</sup>, µ = 0).

Q05.subtopic: Qualitative Test for SO2 using Acidified K2Cr2O7
Q05.conceptHtml: SO<sub>2</sub> is a reducing agent that reduces orange acidified K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> (Cr<sup>6+</sup>) to green Cr<sub>2</sub>(SO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>3</sub> (Cr<sup>3+</sup>).
Q05.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the role of $\text{SO}_2$ gas: Sulphur dioxide ($\text{SO}_2$) acts as a strong reducing agent in aqueous acidic medium, getting oxidised to sulphate ion ($\text{SO}_4^{2-}$).
  2. Step 2 — Check the colour change with acidified $\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$: When $\text{SO}_2$ gas is passed over filter paper dipped in acidified potassium dichromate ($\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7 + \text{dil. H}_2\text{SO}_4$, orange), the dichromate ion ($\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}$) is reduced to green chromium(III) sulphate: $\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7 + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 + 3\text{SO}_2 \rightarrow \text{K}_2\text{SO}_4 + \text{Cr}_2(\text{SO}_4)_3\text{ (green)} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$.
  3. Step 3 — Rule out the other options: Acidified $\text{KMnO}_4$ gets decolourised (purple to colourless $\text{Mn}^{2+}$), $\text{KI}$–starch tests for oxidising gases like $\text{Cl}_2/\text{O}_3$, and lead acetate paper turns black with $\text{H}_2\text{S}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Compound X is $\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$, so the correct option is (d).
Q05.stepsLatex:
Step 1: Reaction:
K2Cr2O7 + H2SO4 + 3SO2 → K2SO4 + Cr2(SO4)3 (green) + H2O.
Step 2: Thus ‘X’ is K2Cr2O7. (KMnO4 would be decolourised from purple to colourless, and Pb(CH3COO)2 turns
black with H2S).
Q05.trapHtml: Don’t confuse SO<sub>2</sub> (turns K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> paper green) with H<sub>2</sub>S (turns lead acetate paper black).

Q06.conceptHtml: Interstitial compounds are formed when small atoms (H, C, N) occupy interstitial voids of transition metal lattices.
Q06.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall what interstitial compounds are: Interstitial compounds are formed when small non-metal atoms such as $\text{H}$, $\text{B}$, $\text{C}$, or $\text{N}$ get trapped inside the crystal lattice voids of transition metals (e.g., $\text{TiC}$, $\text{Mn}_4\text{N}$, $\text{Fe}_3\text{H}$).
  2. Step 2 — Review their standard physical and chemical properties: Interstitial compounds have very high melting points (higher than pure metals), retain metallic conductivity, are chemically inert, and are usually non-stoichiometric (neither typically ionic nor covalent).
  3. Step 3 — Spot the false statement: Interstitial compounds are extremely hard (some transition metal borides approach diamond in hardness) and are not ionic. Therefore, saying they are "very soft and ionic in nature" is false.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The statement that is NOT a characteristic of interstitial compounds is option (b).
Q06.stepsLatex:
Step 1: Per NCERT, interstitial compounds have: (i) high melting points (higher than pure metals), (ii) very hard
(some borides approach diamond in hardness, NOT soft), (iii) retain metallic conductivity, and (iv) are chemically
inert and non-stoichiometric.
Step 2: Therefore, “They are very soft and ionic in nature” is NOT a characteristic of interstitial compounds.
Q06.trapHtml: Interstitial compounds are metallic/covalent-like and hard, never soft and ionic.
Q06.finalAnsHtml: (B) They are very soft and ionic in nature.

Q07.conceptHtml: Write exact ground-state configurations noting 5d<sup>1</sup> exceptions at La, Ce, Gd, Lu, and remember Hf (Z = 72) has a filled 4f<sup>14</sup> core.
Q07.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Write the $4f$ subshell occupancy for each element: Using the atomic numbers provided, the ground-state configurations are: $\text{Eu}$ ($63$): $[\text{Xe}]4f^7 6s^2$; $\text{Gd}$ ($64$): $[\text{Xe}]4f^7 5d^1 6s^2$; $\text{Dy}$ ($66$): $[\text{Xe}]4f^{10} 6s^2$; $\text{Ho}$ ($67$): $[\text{Xe}]4f^{11} 6s^2$; $\text{Tm}$ ($69$): $[\text{Xe}]4f^{13} 6s^2$; $\text{Yb}$ ($70$): $[\text{Xe}]4f^{14} 6s^2$; $\text{Lu}$ ($71$): $[\text{Xe}]4f^{14} 5d^1 6s^2$; $\text{Hf}$ ($72$): $[\text{Xe}]4f^{14} 5d^2 6s^2$.
  2. Step 2 — Check pairs A and B: In pair A ($\text{Eu}$ and $\text{Gd}$), both elements have $7$ electrons in their $4f$ orbital ($4f^7$) because $\text{Gd}$ places its extra electron into $5d^1$ to preserve the half-filled $4f^7$ stability. Thus, A is correct. In pair B ($\text{Dy}$ has $4f^{10}$, $\text{Ho}$ has $4f^{11}$), the counts differ, so B is incorrect.
  3. Step 3 — Check pairs C and D: In pair C ($\text{Yb}$ and $\text{Hf}$), both elements have a completely filled $4f^{14}$ subshell ($14$ electrons each), so C is correct. In pair D ($\text{Lu}$ has $4f^{14}$, $\text{Tm}$ has $4f^{13}$), the counts differ, so D is incorrect.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Pairs A and C have the same number of $4f$ electrons, matching option (d).

• Eu (63) : [Xe]4f76s2 (7); Gd (64) : [Xe]4f75d16s2 (7) =⇒ Pair A matches (4f7).
• Dy (66) : [Xe]4f106s2 (10); Ho (67) : [Xe]4f116s2 (11) =⇒ B does not match.
• Yb (70) : [Xe]4f146s2 (14); Hf (72) : [Xe]4f145d26s2 (14) =⇒ Pair C matches (4f14).
• Lu (71) : [Xe]4f145d16s2 (14); Tm (69) : [Xe]4f136s2 (13) =⇒ D does not match.
Step 2: Pairs with the same number of 4f electrons are A and C only.
Q07.trapHtml: Remember Gd (64) puts its extra electron in 5d<sup>1</sup> to keep 4f<sup>7</sup>, and Hf (72) retains the 4f<sup>14</sup> core.

Q08.subtopic: Highest Mn Fluoride vs Oxide & Unpaired Electrons
Q08.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Oxidation state + magnetic count
Q08.conceptHtml: Oxygen stabilizes higher oxidation states (+7 in Mn<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub>) than fluorine (+4 in MnF<sub>4</sub>) due to pπ–dπ multiple bonding.
Q08.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Find the highest oxidation states of $\text{Mn}$ in its fluoride and oxide: The highest fluoride of manganese is $\text{MnF}_4$ (oxidation state $= +4$), because fluorine can only form single bonds. The highest oxide is $\text{Mn}_2\text{O}_7$ (oxidation state $= +7$), because oxygen stabilises higher states through multiple ($p\pi\text{--}d\pi$) bonds.
  2. Step 2 — Calculate $|x|$: The difference between the two oxidation states is $|x| = |7 - 4| = 3$. We need ions with exactly $3$ unpaired electrons.
  3. Step 3 — Count unpaired electrons in each given ion: $\text{Sc}^{3+}$ ($3d^0 \rightarrow 0$ unpaired), $\text{Zn}^{2+}$ ($3d^{10} \rightarrow 0$ unpaired), $\text{V}^{2+}$ ($3d^3 \rightarrow 3$ unpaired), $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ ($3d^6 \rightarrow 4$ unpaired), and $\text{Co}^{2+}$ ($3d^7 \rightarrow 3$ unpaired).
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Only $\text{V}^{2+}$ (C) and $\text{Co}^{2+}$ (E) have $3$ unpaired electrons, so the correct option is (c).
Q08.stepsLatex:
Step 1: Highest manganese fluoride is MnF4 (Mn OS = +4) and highest manganese oxide is Mn2O7 (Mn OS = +7).
|x| = |4 − 7| = 3.
Step 2: Find ions with n = 3 unpaired electrons:
• Sc3+: 3d0 =⇒ n = 0. Zn2+: 3d10 =⇒ n = 0.
• V2+: 3d3 =⇒ n = 3 (C).
• Fe2+: 3d6 =⇒ n = 4.
• Co2+: 3d7 =⇒ n = 3 (E).
Thus, C and E only have 3 unpaired electrons.
Q08.trapHtml: Highest fluoride of Mn is MnF<sub>4</sub>, NOT MnF<sub>7</sub> (fluorine cannot form multiple bonds like oxygen).

Q09.subtopic: Group 6 Stability, f-Block Redox & Actinoid Contraction
Q09.conceptHtml: In d-block, higher oxidation states become more stable down a group. Actinoid contraction is greater than lanthanoid contraction due to poorer shielding of 5f vs 4f electrons.
Q09.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement A: In the $d$-block, heavier transition metals stabilise higher oxidation states better than $3d$ metals. Thus, $\text{Mo(VI)}$ and $\text{W(VI)}$ are more stable (not less stable) than $\text{Cr(VI)}$. Hence, A is incorrect.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement B: The most stable oxidation state for lanthanoids is $+3$. Therefore, $\text{Ce}^{4+}$ and $\text{Tb}^{4+}$ readily gain an electron to become $+3$ (acting as strong oxidants), whereas $\text{Eu}^{2+}$ and $\text{Yb}^{2+}$ readily lose an electron to become $+3$ (acting as strong reductants). Hence, B is correct.
  3. Step 3 — Evaluate Statement C: Americium ($\text{Am}$, $Z = 95$) has configuration $[\text{Rn}]5f^7 7s^2$ ($7$ unpaired electrons), whereas Curium ($\text{Cm}$, $Z = 96$) has $[\text{Rn}]5f^7 6d^1 7s^2$, which has $7 + 1 = 8$ unpaired electrons (not $7$). Hence, C is incorrect.
  4. Step 4 — Evaluate Statement D and conclude: Because $5f$ orbitals are more diffuse and provide poorer nuclear shielding than $4f$ orbitals, the actinoid contraction from element to element is greater than the lanthanoid contraction. Thus, D is correct. Only B and D are correct, giving option (c).

Step 1: Evaluate each statement:
• A (False): Mo(VI) and W(VI) are more stable than Cr(VI).
• B (True): Ce4+ and Tb4+ readily reduce to +3 (strong oxidants), while Eu2+ and Yb2+ readily oxidise to +3
(strong reductants).
• C (False): Am (95) : [Rn]5f77s2 (7 unpaired e−), but Cm (96) : [Rn]5f76d17s2 has 7 + 1 = 8 unpaired
electrons!
• D (True): Actinoid contraction is greater from element to element than lanthanoid contraction because 5f
electrons have poorer shielding than 4f electrons.
Step 2: Correct statements are B and D only.
Q09.trapHtml: Cm (Z = 96) has 5f<sup>7</sup>6d<sup>1</sup>7s<sup>2</sup> (8 unpaired electrons), just like Gd (Z = 64) has 4f<sup>7</sup>5d<sup>1</sup>6s<sup>2</sup> (8 unpaired electrons).

Q10.conceptHtml: K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> is used as a primary standard (unlike Na<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> which is hygroscopic). Chromate and dichromate interconvert with pH, and ∠Cr − O − Cr = 126<sup>°</sup>.
Q10.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement A: Potassium dichromate ($\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$) is a strong oxidising agent in acidic medium and oxidises ferrous sulphate ($\text{Fe}^{2+}$) to ferric sulphate ($\text{Fe}^{3+}$): $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-} + 6\text{Fe}^{2+} + 14\text{H}^+ \rightarrow 2\text{Cr}^{3+} + 6\text{Fe}^{3+} + 7\text{H}_2\text{O}$. Thus, A is correct.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement B: Sodium dichromate ($\text{Na}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$) is deliquescent/hygroscopic (absorbs moisture from air), so it cannot be weighed accurately and is not used as a primary standard (unlike $\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$). Thus, B is incorrect.
  3. Step 3 — Evaluate Statements C and D: Chromate ($\text{CrO}_4^{2-}$, yellow in base) and dichromate ($\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}$, orange in acid) interconvert with pH: $2\text{CrO}_4^{2-} + 2\text{H}^+ \rightleftharpoons \text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$, so C is correct. Structurally, $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}$ consists of two tetrahedral $\text{CrO}_4$ units sharing one oxygen atom with a $\text{Cr}-\text{O}-\text{Cr}$ bond angle of $126^\circ$, so D is correct.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Statements A, C, and D are correct, matching option (b).

Q11.conceptHtml: Coloured transition metal ions give a positive borax bead test; Zn<sup>2+</sup> (3d<sup>10</sup>, colourless) does not. Removing an electron from a +3 ion requires the 4th IE, which is much higher than 3rd IE of +2 ions.
Q11.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Check which ions give a positive borax bead test: The borax bead test identifies coloured transition metal metaborates formed by ions with unpaired $d$-electrons. Since $\text{Zn}^{2+}$ has a completely filled $3d^{10}$ configuration, it forms a colourless bead and does not give a positive borax bead test. In contrast, $\text{Fe}^{2+}$, $\text{Fe}^{3+}$, and $\text{Cr}^{2+}$ all give characteristic coloured beads.
  2. Step 2 — Compare the ionisation enthalpies of the remaining ions: Ionisation enthalpy of an ion is the energy required to remove an electron from that ion. Removing an electron from $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ (forming $\text{Fe}^{4+}$) corresponds to the $4\text{th}$ ionisation enthalpy of iron, whereas removing an electron from $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ or $\text{Cr}^{2+}$ corresponds to a $3\text{rd}$ ionisation enthalpy.
  3. Step 3 — Factor in electronic configuration stability: Not only does $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ carry a higher positive charge ($+3$ vs $+2$), it also possesses the extra-stable half-filled $[\text{Ar}]3d^5$ configuration, making removal of another electron extremely endothermic.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Therefore, $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ shows a positive borax bead test and has the highest ionisation enthalpy, corresponding to option (d).
Q11.stepsLatex:
Step 1: Fe2+, Fe3+, Cr2+ are coloured transition metal ions and give positive borax bead tests; Zn2+ (3d10) does
not.
Step 2: Among Fe2+, Cr2+, Fe3+, Fe3+ already carries +3 charge and has a stable half-filled 3d5 configuration, so
its ionisation enthalpy (removing the 4th electron from Fe3+) is the highest.
Q11.trapHtml: Ionisation enthalpy of an already formed cation M<sup>n+</sup> increases sharply with positive charge (+3 ≫ +2) and half-filled stability (3d<sup>5</sup>).

Q12.conceptHtml: Acidified K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> (orange) turns green (Cr<sup>3+</sup>) only when reacted with species that can be oxidised (reducing agents).
Q12.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Understand the condition for colour change: Acidified $\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$ (orange, $\text{Cr}^{6+}$) acts as an oxidising agent and turns green ($\text{Cr}^{3+}$) only when it reacts with a reducing agent (a species that can be further oxidised).
  2. Step 2 — Check Option (a): In the set $\{\text{Fe}^{2+}, \text{Sn}^{2+}, \text{I}^-, \text{S}^{2-}\}$, every species is a reducing agent in acidic medium: $\text{Fe}^{2+} \rightarrow \text{Fe}^{3+}$, $\text{Sn}^{2+} \rightarrow \text{Sn}^{4+}$, $\text{I}^- \rightarrow \text{I}_2$, and $\text{S}^{2-} \rightarrow \text{S}$. Hence, all four will turn orange $\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$ green.
  3. Step 3 — Eliminate Options (b), (c), and (d): Option (b) contains $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ (already in its stable oxidised state), option (c) contains $\text{Sn}^{4+}$ (already in its maximum $+4$ state), and option (d) contains $\text{Fe}^{3+}$, $\text{SO}_4^{2-}$, and $\text{Sn}^{4+}$, none of which can reduce $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The only set where all species change the orange colour of acidified $\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$ is option (a).

Q13.subtopic: Structure, Magnetism & Redox of Manganate and
Q13.conceptHtml: MnO<sup>2</sup><sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup> (manganate, Mn +6, d<sup>1</sup>, paramagnetic, green) and MnO<sup>−</sup><sub>4</sub> (permanganate, Mn +7, d<sup>0</sup>, diamagnetic, purple) are both tetrahedral.
Q13.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Check Statements A and B (geometry and oxidation states): Both manganate ($\text{MnO}_4^{2-}$) and permanganate ($\text{MnO}_4^-$) ions have four $\text{Mn}-\text{O}$ bonds with no lone pairs on $\text{Mn}$, so both are tetrahedral (A is correct). The oxidation state of $\text{Mn}$ is $+6$ in manganate ($\text{MnO}_4^{2-}$) and $+7$ in permanganate ($\text{MnO}_4^-$), which is the opposite of what Statement B claims (B is incorrect).
  2. Step 2 — Check Statement C (preparation): In the laboratory, oxidising a $\text{Mn(II)}$ salt with peroxodisulphate ($\text{S}_2\text{O}_8^{2-}$) produces permanganate ($\text{MnO}_4^-$), not manganate: $2\text{Mn}^{2+} + 5\text{S}_2\text{O}_8^{2-} + 8\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow 2\text{MnO}_4^- + 10\text{SO}_4^{2-} + 16\text{H}^+$. Thus, C is incorrect.
  3. Step 3 — Check Statements D and E (magnetism and redox role): In $\text{MnO}_4^{2-}$ ($\text{Mn}^{6+}$, $3d^1$), there is $1$ unpaired electron, so it is paramagnetic; in $\text{MnO}_4^-$ ($\text{Mn}^{7+}$, $3d^0$), there are $0$ unpaired electrons, so it is diamagnetic (D is correct). Acidified $\text{MnO}_4^-$ is a strong oxidising agent that oxidises (not reduces) oxalate, nitrite, and iodide ions (E is incorrect).
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Only statements A and D are correct, giving option (a).

Q14.subtopic: Colour of 3d Ions & f-Block Reducing Strength
Q14.conceptHtml: Ions with d<sup>0</sup> (Sc<sup>3+</sup>, Ti<sup>4+</sup>) or d<sup>10</sup> (Zn<sup>2+</sup>) are colourless in aqueous solution. Eu<sup>2+</sup> (4f<sup>7</sup>) is a strong reducing agent. Step 1 (Statement I): Check the four pairs: • [Sc3+, Ti3+]: Sc3+ (3d0) is colourless =⇒ not both coloured. • [Mn2+, Cr2+]: 3d5 and 3d4 =⇒ both coloured (1 pair). • [Cu2+, Zn2+]: Zn2+ (3d10) is colourless =⇒ not both coloured. • [Ni2+, Ti4+]: Ti4+ (3d0) is colourless =⇒ not both coloured. Only 1 pair has both ions coloured (not 3). Statement I is false. Step 2 (Statement II): Among Th4+, Ce4+, Gd3+, Eu2+, Eu2+ is the strongest reducing agent (readily oxidises to +3). Th4+ is already in its maximum +4 state and cannot act as a reducing agent. Statement II is false.
Q14.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Check the $d$-electron configurations in Statement I: An ion is coloured in aqueous solution if it has $d^1\text{--}d^9$ electrons and colourless if it is $d^0$ or $d^{10}$. Checking each pair: $[\text{Sc}^{3+}(3d^0\text{, colourless}), \text{Ti}^{3+}(3d^1)]$, $[\text{Mn}^{2+}(3d^5\text{, coloured}), \text{Cr}^{2+}(3d^4\text{, coloured})]$, $[\text{Cu}^{2+}(3d^9), \text{Zn}^{2+}(3d^{10}\text{, colourless})]$, and $[\text{Ni}^{2+}(3d^8), \text{Ti}^{4+}(3d^0\text{, colourless})]$.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement I: Only $1$ pair ($[\text{Mn}^{2+}, \text{Cr}^{2+}]$) has both ions coloured, not $3$. Therefore, Statement I is false.
  3. Step 3 — Evaluate Statement II: Among $\text{Th}^{4+}$, $\text{Ce}^{4+}$, $\text{Gd}^{3+}$, and $\text{Eu}^{2+}$, the strongest reducing agent is $\text{Eu}^{2+}$ because it strongly tends to lose an electron to reach the stable $+3$ lanthanoid state ($\text{Eu}^{3+}$). $\text{Th}^{4+}$ is already in its highest stable $+4$ state ($5f^0$) and cannot lose more electrons to act as a reducing agent. Therefore, Statement II is false.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Since both Statement I and Statement II are false, the correct option is (b).

Q15.conceptHtml: Lightest element of Group 7 is Manganese (Mn). Its +6 oxoanion is manganate (MnO<sup>2</sup><sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup>), whose potassium salt K<sub>2</sub>MnO<sub>4</sub> is dark green.
Q15.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the lightest element of Group 7: Group 7 consists of $\text{Mn}$, $\text{Tc}$, $\text{Re}$, and $\text{Bh}$. The lightest element in Group 7 is manganese ($\text{Mn}$).
  2. Step 2 — Identify the oxoanion X in the $+6$ oxidation state: Manganese forms two famous oxoanions: permanganate ($\text{MnO}_4^-$, where $\text{Mn}$ is $+7$) and manganate ($\text{MnO}_4^{2-}$, where $\text{Mn}$ is $+6$). Hence, X is the manganate ion, $\text{MnO}_4^{2-}$.
  3. Step 3 — Recall the colour of its potassium salt: The potassium salt of $\text{MnO}_4^{2-}$ is potassium manganate ($\text{K}_2\text{MnO}_4$), which is characteristically dark green in colour (whereas $\text{KMnO}_4$ is dark purple).
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The colour of the potassium salt of X is green, matching option (d).

Step 2: Oxoanion of Mn in +6 OS is MnO2−, and K2MnO4 is green (dark green).

Q16.subtopic: 1st, 2nd & 3rd Ionisation Enthalpies of Cr vs Mn
Q16.conceptHtml: ∆<sub>i</sub>H<sub>1</sub>(Cr) < ∆<sub>i</sub>H<sub>1</sub>(Mn), ∆<sub>i</sub>H<sub>2</sub>(Cr) > ∆<sub>i</sub>H<sub>2</sub>(Mn), and ∆<sub>i</sub>H<sub>3</sub>(Mn) > ∆<sub>i</sub>H<sub>3</sub>(Cr). Step 1 (Statement I): Cr (3d54s1) has lower ∆<sub>i</sub>H<sub>1</sub> (653 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>) than Mn (3d54s2) (717 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>). Thus, Statement I is true. Step 2 (Statement II): ∆<sub>i</sub>H<sub>2</sub>(Cr) > ∆<sub>i</sub>H<sub>2</sub>(Mn) (1592 > 1509 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>, removing from 3d5 vs 4s1). However, for ∆<sub>i</sub>H<sub>3</sub>, Mn2+ is 3d5 (half-filled) while Cr2+ is 3d4, so ∆<sub>i</sub>H<sub>3</sub>(Mn) > ∆<sub>i</sub>H<sub>3</sub>(Cr) (3248 > 2987 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>). Thus, Statement II is false.
Q16.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Compare the first ionisation enthalpies (Statement I): $\text{Cr}$ ($[\text{Ar}]3d^5 4s^1$) readily loses its single $4s$ electron, while $\text{Mn}$ ($[\text{Ar}]3d^5 4s^2$) must lose an electron from a stable, fully filled $4s^2$ subshell with higher nuclear charge. Thus, $\Delta_i H_1(\text{Cr}) = 653\text{ kJ/mol} < \Delta_i H_1(\text{Mn}) = 717\text{ kJ/mol}$, making Statement I true.
  2. Step 2 — Compare the second ionisation enthalpies: Removing a second electron from $\text{Cr}^+$ ($3d^5$) breaks the half-filled $3d^5$ shell, whereas $\text{Mn}^+$ ($3d^5 4s^1$) easily loses its $4s^1$ electron. So $\Delta_i H_2(\text{Cr}) = 1592\text{ kJ/mol} > \Delta_i H_2(\text{Mn}) = 1509\text{ kJ/mol}$.
  3. Step 3 — Compare the third ionisation enthalpies (the key check for Statement II): For the third ionisation, $\text{Mn}^{2+}$ has the extra-stable half-filled $3d^5$ configuration, whereas $\text{Cr}^{2+}$ is $3d^4$. Breaking $\text{Mn}^{2+}$ ($3d^5$) requires much more energy: $\Delta_i H_3(\text{Mn}) = 3260\text{ kJ/mol} > \Delta_i H_3(\text{Cr}) = 2990\text{ kJ/mol}$. Because $\Delta_i H_3$ of $\text{Cr}$ is lower than that of $\text{Mn}$, Statement II is false.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Statement I is true and Statement II is false, corresponding to option (a).

However, for ∆<sub>i</sub>H<sub>3</sub>, Mn2+ is 3d5 (half-filled) while Cr2+ is 3d4, so ∆<sub>i</sub>H<sub>3</sub>(Mn) > ∆<sub>i</sub>H<sub>3</sub>(Cr) (3248 > 2987 kJ mol−1). Thus, Statement II is false.

Q16.finalAnsHtml: (A) Statement I is true but Statement II is false

Q17.conceptHtml: Mn<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> is a covalent green oil with two tetrahedral MnO<sub>4</sub> units sharing one bridging oxygen (O<sub>3</sub>Mn − O − MnO<sub>3</sub>).
Q17.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statements A and B: In $\text{Mn}_2\text{O}_7$, manganese is in its highest possible oxidation state of $+7$ (using all $3d^5 4s^2$ valence electrons), so A is correct. Oxygen is able to stabilise such high oxidation states better than fluorine because it can form $p\pi\text{--}d\pi$ multiple bonds with $\text{Mn}$, so B is correct.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement C: As the oxidation state of a transition metal increases, the polarising power of the metal increases and ionic character decreases (Fajans\' rule). Hence, $\text{Mn}_2\text{O}_7$ is a covalent green oil, not an ionic oxide. Thus, C is incorrect.
  3. Step 3 — Evaluate Statement D: The molecular structure of $\text{Mn}_2\text{O}_7$ consists of two tetrahedral $\text{MnO}_4$ units linked together through a single bridging oxygen atom ($\text{O}_3\text{Mn}-\text{O}-\text{MnO}_3$). Thus, D is correct.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Statements A, B, and D are correct, matching option (b).

Step 1: Evaluate each statement:
• A (True): Mn is in +7 OS (its highest oxidation state).
• B (True): Oxygen stabilizes high OS via pπ–dπ multiple bonds (Mn = O).
• C (False): Mn2O7 is a covalent oxide (volatile green oil), NOT ionic.
• D (True): Its structure has one bridging oxygen (Mn − O − Mn) and six terminal oxygens.
Q17.trapHtml: Oxides of transition metals in very high OS (+6, +7) like CrO<sub>3</sub> and Mn<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> are covalent and acidic, never ionic.

Q18.conceptHtml: Manganate ion (MnO<sup>2</sup><sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup>, +6) is unstable in neutral or acidic medium and disproportionates to permanganate (+7) and manganese dioxide (+4).
Q18.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the oxidation state of $\text{Mn}$ in manganate ion: In $\text{MnO}_4^{2-}$, manganese is in the $+6$ oxidation state, which is an intermediate state between $+4$ and $+7$ and is unstable in acidic or neutral solutions.
  2. Step 2 — Write the disproportionation reaction in acidic medium: In acidic medium, $\text{MnO}_4^{2-}$ simultaneously oxidises to permanganate ($\text{MnO}_4^-$, $+7$) and reduces to manganese dioxide ($\text{MnO}_2$, $+4$): $3\text{MnO}_4^{2-} + 4\text{H}^+ \rightarrow 2\text{MnO}_4^- + \text{MnO}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$.
  3. Step 3 — Verify atom and charge balance: On both sides there are $3\text{ Mn}$, $12\text{ O}$, $4\text{ H}$, and a net charge of $-2$, confirming the balanced products are $\text{MnO}_4^-$ and $\text{MnO}_2$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The disproportionation products are $\text{MnO}_4^-$ and $\text{MnO}_2$, which corresponds to option (b).

Q19.subtopic: Decreasing Order of Spin-Only Magnetic Moment
Q19.conceptHtml: µ = n(n + 2) BM increases monotonically with the number of unpaired electrons n.
Q19.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the spin-only magnetic moment formula: The spin-only magnetic moment is $\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)}\text{ BM}$, where $n$ is the number of unpaired electrons. Greater $n$ directly means a larger $\mu$.
  2. Step 2 — Find $n$ for each ion: $\text{Cr}^{2+}$ ($[\text{Ar}]3d^4 \rightarrow n = 4$, $\mu = 4.90\text{ BM}$), $\text{Cr}^{3+}$ ($[\text{Ar}]3d^3 \rightarrow n = 3$, $\mu = 3.87\text{ BM}$), $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ ($[\text{Ar}]3d^9 \rightarrow n = 1$, $\mu = 1.73\text{ BM}$), and $\text{Cu}^+$ ($[\text{Ar}]3d^{10} \rightarrow n = 0$, $\mu = 0\text{ BM}$).
  3. Step 3 — Arrange in decreasing order of $\mu$: Ordering from highest $n$ to lowest $n$ gives $\text{Cr}^{2+} > \text{Cr}^{3+} > \text{Cu}^{2+} > \text{Cu}^+$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The decreasing order matches option (c).
Q19.stepsLatex:
Step 1: Count unpaired electrons n for each ion:
• Cr2+: [Ar]3d4 =⇒ n = 4 (µ = 4.90 BM)
• Cr3+: [Ar]3d3 =⇒ n = 3 (µ = 3.87 BM)
• Cu2+: [Ar]3d9 =⇒ n = 1 (µ = 1.73 BM)
• Cu+: [Ar]3d10 =⇒ n = 0 (µ = 0 BM)
Step 2: Decreasing order: Cr2+ > Cr3+ > Cu2+ > Cu+.
Q19.trapHtml: Always remove 4s electrons first when forming transition metal cations.

Q20.subtopic: Enthalpy of Atomisation, Aquated Ion Colour & Oxide
Q20.conceptHtml: Among 3d metals, Vanadium (V) has the highest enthalpy of atomisation (515 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>). V<sup>3+</sup>(aq) is green, and its oxide V<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> is basic.
Q20.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify metal M from the $3d$ series: Among the first transition series elements ($\text{Sc}$ to $\text{Zn}$), vanadium ($\text{V}$) has the highest enthalpy of atomisation ($\Delta_a H^\circ = 515\text{ kJ/mol}$). Therefore, $\text{M} = \text{V}$.
  2. Step 2 — Identify the green aquated ion $\text{M}^{n+}$: The aqueous ions of vanadium have characteristic colours: $\text{V}^{2+}(\text{aq})$ is violet, $\text{V}^{3+}(\text{aq})$ is green, and $\text{VO}^{2+}(\text{aq})$ is blue. Hence, the green aquated ion is $\text{V}^{3+}$.
  3. Step 3 — Determine the nature of the oxide of $\text{V}^{3+}$: The oxide corresponding to $\text{V}^{3+}$ is $\text{V}_2\text{O}_3$. Across the vanadium oxides, acidity increases with oxidation state: $\text{V}_2\text{O}_3$ ($+3$) is basic, $\text{V}_2\text{O}_4$ ($+4$) is less basic/weakly amphoteric, and $\text{V}_2\text{O}_5$ ($+5$) is amphoteric (mainly acidic).
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The oxide $\text{V}_2\text{O}_3$ is basic, so the correct option is (a).
