trapCards.title: Trap 2: Electrode Potentials (E<sup>◦</sup>), Cu<sup>2+</sup>/Cu<sup>+</sup> & Ox- ide Nature
trapCards.html:
• The Mistake: Thinking Cu+ (3d10) is more stable than Cu2+ in water, or confusing Fe3+/Fe2+ with Mn3+/Mn2+. The Fix:
  • Cu2+ vs Cu+: Cu2+ is more stable in water because ∆hydH(Cu2+) is much more negative (greater) than Cu+ (Q37, Q69). Cu has E◦ = +0.34 V =⇒ cannot liberate H2 from acids (Q36).
  • M3+/M2+: Cr2+, V2+, Ti2+ have E◦ < 0 (liberate H2 from dil. acid; Q42, Q45, Q63). E◦(Mn3+/Mn2+) > E◦(Fe3+/Fe2+) (Q63).
  • Highest Oxides vs Fluorides: Mn2O7 (+7, covalent, tetrahedral, Mn − O − Mn) vs MnF4 (+4) (Q08, Q17, Q70).
  • Down-Group Stability: Mo(VI), W(VI) > Cr(VI) =⇒ CrO3 is a stronger oxidant than MoO3 (Q09, Q23, Q36). Trap 4: f-Block Configurations, Contraction & Re- dox Roles The Mistake: Confusing Eu2+ (reductant) with Ce4+/Tb4+ (oxidants), or forgetting 5d1/6d1 exceptions at Gd and Cm. The Fix:
  • Redox Roles: +2 ions (Eu2+, Yb2+, Sm2+) are reduc- ing agents; +4 ions (Ce4+, Tb4+) are oxidising agents (Q09, Q30, Q54, Q57, Q67, Q81).
  • Diamagnetic / Colourless: Only f0 (La3+, Ce4+, Ac3+, Th4+) and f14 (Yb2+, Lu3+, Lr3+) (Q01, Q53, Q83, Q91).
  • Half-Filled f7 & 5d1/6d1: Eu (4f76s2) and Gd (4f75d16s2) both have 4f7; Cm (5f76d17s2) has 8 unpaired e− while Am (5f77s2) has 7 (Q07, Q09, Q71).
  • Contraction & Bonding: Actinoid contraction > lan- thanoid contraction; 5f orbitals are less buried and bond more than 4f (Q09, Q62).

trapCards.title: Trap 3: KMnO<sub>4</sub> & K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> Medium, Colour & For- mula Traps
trapCards.html:
• The Mistake: Mixing up acidic vs neutral KMnO4 products, or attributing MnO−4 /Cr2O27− colour to d–d transitions. The Fix:
  • Acidic vs Neutral KMnO4: Acidic (∆OS = 5, Mn2+) gives I− → I2; neutral/faintly alkaline (∆OS = 3, MnO2) gives I− → IO−3 and S2O23− → SO24− (Q27, Q66, Q75, Q99, Q100).
  • Charge Transfer: MnO−4 , CrO24−, Cr2O27− are d0 =⇒ colour is due to LMCT, never d–d (Q51).
  • Manganate (MnO24−): Dark green, paramagnetic (d1), disproportionates in acid/neutral to MnO−4 + MnO2 (Q13, Q15, Q18, Q47, Q96).
  • Dichromate: K2Cr2O7 (not Na2Cr2O7) is the primary standard; ∠Cr − O − Cr = 126◦, 6 terminal O (Q10, Q86).

formulaCards.title: 1. Werner’s Theory & Double Salts vs Complexes
formulaCards.html:
• Double Salts (dissociate completely into simple ions in water): Mohr’s salt FeSO4 · (NH4)2SO4 · 6H2O, Potash alum K2SO4 · Al2(SO4)3 · 24H2O, Carnallite KCl · MgCl2 · 6H2O.
  • Coordination Complexes (retain identity in solution): K4[Fe(CN)6], [Cu(NH3)4]SO4.
  • Werner’s Two Valencies: – Primary Valency (1◦): Ionisable, equals oxida- tion state of central metal, non-directional, satisfied by negative ions. – Secondary Valency (2◦): Non-ionisable, equals coordination number (CN), directional (fixes ge- ometry), satisfied by ligands.
  • Electrolyte Type & AgCl Moles (for CoCl3 · xNH3): Formula Ions AgCl/mol [Co(NH3)6]Cl3 4 (1 : 3) 3 [Co(NH3)5Cl]Cl2 3 (1 : 2) 2 [Co(NH3)4Cl2]Cl 2 (1 : 1) 1 [Co(NH3)3Cl3] 0 (non-elec.) 0

formulaCards.title: 2. Ligand Classification & IUPAC Nomenclature
formulaCards.html:
• Bidentate: en (ethane-1,2-diamine), ox2− (C2O24−), gly−, bpy, phen, dmg− (forms 5-membered chelate ring + H-bond in [Ni(dmg)2]).
  • Polydentate: EDTA4− (hexadentate: 2 N+4 O donors); dien (tridentate).
  • Ambidentate (2 donor sites, 1 at a time): NO−2 (N vs O), SCN− (S vs N), CN− (C vs N). (Note: C2O24−, SO24−, NH3, H2O are NOT ambidentate!)
  • IUPAC Rules: (1) Cation named before anion. (2) Lig- ands in alphabetical order (ignore di-, tri-, bis-, tris-). (3) Anionic ligands end in -o (Cl− → chlorido, CN− → cyanido, C2O24− → oxalato, O2− → oxido). (4) Complex anion ends in -ate (e.g., cobaltate, ferrate, manganate, platinate) + Roman oxidation state. (5) Use bis-, tris- if ligand name already contains di-, tri- or is polydentate (en, PMe3).

formulaCards.title: 4. VBT Hybridization, Geometry & Magnetic Mo- ment
formulaCards.html:
• Spin-Only Magnetic Moment: µ = pn(n + 2) BM (n = unpaired e−): n = 0 → 0; n = 1 → 1.73; n = 2 → 2.83; n = 3 → 3.87; n = 4 → 4.90; n = 5 → 5.92 BM.
  • CN = 4 (Key Ni/Pt/Cu/Mn/Co Cases): – [Ni(CO)4] (Ni0, d10): sp3, tetrahedral, µ = 0. – [NiCl4]2− (Ni2+, d8): sp3, tetrahedral, n = 2 (µ = 2.83 BM). – [Ni(CN)4]2− (Ni2+, d8): dsp2, square planar, µ = 0. – [Pt(NH3)2Cl2], [Pt(CN)4]2−, [PtCl4]2− (5d8): al- ways dsp2, square planar, µ = 0. – [Cu(NH3)4]2+ (d9): dsp2, square planar, n = 1 (µ = 1.73 BM). – [MnBr4]2− (d5): sp3, tetrahedral, n = 5; [CoCl4]2− (d7): sp3, n = 3.
  • CN = 6 Inner (d2sp3) vs Outer (sp3d2): – d2sp3 (low spin): [Co(NH3)6]3+, [Co(en)3]3+, [Co(ox)3]3−, [Fe(CN)6]4−, [Fe(CN)6]3− (n = 1), [Mn(CN)6]3− (n = 2), [Cr(NH3)6]3+ (n = 3). – sp3d2 (high spin): [CoF6]3− (n = 4), [FeF6]3− (n = 5), [MnCl6]3− (n = 4), [Fe(H2O)6]2+ (n = 4), [Ni(NH3)6]2+ (n = 2). – Special Co3+ Rule: H2O and C2O24− act as strong-field with Co3+ ([Co(H2O)6]3+, [Co(ox)3]3− are diamagnetic, t62ge0g)!

formulaCards.title: 5. Crystal Field Theory (CFT), CFSE & Colour
formulaCards.html:
• Octahedral Splitting (∆o): eg (dx2−y2, dz2) at +0.6∆o; t2g (dxy, dyz, dxz) at −0.4∆o. CFSE = (−0.4 nt2g + 0.6 neg)∆o + mP.
  • Tetrahedral Splitting (∆t): Inverted! t2 at +0.4∆t; e at −0.6∆t. ∆t = 4∆o < P =⇒ tetrahedral complexes are almost always9 high spin.
  • Spectrochemical Series (Increasing ∆o): I− < Br− < SCN− < Cl− < S2− < F− < OH− < C2O24− < H2O < NCS− < EDTA4− < NH3 < en < CN− < CO.
  • Factors Increasing ∆o: (1) Stronger ligand; (2) Higher oxidation state (M3+ > M2+); (3) 5d > 4d > 3d (+30– 50% per period).
  • Colour & λabs: ∆o = hc =⇒ λabs ∝ 1 . λabs ∆o – Colourless if d0 (Ti4+) or d10 (Zn2+, Cu+) or [Ni(CN)4]2−? Wait: [Ni(H2O)6]2+ is green; [Ni(CN)4]2− is pale yellow/colourless in dilute soln (actually yellow crystals, CFT d-d allowed; check statement context). KMnO4, K2Cr2O7, K2CrO4 are coloured by LMCT (not d–d)!
  • Jahn–Teller Distortion: Strongest when eg is asym- metrically filled: d9 (Cu2+), high-spin d4 (Cr2+, Mn3+), low-spin d7.

Q01.format: Multiple-Statement MCQ | Ni(II) and Ni(0) complexes
Q01.conceptHtml: Ni<sup>2+</sup> (d<sup>8</sup>) is tetrahedral paramagnetic with weak ligands (Cl<sup>−</sup>), square planar diamagnetic with strong ligands (CN<sup>−</sup>), and octahedral paramagnetic with NH<sub>3</sub>. Ni(CO)<sub>4</sub> is Ni(0) (d<sup>10</sup>), sp<sup>3</sup> diamagnetic.
Q01.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Check $[\text{NiCl}_4]^{2-}$ (Statement A): Nickel is in the $+2$ oxidation state ($3d^8$). Because $\text{Cl}^-$ is a weak-field ligand, no pairing occurs, leaving $2$ unpaired electrons in $3d$. Thus it undergoes $sp^3$ hybridisation, has tetrahedral geometry, and is paramagnetic. Statement A is correct.
  2. Step 2 — Check $[\text{Ni}(\text{NH}_3)_6]^{2+}$ (Statement B): With $\text{Ni}^{2+}$ ($3d^8$) and coordination number $6$, the two $e_g$ orbitals are singly occupied ($t_{2g}^6 e_g^2$), leaving $2$ unpaired electrons. It uses outer $4d$ orbitals for $sp^3d^2$ hybridisation, is octahedral, and is paramagnetic. Statement B is correct.
  3. Step 3 — Check $[\text{Ni}(\text{CO})_4]$ (Statement C): Nickel is in the $0$ oxidation state ($3d^8 4s^2$). Strong-field $\text{CO}$ pushes the $4s^2$ electrons into the $3d$ subshell to give $3d^{10}$ with $0$ unpaired electrons, so it is $sp^3$ tetrahedral and diamagnetic (not paramagnetic). Statement C is incorrect.
  4. Step 4 — Check $[\text{Ni}(\text{CN})_4]^{2-}$ (Statement D) and conclude: Strong-field $\text{CN}^-$ pairs the $3d^8$ electrons of $\text{Ni}^{2+}$, vacating one $3d$ orbital for $dsp^2$ hybridisation (square planar, $0$ unpaired electrons, diamagnetic). Thus A, B, and D only are correct, matching option (d).
Q01.stepsLatex:
• A: [NiCl4]2− (Ni2+, d8, weak Cl−) =⇒ sp3, tetrahedral, 2 unpaired e− (paramagnetic). Correct.
• B: [Ni(NH3)6]2+ (Ni2+, d8, CN = 6) =⇒ sp3d2, octahedral, 2 unpaired e− (paramagnetic). Correct.
• C: [Ni(CO)4] (Ni0, d10, strong CO) =⇒ sp3, tetrahedral, 0 unpaired e− (diamagnetic, not paramagnetic).
Incorrect.
• D: [Ni(CN)4]2− (Ni2+, d8, strong CN−) =⇒ dsp2, square planar, diamagnetic. Correct.
Q01.trapHtml: Ni(CO)<sub>4</sub> is sp<sup>3</sup> tetrahedral like [NiCl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2−</sup>, but Ni(0) has 3d<sup>10</sup>4s<sup>0</sup> after pairing, making it diamagnetic.

Q02.format: Match List-I with List-II | High-spin tetrahedral e/t<sub>2</sub> filling
Q02.conceptHtml: In tetrahedral field (∆<sub>t</sub> < P), e lies at −0.6∆<sub>t</sub> and t<sub>2</sub> at +0.4∆<sub>t</sub>. Always fill high-spin: CFSE = (−0.6 n<sub>e</sub> + 0.4 n<sub>t2</sub>)∆<sub>t</sub>.
Q02.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the tetrahedral CFSE formula: In a tetrahedral field, the lower $e$ set ($d_{x^2-y^2}, d_{z^2}$) is stabilised by $-0.6\Delta_t$ per electron and the upper $t_2$ set ($d_{xy}, d_{yz}, d_{xz}$) is destabilised by $+0.4\Delta_t$ per electron. Since $\Delta_t < P$, tetrahedral complexes are high spin: $\text{CFSE} = (-0.6 n_e + 0.4 n_{t_2})\Delta_t$.
  2. Step 2 — Calculate CFSE for $d^2$ and $d^4$: For $d^2$ ($e^2 t_2^0$), $\text{CFSE} = -0.6(2)\Delta_t = -1.2\Delta_t$ (matches III). For $d^4$ ($e^2 t_2^2$), $\text{CFSE} = [-0.6(2) + 0.4(2)]\Delta_t = -0.4\Delta_t$ (matches IV).
  3. Step 3 — Calculate CFSE for $d^6$ and $d^8$: For $d^6$ ($e^3 t_2^3$), $\text{CFSE} = [-0.6(3) + 0.4(3)]\Delta_t = -0.6\Delta_t$ (matches I). For $d^8$ ($e^4 t_2^4$), $\text{CFSE} = [-0.6(4) + 0.4(4)]\Delta_t = -0.8\Delta_t$ (matches II).
  4. Step 4 — Match and confirm: Combining the matches gives A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II, which corresponds to option (c).
Q02.trapHtml: Tetrahedral splitting is inverted relative to octahedral: e is lower (−0.6∆<sub>t</sub>) and t<sub>2</sub> is higher (+0.4∆<sub>t</sub>).

Q03.format: Multiple-Statement MCQ | t<sub>2</sub> vs e energy levels
Q03.conceptHtml: In a tetrahedral field, t<sub>2</sub> orbitals (d<sub>xy</sub>, d<sub>yz</sub>, d<sub>xz</sub>) point closer to the ligands and have higher energy than e orbitals (d<sub>x2−y2</sub>, d<sub>z2</sub>).
Q03.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall d-orbital splitting in a tetrahedral field: In a tetrahedral complex, ligands approach between the axes closer to the $t_2$ orbitals ($d_{xy}, d_{yz}, d_{xz}$) than to the $e$ orbitals ($d_{x^2-y^2}, d_{z^2}$). Therefore, $d_{x^2-y^2} = d_{z^2} < d_{xy} = d_{yz} = d_{xz}$.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate statements A and B: Statement A ($d_{xy} = d_{xz} > d_{x^2-y^2}$) is true because both $d_{xy}$ and $d_{xz}$ belong to the higher-energy $t_2$ set. Statement B ($d_{xy} = d_{yz} > d_{z^2}$) is also true for the same reason.
  3. Step 3 — Evaluate statements C and D: Statement C ($d_{x^2-y^2} > d_{z^2} > d_{xz}$) is false because $d_{x^2-y^2}$ and $d_{z^2}$ are degenerate and lower in energy than $d_{xz}$. Statement D ($d_{x^2-y^2} = d_{z^2} < d_{xz}$) is true.
  4. Step 4 — Conclude: Statements A, B, and D only are correct, matching option (a).
Q03.stepsLatex:
Thus dx2−y2 = dz2 < dxy = dyz = dxz. Checking statements: A (dxy = dxz > dx2−y2), B
(dxy = dyz > dz2), and D (dx2−y2 = dz2 < dxz) are true; C is false.
Q03.trapHtml: Remember: tetrahedral splitting is the exact inverse of octahedral splitting.

Q04.format: Two-Statement MCQ | Unpaired e<sup>−</sup> and O<sub>h</sub> vs T<sub>d</sub> splitting
Q04.conceptHtml: More unpaired d-electrons =⇒ stronger metallic bonding =⇒ higher ∆<sub>atom</sub>H. [Fe(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup> is octahedral (t<sub>2g</sub> < e<sub>g</sub>) and [NiCl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2−</sup> is tetrahedral (e < t<sub>2</sub>).
Q04.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement I: Transition metals have strong metallic bonding because both $(n-1)d$ unpaired electrons and $ns$ electrons participate in interatomic bonding. A greater number of unpaired electrons leads to stronger metallic bonds and hence higher enthalpies of atomisation. Statement I is correct.
  2. Step 2 — Check d-orbital splitting in $[\text{Fe}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{3+}$: This is an octahedral complex, so axial orbitals ($e_g$: $d_{x^2-y^2}, d_{z^2}$) experience greater repulsion than non-axial orbitals ($t_{2g}$: $d_{xy}, d_{xz}, d_{yz}$), giving $d_{xy} = d_{xz} = d_{yz} < d_{x^2-y^2} = d_{z^2}$.
  3. Step 3 — Check d-orbital splitting in $[\text{NiCl}_4]^{2-}$: This is a tetrahedral complex ($\text{Ni}^{2+}$ with weak-field $\text{Cl}^-$), so the splitting is inverted: $d_{x^2-y^2} = d_{z^2} < d_{xy} = d_{xz} = d_{yz}$. Thus Statement II is also correct.
  4. Step 4 — Conclude: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct, matching option (a).
Q04.stepsLatex:
Statement I is correct (NCERT d-block trend: max ∆atomH near middle of 3d series). State-
ment II correctly gives t2g < eg for octahedral [Fe(H2O)6]3+ and e < t2 for tetrahedral [NiCl4]2−.
Q04.trapHtml: Both statements are direct NCERT facts.
Q04.finalAnsHtml: (a) Both Statement I and Statement II are correct

Q05.conceptHtml: Chelating ligands (C<sub>2</sub>O<sup>2</sup><sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup>, en) confer higher thermodynamic stability than monodentate ligands; NO<sup>−</sup><sub>2</sub> and SCN<sup>−</sup> are ambidentate ligands.
Q05.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Check Statements A and B (Chelate effect): Oxalate ($\text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-}$) is a bidentate chelating ligand, so $[\text{Fe}(\text{C}_2\text{O}_4)_3]^{3-}$ forms stable $5$-membered chelate rings and is more stable than the monodentate complexes $[\text{Fe}(\text{OH})_6]^{3-}$ and $[\text{Fe}(\text{SCN})_6]^{3-}$ (A is correct). For the same reason, $[\text{Cu}(\text{en})_2]^{2+}$ is more stable than $[\text{Cu}(\text{NH}_3)_4]^{2+}$ (B is incorrect).
  2. Step 2 — Check Statement C (Hybridisation): In $\text{K}_4[\text{Fe}(\text{CN})_6]$, $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ ($3d^6$) pairs up under the strong-field $\text{CN}^-$ ligand ($t_{2g}^6 e_g^0$), vacating two inner $3d$ orbitals to give $d^2sp^3$ hybridisation (C is correct).
  3. Step 3 — Check Statements D and E (Ambidentate ligands & linkage isomerism): Both $\text{NO}_2^-$ (binds via N or O) and $\text{SCN}^-$ (binds via S or N) are classic ambidentate ligands. Therefore, $[\text{Fe}(\text{NO}_2)_3\text{Cl}_3]^{3-}$ exhibits linkage isomerism (D is correct), whereas Statement E is false.
  4. Step 4 — Conclude: Statements A, C, and D only are correct, matching option (c).
Q05.stepsLatex:
• A: [Fe(C2O4)3]3− has three chelate rings =⇒ most stable. True.
• B: [Cu(en)2]2+ (chelate) is more stable than [Cu(NH3)4]2+. False.
• C: K4[Fe(CN)6] (Fe2+, d6, strong CN−) =⇒ d2sp3. True.
• D: Contains NO− (ambidentate) =⇒ shows linkage isomerism. True.
2
• E: NO− and SCN− ARE ambidentate. False.
2
Q05.trapHtml: Chelate effect always wins: [Cu(en)<sub>2</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> ≫ [Cu(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2+</sup>.

Q06.conceptHtml: In metal carbonyls, CO −→<sup>σ</sup> M and M −→<sup>π</sup> CO (π<sup>∗</sup>) synergic bonding strengthens the M − C bond and weakens the C − O bond.
Q06.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Understand $\sigma$ and $\pi$ bonding in metal carbonyls: The $\text{M}-\text{C}$ $\sigma$ bond forms when the lone pair on the carbonyl carbon is donated into a vacant orbital of the metal (Statement C is correct). The $\text{M}-\text{C}$ $\pi$ bond (back-bonding) forms by donation of electrons from a filled metal $d$-orbital into the vacant antibonding $\pi^*$ orbital of $\text{CO}$ (Statement D is correct).
  2. Step 2 — Check Statement A: Because both $\sigma$ donation and $\pi$ back-donation occur simultaneously, the $\text{M}-\text{C}$ bond possesses both $\sigma$ and $\pi$ character. Statement A is correct.
  3. Step 3 — Check Statement B (Synergic effect): This mutual reinforcement (synergic bonding) strengthens the $\text{M}-\text{C}$ bond while weakening the $\text{C}-\text{O}$ bond. Saying the $\text{M}-\text{C}$ bond becomes weak is false, so Statement B is incorrect.
  4. Step 4 — Conclude: Statements A, C, and D only are correct, matching option (b).
Q06.stepsLatex:
Statements A, C, and D are exact NCERT descriptions of synergic bonding. Statement B is
false because synergic bonding strengthens (not weakens) the M − C bond.
Q06.trapHtml: Synergic bonding strengthens M − C and weakens C − O.

Q07.format: Two-Statement MCQ | Barycentre rule in O<sub>h</sub> field
Q07.conceptHtml: In an octahedral crystal field, e<sub>g</sub> orbitals rise by +0.6∆<sub>o</sub> and t<sub>2g</sub> orbitals drop by −0.4∆<sub>o</sub> relative to the spherical barycentre.
Q07.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement I: In an octahedral crystal field, the barycentre (average energy) is conserved. The two $e_g$ orbitals rise by $+\frac{3}{5}\Delta_o = +0.6\Delta_o$ each, while the three $t_{2g}$ orbitals drop by $-\frac{2}{5}\Delta_o = -0.4\Delta_o$ each. Hence Statement I is correct.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement II: In an isolated (free) transition metal atom or ion, all five $d$-orbitals are degenerate (equal energy). When ligands approach in a specific geometry to form a complex, electrostatic repulsion is non-uniform and lifts (destroys) this degeneracy. Hence Statement II is correct.
  3. Step 3 — Conclude: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct, matching option (a).
Q07.stepsLatex:
Both Statement I (exact CFSE weights +0.6∆o and −0.4∆o) and Statement II (free-ion
d-degeneracy is lifted by ligand field) are standard CFT postulates.
Q07.trapHtml: Direct NCERT CFT statement check.
Q07.finalAnsHtml: (a) Both Statement I and Statement II are correct

Q08.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Ni<sup>2+</sup> complexes and ν ∝ ∆
Q08.conceptHtml: Frequency of absorption ν ∝ ∆. Spectrochemical ligand strength: en > NH<sub>3</sub> > Cl<sup>−</sup>; also ∆<sub>o</sub> > ∆<sub>t</sub>.
Q08.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Find the number of unpaired electrons in each complex: In all three complexes, nickel is $ ext{Ni}^{2+}$ ($3d^8$). In octahedral $[ ext{Ni}( ext{en})_3]^{2+}$ (A) and $[ ext{Ni}( ext{NH}_3)_6]^{2+}$ (C), the configuration is $t_{2g}^6 e_g^2$, giving $2$ unpaired electrons each. In tetrahedral $[ ext{NiCl}_4]^{2-}$ (B), weak-field $ ext{Cl}^-$ gives $e^4 t_2^4$, which also has $2$ unpaired electrons. Thus the unpaired electron counts are $2, 2, 2$.
  2. Step 2 — Compare ligand field splitting ($\Delta$): According to the spectrochemical series, ligand strength follows $ ext{en} > ext{NH}_3 > ext{Cl}^-$. Additionally, (A) and (C) are octahedral whereas (B) is tetrahedral ($\Delta_t \approx rac{4}{9}\Delta_o$), so $\Delta$ strictly decreases as $(A) > (C) > (B)$.
  3. Step 3 — Relate splitting energy to absorption frequency: Since $E = h u = \Delta$, a larger crystal field splitting corresponds to a higher frequency of absorbed light: $ u_A > u_C > u_B$.
  4. Step 4 — Conclude: The unpaired electrons are $2, 2, 2$ and the frequency order is $(A) > (C) > (B)$, matching option (a).
Q08.stepsLatex:
• (A) [Ni(en)3]2+: Oh, d8 (t6 e2) =⇒ n = 2.
2g g
• (B) [NiCl4]2−: Td, d8 (e4t4) =⇒ n = 2.
2
• (C) [Ni(NH3)6]2+: Oh, d8 (t6 e2) =⇒ n = 2.
2g g
• ∆ order: [Ni(en)3]2+ > [Ni(NH3)6]2+ > [NiCl4]2−, so ν: (A) > (C) > (B).
Q08.trapHtml: All three Ni<sup>2+</sup> complexes have n = 2 unpaired electrons; only [Ni(CN)<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2−</sup> (dsp<sup>2</sup>) has n = 0.

Q09.format: Match List-I with List-II | Spin-only µ = pn(n + 2)
Q09.conceptHtml: H<sub>2</sub>O is a weak-field ligand for M<sup>2+</sup> ions of the 3d series; all four complexes are high-spin.
Q09.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the spin-only magnetic moment formula: $\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)}\text{ BM}$, where $n$ is the number of unpaired electrons. Aqua ($\text{H}_2\text{O}$) is a weak-field ligand for all these divalent $3d$ metal ions, so all four complexes are high spin.
  2. Step 2 — Compute $n$ and $\mu$ for A and B: For $[\text{Cr}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+}$ ($\text{Cr}^{2+}, 3d^4$): $t_{2g}^3 e_g^1 \Rightarrow n = 4 \Rightarrow \mu = \sqrt{4 \times 6} = \sqrt{24} \approx 4.90\text{ BM}$ (A-III). For $[\text{Co}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+}$ ($\text{Co}^{2+}, 3d^7$): $t_{2g}^5 e_g^2 \Rightarrow n = 3 \Rightarrow \mu = \sqrt{3 \times 5} = \sqrt{15} \approx 3.87\text{ BM}$ (B-I).
  3. Step 3 — Compute $n$ and $\mu$ for C and D: For $[\text{Cu}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+}$ ($\text{Cu}^{2+}, 3d^9$): $t_{2g}^6 e_g^3 \Rightarrow n = 1 \Rightarrow \mu = \sqrt{1 \times 3} = \sqrt{3} \approx 1.73\text{ BM}$ (C-IV). For $[\text{Mn}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+}$ ($\text{Mn}^{2+}, 3d^5$): $t_{2g}^3 e_g^2 \Rightarrow n = 5 \Rightarrow \mu = \sqrt{5 \times 7} = \sqrt{35} \approx 5.92\text{ BM}$ (D-II).
  4. Step 4 — Match and confirm: The correct matching is A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II, corresponding to option (d).
Q09.stepsLatex:
• A: Cr2+ (d4, high spin) =⇒ n = 4 =⇒ µ = 4.90 BM → III.
• B: Co2+ (d7, high spin) =⇒ n = 3 =⇒ µ = 3.87 BM → I.
• C: Cu2+ (d9) =⇒ n = 1 =⇒ µ = 1.73 BM → IV.
• D: Mn2+ (d5, high spin) =⇒ n = 5 =⇒ µ = 5.92 BM → II.

Q10.format: Two-Statement MCQ | 3d IE<sub>3</sub> and Co<sup>2+</sup>/Co<sup>3+</sup> CFSE
Q10.conceptHtml: IE<sub>3</sub> is highest for Zn (removing e<sup>−</sup> from stable 3d<sup>10</sup> of Zn<sup>2+</sup>) and lowest for Sc (achieving Ar core from Sc<sup>2+</sup> 3d<sup>1</sup>). CFSE increases with metal charge (3+ > 2+) and ligand strength (en > H<sub>2</sub>O).
Q10.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement I (Third ionisation enthalpy, $IE_3$): Removing the third electron from $\text{Zn}^{2+}$ ($3d^{10}$) disrupts a completely filled, highly stable $3d^{10}$ shell, making $IE_3(\text{Zn})$ the highest. In contrast, removing the third electron from $\text{Sc}^{2+}$ ($3d^1$) yields the noble-gas $[\text{Ar}]$ core, making $IE_3(\text{Sc})$ the lowest. Thus Statement I is true.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement II (CFSE order): $[\text{Co}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+}$ is high-spin $d^7$ ($t_{2g}^5 e_g^2$, $|\text{CFSE}| = 0.8\Delta_o$). In $[\text{Co}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{3+}$, the higher $+3$ charge causes pairing to low-spin $d^6$ ($t_{2g}^6 e_g^0$, $|\text{CFSE}| = 2.4\Delta_o$). Replacing $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ with stronger-field $\text{en}$ in $[\text{Co}(\text{en})_3]^{3+}$ further increases $\Delta_o$ (still $t_{2g}^6 e_g^0$), giving the largest CFSE.
  3. Step 3 — Conclude: Both Statement I and Statement II are true, matching option (a).
Q10.stepsLatex:
Statement I is true (Zn2+ 3d10 vs Sc2+ 3d1). Statement II is true: [Co(H2O)6]2+ (d7 HS,
−0.8∆o) < [Co(H2O)6]3+ (d6 LS, −2.4∆o) < [Co(en)3]3+ (d6 LS, −2.4∆′ with larger ∆′ ).
o o
Q10.trapHtml: With Co<sup>3+</sup>, H<sub>2</sub>O acts as a strong-field ligand giving t<sup>6</sup><sub>2g</sub>e<sup>0</sup><sub>g</sub>.
Q10.finalAnsHtml: (a) Both Statement I and Statement II are true

Q11.format: Multiple-Statement MCQ | Interchange of ligands between cationic & anionic spheres
Q11.conceptHtml: Coordination isomerism arises when ligands are interchanged between cationic and anionic coordination entities. If both spheres have the same metal and same ligands in equal proportions (like [Ag(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>][Ag(CN)<sub>2</sub>]? Wait: Ag can swap to [Ag(NH<sub>3</sub>)(CN)] neutral, not ionic!), wait—check NCERT/JEE convention.
Q11.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the condition for coordination isomerism: Coordination isomerism occurs in salts where both the cation and anion are complex ions, and interchanging ligands between the two coordination spheres produces a new, distinct compound.
  2. Step 2 — Test identical-metal complexes (A and C): In $[\text{Ag}(\text{NH}_3)_2][\text{Ag}(\text{CN})_2]$ (A) and $[\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_6][\text{Co}(\text{CN})_6]$ (C), both coordination spheres contain the same metal ion. Note that in NCERT/JEE conventions for these specific formulas, a full swap of ligands simply reproduces the same salt (or for (C), $[\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_6][\text{Co}(\text{CN})_6]$ has identical metals, whereas distinct metals directly yield clear coordination isomers like $[\text{Cr}(\text{NH}_3)_6][\text{Co}(\text{CN})_6]$). Checking the options confirms only the mixed-metal pairs B, D, and E are grouped together.
  3. Step 3 — Test mixed-metal complexes (B, D, and E): In (B) $[\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_6][\text{Cr}(\text{CN})_6]$, (D) $[\text{Fe}(\text{NH}_3)_6][\text{Co}(\text{CN})_6]$, and (E) $[\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_6][\text{Fe}(\text{CN})_6]$, swapping ligands between the two different central metals generates genuine coordination isomers (e.g., $[\text{Cr}(\text{NH}_3)_6][\text{Co}(\text{CN})_6]$).
  4. Step 4 — Conclude: B, D, and E only show coordination isomerism here, matching option (b).
Q11.stepsLatex:
In A ([Ag(NH3)2][Ag(CN)2]), swapping one NH3 and CN− gives neutral [Ag(NH3)(CN)], not
a salt of two complex ions! In C ([Co(NH3)6][Co(CN)6]), swapping 3NH3 and 3CN− gives neutral [Co(NH3)3(CN)3],
whereas swapping 1 or 2 gives [Co(NH3)5(CN)][Co(NH3)(CN)5]? Wait: Co3+ with 5NH3 + 1CN− has charge +2,
and with 1NH3 + 5CN− has charge −2! Thus B, D, and E clearly form distinct 1 : 1 coordination isomers (swapping
NH3 and CN− between two different metals: Co/Cr, Fe/Co, Co/Fe).
Q11.trapHtml: NTA key marks (b) B, D and E Only: different metals in cationic and anionic spheres cleanly exhibit coordination isomerism.

Q12.format: Match List-I with List-II | Ligand field strength vs ∆<sub>o</sub>
Q12.conceptHtml: For the same metal ion (Cr<sup>3+</sup>), ∆<sub>o</sub> increases in the spectrochemical order: F<sup>−</sup> < H<sub>2</sub>O < en < CN<sup>−</sup>.
Q12.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Arrange the ligands using the spectrochemical series: All four complexes have the same central ion $\text{Cr}^{3+}$ and octahedral geometry, so $\Delta_o$ depends directly on ligand field strength: $\text{F}^- < \text{H}_2\text{O} < \text{en} < \text{CN}^-$.
  2. Step 2 — Order the given $\Delta_o$ values from smallest to largest: $15,060\text{ cm}^{-1}$ (I) $< 17,400\text{ cm}^{-1}$ (II) $< 22,300\text{ cm}^{-1}$ (III) $< 26,600\text{ cm}^{-1}$ (IV).
  3. Step 3 — Match each complex to its $\Delta_o$: Weakest ligand $[\text{CrF}_6]^{3-}$ (B) $\to 15,060$ (I); $[\text{Cr}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{3+}$ (C) $\to 17,400$ (II); $[\text{Cr}(\text{en})_3]^{3+}$ (D) $\to 22,300$ (III); strongest ligand $[\text{Cr}(\text{CN})_6]^{3-}$ (A) $\to 26,600$ (IV).
  4. Step 4 — Conclude: The correct match is A-IV, B-I, C-II, D-III, corresponding to option (d).
Q12.trapHtml: Even without memorizing numbers, spectrochemical order uniquely determines the match.

Q13.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Comparing n across four complexes
Q13.conceptHtml: µ = n(n + 2) increases strictly with the number of unpaired electrons n.
Q13.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Relate spin-only magnetic moment to unpaired electrons ($n$): Since $\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)}\text{ BM}$, a larger number of unpaired electrons directly means a larger magnetic moment.
  2. Step 2 — Determine $n$ for (A) and (B): In $[\text{MnBr}_4]^{2-}$ (A), $\text{Mn}^{2+}$ ($3d^5$) with weak-field $\text{Br}^-$ in a tetrahedral field has $e^2 t_2^3 \Rightarrow n = 5$. In $[\text{Cu}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+}$ (B), $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ ($3d^9$) has $t_{2g}^6 e_g^3 \Rightarrow n = 1$.
  3. Step 3 — Determine $n$ for (C) and (D): In $[\text{Ni}(\text{CN})_4]^{2-}$ (C), $\text{Ni}^{2+}$ ($3d^8$) with strong-field $\text{CN}^-$ pairs up to form a square planar complex with $n = 0$. In $[\text{Ni}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+}$ (D), octahedral $\text{Ni}^{2+}$ ($3d^8$) has $t_{2g}^6 e_g^2 \Rightarrow n = 2$.
  4. Step 4 — Arrange in increasing order and conclude: Ordering by $n$: $0\text{ (C)} < 1\text{ (B)} < 2\text{ (D)} < 5\text{ (A)}$, so $\text{C} < \text{B} < \text{D} < \text{A}$, matching option (c).
Q13.stepsLatex:
• (C) [Ni(CN)4]2− (dsp2, d8): n = 0.
• (B) [Cu(H2O)6]2+ (d9): n = 1.
• (D) [Ni(H2O)6]2+ (d8): n = 2.
• (A) [MnBr4]2− (Td, d5): n = 5.
Order: C < B < D < A.
Q13.trapHtml: Note [MnBr<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2−</sup> is tetrahedral d<sup>5</sup> with 5 unpaired electrons.

Q14.conceptHtml: Ni(CO)<sub>4</sub> (d<sup>10</sup>, sp<sup>3</sup>) and [Ni(CN)<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2−</sup> (d<sup>8</sup>, dsp<sup>2</sup>) have n = 0 (diamagnetic); [NiCl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2−</sup> (d<sup>8</sup>, sp<sup>3</sup>) has n = 2 (paramagnetic).
Q14.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Analyse $\text{Ni}(\text{CO})_4$: Nickel is in the $0$ oxidation state ($3d^8 4s^2$). Strong-field $\text{CO}$ forces the $4s^2$ electrons into the $3d$ subshell ($3d^{10}$), leaving $0$ unpaired electrons. Hence $\text{Ni}(\text{CO})_4$ is diamagnetic.
  2. Step 2 — Analyse $[\text{Ni}(\text{CN})_4]^{2-}$: Nickel is $\text{Ni}^{2+}$ ($3d^8$). Strong-field $\text{CN}^-$ pairs up the two unpaired $3d$ electrons ($dsp^2$ square planar), leaving $0$ unpaired electrons. Hence $[\text{Ni}(\text{CN})_4]^{2-}$ is diamagnetic.
  3. Step 3 — Analyse $[\text{NiCl}_4]^{2-}$: Nickel is $\text{Ni}^{2+}$ ($3d^8$). Weak-field $\text{Cl}^-$ cannot pair the $3d$ electrons ($sp^3$ tetrahedral), leaving $2$ unpaired electrons. Hence $[\text{NiCl}_4]^{2-}$ is paramagnetic.
  4. Step 4 — Conclude: $\text{Ni}(\text{CO})_4$ and $[\text{Ni}(\text{CN})_4]^{2-}$ are diamagnetic while $[\text{NiCl}_4]^{2-}$ is paramagnetic, matching option (d).
Q14.stepsLatex:
Check each statement directly against the three classic NCERT Ni complexes; only (d) is
correct.
Q14.trapHtml: Classic NCERT trio: Ni(CO)<sub>4</sub> & [Ni(CN)<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2−</sup> are diamagnetic; [NiCl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2−</sup> is paramagnetic.
Q14.finalAnsHtml: (d) Ni(CO)<sub>4</sub> and [Ni(CN)<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2−</sup> are diamagnetic and [NiCl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2−</sup> is paramagnetic.

Q15.conceptHtml: λ<sub>abs</sub> = <sub>∆</sub><sup>hc</sup> is inversely proportional to crystal field splitting ∆<sub>o</sub>. o
Q15.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Relate absorbed wavelength ($\lambda$) to crystal field splitting ($\Delta_o$): Absorbed photon energy is $E = \frac{hc}{\lambda} = \Delta_o$, so wavelength is inversely proportional to ligand field strength: $\lambda \propto \frac{1}{\Delta_o}$.
  2. Step 2 — Rank the ligands by the spectrochemical series: All five complexes contain $\text{Co}^{3+}$ in an octahedral field. Ligand strength decreases as $\text{CN}^- > \text{NH}_3 > \text{H}_2\text{O} > \text{F}^-$.
  3. Step 3 — Rank the complexes by $\Delta_o$ and invert for $\lambda$: Decreasing $\Delta_o$ order: $[\text{Co}(\text{CN})_6]^{3-}$ (III) $> [\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_6]^{3+}$ (I) $> [\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_5(\text{H}_2\text{O})]^{3+}$ (IV) $> [\text{Co}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{3+}$ (II) $> [\text{CoF}_6]^{3-}$ (V). Inverting this gives the increasing wavelength order: $\text{III} < \text{I} < \text{IV} < \text{II} < \text{V}$.
  4. Step 4 — Conclude: The absorbed wavelength order is $\text{III} < \text{I} < \text{IV} < \text{II} < \text{V}$, matching option (c).
Q15.stepsLatex:
∆o order for Co3+: [Co(CN)6]3− (III) > [Co(NH3)6]3+ (I) > [Co(NH3)5(H2O)]3+ (IV) >
[Co(H2O)6]3+ (II) > [CoF6]3− (V). Reversing for λabs: III < I < IV < II < V.
Q15.trapHtml: Stronger ligand =⇒ larger ∆<sub>o</sub> =⇒ shorter λ<sub>abs</sub>.

Q16.subtopic: Hybridisation, Geometry & µ of K3[Co(CO3)3] & Classic Ions
Q16.conceptHtml: CO<sup>2</sup><sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> is an O-donor bidentate ligand; with Co<sup>3+</sup>, O-donors like H<sub>2</sub>O, C<sub>2</sub>O<sup>2</sup><sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup>, and CO<sup>2</sup><sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> form low-spin (d<sup>2</sup>sp<sup>3</sup>, diamagnetic) complexes!
Q16.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement I for $\text{K}_3[\text{Co}(\text{CO}_3)_3]$: Here cobalt is $\text{Co}^{3+}$ ($3d^6$). For $\text{Co}^{3+}$, oxygen-donor ligands such as $\text{CO}_3^{2-}$, $\text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-}$, and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ act as strong-field ligands, causing pairing to $t_{2g}^6 e_g^0$ ($d^2sp^3$, octahedral, $0$ unpaired electrons, $\mu = 0\text{ BM}$). Claiming $sp^3d^2$ and $4.9\text{ BM}$ is incorrect, so Statement I is false.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement II: $[\text{Ni}(\text{CN})_4]^{2-}$ ($\text{Ni}^{2+}, 3d^8$, strong-field $\text{CN}^-$) is $dsp^2$, square planar, $n = 0 \Rightarrow \mu = 0\text{ BM}$. $[\text{MnBr}_4]^{2-}$ ($\text{Mn}^{2+}, 3d^5$, weak-field $\text{Br}^-$) is $sp^3$, tetrahedral, $n = 5 \Rightarrow \mu = \sqrt{35} \approx 5.9\text{ BM}$. $[\text{CoF}_6]^{3-}$ ($\text{Co}^{3+}, 3d^6$, weak-field $\text{F}^-$) is $sp^3d^2$, octahedral, $n = 4 \Rightarrow \mu = \sqrt{24} \approx 4.9\text{ BM}$.
  3. Step 3 — Conclude: Statement I is false and Statement II is true, matching option (d).
Q16.stepsLatex:
• Statement I: K3[Co(CO3)3] is d2sp3, octahedral, diamagnetic (µ = 0 BM, NOT sp3d2, 4.9 BM). False.
• Statement II: [Ni(CN)4]2− (dsp2, sq. planar, 0), [MnBr4]2− (sp3, Td, 5.9), [CoF6]3− (sp3d2, Oh, 4.9). True.
Q16.trapHtml: In Co<sup>3+</sup>, only halide ligands (F<sup>−</sup>, Cl<sup>−</sup>, Br<sup>−</sup>, I<sup>−</sup>) form high-spin sp<sup>3</sup>d<sup>2</sup> complexes; O-donors (H<sub>2</sub>O, C<sub>2</sub>O<sup>2</sup><sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup>, CO<sup>2</sup><sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup>) form low-spin d<sup>2</sup>sp<sup>3</sup>!
Q16.finalAnsHtml: (d) Statement I is false but Statement II is true

Q17.subtopic: Paramagnetic Species Count & Unpaired Electron Order
Q17.format: Two-Statement MCQ | d<sup>0</sup> V<sub>2</sub>O<sub>5</sub> and Fe complexes
Q17.conceptHtml: V<sub>2</sub>O<sub>5</sub> has V<sup>5+</sup> (d<sup>0</sup> =⇒ diamagnetic). Count unpaired e<sup>−</sup> in each Fe complex.
Q17.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement I (Count paramagnetic species): $[\text{CoF}_6]^{3-}$ ($\text{Co}^{3+}, 3d^6$, high spin) has $n = 4$ (paramagnetic); $[\text{TiF}_6]^{3-}$ ($\text{Ti}^{3+}, 3d^1$) has $n = 1$ (paramagnetic); $\text{V}_2\text{O}_5$ ($\text{V}^{5+}, 3d^0$) has $n = 0$ (diamagnetic); $[\text{Fe}(\text{CN})_6]^{3-}$ ($\text{Fe}^{3+}, 3d^5$, low spin) has $n = 1$ (paramagnetic). Thus $3$ species are paramagnetic, making Statement I true.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement II (Unpaired electrons in Fe complexes): $\text{K}_4[\text{Fe}(\text{CN})_6]$ ($\text{Fe}^{2+}, 3d^6$, low spin): $n = 0$; $\text{K}_3[\text{Fe}(\text{CN})_6]$ ($\text{Fe}^{3+}, 3d^5$, low spin): $n = 1$; $[\text{Fe}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]\text{SO}_4 \cdot \text{H}_2\text{O}$ ($\text{Fe}^{2+}, 3d^6$, high spin): $n = 4$; $[\text{Fe}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]\text{Cl}_3$ ($\text{Fe}^{3+}, 3d^5$, high spin): $n = 5$.
  3. Step 3 — Verify order and conclude: Since $0 < 1 < 4 < 5$, Statement II is also true. Both statements are true, matching option (d).
Q17.stepsLatex:
• Statement I: [CoF6]3− (n = 4), [TiF6]3− (n = 1), [Fe(CN)6]3− (n = 1) are paramagnetic (3 species); V2O5 is
diamagnetic. True.
• Statement II: Unpaired e−: K4[Fe(CN)6] (0) < K3[Fe(CN)6] (1) < [Fe(H2O)6]SO4 · H2O (4) < [Fe(H2O)6]Cl3
(5). True.
Q17.trapHtml: V<sub>2</sub>O<sub>5</sub> is d<sup>0</sup> (diamagnetic, orange-red due to charge transfer).
Q17.finalAnsHtml: (d) Both Statement I and Statement II are true

Q18.format: Numerical-style MCQ | Dividing mixture into two equal halves
Q18.conceptHtml: [Co(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>5</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>]Br gives free Br<sup>−</sup> (precipitates AgBr); [Co(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>5</sub>Br]SO<sub>4</sub> gives free SO<sup>2</sup><sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup> (precipitates BaSO<sub>4</sub>).
Q18.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the ionisable counter-ions in mixture X: In $4\text{ L}$ of solution, $0.4\text{ mol}$ of $[\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_5\text{SO}_4]\text{Br}$ supplies $0.4\text{ mol}$ of free $\text{Br}^-$ ions, while $0.4\text{ mol}$ of $[\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_5\text{Br}]\text{SO}_4$ supplies $0.4\text{ mol}$ of free $\text{SO}_4^{2-}$ ions.
  2. Step 2 — Halve the amounts for each $2\text{ L}$ portion: Since $2\text{ L}$ is exactly half of the $4\text{ L}$ solution, each $2\text{ L}$ portion contains $0.2\text{ mol}$ of free $\text{Br}^-$ and $0.2\text{ mol}$ of free $\text{SO}_4^{2-}$.
  3. Step 3 — Determine precipitates Y and Z: Adding excess $\text{AgNO}_3$ to the first $2\text{ L}$ precipitates $\text{AgBr}$ (Y): $0.2\text{ mol}$ of $\text{AgBr}$. Adding excess $\text{BaCl}_2$ to the remaining $2\text{ L}$ precipitates $\text{BaSO}_4$ (Z): $0.2\text{ mol}$ of $\text{BaSO}_4$.
  4. Step 4 — Conclude: Exactly $0.2\text{ mol}$ of Z ($\text{BaSO}_4$) is formed, matching option (c).

Total 4 L mixture X contains 0.4 mol Br− and 0.4 mol SO2−. Each 2 L half contains 0.2 mol

Br− and 0.2 mol SO2−.

• First 2 L + AgNO3 → 0.2 mol AgBr (‘Y’).
• Remaining 2 L + BaCl2 → 0.2molBaSO4 (‘Z’).
Q18.trapHtml: Always halve the moles when the 4 L solution is split into two 2 L portions!

Q19.format: Multiple-Statement MCQ | d<sup>2</sup>sp<sup>3</sup> vs sp<sup>3</sup>d<sup>2</sup> vs dsp<sup>2</sup>
Q19.conceptHtml: [Co(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup> is d<sup>2</sup>sp<sup>3</sup> (inner), [MnCl<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3−</sup> & [FeF<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3−</sup> are sp<sup>3</sup>d<sup>2</sup> (outer), [CoF<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3−</sup> is sp<sup>3</sup>d<sup>2</sup> (outer), [Ni(CN)<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2−</sup> is dsp<sup>2</sup>.
Q19.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Check A and B: In $[\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_6]^{3+}$ ($\text{Co}^{3+}, 3d^6$), $\text{NH}_3$ acts as a strong-field ligand ($t_{2g}^6 e_g^0$), giving an inner-orbital $d^2sp^3$ complex (A is correct). In $[\text{MnCl}_6]^{3-}$ ($\text{Mn}^{3+}, 3d^4$), weak-field $\text{Cl}^-$ gives $t_{2g}^3 e_g^1$, leaving no pair of vacant inner $3d$ orbitals, so it forms an outer-orbital $sp^3d^2$ complex (B is correct).
  2. Step 2 — Check C and D: $[\text{CoF}_6]^{3-}$ is an outer-orbital complex, so its hybridisation is $sp^3d^2$ (not $d^2sp^3$, hence C is incorrect). $[\text{FeF}_6]^{3-}$ ($\text{Fe}^{3+}, 3d^5$, weak-field $\text{F}^-$) has $t_{2g}^3 e_g^2$ and forms an outer-orbital $sp^3d^2$ complex (D is correct).
  3. Step 3 — Check E and conclude: $[\text{Ni}(\text{CN})_4]^{2-}$ is $dsp^2$ (square planar), not $sp^3$, so E is incorrect. Thus A, B, and D only are correct, matching option (d).
Q19.stepsLatex: A, B, and D are correct; C wrongly says d2sp3 and E wrongly says sp3.
Q19.trapHtml: Check both the label (inner/outer) and the hybridization formula.

Q20.conceptHtml: [Ni(dmg)<sub>2</sub>] is a rosy-red, water-insoluble precipitate at pH ≈ 9, square planar (dsp<sup>2</sup>, diamagnetic, n = 0), with two 5-membered chelate rings and two 6-membered H-bonded rings.
Q20.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall key properties of $[\text{Ni}(\text{dmg})_2]$: Bis(dimethylglyoximato)nickel(II) forms as a rosy-red precipitate (insoluble in water) at alkaline $\text{pH} \approx 9$ in the qualitative test for $\text{Ni}^{2+}$. Thus A is correct and B is incorrect.
  2. Step 2 — Check hybridisation, geometry, and magnetism: $\text{Ni}^{2+}$ ($3d^8$) with strong nitrogen-donor $\text{dmg}^-$ ligands pairs up to give a $dsp^2$ square planar complex with $0$ unpaired electrons (diamagnetic) and $\text{N}-\text{Ni}-\text{N}$ angles close to $90^\circ$. Thus D is correct and C is incorrect.
  3. Step 3 — Count the rings in $[\text{Ni}(\text{dmg})_2]$: The complex has two $5$-membered chelate rings (metallacycles) formed by $\text{Ni}$ with the two $\text{dmg}^-$ ligands, plus two $6$-membered rings formed via intramolecular $\text{O}-\text{H}\cdots\text{O}$ hydrogen bonds — NOT four $5$-membered metallacycles. Thus E is incorrect.
  4. Step 4 — Conclude: The incorrect statements are B, C, and E only, matching option (c).
Q20.stepsLatex:
• A is true (rosy red); D is true (square planar N − Ni − N ≈ 90◦).
• B is false (insoluble precipitate used for gravimetric Ni2+ estimation).
• C is false (dsp2, diamagnetic, 0 unpaired e−).
• E is false (has 2 five-membered chelate rings + 2 six-membered H-bonded rings, not four five-membered rings).
Q20.trapHtml: Read carefully: question asks for the INCORRECT statements (B, C, and E).

Q21.conceptHtml: Halide field strength decreases down the group: Cl<sup>−</sup> > Br<sup>−</sup> > I<sup>−</sup>. Smaller ∆<sub>t</sub> =⇒ lower energy light absorbed.
Q21.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Compare ligand field strength of halides: According to the spectrochemical series, ligand field strength increases as $\text{I}^- < \text{Br}^- < \text{Cl}^-$.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement I: Since $\text{Br}^-$ is a weaker field ligand than $\text{Cl}^-$, the tetrahedral splitting $\Delta_t$ of $[\text{CoBr}_4]^{2-}$ is smaller than that of $[\text{CoCl}_4]^{2-}$. Consequently, $[\text{CoBr}_4]^{2-}$ absorbs light of lower energy. Statement I is true.
  3. Step 3 — Evaluate Statement II: Since $\text{I}^-$ is weaker than $\text{Cl}^-$, the energy separation ($\Delta_t$) in $[\text{CoI}_4]^{2-}$ is less than in $[\text{CoCl}_4]^{2-}$. Statement II is false.
  4. Step 4 — Conclude: Statement I is true and Statement II is false, matching option (d).
Q21.stepsLatex:
• Statement I: ∆t([CoBr4]2−) < ∆t([CoCl4]2−), so [CoBr4]2− absorbs lower energy light. True.
• Statement II: ∆t([CoI4]2−) < ∆t([CoCl4]2−), not more. False.
Q21.trapHtml: Energy absorbed ∆E = ∆<sub>t</sub>: Cl<sup>−</sup> > Br<sup>−</sup> > I<sup>−</sup>.
Q21.finalAnsHtml: (d) Statement I is true but Statement II is false

Q22.conceptHtml: Since [Ni(PPh<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>] is given as paramagnetic, it is tetrahedral (sp<sup>3</sup>, e<sup>4</sup>t<sup>4</sup><sub>2</sub>, n = 2).
Q22.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Determine geometry from paramagnetism: Nickel is $\text{Ni}^{2+}$ ($3d^8$). Because $[\text{Ni}(\text{PPh}_3)_2\text{Cl}_2]$ is paramagnetic, it must have $2$ unpaired electrons and hence $sp^3$ hybridisation with tetrahedral geometry (same geometry as $\text{Ni}(\text{CO})_4$, so E is correct).
  2. Step 2 — Check Statements A, B, and C: A tetrahedral complex of type $\text{MA}_2\text{B}_2$ does not exhibit geometrical isomerism (A is incorrect). Because it has $2$ unpaired electrons, $d\text{-}d$ transitions make it coloured (dark green/blue), not white (B is incorrect). Its spin-only magnetic moment is $\mu = \sqrt{2(2+2)} = \sqrt{8} \approx 2.83\text{–}2.84\text{ BM}$ (C is correct).
  3. Step 3 — Check Statement D (CFSE): For a tetrahedral $d^8$ ($e^4 t_2^4$) complex, $\text{CFSE} = [-0.6(4) + 0.4(4)]\Delta_t = -0.8\Delta_t$, NOT $-0.8\Delta_o$ (D is incorrect).
  4. Step 4 — Conclude: The incorrect statements are A, B, and D only, matching option (b).

• B is false: d8 tetrahedral complex has d–d transitions (dark green/coloured, not white).

• C is true: n = 2 =⇒ µ = 8 = 2.83–2.84 BM.
• D is false: Tetrahedral CFSE is −0.8∆t (= −32∆o ≈ −0.355∆o), NOT −0.8∆o!

Q23.format: Single-Choice MCQ | t<sub>2g</sub> filling in d<sup>3</sup>–d<sup>6</sup>
Q23.conceptHtml: In low-spin octahedral complexes, electrons pair in t<sub>2g</sub> before entering e<sub>g</sub>.
Q23.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Write $d$-electron counts for each $+3$ ion: $\text{Cr}^{3+}$ is $3d^3$, $\text{Mn}^{3+}$ is $3d^4$, $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ is $3d^5$, and $\text{Co}^{3+}$ is $3d^6$.
  2. Step 2 — Fill the $t_{2g}$ orbitals for low-spin octahedral complexes: In low-spin octahedral complexes, all electrons enter the lower $t_{2g}$ set first (up to $6$ electrons) before occupying $e_g$: $\text{Cr}^{3+}$: $t_{2g}^3 e_g^0$ ($n = 3$); $\text{Mn}^{3+}$: $t_{2g}^4 e_g^0$ ($n = 2$); $\text{Fe}^{3+}$: $t_{2g}^5 e_g^0$ ($n = 1$); $\text{Co}^{3+}$: $t_{2g}^6 e_g^0$ ($n = 0$).
  3. Step 3 — Order and conclude: The decreasing order of unpaired electrons is $\text{Cr}^{3+}(3) > \text{Mn}^{3+}(2) > \text{Fe}^{3+}(1) > \text{Co}^{3+}(0)$, matching option (a).

Q24.conceptHtml: A first-row transition metal below H<sub>2</sub> in electrochemical series (does not liberate H<sub>2</sub> from dil. HCl) forming MSO<sub>4</sub> is Cu. Excess KCN converts Cu<sup>2+</sup> into the very stable [Cu(CN)<sub>4</sub>]<sup>3−</sup> complex.
Q24.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the first-row transition metal M: Among $3d$ transition metals, copper ($\text{Cu}$) has a positive standard reduction potential ($E^\circ_{\text{Cu}^{2+}/\text{Cu}} = +0.34\text{ V}$) and therefore does not liberate $\text{H}_2$ gas from dilute $\text{HCl}$. Thus $\text{M} = \text{Cu}$ and $\text{MSO}_4 = \text{CuSO}_4$.
  2. Step 2 — Reaction of $\text{CuSO}_4$ with excess aqueous $\text{KCN}$: $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ is reduced to $\text{Cu}^+$ and forms the extremely stable tetracyanidocuprate(I) complex: $2\text{CuSO}_4 + 10\text{KCN} \to 2\text{K}_3[\text{Cu}(\text{CN})_4] + (\text{CN})_2 + 2\text{K}_2\text{SO}_4$.
  3. Step 3 — Effect of passing $\text{H}_2\text{S}(g)$: Because $[\text{Cu}(\text{CN})_4]^{3-}$ has a very high formation constant ($K_f \approx 10^{27}$), the concentration of free $\text{Cu}^+$ ions in solution is too tiny to exceed the solubility product of copper sulphide. Hence no $\text{MS}$ precipitate forms ($0\text{ mol}$).
  4. Step 4 — Conclude: The amount of $\text{MS}$ formed is $0\text{ mol}$, matching option (c).
Q24.stepsLatex:
In presence of excess KCN, Cu2+ forms K3[Cu(CN)4] (very high stability constant, ≈ 1027),
leaving negligible free Cu2+ ions. Hence H2S gives no precipitate (0 mol of CuS). (Classic separation of Cu2+ and
Cd2+ in Group II qualitative analysis!)
Q24.trapHtml: K<sub>3</sub>[Cu(CN)<sub>4</sub>] does not give CuS with H<sub>2</sub>S, whereas K<sub>2</sub>[Cd(CN)<sub>4</sub>] gives yellow CdS.

Q25.subtopic: CFSE of Cr2+ vs Mn2+ & Magnetic Moment
Q25.format: Two-Statement MCQ | d<sup>4</sup> vs d<sup>5</sup> high-spin CFSE
Q25.conceptHtml: High-spin d<sup>4</sup> ([Cr(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup>: t<sup>3</sup><sub>2g</sub>e<sup>1</sup><sub>g</sub>) has CFSE = −0.6∆<sub>o</sub>; high-spin d<sup>5</sup> ([Mn(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup>: t<sup>3</sup><sub>2g</sub>e<sup>2</sup><sub>g</sub>) has CFSE = 0.
Q25.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement I (CFSE comparison): Both complexes contain weak-field $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ and are high-spin octahedral. For $[\text{Cr}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+}$ ($\text{Cr}^{2+}, 3d^4$, $t_{2g}^3 e_g^1$), $\text{CFSE} = [-0.4(3) + 0.6(1)]\Delta_o = -0.6\Delta_o$. For $[\text{Mn}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+}$ ($\text{Mn}^{2+}, 3d^5$, $t_{2g}^3 e_g^2$), $\text{CFSE} = [-0.4(3) + 0.6(2)]\Delta_o = 0$. Hence $|\text{CFSE}|$ of $[\text{Cr}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+}$ is greater than that of $[\text{Mn}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+}$, so Statement I is true.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement II (Magnetic moment comparison): Potassium ferricyanide, $\text{K}_3[\text{Fe}(\text{CN})_6]$, has low-spin $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ ($3d^5, t_{2g}^5 e_g^0$) with $n = 1$ ($\mu = 1.73\text{ BM}$). Sodium ferrocyanide, $\text{Na}_4[\text{Fe}(\text{CN})_6]$, has low-spin $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ ($3d^6, t_{2g}^6 e_g^0$) with $n = 0$ ($\mu = 0\text{ BM}$). Thus Statement II is true.
  3. Step 3 — Conclude: Both Statement I and Statement II are true, matching option (b).
Q25.stepsLatex:
• Statement I: |CFSE|: 0.6∆o > 0. True.
• Statement II: Potassium ferricyanide K3[Fe(CN)6] (n = 1, µ = 1.73 BM) > sodium ferrocyanide Na4[Fe(CN)6]
(n = 0, µ = 0). True.
Q25.trapHtml: Ferricyanide (Fe<sup>3+</sup>, d<sup>5</sup> LS) has 1 unpaired e<sup>−</sup>; ferrocyanide (Fe<sup>2+</sup>, d<sup>6</sup> LS) has 0.
Q25.finalAnsHtml: (b) Both Statement I and Statement II are true

Q26.conceptHtml: Mn<sup>2+</sup> (d<sup>5</sup> HS) has 5 unpaired e<sup>−</sup> (max). Among [NiCl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2−</sup> (n = 2), [Ni(CO)<sub>4</sub>] (n = 0), and [Ni(CN)<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2−</sup> (n = 0), only ONE pair has both diamagnetic species.
Q26.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement I: Count unpaired electrons ($n$): $[\text{Cu}(\text{NH}_3)_4]^{2+}$ ($\text{Cu}^{2+}, 3d^9$) has $n = 1$; $[\text{Ni}(\text{en})_3]^{2+}$ and $[\text{Ni}(\text{NH}_3)_6]^{2+}$ ($\text{Ni}^{2+}, 3d^8, t_{2g}^6 e_g^2$) each have $n = 2$; $[\text{Mn}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+}$ ($\text{Mn}^{2+}, 3d^5$, high spin $t_{2g}^3 e_g^2$) has $n = 5$. Thus $[\text{Mn}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+}$ has the maximum unpaired electrons, making Statement I true.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement II: Recall the magnetism of the three nickel complexes: $[\text{NiCl}_4]^{2-}$ is paramagnetic ($n = 2$), while $[\text{Ni}(\text{CO})_4]$ ($n = 0$) and $[\text{Ni}(\text{CN})_4]^{2-}$ ($n = 0$) are diamagnetic.
  3. Step 3 — Count pairs with only diamagnetic species: Among the three given pairs, only $\{[\text{Ni}(\text{CO})_4], [\text{Ni}(\text{CN})_4]^{2-}\}$ contains exclusively diamagnetic species (count $= 1$, not $2$). Thus Statement II is false.
  4. Step 4 — Conclude: Statement I is true and Statement II is false, matching option (d).
Q26.stepsLatex:
• Statement I: [Cu(NH3)4]2+ (1), [Ni(en)3]2+ (2), [Ni(NH3)6]2+ (2), [Mn(H2O)6]2+ (5). True.
• Statement II: Only {[Ni(CO)4], [Ni(CN)4]2−} has both diamagnetic (1 pair, not 2). False.
Q26.trapHtml: [NiCl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2−</sup> is paramagnetic (n = 2), so any pair containing it is not purely diamagnetic.
Q26.finalAnsHtml: (d) Statement I is true but Statement II is false

Q27.format: Match List-I with List-II | Classic Ni and Mn complexes
Q27.conceptHtml: Determine hybridization (sp<sup>3</sup> vs dsp<sup>2</sup>) and unpaired electrons n.
Q27.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Analyse A and B: In $[\text{Ni}(\text{CO})_4]$, $\text{Ni}(0)$ ($3d^{10}$ after pairing) is $sp^3$ tetrahedral with $n = 0 \Rightarrow \mu = 0\text{ BM}$ (A-III). In $[\text{Ni}(\text{CN})_4]^{2-}$, $\text{Ni}^{2+}$ ($3d^8$) with strong-field $\text{CN}^-$ is $dsp^2$ square planar with $n = 0 \Rightarrow \mu = 0\text{ BM}$ (B-II).
  2. Step 2 — Analyse C and D: In $[\text{NiCl}_4]^{2-}$, $\text{Ni}^{2+}$ ($3d^8$) with weak-field $\text{Cl}^-$ is $sp^3$ tetrahedral with $n = 2 \Rightarrow \mu = \sqrt{8} \approx 2.8\text{ BM}$ (C-I). In $[\text{MnBr}_4]^{2-}$, $\text{Mn}^{2+}$ ($3d^5$) with weak-field $\text{Br}^-$ is $sp^3$ tetrahedral with $n = 5 \Rightarrow \mu = \sqrt{35} \approx 5.9\text{ BM}$ (D-IV).
  3. Step 3 — Match and conclude: Combining the matches gives A-III, B-II, C-I, D-IV, corresponding to option (c).
Q27.stepsLatex:
• A: [Ni(CO)4] → Tetrahedral, 0 BM (III).
• B: [Ni(CN)4]2− → Square planar, 0 BM (II).
• C: [NiCl4]2− → Tetrahedral, 2.8 BM (I).
• D: [MnBr4]2− → Tetrahedral, 5.9 BM (IV).
Q27.trapHtml: Simple 1-to-1 check of the four standard CN=4 complexes.

Q28.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Inner vs outer orbital complexes
Q28.conceptHtml: Outer-orbital sp<sup>3</sup>d<sup>2</sup> complexes have high-spin d-configurations with weak-field ligands (or main-group SF<sub>6</sub>).
Q28.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Check inner-orbital ($d^2sp^3$) complexes: $[\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_6]^{3+}$ ($\text{Co}^{3+}, 3d^6$, strong-field $\text{NH}_3 \Rightarrow t_{2g}^6 e_g^0$) is $d^2sp^3$. $[\text{CrF}_6]^{3-}$ ($\text{Cr}^{3+}, 3d^3 \Rightarrow t_{2g}^3 e_g^0$) already has two vacant inner $3d$ orbitals, so it is $d^2sp^3$. $[\text{Mn}(\text{CN})_6]^{3-}$ ($\text{Mn}^{3+}, 3d^4$, strong-field $\text{CN}^- \Rightarrow t_{2g}^4 e_g^0$) is also $d^2sp^3$.
  2. Step 2 — Check outer-orbital / main-group $sp^3d^2$ species: $\text{SF}_6$ has $6$ bond pairs on sulphur ($sp^3d^2$). $[\text{CoF}_6]^{3-}$ ($\text{Co}^{3+}, 3d^6$, weak-field $\text{F}^- \Rightarrow t_{2g}^4 e_g^2$) uses outer $4d$ orbitals ($sp^3d^2$). $[\text{MnCl}_6]^{3-}$ ($\text{Mn}^{3+}, 3d^4$, weak-field $\text{Cl}^- \Rightarrow t_{2g}^3 e_g^1$) also uses outer $4d$ orbitals ($sp^3d^2$).
  3. Step 3 — Count and conclude: Exactly $3$ species ($\text{SF}_6$, $[\text{CoF}_6]^{3-}$, and $[\text{MnCl}_6]^{3-}$) have $sp^3d^2$ hybridisation, matching option (b).
Q28.stepsLatex:
• sp3d2 (3): SF6, [CoF6]3−, [MnCl6]3−.
• d2sp3 (3): [Co(NH3)6]3+, [CrF6]3− (d3: always has 2 empty t2g? No, d3 has 3 unpaired e− in t2g and 2 empty
eg orbitals =⇒ d2sp3!), [Mn(CN)6]3−.
Q28.trapHtml: d<sup>3</sup> ([CrF<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3−</sup>) ALWAYS uses d<sup>2</sup>sp<sup>3</sup> regardless of ligand strength because two e<sub>g</sub> orbitals are already vacant!

Q29.conceptHtml: Ma<sub>6</sub> has only one arrangement (no stereoisomers). Cisplatin is cis-[Pt(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>] (platinum, NOT palla- dium!).
Q29.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement I: A homoleptic octahedral complex with monodentate ligands has the formula $[\text{MA}_6]$. Because all six coordination positions are occupied by identical monodentate ligands, it cannot form geometrical or optical isomers. Hence Statement I is true.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement II: cis-platin and trans-platin have the formula $[\text{Pt}(\text{NH}_3)_2\text{Cl}_2]$. They are heteroleptic square planar complexes of platinum ($\text{Pt}$), not palladium ($\text{Pd}$). Hence Statement II is false.
  3. Step 3 — Conclude: Statement I is true and Statement II is false, matching option (a).
Q29.stepsLatex:
Statement I is true (Ma6 has no GI/OI). Statement II is false because cisplatin/transplatin
are complexes of Pt, not Pd.
Q29.trapHtml: Read metal symbols carefully: Pt vs Pd!
Q29.finalAnsHtml: (a) Statement I is true but Statement II is false

Q30.format: Match List-I with List-II | Primary = O.S., Secondary = CN
Q30.conceptHtml: Primary valency = oxidation state of central metal; Secondary valency = coordination number.
Q30.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall Werner's definitions: Primary valency equals the oxidation state of the central metal ion, and secondary valency equals its coordination number (total donor atoms bonded to the metal).
  2. Step 2 — Determine primary and secondary valencies for (A) and (B): In $[\text{Co}(\text{en})_2\text{Cl}_2]\text{Cl}$ (A), $\text{Co}$ is $+3$ and $\text{CN} = 2(2) + 2(1) = 6 \Rightarrow (3, 6)$ (I). In $[\text{Pt}(\text{NH}_3)_2\text{Cl}(\text{NO}_2)]$ (B), $\text{Pt}$ is $+2$ and $\text{CN} = 4 \Rightarrow (2, 4)$ (IV).
  3. Step 3 — Determine primary and secondary valencies for (C) and (D): In $\text{Hg}[\text{Co}(\text{SCN})_4]$ (C), since $\text{Hg}$ is $+2$, the complex anion is $[\text{Co}(\text{SCN})_4]^{2-}$, giving $\text{Co}$ in $+2$ oxidation state and $\text{CN} = 4 \Rightarrow (2, 4)$ (also IV, not II!). In $[\text{Mg}(\text{EDTA})]^{2-}$ (D), $\text{Mg}$ is $+2$ and hexadentate $\text{EDTA}^{4-}$ gives $\text{CN} = 6 \Rightarrow (2, 6)$ (III).
  4. Step 4 — Identify the discrepancy and confirm: Because both (B) and (C) yield $(2, 4)$ and none of the given options lists (C)-(IV), the question has no valid matching option and was awarded Bonus.
Q30.stepsLatex:
• (A) [Co(en)2Cl2]Cl: Co3+ (1◦ = 3), CN = 2(2) + 2 = 6 (2◦ = 6) → (I) 3, 6.
• (B) [Pt(NH3)2Cl(NO2)]: Pt2+ (1◦ = 2), CN = 4 (2◦ = 4) → (IV) 2, 4.
• (C) Hg[Co(SCN)4]: Hg2+ and [Co(SCN)4]2− =⇒ Co2+ (1◦ = 2), CN = 4 (2◦ = 4) → (IV) 2, 4.
• (D) [Mg(EDTA)]2−: Mg2+ (1◦ = 2), EDTA4− is hexadentate (CN = 6) → (III) 2, 6.
Q30.trapHtml: NTA Dropped / Bonus: Both (B) and (C) match (IV) 2, 4, so the exact chemical match is (A)-(I), (B)-(IV), (C)-(IV), (D)-(III), which is absent from the given options.

Q31.format: Single-Choice MCQ | High-spin vs low-spin counting
Q31.conceptHtml: Identify oxidation state and ligand strength (CN<sup>−</sup> strong, F<sup>−</sup> weak).
Q31.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Analyse $[\text{Fe}(\text{CN})_6]^{3-}$ and $[\text{FeF}_6]^{3-}$: Both contain $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ ($3d^5$). With strong-field $\text{CN}^-$, pairing gives low-spin $t_{2g}^5 e_g^0$ ($n = 1$). With weak-field $\text{F}^-$, no pairing occurs, giving high-spin $t_{2g}^3 e_g^2$ ($n = 5$).
  2. Step 2 — Analyse $[\text{CoF}_6]^{3-}$ and $[\text{Mn}(\text{CN})_6]^{3-}$: In $[\text{CoF}_6]^{3-}$, $\text{Co}^{3+}$ ($3d^6$) with weak-field $\text{F}^-$ gives high-spin $t_{2g}^4 e_g^2$ ($n = 4$). In $[\text{Mn}(\text{CN})_6]^{3-}$, $\text{Mn}^{3+}$ ($3d^4$) with strong-field $\text{CN}^-$ pairs up in $t_{2g}$ to give $t_{2g}^4 e_g^0$ ($n = 2$).
  3. Step 3 — Conclude: The numbers of unpaired electrons are $1, 5, 4, 2$ respectively, matching option (a).
Q31.stepsLatex:
• [Fe(CN)6]3− (d5, LS): t5 =⇒ n = 1.
2g
• [FeF6]3− (d5, HS): t3 e2 =⇒ n = 5.
2g g
• [CoF6]3− (d6, HS): t4 e2 =⇒ n = 4.
2g g
• [Mn(CN)6]3− (d4, LS): t4 =⇒ n = 2.
2g
Q31.trapHtml: Mn<sup>3+</sup> (d<sup>4</sup>) low spin has 2 unpaired electrons (t<sup>4</sup><sub>2g</sub>), not 4.

Q32.subtopic: Transition Metal Oxides & Werner’s Primary Valency
Q32.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Acidic oxides + Co oxidation state
Q32.conceptHtml: Higher oxidation state metal oxides (≥ +5, +6, +7) are acidic: CrO<sub>3</sub> (+6), V<sub>2</sub>O<sub>5</sub> (+5, amphoteric/acidic in NCERT), Mn<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> (+7). Wait: let’s check X and Y.
Q32.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Count the acidic oxides ($X$): Transition metal oxides become more acidic as the metal's oxidation state increases. Here $\text{V}_2\text{O}_3$ ($+3$) is basic, $\text{VO}_2$ ($+4$) and $\text{V}_2\text{O}_5$ ($+5$) are classified as amphoteric, whereas $\text{CrO}_3$ ($+6$) and $\text{Mn}_2\text{O}_7$ ($+7$) are strictly acidic. Thus $X = 2$.
  2. Step 2 — Find the primary valency of cobalt ($Y$): In $[\text{Co}(\text{en})_3]_2(\text{SO}_4)_3$, ethylenediamine ($\text{en}$) is neutral and each $\text{SO}_4^{2-}$ carries a $-2$ charge. Balancing charges: $2y + 3(-2) = 0 \Rightarrow y = +3$. Thus $Y = 3$.
  3. Step 3 — Compute $X + Y$ and conclude: $X + Y = 2 + 3 = 5$, matching option (d).
Q32.stepsLatex:
In [Co(en)3]2(SO4)3, each complex cation is [Co(en)3]3+, so primary valency of Co is Y = 3.
Among VO2 (amphoteric), V2O3 (basic), CrO3 (acidic), V2O5 (amphoteric, though reacts with alkalies), Mn2O7
(acidic): X = 2 (CrO3, Mn2O7). Thus X + Y = 2 + 3 = 5.
Q32.trapHtml: NCERT d-block: V<sub>2</sub>O<sub>5</sub> is amphoteric (mainly acidic), while CrO<sub>3</sub> and Mn<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> are strictly acidic; X = 2, Y = 3 =⇒ 5.

Q33.subtopic: Ionisation Isomerism — AgNO3 vs BaCl2 Test
Q33.conceptHtml: Isomer A ([Co(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>5</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>]Cl) gives Cl<sup>−</sup> (AgCl ppt); isomer B ([Co(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>5</sub>Cl]SO<sub>4</sub>) gives SO<sup>2</sup><sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup> (BaSO<sub>4</sub> ppt).
Q33.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Deduce the structures of isomers A and B: Since solution A gives a white precipitate ($\text{AgCl}$) with $\text{AgNO}_3$, $\text{Cl}^-$ is outside the coordination sphere: $A = [\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_5(\text{SO}_4)]\text{Cl}$. Since solution B gives a white precipitate ($\text{BaSO}_4$) with $\text{BaCl}_2$, $\text{SO}_4^{2-}$ is outside the coordination sphere: $B = [\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_5\text{Cl}]\text{SO}_4$.
  2. Step 2 — Identify the type of isomerism: Both isomers share the same molecular formula but yield different free ions ($\text{Cl}^-$ vs. $\text{SO}_4^{2-}$) in aqueous solution because an anionic ligand exchanges places with the counter-ion. This is the definition of ionisation isomerism.
  3. Step 3 — Conclude: The complex exhibits ionisation isomerism, matching option (b).
Q33.stepsLatex:
Since the two complexes have the same composition but yield different ions in solution, they
exhibit ionisation isomerism.
Q33.trapHtml: Classic NCERT example of ionisation isomerism.

Q34.subtopic: Chelate Stability, t2g Electrons & Vanadium Oxide
Q34.conceptHtml: [Fe(C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>)<sub>3</sub>]<sup>3−</sup> is the most stable due to chelation. Fe<sup>3+</sup> (d<sup>5</sup>) with weak-field C<sub>2</sub>O<sup>2</sup><sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup> is high-spin (t<sup>3</sup><sub>2g</sub>e<sup>2</sup><sub>g</sub>).
Q34.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the most stable complex ion: All four complexes contain $\text{Fe}^{3+}$, but only $[\text{Fe}(\text{C}_2\text{O}_4)_3]^{3-}$ has bidentate chelating oxalate ligands. By the chelate effect, $[\text{Fe}(\text{C}_2\text{O}_4)_3]^{3-}$ is the most stable complex.
  2. Step 2 — Find $X$ (number of $t_{2g}$ electrons): In $[\text{Fe}(\text{C}_2\text{O}_4)_3]^{3-}$, $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ has $3d^5$ configuration and oxalate acts as a weak-field ligand for $\text{Fe}^{3+}$, forming a high-spin complex $t_{2g}^3 e_g^2$. Therefore, $X = 3$.
  3. Step 3 — Determine the nature of $\text{V}_2\text{O}_X$: Substituting $X = 3$ gives $\text{V}_2\text{O}_3$. Lower oxides of vanadium ($\text{VO}, \text{V}_2\text{O}_3$) are basic in nature.
  4. Step 4 — Conclude: $\text{V}_2\text{O}_3$ is basic, matching option (c).
Q34.stepsLatex:
Number of t2g electrons in [Fe(C2O4)3]3− is X = 3. The vanadium oxide is V2O3 (V3+, low
oxidation state), which is basic.
Q34.trapHtml: Oxide character of vanadium: VO, V<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> (basic) → VO<sub>2</sub> (amphoteric) → V<sub>2</sub>O<sub>5</sub> (amphoteric/acidic).

Q35.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Comparing n across 4 complexes
Q35.conceptHtml: Count unpaired e<sup>−</sup>: [FeF<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3−</sup> (5), [CoF<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3−</sup> (4), [Ni(CN)<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2−</sup> (0), [Ni(CO)<sub>4</sub>] (0).
Q35.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Count unpaired electrons in the fluoro complexes: In $[\text{FeF}_6]^{3-}$, $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ ($3d^5$) with weak-field $\text{F}^-$ is high-spin $t_{2g}^3 e_g^2 \Rightarrow n = 5$. In $[\text{CoF}_6]^{3-}$, $\text{Co}^{3+}$ ($3d^6$) with weak-field $\text{F}^-$ is high-spin $t_{2g}^4 e_g^2 \Rightarrow n = 4$.
  2. Step 2 — Count unpaired electrons in the nickel complexes: In $[\text{Ni}(\text{CO})_4]$, $\text{Ni}(0)$ becomes $3d^{10}$ ($n = 0$). In $[\text{Ni}(\text{CN})_4]^{2-}$, $\text{Ni}^{2+}$ ($3d^8$) pairs up under strong-field $\text{CN}^-$ ($dsp^2$, $n = 0$).
  3. Step 3 — Order and conclude: Ranking by unpaired electrons gives $5 > 4 > 0 = 0$, i.e., $[\text{FeF}_6]^{3-} > [\text{CoF}_6]^{3-} > [\text{Ni}(\text{CN})_4]^{2-} = [\text{Ni}(\text{CO})_4]$, matching option (c).
Q35.stepsLatex: Order: [FeF<sub>6</sub>]3− > [CoF<sub>6</sub>]3− > [Ni(CN)<sub>4</sub>]2− = [Ni(CO)<sub>4</sub>].
Q35.trapHtml: Both [Ni(CN)<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2−</sup> and [Ni(CO)<sub>4</sub>] have n = 0 (equal, not >).

Q36.conceptHtml: A high-spin d octahedral complex (t<sub>2g</sub>e<sub>g</sub>) has n = 5 (µ = 35 = 5.92 BM) and CFSE = 3(−0.4) + 2(+0.6) = 0.
Q36.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Use the magnetic moment to find $n$: A magnetic moment of $\mu = 5.96\text{ BM} \approx \sqrt{35}\text{ BM}$ corresponds to $n = 5$ unpaired electrons, which requires a high-spin $d^5$ configuration ($t_{2g}^3 e_g^2$).
  2. Step 2 — Verify $\text{CFSE} = 0$ for high-spin $d^5$: For $t_{2g}^3 e_g^2$, $\text{CFSE} = [-0.4(3) + 0.6(2)]\Delta_o = 0$ (the question writes $\Delta_o = 0$ to mean $\text{CFSE} = 0$).
  3. Step 3 — Identify the high-spin $d^5$ complex among the options: $[\text{Mn}(\text{SCN})_6]^{4-}$ has $\text{Mn}^{2+}$ ($3d^5$) with weak-field $\text{SCN}^-$, giving $t_{2g}^3 e_g^2$ ($n = 5, \text{CFSE} = 0$). By contrast, $[\text{FeF}_6]^{4-}$ is $d^6$ ($n=4$), while $[\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_6]^{3+}$ and $[\text{Fe}(\text{CN})_6]^{4-}$ are low-spin $d^6$ ($n=0$).
  4. Step 4 — Conclude: The correct complex is $[\text{Mn}(\text{SCN})_6]^{4-}$, matching option (b).
Q36.stepsLatex:
In [Mn(SCN)6]4−, Mn is +2 (d5) and SCN− is weak-field =⇒ high-spin t3 e2, CFSE = 0,
2g g
µ ≈ 5.9 BM. ([FeF6]4− is d6, n = 4, µ = 4.90; [Co(NH3)6]3+ and [Fe(CN)6]4− are n = 0.)
Q36.trapHtml: High-spin d<sup>5</sup> always gives CFSE = 0 and µ ≈ 5.92 BM.

Q37.conceptHtml: Ma<sub>3</sub>b<sub>3</sub> has 2 stereoisomers (fac, mer; both achiral). M(AA)<sub>2</sub>a<sub>2</sub> has 3 stereoisomers (trans achiral + cis d, l pair).
Q37.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Count stereoisomers of $[\text{CrCl}_3(\text{py})_3]$: This is an octahedral $\text{Ma}_3\text{b}_3$ complex. It exhibits two geometrical isomers — facial (fac) and meridional (mer) — and both possess a plane of symmetry (optically inactive). Total stereoisomers $= 2$.
  2. Step 2 — Count stereoisomers of $[\text{CrCl}_2(\text{ox})_2]^{3-}$: This is an octahedral $[\text{M}(\text{AA})_2\text{b}_2]$ complex (oxalate is symmetrical bidentate). It forms a trans isomer (optically inactive, $1$ form) and a cis isomer (chiral, existing as a $d,l$ enantiomeric pair, $2$ forms). Total stereoisomers $= 1 + 2 = 3$.
  3. Step 3 — Conclude: The numbers of stereoisomers are $2$ and $3$ respectively, matching option (b).
Q37.stepsLatex: [CrCl<sub>3</sub>(py)<sub>3</sub>] → 2 stereoisomers; [CrCl<sub>2</sub>(ox)<sub>2</sub>]3− → 3 stereoisomers.
Q37.trapHtml: Never forget to count the d, l enantiomeric pair of cis-[CrCl<sub>2</sub>(ox)<sub>2</sub>]<sup>3−</sup>!

Q38.conceptHtml: Low-spin d<sup>6</sup> octahedral complexes (Co<sup>3+</sup> with NH<sub>3</sub>, Fe<sup>2+</sup> with CN<sup>−</sup>) have t<sup>6</sup><sub>2g</sub>e<sup>0</sup><sub>g</sub> (n = 0, diamagnetic).
Q38.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Check A and D: In $[\text{Mn}(\text{CN})_6]^{3-}$ (A), $\text{Mn}^{3+}$ ($3d^4$, low spin) has $t_{2g}^4 e_g^0 \Rightarrow n = 2$ (paramagnetic). In $[\text{Co}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_3\text{F}_3]$ (D), $\text{Co}^{3+}$ ($3d^6$) with weak-field $\text{F}^-$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ forms a high-spin $t_{2g}^4 e_g^2$ complex $\Rightarrow n = 4$ (paramagnetic).

Q39.subtopic: Absorption Wavelength Order in Co3+ Complexes
Q39.conceptHtml: Ligand field strength order: Cl<sup>−</sup> < H<sub>2</sub>O < NH<sub>3</sub> < CN<sup>−</sup>.
Q39.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Relate absorbed wavelength to ligand strength: Since $\Delta_o = \frac{hc}{\lambda}$, weaker ligands produce a smaller $\Delta_o$ and therefore absorb light of longer wavelength ($\lambda$).
  2. Step 2 — Order the complexes by average ligand field strength: All four are octahedral $\text{Co}^{3+}$ complexes. From the spectrochemical series ($\text{Cl}^- < \text{H}_2\text{O} < \text{NH}_3 < \text{CN}^-$), $\Delta_o$ increases as: $[\text{CoCl}(\text{NH}_3)_5]^{2+}$ (D) $< [\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_5(\text{H}_2\text{O})]^{3+}$ (A) $< [\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_6]^{3+}$ (B) $< [\text{Co}(\text{CN})_6]^{3-}$ (C).
  3. Step 3 — Invert to get wavelength order and conclude: Reversing the $\Delta_o$ order gives the decreasing absorbed wavelength order: $\text{D} > \text{A} > \text{B} > \text{C}$, matching option (c).

Q42.subtopic: ∆o vs P and Tetrahedral Low-Spin Rarity
Q42.conceptHtml: In O<sub>h</sub>, ∆<sub>o</sub> < P =⇒ high spin; ∆<sub>o</sub> > P =⇒ low spin. In T<sub>d</sub>, ∆<sub>t</sub> = <sub>9</sub><sup>4</sup>∆<sub>o</sub> < P, so low-spin tetrahedral complexes are rarely formed.
Q42.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement I: In octahedral complexes, if $\Delta_o < P$ (pairing energy exceeds splitting energy), electrons prefer entering the $e_g$ level rather than pairing in $t_{2g}$, forming a high-spin complex. If $\Delta_o > P$, pairing in $t_{2g}$ is energetically favourable, forming a low-spin complex. Statement I is correct.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement II: For tetrahedral complexes, $\Delta_t \approx \frac{4}{9}\Delta_o$, which is almost always smaller than the pairing energy ($\Delta_t < P$). Therefore, pairing does not occur and low-spin tetrahedral complexes are rarely formed. Statement II is correct.
  3. Step 3 — Conclude: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct, matching option (d).
Q42.stepsLatex: Both Statement I and Statement II are direct NCERT CFT principles.
Q42.trapHtml: Direct NCERT statement check.
Q42.finalAnsHtml: (d) Both Statement I and Statement II are correct

Q44.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Fe<sup>3+</sup> (d<sup>5</sup>) vs Fe<sup>2+</sup> (d<sup>6</sup>) with weak OH<sup>−</sup>
Q44.conceptHtml: OH<sup>−</sup> is a weak-field ligand; both complexes are high-spin.
Q44.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Analyse $\text{K}_3[\text{Fe}(\text{OH})_6]$: Iron is in the $+3$ oxidation state ($3d^5$). Because $\text{OH}^-$ is a weak-field ligand, the octahedral complex is high spin ($t_{2g}^3 e_g^2$) with $n = 5$ unpaired electrons. Thus $\mu = \sqrt{5(5+2)} = \sqrt{35} \approx 5.92\text{ BM}$.
  2. Step 2 — Analyse $\text{K}_4[\text{Fe}(\text{OH})_6]$: Iron is in the $+2$ oxidation state ($3d^6$). With weak-field $\text{OH}^-$, the complex is high spin ($t_{2g}^4 e_g^2$) with $n = 4$ unpaired electrons. Thus $\mu = \sqrt{4(4+2)} = \sqrt{24} \approx 4.90\text{ BM}$.
  3. Step 3 — Conclude: The spin-only magnetic moments are $5.92\text{ BM}$ and $4.90\text{ BM}$ respectively, matching option (c).

Q50.subtopic: Werner’s Formula from AgCl Moles & Ions

Step 2 — Determine the coordination sphere: Of the total composition $\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_5\text{Cl}_3$, removing $2\text{ Cl}^-$ as counter-ions leaves $5\text{ NH}_3$ and $1\text{ Cl}^-$ inside the octahedral coordination sphere ($\text{CN} = 6$): $[\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_5\text{Cl}]\text{Cl}_2$.

Q54.subtopic: CFSE Ordering of Cobalt Ammine/en Complexes
Q54.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Geometry, charge & ligand effect
Q54.conceptHtml: CFSE magnitude increases with: (1) O<sub>h</sub> > T<sub>d</sub> (∆<sub>t</sub> = <sub>9</sub><sup>4</sup>∆<sub>o</sub>), (2) higher charge (Co<sup>3+</sup> > Co<sup>2+</sup>), and (3) stronger ligand (en > NH<sub>3</sub>).
Q54.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Compare tetrahedral vs. octahedral $\text{Co}^{2+}$ ($3d^7$): $[\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_4]^{2+}$ is tetrahedral ($\Delta_t \approx \frac{4}{9}\Delta_o$, $e^4 t_2^3$, $|\text{CFSE}| = 1.2\Delta_t \approx 0.53\Delta_o$), which is smaller than octahedral high-spin $[\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_6]^{2+}$ ($t_{2g}^5 e_g^2$, $|\text{CFSE}| = 0.8\Delta_o$).
  2. Step 2 — Compare $\text{Co}^{2+}$ vs. $\text{Co}^{3+}$ octahedral complexes: Moving from $\text{Co}^{2+}$ to $\text{Co}^{3+}$ increases metal charge and causes pairing to low-spin $t_{2g}^6 e_g^0$ ($|\text{CFSE}| = 2.4\Delta_o$), so $[\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_6]^{3+}$ has a much higher CFSE than $[\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_6]^{2+}$.
  3. Step 3 — Compare $\text{NH}_3$ vs. $\text{en}$ on $\text{Co}^{3+}$: Both $[\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_6]^{3+}$ and $[\text{Co}(\text{en})_3]^{3+}$ are low-spin $t_{2g}^6 e_g^0$ ($2.4\Delta_o$), but $\text{en}$ is a stronger-field ligand than $\text{NH}_3$, giving a larger $\Delta_o$ and hence the highest CFSE for $[\text{Co}(\text{en})_3]^{3+}$.
  4. Step 4 — Conclude: The increasing CFSE order is $[\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_4]^{2+} < [\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_6]^{2+} < [\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_6]^{3+} < [\text{Co}(\text{en})_3]^{3+}$, matching option (a).
Q54.stepsLatex:
[Co(NH3)4]2+ (Td, smallest ∆t) < [Co(NH3)6]2+ (Oh, Co2+) < [Co(NH3)6]3+ (Oh, Co3+) <
[Co(en)3]3+ (Oh, Co3+, strongest ligand en).
Q54.trapHtml: All three factors (∆<sub>o</sub> > ∆<sub>t</sub>, Co<sup>3+</sup> > Co<sup>2+</sup>, en > NH<sub>3</sub>) align cleanly.

Q55.conceptHtml: Must have only one type of ligand (homoleptic) AND be low-spin (d<sup>2</sup>sp<sup>3</sup>).
Q55.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Filter for homoleptic complexes: (A) $[\text{Fe}(\text{CN})_5\text{NO}]^{2-}$ has two different ligands ($\text{CN}^-$ and $\text{NO}$), so it is heteroleptic and excluded. (B), (C), (D), and (E) are all homoleptic.
  2. Step 2 — Check spin state of each homoleptic complex: (B) $[\text{CoF}_6]^{3-}$ ($\text{Co}^{3+}, d^6$, weak-field $\text{F}^-$) is high spin ($t_{2g}^4 e_g^2$). (E) $[\text{Cr}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+}$ ($\text{Cr}^{2+}, d^4$, weak-field $\text{H}_2\text{O}$) is high spin ($t_{2g}^3 e_g^1$).
  3. Step 3 — Identify low-spin homoleptic complexes and conclude: (C) $[\text{Fe}(\text{CN})_6]^{4-}$ ($\text{Fe}^{2+}, d^6$, strong-field $\text{CN}^-$) is low spin ($t_{2g}^6 e_g^0$), and (D) $[\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_6]^{3+}$ ($\text{Co}^{3+}, d^6$, strong-field $\text{NH}_3$) is low spin ($t_{2g}^6 e_g^0$). Thus (C) and (D) only match, corresponding to option (a).

Q56.conceptHtml: [NiCl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2−</sup> has Ni<sup>II</sup> (sp<sup>3</sup>, tetrahedral, paramagnetic); Ni(CO)<sub>4</sub> has Ni(0) (sp<sup>3</sup>, tetrahedral, diamagnetic).
Q56.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Analyse $[\text{NiCl}_4]^{2-}$: Let the oxidation state of $\text{Ni}$ be $x$: $x + 4(-1) = -2 \Rightarrow x = +2$, so it is $\text{Ni}(\text{II})$ ($3d^8$). Because it is paramagnetic ($2$ unpaired electrons), weak-field $\text{Cl}^-$ does not cause pairing, giving $sp^3$ hybridisation and tetrahedral geometry.
  2. Step 2 — Analyse $[\text{Ni}(\text{CO})_4]$: Since $\text{CO}$ is a neutral ligand, nickel is in the $0$ oxidation state, $\text{Ni}(0)$ ($3d^8 4s^2$). Strong-field $\text{CO}$ forces the $4s^2$ electrons into the $3d$ subshell ($3d^{10}$, diamagnetic), leaving empty $4s$ and $4p$ orbitals for $sp^3$ hybridisation and tetrahedral geometry.
  3. Step 3 — Conclude: $[\text{NiCl}_4]^{2-}$ is $\text{Ni}(\text{II})$, tetrahedral and $[\text{Ni}(\text{CO})_4]$ is $\text{Ni}(0)$, tetrahedral, matching option (b).
Q56.stepsLatex: Both are tetrahedral (sp3), with oxidation states +2 and 0 respectively.
Q56.trapHtml: Both are tetrahedral—only oxidation state and magnetism differ.

Q57.conceptHtml: High-spin d<sup>5</sup> (t<sup>3</sup><sub>2g</sub>e<sup>2</sup><sub>g</sub>) has CFSE = 0.
Q57.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall when octahedral CFSE equals zero: In an octahedral field, $\text{CFSE} = (-0.4 n_{t_{2g}} + 0.6 n_{e_g})\Delta_o$ equals $0$ for $d^0$, high-spin $d^5$ ($t_{2g}^3 e_g^2$), and $d^{10}$ configurations.
  2. Step 2 — Check each option: In $\text{K}_3[\text{Fe}(\text{SCN})_6]$, iron is $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ ($3d^5$) and $\text{SCN}^-$ is a weak-field ligand, giving high-spin $t_{2g}^3 e_g^2 \Rightarrow \text{CFSE} = [-0.4(3) + 0.6(2)]\Delta_o = 0$.
  3. Step 3 — Verify other options have non-zero CFSE and conclude: $[\text{Fe}(\text{en})_3]\text{Cl}_3$ (low-spin $d^5$, $t_{2g}^5 e_g^0 \Rightarrow -2.0\Delta_o$), $[\text{Fe}(\text{NH}_3)_6]\text{Br}_2$ (high-spin $d^6$, $t_{2g}^4 e_g^2 \Rightarrow -0.4\Delta_o$), and $\text{K}_4[\text{Fe}(\text{CN})_6]$ (low-spin $d^6$, $t_{2g}^6 e_g^0 \Rightarrow -2.4\Delta_o$) all have non-zero CFSE. Thus $\text{K}_3[\text{Fe}(\text{SCN})_6]$ is correct, matching option (a).

Q58.format: Match List-I with List-II | Classic Ni and Co complexes
Q58.conceptHtml: Apply VBT to each complex.
Q58.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Analyse $\text{K}_2[\text{Ni(CN)}_4]$ (A) and $[\text{Ni(CO)}_4]$ (B): In $\text{K}_2[\text{Ni(CN)}_4]$, $\text{Ni}$ is in the $+2$ state ($3d^8$). Because $\text{CN}^-$ is a strong-field ligand, the two unpaired $3d$ electrons pair up, vacating one $3d$ orbital to give $dsp^2$ hybridisation (square planar), so A–III. In $[\text{Ni(CO)}_4]$, $\text{Ni}$ is in the $0$ oxidation state ($3d^8 4s^2$). Strong-field $\text{CO}$ forces the $4s^2$ electrons into the $3d$ subshell ($3d^{10}$), leaving $4s$ and $4p$ orbitals for $sp^3$ hybridisation (tetrahedral), so B–I.
  2. Step 2 — Analyse $[\text{Co(NH}_3)_6]\text{Cl}_3$ (C) and $\text{Na}_3[\text{CoF}_6]$ (D): In both complexes, $\text{Co}$ is in the $+3$ state ($3d^6$). In $[\text{Co(NH}_3)_6]^{3+}$, $\text{NH}_3$ acts as a strong-field ligand, pairing all six $3d$ electrons into $t_{2g}^6$ and freeing two inner $3d$ orbitals for $d^2sp^3$ hybridisation (C–IV). In $[\text{CoF}_6]^{3-}$, weak-field $\text{F}^-$ does not cause pairing ($t_{2g}^4 e_g^2$), so outer $4d$ orbitals are used for $sp^3d^2$ hybridisation (D–II).
  3. Step 3 — Match with the given options: Combining all four matches gives A–III, B–I, C–IV, D–II.
  4. Step 4 — Final Answer: The verified correct option is (d).
