Q114.format: Assertion–Reason MCQ | Difference is ligand field strength, not O.S.
Q114.conceptHtml: Both complexes have Fe<sup>3+</sup> (+3), but [Fe(CN)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3−</sup> is low-spin (n = 1, 1.74 BM) while [Fe(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup> is high-spin (n = 5, 5.92 BM) due to different ligand field strengths.
Q114.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Check oxidation state of Fe (Reason R): In $[\text{Fe(CN)}_6]^{3-}$, $x + 6(-1) = -3 \Rightarrow x = +3$. In $[\text{Fe(H}_2\text{O)}_6]^{3+}$, $x + 6(0) = +3 \Rightarrow x = +3$. Thus Fe is in the $+3$ oxidation state ($3d^5$) in both complexes, so Reason R is true.
  2. Step 2 — Find unpaired electrons in $[\text{Fe(CN)}_6]^{3-}$: $\text{CN}^-$ is a strong-field ligand, so it pairs electrons in $3d^5$ to give low-spin $t_{2g}^5 e_g^0$ with $n = 1$ unpaired electron. Its spin-only magnetic moment is $\mu = \sqrt{1(1+2)} = \sqrt{3} \approx 1.73\text{ BM}$ (matches $1.74\text{ BM}$).
  3. Step 3 — Find unpaired electrons in $[\text{Fe(H}_2\text{O)}_6]^{3+}$: $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ is a weak-field ligand for $\text{Fe}^{3+}$, giving high-spin $t_{2g}^3 e_g^2$ with $n = 5$ unpaired electrons. Its spin-only magnetic moment is $\mu = \sqrt{5(5+2)} = \sqrt{35} \approx 5.92\text{ BM}$, so Assertion A is true.
  4. Step 4 — Evaluate explanation & conclude: The difference in magnetic moments arises from the difference in ligand field strength ($\text{CN}^-$ vs $\text{H}_2\text{O}$), not merely from Fe having a $+3$ oxidation state. Therefore, both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A — Option (d).
Q114.stepsLatex:
Both A and R are true, but R (same +3 oxidation state) does NOT explain why their magnetic
moments differ!
Q114.trapHtml: Same oxidation state cannot explain different spin states—ligand strength (CN<sup>−</sup> > H<sub>2</sub>O) does.
Q114.finalAnsHtml: (d) Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A

Q115.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Linkage isomerism of NO<sup>−</sup><sub>2</sub>
Q115.conceptHtml: [Co(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>5</sub>NO<sub>2</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> contains the ambidentate NO<sup>−</sup><sub>2</sub> ligand, so it exists as two linkage isomers: [Co(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>5</sub>(NO<sub>2</sub>)]<sup>2+</sup> (yellow, N-bound) and [Co(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>5</sub>(ONO)]<sup>2+</sup> (red, O-bound).
Q115.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Check for geometrical and optical isomerism: Complexes of the type $[Ma_6]$ like $[\text{Co(H}_2\text{O)}_6]^{3+}$ and $[Ma_5b]$ like $[\text{Co(NH}_3)_5\text{Cl}]^{+}$ or $[\text{Co(NH}_3)_5\text{Cl}]^{2+}$ cannot show geometrical or optical isomerism because all positions are equivalent after placing $b$.
  2. Step 2 — Check for ambidentate ligands (linkage isomerism): In $[\text{Co(NH}_3)_5\text{NO}_2]^{2+}$, the $\text{NO}_2^-$ ligand is ambidentate—it can coordinate through nitrogen ($-\text{NO}_2$, nitro isomer) or through oxygen ($-\text{ONO}$, nitrito isomer).
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the exact answer: Because $[\text{Co(NH}_3)_5\text{NO}_2]^{2+}$ forms exactly two linkage isomers, the correct choice is Option (c).
Q115.stepsLatex:
Ma6 and Ma5b show no geometrical or optical isomerism; only [Co(NH3)5NO2]2+ has 2 linkage
isomers.
Q115.trapHtml: Linkage isomerism works even in Ma<sub>5</sub>b complexes!

Q116.conceptHtml: For the same metal ion (Fe<sup>3+</sup>), ∆<sub>o</sub> is largest for the strongest-field ligand in the spectrochemical series.
Q116.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Compare the central metal ion: All four given complexes contain the same central metal ion, $\text{Fe}^{3+}$, in an octahedral geometry, so crystal field splitting ($\Delta_o$) depends directly on the ligand field strength.
  2. Step 2 — Apply the spectrochemical series: Ordering the four ligands from weakest to strongest field gives $\text{F}^- < \text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-} < \text{NH}_3 < \text{CN}^-$.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the exact answer: Since $\text{CN}^-$ is the strongest-field ligand among the choices, $[\text{Fe(CN)}_6]^{3-}$ exhibits the largest $d$-orbital splitting — Option (b).
Q116.stepsLatex:
F− < C2O2− < NH3 < CN− =⇒ [Fe(CN)6]3− has the largest ∆o.
4
Q116.trapHtml: CN<sup>−</sup> is at the top of the spectrochemical series (just below CO).

Q117.format: Multiple-Statement MCQ | Mohr’s salt & Potash alum
Q117.conceptHtml: Double salts dissociate completely into simple ions in water; coordination complexes retain their complex ion.
Q117.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the definition of a double salt: A double salt is a stoichiometric addition compound that is stable in the solid state but dissociates completely into its constituent simple ions in water.
  2. Step 2 — Classify each given compound: A is Mohr's salt, $\text{FeSO}_4\cdot(\text{NH}_4)_2\text{SO}_4\cdot 6\text{H}_2\text{O}$ (double salt); C is potash alum, $\text{K}_2\text{SO}_4\cdot\text{Al}_2(\text{SO}_4)_3\cdot 24\text{H}_2\text{O}$ (double salt). By contrast, B is $[\text{Cu(NH}_3)_4]\text{SO}_4\cdot\text{H}_2\text{O}$ and D is $\text{K}_4[\text{Fe(CN)}_6]$, which retain their complex ions in solution (coordination compounds).
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the exact answer: Only A and C are double salts, matching Option (d).
Q117.stepsLatex:
A (FeSO4 · (NH4)2SO4 · 6H2O, Mohr’s salt) and C (K2SO4 · Al2(SO4)3 · 24H2O, potash alum)
are double salts. B ([Cu(NH3)4]SO4 · H2O) and D (K4[Fe(CN)6]) are coordination compounds.

Q118.conceptHtml: Fe<sup>3+</sup> reacts with [Fe(CN)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>4−</sup> to form insoluble Prussian blue: Fe<sub>4</sub>[Fe(CN)<sub>6</sub>]<sub>3</sub>.
Q118.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the reacting ions: $\text{FeCl}_3$ supplies $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ ions, while potassium ferrocyanide $\text{K}_4[\text{Fe(CN)}_6]$ supplies the $[\text{Fe(CN)}_6]^{4-}$ complex anion.
  2. Step 2 — Balance charges to get the precipitate formula: Combining $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ and $[\text{Fe(CN)}_6]^{4-}$ in a $4:3$ molar ratio gives the electrically neutral ferric ferrocyanide complex: $4\text{FeCl}_3 + 3\text{K}_4[\text{Fe(CN)}_6] \rightarrow \text{Fe}_4[\text{Fe(CN)}_6]_3\downarrow + 12\text{KCl}$.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the exact answer: The intense Prussian blue precipitate is $\text{Fe}_4[\text{Fe(CN)}_6]_3$, corresponding to Option (b).
Q118.trapHtml: Prussian blue is Fe<sup>I</sup><sub>4</sub><sup>II</sup>[Fe<sup>II</sup>(CN)<sub>6</sub>]<sub>3</sub>, not Fe<sub>3</sub>[Fe(CN)<sub>6</sub>]<sub>2</sub> (Turnbull’s blue formula).

Q119.subtopic: CoCl2 Colour Change in Water vs Conc. HCl
Q119.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Pink O<sub>h</sub> [Co(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> ↔ Blue T<sub>d</sub> [CoCl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2−</sup>
Q119.conceptHtml: Co<sup>2+</sup> in water forms pink octahedral [Co(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup>; excess Cl<sup>−</sup> (conc. HCl) shifts equilibrium to deep blue tetrahedral [CoCl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2−</sup>.
Q119.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the aqueous pink complex X: Dissolving $\text{CoCl}_2$ in water hydrates $\text{Co}^{2+}$ to form the pink octahedral hexaaquacobalt(II) ion, $\text{X} = [\text{Co(H}_2\text{O)}_6]^{2+}$.
  2. Step 2 — Identify complex Y formed with conc. HCl: Adding concentrated $\text{HCl}$ supplies excess $\text{Cl}^-$ ions, displacing water to establish the equilibrium $[\text{Co(H}_2\text{O)}_6]^{2+} + 4\text{Cl}^- \rightleftharpoons [\text{CoCl}_4]^{2-} + 6\text{H}_2\text{O}$, giving deep blue $\text{Y} = [\text{CoCl}_4]^{2-}$.
  3. Step 3 — Determine geometry Z & conclude: With coordination number $4$ and weak-field $\text{Cl}^-$ ligands around $\text{Co}^{2+}$ ($3d^7$), $[\text{CoCl}_4]^{2-}$ is $sp^3$ hybridised with tetrahedral geometry ($\text{Z}$). Thus $\text{X} = [\text{Co(H}_2\text{O)}_6]^{2+}$, $\text{Y} = [\text{CoCl}_4]^{2-}$, $\text{Z} = \text{Tetrahedral}$ — Option (a).
Q119.stepsLatex: X = [Co(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]2+ (pink, O<sub>h</sub>), Y = [CoCl<sub>4</sub>]2− (deep blue), Z = Tetrahedral.
Q119.trapHtml: Classic NCERT / lab equilibrium: pink octahedral ↔ blue tetrahedral.

Q120.format: Match List-I with List-II | Fe<sup>2+</sup> with NH<sub>3</sub> vs H<sub>2</sub>O
Q120.conceptHtml: Both NH<sub>3</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>O are weak-field ligands for Fe<sup>2+</sup> (d<sup>6</sup>), forming high-spin outer-orbital sp<sup>3</sup>d<sup>2</sup> complexes ([Fe(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> and [Fe(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup>).
Q120.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Determine hybridisation of A and B: In $[\text{Ni(CO)}_4]$, $\text{Ni}(0)$ ($3d^8 4s^2$) undergoes pairing under strong-field $\text{CO}$ to $3d^{10}$, giving $sp^3$ hybridisation (A–I). In $[\text{Cu(NH}_3)_4]^{2+}$, $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ ($3d^9$) adopts square planar $dsp^2$ hybridisation (B–II).
  2. Step 2 — Determine hybridisation of C and D: Both $[\text{Fe(NH}_3)_6]^{2+}$ and $[\text{Fe(H}_2\text{O)}_6]^{2+}$ contain $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ ($3d^6$). Neither $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ nor $\text{NH}_3$ is strong enough to pair $3d^6$ electrons in $\text{Fe}^{2+}$, so BOTH complexes are high-spin outer-orbital complexes with $sp^3d^2$ hybridisation (C–III and D–III).
  3. Step 3 — Compare with options & confirm official verdict: Since both C and D map to III ($sp^3d^2$), none of the given options (which pair C and D with III and IV separately) is chemically correct. Therefore, NTA awarded this question as Bonus.
Q120.stepsLatex:
• A. [Ni(CO)4] (d10) → sp3 (I).
• B. [Cu(NH3)4]2+ (d9) → dsp2 (II).
• C. [Fe(NH3)6]2+ (d6 HS) → sp3d2 (III).
• D. [Fe(H2O)6]2+ (d6 HS) → sp3d2 (III).
Q120.trapHtml: NTA Dropped / Bonus: Both C and D are sp<sup>3</sup>d<sup>2</sup> (III), so the exact chemical match is A-I, B-II, C-III, D-III, which is absent from all options (option (c) A-I, B-II, C-IV, D-III erroneously assumes NH<sub>3</sub> pairs Fe<sup>2+</sup>).
Q120.finalAnsHtml: NTA Dropped / Bonus [Verified Match: A-I, B-II, C-III, D-III]

Q121.subtopic: Cl − Co − Cl Bond Angle in fac-[Co(NH3)3Cl3]
Q121.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Facial vs meridional angles
Q121.conceptHtml: In the fac (facial) isomer, three identical ligands occupy three corners of one triangular face of the octahedron, so every pair is mutually cis (90<sup>°</sup>).
Q121.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the facial ($fac$) geometry of $[Ma_3b_3]$: In the $fac$ isomer of an octahedral complex $[\text{Co(NH}_3)_3\text{Cl}_3]$, the three identical $\text{Cl}^-$ ligands occupy three mutually adjacent corners forming one triangular face of the octahedron.
  2. Step 2 — Measure the $\text{Cl}-\text{Co}-\text{Cl}$ bond angles: Because every pair of $\text{Cl}^-$ ligands is adjacent (cis to one another), all three $\text{Cl}-\text{Co}-\text{Cl}$ bond angles are strictly $90^\circ$ (there is no $180^\circ$ trans pair, unlike in the $mer$ isomer).
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the exact answer: The $\text{Cl}-\text{Co}-\text{Cl}$ bond angle value is $90^\circ$ only — Option (b).
Q121.stepsLatex:
All three Cl − Co − Cl bond angles in fac-[Co(NH3)3Cl3] are 90◦. (In mer, two angles are 90◦
and one is 180◦.)

Q122.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Dividing 2 L into two 1 L parts
Q122.conceptHtml: 1 L × 0.02 M = 0.02 mol of each isomer. Total 2 L solution has 0.02 mol free Br<sup>−</sup> and 0.02 mol free SO<sup>2</sup><sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup>.
Q122.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Find total moles of ionisable ions after mixing: $1\text{ L}$ of $0.02\text{ M}$ $[\text{Co(NH}_3)_5\text{SO}_4]\text{Br}$ provides $0.02\text{ mol}$ of free $\text{Br}^-$ ions. $1\text{ L}$ of $0.02\text{ M}$ $[\text{Co(NH}_3)_5\text{Br}]\text{SO}_4$ provides $0.02\text{ mol}$ of free $\text{SO}_4^{2-}$ ions. The combined $2\text{ L}$ mixture contains $0.02\text{ mol}$ $\text{Br}^-$ and $0.02\text{ mol}$ $\text{SO}_4^{2-}$.
  2. Step 2 — Divide into two equal $1\text{ L}$ parts (X): Each $1\text{ L}$ portion (X) contains half of each free counter-ion: $0.01\text{ mol}$ of $\text{Br}^-$ and $0.01\text{ mol}$ of $\text{SO}_4^{2-}$.
  3. Step 3 — Precipitate with excess $\text{AgNO}_3$ and $\text{BaCl}_2$: Excess $\text{AgNO}_3$ reacts only with free $\text{Br}^-$ to form $0.01\text{ mol}$ of $\text{AgBr}$ (Y). Excess $\text{BaCl}_2$ reacts only with free $\text{SO}_4^{2-}$ to form $0.01\text{ mol}$ of $\text{BaSO}_4$ (Z).
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the exact answer: Moles of Y and Z are $0.01$ and $0.01$ respectively — Option (a).
Q122.stepsLatex:
Dividing into two equal 1 L parts (X) gives 0.01 mol Br− and 0.01 mol SO2− in each part.
4
Hence AgNO3 gives 0.01 mol AgBr (Y) and BaCl2 gives 0.01molBaSO4 (Z).
Q122.trapHtml: Don’t forget to divide moles by 2 when splitting into two equal parts!

Q123.conceptHtml: NCERT Biological Importance: cis-platin ([Pt(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>]) and related Pt coordination compounds inhibit tumour growth. (EDTA treats Pb poisoning; D-penicillamine treats Cu/Wilson’s disease.)
Q123.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall medicinal uses of coordination compounds (NCERT): Coordination compounds of platinum (B), specifically cis-platin ($cis\text{-[Pt(NH}_3)_2\text{Cl}_2]$, D), are used in chemotherapy to inhibit the growth of tumours.
  2. Step 2 — Eliminate chelation-therapy agents: EDTA (A) is used to treat lead poisoning, while D-penicillamine (C) is used to remove excess copper and iron from the body (not for inhibiting tumour growth).
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the exact answer: Thus B and D only are used to inhibit tumour growth — Option (c).
Q123.stepsLatex: B (Coordination compounds of Pt) and D (Cis-platin) are used to inhibit tumour growth.
Q123.trapHtml: NCERT uses: Cisplatin (Pt) → cancer; EDTA → Pb; D-penicillamine/desferrioxamine B → Cu/Fe.

Q124.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Increasing ligand field strength
Q124.conceptHtml: Standard spectrochemical series: S<sup>2−</sup> < C<sub>2</sub>O<sup>2</sup><sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup> < NH<sub>3</sub> < en < CO.
Q124.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the spectrochemical series: Ligands arranged in increasing order of crystal field splitting strength follow: $\text{I}^- < \text{Br}^- < \text{SCN}^- < \text{Cl}^- < \text{S}^{2-} < \text{F}^- < \text{OH}^- < \text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-} < \text{H}_2\text{O} < \text{NCS}^- < \text{edta}^{4-} < \text{NH}_3 < \text{en} < \text{CN}^- < \text{CO}$.
  2. Step 2 — Pick out the five given ligands in order: From weakest to strongest, the order is $\text{S}^{2-} < \text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-} < \text{NH}_3 < \text{en} < \text{CO}$.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the exact answer: This matches Option (a).

Q125.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Analyse $[\text{FeF}_6]^{3-}$: $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ has a $3d^5$ configuration. With weak-field $\text{F}^-$, it forms a high-spin complex ($t_{2g}^3 e_g^2$) with $n = 5$ unpaired electrons ($\mu = \sqrt{35} \approx 5.92\text{ BM}$).
  2. Step 2 — Analyse $[\text{CoF}_6]^{3-}$: $\text{Co}^{3+}$ has a $3d^6$ configuration. With weak-field $\text{F}^-$, it forms a high-spin complex ($t_{2g}^4 e_g^2$) with $n = 4$ unpaired electrons ($\mu = \sqrt{24} \approx 4.90\text{ BM}$).
  3. Step 3 — Analyse $[\text{Co(C}_2\text{O}_4)_3]^{3-}$: Oxalate ($\text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-}$) acts as a strong-field ligand for $\text{Co}^{3+}$ ($3d^6$), pairing all electrons into $t_{2g}^6 e_g^0$ with $n = 0$ unpaired electrons ($\mu = 0\text{ BM}$).
  4. Step 4 — Rank & confirm the exact answer: Since $\mu \propto \sqrt{n(n+2)}$, the decreasing order is $[\text{FeF}_6]^{3-} > [\text{CoF}_6]^{3-} > [\text{Co(C}_2\text{O}_4)_3]^{3-}$ — Option (c).
Q125.stepsLatex: [FeF<sub>6</sub>]3− (d5 HS, n = 5) > [CoF<sub>6</sub>]3− (d6 HS, n = 4) > [Co(C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>)<sub>3</sub>]3− (d6 LS, n = 0).
Q125.trapHtml: C<sub>2</sub>O<sup>2</sup><sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup> pairs Co<sup>3+</sup> (n = 0), whereas F<sup>−</sup> leaves it high-spin (n = 4).

Q126.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Lack of plane/centre of symmetry
Q126.conceptHtml: Square planar complexes always have a molecular mirror plane (achiral). trans-M(AA)<sub>2</sub>a<sub>2</sub> and trans-Ma<sub>4</sub>b<sub>2</sub> also have planes/centres of symmetry. Only cis-M(AA)<sub>2</sub>a<sub>2</sub> is chiral.
Q126.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the condition for chirality: A coordination complex is chiral (optically active) if it lacks a plane of symmetry (POS) and a centre of symmetry (COS), making its mirror image non-superimposable.
  2. Step 2 — Check each complex for symmetry elements: $trans\text{-[Co(NH}_3)_4\text{Cl}_2]^+$ and $trans\text{-[PtCl}_2(\text{en})_2]^{2+}$ both possess a plane of symmetry and a centre of symmetry, so they are achiral. Square planar $cis\text{-[PtCl}_2(\text{NH}_3)_2]$ lies in a single molecular plane, which is itself a plane of symmetry (achiral).
  3. Step 3 — Check $cis\text{-[PtCl}_2(\text{en})_2]^{2+}$ & conclude: Octahedral $cis\text{-[M(AA)}_2\text{X}_2]$ has no plane or centre of symmetry, so $cis\text{-[PtCl}_2(\text{en})_2]^{2+}$ is chiral — Option (a).
Q126.stepsLatex: cis-[PtCl<sub>2</sub>(en)<sub>2</sub>]2+ lacks any plane or centre of symmetry =⇒ chiral (optically active).
Q126.trapHtml: Square planar cis-[PtCl<sub>2</sub>(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>] is achiral because the molecular plane itself is a σ-plane.

Q127.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Relate absorbed wavelength to crystal field splitting: The energy absorbed is $E = \Delta = \frac{hc}{\lambda}$, so a stronger ligand (larger $\Delta$) absorbs a shorter wavelength $\lambda$.
  2. Step 2 — Order the complexes by ligand strength and metal charge: Among the $\text{Co}^{3+}$ complexes, ligand strength is $\text{CN}^- > \text{NH}_3 > \text{Cl}^-$, so $\lambda$ increases as $[\text{Co(CN)}_6]^{3-} < [\text{Co(NH}_3)_6]^{3+} < [\text{CoCl(NH}_3)_5]^{2+}$. Meanwhile, $[\text{Cu(H}_2\text{O)}_4]^{2+}$ has a lower $+2$ charge and weak-field $\text{H}_2\text{O}$, giving the smallest $\Delta$ and longest $\lambda$.
  3. Step 3 — Match exact NCERT values & conclude: C. $[\text{Co(CN)}_6]^{3-}$ — $310\text{ nm}$ (I); B. $[\text{Co(NH}_3)_6]^{3+}$ — $475\text{ nm}$ (II); A. $[\text{CoCl(NH}_3)_5]^{2+}$ — $535\text{ nm}$ (III); D. $[\text{Cu(H}_2\text{O)}_4]^{2+}$ — $600\text{ nm}$ (IV). Thus A–III, B–II, C–I, D–IV — Option (b).
Q127.stepsLatex:
∆ order: [Co(CN)6]3− > [Co(NH3)6]3+ > [CoCl(NH3)5]2+ > [Cu(H2O)4]2+. Matching λabs
(increasing): C → 310 nm (I), B → 475 nm (II), A → 535 nm (III), D → 600 nm (IV).
Q127.trapHtml: You don’t need to memorize the exact wavelengths—ordering ∆ gives the unique match!

Q128.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Find the oxidation state and $d$-electron count: In $[\text{Co(NH}_3)_6]^{3+}$, $\text{NH}_3$ is neutral, so cobalt is in the $+3$ state: $\text{Co}^{3+} = [\text{Ar}]3d^6$.
  2. Step 2 — Apply ligand field pairing: $\text{NH}_3$ acts as a strong-field ligand for $\text{Co}^{3+}$, forcing all $6$ electrons to pair in the lower $t_{2g}$ orbitals ($t_{2g}^6 e_g^0$). This leaves two inner $3d$ orbitals empty.
  3. Step 3 — Determine hybridisation, magnetism & conclude: Using the two vacant inner $3d$ orbitals along with one $4s$ and three $4p$ orbitals yields $d^2sp^3$ hybridisation, and with $n = 0$ unpaired electrons the complex is diamagnetic — Option (c).
Q128.stepsLatex: Two 3d orbitals are vacated for d2sp3 hybridization; all 6 electrons are paired =⇒ diamagnetic.

Q129.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Spectrochemical series cannot be explained by CFT
Q129.conceptHtml: Pure electrostatic CFT predicts anionic ligands should exert the strongest field, contradicting the observed spectrochemical series (where CO is strongest and I<sup>−</sup> is weakest).
Q129.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall what Crystal Field Theory (CFT) explains well: By modelling electrostatic repulsion between $d$-electrons and ligands, CFT successfully explains $d$-orbital splitting, colours ($d\text{–}d$ transitions), magnetic properties (high-spin vs low-spin), and relative stability (CFSE) of complexes.
  2. Step 2 — Identify the key limitation of CFT: Because CFT treats ligands purely as point charges or dipoles, it predicts that anionic ligands (like $\text{F}^-$ or $\text{OH}^-$) should cause stronger splitting than neutral ligands (like $\text{CO}$ or $\text{NH}_3$). It cannot explain the actual order of the spectrochemical series, which requires covalent $\pi$-bonding (Ligand Field / Molecular Orbital Theory).
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the exact answer: CFT cannot explain the order of the spectrochemical series — Option (a).
Q129.stepsLatex:
CFT explains colour, magnetic properties, and relative stability (CFSE), but cannot
explain the order of the spectrochemical series (requires π-bonding / LFT).

Q130.conceptHtml: Primary valency = oxidation state; Secondary valency = coordination number.
Q130.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Determine primary valency (oxidation state): Let the oxidation state of Co in $[\text{Co(NH}_3)_5\text{Cl}]\text{Cl}_2$ be $x$. Then $x + 5(0) + 1(-1) + 2(-1) = 0 \Rightarrow x = +3$. So primary valency $= 3$.
  2. Step 2 — Determine secondary valency (coordination number): Inside the coordination sphere $[\text{Co(NH}_3)_5\text{Cl}]^{2+}$, Co is bonded to $5$ monodentate $\text{NH}_3$ ligands and $1$ monodentate $\text{Cl}^-$ ligand, giving coordination number $= 5 + 1 = 6$. So secondary valency $= 6$.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the exact answer: Primary and secondary valencies are $3$ and $6$ respectively — Option (d).
Q130.stepsLatex:
Co oxidation state = +3 (primary valency = 3); ligands attached = 5 NH3 + 1 Cl− = 6
(secondary valency = 6).
Q130.trapHtml: Don’t count only the 2 outer Cl<sup>−</sup> ions for primary valency—the inner Cl<sup>−</sup> also satisfies 1<sup>°</sup> valency!

Q131.conceptHtml: A complex is paramagnetic if it has at least one unpaired electron (n ≥ 1).
Q131.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Check the four 4-coordinate complexes: $[\text{MnBr}_4]^{2-}$ ($\text{Mn}^{2+}, 3d^5$, tetrahedral) has $n = 5$ (paramagnetic); $[\text{NiCl}_4]^{2-}$ ($\text{Ni}^{2+}, 3d^8$, tetrahedral) has $n = 2$ (paramagnetic); $[\text{Ni(CN)}_4]^{2-}$ ($\text{Ni}^{2+}, 3d^8$, square planar) has $n = 0$ (diamagnetic); $[\text{Ni(CO)}_4]$ ($\text{Ni}(0), 3d^{10}$, tetrahedral) has $n = 0$ (diamagnetic).
  2. Step 2 — Check the first three octahedral complexes: $[\text{CoF}_6]^{3-}$ ($\text{Co}^{3+}, 3d^6$, high-spin $t_{2g}^4 e_g^2$) has $n = 4$ (paramagnetic); $[\text{Fe(CN)}_6]^{4-}$ ($\text{Fe}^{2+}, 3d^6$, low-spin $t_{2g}^6 e_g^0$) has $n = 0$ (diamagnetic); $[\text{Mn(CN)}_6]^{3-}$ ($\text{Mn}^{3+}, 3d^4$, low-spin $t_{2g}^4 e_g^0$) has $n = 2$ (paramagnetic).
  3. Step 3 — Check the remaining three octahedral complexes: $[\text{Ti(CN)}_6]^{3-}$ ($\text{Ti}^{3+}, 3d^1$) has $n = 1$ (paramagnetic); $[\text{Cu(H}_2\text{O)}_6]^{2+}$ ($\text{Cu}^{2+}, 3d^9$) has $n = 1$ (paramagnetic); $[\text{Co(C}_2\text{O}_4)_3]^{3-}$ ($\text{Co}^{3+}, 3d^6$, low-spin $t_{2g}^6 e_g^0$) has $n = 0$ (diamagnetic).
  4. Step 4 — Count & confirm the exact answer: The paramagnetic complexes are $[\text{MnBr}_4]^{2-}$, $[\text{NiCl}_4]^{2-}$, $[\text{CoF}_6]^{3-}$, $[\text{Mn(CN)}_6]^{3-}$, $[\text{Ti(CN)}_6]^{3-}$, and $[\text{Cu(H}_2\text{O)}_6]^{2+}$, giving a total of 6.
Q131.trapHtml: [Co(C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>)<sub>3</sub>]<sup>3−</sup> is low-spin diamagnetic; [Ti(CN)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3−</sup> (d<sup>1</sup>) always has 1 unpaired electron.

Q132.conceptHtml: Tetraaquadichloridochromium(III) chloride is [Cr(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>4</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>]Cl, which has 1 ionisable Cl<sup>−</sup> per mole of complex.
Q132.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Write the formula of the complex: Tetraaquadichloridochromium(III) chloride has $4\text{ H}_2\text{O}$ and $2\text{ Cl}^-$ inside the coordination sphere with $\text{Cr}^{3+}$, leaving $1\text{ Cl}^-$ outside: $[\text{Cr(H}_2\text{O)}_4\text{Cl}_2]\text{Cl}$.
  2. Step 2 — Calculate moles of the complex in solution: $\text{Moles of complex} = \text{Molarity} \times \text{Volume (L)} = 0.05\text{ M} \times 0.100\text{ L} = 0.005\text{ mol} = 5 \times 10^{-3}\text{ mol}$.
  3. Step 3 — Find moles of $\text{AgCl}$ precipitated & conclude: Each mole of $[\text{Cr(H}_2\text{O)}_4\text{Cl}_2]\text{Cl}$ releases $1\text{ mol}$ of ionisable $\text{Cl}^-$, precipitating $5 \times 10^{-3}\text{ mol}$ of $\text{AgCl}$. Hence the answer is 5.
Q132.stepsLatex:
Moles of complex = 0.05 M × 0.1 L = 5 × 10−3 mol. Each mole releases 1 mol Cl− =⇒
moles of AgCl = 5 × 10−3 mol.
Q132.trapHtml: Only the counter-ion Cl<sup>−</sup> outside the bracket precipitates with AgNO<sub>3</sub>.

Q133.subtopic: Numerical — Sum of Unpaired Electrons in Octahedral
Q133.format: Numerical | Counting n for 5 d<sup>n</sup> configurations
Q133.conceptHtml: Fill t<sub>2g</sub> and e<sub>g</sub> according to high-spin vs low-spin.
Q133.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Write the $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ configurations for each system:
    • $d^3$: $t_{2g}^3 e_g^0 \Rightarrow 3$ unpaired electrons.
    • $d^4$ (low spin): $t_{2g}^4 e_g^0 \Rightarrow 2$ unpaired electrons.
    • $d^5$ (high spin): $t_{2g}^3 e_g^2 \Rightarrow 5$ unpaired electrons.
  2. Step 2 — Write configurations for the remaining two systems:
    • $d^6$ (high spin): $t_{2g}^4 e_g^2 \Rightarrow 4$ unpaired electrons.
    • $d^7$ (low spin): $t_{2g}^6 e_g^1 \Rightarrow 1$ unpaired electron.
  3. Step 3 — Sum & confirm the exact answer: Total unpaired electrons $= 3 + 2 + 5 + 4 + 1 =$ 15.
Q133.stepsLatex:
• d3: t3 =⇒ n = 3.
2g
• d4 (low spin): t4 =⇒ n = 2.
2g
• d5 (high spin): t3 e2 =⇒ n = 5.
2g g
• d6 (high spin): t4 e2 =⇒ n = 4.
2g g
• d7 (low spin): t6 e1 =⇒ n = 1.
2g g
Total = 3 + 2 + 5 + 4 + 1 = 15.
Q133.trapHtml: Low-spin d<sup>7</sup> puts the 7th electron in e<sub>g</sub>, leaving 1 unpaired electron.

Q134.subtopic: Numerical — Mole Ratio of Complex to AgCl
Q134.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Compute molar masses: For $\text{CrCl}_3\cdot 6\text{H}_2\text{O}$, $M = 52 + 3(35.5) + 6(18) = 266.5\text{ g mol}^{-1}$. For $\text{AgCl}$, $M = 108 + 35.5 = 143.5\text{ g mol}^{-1}$.
  2. Step 2 — Calculate moles of complex and $\text{AgCl}$: Moles of complex $= \frac{5.33}{266.5} = 0.02\text{ mol}$. Moles of $\text{AgCl} = \frac{8.61}{143.5} = 0.06\text{ mol}$ (consistent with the $1:3$ electrolyte $[\text{Cr(H}_2\text{O)}_6]\text{Cl}_3$ releasing $3\text{ Cl}^-$ per formula unit).
  3. Step 3 — Compute the ratio & conclude: $\frac{\text{Moles of complex}}{\text{Moles of AgCl}} = \frac{0.02}{0.06} = \frac{1}{3} \approx 0.3333 = 33.33 \times 10^{-2}$. Rounding to the nearest integer gives 33.
Q134.stepsLatex:
Moles of complex = 5.33 = 0.02 mol. Moles of AgCl = 8.61 = 0.06 mol (consistent with 1 : 3
electrolyte giving 3Cl−). Ratio = 0.02 = 1 2≈660.5.3333 = 33 × 10−2. 143.5
0.06 3
Q134.trapHtml: Check which way the ratio is asked: moles of complex / moles of AgCl, not AgCl / complex!

Q135.conceptHtml: Count d-electrons in the given 3d ions to find ‘n’, then determine the complex formula.
Q135.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Find the number of isoelectronic species ($n$): Count total electrons: $\text{Sc}^{3+} = 21 - 3 = 18$; $\text{Cr}^{2+} = 24 - 2 = 22$; $\text{Mn}^{3+} = 25 - 3 = 22$; $\text{Co}^{3+} = 27 - 3 = 24$; $\text{Fe}^{3+} = 26 - 3 = 23$. Only $\text{Cr}^{2+}$ and $\text{Mn}^{3+}$ share the same electron count ($22$), so $n = 2$.
  2. Step 2 — Write the coordination formula of the Co complex: Since $n = 2$ moles of $\text{AgCl}$ are precipitated, $2\text{ Cl}^-$ ions lie outside the coordination sphere: $[\text{Co(en)}_2(\text{NH}_3)\text{Cl}]\text{Cl}_2$ (coordination number $= 4 + 1 + 1 = 6$, octahedral).
  3. Step 3 — Find $t_{2g}$ electrons & conclude: Cobalt is in the $+3$ state ($3d^6$). With strong-field ligands $\text{en}$ and $\text{NH}_3$ dominating the field around $\text{Co}^{3+}$, the complex is low-spin with configuration $t_{2g}^6 e_g^0$. Hence the number of electrons in $t_{2g}$ is 6.
Q135.stepsLatex:
Sc3+ (18e−), Cr2+ (22e−), Mn3+ (22e−), Co3+ (24e−), Fe3+ (23e−). Only Cr2+ and Mn3+
are isoelectronic (22e−, d4), so n = 2. Since 2 mol AgCl precipitates, the complex is [Co(en)2(NH3)Cl]Cl2 (Co3+, d6
with strong-field en, NH3 =⇒ low-spin t6 e0). Number of electrons in t2g orbital = 6.
2g g
Q135.trapHtml: Even if n were different, Co<sup>3+</sup> with en and NH<sub>3</sub> is always low-spin t<sup>6</sup><sub>2g</sub>e<sup>0</sup><sub>g</sub>.

Q136.subtopic: Numerical — Sum of Isomer Counts (X + Y + Z)
Q136.format: Numerical | Square planar Mabcd + octahedral M(AA)<sub>2</sub>a<sub>2</sub> + Ma<sub>3</sub>b<sub>3</sub>
Q136.conceptHtml: Recall isomer counts: square planar Mabcd has 3 GI; octahedral M(AA)<sub>2</sub>a<sub>2</sub> has 1 optically inactive (trans) isomer; Ma<sub>3</sub>b<sub>3</sub> has 2 GI (fac, mer).
Q136.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Find $X$: $[\text{Pt(NH}_3)(\text{H}_2\text{O})\text{BrCl}]$ is a square planar complex of the type $[Mabcd]$. Fixing one ligand (say $\text{NH}_3$), any of the other $3$ ligands can be placed trans to it, giving $X = 3$ geometrical isomers.
  2. Step 2 — Find $Y$: $[\text{CrCl}_2(\text{ox})_2]^{3-}$ is an octahedral $[M(AA)_2b_2]$ complex with $cis$ and $trans$ forms. The $cis$ form is optically active ($d, l$ pair), whereas the $trans$ form has a plane and centre of symmetry and is optically inactive, giving $Y = 1$.
  3. Step 3 — Find $Z$ & sum: $[\text{Co(NH}_3)_3(\text{NO}_2)_3]$ is an octahedral $[Ma_3b_3]$ complex, which exhibits $Z = 2$ geometrical isomers ($fac$ and $mer$). Therefore, $X + Y + Z = 3 + 1 + 2 =$ 6.
Q136.stepsLatex:
• X = 3 (three geometrical isomers for square planar [Pt(NH3)(H2O)BrCl]).
• Y = 1 (only trans-[CrCl2(ox)2]3− is optically inactive; cis is optically active).
• Z = 2 (fac and mer for [Co(NH3)3(NO2)3]).
X + Y + Z = 3 + 1 + 2 = 6.
Q136.trapHtml: Read Y carefully: “optically inactive isomer(s)”, which is 1 (trans), not 2 or 3!

Q137.subtopic: Numerical — Mass of AgCl from 1 : 2 Electrolyte CrCl3 · 6H2O
Q137.conceptHtml: 1: 2 electrolyte =⇒ [Cr(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>5</sub>Cl]Cl<sub>2</sub> · H<sub>2</sub>O, which gives 2 mol free Cl<sup>−</sup> per mole of complex.
Q137.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the complex formula: A $1:2$ electrolyte with composition $\text{CrCl}_3\cdot 6\text{H}_2\text{O}$ must dissociate into $1$ complex cation and $2$ chloride counter-ions: $[\text{Cr(H}_2\text{O)}_5\text{Cl}]\text{Cl}_2\cdot\text{H}_2\text{O}$ (its $\text{Cr}^{3+}$ ion is $3d^3$ with $n = 3$, matching $\mu = \sqrt{15} = 3.87\text{ BM}$).
  2. Step 2 — Calculate moles of complex and $\text{AgCl}$: Molar mass of $\text{CrCl}_3\cdot 6\text{H}_2\text{O} = 52 + 3(35.5) + 6(18) = 266.5\text{ g mol}^{-1}$. Moles of complex $= \frac{2.75}{266.5} \approx 0.01032\text{ mol}$. Since each mole releases $2\text{ mol}$ of free $\text{Cl}^-$, moles of $\text{AgCl} = 2 \times 0.01032 = 0.02064\text{ mol}$.
  3. Step 3 — Find mass of $\text{AgCl}$ & conclude: Molar mass of $\text{AgCl} = 108 + 35.5 = 143.5\text{ g mol}^{-1}$. Mass of $\text{AgCl} = 0.02064 \times 143.5 \approx 2.96\text{ g}$. Rounding to the nearest integer gives 3.
Q137.stepsLatex:
M(CrCl3 · 6H2O) = 266.5 g/mol; M(AgCl) = 143.5 g/mol. Moles of complex = 2.75 ≈
0.01032 mol. Moles of AgCl = 2 × 0.01032 = 0.02064 mol. Mass of AgCl = 0.02064 × 143.5 ≈ 2.96 g ≈ 3 g. 266.5
Q137.trapHtml: A 1: 2 electrolyte produces 3 ions total (1 complex cation +2 Cl<sup>−</sup> anions).

Q138.subtopic: Numerical — Total Unpaired Electrons in 5 Complexes
Q138.conceptHtml: All Pt<sup>2+</sup> (5d<sup>8</sup>) CN = 4 complexes are square planar diamagnetic (n = 0).
Q138.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Check the nickel complexes:
    • $[\text{Ni(CO)}_4]$: $\text{Ni}(0)$ ($3d^8 4s^2 \rightarrow 3d^{10}$ under strong-field $\text{CO}$), tetrahedral $sp^3 \Rightarrow 0$ unpaired electrons.
    • $[\text{NiCl}_4]^{2-}$: $\text{Ni}^{2+}$ ($3d^8$), weak-field $\text{Cl}^-$, tetrahedral $sp^3$ ($e^4 t_2^4$) $\Rightarrow 2$ unpaired electrons.
    • $[\text{Ni(CN)}_4]^{2-}$: $\text{Ni}^{2+}$ ($3d^8$), strong-field $\text{CN}^-$, square planar $dsp^2 \Rightarrow 0$ unpaired electrons.
  2. Step 2 — Check the platinum complexes: Both $[\text{PtCl}_2(\text{NH}_3)_2]$ and $[\text{Pt(CN)}_4]^{2-}$ contain $\text{Pt}^{2+}$ ($5d^8$). All $5d^8$ complexes are square planar ($dsp^2$) with all $d$-electrons paired $\Rightarrow 0$ unpaired electrons each.
  3. Step 3 — Sum & confirm the exact answer: Total unpaired electrons $= 0 + 2 + 0 + 0 + 0 =$ 2.
Q138.trapHtml: Only [NiCl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2−</sup> is paramagnetic among these five.

Q139.conceptHtml: With ∆<sub>o</sub> ≫ P, Co<sup>3+</sup> (d<sup>6</sup>) is t<sup>6</sup><sub>2g</sub>e<sup>0</sup><sub>g</sub> (CFSE = −2.4∆<sub>o</sub>) and Cr<sup>3+</sup> (d<sup>3</sup>) is t<sup>3</sup><sub>2g</sub>e<sup>0</sup><sub>g</sub> (CFSE = −1.2∆<sub>o</sub>).
Q139.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Calculate CFSE of $[\text{Co(oxalate)}_3]^{3-}$: $\text{Co}^{3+}$ is $3d^6$. Given $\Delta_o \gg P$, it forms a low-spin complex ($t_{2g}^6 e_g^0$). Neglecting pairing energy as $\Delta_o \gg P$, $\text{CFSE}_1 = 6(-0.4\Delta_o) = -2.4\Delta_o$.
  2. Step 2 — Calculate CFSE of $[\text{Cr(oxalate)}_3]^{3-}$: $\text{Cr}^{3+}$ is $3d^3$, which always has configuration $t_{2g}^3 e_g^0$. Its CFSE is $\text{CFSE}_2 = 3(-0.4\Delta_o) = -1.2\Delta_o$.
  3. Step 3 — Take the ratio & conclude: $n = \frac{\text{CFSE}_1}{\text{CFSE}_2} = \frac{-2.4\Delta_o}{-1.2\Delta_o} =$ 2.
Q139.trapHtml: Note: JEE refers to CFSE here as “crystal field splitting energy”; 2.4/1.2 = 2.

Q140.subtopic: Numerical — Sum of Unpaired e− for Ions with µ > 3.0 BM
Q140.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Find the threshold for $\mu > 3.0\text{ BM}$: Using $\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)}$, $n = 2$ gives $\sqrt{8} = 2.83\text{ BM}$ ($< 3.0$), whereas $n = 3$ gives $\sqrt{15} = 3.87\text{ BM}$ ($> 3.0$). Thus qualifying ions must have $n \ge 3$.
  2. Step 2 — Count unpaired electrons in high-spin octahedral complexes:
    • $\text{Co}^{2+}$ ($3d^7$, $t_{2g}^5 e_g^2$): $n = 3$ ($\mu = 3.87\text{ BM} > 3.0$) — qualifies.
    • $\text{Ni}^{2+}$ ($3d^8$, $t_{2g}^6 e_g^2$): $n = 2$ ($\mu = 2.83\text{ BM}$) — does not qualify.
    • $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ ($3d^6$, $t_{2g}^4 e_g^2$): $n = 4$ ($\mu = 4.90\text{ BM} > 3.0$) — qualifies.
    • $\text{V}^{3+}$ ($3d^2$, $t_{2g}^2 e_g^0$): $n = 2$ ($\mu = 2.83\text{ BM}$) — does not qualify.
    • $\text{Ti}^{2+}$ ($3d^2$, $t_{2g}^2 e_g^0$): $n = 2$ ($\mu = 2.83\text{ BM}$) — does not qualify.
  3. Step 3 — Sum & confirm the exact answer: Adding the unpaired electrons of the qualifying ions ($\text{Co}^{2+}$ and $\text{Fe}^{2+}$) gives $3 + 4 =$ 7.
Q140.stepsLatex:
• Co2+ (d7 HS): n = 3 (µ = 3.87 > 3.0). Include.
• Ni2+ (d8): n = 2 (µ = 2.83 < 3.0). Exclude.
• Fe2+ (d6 HS): n = 4 (µ = 4.90 > 3.0). Include.
• V3+ (d2): n = 2 (µ = 2.83 < 3.0). Exclude.
• Ti2+ (d2): n = 2 (µ = 2.83 < 3.0). Exclude.
Sum of unpaired electrons = 3 + 4 = 7.
Q140.trapHtml: Filter out n = 2 ions (µ = 2.83 BM) before summing!

Q141.subtopic: Numerical — Paramagnetic Species with Same Unpaired e−
Q141.conceptHtml: List n for each paramagnetic complex: [Co(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup> (0), [Co(C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>)<sub>3</sub>]<sup>3−</sup> (0), [MnCl<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3−</sup> (4), [Mn(CN)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3−</sup> (2), [CoF<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3−</sup> (4), [Fe(CN)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3−</sup> (1), [FeF<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3−</sup> (5).
Q141.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Find unpaired electrons for each complex:
    • $[\text{Co(NH}_3)_6]^{3+}$ ($\text{Co}^{3+}, d^6$, low-spin $t_{2g}^6 e_g^0$): $n = 0$ (diamagnetic).
    • $[\text{Co(C}_2\text{O}_4)_3]^{3-}$ ($\text{Co}^{3+}, d^6$, low-spin $t_{2g}^6 e_g^0$): $n = 0$ (diamagnetic).
    • $[\text{MnCl}_6]^{3-}$ ($\text{Mn}^{3+}, d^4$, high-spin $t_{2g}^3 e_g^1$): $n = 4$ (paramagnetic).
    • $[\text{Mn(CN)}_6]^{3-}$ ($\text{Mn}^{3+}, d^4$, low-spin $t_{2g}^4 e_g^0$): $n = 2$ (paramagnetic).
  2. Step 2 — Check the remaining three complexes:
    • $[\text{CoF}_6]^{3-}$ ($\text{Co}^{3+}, d^6$, high-spin $t_{2g}^4 e_g^2$): $n = 4$ (paramagnetic).
    • $[\text{Fe(CN)}_6]^{3-}$ ($\text{Fe}^{3+}, d^5$, low-spin $t_{2g}^5 e_g^0$): $n = 1$ (paramagnetic).
    • $[\text{FeF}_6]^{3-}$ ($\text{Fe}^{3+}, d^5$, high-spin $t_{2g}^3 e_g^2$): $n = 5$ (paramagnetic).
  3. Step 3 — Match & confirm the exact answer: Among the paramagnetic species, only $[\text{MnCl}_6]^{3-}$ and $[\text{CoF}_6]^{3-}$ share the same number of unpaired electrons ($n = 4$). Hence the count is 2.
Q141.stepsLatex:
Both [MnCl6]3− and [CoF6]3− are paramagnetic with the same number of unpaired electrons
(n = 4). Thus count = 2.
Q141.trapHtml: Exclude the two diamagnetic (n = 0) complexes since the question asks for paramagnetic species!

Q142.conceptHtml: Filter for both d<sup>2</sup>sp<sup>3</sup> (low spin) AND n ≥ 1 (paramagnetic).
Q142.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Separate inner-orbital ($d^2sp^3$) from outer-orbital ($sp^3d^2$) complexes: Weak-field halide complexes $[\text{FeF}_6]^{3-}$, $[\text{MnCl}_6]^{3-}$, and $[\text{CoF}_6]^{3-}$ are high-spin outer-orbital ($sp^3d^2$) complexes, so they are excluded.
  2. Step 2 — Check magnetism of the $d^2sp^3$ complexes:
    • $[\text{Fe(CN)}_6]^{3-}$: $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ ($3d^5$), low-spin $t_{2g}^5 e_g^0$ ($d^2sp^3$), $n = 1$ (paramagnetic).
    • $[\text{Mn(CN)}_6]^{3-}$: $\text{Mn}^{3+}$ ($3d^4$), low-spin $t_{2g}^4 e_g^0$ ($d^2sp^3$), $n = 2$ (paramagnetic).
    • $[\text{Co(C}_2\text{O}_4)_3]^{3-}$: $\text{Co}^{3+}$ ($3d^6$), low-spin $t_{2g}^6 e_g^0$ ($d^2sp^3$), $n = 0$ (diamagnetic).
  3. Step 3 — Count & confirm the exact answer: Exactly 2 complexes ($[\text{Fe(CN)}_6]^{3-}$ and $[\text{Mn(CN)}_6]^{3-}$) are both paramagnetic and $d^2sp^3$ hybridised.
Q142.stepsLatex:
• [Fe(CN)6]3− (d5 LS): d2sp3, n = 1 (Yes).
• [Mn(CN)6]3− (d4 LS): d2sp3, n = 2 (Yes).
• [Co(C2O4)3]3−: d2sp3, n = 0 (diamagnetic, No).
• [FeF6]3−, [MnCl6]3−, [CoF6]3−: all sp3d2 (outer orbital, No).
Count = 2.
Q142.trapHtml: Check both filters: paramagnetic AND d<sup>2</sup>sp<sup>3</sup>!

Q143.format: Numerical | Lone pairs in BrF<sub>5</sub> + Ma<sub>3</sub>b<sub>3</sub> GI
Q143.conceptHtml: In BrF<sub>5</sub>, SN = <sub>2</sub><sup>1</sup>(7 + 5) = 6 (5 bp + 1 lp), so x = 1.
Q143.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Find $x$ from the lone pairs on $\text{Br}$ in $\text{BrF}_5$: Bromine has $7$ valence electrons and forms $5$ single bonds with fluorine, leaving $\frac{7 - 5}{2} = 1$ lone pair on Br. Thus $x = 1$.
  2. Step 2 — Deduce the coordination formula: Since $1$ mole of $\text{AgCl}$ precipitates, $1\text{ Cl}^-$ lies outside the coordination sphere. From $\text{MCl}_4\cdot 3\text{NH}_3$, the complex is $[\text{M(NH}_3)_3\text{Cl}_3]\text{Cl}$ (coordination number $6$, octahedral $sp^3d^2$).
  3. Step 3 — Count geometrical isomers & conclude: An octahedral complex of the type $[Ma_3b_3]$ exhibits exactly 2 geometrical isomers: facial ($fac$) and meridional ($mer$).
Q143.stepsLatex:
Since 1 mol AgCl is formed, the complex is [M(NH3)3Cl3]Cl, i.e., [M(NH3)3Cl3]+ of type
Ma3b3, which exhibits 2 geometrical isomers (fac and mer).

Q144.conceptHtml: FeCl<sub>3</sub> + 3KOH + 3H<sub>2</sub>C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> → K<sub>3</sub>[Fe(C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>)<sub>3</sub>] + 3KCl + 3H<sub>2</sub>O (Wait: with K<sub>2</sub>C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>/excess KOH, product A is K<sub>3</sub>[Fe(C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>)<sub>3</sub>]).
Q144.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify complex (A): Treating $\text{FeCl}_3$ with $\text{KOH}$ and oxalic acid ($\text{H}_2\text{C}_2\text{O}_4$) produces potassium trioxalatoferrate(III): $\text{FeCl}_3 + 3\text{KOH} + 3\text{H}_2\text{C}_2\text{O}_4 \rightarrow \text{K}_3[\text{Fe(C}_2\text{O}_4)_3] + 3\text{HCl} + 3\text{H}_2\text{O}$.
  2. Step 2 — Check chirality of $[\text{Fe(ox)}_3]^{3-}$: This is an octahedral $[M(AA)_3]$ complex with three symmetrical bidentate oxalate ligands. It has no plane of symmetry and no centre of symmetry, so it is optically active.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the exact answer: It exists as a non-superimposable $d$ and $l$ enantiomeric pair, giving 2 optical isomers.
Q144.stepsLatex:
[Fe(C2O4)3]3− is of type M(AA)3, which exists as a d, l enantiomeric pair =⇒ 2 optical
isomers.
Q144.trapHtml: All M(AA)<sub>3</sub> complexes are chiral and have 2 optical isomers.

Q145.subtopic: Numerical — Least Enthalpy of Atomisation Metal (Zn)
Q145.conceptHtml: Among Ni, Zn, Mn, Cu, Zn (3d<sup>10</sup>4s<sup>2</sup>, zero unpaired e<sup>−</sup>) has the least enthalpy of atomisation (126 kJ/mol).
Q145.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify metal $M$ with the least enthalpy of atomisation: Among Ni, Zn, Mn, and Cu, zinc ($\text{Zn}$, $3d^{10} 4s^2$) has no unpaired $d$-electrons available for metallic bonding and therefore has the lowest enthalpy of atomisation. Thus $M = \text{Zn}$.
  2. Step 2 — Find $n$ by counting diamagnetic complexes:
    • $\text{K}_2[\text{NiCl}_4]$ ($\text{Ni}^{2+}, 3d^8$, tetrahedral): $n_u = 2$ (paramagnetic).
    • $[\text{Zn(H}_2\text{O)}_6]\text{Cl}_2$ ($\text{Zn}^{2+}, 3d^{10}$): $n_u = 0$ (diamagnetic).
    • $\text{K}_3[\text{Mn(CN)}_6]$ ($\text{Mn}^{3+}, 3d^4$, low-spin $t_{2g}^4$): $n_u = 2$ (paramagnetic).
    • $[\text{Cu(PPh}_3)_3\text{I}]$ ($\text{Cu}^{+}, 3d^{10}$): $n_u = 0$ (diamagnetic).
    Hence $n = 2$.
  3. Step 3 — Calculate spin-only magnetic moment of $M^{n+}$ & conclude: The ion is $\text{Zn}^{2+}$ ($3d^{10}$), which has $0$ unpaired electrons. Therefore, $\mu = \sqrt{0(0+2)} =$ 0 BM.
Q145.stepsLatex:
Diamagnetic complexes: [Zn(H2O)6]Cl2 (d10, n = 0) and [Cu(PPh3)3I] (Cu+, d10, n = 0)
=⇒ n = 2. (K2[NiCl4] has n = 2, K3[Mn(CN)6] has n = 2.) Thus Mn+ = Zn2+ (3d10), which has 0 unpaired
electrons =⇒ µ = 0 BM.
Q145.trapHtml: Zn has the lowest ∆<sub>atom</sub>H in the 3d series, and Zn<sup>2+</sup> is always d<sup>10</sup> (µ = 0).

Q146.format: Numerical | Highest E<sup>◦</sup>(M<sup>3+</sup>/M<sup>2+</sup>) among Mn, Cr, Co, Fe
Q146.conceptHtml: Among Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, Co has the highest E<sup>°</sup>(Co<sup>3+</sup>/Co<sup>2+</sup>) = +1.97 V (NCERT d-block).
Q146.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify metal $M$ with the highest $E^\circ(M^{3+}/M^{2+})$: Standard electrode potentials are $\text{Cr}$ ($-0.41\text{ V}$), $\text{Fe}$ ($+0.77\text{ V}$), $\text{Mn}$ ($+1.57\text{ V}$), and $\text{Co}$ ($+1.97\text{ V}$). Thus $M = \text{Co}$.
  2. Step 2 — Determine oxidation state and $d$-configuration in $[\text{Co(CN)}_6]^{4-}$: $x + 6(-1) = -4 \Rightarrow x = +2$, so $\text{Co}^{2+}$ has a $3d^7$ configuration.
  3. Step 3 — Fill octahedral orbitals & conclude: Because $\text{CN}^-$ is a strong-field ligand, the $7$ electrons fill in low-spin order: $t_{2g}^6 e_g^1$. Hence there is 1 electron in the $e_g$ orbital.
Q146.stepsLatex:
In [Co(CN)6]4−, Co is +2 (d7). With strong-field CN−, low-spin configuration is t6 e1. Number
2g g
of electrons in eg orbital = 1.
Q146.trapHtml: Notice the complex charge is 4− (Co<sup>2+</sup>, d<sup>7</sup>), not 3− (Co<sup>3+</sup>, d<sup>6</sup>).

Q147.conceptHtml: Among the five: K<sub>3</sub>[Co(NO<sub>2</sub>)<sub>6</sub>] (yellow, Co<sup>3+</sup>, d<sup>6</sup> LS, n = 0), K<sub>4</sub>[Fe(CN)<sub>6</sub>] (pale yellow, Fe<sup>2+</sup>, d<sup>6</sup> LS, n = 0), K<sub>3</sub>[Fe(CN)<sub>6</sub>] (red), Cu<sub>2</sub>[Fe(CN)<sub>6</sub>] (chocolate brown), Zn<sub>2</sub>[Fe(CN)<sub>6</sub>] (white).
Q147.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the colours of the five given complexes:
    • $\text{K}_3[\text{Co(NO}_2)_6]$ (Fischer's salt): yellow.
    • $\text{K}_4[\text{Fe(CN)}_6]$ (potassium ferrocyanide): yellow.
    • $\text{K}_3[\text{Fe(CN)}_6]$: red / orange-red.
    • $\text{Cu}_2[\text{Fe(CN)}_6]$: chocolate brown.
    • $\text{Zn}_2[\text{Fe(CN)}_6]$: white.
  2. Step 2 — Find spin-only magnetic moments of the yellow complexes: In $\text{K}_3[\text{Co(NO}_2)_6]$, $\text{Co}^{3+}$ ($3d^6$, low-spin $t_{2g}^6 e_g^0$) has $n = 0 \Rightarrow \mu = 0\text{ BM}$. In $\text{K}_4[\text{Fe(CN)}_6]$, $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ ($3d^6$, low-spin $t_{2g}^6 e_g^0$) also has $n = 0 \Rightarrow \mu = 0\text{ BM}$.
  3. Step 3 — Sum & confirm the exact answer: The sum of spin-only magnetic moments of the yellow complexes is $0 + 0 =$ 0 BM.

of their spin-only magnetic moments is 0 + 0 = 0 BM.

Q148.conceptHtml: Dimethylglyoxime (H<sub>2</sub>dmg) is CH<sub>3</sub> − C(=NOH) − C(=NOH) − CH<sub>3</sub> (C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub>N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>). On monodeprotona- tion, Hdmg<sup>−</sup> is C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>7</sub>N<sub>2</sub>O<sup>−</sup><sub>2</sub> (7 H atoms).
Q148.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Write the formula of the complex: $\text{Ni}^{2+}$ reacts with two molecules of dimethylglyoxime ($\text{dmgH}_2$, $\text{C}_4\text{H}_8\text{N}_2\text{O}_2$) in slightly alkaline medium to form the rosy-red chelate $[\text{Ni(dmgH)}_2]$ by losing one $\text{H}^+$ per ligand.
  2. Step 2 — Count hydrogen atoms per $\text{dmgH}^-$ ligand: Each $\text{dmgH}^-$ ligand has two $-\text{CH}_3$ groups ($6\text{ H}$) and one $-\text{OH}$ group ($1\text{ H}$, involved in intramolecular H-bonding), giving $7$ hydrogen atoms per ligand ($\text{C}_4\text{H}_7\text{N}_2\text{O}_2^-$).
  3. Step 3 — Multiply & confirm the exact answer: With $2$ $\text{dmgH}^-$ ligands in $[\text{Ni(dmgH)}_2]$, the total number of hydrogen atoms is $2 \times 7 =$ 14.

(12 from four CH3 groups +2 from two O − H · · · O bridges).

Q149.conceptHtml: Ambidentate ligands can coordinate through either of two different donor atoms.
Q149.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall what an ambidentate ligand is: An ambidentate ligand is a monodentate ligand that possesses two different donor atoms and can coordinate through either one (but only one at a time).
  2. Step 2 — Check each listed ligand:
    • $\text{NO}_2^-$: binds via $\text{N}$ or $\text{O}$ (ambidentate).
    • $\text{SCN}^-$: binds via $\text{S}$ or $\text{N}$ (ambidentate).
    • $\text{CN}^-$: binds via $\text{C}$ or $\text{N}$ (ambidentate).
    • $\text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-}$ (bidentate via two O), $\text{SO}_4^{2-}$ (only O donors), $\text{NH}_3$ (only N), and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ (only O) are NOT ambidentate.
  3. Step 3 — Count & confirm the exact answer: There are 3 ambidentate ligands ($\text{NO}_2^-$, $\text{SCN}^-$, and $\text{CN}^-$).

Ambidentate (3): NO− (N/O), SCN− (S/N), CN− (C/N). Non-ambidentate (4): C2O2−,
2 4
NH3, SO2−, H2O. Count = 3.
4

Q150.conceptHtml: [Co(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup> (d<sup>6</sup> LS) has n = 0; [NiCl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2−</sup> (d<sup>8</sup>, T<sub>d</sub>) has n = 2.
Q150.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Find unpaired electrons in $[\text{Co(NH}_3)_6]^{3+}$: $\text{Co}^{3+}$ is $3d^6$. With strong-field $\text{NH}_3$, it is low-spin ($t_{2g}^6 e_g^0$), so $n_1 = 0$.
  2. Step 2 — Find unpaired electrons in $[\text{NiCl}_4]^{2-}$: $\text{Ni}^{2+}$ is $3d^8$. With weak-field $\text{Cl}^-$, it forms a tetrahedral complex ($e^4 t_2^4$), so $n_2 = 2$.
  3. Step 3 — Sum & confirm the exact answer: Total unpaired electrons $= 0 + 2 =$ 2.

Q151.subtopic: Numerical — Magnetic Moment of MO24− (Least Metallic
Q151.format: Numerical | Mn vs Cr radius + MnO<sup>2</sup><sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup> vs CrO<sup>2</sup><sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup>
Q151.conceptHtml: Among Sc, Ti, V, Cr, Mn, Zn, metallic radii (NCERT d-block): Sc (164), Ti (147), V (135), Cr (129), Mn (137), Zn (137 pm). Thus M = Cr (least metallic radius)!
Q151.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify metal $M$ with the least metallic radius: Across the $3d$ series, metallic radii decrease from Sc ($164\text{ pm}$) to Ti ($147\text{ pm}$) to V ($135\text{ pm}$) to Cr ($129\text{ pm}$), then rise at Mn ($137\text{ pm}$) and Zn ($137\text{ pm}$). Thus $M = \text{Cr}$.
  2. Step 2 — Find the oxidation state and $d$-electrons in $\text{CrO}_4^{2-}$: $x + 4(-2) = -2 \Rightarrow x = +6$. Since $\text{Cr}$ is $[\text{Ar}]3d^5 4s^1$, $\text{Cr}^{6+}$ has a $3d^0$ configuration with $n = 0$ unpaired electrons.
  3. Step 3 — Calculate $\mu$ & conclude: $\mu = \sqrt{0(0+2)} =$ 0 BM.
Q151.stepsLatex:
CrO2− has Cr6+ (d0, 0 unpaired electrons) =⇒ µ = 0 BM.
4
Q151.trapHtml: In 3d metals, Mn has a larger metallic radius (137 pm) than Cr (129 pm) due to weaker metallic bonding from half-filled d<sup>5</sup>!

Q152.subtopic: Numerical — ∆µ in KMnO4 vs Oxalic Acid Titration
Q152.conceptHtml: In acidic medium, MnO<sup>−</sup><sub>4</sub> (Mn<sup>7+</sup>, d<sup>0</sup> =⇒ µ = 0) is reduced to Mn<sup>2+</sup> (d<sup>5</sup> HS =⇒ n = 5, µ = 5.92 BM).
Q152.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Find $\mu$ for $\text{KMnO}_4$: In $\text{KMnO}_4$, Mn is in the $+7$ oxidation state ($3d^0$), giving $n = 0$ unpaired electrons and $\mu_1 = 0\text{ BM}$.
  2. Step 2 — Find $\mu$ for the manganese product in acidic titration: During titration against oxalic acid in acidic medium, $\text{MnO}_4^-$ is reduced to $\text{Mn}^{2+}$ ($3d^5$, $n = 5$ unpaired electrons). Thus $\mu_2 = \sqrt{5(5+2)} = \sqrt{35} \approx 5.92\text{ BM}$.
  3. Step 3 — Take the difference & conclude: $|\mu_2 - \mu_1| = 5.92 - 0 = 5.92\text{ BM}$, which rounds to the nearest integer 6.

Q153.subtopic: Numerical — Magnetic Moment of Strong Oxidising Agent
Q153.conceptHtml: Among Ti<sup>2+</sup>, V<sup>2+</sup>, Co<sup>3+</sup>, Cr<sup>2+</sup>, Co<sup>3+</sup> is a very strong oxidising agent (E<sup>°</sup>(Co<sup>3+</sup>/Co<sup>2+</sup>) = +1.97 V). Wait: [Co(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup> is diamagnetic (n = 0), whereas free Co<sup>3+</sup> (3d<sup>6</sup>) has n = 4 (µ = 4.90 ≈ 5 BM)!
Q153.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the strong oxidising agent in aqueous solution: $\text{Ti}^{2+}$, $\text{V}^{2+}$, and $\text{Cr}^{2+}$ are strong reducing agents (easily oxidised to $+3$). By contrast, $\text{Co}^{3+}$ has a very high reduction potential ($E^\circ(\text{Co}^{3+}/\text{Co}^{2+}) = +1.97\text{ V}$) and acts as a strong oxidising agent.
  2. Step 2 — Find unpaired electrons in $\text{Co}^{3+}$: Cobalt ($Z = 27$) is $[\text{Ar}]3d^7 4s^2$, so $\text{Co}^{3+}$ is $3d^6$. As a free ion (high-spin $3d^6$), it has $n = 4$ unpaired electrons.
  3. Step 3 — Compute $\mu$ & conclude: $\mu = \sqrt{4(4+2)} = \sqrt{24} \approx 4.90\text{ BM}$, which rounds to the nearest integer 5.
Q153.stepsLatex:
For free Co3+ ion (3d6), Hund’s rule gives n = 4 unpaired electrons =⇒ µ = p4(4 + 2) =
√
24 = 4.90 BM ≈ 5 BM (nearest integer).
Q153.trapHtml: The question asks for the free ion Co<sup>3+</sup> (d<sup>6</sup>, n = 4 =⇒ 4.90 ≈ 5 BM), NOT the aqua complex [Co(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup>!

Q154.conceptHtml: Ni<sup>2+</sup> (d<sup>8</sup>) in octahedral field is always t<sup>6</sup><sub>2g</sub>e<sup>2</sup><sub>g</sub> (n = 2).
Q154.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Determine the $d$-electron configuration of Ni: In $[\text{Ni(NH}_3)_6]^{2+}$, $\text{NH}_3$ is neutral, so Ni is in the $+2$ oxidation state: $\text{Ni}^{2+} = [\text{Ar}]3d^8$.
  2. Step 2 — Count unpaired electrons in an octahedral field: Any octahedral $d^8$ complex has the unique configuration $t_{2g}^6 e_g^2$ regardless of ligand strength, giving $n = 2$ unpaired electrons.
  3. Step 3 — Compute $\mu$ & format the answer: $\mu = \sqrt{2(2+2)} = \sqrt{8} \approx 2.83\text{ BM} = 28.3 \times 10^{-1}\text{ BM}$. Rounding to the nearest integer gives 28.
Q154.trapHtml: Express in ×10<sup>−1</sup> BM and round to nearest integer (28.3 → 28).

Q155.format: Numerical | cis-M(AA)<sub>2</sub>a<sub>2</sub> and M(AA)<sub>3</sub> are chiral
Q155.conceptHtml: cis-M(AA)<sub>2</sub>a<sub>2</sub> and M(AA)<sub>3</sub> lack planes/centres of symmetry (optically active); trans-M(AA)<sub>2</sub>a<sub>2</sub> has a plane of symmetry (inactive).
Q155.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall optical activity rules for octahedral bidentate complexes: Tris-bidentate $[M(AA)_3]$ and $cis\text{-[M(AA)}_2\text{X}_2]$ complexes lack a plane and centre of symmetry and are optically active, whereas $trans\text{-[M(AA)}_2\text{X}_2]$ complexes possess both symmetry elements and are optically inactive.
  2. Step 2 — Classify each of the six complexes:
    • Optically active: $cis\text{-[Cr(ox)}_2\text{Cl}_2]^{3-}$, $[\text{Co(en)}_3]^{3+}$, $cis\text{-[Pt(en)}_2\text{Cl}_2]^{2+}$, and $cis\text{-[Co(en)}_2\text{Cl}_2]^+$ ($4$ complexes).
    • Optically inactive: $trans\text{-[Pt(en)}_2\text{Cl}_2]^{2+}$ and $trans\text{-[Cr(ox)}_2\text{Cl}_2]^{3-}$ ($2$ complexes).
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the exact answer: The number of complexes showing optical isomerism is 4.
Q155.stepsLatex:
Optically active (4): cis-[Cr(ox)2Cl2]3−, [Co(en)3]3+, cis-[Pt(en)2Cl2]2+, cis-[Co(en)2Cl2]+.
Optically inactive (2): trans-[Pt(en)2Cl2]2+, trans-[Cr(ox)2Cl2]3−. Count = 4.
Q155.trapHtml: trans isomers of M(AA)<sub>2</sub>a<sub>2</sub> are always optically inactive.

Q156.conceptHtml: All square planar d<sup>8</sup> complexes are diamagnetic (n = 0).
Q156.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Determine the oxidation state of Pt: In $[\text{Pt(NH}_3)_2\text{Cl(NH}_2\text{CH}_3)]\text{Cl}$, $\text{NH}_3$ and $\text{NH}_2\text{CH}_3$ are neutral while each $\text{Cl}^-$ has $-1$ charge. Thus $x + 0 - 1 + 0 - 1 = 0 \Rightarrow x = +2$, so $\text{Pt}^{2+}$ is $5d^8$.
  2. Step 2 — Determine unpaired electrons in square planar geometry: In a square planar $5d^8$ complex ($dsp^2$), crystal field splitting is large and all $8$ $d$-electrons occupy the four lower-energy $d$-orbitals in pairs, leaving the high-energy $d_{x^2-y^2}$ orbital empty ($n = 0$).
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the exact answer: With $n = 0$, the spin-only magnetic moment is $\mu =$ 0 BM.
Q156.stepsLatex:
Pt2+ (5d8) in square planar field pairs all 8 electrons in the lower 4 orbitals (dxz, dyz, dz2, dxy),
leaving dx2−y2 empty =⇒ n = 0 =⇒ µ = 0 BM.
Q156.trapHtml: Square planar d<sup>8</sup> is always diamagnetic.

Q157.subtopic: Numerical — Unpaired Electrons in t2g of [Co(H2O)6]2+
Q157.conceptHtml: Co<sup>2+</sup> (d<sup>7</sup>) with weak-field H<sub>2</sub>O is high-spin: t<sup>5</sup><sub>2g</sub>e<sup>2</sup><sub>g</sub>.
Q157.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Write the complex formula and $d$-electron count: The homoleptic octahedral complex of $\text{Co}^{2+}$ with $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ is $[\text{Co(H}_2\text{O)}_6]^{2+}$, where $\text{Co}^{2+}$ has a $3d^7$ configuration.
  2. Step 2 — Write the high-spin octahedral configuration: Since $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ is a weak-field ligand for $\text{Co}^{2+}$, the electrons distribute as high-spin $t_{2g}^5 e_g^2$.
  3. Step 3 — Count unpaired electrons in $t_{2g}$ & conclude: Putting $5$ electrons into the $3$ orbitals of the $t_{2g}$ set gives two paired orbitals and one singly occupied orbital ($\uparrow\downarrow, \uparrow\downarrow, \uparrow$). Hence there is 1 unpaired electron in $t_{2g}$.
Q157.stepsLatex:
In t5 (2 paired pairs +1 single electron), there is 1 unpaired electron in t2g (and 2 in eg).
2g
Q157.trapHtml: Read carefully: unpaired electrons in the t<sub>2g</sub> set only (1), not total unpaired electrons (3)!

Q158.conceptHtml: For d<sup>3</sup> (Cr<sup>3+</sup>), all 3 electrons occupy separate t<sub>2g</sub> orbitals (t<sup>3</sup><sub>2g</sub>e<sup>0</sup><sub>g</sub>) regardless of ligand strength!
Q158.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Find the oxidation state and $d$-count of Cr in both complexes: In $[\text{Cr(CN)}_6]^{3-}$, $x - 6 = -3 \Rightarrow x = +3$. In $[\text{Cr(H}_2\text{O)}_6]^{3+}$, $x + 0 = +3 \Rightarrow x = +3$. Thus both contain $\text{Cr}^{3+}$ ($3d^3$).
  2. Step 2 — Compare unpaired electrons: In an octahedral field, a $3d^3$ ion always has the configuration $t_{2g}^3 e_g^0$ ($n = 3$ unpaired electrons) regardless of whether the ligand is strong-field ($\text{CN}^-$) or weak-field ($\text{H}_2\text{O}$).
  3. Step 3 — Take the ratio & conclude: Both complexes have $\mu_{\text{eff}} = \sqrt{3(3+2)} = \sqrt{15}\text{ BM}$, so their ratio is $\frac{\sqrt{15}}{\sqrt{15}} =$ 1.
Q158.stepsLatex:
Both complexes have n = 3 (µ = 15 BM), so the ratio is √15 = 1.
15
Q158.trapHtml: d<sup>3</sup> never pairs—its unpaired count is 3 for both strong and weak ligands.

Q159.subtopic: Numerical — Unpaired Electrons from µ = 4.90 BM
Q159.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Apply the spin-only magnetic moment formula: $\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)}\text{ BM}$, where $n$ is the number of unpaired electrons.
  2. Step 2 — Solve for $n$: Squaring both sides gives $n(n+2) = (4.90)^2 \approx 24.01 \approx 24$.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the exact answer: Since $4 \times (4 + 2) = 24$, the metal ion has 4 unpaired electrons.
Q159.trapHtml: Nearest integer rule shortcut: µ ≈ n + 0.9 for n = 1..5, so the integer part of 4.90 is 4!

Q160.subtopic: Numerical — Electron Pairs in t2g of K4[Fe(CN)6]
Q160.conceptHtml: In potassium ferrocyanide K<sub>4</sub>[Fe(CN)<sub>6</sub>], Fe<sup>2+</sup> (d<sup>6</sup>) with strong-field CN<sup>−</sup> is t<sup>6</sup><sub>2g</sub>e<sup>0</sup><sub>g</sub>.
Q160.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Write the formula and oxidation state: Potassium ferrocyanide is $\text{K}_4[\text{Fe(CN)}_6]$, in which iron is in the $+2$ oxidation state ($\text{Fe}^{2+} = 3d^6$).
  2. Step 2 — Determine the crystal field configuration: $\text{CN}^-$ is a strong-field ligand, so all $6$ $d$-electrons pair in the lower $t_{2g}$ orbitals to give $t_{2g}^6 e_g^0$.
  3. Step 3 — Count electron pairs & conclude: Six paired electrons in three $t_{2g}$ orbitals correspond to $\frac{6}{2} =$ 3 pairs of electrons.
Q160.stepsLatex: 6 electrons in three t<sub>2g</sub> orbitals form 3 pairs of electrons.

Q161.subtopic: Numerical — Charge x on [Mn(NCS)6]x− from µ = 6.06 BM
Q161.conceptHtml: µ ≈ 6.0 BM =⇒ n = 5 unpaired electrons =⇒ Mn<sup>2+</sup> (d<sup>5</sup> high-spin).
Q161.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Deduce unpaired electrons from $\mu_{\text{obs}}$: An observed magnetic moment of $6.06\text{ BM}$ is closest to the spin-only value for $n = 5$ unpaired electrons ($\sqrt{5(5+2)} = \sqrt{35} \approx 5.92\text{ BM}$).
  2. Step 2 — Identify the oxidation state of Mn: With weak-field $\text{NCS}^-$ ligands in an octahedral complex, $\text{Mn}^{2+}$ ($3d^5$, high-spin $t_{2g}^3 e_g^2$) provides exactly $5$ unpaired electrons.
  3. Step 3 — Compute charge $x$ & conclude: Each $\text{NCS}^-$ carries a $-1$ charge, so the overall charge on $[\text{Mn(NCS)}_6]^{x-}$ is $+2 + 6(-1) = -4$. Therefore, $x =$ 4.
Q161.stepsLatex: With Mn in +2 oxidation state and six NCS− (−1 each): +2 + 6(−1) = −4 =⇒ x = 4.
Q161.trapHtml: Note Mn is +2 (d<sup>5</sup>), giving −4 total charge.

Q162.conceptHtml: en is a bidentate chelating ligand (not ambidentate); SCN<sup>−</sup> is ambidentate (S or N donor).
Q162.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Check each ligand type in $[\text{M(en)(SCN)}_4]$: Ethylenediamine ($\text{en}$) is a symmetrical bidentate ligand (coordinates via both N atoms simultaneously) and is NOT ambidentate. Thiocyanate ($\text{SCN}^-$) is an ambidentate ligand because it can coordinate through either S or N.
  2. Step 2 — Count the ambidentate ligands present: The formula $[\text{M(en)(SCN)}_4]$ contains $4$ $\text{SCN}^-$ ligands.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the exact answer: The number of ambidentate ligands in the complex is 4.
Q162.stepsLatex: There are 4 ambidentate SCN− ligands in [M(en)(SCN)<sub>4</sub>].
Q162.trapHtml: Count the stoichiometry (4 SCN<sup>−</sup> ligands), not just the number of types (1).

Q163.conceptHtml: Mn<sup>2+</sup> (d<sup>5</sup>) with weak-field H<sub>2</sub>O is high-spin (t<sup>3</sup><sub>2g</sub>e<sup>2</sup><sub>g</sub>, n = 5).
Q163.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Determine the $d$-electron configuration of Mn: In $[\text{Mn(H}_2\text{O)}_6]^{2+}$, Mn is in the $+2$ oxidation state: $\text{Mn}^{2+} = [\text{Ar}]3d^5$.
  2. Step 2 — Count unpaired electrons: $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ is a weak-field ligand for $\text{Mn}^{2+}$, yielding a high-spin octahedral configuration $t_{2g}^3 e_g^2$ with $n = 5$ unpaired electrons.
  3. Step 3 — Calculate $\mu$ & conclude: $\mu = \sqrt{5(5+2)} = \sqrt{35} \approx 5.92\text{ BM}$. Rounding to the nearest integer gives 6.

Q164.subtopic: Numerical — Absorption Wavelength from CFSE of
Q164.conceptHtml: For Ti<sup>3+</sup> (d<sup>1</sup>), t<sup>1</sup><sub>2g</sub>e<sup>0</sup><sub>g</sub> has CFSE = −0.4∆<sub>o</sub>, so ∆<sub>o</sub> = <sup>9</sup><sub>0</sub><sup>6</sup><sub>.</sub><sup>.</sup><sub>4</sub><sup>0</sup> = 240 kJ/mol.
Q164.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Relate CFSE to $\Delta_o$ for $[\text{Ti(H}_2\text{O)}_6]^{3+}$: $\text{Ti}^{3+}$ has a $3d^1$ ($t_{2g}^1 e_g^0$) configuration, so $\text{CFSE} = -0.4\Delta_o$. Given $\text{CFSE} = -96.0\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$, we get $\Delta_o = \frac{96.0}{0.4} = 240\text{ kJ mol}^{-1} = 2.4 \times 10^5\text{ J mol}^{-1}$.
  2. Step 2 — Relate molar splitting energy $\Delta_o$ to wavelength $\lambda$: Using $\Delta_o = \frac{N_A h c}{\lambda}$, solve for $\lambda$: $\lambda = \frac{N_A h c}{\Delta_o}$.
  3. Step 3 — Substitute values & conclude: $\lambda = \frac{(6 \times 10^{23}) \times (6.4 \times 10^{-34}) \times (3.0 \times 10^8)}{2.4 \times 10^5} = \frac{115.2 \times 10^{-3}}{2.4 \times 10^5} = 48 \times 10^{-8}\text{ m} = 480 \times 10^{-9}\text{ m} =$ 480 nm.
Q164.trapHtml: Classic trap: CFSE = −0.4∆<sub>o</sub>, so divide 96.0 by 0.4 to get ∆<sub>o</sub> = 240 kJ/mol before using λ = hc/∆<sub>o</sub>!

Q165.subtopic: Numerical — Denticity of Ligand in Fehling’s Reagent
Q165.conceptHtml: Fehling’s B contains Rochelle salt (sodium potassium tartrate); in alkaline Cu<sup>2+</sup> complex [Cu(tartrate)<sub>2</sub>]<sup>2−</sup>, each tartrate dianion (or tetranion) coordinates via two carboxylate O atoms and two deprotonated alkoxide O atoms (or 2 carboxylate + 2 OH). Wait: check NTA key!
Q165.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the ligand in Fehling's reagent: Fehling's solution B contains alkaline sodium potassium tartrate (Rochelle salt), which supplies the tartrate ligand to complex $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ and prevent $\text{Cu(OH)}_2$ precipitation.
  2. Step 2 — Count the donor atoms of the tartrate ligand: The tartrate ion ($^-\text{OOC}-\text{CH(OH)}-\text{CH(OH)}-\text{COO}^-$) has $4$ oxygen donor sites (two carboxylate oxygens and two hydroxyl/alkoxide oxygens) that can coordinate to metal centres.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the exact answer: Therefore, the denticity of the tartrate ligand in Fehling's reagent is 4.

In alkaline Fehling’s solution, tartrate acts as a tetradentate ligand (coordinating via
2 −COO− and 2 −O− groups, denticity = 4) — or in bis(tartrato)cuprate(II), each tartrate binds through 4
O-donor sites (two chelated Cu2+ or 4 donor atoms). Official NTA key is 4.

Q166.subtopic: Numerical — Bridging Carbonyls in W(CO)6 & Mn2(CO)10
Q166.conceptHtml: Both W(CO)<sub>6</sub> (mononuclear octahedral) and Mn<sub>2</sub>(CO)<sub>10</sub> (binuclear with Mn − Mn bond) have zero bridging CO ligands.
Q166.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Check bridging carbonyls in $\text{W(CO)}_6$: $\text{W(CO)}_6$ is a mononuclear octahedral carbonyl containing only $1$ metal atom, so all $6$ $\text{CO}$ ligands are terminal ($0$ bridging carbonyls).
  2. Step 2 — Check bridging carbonyls in $\text{Mn}_2(\text{CO})_{10}$: Dimanganese decacarbonyl consists of two square-pyramidal $\text{Mn(CO)}_5$ units joined directly by a single $\text{Mn}-\text{Mn}$ metallic bond, with all $10$ $\text{CO}$ ligands terminal ($0$ bridging carbonyls).
  3. Step 3 — Sum & confirm the exact answer: The sum of bridging carbonyls is $0 + 0 =$ 0.
Q166.trapHtml: Remember: Mn<sub>2</sub>(CO)<sub>10</sub> has NO bridging CO, unlike Co<sub>2</sub>(CO)<sub>8</sub> (2) and Fe<sub>2</sub>(CO)<sub>9</sub> (3).

Q167.subtopic: Numerical — Total AgCl Precipitated from 4 Complexes
Q167.format: Numerical | Sum of outer-sphere Cl<sup>−</sup> ions
Q167.conceptHtml: Only counter-ion Cl<sup>−</sup> outside the square bracket precipitates with AgNO<sub>3</sub>.
Q167.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall which chloride ions precipitate with $\text{AgNO}_3$: Only ionisable $\text{Cl}^-$ counter-ions located outside the square coordination bracket react with excess $\text{AgNO}_3$ to form $\text{AgCl}$.
  2. Step 2 — Count ionisable $\text{Cl}^-$ per mole of each complex:
    • $[\text{Co(NH}_3)_4\text{Cl}_2]\text{Cl}$: $1\text{ mol}$ $\text{AgCl}$.
    • $[\text{Ni(H}_2\text{O)}_6]\text{Cl}_2$: $2\text{ mol}$ $\text{AgCl}$.
    • $[\text{Pt(NH}_3)_2\text{Cl}_2]$: $0\text{ mol}$ $\text{AgCl}$.
    • $[\text{Pd(NH}_3)_4]\text{Cl}_2$: $2\text{ mol}$ $\text{AgCl}$.
  3. Step 3 — Sum & confirm the exact answer: Total moles of $\text{AgCl}$ precipitated $= 1 + 2 + 0 + 2 =$ 5.
Q167.trapHtml: [Pt(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>] is neutral and gives 0 mol AgCl.

Q168.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Check the nickel and copper complexes:
    • $[\text{Ni(CN)}_4]^{2-}$ ($\text{Ni}^{2+}, d^8$, square planar): $n = 0$ (diamagnetic).
    • $[\text{Ni(CO)}_4]$ ($\text{Ni}(0), d^{10}$, tetrahedral): $n = 0$ (diamagnetic).
    • $[\text{NiCl}_4]^{2-}$ ($\text{Ni}^{2+}, d^8$, tetrahedral): $n = 2$ (paramagnetic).
    • $[\text{Cu(NH}_3)_4]^{2+}$ ($\text{Cu}^{2+}, d^9$, square planar): $n = 1$ (paramagnetic).
  2. Step 2 — Check the iron complexes:
    • $[\text{Fe(CN)}_6]^{4-}$ ($\text{Fe}^{2+}, d^6$, low-spin $t_{2g}^6 e_g^0$): $n = 0$ (diamagnetic).
    • $[\text{Fe(CN)}_6]^{3-}$ ($\text{Fe}^{3+}, d^5$, low-spin $t_{2g}^5 e_g^0$): $n = 1$ (paramagnetic).
    • $[\text{Fe(H}_2\text{O)}_6]^{2+}$ ($\text{Fe}^{2+}, d^6$, high-spin $t_{2g}^4 e_g^2$): $n = 4$ (paramagnetic).
  3. Step 3 — Count & confirm the exact answer: The paramagnetic species are $[\text{NiCl}_4]^{2-}$, $[\text{Cu(NH}_3)_4]^{2+}$, $[\text{Fe(CN)}_6]^{3-}$, and $[\text{Fe(H}_2\text{O)}_6]^{2+}$, giving a total of 4.

Q169.conceptHtml: In [CoCl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2−</sup>, Co<sup>2+</sup> is d<sup>7</sup> in a tetrahedral field (e lower, t<sub>2</sub> higher, always high-spin).
Q169.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Find the oxidation state and $d$-electron count of Co: In $[\text{CoCl}_4]^{2-}$, $x + 4(-1) = -2 \Rightarrow x = +2$, so $\text{Co}^{2+}$ has a $3d^7$ configuration.
  2. Step 2 — Fill the tetrahedral crystal field orbitals: In a tetrahedral field, splitting $\Delta_t$ is always smaller than pairing energy $P$, so all tetrahedral complexes are high-spin. Filling $7$ electrons into lower $e$ (2 orbitals) and higher $t_2$ (3 orbitals) gives $e^4 t_2^3$.
  3. Step 3 — Extract $m$ and unpaired electrons & conclude: Comparing $e^4 t_2^3$ with $e^m t_2^n$ gives $m = 4$. All $4$ electrons in $e$ are paired, while the $3$ electrons in $t_2$ are unpaired ($3$ unpaired electrons). Thus the sum is $4 + 3 =$ 7.
Q169.stepsLatex:
Configuration is e4t3, so m = 4 and number of unpaired electrons = 3. Sum = 4 + 3 = 7.
2
Q169.trapHtml: In tetrahedral d<sup>7</sup> (e<sup>4</sup>t<sup>3</sup><sub>2</sub>), all 3 unpaired electrons are in t<sub>2</sub>.

formulaCards.title: 1. Dry Tests: Flame & Borax Bead Tests ⋆ High- ROI
formulaCards.html:
• Flame Test (conc. HCl paste on Pt wire): – Na+: Golden Yellow | K+: Lilac / Violet – Ca2+: Brick Red | Sr2+: Crimson Red – Ba2+: Apple Green | Cu2+: Bluish-Green (green flame with blue centre) – No characteristic flame: Mg2+, Be2+, Zn2+, Fe2+, Co2+.
  • Borax Bead Test (Na2B4O7 · 10H2O −∆→ 2NaBO2 + B2O3): B2O3 forms coloured metaborates M(BO2)n in outer oxidising (non-luminous) flame, reduced to lower OS / metal in inner reducing (luminous) flame: – Cu2+: Oxidising → Green (hot), Sky Blue (cold) as Cu(BO2)2; Reducing → Colourless (hot) as CuBO2, Opaque Red (cold, Cu). – Fe3+/Fe2+: Oxidising → Yellow/Brown (hot), Pale Yellow (cold); Reducing → Bottle Green (hot & cold). – Cr3+: Green (hot & cold, both flames). – Mn2+: Oxidising → Violet / Amethyst (hot & cold); Reducing → Colourless. – Co2+: Deep Blue (hot & cold, both flames). – Ni2+: Oxidising → Reddish-Brown (cold); Reducing → Grey.
  • Charcoal Cavity + Na2CO3 / Co(NO3)2 Test: MSO −N−−a2−C−O−3−,−∆→ MCO → MO → M. With Co(NO ) : 3+4 3 2+ 3 2 Al gives Thenard’s Blue (CoO · Al2O3); Zn gives Rin- mann’s Green (CoO · ZnO); Mg2+ gives Pink.

formulaCards.title: 2. Cation Groups 0–VI: Reagents & Precipitates
formulaCards.html:
• Group 0 (NH+4 ): NaOH + heat → NH3(g). With Nessler’s reagent (K2HgI4 + KOH): brown ppt of H2N · HgO · HgI (iodide of Millon’s base).
  • Group I (Pb2+, Ag+, Hg22+): Reagent = dil. HCl. Pre- cipitates white chlorides: PbCl2 (soluble in hot water), AgCl (curdy white, soluble in NH4OH as [Ag(NH3)2]Cl), Hg2Cl2 (blackens with NH4OH).
  • Group II (Pb2+, Cu2+, Bi3+, Cd2+, Hg2+, As3+, Sb3+, Sn2+ Reagent = H2S in dil. HCl (common ion H+ suppresses [S2−] so only low-Ksp sulphides ppt). – Black: PbS, CuS, HgS, Bi2S3 (brownish-black). – Yellow: CdS, As2S3, As2S5, SnS2. Orange: Sb2S3. Brown: SnS.
  • Group III (Fe3+, Al3+, Cr3+): Reagent = NH4OH in presence of NH4Cl. NH+4 suppresses [OH−] via common ion effect so Group IV/V/Mg2+ do not ppt. – Fe(OH)3: Reddish-brown | Al(OH)3: Gelatinous white | Cr(OH)3: Dirty green.
  • Group IV (Co2+, Ni2+, Mn2+, Zn2+): Reagent = H2S in NH4OH (+NH4Cl). High [S2−] precipitates higher- Ksp sulphides: – CoS, NiS: Black (dissolve in aqua regia) | MnS: Buff/Flesh-pink | ZnS: Dirty white.
  • Group V (Ba2+, Sr2+, Ca2+): Reagent = (NH4)2CO3 in NH4OH + NH4Cl. White carbon- ates BaCO3, SrCO3, CaCO3; dissolved in acetic acid and tested sequentially: K2CrO4 ppts BaCrO4 (yellow), (NH4)2SO4 ppts SrSO4 (white), (NH4)2C2O4 ppts CaC2O4 (white).
  • Group VI (Mg2+): NH4OH + Na2HPO4 → white crys- talline ppt of Mg(NH4)PO4.

formulaCards.title: 4. Anion Analysis: Dilute H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> Group
formulaCards.html:
• CO23−: Colourless, odourless CO2 with brisk efferves- cence; turns lime water milky (CaCO3), excess gives solu- ble Ca(HCO3)2.
  • S2−: Rotten-egg smelling H2S; turns lead acetate pa- per black (PbS); sodium carbonate extract + sodium nitroprusside (Na2[Fe(CN)5NO]) gives purple/violet Na4[Fe(CN)5NOS].
  • SO23−: Pungent SO2 (burning sulphur); turns acidi- fied K2Cr2O7 paper/solution green (Cr3+); gives white BaSO3 with BaCl2 that dissolves in dil. HCl liberating SO2.
  • NO−2 : Reddish-brown NO2 fumes; turns acidified KI- starch paper blue; Griess-Ilosvay test: sulphanilic acid + NO−2 /H+ (diazotisation) + α-naphthylamine → red azo- dye.
  • CH3COO−: Vinegar smell (CH3COOH); neutral FeCl3 gives deep red colour → reddish-brown ppt on boiling.

formulaCards.title: 5. Anion Analysis: Conc. H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> & Independent Groups
formulaCards.html:
• Cl−: Colourless pungent HCl gas (white fumes with NH3); with MnO2 + H2SO4 → greenish-yellow Cl2 gas. – Chromyl Chloride Test: 4NaCl + K2Cr2O7 + 6H2SO4 −∆→ 2CrO2Cl2 ↑ (reddish-brown vapours, Cr in +6) + 2KHSO4 + 4NaHSO4 + 3H2O. – CrO2Cl2 + 4NaOH → Na2CrO4 (yellow) +2NaCl + 2H2O. – Acidify Na2CrO4 + H2O2 + amyl alcohol → blue organic layer of CrO5 (two O22− peroxo bridges, Cr in +6). – Fails for covalent chlorides: AgCl, Hg2Cl2, PbCl2, SnCl2.
  • Br−: Reddish-brown Br2 vapours; AgNO3 gives pale yel- low AgBr (soluble with difficulty in NH4OH).
  • I−: Violet I2 vapours; AgNO3 gives bright yellow AgI (insoluble in NH4OH).
  • F− (CaF2): Evolves colourless HF (no coloured vapours).
  • NO−3 : Conc. H2SO4 + Cu turnings → brown NO2 fumes. ): Brown Ring Test: Salt soln + freshly prepared FeSO4 + conc. H2SO4 along test-tube wall → dark brown ring of [Fe(H2O)5(NO)]SO4 at junction.
  • SO24−: BaCl2 gives white BaSO4 (insoluble in conc. HCl/HNO3).
  • PO34−: Na2CO3 extract + conc. HNO3 + ammo- nium molybdate + heat → canary yellow ppt of (NH4)3PO4 · 12MoO3.

formulaCards.title: 6. Titrimetric Primary Standards & Colour Sum- mary
formulaCards.html:
• Primary Standards (Stable, non-hygroscopic, high purity): K2Cr2O7, Oxalic acid (H2C2O4 · 2H2O), Borax (Na2B4O7 · 10H2O), Anhydrous Na2CO3, Mohr’s salt.
  • NOT Primary Standards: Na2Cr2O7 (hygroscopic), NaOH (deliquescent, absorbs CO2), FeSO4 · 6H2O (air- oxidises), KMnO4 (self-decomposes).
  • Quick White vs Yellow Salt Checklist: – White: SrSO4, PbSO4, BaSO4, Mg(NH4)PO4, Mn(OH)2, CaC2O4 – Yellow: BaCrO4, PbCrO4, PbI2, AgI, As2S3, As2S5, CdS, (NH4)3P

Q01.subtopic: Cation Group IV Reagent & Manganese OS
Q01.conceptHtml: H<sub>2</sub>S gas in the presence of NH<sub>4</sub>OH (and NH<sub>4</sub>Cl) is the Group IV reagent, precipitating Co<sup>2+</sup>, Ni<sup>2+</sup>, Mn<sup>2+</sup>, Zn<sup>2+</sup> as sulphides.
Q01.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the analytical group: Passing $\text{H}_2\text{S}$ gas in the presence of $\text{NH}_4\text{OH}$ (basic medium) is the group reagent for Group IV cations ($\text{Zn}^{2+}, \text{Mn}^{2+}, \text{Co}^{2+}, \text{Ni}^{2+}$).
  2. Step 2 — Classify the given cations: $\text{Pb}^{2+}$ belongs to Group I/II, $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ belongs to Group II (precipitated by $\text{H}_2\text{S}$ in acidic medium), $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ belongs to Group III (precipitated by $\text{NH}_4\text{OH}$ in presence of $\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$), and $\text{Mn}^{2+}$ belongs to Group IV (precipitates as buff/flesh-coloured $\text{MnS}$).
  3. Step 3 — Find the highest oxidation state of Mn: Manganese ($Z = 25$) has the ground-state electronic configuration $[\text{Ar}]\,3d^5 4s^2$. By losing all $7$ valence electrons ($2$ from $4s$ and $5$ from $3d$), it attains a maximum oxidation state of $+7$ (as in $\text{MnO}_4^-$).
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: The highest possible oxidation state is $+7$, which corresponds to option (d).

HCl), Fe3+ belongs to Group III (NH4OH + NH4Cl), and Mn2+ belongs to Group IV (H2S + NH4OH).
Step 2: Passing H2S in ammoniacal medium precipitates Mn2+ as buff/flesh-coloured MnS. Manganese ([Ar] 3d54s2)
exhibits a maximum oxidation state of +7 (as in MnO−).

Q01.trapHtml: Do not confuse Group II (H<sub>2</sub>S + dil. HCl) with Group IV (H<sub>2</sub>S + NH<sub>4</sub>OH); Fe<sup>3+</sup> precipitates as Fe(OH)<sub>3</sub> in Group III before H<sub>2</sub>S is passed. Verified Answer: (D) +7

Q02.subtopic: Flame Test, Group V & Phosphate Anion
Q02.conceptHtml: Ba<sup>2+</sup> imparts an apple green flame and forms yellow BaCrO<sub>4</sub>; PO<sup>3</sup><sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup> gives canary yellow (NH<sub>4</sub>)<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>4</sub> · 12MoO<sub>3</sub> with ammonium molybdate.
Q02.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the cation from the flame and chromate tests: An apple-green colour in the flame test is characteristic of $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ ions. Dissolving its Group V carbonate precipitate ($\text{BaCO}_3$) in acetic acid and adding $\text{K}_2\text{CrO}_4$ gives a yellow precipitate of barium chromate: $\text{Ba}^{2+} + \text{CrO}_4^{2-} \rightarrow \text{BaCrO}_4\downarrow$ (yellow).
  2. Step 2 — Identify the anion from the ammonium molybdate test: Heating the sodium carbonate extract with conc. $\text{HNO}_3$ and ammonium molybdate gives a canary-yellow precipitate of ammonium phosphomolybdate, confirming the phosphate ion ($\text{PO}_4^{3-}$): $\text{PO}_4^{3-} + 12(\text{NH}_4)_2\text{MoO}_4 + 24\text{HNO}_3 \rightarrow (\text{NH}_4)_3\text{PO}_4\cdot 12\text{MoO}_3\downarrow + 21\text{NH}_4\text{NO}_3 + 12\text{H}_2\text{O} + 3\text{NO}_3^-$.
  3. Step 3 — Combine the cation and anion: The cation is $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ and the anion is $\text{PO}_4^{3-}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: The salt contains $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ and $\text{PO}_4^{3-}$, matching option (b).

and adding K2CrO4 gives yellow BaCrO4 ppt.

precipitate of ammonium phosphomolybdate, (NH4)3PO4 · 12MoO3, confirming PO3−.
4
Q02.trapHtml: Sulphate (SO<sup>2</sup><sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup>) gives a white BaSO<sub>4</sub> ppt with BaCl<sub>2</sub>, not a canary yellow ppt with ammonium molybdate. Verified Answer: (B) Ba<sup>2+</sup> and PO<sup>3</sup><sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup>

Q03.conceptHtml: Borax decomposes on heating to NaBO<sub>2</sub> (X) and B<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> (Y ). In the oxidising (non-luminous) flame, Cu<sup>2+</sup> forms Cu(BO<sub>2</sub>)<sub>2</sub>; in the reducing (luminous) flame, it reduces to CuBO<sub>2</sub>.
Q03.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Thermal decomposition of borax: On heating, anhydrous borax decomposes into sodium metaborate ($X$) and boric anhydride ($Y$): $\text{Na}_2\text{B}_4\text{O}_7 \xrightarrow{\Delta} 2\text{NaBO}_2\,(X) + \text{B}_2\text{O}_3\,(Y)$.
  2. Step 2 — Reaction in the non-luminous (oxidising) flame: $\text{CuSO}_4$ reacts with boric anhydride ($Y$) to form blue-green copper(II) metaborate ($Z$): $\text{CuSO}_4 + \text{B}_2\text{O}_3 \rightarrow \text{Cu(BO}_2)_2\,(Z) + \text{SO}_3$. Since each $\text{BO}_2^-$ carries a $-1$ charge, the oxidation state of $\text{Cu}$ in $Z$ is $+2$.
  3. Step 3 — Reaction in the luminous (reducing) flame: In the presence of carbon, $Z$ is reduced to colourless copper(I) metaborate ($Q$): $2\text{Cu(BO}_2)_2 + 2\text{NaBO}_2 + \text{C} \rightarrow 2\text{CuBO}_2\,(Q) + \text{Na}_2\text{B}_4\text{O}_7 + \text{CO}$. Here, the oxidation state of $\text{Cu}$ in $Q$ is $+1$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: The oxidation states of $\text{Cu}$ in $Z$ and $Q$ are $+2$ and $+1$ respectively, which is option (a).

Step 1: Na2B4O7 −∆→ 2NaBO2 (X) + B2O3 (Y).
Step 2: In the non-luminous (oxidising) flame: CuSO4 + B2O3 → Cu(BO2)2 (Z) + SO3. Here Cu is in the +2
oxidation state.
Step 3: In the luminous (reducing) flame with carbon: 2Cu(BO2)2 +2NaBO2 +C → 2CuBO2 (Q)+Na2B4O7 +CO.
In CuBO2, Cu is in the +1 oxidation state.
Verified Answer: (A) +2 and +1

Q04.conceptHtml: The Griess-Ilosvay test detects NO<sup>−</sup><sub>2</sub> by diazotising sulphanilic acid in acidic medium and coupling with α-naphthylamine to produce a red azo-dye.
Q04.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement I: The Griess-Ilosvay test is a classic, highly sensitive confirmatory test for nitrite ions ($\text{NO}_2^-$). It uses Griess-Ilosvay reagent, which is a mixture of sulphanilic acid and $\alpha$-naphthylamine in acetic acid. Therefore, Statement I is true.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement II: In acidic medium, $\text{NO}_2^-$ forms nitrous acid ($\text{HNO}_2$), which diazotizes the $-\text{NH}_2$ group of sulphanilic acid to form a diazonium salt. This diazonium salt then undergoes electrophilic azo-coupling with $\alpha$-naphthylamine to produce an intense red azo-dye. Therefore, Statement II is true.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the answer: Both Statement I and Statement II are true, matching option (d).

2

Q05.conceptHtml: Group V cations (Ba<sup>2+</sup>, Sr<sup>2+</sup>, Ca<sup>2+</sup>) are precipitated as carbonates using (NH<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> in NH<sub>4</sub>OH/NH<sub>4</sub>Cl.
Q05.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the analytical group of $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ and $\text{Ca}^{2+}$: Both $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ and $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ (along with $\text{Sr}^{2+}$) belong to Group V of qualitative cation analysis.
  2. Step 2 — Recall the Group V reagent and precipitates: The group reagent for Group V is ammonium carbonate, $(\text{NH}_4)_2\text{CO}_3$, in the presence of $\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$ and $\text{NH}_4\text{OH}$. This precipitates $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ and $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ as their insoluble white carbonates: $\text{BaCO}_3\downarrow$ and $\text{CaCO}_3\downarrow$.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the answer: Both cations are precipitated as carbonate and carbonate, which corresponds to option (d).

Q06.conceptHtml: CuCl<sub>2</sub> is freely water-soluble; AgCl is sparingly soluble/insoluble at room temperature (K<sub>sp</sub> ≈ 1.8×10<sup>−10</sup>); PbCl<sub>2</sub> dissolves in hot water.
Q06.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Analyse solubility of Group I chlorides vs other chlorides: Group I cations ($\text{Ag}^+, \text{Hg}_2^{2+}, \text{Pb}^{2+}$) form sparingly soluble chlorides in cold water, whereas $\text{CuCl}_2$ (a Group II cation chloride) is freely soluble in water at room temperature. Thus $x = \text{CuCl}_2$.
  2. Step 2 — Distinguish $y$ and $z$: $\text{AgCl}$ is sparingly soluble in water at room temperature and remains insoluble even in hot water, so $y = \text{AgCl}$. In contrast, $\text{PbCl}_2$ is sparingly soluble in cold water but dissolves readily in hot water (a key step used to separate $\text{PbCl}_2$ from $\text{AgCl}$ and $\text{Hg}_2\text{Cl}_2$), so $z = \text{PbCl}_2$.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the answer: Hence $x, y, z$ are $\text{CuCl}_2, \text{AgCl}, \text{PbCl}_2$ respectively, which matches option (b).
