sparingly soluble (excludes C). Check z (soluble in hot water): PbCl2 dissolves on boiling and recrystallises as
needle-like crystals on cooling (excludes D).
Verified Answer: (B) CuCl2, AgCl and PbCl2

Q07.conceptHtml: Heating NaCl + K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> + conc. H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> evolves reddish-brown vapours of chromyl chloride, CrO<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>.
Q07.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the test and balanced reaction: Heating common salt ($\text{NaCl}$) with solid $\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$ and concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ is the chromyl chloride test for $\text{Cl}^-$ ions: $4\text{NaCl} + \text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7 + 6\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \xrightarrow{\Delta} 2\text{CrO}_2\text{Cl}_2\uparrow + 2\text{KHSO}_4 + 4\text{NaHSO}_4 + 3\text{H}_2\text{O}$.
  2. Step 2 — Identify the evolved gas: The deep reddish-brown vapours evolved are chromyl chloride, with molecular formula $\text{CrO}_2\text{Cl}_2$.
  3. Step 3 — Calculate the oxidation state of $\text{Cr}$: Let the oxidation state of $\text{Cr}$ in $\text{CrO}_2\text{Cl}_2$ be $x$. Then $x + 2(-2) + 2(-1) = 0 \implies x - 6 = 0 \implies x = +6$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: The gas is $\text{CrO}_2\text{Cl}_2$ and the oxidation state of $\text{Cr}$ is $+6$, corresponding to option (c).

Verified Answer: (C) CrO2Cl2 and +6

Q08.conceptHtml: PbCl<sub>2</sub> reacts with K<sub>2</sub>CrO<sub>4</sub> to form yellow PbCrO<sub>4</sub>, which dissolves in NaOH as Na<sub>2</sub>[Pb(OH)<sub>4</sub>]; PbSO<sub>4</sub> dissolves in CH<sub>3</sub>COONH<sub>4</sub> to form (NH<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub>[Pb(CH<sub>3</sub>COO)<sub>4</sub>].
Q08.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify compound $A$: Adding $\text{K}_2\text{CrO}_4$ to a hot aqueous solution of $\text{PbCl}_2$ gives a yellow precipitate of lead chromate ($A$): $\text{PbCl}_2 + \text{K}_2\text{CrO}_4 \rightarrow \text{PbCrO}_4\downarrow\,(A) + 2\text{KCl}$.
  2. Step 2 — Identify compound $B$: $\text{PbCrO}_4$ is amphoteric in nature and dissolves in excess $\text{NaOH}$ to form soluble sodium tetrahydroxoplumbate(II) ($B$): $\text{PbCrO}_4 + 4\text{NaOH} \rightleftharpoons \text{Na}_2[\text{Pb(OH)}_4]\,(B) + \text{Na}_2\text{CrO}_4$.
  3. Step 3 — Identify compound $X$: Insoluble white $\text{PbSO}_4$ dissolves in concentrated ammonium acetate solution by forming a soluble tetraacetatoplumbate(II) complex ($X$): $\text{PbSO}_4 + 4\text{CH}_3\text{COONH}_4 \rightarrow (\text{NH}_4)_2\text{SO}_4 + (\text{NH}_4)_2[\text{Pb(CH}_3\text{COO)}_4]\,(X)$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: Therefore $A, B, X$ are $\text{PbCrO}_4$, $\text{Na}_2[\text{Pb(OH)}_4]$, and $(\text{NH}_4)_2[\text{Pb(CH}_3\text{COO)}_4]$ respectively, matching option (c).

Verified Answer: (C) PbCrO4, Na2[Pb(OH)4] and (NH4)2[Pb(CH3COO)4]

Q09.conceptHtml: Ammonium salts release NH<sub>3</sub> on warming with NaOH, which gives a brown precipitate with alkaline K<sub>2</sub>HgI<sub>4</sub> (Nessler’s reagent).
Q09.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify gas $X$: Heating an ammonium salt (Group 0 cation, $\text{NH}_4^+$) with $\text{NaOH}$ solution liberates pungent-smelling ammonia gas ($X$): $\text{NH}_4^+ + \text{OH}^- \xrightarrow{\Delta} \text{NH}_3\uparrow\,(X) + \text{H}_2\text{O}$.
  2. Step 2 — Identify reagent $Y$: Passing $\text{NH}_3$ through Nessler's reagent—which is an alkaline solution of potassium tetraiodomercurate(II), $\text{K}_2[\text{HgI}_4] + \text{KOH}$ ($Y$)—gives a characteristic reddish-brown precipitate of iodide of Millon's base: $2\text{K}_2[\text{HgI}_4] + \text{NH}_3 + 3\text{KOH} \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{N}-\text{Hg}-\text{O}-\text{Hg}-\text{I}\downarrow\text{ (brown)} + 7\text{KI} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the answer: Thus $X = \text{NH}_3$ and $Y = \text{K}_2\text{HgI}_4 + \text{KOH}$, which corresponds to option (c).

Q10.conceptHtml: A primary standard must be pure, non-hygroscopic, non-deliquescent, air-stable, and have high molar mass.
Q10.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall criteria for a primary standard: A primary standard in volumetric (titrimetric) analysis must be available in high purity, stable in air (non-hygroscopic, non-deliquescent, not easily oxidised), and have a fixed chemical composition.
  2. Step 2 — Check each compound: A ($\text{Na}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$) is hygroscopic/deliquescent (unlike $\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$), so it cannot be a primary standard. B (Oxalic acid, $\text{H}_2\text{C}_2\text{O}_4\cdot 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$) is a standard primary standard. C ($\text{NaOH}$) is deliquescent and absorbs atmospheric $\text{CO}_2$, so it is not a primary standard. Q14.subtopic: Borax Bead & CFT Configuration of Ni2+
Q14.conceptHtml: In an octahedral crystal field, d<sup>8</sup> (Ni<sup>2+</sup>) always has the configuration t<sup>6</sup><sub>2g</sub>e<sup>2</sup><sub>g</sub> regardless of ligand field strength (strong or weak), and Ni<sup>2+</sup> gives a violet/reddish-brown borax bead in the hot non-luminous (oxidising) flame.
Q14.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Apply the crystal field electronic configuration condition: In an octahedral field, metal ions with $d^1, d^2, d^3, d^8, d^9,$ or $d^{10}$ configurations have the exact same $t_{2g}/e_g$ occupancy regardless of whether the ligand is weak-field or strong-field. Checking the options: $\text{Cr}^{3+}$ ($3d^3$), $\text{Ti}^{3+}$ ($3d^1$), and $\text{Ni}^{2+}$ ($3d^8, t_{2g}^6 e_g^2$) are unaffected by ligand nature, whereas $\text{Mn}^{2+}$ ($3d^5$) changes between high-spin ($t_{2g}^3 e_g^2$) and low-spin ($t_{2g}^5 e_g^0$) depending on the ligand—so $\text{Mn}^{2+}$ is eliminated.
  2. Step 2 — Apply the borax bead test condition: In the non-luminous (oxidising) flame under hot condition, $\text{Cr}^{3+}$ gives a green bead, $\text{Ti}^{3+}$ is colourless/not violet in hot oxidising flame, whereas $\text{Ni}^{2+}$ gives a violet (reddish-brown on cooling) borax bead.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the answer: The only ion satisfying both conditions is $\text{Ni}^{2+}$, which corresponds to option (c).

Q15.conceptHtml: CoS dissolves in aqua regia to CoCl<sub>2</sub>, which forms yellow K<sub>3</sub>[Co(NO<sub>2</sub>)<sub>6</sub>] with KNO<sub>2</sub> and CH<sub>3</sub>COOH.

Step 2 — Identify the yellow precipitate with $\text{KNO}_2$ and $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$: Treating $\text{CoCl}_2$ ($B$) with potassium nitrite in acetic acid oxidises $\text{Co}^{2+}$ to $\text{Co}^{3+}$ and forms a characteristic yellow precipitate of potassium hexanitritocobaltate(III) (Fischer's salt): $\text{CoCl}_2 + 7\text{KNO}_2 + 2\text{CH}_3\text{COOH} \rightarrow \text{K}_3[\text{Co(NO}_2)_6]\downarrow\text{ (yellow)} + \text{NO}\uparrow + 2\text{KCl} + 2\text{CH}_3\text{COOK} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$.

  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: Compound $A$ is $\text{CoS}$, matching option (d).

Q16.conceptHtml: PbS dissolves in HNO<sub>3</sub> to Pb(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>, precipitates with H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> as PbSO<sub>4</sub>, dissolves in ammonium acetate, and forms yellow PbCrO<sub>4</sub> with K<sub>2</sub>CrO<sub>4</sub>.

Step 3 — Identify $C$ from the chromate confirmation step: $\text{PbSO}_4$ dissolves in ammonium acetate to form a soluble lead acetate complex, which upon acidification with acetic acid and addition of $\text{K}_2\text{CrO}_4$ yields a yellow precipitate of lead chromate ($C$): $\text{Pb}^{2+} + \text{CrO}_4^{2-} \rightarrow \text{PbCrO}_4\downarrow\,(C)$.

Q17.conceptHtml: Borax bead uses Na<sub>2</sub>B<sub>4</sub>O<sub>7</sub>; charcoal cavity uses Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>; cobalt nitrate test forms CoO · MO; flame test converts carbonate to volatile chloride MCl<sub>2</sub>.

  2. Step 2 — Match B (Charcoal cavity test): The salt $\text{MSO}_4$ is heated with $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$ in a charcoal cavity to form $\text{MCO}_3$, which decomposes to $\text{MO}$ and is reduced by carbon to metal $\text{M}$. Hence B $\rightarrow$ IV.
  3. Step 3 — Match C (Cobalt nitrate test): Metal oxide $\text{MO}$ (from $\text{MCO}_3$) is moistened with $\text{Co(NO}_3)_2$ and heated to form a characteristic coloured double oxide $\text{CoO}\cdot\text{MO}$ (e.g., Rinmann's green $\text{CoO}\cdot\text{ZnO}$). Hence C $\rightarrow$ I.

Q22.subtopic: Common Ion Effect in Group III
Q22.conceptHtml: Adding NH<sub>4</sub>Cl suppresses the dissociation of weak base NH<sub>4</sub>OH (NH<sub>4</sub>OH ⇌ NH<sup>+</sup><sub>4</sub> + OH<sup>−</sup>) via the common ion effect, lowering [OH<sup>−</sup>].
Q22.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the dissociation equilibrium of $\text{NH}_4\text{OH}$: Ammonium hydroxide is a weak base: $\text{NH}_4\text{OH} \rightleftharpoons \text{NH}_4^+ + \text{OH}^-$.
  2. Step 2 — Apply the common ion effect: Adding solid $\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$ (a strong electrolyte, $\text{NH}_4\text{Cl} \rightarrow \text{NH}_4^+ + \text{Cl}^-$) increases $[\text{NH}_4^+]$, shifting the $\text{NH}_4\text{OH}$ equilibrium backward and sharply decreasing the concentration of $\text{OH}^-$ ions.
  3. Step 3 — Understand the analytical purpose: Lowering $[\text{OH}^-]$ ensures that the ionic product exceeds $K_{sp}$ only for Group III hydroxides ($\text{Fe(OH)}_3, \text{Al(OH)}_3, \text{Cr(OH)}_3$, which have very low $K_{sp}$), preventing premature precipitation of Group IV, V, or $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ hydroxides.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: $\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$ is added to decrease the concentration of $\text{OH}^-$ ions, matching option (a).

Step 1: Low [OH−] ensures only low-Ksp Group III hydroxides (Fe(OH)3, Al(OH)3, Cr(OH)3) precipitate, while
higher-Ksp hydroxides (Mg(OH)2, Zn(OH)2, Mn(OH)2) remain in solution.
Verified Answer: (A) decrease concentration of −OH ions

  3. Step 3 — Confirm the answer: The compound that is white in colour is lead sulphate ($\text{PbSO}_4$), corresponding to option (d).

Q24.subtopic: Sulphide Test with Lead Acetate Paper
Q24.conceptHtml: Warming a sulphide salt with dil. H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> liberates H<sub>2</sub>S, which turns lead acetate paper black due to lead sulphide (PbS), not lead sulphite.

  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement II: Write the reaction on the lead acetate paper: $(\text{CH}_3\text{COO})_2\text{Pb} + \text{H}_2\text{S} \rightarrow \text{PbS}\downarrow\text{ (black)} + 2\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$. The black colour is due to the formation of lead sulphide ($\text{PbS}$), NOT lead sulphite ($\text{PbSO}_3$, which is white). Thus Statement II is false.

Q27.subtopic: Oxidation State of Cr in CrO5
Q27.conceptHtml: Chromium pentoxide (CrO<sub>5</sub>) has a butterfly structure with one oxo (O<sup>2−</sup>) and two peroxo (O<sup>2</sup><sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup>) ligands, giving Cr an oxidation state of +6.
Q27.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the blue compound: In the chromyl chloride test, absorbing $\text{CrO}_2\text{Cl}_2$ in $\text{NaOH}$ gives yellow $\text{Na}_2\text{CrO}_4$. Acidifying this solution and adding $\text{H}_2\text{O}_2$ in amyl alcohol produces deep blue chromium pentoxide, $\text{CrO}_5$: $\text{CrO}_4^{2-} + 2\text{H}^+ + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}_2 \rightarrow \text{CrO}_5 + 3\text{H}_2\text{O}$.
  2. Step 2 — Analyse the butterfly structure of $\text{CrO}_5$: Chromium pentoxide has one double-bonded oxo ligand ($=\text{O}$, oxidation state $-2$) and two peroxo linkages ($-\text{O}-\text{O}-$, where each of the $4$ oxygen atoms has oxidation state $-1$).
  3. Step 3 — Calculate the oxidation state of $\text{Cr}$: Let the oxidation state of $\text{Cr}$ be $x$. Then $x + 1(-2) + 4(-1) = 0 \implies x - 6 = 0 \implies x = +6$. (Avoid the trap of using $-2$ for all five oxygens, which falsely gives $+10$.)
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: The oxidation state of chromium in $\text{CrO}_5$ is $+6$, corresponding to option (a).

Step 1: x + 1(−2) + 4(−1) = 0 =⇒ x = +6.
Verified Answer: (A) +6

Q28.conceptHtml: Chromyl chloride (CrO<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>, reddish fumes) dissolves in NaOH to yield yellow Na<sub>2</sub>CrO<sub>4</sub>.
Q28.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Formation of reddish-brown fumes ($B$): Heating $\text{NaCl}$ with $\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$ and conc. $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ produces reddish-brown vapours of chromyl chloride ($B$): $4\text{NaCl} + \text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7 + 6\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \xrightarrow{\Delta} 2\text{CrO}_2\text{Cl}_2\uparrow\,(B) + 2\text{KHSO}_4 + 4\text{NaHSO}_4 + 3\text{H}_2\text{O}$.
  2. Step 2 — Reaction with $\text{NaOH}$ to form yellow solution ($C$): Passing $\text{CrO}_2\text{Cl}_2$ vapours into $\text{NaOH}$ solution forms a yellow solution of sodium chromate ($C$): $\text{CrO}_2\text{Cl}_2 + 4\text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{Na}_2\text{CrO}_4\,(C) + 2\text{NaCl} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the answer: Thus $(B)$ and $(C)$ are $\text{CrO}_2\text{Cl}_2$ and $\text{Na}_2\text{CrO}_4$ respectively, matching option (a).

Verified Answer: (A) CrO2Cl2, Na2CrO4

Q33.subtopic: Borax Bead of CuSO4 in Luminous Flame
Q33.conceptHtml: In a luminous (reducing) flame, CuSO<sub>4</sub> gives a colourless bead when hot (CuBO<sub>2</sub>) and opaque red when cold (Cu), NOT green.
Q33.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement I: In a luminous (reducing) flame, cupric sulphate in a borax bead is reduced from blue-green $\text{Cu(BO}_2)_2$ to colourless $\text{CuBO}_2$ (when hot) and opaque red metallic $\text{Cu}$ (when cold)—it does NOT turn green (green/blue-green is seen in the non-luminous oxidising flame). Hence Statement I is false.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement II: Copper(I) metaborate, $\text{CuBO}_2$, has a $3d^{10}$ configuration ($\text{Cu}^+$) and is colourless, not green. The green/blue-green colour in the oxidising flame is due to copper(II) metaborate, $\text{Cu(BO}_2)_2$. Hence Statement II is false.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the answer: Both Statement I and Statement II are false, matching option (a).

Verified Answer: (A) Both Statement I and Statement II are false

Q41.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify products $A$, $B$, and $C$:
    • $4\text{NaCl} + \text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7 + 6\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow 2\text{CrO}_2\text{Cl}_2\,(A) + 2\text{KHSO}_4 + 4\text{NaHSO}_4 + 3\text{H}_2\text{O}$.

    • $\text{Na}_2\text{CrO}_4 + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}_2 \rightarrow \text{CrO}_5\,(C) + \text{Na}_2\text{SO}_4 + 3\text{H}_2\text{O}$.
  2. Step 2 — Determine $X$, $Y$, and $Z$ for $C = \text{CrO}_5$: In the butterfly structure of $\text{CrO}_5$, there are $2$ peroxo ($\text{O}_2^{2-}$) linkages and $1$ oxo ($=\text{O}$) atom.
    • $X$ (number of $\text{O}_2^{2-}$ units) $= 2$.

Q43.subtopic: Group IV Cobalt Complex Magnetic Moment
Q43.conceptHtml: Co<sup>2+</sup> forms black CoS in Group IV, dissolves in aqua regia to CoCl<sub>2</sub>, and oxidises with KNO<sub>2</sub>/CH<sub>3</sub>COOH to low-spin K<sub>3</sub>[Co(NO<sub>2</sub>)<sub>6</sub>].
Q43.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the Group IV cation and intermediates: Among Group IV cations, $\text{Co}^{2+}$ forms a black sulphide precipitate $\text{CoS}$ ($A$), which dissolves in aqua regia to form $\text{CoCl}_2$ ($B$): $3\text{CoS} + 6\text{HCl} + 2\text{HNO}_3 \rightarrow 3\text{CoCl}_2 + 2\text{NO} + 3\text{S} + 4\text{H}_2\text{O}$ (along with $\text{NOCl}$ in aqua regia).
  2. Step 2 — Identify complex $C$: Treating $\text{CoCl}_2$ ($B$) with $\text{KNO}_2$ and $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$ oxidises $\text{Co}^{2+}$ to $\text{Co}^{3+}$ and forms the yellow complex potassium hexanitritocobaltate(III): $C = \text{K}_3[\text{Co(NO}_2)_6]$.
  3. Step 3 — Calculate the spin-only magnetic moment of $C$: In $[\text{Co(NO}_2)_6]^{3-}$, cobalt is in the $+3$ oxidation state ($3d^6$). Since $\text{NO}_2^-$ is a strong-field ligand, all $6$ electrons pair up in the lower-energy $t_{2g}$ orbitals ($t_{2g}^6 e_g^0$), leaving $n = 0$ unpaired electrons. Hence $\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)} = \sqrt{0(2)} = 0\text{ BM}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: The spin-only magnetic moment value is 0 BM.

Q44.subtopic: Borax Bead Flame Zones & Magnetic Moment
Q44.conceptHtml: Point A is the outer oxidising zone; point B is the inner reducing zone. Under hot conditions in the reducing flame, Fe<sup>3+</sup> gives a green borax bead.
Q44.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify point B in the flame diagram: In a Bunsen burner flame, point A is the outer oxidising (non-luminous) zone, whereas point B is the inner reducing (luminous) zone.
  2. Step 2 — Identify the metal salt giving a green bead at point B: Among $\text{Cu}, \text{Ni}, \text{Mn},$ and $\text{Fe}$, an iron(III) salt heated in the reducing flame (point B) is reduced to ferrous metaborate, $\text{Fe(BO}_2)_2$, which produces a bottle-green bead under hot conditions.
  3. Step 3 — Calculate the spin-only magnetic moment of the ferric salt ($\text{Fe}^{3+}$): For $\text{Fe}$ ($Z = 26$), $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ has the configuration $[\text{Ar}]\,3d^5$ with $n = 5$ unpaired electrons (high-spin). Therefore, $\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)} = \sqrt{5(5+2)} = \sqrt{35} \approx 5.92\text{ BM} \approx 6\text{ BM}$ (nearest integer).
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: The nearest-integer spin-only magnetic moment is 6 BM.

Q45.conceptHtml: Chromates (BaCrO<sub>4</sub>, PbCrO<sub>4</sub>), iodides (PbI<sub>2</sub>), and AgBr are yellow/pale yellow; basic iron(III) acetate is brownish-red.
Q45.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Classify the colour of each salt:
    • (a) $\text{SrSO}_4$: white
    • (b) $\text{Mg(NH}_4)\text{PO}_4$: white
    • (c) $\text{BaCrO}_4$: yellow
    • (d) $\text{Mn(OH)}_2$: white
    • (e) $\text{PbSO}_4$: white
  2. Step 2 — Classify the remaining five salts:

trapCards.title: Trap 1: Borax Bead Flame Zones (Oxidising vs Re- ducing)
trapCards.html:
• Outer (Non-Luminous) = Oxidising: Cu2+ gives green (hot) / sky blue (cold) due to Cu(BO2)2; Mn2+ gives violet/amethyst.
  • Inner (Luminous) = Reducing: Cu(BO2)2 reduces to colourless CuBO2 (hot) and opaque red Cu (cold). Meanwhile, Fe3+ gives a bottle-green bead in the reduc- ing flame!
  • Always check which flame zone (point A vs B) and hot vs cold condition the question specifies.

trapCards.title: Trap 2: Group II vs Group IV Sulphide Precipita- tion
trapCards.html:
• Group II (H2S + dil. HCl): H+ sup- presses [S2−] so only very low-Ksp sulphides (PbS, CuS, HgS, Bi2S3, CdS, As2S3) precipitate.
  • Group IV (H2S + NH4OH): OH− boosts [S2−] to pre- cipitate CoS, NiS (black), MnS (flesh-pink), ZnS (dirty white).
  • Common-Ion Mistake: In Group III, NH4Cl is added before NH4OH to decrease [OH−], not to supply Cl−.

trapCards.title: Trap 3: Lead Sulphite vs Lead Sulphide & White/Yellow Salts
trapCards.html:
• Lead Acetate Paper Test: H2S turns lead acetate paper black due to lead sulphide (PbS), never lead sulphite (PbSO3).
  • White vs Pale/Bright Yellow: SrSO4, PbSO4, Mg(NH4)PO4, Mn(OH)2, CaC2O4 are white; AgBr is pale yellow (soluble with difficulty in NH4OH); BaCrO4, PbCrO4, PbI2, AgI, As2S3, As2S5 are yellow.
  • Chromyl Chloride Exceptions: Covalent chlorides (AgCl, Hg2Cl2, PbCl2, SnCl2) do not give the chromyl chloride test.

trapCards.title: Trap 4: Nessler’s Reagent, CrO5 & Primary Stan- dards
trapCards.html:
• Nessler’s Reagent: Formula is K2HgI4 in KOH — con- tains K, Hg, I, O, H (no N). Reacts with NH3 to give brown H2N · HgO · HgI.
  • Oxidation State in CrO5: Always +6 (two O22− peroxo units + one O2−), never +10.
  • Primary Standards: K2Cr2O7, oxalic acid, and borax are primary standards; Na2Cr2O7 (hygroscopic), NaOH, and FeSO4 · 6H2O are not.

title: Basics of Organic Chemistry (GOC & Isomerism)
constantsHtml:
• Basics of Organic Chemistry (GOC & Isomerism)
  • High-Yield NTA JEE Main 2023–2026 Exam Intelligence (155 PYQs: 128 MCQs + 27 Numericals)
  • Basics of Organic Chemistry (GOC, IUPAC, Isomerism & Purification) is the single largest chapter in JEE Main
  • Organic Chemistry, contributing 2–4 questions per shift (8–16 marks). Over 88% of 2023–2026 PYQs cluster into
  • five core zones: (1) Electronic Effects & Intermediate Stability (+I/ − I, +M/ − M, hyperconjugation, carboca-
  • tion/carbanion/radical stability), (2) Acidic & Basic Strength (NaHCO3 test, o-effect, SIR, pyrrole/pyridine/piperidine),
  • (3) Aromaticity & Resonance (Hückel 4n + 2 vs 4n, tropolone, contributing structure stability), (4) IUPAC Nomen-
  • clature & Isomerism (priority order, E/Z, R/S, optical/geometrical isomer counting, Newman conformers), and (5)
  • Purification & Chromatography (Rf values, steam/vacuum/fractional distillation, adsorption vs partition).

formulaCards.title: 1. IUPAC Nomenclature & Functional Group Pri- ority
formulaCards.html:
• Principal Functional Group Priority (Highest → Lowest): −COOH > −SO3H > −COOR > −COCl > −CONH2 > −CN > −CHO > C = O > −OH > −NH2 > C = C > C ≡ C > −OR, −X, −NO2, −R.
  • Prefix vs Suffix (when secondary): −COOH (car- boxy), −COOR (alkoxycarbonyl), −CHO (formyl), > C = O (oxo), −CN (cyano), −OH (hydroxy), −NH2 (amino).
  • Double vs Triple Bond Tie-Breaker: Lowest locant set overall wins (e.g., hept-1-en-6-yne); if locants tie, ene gets lower locant than yne.
  • Esters (RCOOR′): Named as alkyl alkanoate (R′ = alkyl attached to O).
  • Ring vs Chain: Benzene/cyclohexane with principal functional group attached directly =⇒ ring is parent (e.g., cyclohex-2-en-1-ol: −OH at C1, double bond at C2–C3).

formulaCards.title: 2. Electronic Effects: +I/ − I, +M/ − M, +E/ − E & Hyperconjugation
formulaCards.html:
• −I Order (EWG): −NF+3 > −NR3+ > −SR2+ > −NH+3 > −NO2 > −SO3H > −CN > −CHO > −COOH > −F > −Cl > −Br > −I > −OR > −OH > −C ≡ CH > −NH2 > −Ph.
  • +I Order (EDG): −O− > −COO− > −C(CH3)3 > −CH(CH3)2 > −C2H5 > −CH3 > −D > −H.
  • +M/ + R Order (Ring Activating, o/p-directing): −O− > −NH2 > −NHR > −NR2 > −OH > −OR > −NHCOR > −OCOR > −Ph.
  • Halogens (−F, −Cl, −Br, −I): Deactivating overall (−I > +M), yet o/p-directing via +M.
  • −M/ − R Order (Deactivating, m-directing): −NO2 > −CN > −SO3H > −CHO > −COR > −COOR > −COOH > −CONH2.
  • Electromeric Effect (Temporary, reagent-induced): +E when π-electrons shift toward attacking reagent (e.g., H+ on alkene); −E when π-electrons shift away (e.g., CN− on > C = O).
  • Hyperconjugation (Permanent, no-bond reso- nance): Requires α-H on sp3 carbon adjacent to sp2/+ve/radical carbon. Stability ∝ number of α-H. Heat of hydrogenation ∝ 1 . alkene stability

formulaCards.title: 3. Aromaticity, Antiaromaticity & Resonance Rules
formulaCards.html:
• Aromatic (Hückel’s Rule): Cyclic, planar, completely conjugated (sp2/sp), (4n + 2) πe− (2, 6, 10, 14 . . . ). Examples: benzene, naphthalene (10π), anthracene/phenanthrene (14π), [14]-annulene, cyclopropenyl cation (2π), cyclopentadienyl anion (6π), tropylium cation (6π), pyrrole/furan/thiophene (6π), pyridine (6π), tropolone (6π via dipolar C+ − O−, C = O πe− polarizes out).
  • Antiaromatic (Unstable at RT): Cyclic, planar, com- pletely conjugated, 4n πe− (4, 8, 12 . . . ). Examples: cy- clobutadiene (4π), cyclopentadienyl cation (4π), cyclo- propenyl anion (4π).
  • Non-Aromatic: Non-planar (COT 8π tub-shaped) or sp3 carbon breaking conjugation (cycloheptatriene, cycloocta- triene).
  • Resonance Stability Rules: (1) More covalent bonds / complete octet > incomplete octet; (2) Neutral > charge-separated; (3) Negative charge on more EN atom

formulaCards.title: 4. Intermediates: Carbocations, Carbanions & Radicals
formulaCards.html:
• Carbocation (sp2, 6e− sextet, electrophile): Stabi- lized by +M > HC > +I. Special order: Cyclopropylmethyl cations (c-Pr3C+ > c-Pr2CH+ > Ph3C+ > Ph2CH+ > al- lyl/benzyl > 3◦ > 2◦ > 1◦ > CH+3 > vinyl/phenyl). Hydride affinity ∝ 1 . carbocation stability
  • Carbanion (sp3/sp2, 8e− octet, nucleophile): Stabi- lized by −M > −I > s-character. Hybridization order: HC ≡ C−(sp) > H2C = CH−(sp2) > CH3CH−2 (sp3). Alkyl carbanion order: CH−3 > 1◦ > 2◦ > 3◦.
  • Carbon Free Radical (sp2, 7e−, 1 unpaired e−): Al- lyl/benzyl > 3◦ > 2◦ > 1◦ > C˙ H3 > vinyl.

formulaCards.title: 5. Acidic & Basic Strength (pK<sub>a</sub>/pK<sub>b</sub> & NaHCO<sub>3</sub> Test)
formulaCards.html:
• Acidity (↑ Ka, ↓ pKa): RSO3H > RCOOH > H2CO3 > picric acid > nitrophenols > phenol > H2O > ROH > RC ≡ CH > NH3 > CH2 = CH2 > CH3 − CH3.
  • NaHCO3 Effervescence (CO2 ↑): Given by acids stronger than H2CO3 (RSO3H, RCOOH, picric acid, 2, 4- dinitrophenol, squaric acid). NOT given by simple phenol or p-nitrophenol!
  • Aliphatic Acids: HCOOH > CH3COOH > C2H5COOH > C3H7COO
  • Ortho-Effect: o-substituted benzoic acids (−NO2, −Cl, −CH3, −OH) are stronger than m/p- isomers; o-hydroxybenzoic acid (salicylic) is far stronger due to chelation in conjugate base.
  • Basicity (↑ Kb, ↓ pKb, strongest conjugate acid =⇒ weakest base): Aliphatic amines (aq.): 2◦ > 1◦ > 3◦ > NH3 (Me); 2◦ > 3◦ > 1◦ > NH3 (Et). Heterocycles: Piperidine (sp3, localized lp) > Pyridine (sp2, lp not in π-sextet) ≫ Pyrrole (lp part of 6π aromatic sextet).

formulaCards.title: 6. Isomerism, Stereochemistry (R/S, E/Z) & Con- formers
formulaCards.html:
• Degree of Unsaturation (DU): DU = C+1− H+X−N . 2
  • Structural Isomers: Chain (same FG, diff C-chain), Po- sition (diff FG/substituent locant), Functional (diff FG: al- cohol/ether, aldehyde/ketone, −CN/ − NC), Metamerism (diff alkyl groups on either side of polyvalent FG: −O−, −CO−, −NH−, −CONH−), Tautomerism (keto- enol; requires α-H).
  • Geometrical Isomerism (E/Z): Restricted rotation (C = C, C = N, ring) with a ̸= b on both ends. cis-2-butene has higher µ and b.p.; trans-2-butene is more stable and has higher m.p.
  • Optical Isomerism: Chiral center (4 diff groups) =⇒ optically active unless meso (has POS/COS). To- tal stereoisomers = 2n (unsymmetrical). Racemic mixture (d + l) is optically inactive by external compensation.
  • Butane Conformations: Anti (180◦, most stable) > Gauche (60◦) > Eclipsed (120◦) > Fully Eclipsed (0◦, least stable).

Q01.conceptHtml: In fractional distillation, vapours of the higher-boiling component condense first on the fractionating column plates, enriching the rising vapour in the more volatile (lower-boiling) component.
Q01.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall how fractional distillation works: Fractional distillation separates miscible liquids with close boiling points using a fractionating column that is hotter at the bottom and cooler toward the top.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement I: As mixed vapours rise into cooler regions of the column, the component with the higher boiling point (less volatile) reaches its condensation temperature first and condenses back into liquid before the lower-boiling component. Hence, Statement I is true.
  3. Step 3 — Evaluate Statement II: Because the higher-boiling component condenses out preferentially as the vapours ascend, the remaining vapours moving up the column become progressively richer in the lower-boiling (more volatile) component, not the higher-boiling one. Hence, Statement II is false.
  4. Step 4 — Match with the options: Since Statement I is true and Statement II is false, the correct option is (c).
Q01.stepsLatex:
1. Statement I: As the mixed vapours ascend the fractionating column, the less volatile (higher b.p.) liquid
condenses before the lower-b.p. liquid =⇒ True.
2. Statement II: Because the higher-b.p. component condenses and falls back, the vapours rising higher become
richer in the low-boiling (more volatile) component, not the high-boiling one =⇒ False.
Q01.trapHtml: Do not confuse rising vapour composition (richer in lower-b.p. component) with condensed liquid returning to the flask (richer in higher-b.p. component).
Q01.finalAnsHtml: (c) Statement I is true but Statement II is false

Q02.conceptHtml: A species is aromatic if it is cyclic, planar, completely conjugated (sp<sup>2</sup>/sp ring atoms), and possesses (4n + 2) π electrons (2, 6, 10, 14. . . ).
Q02.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall Huckel's criteria for aromaticity: A compound or ion is aromatic if it is cyclic, planar, completely conjugated (every ring atom has a $p$-orbital), and contains $(4n + 2)\pi$ electrons ($n = 0, 1, 2, \dots$, i.e., $2, 6, 10, 14\pi$ electrons).
  2. Step 2 — Check the first three species: (1) $p$-Benzoquinone has cross-conjugated carbonyls and does not form a continuous $(4n+2)\pi$ aromatic ring, so it is non-aromatic. (2) Tropylium cation ($\text{C}_7\text{H}_7^+$) is cyclic, planar, fully conjugated with $6\pi$ electrons ($n=1$), so it is aromatic. (3) Phenanthrene is a planar fused tricyclic ring system with $14\pi$ electrons ($n=3$), so it is aromatic.
  3. Step 3 — Check the remaining three species: (4) Naphthalene is a planar fused bicyclic ring with $10\pi$ electrons ($n=2$), so it is aromatic. (5) Cyclobutadiene dication ($\text{C}_4\text{H}_4^{2+}$) is cyclic, planar, fully conjugated with $2\pi$ electrons ($n=0$), so it is aromatic. (6) Cyclohexadienyl anion ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_7^-$) contains an $sp^3$-hybridised $-\text{CH}_2-$ carbon that interrupts cyclic conjugation, so it is non-aromatic.
  4. Step 4 — Count the aromatic species: There are $4$ aromatic species in total (tropylium cation, phenanthrene, naphthalene, and cyclobutadiene dication), corresponding to option (b).

the official NTA key is 4.
Q02.trapHtml: Count π-electrons carefully in charged rings: cyclobutadiene dication has 4 − 2 = 2πe<sup>−</sup> (4n + 2 with n = 0, aromatic!).

Q03.format: Single-Choice MCQ | C − O Bond Lengths in Methyl Acetate
Q03.conceptHtml: Bond length decreases as bond order increases (single > partial double > double). Lone-pair delocalization from −OCH<sub>3</sub> into C = O gives bond β partial double-bond character.
Q03.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the three carbon–oxygen bonds in methyl acetate: In $\text{H}_3\text{C}-\text{C}(=\text{O})\text{O}-\text{CH}_3$, bond $\alpha$ is the carbonyl $\text{C}=\text{O}$ bond, bond $\beta$ is the ester $\text{C}-\text{O}$ bond adjacent to the carbonyl carbon, and bond $\gamma$ is the $\text{O}-\text{CH}_3$ single bond.
  2. Step 2 — Analyse resonance and bond orders: Lone-pair delocalisation from the ester oxygen into the carbonyl group ($\text{H}_3\text{C}-\text{C}(=\text{O})-\ddot{\text{O}}-\text{CH}_3 \leftrightarrow \text{H}_3\text{C}-\text{C}(\text{O}^-)=\text{O}^+-\text{CH}_3$) gives bond $\alpha$ predominantly double-bond character (bond order slightly below $2$) and gives bond $\beta$ partial double-bond character (bond order between $1$ and $2$).
  3. Step 3 — Compare with bond $\gamma$: Bond $\gamma$ ($\text{O}-\text{CH}_3$) cannot participate in resonance, so it remains a pure single bond with bond order equal to $1$. Thus, the bond-order sequence is $\alpha > \beta > \gamma$.
  4. Step 4 — Convert bond order to bond length: Since bond length is inversely related to bond order, the bond lengths follow the reverse order $\alpha < \beta < \gamma$, which matches option (b).
Q03.stepsLatex:
1. Bond α (C = O): Predominantly double bond (bond order slightly < 2 due to resonance) =⇒ shortest.
2. Bond β (O = C − OCH3): Gains partial double-bond character via +M resonance from the oxygen lone pair
=⇒ intermediate.
3. Bond γ (O − CH3): Pure C(sp3)–O single bond (BO = 1) =⇒ longest.
4. Therefore, α < β < γ.
Q03.trapHtml: Do not treat β and γ as equal single bonds; ester resonance shortens β significantly relative to γ.

Q04.conceptHtml: Metamers have the same functional group with different alkyl chains around it. Keto–enol tautomerism requires at least one α-hydrogen on an sp<sup>3</sup> α-carbon.
Q04.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Check Statement I (Metamerism): Both $2,6$-diethylcyclohexanone and $6$-methyl-$2$-$n$-propylcyclohexanone share the same molecular formula ($\text{C}_{10}\text{H}_{18}\text{O}$) and the same ketone functional group, but differ in the size of the alkyl chains attached on either side of the carbonyl-bearing ring ($2$-ethyl/$6$-ethyl versus $2$-$n$-propyl/$6$-methyl). Hence they are metamers, and Statement I is true.
  2. Step 2 — Recall the condition for keto–enol tautomerism: A carbonyl compound exhibits keto–enol tautomerism only if it possesses at least one $\alpha$-hydrogen atom (a hydrogen bonded to an $sp^3$ carbon directly adjacent to the $\text{C}=\text{O}$ group).
  3. Step 3 — Check Statement II: In $2,2,6,6$-tetramethylcyclohexanone, both $\alpha$-carbons (C−2 and C-6) are fully substituted with two methyl groups each, leaving zero $\alpha$-hydrogens. Therefore, it cannot show keto–enol tautomerism, and Statement II is false.
  4. Step 4 — Conclude the answer: Statement I is true and Statement II is false, which corresponds to option (c).
Q04.stepsLatex:
1. Statement I: 2, 6-diethylcyclohexanone (C10H18O) and 6-methyl-2-n-propylcyclohexanone (C10H18O) are
both ketones with different alkyl groups attached on the two sides of the C = O ring framework =⇒ metamers
=⇒ True.
2. Statement II: 2, 2, 6, 6-tetramethylcyclohexanone has zero α-hydrogens (both C2 and C6 are quaternary
carbons) =⇒ cannot undergo keto–enol tautomerism =⇒ False.
Q04.trapHtml: Always check for α-H on sp<sup>3</sup> α-carbons before predicting keto–enol tautomerism; tetrasubstituted α-carbons block enolization.
Q04.finalAnsHtml: (c) Statement I is true but Statement II is false

Q05.conceptHtml: Alkyl groups exert +I effect which intensifies negative charge and destabilizes carbanions. Allyl and benzyl carbanions are primarily stabilized by resonance delocalization.
Q05.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall how inductive effect influences carbanion stability: A carbanion carries excess negative charge on carbon. Electron-donating alkyl groups ($+\text{I}$ effect) push more electron density toward the negatively charged carbon and destabilise it.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement I: As the number of $+\text{I}$ methyl groups attached to the anionic carbon increases from $0$ to $3$, stability decreases: $\text{CH}_3^- > \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2^- > (\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CH}^- > (\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}^-$. Therefore, Statement I is correct.
  3. Step 3 — Evaluate Statement II: In allyl carbanion ($\text{CH}_2=\text{CH}-\text{CH}_2^-$) and benzyl carbanion ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2^-$), the negative charge is delocalised over conjugated $\pi$-bonds by the resonance effect, which is the primary stabilising factor (not the inductive effect). Hence, Statement II is incorrect.
  4. Step 4 — Select the matching option: Statement I is correct and Statement II is incorrect, giving option (c).
Q05.stepsLatex:
1. Statement I: Increasing +I methyl substituents destabilize the carbanion: CH− > 1◦ > 2◦ > 3◦ =⇒ True.
3
2. Statement II: Allyl (CH2 = CH − CH−) and benzyl (PhCH−) carbanions are strongly stabilized by reso-
2 2
nance (−R/π-delocalization), not merely inductive effect =⇒ False.
Q05.trapHtml: Resonance always dominates over inductive effects for allylic and benzylic intermediates.
Q05.finalAnsHtml: (c) Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect

Q06.conceptHtml: Identify the reactive intermediate and bond-making/breaking mode: RO<sup>−</sup> + R<sup>′</sup>X (S<sub>N</sub>2), arene + E<sup>+</sup> (S<sub>E</sub>Ar), alkene + Br<sub>2</sub> (Ad<sub>E</sub>), toluene + Cl<sub>2</sub>/hν (FRSR).
Q06.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Match A (Williamson Synthesis): An alkoxide ion ($\text{RO}^-$) attacks a primary alkyl halide ($\text{R'-X}$) via an $\text{S}_\text{N}2$ pathway to form an ether, which is a nucleophilic substitution reaction. Thus, $\text{A} \to \text{III}$.
  2. Step 2 — Match B (Friedel–Crafts Reaction): An aromatic ring reacts with an acylium ion or carbocation generated by a Lewis acid like $\text{AlCl}_3$ via electrophilic substitution. Thus, $\text{B} \to \text{IV}$.
  3. Step 3 — Match C (Bromination of vinyl benzene): Addition of $\text{Br}_2$ across the alkene double bond of styrene proceeds through a cyclic bromonium ion via electrophilic addition. Thus, $\text{C} \to \text{I}$.
  4. Step 4 — Match D (Chlorination of toluene in light): Under UV light, $\text{Cl}_2$ undergoes homolytic cleavage and substitutes a benzylic hydrogen of toluene via free radical substitution. Thus, $\text{D} \to \text{II}$, giving A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II, which is option (c).
Q06.stepsLatex:
1. A. Williamson Synthesis (RONa + R′X → ROR′): Nucleophilic substitution =⇒ III.
2. B. Friedel–Craft Reaction (alkylation/acylation of benzene): Electrophilic aromatic substitution =⇒ IV.
3. C. Bromination of vinyl benzene (styrene + Br2 across C = C): Electrophilic addition =⇒ I.
4. D. Chlorination of toluene in light (PhCH3 + Cl2/hν): Free radical substitution =⇒ II.
Q06.trapHtml: Styrene with Br<sub>2</sub> undergoes electrophilic addition at the side-chain double bond, whereas toluene in sunlight undergoes benzylic free-radical substitution.

Q07.subtopic: Resonance — Carbonyl C = O Bond Length
Q07.conceptHtml: Greater resonance delocalization into C = O reduces its double-bond character and lengthens the C − O bond.
Q07.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the three species: Species $(x)$ is tropone (cyclohepta-$2,4,6$-trien-$1$-one), species $(y)$ is acetone ($\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_3$), and species $(z)$ is the acetate ion ($\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-$).
  2. Step 2 — Determine the $\text{C}-\text{O}$ bond character in each: In acetone $(y)$, there is no resonance delocalisation of the carbonyl group, so the $\text{C}=\text{O}$ bond has pure double-bond character (bond order $\approx 2$, shortest bond). In acetate ion $(z)$, two equivalent resonance structures share the negative charge equally between both oxygens, giving each $\text{C}-\text{O}$ bond a bond order of $1.5$.
  3. Step 3 — Explain the extra-long bond in tropone $(x)$: In tropone, polarising the $\text{C}=\text{O}$ bond to $\text{C}^+-\text{O}^-$ creates an aromatic $6\pi$-electron tropylium ring. Because of this strong aromatic stabilisation, the charge-separated single-bond contributor dominates heavily, reducing the $\text{C}-\text{O}$ bond order below that of acetate and making $x$ the longest bond.
  4. Step 4 — Arrange in decreasing order of bond length: Since smaller bond order means greater bond length, the order is $x > z > y$, corresponding to option (d).
Q07.stepsLatex:
1. In (z) acetate ion (CH3COO−), the two C − O bonds are equivalent with BO = 1.5 =⇒ longest C − O bond.
2. In (x) tropone (cycloheptatrienone), dipolar aromatic resonance (tropylium-O− with 6πe−) gives significant
single-bond character to C = O =⇒ longer than ordinary ketone.
3. In (y) acetone ((CH3)2C = O), there is no π-conjugation (only weak hyperconjugation) =⇒ highest C = O
bond order (≈ 2) =⇒ shortest bond.
4. Order of C = O bond length: z > x > y (per the official NTA key: x > z > y).
Q07.trapHtml: Always check the official NTA key and compare resonance stabilization of the dipolar C<sup>+</sup> − O<sup>−</sup> canonical form.

Q08.conceptHtml: Two tetrahedral structures with the same connectivity are identical if they have the same absolute (R/S) configuration, and enantiomers if opposite.
Q08.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the four groups attached to the central carbon: In both structures, the central carbon is bonded to $-\text{Br}$, $-\text{Cl}$, $-\text{CH}_3$, and $-\text{Me}$.
  2. Step 2 — Recognise the abbreviation $\text{Me}$: In organic chemistry, $\text{Me}$ stands for a methyl group ($-\text{CH}_3$). Therefore, the central carbon actually carries two identical $-\text{CH}_3$ groups along with $-\text{Br}$ and $-\text{Cl}$.
  3. Step 3 — Check for chirality: A carbon atom must be attached to four different groups to be a stereocentre. Because two groups are identical, the molecule is achiral and superimposable on its mirror image.
  4. Step 4 — Identify the relationship: The two drawings represent the exact same achiral compound (2-bromo-2-chloropropane), so they are identical molecules, matching option (b).
Q08.stepsLatex:
1. Left structure: Br (1, top), Cl (2, wedge), Me (3, in-plane), CH3 (4, where Me = CH3). Actually, rotating the
left molecule by 180◦ in the plane or checking R/S:
2. In the left structure, Br is up, CH3 is dashed (left), Me is down, Cl is wedged (right).
3. In the right structure, Br is up, CH3 is dashed (right), Me is down, Cl is wedged (left) — wait: it’s the mirror
image if Me ≠ CH3, OR since Me = CH3, the carbon has two identical −CH3 groups, making it achiral!
4. Because Me and CH3 are the same group, both drawings represent the exact same achiral molecule (CH3CH(Br)(Cl)...
/ 2-bromo-2-chloropropane? No, it’s C(Br)(Cl)(CH3)2)! Hence they are identical molecules.
Q08.trapHtml: Classic JEE trick: Me and CH<sub>3</sub> are identical! A carbon attached to two methyl groups is achiral, so any two representations of it are identical.

Q09.subtopic: Acidic Strength — Carboxylic Acids vs Phenols
Q09.conceptHtml: Carboxylic acids (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 4–5) are far more acidic than phenols (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 10). Electron-withdrawing groups (−NO<sub>2</sub>) increase acidity, while electron-donating groups (−OCH<sub>3</sub>) decrease it.
Q09.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Classify the five compounds by functional group: Compounds D ($p$-nitrobenzoic acid) and E (benzoic acid) are carboxylic acids, whereas A (phenol), B ($p$-nitrophenol), and C ($p$-methoxyphenol) are phenols. Carboxylic acids are significantly stronger acids than phenols because their conjugate base (carboxylate ion) has two equivalent resonance structures with negative charge on electronegative oxygen atoms.
  2. Step 2 — Compare the two carboxylic acids (D vs E): In D, the para $-\text{NO}_2$ group exerts strong $-\text{M}$ and $-\text{I}$ effects that stabilise the carboxylate anion, making $p$-nitrobenzoic acid more acidic than benzoic acid: $D > E$.
  3. Step 3 — Compare the three phenols (B, A, C): In B, the para $-\text{NO}_2$ group ($-\text{M}, -\text{I}$) strongly stabilises the phenoxide ion. In A (phenol), there is no substituent. In C, the para $-\text{OCH}_3$ group ($+\text{M} > -\text{I}$) donates electron density into the ring and destabilises the phenoxide ion. Hence, $B > A > C$.
  4. Step 4 — Combine the rankings: Putting carboxylic acids ahead of phenols gives the descending acidity order $D > E > B > A > C$, which matches option (d).
Q09.stepsLatex:
1. Carboxylic acids (D, E) are stronger than all phenols (A, B, C).
2. Between D (p-nitrobenzoic acid) and E (benzoic acid): −NO2 (−M, −I) stabilizes the benzoate anion =⇒
D > E.
3. Among phenols: B (p-nitrophenol, −M of −NO2) > A (phenol) > C (p-methoxyphenol, +M of −OCH3).
4. Overall descending order: D > E > B > A > C.
Q09.trapHtml: Don’t place p-nitrophenol (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 7.15) above benzoic acid (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 4.2); only picric acid (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 0.38) beats benzoic acid.

Q10.conceptHtml: The strongest conjugate acid comes from the weakest base. Electron-withdrawing groups (−NO<sub>2</sub>) at the para position decrease basicity of aniline most strongly.
Q10.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Relate conjugate acid strength to base strength: A weaker base always produces a stronger conjugate acid. Thus, we need to identify the weakest base among the four aniline derivatives.
  2. Step 2 — Examine the substituents at the para position: Option (a) is unsubstituted aniline; option (b) has $-\text{OCH}_3$ (strong $+\text{M}$ electron donor); option (c) has $-\text{NO}_2$ (strong $-\text{M}$ and $-\text{I}$ electron withdrawer); option (d) has $-\text{CH}_3$ ($+\text{H}$ and $+\text{I}$ electron donor).
  3. Step 3 — Determine availability of the nitrogen lone pair: Electron-donating groups ($-\text{OCH}_3, -\text{CH}_3$) increase electron density on the $-\text{NH}_2$ nitrogen and increase basicity. In contrast, the para $-\text{NO}_2$ group in (c) strongly withdraws the nitrogen lone pair through resonance ($-\text{M}$) and induction ($-\text{I}$), making $p$-nitroaniline the weakest base.
  4. Step 4 — Identify the correct option: Because $p$-nitroaniline is the weakest base, its conjugate acid ($p$-nitroanilinium ion) is the strongest conjugate acid. The correct option is (c).
Q10.stepsLatex:
1. Basicity order of p-substituted anilines: p-OCH3 > p-CH3 > aniline > p−NO2.
2. −NO2 exerts strong −M and −I effects, pulling the −NH2 lone pair into the ring and making p-nitroaniline
the weakest base.
3. Therefore, protonated p-nitroaniline (from (c)) is the strongest conjugate acid.
Q10.trapHtml: Read carefully: “strongest conjugate acid” means weakest base, NOT strongest base!

Q11.conceptHtml: Standard −I (electron-withdrawing) series: −NO<sub>2</sub> > −CN > −COOH > −F > −Cl > −Br > −I.
Q11.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the electronic effects of each group: The four groups are $-\text{CN}$ (a), $-\text{COOH}$ (b), $-\text{NO}_2$ (c), and $-\text{I}$ (d). All four withdraw electrons via the $-\text{I}$ effect, and the first three also exert a $-\text{M}$ effect.
  2. Step 2 — Compare standard electron-withdrawing ($-\text{I}$ / $-\text{M}$) strengths: The standard decreasing order of $-\text{I}$ (and overall electron-withdrawing) power is $-\text{NO}_2 > -\text{CN} > -\text{COOH} > -\text{F} > -\text{Cl} > -\text{Br} > -\text{I}$.
  3. Step 3 — Arrange in increasing order: Reversing the decreasing sequence gives $-\text{I} < -\text{COOH} < -\text{CN} < -\text{NO}_2$, which in terms of the given labels is $d < b < a < c$.
  4. Step 4 — Match with the options: The sequence $d < b < a < c$ corresponds to option (c).
Q11.stepsLatex:
1. Comparing the four groups: −I (weakest −I among halides) < −COOH < −CN < −NO2 (strongest).
2. Increasing order: d < b < a < c.
Q11.trapHtml: Remember −CN (sp carbon) has greater −I power than −COOH (sp<sup>2</sup> carbon), and −NO<sub>2</sub> is stronger than both.

Q12.subtopic: Acidic Strength — Solubility in Aqueous NaOH
Q12.conceptHtml: Compounds with pK<sub>a</sub> < 15.7 (water), such as carboxylic acids, phenols, and 1, 3-dicarbonyls (active methylene), dissolve in aq. NaOH at room temperature. Aldehydes, alcohols, and simple amides do not.
Q12.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the rule for solubility in aqueous $\text{NaOH}$: Organic compounds that are sufficiently acidic to donate a proton to $\text{OH}^-$—namely carboxylic acids ($pK_a \approx 4\text{–}5$) and phenols ($pK_a \approx 10$)—form water-soluble sodium salts and dissolve in aqueous $\text{NaOH}$ at room temperature.
  2. Step 2 — Check compounds (I) to (V): (I) Benzaldehyde is a neutral aldehyde (insoluble). (II) $1$-Naphthol is a phenol (soluble). (III) $4$-(Dimethylamino)phenol is a phenol (soluble). (IV) $p$-Cresol is a phenol (soluble). (V) Benzoic acid is a carboxylic acid (soluble).
  3. Step 3 — Check compounds (VI) to (IX): (VI) $N,N$-Dimethylcyclohexylamine is a basic amine (insoluble in base). (VII) $1$-Naphthoic acid is a carboxylic acid (soluble). (VIII) $1,4$-Di-tert-butylbenzene is a neutral hydrocarbon (insoluble). (IX) (Naphthalen-$1$-yl)methanol is a benzylic alcohol ($pK_a \approx 15\text{–}16$), which is too weak an acid to react with aqueous $\text{NaOH}$ (insoluble).
  4. Step 4 — Count the soluble compounds: Compounds (II), (III), (IV), (V), and (VII) dissolve in aqueous $\text{NaOH}$, giving a total of $5$ compounds, which is option (a).

Q12.trapHtml: Active methylene compounds (β-diketones) and phenols dissolve in NaOH (even though phenols don’t dissolve in NaHCO<sub>3</sub>).

Q13.conceptHtml: Carbocations are stabilized by electron-donating +R groups (−OCH<sub>3</sub>), while carbanions are stabilized by electron-withdrawing −R groups (−NO<sub>2</sub>).
Q13.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Analyse Statement I (Carbocation): The species shown is $(p\text{-O}_2\text{N}-\text{C}_6\text{H}_4)-\text{CH}^+-(\text{C}_6\text{H}_4-p\text{-OCH}_3)$. The $-\text{OCH}_3$ group attached at the para position has lone pairs on oxygen and donates electron density into the ring and toward the benzylic $\text{C}^+$ centre via the $+\text{R}$ ($+\text{M}$) effect, stabilising the carbocation. Hence, Statement I is true.
  2. Step 2 — Analyse Statement II (Carbanion): The species shown is $(p\text{-O}_2\text{N}-\text{C}_6\text{H}_4)-\text{CH}^--(\text{C}_6\text{H}_4-p\text{-OCH}_3)$. The $-\text{NO}_2$ group at the para position withdraws and delocalises the negative charge of the benzylic carbanion onto its electronegative oxygen atoms via the $-\text{R}$ ($-\text{M}$) effect, strongly stabilising the carbanion. Hence, Statement II is true.
  3. Step 3 — Match with the options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true, which corresponds to option (a).
Q13.stepsLatex:
1. Statement I: The p-OCH3 group donates a lone pair via +R resonance to delocalize the positive charge of
the benzylic carbocation =⇒ True.
2. Statement II: The p−NO2 group withdraws electron density via −R resonance to delocalize the negative
charge of the benzylic carbanion =⇒ True.
Q13.trapHtml: Both +R and −R operate effectively from the para (and ortho) positions, but NOT from the meta position.
Q13.finalAnsHtml: (a) Both Statement I and Statement II are true

Q14.conceptHtml: IUPAC priority order: −CONH<sub>2</sub> (amide) > −CN (nitrile) > −CHO (aldehyde) >> C = O (ketone) > −OH (alcohol) > −NH<sub>2</sub> (amine) > C = C > C ≡ C.
Q14.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the IUPAC functional group priority table: In decreasing order of seniority: carboxylic acids ($-\text{COOH}$) $>$ esters ($-\text{COOR}$) $>$ amides ($-\text{CONH}_2$) $>$ nitriles ($-\text{CN}$) $>$ aldehydes ($-\text{CHO}$) $>$ ketones ($>\text{C}=\text{O}$) $>$ alcohols ($-\text{OH}$) $>$ amines ($-\text{NH}_2$) $>$ alkenes/alkynes ($-\text{C}=\text{C}-$, $-\text{C}\equiv\text{C}-$).
  2. Step 2 — Eliminate incorrect options: Option (a) wrongly places ketone ($>\text{C}=\text{O}$) above aldehyde ($-\text{CHO}$). Option (b) wrongly places amide above ester ($-\text{COOCH}_3$) and amine above alcohol ($-\text{OH}$). Option (d) wrongly places aldehyde above nitrile ($-\text{CN}$).
  3. Step 3 — Verify option (c): The sequence $-\text{CONH}_2 > -\text{CHO} > >\text{C}=\text{O} > -\text{NH}_2 > -\text{C}\equiv\text{C}-$ follows the IUPAC priority order strictly from highest to lowest.
  4. Step 4 — Conclude the answer: The correct option is (c).
Q14.stepsLatex:
1. Option (a) puts > C = O before −CHO (wrong).
2. Option (b) puts −CONH2 before −COOCH3 (wrong; ester > amide).
3. Option (c): −CONH2 > −CHO >> C = O > −NH2 > −C ≡ C− =⇒ Correct.
4. Option (d) puts −CHO before −CN (wrong; nitrile > aldehyde).
Q14.trapHtml: Remember: Ester (−COOR) > Amide (−CONH<sub>2</sub>) > Nitrile (−CN) > Aldehyde (−CHO) > Ketone (> C = O).

Q15.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Preferred Site in Benzamide
Q15.conceptHtml: In N-phenylbenzamide (Ph − C(= O) − NH − Ph), the ring attached to −NH− is strongly activated (+M, o/p-directing), whereas the ring attached to −C = O− is deactivated (−M, m-directing).
Q15.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Compare the two benzene rings in benzanilide ($x$): The left benzene ring is bonded to the carbonyl carbon ($-\text{CONHPh}$), which is an electron-withdrawing ($-\text{M}$) deactivating group. The right benzene ring is bonded to the amide nitrogen ($-\text{NHCOPh}$), whose lone pair donates electron density into the ring ($+\text{M}$), making it an activating, ortho/para-directing group.
  2. Step 2 — Identify the ring that reacts with an electrophile: Electrophilic aromatic substitution occurs preferentially on the more electron-rich, activated ring—the right-hand ring containing positions "s" (ortho) and "u" (para).
  3. Step 3 — Choose between ortho ("s") and para ("u"): Because the $-\text{NHCOPh}$ group is bulky, attack at the ortho position ("s") suffers significant steric hindrance, whereas the para position ("u") is sterically unhindered.
  4. Step 4 — Conclude the preferred site: Electrophilic attack occurs predominantly at position "u", matching option (d).
Q15.stepsLatex:
1. Left ring is attached to −C(= O)− (−M group) =⇒ deactivated toward SEAr.
2. Right ring is attached to −NH− (+M group) =⇒ strongly activated toward SEAr at ortho/para positions.
3. Between ortho (‘s‘) and para (‘u‘) on the activated ring, the para position (‘u‘) is sterically unhindered and
preferred predominantly.
Q15.trapHtml: Always split unsymmetrical amides/esters into the −C = O side (deactivated) and the −NH−/−O− side (activated).

Q16.conceptHtml: An electron-withdrawing −NO<sub>2</sub> group (−M, −I) decreases ring electron density, deactivating S<sub>E</sub>Ar and activating S<sub>N</sub>Ar (via Meisenheimer complex stabilization).
Q16.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Determine the electronic nature of the $-\text{NO}_2$ group: The nitro group ($-\text{NO}_2$) is strongly electron-withdrawing through both $-\text{M}$ (resonance) and $-\text{I}$ (inductive) effects, reducing electron density in the benzene ring.
  2. Step 2 — Effect on electrophilic substitution (A vs B): Electrophiles seek electron-rich rings. Because $-\text{NO}_2$ depletes electron density from the ring, it strongly deactivates the ring toward electrophilic substitution. Thus, B is correct and A is incorrect.
  3. Step 3 — Effect on nucleophilic substitution (C vs D): Nucleophiles attack electron-deficient rings, and the $-\text{NO}_2$ group stabilises the negatively charged Meisenheimer intermediate formed during nucleophilic aromatic substitution ($\text{S}_\text{N}\text{Ar}$). Therefore, $-\text{NO}_2$ activates the ring toward nucleophilic substitution. Thus, C is correct and D is incorrect.
  4. Step 4 — Select the matching option: Statements B and C are correct, corresponding to option (d).
Q16.stepsLatex:
1. −NO2 deactivates benzene toward electrophilic substitution (B is true, A is false).
2. −NO2 activates benzene toward nucleophilic aromatic substitution (C is true, D is false).
Q16.trapHtml: Activating/deactivating depends on the reagent: EWGs deactivate S<sub>E</sub>Ar but activate S<sub>N</sub>Ar.

Q17.subtopic: Hyperconjugation — α-Hydrogen Counting in Cyclic Cations
Q17.conceptHtml: Number of hyperconjugable α-hydrogens = total C − H bonds on sp<sup>3</sup> carbons directly adjacent to the positively charged carbon.
Q17.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall how to count hyperconjugation interactions: For a carbocation, the number of hyperconjugating structures equals the total number of $\alpha$-hydrogen atoms (hydrogens bonded to $sp^3$ carbons directly adjacent to the positively charged carbon).
  2. Step 2 — Count $\alpha$-H in cations A and B: In A ($1$-methyl-$2$-ethylcyclohex-$1$-yl cation), the $\text{C}^+$ is adjacent to a $-\text{CH}_3$ ($3\,\alpha\text{-H}$), a ring $-\text{CH}_2-$ ($2\,\alpha\text{-H}$), and a ring $-\text{CH(Et)}-$ ($1\,\alpha\text{-H}$), giving $3 + 2 + 1 = 6\,\alpha\text{-H}$. In B ($1$-methyl-$3$-ethylcyclohex-$1$-yl cation), $\text{C}^+$ is adjacent to $-\text{CH}_3$ ($3\,\alpha\text{-H}$) and two ring $-\text{CH}_2-$ groups ($2 + 2 = 4\,\alpha\text{-H}$), giving $3 + 4 = 7\,\alpha\text{-H}$.
  3. Step 3 — Count $\alpha$-H in cations C and D: In C ($1,3$-diethylcyclohex-$1$-yl cation), $\text{C}^+$ is adjacent to an exocyclic $-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ ($2\,\alpha\text{-H}$) and two ring $-\text{CH}_2-$ groups ($2 + 2 = 4\,\alpha\text{-H}$), giving $2 + 4 = 6\,\alpha\text{-H}$. In D ($1,2$-diethylcyclohex-$1$-yl cation), $\text{C}^+$ is adjacent to $-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ ($2\,\alpha\text{-H}$), one ring $-\text{CH}_2-$ ($2\,\alpha\text{-H}$), and one ring $-\text{CH(Et)}-$ ($1\,\alpha\text{-H}$), giving $2 + 2 + 1 = 5\,\alpha\text{-H}$.
  4. Step 4 — Identify the matching pair: Both cations A and C have $6$ hyperconjugating structures, which corresponds to option (c).
Q17.stepsLatex:
1. Structure A (1-ethylcyclohexyl cation? Look at the rendered figure: A has +-charge at C1 with ethyl substituent
=⇒ 2 ring CH2’s + 1 ethyl CH2 = 2 + 2 + 2 = 6 α-H).
2. Structure B (+ at C2 adjacent to ethyl at C1 =⇒ 1 CH + 1 CH2 = 3 α-H).
3. Structure C (+ at C1 with isopropyl/propyl? In the rendered figure, C has + on the ring carbon bearing
−CH(CH3)2 or −CH2CH3: wait, C has 2 + 2 + 2 = 6 or 5 α-H; A and C both have the exact same number of
α-H!).
Q17.trapHtml: Count only hydrogens on sp<sup>3</sup> carbons directly bonded to the C<sup>+</sup> center, not β-hydrogens.

Q18.conceptHtml: Higher s-character increases electronegativity of carbon, stabilizing the negative charge closer to the nucleus: sp (50%) > sp<sup>2</sup> (33.3%) > sp<sup>3</sup> (25%).
Q18.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Determine the hybridisation of the negatively charged carbon: In $\text{CH}\equiv\text{C}^-$, the anionic carbon is $sp$-hybridised ($50\%$ $s$-character). In $\text{CH}_2=\text{CH}^-$, it is $sp^2$-hybridised ($33.3\%$ $s$-character). In $\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}_2^-$, it is $sp^3$-hybridised ($25\%$ $s$-character).
  2. Step 2 — Relate $s$-character to electronegativity and stability: Higher $s$-character pulls the lone pair closer to the nucleus, making the carbon atom more electronegative and better able to hold a negative charge.
  3. Step 3 — Order the carbanions by stability: Decreasing $s$-character ($50\% > 33.3\% > 25\%$) gives the stability order $\text{CH}\equiv\text{C}^- > \text{CH}_2=\text{CH}^- > \text{CH}_3-\text{CH}_2^-$.
  4. Step 4 — Match with the options: This order matches option (c).
Q18.stepsLatex:
1. CH ≡ C− (sp) > CH2 = CH− (sp2) > CH3 − CH− (sp3).
2
Q18.trapHtml: This is the exact reverse of carbocation stability, where sp<sup>3</sup> alkyl is far more stable than vinyl/alkynyl cations.
Q18.finalAnsHtml: (c) CH ≡ C<sup>−</sup> > CH<sub>2</sub> = CH<sup>−</sup> > CH<sub>3</sub> − CH<sup>−</sup><sub>2</sub>

Q19.conceptHtml: In n-butane, the fully eclipsed conformer (θ = 0<sup>°</sup>) has maximum torsional + steric strain (least stable), while the anti conformer (θ = 180<sup>°</sup>) has minimum strain (most stable).
Q19.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify conformers (X) and (Y) of $n$-butane: In the Newman projections shown, conformer (X) has both $-\text{CH}_3$ groups directly overlapping at a dihedral angle of $0^\circ$ (fully eclipsed), while conformer (Y) has the two $-\text{CH}_3$ groups opposite each other at a dihedral angle of $180^\circ$ (anti / staggered).
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement I: Fully eclipsed (X) suffers maximum torsional and van der Waals steric repulsion, making it the least stable conformer; anti (Y) has minimum steric and torsional repulsion, making it the most stable conformer. Thus, Statement I is true.
  3. Step 3 — Evaluate Statement II: As the dihedral angle increases from $0^\circ$ (eclipsed X) toward staggered conformations like anti (Y, $180^\circ$), bond-pair repulsions decrease and torsional strain decreases. Thus, Statement II is also true.
  4. Step 4 — Match with the options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true, corresponding to option (d).
Q19.stepsLatex:
1. Statement I: (X) is fully eclipsed (θ = 0◦, least stable) and (Y) is anti (θ = 180◦, most stable) =⇒ True.
2. Statement II: As dihedral angle increases from 0◦ (X) to 180◦ (Y), torsional strain decreases overall (reaching
minimum at anti) =⇒ True.
Q19.trapHtml: Gauche (θ = 60<sup>°</sup>) is staggered (zero torsional strain) but has slight van der Waals steric repulsion between CH<sub>3</sub> groups; anti (θ = 180<sup>°</sup>) is the global minimum.
Q19.finalAnsHtml: (d) Both Statement I and Statement II are true

Q20.conceptHtml: Electromeric +E: π-electrons move toward reagent (electrophile); −E: π-electrons move away (nucleophile). More alkyl groups on C = C =⇒ more stable alkene =⇒ lower heat of hydrogenation.
Q20.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Check statements A, C, and E: Statement A is true (more covalent bonds and less charge separation stabilise a resonance contributor). Statement C is true (permanent bond polarity from inductive effect raises dipole moment, boiling point, and melting point). Statement E is true (higher $s$-character increases carbon electronegativity and stabilises a carbanion).
  2. Step 2 — Check statement B (Electromeric effect): In $+\text{E}$ effect, $\pi$-electrons shift toward the attacking reagent (which happens with an electrophile like $\text{H}^+$), whereas in $-\text{E}$ effect, $\pi$-electrons shift away from the attacking reagent (which happens with a nucleophile like $\text{CN}^-$). Statement B reverses this, so B is not true.
  3. Step 3 — Check statement D (Heat of hydrogenation): More alkyl groups on a $\text{C}=\text{C}$ bond increase alkene stability via hyperconjugation. A more stable alkene has lower potential energy and releases less heat on hydrogenation (lower heat of hydrogenation), not higher. So D is not true.
  4. Step 4 — Identify the incorrect statements: Only statements B and D are not true, which matches option (c).
Q20.stepsLatex:
1. A: True (standard resonance rule).
2. B: False (+E is with electrophile, −E is with nucleophile — reversed in statement!).
3. C: True (polarity increases dipole moment and intermolecular forces).
4. D: False (more substituted alkene is more stable, so heat of hydrogenation is lower, not higher).
5. E: True (higher s-character stabilizes carbanion).
Q20.trapHtml: Always check whether the question asks for true or not true statements!

Q21.conceptHtml: Carbanions are stabilized by −M and −I groups and destabilized by +I and +M groups.
Q21.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Understand what stabilises benzyl carbanions: All five ions are para-substituted benzyl carbanions ($p\text{-G}-\text{C}_6\text{H}_4-\text{CH}_2^-$). Electron-withdrawing groups ($-\text{M}, -\text{I}$) disperse the negative charge and stabilise the carbanion, whereas electron-donating groups ($+\text{M}, +\text{H}, +\text{I}$) destabilise it.
  2. Step 2 — Rank the electron-withdrawing substituents (IV and I): In IV, $-\text{CHO}$ exerts both strong $-\text{M}$ and $-\text{I}$ effects, making IV the most stable. In I, $-\text{Br}$ exerts a net electron-withdrawing effect ($-\text{I} > +\text{M}$), stabilising it relative to unsubstituted benzyl carbanion II. Thus, $\text{IV} > \text{I} > \text{II}$.
  3. Step 3 — Rank the electron-donating substituents (V and III): In V, $-\text{CH}_3$ destabilises the carbanion moderately via $+\text{H}$ and $+\text{I}$ effects. In III, $-\text{OCH}_3$ destabilises it strongly via the $+\text{M}$ resonance effect ($+\text{M} > -\text{I}$), making III the least stable. Thus, $\text{II} > \text{V} > \text{III}$.
  4. Step 4 — Combine the full sequence: The decreasing order of carbanion stability is $\text{IV} > \text{I} > \text{II} > \text{V} > \text{III}$, which matches option (d).
Q21.stepsLatex:
1. IV (p−CHO): Strong −M and −I =⇒ most stable.
2. I (p−Br): Weak −I > +M (overall electron-withdrawing) =⇒ 2nd.
3. II (C6H5CH−): Unsubstituted reference =⇒ 3rd.
2
4. V (p−CH3): +I and weak +HC destabilizes carbanion =⇒ 4th.
5. III (p−OCH3): Strong +M donates electron density, strongly destabilizing carbanion =⇒ least stable.
Q21.trapHtml: For halogens at the para position of a carbanion, −I dominates over +M, so p−Br − C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>4</sub>CH<sup>−</sup><sub>2</sub> is more stable than C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CH<sup>−</sup><sub>2</sub> .

Q22.conceptHtml: (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>C<sup>+</sup> has 9 α-H atoms (9 hyperconjugative structures), whereas CH<sup>+</sup><sub>3</sub> has 0 α-H atoms (zero hyper- conjugation).
Q22.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Count $\alpha$-hydrogens in $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}^+$: In the tert-butyl carbocation, the positively charged carbon is attached to three $-\text{CH}_3$ groups, providing $3 \times 3 = 9$ $\alpha$-hydrogens and therefore $9$ hyperconjugation interactions. This makes it much more stable than $\text{CH}_3^+$. Hence, Statement I is true.
  2. Step 2 — Count $\alpha$-hydrogens in $\text{CH}_3^+$: For hyperconjugation, there must be a $\text{C}-\text{H}$ bond on a carbon adjacent ($\alpha$-carbon) to the positively charged carbon. In $\text{CH}_3^+$, the three hydrogens are bonded directly to the $\text{C}^+$ atom itself—there are zero $\alpha$-carbons and zero hyperconjugation interactions (not three).
  3. Step 3 — Evaluate Statement II: Because $\text{CH}_3^+$ has zero hyperconjugation interactions rather than three, Statement II is false.
  4. Step 4 — Match with the options: Statement I is true and Statement II is false, which corresponds to option (b).
Q22.stepsLatex:
1. Statement I: (CH3)3C+ has 9 hyperconjugation interactions =⇒ True.
2. Statement II: Claims CH+ has 3 hyperconjugation interactions — false! CH+ has zero α-carbons and zero
3 3
hyperconjugation =⇒ False.
Q22.trapHtml: Hydrogens attached directly to the C<sup>+</sup> atom are NOT α-hydrogens; CH<sup>+</sup><sub>3</sub> has 0 hyperconjugative structures.
Q22.finalAnsHtml: (b) Statement I is true but Statement II is false

Q23.conceptHtml: Sublimation separates sublimable solids (high vapour pressure below m.p.) from non-sublimable impurities, regardless of low m.p. Boiling point decreases when external pressure is reduced.
Q23.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement I (Sublimation): Sublimation is used to separate sublimable volatile solids (which pass directly from solid to vapour on heating, such as camphor, naphthalene, or benzoic acid) from non-sublimable impurities. It is based on high vapour pressure of the solid below its triple point, not simply on having a "low melting point". Hence, Statement I is false.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement II (Effect of pressure on boiling point): A liquid boils when its vapour pressure equals the external atmospheric pressure. When the external pressure is reduced, the liquid reaches that lower pressure at a lower temperature, so its boiling point decreases (which is the basis of distillation under reduced pressure), not increases. Hence, Statement II is false.
  3. Step 3 — Conclude the answer: Both Statement I and Statement II are false, matching option (a).
Q23.stepsLatex:
1. Statement I: Sublimation is based on direct solid-to-vapour transition (high vapour pressure), not low melting
point =⇒ False.
2. Statement II: Boiling point decreases (not increases) as external pressure is reduced (principle of vacuum
distillation) =⇒ False.
Q23.trapHtml: Reduced pressure =⇒ lower boiling point (used for glycerol so it distills before decomposing).
Q23.finalAnsHtml: (a) Both Statement I and Statement II are false

Q24.conceptHtml: In esters (R − C(= O) − O − R<sup>′</sup>), the alkyl group on oxygen (R<sup>′</sup>) is named first as a prefix, followed by the parent alkanoate chain numbered from C1 = O.
Q24.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the functional group and alkyl part on oxygen: The molecule is an ester ($\text{R}-\text{COO}-\text{R'}$). The group attached directly to the single-bonded oxygen is a straight $3$-carbon chain ($-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$), which is named first as $n$-propyl.
  2. Step 2 — Find the longest carbon chain starting from the carbonyl carbon (C−1): Starting at C−1 ($\text{C}=\text{O}$), trace along C−2 ($-\text{CH(Br)}-$), C−3 ($-\text{CH}_2-$), C−4 ($-\text{CH}_2-$), C-5 ($-\text{CH(CH}_3)-$), and follow the longer ethyl branch to C-6 and C-7. The parent chain has $7$ carbons, giving the root name heptanoate.
  3. Step 3 — Locate and alphabetise the substituents: There is a bromo group at C−2 and a methyl group at C-5. Listed alphabetically, the acyl part is $2$-bromo-$5$-methylheptanoate.
  4. Step 4 — Assemble the complete IUPAC name: Combining the ester alkyl prefix and acyl root gives $n$-propyl-$2$-bromo-$5$-methylheptanoate, which matches option (c).
Q24.stepsLatex:
1. Group attached to −O− has 3 carbons in a straight chain =⇒ n-propyl.
2. Acyl chain from C1(= O): C1(= O) − C2(Br) − C3H2 − C4H2 − C5(CH3) − C6H2 − C7H3 =⇒ 7-carbon
chain (heptanoate) with −Br at C2 and −CH3 at C5.
3. Name: n-propyl-2-bromo-5-methylheptanoate.
Q24.trapHtml: Count the carbonyl carbon (C = O) as C1 and trace the longest chain carefully so you don’t miscount 7 carbons as 6.

Q25.conceptHtml: Match pairs by comparing carbon skeleton (chain), substituent locant (position), functional group (func- tional), and 3D arrangement (stereoisomers).
Q25.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Match A ($2$-Methylpropene and but-$1$-ene): Both have formula $\text{C}_4\text{H}_8$ and a double bond at C−1, but differ in the carbon skeleton (branched $3$-carbon chain vs straight $4$-carbon chain), so they are chain isomers ($\text{A} \to \text{III}$).
  2. Step 2 — Match B (cis-but-$2$-ene and trans-but-$2$-ene): They have identical connectivity but different spatial arrangements around the $\text{C}=\text{C}$ bond, making them geometrical stereoisomers ($\text{B} \to \text{I}$).
  3. Step 3 — Match C ($2$-Butanol and diethyl ether): Both have formula $\text{C}_4\text{H}_{10}\text{O}$ but different functional groups (alcohol vs ether), so they are functional group isomers ($\text{C} \to \text{IV}$).
  4. Step 4 — Match D (But-$1$-ene and but-$2$-ene): Both have the same $4$-carbon straight chain but differ in the position of the double bond, so they are position isomers ($\text{D} \to \text{II}$). Thus A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II matches option (a).
Q25.stepsLatex:
1. A. 2-Methylpropene (3-C chain) and but-1-ene (4-C chain) =⇒ Chain isomers (III).
2. B. cis-but-2-ene and trans-but-2-ene =⇒ Stereoisomers (I).
3. C. 2-Butanol (alcohol) and diethyl ether (ether) =⇒ Functional group isomers (IV).
4. D. But-1-ene and but-2-ene (double bond position) =⇒ Position isomers (II).
Q25.trapHtml: Double-bond position shift without changing the carbon chain length is position isomerism, not chain isomerism.

Q26.conceptHtml: Only a molecule with a chiral center (4 different groups on carbon) exhibits optical isomerism.
Q26.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify which compound exhibits optical isomerism: Check each chloride for a chiral carbon (bonded to four different groups): $n$-propyl chloride ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$), iso-propyl chloride ($(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CHCl}$), and neo-pentyl chloride ($(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{CCH}_2\text{Cl}$) have no chiral centre. Only sec-butyl chloride ($\text{CH}_3-\text{CH(Cl)}-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$) has a chiral carbon (attached to $-\text{H}, -\text{Cl}, -\text{CH}_3, -\text{C}_2\text{H}_5$).
  2. Step 2 — Calculate the molar mass of sec-butyl chloride ($\text{C}_4\text{H}_9\text{Cl}$): Using atomic masses $\text{C} = 12$, $\text{H} = 1$, and $\text{Cl} = 35.5$, the molar mass is $4(12) + 9(1) + 35.5 = 48 + 9 + 35.5 = 92.5\text{ g mol}^{-1}$.
  3. Step 3 — Compute the percentage of carbon: $\%\text{C} = \frac{48}{92.5} \times 100 = 51.89\% \approx 52\%$.
  4. Step 4 — Match with the options: The value $52$ corresponds to option (c).
Q26.stepsLatex:
∗
1. Among n-propyl chloride, iso-propyl chloride, sec-butyl chloride (CH3 − CH(Cl) − CH2CH3), and neo-pentyl
chloride, only sec-butyl chloride (C4H9Cl) has a chiral carbon.
2. Molar mass of C4H9Cl = 4(12) + 9(1) + 35.5 = 92.5 g mol−1.
3. %C = 48 × 100 ≈ 51.89% ≈ 52%.
92.5
Q26.trapHtml: Don’t forget to round 51.89% to the nearest integer 52.

Q27.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Least Stable Canonical Form
Q27.conceptHtml: Resonance structures with adjacent like charges (+ next to +) are extremely unstable due to electrostatic repulsion.
Q27.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the key stability rule for charged resonance structures: Structures that place like charges (such as two positive charges) on directly adjacent atoms experience strong electrostatic repulsion and are extremely unstable.
  2. Step 2 — Examine the charge positions in all four structures: In each structure, the nitrogen atom of the $-\text{NO}_2$ group bears a formal positive charge ($+1$). In structures (a), (b), and (c), the carbocationic positive charge is separated from the $\text{N}^+$ atom by one or more carbon atoms.
  3. Step 3 — Inspect structure (d): In structure (d), the carbocationic positive charge sits on the carbon atom directly bonded to the positively charged nitrogen of the $-\text{NO}_2$ group ($-\text{CH}^+-\text{N}^+(= ext{O})\text{O}^-$), causing severe adjacent-charge repulsion.
  4. Step 4 — Conclude the least stable structure: Because of this adjacent positive–positive repulsion, structure (d) is the least stable.
Q27.stepsLatex:
1. In all four structures, the nitro group has a formal +1 charge on N.
2. In option (d), the carbocation + charge sits on the carbon directly adjacent to N+, creating adjacent +/+
repulsion!
3. Hence (d) is the least stable contributing structure.
Q27.trapHtml: Adjacent like charges (+ on C1 next to N<sup>+</sup>) always make a canonical structure the least stable.

Q28.conceptHtml: But-2-ene is achiral (no optical isomerism); but-1-ene and but-2-ene are position isomers, not functional isomers.
Q28.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Check statements A and B: Propanal ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CHO}$) and propanone ($\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_3$) both have formula $\text{C}_3\text{H}_6\text{O}$ with different functional groups (aldehyde vs ketone), so A is correct. Ethoxyethane ($\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OC}_2\text{H}_5$) and methoxypropane ($\text{CH}_3\text{OC}_3\text{H}_7$) differ in alkyl chains around the ether oxygen, so they are metamers; B is correct.
  2. Step 2 — Check statements C and D: But-$2$-ene is planar with no chiral carbon; it shows geometrical (cis–trans) isomerism, not optical isomerism, so C is incorrect. But-$1$-ene and but-$2$-ene have the same alkene functional group at different positions, so they are position isomers (not functional isomers), making D incorrect.
  3. Step 3 — Check statement E: Pentane and $2,2$-dimethylpropane share formula $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{12}$ and differ in carbon chain branching, so they are chain isomers; E is correct.
  4. Step 4 — Select the matching option: Statements A, B, and E are correct, which matches option (a).
Q28.stepsLatex:
1. A: Propanal & propanone (C3H6O) = functional isomers =⇒ True.
2. B: Ethoxyethane & methoxypropane (C4H10O) = metamers =⇒ True.
3. C: But-2-ene shows geometrical, NOT optical isomerism =⇒ False.
4. D: But-1-ene & but-2-ene are position isomers, NOT functional =⇒ False.
5. E: Pentane & 2, 2-dimethylpropane (C5H12) = chain isomers =⇒ True.
Q28.trapHtml: Alkenes like but-2-ene are planar at the double bond and show geometrical isomerism, not optical isomerism.

Q29.conceptHtml: Carbocations are sp<sup>2</sup> with an empty p-orbital (6e<sup>−</sup>); C-free radicals are sp<sup>2</sup> (or sp<sup>3</sup> when bridged/strained) with 1 unpaired e<sup>−</sup>; nucleophiles donate e<sup>−</sup> pairs; electrophiles accept e<sup>−</sup> pairs.
Q29.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Match A (Carbocation): A carbocation ($\text{R}_3\text{C}^+$) has three $\sigma$-bonds and $6$ valence electrons, so the central carbon is $sp^2$-hybridised with a vacant unhybridised $p$-orbital. Thus, $\text{A} \to \text{III}$.
  2. Step 2 — Match B (C-Free radical): A carbon free radical ($\text{R}_3\text{C}^\cdot$) is typically $sp^2$-hybridised (or shallow pyramidal $sp^3$-like when substituted with electronegative atoms) and contains one unpaired electron. Thus, $\text{B} \to \text{IV}$.
  3. Step 3 — Match C (Nucleophile) and D (Electrophile): A nucleophile ("nucleus-loving") is an electron-rich species that can donate/supply an electron pair ($\text{C} \to \text{I}$). An electrophile ("electron-loving") is an electron-deficient species that can accept/receive an electron pair ($\text{D} \to \text{II}$).
  4. Step 4 — Match with the options: The combination A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II corresponds to option (c).
Q29.stepsLatex:
1. A. Carbocation → sp2 hybridized carbon with empty p-orbital (III).
2. B. C-Free radical → sp2/sp3 hybridized carbon with one unpaired electron (IV).
3. C. Nucleophile → Species that can supply a pair of electrons (I).
4. D. Electrophile → Species that can receive a pair of electrons (II).
Q29.trapHtml: Don’t swap Nucleophile (electron-pair donor) and Electrophile (electron-pair acceptor).

Q30.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Priority of −OH over C = C
Q30.conceptHtml: The principal functional group (−OH) gets locant 1; numbering then proceeds through the double bond to give C = C the lowest locant (2, 3).
Q30.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the principal functional group: The ring contains both an alcohol ($-\text{OH}$) and a double bond ($\text{C}=\text{C}$). Since $-\text{OH}$ has higher IUPAC priority than an alkene, it receives locant $1$ and the suffix -ol.
  2. Step 2 — Number the cyclopentene ring: Starting at C−1 (carbon bearing $-\text{OH}$), number toward the double bond to give the alkene the lowest possible locants (C−2 and C−3). Continuing around the ring places the ethyl substituent at C−4.
  3. Step 3 — Assemble the IUPAC name: Combining substituent ($4$-ethyl), ring root (cyclopent), unsaturation ($2$-en), and principal suffix ($1$-ol) gives $4$-Ethylcyclopent-$2$-en-$1$-ol.
  4. Step 4 — Match with the options: This matches option (b).
Q30.stepsLatex:
1. −OH is at C1.
2. Numbering through the double bond gives C2 = C3 and puts the ethyl group at C4.
3. Name: 4-Ethylcyclopent-2-en-1-ol.
Q30.trapHtml: Never number from the ethyl substituent or double bond when −OH is present; −OH is the principal functional group and must be C1.

Q31.conceptHtml: Reductive ozonolysis cleaves C = C into C = O groups. Check if the resulting fragments retain any chiral centers without internal symmetry.
Q31.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Write the structure of the given triene: The compound is $\text{H}_3\text{C}-\text{CH}=\text{CH}-\text{CH(CH}_3)-\text{CH}=\text{CH}-\text{CH(CH}_3)-\text{CH}=\text{CH}-\text{CH}_3$.
  2. Step 2 — Perform complete ozonolysis: Cleaving all three $\text{C}=\text{C}$ double bonds and replacing each $=\text{CH}-$ end with $=\text{O}$ yields: two molecules of acetaldehyde ($\text{CH}_3\text{CHO}$) from the two terminal double bonds, and two molecules of $2$-methylpropanedial ($\text{OHC}-\text{CH(CH}_3)-\text{CHO}$) from the internal fragments.
  3. Step 3 — Check every product for optical activity: Acetaldehyde ($\text{CH}_3\text{CHO}$) has no chiral carbon, so it is optically inactive. In $2$-methylpropanedial ($\text{OHC}-\text{CH(CH}_3)-\text{CHO}$), the central carbon is bonded to two identical $-\text{CHO}$ groups (along with $-\text{CH}_3$ and $-\text{H}$), so it is also achiral and optically inactive.
  4. Step 4 — Count the optically active products: Neither product is chiral, so the number of optically active products is $0$, matching option (b).
Q31.stepsLatex:
1. Cleaving the three C = C bonds gives: CH3CHO (achiral) from both ends, and the central fragments OHC − CH(CH3) − CH

Q32.conceptHtml: Only acids stronger than H<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 6.35) liberate CO<sub>2</sub> with NaHCO<sub>3</sub>: RCOOH, picric acid (pK<sub>a</sub> = 0.38), and anilinium chloride (PhNH<sup>+</sup><sub>3</sub> Cl<sup>−</sup>, pK<sub>a</sub> = 4.6). Simple nitrophenols (p-nitrophenol, pK<sub>a</sub> = 7.15) do NOT.

1. Step 1 — Recall the condition for the $\text{NaHCO}_3$ effervescence test: An organic acid liberates $\text{CO}_2$ gas with aqueous $\text{NaHCO}_3$ only if it is a stronger acid than carbonic acid ($\text{H}_2\text{CO}_3$, $pK_a \approx 6.35$).

Step 2 — Evaluate options (a), (b), and (c): Strong organic acids such as sulfonic/ammonium acids in (a), $p$-nitrobenzoic acid in (b) ($pK_a \approx 3.4$), and picric acid ($2,4,6$-trinitrophenol) in (c) ($pK_a \approx 0.4$, strongly acidified by three $-\text{NO}_2$ groups) all have $pK_a < 6.35$ and readily give $\text{CO}_2$ effervescence.

Step 3 — Evaluate option (d) ($m$-nitrophenol): In $m$-nitrophenol, the single $-\text{NO}_2$ group at the meta position exerts only a $-\text{I}$ effect (no $-\text{M}$ resonance stabilisation of the phenoxide ion). Its $pK_a \approx 8.4$, which is weaker than $\text{H}_2\text{CO}_3$, so it does not liberate $\text{CO}_2$ with aqueous $\text{NaHCO}_3$.
  4. Step 4 — Conclude the answer: The compound least likely to give $\text{CO}_2$ effervescence is $m$-nitrophenol, which is option (d).
