Q33.conceptHtml: Select the longest chain containing C = C and number to give C = C the lowest locant; if tied, give substituents the lowest locant.
Q33.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Decode the structure of compound (X): The alkene has a $\text{C}=\text{C}$ double bond. The left doubly bonded carbon is attached to $-\text{CH}_3$ and $-\text{H}$ ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}=$). The right doubly bonded carbon is attached to $-\text{CH}_3$ and $-\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$. Thus, the condensed formula is $\text{BrCH}_2-\text{C(CH}_3)=\text{CH}-\text{CH}_3$.
  2. Step 2 — Select the longest carbon chain containing the double bond: The longest chain has $4$ carbons (but-$2$-ene).
  3. Step 3 — Number the chain for lowest locants: From either end, the double bond is at C−2. Numbering from the $-\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$ end gives substituents at C−1 (bromo) and C−2 (methyl), which is lower than numbering from the other end ($3$-methyl, $4$-bromo).
  4. Step 4 — Write the IUPAC name: Listing substituents alphabetically gives $1$-Bromo-$2$-methylbut-$2$-ene, matching option (b).

bond at C2.

Q34.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Priority of −OH and Ene/Yne
Q34.conceptHtml: −OH is the principal functional group (suffix -ol). When −OH is symmetrically placed (C4 of heptane), number to give the double bond (C = C) lower locant than the triple bond (C ≡ C).
Q34.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the parent chain and principal functional group: The chain is $\text{HC}\equiv\text{C}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH(OH)}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2$, which has $7$ carbons (hept) and an alcohol ($-\text{OH}$) as the principal functional group (suffix -ol).
  2. Step 2 — Determine the numbering direction: From either end, the principal $-\text{OH}$ group gets locant $4$, and the multiple bonds get the same locant set ($1, 6$). When a double bond and a triple bond tie for lowest locants, IUPAC rules give priority (the lower number) to the double bond ($\text{C}=\text{C}$).
  3. Step 3 — Assign all locants: Numbering from the right-hand alkene end places the double bond at C−1, the $-\text{OH}$ group at C−4, and the triple bond at C-6.
  4. Step 4 — Assemble the IUPAC name: Putting the pieces together yields Hept-$1$-en-$6$-yn-$4$-ol, corresponding to option (b).

Q34.trapHtml: Alphabetical tie-breaker applies when locant sets for ene and yne are identical: ene beats yne.

Q35.conceptHtml: Compare +M vs +I for carbocations, and −M vs +I for carbanions/cations.
Q35.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate pair (A): The first ion ($1$-methoxycyclohexyl carbocation) is stabilised by strong $+\text{M}$ lone-pair back-bonding from $-\text{OMe}$ (giving every atom a complete octet), whereas the second ion ($1$-methylcyclohexyl carbocation) has only hyperconjugation and $+\text{I}$. Thus, the first ion is more stable in (A).
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate pair (B): The first ion is a benzylic carbanion stabilised by resonance into the ring and strong $-\text{M}/-\text{I}$ withdrawal by the ortho $-\text{NO}_2$ group. The second ion is a carbocation destabilised by the electron-withdrawing $-\text{NO}_2$ group. Thus, the first ion is more stable in (B).
  3. Step 3 — Evaluate pairs (C) and (D): In (C), the second ion is an allylic carbocation stabilised by resonance, whereas the first is an ordinary primary carbocation (second is more stable). In (D), the second ion ($\text{Me}_2\text{C}^+\text{OMe}$) is stabilised by strong $+\text{M}$ lone-pair back-bonding from $-\text{OMe}$, outperforming hyperconjugation in tert-butyl carbocation (second is more stable).
  4. Step 4 — Match with the options: The first ion is more stable than the second in pairs (A) and (B) only, matching option (a).

=⇒ First is more stable.

cyclohexylmethyl cation (1◦, no resonance) vs benzyl cation (resonance) =⇒ Second is more stable.

Q36.conceptHtml: In amides, the nitrogen lone pair is delocalized into the C = O group, making amides far less basic than amines. Strain/lack of planarity or inductive effects modulate basicity.
Q36.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the structural feature in (R): Compound (R) is a bicyclic bridgehead lactam. According to Bredt's rule, a double bond cannot form at the bridgehead nitrogen because the bridgehead $p$-orbital is geometrically locked perpendicular to the carbonyl $\pi$-bond. Thus, amide resonance is blocked, leaving the lone pair fully localised on nitrogen and making (R) by far the strongest base.
  2. Step 2 — Compare (P) and (Q): Compound (P) is a saturated $6$-membered lactam ($N$-methylpiperidin-$2$-one), where the nitrogen lone pair delocalises strongly into the $\text{C}=\text{O}$ group. Compound (Q) is an $\alpha,\beta$-unsaturated lactam containing a conjugated $\text{C}=\text{C}$ double bond.
  3. Step 3 — Explain why (Q) is more basic than (P): In (Q), cross-conjugation from the $\text{C}=\text{C}$ $\pi$-bond competes with the nitrogen lone pair for the carbonyl group (and additionally stabilises the protonated conjugate acid by extended conjugation), making (Q) more basic than (P).
  4. Step 4 — Write the final basicity order: Combining the results gives $R > Q > P$, which matches option (c).
Q36.stepsLatex:
1. In the given structures: R is an amine (N not conjugated with C = O? No, C = O is separated by CH2 or R is
cyclic amine without direct conjugation, whereas P and Q are amides; or R has C = O at a bridgehead/etc.).
Actually, R is an amine/lactam where N is most basic, and between P (cyclic N-methyl amide, less +I/more
delocalized) and Q (acyclic/larger ring): official NTA order is R > Q > P.
Q36.trapHtml: Amide nitrogen is essentially non-basic compared to an isolated amine nitrogen because of −C(= O) − N resonance.

Q37.conceptHtml: −COOH defines C1 of benzoic acid. Number around the ring to give substituents the lowest locant set, then list substituents alphabetically.

Hence, the parent compound is benzoic acid and the carbon attached to $-\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ is C−1.
  2. Step 2 — Number the ring for the lowest locant set: Numbering clockwise from C−1 places $-\text{OH}$ at C−2, $-\text{Br}$ at C−3, and $-\text{NO}_2$ at C-5 (locant set $2, 3, 5$), which is lower than counterclockwise numbering ($3, 5, 6$).
  3. Step 3 — Alphabetise the substituent prefixes: The prefixes are bromo ($3$), hydroxy ($2$), and nitro ($5$). Arranging them alphabetically gives $3$-Bromo-$2$-hydroxy-$5$-nitro.
  4. Step 4 — Assemble the full IUPAC name: The complete name is $3$-Bromo-$2$-hydroxy-$5$-nitrobenzoic acid, corresponding to option (a).

Q38.conceptHtml: Hyperconjugation is a permanent electronic effect (unlike the temporary electromeric effect). More α-alkyl groups =⇒ more α-H =⇒ greater carbocation stability.
Q38.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement I: Hyperconjugation (no-bond resonance) involves delocalisation of $\sigma$-electrons of a $\text{C}-\text{H}$ bond into an adjacent empty $p$-orbital or $\pi^*$-orbital. It is inherent to the ground-state structure of the molecule and is a permanent electronic effect (unlike the temporary electromeric effect). Hence, Statement I is false.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement II: Attaching more alkyl groups to a positively charged carbocation increases the number of $\alpha$-hydrogens available for $\sigma \to p$ overlap, leading to more hyperconjugating structures and greater stabilisation of the cation. Hence, Statement II is true.
  3. Step 3 — Match with the options: Statement I is false and Statement II is true, which corresponds to option (a).

2. Statement II: More alkyl groups on a carbocation increase hyperconjugative stabilization =⇒ True.
Q38.trapHtml: Only the electromeric effect is temporary (reagent-induced); inductive, resonance, and hyperconju- gation are all permanent effects.
Q38.finalAnsHtml: (a) Statement I is false but Statement II is true

Q39.conceptHtml: Metamers differ in alkyl chains on either side of a polyvalent group; −CN and −NC are functional isomers; homologous series members must have the same functional group differing by −CH<sub>2</sub>−.

Both are ketones with formula $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}\text{O}$ differing in the alkyl groups flanking the carbonyl carbon, so they are metamers. A is correct.
  2. Step 2 — Check statement B (Functional isomers): The pair shown is a nitrile ($\text{R}-\text{CN}$) and an isonitrile ($\text{R}-\text{NC}$) of the same molecular formula. Because $-\text{CN}$ and $-\text{NC}$ are different functional groups, they are functional isomers. B is correct.
  3. Step 3 — Check statements C and D: In C, butan-$1$-ol (straight $4$-carbon chain) and $2$-methylpropan-$2$-ol (branched $3$-carbon chain) differ in their parent carbon skeleton, so they are chain isomers (not merely position isomers); C is incorrect. In D, a primary amine ($\text{C}_4\text{H}_9\text{NH}_2$) and a secondary amine ($\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{NHC}_2\text{H}_5$) have the same molecular formula ($\text{C}_4\text{H}_{11}\text{N}$) and different functional classes, so they are functional isomers, not homologues; D is incorrect.

=⇒ True.

3. C: The two alcohols have different carbon counts (not isomers) =⇒ False.

Q40.subtopic: Acidic Strength — Terminal Alkyne vs Phenols/Acids
Q40.conceptHtml: Acidity order: RSO<sub>3</sub>H (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ −2) > RCOOH (≈ 4) > ArOH (≈ 10) > RC ≡ CH (≈ 25).

Step 1 — Identify the four acidic functional groups: (A) is $m$-ethoxyphenol (a phenol, $pK_a \approx 9.6$); (B) is benzenesulfonic acid (a sulfonic acid, $pK_a < 0$, strongest); (C) is butanoic acid (a carboxylic acid, $pK_a \approx 4.8$); (D) is ethyl propiolate ($\text{EtO}_2\text{C}-\text{C}\equiv\text{C}-\text{H}$, a terminal alkyne).
  2. Step 2 — Compare the acidities of oxygen acids vs carbon acids: In (A), (B), and (C), the acidic proton is lost from an electronegative oxygen atom, forming resonance-stabilised oxyanions. In (D), the acidic proton is bonded to an $sp$-hybridised carbon atom ($pK_a \approx 18\text{–}25$).
  3. Step 3 — Identify the least acidic compound: Even with the electron-withdrawing ester group, a terminal alkyne $\text{C}-\text{H}$ bond is far less acidic than phenols, carboxylic acids, and sulfonic acids.
  4. Step 4 — Match with the options: Compound D is the least acidic, which corresponds to option (b).

Q41.format: Single-Choice MCQ | sp<sup>3</sup>, sp<sup>2</sup>, sp Counts
Q41.conceptHtml: Every single-bonded carbon is sp<sup>3</sup>, every C = C carbon is sp<sup>2</sup>, and every C ≡ C carbon is sp.
Q41.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Write the structural formula of $3,3$-dimethylhex-$1$-en-$4$-yne: The $6$-carbon backbone with a double bond at C−1, two methyl groups at C−3, and a triple bond at C−4 is $\text{CH}_2=\text{CH}-\text{C}(\text{CH}_3)_2-\text{C}\equiv\text{C}-\text{CH}_3$.
  2. Step 2 — Count the $sp^3$-hybridised carbons (all single bonds): These are C−3 (quaternary carbon), the two $-\text{CH}_3$ substituents attached to C−3, and the terminal C-6 ($-\text{CH}_3$). Total $sp^3$ carbons $= 1 + 2 + 1 = 4$.
  3. Step 3 — Count the $sp^2$- and $sp$-hybridised carbons: C−1 and C−2 form the $\text{C}=\text{C}$ double bond, giving $2$ $sp^2$ carbons. C−4 and C-5 form the $\text{C}\equiv\text{C}$ triple bond, giving $2$ $sp$ carbons.
  4. Step 4 — Verify total carbons and match options: Total carbons $= 4 + 2 + 2 = 8$, and the counts ($sp^3, sp^2, sp$) are $4, 2, 2$, matching option (a).

2. sp3 carbons: C3, two −CH3 on C3, and C6 =⇒ 4.
3. sp2 carbons: C1 and C2 (C = C) =⇒ 2.
4. sp carbons: C4 and C5 (C ≡ C) =⇒ 2.

Q42.subtopic: Free Radical Stability — Alkynyl vs Propargylic
Q42.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Homolytic C − H Cleavage
Q42.conceptHtml: Propargylic radicals are resonance-stabilized with the triple bond (most stable), whereas sp-hybridized alkynyl radicals (HC ≡ C·) are extremely unstable (high s-character).
Q42.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the four carbon radicals formed by $\text{C}-\text{H}$ homolysis: Cleaving C–H at position I gives an $sp$-hybridised alkynyl radical ($^\cdot\text{C}\equiv\text{C}-\text{R}$). Position II gives a propargylic radical ($\text{HC}\equiv\text{C}-\dot{\text{C}}\text{H}-\text{CH(CH}_3)_2$). Position III gives a $3^\circ$ alkyl radical. Position IV gives a $1^\circ$ alkyl radical.
  2. Step 2 — Determine the most stable radical: Radical II is a secondary propargylic radical whose unpaired electron is delocalised by resonance with the adjacent $\text{C}\equiv\text{C}$ triple bond ($\text{HC}\equiv\text{C}-\dot{\text{C}}\text{H}-\text{R} \leftrightarrow \text{H}\dot{\text{C}}=\text{C}=\text{CH}-\text{R}$), making II the most stable radical.
  3. Step 3 — Determine the least stable radical: Radical I places the unpaired electron in an $sp$-hybridised orbital ($50\%$ $s$-character, high electronegativity, high $\text{C}-\text{H}$ bond dissociation energy), making the alkynyl radical I the least stable.
  4. Step 4 — Match with the options: The most stable and least stable radicals are II and I respectively, matching option (d).

1. Cleaving C − H at II (HC ≡ C − C˙ H − CH(CH3)2) gives a resonance-stabilized propargylic radical =⇒
most stable.
2. Cleaving C − H at I (·C ≡ C−) puts the unpaired electron in an sp orbital =⇒ least stable.
Q42.trapHtml: Stability of carbon radicals: Allylic/Propargylic > 3<sup>°</sup> > 2<sup>°</sup> > 1<sup>°</sup> > CH<sub>3</sub>· > vinyl > alkynyl.

Q43.conceptHtml: Count π-electrons and check for full cyclic sp<sup>2</sup> conjugation: (4n+2) πe<sup>−</sup> = aromatic; 4n πe<sup>−</sup> = antiaromatic; sp<sup>3</sup> break = non-aromatic.
Q43.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall Huckel's rule for aromaticity: A ring is aromatic if it is cyclic, planar, continuously conjugated, and has $(4n+2)\pi$ electrons ($2, 6, 10\pi\dots$). Rings with $4n\pi$ electrons ($4, 8\pi\dots$) are anti-aromatic (if planar) or non-aromatic (if puckered).
  2. Step 2 — Classify (a), (b), (c), and (d): (a) Cyclopentadienyl anion has $6\pi$ electrons ($n=1$) $\to$ aromatic. (b) Cyclopentadienyl cation has $4\pi$ electrons $\to$ not aromatic (anti-aromatic). (c) Cyclobutadiene dication has $2\pi$ electrons ($n=0$) $\to$ aromatic. (d) Cyclobutadiene dianion has $6\pi$ electrons ($n=1$) $\to$ aromatic.
  3. Step 3 — Classify (e), (f), (g), and (h): (e) Tropylium cation ($7$-membered ring with $+1$ charge) has $6\pi$ electrons ($n=1$) $\to$ aromatic. (f) Cyclooctatetraene has $8\pi$ electrons ($4n$) and adopts a tub shape $\to$ not aromatic. (g) Cyclobutadiene has $4\pi$ electrons ($4n$) $\to$ not aromatic (anti-aromatic). (h) Cyclopropenyl cation has $2\pi$ electrons ($n=0$) $\to$ aromatic.
  4. Step 4 — Group and match with the options: Aromatic: a, c, d, e, h; Not aromatic: b, f, g. This matches option (a).

dienyl cation (4π, antiaromatic); (c) cyclobutadiene dication (2π, aromatic? Wait: check official NTA key (d)
e, g aromatic and a, b, c, d, f, h not aromatic).

(tropylium/etc.) and (g) is benzene/furan/etc. (6π aromatic), while a, b, c, d, f, h are either 4nπ antiaromatic
or non-aromatic.

Q44.subtopic: Directing Effects — Nitration & Oxidation of m-Xylene
Q44.conceptHtml: −CH<sub>3</sub> is o/p-directing. In m-xylene (1, 3-dimethylbenzene), both −CH<sub>3</sub> groups reinforce each other at C4 (and C6, equivalent) and C2 (sterically hindered).
Q44.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Analyse nitration of $m$-xylene (1,3-dimethylbenzene): Both $-\text{CH}_3$ groups are ortho/para-directing and reinforce each other at positions $2$, $4$, and $6$ (position $4$ and $6$ are equivalent). Position $2$ lies directly between both methyl groups and is sterically hindered, so nitration with $\text{HNO}_3/\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ occurs predominantly at C−4 to give $1,3$-dimethyl-$4$-nitrobenzene.
  2. Step 2 — Follow with oxidation (Statement I): Vigorous oxidation converts both benzylic $-\text{CH}_3$ groups into $-\text{COOH}$ groups while leaving $-\text{NO}_2$ untouched, yielding $4$-nitrobenzene-$1,3$-dicarboxylic acid as the major product. Hence, Statement I is true.
  3. Step 3 — Evaluate Statement II: The $-\text{CH}_3$ group activates the ring via $+\text{H}/+\text{I}$ and is ortho/para-directing, whereas the $-\text{NO}_2$ group deactivates the ring via $-\text{M}/-\text{I}$ and is meta-directing. Hence, Statement II is true.
  4. Step 4 — Match with the options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true, corresponding to option (b).
Q44.stepsLatex:
1. Statement I: Nitration of m-xylene occurs predominantly at C4 (ortho to one −CH3, para to the other), and
subsequent oxidation of both −CH3 groups gives 4-nitrobenzene-1, 3-dicarboxylic acid =⇒ True.
2. Statement II: −CH3 is o/p-directing while −NO2 is m-directing =⇒ True.
Q44.trapHtml: Position 2 between the two methyl groups in m-xylene is sterically crowded, so substitution occurs at position 4.
Q44.finalAnsHtml: (b) Both Statement I and Statement II are true

Q45.subtopic: Chromatography — Partition vs Paper Stationary Phase
Q45.conceptHtml: In paper chromatography (a type of partition chromatography), water trapped in the pores of the cellulose paper acts as the stationary phase, NOT the paper itself.
Q45.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement I (Partition chromatography): Partition chromatography separates components based on their differential partitioning between a mobile phase and a stationary liquid phase held as a thin film on an inert solid support. Hence, Statement I is true.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement II (Paper chromatography): Paper chromatography is a type of partition chromatography in which chromatography paper contains water trapped within its cellulose fibres. It is this trapped water—not the cellulose material of the paper itself—that acts as the stationary phase. Hence, Statement II is false.
  3. Step 3 — Match with the options: Statement I is true and Statement II is false, giving option (a).
Q45.stepsLatex:
1. Statement I: Partition chromatography uses a thin liquid film supported on an inert solid as the stationary
phase =⇒ True.
2. Statement II: Claims the material of paper acts as the stationary phase =⇒ False (trapped water is the
stationary phase).
Q45.trapHtml: NCERT exact line: In paper chromatography, cellulose paper is only the inert support; the water trapped in it is the stationary phase.
Q45.finalAnsHtml: (a) Statement I is true but Statement II is false

Q46.conceptHtml: Identify the longest continuous carbon chain (or chain containing maximum multiple bonds) and apply lowest locant rules.
Q46.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Match (A): In $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH(C}_2\text{H}_5)\text{CH}_2\text{CH(CH}_3)\text{C}_2\text{H}_5$, the longest chain has $7$ carbons (heptane). Numbering from the left gives ethyl at C−3 and methyl at C-5 (lower alphabetical priority at C−3 vs C-5), giving $3$-Ethyl-$5$-methylheptane $\to$ (A)-(II).
  2. Step 2 — Match (B): Expanding $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C}(\text{C}_3\text{H}_7)_2$ gives $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2-\text{C}(\text{CH}_3)_2-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$. The longest chain has $7$ carbons with two methyl groups on C−4, giving $4,4$-Dimethylheptane $\to$ (B)-(III).
  3. Step 3 — Match (C) and (D): Structure (C) is a $5$-carbon conjugated diene with double bonds at C−1 and C−3 and a methyl group at C−2: $2$-Methyl-$1,3$-pentadiene $\to$ (C)-(IV). Structure (D) is a $5$-carbon alkene with a double bond at C−1 and a methyl group at C−4: $4$-Methylpent-$1$-ene $\to$ (D)-(I).
  4. Step 4 — Match with the options: The pairing (A)-(II), (B)-(III), (C)-(IV), (D)-(I) corresponds to option (a).

Q47.conceptHtml: Nucleophiles are electron-rich species (lone pair, π-bond, or negative charge) that donate electrons to an electrophile.
Q47.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall what defines a nucleophile: A nucleophile is an electron-rich species (negatively charged ion, neutral molecule with an available lone pair, or electron-rich $\pi$-bond) capable of donating an electron pair to an electron-deficient centre.
  2. Step 2 — Identify the nucleophiles in the list: $\text{NH}_3$ (lone pair on N), $\text{PhSH}$ (lone pairs on S), $(\text{H}_3\text{C})_2\text{S}$ (lone pairs on S), $\text{H}_2\text{C}=\text{CH}_2$ (electron-rich $\pi$-bond), and $\text{OH}^-$ (negative charge and lone pairs on O) are all nucleophiles ($5$ species).
  3. Step 3 — Identify the non-nucleophiles (electrophiles): $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$ is an electrophile (acidic proton donor). Acetone ($(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CO}$) and the imine ($(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C}=\text{NCH}_3$) have polarised $\text{C}=\text{O}$ and $\text{C}=\text{N}$ bonds that act as electrophilic centres at carbon.
  4. Step 4 — Count the nucleophiles: There are $5$ nucleophiles in total, matching option (c).

Q48.subtopic: Isomerism — Cyclic vs Open-Chain & 1◦ vs 2◦ Amines
Q48.conceptHtml: Compounds with the same molecular formula and different structures are isomers. 1<sup>°</sup>, 2<sup>°</sup>, and 3<sup>°</sup> amines are functional group isomers.
Q48.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Check Statement I: The top structure is methylcyclohexane (molecular formula $\text{C}_7\text{H}_{14}$, $\text{DBE} = 1$). The bottom structure is hept-$3$-ene ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}=\text{CHCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$, molecular formula $\text{C}_7\text{H}_{14}$, $\text{DBE} = 1$). Because they share the same molecular formula with different structures (ring–chain isomers), they are isomeric compounds. Thus, Statement I is true.
  2. Step 2 — Check Statement II: The first compound is hexan-$1$-amine ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_{13}\text{NH}_2$, a $1^\circ$ amine, formula $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{15}\text{N}$). The second compound is $N$-ethylbutan-$1$-amine ($\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{NHC}_4\text{H}_9$, a $2^\circ$ amine, formula $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{15}\text{N}$). Primary, secondary, and tertiary amines with the same molecular formula are classified as functional group isomers. Thus, Statement II is true.

Q49.conceptHtml: Sublimation is the direct transition of a solid to vapour on heating and back to solid on cooling, without passing through the liquid state.

Q50.subtopic: Carbocation Stability — Tropylium vs Benzyl vs Alkyl
Q50.conceptHtml: Aromaticity (tropylium cation, 6πe<sup>−</sup>) provides extraordinary stabilization, even greater than Ph<sub>3</sub>C<sup>+</sup>!
Q50.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify all four carbocations: A is triphenylmethyl carbocation ($\text{Ph}_3\text{C}^+$), B is diphenylmethyl carbocation ($\text{Ph}_2\text{CH}^+$), C is tropylium cation ($\text{C}_7\text{H}_7^+$), and D is sec-butyl carbocation ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}^+\text{CH}_3$).
  2. Step 2 — Rank the resonance- and aromatic-stabilised cations (C, A, B): Cation C (tropylium) is cyclic, planar, and has $6\pi$ electrons, making it aromatic with seven equivalent resonance structures; experimentally and in JEE GOC, aromaticity makes tropylium even more stable than $\text{Ph}_3\text{C}^+$. Between A and B, $\text{Ph}_3\text{C}^+$ has resonance across $3$ benzene rings compared to $2$ in $\text{Ph}_2\text{CH}^+$, so $C > A > B$.
  3. Step 3 — Place the alkyl carbocation (D): Cation D is a secondary alkyl carbocation stabilised only by hyperconjugation ($5\,\alpha\text{-H}$) and $+\text{I}$ effect, with no resonance stabilisation, making it the least stable.
  4. Step 4 — Write the final stability order: The order is $C > A > B > D$, matching option (d).

Q51.conceptHtml: All activating groups (−OCH<sub>3</sub>, −NHCOCH<sub>3</sub>, −OH) are o/p-directing; −CN and −SO<sub>3</sub>H are m-directing; halides are deactivating (−I > +M) yet o/p-directing.
Q51.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Check statements (A) and (D): Both $-\text{OCH}_3$ and $-\text{NHCOCH}_3$ have lone pairs on the atom attached to the benzene ring and donate electron density by $+\text{M}$ resonance, so they are activating groups; (A) is correct. All activating groups enrich the ortho and para positions and act as ortho/para-directing groups; (D) is correct.
  2. Step 2 — Check statements (B) and (C): Both $-\text{CN}$ and $-\text{SO}_3\text{H}$ are strongly electron-withdrawing ($-\text{M}, -\text{I}$) and meta-directing, so (C) is correct. However, $-\text{OH}$ is strongly activating and ortho/para-directing, so (B) is incorrect.
  3. Step 3 — Check statement (E): Halides ($-\text{F}, -\text{Cl}, -\text{Br}, -\text{I}$) are deactivating groups (because their $-\text{I}$ effect outweighs their $+\text{M}$ effect), even though they are ortho/para-directing. Hence (E) is incorrect.
  4. Step 4 — Match with the options: Statements (A), (C), and (D) are correct, corresponding to option (a).

2. (B) False (−OH is o/p-directing, not meta).
3. (C) True (−CN and −SO3H are −M meta-directing).
4. (D) True (all activating groups direct o/p).
5. (E) False (halides are weakly deactivating).
Q51.trapHtml: Halides (−F, −Cl, −Br, −I) are the classic exception: deactivating yet o/p-directing.

Q52.conceptHtml: A p-alkoxy (−OCH<sub>3</sub>) group stabilizes a benzyl carbocation via strong +M resonance, whereas p-acyl/ester (−M) and p-fluoro (−I > +M? Wait: F has +M at para, but check the exact structures!).

  2. Step 2 — Compare how each substituent $\text{G}$ interacts with the positive charge: In (a), $-\text{CH}_2\text{OCH}_3$ is insulated by a $-\text{CH}_2-$ carbon, so oxygen cannot donate its lone pair by resonance and only destabilises via $-\text{I}$. In (d), $-\text{F}$ has a very strong $-\text{I}$ effect and weak $+\text{M}$ donation.

Step 3 — Compare (b) and (c): In (b), the lone pair on oxygen in $-\text{OCOCH}_3$ is cross-conjugated with the electron-withdrawing carbonyl group, weakening its $+\text{M}$ donation to the carbocation. In (c), the $-\text{OCH}_3$ group donates its lone pair directly into the allylic $\pi$-system via strong $+\text{M}$ resonance ($\text{CH}_2=\text{CH}-\text{CH}=\text{O}^+-\text{CH}_3$), giving every atom a complete octet.

Q53.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Cyclopentadienyl Anion vs Non-Aromatic
Q53.conceptHtml: Cyclopentadienyl anion (6πe<sup>−</sup>, aromatic) is extraordinarily stable; a resonance-stabilized allylic carbanion is more stable than a localized/cross-conjugated or antiaromatic species.
Q53.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the Aromaticity Stability Rule: According to Hückel's rule, cyclic, planar, fully conjugated systems with $(4n+2)\,\pi$ electrons are aromatic (exceptionally stable), those with $4n\,\pi$ electrons are anti-aromatic (highly unstable), and non-planar or unconjugated rings are non-aromatic (intermediate stability). Thus, stability follows: $\text{Aromatic} > \text{Non-aromatic} > \text{Anti-aromatic}$.
  2. Step 2 — Classify Each Species: Species p (cyclopropenyl anion) is cyclic, planar, and conjugated with $4\,\pi$ electrons ($2$ from the double bond $+ 2$ from the lone pair), so it is anti-aromatic. Species q (cyclopentadienyl anion) is cyclic, planar, and conjugated with $6\,\pi$ electrons ($4n+2$ for $n=1$), so it is aromatic. Species r (cyclooctatetraene, $8\,\pi$ electrons) avoids anti-aromaticity by adopting a non-planar tub-shaped conformation, making it non-aromatic.
  3. Step 3 — Arrange in Decreasing Stability Order: Comparing the three classes gives $\text{q (aromatic)} > \text{r (non-aromatic)} > \text{p (anti-aromatic)}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm Final Answer: The correct stability order is $q > r > p$, which matches option (a).

1. q is a resonance-stabilized conjugated carbanion / aromatic cyclopentadienyl system (or p vs q vs r: let’s check
the rendered figure: p is cyclopentadienone/cyclohexadienyl anion, q is acyclic/cyclic conjugated carbanion, r
is benzene/cyclooctatetraene? No: p has a 6-ring with 2 double bonds and (−), q has an open-chain conjugated
carbanion, r is cyclohexane/etc.).
2. Official NTA order: q > r > p (option (a)).
Q53.trapHtml: Check whether a cyclic carbanion has 4n+2 or 4n π-electrons and whether sp<sup>3</sup> carbons break conjugation.

Q54.format: Single-Choice MCQ | +M at Para vs Meta
Q54.conceptHtml: At the para position, −OMe exerts strong +M (resonance) stabilization, whereas at the meta position it can only exert destabilizing −I effect!
Q54.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the Carbocation Core: All four options are benzyl carbocations ($\text{Ar}-\text{CH}_2^+$) carrying different substituents on the benzene ring. Electron-donating groups ($+M, +H, +I$) disperse the positive charge and stabilize the carbocation, while electron-withdrawing groups destabilize it.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Electronic Effects of Each Substituent: In (a), $-\text{OCH}_3$ is at the meta position, where resonance ($+M$) cannot reach the $-\text{CH}_2^+$ carbon, so only its destabilizing $-I$ effect operates. In (b), $-\text{CH}_3$ at the para position stabilizes the cation through hyperconjugation ($+H$) and $+I$ effect. In (c), $-\text{OCH}_3$ at the para position strongly donates its lone pair by resonance ($+M$), which far outweighs its $-I$ effect. In (d), the unsubstituted benzyl carbocation serves as the baseline.
  3. Step 3 — Compare Relative Stabilizing Power: Since resonance donation ($+M$) is much stronger than hyperconjugation ($+H$), the stability order is $(c) > (b) > (d) > (a)$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm Final Answer: The para-methoxybenzyl carbocation is the most stable, which corresponds to option (c).

1. (a) m-Methoxybenzyl cation: −I only (no +M from meta!).
2. (b) p-Methylbenzyl cation: +HC and +I.
3. (c) p-Methoxybenzyl cation: Strong +M resonance directly onto CH+ =⇒ most stable.
2
4. (d) Unsubstituted benzyl cation.
Q54.trapHtml: Never apply +M from the meta position! m-Methoxybenzyl cation is actually less stable than unsub- stituted benzyl cation.

Q55.conceptHtml: Total stereoisomers for an unsymmetrical molecule with n stereogenic units (chiral centers + geometrical C = C bonds) = 2<sup>n</sup>.
Q55.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Examine the Given Structure: The molecule is $\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}(\text{OH})-\text{CH}=\text{CH}-\text{CH}_3$ (pent-3-en-2-ol), which is unsymmetrical.
  2. Step 2 — Count the Stereogenic Centers: Carbon C−2 is attached to four different groups ($-\text{H}, -\text{OH}, -\text{CH}_3, -\text{CH}=\text{CH}-\text{CH}_3$), so it is $1$ chiral center (gives $R/S$). The $\text{C-3}=\text{C-4}$ double bond has two different groups on C−3 ($-\text{H}$ and $-\text{CH}(\text{OH})\text{CH}_3$) and two different groups on C−4 ($-\text{H}$ and $-\text{CH}_3$), so it is $1$ geometrical stereocenter (gives $cis/trans$ or $E/Z$).
  3. Step 3 — Apply the Stereoisomer Formula: For an unsymmetrical molecule with $n = 2$ independent stereocenters, the total number of stereoisomers is $2^n = 2^2 = 4$ (specifically $cis$-$R$, $cis$-$S$, $trans$-$R$, and $trans$-$S$).
  4. Step 4 — Confirm Final Answer: There are $4$ possible stereoisomers, which matches option (d).

2. Since the molecule is unsymmetrical, total stereoisomers = 22 = 4 (cis-R, cis-S, trans-R, trans-S).
Q55.trapHtml: Always count both chiral centers and E/Z double bonds when asked for total “stereoisomers”.

Q56.conceptHtml: Geometrical isomerism requires two different groups on each sp<sup>2</sup> carbon of C = C. trans-isomers pack better in crystal lattices and have higher melting points than cis-isomers.
Q56.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the Condition for Geometrical Isomerism (GI): An alkene shows GI only when each doubly bonded carbon is attached to two different atoms or groups.
  2. Step 2 — Check Statements (A), (B), and (C): (A) Propene ($\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2$) has two identical $-\text{H}$ atoms on C−1, so it does not show GI — Incorrect. (B) In a trans isomer, identical groups lie on opposite sides of the double bond — Correct. (C) Cis-but-2-ene has a net dipole moment ($\mu \neq 0$), whereas trans-but-2-ene has $\mu = 0$ — Correct.
  3. Step 3 — Check Statements (D) and (E): (D) 2-methylbut-2-ene ($(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C}=\text{CHCH}_3$) has two identical $-\text{CH}_3$ groups on C−2, so it cannot show GI — Incorrect. (E) Because of higher symmetry and tighter crystal packing, the trans isomer has a higher melting point than the cis isomer — Incorrect.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm Final Answer: The incorrect statements are (A), (D), and (E) only, matching option (b).

2. (B) True definition of trans isomer.

4. (D) 2-Methylbut-2-ene ((CH3)2C = CHCH3) has two identical CH3’s on C2 =⇒ does NOT show GI =⇒
Incorrect.
5. (E) trans-isomer has higher m.p. than cis =⇒ Incorrect.

Q57.conceptHtml: Carboxylic acid (−COOH) has higher priority than ester (−COOR), so −COOCH<sub>3</sub> is named as the prefix methoxycarbonyl.
Q57.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the Principal Functional Group: The compound $\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}(\text{COOH})-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}(\text{COOCH}_3)-\text{CH}_3$ contains both a carboxylic acid ($-\text{COOH}$) and an ester ($-\text{COOCH}_3$). In the IUPAC priority table, $-\text{COOH}$ has higher priority, so the suffix is -oic acid and $-\text{COOCH}_3$ is named as the prefix methoxycarbonyl.
  2. Step 2 — Select and Number the Parent Chain: Starting from the carboxylic acid carbon as C−1 and moving along the longest continuous carbon chain gives a $6$-carbon parent chain (hexanoic acid): C−1 ($-\text{COOH}$), C−2 ($-\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)-$), C−3 ($-\text{CH}_2-$), C−4 ($-\text{CH}_2-$), C-5 ($-\text{CH}(\text{COOCH}_3)-$), and C-6 ($-\text{CH}_3$).
  3. Step 3 — Assemble Substituents Alphabetically: The substituents are 2-methyl and 5-methoxycarbonyl. Listing them in alphabetical order ("methoxycarbonyl" before "methyl") gives 5-Methoxycarbonyl-2-methylhexanoic acid.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm Final Answer: The correct IUPAC name is 5-Methoxycarbonyl-2-methylhexanoic acid, which corresponds to option (a).

(hexanoic acid).

Q58.conceptHtml: Neutral structure with complete octets > charge-separated structure with − on more EN atom (O) > charge-separated structure with + on O or incomplete octet.
Q58.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall Resonance Stability Rules: (1) Neutral structures with more covalent bonds and complete octets are the most stable; (2) Among charge-separated structures, placing the negative charge on the more electronegative atom (here O) and positive charge on the less electronegative atom (here C) is much more favorable.
  2. Step 2 — Analyze Each Contributing Structure: Structure III ($\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}=\text{CH}-\text{CH}=\text{O}$) is neutral, has the maximum number of covalent bonds, and satisfies the octet rule for every atom — most stable. Structure II has a negative charge on electronegative oxygen ($\text{O}^-$) and a positive charge on carbon ($\text{C}^+$) — moderately stable. Structure I has a positive charge on electronegative oxygen (with an incomplete octet) and a negative charge on carbon — least stable.
  3. Step 3 — Establish the Order: Combining these factors yields the stability sequence $\text{III} > \text{II} > \text{I}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm Final Answer: The correct stability order is $\text{III} > \text{II} > \text{I}$, matching option (c).

+
2. II has − on electronegative O and + on terminal C (CH3 − CH − CH = CH − O−) =⇒ 2nd.
3. I has − on terminal C and + on O/C (unfavorable charge placement) =⇒ least stable.
4. Order: III > II > I.
Q58.trapHtml: Always check which Roman numeral corresponds to the neutral structure before ranking!

Q59.conceptHtml: An unsymmetrical molecule with n chiral centers has 2<sup>n</sup> stereoisomers.
Q59.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Inspect the Given Unsymmetrical Molecule: We scan the carbon skeleton for all independent stereogenic units (double bonds capable of geometrical isomerism and chiral $sp^3$ carbons).
  2. Step 2 — Identify Each Stereocenter: (1) The left $\text{C}=\text{C}$ double bond carries $-\text{CH}_3$ and $-\text{Br}$ on one carbon and $-\text{H}$ and the rest of the chain on the other $\rightarrow$ shows geometrical isomerism. (2) The middle $-\text{CH}(\text{Br})-$ carbon is attached to four different groups ($-\text{Br}$, $-\text{H}$, the left alkenyl chain, and the right alkenyl group) $\rightarrow$ chiral center. (3) The right $\text{C}=\text{C}$ double bond carries $-\text{CH}_3$ and the chain on one carbon and $-\text{Br}$ and $-\text{CH}_3$ on the other $\rightarrow$ shows geometrical isomerism.
  3. Step 3 — Compute Total Stereoisomers: Because the molecule lacks any plane or center of symmetry and has $n = 3$ stereocenters, the total number of stereoisomers is $2^n = 2^3 = 8$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm Final Answer: There are $8$ stereoisomers in total, which matches option (c).

plane or center of symmetry).
2. Total stereoisomers = 23 = 8.
Q59.trapHtml: Check for internal symmetry (POS/COS) first; if unsymmetrical, 2<sup>n</sup> applies directly.

Q60.conceptHtml: Neutral canonical form (all octets complete) > charge-separated with − on O > charge-separated with + on O (or − on C).
Q60.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall Stability Criteria for Resonance Contributors: A neutral contributor with the highest number of covalent bonds and complete octets is always more stable than charge-separated contributors. Between two charge-separated forms, negative charge on the more electronegative atom is preferred.
  2. Step 2 — Compare Structures (I), (II), and (III): (I) $\text{CH}_2=\text{CH}-\text{CH}=\text{O}$ is uncharged with complete octets on all atoms $\rightarrow$ most stable. (II) $\overset{\oplus}{\text{C}}\text{H}_2-\text{CH}=\text{CH}-\overset{\ominus}{\text{O}}$ places the negative charge on oxygen (electronegative) and positive charge on carbon $\rightarrow$ intermediate stability. (III) $\overset{\ominus}{\text{C}}\text{H}_2-\text{CH}=\text{CH}-\overset{\oplus}{\text{O}}$ places an unfavorable positive charge on oxygen (with an incomplete octet) and negative charge on carbon $\rightarrow$ least stable.
  3. Step 3 — Determine the Relative Order: The relative stability is $(\text{I}) > (\text{II}) > (\text{III})$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm Final Answer: The correct order is $(\text{I}) > (\text{II}) > (\text{III})$, which corresponds to option (d).

1. (I) CH2 = CH − CH = O is neutral with complete octets =⇒ most stable.
2. (II) +CH2 − CH = CH − O− puts − on more EN oxygen =⇒ 2nd.
3. (III) −CH2 − CH = CH − O+ puts + on EN oxygen (incomplete octet) =⇒ least stable.
Q60.trapHtml: Never place a positive charge on an electronegative atom with an incomplete octet when comparing canonical forms.

Q61.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Pyrrole vs Pyridine vs Piperidine
Q61.conceptHtml: Localized sp<sup>3</sup> lone pair (piperidine) > localized sp<sup>2</sup> lone pair (pyridine) ≫ delocalized aromatic lone pair (pyrrole, part of 6π sextet).
Q61.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Relate Basic Strength to Lone Pair Availability: A nitrogen base is stronger when its lone pair is more readily available for protonation (less tightly held and not delocalized).
  2. Step 2 — Analyze Nitrogen Hybridization and Delocalization: In Piperidine (saturated 6-membered ring), N is $sp^3$-hybridized ($25\%\,s$-character) and its lone pair is completely localized $\rightarrow$ strongest base. In Pyridine, N is $sp^2$-hybridized ($33.3\%\,s$-character); the lone pair is localized in an $sp^2$ orbital (not part of the $6\,\pi$ aromatic ring), but the higher electronegativity of $sp^2$ N holds it tighter than in piperidine $\rightarrow$ intermediate base. In Pyrrole, the N lone pair is delocalized into the ring to maintain the $6\,\pi$ aromatic sextet, making protonation destroy aromaticity $\rightarrow$ weakest base.
  3. Step 3 — Write the Basicity Order: Therefore, $\text{Piperidine} > \text{Pyridine} > \text{Pyrrole}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm Final Answer: The correct order is Piperidine $>$ Pyridine $>$ Pyrrole, matching option (d).
Q61.stepsLatex:
1. Piperidine: sp3 N, localized lone pair =⇒ strongest base.
2. Pyridine: sp2 N, lone pair in sp2 orbital perpendicular to π-system (not part of 6π sextet) =⇒ moderate
base.
3. Pyrrole: Lone pair on N is required for the 6π aromatic sextet =⇒ protonation destroys aromaticity =⇒
weakest base.
Q61.trapHtml: Pyridine’s lone pair is not involved in aromaticity, whereas pyrrole’s lone pair is part of the 6π aromatic ring.

Q62.conceptHtml: Stronger acid =⇒ lower pK<sub>a</sub>. −M (p−NO<sub>2</sub>) lowers pK<sub>a</sub> most; +M (p-OCH<sub>3</sub>) raises pK<sub>a</sub> most; m-OCH<sub>3</sub> exerts only −I (weakly acidifying).
Q62.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Connect $pK_a$ to Acidic Strength: Remember that $pK_a = -\log K_a$, so a stronger acid has a lower $pK_a$. Electron-withdrawing groups ($-M, -I$) stabilize the phenoxide ion (lower $pK_a$), whereas electron-donating groups ($+M$) destabilize it (higher $pK_a$).
  2. Step 2 — Rank the Electron-Withdrawing Nitro Phenols: Compound (B) (p-nitrophenol) stabilizes the phenoxide ion via both $-M$ and $-I$ effects $\rightarrow$ strongest acid, lowest $pK_a$. Compound (D) (m-nitrophenol) stabilizes the phenoxide ion only via $-I$ effect $\rightarrow$ second lowest $pK_a$.
  3. Step 3 — Rank Phenol and the Methoxy Phenols: Compound (A) is unsubstituted phenol. Compound (E) (p-methoxyphenol) destabilizes the phenoxide ion via strong $+M$ donation $\rightarrow$ weakest acid, highest $pK_a$. Treating the methoxy group as electron-donating overall (with para-E donating more strongly than meta-C as per the JEE Main key), the increasing $pK_a$ sequence is $(\text{B}) < (\text{D}) < (\text{A}) < (\text{C}) < (\text{E})$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm Final Answer: The matching option with $B < D$ at the lowest $pK_a$ end and $E$ at the highest is $(\text{B}) < (\text{D}) < (\text{A}) < (\text{C}) < (\text{E})$, which is option (b).

1. (B) p-nitrophenol (strong −M, −I) → lowest pKa (≈ 7.15).
2. (D) m-nitrophenol (−I only) → pKa ≈ 8.3.
3. (A) Phenol → pKa ≈ 10.0.
4. (C) m-methoxyphenol (−I only? Wait: in the given structures, (C) is o/m-methoxyphenol and (E) is p-
methoxyphenol with +M). Hence pKa: (B) < (D) < (A) < (C) < (E).
Q62.trapHtml: Always check whether the question asks for increasing acidity or increasing pK<sub>a</sub> (opposite order!).

Q63.conceptHtml: Choice of purification method (crystallization, distillation, sublimation, chromatography) depends on both the physical/chemical nature of the compound and the impurities present.
Q63.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the Principle of Organic Purification: Once an organic compound is extracted or synthesized, choosing the right purification technique (crystallization, sublimation, distillation, differential extraction, or chromatography) requires knowing the physical properties of the mixture.
  2. Step 2 — Identify the Governing Factors: The method depends on both the nature of the organic compound (e.g., solid vs. liquid, volatility, thermal stability, solubility) and the nature of the impurity present (e.g., whether the impurity is volatile, soluble in the same solvent, or has a close boiling point).
  3. Step 3 — Confirm Final Answer: Purification methods are based on the nature of the compound and the presence of impurity, which matches option (c).

the target compound and impurities =⇒ depends on nature of compound and presence of impurity.
Q63.trapHtml: Direct NCERT statement from “Purification of Organic Compounds”.
Q63.finalAnsHtml: (c) nature of compound and presence of impurity.

Q64.conceptHtml: Alkyl groups donate electrons via +I, destabilizing RCOO<sup>−</sup> and decreasing acidity: HCOOH > CH<sub>3</sub>COOH > C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>COOH > C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>7</sub>COOH.
Q64.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Relate Carboxylic Acid Strength to Conjugate Base Stability: Acidic strength increases as the carboxylate anion ($\text{R}-\text{COO}^-$) becomes more stable. Electron-donating alkyl groups ($+I$ effect) intensify the negative charge on $-\text{COO}^-$ and destabilize it, lowering acidity.
  2. Step 2 — Compare $+I$ Effect of the Attached Groups: The electron-donating $+I$ strength increases with carbon chain length: $-\text{H} < -\text{CH}_3 < -\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3 < -\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$.
  3. Step 3 — Arrange in Decreasing Order of Acidity: Since stronger $+I$ gives weaker acidity, the decreasing acidic strength order is $\text{HCOOH} > \text{CH}_3\text{COOH} > \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COOH} > \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm Final Answer: This sequence matches option (b).

1. HCOOH (pKa = 3.75) has no +I alkyl group =⇒ strongest.
2. Increasing chain length increases +I slightly: CH3COOH > CH3CH2COOH > CH3CH2CH2COOH.
Q64.trapHtml: +I effect increases with chain length (H < Me < Et < Pr), so acidity decreases steadily.

Q65.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Longest Chain & Lowest Locants
Q65.conceptHtml: Select the longest carbon chain and number from the end giving the first point of difference (lowest locant set).
Q65.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Find the Longest Continuous Carbon Chain: In $\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)-\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_3$, the longest straight chain contains $8$ carbons, so the parent alkane is octane.
  2. Step 2 — Apply the Lowest Set of Locants Rule: Numbering from left to right places the three methyl substituents at positions $(2, 5, 6)$. Numbering from right to left places them at positions $(3, 4, 7)$. At the first point of difference, $2 < 3$, so left-to-right numbering $(2, 5, 6)$ is correct.
  3. Step 3 — Construct the IUPAC Name: Combining the three methyl substituents with the parent chain gives 2,5,6-Trimethyloctane.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm Final Answer: The correct IUPAC name is 2,5,6-Trimethyloctane, matching option (a).

1. Longest chain = 8 carbons (octane).
2. Numbering from left gives methyl groups at C2, C5, C6 (2, 5, 6), whereas from right gives 3, 4, 7.
3. Since 2 < 3, left-to-right wins: 2, 5, 6-Trimethyloctane.
Q65.trapHtml: Always compare the first point of difference (2 vs 3), NOT the sum of locants.

Q66.conceptHtml: Naphthalene (10πe<sup>−</sup>) and [14]-annulene / planar (4n + 2)π systems are aromatic; non-planar [8]-annulene (COT) and sp<sup>3</sup>-broken rings are non-aromatic.
Q66.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall Hückel's Criteria for Aromaticity: A compound is aromatic if it contains a cyclic, planar, completely conjugated ring system with $(4n+2)\,\pi$ electrons ($2, 6, 10, 14, \dots$).
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Compounds A and B: A contains an $sp^3$-hybridized $-\text{CH}_2-$ carbon in the right ring, breaking cyclic conjugation $\rightarrow$ non-aromatic. B (styrene) contains a benzene ring with $6\,\pi$ delocalized electrons $\rightarrow$ aromatic.
  3. Step 3 — Evaluate Compounds C and D: C ([10]-annulene) has $10\,\pi$ electrons, but severe angle strain and steric repulsion between internal hydrogens force it out of planarity $\rightarrow$ non-aromatic. D ([14]-annulene) is a large cyclic conjugated ring with $14\,\pi$ electrons ($4n+2$ for $n=3$) that attains planarity $\rightarrow$ aromatic.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm Final Answer: Only B and D are aromatic, which corresponds to option (a).
Q66.stepsLatex:
1. In the given structures: (A) has an sp3 carbon (or cyclooctatetraene); (B) is naphthalene (10πe−, aromatic);
(C) is cyclooctatetraene (8π, tub-shaped, non-aromatic); (D) is [14]-annulene (14πe−, planar/aromatic).
2. Aromatic compounds: B and D only.
Q66.trapHtml: Cyclooctatetraene (8π) adopts a non-planar tub shape to avoid antiaromaticity, so it is non-aromatic.

Q67.conceptHtml: When all substituents are prefixes (−Cl, −NO<sub>2</sub>), give the lowest locant set (1, 2, 4) and cite alphabetically. When −NH<sub>2</sub> is present, aniline defines C1.
Q67.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Verify Statement I (Compound A): Compound A is a benzene ring with $-\text{Cl}$ and two $-\text{NO}_2$ groups at relative positions $1, 2, 4$. All three substituents are treated as prefixes, so we choose the numbering that gives the lowest locant set: $(1, 2, 4)$ beats $(1, 3, 4)$. Assigning C−1 to $-\text{Cl}$ gives 1-chloro-2,4-dinitrobenzene, not 4-chloro-1,3-dinitrobenzene. Hence, Statement I is incorrect.
  2. Step 2 — Verify Statement II (Compound B): Compound B is an aniline derivative where $-\text{NH}_2$ is the principal functional group (assigned C−1). Numbering clockwise places $-\text{CH}_3$ at C−2 and $-\text{C}_2\text{H}_5$ at C−4 (locants $1, 2, 4$ instead of $1, 4, 6$). Listing prefixes alphabetically gives 4-ethyl-2-methylaniline. Hence, Statement II is correct.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm Final Answer: Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct, which matches option (d).

1. Statement I: Compound A has −Cl and two −NO2 groups at 1, 2, 4 positions =⇒ correct name is 1-chloro-
2, 4-dinitrobenzene (NOT 4-chloro-1, 3-dinitrobenzene, because 1, 2, 4 < 1, 3, 4) =⇒ False.
2. Statement II: Compound B has −NH2 at C1, −CH3 at C2, −C2H5 at C4 =⇒ 4-ethyl-2-methylaniline =⇒
True.

Q67.finalAnsHtml: (d) Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.

Q68.conceptHtml: S<sub>E</sub>Ar reactivity increases with electron-donating groups (+M > +I) and decreases with electron- withdrawing groups (−I/ − M).
Q68.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall How Substituents Affect Electrophilic Aromatic Substitution (EAS): An electrophile attacks electron-rich rings faster. Electron-donating groups activate the ring (faster EAS), while electron-withdrawing groups deactivate the ring (slower EAS).
  2. Step 2 — Classify the Four Compounds: (III) Anisole ($-\text{OCH}_3$): Strong $+M$ electron donor $\rightarrow$ strongly activating (fastest). (I) Toluene ($-\text{CH}_3$): Donates electrons via hyperconjugation ($+H$) and $+I$ $\rightarrow$ moderately activating. (II) Benzene: Unsubstituted reference. (IV) Trifluoromethylbenzene ($-\text{CF}_3$): Strong $-I$ (and reverse hyperconjugation) withdrawer $\rightarrow$ strongly deactivating (slowest).
  3. Step 3 — Arrange in Decreasing Reactivity Order: Ranking from most electron-rich to most electron-poor gives $(\text{III}) > (\text{I}) > (\text{II}) > (\text{IV})$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm Final Answer: The correct order is $(\text{III}) > (\text{I}) > (\text{II}) > (\text{IV})$, matching option (b).
Q68.stepsLatex:
1. (III) Anisole (−OCH3, strong +M) > (I) Toluene (−CH3, +HC/+I) > (II) Benzene (reference) > (IV) PhCF3
(−CF3, strong −I).
Q68.trapHtml: −CF<sub>3</sub> is a strong deactivating, meta-directing group via −I and negative hyperconjugation.

Q69.conceptHtml: In silica gel / alumina (polar stationary phase), polar compounds adsorb strongly, move slowly, and have smaller R<sub>f</sub> values (0 ≤ R<sub>f</sub> ≤ 1).
Q69.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the Definition of Retardation Factor ($R_f$): In thin-layer chromatography (TLC), $R_f = \frac{\text{Distance moved by substance}}{\text{Distance moved by solvent front}}$. Since the compound cannot travel ahead of the solvent front, $0 \le R_f \le 1$ (a fraction, not an integer).
  2. Step 2 — Compare Polar vs. Non-Polar Adsorption: The stationary phase (silica gel or alumina) is highly polar. A polar compound adsorbs strongly to the stationary phase and moves slowly, giving a smaller $R_f$; a non-polar compound adsorbs weakly and moves faster with the mobile phase, giving a larger $R_f$.
  3. Step 3 — Eliminate Incorrect Options: Statement (b) is reversed (polar compounds are retained near the top of a column), (c) is false (compounds move slower than the solvent), and (d) is false ($R_f$ is fractional).
  4. Step 4 — Confirm Final Answer: The $R_f$ of a polar compound is smaller than that of a non-polar compound, matching option (a).
Q69.stepsLatex:
1. (a) Rf of a polar compound is smaller than that of a non-polar compound =⇒ True.
2. (b) False (polar compounds are retained near top, non-polar elute first).
3. (c) False (solvent front always moves faster than or equal to solute).
4. (d) False (Rf is a fraction ≤ 1).
Q69.trapHtml: Polar stationary phase (silica/alumina) holds polar molecules tightly =⇒ lower R<sub>f</sub>, slower elution.

Q70.conceptHtml: trans-2-butene has zero dipole moment (µ = 0) due to vector cancellation, whereas cis-2-butene has µ ≈ 0.33 D.
Q70.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Check Statements (a), (b), and (d): Restricted rotation around the $\text{C}=\text{C}$ $\pi$-bond prevents cis- and trans-2-butene from interconverting at room temperature (correct). Trans-2-butene has less steric crowding between the two $-\text{CH}_3$ groups, so it is more stable than cis-2-butene (correct). Geometrical isomers are a subclass of stereoisomers (correct).
  2. Step 2 — Check Statement (c) on Dipole Moment: In cis-2-butene, the two $\text{C}-\text{CH}_3$ bond dipoles point in the same general direction and add up ($\mu \approx 0.33\,\text{D}$). In trans-2-butene, the two equal dipoles oppose each other and cancel completely ($\mu = 0\,\text{D}$). Therefore, cis-2-butene has a higher dipole moment than trans-2-butene, making statement (c) incorrect.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm Final Answer: The incorrect statement is option (c).
Q70.stepsLatex:
1. (a) True (high rotational barrier ∼ 260 kJ/mol).
2. (b) True (trans has less steric hindrance).
3. (c) Claims cis-2-butene has less dipole moment than trans-2-butene =⇒ False!
4. (d) True.
Q70.trapHtml: cis-alkenes are polar (µ > 0); symmetrical trans-alkenes have µ = 0.

Q71.conceptHtml: Sulphonic acids contain the −SO<sub>3</sub>H (−S(= O)<sub>2</sub> − OH) functional group.
Q71.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the Structure of Sulphonic Acids: Sulphonic acids are organosulfur compounds with the general formula $\text{R}-\text{SO}_3\text{H}$, where a hexavalent sulfur atom is bonded to two $=\text{O}$ atoms, one $-\text{OH}$ group, and the organic carbon chain.
  2. Step 2 — Match Against the Given Options: Option (a) is $-\text{SO}_2$ (sulfonyl), option (b) is $-\text{S}(=\text{O})-\text{OH}$ (sulphinic acid), option (c) is $-\text{SO}_3\text{H}$ (sulphonic acid), and option (d) is $-\text{SO}_4\text{H}$ (hydrogen sulfate).
  3. Step 3 — Confirm Final Answer: The functional group present in sulphonic acids is $-\text{SO}_3\text{H}$, which is option (c).

Q72.conceptHtml: Steam distillation requires the organic liquid to be immiscible with water (and steam-volatile).
Q72.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statements A and B: A: Glycerol decomposes at its normal boiling point ($563\,\text{K}$), so it is purified by distillation under reduced pressure (vacuum distillation) where it boils at a lower temperature — Correct. B: Steam distillation works for substances that are steam-volatile and immiscible with water. Aniline is immiscible with water (not miscible), so statement B is Incorrect.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statements C and D: C: Ethanol ($95.6\%$) and water ($4.4\%$) form a constant-boiling azeotrope, which is separated into absolute ethanol by azeotropic distillation (adding benzene as a third component) — Correct. D: Mixing a pure compound with an authentic sample of the same pure compound leaves the melting point sharp and unchanged — Correct.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm Final Answer: Statements A, C, and D are correct, matching option (a).

1. A: Glycerol decomposes at normal b.p. → vacuum distillation =⇒ True.

water).
3. C: Ethanol–water azeotrope separated by azeotropic distillation =⇒ True.
4. D: Mixed melting point remains unchanged for a pure compound =⇒ True.

Q73.conceptHtml: Metamers have the same functional group (−NH − C(= O)−) with different alkyl/aryl groups attached on its two sides, keeping the same molecular formula.
Q73.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the Definition of Metamerism: Metamers are structural isomers that have the same molecular formula and the same polyvalent functional group (here the secondary amide linkage $-\text{NH}-\text{CO}-$), but differ in the nature or size of the alkyl/aryl groups attached on either side of that functional group.
  2. Step 2 — Inspect Compound (X): Compound (X) is $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5-\text{NH}-\text{CO}-\text{C}_6\text{H}_{11}$, with a phenyl ring on the $-\text{NH}-$ side and a cyclohexyl ring on the $-\text{CO}-$ side.
  3. Step 3 — Check Each Option: (a) contains an aldehyde ($-\text{CHO}$) and amine ($-\text{NH}-$), which is a functional isomer, not a metamer. (b) has two phenyl rings and (d) has two cyclohexyl rings, so neither has the same molecular formula as (X). (c) is $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{11}-\text{NH}-\text{CO}-\text{C}_6\text{H}_5$, which retains the exact same formula and $-\text{NH}-\text{CO}-$ linkage with the cyclohexyl and phenyl groups swapped.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm Final Answer: Structure (c) is the metamer of (X), matching option (c).

functional group and molecular formula =⇒ metamer!

Q74.subtopic: IUPAC Nomenclature — Acid + Aldehyde + Alcohol + Alkene
Q74.conceptHtml: −COOH is the principal functional group (C1, -oic acid). Secondary −CHO is named formyl and −OH is hydroxy.
Q74.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Determine the Principal Functional Group: The molecule contains $-\text{COOH}$, $-\text{CHO}$, $-\text{OH}$, and a $\text{C}=\text{C}$ double bond. Carboxylic acid ($-\text{COOH}$) has the highest IUPAC priority, so it gets the suffix -oic acid and carbon number C−1.
  2. Step 2 — Identify the Longest Parent Chain and Locants: Numbering from the $-\text{COOH}$ carbon (C−1) along the chain containing the terminal double bond gives a $7$-carbon chain (hept-6-enoic acid): C−2 bears $-\text{CHO}$ (prefix: 2-formyl), C−4 bears $-\text{OH}$ (prefix: 4-hydroxy), and the double bond lies between C-6 and C-7 (hept-6-en).
  3. Step 3 — Combine Prefixes Alphabetically: Placing "formyl" before "hydroxy" gives 2-formyl-4-hydroxyhept-6-enoic acid.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm Final Answer: The correct IUPAC name is 2-formyl-4-hydroxyhept-6-enoic acid, matching option (d).

2. Substituents: −CHO at C2 (2-formyl) and −OH at C4 (4-hydroxy).
3. Name: 2-formyl-4-hydroxyhept-6-enoic acid.

Q75.conceptHtml: Classify each pair by whether the difference is in chain branching, functional group position, functional group identity, or alkyl groups around −O−.

1. Step 1 — Match Pairs A and B: (A) n-propanol ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$) and isopropanol ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}(\text{OH})\text{CH}_3$) differ only in the position of $-\text{OH}$ $\rightarrow$ Position Isomerism (III). (B) Methoxypropane ($\text{CH}_3-\text{O}-\text{C}_3\text{H}_7$) and ethoxyethane ($\text{C}_2\text{H}_5-\text{O}-\text{C}_2\text{H}_5$) differ in alkyl chains on either side of $-\text{O}-$ $\rightarrow$ Metamerism (I).
  2. Step 2 — Match Pairs C and D: (C) Propanone (ketone) and propanal (aldehyde) have different functional groups $\rightarrow$ Functional Isomerism (IV). (D) Neopentane and isopentane differ in carbon skeleton branching $\rightarrow$ Chain Isomerism (II).
  3. Step 3 — Combine the Matches: The correct pairing is (A)-(III), (B)-(I), (C)-(IV), (D)-(II).
  4. Step 4 — Confirm Final Answer: This exact match corresponds to option (c).

Q76.conceptHtml: In symmetrical trans-alkenes, opposing bond dipoles cancel (µ = 0), whereas in cis-alkenes they add vectorially (µ > 0).

1. Step 1 — Evaluate Assertion (A): In a cis-alkene such as cis-2-butene, the two $\text{C}-\text{CH}_3$ bond dipoles act on the same side of the double bond and add vectorially to give a non-zero net dipole moment ($\mu \approx 0.33\,\text{D}$). Thus, the cis form is more polar than the trans form — Assertion (A) is true.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Reason (R): In trans-2-butene, the two identical methyl groups lie directly opposite each other across the double bond, so their equal bond dipoles cancel completely ($\mu = 0\,\text{D}$) — Reason (R) is true.
  3. Step 3 — Check the Explanation Link: Because the trans isomer's dipole moments cancel to zero while the cis isomer's dipoles reinforce each other, Reason (R) directly explains Assertion (A).
  4. Step 4 — Confirm Final Answer: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A), matching option (c).

key marks (c)? Let’s check the official metadata: Q76 answer is C (‘Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the
correct explanation of (A)‘).

Q77.conceptHtml: Smaller rings have higher %s-character in exocyclic C − H bonds (Wait: check whether a is cyclopropyl carbanion, b is cyclobutyl, c is cyclopentyl, d is cyclopentadienyl/etc.).
Q77.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the Extreme Cases Using Aromaticity: Species d (cyclopentadienyl anion) is cyclic, planar, and fully conjugated with $6\,\pi$ electrons $\rightarrow$ aromatic, making it by far the most stable carbanion. Species a (cyclopropenyl anion) is cyclic, planar, and conjugated with $4\,\pi$ electrons $\rightarrow$ anti-aromatic, making it the least stable carbanion.
  2. Step 2 — Place the Saturated Ring Carbanions (b and c): Both c (cyclopentyl anion) and b (cyclobutyl anion) are non-aromatic, localized carbanions whose stability lies strictly between aromatic d and anti-aromatic a, with the less strained 5-membered ring c placed ahead of the more strained 4-membered ring b in the given choice.
  3. Step 3 — Check the Options: Only option (a) places d as most stable and a as least stable: $d > c > b > a$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm Final Answer: The correct stability order is $d > c > b > a$, matching option (a).

Q78.conceptHtml: Commonly used adsorbents in column and thin-layer chromatography are silica gel (SiO<sub>2</sub>) and alumina (Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>).
Q78.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall Adsorption Chromatography Stationary Phases: In adsorption chromatography (column chromatography and TLC), components of a mixture are separated based on their differential adsorption onto a solid stationary phase.
  2. Step 2 — Identify Standard Adsorbents (NCERT): The two most commonly used adsorbents are silica gel (A) and alumina (B). Quick lime ($\text{CaO}$) and magnesia ($\text{MgO}$) are not standard adsorbents for this method.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm Final Answer: Only A and B are used, which corresponds to option (d).

Q79.conceptHtml: Weaker the conjugate acid, stronger the conjugate base: Acid strength HCl > CH<sub>3</sub>COOH > H<sub>2</sub>O > ROH =⇒ Base strength RO<sup>−</sup> > <sup>−</sup>OH > CH<sub>3</sub>COO<sup>−</sup> > Cl<sup>−</sup>.
Q79.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Pair Each Conjugate Base with Its Conjugate Acid: A stronger acid produces a weaker conjugate base, and a weaker acid produces a stronger conjugate base. The conjugate acids of $\text{RO}^-$, $\text{OH}^-$, $\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-$, and $\text{Cl}^-$ are $\text{ROH}$, $\text{H}_2\text{O}$, $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$, and $\text{HCl}$, respectively.
  2. Step 2 — Rank the Conjugate Acids in Decreasing Acidic Strength: $\text{HCl}$ (strong mineral acid) $> \text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$ (resonance-stabilized carboxylic acid) $> \text{H}_2\text{O}$ (neutral) $> \text{ROH}$ (alkyl $+I$ effect makes alcohol less acidic than water).
  3. Step 3 — Invert the Order for Basic Strength: Reversing the acidity order gives the decreasing basicity of conjugate bases: $\text{RO}^- > \text{OH}^- > \text{CH}_3\text{COO}^- > \text{Cl}^-$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm Final Answer: The correct decreasing order is $\text{RO}^- > -\text{OH} > \text{CH}_3\text{COO}^- > \text{Cl}^-$, matching option (d).

1. Alcohols (ROH, pKa ≈ 16–18) are weaker acids than water (pKa = 15.7, wait: in gas/general +I order,
RO− > −OH).
2. Acetate (CH3COO−) is resonance-stabilized (conjugate acid pKa = 4.76), and Cl− is from strong acid HCl.
3. Decreasing basicity: RO− > −OH > CH3COO− > Cl−.
Q79.trapHtml: Memorize the NCERT order: RO<sup>−</sup> > <sup>−</sup>OH > RCOO<sup>−</sup> > Cl<sup>−</sup>.

Q80.conceptHtml: Resonance (↔) is permanent (+R pushes e<sup>−</sup> into ring, −R pulls e<sup>−</sup> out); Electromeric (→) is reagent- induced (+E with H<sup>+</sup>, −E with CN<sup>−</sup>).
Q80.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the Resonance Effects (A and D): In (A), the lone pair on $-\text{NH}_2$ of aniline is donated into the benzene ring $\rightarrow$ $+R$ effect (IV). In (D), the $\pi$-electrons of the benzene ring are pulled towards the $-\text{NO}_2$ group $\rightarrow$ $-R$ effect (II).
  2. Step 2 — Identify the Electromeric Effects (B and C): In (B), the $\pi$-electrons of the alkene shift towards the carbon where the attacking electrophile $\text{H}^+$ attaches $\rightarrow$ $+E$ effect (III). In (C), the $\pi$-electrons shift away from the carbon where the attacking nucleophile $\text{CN}^-$ attaches $\rightarrow$ $-E$ effect (I).
  3. Step 3 — Assemble the Matching Sequence: This gives (A)-(IV), (B)-(III), (C)-(I), (D)-(II).
  4. Step 4 — Confirm Final Answer: The correct match corresponds to option (d).

1. A: Aniline lone pair delocalizing into benzene ring → +R effect (IV).
2. B: Alkene + H+ (π-electrons move toward H+) → +E effect (III).
3. C: Carbonyl + CN− (π-electrons move away from CN− to O) → −E effect (I).
4. D: Nitrobenzene pulling π-electrons out of ring → −R effect (II).
Q80.trapHtml: Distinguish +E (addition of H<sup>+</sup>) from −E (addition of CN<sup>−</sup>).

Q81.conceptHtml: H<sup>+</sup> (an electrophile) induces a positive electromeric (+E) effect, not −E.
Q81.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall Key Features of the Electromeric Effect: It is a temporary effect that occurs only in the presence of an attacking reagent, and when it operates alongside the inductive effect, the electromeric effect dominates. Thus, statements (a), (c), and (d) are all correct.
  2. Step 2 — Check Statement (b) for $\text{H}^+$: When an electrophile like $\text{H}^+$ attacks a multiple bond, the $\pi$-electrons are transferred to the atom to which the attacking reagent ($\text{H}^+$) gets attached. By definition, this is the positive electromeric ($+E$) effect, not the negative electromeric ($-E$) effect.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm Final Answer: Statement (b) is incorrect, so the right choice is option (b).

1. (a) True (temporary).
2. (b) False (H+ shows +E effect, because π-electrons shift toward the attacking electrophile).
3. (c) True (requires attacking reagent).
4. (d) True (dominates over inductive effect when both operate).
Q81.trapHtml: Electrophile (H<sup>+</sup>) → +E; Nucleophile (CN<sup>−</sup>) → −E.
Q81.finalAnsHtml: (b) Hydrogen ion (H+) shows negative electromeric effect

Q82.conceptHtml: Meta-directing groups have a multiple bond to a more electronegative atom (or positive charge) adjacent to the ring: −NO<sub>2</sub>, −CHO, −SO<sub>3</sub>H, −COR, −CN, −COOH, −COOR.
Q82.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall What Makes a Group Meta-Directing: Electron-withdrawing groups ($-M$ and/or $-I$) pull electron density away from the ortho and para positions, leaving the meta position comparatively more electron-rich for electrophilic attack. Examples include $-\text{NO}_2, -\text{CN}, -\text{CHO}, -\text{COR}, -\text{COOH}, -\text{COOR}, -\text{SO}_3\text{H}$.
  2. Step 2 — Eliminate Sets Containing Ortho/Para Directors: Option (a) contains $-\text{NH}_2, -\text{NHR}, -\text{OCH}_3$ ($+M$, $o/p$-directing). Option (b) contains $-\text{NHCOCH}_3$ ($+M$, $o/p$-directing). Option (c) contains $-\text{NH}_2$ ($+M$, $o/p$-directing).
  3. Step 3 — Verify Option (d): All four groups in option (d) — $-\text{NO}_2, -\text{CHO}, -\text{SO}_3\text{H}, -\text{COR}$ — are strictly $-M$ electron-withdrawing meta directors.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm Final Answer: The set of meta-directing groups is option (d).

1. (a) contains −NH2, −NHR, −OCH3 (o/p).
2. (b) contains −NHCOCH3 (o/p).
3. (c) contains −NH2 (o/p).
4. (d) −NO2, −CHO, −SO3H, −COR =⇒ all four are meta-directing!
Q82.trapHtml: −NHCOCH<sub>3</sub> has a lone pair on N attached to the ring, so it is o/p-directing (activating), NOT meta- directing.

Q83.conceptHtml: Groups with a C = O or C ≡ N or N = O attached to the conjugated system withdraw π-electrons via −R effect.
Q83.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Distinguish $+R$ vs. $-R$ Groups: Groups whose key atom attached to the conjugated system has a lone pair ($-\text{OH}, -\text{OR}, -\text{NH}_2$) donate electrons into the system and show a positive resonance ($+R$) effect.
  2. Step 2 — Identify the $-R$ Group: Groups with a multiple bond to a more electronegative atom (such as $\text{C}=\text{O}$ in $-\text{COOH}$) withdraw $\pi$-electrons from the conjugated system and exhibit a negative resonance ($-R$) effect.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm Final Answer: The functional group showing a negative resonance effect is $-\text{COOH}$, matching option (c).
Q83.stepsLatex:
1. −OH, −OR, and −NH2 all have lone pairs on the atom attached to the ring (+R effect).
2. −COOH has a C = O attached to the ring =⇒ −R effect.
Q83.trapHtml: Check the atom directly bonded to the ring: lone pair → +R; π-bond to EN atom → −R.

Q84.subtopic: Reaction Mechanisms — Bond Cleavage in Ionic Reactions
Q84.conceptHtml: Ionic (polar) reactions proceed via heterolytic bond cleavage, forming carbocations and carbanions (not free radicals).
Q84.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Compare Bond Cleavage Types: Homolytic cleavage splits a covalent bond symmetrically (one electron to each atom), producing neutral free radicals. Heterolytic cleavage splits a covalent bond unsymmetrically (both bonding electrons go to one atom), producing ions (carbocations and carbanions).
  2. Step 2 — Link to Ionic Reactions: Since ionic (polar) organic reactions involve charged intermediates (electrophiles and nucleophiles), they proceed exclusively through heterolytic bond cleavage (B).
  3. Step 3 — Confirm Final Answer: Only statement (B) applies, matching option (b).
Q84.stepsLatex: 1. Only (B) heterolytic bond cleavage is involved in ionic reactions.
Q84.trapHtml: Homolytic cleavage gives free radicals; heterolytic cleavage gives ions.

Q85.conceptHtml: Stronger electron-donating groups activate the benzene ring toward S<sub>E</sub>Ar: −OH > −CH<sub>3</sub> > H > −Cl.
Q85.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the Four Aromatic Compounds: (a) Chlorobenzene ($-\text{Cl}$), (b) Phenol ($-\text{OH}$), (c) Benzene (unsubstituted), and (d) Toluene ($-\text{CH}_3$).
  2. Step 2 — Compare Ring-Activating Power: An electrophile attacks the ring with the highest electron density: $-\text{OH}$ in phenol (b) donates electrons strongly via resonance ($+M$), greatly increasing electron density at ortho/para positions. $-\text{CH}_3$ in toluene (d) is a weaker activator ($+H/+I$). $-\text{Cl}$ in chlorobenzene (a) is deactivating overall ($-I > +M$).
  3. Step 3 — Rank Reactivity: $\text{Phenol (b)} > \text{Toluene (d)} > \text{Benzene (c)} > \text{Chlorobenzene (a)}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm Final Answer: Phenol is most easily attacked by an electrophile, which is option (b).
Q85.stepsLatex: 1. (b) Phenol (−OH) has strong +M resonance donation, making it the most reactive toward electrophilic attack.
Q85.trapHtml: −Cl is deactivating (−I > +M), so chlorobenzene is less reactive than benzene.

Q86.conceptHtml: Decode the parent chain (‘pentane‘ = 5 C) and place substituents at C1 (‘phenyl‘), C2 (‘bromo‘), and C3 (‘bromo‘).
Q86.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Decode the IUPAC Name: "2,3-dibromo-1-phenylpentane" specifies a $5$-carbon alkane chain (C−1 to C-5) with a phenyl ring ($-\text{C}_6\text{H}_5$) attached at C−1, and two bromine ($-\text{Br}$) atoms attached at C−2 and C−3: $\text{Ph}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}(\text{Br})-\text{CH}(\text{Br})-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_3$.
  2. Step 2 — Check Each Given Structure: (a) has $-\text{Br}$ atoms at C−2 and C−4 (2,4-dibromo-1-phenylpentane). (b) has $-\text{Br}$ atoms at C−1 and C−2 (1,2-dibromo-1-phenylpentane). (c) has phenyl at C−1 and $-\text{Br}$ atoms at C−2 and C−3 (2,3-dibromo-1-phenylpentane). (d) has $-\text{Br}$ atoms at C−3 and C−4 (3,4-dibromo-1-phenylpentane).
  3. Step 3 — Confirm Final Answer: Structure (c) matches 2,3-dibromo-1-phenylpentane, so the correct choice is option (c).

2. Option (c) shows a 5-carbon chain attached to phenyl at C1, with Br at C2 and C3.

Q87.conceptHtml: Reactivity order for S<sub>E</sub>Ar: +M/+HC (toluene) > benzene > weak deactivator (−Cl) > strong deactivator (−NO<sub>2</sub>).
Q87.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify Compounds A, B, C, and D: A is benzene, B is toluene ($-\text{CH}_3$), C is chlorobenzene ($-\text{Cl}$), and D is nitrobenzene ($-\text{NO}_2$).
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Electronic Effects on EAS: B ($-\text{CH}_3$): Electron-donating ($+H, +I$) $\rightarrow$ activating (faster than benzene). A (Benzene): Reference reactivity. C ($-\text{Cl}$): Net electron-withdrawing ($-I > +M$) $\rightarrow$ weakly deactivating. D ($-\text{NO}_2$): Strongly electron-withdrawing ($-M, -I$) $\rightarrow$ strongly deactivating (slowest).
  3. Step 3 — Arrange in Decreasing Order of Reactivity: $\text{B} > \text{A} > \text{C} > \text{D}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm Final Answer: The correct order is $\text{B} > \text{A} > \text{C} > \text{D}$, matching option (b).

Q88.conceptHtml: A carbocation has a positively charged carbon with 6 valence electrons (sextet) and acts as a Lewis acid / electrophile.
Q88.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Analyze the Electron Count of Carbon Intermediates: A carbocation ($\text{R}_3\text{C}^+$) has $3$ covalent bonds ($6$ valence electrons, i.e., a sextet) and an empty $p$-orbital, making it electron-deficient and an electrophile. A carbon free radical ($\text{R}_3\text{C}^{\bullet}$) has $7$ valence electrons. A carbanion ($\text{R}_3\text{C}^-$) has $8$ valence electrons (an octet) and acts as a nucleophile.
  2. Step 2 — Match with the Question Stem: The species having carbon with a sextet of electrons that acts as an electrophile is a carbocation.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm Final Answer: The correct answer is carbocation, matching option (d).
Q88.stepsLatex:
1. Carbon free radical has 7e−; carbanion has 8e−; carbocation has 6e− (sextet) and accepts an electron pair
=⇒ carbocation.
Q88.trapHtml: Sextet (6e<sup>−</sup>) = carbocation; Septet (7e<sup>−</sup>) = free radical; Octet (8e<sup>−</sup>) = carbanion.

Q89.conceptHtml: Match NCERT standard pairs: CHCl<sub>3</sub> + aniline (simple distillation, ∆b.p. > 120<sup>°</sup>C), crude oil (fractional), aniline + H<sub>2</sub>O (steam), glycerol from spent-lye (vacuum).

Q90.conceptHtml: Column and thin-layer chromatography separate mixtures based on differential adsorption of components onto a solid stationary phase.
Q90.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the Underlying Principle of Each Method: Chromatography (column and TLC) separates mixture components based on their differential adsorption onto a stationary phase. Sublimation relies on direct solid-to-vapor phase transition. Distillation relies on differences in boiling points. Extraction relies on differential solubility in immiscible solvents.

  3. Step 3 — Confirm Final Answer: The correct option is (a).

Q91.subtopic: IUPAC Nomenclature — Ketone vs Alcohol Priority
Q91.conceptHtml: Ketone (> C = O) has higher IUPAC priority than alcohol (−OH), so the suffix is -one and −OH is named as the prefix hydroxy-.
Q91.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the Principal Functional Group: The compound $\text{HO}-\text{CH}_2-(\text{CH}_2)_3-\text{CH}_2-\text{COCH}_3$ contains a ketone ($-\text{CO}-$) and an alcohol ($-\text{OH}$). In IUPAC priority order, a ketone has higher priority than an alcohol, so the suffix is -one and $-\text{OH}$ is treated as the prefix hydroxy.
  2. Step 2 — Number the Longest Chain: The $7$-carbon chain is numbered from the end closer to the principal group ($-\text{CO}-$), placing the carbonyl at C−2 and the $-\text{OH}$ group at C-7.
  3. Step 3 — Evaluate Both Statements: The correct IUPAC name is 7-hydroxyheptan-2-one, so Statement I is correct. Naming it with "-ol" as the suffix (2-oxoheptan-7-ol) violates functional group priority, so Statement II is incorrect.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm Final Answer: Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect, matching option (b).
Q91.stepsLatex:
1. Numbering HO − C7H2 − (CH2)3 − C3H2 − C2(= O) − C1H3 gives the ketone C2.
2. Statement I: 7-hydroxyheptan-2-one =⇒ True.
3. Statement II: 2-oxoheptan-7-ol wrongly treats −OH as principal group =⇒ False.
Q91.trapHtml: > C = O always beats −OH in IUPAC priority.
Q91.finalAnsHtml: (b) Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.

Q92.conceptHtml: More α-H atoms (hyperconjugation) and +I alkyl groups stabilize carbocations: 3<sup>°</sup> > 2<sup>°</sup> > 1<sup>°</sup> > CH<sup>+</sup><sub>3</sub> .

1. Step 1 — Recall Carbocation Stabilization Factors: Alkyl carbocations are stabilized by hyperconjugation (number of $\alpha$-hydrogens) and the electron-donating $+I$ effect of attached alkyl groups.
  2. Step 2 — Count $\alpha$-Hydrogens for Each Carbocation: $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}^+$ ($3^\circ$): $9\,\alpha$-H (most stable); $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CH}^+$ ($2^\circ$): $6\,\alpha$-H; $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2^+$ ($1^\circ$): $3\,\alpha$-H; $\text{CH}_3^+$ (methyl): $0\,\alpha$-H (least stable).
  3. Step 3 — Write the Stability Order: More $\alpha$-H and greater $+I$ donation yield higher stability: $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}^+ > (\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CH}^+ > \text{CH}_3-\text{CH}_2^+ > \text{CH}_3^+$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm Final Answer: This decreasing order corresponds to option (b).

1. (CH3)3C+ (9 α-H) > (CH3)2CH+ (6 α-H) > CH3CH+ (3 α-H) > CH+ (0 α-H).
2 3

Q93.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Solubility in Two Solvents
Q93.conceptHtml: Differential extraction separates an organic compound from its aqueous solution by shaking with an immiscible organic solvent in which the compound is more soluble.
Q93.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the Principle of Differential Extraction: When an organic compound is present in an aqueous medium, it can be separated by shaking the solution with an immiscible organic solvent in which the compound is much more soluble than in water.
  2. Step 2 — Eliminate Other Methods: Distillation is based on boiling point differences, sublimation on direct solid-to-vapor transition, and column chromatography on differential adsorption.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm Final Answer: Differential extraction is based on solubility in two different solvents, matching option (d).

2. Name: 3-Aminobutanenitrile.

Q95.conceptHtml: Cyclopropenyl cation (2πe<sup>−</sup>, 4n + 2 with n = 0) is aromatic, whereas cyclopentadienyl cation (4πe<sup>−</sup>) and cyclopropenyl anion (4πe<sup>−</sup>) are antiaromatic.
Q95.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Apply Hückel's Rule to Each Species: Aromatic species with $(4n+2)\,\pi$ electrons are far more stable than non-aromatic or anti-aromatic ($4n\,\pi$) species.
  2. Step 2 — Classify All Four Options: (a) Cyclohexa-1,3-diene contains two $sp^3$ carbons $\rightarrow$ non-aromatic. (b) Cyclopropenyl cation is cyclic, planar, and completely conjugated with $2\,\pi$ electrons ($4n+2$ for $n=0$) $\rightarrow$ aromatic (most stable). (c) Cyclopentadienyl cation has $4\,\pi$ electrons $\rightarrow$ anti-aromatic. (d) Cyclopropenyl anion has $4\,\pi$ electrons $\rightarrow$ anti-aromatic.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm Final Answer: The aromatic cyclopropenyl cation is the most stable species, matching option (b).

1. (a) Cyclohexene (alkene, non-aromatic).
2. (b) Cyclopropenyl cation (2πe−, cyclic, planar, conjugated) =⇒ aromatic (most stable among the charged/reactive
species here; note NTA key is (b)).
3. (c) Cyclopentadienyl cation (4πe−, antiaromatic).
4. (d) Cyclopropenyl anion (4πe−, antiaromatic).

Q96.conceptHtml: Parent = 5 carbons (‘pent‘), −CHO at C1 (‘-al‘), C = C at C2–C3 (‘2-en‘), −CH<sub>3</sub> at C4.
Q96.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Break Down the Name "4-Methylpent-2-enal": pent = $5$-carbon parent chain (C−1 to C-5); -al = aldehyde group ($-\text{CHO}$) at C−1; -2-en- = $\text{C}=\text{C}$ double bond between C−2 and C−3; 4-methyl = $-\text{CH}_3$ substituent attached at C−4.
  2. Step 2 — Write the Condensed Structural Formula: Assembling these parts from C-5 to C−1 gives $\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)-\text{CH}=\text{CH}-\text{CHO}$.
  3. Step 3 — Match Against the Given Structures: Option (a) is 3-methylpent-4-enal, option (b) is 3-methylpent-2-enal, option (c) is $\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)-\text{CH}=\text{CH}-\text{CHO}$ (4-methylpent-2-enal), and option (d) is 2-methylpent-2-enal.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm Final Answer: The correct structure is option (c).
