Q97.conceptHtml: −OH gets C1; number through the double bond to give C2 = C3.
Q97.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the Principal Functional Group: The molecule is a cyclohexene ring with an $-\text{OH}$ group. Alcohol ($-\text{OH}$) has higher priority than a double bond, so it takes the suffix -ol and gets position C−1.
  2. Step 2 — Number the Ring for Lowest Locant of the Double Bond: Starting at C−1 ($-\text{OH}$) and numbering clockwise places the double bond between C−2 and C−3 (locant $2$), whereas counterclockwise would place it at C-5.
  3. Step 3 — Assemble the IUPAC Name: Combining the ring root (cyclohex), double bond position (2-en), and alcohol suffix (1-ol) gives Cyclohex-2-en-1-ol.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm Final Answer: The correct IUPAC name is Cyclohex-2-en-1-ol, matching option (a).
Q97.stepsLatex: 1. −OH at C1, double bond at C2–C3 =⇒ Cyclohex-2-en-1-ol.
Q97.trapHtml: Never give C1 to the double bond when −OH is present on the ring.

Q98.subtopic: Acidic Strength — Hydrocarbon C − H Acidity
Q98.conceptHtml: C − H acidity increases with %s-character (sp > sp<sup>2</sup> > sp<sup>3</sup>) and decreases with +I alkyl groups.
Q98.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Relate C–H Acidity to Carbon Hybridization ($s$-Character): Higher $s$-character makes carbon more electronegative, stabilizing the resulting carbanion after $\text{H}^+$ loss and increasing acidity: $sp\,(50\%\,s) > sp^2\,(33.3\%\,s) > sp^3\,(25\%\,s)$.
  2. Step 2 — Classify Hydrogens A and B: A is attached to an $sp$ carbon (acetylene) $\rightarrow$ most acidic. B is attached to an $sp^2$ carbon (ethene) $\rightarrow$ second most acidic.
  3. Step 3 — Compare the Two $sp^3$ Hydrogens (C and D): Removing H from C (isobutane) forms a $3^\circ$ carbanion $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}^-$, which is strongly destabilized by the $+I$ effect of three $-\text{CH}_3$ groups $\rightarrow$ least acidic. Removing H from D (ethane) forms a $1^\circ$ carbanion $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2^-$ with only one $-\text{CH}_3$ group, so D is more acidic than C.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm Final Answer: The ascending order of acidity is $\text{C} < \text{D} < \text{B} < \text{A}$, which matches option (d).
Q98.stepsLatex:
1. A (HC ≡ C − H, sp, 50%s) > B (H2C = CH − H, sp2, 33.3%s) > D (H3C − CH2 − H, 1◦ sp3) > C ((CH3)3C − H,
3◦ sp3, three +I methyls destabilize 3◦ carbanion).
2. Ascending order: C < D < B < A.
Q98.trapHtml: Check whether the question asks for ascending (<) or descending (>) order!

Q99.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Column & TLC vs Paper
Q99.conceptHtml: Column chromatography and TLC are based on differential adsorption; paper chromatography is based on partition.
Q99.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Classify the Chromatographic Techniques (NCERT): Chromatography is broadly divided into adsorption chromatography and partition chromatography.
  2. Step 2 — Check Each Technique: (A) Column chromatography and (B) Thin layer chromatography (TLC) both rely on differential adsorption of components on a solid adsorbent (silica gel or alumina). (C) Paper chromatography is a type of partition chromatography, based on continuous differential partitioning between water trapped in paper and the mobile phase.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm Final Answer: Only A and B are based on differential adsorption, matching option (c).
Q99.stepsLatex: 1. A (Column) and B (TLC) use differential adsorption; C (Paper) uses partition =⇒ A & B only.
Q99.trapHtml: Paper chromatography = partition; Column & TLC = adsorption.

Q100.conceptHtml: An exocyclic double bond shows geometrical isomerism only if both ends have two different groups (including non-identical ring paths!).
Q100.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the Condition for Geometrical Isomerism in Exocyclic Alkenes: Both carbons of the $\text{C}=\text{C}$ double bond must carry two different groups (or two unsymmetrical paths around the ring).
  2. Step 2 — Eliminate Options (b), (c), and (d): In (b) and (c), the exocyclic carbon is $=\text{CH}_2$, which has two identical $-\text{H}$ atoms $\rightarrow$ no GI. In (d), the $-\text{Br}$ is at C−4 (directly opposite C−1), making the clockwise and counterclockwise ring paths from C−1 completely identical $\rightarrow$ no GI.
  3. Step 3 — Verify Option (a): In (a) (1-(bromomethylidene)-3-bromocyclohexane), the exocyclic carbon has two different groups ($-\text{H}$ and $-\text{Br}$), and because the ring $-\text{Br}$ sits at C−3, the two ring paths from C−1 are unsymmetrical (different). Hence, it exhibits $E/Z$ geometrical isomerism.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm Final Answer: Only compound (a) shows geometrical isomerism, matching option (a).
Q100.stepsLatex:
1. In (b) and (c), the exocyclic carbon is = CH2 (two identical H’s =⇒ no GI).
2. In (d), the ring is symmetrically substituted at C4 (Br is para to = CHBr), so both ring paths are identical
=⇒ no GI.
3. In (a), = CHBr has H ≠ Br, and the ring has −Br at C3 (unsymmetrical ring paths!) =⇒ shows geometrical
isomerism!
Q100.trapHtml: For exocyclic = CHBr on a substituted cyclohexane, check if the ring substituent breaks the left–right symmetry of the ring!

Q101.conceptHtml: Delocalization involving interaction between a π-bond and an adjacent lone pair (or another π-bond) is the resonance effect (mesomeric effect).
Q101.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the Definition of Resonance (Mesomeric) Effect: The resonance effect is the polarity produced in a molecule by the interaction of two $\pi$-bonds or between a $\pi$-bond and a lone pair of electrons present on an adjacent atom (e.g., $\text{CH}_2=\text{CH}-\ddot{\text{O}}\text{H}$).
  2. Step 2 — Distinguish from Other Electronic Effects: Inductive effect operates through $\sigma$-bonds, hyperconjugation involves $\sigma\text{–}\pi$ (or $\sigma\text{–}p$) delocalization, and electromeric effect is a temporary reagent-induced shift of $\pi$-electrons.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm Final Answer: The interaction between a $\pi$-bond and an adjacent lone pair causes the Resonance effect, matching option (a).
Q101.stepsLatex: 1. π-bond + adjacent lone pair =⇒ Resonance effect.
Q101.trapHtml: Hyperconjugation is σ–π or σ–p interaction; resonance is π–π or π–lp interaction.

Q102.conceptHtml: Neutral structure with complete octets (I) > charge-separated with − on O (II) > charge-separated with + on O (III).
Q102.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Apply Resonance Stability Rules to Acrolein ($\text{CH}_2=\text{CH}-\text{CHO}$): Neutral structures with maximum covalent bonds and complete octets are most stable; among charge-separated structures, negative charge on the more electronegative atom is preferred.
  2. Step 2 — Compare Structures I, II, and III: I ($\text{CH}_2=\text{CH}-\text{CH}=\text{O}$) is neutral with complete octets on every atom $\rightarrow$ most stable. II ($\overset{\oplus}{\text{C}}\text{H}_2-\text{CH}=\text{CH}-\overset{\ominus}{\text{O}}$) places the negative charge on electronegative oxygen and positive charge on carbon $\rightarrow$ intermediate stability. III ($\overset{\ominus}{\text{C}}\text{H}_2-\text{CH}=\text{CH}-\overset{\oplus}{\text{O}}$) places a positive charge on electronegative oxygen (incomplete octet) and negative charge on carbon $\rightarrow$ least stable.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm Final Answer: The relative stability order is $\text{I} > \text{II} > \text{III}$, which matches option (b).
Q102.stepsLatex: 1. I (neutral) > II (− on O, + on C) > III (+ on O, − on C).
Q102.trapHtml: Same classic acrolein stability order as Q60: neutral > (− on O) > (+ on O).

Q103.conceptHtml: In ethane, the staggered conformation is the most stable (lowest energy), while the eclipsed conformation is the least stable (highest torsional strain).
Q103.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Verify the True Statements About Ethane Conformations: Rotation around the $\text{C}-\text{C}$ single bond gives an infinite number of conformations (statement b is correct) that rapidly interconvert at room temperature (statement d is correct). In the staggered conformation, adjacent $\text{C}-\text{H}$ bonds are separated by a dihedral angle of $60^\circ$ (statement a is correct).
  2. Step 2 — Check Stability of Eclipsed vs. Staggered Conformation: In the eclipsed conformation (dihedral angle $0^\circ$), the $\text{C}-\text{H}$ bonding electron clouds are closest together, creating maximum torsional strain. Therefore, the eclipsed conformation is the least stable (highest energy), whereas the staggered conformation is the most stable.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm Final Answer: Statement (c) claiming that the eclipsed conformation is the most stable is incorrect, matching option (c).
Q103.stepsLatex: 1. Option (c) claims “Eclipsed conformation is the most stable conformation” =⇒ False.
Q103.trapHtml: Staggered = minimum energy (most stable); Eclipsed = maximum energy (least stable).

Q104.conceptHtml: In bond-line formulas, carbon atoms and C − H hydrogens are omitted; vertices/intersections represent carbons.
Q104.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall Bond-Line Formula Rules: In a bond-line representation, carbon atoms and hydrogen atoms directly bonded to carbon are omitted (represented by vertices/intersections of lines), while heteroatoms and functional groups like $-\text{OH}$ and $-\text{CN}$ are explicitly shown.
  2. Step 2 — Convert $\text{HOCH}(\text{CN})_2$ to Bond-Line Form: The central $-\text{CH}-$ group becomes a simple vertex (junction of three lines) without writing "C" or "H", connected to one $-\text{OH}$ group and two $-\text{CN}$ groups.
  3. Step 3 — Eliminate Condensed/Expanded Structures: Options (a), (b), and (c) explicitly write out the central C and H atoms, so they are not bond-line formulas. Only option (d) omits the central C and H and shows the vertex bonded to $-\text{OH}$ and two $-\text{CN}$ groups.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm Final Answer: The correct bond-line formula is option (d).
Q104.stepsLatex: 1. HOCH(CN)<sub>2</sub> has a central CH vertex bonded to −OH and two −CN groups =⇒ option (d).
Q104.trapHtml: In a true bond-line formula, the central CH is shown as a vertex, not written out as ‘CH‘.

Q105.subtopic: Basic Strength — Aliphatic vs Aromatic/Heterocyclic Amines
Q105.conceptHtml: Localized sp<sup>3</sup> lone pair on an aliphatic secondary amine (pyrrolidine) is far more available for protonation than delocalized lone pairs in aniline, diphenylamine, or pyrrole.
Q105.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall what makes a strong Brønsted base: A Brønsted base accepts a proton ($\text{H}^+$) using its lone pair of electrons. The more localized and readily available the nitrogen lone pair is, the stronger the base.
  2. Step 2 — Analyze options (a), (b), and (c): In aniline (a) and diphenylamine (b), the nitrogen lone pair is delocalized into one or two benzene rings by resonance, which sharply lowers basicity. In pyrrole (c), the nitrogen lone pair is part of the aromatic $6\pi$ electron sextet, so protonating nitrogen would destroy aromaticity, making it a very weak base.
  3. Step 3 — Analyze option (d) (pyrrolidine): Pyrrolidine is a saturated cyclic secondary amine where nitrogen is $sp^3$-hybridized. Its lone pair is completely localized (not involved in resonance) and is further enriched by the $+I$ (electron-donating) effect of the two ring $-\text{CH}_2-$ groups.
  4. Step 4 — Conclude the strongest base: Because pyrrolidine has a fully localized, electron-rich lone pair, it is the strongest Brønsted base among the four. Hence, the correct option is (d).
Q105.stepsLatex:
1. (a) Aniline (lone pair delocalized into 1 benzene ring).
2. (b) Diphenylamine (lone pair delocalized into 2 benzene rings).
3. (c) Pyrrole (lone pair part of 6π aromatic sextet).
4. (d) Pyrrolidine (sp3 cyclic 2◦ amine, localized lone pair + +I of ring carbons) =⇒ strongest Brønsted
base.
Q105.trapHtml: Aliphatic cyclic amines (pyrrolidine, piperidine) are always much stronger bases than aryl amines or pyrrole.

Q106.conceptHtml: A −CH<sub>2</sub>− flanked by two carbonyl groups (β-diketone) has highly acidic α-hydrogens (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 9) because its conjugate base is stabilized by two C = O groups.
Q106.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the criterion for highly acidic $\text{C}-\text{H}$ hydrogens: A hydrogen atom is highly acidic if the carbanion (conjugate base) formed after losing $\text{H}^+$ is strongly stabilized by resonance and inductive ($-M, -I$) electron-withdrawing groups.
  2. Step 2 — Compare the structures of the four carbonyl compounds: Options (a) (pentane-2,3-dione), (b) (hexane-2,5-dione), and (c) (a monoketone) only have $\alpha$-hydrogens adjacent to a single carbonyl ($>\text{C}=\text{O}$) group, so their conjugate bases are stabilized by only one carbonyl group.
  3. Step 3 — Examine option (d) (hexane-2,4-dione): Option (d) is a $\beta$-diketone ($\text{CH}_3\text{CO}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CO}-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$) containing an active methylene ($-\text{CH}_2-$) group flanked directly by two $-\text{C}(=\text{O})-$ groups. Removing a proton from this central $-\text{CH}_2-$ produces an enolate carbanion delocalized over both carbonyl oxygens.
  4. Step 4 — Conclude the answer: Due to strong dual $-M$ stabilization of its conjugate base, the $\beta$-diketone in option (d) has the most acidic hydrogen. Hence, the correct option is (d).

1. (a) 1, 2-diketone (no −CH2− between carbonyls).
2. (b) 1, 4-diketone (−CH2CH2− between carbonyls; α-H stabilized by only 1 C = O).
3. (c) Monoketone (acetone).
4. (d) check the given structures: (b) has −CO − CH2 − CH2 − CO− (1, 4-diketone), whereas (d) has −CO − CH2 − CO−?
Look closely at the given structures: (b) is H3C − C(= O) − CH2 − CH2 − C(= O) − CH3 (1, 4-diketone), and
(d) is H3C − C(= O) − CH2 − C(= O) − CH2 − CH3? Actually in the given structures, (d) has H3C − C(= O) − CH2 − C(
(1, 3-diketone, active methylene −CH2− between two C = O’s)! Wait: let’s check option (d): yes! In (d) the
two C = O groups are separated by a single CH2? No, let’s check: in (b) there are two CH2’s between the
two C = O’s, whereas in (d) there is one CH2 between the two C = O’s (β-diketone)! Hence (d) has the highly
acidic active methylene hydrogen.

Q107.conceptHtml: Alicyclic compounds are aliphatic cyclic compounds (rings of carbon atoms that are not aromatic).
Q107.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Inspect the structure of cyclohexene: Cyclohexene ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_{10}$) consists of a six-membered carbon ring containing one $\text{C}=\text{C}$ double bond and four $sp^3$-hybridized $-\text{CH}_2-$ carbons.
  2. Step 2 — Check cyclic vs. acyclic and aromaticity: Because its carbon atoms form a closed ring, it is cyclic (ruling out acyclic). Because it lacks continuous conjugation and does not have a benzene ring, it is neither benzenoid nor aromatic.
  3. Step 3 — Classify as an alicyclic compound: Organic compounds that contain a carbon ring but exhibit properties similar to aliphatic (open-chain) compounds are classified as alicyclic (aliphatic cyclic) compounds.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the correct option: Cyclohexene is an alicyclic compound. Hence, the correct option is (d).
Q107.stepsLatex: 1. Cyclohexene is a non-aromatic, carbocyclic 6-membered ring with one double bond =⇒ Alicyclic.
Q107.trapHtml: Do not confuse alicyclic (non-aromatic rings) with benzenoid/aromatic rings.

Q108.conceptHtml: Give the ring carbon with two substituents (geminal dimethyl) locant 1 so the locant set is (1, 1, 3) rather than (1, 3, 3).
Q108.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the parent ring and substituents in (P): The parent hydrocarbon is a six-membered saturated ring (cyclohexane). One ring carbon bears two methyl ($-\text{CH}_3$) groups, and another carbon separated by one $-\text{CH}_2-$ bears an ethyl ($-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$) group.
  2. Step 2 — Apply the lowest set of locants rule: Numbering from the gem-dimethyl carbon gives locants $(1, 1, 3)$, whereas numbering from the ethyl carbon gives locants $(1, 3, 3)$ or $(1, 5, 5)$. Comparing at the first point of difference, $(1, 1, 3) < (1, 3, 3)$, so the two methyl groups must get position $1$ and the ethyl group gets position $3$.
  3. Step 3 — Arrange substituents in alphabetical order: Prefixes like "di" are ignored when alphabetizing, so "ethyl" comes before "methyl". Thus, the IUPAC name is 3-ethyl-1,1-dimethylcyclohexane.
  4. Step 4 — Match with the options: This matches 3-Ethyl-1, 1-dimethylcyclohexane. Hence, the correct option is (b).
Q108.stepsLatex:
1. Locant set (1, 1, 3) < (1, 3, 3) at the second point of difference (1 < 3).
2. Cite substituents alphabetically (ethyl before dimethyl): 3-Ethyl-1, 1-dimethylcyclohexane.
Q108.trapHtml: Alphabetical order does NOT override the lowest locant set rule: (1, 1, 3) always beats (1, 3, 3).

Q109.conceptHtml: Paper chromatography is a type of partition chromatography in which water trapped in the pores of the paper acts as the stationary phase.
Q109.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the principle of paper chromatography: Paper chromatography is a type of partition chromatography, not simple adsorption chromatography.
  2. Step 2 — Identify the stationary phase: Special quality chromatography paper (cellulose) traps water molecules inside its microscopic pores. It is this trapped water—not the cellulose sheet itself—that acts as the liquid stationary phase.
  3. Step 3 — Identify the mobile phase and separation mechanism: A suitable solvent (or solvent mixture) acts as the mobile phase and rises up the paper by capillary action, partitioning components between the mobile solvent and the stationary water trapped in the pores.
  4. Step 4 — Match with the given statements: Only statement (b) accurately states that water present in the pores of the paper forms the stationary phase. Hence, the correct option is (b).
Q109.stepsLatex: 1. Option (b) “Water present in the pores of the paper forms the stationary phase” is the exact NCERT statement.
Q109.trapHtml: The cellulose paper itself is only an inert support, NOT the stationary phase.

Q110.conceptHtml: Tropolone has a 7-membered ring with 6π electrons delocalized in the ring (aromatic via dipolar tropylium- like resonance); the π-electrons of C = O polarize onto O and are not part of the 6π aromatic sextet.
Q110.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Analyze the structure and aromaticity of tropolone: Tropolone (2-hydroxycyclohepta-2,4,6-trien-1-one) is a non-benzenoid aromatic compound. When the exocyclic $>\text{C}=\text{O}$ bond polarizes as $>\text{C}^+-\text{O}^-$, the seven-membered ring forms a planar, cyclic, completely conjugated tropylium-like system with $6\pi$ electrons ($4n+2$ for $n=1$).
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement I: Although tropolone is aromatic, its aromatic ring sextet consists of $6\pi$ electrons (not $8\pi$ electrons—$8\pi$ electrons would violate Hückel's $4n+2$ rule). Therefore, Statement I is false.
  3. Step 3 — Evaluate Statement II: In the dipolar aromatic resonance form, the $\pi$ electrons of the $>\text{C}=\text{O}$ group shift completely onto the exocyclic oxygen atom ($-\text{O}^-$), leaving an empty $p$-orbital on the ring carbon. Thus, the carbonyl $\pi$ electrons are NOT part of the cyclic $6\pi$ aromatic sextet. Therefore, Statement II is also false.
  4. Step 4 — Conclude the answer: Since both Statement I and Statement II are false, the correct option is (b).
Q110.stepsLatex:
1. Statement I: Tropolone is aromatic, but its aromatic ring has 6π electrons (not 8π in the ring) =⇒ False.
2. Statement II: The π-electrons of the > C = O group polarize onto oxygen (C+ − O−) so that the ring retains
6π electrons; they are not counted inside the aromatic sextet =⇒ False.
Q110.trapHtml: Tropolone is 6π aromatic (like tropylium cation), NOT 8π!
Q110.finalAnsHtml: (b) Both Statement I and Statement II are false

Q111.conceptHtml: Compounds whose dipolar resonance structure (C<sup>+</sup> − C<sup>−</sup>) creates two aromatic rings (or a 6π / 2π aromatic system) have exceptionally high dipole moments.
Q111.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the dipole moment principle for hydrocarbons: Symmetrical alkenes have canceling bond dipoles ($\mu = 0$), whereas conjugated hydrocarbons that gain aromatic stabilization upon charge separation exhibit unusually large dipole moments.
  2. Step 2 — Eliminate symmetrical and non-aromatic options: Compounds (a) and (b) are symmetrical about their central double bond, so their net dipole moment is zero. Compound (c) is cyclopropanone (a saturated three-membered ring ketone) with only a normal carbonyl dipole and no aromatic charge-separated contributor.
  3. Step 3 — Analyze option (d) (calicene): Compound (d) consists of a cyclopropene ring linked by an exocyclic double bond to a cyclopentadiene ring. Polarizing the central $\pi$ bond toward the five-membered ring creates a $2\pi$ cyclopropenylium cation ($4n+2, n=0$) and a $6\pi$ cyclopentadienyl anion ($4n+2, n=1$) simultaneously.
  4. Step 4 — Conclude the highest dipole moment: Because both rings become aromatic in the dipolar resonance contributor, compound (d) has substantial permanent charge separation and therefore the highest dipole moment. Hence, the correct option is (d).
Q111.stepsLatex:
1. In (d), polarizing the exocyclic double bond between the 3-membered ring and 5-membered ring (calicene)
gives a 2π aromatic cyclopropenyl cation + a 6π aromatic cyclopentadienyl anion!
2. In (d) (sesquifulvalene (5-ring = 7-ring: polarizing C = C gives 6π cyclopentadienyl anion + 6π tropylium
cation — BOTH rings aromatic!) =⇒ highest dipole moment.
Q111.trapHtml: Check if dipolar π-bond polarization makes both rings aromatic (6π anion + 6π or 2π cation)!

Q112.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Reaction with 2 eq OH<sup>−</sup>
Q112.conceptHtml: Squaric acid (C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>) is a strong dibasic acid (pK<sub>a1</sub> ≈ 1.5, pK<sub>a2</sub> ≈ 3.5) that reacts rapidly with 2 eq OH<sup>−</sup> to form the squarate dianion (C<sub>4</sub>O<sup>2</sup><sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup>), which is 2π-aromatic with all C − C bonds equal.
Q112.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify compounds A and B: Compound A is squaric acid (3,4-dihydroxycyclobut-3-ene-1,2-dione). Treating A with $2\text{ eq.}$ of $\text{OH}^-$ removes both acidic protons to give the squarate dianion, $\text{C}_4\text{O}_4^{2-}$ (compound B).
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate statements A and D: In the squarate dianion (B), the four-membered ring is planar and fully conjugated with $2\pi$ electrons in the ring ($4n+2$ with $n=0$), making B aromatic (statement A is true). Resonance delocalizes the negative charges equally across all four oxygens and ring carbons, so all four $\text{C}-\text{C}$ bond lengths in B are identical (statement D is true).
  3. Step 3 — Evaluate statements B and C: Acid-base neutralization between a strong organic acid (squaric acid) and $\text{OH}^-$ is virtually instantaneous, not slow (so statement B is false). Compound A contains an enediol ($-\text{C(OH)}=\text{C(OH)}-$) adjacent to carbonyl groups and exhibits keto-enol tautomerism (statement C is true).
  4. Step 4 — Combine the correct statements: Statements A, C, and D are correct. Hence, the correct option is (b).
Q112.stepsLatex:
1. A: Compound ‘B’ (squarate dianion, 2πe− in 4-ring) is aromatic =⇒ True.
2. B: Acid–base neutralization is extremely fast, not slow =⇒ False.
3. C: ‘A’ (squaric acid) has enolizable O = C − C = C(OH)− system (tautomerism) =⇒ True.
4. D: Resonance symmetry makes all four C − C bond lengths in ‘B’ identical =⇒ True.
Q112.trapHtml: Acid–base reactions are among the fastest reactions in chemistry (diffusion-controlled), never slow!

Q113.subtopic: Chromatography — TLC to Column Elution Order
Q113.conceptHtml: Higher R<sub>f</sub> in TLC = weaker adsorption = faster movement = elutes first in column chromatography.
Q113.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Relate TLC spot height to adsorption strength: On a polar silica gel TLC plate, a compound that travels farther up the plate (higher $R_f$) is less polar and more weakly adsorbed on silica gel.
  2. Step 2 — Read the heights of spots A, B, and C from the TLC plate: From the diagram, spot A has moved the farthest (highest $R_f$), spot C is at an intermediate height, and spot B is closest to the baseline (lowest $R_f$). Thus, the order of $R_f$ is $R_{f,A} > R_{f,C} > R_{f,B}$.
  3. Step 3 — Connect $R_f$ order to silica gel column elution order: In silica gel column chromatography, the least strongly adsorbed (highest $R_f$) compound moves down the column fastest and elutes first, while the most strongly adsorbed (lowest $R_f$) compound elutes last.
  4. Step 4 — State the elution order: The compounds elute in the order A, C, B. Hence, the correct option is (c).
Q113.stepsLatex:
1. From the TLC plate, spot heights from baseline: A > C > B (Rf order: A > C > B).
2. Therefore, elution order from the silica gel column is A, C, B.
Q113.trapHtml: In TLC, the spot closest to the solvent front (highest R<sub>f</sub>) is the least polar and elutes first from a column.

Q114.conceptHtml: Hydride affinity (R+ + H− → R − H) is inversely proportional to carbocation stability: least stable carbocation has the highest hydride affinity.
Q114.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Understand hydride affinity of a carbocation: Hydride affinity is the enthalpy released when a carbocation accepts a hydride ion ($\text{H}^-$). A less stable carbocation is more eager to accept $\text{H}^-$ and therefore has a higher hydride affinity (hydride affinity $\propto \frac{1}{\text{carbocation stability}}$).
  2. Step 2 — Rank the stability of carbocations A, B, C, and D: D (tricyclopropylmethyl cation) is exceptionally stabilized by dancing resonance ($\sigma$-conjugation from three cyclopropyl rings). B (triphenylmethyl cation, $\text{Ph}_3\text{C}^+$) is strongly stabilized by resonance across three phenyl rings. A ($\text{CH}_2=\text{CH}-\text{C}^+(\text{CH}_3)_2$) is a tertiary allylic carbocation stabilized by resonance plus $6\,\alpha\text{-H}$ hyperconjugation. C (tert-butyl cation, $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}^+$) has no resonance and is stabilized only by $9\,\alpha\text{-H}$ hyperconjugation and $+I$ effect.
  3. Step 3 — Write stability and invert for hydride affinity: The stability order is $\text{D} > \text{B} > \text{A} > \text{C}$. Reversing this gives the decreasing order of hydride affinity: $\text{C} > \text{A} > \text{B} > \text{D}$.
  4. Step 4 — Match with the options: The decreasing order of hydride affinity is C, A, B, D. Hence, the correct option is (b).
Q114.stepsLatex:
+
1. Carbocation stability order: D (tricyclopropylmethyl cation, dancing resonance) > B (Ph3C+) > A (CH2 = CH − C(CH3)2
3◦ allylic) > C ((CH3)3C+, 3◦ alkyl).
2. Hydride affinity is the reverse of stability: C > A > B > D.
Q114.trapHtml: Tricyclopropylmethyl cation (D) is even more stable than Ph<sub>3</sub>C<sup>+</sup> (B), and hydride affinity is opposite to stability!

Q115.conceptHtml: If ‘A’ elutes first, ‘B’ is more strongly adsorbed onto the stationary phase and therefore has a lower R<sub>f</sub>.
Q115.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall how separation works in column chromatography: Components of a mixture separate based on their differential adsorption onto the stationary phase (such as silica gel or alumina).
  2. Step 2 — Compare compounds A and B: Since compound A elutes first, A interacts weakly with the stationary phase (weaker adsorption) and moves rapidly with the mobile phase (high $R_f$).
  3. Step 3 — Deduce the properties of compound B: Because compound B elutes after A, B is retained more strongly by the stationary phase (stronger adsorption) and travels more slowly (low $R_f$).
  4. Step 4 — Match with the options: Compound B has low $R_f$ and stronger adsorption. Hence, the correct option is (d).
Q115.stepsLatex: 1. ‘B’ elutes after ‘A’ =⇒ ‘B’ has low R<sub>f</sub>, stronger adsorption.
Q115.trapHtml: Elutes last = stronger adsorption = lower R<sub>f</sub>.

Q116.conceptHtml: Number from −COOH as C1; the internal ketone > C = O is named with the prefix oxo-.
Q116.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the principal functional group: The molecule contains both a carboxylic acid ($-\text{COOH}$) and a ketone ($>\text{C}=\text{O}$). According to IUPAC priority rules, $-\text{COOH}$ takes precedence as the principal functional group (suffix "-oic acid"), while the ketone is treated as a substituent (prefix "oxo-").
  2. Step 2 — Choose and number the longest carbon chain containing $-\text{COOH}$: Starting with the carboxylic acid carbon as $\text{C-1}$, the longest continuous chain has 6 carbons: $\text{HOOC(1)}-\text{CH(CH}_3)(2)-\text{CH}_2(3)-\text{CH}_2(4)-\text{CO}(5)-\text{CH}_3(6)$ (a hexanoic acid backbone).
  3. Step 3 — Locate and alphabetize the substituents: There is a methyl group at $\text{C-2}$ and an oxo (ketone) group at $\text{C-5}$. Alphabetically, "methyl" comes before "oxo", giving 2-methyl-5-oxohexanoic acid.
  4. Step 4 — Match with the options: This corresponds to 2-Methyl-5-oxohexanoic acid. Hence, the correct option is (d).

1. Longest chain from −COOH (C1): HOOC − C2H(CH3) − C3H2 − C4H2 − C5(= O) − C6H3 (6 carbons, hex-
anoic acid).
2. Methyl at C2, oxo at C5 =⇒ 2-Methyl-5-oxohexanoic acid.
Q116.trapHtml: Use oxo- for a ketonic > C = O substituent; formyl- is only for −CHO outside the main chain.

Q117.conceptHtml: More −I groups and higher halogen electronegativity (F > Cl > Br) stabilize the carboxylate anion and increase acidity.
Q117.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall how substituents affect carboxylic acid acidity: Acid strength increases as the carboxylate conjugate base ($\text{RCOO}^-$) is stabilized by electron-withdrawing ($-I$) groups, and decreases with electron-donating ($+I$) groups.
  2. Step 2 — Compare the $-I$ effects of the halogens: Electronegativity follows $\text{F} > \text{Cl} > \text{Br}$, so the $-I$ strength follows $-\text{F} > -\text{Cl} > -\text{Br}$. Furthermore, inductive effects are additive, so three fluorine atoms in $\text{F}_3\text{C}-\text{COOH}$ (B) exert a much stronger $-I$ pull than a single fluorine in $\text{FCH}_2\text{COOH}$ (D).
  3. Step 3 — Rank all five acids: Comparing all five compounds, $\text{F}_3\text{CCOOH}$ (B) is the strongest, followed by $\text{FCH}_2\text{COOH}$ (D), $\text{ClCH}_2\text{COOH}$ (C), $\text{BrCH}_2\text{COOH}$ (E), and finally unsubstituted $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$ (A), which has a $+I$ methyl group.
  4. Step 4 — Write the descending order: The decreasing acidity order is $\text{B} > \text{D} > \text{C} > \text{E} > \text{A}$. Hence, the correct option is (c).

Q118.conceptHtml: In a silica gel column, the most polar band stays nearest the top (‘a‘), while the least polar band travels fastest toward the bottom (‘c‘) and elutes first.
Q118.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Interpret the bands in the column chromatography diagram: Band 'a' is near the top of the polar stationary phase column, 'b' is in the middle, and 'c' is closest to the bottom exit.
  2. Step 2 — Determine polarity and elution order: Since 'a' moves the slowest and stays near the top, 'a' is the most polar (strongest adsorption) and spends the most time in the column. Conversely, 'c' moves fastest, is the least polar, and elutes first, followed by 'b', and finally 'a'.
  3. Step 3 — Check each statement for correctness: Statement A ("c is more polar than a and b") is incorrect. Statement B ("a is least polar") is incorrect. Statement C ("b comes out before c and after a") is incorrect (actual elution order is c, then b, then a). Statement D ("a spends more time in the column") is correct.
  4. Step 4 — Identify the incorrect statements: The incorrect statements are A, B, and C only. Hence, the correct option is (d).

1. From the column: ‘a‘ is at top (most polar, spends most time in column), ‘b‘ is middle, ‘c‘ is at bottom (least
polar, elutes first).
2. A: Claims ‘c‘ is more polar than ‘a‘ and ‘b‘ =⇒ Incorrect.
3. B: Claims ‘a‘ is least polar =⇒ Incorrect.
4. C: Claims ‘b‘ comes out before ‘c‘ =⇒ Incorrect (‘c‘ comes out first).
5. D: ‘a‘ spends more time in column =⇒ Correct.
Q118.trapHtml: Column chromatography runs top-to-bottom: the band at the bottom (‘c‘) elutes first (least polar).

Q119.conceptHtml: Canonical (contributing) structures are hypothetical; the actual molecule is a single resonance hybrid (not a dynamic equilibrium).
Q119.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the fundamental concept of resonance: Canonical (resonating) structures are hypothetical Lewis structures used to represent electron delocalization; they do NOT have independent physical existence.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate options (a), (b), and (c): Because canonical structures are imaginary, they cannot be isolated or detected individually (a is false), they are not in dynamic equilibrium like tautomers (b is false), and the ion does not spend time switching between them (c is false).
  3. Step 3 — Evaluate option (d): The carbonate ion ($\text{CO}_3^{2-}$) exists as a single actual structure—the resonance hybrid of the three equivalent canonical forms—in which all three $\text{C}-\text{O}$ bonds have equal length and bond order $\frac{4}{3}$.
  4. Step 4 — Conclude the correct statement: Option (d) accurately describes resonance in $\text{CO}_3^{2-}$. Hence, the correct option is (d).

1. CO2− exists as a single resonance hybrid of the three equivalent canonical forms, with all C − O bonds equal
3
(BO = 1.33).
Q119.trapHtml: Resonance is NOT a rapid equilibrium between real structures; canonical forms have no independent physical existence.

Q120.conceptHtml: Immiscible liquids → differential solvent extraction; ortho/para isomers → column chromatography; kerosene/naphthalene → fractional distillation; glucose/NaCl → crystallization.
Q120.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Match A ($\text{H}_2\text{O} / \text{CH}_2\text{Cl}_2$): Water and dichloromethane are immiscible liquids (forming two distinct layers), which are separated by differential solvent extraction using a separating funnel $\Rightarrow \text{A-(ii)}$.
  2. Step 2 — Match B (1-tetralone / 4-nitrophenol): This is a mixture of two non-volatile organic solids with different polarities (a ketone and a polar nitrophenol), best separated by column chromatography $\Rightarrow \text{B-(iii)}$.
  3. Step 3 — Match C (Kerosene / Naphthalene) and D ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6 / \text{NaCl}$): Kerosene (liquid mixture) and naphthalene (higher-boiling component) are separated by fractional distillation $\Rightarrow \text{C-(iv)}$. Glucose and $\text{NaCl}$ are two water-soluble solids separated by fractional crystallization based on solubility differences $\Rightarrow \text{D-(i)}$.
  4. Step 4 — Combine the matches: The correct matching is A-(ii), B-(iii), C-(iv), D-(i). Hence, the correct option is (d).

1. A. H2O/CH2Cl2 (immiscible) → Differential solvent extraction (ii).
2. B. o- vs p-nitrophenol/etc. → Column chromatography (iii).
3. C. Kerosene / Naphthalene → Fractional distillation (iv).
4. D. C6H12O6/NaCl → Crystallization (i).
Q120.trapHtml: Water and dichloromethane (CH<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>) are immiscible and separated using a separating funnel (differential extraction).

Q121.conceptHtml: Match NCERT mixtures to their standard purification techniques.
Q121.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Match A ($\text{CHCl}_3 + \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2$): Chloroform ($\text{b.p. } 334\text{ K}$) and aniline ($\text{b.p. } 457\text{ K}$) are miscible liquids with a large boiling point difference ($>40\text{ K}$), so they are separated by simple distillation $\Rightarrow \text{A-III}$.
  2. Step 2 — Match B ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_{14} + \text{C}_5\text{H}_{12}$): Hexane ($\text{b.p. } 342\text{ K}$) and pentane ($\text{b.p. } 309\text{ K}$) are miscible liquids with close boiling points, requiring fractional distillation $\Rightarrow \text{B-IV}$.
  3. Step 3 — Match C ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$) and D (Organic compound in $\text{H}_2\text{O}$): Aniline is steam-volatile and immiscible with water, so aniline-water mixtures are separated by steam distillation $\Rightarrow \text{C-I}$. An organic compound dissolved in water is recovered using an immiscible organic solvent via differential extraction $\Rightarrow \text{D-II}$.
  4. Step 4 — Combine the matches: The correct sequence is A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II. Hence, the correct option is (d).

3. C. C6H5NH2 + H2O (immiscible, steam-volatile) → Steam distillation (I).
4. D. Organic compound in H2O → Differential extraction (II).

Q122.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Carboxylic Acid vs Phenol vs Alkyne
Q122.conceptHtml: Acidity order: −COOH (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 4) > phenol −OH (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 10) > terminal alkyne ≡ C − H (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 25) > alkene = C − H (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 44).
Q122.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the chemical environment of each marked proton: $\text{H}_C$ is a carboxylic acid proton ($-\text{CO}_2\text{H}_C$). $\text{H}_D$ is an $\alpha$-benzylic proton attached to a carbon bonded to both a benzene ring and a $-\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ group. $\text{H}_A$ is a terminal alkyne proton ($-\text{C}\equiv\text{C}-\text{H}_A$, $sp$-hybridized carbon). $\text{H}_B$ is a benzylic/propargylic $sp^3$ $\text{C}-\text{H}$ proton.
  2. Step 2 — Compare $\text{H}_C$ and $\text{H}_D$: Removing $\text{H}_C$ gives a resonance-stabilized carboxylate anion ($-\text{COO}^-$) with negative charge on electronegative oxygens ($\text{p}K_a \approx 4\text{--}5$), making $\text{H}_C$ the most acidic. Removing $\text{H}_D$ gives a carbanion stabilized simultaneously by the benzene ring and the adjacent carbonyl ($-M$), making $\text{H}_D$ second most acidic.
  3. Step 3 — Compare $\text{H}_A$ and $\text{H}_B$: $\text{H}_A$ is bonded to an $sp$-hybridized carbon ($50\%$ $s$-character, $\text{p}K_a \approx 25$), which holds the conjugate base lone pair tightly and is more acidic than the $sp^3$ $\text{C}-\text{H}$ proton $\text{H}_B$ ($\text{p}K_a \approx 35\text{--}40$).
  4. Step 4 — Arrange in decreasing order of acidity: The acidity order is $\text{H}_C > \text{H}_D > \text{H}_A > \text{H}_B$. Hence, the correct option is (d).
Q122.stepsLatex: 1. H<sub>C</sub> (−CO<sub>2</sub>H) > H<sub>D</sub> (phenolic −OH) > H<sub>A</sub> (terminal alkyne ≡ C − H) > H<sub>B</sub> (aromatic/vinylic C − H).
Q122.trapHtml: Terminal alkyne H<sub>A</sub> (sp) is vastly more acidic than aromatic/alkene H<sub>B</sub> (sp<sup>2</sup>).

Q123.subtopic: Optical Isomerism — Chiral Centers in C4H8DBr
Q123.conceptHtml: Deuterium (D) and Hydrogen (H) are treated as different groups for chirality!
Q123.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the condition for a chiral carbon: A carbon atom is chiral (asymmetric) if it is $sp^3$-hybridized and bonded to four different atoms or groups (note that $\text{H}$ and $\text{D}$ count as different groups).
  2. Step 2 — Check options (a), (b), and (d): In 2-bromo-1-deuterobutane ($\text{DCH}_2-\text{CH(Br)}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_3$), only $\text{C-2}$ is chiral ($1$ chiral carbon). In 2-bromo-1-deutero-2-methylpropane ($\text{DCH}_2-\text{C(Br)(CH}_3)_2$), there are $0$ chiral carbons because $\text{C-2}$ has two identical $-\text{CH}_3$ groups. In 2-bromo-2-deuterobutane ($\text{CH}_3-\text{C(Br)(D)}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_3$), only $\text{C-2}$ is chiral ($1$ chiral carbon).
  3. Step 3 — Check option (c) (2-bromo-3-deuterobutane): Its structure is $\text{CH}_3-\text{C}^*\text{H(Br)}-\text{C}^*\text{H(D)}-\text{CH}_3$. Here, $\text{C-2}$ is bonded to $-\text{H}, -\text{Br}, -\text{CH}_3, -\text{CHDCH}_3$ (chiral), and $\text{C-3}$ is bonded to $-\text{H}, -\text{D}, -\text{CH}_3, -\text{CH(Br)CH}_3$ (chiral), giving two chiral carbon atoms.
  4. Step 4 — Conclude the answer: 2-Bromo-3-deuterobutane has two chiral carbon atoms. Hence, the correct option is (c).

∗ ∗
1. In 2-Bromo-3-deuterobutane (CH3 − CH(Br) − CH(D) − CH3):
2. C2 is bonded to −H, −Br, −CH3, −CHDCH3 (chiral).
3. C3 is bonded to −H, −D, −CH3, −CHBrCH3 (chiral).
4. Hence it has two chiral carbons.
Q123.trapHtml: D vs H creates a genuine chiral center when the other two groups are also distinct.

Q124.subtopic: Isomerism — Amines, Ketones, Amide–Imidic Acid, Phenols
Q124.conceptHtml: Classify each pair: 1<sup>°</sup>/2<sup>°</sup> amines (functional), ketones with shifted C = O (metamers), amide/hydroxyimine (tautomers), o/p-nitrophenol (positional).
Q124.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Match A (Propanamine and N-Methylethanamine): Propanamine ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$) is a $1^\circ$ amine, whereas N-methylethanamine ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{NHCH}_3$) is a $2^\circ$ amine. Primary, secondary, and tertiary amines with the same formula are functional isomers $\Rightarrow \text{A-III}$.
  2. Step 2 — Match B (Hexan-2-one and Hexan-3-one): Both are ketones ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}$) differing in the alkyl chains attached on either side of the divalent $-\text{CO}-$ group ($\text{CH}_3$ & $\text{C}_4\text{H}_9$ vs. $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5$ & $\text{C}_3\text{H}_7$), making them metamers $\Rightarrow \text{B-I}$.
  3. Step 3 — Match C and D: Ethanamide ($\text{CH}_3\text{CONH}_2$) and hydroxyethanimine ($\text{CH}_3\text{C(OH)}=\text{NH}$) interconvert via 1,3-proton migration (amide-imidic acid tautomerism), so they are tautomers $\Rightarrow \text{C-IV}$. $o$-Nitrophenol and $p$-nitrophenol differ only in the position of the $-\text{NO}_2$ group on the benzene ring, so they are positional isomers $\Rightarrow \text{D-II}$.
  4. Step 4 — Combine the matches: The correct matching is A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II. Hence, the correct option is (a).

1. A. Propanamine (1◦) & N-Methylethanamine (2◦) → Functional isomers (III).
2. B. Hexan-2-one & Hexan-3-one → Metamers (I).
3. C. Ethanamide & Hydroxyethanimine → Tautomers (IV).
4. D. o-nitrophenol & p-nitrophenol → Positional isomers (II).
Q124.trapHtml: Hexan-2-one and hexan-3-one are classified as metamers (different alkyl chains on either side of C = O).

Q125.subtopic: Conformational Analysis — Newman Projections of n-Butane
Q125.conceptHtml: The anti conformation (θ = 180<sup>°</sup> between the two Me groups) minimizes both torsional strain and steric repulsion.
Q125.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall Newman projection stability rules for $n$-butane: Conformational stability depends on minimizing torsional strain (eclipsing of bonds) and steric/van der Waals repulsion between bulky methyl ($-\text{Me}$) groups.
  2. Step 2 — Identify each conformation shown in the options: Option (a) is the anti (staggered) conformation where the two $-\text{Me}$ groups are at a dihedral angle of $180^\circ$. Option (b) is partially eclipsed ($120^\circ$), option (c) is gauche staggered ($60^\circ$), and option (d) is fully eclipsed ($0^\circ$).
  3. Step 3 — Compare energies: In the anti conformation (a), all bonds are staggered (zero torsional strain) and the two bulky $-\text{Me}$ groups are maximally separated at $180^\circ$ (minimum steric repulsion), giving the lowest potential energy.
  4. Step 4 — Conclude the most stable conformation: The anti staggered conformation in option (a) is the most stable. Hence, the correct option is (a).

1. (a) Anti conformation (Me groups 180◦ apart) =⇒ most stable.
2. (b) Eclipsed; (c) Gauche (60◦); (d) Fully eclipsed (0◦).

Q126.conceptHtml: Benzene is stabilized by ∼ 150 kJ/mol of resonance energy because delocalized π-electrons are shared over all 6 carbon nuclei (lowering kinetic/potential energy).
Q126.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Assertion A: Experimental enthalpy of hydrogenation data show that benzene is about $150\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$ ($36\text{ kcal mol}^{-1}$) lower in energy (more stable) than hypothetical cyclohexa-1,3,5-triene. Thus, Assertion A is correct.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Reason R: In benzene, the six $\pi$ electrons are delocalized over all six carbon nuclei rather than confined between pairs of carbons. This delocalization allows the $\pi$ electron cloud to experience stronger net electrostatic attraction from all six carbon nuclei, lowering the overall potential energy. Thus, Reason R is correct.
  3. Step 3 — Check whether R explains A: This increased nuclear attraction from $\pi$-electron delocalization is precisely the physical origin of benzene's resonance (aromatic) stabilization energy over localized cyclohexatriene.
  4. Step 4 — Conclude the answer: Both A and R are correct, and R is the correct explanation of A. Hence, the correct option is (b).
Q126.stepsLatex:
1. Both Assertion A and Reason R are true, and R (stronger nuclear attraction of delocalized π-cloud) is the
correct explanation of A.
Q126.trapHtml: Resonance stabilization lowers the potential energy of delocalized π-electrons.
Q126.finalAnsHtml: (b) Both A and R are correct and R is the correct explanation of A

Q127.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Active Methylene vs Ester
Q127.conceptHtml: Ketones withdraw electron density more strongly than esters (where the −OMe lone pair competes via cross-conjugation), making β-diketones more acidic than β-ketoesters and diesters.
Q127.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the three $\beta$-dicarbonyl compounds: Compound (a) is pentane-2,4-dione (a $\beta$-diketone, $\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_2\text{COCH}_3$), compound (b) is dimethyl malonate (a $\beta$-diester, $\text{MeOOC}-\text{CH}_2-\text{COOMe}$), and compound (c) is methyl acetoacetate (a $\beta$-ketoester, $\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_2\text{COOMe}$).
  2. Step 2 — Compare how effectively each group stabilizes the central carbanion: In an ester group ($-\text{COOMe}$), the lone pair on the $-\text{OMe}$ oxygen undergoes cross-conjugation ($+M$) with the carbonyl group, reducing the carbonyl's ability to accept negative charge from the central $-\text{CH}^--$ carbanion.
  3. Step 3 — Rank the acidity of the active methylene protons: Because ketone carbonyls have no competing cross-conjugation, a ketone $-\text{COR}$ stabilizes the carbanion much better than an ester $-\text{COOR}$. Therefore, acidity follows: diketone (a, $\text{p}K_a \approx 9$) $>$ ketoester (c, $\text{p}K_a \approx 11$) $>$ diester (b, $\text{p}K_a \approx 13$).
  4. Step 4 — Conclude the answer: Compound (a) undergoes deprotonation most readily in basic medium. Hence, the correct option is (a).
Q127.stepsLatex:
1. Acidity of active methylene −CH2− decreases as −C = O groups are replaced by −COOMe: a (β-diketone,
pKa ≈ 9) > b (β-ketoester, pKa ≈ 11) > c (malonate diester, pKa ≈ 13).
2. Hence ‘a only’ undergoes deprotonation most readily.
Q127.trapHtml: Cross-conjugation from −OMe in esters reduces the stabilization of the enolate carbanion.

Q128.conceptHtml: Neutral structure with complete octets (D) > charge-separated with all octets complete (B, + on N, − on O? Wait: check charges in the given structures) > incomplete octet / unfavorable charges.
Q128.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Apply the priority rules for resonance structure stability: (1) Structures with complete octets on all atoms are most stable; (2) positive charge is better tolerated on less electronegative atoms and destabilized on electronegative atoms (especially with an incomplete octet); (3) charges stabilized by adjacent groups ($-M$ stabilizing $-$, $+M$ stabilizing $+$) are favored.
  2. Step 2 — Identify the most stable structure (D): In structure D ($\text{OHC}-\text{CH}^--\text{CH}=\text{CH}-\text{CH}=\text{NH}_2^+$), every heavy atom has a complete octet (nitrogen forms 4 bonds with a $+$ charge) and the carbanion is stabilized by $-\text{CHO}$. Thus, D is the most stable.
  3. Step 3 — Compare structures B, A, and C: In B, the carbocation is adjacent to $+M$ $-\text{NH}_2$ and the carbanion is adjacent to $-M$ $-\text{CHO}$ (favorable charge placement, though $\text{C}^+$ has an incomplete octet). In A, the polarity is reversed ($\text{C}^+$ next to electron-withdrawing $-\text{CHO}$ and $\text{C}^-$ next to $-\text{NH}_2$), making A less stable than B. In C, highly electronegative oxygen carries a positive charge with an unfavorable electronic arrangement, making C the least stable.
  4. Step 4 — Write the increasing order of stability: The increasing stability order is $\text{C} < \text{A} < \text{B} < \text{D}$. Hence, the correct option is (c).

1. In the given structures: D is the neutral structure (most stable); B has + on N (actually N+ has 4 bonds =
complete octet!) and − on C/O; A has + on C (sextet) and − on C; C has + on O/C and − on C (least
stable).
2. Increasing order: C < A < B < D (i.e. ‘C, A, B, D‘).
Q128.trapHtml: Always check whether the question asks for increasing or decreasing order!

Q129.conceptHtml: Count monosubstituted (−C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>7</sub>), disubstituted (−CH<sub>3</sub>, −C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>), and trisubstituted (3 × −CH<sub>3</sub>) benzene isomers.
Q129.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Determine the substituent carbons on the benzene ring: Subtracting the benzene ring skeleton ($\text{C}_6$) from $\text{C}_9\text{H}_{12}$ leaves $3$ saturated carbon atoms to distribute as alkyl substituents on the ring.
  2. Step 2 — Count monosubstituted benzene derivatives ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5-\text{C}_3\text{H}_7$): A propyl group has two structural isomers: $n$-propylbenzene and isopropylbenzene (cumene). Count $= 2$.
  3. Step 3 — Count disubstituted benzene derivatives ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_4(\text{CH}_3)(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5)$): One methyl and one ethyl group can be arranged in ortho (1,2), meta (1,3), or para (1,4) positions. Count $= 3$.
  4. Step 4 — Count trisubstituted benzene derivatives ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_3(\text{CH}_3)_3$) and sum: Three methyl groups give 1,2,3-trimethylbenzene, 1,2,4-trimethylbenzene, and 1,3,5-trimethylbenzene (Count $= 3$). Total structural isomers $= 2 + 3 + 3 = 8$. Therefore, the answer is 8.

1. Monosubstituted (C6H5 − C3H7): n-propylbenzene, isopropylbenzene =⇒ 2.
2. Disubstituted (C6H4(CH3)(C2H5)): o-, m-, p-ethyltoluene =⇒ 3.
3. Trisubstituted (C6H3(CH3)3): 1, 2, 3-, 1, 2, 4-, 1, 3, 5-trimethylbenzene =⇒ 3.

Q130.conceptHtml: DU = C + 1 − <sup>H</sup><sub>2</sub> for a hydrocarbon C<sub>x</sub>H<sub>y</sub>.
Q130.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Find the mass of carbon and hydrogen in $1\text{ mol}$ of (X): The molar mass is $80\text{ g mol}^{-1}$ and carbon is $90\%$ by mass, so mass of $\text{C} = 0.90 \times 80 = 72\text{ g}$ and mass of $\text{H} = 80 - 72 = 8\text{ g}$.
  2. Step 2 — Determine the molecular formula: Number of carbon atoms $= \frac{72}{12} = 6$ and number of hydrogen atoms $= \frac{8}{1} = 8$. Thus, the molecular formula of hydrocarbon (X) is $\text{C}_6\text{H}_8$.
  3. Step 3 — Calculate the Degree of Unsaturation (DU / IHD): Using the formula $\text{DU} = C + 1 - \frac{H}{2}$, we get $\text{DU} = 6 + 1 - \frac{8}{2} = 7 - 4 = 3$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final numerical value: The degree of unsaturation of hydrocarbon (X) is 3.

Q131.conceptHtml: Total stereoisomers = 2<sup>n</sup> for an unsymmetrical molecule with n stereocenters/C = C bonds.
Q131.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Draw the structure of 5-phenylpent-4-en-2-ol: The structural formula is $\text{Ph}-\text{CH}=\text{CH}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH(OH)}-\text{CH}_3$.
  2. Step 2 — Identify all stereogenic centers: First, the $\text{C-4}=\text{C-5}$ double bond has two different groups on $\text{C-5}$ ($-\text{Ph}, -\text{H}$) and two different groups on $\text{C-4}$ ($-\text{H}, -\text{CH}_2\text{CH(OH)CH}_3$), so it shows geometrical isomerism ($E/Z$, $1$ stereogenic unit). Second, $\text{C-2}$ is attached to four different groups ($-\text{H}, -\text{OH}, -\text{CH}_3, -\text{CH}_2\text{CH}=\text{CHPh}$), so it is a chiral center ($R/S$, $1$ stereogenic unit).
  3. Step 3 — Calculate the total number of stereoisomers: Because the molecule is unsymmetrical and has $n = 2$ independent stereocenters ($1$ double bond $+ 1$ chiral carbon), the total number of stereoisomers is $2^n = 2^2 = 4$ (specifically $(E,R)$, $(E,S)$, $(Z,R)$, and $(Z,S)$).
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final numerical value: The possible number of stereoisomers is 4.

Q132.subtopic: Chromatography — Rf Ratio from TLC Plate
Q132.conceptHtml: R<sub>f</sub> = <sub>dista</sub><sup>d</sup><sub>n</sub><sup>is</sup><sub>c</sub><sup>t</sup><sub>e</sub><sup>a</sup><sub>m</sub><sup>nc</sup><sub>o</sub><sup>e</sup><sub>ve</sub><sup>m</sup><sub>d</sub><sup>ov</sup><sub>b</sub><sup>e</sup><sub>y</sub><sup>d</sup><sub>so</sub><sup>b</sup><sub>l</sub><sup>y</sup><sub>ve</sub><sup>s</sup><sub>n</sub><sup>p</sup><sub>t</sub><sup>ot</sup><sub>fr</sub><sup>f</sup><sub>o</sub><sup>r</sup><sub>n</sub><sup>o</sup><sub>t</sub><sup>m</sup><sub>fr</sub><sup>b</sup><sub>o</sub><sup>a</sup><sub>m</sub><sup>se</sup><sub>b</sub><sup>li</sup><sub>a</sub><sup>n</sup><sub>s</sub><sup>e</sup><sub>eline</sub>. Always subtract the baseline offset!
Q132.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Find the solvent front distance from the baseline: From the TLC diagram, the total plate height is $10\text{ cm}$, the baseline is $1\text{ cm}$ above the bottom edge, and the solvent front is $1\text{ cm}$ below the top edge. Thus, distance moved by the solvent front from the baseline $= 10 - 1 - 1 = 8\text{ cm}$.
  2. Step 2 — Find the distances moved by spots A and B from the baseline: Since spots A and B are at $5\text{ cm}$ and $7\text{ cm}$ from the bottom edge, their distances from the baseline ($1\text{ cm}$ mark) are $d_A = 5 - 1 = 4\text{ cm}$ and $d_B = 7 - 1 = 6\text{ cm}$.
  3. Step 3 — Compute $R_{f,A}$, $R_{f,B}$, and their ratio: $R_{f,A} = \frac{4}{8} = 0.5$ and $R_{f,B} = \frac{6}{8} = 0.75$. Therefore, the ratio is $\frac{R_{f,B}}{R_{f,A}} = \frac{0.75}{0.5} = 1.5 = 15 \times 10^{-1}$.

Q133.conceptHtml: A compound shows all three effects (I, M, and hyperconjugation) when it has a conjugated π-system attached to a group with lone pairs/π-bond (M) AND an α-C − H adjacent to an sp<sup>2</sup> carbon (HC).
Q133.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — State the requirements for all three effects: To show inductive ($I$), mesomeric ($M$), and hyperconjugation ($H$) effects simultaneously, a molecule needs a polar substituent/bond (for $I$), a conjugated $\pi$-system with a $+M$ or $-M$ group (for $M$), and at least one $sp^3$ $\alpha$-$\text{C}-\text{H}$ bond adjacent to a $\pi$-bond or benzene ring (for $H$).
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate the four compounds in the top row: (1) Anisole ($\text{Ph}-\text{OCH}_3$) has $-I$ and $+M$, but no $\alpha$-$\text{H}$ on a ring-attached carbon (no $H$). (2) 5-Methylhex-3-en-2-one has $I$, $M$ (conjugation of $\text{C}=\text{C}$ with $\text{C}=\text{O}$), and $H$ ($1\,\alpha\text{-H}$ on the isopropyl $\text{CH}$ next to $\text{C}=\text{C}$) $\Rightarrow$ Yes (1). (3) Benzene has neither $I$ nor $H$. (4) Chlorocyclohexane has only $-I$ (no $\pi$-system).
  3. Step 3 — Evaluate the four compounds in the bottom row: (5) $o$-Nitrocumene has $-I/-M$ ($-\text{NO}_2$) and $+I/H$ ($1\,\alpha\text{-H}$ on isopropyl) $\Rightarrow$ Yes (2). (6) 1-(But-3-en-2-yl)-2-nitrobenzene has $-I/-M$ ($-\text{NO}_2$) and $+I/H$ ($1\,\alpha\text{-H}$ on the benzylic/allylic $\text{CH}$) $\Rightarrow$ Yes (3). (7) $m$-Xylene has $+I$ and $H$ ($6\,\alpha\text{-H}$), but no mesomeric substituent. (8) 1-(2-Methylcyclohex-1-en-1-yl)ethan-1-one has $-I/-M$ ($-\text{COCH}_3$ conjugated with ring $\text{C}=\text{C}$) and $H$ (allylic $\alpha\text{-H}$ atoms) $\Rightarrow$ Yes (4).
  4. Step 4 — Count the qualifying compounds: Exactly 4 compounds exhibit inductive, mesomeric, and hyperconjugation effects together.

someric, and α-H hyperconjugation =⇒ 4 compounds qualify (official NTA key = 4).
Q133.trapHtml: Hyperconjugation requires at least one α-H on an sp<sup>3</sup> carbon adjacent to the π-system.

Q134.conceptHtml: Check planarity, full cyclic conjugation, and (4n + 2)π electrons.
Q134.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall Hückel's criteria for aromaticity: A compound is aromatic if it is cyclic, planar, completely conjugated around the ring, and contains $(4n + 2)\pi$ delocalized electrons ($n = 0, 1, 2, \dots$).
  2. Step 2 — Check the first four structures: (1) The fused bicyclic diene/triene contains $sp^3$ ring carbons that break cyclic conjugation $\Rightarrow$ non-aromatic. (2) The bicyclic structure with two five-membered rings joined by a double bond contains $sp^3$ carbons $\Rightarrow$ non-aromatic. (3) Cyclopentadienyl cation ($\text{C}_5\text{H}_5^+$) is cyclic, planar, and conjugated with $4\pi$ electrons ($4n\pi$) $\Rightarrow$ anti-aromatic. (4) Cyclooctatetraene ($\text{C}_8\text{H}_8$) has $8\pi$ electrons and adopts a non-planar tub shape $\Rightarrow$ non-aromatic.
  3. Step 3 — Check the last two structures: (5) Pyridine ($\text{C}_5\text{H}_5\text{N}$) is cyclic, planar, completely conjugated, and has $6\pi$ electrons ($n = 1$; nitrogen's lone pair resides in an $sp^2$ orbital outside the $\pi$ cloud) $\Rightarrow$ Aromatic (1). (6) Cycloheptatriene ($\text{C}_7\text{H}_8$) has an $sp^3$ $-\text{CH}_2-$ carbon that breaks conjugation $\Rightarrow$ non-aromatic.
  4. Step 4 — Conclude the total count: Only pyridine is aromatic, so the total number of aromatic compounds is 1.

heterocycle/cation, while the others have sp3 carbons or 4nπ electrons).
Q134.trapHtml: An sp<sup>3</sup> CH<sub>2</sub> in the ring breaks cyclic conjugation (non-aromatic), even if the ring has 6π electrons.

Q135.subtopic: Optical Activity — Meso vs Chiral Compounds
Q135.conceptHtml: A compound is optically active only if it is chiral (lacks a plane/center of symmetry).
Q135.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the condition for optical activity: A compound is optically active if it is chiral (non-superimposable on its mirror image, lacking a plane of symmetry and center of symmetry).
  2. Step 2 — Inspect the first three compounds: (1) meso-Butane-2,3-diol (both $-\text{OH}$ on the same side in the Fischer projection) has an internal plane of symmetry $\Rightarrow$ optically inactive. (2) Propane-1,2,3-triol (glycerol, $\text{HOCH}_2\text{CH(OH)CH}_2\text{OH}$) has two identical $-\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ groups on $\text{C-2}$ (no chiral center) $\Rightarrow$ optically inactive. (3) Butan-1-ol ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$) has no chiral center $\Rightarrow$ optically inactive.
  3. Step 3 — Inspect the last three compounds: (4) 2-Chlorobutane ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{C}^*\text{H(Cl)CH}_3$) has one chiral carbon ($\text{C-2}$ bonded to $-\text{H}, -\text{Cl}, -\text{CH}_3, -\text{C}_2\text{H}_5$) and is optically active (1). (5) 1-Chlorobutane ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$) has no chiral center $\Rightarrow$ optically inactive. (6) 1-Chloro-3-methylbutane ($(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CHCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$) has no chiral center $\Rightarrow$ optically inactive.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the count: Only 2-chlorobutane is optically active, so the answer is 1.

Q136.conceptHtml: Count all stereogenic (chiral) carbons in the unsymmetrical bicyclic framework and apply 2<sup>n</sup>.
Q136.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Locate every chiral carbon in the tricyclic structure: The molecule consists of three linearly fused cyclohexane rings with a $-\text{Br}$ substituent at one ring-junction carbon and a $-\text{CH}_3$ substituent on a carbon of the terminal right ring.
  2. Step 2 — Count the chiral centers ($n$): Because the $-\text{Br}$ and $-\text{CH}_3$ substituents break all molecular symmetry, all $4$ ring-junction carbons are asymmetric (each is bonded to four distinct paths/groups). In addition, the carbon bearing the $-\text{CH}_3$ group is also bonded to four different groups ($-\text{H}, -\text{CH}_3$, and two unequal ring paths). Thus, the total number of chiral centers is $n = 4 + 1 = 5$.
  3. Step 3 — Apply the optical isomer formula for an unsymmetrical molecule: Since the molecule has no symmetry element that could produce meso forms, the number of optical isomers is $2^n = 2^5 = 32$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final numerical value: The number of optical isomers is 32.

Q137.conceptHtml: A carbocation is stabilized by hyperconjugation only if there is at least one α-H on an sp<sup>3</sup> carbon directly attached to C<sup>+</sup>.
Q137.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the requirement for hyperconjugation in a carbocation: A carbocation is stabilized by hyperconjugation only if it has at least one $sp^3$-hybridized $\alpha$-carbon carrying an $\alpha$-hydrogen atom ($\text{C}-\text{H}$ $\sigma$-bond adjacent to the empty $p$-orbital).
  2. Step 2 — Check the first three carbocations: (1) 2-Methylbutyl / secondary-alkyl carbocation has $sp^3$ $\alpha$-carbons with $\alpha$-hydrogens $\Rightarrow$ IS stabilized by hyperconjugation. (2) Di-tert-butylmethyl cation ($(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}-\text{CH}^+-\text{C(CH}_3)_3$) has quaternary $\alpha$-carbons with $0\,\alpha\text{-H}$ $\Rightarrow$ NOT stabilized by hyperconjugation (1). (3) Methyl carbocation ($\text{CH}_3^+$) has no $\alpha$-carbon at all $\Rightarrow$ NOT stabilized by hyperconjugation (2).
  3. Step 3 — Check the last three carbocations: (4) Cyclopentadienyl cation ($\text{C}_5\text{H}_5^+$) has only $sp^2$ $\alpha$-carbons (no $sp^3$ $\alpha\text{-C}-\text{H}$ bond) $\Rightarrow$ NOT stabilized by hyperconjugation (3). (5) Methoxymethyl cation ($^+\text{CH}_2-\text{OCH}_3$) is stabilized by $+M$ lone-pair resonance from oxygen, with no $\alpha\text{-C}-\text{H}$ bond $\Rightarrow$ NOT stabilized by hyperconjugation (4). (6) $N,N$-Dimethyliminium/aminomethyl cation ($(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{N}-\text{CH}_2^+$) is stabilized by $+M$ resonance from nitrogen, with no $\alpha\text{-C}-\text{H}$ bond $\Rightarrow$ NOT stabilized by hyperconjugation (5).
  4. Step 4 — Sum the non-hyperconjugated carbocations: In total, 5 carbocations are not stabilized by hyperconjugation.

Q138.subtopic: Chromatography — Rf Ratio in Paper Chromatography
Q138.conceptHtml: R<sub>f</sub>(A)/R<sub>f</sub>(C) = <sub>d</sub><sup>d</sup>A (since solvent front distance cancels out). C

  4. Step 4 — State the value of $x$: Matching $50 \times 10^{-2}$ with $x \times 10^{-2}$ gives $x = \mathbf{50}$.

Q139.conceptHtml: Single bond = 1σ; double bond = 1σ + 1π; triple bond = 1σ + 2π.
Q139.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Write the structural and molecular formula of 2-oxohex-4-ynoic acid: The structure is $\text{CH}_3-\text{C}\equiv\text{C}-\text{CH}_2-\text{C}(=\text{O})-\text{COOH}$. Counting all atoms gives $6\text{ C}$, $6\text{ H}$, and $3\text{ O}$ (molecular formula $\text{C}_6\text{H}_6\text{O}_3$, total $15$ atoms).
  2. Step 2 — Count the $\sigma$ bonds: For any acyclic (open-chain) molecule, the number of $\sigma$ bonds equals $(\text{total atoms} - 1) = 15 - 1 = 14$.
  3. Step 3 — Count the $\pi$ bonds: There is $1\,\pi$ bond in the $-\text{COOH}$ carbonyl, $1\,\pi$ bond in the $\text{C-2}$ ketone carbonyl ($>\text{C}=\text{O}$), and $2\,\pi$ bonds in the $\text{C-4}\equiv\text{C-5}$ triple bond, giving $1 + 1 + 2 = 4\,\pi$ bonds.
  4. Step 4 — Add $\sigma$ and $\pi$ bonds: Total number of bonds $= 14 + 4 = \mathbf{18}$.

  2. Step 2 — List the 5-carbon main-chain isomers: With two methyl groups ($4$): 2,2-dimethylpentane, 2,3-dimethylpentane, 2,4-dimethylpentane, and 3,3-dimethylpentane. With one ethyl group ($1$): 3-ethylpentane.
  3. Step 3 — List the 4-carbon main-chain isomer: With three methyl groups ($1$): 2,2,3-trimethylbutane.
  4. Step 4 — Sum all chain isomers: Total chain isomers of heptane ($\text{C}_7\text{H}_{16}$) $= 1 + 2 + 4 + 1 + 1 = \mathbf{9}$.

Q141.conceptHtml: Identify every distinct H position in 2-methylbutane (CH<sub>3</sub> − CH(CH<sub>3</sub>) − CH<sub>2</sub> − CH<sub>3</sub>) and check each product for chirality.

1. Step 1 — Draw 2-methylbutane and identify distinct types of hydrogens: The structure is $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CH}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_3$. It has $4$ chemically distinct sets of hydrogens: at $\text{C-1}$ (either of the two equivalent methyls on $\text{C-2}$), $\text{C-2}$ (tertiary $\text{CH}$), $\text{C-3}$ (secondary $\text{CH}_2$), and $\text{C-4}$ (terminal $\text{CH}_3$).
  2. Step 2 — Check stereoisomerism for each of the $4$ structural monochloro products: (1) Chlorination at $\text{C-1}$ gives 1-chloro-2-methylbutane ($\text{ClCH}_2-\text{C}^*\text{H(CH}_3)-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$): $1$ chiral center $\Rightarrow 2$ enantiomers ($d, l$). Step 3 — Check chlorination at $\text{C-3}$ and $\text{C-4}$: (3) Chlorination at $\text{C-3}$ gives 2-chloro-3-methylbutane ($(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CH}-\text{C}^*\text{H(Cl)}-\text{CH}_3$): $1$ chiral center $\Rightarrow 2$ enantiomers ($d, l$). (4) Chlorination at $\text{C-4}$ gives 1-chloro-3-methylbutane: $0$ chiral centers $\Rightarrow 1$ isomer.

Q142.subtopic: Directing Effects — Deactivating Groups in SEAr
Q142.conceptHtml: Groups that withdraw electron density from the benzene ring (−M or −I > +M) deactivate S<sub>E</sub>Ar.
Q142.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall what makes a group activating vs. deactivating in EAS: Groups attached to the benzene ring via an atom carrying a lone pair (like $-\text{O}-$, $-\text{N}<$) donate electron density by $+M$ and are activating. Groups attached via a multiple-bonded electronegative center (like $-\text{C}(=\text{O})-$, $-\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$) withdraw electron density by $-M$ and $-I$, making them deactivating.
  2. Step 2 — Classify each of the five given groups: (1) $-\text{COOCH}_3$ (attached through carbonyl carbon) $\Rightarrow -M, -I$ (Deactivating, 1). (2) $-\text{NHCOCH}_3$ (attached through $\text{N}$ with a lone pair) $\Rightarrow +M$ (Activating). (3) $-\text{NHCH}_3$ (attached through $\text{N}$ with a lone pair) $\Rightarrow +M$ (Activating). (4) $-\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$ (cyano group) $\Rightarrow -M, -I$ (Deactivating, 2). (5) $-\text{OCH}_3$ (attached through $\text{O}$ with lone pairs) $\Rightarrow +M$ (Activating).
  3. Step 3 — Count the deactivating groups: Only $-\text{COOCH}_3$ and $-\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$ are deactivating groups.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final numerical value: The total number of deactivating groups is 2.

Q144.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the four non-equivalent hydrogen positions in 2-methylbutane: In $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CH}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_3$, free-radical monochlorination in sunlight can substitute $\text{H}$ at $\text{C-1}$, $\text{C-2}$, $\text{C-3}$, or $\text{C-4}$, producing $4$ structural isomers.
  2. Step 2 — Account for enantiomeric pairs (stereoisomers): 1-Chloro-2-methylbutane has $1$ chiral center ($\text{C-2}$) $\Rightarrow 2$ stereoisomers. 2-Chloro-2-methylbutane has $0$ chiral centers $\Rightarrow 1$ isomer. 2-Chloro-3-methylbutane has $1$ chiral center ($\text{C-2}$) $\Rightarrow 2$ stereoisomers. 1-Chloro-3-methylbutane has $0$ chiral centers $\Rightarrow 1$ isomer.
  3. Step 3 — Sum all isomeric products: Total isomeric products $= 2 + 1 + 2 + 1 = 6$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final numerical value: The number of isomeric products formed is 6.
Q144.trapHtml: In JEE Main, “isomeric products” without “structural” includes stereoisomers (6).

Q145.format: Numerical | E/Z at Two Double Bonds
Q145.conceptHtml: Count independent stereogenic double bonds (or rings with H ̸= D) that give distinct geometrical isomers.
Q145.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Analyze the symmetry of the triene structure: The molecule has a central $\text{C}=\text{CH}-\text{CH}_3$ double bond whose upper carbon is bonded to two structurally identical alkenyl branches: $-\text{CH}_2-\text{C(CH}_3)=\text{CHD}$. Each of these two terminal double bonds can independently exist in the $E$ or $Z$ configuration.
  2. Step 2 — Count isomers when both terminal branches have the same configuration: If both branches are $(E, E)$, the two groups on the upper carbon of the central double bond are identical, so the central double bond cannot show geometrical isomerism $\Rightarrow 1$ isomer. Similarly, if both branches are $(Z, Z)$, the central double bond is inactive $\Rightarrow 1$ isomer.
  3. Step 3 — Count isomers when the two terminal branches differ ($E$ and $Z$): When one branch is $E$ and the other is $Z$, the upper carbon of the central double bond now carries two stereochemically different groups ($E$-branch vs. $Z$-branch), while its lower carbon carries $-\text{H}$ and $-\text{CH}_3$. Hence, the central double bond becomes geometrically active (pseudo-asymmetric), giving $2$ distinct isomers ($-\text{CH}_3$ cis to the $E$-branch or cis to the $Z$-branch).
  4. Step 4 — Sum all geometrical isomers: Total geometrical isomers $= 1 + 1 + 2 = \mathbf{4}$.
Q145.stepsLatex:
1. In the given structure, there are 2 stereogenic centers/double bonds with H and D substituents giving 22 = 4
geometrical isomers (cis/cis, cis/trans, trans/cis, trans/trans).
Q145.trapHtml: Check symmetry carefully; here the two ends are distinguishable, giving 4 distinct isomers.

Q146.conceptHtml: Substitute each H of 2-chlorobutane with Cl and count optically active stereoisomers (exclude achiral and meso forms!).
Q146.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — List all four structural isomers formed by chlorinating 2-chlorobutane: Substituting a second $-\text{Cl}$ on $\text{CH}_3-\text{CH(Cl)}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_3$ gives: (1) 1,2-dichlorobutane, (2) 2,2-dichlorobutane, (3) 2,3-dichlorobutane, and (4) 1,3-dichlorobutane.
  2. Step 2 — Count optically active isomers for 1,2-, 2,2-, and 1,3-dichlorobutane: 1,2-Dichlorobutane ($\text{ClCH}_2\text{C}^*\text{H(Cl)CH}_2\text{CH}_3$) has $1$ chiral center $\Rightarrow 2$ optically active enantiomers. 2,2-Dichlorobutane ($\text{CH}_3\text{CCl}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$) has $0$ chiral centers $\Rightarrow 0$ optically active isomers. 1,3-Dichlorobutane ($\text{ClCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{C}^*\text{H(Cl)CH}_3$) has $1$ chiral center $\Rightarrow 2$ optically active enantiomers.
  3. Step 3 — Count optically active isomers for 2,3-dichlorobutane: 2,3-Dichlorobutane ($\text{CH}_3\text{C}^*\text{H(Cl)C}^*\text{H(Cl)CH}_3$) has $2$ identical chiral centers, forming $1$ optically inactive meso isomer and $2$ optically active enantiomers ($(2R,3R)$ and $(2S,3S)$).
  4. Step 4 — Sum all optically active isomers: Total optically active isomers $= 2 + 0 + 2 + 2 = \mathbf{6}$.
Q146.stepsLatex:
1. 1, 2-dichlorobutane: 1 chiral center =⇒ 2 optically active (R, S).
2. 2, 2-dichlorobutane: achiral =⇒ 0.
3. 2, 3-dichlorobutane: (2R, 3R) and (2S, 3S) are optically active (2), while (2R, 3S) is meso (inactive!).
4. 1, 3-dichlorobutane: 1 chiral center =⇒ 2 optically active (R, S).
5. Total optically active isomers = 2 + 0 + 2 + 2 = 6.
Q146.trapHtml: Do NOT count the meso form of 2, 3-dichlorobutane as optically active!

Q147.conceptHtml: R<sub>f</sub> = distance moved by compound. distance moved by solvent
Q147.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the retardation factor ($R_f$) formula: $R_f = \frac{\text{Distance moved by the substance from baseline}}{\text{Distance moved by the solvent front from baseline}}$.
  2. Step 2 — Substitute the given values: Distance moved by the organic compound $= 3.5\text{ cm}$ and distance moved by the solvent $= 5\text{ cm}$.
  3. Step 3 — Calculate $R_f$: $R_f = \frac{3.5}{5} = 0.7 = 7 \times 10^{-1}$.
  4. Step 4 — Match the requested format: Expressing $R_f$ as $\text{____} \times 10^{-1}$ gives 7.

Q148.subtopic: Optical Isomerism — Counting Compounds with Chiral
Q148.conceptHtml: A carbon atom bonded to 4 different groups is a chiral carbon.
Q148.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Check the two cyclic ketones in the top row: (1) 2-Methylcyclohexan-1-one has a chiral carbon at $\text{C-2}$ (bonded to $-\text{H}, -\text{CH}_3$, and two unequal ring paths) $\Rightarrow$ Yes (1). (2) Cyclopentane-1,3-dione has only $-\text{CH}_2-$ and $>\text{C}=\text{O}$ carbons (no chiral carbon) $\Rightarrow$ No.
  2. Step 2 — Check the first three acyclic compounds: (3) $\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}_2-\text{C}^*\text{H(NO}_2)-\text{COOH}$ has a chiral carbon at $\text{C-2}$ $\Rightarrow$ Yes (2). (4) $\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH(Br)}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_3$ (3-bromopentane) has two identical ethyl groups on $\text{C-3}$ (no chiral carbon) $\Rightarrow$ No. (5) $\text{CH}_3-\text{C}^*\text{H(I)}-\text{CH}_2-\text{NO}_2$ has a chiral carbon at $\text{C-2}$ $\Rightarrow$ Yes (3).
  3. Step 3 — Check the last two acyclic compounds: (6) $\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}_2-\text{C}^*\text{H(OH)}-\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ has a chiral carbon at $\text{C-2}$ $\Rightarrow$ Yes (4). (7) $\text{CH}_3-\text{C}^*\text{H(I)}-\text{C}^*\text{H(I)}-\text{C}_2\text{H}_5$ has two chiral carbons ($\text{C-2}$ and $\text{C-3}$) $\Rightarrow$ Yes (5).
  4. Step 4 — Count the compounds with chiral carbons: Exactly 5 compounds contain chiral carbon atoms.

Q148.trapHtml: CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CHBrCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> (3-bromopentane) has two identical ethyl groups, so C3 is NOT chiral!

Q149.conceptHtml: In the presence of peroxide, HBr adds anti-Markovnikov across C = C (Br goes to the less substituted C2, H goes to the more substituted C3).
Q149.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Predict the addition product (A) via peroxide effect: 3-Methylhex-2-ene ($\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}=\text{C(CH}_3)-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$) reacts with $\text{HBr}$ in the presence of peroxide via free-radical anti-Markovnikov addition, placing $-\text{Br}$ on the less substituted alkene carbon ($\text{C-2}$) and $-\text{H}$ on the more substituted carbon ($\text{C-3}$).
  2. Step 2 — Write the structure of product (A): Product (A) is 2-bromo-3-methylhexane: $\text{CH}_3-\text{C}^*\text{H(Br)}-\text{C}^*\text{H(CH}_3)-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$.
  3. Step 3 — Count chiral centers and calculate stereoisomers: Both $\text{C-2}$ and $\text{C-3}$ are bonded to four different groups, so there are $n = 2$ chiral centers. Because the molecule is unsymmetrical, the number of possible stereoisomers is $2^n = 2^2 = 4$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final numerical value: The number of possible stereoisomers for (A) is 4.

∗ ∗
1. Product (A): CH3 − CH(Br) − CH(CH3) − CH2CH2CH3 (2-bromo-3-methylhexane).
2. It has 2 distinct chiral centers (C2 and C3) and is unsymmetrical.
3. Total possible stereoisomers = 22 = 4.
Q149.trapHtml: Without peroxide, Br goes to C3 (1 chiral center → 2 isomers); WITH peroxide, Br goes to C2 (2 chiral centers → 4 isomers)!

Q150.conceptHtml: Check each ring for planarity, complete conjugation, and (4n + 2)π electrons.
Q150.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Check compound (A): Compound (A) has no double bond at the central ring-fusion bond; both bridgehead carbons are $sp^3$-hybridized, breaking cyclic conjugation (only $8\pi$ electrons) $\Rightarrow$ Non-aromatic.
  2. Step 2 — Check compound (B): Compound (B) contains a benzene ring ($6\pi$ electrons, $4n+2$ with $n=1$) attached to a $-\text{CH}_2$-cyclohexenyl group, so it is an aromatic compound (1).
  3. Step 3 — Check compounds (C) and (D): Compound (C) has a planar, completely conjugated bicyclic perimeter with $4$ double bonds plus $1$ lone pair ($10\pi$ electrons, $4n+2$ with $n=2$) $\Rightarrow$ Aromatic (2). Compound (D) is the fluorenyl anion, which is cyclic, planar, and completely conjugated with $6$ double bonds plus $1$ negative charge lone pair ($14\pi$ electrons, $4n+2$ with $n=3$) $\Rightarrow$ Aromatic (3).
  4. Step 4 — Count the aromatic compounds: Compounds (B), (C), and (D) are aromatic, giving a total of 3.

cyclopentadiene? No, (C) is bicyclic/azulene or furan/cyclopentadienyl? Look at the rendered figure: (A)
naphthalene (aromatic), (B) bicyclic non-aromatic, (C) 6π aromatic, (D) fluorenyl anion (14π, aromatic)).
4. Total aromatic compounds = 3.
Q150.trapHtml: Fluorenyl anion (D) has 6 + 6 + 2 = 14πe<sup>−</sup> (n = 3) and is planar =⇒ aromatic!

Q151.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the rule for meta-directing groups: Strongly deactivating groups that withdraw electron density by $-M$ (resonance) and $-I$ effects direct incoming electrophiles to the meta position, whereas $+M$ groups and halogens ($-\text{Cl}$) are ortho/para directors.
  2. Step 2 — Identify the ortho/para-directing groups in the list: $-\text{OCH}_3$ ($+M$), $-\text{CH}_3$ ($+H, +I$), $-\text{NHCOCH}_3$ ($+M$), $-\text{OH}$ ($+M$), and $-\text{Cl}$ ($+M$ directs $o/p$ despite $-I$ deactivation) are all ortho/para directors ($5$ groups).
  3. Step 3 — Identify the meta-directing groups in the list: $-\text{NO}_2$, $-\text{CN}$, $-\text{COR}$, and $-\text{COOH}$ all withdraw electron density via $-M$ and $-I$ effects and are meta directors.
  4. Step 4 — Count the meta-directing groups: There are 4 meta-directing functional groups.
Q151.trapHtml: −Cl is deactivating, yet it is o/p-directing, NOT meta-directing!

Q152.subtopic: Chromatography — Rf of Most Polar Compound
Q152.conceptHtml: The most polar compound adsorbs most strongly to silica gel and travels the shortest distance (lowest R<sub>f</sub>).
Q152.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the most polar compound from the TLC plate: Hexane is a non-polar mobile phase, while the TLC stationary phase (silica gel) is polar. Therefore, the most polar compound is adsorbed most strongly on the plate and travels the shortest distance.
  2. Step 2 — Read the distances from the figure: Spot A traveled $6\text{ cm}$, spot B traveled $4\text{ cm}$, and spot C traveled $2\text{ cm}$, while the solvent front traveled $8\text{ cm}$. Hence, compound C is the most polar.
  3. Step 3 — Calculate the $R_f$ value of compound C: $R_{f,C} = \frac{2\text{ cm}}{8\text{ cm}} = 0.25 = 25 \times 10^{-2}$.
  4. Step 4 — Match the requested format: Comparing $25 \times 10^{-2}$ with $\text{____} \times 10^{-2}$ gives 25.

2. Spot distances from baseline: A = 6 cm, B = 4 cm, C = 2 cm.
3. Most polar compound = C (shortest distance = 2 cm).

Q152.trapHtml: Do not compute R<sub>f</sub> of A (0.75); the most polar compound is the lowest spot C.

Q153.subtopic: Optical Isomerism — Asymmetric Carbons in Testosterone
Q153.conceptHtml: An asymmetric (chiral) carbon is an sp<sup>3</sup> carbon bonded to 4 different groups.
Q153.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall what qualifies as an asymmetric (chiral) carbon: An asymmetric carbon must be $sp^3$-hybridized and bonded to four different atoms or groups; $sp^2$ carbons (the carbonyl carbon and the two $\text{C}=\text{C}$ alkene carbons) and $-\text{CH}_2-$ / $-\text{CH}_3$ carbons cannot be chiral.
  2. Step 2 — Inspect the ring-junction carbons of testosterone: Out of the $6$ ring-junction carbons in the steroid A-B-C-D skeleton, one (C-5, part of the $\text{C}=\text{C}$ double bond in ring A) is $sp^2$-hybridized and achiral. The remaining $5$ ring-junction carbons (C-8, C-9, C-10 bearing $-\text{CH}_3$, C-13 bearing $-\text{CH}_3$, and C-14) are all $sp^3$-hybridized with four distinct substituents/paths $\Rightarrow 5$ chiral carbons.
  3. Step 3 — Inspect the non-junction substituted carbons: In ring D, carbon C-17 bears $-\text{OH}$, $-\text{H}$, and two unequal ring paths, making it $1$ additional chiral carbon.
  4. Step 4 — Sum all asymmetric carbons: Total asymmetric carbon atoms in testosterone $= 5 + 1 = \mathbf{6}$.
