are achiral.
2. Chiral carbons are the 6 sp3 methine/quaternary stereocenters: C8, C9, C10 (bearing CH3), C13 (bearing
CH3), C14, and C17 (bearing −OH).
3. Total asymmetric carbons = 6.
Q153.trapHtml: Count every ring-junction sp<sup>3</sup> carbon systematically from left to right (C10, C9, C8, C14, C13, C17).

Q154.conceptHtml: A molecule is chiral if it lacks a plane of symmetry (σ) and center of symmetry (i).
Q154.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Check compounds 1 and 2 (top row): (1) 4-Benzylidenecyclohexanecarboxylic acid exhibits axial chirality (like an even-cumulene/alkylidenecycloalkane): the $=\text{CHPh}$ group and the $-\text{CH(COOH)}-$ group lie in perpendicular planes, so the molecule has no plane or center of symmetry $\Rightarrow$ Chiral (1). (2) 1-(8-Chloronaphthalen-1-yloxy)-3-(naphthalen-2-yloxy)propan-2-ol has a central $-\text{C}^*\text{H(OH)}-$ carbon attached to four different groups ($-\text{H}, -\text{OH}$, and two different naphthyloxy-methyl groups) $\Rightarrow$ Chiral (2).
  2. Step 2 — Check compounds 3, 4, and 5 (bottom row): (3) meso-Tartaric acid has a horizontal plane of symmetry bisecting the $\text{C-2}-\text{C-3}$ bond $\Rightarrow$ achiral. (4) The cyclohexane-1,2,3,4,5,6-hexol isomer (two adjacent dashed $-\text{OH}$ groups and four wedged $-\text{OH}$ groups) has a plane of symmetry bisecting the bond between the two dashed $-\text{OH}$ carbons and the opposite bond $\Rightarrow$ achiral. (5) cis-Cyclopropane-1,2-dicarboxylic acid has a vertical plane of symmetry bisecting the $\text{C-1}-\text{C-2}$ bond $\Rightarrow$ achiral.
  3. Step 3 — Count the chiral compounds: Only the first two compounds lack internal symmetry elements and are chiral.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final numerical value: The total number of chiral compounds is 2.

Q155.conceptHtml: Subtract both the baseline offset and top margin from the total plate length (6 cm) to get the solvent front travel distance.
Q155.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Find the solvent front distance from the baseline: The TLC glass plate is $6\text{ cm}$ tall. The baseline is $0.5\text{ cm}$ from the bottom edge and the solvent front is $0.5\text{ cm}$ from the top edge, so the solvent front traveled $6.0 - 0.5 - 0.5 = 5.0\text{ cm}$ from the baseline.
  2. Step 2 — Find the distance traveled by compound A from the baseline: The diagram shows compound A is $3.5\text{ cm}$ above the bottom edge of the plate. Subtracting the $0.5\text{ cm}$ baseline offset gives $d_A = 3.5 - 0.5 = 3.0\text{ cm}$.
  3. Step 3 — Calculate the retardation factor ($R_f$): $R_f = \frac{3.0\text{ cm}}{5.0\text{ cm}} = 0.6 = 6 \times 10^{-1}$.
  4. Step 4 — Match the requested format: Expressing $R_f$ as $\text{____} \times 10^{-1}$ gives 6.

trapCards.title: Trap 1: Electronic Effects & Intermediate Stability
trapCards.html:
• Meta-Position +M Illusion (Q54): −OCH3 at the meta position exerts ONLY −I (destabilizes benzyl car- bocation), whereas at para it exerts strong +M.
  • Tropolone π-Count (Q110): Tropolone is 6π aromatic (not 8π); the C = O π-electrons polarize onto oxygen (C+ − O−) outside the 6π ring sextet.
  • Halogens in SEAr (Q51, Q85, Q87, Q151): Halogens (−F, −Cl, −Br, −I) are deactivating (−I > +M), yet o/p-directing.
  • Hydride Affinity vs Stability (Q114): Hydride affin- ity is inversely proportional to carbocation stability; cyclopropylmethyl > Ph3C+.

trapCards.title: Trap 2: Acid–Base & NaHCO<sub>3</sub> Effervescence Traps
trapCards.html:
• NaHCO3 Cutoff (pKa < 6.35) (Q32): RCOOH, picric acid, and PhNH+3 Cl− (pKa ≈ 4.6) liberate CO2; simple phenols and p-nitrophenol (pKa = 7.15) do not.
  • Strongest Conjugate Acid = Weakest Base (Q10): Always invert the basicity order when asked for the strongest conjugate acid.
  • Pyridine vs Pyrrole vs Piperidine (Q61, Q105): Piperidine (sp3) > Pyridine (sp2, lp outside sextet) ≫ Pyrrole (lp inside 6π sextet). Final Pre-Submission Self-Audit for Basics of Organic Before moving to Chapter 17, verify you can recall without pe (2) +M/ − M and +I/ − I orders including halogen deactiv (tropolone 6π, squarate 2π); (4) NaHCO3 effervescence cutoff and NCERT purification pairs.

trapCards.title: Trap 3: IUPAC & Isomerism Counting Traps
trapCards.html:
• Priority & Locant Ties (Q14, Q34, Q67, Q108): Ester > Amide > Nitrile > Aldehyde > Ketone > Alcohol. If ene/yne locants tie, ene gets the lower locant.
  • Meso & Achiral Traps (Q08, Q31, Q135, Q146): Check for identical groups (Me = CH3) and internal planes of symmetry (meso 2, 3-dichlorobutane is optically inac- tive).
  • Including Stereoisomers (Q55, Q131, Q141, Q149): Count both chiral centers and E/Z double bonds (2n for unsymmetrical molecules).
  • Keto–Enol α-H Check (Q04): Tetrasubstituted α- carbons (2, 2, 6, 6-tetramethylcyclohexanone) have 0 α-H and cannot enolize.

trapCards.title: Trap 4: Purification & Chromatography Traps
trapCards.html:
• Paper vs TLC/Column (Q45, Q69, Q99, Q109): Paper chromatography is partition (water in paper pores = stationary phase); TLC & column are adsorption (sil- ica/alumina).
  • TLC Baseline & Solvent Front Offsets (Q132, Q155): Always subtract the baseline margin from spot distances AND subtract both top and bottom margins from total plate height!
  • Distillation Selection (Q01, Q72, Q89, Q121): Glyc- erol from spent-lye → vacuum distillation; Aniline + H2O (immiscible) → steam distillation; CHCl3 + aniline → simple distillation. Chemistry king: (1) Full IUPAC priority table and ene/yne tie-breaker; ting-o/p exception; (3) Hückel (4n + 2)π vs 4nπ aromaticity and pyridine vs pyrrole basicity; (5) TLC Rf offset formula

formulaCards.title: 1. Alkanes: Preparation, Wurtz, Kolbe & Aromati- zation
formulaCards.html:
• Soda-Lime Decarboxylation: RCOONa + NaOH −C−a−O−,−∆→ R − H + Na CO (1 C less). Note: 2 3 CH3COONa → CH4.
  • Kolbe’s Electrolysis: 2RCOONa + 2H O −e−le−c−tr−o−ly−si→s 2 R − R + 2CO2 ↑ (anode) + H2 ↑ +2NaOH (cathode). Cannot form CH4; mixture of two acids gives 3 alkanes.
  • Wurtz Reaction: 2R − X+2Na −d−r−y−e−th−e→r R − R+2NaX (even-carbon symmetrical alkanes; cannot form CH4; 3◦ R − X gives elimination).
  • Grignard Hydrolysis: CH3MgBr + H2O → CH4 + Mg(OH)Br (acid-base!).
  • Isomerization: n-alkane −A−−nh−y−d−.−A−lC−l−3−/H−−C−l,−∆→ branched alkane (n-hexane → 2-methylpentane + 3-methylpentane).
  • Aromatization: n-hexane −C−−r2−O−3−−or−V−−2O−−5,−7−7−3−K−,−1−0−–2−0−a−t−m→ C H ; n-heptane → 6 6 toluene.

formulaCards.title: 2. Free-Radical Halogenation & Selectivity ⋆ High- ROI
formulaCards.html:
• Reactivity of Halogens: F2 > Cl2 > Br2 > I2.
  • Relative Selectivity (3◦ : 2◦ : 1◦ H): – Cl2/hν: 5 : 3.8 : 1 (fast, less selective; CH4 gives CH3Cl → CH2Cl2 → CHCl3 → CCl4). – Br2/hν: 1600 : 82 : 1 (highly selective for 3◦ or benzylic/allylic H!).
  • Isomer Counting: Count chemically non-equivalent H sets for monochlorination; for n-butane → 2-chlorobutane (optically active, d/l pair) → further chlorination gives 5 structural dichloro isomers (1, 2; 2, 2; 2, 3; 1, 3; 2, 4? i.e. 1, 2; 2, 2; 2, 3; 1, 3; wait: 1, 2-, 2, 2-, 2, 3-, 1, 3- dichlorobutane = 4!).
  • Physical Properties: Boiling point ∝ molar mass / surface area (decreases with branching: n-pentane > isopentane > neopentane). Melting point: neopentane > n-pentane (high symmetry).

formulaCards.title: 3. Conformations & Alkene Stability
formulaCards.html:
• Ethane / Butane Conformations: Staggered (anti > gauche) > Skew > Partially eclipsed > Fully eclipsed (∆E ≈ 12.5 kJ/mol in ethane).
  • Alkene Stability: ∝ number of α-H atoms (hy- perconjugation) > substitution > trans > cis: R2C = CR2 > R2C = CHR > R2C = CH2 > trans-RCH = C
  • Heat of Hydrogenation (HOH): ∝ 1 stability of alkene (per π-bond).

formulaCards.title: 4. Alkenes: Addition, Hydration & Ozonolysis
formulaCards.html:
• HX Addition (Markovnikov): Via most stable carbo- cation (C+); hydride/methyl shift & ring expansion occur!
  • Peroxide / Kharasch Effect: R − CH = CH2 + HBr −(−P−h−C−O−O−)→2 R − CH − CH Br (Anti-Markovnikov ◦ 2 2 via 2 radical; ONLY with HBr, NOT HCl or HI).
  • Hydration Triad: – H2O/H+: Markovnikov with rearrangement. – Hg(OAc)2, H2O/NaBH4 (OMDM): Markovnikov, NO rearrangement. – B2H6, THF/H2O2, OH− (HBO): Anti-Markovnikov, syn-addition, NO rearrangement.
  • Halogenation: Br2/CCl4 gives anti-addition via cyclic bromonium ion (cis-alkene → d/l; trans-alkene → meso). Br2/hν or NBS gives allylic substitution.
  • Ozonolysis: O3/Zn, H2O (reductive) cleaves C = C to aldehydes/ketones; KMnO4/∆ (oxidative) gives ke- tones/carboxylic acids (= CH2 → CO2).
  • Baeyer’s Reagent: Cold dil. alk. KMnO4 (273 K) gives syn-1,2-diol (decolorizes purple KMnO4).

formulaCards.title: 5. Alkynes: Acidity, Reduction & Hydration
formulaCards.html:
• Terminal Alkyne Acidity: sp-C (EN ≈ 3.25) reacts with Na, NaNH2, Ag(NH3)+2 (white ppt), Cu(NH3)+2 (red ppt). RC ≡ C−Na+ + 1◦ R′X → RC ≡ CR′.
  • Partial Reduction: – H2 / Lindlar (Pd/CaCO3, quinoline) → cis-alkene (syn). – Na/liq. NH3 (Birch) → trans-alkene (anti).
  • Kucherov Hydration: HgSO4/H2SO4: C2H2 → CH3CHO; terminal alkynes → methyl ke- tones (RC(= O)CH3).
  • Polymerization: 3 HC ≡ CH −r−ed−−h−ot−−Fe−−tu−b−e−,8−7−3−K→ C6H6.

formulaCards.title: 6. Benzene: EAS, Directing Effects & Side-Chain
formulaCards.html:
• EAS Reagents: Nitration (HNO3/H2SO4, NO+2 ); Sul- fonation (H2SO4/SO3); Halogenation (X2/FeX3); FC Alkylation (RX/AlCl3 — carbocation rearranges!); FC Acylation (RCOCl/AlCl3 — NO rearrangement).
  • FC Failure: Fails on strongly deactivated rings (−NO2, −CF3, −COR, −COOH, −SO3H) AND on −NH2, −NHR, −NR2 (forms Lewis acid-base adduct with HR > cisA-RlCCl3H!)=. CHR > RCH = CH2 > CH2 = CH2.
  • Directing Groups: o/p-activating (−NR2 > −OH > −OR > −NHCOR > −R); o/p- deactivating (−F, −Cl, −Br, −I); m-deactivating (−NO2, −CN, −CHO, −COR, −COOH, −CF3).
  • Side-Chain Oxidation: Any alkylbenzene with ≥ 1 ben- zylic H −K−−M−n−O−4−/−K−O−H−,−∆→ PhCOO−K+ −H−+→ PhCOOH.
  • BHC: C6H6 + 3Cl2 −h−→ν C6H6Cl6 (Gammaxene, 6 H atoms).

Q01.conceptHtml: Friedel–Crafts alkylation with 1<sup>°</sup> halides, n-alkane isomerization with AlCl<sub>3</sub>/HCl, and dehydration of neopentyl/pinacolyl alcohols proceed via carbocation or skeletal rearrangements.
Q01.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Check option (a) — Friedel-Crafts alkylation: Treating benzene with 1-chloropropane ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$) and anhydrous $\text{AlCl}_3$ initially forms a $1^\circ$ propyl carbocation, which rearranges via a 1,2-hydride shift to the more stable $2^\circ$ isopropyl carbocation to yield cumene (isopropylbenzene).
  2. Step 2 — Check option (b) — Dehydration of tert-butanol: Acid-catalyzed dehydration of 2-methylpropan-2-ol ($(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{COH}$) with $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$ directly generates a highly stable $3^\circ$ tert-butyl carbocation ($(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}^+$). No carbocation rearrangement is needed before losing $\text{H}^+$ to give 2-methylpropene.
  3. Step 3 — Check options (c) and (d): In (c), heating $n$-hexane with anhydrous $\text{AlCl}_3/\text{HCl}$ causes skeletal isomerization (rearrangement) to 2-methylpentane. In (d), dehydrating neopentyl alcohol ($(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{CCH}_2\text{OH}$) forms a $1^\circ$ carbocation that undergoes a 1,2-methyl shift to a $3^\circ$ carbocation before giving 2-methylbut-2-ene.
  4. Step 4 — Final Answer: Only reaction (b) gives its major product without any rearrangement, so the correct option is (b).

Q02.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Dichloro isomers from optically active 2-chlorobutane
Q02.conceptHtml: Monochlorination of n-butane gives 1-chlorobutane (achiral) and 2-chlorobutane (chiral, P”). Further chlorination of 2-chlorobutane replaces any of the 4 chemically non-equivalent carbon positions.
Q02.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the optically active monochloro compound P: Photochemical monochlorination of $n$-butane ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$) yields 1-chlorobutane (achiral) and 2-chlorobutane ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH(Cl)CH}_2\text{CH}_3$). Since C2 in 2-chlorobutane is bonded to four different groups ($-\text{H}$, $-\text{Cl}$, $-\text{CH}_3$, $-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$), compound P is 2-chlorobutane.
  2. Step 2 — List all possible positions for the second chlorine atom: Replacing one hydrogen atom in $\text{C}^1\text{H}_3-\text{C}^2\text{H(Cl)}-\text{C}^3\text{H}_2-\text{C}^4\text{H}_3$ can occur at four non-equivalent carbon positions: C1, C2, C3, or C4.
  3. Step 3 — Name the resulting structural dichloro isomers: Chlorination at C1 gives 1,2-dichlorobutane; at C2 gives 2,2-dichlorobutane; at C3 gives 2,3-dichlorobutane; and at C4 gives 1,3-dichlorobutane.
  4. Step 4 — Final Answer: Ignoring stereoisomers, exactly 4 structural dichloro compounds are obtained, so the correct option is (b).

Q03.format: Multi-Step Scheme MCQ | Count π and lone-pair electrons in (X)
Q03.conceptHtml: Glucose + HI/∆ → n-hexane; n-hexane + V<sub>2</sub>O<sub>5</sub>/773 K → benzene; benzene + benzoyl chloride / AlCl<sub>3</sub> → benzophenone.
Q03.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Step (i) — Reduction of glucose with HI: Prolonged heating of glucose ($\text{CHO}-(\text{CHOH})_4-\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$) with $\text{HI}, \Delta$ completely reduces all oxygen-containing groups to give $n$-hexane ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_{14}$).
  2. Step 2 — Step (ii) — Aromatization: Heating $n$-hexane over $\text{V}_2\text{O}_5$ at $10\text{–}20\text{ atm}$ and $773\text{ K}$ causes dehydrocyclization (aromatization) to produce benzene ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_6$).
  3. Step 3 — Step (iii) — Friedel-Crafts acylation to form (X): Benzene reacts with benzoyl chloride ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COCl}$) in the presence of anhydrous $\text{AlCl}_3$ to yield benzophenone ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5-\text{CO}-\text{C}_6\text{H}_5$) as the major product (X).
  4. Step 4 — Count π-bond electrons and lone-pair electrons: Benzophenone contains $3 + 3 = 6$ $\pi$ bonds in the two benzene rings and $1$ $\pi$ bond in the $\text{C=O}$ group, giving $7 \times 2 = 14$ $\pi$-electrons. The carbonyl oxygen also carries $2$ lone pairs, contributing $2 \times 2 = 4$ lone-pair electrons. Total $= 14 + 4 = 18$.
  5. Step 5 — Final Answer: The total number of $\pi$-bond and lone-pair electrons in (X) is $18$, so the correct option is (d).

2. Step (ii): n-Hexane −V−2−O−5−,1−0−–−20−a−t−m−,−77−3−→K C6H6 (benzene).
3. Step (iii): C6H6 + PhCOCl −A−n−h−yd−.−A−lC−l→3 Ph − C(= O) − Ph (benzophenone, X).
4. Count in benzophenone: 6 ring π-bonds +1 C = O π-bond = 7 π-bonds (14 π e−); oxygen has 2 lone pairs
(4 e−). Total = 14 + 4 = 18.
Q03.trapHtml: Don’t forget the 2 lone pairs (4 electrons) on the carbonyl oxygen of benzophenone!

Q04.format: Statement I & II MCQ | Soda-lime, Kolbe, Grignard, Wurtz
Q04.conceptHtml: Methane (CH<sub>4</sub>) has only 1 carbon; reactions that couple two alkyl/acyl radicals (Wurtz, Kolbe’s electrolysis) always yield alkanes with ≥ 2 carbons.
Q04.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement I: Decarboxylation of sodium ethanoate ($\text{CH}_3\text{COONa}$) with soda lime gives $\text{CH}_4$, and hydrolysis of $\text{CH}_3\text{MgBr}$ with $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ also gives $\text{CH}_4$. However, Kolbe's electrolysis of sodium acetate couples two $\text{CH}_3^\bullet$ radicals to produce ethane ($\text{C}_2\text{H}_6$), not methane. Hence, Statement I is false.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement II: Hydrogenation of unsaturated hydrocarbons (alkenes/alkynes, which have at least 2 carbons) always produces alkanes with $\ge 2$ carbons. Similarly, the Wurtz reaction ($2\text{R}-\text{X} + 2\text{Na} \to \text{R}-\text{R} + 2\text{NaX}$) forms a new $\text{C}-\text{C}$ bond, so it cannot produce methane. Hence, Statement II is true.
  3. Step 3 — Final Answer: Statement I is false and Statement II is true, so the correct option is (d).
Q04.stepsLatex:
• Statement I is false: Decarboxylation of sodium ethanoate (CH3COONa) and hydrolysis of CH3MgBr give
CH4, but Kolbe’s electrolysis of CH3COONa gives ethane (C2H6), NOT methane.
• Statement II is true: Catalytic hydrogenation of unsaturated hydrocarbons (≥ 2 C) and Wurtz reaction
(R − X + Na) both produce alkanes with ≥ 2 carbons, never CH4.
Q04.trapHtml: Kolbe’s electrolysis and Wurtz reaction both fail to prepare methane.
Q04.finalAnsHtml: (d) Statement I is false but Statement II is true

Q05.format: Ranking MCQ | Compare α-H count in 4 alkenes
Q05.conceptHtml: Alkene stability increases with the number of α-hydrogens available for hyperconjugation.
Q05.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the stability rule for alkenes: Alkene stability increases with the number of $\alpha$-hydrogens available for hyperconjugation with the $\text{C=C}$ double bond.
  2. Step 2 — Count α-hydrogens for each alkene: C (2,3-dimethylbut-2-ene, $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C=C}(\text{CH}_3)_2$) has $12$ $\alpha$-H; A (2-methylbut-2-ene, $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C=CHCH}_3$) has $9$ $\alpha$-H; B (cis-but-2-ene, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH=CHCH}_3$) has $6$ $\alpha$-H; and D (prop-1-ene, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH=CH}_2$) has $3$ $\alpha$-H.
  3. Step 3 — Arrange in decreasing order of stability: Ordering from highest to lowest $\alpha$-H count gives $\text{C} (12) > \text{A} (9) > \text{B} (6) > \text{D} (3)$.
  4. Step 4 — Final Answer: The correct stability order is $\text{C} > \text{A} > \text{B} > \text{D}$, so the correct option is (a).

• C (2, 3-dimethylbut-2-ene): 12 α-H
• A (2-methylbut-2-ene): 9 α-H
• B (cis-but-2-ene): 6 α-H
• D (prop-1-ene): 3 α-H
Stability order: C > A > B > D.
Q05.trapHtml: Count α-H atoms attached to sp<sup>3</sup> carbons directly bonded to the C = C double bond.

Q06.format: Single-Choice MCQ | C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub> with 3 primary carbons
Q06.conceptHtml: A molar mass of 72 g mol<sup>−1</sup> corresponds to C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub> (5 × 12 + 12 = 72).
Q06.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Determine the molecular formula from molar mass: For an alkane $\text{C}_n\text{H}_{2n+2}$ with molar mass $72\text{ g mol}^{-1}$, we have $14n + 2 = 72 \implies 14n = 70 \implies n = 5$. Thus, hydrocarbon (x) has the formula $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{12}$ (eliminating 1,1-dimethylcyclopropane, $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}$, which has molar mass $70\text{ g mol}^{-1}$).
  2. Step 2 — Count primary (1°) carbons in each C5H12 isomer: In $n$-pentane ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$), there are $2$ primary carbons. In 2,2-dimethylpropane ($\text{C}(\text{CH}_3)_4$), there are $4$ primary carbons. In 2-methylbutane ($(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CHCH}_2\text{CH}_3$), there are exactly $3$ primary ($-\text{CH}_3$) carbons.
  3. Step 3 — Final Answer: The hydrocarbon with molar mass $72\text{ g mol}^{-1}$ and three primary carbons is 2-methylbutane, so the correct option is (c).
Q06.stepsLatex:
• 1, 1-Dimethylcyclopropane: C5H10 (M = 70).
• 2, 2-Dimethylpropane (neopentane): C5H12 with 4 primary (1◦) carbons.
• 2-Methylbutane (isopentane): CH3 − CH(CH3) − CH2 − CH3 (C5H12, M = 72) has 3 primary (1◦) carbons.
• n-Pentane: 2 primary carbons.
Q06.trapHtml: 1, 1-Dimethylcyclopropane also has 3 1<sup>°</sup> carbons, but its formula is C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub> (70 g mol<sup>−1</sup>), not 72!

Q07.conceptHtml: Friedel–Crafts alkylation with 1<sup>°</sup> alkyl halides undergoes 1, 2-hydride shift to form a more stable 2<sup>°</sup> carbocation and suffers from polyalkylation.
Q07.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Analyze the electrophile and rearrangement (Statements A and B): In Friedel-Crafts alkylation of benzene with 1-chloropropane and anhydrous $\text{AlCl}_3$, the initially formed $1^\circ$ $n$-propyl carbocation ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2^+$) undergoes a rapid 1,2-hydride shift to form the more stable $2^\circ$ isopropyl carbocation ($\text{CH}_3\stackrel{+}{\text{C}}\text{HCH}_3$). Therefore, isopropylbenzene (cumene) is the major product, making Statement A incorrect and Statement B correct.
  2. Step 2 — Check polyalkylation (Statement C): Once an alkyl group is attached to benzene, its electron-donating ($+I$ and hyperconjugation) effect activates the ring relative to unsubstituted benzene, making further alkylation (multiple substitution) inevitable. Thus, Statement C is correct.
  3. Step 3 — Evaluate substituent effects (Statement D): Introducing an electron-donating group (such as $-\text{CH}_3$ or $-\text{OCH}_3$) increases electron density on the benzene ring and accelerates electrophilic alkylation rather than preventing it. Thus, Statement D is incorrect.
  4. Step 4 — Final Answer: Statements B and C only are correct, so the correct option is (b).
Q07.stepsLatex:
• A (False): Major product is isopropylbenzene (cumene), not n-propylbenzene.
• B (True): 1◦ CH3CH2CH+ rearranges to 2◦ isopropyl carbocation.
2
• C (True): The alkyl group activates the benzene ring, making multiple substitution (polyalkylation) inevitable.
• D (False): Electron-donating groups (e.g., −CH3, −OCH3) accelerate FC alkylation (only strong EWG like
−NO2 or −NH2 prevent it).
Q07.trapHtml: Alkylbenzenes are more reactive than benzene toward EAS, so polysubstitution occurs unless benzene is in large excess.

Q08.format: Multi-Step Scheme MCQ | Calculate molar mass of product (Y)
Q08.conceptHtml: Dibromination + double dehydrohalogenation (NaNH<sub>2</sub> excess) converts cyclohexene? No: terminal alkyne? Wait: 1-methyl-something! Let’s trace carefully.
Q08.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Step (i) — Bromination of styrene (X): Styrene ($\text{Ph}-\text{CH=CH}_2$) undergoes electrophilic addition of $\text{Br}_2/\text{CHCl}_3$ across the double bond to form the vicinal dibromide $\text{Ph}-\text{CH(Br)}-\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$.
  2. Step 2 — Step (ii) and (iii) — Double elimination and alkylation: Excess $\text{NaNH}_2$ eliminates two equivalents of $\text{HBr}$ and deprotonates the resulting terminal alkyne to form sodium phenylacetylide ($\text{Ph}-\text{C}\equiv\text{C}^-\text{Na}^+$). Subsequent $\text{S}_\text{N}2$ reaction with $\text{CH}_3\text{I}$ yields 1-phenylprop-1-yne ($\text{Ph}-\text{C}\equiv\text{C}-\text{CH}_3$).
  3. Step 3 — Step (iv) — Dissolving-metal reduction to (Y): Treatment with $\text{Na}/\text{NH}_3(l)$ reduces the internal alkyne to the corresponding trans-alkene: trans-1-phenylprop-1-ene ($\text{Ph}-\text{CH=CH}-\text{CH}_3$), which has molecular formula $\text{C}_9\text{H}_{10}$.
  4. Step 4 — Calculate the molar mass of (Y): Using $\text{C} = 12$ and $\text{H} = 1$, the molar mass of $\text{C}_9\text{H}_{10}$ is $9(12) + 10(1) = 108 + 10 = 118\text{ g mol}^{-1}$.
  5. Step 5 — Final Answer: The molar mass of major product (Y) is $118\text{ g mol}^{-1}$, so the correct option is (b).

membered ring, if (X) is cyclohexene, NaNH2 gives cyclohexyne / 1-alkyne; Wait: with CH3I followed by
H2, Na/NH3(l) (Birch reduction), the carbon count increases by 1 CH3 group? Wait: 118 g mol−1 is C9H10 or

Q09.format: Structure Identification MCQ | Reconstruct alkene (X) from ozonolysis fragments
Q09.conceptHtml: Reconnect = O carbons pairwise to reconstruct C = C double bonds: each HCHO (2 moles) comes from an exocyclic = CH<sub>2</sub> group.
Q09.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Interpret the reductive ozonolysis products: Reductive ozonolysis cleaves every $\text{C=C}$ bond and places an $=\text{O}$ atom on each alkene carbon. The products are $2\text{ mol}$ of $\text{HCHO}$ (indicating two terminal $=\text{CH}_2$ groups), $1\text{ mol}$ of $\text{OHC}-\text{CO}-\text{CHO}$ ($3$ carbons), and $1\text{ mol}$ of $\text{CH}_3-\text{CO}-\text{CO}-\text{CO}-\text{CH}_3$ ($5$ carbons). Total carbon count $= 2 + 3 + 5 = 10$.
  2. Step 2 — Identify the structural features of alkene (X): To yield both a 3-carbon tricarbonyl ($\text{OHC}-\text{CO}-\text{CHO}$) and a 5-carbon tricarbonyl ($\text{CH}_3\text{COCOCOCH}_3$) along with $2\text{ HCHO}$, the central carbonyls of both tricarbonyls must come from two exocyclic $=\text{CH}_2$ groups on a 6-membered ring, while the outer carbonyls come from two endocyclic double bonds.
  3. Step 3 — Verify option (d): In structure (d), the 6-membered ring has two exocyclic $=\text{CH}_2$ groups at opposite positions (C2 and C5) and two endocyclic double bonds bearing methyl groups on the same side of the ring ($\text{CH}_3-\text{C1=C6H}$ and $\text{CH}_3-\text{C3=C4H}$). Cleaving all four double bonds gives $2\text{ HCHO}$, $\text{CH}_3\text{COCOCOCH}_3$ (from C1–C2–C3), and $\text{OHC}-\text{CO}-\text{CHO}$ (from C6–C5–C4).
  4. Step 4 — Final Answer: Structure (d) matches all ozonolysis products exactly, so the correct option is (d).
Q09.stepsLatex:
1. Ozonolysis yields: 2 mol HCHO (two = CH2 groups), 1 mol OHC − C(= O) − CHO (3-carbon dicarbonyl with
central ketone), and 1 mol CH3 − C(= O) − C(= O) − C(= O) − CH3 (5-carbon tricarbonyl).
2. Total carbons in (X) = 2(1) + 3 + 5 = 10 carbons.
3. In option (d), cleaving all three C = C bonds yields exactly 2 mol HCHO, the 3-carbon keto-dialdehyde, and
the 5-carbon CH3(CO)3CH3 fragment.
Q09.trapHtml: Count total carbons (10) and match the number of HCHO moles (2 =⇒ two = CH<sub>2</sub> termini) first to eliminate wrong rings.

Q10.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Identify n-heptane from 3 reactions
Q10.conceptHtml: n-Heptane (C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>16</sub>) isomerizes with AlCl<sub>3</sub>/HCl to branched heptanes (2, 4-dimethylpentane) and aroma- tizes/cyclizes to toluene and methylcyclohexane.
Q10.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Use the carbon count from the products: All three reactions preserve the 7-carbon skeleton: 2,4-dimethylpentane ($\text{C}_7\text{H}_{16}$), toluene ($\text{C}_7\text{H}_8$), and methylcyclohexane ($\text{C}_7\text{H}_{14}$).
  2. Step 2 — Match the three classic alkane reactions: Heating a straight-chain alkane with anhydrous $\text{AlCl}_3$ and $\text{HCl}$ gas causes skeletal isomerization ($n$-heptane $\to$ 2,4-dimethylpentane). Under catalytic reforming conditions, $n$-heptane undergoes cyclization to methylcyclohexane and aromatization (dehydrocyclization) to toluene.
  3. Step 3 — Final Answer: Compound (X) is $n$-heptane (Heptane), so the correct option is (c).
Q10.stepsLatex:
• (i) n-Heptane −A−l−C−l3−/−H−C−l,−∆→ 2, 4-dimethylpentane (skeletal isomerization).
• (ii) n-Heptane −C−r−2O−−3/−A−l2−O−3−,−77−3−→K toluene (C7H8).
• (iii) n-Heptane cyclization gives methylcyclohexane (C7H14).
Thus, (X) is Heptane.
Q10.trapHtml: Toluene has 7 carbons, immediately ruling out hexane and pointing to C<sub>7</sub> saturated alkane (heptane).

Q11.conceptHtml: Peroxide-initiated addition of HBr to alkenes is a free-radical chain reaction: PhCOO<sup>•</sup> → Ph<sup>•</sup> + CO<sub>2</sub>; Ph<sup>•</sup> + HBr → PhH + Br<sup>•</sup>.
Q11.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Analyze the radical chain mechanism (Statements A, B, and C): With benzoyl peroxide $(\text{PhCOO})_2$, homolysis followed by decarboxylation produces phenyl radicals ($\text{Ph}^\bullet$). $\text{Ph}^\bullet$ abstracts $\text{H}$ from $\text{HBr}$ to form benzene ($\text{Ph}-\text{H}$) as a byproduct and a bromine radical ($\text{Br}^\bullet$)—not $\text{H}^\bullet$. Thus, Statement B is false and Statement C is true. $\text{Br}^\bullet$ then adds to the terminal carbon of styrene to form the more stable $2^\circ$ benzylic radical ($\text{Ph}-\dot{\text{C}}\text{H}-\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$), so Statement A is true.
  2. Step 2 — Identify the major product (Statement D): Hydrogen abstraction by $\text{Ph}-\dot{\text{C}}\text{H}-\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$ from $\text{HBr}$ yields 1-bromo-2-phenylethane ($\text{Ph}-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$) as the major anti-Markovnikov product, making Statement D false.
  3. Step 3 — Compare with reaction in absence of peroxide (Statement E): Without peroxide, $\text{HBr}$ adds to styrene via an ionic electrophilic addition mechanism through the $2^\circ$ benzylic carbocation ($\text{Ph}-\stackrel{+}{\text{C}}\text{H}-\text{CH}_3$). Thus, Statement E is true.
  4. Step 4 — Final Answer: Statements A, C, and E only are correct, so the correct option is (c).
Q11.stepsLatex:
• A (True): Br• adds to = CH2 to give the more stable 2◦ benzylic radical Ph − C˙ H − CH2Br.
• B (False): Peroxide generates Br• (via Ph• + HBr → PhH + Br•), NOT H•.
• C (True): Benzene (PhH) is formed as a byproduct in the initiation step!
• D (False): 1-Bromo-2-phenylethane (Ph − CH2 − CH2Br) is the major product, not minor.
• E (True): Without peroxide, HBr adds ionically via the 2◦ benzylic carbocation.
Q11.trapHtml: Statement C is a classic NCERT detail: C<sub>6</sub>H<sup>•</sup><sub>5</sub> + H − Br → C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>6</sub> + Br<sup>•</sup>, so benzene is indeed a byproduct!

Q12.format: Ranking MCQ | Order of alkene stability
Q12.conceptHtml: More substituted alkenes are more stable (α-H hyperconjugation); for disubstituted alkenes, trans > cis (less steric repulsion), and geminal/internal > terminal.
Q12.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Count α-hydrogens for each alkene: From the diagram: I is 2,3-dimethylbut-2-ene ($12$ $\alpha$-H), III is 2-methylbut-2-ene ($9$ $\alpha$-H), II is trans-but-2-ene ($6$ $\alpha$-H), and IV is cis-but-2-ene ($6$ $\alpha$-H).
  2. Step 2 — Compare hyperconjugation and steric effects: More $\alpha$-hydrogens provide greater hyperconjugative stabilization, so $\text{I} > \text{III} > (\text{II}, \text{IV})$. Between the two geometric isomers with $6$ $\alpha$-H, trans-but-2-ene (II) is more stable than cis-but-2-ene (IV) because the bulky methyl groups are farther apart, reducing steric repulsion.
  3. Step 3 — Final Answer: The decreasing order of stability is $\text{I} > \text{III} > \text{II} > \text{IV}$, so the correct option is (c).
Q12.stepsLatex:
• I: Tetrasubstituted (2, 3-dimethylbut-2-ene, 12 α-H) — most stable.
• III: Trisubstituted (2-methylbut-2-ene, 9 α-H).
• II: trans-But-2-ene (6 α-H, lower steric hindrance).
• IV: cis-But-2-ene (6 α-H, methyl-methyl steric clash).
Decreasing stability: I > III > II > IV.
Q12.trapHtml: trans-Alkene (II) is more stable than cis-alkene (IV) because bulky groups are on opposite sides.

Q13.subtopic: Debromination with Zn & HBr Addition with Ring/Hydride
Q13.conceptHtml: Heating a vicinal dibromide with Zn dust eliminates Br<sub>2</sub> to form an alkene; subsequent HBr addition forms the most stable 3<sup>°</sup> carbocation via hydride shift if needed.
Q13.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Step (i) — Debromination with Zn, Δ: Heating the vicinal dibromide with $\text{Zn}$ dust eliminates $\text{ZnBr}_2$ to introduce a double bond between the two bromine-bearing carbons, giving 3-ethyl-5-methylcyclopentene.
  2. Step 2 — Step (ii) — Protonation and 1,2-hydride shift: Addition of $\text{H}^+$ from $\text{HBr}$ initially forms a $2^\circ$ carbocation on either side of the double bond, which rapidly rearranges via a 1,2-hydride shift to a more stable $3^\circ$ carbocation at either the methyl-bearing carbon or the ethyl-bearing carbon.
  3. Step 3 — Select the more stable 3° carbocation: The $3^\circ$ carbocation at the methyl-bearing ring carbon has $3\text{ (from }-\text{CH}_3) + 2 + 2\text{ (from two ring }-\text{CH}_2-) = 7$ $\alpha$-hydrogens. The $3^\circ$ carbocation at the ethyl-bearing ring carbon has $2\text{ (from }-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3) + 2 + 2 = 6$ $\alpha$-hydrogens. Because $7 > 6$, the carbocation at the methyl-bearing carbon is more stable.
  4. Step 4 — Nucleophilic attack by Br⁻ and Final Answer: $\text{Br}^-$ attacks the more stable $3^\circ$ carbocation at the methyl-bearing carbon to form 1-bromo-3-ethyl-1-methylcyclopentane, matching structure (d).
Q13.stepsLatex:
1. Step (i): Zn/∆ removes both Br atoms to form 1, 3-dimethylcyclopentene (or 3, 4-dimethylcyclopentene de-
pending on substituent positions).
2. Step (ii): Protonation by HBr followed by 1, 2-hydride shift places the positive charge at the tertiary (3◦) ring
carbon bearing the methyl group, and Br− attacks there to give (d).
Q13.trapHtml: Always check if a 1, 2-hydride shift converts a 2<sup>°</sup> ring carbocation into a more stable 3<sup>°</sup> carbocation.

Q14.subtopic: Nitration Reactivity: Activating vs Deactivating Groups
Q14.conceptHtml: Electrophilic aromatic substitution (nitration) rate increases with electron-donating groups (+M) and decreases with electron-withdrawing groups (−I, −M).
Q14.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the substituents and their electronic effects: Compound a is chlorobenzene ($-\text{Cl}$: weakly deactivating because $-I > +M$), compound b is nitrobenzene ($-\text{NO}_2$: strongly deactivating due to both $-M$ and $-I$), and compound c is anisole ($-\text{OCH}_3$: strongly activating because $+M > -I$).
  2. Step 2 — Relate ring electron density to nitration rate: Nitration with a nitrating mixture ($\text{conc. HNO}_3 + \text{conc. H}_2\text{SO}_4$) is an electrophilic aromatic substitution ($\text{NO}_2^+$ attack), so higher electron density in the benzene ring gives a faster reaction.
  3. Step 3 — Order from least reactive to most reactive: Strongly deactivated nitrobenzene (b) reacts slowest, followed by weakly deactivated chlorobenzene (a), and strongly activated anisole (c) reacts fastest: $\text{b} < \text{a} < \text{c}$.
  4. Step 4 — Final Answer: The increasing order of reactivity is $\text{b} < \text{a} < \text{c}$, so the correct option is (d).
Q14.stepsLatex:
• b (Ph − NO2): Strong −M, −I deactivator (slowest).
• a (Ph − Cl): −I > +M, weakly deactivating.
• c (Ph − OCH3): Strong +M > −I activator (fastest).
Increasing order: b < a < c.
Q14.trapHtml: Read the question direction carefully: increasing order” means slowest first (b < a < c).

Q15.subtopic: Lindlar vs Birch Reduction of But-2-yne
Q15.conceptHtml: But-2-yne + H<sub>2</sub>/Pd − C (or Lindlar) → cis-but-2-ene (X); But-2-yne + Na/liq. NH<sub>3</sub> → trans-but-2-ene (Y).
Q15.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify products X and Y: Partial syn-hydrogenation of but-2-yne with $1\text{ mol }\text{H}_2$ over $\text{Pd/C}$ gives X = cis-but-2-ene, whereas anti-reduction with $\text{Na}/\text{liq. NH}_3$ gives Y = trans-but-2-ene.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statements A and C: cis-But-2-ene and trans-but-2-ene are geometrical isomers (a subclass of stereoisomers), so Statement A is correct. Because cis-but-2-ene (X) is polar while trans-but-2-ene (Y) is non-polar, X has stronger dipole–dipole interactions and a higher boiling point than Y, so Statement C is correct.
  3. Step 3 — Evaluate Statements B and D: In cis-but-2-ene (X), the bond dipoles do not cancel, so its dipole moment is non-zero ($\mu \neq 0$, whereas $\mu = 0$ for Y); thus Statement B is incorrect. Reductive ozonolysis ($\text{O}_3/\text{Zn}+\text{H}_2\text{O}$) cleaves the $\text{C=C}$ bond of both X and Y to give the exact same product ($2\text{ mol}$ of $\text{CH}_3\text{CHO}$); thus Statement D is incorrect.
  4. Step 4 — Final Answer: The incorrect statements are B and D only, so the correct option is (a).
Q15.stepsLatex:
• A (True): cis- and trans-but-2-ene are geometrical (stereo) isomers.
• B (False): X (cis-but-2-ene) has a non-zero dipole moment (µ ≠ 0); Y (trans) has µ = 0.
• C (True): Polar cis-isomer (X) has a higher boiling point than non-polar trans-isomer (Y).
• D (False): Both X and Y give the same ozonolysis product (2 mol CH3CHO).
Incorrect statements: B and D Only.
Q15.trapHtml: Notice the prompt asks for the incorrect statements (B and D), not the correct ones!

Q16.format: Reaction-Scheme MCQ | Vicinal dibromide + NaNH<sub>2</sub>, then i-PrCH<sub>2</sub>Br
Q16.conceptHtml: Vicinal dibromide + 2 NaNH<sub>2</sub> gives a terminal alkyne (X); a third equivalent of NaNH<sub>2</sub> forms acetylide, which undergoes S<sub>N</sub>2 with 1<sup>°</sup> alkyl bromide.
Q16.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Step 1 — Double dehydrohalogenation to form X: The starting material is 1,1-dibromobutane ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CHBr}_2$). Heating with $2\text{ equivalents}$ of strong base $\text{NaNH}_2$ eliminates $2\text{ HBr}$ to yield the terminal alkyne X = but-1-yne ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{C}\equiv\text{CH}$).
  2. Step 2 — Step 2 — Alkynide formation and alkylation to form Y: Treatment of but-1-yne with $\text{NaNH}_2$ removes the acidic terminal proton to form $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{C}\equiv\text{C}^-\text{Na}^+$. Subsequent nucleophilic substitution with isopropyl bromide ($(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CH}-\text{Br}$) yields $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{C}\equiv\text{C}-\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)_2$.
  3. Step 3 — Assign the IUPAC name of Y: The longest continuous chain containing the triple bond has $6$ carbons; numbering from the end closer to the methyl substituent (both ends place the triple bond at C3) gives 2-methylhex-3-yne.
  4. Step 4 — Final Answer: Product Y is 2-methylhex-3-yne, so the correct option is (a).
Q16.stepsLatex:
1. 1, 2-Dibromopropane + 2 NaNH2 → CH3 − C ≡ CH (propyne, X).
2. (i) NaNH2 forms CH3 − C ≡ C−Na+.
3. (ii) SN2 alkylation of the acetylide anion with the alkyl bromide extends the carbon chain to give 2-methylhex-
3-yne.
Q16.trapHtml: Number the longest chain containing the triple bond from the end giving the triple bond the lowest locant (3-yne vs 2-methyl).

Q17.conceptHtml: Positive iodoform test + negative Tollen’s test indicates a methyl ketone (−COCH<sub>3</sub>), NOT an aldehyde.
Q17.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Deduce the functional group in [R]: Product [R] gives a positive iodoform test (indicating a methyl ketone $-\text{COCH}_3$ or $-\text{CH(OH)CH}_3$ group) and a negative Tollen's test (confirming it is a ketone, not an aldehyde).
  2. Step 2 — Work backward from [R] to alkyne [Q]: Kucherov hydration ($\text{HgSO}_4/\text{dil. H}_2\text{SO}_4$) of a terminal alkyne ($\text{Ar}-\text{C}\equiv\text{CH}$) adds water in Markovnikov fashion to yield an aryl methyl ketone ($\text{Ar}-\text{COCH}_3$). With formula $\text{C}_9\text{H}_{10}\text{Br}_2$ for [P], losing $2\text{ HBr}$ gives [Q] as $\text{C}_9\text{H}_8$, i.e., $p$-tolylacetylene ($p-\text{CH}_3\text{C}_6\text{H}_4-\text{C}\equiv\text{CH}$), which hydrates to 4-methylacetophenone.
  3. Step 3 — Verify which dibromide [P] gives [Q]: Structure (d) is 1-(1,1-dibromoethyl)-4-methylbenzene ($p-\text{CH}_3\text{C}_6\text{H}_4-\text{CBr}_2\text{CH}_3$, formula $\text{C}_9\text{H}_{10}\text{Br}_2$). Heating with excess $\text{NaNH}_2$ followed by dil. $\text{HCl}$ eliminates $2\text{ HBr}$ from the gem-dibromide to give $p$-tolylacetylene [Q]. None of the other options can eliminate $2\text{ HBr}$ to form a terminal aryl alkyne.
  4. Step 4 — Final Answer: Compound [P] is structure (d).
Q17.stepsLatex:
1. [P] (C9H10Br2) + excess NaNH2 / HCl gives alkyne [Q].
2. Hydration of [Q] (HgSO4/H2SO4) gives ketone [R] with a −COCH3 group (positive iodoform, negative Tollen’s).
3. Dehydrohalogenation of (d) with excess NaNH2 followed by HCl yields the terminal alkyne [Q], whose hydration
with HgSO4/H2SO4 gives a methyl ketone [R] that answers the iodoform test positively and Tollen’s test
negatively.
Q17.trapHtml: Positive iodoform + negative Tollen’s rules out aldehydes (which give Tollen’s) and non-methyl ketones.

Q18.format: Statement I & II MCQ | Nitration followed by FC acylation
Q18.conceptHtml: Nitrobenzene is so strongly deactivated by the −NO<sub>2</sub> group (−M, −I) that it does NOT undergo Friedel–Crafts alkylation or acylation.
Q18.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement I: Nitration of benzene yields nitrobenzene. However, nitrobenzene does not undergo Friedel-Crafts acylation with $\text{CH}_3\text{COCl}/\text{AlCl}_3$ because the strongly electron-withdrawing $-\text{NO}_2$ group deactivates the ring and coordinates with the Lewis acid catalyst $\text{AlCl}_3$. Therefore, m-nitroacetophenone is not formed, and Statement I is incorrect.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement II: The $-\text{NO}_2$ group withdraws electron density from the benzene ring via both $-M$ and $-I$ effects, especially at the ortho and para positions, making it a strongly deactivating and meta-directing group. Thus, Statement II is correct.
  3. Step 3 — Final Answer: Statement I is incorrect and Statement II is correct, so the correct option is (a).
Q18.stepsLatex:
• Statement I is incorrect: Nitrobenzene does not react with CH3COCl/AlCl3 (nitrobenzene is actually used
as a solvent for Friedel–Crafts reactions!).
• Statement II is correct: −NO2 is a strong m-directing and deactivating group.
Q18.trapHtml: Even though −NO<sub>2</sub> is m-directing, Friedel–Crafts reactions fail completely on nitrobenzene!
Q18.finalAnsHtml: (a) Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

Q19.subtopic: Hydrogenation & Oxidative Cleavage of Bicyclic Diene
Q19.format: Structure Identification MCQ | Identify bicyclic diene A
Q19.conceptHtml: 2 mol H<sub>2</sub>/Pt saturates two C = C bonds to decalin; KMnO<sub>4</sub>/∆ cleaves both C = C bonds to a cyclohexane- tricarboxylic acid + oxalic acid (HOOC − COOH).
Q19.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Determine the carbon skeleton and unsaturation of A: Catalytic hydrogenation of A with $2\text{ mol }\text{H}_2/\text{Pt}$ produces decalin (bicyclo[4.4.0]decane, $\text{C}_{10}\text{H}_{18}$). This shows A is a bicyclic diene ($\text{C}_{10}\text{H}_{14}$) with two fused 6-membered rings.
  2. Step 2 — Analyze the hot KMnO4 oxidation products: Oxidative cleavage with hot $\text{KMnO}_4$ yields cyclohexane-1,2-dicarboxylic acid ($8$ carbons) plus oxalic acid ($\text{HOOC}-\text{COOH}$, $2$ carbons). Because an intact cyclohexane ring survives, one of the two fused rings in A must be completely saturated.
  3. Step 3 — Locate the two double bonds in the unsaturated ring: To obtain two $-\text{COOH}$ groups directly attached to the two bridgehead carbons of the cyclohexane ring alongside a 2-carbon oxalic acid fragment, the two double bonds must lie in the second ring separated by a single $\text{C}-\text{C}$ bond away from the ring junction (a conjugated 1,3-diene across the four non-junction carbons, i.e., $-\text{CH}=\text{CH}-\text{CH}=\text{CH}-$ attached to the two bridgeheads). Cleavage breaks out the middle 2-carbon unit as oxalic acid and oxidizes the two carbons attached to the bridgeheads into $-\text{COOH}$ groups.
  4. Step 4 — Final Answer: This bicyclic conjugated diene matches structure (a).
Q19.stepsLatex:
1. Formation of oxalic acid (HOOC − COOH, 2 carbons) requires a = CH − CH = unit flanked by two C = C
bonds!
2. In (a), the right ring is a 1, 3-cyclohexadiene: cleaving both C = C bonds releases the two-carbon = CH − CH =
bridge as HOOC − COOH and oxidizes the remaining ring carbons to the tricarboxylic acid.
Q19.trapHtml: Oxalic acid (HOOC − COOH) from KMnO<sub>4</sub>/∆ is the telltale signature of a conjugated 1, 3-diene unit (−CH = CH − CH = CH−).

Q20.conceptHtml: Alkyne hydration (Hg<sup>2+</sup>/H<sup>+</sup>) forms a ketone, and Clemmensen reduction (Zn − Hg/H<sup>+</sup>) reduces C = O completely to −CH<sub>2</sub>−.
Q20.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Steps (i) and (ii) — Double dehydrohalogenation: Treating 1,2-dibromocyclooctane with alcoholic $\text{KOH}$ eliminates one $\text{HBr}$ to form 1-bromocyclooctene. Stronger base $\text{NaNH}_2$ then eliminates the second $\text{HBr}$ to give cyclooctyne.
  2. Step 2 — Step (iii) — Acid-catalyzed hydration of the alkyne: Hydration of cyclooctyne with $\text{Hg}^{2+}/\text{H}^+$ forms an enol intermediate (cyclooct-1-en-1-ol), which tautomerizes to cyclooctanone.
  3. Step 3 — Step (iv) — Clemmensen reduction: Treating cyclooctanone with $\text{Zn}-\text{Hg}/\text{H}^+$ (Clemmensen reduction) completely reduces the carbonyl group ($\text{C=O}$) to a methylene group ($-\text{CH}_2-$), yielding cyclooctane.
  4. Step 4 — Final Answer: Major product P is cyclooctane, which corresponds to option (c).
Q20.stepsLatex:
1. (i) KOH (alc.) + (ii) NaNH2 on 1, 2-dibromocyclooctane → cyclooctyne.
2. (iii) Hg2+/H+ hydrates cyclooctyne to cyclooctanone.
3. (iv) Zn − Hg/H+ (Clemmensen reduction) reduces cyclooctanone to cyclooctane (c).
Q20.trapHtml: Don’t stop at cyclooctanone (b) — step (iv) Zn − Hg/H<sup>+</sup> reduces the carbonyl all the way to −CH<sub>2</sub>−!

Q21.subtopic: Reactions That Do NOT Give Alkene by Elimination
Q21.conceptHtml: Aqueous KOH favors S<sub>N</sub>2 substitution (alcohol), not elimination; Na<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub>/H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> is an oxidizing agent (ketone), not a dehydrating/eliminating agent.
Q21.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Check reactions A, C, and E: In A, 1-bromo-2-methylcyclohexane reacts with strong base $\text{NaOEt}$ via E2 elimination to give an alkene. In C, tert-butyl bromide ($3^\circ$ halide) reacts with strong base $\text{NaOMe}$ exclusively via E2 elimination to give 2-methylpropene. In E, passing tert-butyl alcohol over $\text{Cu}$ at $573\text{ K}$ causes dehydration (elimination) to 2-methylpropene.
  2. Step 2 — Check reactions B and D: In B, 2-bromobutane with aqueous $\text{KOH}$ undergoes nucleophilic substitution to give butan-2-ol rather than elimination (alcoholic $\text{KOH}$ is required for elimination). In D, phenol with $\text{Na}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7/\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ undergoes oxidation to p-benzoquinone, not elimination to an alkene.
  3. Step 3 — Final Answer: Reactions B and D cannot be applied to prepare an alkene by elimination, so the correct option is (d).
Q21.stepsLatex:
• A: 2◦ bromide + NaOEt → E2 elimination (alkene).
• B: 2-Bromobutane + KOH (aq) → SN2 substitution to butan-2-ol (NOT elimination).
• C: 3◦ bromide + NaOMe → E2 elimination (alkene).
• D: Cyclohexanol + Na2Cr2O7/H2SO4 → oxidation to cyclohexanone (NOT elimination).
• E: 3◦ alcohol + Cu/573 K → dehydration to alkene (note: 3◦ alcohols dehydrate with Cu/573 K!).
Thus B & D Only cannot be applied to prepare an alkene.
Q21.trapHtml: 3<sup>°</sup> alcohols undergo dehydration (not dehydrogenation) over Cu/573 K because they lack an α-H!

Q22.format: Statement I & II MCQ | cis-2-butene and 3,6-dimethyloct-4-ene
Q22.conceptHtml: Ozonolysis cleaves C = C into C = O; check whether the resulting carbonyl product retains any chiral carbon (4 different groups).
Q22.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement I: Reductive ozonolysis ($\text{O}_3$ followed by $\text{Zn}/\text{H}_2\text{O}$) of cis-2-butene ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH=CHCH}_3$) cleaves the $\text{C=C}$ bond to yield $2\text{ moles}$ of ethanal ($\text{CH}_3\text{CHO}$). Hence, Statement I is true.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement II: Reductive ozonolysis of 3,6-dimethyloct-4-ene ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH(CH}_3)\text{CH=CHCH(CH}_3)\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$) yields $2\text{ moles}$ of 2-methylbutanal ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH(CH}_3)\text{CHO}$). Carbon-2 is bonded to four different groups ($-\text{H}$, $-\text{CH}_3$, $-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$, and $-\text{CHO}$), so the product does contain a chiral carbon atom. Hence, Statement II is false.
  3. Step 3 — Final Answer: Statement I is true and Statement II is false, so the correct option is (c).
Q22.stepsLatex:
• Statement I is true: CH3 − CH = CH − CH3 −O−3−/−Zn−,−H−2O→ 2 CH3CHO (ethanal).
• Statement II is false: Reductive ozonolysis of 3, 6-dimethyloct-4-ene (CH3 − CH2 − CH(CH3) − CH = CH − CH(CH3) −
∗
yields 2-methylbutanal (CH3 − CH2 − CH(CH3) − CHO), where C2 is a chiral carbon bonded to −H, −CH3,
−CH2CH3, and −CHO.
Q22.trapHtml: Always draw out the ozonolysis product and check all 4 valencies of every sp<sup>3</sup> carbon for chirality!
Q22.finalAnsHtml: (c) Statement I is true but Statement II is false

Q23.format: Multi-Step Scheme MCQ | Methylcyclohexane reaction sequence
Q23.conceptHtml: Br<sub>2</sub>/hν selectively brominates the 3<sup>°</sup> carbon; alc. KOH gives the Zaitsev alkene (1-methylcyclohexene); HBr/ROOR adds Br anti-Markovnikov to the less substituted C = C carbon.
Q23.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Step (1) — Free-radical bromination: Bromination of methylcyclohexane with $\text{Br}_2/h\nu$ is highly regioselective for the $3^\circ$ C–H bond (forming the most stable $3^\circ$ radical), giving 1-bromo-1-methylcyclohexane as the major product.
  2. Step 2 — Step (2) — Dehydrohalogenation: Heating 1-bromo-1-methylcyclohexane with alcoholic $\text{KOH}$ induces E2 elimination to give the more substituted Saytzeff alkene, 1-methylcyclohexene.
  3. Step 3 — Step (3) — Peroxide-assisted HBr addition: Addition of $\text{HBr}$ in the presence of peroxide ($\text{R}-\text{O}-\text{O}-\text{R}, h\nu$) follows the Kharasch anti-Markovnikov free-radical mechanism: $\text{Br}^\bullet$ adds to the less substituted alkene carbon (C2) to form the more stable $3^\circ$ radical at C1, yielding 1-bromo-2-methylcyclohexane.
  4. Step 4 — Final Answer: The major product is 1-bromo-2-methylcyclohexane, matching option (b).
Q23.stepsLatex:
1. (1) Methylcyclohexane + Br2/hν → 1-bromo-1-methylcyclohexane (3◦ radical).
2. (2) Alc. KOH/∆ → 1-methylcyclohexene (Zaitsev product).
3. (3) HBr/R − O − O − R, hν (Kharasch effect) → 1-bromo-2-methylcyclohexane (b).
Q23.trapHtml: Step (3) uses peroxide (R − O − O − R), so Br goes to C2 (less substituted), NOT C1 (3<sup>°</sup>)!

Q24.format: Structure Identification MCQ | Identify cyclic alkene
Q24.conceptHtml: 3-Methyl-6-oxoheptanal has 8 carbons (C<sub>8</sub>): C1 (−CHO) and C6 (−C(= O)CH<sub>3</sub>) were joined by the C = C bond in a 6-membered ring.
Q24.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Write the structure of the ozonolysis product: 3-Methyl-6-oxoheptanal has the open-chain structure $\text{OHC}^1-\text{CH}_2^2-\text{CH}^3(\text{CH}_3)-\text{CH}_2^4-\text{CH}_2^5-\text{C}^6(=\text{O})-\text{CH}_3^7$.
  2. Step 2 — Apply reverse ozonolysis: Because a single dicarbonyl molecule is formed, the starting alkene must be cyclic. Remove the $=\text{O}$ atoms from C1 (aldehyde) and C6 (ketone) and reconnect C1 and C6 with a $\text{C=C}$ double bond.
  3. Step 3 — Identify the resulting cycloalkene: Joining C1 and C6 forms a 6-membered cyclohexene ring with one $-\text{CH}_3$ group on the double-bonded carbon (C6) and the second $-\text{CH}_3$ group directly across the ring at the 4-position (C3), giving 1,4-dimethylcyclohexene.
  4. Step 4 — Final Answer: 1,4-Dimethylcyclohexene corresponds to option (a).
Q24.stepsLatex:
1 2 3 4 5 6 7
1. Numbering 3-methyl-6-oxoheptanal: CHO − CH2 − CH(CH3) − CH2 − CH2 − C(= O) − CH3.
2. Joining C1 and C6 forms a 6-membered ring with a C = C between C1 and C6, a methyl at C6 (i.e., C1 of
cyclohexene), and a methyl at C3 (i.e., C4 of cyclohexene): 1, 4-dimethylcyclohexene (a).
Q24.trapHtml: Verify the distance between the two methyls: C1 and C4 are para to each other in (a), not C1,C3 or C1,C5.

Q25.format: Statement I & II MCQ | Monosubstitution and melting point
Q25.conceptHtml: Neopentane (C(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>) has 12 equivalent 1<sup>°</sup> hydrogens and high tetrahedral symmetry, allowing tight crystal packing.
Q25.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement I: Neopentane ($\text{C}(\text{CH}_3)_4$, 2,2-dimethylpropane) has $12$ completely equivalent primary hydrogen atoms. Replacing any one of them gives the exact same compound, so it forms only one monosubstituted derivative. Statement I is correct.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement II: Neopentane has a compact, highly symmetrical spherical shape that packs much more tightly in a solid crystal lattice than linear $n$-pentane. Consequently, neopentane has a significantly higher melting point ($256.4\text{ K}$) than $n$-pentane ($143.3\text{ K}$). Statement II is correct.
  3. Step 3 — Final Answer: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct, so the correct option is (b).
Q25.stepsLatex:
• Statement I is true: All 12 H atoms in neopentane are equivalent =⇒ only 1 monosubstituted derivative.
• Statement II is true: Neopentane packs much more efficiently in the solid state than n-pentane, giving it a
much higher melting point (256.5 K vs 143 K).
Q25.trapHtml: Branching lowers boiling point, but high symmetry (like neopentane) raises melting point!
Q25.finalAnsHtml: (b) Both Statement I and Statement II are correct

Q26.subtopic: Counting σ and π Bonds in Hex-1-en-4-yne
Q26.format: Single-Choice MCQ | CH<sub>2</sub> = CH − CH<sub>2</sub> − C ≡ C − CH<sub>3</sub>
Q26.conceptHtml: Number of σ bonds in an acyclic hydrocarbon = (Total atoms) − 1.
Q26.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Write the structural and molecular formula: Hex-1-en-4-yne has the structure $\text{CH}_2=\text{CH}-\text{CH}_2-\text{C}\equiv\text{C}-\text{CH}_3$, which corresponds to the molecular formula $\text{C}_6\text{H}_8$.
  2. Step 2 — Count the sigma (σ) bonds: In an open-chain hydrocarbon with $6$ carbons and $8$ hydrogens, there are $6 - 1 = 5$ $\text{C}-\text{C}$ $\sigma$ bonds and $8$ $\text{C}-\text{H}$ $\sigma$ bonds, giving a total of $5 + 8 = 13$ $\sigma$ bonds.
  3. Step 3 — Count the pi (π) bonds: The $\text{C=C}$ double bond at C1 contributes $1$ $\pi$ bond, and the $\text{C}\equiv\text{C}$ triple bond at C4 contributes $2$ $\pi$ bonds, giving a total of $1 + 2 = 3$ $\pi$ bonds.
  4. Step 4 — Final Answer: Hex-1-en-4-yne contains $13$ $\sigma$ bonds and $3$ $\pi$ bonds, so the correct option is (c).
Q26.stepsLatex:
1. Formula of hex-1-en-4-yne (CH2 = CH − CH2 − C ≡ C − CH3): C6H8 (14 atoms).
2. σ bonds = 14 − 1 = 13.
3. π bonds = 1 (from C=C) + 2 (from C ≡ C) = 3.
Q26.trapHtml: Always use (atoms − 1) for acyclic σ-bond counts to avoid missing C–H bonds.

Q27.subtopic: Alkene + HCl Followed by AgCN (Isocyanide Formation)
Q27.conceptHtml: HCl adds to the alkene via the more stable benzylic carbocation; AgCN (covalent) attacks via the nitrogen lone pair to give an isocyanide (−NC).
Q27.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Step 1 — Electrophilic addition of HCl to form (A): Protonation of 1-methyl-4-(prop-1-en-1-yl)benzene ($p-\text{CH}_3\text{C}_6\text{H}_4-\text{CH=CH}-\text{CH}_3$) preferentially generates the resonance-stabilized benzylic carbocation $p-\text{CH}_3\text{C}_6\text{H}_4-\stackrel{+}{\text{C}}\text{H}-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$. Q33.subtopic: Selectivity of Radical Bromination (3◦ vs 2◦ H)

Q42.format: Reaction-Scheme MCQ | Identify dicarboxylic acid D
Q42.conceptHtml: Dehydrohalogenation → dibromination → S<sub>N</sub>2 with excess KCN → complete acidic hydrolysis (H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>) gives a 4-carbon dicarboxylic acid.
Q42.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify intermediates A and B: Dehydrohalogenation of bromoethane ($\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{Br}$) with alcoholic $\text{KOH}$ gives A = ethene ($\text{CH}_2=\text{CH}_2$). Electrophilic addition of $\text{Br}_2/\text{CCl}_4$ across ethene yields B = 1,2-dibromoethane ($\text{BrCH}_2-\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$).
  2. Step 2 — Identify intermediate C — Nucleophilic substitution: Reacting 1,2-dibromoethane with excess $\text{KCN}$ replaces both $-\text{Br}$ atoms with $-\text{CN}$ groups via $\text{S}_\text{N}2$ substitution, forming C = butane-1,4-dinitrile ($\text{NC}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{CN}$).
  3. Step 3 — Identify acid D — Complete acid hydrolysis: Complete hydrolysis of both nitrile groups with excess $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$ converts $-\text{CN}$ into $-\text{COOH}$, yielding butane-1,4-dioic acid ($\text{HOOC}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{COOH}$), commonly known as succinic acid.
  4. Step 4 — Final Answer: Acid D is succinic acid, so the correct option is (c).

1. C2H5Br −a−l−c.−K−O−→H CH2 = CH2 (A).
2. CH2 = CH2 −B−r−2/−C−C−l→4 BrCH2 − CH2Br (B).
3. BrCH2 − CH2Br −K−C−N−−(e−xc−e−ss→) NC − CH2 − CH2 − CN (C).
4. NC − CH2 − CH2 − CN −H−3−O−+−(−e−xc−e−ss→) HOOC − CH2 − CH2 − COOH (Succinic acid, D).
Q42.trapHtml: Count the carbons: 2 from ethene +2 from two −CN groups = 4 carbons =⇒ succinic acid (not oxalic or malonic).

Q43.format: Reaction-Scheme MCQ | Markovnikov vs Anti-Markovnikov hydration
Q43.conceptHtml: H<sup>+</sup>/H<sub>2</sub>O adds −OH at the more substituted (3<sup>°</sup>) ring carbon; B<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub>/H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>, NaOH adds −OH at the less substituted (2<sup>°</sup>) ring carbon.
Q43.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the starting alkene: The reactant is 1-methylcyclohexene, an unsymmetrical trisubstituted cyclic alkene where C1 carries a methyl group and C2 carries a hydrogen atom.
  2. Step 2 — Acid-catalyzed hydration to form A: Treating 1-methylcyclohexene with $\text{H}^+/\text{H}_2\text{O}$ proceeds via the more stable $3^\circ$ carbocation at C1 (Markovnikov addition). Water attacks C1, giving A = 1-methylcyclohexan-1-ol (both $-\text{CH}_3$ and $-\text{OH}$ on the same carbon).
  3. Step 3 — Hydroboration–oxidation to form B: Reaction with $\text{B}_2\text{H}_6$ followed by $\text{H}_2\text{O}_2, \text{NaOH(aq)}$ adds $-\text{H}$ and $-\text{OH}$ in a syn, anti-Markovnikov fashion without rearrangement, placing $-\text{OH}$ at the less substituted C2 carbon to give B = 2-methylcyclohexan-1-ol.
  4. Step 4 — Match with options: A = 1-methylcyclohexan-1-ol and B = 2-methylcyclohexan-1-ol match Option (d).

1. A (H+/H2O): 1-methylcyclohexan-1-ol (−OH and −CH3 on the same carbon).
2. B (B2H6/H2O2, NaOH): 2-methylcyclohexan-1-ol (−OH on the adjacent −CH− carbon).
Q43.trapHtml: Check the arrow directions: right arrow gives A (H<sup>+</sup>/H<sub>2</sub>O), left arrow gives B (B<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub>)!

Q44.subtopic: Terminal Alkyne Alkylation with 1° Alkyl Bromide
Q44.format: Reaction-Scheme MCQ | Identify A and B
Q44.conceptHtml: Propyne + Na forms sodium propynide (CH<sub>3</sub> − C ≡ C<sup>−</sup>Na<sup>+</sup>), which attacks 1-bromopropane via S<sub>N</sub>2 to extend the chain.
Q44.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Formation of sodium alkynide (A): Propyne ($\text{CH}_3-\text{C}\equiv\text{CH}$) is a terminal alkyne with an acidic $sp$-hybridized $\text{C}-\text{H}$ proton. Reacting it with $\text{Na}$ metal replaces this proton to give sodium propynide, A = $\text{CH}_3-\text{C}\equiv\text{C}^-\text{Na}^+$.
  2. Step 2 — Analyze the alkylation product (C): Product C is hex-2-yne ($\text{CH}_3-\text{C}\equiv\text{C}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_3$) formed alongside $\text{NaBr}$, showing that a 3-carbon $n$-propyl group has been attached to the alkynide carbon.
  3. Step 3 — Identify reagent B: Alkylation of a sodium alkynide proceeds via an $\text{S}_\text{N}2$ reaction with a primary alkyl halide. To introduce $-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ and release $\text{NaBr}$, reagent B must be 1-bromopropane, B = $\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{Br}$.
  4. Step 4 — Match with options: $\text{A} = \text{CH}_3-\text{C}\equiv\text{C}^-\text{Na}^+$ and $\text{B} = \text{CH}_3-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{Br}$ correspond to Option (a).
Q44.stepsLatex:
1. CH3 − C ≡ CH + Na → CH3 − C ≡ C−Na+ (A).
2. A reacts with CH3 − CH2 − CH2 − Br (B) to give CH3 − C ≡ C − CH2 − CH2 − CH3 + NaBr (C).
Q44.trapHtml: Note that CH<sub>3</sub> − CH<sub>2</sub> − CH<sub>3</sub> (alkane) in option (c) has no leaving group and cannot undergo S<sub>N</sub>2.
Q44.finalAnsHtml: (a) A = CH<sub>3</sub> − C ≡ C<sup>−</sup>Na<sup>+</sup>, B = CH<sub>3</sub> − CH<sub>2</sub> − CH<sub>2</sub> − Br

Q45.subtopic: Allylic Radical Chlorination (hν) vs Electrophilic Addition
Q45.format: Reaction-Scheme MCQ | Cyclohexene + Cl<sub>2</sub> under hν vs CCl<sub>4</sub>
Q45.conceptHtml: Under hν (free-radical conditions), Cl<sub>2</sub> substitutes at the allylic positions (3, 6-dichlorocyclohexene if 2 mol, or allylic substitution leaving C = C intact); in CCl<sub>4</sub> (dark/ionic), Cl<sub>2</sub> adds across C = C to give 1, 2-dichlorocyclohexane.
Q45.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Reaction under UV light ($h\nu$) to form Product A: Treating cyclohexene with $\text{Cl}_2$ in the presence of light ($h\nu$) favors free-radical substitution at the weak allylic $\text{C}-\text{H}$ bond via a resonance-stabilized allylic radical, leaving the double bond intact to give Product A = 3-chlorocyclohexene.
  2. Step 2 — Reaction in $\text{CCl}_4$ to form Product B: In the inert, non-polar solvent $\text{CCl}_4$ without light, $\text{Cl}_2$ undergoes electrophilic anti-addition across the $\text{C}=\text{C}$ double bond via a cyclic chloronium ion intermediate to give Product B = 1,2-dichlorocyclohexane.
  3. Step 3 — Match with options: Comparing the structures of A (3-chlorocyclohexene) and B (1,2-dichlorocyclohexane) with the given choices confirms Option (a).
Q45.stepsLatex:
• Product A (hν) retains the C = C double bond with Cl at the two allylic carbons; Product B (CCl4) is the
1, 2-addition product (1, 2-dichlorocyclohexane).
Q45.trapHtml: hν triggers free-radical allylic substitution (double bond stays!), while CCl<sub>4</sub> gives electrophilic anti- addition across C = C.

Q46.subtopic: Hydration, Oxidation & Wolff–Kishner Reduction of Styrene
Q46.conceptHtml: H<sub>2</sub>O/H<sup>+</sup> gives 1-phenylethanol; CrO<sub>3</sub> oxidizes 2<sup>°</sup> alcohol to acetophenone; Wolff–Kishner (H<sub>2</sub>N − NH<sub>2</sub>, KOH/∆) reduces C = O to −CH<sub>2</sub>−.
Q46.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Acid-catalyzed hydration (step i): Styrene ($\text{Ph}-\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2$) reacts with $\text{H}_2\text{O}/\text{H}^+$ via the resonance-stabilized $2^\circ$ benzylic carbocation ($\text{Ph}-\text{CH}^+-\text{CH}_3$) to yield the Markovnikov alcohol, 1-phenylethanol ($\text{Ph}-\text{CH(OH)}-\text{CH}_3$).
  2. Step 2 — Oxidation with $\text{CrO}_3$ (step ii): Chromium trioxide oxidizes the secondary alcohol 1-phenylethanol to the corresponding ketone, acetophenone ($\text{Ph}-\text{CO}-\text{CH}_3$).
  3. Step 3 — Wolff–Kishner reduction (step iii): Heating acetophenone with hydrazine ($\text{H}_2\text{N}-\text{NH}_2$) and $\text{KOH}$ completely reduces the carbonyl group ($>\text{C}=\text{O}$) to a methylene group ($-\text{CH}_2-$), forming ethylbenzene ($\text{Ph}-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$).
  4. Step 4 — Match with options: Ethylbenzene is shown in Option (a).
Q46.stepsLatex:
1. (i) Ph − CH = CH2 −H−2−O−,−H→+ Ph − CH(OH) − CH3.
2. (ii) −C−r−O→3 Ph − C(= O) − CH3 (acetophenone).
3. (iii) −H−2−N−−−N−H−2−,K−−O−H−,∆→ Ph − CH2 − CH3 (ethylbenzene, (a)).
Q46.trapHtml: Don’t stop at the hydrazone (d)! Heating with KOH completes the Wolff–Kishner reduction to the alkane.

Q47.conceptHtml: HBO gives 1<sup>°</sup> alcohol; PCC stops oxidation at the aldehyde; CH<sub>3</sub>MgBr adds a methyl group to give a 2<sup>°</sup> alcohol.
Q47.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Hydroboration–oxidation (steps i & ii): Propene ($\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2$) treated with $\text{B}_2\text{H}_6$ followed by $\text{H}_2\text{O}_2/\text{NaOH}$ undergoes anti-Markovnikov hydration to give the primary alcohol propan-1-ol ($\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{OH}$).
  2. Step 2 — Selective oxidation with PCC (step iii): Pyridinium chlorochromate (PCC) is a mild oxidizing agent that converts a $1^\circ$ alcohol selectively to an aldehyde without over-oxidation, giving propanal ($\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}_2-\text{CHO}$).
  3. Step 3 — Grignard addition (step iv): Methylmagnesium bromide ($\text{CH}_3\text{MgBr}$) adds nucleophilically to the electrophilic carbonyl carbon of propanal; subsequent protonation yields the $2^\circ$ alcohol butan-2-ol, $\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH(OH)}-\text{CH}_3$.
  4. Step 4 — Match with options: $\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH(OH)}-\text{CH}_3$ matches Option (d).

1. (i)–(ii) CH3 − CH = CH2 −B−2−H−6−/H−2−O−2−,N−a−O−→H CH3 − CH2 − CH2 − OH.
2. (iii) −P−C−→C CH3 − CH2 − CHO (propanal).
3. (iv) −C−H−3−M−g−B−r−,H−3−O−→+ CH3 − CH2 − CH(OH) − CH3 (butan-2-ol, (d)).

Q48.subtopic: EAS Reactivity Order of Substituted Benzenes
Q48.conceptHtml: EAS reactivity follows the electron-donating strength of the substituent: +M (−NMe<sub>2</sub> > −OCH<sub>3</sub>) > +I/hyperconjugation (−CH<sub>3</sub>) > −H > −I (−CF<sub>3</sub>).
Q48.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the rule for EAS reactivity: Electron-donating groups (EDGs) increase electron density on the benzene ring and accelerate electrophilic aromatic substitution (EAS), whereas electron-withdrawing groups (EWGs) deactivate the ring.
  2. Step 2 — Classify each substituent: (e) $-\text{NMe}_2$ is a very strong activator ($+M$), (d) $-\text{OCH}_3$ is a strong activator ($+M$, weaker than $-\text{NMe}_2$ because oxygen is more electronegative than nitrogen), (a) $-\text{CH}_3$ is a weak activator ($+H/+I$), (b) $-\text{H}$ is the benzene reference, and (c) $-\text{CF}_3$ is a strong deactivator ($-I$ and reverse hyperconjugation).
  3. Step 3 — Arrange in decreasing order: Ranking from most electron-rich to most electron-poor gives $\text{e} > \text{d} > \text{a} > \text{b} > \text{c}$.
  4. Step 4 — Match with options: The order $\text{e} > \text{d} > \text{a} > \text{b} > \text{c}$ corresponds to Option (d).
Q48.stepsLatex:
• (e) Ph − NMe2 (+M, strongest activator) > (d) Ph − OCH3 (+M) > (a) Ph − CH3 (+I/HC) > (b) C6H6 >
(c) Ph − CF3 (−I, deactivator).
Decreasing order: e > d > a > b > c.
Q48.trapHtml: −NMe<sub>2</sub> is a stronger +M donor than −OCH<sub>3</sub> because N is less electronegative than O and donates its lone pair more readily.

Q49.subtopic: Isomerization of n-Hexane with Anhyd. AlCl3 / HCl
Q49.conceptHtml: Heating straight-chain alkanes with Anhyd. AlCl<sub>3</sub> and HCl gas causes skeletal isomerization to branched- chain alkanes.
Q49.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recognize the reaction type: Heating a straight-chain alkane like $n$-hexane ($\text{CH}_3(\text{CH}_2)_4\text{CH}_3$) with anhydrous $\text{AlCl}_3$ and $\text{HCl}$ gas catalyzes alkane isomerization.
  2. Step 2 — Apply the driving force: Straight-chain alkanes rearrange via carbocation intermediates into more thermodynamically stable branched-chain isomers with the same molecular formula ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_{14}$).
  3. Step 3 — Identify the major product X: $n$-Hexane isomerizes to branched hexanes, with 2-methylpentane, $\text{CH}_3-\text{CH(CH}_3)-(\text{CH}_2)_2\text{CH}_3$, listed among the options as the major branched isomer.
  4. Step 4 — Match with options: $\text{CH}_3-\text{CH(CH}_3)-(\text{CH}_2)_2\text{CH}_3$ matches Option (b).
Q49.stepsLatex:
CH3(CH2)4CH3 −A−n−h−yd−.−A−lC−l−3/−H−C−l−,∆→ CH3 − CH(CH3) − (CH2)2 − CH3 (2-methylpentane, ma-
jor isomer (b)).
Q49.trapHtml: This is a direct NCERT Hydrocarbons reaction — no chlorination or cyclization occurs.

Q50.subtopic: Double Ring Expansion of Spiro/Bicyclic Alcohol
Q50.conceptHtml: Carbocations adjacent to strained 4- and 5-membered rings undergo sequential 1, 2-alkyl shifts (ring expansion) to relieve angle strain until stable 6-membered rings are formed.
Q50.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Initial carbocation formation: Protonation of the $-\text{OH}$ group in cyclobutyl(cyclopentyl)methanol by $\text{H}^+$ followed by loss of $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ generates a $2^\circ$ carbocation directly attached to both the 4-membered ring (A) and the 5-membered ring (B).
  2. Step 2 — First ring expansion (Ring A): Because a 4-membered ring has much higher angle strain than a 5-membered ring, ring A expands first (4-membered $\to$ 5-membered) to relieve strain, followed by a 1,2-hydride shift to place the positive charge on the $3^\circ$ carbon attached to ring B.
  3. Step 3 — Subsequent ring expansions to strain-free 6-membered rings: With the carbocation adjacent to the 5-membered ring B, ring B expands to a 6-membered ring (5 $\to$ 6). Another hydride shift brings the carbocation adjacent to the remaining 5-membered ring A, which also expands to a 6-membered ring (5 $\to$ 6), giving a strain-free system of two 6-membered rings prior to $\beta$-deprotonation.
  4. Step 4 — Match with options: Finally, both rings become six-membered each, confirming Option (a).
Q50.stepsLatex:
1. Protonation of −OH and loss of H2O forms a 2◦ carbocation between the 4-membered (A) and 5-membered
(B) rings.
2. First ring expansion relieves the 4-membered ring strain (A: 4 → 5), and a subsequent hydride/alkyl shift
expands B (5 → 6) and A (5 → 6), forming a fused 6, 6-bicyclic alkene (octalin).
3. Thus, finally both rings become six-membered each.
Q50.trapHtml: A 6-membered ring has minimal angle/torsional strain; expansion does NOT proceed to 7-membered rings.
Q50.finalAnsHtml: (a) Finally both rings will become six membered each.

Q51.conceptHtml: NaHCO<sub>3</sub> deprotonates −COOH to −COO<sup>−</sup>; Br<sub>2</sub> forms a cyclic bromonium ion on the alkene, which is attacked intramolecularly by −COO<sup>−</sup> (5-exo-trig) to form a γ-lactone.
Q51.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Deprotonation of the carboxylic acid: Pent-4-enoic acid ($\text{CH}_2=\text{CH}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{COOH}$) reacts with the mild base $\text{NaHCO}_3$ to form the nucleophilic carboxylate anion ($\text{CH}_2=\text{CH}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{COO}^-$).
  2. Step 2 — Bromonium ion formation: Electrophilic addition of $\text{Br}_2$ across the terminal $\text{C}=\text{C}$ double bond generates a cyclic 3-membered bromonium ion intermediate.
  3. Step 3 — Intramolecular bromolactonization: The tethered carboxylate oxygen attacks the more substituted internal carbon of the bromonium ion intramolecularly (a kinetically favored 5-exo-tet cyclization, much faster than external $\text{Br}^-$ attack) to form the 5-membered cyclic ester (bromolactone) with a $-\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$ substituent.
  4. Step 4 — Match with options: This 5-membered bromolactone is depicted in Option (c).
Q51.stepsLatex:
1. CH2 = CH − CH2 − CH2 − COOH + NaHCO3 → CH2 = CH − CH2 − CH2 − COO−.
2. Br2 forms the terminal bromonium ion; intramolecular nucleophilic attack at the internal carbon C4 closes a
5-membered γ-lactone ring with a −CH2Br substituent (c).
Q51.trapHtml: Intramolecular 5-membered lactone formation is much faster than intermolecular Br<sup>−</sup> attack!

Q52.conceptHtml: Protonation of the alkene generates a 3<sup>°</sup> carbocation on the ring, which is trapped intramolecularly by the −OH group to form a 6-membered cyclic ether (pyran ring).
Q52.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Carbocation generation from the alcohol: Protonation of the secondary $-\text{OH}$ group by $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$ followed by loss of $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ forms a $2^\circ$ carbocation directly adjacent to the bulky tert-butyl ($-\text{C}(\text{CH}_3)_3$) group.
  2. Step 2 — 1,2-Methyl shift to a $3^\circ$ carbocation: A rapid 1,2-methyl migration from the tert-butyl carbon converts the $2^\circ$ carbocation into a more stable $3^\circ$ carbocation, $-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH(CH}_3)\text{C}^+(\text{CH}_3)_2$.
  3. Step 3 — Intramolecular electrophilic cyclization: The electron-rich cyclohexene $\pi$-bond attacks this $3^\circ$ carbocation intramolecularly to close a strain-free fused 6-membered ring (forming a 6,6-bicyclic octalin skeleton with a $3^\circ$ bridgehead carbocation).
  4. Step 4 — Deprotonation to the Zaitsev alkene: Loss of a bridgehead $\beta$-proton yields the most substituted (tetrasubstituted) bridgehead alkene, which matches Option (b).
Q52.stepsLatex:
1. Protonation of the cyclohexene C = C gives the 3◦ carbocation at the carbon bearing the side chain.
2. The side-chain −OH (with a tert-butyl/isopropyl group adjacent) attacks the 3◦ carbocation intramolecularly
to close a stable 6-membered oxane/chromane-type ring (b).
Q52.trapHtml: Intramolecular nucleophilic trapping of a 3<sup>°</sup> carbocation by −OH beats external H<sub>2</sub>O attack.

Q53.conceptHtml: HF protonates methylenecyclohexane to give the 3<sup>°</sup> 1-methylcyclohexyl carbocation, which alkylates benzene.
Q53.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Protonation of the alkene: In the presence of $\text{HF}$ and heat, the exocyclic double bond of methylenecyclohexane is protonated at the terminal $=\text{CH}_2$ carbon to generate the stable $3^\circ$ 1-methylcyclohexyl carbocation.
  2. Step 2 — Friedel–Crafts alkylation of benzene: Benzene acts as a nucleophile and attacks the $3^\circ$ 1-methylcyclohexyl carbocation via electrophilic aromatic substitution, followed by loss of $\text{H}^+$ to restore aromaticity.
  3. Step 3 — Identify the major product X: Both the phenyl ring and the methyl group end up attached to the same carbon (C1) of the cyclohexane ring, forming (1-methylcyclohexyl)benzene.
  4. Step 4 — Match with options: (1-Methylcyclohexyl)benzene is shown in Option (d).
Q53.stepsLatex:
1. Methylenecyclohexane + H+ → 1-methylcyclohexyl cation (3◦).
2. Electrophilic attack on benzene yields 1-methyl-1-phenylcyclohexane (d).
Q53.trapHtml: Protonation gives the 3<sup>°</sup> carbocation inside the ring, so the phenyl ring attaches to the same carbon as the methyl group!

Q54.subtopic: Cis vs Trans But-2-yne Reduction Properties
Q54.conceptHtml: But-2-yne + H<sub>2</sub>/Pd − C gives cis-but-2-ene (A, µ ̸= 0, higher b.p., lower m.p.); Na/liq. NH<sub>3</sub> gives trans- but-2-ene (B, µ = 0, lower b.p., higher m.p.).
Q54.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify products A and B: Partial hydrogenation of but-2-yne with 1 mol $\text{H}_2$ over $\text{Pd/C}$ gives syn-addition, so A = cis-but-2-ene. Reduction with $\text{Na/liq. NH}_3$ (Birch reduction) gives anti-addition, so B = trans-but-2-ene.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate statements A and B: Cis-but-2-ene (A) has a net dipole moment ($\mu \neq 0$), making it more polar and more soluble in polar solvents than non-polar trans-but-2-ene (B, $\mu = 0$) — so statement A is correct. Due to dipole–dipole attractions and poorer crystal packing, cis-but-2-ene (A) has a higher boiling point and lower melting point than trans-but-2-ene (B) — so statement B is correct.
  3. Step 3 — Evaluate statements C and D: Statement C wrongly claims the dipole moment of A is zero (in fact, $\mu_A > 0$ and $\mu_B = 0$) — incorrect. Statement D wrongly claims $\text{Br}_2$ adds more easily to B than A; cis-but-2-ene (A) is higher in energy due to steric repulsion and reacts faster with $\text{Br}_2$ than the more stable trans isomer (B) — incorrect.
  4. Step 4 — Match with options: The incorrect statements are C and D only, confirming Option (d).
Q54.stepsLatex:
• A (True): Polar cis-isomer (A) is more soluble in polar solvents than non-polar B.
• B (True): b.p. of A > B; m.p. of A < B (better packing in trans).
• C (False): Dipole moment of A (cis) is non-zero (not zero!).
• D (False): More electron-rich/strained cis (A) adds Br2 faster than trans (B).
Incorrect statements: C and D only.
Q54.trapHtml: Verify both parts of every statement: C falsely claims µ(A) = 0, and D reverses Br<sub>2</sub> addition reactivity.

Q55.format: Single-Choice MCQ | C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>8</sub> → 2 mol OHC − CH<sub>2</sub> − CHO
Q55.conceptHtml: Methane dicarbaldehyde is malondialdehyde (OHC − CH<sub>2</sub> − CHO, 3 carbons). Two moles require a sym- metrical 6-membered diene with two isolated = CH − CH<sub>2</sub> − CH = units.
Q55.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Calculate Degree of Unsaturation (DBE): For $\text{C}_6\text{H}_8$, $\text{DBE} = 6 + 1 - \frac{8}{2} = 3$.
  2. Step 2 — Determine rings and double bonds: Since 1 mole of X absorbs 2 moles of $\text{H}_2$ on catalytic hydrogenation, X contains 2 $\pi$-bonds (two $\text{C}=\text{C}$ double bonds) and therefore $3 - 2 = 1$ ring.
  3. Step 3 — Reconstruct X from ozonolysis: Ozonolysis yields 2 moles of methane dicarbaldehyde (malondialdehyde, $\text{OHC}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CHO}$). Joining two $\text{O}=\text{CH}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}=\text{O}$ units by removing the oxygens and forming $\text{C}=\text{C}$ bonds connects them into a 6-membered ring with double bonds at C1–C2 and C4–C5, which is cyclohexa-1,4-diene.
  4. Step 4 — Match with options: Cyclohexa-1,4-diene matches Option (b).
Q55.stepsLatex:
1. C6H8 absorbs 2 mol H2 =⇒ 2 π-bonds and 1 ring (DBE = 3).
2. Reductive ozonolysis of cyclohexa-1, 4-diene cleaves C1=C2 and C4=C5 to give 2 moles of OHC − CH2 − CHO
(methane dicarbaldehyde).
Q55.trapHtml: Cyclohexa-1, 3-diene would give glyoxal (OHC − CHO) + butanedial, NOT two moles of malondialde- hyde!

Q56.format: Single-Choice MCQ | trans-Ph − CH = CH − CH<sub>3</sub> → cis-Ph − CH = CH − CH<sub>3</sub>
Q56.conceptHtml: Convert alkene → vicinal dibromide (Br<sub>2</sub>) → internal alkyne (alc. KOH + NaNH<sub>2</sub>) → cis-alkene (H<sub>2</sub>/Lindlar catalyst).
Q56.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Plan the trans-to-cis conversion: Converting a trans-alkene to a cis-alkene requires first converting the alkene into an internal alkyne (removing stereochemistry) and then performing stereoselective syn-hydrogenation.
  2. Step 2 — Convert trans-alkene to alkyne: First, add $\text{Br}_2$ to $\text{Ph}-\text{CH}=\text{CH}-\text{CH}_3$ to form the vicinal dibromide ($\text{Ph}-\text{CHBr}-\text{CHBr}-\text{CH}_3$). Next, eliminate 2 equivalents of $\text{HBr}$ using alc. KOH (first elimination to vinyl bromide) followed by the stronger base $\text{NaNH}_2$ (second elimination) to obtain 1-phenylpropyne ($\text{Ph}-\text{C}\equiv\text{C}-\text{CH}_3$).
  3. Step 3 — Stereoselective reduction to the cis-alkene: Treating the internal alkyne with $\text{H}_2$ / Lindlar's catalyst performs syn-addition of 1 mole of $\text{H}_2$ to give cis-$\text{Ph}-\text{CH}=\text{CH}-\text{CH}_3$. (Using $\text{Na/liq. NH}_3$ would regenerate the trans isomer, and aq. $\text{KOH}$ favors substitution over elimination.)
  4. Step 4 — Match with options: The reagent sequence $\text{Br}_2$, alc. $\text{KOH}$, $\text{NaNH}_2$, $\text{H}_2$/Lindlar catalyst matches Option (a).

Q57.conceptHtml: Isobutene + cold H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> forms tert-butyl hydrogen sulfate (A); heating with H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> at 80<sup>°</sup>C dimerizes isobutene via (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>C<sup>+</sup> attack on another isobutene to 2, 4, 4-trimethylpent-2-ene (B).

Q58.format: Single-Choice MCQ | Count E2 alkene isomers (incl. cis/trans)

  2. Step 2 — Check options (a), (b), and (c): 2-Bromo-3,3-dimethylpentane has no $\beta$-H on C3, giving only 1 alkene (3,3-dimethylpent-1-ene). 2-Bromopropane has equivalent $\beta$-carbons, giving only 1 alkene (propene). 1-Bromo-2-methylbutane has only one $\beta$-carbon (C2), giving only 1 alkene (2-methylbut-1-ene).
  3. Step 3 — Check option (d), 2-bromopentane: Elimination toward C1 gives pent-1-ene (1 isomer), while elimination toward C3 gives pent-2-ene, which exists as both cis-pent-2-ene and trans-pent-2-ene (2 isomers), giving a total of 3 isomeric alkenes.
  4. Step 4 — Match with options: 2-Bromopentane gives the maximum number of isomeric alkenes (3), confirming Option (d).

Q60.subtopic: Carbocation Ring Expansion (4 → 5) on HBr Addition
Q60.conceptHtml: Protonation of a vinyl group attached to a strained 4-membered ring generates a 3<sup>°</sup> cyclobutylcarbinyl cation, which undergoes 1, 2-alkyl shift (ring expansion to 5-membered ring) followed by hydride shift?   2. Step 2 — Ring expansion to relieve angle strain: A ring $\text{C}-\text{C}$ bond migrates onto the carbocation carbon (4-membered $\to$ 5-membered ring expansion), forming the 2,2-dimethylcyclopentyl $2^\circ$ carbocation.
  3. Step 3 — 1,2-Methyl shift and bromide capture: The $2^\circ$ cyclopentyl carbocation undergoes a rapid 1,2-methyl shift to form the much more stable $3^\circ$ 1,2-dimethylcyclopentyl carbocation. Attack by $\text{Br}^-$ gives the major product A = 1-bromo-1,2-dimethylcyclopentane.
  4. Step 4 — Match with options: 1-Bromo-1,2-dimethylcyclopentane is shown in Option (b).
