Q62.format: Numerical | Alkane requiring 8 mol O<sub>2</sub> with 1 monochloro product
Q62.conceptHtml: Combustion of C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n+2</sub>: n + <sup>2n</sup><sub>4</sub><sup>+2</sup> = <sup>3n</sup><sub>2</sub><sup>+1</sup> = 8 =⇒ n = 5 (C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub>).
Q62.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Find the molecular formula from combustion: The balanced combustion of an alkane $\text{C}_n\text{H}_{2n+2}$ requires $\frac{3n+1}{2}$ moles of $\text{O}_2$ per mole of alkane. Setting $\frac{3n+1}{2} = 8$ gives $3n + 1 = 16 \implies n = 5$, so alkane (Y) is an isomer of $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{12}$.
  2. Step 2 — Identify the exact isomer (Y): Since free-radical chlorination ($\text{Cl}_2/h\nu$) gives only one monochlorinated product (Z), all 12 hydrogen atoms in (Y) must be chemically equivalent. The only $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{12}$ isomer with all equivalent hydrogens is neopentane (2,2-dimethylpropane), $\text{C}(\text{CH}_3)_4$.
  3. Step 3 — Count primary ($1^\circ$) carbon atoms: In $\text{C}(\text{CH}_3)_4$, the central carbon is quaternary ($4^\circ$) and each of the four outer $-\text{CH}_3$ carbons is bonded to only one other carbon, making them primary ($1^\circ$) carbons.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The total number of primary carbon atoms in (Y) is 4.

Q63.format: Numerical | Total structural monochloro isomers from all C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub> cycloalkanes
Q63.conceptHtml: Isomers of C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub> that do NOT decolorize KMnO<sub>4</sub> are the saturated cycloalkanes (DBE = 1).
Q63.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the class of isomers: For $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}$, $\text{DBE} = 1$. Because these isomers do not decolorize $\text{KMnO}_4$ (no $\text{C}=\text{C}$ double bonds), they must be cycloalkanes.
  2. Step 2 — List all 5 structural cycloalkane isomers of $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}$: The five cycloalkanes are (1) cyclopentane, (2) methylcyclobutane, (3) ethylcyclopropane, (4) 1,1-dimethylcyclopropane, and (5) 1,2-dimethylcyclopropane.
  3. Step 3 — Count distinct structural monochloro derivatives for each: Cyclopentane gives 1; methylcyclobutane gives 4 (methyl, C1, C2/C4, C3); ethylcyclopropane gives 4 ($-\text{CH}_3$, $-\text{CH}_2-$, C1, C2/C3); 1,1-dimethylcyclopropane gives 2 (methyl, ring $\text{CH}_2$); and 1,2-dimethylcyclopropane gives 3 (methyl, C1/C2, C3).
  4. Step 4 — Sum and confirm the final answer: Total structural monochloro compounds $= 1 + 4 + 4 + 2 + 3 =$ 14.

Q64.subtopic: Numerical — Total Atoms in Alkane from Combustion
Q64.conceptHtml: <sup>3n</sup><sub>2</sub><sup>+1</sup> = 8 =⇒ n = 5 (C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub>).
Q64.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Write the general combustion equation: For an alkane $\text{C}_n\text{H}_{2n+2}$, complete combustion is $\text{C}_n\text{H}_{2n+2} + \left(\frac{3n+1}{2}\right)\text{O}_2 \to n\text{CO}_2 + (n+1)\text{H}_2\text{O}$.
  2. Step 2 — Solve for $n$: Given that 1 mole of alkane requires 8 moles of $\text{O}_2$, we have $\frac{3n+1}{2} = 8 \implies 3n + 1 = 16 \implies n = 5$.
  3. Step 3 — Determine the formula and total atoms: Substituting $n = 5$ gives pentane, $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{12}$, which has 5 carbon atoms and 12 hydrogen atoms.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The sum of carbon and hydrogen atoms is $5 + 12 =$ 17.

Q64.trapHtml: Check the wording: Sum of number of carbon and hydrogen atoms”, not molar mass.

Q65.conceptHtml: Benzene + CH<sub>3</sub> − C(= O) − CH<sub>2</sub> − CH<sub>2</sub> − C(= O)Cl/AlCl<sub>3</sub> gives the 1, 4-diketone Ph − C(= O) − CH<sub>2</sub> − CH<sub>2</sub> − C(= O) − CH<sub>3</sub> (P); heating with aq. NaOH performs intramolecular aldol condensa- tion to 3-phenylcyclopent-2-en-1-one (Q).
Q65.stepsHtml:

Step 1 — Friedel–Crafts acylation to form (P): Benzene reacts with 4-oxopentanoyl chloride ($\text{CH}_3-\text{CO}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{COCl}$) in the presence of anhydrous $\text{AlCl}_3$ to give the 1,4-diketone (P) = 1-phenylpentane-1,4-dione ($\text{Ph}-\text{CO}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{CO}-\text{CH}_3$).
  2. Step 2 — Intramolecular aldol condensation to form (Q): Heating (P) with $\text{aq. NaOH}$ deprotonates the terminal $-\text{CH}_3$ (forming an enolate that attacks the benzoyl carbonyl carbon) to close a stable 5-membered ring, followed by dehydration to yield (Q) = 3-phenylcyclopent-2-en-1-one.
  3. Step 3 — Calculate the molecular formula and molar mass of (Q): Combining the phenyl group ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5-$) and cyclopentenone ring ($-\text{C}_5\text{H}_5\text{O}$) gives $\text{C}_{11}\text{H}_{10}\text{O}$, with molar mass $= 11(12) + 10(1) + 16 = 158\text{ g mol}^{-1}$.
  4. Step 4 — Compute % oxygen and confirm the answer: $\%\text{ O} = \frac{16}{158} \times 100\% \approx 10.13\%$, which rounds to the nearest integer 10.

Q66.format: Numerical | C : Br atom ratio 3 : 1 after adding 1 mol Br<sub>2</sub>
Q66.conceptHtml: Adding 1 mol Br<sub>2</sub> gives a dibromide (2 Br atoms); C: Br = 3: 1 =⇒ 6 C atoms (cyclohexene → 1, 2-dibromocyclohexane, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>10</sub>Br<sub>2</sub>).
Q66.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Deduce the formula of dibromide (Y): Since cycloalkene (X) consumes 1 mole of $\text{Br}_2$ per mole of (X), product (Y) is a dibromocycloalkane of formula $\text{C}_n\text{H}_{2n-2}\text{Br}_2$ containing exactly 2 bromine atoms.
  2. Step 2 — Use the $\text{C}:\text{Br}$ atomic ratio: Given $\text{C}:\text{Br} = 3:1$ in (Y) and 2 $\text{Br}$ atoms per molecule, the number of carbon atoms is $n = 3 \times 2 = 6$. Thus, (Y) is 1,2-dibromocyclohexane, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{10}\text{Br}_2$.
  3. Step 3 — Calculate the molar mass of (Y): $M(\text{C}_6\text{H}_{10}\text{Br}_2) = 6(12) + 10(1) + 2(80) = 72 + 10 + 160 = 242\text{ g mol}^{-1}$.
  4. Step 4 — Compute % bromine and confirm the answer: $\%\text{ Br} = \frac{160}{242} \times 100\% \approx 66.12\%$, which rounds to the nearest integer 66.
Q66.trapHtml: A cycloalkene C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>10</sub> has 10 H atoms (not 12!), so M = 242 g mol<sup>−1</sup>.

Q67.subtopic: Numerical — Aromatic C9H12 Isomers with 4 Non-Aliphatic
Q67.conceptHtml: Negative Baeyer’s test with C<sub>9</sub>H<sub>12</sub> (DBE = 4) means benzene derivatives (aromatic hydrocarbons). Four different non-aliphatic substitution sites” means 4 chemically non-equivalent aromatic ring C–H positions.

  2. Step 2 — List all 8 aromatic isomers of $\text{C}_9\text{H}_{12}$: They are propylbenzene, isopropylbenzene, o-ethylmethylbenzene, m-ethylmethylbenzene, p-ethylmethylbenzene, 1,2,3-trimethylbenzene, 1,2,4-trimethylbenzene, and 1,3,5-trimethylbenzene.
  3. Step 3 — Count distinct non-aliphatic (aromatic ring) substitution sites for each: Monosubstituted benzenes have 3 distinct ring sites (o, m, p); p-ethylmethylbenzene has 2; 1,2,3-trimethylbenzene has 2; 1,2,4-trimethylbenzene has 3; and 1,3,5-trimethylbenzene has 1. Only o-ethylmethylbenzene (C3, C4, C5, C6 all distinct) and m-ethylmethylbenzene (C2, C4, C5, C6 all distinct) have exactly 4 different aromatic ring substitution sites.

Q68.subtopic: Numerical — Sum of σ and π Bonds in Hex-1,3-dien-5-yne
Q68.format: Numerical | CH<sub>2</sub> = CH − CH = CH − C ≡ CH
Q68.conceptHtml: Formula of hex-1, 3-dien-5-yne: C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>6</sub> (12 atoms, acyclic).
Q68.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Write the condensed structure: Hex-1,3-dien-5-yne is $\text{CH}_2=\text{CH}-\text{CH}=\text{CH}-\text{C}\equiv\text{CH}$, which has the molecular formula $\text{C}_6\text{H}_6$ (6 carbons and 6 hydrogens).
  2. Step 2 — Count the $\sigma$ bonds: An open-chain molecule with $N$ atoms has $N - 1$ $\sigma$ bonds. Here, there are $5\text{ C}-\text{C}$ and $6\text{ C}-\text{H}$ $\sigma$ bonds, giving $5 + 6 = 11\ \sigma$ bonds.
  3. Step 3 — Count the $\pi$ bonds: Each $\text{C}=\text{C}$ double bond has $1\ \pi$ bond (2 double bonds $\to 2\ \pi$ bonds) and the $\text{C}\equiv\text{C}$ triple bond has $2\ \pi$ bonds, giving $2 + 2 = 4\ \pi$ bonds.
  4. Step 4 — Sum and confirm the final answer: Total $\sigma + \pi$ bonds $= 11 + 4 =$ 15.
Q68.stepsLatex:
1. σ bonds = 12 − 1 = 11.
2. π bonds = 2 (two C=C) + 2 (one C ≡ C) = 4.
3. Total (σ + π) = 11 + 4 = 15.
Q68.trapHtml: Count carefully: 2 double bonds (2π) + 1 triple bond (2π) = 4 π bonds.

Q69.subtopic: Numerical — Reconstruction of Diene from KMnO4/H+
Q69.format: Numerical | Total σ bonds in compound ’X’
Q69.conceptHtml: ’X’ absorbs 2 mol H<sub>2</sub> (2 π-bonds). Oxidative cleavage (KMnO<sub>4</sub>/H<sup>+</sup>) gives acetone, acetic acid, and 4-oxopentanoic acid.
Q69.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Determine the unsaturation in X: Compound X absorbs 2 moles of $\text{H}_2$ on hydrogenation, indicating it contains 2 $\text{C}=\text{C}$ double bonds (and is acyclic since oxidative cleavage breaks it into 3 separate fragments).
  2. Step 2 — Reconstruct X from the $\text{KMnO}_4/\text{H}^+$ cleavage products: The three products are acetone ($\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_3$, 3 C), acetic acid ($\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$, 2 C), and 4-oxopentanoic acid ($\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$, 5 C). Joining the carbonyl/carboxyl ends back into double bonds gives $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C}=\text{C}(\text{CH}_3)-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}=\text{CH}-\text{CH}_3$ (2,3-dimethylocta-2,6-diene).
  3. Step 3 — Find the molecular formula and $\sigma$ bond count: Total carbons $= 3 + 2 + 5 = 10$. An open-chain diene ($\text{C}_n\text{H}_{2n-2}$) has formula $\text{C}_{10}\text{H}_{18}$, containing $10 + 18 = 28$ atoms in total.
  4. Step 4 — Compute $\sigma$ bonds and confirm the answer: For any acyclic molecule, number of $\sigma$ bonds $= (\text{total atoms}) - 1 = 28 - 1 =$ 27.

Q70.subtopic: Numerical — π Electrons in Symmetric C6H6 Isomer
Q70.format: Numerical | C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>6</sub> taking 4 mol H<sub>2</sub> and giving 1 monobromo product
Q70.conceptHtml: C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>6</sub> has DBE = 4. Taking 4 mol H<sub>2</sub> means all 4 degrees of unsaturation are π-bonds (acyclic)!
Q70.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Calculate Degree of Unsaturation (DBE): For $\text{C}_6\text{H}_6$, $\text{DBE} = 6 + 1 - \frac{6}{2} = 4$.
  2. Step 2 — Determine the number of $\pi$ bonds: Taking up 4 moles of $\text{H}_2$ per mole for complete hydrogenation means all 4 degrees of unsaturation are $\pi$ bonds (0 rings, i.e., an acyclic hydrocarbon).
  3. Step 3 — Verify the symmetric structure: Because it gives only one monobromo derivative, all 6 hydrogens must be equivalent — matching hexa-2,4-diyne ($\text{CH}_3-\text{C}\equiv\text{C}-\text{C}\equiv\text{C}-\text{CH}_3$), which has 2 triple bonds $= 4\ \pi$ bonds.
  4. Step 4 — Count $\pi$ electrons and confirm the answer: Each $\pi$ bond contains $2\ \pi$ electrons, so $4 \times 2 =$ 8 $\pi$ electrons.
Q70.stepsLatex:
1. CH3 − C ≡ C − C ≡ C − CH3 (hexa-2, 4-diyne) has 4 π-bonds (= 8 π electrons), absorbs 4 mol H2, and has all
6 H atoms equivalent (1 monobromo derivative).
2. Note: NTA also accepted 6 in the official final key.
Q70.trapHtml: Benzene only takes 3 mol H<sub>2</sub> (not 4), so hexa-2, 4-diyne (8 π e<sup>−</sup>) is the exact chemical match; NTA keyed 8 or 6”.

Q71.format: Numerical | Count compounds unable to undergo FC reaction
Q71.conceptHtml: Friedel–Crafts reactions fail for strongly deactivated rings (−NO<sub>2</sub>) and for anilines (−NH<sub>2</sub> forms an insoluble salt/adduct with AlCl<sub>3</sub>).
Q71.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall why certain arenes fail Friedel–Crafts reactions: Strongly electron-withdrawing meta-directors (like $-\text{NO}_2$) deactivate the ring too strongly, while basic amino groups ($-\text{NH}_2$) form an acid–base complex ($-\text{NH}_2^+\text{AlCl}_3^-$) with the Lewis acid catalyst $\text{AlCl}_3$ that strongly deactivates the ring.
  2. Step 2 — Check compounds that DO undergo Friedel–Crafts reactions: Toluene, xylene, and cumene have activating alkyl groups and react readily; chlorobenzene is weakly deactivated ($-I > +M$) but still undergoes Friedel–Crafts reactions.
  3. Step 3 — Identify compounds that CANNOT undergo Friedel–Crafts reactions: The four unreactive compounds are nitrobenzene, aniline, m-nitroaniline, and m-dinitrobenzene.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The number of compounds that cannot undergo Friedel–Crafts reactions is 4.
Q71.stepsLatex:
• Cannot undergo FC (4): nitrobenzene, aniline, m-nitroaniline, m-dinitrobenzene.
• Can undergo FC (4): toluene, xylene, cumene, chlorobenzene.
Q71.trapHtml: Chlorobenzene is weakly deactivated (−I > +M) and still undergoes Friedel–Crafts reactions; aniline fails due to Lewis acid-base complexation with AlCl<sub>3</sub>!

Q72.conceptHtml: KMnO<sub>4</sub> − KOH/∆ oxidizes ethylbenzene to benzoic acid (after acidification/nitration); −COOH is m- directing.
Q72.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Side-chain oxidation to form (A): Heating ethylbenzene ($\text{Ph}-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$) with alkaline $\text{KMnO}_4$ ($\text{KMnO}_4-\text{KOH}, \Delta$) oxidizes the entire benzylic alkyl side chain to a carboxyl group, yielding (A) = benzoic acid ($\text{Ph}-\text{COOH}$, upon acidification).
  2. Step 2 — Nitration to form (B): Since $-\text{COOH}$ is a meta-directing deactivating group, nitrating benzoic acid with $\text{HNO}_3/\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ produces (B) = m-nitrobenzoic acid.
  3. Step 3 — Count all $\pi$ bonds in (B): The benzene ring contributes $3\ \pi$ bonds, the $-\text{COOH}$ group ($\text{C}=\text{O}$) contributes $1\ \pi$ bond, and the $-\text{NO}_2$ group ($\text{N}=\text{O}$) contributes $1\ \pi$ bond.
  4. Step 4 — Sum and confirm the final answer: Total $\pi$ bonds in B $= 3 + 1 + 1 =$ 5.

Q73.format: Numerical | Ratio of O to Br atoms in Q (×10<sup>−1</sup>)
Q73.conceptHtml: −OC<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub> is a strong o/p-directing activator (p-product major due to sterics); subsequent 2 Br<sub>2</sub>/Fe bromi- nates both ortho positions to −OC<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>.

Due to steric hindrance at the ortho positions, nitration with $\text{HNO}_3/\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ gives P = 4-nitrophenetole (1-ethoxy-4-nitrobenzene) as the major product.
  2. Step 2 — Dibromination to form Q: In P, the activating $-\text{OC}_2\text{H}_5$ directs electrophiles to C2 and C6 (which are also meta to the $-\text{NO}_2$ group, so both groups reinforce the same sites). Treating P with $2\text{Br}_2/\text{Fe}$ yields Q = 2,6-dibromo-1-ethoxy-4-nitrobenzene.

  4. Step 4 — Compute the ratio and confirm the answer: $\frac{\text{Number of O atoms}}{\text{Number of Br atoms}} = \frac{3}{2} = 1.5 = \mathbf{15} \times 10^{-1}$, so the answer is 15.

Q74.conceptHtml: But-2-yne + Na/liq. NH<sub>3</sub> gives trans-but-2-ene; cold dil. KMnO<sub>4</sub> (273 K) performs syn-dihydroxylation to a 1, 2-diol.

  2. Step 2 — Cold dilute $\text{KMnO}_4$ oxidation (step ii): Cold, dilute alkaline $\text{KMnO}_4$ at $273\text{ K}$ (Baeyer's reagent) performs mild syn-dihydroxylation across the $\text{C}=\text{C}$ double bond without cleaving the carbon chain, giving P = butane-2,3-diol ($\text{CH}_3-\text{CH(OH)}-\text{CH(OH)}-\text{CH}_3$).
  3. Step 3 — Count oxygen atoms and confirm the answer: Each molecule of butane-2,3-diol contains two $-\text{OH}$ groups, so the number of oxygen atoms in P is 2.

Q75.subtopic: Numerical — E2 Elimination vs Substitution of
Q75.format: Numerical | Total π electrons in A and B
Q75.conceptHtml: Cyclohexene + Br<sub>2</sub> → 1, 2-dibromocyclohexane. With 3 eq. alc. KOH, double dehydrohalogenation gives cyclohexa-1, 3-diene (B); with 1 eq. EtO<sup>−</sup>Na<sup>+</sup>, mono-elimination gives 1-bromocyclohexene (A)? Wait: 2 π-bonds in B (4 π e<sup>−</sup>) + 1 π-bond in A? Let’s check!

1. Step 1 — Common bromination step: Cyclohexene reacts with $\text{Br}_2$ in both pathways to form trans-1,2-dibromocyclohexane.
  2. Step 2 — Determine Product B and its $\pi$ electrons: Treating trans-1,2-dibromocyclohexane with excess alc. $\text{KOH}$ (3 eq.) eliminates 2 equivalents of $\text{HBr}$ to form B = cyclohexa-1,3-diene, which contains $2\ \pi$ bonds $= 4\ \pi$ electrons.
  3. Step 3 — Determine Product A and its $\pi$ electrons: Treating trans-1,2-dibromocyclohexane with 1.0 eq. of sodium propargyloxide ($\text{HC}\equiv\text{C}-\text{CH}_2\text{O}^-\text{Na}^+$) undergoes nucleophilic substitution ($\text{S}_\text{N}2$) replacing one $-\text{Br}$ to form A = 1-bromo-2-(prop-2-yn-1-yloxy)cyclohexane, which contains one $\text{C}\equiv\text{C}$ triple bond ($2\ \pi$ bonds $= 4\ \pi$ electrons).
  4. Step 4 — Sum and confirm the final answer: Total $\pi$ electrons in A and B $= 4 + 4 =$ 8.

Q76.conceptHtml: Kolbe’s electrolysis of two carboxylates R<sub>1</sub>COONa and R<sub>2</sub>COONa produces three radical-coupling alkanes: R<sub>1</sub> − R<sub>1</sub>, R<sub>2</sub> − R<sub>2</sub>, and R<sub>1</sub> − R<sub>2</sub>.

Q78.conceptHtml: Loss of H<sub>2</sub>O gives a 2<sup>°</sup> carbocation flanked by a tert-butyl group and an isopropyl group; 1, 2-methyl shift gives a 3<sup>°</sup> carbocation that can lose β-H in multiple ways (including E/Z stereoisomers).
Q78.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Form the initial $2^\circ$ carbocation: Protonation and dehydration ($\text{H}^+, \Delta$) of alcohol A, $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}-\text{CH(OH)}-\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)_2$, produces the $2^\circ$ carbocation $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}-\text{CH}^+-\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)_2$.
  2. Step 2 — Pathway 1 (1,2-hydride shift): Shifting the tertiary $\text{H}$ from the isopropyl group forms the $3^\circ$ carbocation $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}-\text{CH}_2-\text{C}^+(\text{CH}_3)_2$. Loss of a $\beta$-proton yields 2 alkenes: $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}-\text{CH}=\text{C}(\text{CH}_3)_2$ and $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}-\text{CH}_2-\text{C}(\text{CH}_3)=\text{CH}_2$ (neither shows geometrical isomerism).
  3. Step 3 — Pathway 2 (1,2-methyl shift): Shifting a $-\text{CH}_3$ from the tert-butyl group forms the $3^\circ$ carbocation $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C}^+-\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)-\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)_2$. Loss of a $\beta$-proton yields 2 more alkenes: $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C}=\text{C}(\text{CH}_3)-\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)_2$ and $\text{CH}_2=\text{C}(\text{CH}_3)-\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)-\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)_2$ (neither shows geometrical isomerism).
  4. Step 4 — Sum and confirm the final answer: Total possible alkene products from the tertiary carbocations $= 2 + 2 =$ 4.

1. Step 1 — Calculate moles of hydrocarbon ($\text{C}_{10}\text{H}_{16}$): Molar mass $= 10(12) + 16(1) = 136\text{ g mol}^{-1}$. Moles of hydrocarbon $= \frac{17 \times 10^{-3}\text{ g}}{136\text{ g mol}^{-1}} = 1.25 \times 10^{-4}\text{ mol}$.

(The three ozonolysis fragments—acetone, formaldehyde, and $\text{OHC}-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2-\text{CO}-\text{CHO}$—also confirm an acyclic $\text{C}_{10}\text{H}_{16}$ triene with $\text{DBE} = 3$.)

  3. Step 3 — Count all isomeric monochloro derivatives (including stereoisomers): Chlorinating Set 1 gives achiral 1-chloro-2,2,5,5-tetramethylhexane (1 isomer). Chlorinating Set 2 creates a chiral center at C3, forming 3-chloro-2,2,5,5-tetramethylhexane as a $d/l$ enantiomeric pair (2 stereoisomers).
  4. Step 4 — Sum and confirm the final answer: The maximum number of isomeric monochloro derivatives is $1 + 2 =$ 3.

trapCards.title: Trap 1: Carbocation Rearrangements & Hydration Triad
trapCards.html:
• Ring Expansion & Hydride/Methyl Shifts (Q01, Q50, Q60, Q78): Acid-catalyzed hydration (H2O/H+), HX addition, and Friedel–Crafts alkylation ALWAYS re- arrange to the most stable carbocation (4 → 5 or 5 → 6 ring expansion).
  • No-Rearrangement Reagents (Q37, Q43, Q59): Oxymercuration–demercuration (OMDM, Markovnikov) and Hydroboration–oxidation (HBO, Anti-Markovnikov) proceed without carbocation rearrangement.
  • Peroxide Effect (Q11, Q23): Kharasch anti- Markovnikov addition works ONLY with HBr (never HCl or HI), and generates benzene (PhH) as a byprod- uct from (PhCOO)2.

trapCards.title: Trap 2: Ozonolysis, Oxidation & Alkyne Reduc- tions
trapCards.html:
• Reductive vs Oxidative Cleavage (Q09, Q24, Q55, Q69): O3/Zn, H2O stops at aldehy- des/ketones (= CH2 → HCHO); KMnO4/∆ oxidizes −CHO → −COOH and = CH2 → CO2.
  • Lindlar vs Birch Stereochemistry (Q15, Q41, Q54, Q56): H2/Lindlar gives cis-alkene (µ ̸= 0, higher b.p., lower m.p.); Na/liq. NH3 gives trans-alkene (µ = 0, lower b.p., higher m.p.).
  • Cold KMnO4 vs KMnO4/∆ (Q72, Q74): Cold dil. KMnO4 (273 K) gives a syn-diol; hot alk. KMnO4/∆ ox- idizes alkylbenzene side chains (with ≥ 1 benzylic H) to benzoic acid. trapCards.title: Trap 3: Benzene EAS, Friedel–Crafts & Selectivity
trapCards.html:
• Friedel–Crafts Failures (Q18, Q71): FC alky- lation/acylation fail on strongly deactivated rings (−NO2, −CF3, −COR) AND on anilines (−NH2 forms an adduct with AlCl3). Chlorobenzene does undergo FC!
  • hν vs CCl4 with Halogens (Q33, Q45): X2/hν gives free-radical substitution (3◦ > 2◦ > 1◦, or al- lylic/benzylic); X2/CCl4 gives ionic anti-addition across C = C.
  • AgCN vs KCN (Q27): AgCN yields an isocyanide (−NC), whereas KCN yields a nitrile (−CN).

trapCards.title: Trap 4: Isomer Counting & Question-Wording Traps
trapCards.html:
• Ignore Stereoisomers” vs Maximum Isomers” (Q02, Q32, Q58, Q83): Read the parenthetical! When stereoisomers are included, count cis/trans alkenes and d/l enantiomer pairs; when ignored, count constitutional isomers only.
  • Methane Exclusions (Q04): Wurtz reaction and Kolbe’s electrolysis cannot prepare CH4.

subject: Chemistry
title: Haloalkanes & Haloarenes
constantsHtml:
• Haloalkanes & Haloarenes
  • Chapter DNA & High-Yield Focus (77 Qs: 71 MCQ + 6 Numerical | 2023–2026)
  • Haloalkanes and Haloarenes is one of the highest-ROI chapters in Organic Chemistry I. Over 70% of 2023–2026 JEE Main
  • questions test: (1) SN1 vs SN2 rate orders, carbocation stability, bridgehead/vinylic/aryl inertness, and solvent effects; (2)
  • KCN vs AgCN and KNO2 vs AgNO2 ambident nucleophiles; (3) alc. KOH (E2 elimination) vs aq. KOH (SN substitution);
  • (4) named halogen-exchange and diazonium reactions (Finkelstein, Swarts, Sandmeyer, Gattermann, Wurtz–Fittig); and (5)
  • SNAr activation by o/p-NO2 groups and physical property trends (b.p., m.p., density).

formulaCards.title: 1. Classification, C–X Bond & Physical Trends
formulaCards.html:
• Allylic: CH2 = CH − CH2 − X (sp3 C next to C = C). Benzylic: Ar − CH2 − X (sp3 C next to ring).
  • Vinylic: CH2 = CH − X (sp2 C). Aryl: Ar − X (sp2 C). Both are inert to SN1/SN2.
  • C–X Bond Strength: C−F > C−Cl > C−Br > C−I. Vinylic/aryl C−Cl has partial double-bond character (sp2 C + resonance) ⇒ shorter & stronger than alkyl C − Cl.
  • Dipole Moment (µ): CH3Cl > CH3F > CH3Br > CH3I (small C − F bond length lowers q × d).
  • Boiling Point: RI > RBr > RCl > RF; increases with chain length; decreases with branching (n-butyl > isobutyl > tert-butyl).
  • Melting Point of Dichlorobenzenes: para > ortho > meta (symmetric para packs tightly in crystal lattice). Boiling point: ortho > para > meta.
  • Density: Increases with C-count, halogen mass, and poly- halogenation (RI > RBr > RCl; CH2Cl2 > H2O).

formulaCards.title: 2. Preparation & Named Reactions
formulaCards.html:
• Darzens Process: R − OH + SOCl −P−→y R − Cl + SO ↑ 2 2 +HCl ↑ (purest R − Cl; Ar − OH does not react with SOCl2/HX).
  • Lucas Reagent (HCl/ZnCl2): 3◦ > 2◦ > 1◦ alcohols.
  • Finkelstein Reaction: R − X + NaI −D−−ry−−A−ce−t−on−→e R − I + NaX ↓ (X = Cl, Br; NaCl/NaBr insoluble in acetone drives equilibrium forward via SN2).
  • Swarts Reaction: R − Br/Cl + AgF/Hg2F2/CoF2/SbF3 → R − F.
  • Hunsdiecker Reaction: RCOOAg + Br −C−C−l−4,−∆→ R − 2 Br + CO2 + AgBr (1 C less).
  • Sandmeyer Reaction: ArN+X− −C−−u2−C−l−2−/H−−C−l,−C−u−2−B−r2−/−H−B−r−,−C−u−C−N−/−K−C−N→ ArCl2, ArBr, ArCN. (ArI via KI; ArF via HBF /∆ 4 Balz–Schiemann).
  • Gattermann Reaction: ArN+X− −C−u−/−H−C−l−o−r−H−B−→r ArCl/ArBr (also Cu/KCN for ArC2N).
  • Benzylic Halogenation: PhCH −B−r−2−,−h→ν PhCH Br 3 2 (radical); PhCH −B−−r2−,−F−e,−d−a−r→k o/p-BrC H CH (EAS). 3 6 4 3

formulaCards.title: 3. S<sub>N</sub>1 vs S<sub>N</sub>2 Mechanisms
formulaCards.html:
• SN2 (Bimolecular): Rate = k[RX][Nu−] (2nd order). Single step, pentacoordinate T.S., 100% Walden inver- sion (stereospecific).
  • SN2 Reactivity: CH3X > 1◦ > 2◦ > 3◦ (sterics). Neopentyl (Me3C − CH2Cl) is 1◦ yet very slow in SN2. Benzyl/allyl halides are fast in SN2 (p-orbital conjugation in T.S.).
  • SN2 Favored By: Strong Nu−, high [Nu−], polar apro- tic solvent (DMSO, DMF, acetone).
  • SN1 (Unimolecular): Rate = k[RX] (1st order). Two steps via planar sp2 carbocation ⇒ racemisation (+ slight inversion).
  • SN1 Reactivity: Ph3C − X > Ph2CH − X > PhCH2 − X ≈ allyl > 3◦ > 2◦ > 1◦. CH3OCH2Cl (1◦) reacts fast via SN1 (resonance-stabilized oxocarbenium ion).
  • SN1 Inertness: Bridgehead halides (Bredt’s rule: cannot become planar), vinylic, and aryl halides do not give SN1 or AgNO3 precipitate.
  • Leaving Group Ability: I− > Br− > Cl− > F−. Adding NaI catalyzes R − Cl hydrolysis (Finkelstein → fast SN2).
  • NGP: β-haloamines (Et2NCH2CH2Cl) hydrolyze rapidly via cyclic aziridinium ion.

formulaCards.title: 4. Stereochemistry & Ambident Nucleophiles
formulaCards.html:
• Retention: Bond to chiral centre is not broken (e.g., R− CH(Me)CH2OH + HCl).
  • Inversion (SN2): Backside attack flips configuration; stereospecific.
  • Racemisation (SN1): Planar carbocation attacked equally from both faces ⇒ optically inactive dl-mixture (zero rotation of plane-polarized light).
  • Ambident Nucleophiles: – KCN/NaCN (ionic, C-attack) → R − CN (alkyl cyanide / nitrile). – AgCN (covalent, N-lone pair attack) → R − NC (alkyl isocyanide). – KNO2 (ionic, O-attack) → R − O − N = O (alkyl nitrite). – AgNO2 (covalent, N-attack) → R − NO2 (ni- troalkane).
  • Nucleophilicity in Polar Protic (MeOH/H2O): I− > Br− > Cl− > F− (larger, less solvated I− is stronger); RO− > PhO− > RCOO− > ClO−4 (stronger base = stronger Nu−).

formulaCards.title: 5. Elimination (E1, E2, E1cb) & Grignard ⋆ High- ROI
formulaCards.html:
• Aqueous KOH ⇒ Substitution (R − OH). Alcoholic KOH / ∆ ⇒ β-Elimination (alkene; E2, anti-periplanar).
  • Zaitsev Rule: More substituted (more stable) alkene is major (e.g., 2-bromopentane + alc. KOH → pent-2-ene).
  • Hofmann Rule: Bulky base (t-BuO−) or poor leaving group (-F, -NR+3 ) gives less substituted alkene.
  • E1 vs E2 vs E1cb: E2 = 1-step, rate = k[RX][B−], 3◦ > 2◦ > 1◦. E1 = 2-step via carbocation. E1cb = via carbanion (needs EWG β to LG).
  • Grignard Reagent (RMgX): Prepared in dry ether (Et2O). Strong base/nucleophile: – RMgX + H2O/ROH → R − H; RMgX + D2O → R − D. – RMgX + CO −H−+→ RCOOH. 2
  • Wurtz: 2RX+2Na −E−t−2−O→ R−R. Fittig: 2ArX+2Na → Ar − Ar. Wurtz–Fittig: ArX + RX + 2Na → Ar − R.

formulaCards.title: 6. Haloarenes (S<sub>N</sub>Ar, EAS) & Polyhalogens ⋆ High- ROI
formulaCards.html:
• Dow’s Process: PhCl −N−−aO−−H−,6−2−3−K−−,3−0−0−a−t−m−;−H−3−O−+→ PhOH.
  • SNAr (Addition–Elimination): Activated by o/p-NO2 groups (stabilize Meisenheimer carbanion): – 1 NO2 (p): NaOH, 443 K. – 2 NO2 (2, 4): NaOH, 368 K. – 3 NO2 (2, 4, 6): Warm H2O (picryl chloride). Meta-NO2 does not stabilize by resonance; EDG (−OMe) deactivates SNAr.
  • EAS of Haloarenes: o/p-directing (+M) but ring- deactivating (−I > +M).
  • Polyhalogen Compounds (NCERT/NTA): – CH2Cl2 (Methylene chloride): Paint remover. – CHCl3: Oxidizes in light/air to phosgene (COCl2). – CCl4: Fire extinguisher (Pyrene). – Freons (CCl2F2): Refrigerants & ACs (ozone deple- tion). – DDT: Non-biodegradable insecticide. – Gammaxene (C6H6Cl6, BHC): 6 Cl; Chloral (CCl3CHO): 3 Cl; Chloropicrin (CCl3NO2): 3 Cl.

Q01.conceptHtml: Boiling point increases with molecular mass (stronger van der Waals forces). For dichlorobenzenes, sym- metric para-isomer has the highest melting point due to close crystal packing, while meta-isomer has a slightly lower boiling point than para (and ortho is highest).
Q01.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement I (Boiling point of alkyl iodides): In the homologous series $\text{CH}_3\text{I}$, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{I}$, and $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{I}$, all three compounds share the same halogen atom ($-\text{I}$), while the alkyl chain length and molecular mass increase progressively. Greater molecular mass and surface area strengthen intermolecular van der Waals (London dispersion) forces, so the boiling point order is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{I} > \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{I} > \text{CH}_3\text{I}$. Hence, Statement I is true.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement II (Melting point comparison): The first structure shown is p-dichlorobenzene ($1,4$-dichlorobenzene) and the second is o-dichlorobenzene ($1,2$-dichlorobenzene). Because p-dichlorobenzene is highly symmetrical, its molecules pack much more tightly in the crystal lattice, requiring more thermal energy to melt (m.p. $\approx 323\text{ K}$ vs. $\approx 256\text{ K}$ for o-dichlorobenzene).
  3. Step 3 — Evaluate Statement II (Boiling point comparison): In the liquid phase, crystal packing no longer dominates; instead, polarity matters. p-Dichlorobenzene has zero net dipole moment ($\mu = 0$) due to symmetry, whereas o-dichlorobenzene is polar ($\mu \neq 0$) and has stronger dipole–dipole attractions, giving p-dichlorobenzene a slightly lower boiling point ($\approx 448\text{ K}$) than o-dichlorobenzene ($\approx 453\text{ K}$). Hence, Statement II is also true.
  4. Step 4 — Final Conclusion: Both Statement I and Statement II are true, which corresponds to option (a).

surface area increases van der Waals dispersion forces, so Statement I is true.
Step 2: Evaluate Statement II: p-Dichlorobenzene is symmetric and packs tightly in the crystal lattice, giving a
higher m.p. (323 K) than o-dichlorobenzene (256 K). Its b.p. (448 K) is higher than m-dichlorobenzene (446 K),
Wait—check NCERT Table: o-dichlorobenzene b.p. = 453 K, m-dichlorobenzene b.p. = 446 K, p-dichlorobenzene
b.p. = 448 K? In NTA/NCERT, Statement II is marked true (or wait: p vs m b.p. is 448 vs 446 K, yet NTA official
key is (A): Both Statement I and Statement II are true, treating p-isomer as lower dipole moment than o-isomer
and lower b.p. in their comparison).

Q02.conceptHtml: 3-Phenylpropene (Ph−CH<sub>2</sub> −CH = CH<sub>2</sub>) undergoes Markovnikov addition with HBr via a 2<sup>°</sup> carbocation, which rearranges via 1,2-hydride shift to a resonance-stabilized benzylic carbocation, giving 1-bromo-1-phenylpropane (which has a chiral carbon!). + 1,2-H<sup>−</sup> shift + Br<sup>−</sup>
Q02.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Analyze Statement I (Addition of $\text{HBr}$ to $3$-phenylpropene): $3$-Phenylpropene ($\text{Ph}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2$) undergoes electrophilic addition with $\text{HBr}$. Protonation at the terminal carbon first forms the $2^\circ$ carbocation $\text{Ph}-\text{CH}_2-\overset{+}{\text{C}}\text{H}-\text{CH}_3$, which quickly undergoes a $1,2$-hydride shift to form the much more stable resonance-stabilized $2^\circ$ benzylic carbocation $\text{Ph}-\overset{+}{\text{C}}\text{H}-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$.
  2. Step 2 — Check product class and chirality: Nucleophilic attack by $\text{Br}^-$ on the benzylic carbocation gives $1$-bromo-$1$-phenylpropane ($\text{Ph}-\text{CH(Br)}-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$). This is a secondary ($2^\circ$) alkyl bromide, and the $\text{C}-1$ carbon is bonded to four different groups ($-\text{Ph}$, $-\text{H}$, $-\text{Br}$, and $-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$), making it chiral. Hence, Statement I is true.
  3. Step 3 — Analyze Statement II (Sandmeyer vs. Gattermann reaction): The Sandmeyer reaction uses $\text{Cu}_2\text{Cl}_2/\text{HCl}$, $\text{Cu}_2\text{Br}_2/\text{HBr}$, or $\text{CuCN}/\text{KCN}$ on diazonium salts ($\text{ArN}_2^+\text{X}^-$) to prepare aryl chlorides, aryl bromides, and aryl cyanides ($\text{ArCN}$). In contrast, the Gattermann reaction uses copper powder with $\text{HCl}$ or $\text{HBr}$ to prepare aryl chlorides and aryl bromides only—it is not used for preparing aryl cyanides. Hence, Statement II is false.
  4. Step 4 — Final Conclusion: Statement I is true but Statement II is false, confirming option (c).
Q02.stepsLatex:
Step 1: Statement I: Ph − CH2 − CH = CH2 + H+ → Ph − CH2 − CH − CH3 −−−−−−−−→ Ph − CH − CH2CH3 −−→
Ph − CH(Br) − CH2CH3. The C-1 carbon has four different groups (Ph, H, Br, Et), so it is chiral! Statement I is
true.
Step 2: Statement II: Both Sandmeyer (Cu2Cl2/HCl, CuCN/KCN) and Gattermann (Cu/HCl) prepare ArCl;
however, per NCERT, Gattermann reaction is restricted to ArCl and ArBr (not aryl cyanides). Thus Statement II
is false.
Q02.trapHtml: Carbocation rearrangement in 3-phenylpropene gives a chiral benzylic bromide, and NCERT restricts Gattermann to Cl/Br only. Verified Answer: (C) Statement I is true but Statement II is false

Q03.conceptHtml: Direct reagent-to-reaction mapping from NCERT.
Q03.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Match Finkelstein and Swarts reactions (Halogen exchange): The Finkelstein reaction converts alkyl chlorides or bromides into alkyl iodides using $\text{NaI}$ in dry acetone: $\text{R}-\text{X} + \text{NaI} \xrightarrow{\text{dry acetone}} \text{R}-\text{I} + \text{NaX}$, so A–III. The Swarts reaction prepares alkyl fluorides by heating alkyl bromides/chlorides with metallic fluorides such as $\text{SbF}_3$, $\text{AgF}$, or $\text{Hg}_2\text{F}_2$, so B–I.
  2. Step 2 — Match Sandmeyer’s reaction: Sandmeyer’s reaction converts an arenediazonium salt ($\text{ArN}_2^+\text{Cl}^-$) into an aryl chloride using cuprous chloride ($\text{Cu}_2\text{Cl}_2/\text{HCl}$), releasing $\text{N}_2$ gas, so C–IV.
  3. Step 3 — Match Fittig reaction: The Fittig reaction couples two aryl halide molecules in the presence of sodium metal in dry ether ($2\text{Ar}-\text{X} + 2\text{Na} \xrightarrow{\text{dry ether}} \text{Ar}-\text{Ar} + 2\text{NaX}$) to form diaryl compounds like biphenyl, so D–II.
  4. Step 4 — Final Conclusion: Combining the matches gives A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II, which is option (b).

Step 2: Swarts reaction uses SbF3 (or AgF, Hg F2, CoF2) ⇒ B–I.

Q04.conceptHtml: Alcoholic KOH favours β-elimination; S<sub>N</sub>1 rate depends on carbocation stability; phenols do not react with SOCl<sub>2</sub> due to partial C − O double bond character.
Q04.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Check Statements A and B: In Statement A, alcohol is less polar than water, and alcoholic $\text{KOH}$ generates alkoxide/hydroxide ions that act primarily as strong bases to favour $\beta$-elimination (dehydrohalogenation) of $\text{R}-\text{X}$ into alkenes. Thus, A is correct. In Statement B, $\text{S}_\text{N}1$ reactivity follows carbocation stability: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5-\overset{+}{\text{C}}\text{H}-\text{C}_6\text{H}_5$ (stabilized by two phenyl rings) is far more stable than $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5-\overset{+}{\text{C}}\text{H}_2$ (one phenyl ring), so $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH(Cl)C}_6\text{H}_5 > \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$. Statement B gives the reverse order, so B is incorrect.
  2. Step 2 — Check Statements C and D: In Statement C, unsubstituted aryl halides ($\text{Ar}-\text{X}$) are far less reactive towards nucleophilic substitution than alkyl halides due to partial double-bond character of $\text{C}-\text{X}$ and $sp^2$ hybridization; thus C is incorrect. In Statement D, both vinyl chloride ($\text{CH}_2=\text{CH}-\text{Cl}$) and allyl chloride ($\text{CH}_2=\text{CH}-\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$) contain a $\text{C}=\text{C}$ double bond (haloalkenes), not a triple bond (haloalkyne); thus D is incorrect.
  3. Step 3 — Check Statement E: Aliphatic alcohols react smoothly with thionyl chloride ($\text{R}-\text{OH} + \text{SOCl}_2 \rightarrow \text{R}-\text{Cl} + \text{SO}_2\uparrow + \text{HCl}\uparrow$). However, phenols ($\text{Ar}-\text{OH}$) do not form $\text{Ar}-\text{Cl}$ with $\text{SOCl}_2$ because the $\text{C}-\text{O}$ bond has partial double-bond character due to resonance with the benzene ring. Thus, E is correct.
  4. Step 4 — Final Conclusion: Only statements A and E are correct, confirming option (c).

Q05.subtopic: SN1 Reactivity: Benzyl vs Ethyl Chloride
Q05.conceptHtml: Resonance stabilization in benzyl carbocation (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CH<sup>+</sup><sub>2</sub> ) is far stronger than hyperconjugation (3 α-H) in ethyl carbocation (CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sup>+</sup><sub>2</sub> ).
Q05.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the rate-determining step of $\text{S}_\text{N}1$: In an $\text{S}_\text{N}1$ reaction, the rate-determining step is the slow ionization of the $\text{C}-\text{X}$ bond to form a carbocation intermediate. The more stable the carbocation, the lower the activation energy and the faster the reaction.
  2. Step 2 — Compare carbocation stability (Statement II): Ethyl chloride ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$) forms the $1^\circ$ ethyl carbocation ($\text{CH}_3\overset{+}{\text{C}}\text{H}_2$), which is weakly stabilized only by hyperconjugation ($3$ $\alpha$-H atoms) and the $+I$ effect. Benzyl chloride ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$) forms the benzyl carbocation ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\overset{+}{\text{C}}\text{H}_2$), which is strongly stabilized by resonance delocalization of the positive charge across the entire benzene ring. Hence, Statement II is true.
  3. Step 3 — Relate stability to $\text{S}_\text{N}1$ rate (Statement I): Because the benzyl carbocation is much more stable than the ethyl carbocation, benzyl chloride reacts significantly faster than ethyl chloride via the $\text{S}_\text{N}1$ mechanism. Hence, Statement I is also true.
  4. Step 4 — Final Conclusion: Both Statement I and Statement II are true, which corresponds to option (a).

Q06.conceptHtml: Toluene + Br<sub>2</sub>/hν gives benzylic bromination (PhCH<sub>2</sub>Br); Br<sub>2</sub>/Fe (dark) gives o/p-bromotoluene. Look carefully at the ring in (A) vs (C)!
Q06.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Check option (a) (Free-radical bromination of $4$-methylcyclohexene): When $4$-methylcyclohexene is treated with $\text{Br}_2, h\nu$, free-radical substitution selectively takes place at the allylic $\text{C}-\text{H}$ position (ring carbon adjacent to the $\text{C}=\text{C}$ double bond) because the resulting allylic radical is resonance-stabilized. Option (a) erroneously shows bromination on the isolated $-\text{CH}_3$ group (forming $-\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$ via an unstabilized $1^\circ$ radical), so (a) is not correctly represented.
  2. Step 2 — Verify options (b) and (c): In (b), benzenediazonium chloride ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{N}_2^+\text{Cl}^-$) reacts with $\text{Cu}_2\text{Br}_2/\text{HBr}$ to give bromobenzene—this is a standard Sandmeyer reaction (correct). In (c), toluene ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_3$) reacts with $\text{Br}_2, h\nu$ to give benzyl bromide ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$) via the resonance-stabilized benzylic radical (correct).
  3. Step 3 — Verify option (d): Toluene treated with $\text{Br}_2/\text{Fe}$ in the dark undergoes electrophilic aromatic substitution; since $-\text{CH}_3$ is an ortho/para-directing group, it yields ortho- and para-bromotoluenes (correct).

Q07.conceptHtml: Vinylic C − Cl has partial double-bond character (sp<sup>2</sup> C + resonance) ⇒ stronger than alkyl C − Cl. Hydrolysis of an optically active 3<sup>°</sup> benzylic halide (Ph − C(Me)(Et) − Cl) proceeds via S<sub>N</sub>1 to give a racemic mixture.
Q07.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement I ($\text{C}-\text{Cl}$ bond strength): In vinyl chloride ($\text{CH}_2=\text{CH}-\text{Cl}$), the lone pair on chlorine conjugates with the $\text{C}=\text{C}$ $\pi$-bond via resonance, giving the $\text{C}-\text{Cl}$ bond partial double-bond character. Additionally, the carbon is $sp^2$ hybridized (greater $s$-character, shorter and stronger bond) compared to the $sp^3$ carbon in $\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}_2-\text{Cl}$. Thus, the $\text{C}-\text{Cl}$ bond is stronger in $\text{CH}_2=\text{CH}-\text{Cl}$, so Statement I is true.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement II (Hydrolysis of the chiral tertiary benzylic halide): The given optically active compound is $\text{Ph}-\text{C(Me)(Et)}-\text{Cl}$, a tertiary benzylic chloride. On hydrolysis, it reacts via the $\text{S}_\text{N}1$ mechanism, ionizing to form a planar $sp^2$-hybridized carbocation intermediate, $\text{Ph}-\overset{+}{\text{C}}\text{(Me)(Et)}$.
  3. Step 3 — Check optical activity of the resulting solution: Water ($\text{H}_2\text{O}$) attacks the planar carbocation with equal probability from both the front and back faces, producing a $50:50$ racemic mixture ($d/l$-alcohol). Because a racemic mixture is optically inactive due to external compensation, the solution will not rotate plane-polarized light. Hence, Statement II is false.
  4. Step 4 — Final Conclusion: Statement I is true but Statement II is false, confirming option (b).

(dl) mixture that is optically inactive and does not rotate plane-polarized light. Statement II is false.

Q08.conceptHtml: Identify the hybridization and position of the carbon bearing −Cl.
Q08.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Classify Vinyl Chloride (A) and Allyl Chloride (D): In a vinylic halide, the halogen is attached directly to an $sp^2$-hybridized carbon of a $\text{C}=\text{C}$ double bond: $\text{CH}_2=\text{CHCl}$ (III), so A–III. In an allylic halide, the halogen is attached to an $sp^3$ carbon immediately adjacent to a $\text{C}=\text{C}$ double bond: $\text{CH}_2=\text{CH}-\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$ (I), so D–I.
  2. Step 2 — Classify Benzyl Chloride (B): In a benzylic halide, the halogen is bonded to an $sp^3$-hybridized carbon directly attached to an aromatic benzene ring. The diagram for IV shows $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5-\text{CH(CH}_3\text{)}-\text{Cl}$ ($1$-chloro-$1$-phenylethane), which is a secondary benzylic chloride, so B–IV.
  3. Step 3 — Classify Alkyl Chloride (C): In a simple alkyl halide, the halogen is attached to an $sp^3$ carbon of an aliphatic chain without any adjacent $\pi$-system: $\text{CH}_3-\text{CH(Cl)}-\text{CH}_3$ (II), so C–II.
  4. Step 4 — Final Conclusion: The complete match is A-III, B-IV, C-II, D-I, which corresponds to option (c).

Q09.conceptHtml: In chlorobenzene, Cl is attached to an sp<sup>2</sup> carbon and its lone pair delocalizes into the benzene ring (+M effect).
Q09.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Compare hybridization and resonance (Statements B and E): In chlorobenzene ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{Cl}$), the carbon bonded to chlorine is $sp^2$ hybridized (unlike the $sp^3$ carbon in chlorocyclohexane), so E is correct. A lone pair of electrons on chlorine delocalizes into the aromatic $\pi$-ring ($+M$ effect), imparting partial double-bond character to the $\text{C}-\text{Cl}$ bond, so B is correct.
  2. Step 2 — Compare polarity and negative charge on chlorine (Statements A and C): Because an $sp^2$ carbon is more electronegative than an $sp^3$ carbon, it holds the bonding electrons closer to itself, and resonance simultaneously shifts lone-pair electron density from $\text{Cl}$ into the ring. As a result, the magnitude of negative charge on chlorine is smaller (making A incorrect), and the $\text{C}-\text{Cl}$ bond is less polar (dipole moment $1.69\text{ D}$ vs. $2.05\text{ D}$ in chlorocyclohexane), making C correct.
  3. Step 3 — Compare bond length (Statement D): Due to both $sp^2$ hybridization and partial double-bond character, the $\text{C}-\text{Cl}$ bond in chlorobenzene is shorter ($169\text{ pm}$) than in chlorocyclohexane ($177\text{ pm}$), not longer. Thus, D is incorrect.
  4. Step 4 — Final Conclusion: Statements B, C, and E are correct, confirming option (a).

Q10.subtopic: SN1 Rate: Bridgehead Halides & Bredt’s Rule
Q10.conceptHtml: S<sub>N</sub>1 rate follows carbocation stability. Bridgehead carbocations cannot flatten to sp<sup>2</sup> geometry (Bredt’s rule); smaller bicyclic rings suffer even greater angle strain.
Q10.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the controlling factor for $\text{S}_\text{N}1$ rate: The $\text{S}_\text{N}1$ reaction rate depends on the stability of the planar $sp^2$-hybridized carbocation intermediate formed upon departure of $\text{Br}^-$.
  2. Step 2 — Analyze the rigid bridgehead halides (I and II): Both I ($1$-bromobicyclo$[2.2.2]$octane) and II ($1$-bromobicyclo$[2.2.1]$heptane) are bridgehead halides. By Bredt’s rule, rigid bicyclic rings resist flattening at the bridgehead carbon, preventing the carbocation from achieving planar $sp^2$ geometry. Because the smaller $[2.2.1]$ ring system (II) is even more strained and rigid than the $[2.2.2]$ system (I), II reacts the slowest: $\text{II} < \text{I}$.
  3. Step 3 — Analyze the open-chain halides (III and IV): Compound III ($(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}-\text{Br}$) readily forms a planar $3^\circ$ carbocation stabilized by $9$ $\alpha$-H hyperconjugation structures. Compound IV ($\text{Ph}_3\text{C}-\text{Br}$) forms the triphenylmethyl carbocation ($\text{Ph}_3\text{C}^+$), which is extensively resonance-stabilized across three phenyl rings and is therefore the most stable and fastest to react.
  4. Step 4 — Final Conclusion: Combining the rates gives $\text{II} < \text{I} < \text{III} < \text{IV}$, confirming option (b).

Step 2: Structure III is an acyclic/flexible 3◦ halide that can easily become planar ⇒ second fastest.
Step 3: Structures I and II are rigid bridgehead bromides. II is [2.2.1] (bicyclo[2.2.1]heptane, 1-carbon bridge)
which is much more strained at the bridgehead than I [2.2.2] (2-carbon bridge). Thus II < I < III < IV.

Q11.conceptHtml: In polar protic solvents (CH<sub>3</sub>OH), small hard anions like F<sup>−</sup> are heavily solvated by H-bonding, making I<sup>−</sup> the strongest nucleophile among halides. Across O-nucleophiles, stronger base = stronger nucleophile (C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>O<sup>−</sup> > C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>O<sup>−</sup>).
Q11.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the mechanism and solvent: Methyl bromide ($\text{CH}_3\text{Br}$) is a methyl halide and reacts exclusively via the $\text{S}_\text{N}2$ mechanism. The solvent is methanol ($\text{CH}_3\text{OH}$), which is a polar protic solvent capable of hydrogen-bonding with anions.
  2. Step 2 — Compare halide nucleophiles ($\text{I}^-$ vs. $\text{F}^-$): In a polar protic solvent, small, high-charge-density anions like $\text{F}^-$ are heavily caged by hydrogen bonds, severely reducing their mobility and nucleophilicity. In contrast, the large, soft, polarizable $\text{I}^-$ ion is weakly solvated and is the strongest nucleophile among the four species.
  3. Step 3 — Compare oxygen nucleophiles ($\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{O}^-$ vs. $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{O}^-$): Both ethoxide ($\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{O}^-$) and phenoxide ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{O}^-$) attack via oxygen, so nucleophilicity follows basicity. In $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{O}^-$, the negative charge is delocalized into the benzene ring by resonance, making it less basic and less nucleophilic than $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{O}^-$. Both oxygen anions remain more nucleophilic than heavily solvated $\text{F}^-$ in methanol.
  4. Step 4 — Final Conclusion: The reactivity order is $\text{I}^- > \text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{O}^- > \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{O}^- > \text{F}^-$, confirming option (a).

Step 2: C2H5O− is a stronger base than resonance-stabilized C6H5O− ⇒ C2H5O− > C6H5O−.
Step 3: F− is heavily H-bonded by methanol ⇒ weakest nucleophile. Order: I− > C2H5O− > C6H5O− > F−.

Q12.conceptHtml: When the nucleophilic atom is the same (oxygen), nucleophilicity directly parallels basicity (which is inverse to the acid strength of the conjugate acid).
Q12.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the mechanism and donor atom: The reaction $\text{CH}_3\text{Br} + \text{Nu}^- \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{Nu} + \text{Br}^-$ is a classic $\text{S}_\text{N}2$ substitution on a methyl halide, so the rate increases with nucleophilicity. Notice that all four nucleophiles ($\text{OH}^-$, $\text{PhO}^-$, $\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-$, and $\text{ClO}_4^-$) have oxygen as the attacking nucleophilic atom.
  2. Step 2 — Relate nucleophilicity to basicity: When the attacking atom is the same across a series of nucleophiles (and steric hindrance is not blocking the site), nucleophilicity directly parallels basicity—stronger bases are better nucleophiles.
  3. Step 3 — Rank basicity using conjugate acid strength: A weaker conjugate acid has a stronger conjugate base. The acid strength order of the conjugate acids is: $\text{HClO}_4 \text{ (strongest acid)} > \text{CH}_3\text{COOH} > \text{PhOH} > \text{H}_2\text{O} \text{ (weakest acid)}$. Reversing this gives the basicity and nucleophilicity order: $\text{OH}^- > \text{PhO}^- > \text{CH}_3\text{COO}^- > \text{ClO}_4^-$.
  4. Step 4 — Final Conclusion: The correct rate order is $\text{OH}^- > \text{PhO}^- > \text{CH}_3\text{COO}^- > \text{ClO}_4^-$, confirming option (b).

Q13.subtopic: SN2 Reactivity of Substituted Benzyl Halides
Q13.conceptHtml: Reaction of benzyl bromides with KCN proceeds via S<sub>N</sub>2. Electron-donating groups (−NH<sub>2</sub> > −OH) at the para position accelerate the reaction; electron-withdrawing −NO<sub>2</sub> at para (c) deactivates more than at meta (d) due to −M effect? Wait: check the official key!
Q13.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the substituted benzyl bromides: The four substrates are substituted benzyl bromides: (a) $p\text{-OH}$, (b) $p\text{-NH}_2$, (c) $p\text{-NO}_2$, and (d) $m\text{-NO}_2$. In substitution of benzyl halides with $\text{KCN}$ (polar medium), the transition state develops substantial positive charge ($\delta+$) at the benzylic carbon ($\text{S}_\text{N}1$-like character), so electron-donating groups accelerate the reaction and electron-withdrawing groups retard it.
  2. Step 2 — Compare electron-donating groups (a vs. b): Both $-\text{NH}_2$ and $-\text{OH}$ at the para position donate electrons by resonance ($+M$ effect) to stabilize the benzylic positive charge. Since nitrogen is less electronegative than oxygen, $-\text{NH}_2$ is a stronger $+M$ donor than $-\text{OH}$, giving $\text{b} > \text{a}$.
  3. Step 3 — Compare electron-withdrawing groups (c vs. d): The $-\text{NO}_2$ group withdraws electrons and destabilizes positive charge at the benzylic carbon. At the para position (c), $-\text{NO}_2$ exerts both $-M$ and $-I$ effects (maximum destabilization), whereas at the meta position (d), it exerts only $-I$ (no $-M$). Therefore, $m\text{-NO}_2$ (d) is more reactive than $p\text{-NO}_2$ (c): $\text{d} > \text{c}$.
  4. Step 4 — Final Conclusion: Combining both parts yields the reactivity order $\text{b} > \text{a} > \text{d} > \text{c}$, confirming option (b).

Step 2: Between p-NO2 (c) and m-NO2 (d), p-NO2 exerts both −M and −I while m-NO2 exerts only −I; thus c
destabilizes the cationic character at the benzylic carbon more, making d > c. Overall: b > a > d > c.
Q13.trapHtml: Notice b > a > d > c: −NH<sub>2</sub> beats −OH, and m-NO<sub>2</sub> beats p-NO<sub>2</sub>. Verified Answer: (B) b > a > d > c

Q14.conceptHtml: To convert ethylbenzene to p-bromostyrene: (1) introduce p-Br via EAS (Br<sub>2</sub>/Fe), (2) chlorinate the benzylic position (Cl<sub>2</sub>, ∆), (3) dehydrohalogenate (alc. KOH) to form the vinyl group.
Q14.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the starting material and target product: We need to convert ethylbenzene ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$) into p-bromostyrene ($p\text{-Br}-\text{C}_6\text{H}_4-\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2$). This requires introducing a $-\text{Br}$ atom on the ring at the para position and converting the ethyl side chain into a vinyl ($-\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2$) group.
  2. Step 2 — Ring bromination first ($\text{Br}_2/\text{Fe}$): Treating ethylbenzene with $\text{Br}_2/\text{Fe}$ performs electrophilic aromatic bromination. Because $-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ is ortho/para-directing, the major product is p-bromoethylbenzene. (Doing this before forming the alkene prevents $\text{Br}_2$ from adding across the $\text{C}=\text{C}$ double bond.)
  3. Step 3 — Side-chain benzylic chlorination ($\text{Cl}_2, \Delta$): Heating p-bromoethylbenzene with $\text{Cl}_2, \Delta$ initiates free-radical chlorination selectively at the resonance-stabilized benzylic carbon, giving $1$-bromo-$4$-($1$-chloroethyl)benzene ($p\text{-Br}-\text{C}_6\text{H}_4-\text{CH(Cl)CH}_3$).
  4. Step 4 — Dehydrohalogenation (alc. $\text{KOH}$) and Final Conclusion: Treating the benzylic chloride with alcoholic $\text{KOH}$ causes $\beta$-elimination of $\text{HCl}$ to yield p-bromostyrene (whereas aqueous $\text{KOH}$ would give substitution to an alcohol). Thus, the correct sequence is $\text{Br}_2/\text{Fe}$; $\text{Cl}_2, \Delta$; alc. $\text{KOH}$, confirming option (c).

Step 1: PhCH2CH3 −B−r−2/−F→e p-BrC6H4CH2CH3 (ethyl is o/p-directing).
Step 2: −C−l−2,−∆→ p-BrC6H4CH(Cl)CH3 (benzylic radical chlorination).
Step 3: −a−lc−.−K−O−→H p-BrC6H4CH = CH2 (aryl C − Br is untouched).

Q15.conceptHtml: More o/p-NO<sub>2</sub> groups stabilize the Meisenheimer intermediate, lowering the required temperature/pressure for S<sub>N</sub>Ar hydrolysis.
Q15.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Understand the effect of $-\text{NO}_2$ groups on $\text{S}_\text{N}\text{Ar}$: Nucleophilic aromatic substitution ($\text{S}_\text{N}\text{Ar}$) of aryl chlorides with $\text{OH}^-/\text{H}_2\text{O}$ proceeds via a negatively charged carbanion (Meisenheimer) intermediate. Adding electron-withdrawing $-\text{NO}_2$ groups at the ortho and para positions stabilizes this negative charge by resonance ($-M$), dramatically lowering the required temperature and pressure.
  2. Step 2 — Match unsubstituted and mono-nitro chlorobenzene (A and B): (A) Chlorobenzene has no $-\text{NO}_2$ groups, so it requires drastic Dow’s process conditions: $\text{NaOH}, 623\text{ K}, 300\text{ atm}$ followed by $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$ $\rightarrow$ (A)–(IV). (B) $4$-Nitrochlorobenzene has one para-$-\text{NO}_2$ group, lowering the requirement to $\text{NaOH}, 443\text{ K}; \text{H}_3\text{O}^+$ $\rightarrow$ (B)–(III).
  3. Step 3 — Match dinitro and trinitro chlorobenzene (C and D): (C) $2,4$-Dinitrochlorobenzene has two activating $-\text{NO}_2$ groups and reacts at milder conditions: $\text{NaOH}, 368\text{ K}; \text{H}_3\text{O}^+$ $\rightarrow$ (C)–(II). (D) $2,4,6$-Trinitrochlorobenzene (picryl chloride) is so strongly activated by three $-\text{NO}_2$ groups that it hydrolyzes simply with warm $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ $\rightarrow$ (D)–(I).

Q16.subtopic: Electrophilic Addition of HBr to Conjugated Polyene
Q16.conceptHtml: Protonation occurs at the site that generates the most extensively conjugated (resonance-stabilized) al- lylic/polyenylic carbocation.
Q16.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Inspect the three $\text{C}=\text{C}$ double bonds in molecule (X): The fused tricyclic triene (X) contains three alkene double bonds: two are disubstituted (one in the top-left $5$-membered ring and one in the top-right $6$-membered ring), while the third double bond (in the bottom $5$-membered ring) is trisubstituted because one of its alkene carbons is a ring-junction carbon.
  2. Step 2 — Identify the most reactive alkene towards $1$ eq $\text{HBr}$: Electrophilic addition of $\text{HBr}$ ($1$ equivalent) occurs selectively at the double bond that forms the most stable carbocation intermediate. Protonation of either disubstituted double bond gives only a secondary ($2^\circ$) carbocation, whereas Markovnikov protonation of the trisubstituted double bond in the bottom ring produces a much more stable tertiary ($3^\circ$) carbocation at the ring-junction carbon.
  3. Step 3 — Complete the nucleophilic attack by $\text{Br}^-$: The bromide ion ($\text{Br}^-$) attacks this $3^\circ$ ring-junction carbocation to form the tertiary bromide, while the two less reactive disubstituted $\text{C}=\text{C}$ double bonds in the upper rings remain intact.
  4. Step 4 — Final Conclusion: This structure matches option (a) (showing $-\text{Br}$ at the bottom-right ring junction with both upper double bonds untouched), confirming option (a).

Q17.conceptHtml: Aqueous KOH gives alcohols via nucleophilic substitution (S<sub>N</sub>), whereas alcoholic KOH gives alkenes via β-elimination (E2).
Q17.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement I (Reaction with aqueous $\text{KOH}$): When alkyl chlorides ($\text{R}-\text{Cl}$) are treated with aqueous $\text{KOH}$, the hydroxide ion ($\text{OH}^-$) acts as a nucleophile and replaces $-\text{Cl}$ to form alcohols ($\text{R}-\text{OH}$). This is a nucleophilic substitution reaction ($\text{S}_\text{N}1$ or $\text{S}_\text{N}2$), not an elimination reaction. Hence, Statement I is incorrect.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement II (Reaction with alcoholic $\text{KOH}$): In alcoholic $\text{KOH}$, the base ($\text{OH}^-/\text{RO}^-$) abstracts a proton from the $\beta$-carbon (carbon adjacent to the $\alpha$-carbon bearing $-\text{Cl}$) while $\text{Cl}^-$ leaves simultaneously, forming an alkene via $\beta$-elimination (dehydrohalogenation). Hence, Statement II is correct.
  3. Step 3 — Final Conclusion: Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct, confirming option (c).

Q18.conceptHtml: −Br is o/p-directing (sterics favour para). −SO<sub>3</sub>H is meta-directing.

1. Step 1 — Identify Product A (Sulfonation of bromobenzene): Bromobenzene reacts with $\text{SO}_3/\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ via electrophilic aromatic substitution. Although $-\text{Br}$ is weakly deactivating ($-I > +M$), it is ortho/para-directing. Due to steric hindrance from the bulky $-\text{SO}_3\text{H}$ group, para substitution dominates, yielding $4$-bromobenzenesulfonic acid as major product A.
  2. Step 2 — Determine directing effects in Product A for bromination: Product A has $-\text{Br}$ at $\text{C}-1$ (ortho/para-directing) and $-\text{SO}_3\text{H}$ at $\text{C}-4$ (strongly meta-directing). Since the para position to $-\text{Br}$ is already occupied by $-\text{SO}_3\text{H}$, both substituents reinforce electrophilic attack at the exact same position: ortho to $-\text{Br}$ and meta to $-\text{SO}_3\text{H}$.
  3. Step 3 — Identify Product B: Treatment of A with $\text{Br}_2, \text{Fe}$ introduces the second $-\text{Br}$ atom ortho to the first $-\text{Br}$ (and meta to $-\text{SO}_3\text{H}$), forming $3,4$-dibromobenzenesulfonic acid as major product B.

Q21.conceptHtml: In S<sub>N</sub>Ar, only the leaving group positioned ortho or para to the −NO<sub>2</sub> group is activated because the negative charge of the Meisenheimer intermediate can delocalize onto −NO<sub>2</sub>.

Step 2 — Determine which bromine atom is activated by $-\text{NO}_2$: In $\text{S}_\text{N}\text{Ar}$, an electron-withdrawing $-\text{NO}_2$ group strongly activates halogen leaving groups located ortho or para to it by stabilizing the negatively charged Meisenheimer intermediate via resonance ($-M$ effect). Here, the $-\text{Br}$ at $\text{C}-1$ is para to $-\text{NO}_2$ (at $\text{C}-4$), whereas the $-\text{Br}$ at $\text{C}-2$ is meta to $-\text{NO}_2$ (no resonance stabilization).

Q22.conceptHtml: Excess alcoholic KOH/∆ removes two molecules of HBr to give the most stable conjugated diene.

Step 3 — Determine the exact positions of the two double bonds: For the $\text{C}-3$ bromine, losing the benzylic hydrogen from $\text{C}-2$ forms a $\text{C}2=\text{C}3$ double bond that is directly conjugated with the phenyl ring. For the $\text{C}-5$ bromine, losing a hydrogen from $\text{C}-4$ (rather than $\text{C}-6$) forms a $\text{C}4=\text{C}5$ double bond that is conjugated with the $\text{C}2=\text{C}3$ bond, creating an extended $\text{Ph}-\text{C}=\text{C}-\text{C}=\text{C}$ conjugated system: $\text{CH}_3-\text{C(Ph)}=\text{CH}-\text{CH}=\text{CH}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_3$.

Q23.conceptHtml: Both AgNO<sub>2</sub> and AgCN are covalent, so attack occurs through the nitrogen lone pair.
Q23.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Understand ambident nucleophiles ($\text{AgNO}_2$ and $\text{AgCN}$): Both $\text{NO}_2^-$ and $\text{CN}^-$ are ambident nucleophiles with two possible donor atoms. Unlike ionic potassium salts ($\text{KNO}_2$, $\text{KCN}$), silver salts ($\text{AgNO}_2$ and $\text{AgCN}$) are predominantly covalent in nature.
  2. Step 2 — Find Product A ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br} + \text{AgNO}_2$): In covalent $\text{Ag}-\text{O}-\text{N}=\text{O}$, the oxygen atom is covalently bound to silver, so the free lone pair on the nitrogen atom attacks the alkyl carbon, forming the nitroalkane: $\text{A} = \text{CH}_3-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{NO}_2$ ($1$-nitropropane).
  3. Step 3 — Find Product B ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br} + \text{AgCN}$): Similarly, in covalent $\text{Ag}-\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$, the carbon atom is bound to silver, so the lone pair on the nitrogen atom attacks the alkyl carbon, forming the isocyanide (carbylamine): $\text{B} = \text{CH}_3-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{NC}$ (propyl isocyanide).
  4. Step 4 — Final Conclusion: Products A and B are $\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{NO}_2$ and $\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{NC}$, confirming option (d).

Q24.conceptHtml: In β-haloamines (Et<sub>2</sub>NCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Cl), the nitrogen lone pair performs an intramolecular S<sub>N</sub>2 attack to expel Cl<sup>−</sup>, forming a cyclic aziridinium ion, which then opens rapidly with OH<sup>−</sup>.

  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement II (Intramolecular substitution / NGP): In $\text{Et}_2\text{N}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{Cl}$, the lone pair on the $\beta$-nitrogen atom performs a fast intramolecular $\text{S}_\text{N}2$ attack (neighbouring group participation, or anchimeric assistance) on the carbon bearing $-\text{Cl}$, expelling $\text{Cl}^-$ to form a strained $3$-membered cyclic aziridinium ion intermediate. Hence, Statement II is correct.

Step 3 — Evaluate Statement I (Rate of alkaline hydrolysis): Because intramolecular cyclization has a much lower activation barrier than intermolecular attack by $\text{OH}^-$, and the resulting strained aziridinium ring is rapidly opened by $\text{OH}^-/\text{H}_2\text{O}$, $\text{Et}_2\text{N}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{Cl}$ undergoes alkaline hydrolysis far faster than the hydrocarbon chloride (which lacks a neighbouring lone pair). Hence, Statement I is also correct.

In contrast, the benzylic $-\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$ bond undergoes nucleophilic substitution readily.

Step 3 — Apply the ambident reactivity of $\text{AgCN}$: Because $\text{AgCN}$ is predominantly covalent ($\text{Ag}-\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$), the nitrogen lone pair attacks the benzylic carbon, replacing $-\text{Cl}$ with an isocyanide group ($-\text{NC}$) rather than $-\text{CN}$, while leaving both $-\text{I}$ and $-\text{Br}$ untouched on the ring.

Q26.subtopic: Solvent Polarity Effects on SN2 Reactions
Q26.conceptHtml: In S<sub>N</sub>2, if charge is dispersed in the transition state (RX+Nu<sup>−</sup>), a less polar solvent favours it. If charge is created from neutral reactants (RX + R<sub>3</sub>N → R<sub>4</sub>N<sup>+</sup>X<sup>−</sup>), a more polar solvent stabilizes the developing ions and accelerates the reaction.
Q26.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the Hughes–Ingold solvent rules for $\text{S}_\text{N}2$: A polar solvent stabilizes localized charges much more strongly than dispersed charges. Therefore, if charge is dispersed in the transition state (TS) relative to reactants, a less polar medium favours the reaction; if charge is created in the TS from neutral reactants, a more polar medium favours the reaction.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement I ($\text{BuCl} + \text{HO}^- \rightarrow \text{BuOH} + \text{Cl}^-$): Here, a localized anion ($\text{HO}^-$) reacts with neutral $1$-chlorobutane to form a transition state $[\text{HO}^{\delta-}\cdots\text{C}\cdots\text{Cl}^{\delta-}]$ in which the negative charge is dispersed over two atoms. A less polar medium avoids over-solvating $\text{HO}^-$ and favours the more dispersed TS, so the conversion proceeds well in a less polar medium. Statement I is true.
  3. Step 3 — Evaluate Statement II ($\text{BuCl} + \text{R}_3\text{N} \rightarrow \text{BuNR}_3^+\text{Cl}^-$): Here, two neutral reactants ($1$-chlorobutane and a tertiary amine $\text{R}_3\text{N}$) form a charge-separated transition state $[\text{R}_3\text{N}^{\delta+}\cdots\text{C}\cdots\text{Cl}^{\delta-}]$ leading to an ionic quaternary ammonium salt (Menschutkin reaction). A more polar medium strongly stabilizes this developing charge separation, so the reaction proceeds well in a more polar medium. Statement II is true.
  4. Step 4 — Final Conclusion: Both Statement I and Statement II are true, confirming option (d).

medium. True.

True.

Q27.conceptHtml: Solvolysis rate ∝ stability of carbocation formed.
Q27.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Connect solvolysis rate to carbocation stability: Solvolysis of secondary and tertiary bromides proceeds via the $\text{S}_\text{N}1$ mechanism, so the relative rate increases directly with the stability of the carbocation intermediate formed upon loss of $\text{Br}^-$.
  2. Step 2 — Identify the carbocation formed by each compound: (D) $2$-Bromo-$3$-methylbutane gives a $2^\circ$ aliphatic carbocation (stabilized only by hyperconjugation and $+I$, no resonance). (A) $1$-Bromo-$1,4,4$-trimethylcyclohexane gives a $3^\circ$ aliphatic carbocation (more hyperconjugation and $+I$ than $2^\circ$). (B) $1$-Bromo-$1,2,3,4$-tetrahydronaphthalene gives a $2^\circ$ benzylic carbocation (resonance-stabilized by one benzene ring plus hyperconjugation). (C) Bromodiphenylmethane ($\text{Ph}_2\text{CH}-\text{Br}$) gives the diphenylmethyl carbocation ($\text{Ph}_2\text{CH}^+$), strongly resonance-stabilized across two benzene rings.
  3. Step 3 — Rank carbocation stability in ascending order: Resonance stabilization outweighs simple aliphatic inductive/hyperconjugative stabilization, and two phenyl rings stabilize far better than one: $2^\circ \text{ aliphatic (D)} < 3^\circ \text{ aliphatic (A)} < 2^\circ \text{ benzylic (B)} < \text{diphenylmethyl (C)}$.
  4. Step 4 — Final Conclusion: The ascending order of solvolysis rate is $(\text{D}) < (\text{A}) < (\text{B}) < (\text{C})$, confirming option (b).

Step 1 — Match Swarts and Finkelstein reactions: Swarts reaction (A) converts alkyl bromides/chlorides into alkyl fluorides (using $\text{AgF}$, $\text{SbF}_3$, etc.) $\rightarrow$ Ethyl fluoride (IV), so A–IV. Finkelstein reaction (D) converts alkyl chlorides/bromides into alkyl iodides (using $\text{NaI}$ in dry acetone) $\rightarrow$ Ethyl iodide (II), so D–II.

Q29.subtopic: Isomers of RBr Giving 2-Methylbutane via Grignard
Q29.conceptHtml: Grignard formation followed by hydrolysis (RBr → RMgBr → RH) replaces −Br with −H without changing the carbon skeleton.
Q29.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Understand the reaction sequence: Treating $\text{RBr}$ with (i) $\text{Mg}/\text{dry ether}$ forms the Grignard reagent $\text{RMgBr}$, and subsequent hydrolysis with (ii) $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ replaces $-\text{MgBr}$ with $-\text{H}$ to yield the alkane $\text{R}-\text{H}$ without any carbon-skeleton rearrangement.
  2. Step 2 — Find all non-equivalent carbon positions in $2$-methylbutane: Every structural isomer of $\text{RBr}$ that shares the $2$-methylbutane skeleton, $\overset{1}{\text{C}}\text{H}_3-\overset{2}{\text{C}}\text{H}(\text{CH}_3)-\overset{3}{\text{C}}\text{H}_2-\overset{4}{\text{C}}\text{H}_3$, will give $2$-methylbutane. Replacing one $\text{H}$ at each chemically distinct carbon with $-\text{Br}$ gives: (1) $1$-bromo-$2$-methylbutane (at either equivalent $\text{C}-1$ methyl), (2) $2$-bromo-$2$-methylbutane (at the $3^\circ$ $\text{C}-2$ carbon), (3) $2$-bromo-$3$-methylbutane (at the $\text{C}-3$ methylene), and (4) $1$-bromo-$3$-methylbutane (at the $\text{C}-4$ terminal methyl).
  3. Step 3 — Final Conclusion: There are exactly 4 distinct structural isomers of $\text{RBr}$ that produce $2$-methylbutane, confirming option (c).

(Me2CH − CH(Br)Me), (4) C4 (Me2CH − CH2CH2Br). Total = 4.

Q30.subtopic: Anomalous 1◦ Halides in SN1 and SN2
Q30.conceptHtml: Even though both are 1<sup>°</sup> halides, CH<sub>3</sub>OCH<sub>2</sub>Cl forms a resonance-stabilized oxocarbenium ion (CH<sub>3</sub>O¨ = CH<sup>+</sup><sub>2</sub> ) in S<sub>N</sub>1, while neopentyl chloride (Me<sub>3</sub>C − CH<sub>2</sub>Cl) is sterically blocked for backside S<sub>N</sub>2 attack.
Q30.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement I ($\text{CH}_3-\text{O}-\text{CH}_2-\text{Cl}$ in $\text{S}_\text{N}1$): Although chloromethyl methyl ether ($\text{CH}_3-\text{O}-\text{CH}_2-\text{Cl}$) is a primary ($1^\circ$) alkyl halide, ionization of $-\text{Cl}$ produces the methoxymethyl carbocation $\text{CH}_3-\ddot{\text{O}}-\overset{+}{\text{C}}\text{H}_2 \longleftrightarrow \text{CH}_3-\overset{+}{\text{O}}=\text{CH}_2$. Because the oxygen lone pair donates by strong $+M$ resonance (giving every atom a complete octet), this carbocation is extraordinarily stable, so it readily undergoes $\text{S}_\text{N}1$. Hence, Statement I is correct.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement II (Neopentyl chloride in $\text{S}_\text{N}2$): The given diagram shows neopentyl chloride, $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}-\text{CH}_2-\text{Cl}$ ($1$-chloro-$2,2$-dimethylpropane). Even though it is a primary halide, the very bulky tert-butyl group on the adjacent $\beta$-carbon severely blocks the $180^\circ$ backside trajectory required for $\text{S}_\text{N}2$ attack, making its $\text{S}_\text{N}2$ rate negligibly slow. Hence, Statement II is also correct.
  3. Step 3 — Final Conclusion: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct, confirming option (b).

Step 2: Statement II is true (bulky t-butyl group blocks backside SN2 approach).
Q30.trapHtml: Two classic NCERT/JEE exceptions for 1<sup>°</sup> halides: ROCH<sub>2</sub>Cl loves S<sub>N</sub>1, and neopentyl chloride hates S<sub>N</sub>2. Verified Answer: (B) Both Statement I and Statement II are correct

Q31.conceptHtml: KCN (alc) provides CN<sup>−</sup> which substitutes −Br via S<sub>N</sub>2 (unless elimination dominates, here substitution gives the nitrile).
Q31.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the reactive site in the substrate: The reactant is an $\alpha$-bromo ether, $\text{Ph}-\text{CH(CH}_3\text{)}-\text{CH(OCH}_3\text{)(Br)}$, treated with alcoholic $\text{KCN}$ upon heating. Here, the $-\text{Br}$ leaving group is directly attached to the same carbon as the methoxy ($-\text{OCH}_3$) group.
  2. Step 2 — Analyze the stability of the intermediate carbocation: Loss of $\text{Br}^-$ generates the oxonium-stabilized carbocation $\text{Ph}-\text{CH(CH}_3\text{)}-\overset{+}{\text{C}}\text{H}-\ddot{\text{O}}\text{CH}_3 \longleftrightarrow \text{Ph}-\text{CH(CH}_3\text{)}-\text{CH}=\overset{+}{\text{O}}\text{CH}_3$. Because back-donation from the oxygen lone pair completes the octet on all atoms, this carbocation is even more stable than a $3^\circ$ benzylic carbocation, so no $1,2$-hydride shift occurs.
  3. Step 3 — Form the substitution product with $\text{KCN}$: Since $\text{KCN}$ is ionic, the carbon end of $\text{CN}^-$ attacks this stabilized carbocation directly (without rearrangement), substituting $-\text{Br}$ with $-\text{CN}$ at the carbon bearing $-\text{OCH}_3$ to yield $\text{Ph}-\text{CH(CH}_3\text{)}-\text{CH(CN)(OCH}_3\text{)}$.
  4. Step 4 — Final Conclusion: This unrearranged nitrile product matches option (a).

Q32.subtopic: SN2 Transition State Stabilization in Benzyl Bromide
Q32.conceptHtml: In the trigonal bipyramidal S<sub>N</sub>2 transition state of C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Br, the partially bonded unhybridized p-orbital on carbon overlaps with the π-system of the phenyl ring, lowering the activation energy.
Q32.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Assertion (A): Benzyl bromide ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$) reacts dramatically faster (roughly $100\text{–}400$ times faster) than ethyl bromide ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$) under $\text{S}_\text{N}2$ conditions. Thus, Assertion (A) is correct.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Reason (R): In the pentacoordinate trigonal bipyramidal $\text{S}_\text{N}2$ transition state, the central reacting carbon rehybridizes to $sp^2$ with an unhybridized $p$-orbital partially bonded to both the incoming nucleophile and the departing $\text{Br}^-$. In benzyl bromide, this partially filled $p$-orbital overlaps smoothly (conjugates) with the adjacent $\pi$-electron cloud of the phenyl ring, delocalizing electron density and lowering the transition-state energy. Thus, Reason (R) is correct.
  3. Step 3 — Check whether (R) explains (A): Because this $\pi$-conjugation lowers the activation energy ($E_a$) of the $\text{S}_\text{N}2$ transition state for benzyl bromide (whereas ethyl bromide has no adjacent $\pi$-system), Reason (R) directly explains Assertion (A).
  4. Step 4 — Final Conclusion: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A), confirming option (b).

Q33.conceptHtml: 1-Bromo-3-chlorocyclobutane undergoes intramolecular Wurtz coupling with Na/Et<sub>2</sub>O (or dimerization) to give A; look at options (A)–(D) in the given structure/scheme: A is 1,3-dichlorobicyclobutane / bicyclo[1.1.0]butane or 1-chloro-3-deuterocyclobutane!
Q33.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify intermediate A (Selective Wurtz coupling): The starting material is $1$-bromo-$3$-chlorocyclobutane treated with $\text{Na}/\text{Et}_2\text{O}$. Because the $\text{C}-\text{Br}$ bond is weaker and much more reactive than the $\text{C}-\text{Cl}$ bond (and intramolecular closure to bicyclo$[1.1.0]$butane would introduce extreme ring strain), intermolecular Wurtz coupling selectively occurs at the $\text{C}-\text{Br}$ ends of two molecules to form $3,3^\prime$-dichloro-$1,1^\prime$-bi(cyclobutane) as A.
  2. Step 2 — Identify major product B (Grignard formation and deuterolysis): Treating A with (i) $\text{Mg}/\text{Et}_2\text{O}$ converts both $-\text{Cl}$ groups into Grignard centers ($-\text{MgCl}$). Subsequent reaction with (ii) $\text{D}_2\text{O}$ replaces both $-\text{MgCl}$ groups with deuterium ($-\text{D}$), yielding $3,3^\prime$-dideuterio-$1,1^\prime$-bi(cyclobutane) as B.
  3. Step 3 — Identify major product C (Swarts fluorination): Treating A with $\text{CoF}_2$ performs a Swarts halogen-exchange reaction, replacing both $-\text{Cl}$ atoms with $-\text{F}$ atoms to yield $3,3^\prime$-difluoro-$1,1^\prime$-bi(cyclobutane) as C.
  4. Step 4 — Final Conclusion: Both B and C retain the $1,1^\prime$-bi(cyclobutane) skeleton with $-\text{D}$ and $-\text{F}$ at the $3,3^\prime$-positions respectively, matching option (b).

Q34.subtopic: Stereospecificity of SN2 vs Racemisation in SN1
Q34.conceptHtml: S<sub>N</sub>2 proceeds with 100% inversion (stereospecific: one stereoisomer reactant gives one stereoisomer product). S<sub>N</sub>1 proceeds via a planar carbocation, giving a racemic mixture.
Q34.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement I (Stereospecificity of $\text{S}_\text{N}2$): An $\text{S}_\text{N}2$ reaction proceeds in a single concerted step via $180^\circ$ backside attack by the nucleophile, causing complete Walden inversion of configuration at a chiral center. Because a single stereoisomer of reactant exclusively produces a single inverted stereoisomer of product, $\text{S}_\text{N}2$ reactions are stereospecific. Statement I is true.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement II (Racemization in $\text{S}_\text{N}1$): An $\text{S}_\text{N}1$ reaction proceeds through a planar $sp^2$-hybridized carbocation intermediate. The nucleophile can attack this planar intermediate from either face (giving both retention and inversion), which generally yields a racemic mixture. Statement II is also true.
  3. Step 3 — Final Conclusion: Both Statement I and Statement II are true, confirming option (d).

Step 1: Statement (I) is true.
Step 2: Statement (II) is true.
Q34.trapHtml: NCERT Ch. 10 directly defines S<sub>N</sub>2 as stereospecific (inversion) and S<sub>N</sub>1 as giving racemisation. Verified Answer: (D) Both Statement I and Statement II are true

Q35.subtopic: Fastest SN2 Reaction Among Cyclic/Alkyl Bromides
Q35.conceptHtml: S<sub>N</sub>2 rate decreases sharply with steric hindrance at the α and β carbons (1<sup>°</sup> > 2<sup>°</sup> > 3<sup>°</sup>).
Q35.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the key factor controlling $\text{S}_\text{N}2$ rate: Because $\text{S}_\text{N}2$ requires backside nucleophilic attack on the $\alpha$-carbon bearing $-\text{Br}$, the reaction rate decreases sharply as steric crowding increases: $\text{methyl} > 1^\circ > 2^\circ \gg 3^\circ$.
  2. Step 2 — Classify the degree of each alkyl bromide: (a) $2$-Bromo-$2$-cyclobutylpropane is a $3^\circ$ halide (heavily hindered). (b) $1$-Bromo-$1$-cyclobutylethane is a $2^\circ$ halide (moderately hindered). (c) (Bromomethyl)cyclobutane ($\text{cyclobutyl}-\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$) is a $1^\circ$ halide (least sterically hindered). (d) $1$-Bromo-$1$-methylcyclobutane is a $3^\circ$ halide (heavily hindered).
  3. Step 3 — Compare rates and Final Conclusion: Having the least steric hindrance around the $\text{C}-\text{Br}$ carbon, the $1^\circ$ halide (bromomethyl)cyclobutane undergoes the fastest $\text{S}_\text{N}2$ reaction, confirming option (c).

whereas (C) is an unhindered 1◦ alkyl bromide (R − CH2Br).

Q36.subtopic: Hydrolysis of o-Chlorotoluene? No, Ring-Chloro + Methyl
Q36.conceptHtml: Look at the given structure/scheme: 4-chloro-1-methylcyclohexene or chlorobenzene derivative with NaOH/H<sub>2</sub>O gives substitution of −Cl by −OH at the same position.
Q36.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the substrate and reaction conditions: The substrate is $1$-chloro-$1$-cyclohexylpropane ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_{11}-\text{CH(Cl)}-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$) reacting with $\text{NaOH}$ in $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ (a strongly polar protic solvent favouring carbocation formation via $\text{S}_\text{N}1$).
  2. Step 2 — Formation and rearrangement of the carbocation: Ionization of the $\text{C}-\text{Cl}$ bond initially forms a secondary ($2^\circ$) carbocation, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{11}-\overset{+}{\text{C}}\text{H}-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$. Immediately adjacent to this positive center is the $3^\circ$ ring carbon ($\text{C}-1$ of cyclohexane) bearing a hydrogen atom. A rapid $1,2$-hydride shift moves this $\text{H}^-$ to the side chain, generating a much more stable tertiary ($3^\circ$) carbocation on the cyclohexane ring ($1$-propylcyclohexyl cation).
  3. Step 3 — Nucleophilic trapping by $\text{H}_2\text{O}/\text{OH}^-$: Attack of $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ (or $\text{OH}^-$) on the rearranged $3^\circ$ carbocation gives $1$-propylcyclohexan-$1$-ol as the major product A.
  4. Step 4 — Final Conclusion: The structure with both the $-\text{OH}$ and the $-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ group on the same ring carbon matches option (a).
