Q37.conceptHtml: With OH<sup>−</sup>/C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH (alcoholic base), a 2<sup>°</sup> cyclic bromide undergoes E2 β-elimination to form the more substituted Zaitsev alkene.
Q37.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the substrate and reaction type: The reactant is $1$-bromo-$1$-methylcyclopentane (a $3^\circ$ alkyl bromide) treated with alcoholic base ($\text{OH}^-/\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}$), which promotes E2 $\beta$-elimination (dehydrohalogenation).
  2. Step 2 — Compare the two possible $\beta$-elimination pathways: Abstracting a $\beta$-hydrogen from the ring $-\text{CH}_2-$ group gives the endocyclic trisubstituted alkene $1$-methylcyclopentene ($7$ $\alpha$-H atoms). Abstracting a $\beta$-hydrogen from the $-\text{CH}_3$ group gives the exocyclic disubstituted alkene methylenecyclopentane ($4$ $\alpha$-H atoms).
  3. Step 3 — Apply Zaitsev’s (Saytzeff’s) rule: With a small, unhindered base ($\text{OH}^-/\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{O}^-$), elimination follows Zaitsev’s rule, favouring the more substituted, more stable alkene—namely $1$-methylcyclopentene.
  4. Step 4 — Final Conclusion: The major product $1$-methylcyclopentene corresponds to option (b).

Q38.subtopic: E2 Elimination on β-Phenylethyl Bromide Derivative
Q38.conceptHtml: Alcoholic KOH/∆ performs E2 elimination; formation of a double bond conjugated with the benzene ring is strongly favoured.
Q38.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the substrate and possible $\beta$-hydrogens: The reactant is $2$-bromo-$3$-methyl-$1$-phenylbutane, $\text{Ph}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH(Br)}-\text{CH(CH}_3)_2$, heated with alcoholic $\text{KOH}$ ($\text{E2}$ elimination). There are two sets of $\beta$-hydrogens: on the benzylic $-\text{CH}_2-$ ($\text{C}-1$) and on the isopropyl methine $-\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)_2$ ($\text{C}-3$).
  2. Step 2 — Compare the stability of the two candidate alkenes: Elimination toward $\text{C}-3$ gives $3$-methyl-$1$-phenylbut-$2$-ene (a trisubstituted but unconjugated alkene). Elimination toward the benzylic $\text{C}-1$ gives (E)-$3$-methyl-$1$-phenylbut-$1$-ene ($\text{Ph}-\text{CH}=\text{CH}-\text{CH(CH}_3)_2$), in which the $\text{C}=\text{C}$ double bond is directly conjugated with the benzene ring.
  3. Step 3 — Choose the thermodynamically favoured major product: Resonance conjugation with the aromatic phenyl ring provides far greater stabilization than one extra alkyl substituent, and the benzylic $\text{C}-\text{H}$ is also more acidic. Moreover, the trans ($E$) isomer minimizes steric repulsion between the $-\text{Ph}$ and $-\text{CH(CH}_3)_2$ groups.
  4. Step 4 — Final Conclusion: The major product P is trans-$3$-methyl-$1$-phenylbut-$1$-ene, confirming option (d).

Q39.conceptHtml: 1-Bromopropane + NaOH/C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH gives propene (Product A). Acid-catalysed hydration (H<sub>2</sub>O/H<sup>+</sup>) is Markovnikov (2-propanol), while hydroboration–oxidation (B<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub>; H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>/OH<sup>−</sup>) is anti-Markovnikov (1-propanol).
Q39.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify Product A (Dehydrohalogenation): When $1$-bromopropane ($\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{Br}$) is treated with $\text{NaOH}$ in ethanol ($\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}$), it undergoes $\beta$-elimination (dehydrohalogenation) to form propene ($\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2$) as Product A.
  2. Step 2 — Identify Product B (Acid-catalyzed hydration): Reacting propene with $\text{H}_2\text{O}/\text{H}^+$ proceeds via a $2^\circ$ isopropyl carbocation ($\text{CH}_3-\overset{+}{\text{C}}\text{H}-\text{CH}_3$), following Markovnikov’s rule. Addition of $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ yields $2$-propanol ($\text{CH}_3-\text{CH(OH)}-\text{CH}_3$) as Product B.
  3. Step 3 — Identify Product C (Hydroboration–oxidation): Reacting propene with diborane ($\text{B}_2\text{H}_6$) followed by $\text{H}_2\text{O}_2/\text{OH}^-$ results in net anti-Markovnikov hydration of the double bond, placing $-\text{OH}$ on the terminal carbon to yield $1$-propanol ($\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$) as Product C.
  4. Step 4 — Final Conclusion: Therefore, $\text{B} = 2\text{-Propanol}$ and $\text{C} = 1\text{-Propanol}$, confirming option (d).

Step 2: CH3CH = CH2 −H−2−O−/−H−→+ CH3CH(OH)CH3 (B = 2-Propanol).

Q40.subtopic: Chemoselective SN2 on Benzylic vs Aryl Bromide
Q40.conceptHtml: Aryl C − Br (sp<sup>2</sup> C) is inert to Me<sub>2</sub>NH at room temperature, whereas benzylic C − Br (sp<sup>3</sup> C) undergoes rapid S<sub>N</sub>2 substitution.

1. Step 1 — Analyze the starting substrate and reagent: The reactant is 3,5-dibromocyclopent-1-ene, which contains two allylic $\text{C}-\text{Br}$ bonds flanking a $\text{C}=\text{C}$ double bond, treated with $2\text{ equiv}$ of the secondary amine nucleophile $\text{Me}_2\text{NH}$ ($\text{Me} = -\text{CH}_3$).
  2. Step 2 — First substitution step: One equivalent of $\text{Me}_2\text{NH}$ displaces the first allylic bromide (say at $\text{C-3}$) via an $\text{S}_\text{N}2$ reaction, forming 5-bromo-3-(dimethylamino)cyclopent-1-ene (with $\text{HBr}$ scavenged in the medium).
  3. Step 3 — Second substitution via $\text{S}_\text{N}2'$ pathway: The second equivalent of $\text{Me}_2\text{NH}$ attacks the allylic $\text{C}=\text{C}$ system via a concerted $\text{S}_\text{N}2'$ mechanism at the vinylic carbon adjacent to the existing $-\text{NMe}_2$ group, shifting the $\pi$-bond and expelling the remaining $\text{Br}^-$ from $\text{C-5}$.
  4. Step 4 — Identify the major product: This shifts the double bond to the opposite side of the ring and places both $-\text{NMe}_2$ groups on adjacent carbons (3,4-bis(dimethylamino)cyclopent-1-ene), matching Option (a).

Q41.conceptHtml: Alcoholic NaOH performs E2 elimination to give alkene B; HBr/ether adds Markovnikov across the double bond to give C.

1. Step 1 — Identify compound A and its reactive site: Compound A is 1-bromo-4-(2-bromoethyl)benzene ($p\text{-BrC}_6\text{H}_4\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$). The aryl $\text{C}-\text{Br}$ bond has partial double-bond character due to resonance and does not react under ordinary elimination conditions, whereas the aliphatic $-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$ chain reacts readily.
  2. Step 2 — Formation of B with alcoholic $\text{NaOH}$: Treatment with $\text{NaOH(alc)}$ causes $\text{E2}$ dehydrohalogenation of the $-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$ side chain to yield 4-bromostyrene ($p\text{-BrC}_6\text{H}_4\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2$) as compound B.
  3. Step 3 — Formation of C with $\text{HBr/Ether}$: In the absence of peroxides, $\text{HBr}$ adds across the double bond of B via Markovnikov electrophilic addition through the resonance-stabilized benzylic carbocation, producing 1-bromo-4-(1-bromoethyl)benzene ($p\text{-BrC}_6\text{H}_4\text{CH(Br)CH}_3$) as compound C.

Step 4 — Relate A and C: Compounds A ($p\text{-BrC}_6\text{H}_4\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$) and C ($p\text{-BrC}_6\text{H}_4\text{CH(Br)CH}_3$) share the same molecular formula and carbon skeleton but differ in the position of the side-chain bromine atom, so they are position isomers. This matches Option (a).

Q44.subtopic: KCN vs AgCN: Ionic vs Covalent Bonding
Q44.conceptHtml: KCN is predominantly ionic (K<sup>+</sup>CN<sup>−</sup>), so attack occurs via the softer/more nucleophilic C atom to give R − CN. AgCN is predominantly covalent (Ag − C ≡ N), so only the N lone pair is free to attack, giving R − NC.

With $\text{KCN}$ (predominantly ionic), free $\text{CN}^-$ attacks mainly through the carbon atom because the resulting $\text{C}-\text{C}$ bond is more stable than a $\text{C}-\text{N}$ bond, forming alkyl cyanides ($\text{R}-\text{CN}$). With $\text{AgCN}$ (predominantly covalent), the carbon end is bonded to $\text{Ag}$, so attack occurs through the nitrogen lone pair to give alkyl isocyanides ($\text{R}-\text{NC}$). Hence, Assertion (A) is correct.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Reason (R): While $\text{KCN}$ is predominantly ionic, $\text{AgCN}$ is predominantly covalent in nature (due to the high polarizing power of $\text{Ag}^+$). Saying both are highly ionic is incorrect. Hence, Reason (R) is not correct.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the answer: Since (A) is correct and (R) is not correct, the answer is Option (a).

Q47.subtopic: Mechanism Selection for Secondary Alkyl Halides
Q47.conceptHtml: Secondary alkyl halides are borderline: a high concentration of a strong nucleophile drives S<sub>N</sub>2, whereas solvolysis in excess weak protic nucleophile (ethanol) proceeds via S<sub>N</sub>1.
Q47.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement-I: Secondary ($2^\circ$) alkyl halides sit at the borderline between $\text{S}_\text{N}1$ and $\text{S}_\text{N}2$. When there are no bulky substituents blocking backside attack and a high concentration of a strong nucleophile is present, the bimolecular rate ($r = k[\text{R}-\text{X}][\text{Nu}^-]$) dominates, so the reaction follows the $\text{S}_\text{N}2$ mechanism. Thus, Statement-I is true.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement-II: Ethanol ($\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}$) is a weak nucleophile and a polar protic solvent. In a large excess of ethanol (solvolysis), the $2^\circ$ alkyl halide ionizes to a carbocation intermediate stabilized by the polar protic solvent, following the $\text{S}_\text{N}1$ mechanism. Thus, Statement-II is true.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the answer: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are true, corresponding to Option (a).

Q51.subtopic: Conversion of Alkyl Halide to Alkyl Isocyanide
Q51.conceptHtml: Covalent AgCN reacts with R − X via the nitrogen lone pair to yield alkyl isocyanide (R − NC).

Q52.subtopic: Phenol Cannot Form Aryl Halide with HX
Q52.conceptHtml: The C − O bond in phenol has partial double-bond character due to resonance of the oxygen lone pair into the benzene ring, making it too strong to be cleaved by HX or SOCl<sub>2</sub>.
Q52.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Assertion A: In phenol ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH}$), lone-pair delocalization from oxygen into the benzene ring gives the $\text{C}-\text{O}$ bond partial double-bond character, making it much stronger than the $\text{C}-\text{O}$ bond in alcohols. Consequently, aryl halides cannot be prepared by replacing the $-\text{OH}$ group of phenol with a halogen using $\text{HX}$. Thus, A is true.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Reason R: Because the aryl $\text{C}-\text{O}$ bond is strong and unreactive towards nucleophilic substitution, phenols do not react with halogen acids—let alone violently. Thus, R is false.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the answer: A is true and R is false, matching Option (a).

Q53.conceptHtml: Vinylic halides (R − CH = CH − Cl) do not undergo S<sub>N</sub>1 because the C − Cl bond has partial double-bond character and the resulting vinylic carbocation is extremely unstable.

1. Step 1 — Recall the requirement for $\text{S}_\text{N}1$ reaction: The rate-determining step of an $\text{S}_\text{N}1$ reaction is heterolytic cleavage of the $\text{C}-\text{Cl}$ bond to form a reasonably stable carbocation.

Step 2 — Check compounds (A), (C), and (D): (A) $\text{H}_2\text{C}=\text{CH}-\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$ forms a resonance-stabilized allyl carbocation; (C) benzyl chloride ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$) forms a resonance-stabilized benzyl carbocation; (D) isopropyl chloride ($(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CHCl}$) forms a secondary carbocation. All three can undergo $\text{S}_\text{N}1$.
  3. Step 3 — Check compound (B): $\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}=\text{CH}-\text{Cl}$ is a vinylic halide. Lone-pair resonance from chlorine gives the $\text{C}-\text{Cl}$ bond partial double-bond character, and loss of $\text{Cl}^-$ would form a highly unstable vinylic carbocation ($sp$-like positive carbon). Hence, (B) will not show $\text{S}_\text{N}1$.

Q54.conceptHtml: In a chiral alkyl halide, S<sub>N</sub>1 forms a planar carbocation leading to racemisation, while S<sub>N</sub>2 proceeds via backside attack leading to inversion of configuration.

  2. Step 2 — Stereochemistry of $\text{S}_\text{N}2$: An $\text{S}_\text{N}2$ reaction is a single-step concerted process in which the nucleophile attacks strictly from the side opposite to the leaving group ($180^\circ$ backside attack), resulting in complete inversion of configuration (Walden inversion).
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the answer: Racemisation occurs in $\text{S}_\text{N}1$ and inversion occurs in $\text{S}_\text{N}2$, which matches Option (d).

Q57.subtopic: 2-Methylpropyl Bromide: SN2 vs SN1 with Rearrangement
Q57.conceptHtml: 2-Methylpropyl bromide (isobutyl bromide, 1<sup>°</sup>) with strong nucleophile C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>O<sup>−</sup> undergoes S<sub>N</sub>2 without rearrangement to give isobutyl ethyl ether. 1. Step 1 — Identify the substrate: 2-Methylpropyl bromide (isobutyl bromide) has the structure $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CH}-\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$, a $1^\circ$ alkyl halide with $\beta$-branching.

Step 2 — Reaction with strong nucleophile $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{O}^-$: Ethoxide is a strong anionic nucleophile, so it directly displaces $\text{Br}^-$ via an $\text{S}_\text{N}2$ mechanism without carbocation rearrangement, yielding A = iso-butyl ethyl ether ($(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CHCH}_2\text{OC}_2\text{H}_5$).

The incipient $1^\circ$ carbocation immediately undergoes a 1,2-hydride shift to form the much more stable $3^\circ$ tert-butyl carbocation ($(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}^+$), which is trapped by $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}$ to give B = tert-butyl ethyl ether ($(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{COC}_2\text{H}_5$).

Q58.conceptHtml: AgNO<sub>3</sub> precipitates AgBr only if the C − Br bond can ionize to a carbocation. Rigid bridgehead bromides (Bredt’s rule) cannot flatten and do NOT precipitate with AgNO<sub>3</sub>.
Q58.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the principle of the $\text{AgNO}_3$ test: An organic bromide gives a pale-yellow precipitate of $\text{AgBr}$ with $\text{AgNO}_3$ only if its $\text{C}-\text{Br}$ bond can heterolytically cleave to form a stabilized carbocation.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate options (a), (c), and (d): (a) Cinnamyl bromide ($\text{PhCH}=\text{CHCH}_2\text{Br}$) forms an extended allylic-benzylic carbocation; (c) benzyl bromide ($\text{PhCH}_2\text{Br}$) forms a resonance-stabilized benzyl carbocation; (d) 3-bromocycloprop-1-ene forms the aromatic cyclopropenyl cation ($2\pi$ electrons, Hückel $4n+2$). All three readily precipitate $\text{AgBr}$.
  3. Step 3 — Evaluate option (b): 1-Bromocyclohex-1-ene is a vinylic bromide whose $\text{C}-\text{Br}$ bond has partial double-bond character due to resonance and would yield an extremely unstable vinylic carbocation. Therefore, it does not give a precipitate with $\text{AgNO}_3$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: The unreactive compound is Option (b).

Step 2: (B) is a rigid bicyclic bridgehead bromide, which cannot form a planar carbocation ⇒ no AgBr precipitate.
Verified Answer: (B)

Q59.subtopic: SN1 vs SN2 Kinetics via Ring Substituents
Q59.conceptHtml: p-MeO (+M) strongly stabilizes the benzyl carbocation, shifting the mechanism to S<sub>N</sub>1 (1st order). p-NO<sub>2</sub> (−M) destabilizes the carbocation, forcing the reaction through S<sub>N</sub>2 (2nd order).
Q59.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Analyze Reaction (I): The substrate is $p$-methoxybenzyl chloride ($p\text{-MeO}-\text{C}_6\text{H}_4-\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$). The strongly electron-donating $-\text{OMe}$ group ($+M$ effect) greatly stabilizes the benzylic carbocation intermediate, favoring the unimolecular $\text{S}_\text{N}1$ mechanism, which follows 1st order kinetics ($r = k[\text{substrate}]$).
  2. Step 2 — Analyze Reaction (II): The substrate is $p$-nitrobenzyl chloride ($p\text{-O}_2\text{N}-\text{C}_6\text{H}_4-\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$). The strongly electron-withdrawing $-\text{NO}_2$ group ($-M, -I$) destabilizes carbocation formation while increasing electrophilicity at the benzylic carbon, favoring the bimolecular $\text{S}_\text{N}2$ mechanism, which follows 2nd order kinetics ($r = k[\text{substrate}][\text{Nu}]$).
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the answer: Reaction (I) is of 1st order and reaction (II) is of 2nd order, matching Option (a).
Q59.stepsLatex:
Step 1: Reaction (I) has p-MeO ⇒ 1st order (SN1).
Step 2: Reaction (II) has p-NO2 ⇒ 2nd order (SN2).
Q59.trapHtml: EDG favours S<sub>N</sub>1 (1st order); EWG disfavours carbocation and favours S<sub>N</sub>2 (2nd order). Verified Answer: (A) Reaction (I) is of 1st order and reaction (II) is of 2nd order

Q60.subtopic: Reactivity Orders Across Mechanisms (SN2, SN1, EAS, SNAr)
Q60.conceptHtml: Verify each pair against its stated mechanism.
Q60.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Check pairs (A) and (B): In (A), 1-bromobutane ($1^\circ$) is far less sterically hindered than 2-bromo-2-methylpropane ($3^\circ$), so it reacts faster via $\text{S}_\text{N}2$ (correct). In (B), 1-bromo-1-phenylethane forms a resonance-stabilized $2^\circ$ benzylic carbocation, whereas 1-bromo-2-phenylethane forms an unstabilized $1^\circ$ carbocation, so the first reacts faster via $\text{S}_\text{N}1$ (correct).
  2. Step 2 — Check pair (C): For electrophilic aromatic substitution, adding a strongly electron-withdrawing $-\text{NO}_2$ group ($-M, -I$) to chlorobenzene reduces ring electron density further, so chlorobenzene is more reactive than 1-chloro-4-nitrobenzene (correct).
  3. Step 3 — Check pair (D): For nucleophilic aromatic substitution ($\text{S}_\text{N}\text{Ar}$), a para $-\text{NO}_2$ group stabilizes the anionic Meisenheimer intermediate by resonance, making 1-bromo-4-nitrobenzene much more reactive than bromobenzene (correct).
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: All four orders (A), (B), (C), and (D) are correct, matching Option (b).

Step 2: (B) SN1: 3◦ bromide > 2◦ bromide ⇒ correct.

Step 4: (D) SNAr: p-nitrobromobenzene > bromobenzene (−NO2 activates SNAr) ⇒ correct.
Verified Answer: (B) (A), (B), (C) and (D)

Q61.subtopic: SNAr Reactivity Order with Aqueous NaOH
Q61.conceptHtml: In S<sub>N</sub>Ar, EWGs (−NO<sub>2</sub> at o/p) accelerate the reaction and EDGs (−OMe) retard it.
Q61.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the electronic rule for $\text{S}_\text{N}\text{Ar}$: Nucleophilic aromatic substitution of haloarenes with aqueous $\text{NaOH}$ proceeds through a negatively charged Meisenheimer complex. Electron-withdrawing groups ($-\text{NO}_2$) at ortho/para positions stabilize this carbanion and accelerate the reaction, whereas electron-donating groups ($-\text{OMe}$) destabilize it and slow the reaction.
  2. Step 2 — Compare all four haloarenes: Compound D (1-chloro-2,4,6-trinitrobenzene) has three ortho/para $-\text{NO}_2$ groups (fastest). Compound B (1-chloro-4-nitrobenzene) has one para $-\text{NO}_2$ group (second). Compound A (chlorobenzene) has no extra substituent (third). Compound C (1-chloro-4-methoxybenzene) has an electron-donating $+M$ $-\text{OMe}$ group (slowest).
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the reactivity order: Decreasing reactivity order is $\text{D} > \text{B} > \text{A} > \text{C}$, which corresponds to Option (b).

Verified Answer: (B) D > B > A > C

Q62.subtopic: Most Reactive Halogen Towards SN1 in Polyhalides
Q62.conceptHtml: Compare the carbocation formed by losing each halogen: benzylic/allylic/tertiary carbocations beat pri- mary/vinylic/aryl ones.
Q62.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Compare halogens in A and B: In A, $\text{Br}_{(a)}$ is at the benzylic carbon (forming a resonance-stabilized benzylic carbocation), whereas $\text{Br}_{(b)}$ gives only a $2^\circ$ aliphatic carbocation $\rightarrow$ $\text{Br}_{(a)}$. In B, $\text{I}_{(a)}$ is at the allylic position (resonance-stabilized allylic carbocation), whereas $\text{I}_{(b)}$ is a simple $1^\circ$ iodide $\rightarrow$ $\text{I}_{(a)}$.
  2. Step 2 — Compare halogens in C: In the bicyclic system C, $\text{Br}_{(a)}$ sits at a bridgehead carbon where a planar $sp^2$ carbocation cannot form due to severe angle strain (Bredt's rule). In contrast, $\text{Br}_{(b)}$ is at a non-bridgehead $3^\circ$ carbon that readily forms a $3^\circ$ carbocation $\rightarrow$ $\text{Br}_{(b)}$.
  3. Step 3 — Compare halogens in D: In D, $\text{Br}_{(a)}$ is attached to a $3^\circ$ carbon (stable $3^\circ$ carbocation), whereas $\text{Br}_{(b)}$ is attached to a $1^\circ$ carbon $\rightarrow$ $\text{Br}_{(a)}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: The most reactive halogens are $\text{A}-\text{Br}_{(a)}$; $\text{B}-\text{I}_{(a)}$; $\text{C}-\text{Br}_{(b)}$; $\text{D}-\text{Br}_{(a)}$, matching Option (d).

Step 3: Compound C: Br(b) is 3◦ (at the carbon bearing Me) whereas Br(a) is aryl ⇒ Br(b).

Q63.conceptHtml: Finkelstein (RCH<sub>2</sub>Br + I<sup>−</sup> <sup>−A</sup><sup>−c</sup><sup>−e</sup><sup>−to</sup><sup>−n</sup>→<sup>e</sup> RCH<sub>2</sub>I + Br<sup>−</sup>) is an S<sub>N</sub>2 reaction in a polar aprotic solvent (acetone). The S<sub>N</sub>2 transition state [I<sup>δ−</sup> · · · CH<sub>2</sub>R · · · Br<sup>δ−</sup>] has dispersed negative charge, making it less polar (and less solvated) than the localized I<sup>−</sup> anion.
Q63.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the reaction and mechanism: $\text{RCH}_2\text{Br} + \text{I}^- \xrightarrow{\text{Acetone}} \text{RCH}_2\text{I} + \text{Br}^-$ is the Finkelstein reaction, proceeding by a concerted $\text{S}_\text{N}2$ mechanism in the polar aprotic solvent acetone.
  2. Step 2 — Analyze the polarity of the transition state: In the reactants, the full negative charge is localized on the small $\text{I}^-$ anion. In the pentacoordinate $\text{S}_\text{N}2$ transition state $[\text{I}^{\delta-}\cdots\text{CH}_2(\text{R})\cdots\text{Br}^{\delta-}]$, this charge is dispersed over two halogen atoms, making the transition state less polar than the localized reactant anion.
  3. Step 3 — Eliminate incorrect statements: Acetone is polar aprotic (poorly solvates anions and precipitates $\text{NaBr}$, preventing $\text{Br}^-$ from competing), and acetic acid is polar protic (which solvates $\text{I}^-$ by hydrogen bonding and dissolves $\text{NaBr}$, suppressing the reaction).
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: Thus, the correct statement is Option (d).

the reaction forward); (C) is false (acetic acid is protic and would solvate I−); (D) is true!
Verified Answer: (D)

Q64.conceptHtml: Alcoholic KOH with tert-butyl bromide undergoes β-elimination (E2) to give isobutene (2-methylpropene), NOT tert-butyl alcohol.

(d) Aqueous $\text{KOH}$ converts 1-bromobutane into butan-1-ol via $\text{S}_\text{N}2$ substitution. All three are valid.
  2. Step 2 — Examine option (c): Treating a tertiary alkyl halide (tert-butyl bromide) with alcoholic $\text{KOH}$ causes $\text{E2}$ dehydrohalogenation to yield an alkene (2-methylpropene), not nucleophilic substitution to tert-butyl alcohol.

Q67.subtopic: SN1 Reactivity of Substituted Benzyl Chlorides
Q67.conceptHtml: S<sub>N</sub>1 rate follows carbocation stability: +M (p-OMe) > unsubstituted (−H) > −I (p-Cl) > −M, −I (p-NO<sub>2</sub>).

Q69.subtopic: Physical Property Trends: Boiling Point & Density

In (C), adding more bromine atoms increases molar mass and dispersion forces, raising the boiling point (correct). In (E), among isomeric butyl chlorides, branching reduces surface area and weakens van der Waals forces, so boiling point decreases with branching: $1\text{-chlorobutane} > \text{isobutyl chloride} > \text{tert-butyl chloride}$ (correct).

Q70.subtopic: Lowest Rate Towards SNAr with OH−
Q70.conceptHtml: In S<sub>N</sub>Ar, a −NO<sub>2</sub> group at the meta position cannot stabilize the Meisenheimer carbanion by resonance (only −I), giving the lowest rate compared to ortho or para −NO<sub>2</sub>.

In (a) 1-chloro-2-nitrobenzene and (c) 1-chloro-4-nitrobenzene, the single ortho or para $-\text{NO}_2$ group stabilizes the carbanion directly via $-M$ resonance.
  3. Step 3 — Identify the slowest substrate: In (b) 1-chloro-3-nitrobenzene, the meta $-\text{NO}_2$ group cannot delocalize the negative charge by resonance (it exerts only a weaker $-I$ effect), so it exhibits the lowest rate of nucleophilic aromatic substitution.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: The compound with the lowest rate is Option (b).

rate.

Q71.subtopic: NaI Catalysis in Alkyl Chloride Hydrolysis

Step 2 — Evaluate Reason R and its explanatory link: $\text{I}^-$ is both a stronger nucleophile (easily displacing $\text{Cl}^-$ via $\text{S}_\text{N}2$ to form $\text{R}-\text{I}$) and a much better leaving group than $\text{Cl}^-$ (so $\text{R}-\text{I}$ hydrolyzes rapidly to $\text{R}-\text{OH}$, regenerating $\text{I}^-$). Thus, Reason R is true and correctly explains A.

Q73.subtopic: Structural Isomers of C5H11Br Giving Chiral Alcohols

Q74.conceptHtml: 2-Bromopentane (M = 151 g mol<sup>−1</sup>) <sup>−a</sup><sup>−lc</sup><sup>−.</sup><sup>−K</sup><sup>−O</sup>−→<sup>H</sup> pent-2-ene (P, 80% yield) <sup>−B</sup><sup>−r</sup>→<sup>2</sup> 2,3-dibromopentane (Q, M = 230 g mol<sup>−1</sup>, 100% yield).
Q74.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Calculate initial moles of 2-bromopentane: Molar mass of 2-bromopentane ($\text{C}_5\text{H}_{11}\text{Br}$) $= 5(12) + 11(1) + 80 = 151\text{ g mol}^{-1}$. Thus, moles reacted $= \frac{151\text{ g}}{151\text{ g mol}^{-1}} = 1\text{ mol}$.
  2. Step 2 — Identify major product P and its moles: Dehydrohalogenation of 2-bromopentane with alcoholic $\text{KOH}$ follows Zaitsev's rule to yield the more substituted alkene, pent-2-ene ($\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}$), as major product P. At $80\%$ yield, moles of $\text{P} = 1 \times 0.80 = 0.80\text{ mol}$.
  3. Step 3 — Identify product Q and its molar mass: Electrophilic addition of $\text{Br}_2$ across the double bond of pent-2-ene gives 2,3-dibromopentane ($\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}\text{Br}_2$) as product Q. Its molar mass is $5(12) + 10(1) + 2(80) = 60 + 10 + 160 = 230\text{ g mol}^{-1}$.
  4. Step 4 — Compute the mass of Q: With $100\%$ yield in the second step, moles of $\text{Q} = 0.80\text{ mol}$, so mass of $\text{Q} = 0.80\text{ mol} \times 230\text{ g mol}^{-1} = 184\text{ g}$. The verified numerical answer is 184.

Verified Answer: 184

Q75.conceptHtml: Sandmeyer’s reaction (ArN<sup>+</sup><sub>2</sub> X<sup>−</sup> + Cu<sub>2</sub>X<sub>2</sub>/HX) prepares only PhCl and PhBr among halobenzenes (PhF uses Balz–Schiemann HBF<sub>4</sub>/∆; PhI uses KI directly without Cu<sub>2</sub>I<sub>2</sub>).
Q75.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the scope of Sandmeyer's reaction: Sandmeyer's reaction replaces the diazonium group of a benzenediazonium salt ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{N}_2^+\text{X}^-$) with $-\text{Cl}$, $-\text{Br}$, or $-\text{CN}$ using the corresponding copper(I) salt ($\text{Cu}_2\text{Cl}_2/\text{HCl}$, $\text{Cu}_2\text{Br}_2/\text{HBr}$, or $\text{CuCN}/\text{KCN}$).
  2. Step 2 — Check the five halobenzenes shown: Chlorobenzene (II) and bromobenzene (III) are directly prepared by Sandmeyer's reaction.
  3. Step 3 — Exclude the others: Fluorobenzene (I) is prepared via the Balz–Schiemann reaction ($\text{HBF}_4/\Delta$), iodobenzene (IV) is prepared simply by warming with $\text{KI}$ (no $\text{Cu(I)}$ catalyst required), and astatobenzene (V) is not prepared by Sandmeyer's reaction.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the count: Only $2$ halobenzenes (II and III) can be prepared by Sandmeyer's reaction. The verified numerical answer is 2.

Q76.subtopic: E2 vs SN2 on Bromoethane: Atom Counting
Q76.conceptHtml: CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Br + NaOH/C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH → CH<sub>2</sub> = CH<sub>2</sub> (A, 4 H); CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Br + NaOH/H<sub>2</sub>O → CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH (B, 6 H).
Q76.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify Product A (alcoholic medium): Treating bromoethane ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$) with $\text{NaOH}$ in ethanol ($\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}$) favors $\text{E2}$ dehydrohalogenation, giving Product A = ethene ($\text{CH}_2=\text{CH}_2$, formula $\text{C}_2\text{H}_4$), which has $4$ hydrogen atoms.
  2. Step 2 — Identify Product B (aqueous medium): Treating bromoethane with $\text{NaOH}$ in water ($\text{H}_2\text{O}$) favors $\text{S}_\text{N}2$ nucleophilic substitution, giving Product B = ethanol ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$, formula $\text{C}_2\text{H}_6\text{O}$), which has $6$ hydrogen atoms.
  3. Step 3 — Sum the hydrogen atoms: Total number of hydrogen atoms in Product A and Product B $= 4 + 6 = 10$. The verified numerical answer is 10.

Q77.subtopic: Moles of AgCl Precipitated with AgNO
Q77.conceptHtml: Only sp<sup>3</sup>-bonded Cl atoms that can form stable carbocations precipitate with AgNO<sub>3</sub>; vinylic and aryl Cl atoms do NOT react.
Q77.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Classify all four chlorine atoms in the molecule: The compound contains (i) an aryl $-\text{Cl}$ attached directly to the benzene ring, (ii) a vinylic $-\text{Cl}$ attached to a $\text{C}=\text{C}$ double bond, (iii) a benzylic $-\text{CH(Cl)}-$ on the side chain, and (iv) a tertiary $-\text{C(CH}_3)_2\text{Cl}$ at the end of the side chain.
  2. Step 2 — Identify unreactive $\text{C}-\text{Cl}$ bonds: Both the aryl $-\text{Cl}$ and vinylic $-\text{Cl}$ bonds possess partial double-bond character due to resonance and would form highly unstable aryl/vinylic carbocations, so neither reacts with $\text{AgNO}_3$.
  3. Step 3 — Identify reactive $\text{C}-\text{Cl}$ bonds: The benzylic $-\text{Cl}$ ionizes readily to give a resonance-stabilized benzylic carbocation, and the tertiary $-\text{Cl}$ ionizes readily to give a stable $3^\circ$ carbocation. Both release $\text{Cl}^-$ to precipitate $\text{AgCl}$ with $\text{AgNO}_3$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the number of moles of $\text{AgCl}$: Exactly $2$ moles of $\text{AgCl}$ are formed per mole of the compound. The verified numerical answer is 2.

trapCards.title: Trap 1: S<sub>N</sub>1 vs S<sub>N</sub>2 & Bredt’s Rule
trapCards.html:
• Vinylic / Aryl / Bridgehead Halides: Completely inert to both SN1 and SN2 (and give no AgNO3 precipi- tate). Smaller bicyclic bridgehead ([2.2.1]) is even slower than [2.2.2].
  • Anomalous 1◦ Halides: CH3OCH2Cl (1◦) reacts rapidly via SN1 (resonance-stabilized oxocarbenium), whereas neopentyl chloride (Me3CCH2Cl) is 1◦ yet prac- tically inert to SN2.
  • Racemisation vs Inversion: SN1 on a chiral halide gives an optically inactive racemic mixture; SN2 gives 100% Walden inversion (stereospecific).

trapCards.title: Trap 2: Ambident Nucleophiles & Solvents
trapCards.html:
• KCN vs AgCN: Ionic KCN → R−CN (nitrile); covalent AgCN → R − NC (isocyanide). Never assume AgCN is ionic!
  • KNO2 vs AgNO2: Ionic KNO2 → R − ONO (alkyl nitrite); covalent AgNO2 → R − NO2 (nitroalkane).
  • Protic Solvents: In MeOH/H2O, I− > Br− > Cl− > F− (F− is heavily H-bonded and drops below PhO−!).
  • Hughes–Ingold: Neutral + neutral → ionic product (RX + R3N) is accelerated in more polar solvents.

trapCards.title: Trap 3: Aq. KOH vs Alc. KOH & Rearrangements
trapCards.html:
• Aqueous KOH = Substitution (R − OH). Alcoholic KOH / ∆ = β-Elimination (E2, Zaitsev alkene).
  • Solvolysis Rearrangement: Isobutyl bromide + EtO− gives SN2 (isobutyl ethyl ether), but with EtOH (SN1) it rearranges via 1, 2-H− shift to tert-butyl ethyl ether!
  • Ring vs Side-Chain: Br2/Fe (dark) brominates the aro- matic ring (o/p), while Br2/hν or Cl2/∆ substitutes the benzylic α-carbon.

trapCards.title: Trap 4: Haloarenes, S<sub>N</sub>Ar & NCERT Memory
trapCards.html:
• SNAr Regioselectivity: Only o/p-NO2 activates C − X substitution; m-NO2 cannot stabilize the Meisenheimer carbanion by resonance!
  • Sandmeyer Scope: Prepares ArCl and ArBr (and ArCN); ArF needs Balz–Schiemann (HBF4/∆), ArI needs KI.
  • Dichlorobenzene Trends: M.P. p > o > m; B.P. o > p ≈ m.
  • Polyhalogens: Gammaxene (C6H6Cl6, 6 Cl); CCl4 (fire extinguisher); CH2Cl2 (paint remover); Freons (AC/refrigerant).

subject: Chemistry
title: Practical Organic Chemistry
constantsHtml:
• Practical Organic Chemistry
  • Chapter Overview & High-Yield Focus (2023–2026: 69 Questions)
  • Practical Organic Chemistry (POC) is one of the highest-ROI chapters in JEE Main Chemistry: nearly every shift features
  • either a purification/separation match, a Lassaigne’s/quantitative estimation calculation (Dumas, Kjeldahl, Car-
  • ius, Liebig), or a functional group / titrimetric test. Mastering the exact precipitate formulas, colour changes, and
  • stoichiometric factors guarantees full marks in under 60 seconds per question.

formulaCards.title: 1. Purification Techniques
formulaCards.html:
• Crystallisation: Based on difference in solubility of com- pound and impurities in a suitable solvent (dissolves more at high T, crystallises on cooling). E.g., sugar + NaCl separated using ethanol.
  • Sublimation: Separates sublimable solids from non- sublimable impurities (camphor, naphthalene, anthracene, benzoic acid, I2).
  • Simple Distillation: Liquids with large ∆Tb (≥ 25 K) and no decomposition. E.g., chloroform (334 K) + aniline (457 K); glycerol/water? No, glycerol decomposes!
  • Fractional Distillation: Miscible liquids with close boiling points (∆Tb < 25 K). E.g., crude oil fractions (petrol + diesel), acetone + methanol. Note: Azeotropic mixtures cannot be separated by fractional distillation.
  • Distillation under Reduced Pressure: Liquids that decompose at or below their normal b.p. E.g., glyc- erol from spent-lye in soap industry.
  • Steam Distillation: Substances that are steam volatile and immiscible with water. E.g., aniline– water mixture, o-nitrophenol vs p-nitrophenol, essential oils (rose essence).
  • Differential Extraction: Organic compound shaken with immiscible organic solvent + water (separating fun- nel); acidic/basic components extracted into aqueous layer using NaOH or HCl.

formulaCards.title: 2. Chromatography & R<sub>f</sub> Value
formulaCards.html:
• Adsorption Chromatography: Column & Thin Layer (TLC). Stationary phase: solid (Al2O3 or silica gel); mo- bile phase: liquid.
  • Partition Chromatography: Paper chromatography (water trapped in cellulose = stationary phase).
  • Retardation Factor (Rf): R = Distance moved by substance from base line ≤ 1 f Distance moved by solvent front from base line
  • Polarity Rule (Silica/Alumina TLC): More polar compounds adsorb more strongly =⇒ travel slower =⇒ lower Rf. Less polar compounds =⇒ higher Rf. (e.g., alkane > alcohol).

formulaCards.title: 3. Lassaigne’s Test (Extra Elements)
formulaCards.html:
• Organic compound fused with Na metal (converts covalent bonds to ionic salts: NaCN, Na2S, NaX).
  • Nitrogen: Extract + FeSO4 + NaOH −b−o−→il Na [Fe(CN) ] −F−e−3+−−,H−+→ Prussian blue Fe [Fe(CN) ] . 4 6 4 6 3
  • N + S together: Forms NaSCN −F−e−3+→ Blood-red [Fe(SCN)]2+. (Excess Na decomposes NaSCN → NaCN+ Na2S).
  • Sulphur: (i) + Sodium nitroprusside Na2[Fe(CN)5NO] → Violet/Purple Na4[Fe(CN)5NOS]. (ii) + Acetic acid + Pb(OAc)2 → black PbS ↓.
  • Halogens: Boil extract with conc. HNO3 first (to expel HCN/H2S as gases so they don’t give AgCN/Ag2S), then + AgNO3: – Cl−: White ppt (AgCl), soluble in NH4OH. – Br−: Pale yellow ppt (AgBr), sparingly soluble in NH4OH. – I−: Yellow ppt (AgI), insoluble in NH4OH.
  • Phosphorus: Fuse with Na2O2 → boil with HNO3 + ammonium molybdate (NH4)2MoO4 → Canary yellow ppt of (NH ) PO · 12MoO .

formulaCards.title: 4. Quantitative Estimation Formulas
formulaCards.html:
• Let m = mass of organic compound taken:
  • Liebig’s Method (C & H): %C = 12 × mCO2 × 100, %H = 2 × mH2O × 100 44 m 18 m
  • Dumas Method (N): Heated with CuO; NOx reduced over copper gauze; N2 collected over KOH: P = P − Aqueous tension, V = PdryV × 273 dry atm STP 760 × T %N = 28 × VSTP (mL) × 100 22400 m (g)
  • Kjeldahl’s Method (N): Heated with conc. H2SO4 + CuSO4 (catalyst) → (NH4)2SO4. %N = 1.4 × Macid × basicity × Vacid (mL) = 1.4 × N × V (mL) m (g) m (g) Fails for: −NO2, −N = N− (azo), and ring-N (e.g., pyri- dine).
  • Carius Method (Halogens & S): Heated with fuming HNO3 (+ AgNO3 for X; + BaCl2 for S): %X = At.wt(X)×mAgX ×100 (AgCl : 143.5, AgBr : 188, AgI : 235) MAgX m %S = 32 × mBaSO4 × 100 233 m
  • Phosphorus Estimation: 62 mMg2P2O7 31 m(NH4)3PO4·12MoO3 %P = 222× m ×100 or 1877× m ×100

formulaCards.title: 5. Functional Group Detection Tests
formulaCards.html:
• Unsaturation: (i) Br2/H2O or Br2/CCl4: reddish- orange decolourises. (ii) Baeyer’s reagent (cold dil. alk. KMnO4): pink colour discharged.
  • Alcoholic −OH: (i) Ceric ammonium nitrate (CAN): red colour. (ii) Lucas test (conc. HCl + anh. ZnCl2): 3◦ immediate turbidity, 2◦ in 5 min, 1◦ no tur- bidity at RT. (iii) Victor Meyer (1◦ blood-red, 2◦ blue, 3◦ colourless).
  • Phenolic −OH: (i) Neutral FeCl3: vio- let/blue/green/red colour (also acetate ion gives red). (ii) Phthalein dye test (phthalic anhydride + conc. H2SO4 −N−a−O−H→ pink phenolphthalein).
  • Aldehydes & Ketones: (i) 2,4-DNP: yellow/orange- red ppt (both). (ii) Tollens’ reagent: silver mirror (alde- hydes + α-hydroxy ketones + HCOOH). (iii) Fehling’s solution: red Cu2O ppt (aliphatic aldehydes only; ben- zaldehyde fails). (iv) Schiff’s reagent: pink/magenta colour (aldehydes).
  • Iodoform Test (I2/NaOH): Yellow CHI3 ↓ for CH3CO− or CH3CH(OH)− groups.
  • Carboxylic Acid: NaHCO3 gives brisk effervescence of CO2.
  • Amines: (i) Carbylamine test (CHCl3 + KOH, ∆): foul-smelling isocyanide (1◦ amines only). (ii) Hinsberg’s reagent (PhSO2Cl): 1◦ → soluble in KOH; 2◦ → insol- uble in KOH; 3◦ → no reaction. (iii) Azo dye test: 1◦ aromatic amine + NaNO2/HCl (0–5◦C) + β-naphthol → orange-red dye.

Q01.conceptHtml: Differential solubility separates sugar from NaCl in ethanol; steam distillation isolates steam-volatile, water-insoluble essential oils.
Q01.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement I (Differential Solubility): Cane sugar ($\text{C}_{12}\text{H}_{22}\text{O}_{11}$) is a covalent organic compound that dissolves in alcohol (ethanol), whereas sodium chloride ($\text{NaCl}$) is an ionic salt that is practically insoluble in alcohol. Because of this difference in solubility, sugar can be extracted into alcohol and filtered away from solid $\text{NaCl}$. Hence, Statement I is true.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement II (Steam Distillation): Steam distillation is used to purify organic compounds that are steam-volatile (high vapour pressure with steam) and immiscible/insoluble in water. Rose essence (essential oil) from rose petals satisfies both conditions, allowing it to distil below $100^\circ\text{C}$ without decomposing. Hence, Statement II is true.
  3. Step 3 — Final Verification: Both Statement I and Statement II are true, which matches option (a).
Q01.stepsLatex:
Step 1: Evaluate Statement I: Sucrose (C12H22O11) is soluble in hot ethanol/alcohol, whereas ionic NaCl is insoluble
in alcohol. Filtering separates NaCl as residue and sugar from the filtrate. Hence, Statement I is true.
Step 2: Evaluate Statement II: Rose essence (essential oil) is steam-volatile and immiscible with water, so it co-distils
with steam at < 100◦C without decomposing. Hence, Statement II is true.
Q01.trapHtml: Do not confuse steam distillation (for water-insoluble, steam-volatile liquids) with distillation under reduced pressure (for high-boiling liquids like glycerol that decompose before boiling). Verified Answer: (A) Both Statement I and Statement II are true

Q02.conceptHtml: On polar stationary phases (silica gel/alumina), more polar molecules adsorb more strongly and have a lower R<sub>f</sub> value.
Q02.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the Major Product $(X)$: Treating 2-methylpropene, $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C}=\text{CH}_2$, with dilute $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ performs acid-catalysed Markovnikov hydration via a stable $3^\circ$ carbocation intermediate to give 2-methylpropan-2-ol (tert-butyl alcohol), $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}-\text{OH}$, as the major product $(X)$.
  2. Step 2 — Compare Polarities of Reactant and Product: 2-Methylpropene is a non-polar hydrocarbon, whereas tert-butyl alcohol $(X)$ contains a polar $-\text{OH}$ group capable of forming strong hydrogen bonds. Therefore, $(X)$ is significantly more polar than 2-methylpropene.
  3. Step 3 — Relate Polarity to $R_f$ Value in Chromatography: In normal-phase chromatography (polar stationary phase such as silica gel or alumina), a more polar compound adsorbs more strongly onto the stationary phase and travels a shorter distance with the mobile phase. Thus, the $R_f$ value of $(X)$ must be much lower than $0.42$.
  4. Step 4 — Final Verification: Among the given choices ($0.42, 0.82, 0.62, 0.12$), the only value smaller than $0.42$ is $0.12$, confirming option (d).

Step 1: Hydration of 2-methylpropene (CH2 = C(CH )2) with dilute H2SO4 follows Markovnikov’s rule to yield
3
tert-butyl alcohol ((CH3)3C-OH) as major product (X).
Step 2: X has a polar −OH group capable of H-bonding with the stationary phase, making it much more polar than
the starting alkene (Rf = 0.42).
Step 3: Stronger adsorption slows migration, so Rf(X) < 0.42. Among the options, only 0.12 is less than 0.42.
Q02.trapHtml: Higher polarity =⇒ stronger adsorption on silica/alumina =⇒ smaller R<sub>f</sub>, not larger. Verified Answer: (D) 0.12

Q03.conceptHtml: Match boiling-point difference, thermal stability, and steam volatility to the corresponding distillation method.
Q03.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Match Simple and Fractional Distillation (A and B): Simple distillation (A) separates two miscible liquids having a large difference in their boiling points ($\Delta T_b > 25\text{ K}$), so A-II. Fractional distillation (B) uses a fractionating column to separate two miscible liquids with close boiling points, so B-IV.
  2. Step 2 — Match Steam Distillation and Reduced-Pressure Distillation (C and D): Steam distillation (C) is used for organic liquids that are steam-volatile and immiscible with water, so C-I. Distillation under reduced pressure (D) lowers the external pressure so that high-boiling liquids which decompose at or below their normal boiling point can distil at a lower temperature, so D-III.
  3. Step 3 — Final Verification: Combining all matches gives A-II, B-IV, C-I, D-III, which corresponds to option (b).
Q03.stepsLatex:
Step 1: Simple distillation (A) separates liquids with a large difference in boiling points =⇒ A–II.
Step 2: Fractional distillation (B) separates miscible liquids with close boiling points =⇒ B–IV.
Step 3: Steam distillation (C) isolates steam-volatile, water-immiscible compounds =⇒ C–I.
Step 4: Distillation under reduced pressure (D) prevents decomposition of liquids that decompose at their normal
b.p. =⇒ D–III.
Q03.trapHtml: Watch the swap between (A) and (B): large ∆T<sub>b</sub> uses simple distillation; small ∆T<sub>b</sub> requires a fractionating column. Verified Answer: (B) A-II, B-IV, C-I, D-III

Q04.conceptHtml: Match cyclohexanol, cyclohexylamine, cyclohexanecarbaldehyde, and phenol to their diagnostic group tests.
Q04.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify Compounds A, B, C, and D from the Diagram: From the given structures: A is cyclohexanol (a secondary aliphatic alcohol), B is cyclohexylamine (a primary amine), C is cyclohexanecarbaldehyde (an aldehyde), and D is phenol (an aromatic $-\text{OH}$ compound).
  2. Step 2 — Match Each Functional Group to Its Qualitative Test: Cyclohexanol (A) is a $2^\circ$ alcohol that responds to the Lucas test ($\text{conc. HCl} + \text{anhydrous ZnCl}_2$, turbidity in $\sim 5\text{ min}$), giving A-III. Cyclohexylamine (B) is a $1^\circ$ amine identified using Hinsberg’s reagent test ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{SO}_2\text{Cl}$), giving B-I.
  3. Step 3 — Match Aldehyde and Phenol: Cyclohexanecarbaldehyde (C) is an aldehyde that reduces ammoniacal silver nitrate to form a silver mirror in Tollen’s test, giving C-IV. Phenol (D) condenses with phthalic anhydride in conc. $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ to form phenolphthalein (pink in alkali) in the phthalein dye test, giving D-II.
  4. Step 4 — Final Verification: The complete matching is A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II, confirming option (a).
Q04.stepsLatex:
Step 1: Compound A is cyclohexanol (2◦ alcohol) → Lucas test (turbidity in ∼ 5 min) =⇒ A–III.
Step 2: Compound B is cyclohexylamine (1◦ amine) → Hinsberg’s reagent test (gives KOH-soluble sulphonamide)
=⇒ B–I.
Step 3: Compound C is cyclohexanecarbaldehyde (−CHO) → Tollen’s test (silver mirror) =⇒ C–IV.
Step 4: Compound D is phenol (Ar-OH) → Phthalein dye test (pink phenolphthalein with phthalic anhydride/H2SO4
+ NaOH) =⇒ D–II.

Q05.conceptHtml: %C = <sub>4</sub><sup>1</sup><sub>4</sub><sup>2</sup> × <sup>mC</sup><sub>X</sub><sup>O</sup>2 × 100 and %H = <sub>1</sub><sup>2</sup><sub>8</sub> × <sup>mH</sup><sub>X</sub>2<sup>O</sup> × 100.
Q05.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Find the Mass of Carbon from $\text{CO}_2$: All carbon in the organic compound is converted into $\text{CO}_2$ (molar mass $44\text{ g mol}^{-1}$). The mass of carbon in $0.25\text{ g}$ of $\text{CO}_2$ is: $m_{\text{C}} = \frac{12}{44} \times 0.25 = \frac{3}{44} \approx 0.06818\text{ g}$.
  2. Step 2 — Calculate Sample Mass $X$ Using Percentage of Carbon: Using $\%\text{C} = \frac{m_{\text{C}}}{X} \times 100$: $25 = \frac{0.06818}{X} \times 100 \implies X = \frac{6.818}{25} = 0.2727\text{ g} = 272.7 \times 10^{-3}\text{ g}$.
  3. Step 3 — Cross-Check Using Percentage of Hydrogen: Mass of hydrogen in $0.12\text{ g}$ of $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ is $m_{\text{H}} = \frac{2}{18} \times 0.12 = 0.01333\text{ g}$. Then $X = \frac{0.01333 \times 100}{4.89} \approx 0.2727\text{ g} = 272.7 \times 10^{-3}\text{ g}$, which agrees completely.
  4. Step 4 — Final Verification: Rounding $272.7$ to the nearest integer gives $273$, so $X = 273 \times 10^{-3}\text{ g}$, confirming option (a).
Q05.trapHtml: Pay attention to the ×10<sup>−3</sup> g multiplier so you don’t pick 27 or 2730. Verified Answer: (A) 273

Q06.conceptHtml: Glycerol (1,2,3-trihydroxypropane) decomposes near its b.p. (290<sup>°</sup>C); azeotropes boil at constant compo- sition.
Q06.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement I (Glycerol Separation): 1,2,3-Trihydroxypropane is glycerol, which has a very high normal boiling point ($290^\circ\text{C}$) and decomposes at its boiling point under atmospheric pressure. Therefore, it cannot be separated from water/spent-lye by simple distillation; it requires distillation under reduced pressure. Hence, Statement I is false.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement II (Azeotropic Mixtures): An azeotropic mixture is a constant-boiling liquid mixture that has the exact same composition in both the liquid and vapour phases. Because the vapour is not enriched in either component, fractional distillation cannot separate an azeotrope. Hence, Statement II is true.
  3. Step 3 — Final Verification: Statement I is false and Statement II is true, which matches option (d).

at atmospheric pressure, so it is purified by distillation under reduced pressure, not simple distillation (or water boils
off leaving glycerol, while NCERT specifies vacuum distillation for glycerol). Thus Statement (I) is false.
Step 2: Statement (II): An azeotropic mixture has identical composition in liquid and vapour phases, so it cannot
be separated by fractional distillation. Statement (II) is true.
Q06.trapHtml: Constant-boiling azeotropes behave like a pure liquid during fractional distillation and require azeotropic/extractive distillation or molecular sieves. Verified Answer: (D) Statement I is false but Statement II is true

Q07.conceptHtml: Pair each mixture with a reagent that reacts selectively with only one component.
Q07.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Distinguish Amines (A) and Carbonyls (B): Diethyl amine ($2^\circ$) and Ethyl amine ($1^\circ$) (A) are distinguished by the carbylamine test using $\text{CHCl}_3 + \text{KOH}, \Delta$: only $1^\circ$ ethyl amine produces a foul-smelling isocyanide, giving A-II. Acetaldehyde and Acetone (B) are distinguished by ammoniacal silver nitrate (Tollen’s reagent): only acetaldehyde gives a silver mirror, giving B-IV.
  2. Step 2 — Distinguish Alcohol/Phenol (C) and Acids (D): Ethanol and Phenol (C) are distinguished by neutral $\text{FeCl}_3$: phenol forms a violet-coloured complex while ethanol does not react, giving C-III. Benzoic acid and Cinnamic acid (D) are distinguished by bromine water: cinnamic acid ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}=\text{CHCOOH}$) contains an olefinic double bond that decolourises bromine water, whereas benzoic acid does not, giving D-I.
  3. Step 3 — Final Verification: The complete match is A-II, B-IV, C-III, D-I, confirming option (d).

D–I.

Q08.conceptHtml: %S = 32 × <sup>m</sup>BaSO<sub>4</sub> × 100. 233 m<sub>comp</sub>
Q08.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the Carius Method Formula for Sulphur: In Carius estimation, all sulphur in the organic compound is oxidised to $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ and precipitated as $\text{BaSO}_4$ (molar mass $233\text{ g mol}^{-1}$, containing $32\text{ g}$ of S per mole): $\%\text{S} = \frac{32}{233} \times \frac{\text{Mass of }\text{BaSO}_4}{\text{Mass of organic compound}} \times 100$.
  2. Step 2 — Substitute the Given Values: Here, mass of compound $= 0.314\text{ g}$ and mass of $\text{BaSO}_4 = 0.4813\text{ g}$: $\%\text{S} = \frac{32}{233} \times \frac{0.4813}{0.314} \times 100$.
  3. Step 3 — Compute the Percentage: $\%\text{S} = \frac{32 \times 48.13}{233 \times 0.314} = \frac{1540.16}{73.162} \approx 21.05\%$.
  4. Step 4 — Final Verification: The calculated sulphur percentage is $21.05\%$, confirming option (b).
Q08.trapHtml: Always use M(BaSO<sub>4</sub>) = 233 g mol<sup>−1</sup> (Ba = 137, S = 32, 4O = 64). Verified Answer: (B) 21.05%

Q09.conceptHtml: Bromination of benzene gives bromobenzene (A); nitration gives o- and p-bromonitrobenzene (B and C), which differ in b.p. and m.p.
Q09.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify Intermediate A and Products B and C: Benzene reacts with $\text{Br}_2 / \text{FeBr}_3$ via electrophilic aromatic substitution to give bromobenzene (A). Since $-\text{Br}$ is an ortho/para-directing group, nitration of bromobenzene with $\text{conc. HNO}_3 + \text{conc. H}_2\text{SO}_4$ yields a mixture of $o$-bromonitrobenzene (B) and $p$-bromonitrobenzene (C).
  2. Step 2 — Analyse Their Physical Properties for Separation: Unlike $o$-nitrophenol and $p$-nitrophenol (where intramolecular H-bonding makes $o$-nitrophenol steam-volatile), neither $o$-bromonitrobenzene nor $p$-bromonitrobenzene forms hydrogen bonds. Instead, they are positional isomers with very close boiling points ($\sim 258^\circ\text{C}$ and $\sim 256^\circ\text{C}$).
  3. Step 3 — Select the Appropriate Separation Method: Two miscible liquids/molten isomers with very close boiling points are separated by fractional distillation (not steam distillation or simple distillation).
  4. Step 4 — Final Verification: Therefore, the mixture of B and C is separated by fractional distillation, confirming option (c).

Step 2: Nitration of bromobenzene with conc. HNO3/H2SO4 yields o-bromonitrobenzene and p-bromonitrobenzene
(B + C).
Step 3: Unlike o-/p-nitrophenol (which have intramolecular vs intermolecular H-bonding and are separated by steam
distillation), o- and p-bromonitrobenzene lack −OH H-bonding and are separated by fractional distillation (or
fractional crystallisation). Among the options, fractional distillation is correct.

Q10.conceptHtml: %Cl = 35.5 × <sup>m</sup><sub>AgCl</sub> × 100. 143.5 m<sub>comp</sub>
Q10.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the Carius Formula for Chlorine: Chlorine in the organic compound is precipitated as $\text{AgCl}$ (molar mass $= 108 + 35.5 = 143.5\text{ g mol}^{-1}$): $\%\text{Cl} = \frac{35.5}{143.5} \times \frac{\text{Mass of AgCl}}{\text{Mass of organic compound}} \times 100$.
  2. Step 2 — Substitute the Given Data: With mass of organic compound $= 0.2425\text{ g}$ and mass of $\text{AgCl} = 0.5253\text{ g}$: $\%\text{Cl} = \frac{35.5}{143.5} \times \frac{0.5253}{0.2425} \times 100$.
  3. Step 3 — Perform the Calculation: $\%\text{Cl} = \frac{35.5 \times 52.53}{143.5 \times 0.2425} = \frac{1864.815}{34.79875} \approx 53.588\% \approx 53.58\%$.
  4. Step 4 — Final Verification: The percentage of chlorine is $53.58\%$, matching option (b).
Q10.trapHtml: Remember M(AgCl) = 108 + 35.5 = 143.5 g mol<sup>−1</sup>. Verified Answer: (B) 53.58%

Q11.conceptHtml: Recall the exact visual endpoint of Baeyer’s, CAN, Tollen’s, and neutral FeCl<sub>3</sub> tests.
Q11.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Match Baeyer’s Test (A) and CAN Test (B): In Baeyer’s test (A) for unsaturation ($\text{C}=\text{C}$ or $\text{C}\equiv\text{C}$), cold dilute alkaline $\text{KMnO}_4$ loses its pink/purple colour as $\text{MnO}_4^-$ is reduced to $\text{MnO}_2$, so A-IV. In the ceric ammonium nitrate (CAN) test (B), alcohols form a red-coloured cerium(IV) alkoxy complex, so B-I.
  2. Step 2 — Match Tollen’s Test (C) and $\text{FeCl}_3$ Test (D): In Tollen’s test (C), aldehydes reduce $[\text{Ag(NH}_3)_2]^+$ to metallic silver, producing a silver mirror on the test tube wall, so C-II. In the neutral $\text{FeCl}_3$ test (D), phenols form a coloured (typically violet) complex with $\text{Fe}^{3+}$, so D-III.
  3. Step 3 — Final Verification: Combining the pairs gives A-IV, B-I, C-II, D-III, confirming option (a).

Step 4: Neutral FeCl3 for phenol: violet colour appears =⇒ D–III.
Q11.trapHtml: CAN gives a red complex with alcohols, whereas FeCl<sub>3</sub> gives a violet complex with phenol. Verified Answer: (A) A-IV, B-I, C-II, D-III

Q12.conceptHtml: A primary standard must be stable in air, react stoichiometrically/instantaneously, be soluble in water, and have high molar mass.
Q12.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Review Essential Characteristics of a Primary Standard: A primary standard must be available in high purity, remain stable in air (non-hygroscopic and unreactive with $\text{O}_2$ or $\text{CO}_2$), react instantaneously and stoichiometrically with the titrant, be readily soluble in water, and possess a high relative molar mass (to minimise relative weighing error).
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statements A, B, and C: A is correct: Stable hydrated salts of definite composition (such as oxalic acid dihydrate, $\text{H}_2\text{C}_2\text{O}_4 \cdot 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$, and Mohr’s salt) are standard primary standards. B is correct: It must not react with air. C is correct: Its titration reaction must be fast and stoichiometric.
  3. Step 3 — Evaluate Statements D and E: D is incorrect: A primary standard for aqueous titrimetry must be readily soluble in water. E is incorrect: It should have a high, not low, molar mass so that weighing errors are minimal.
  4. Step 4 — Final Verification: Only statements A, B, and C are correct, confirming option (d).

Mohr’s salt) can act as primary standards =⇒ Correct.
Step 2: Statement B: Should not react with air (CO2, O2, moisture) =⇒ Correct.
Step 3: Statement C: Titration reaction must be fast/instantaneous and stoichiometric =⇒ Correct.
Step 4: Statement D: Should be soluble in water (so D saying "not soluble" is false). Statement E: Should have high
molar mass to minimize weighing error (so E saying "low" is false).
Q12.trapHtml: High equivalent/molar mass reduces relative weighing error; never confuse low vs high molar mass. Verified Answer: (D) A, B and C Only

Q13.conceptHtml: %N = <sup>1.4×N</sup><sub>m</sub>acid<sup>×V</sup>a<sub>(</sub>c<sub>g</sub>i<sub>)</sub>d <sup>(mL)</sup>, where N = M × basicity. comp
Q13.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall Kjeldahl’s Formula for Percentage of Nitrogen: When evolved $\text{NH}_3$ neutralises $V\text{ mL}$ of $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ of molarity $M$ (basicity $n = 2$, so normality $N = 2M$), the percentage of nitrogen in mass $m\text{ g}$ of compound is: $\%\text{N} = \frac{1.4 \times (2M) \times V}{m}$.
  2. Step 2 — Substitute the Given Values: Here, $M = 1\text{ M}$, $V = 15\text{ mL}$, and $m = 1\text{ g}$: $\%\text{N} = \frac{1.4 \times 2 \times 1 \times 15}{1} = 1.4 \times 30 = 42\%$.
  3. Step 3 — Verify via Mole Stoichiometry: Moles of $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 = 1\text{ M} \times 0.015\text{ L} = 0.015\text{ mol}$. Since $2\text{NH}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \to (\text{NH}_4)_2\text{SO}_4$, moles of $\text{N} = 2 \times 0.015 = 0.030\text{ mol}$, giving $0.030 \times 14 = 0.42\text{ g}$ of N in $1\text{ g}$ sample, i.e., $42\%$.
  4. Step 4 — Final Verification: The percentage of nitrogen is $42$, confirming option (c).

Q14.conceptHtml: %P = 62 × <sup>m</sup>Mg<sub>2</sub>P<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> × 100. 222 m<sub>comp</sub>
Q14.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Calculate the Molar Mass of Magnesium Pyrophosphate ($\text{Mg}_2\text{P}_2\text{O}_7$): Using $\text{Mg} = 24$, $\text{P} = 31$, and $\text{O} = 16\text{ g mol}^{-1}$: $M(\text{Mg}_2\text{P}_2\text{O}_7) = 2(24) + 2(31) + 7(16) = 48 + 62 + 112 = 222\text{ g mol}^{-1}$.
  2. Step 2 — Apply the Percentage of Phosphorus Formula: Each mole of $\text{Mg}_2\text{P}_2\text{O}_7$ contains $2\text{ mol}$ of P ($2 \times 31 = 62\text{ g}$): $\%\text{P} = \frac{62}{222} \times \frac{\text{Mass of }\text{Mg}_2\text{P}_2\text{O}_7}{\text{Mass of compound}} \times 100$.
  3. Step 3 — Compute the Value: Substituting mass of $\text{Mg}_2\text{P}_2\text{O}_7 = 1.79\text{ g}$ and mass of compound $= 1.00\text{ g}$: $\%\text{P} = \frac{62}{222} \times \frac{1.79}{1.00} \times 100 = \frac{11098}{222} \approx 49.99\% \approx 50\%$.
  4. Step 4 — Final Verification: To the nearest integer, the percentage of phosphorus is $50$, confirming option (d).
Q14.trapHtml: Use 62/222 (two P atoms per Mg<sub>2</sub>P<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub>), not 31/222. Verified Answer: (D) 50

Q15.conceptHtml: %S = 32 × <sup>m</sup>BaSO<sub>4</sub> × 100. 233 m<sub>comp</sub>
Q15.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — State the Carius Estimation Formula for Sulphur: Since $1\text{ mol}$ of $\text{BaSO}_4$ ($233\text{ g}$) contains $1\text{ mol}$ of S ($32\text{ g}$): $\%\text{S} = \frac{32}{233} \times \frac{\text{Mass of }\text{BaSO}_4}{\text{Mass of organic compound}} \times 100$.
  2. Step 2 — Substitute the Given Masses: Given mass of organic compound $= 0.75\text{ g}$ and mass of $\text{BaSO}_4 = 1.2\text{ g}$: $\%\text{S} = \frac{32}{233} \times \frac{1.2}{0.75} \times 100$.
  3. Step 3 — Evaluate the Expression: Note that $\frac{1.2}{0.75} = 1.6$. Hence: $\%\text{S} = \frac{32 \times 1.6 \times 100}{233} = \frac{5120}{233} \approx 21.974\% \approx 21.97\%$.
  4. Step 4 — Final Verification: The sulphur percentage is $21.97\%$, confirming option (d).

Q16.conceptHtml: Match standard laboratory reagents to the functional groups they detect.
Q16.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Match Sodium Bicarbonate (A) and Neutral $\text{FeCl}_3$ (B): Sodium bicarbonate solution (A) reacts with carboxylic acids ($-\text{COOH}$) to evolve brisk effervescence of $\text{CO}_2$, giving A-II. Neutral ferric chloride (B) gives a characteristic violet/blue/green colour with a phenolic $-\text{OH}$ group, giving B-III.
  2. Step 2 — Match CAN (C) and Alkaline $\text{KMnO}_4$ (D): Ceric ammonium nitrate (C) produces a red colour with an alcoholic $-\text{OH}$ group, giving C-IV. Cold dilute alkaline $\text{KMnO}_4$ (D) (Baeyer’s reagent) is decolourised by a double bond/unsaturation, giving D-I.
  3. Step 3 — Final Verification: Putting all four together gives A-II, B-III, C-IV, D-I, confirming option (d).

Step 2: Neutral FeCl3 → phenolic −OH (violet complex) =⇒ B–III.

Step 4: Alkaline KMnO4 (Baeyer’s) → double bond/unsaturation =⇒ D–I.

Q17.conceptHtml: Acidic components react with NaOH to form water-soluble sodium salts and move into the aqueous layer; neutral/basic organics stay in the organic layer.
Q17.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Classify the Acid–Base Nature of Each Component: In the ethyl acetate solution: benzoic acid ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COOH}$) is acidic, aniline ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2$) is basic, and chlorobenzene ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{Cl}$) is neutral.
  2. Step 2 — Determine Which Compound Reacts with Aqueous $5\text{ M NaOH}$: When shaken with aqueous $\text{NaOH}$ (a strong base), only acidic benzoic acid reacts: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COOH} + \text{NaOH} \to \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COO}^-\text{Na}^+ + \text{H}_2\text{O}$. The ionic salt sodium benzoate is highly soluble in water and moves completely into the aqueous layer.
  3. Step 3 — Identify What Remains in the Organic (Ethyl Acetate) Layer: Neither neutral chlorobenzene nor basic aniline reacts with $\text{NaOH}$, so both remain un-ionised and stay dissolved in the organic ethyl acetate layer.
  4. Step 4 — Final Verification: The ethyl acetate layer contains chlorobenzene and aniline, confirming option (a).

(organic layer).
Step 2: Adding 5 M NaOH deprotonates benzoic acid to sodium benzoate (C6H5COO−Na+), which dissolves in the
aqueous layer.
Step 3: Chlorobenzene and aniline do not react with NaOH and remain in the ethyl acetate layer.

Q18.conceptHtml: Recall the 4 textbook NCERT distillation examples.
Q18.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Match Aniline–Water (A) and Glycerol–Spent-Lye (B): Aniline is steam-volatile and practically immiscible with water, so aniline is separated from an aniline–water mixture by steam distillation, giving (A)-(IV). Glycerol decomposes at its normal boiling point, so it is separated from spent-lye in the soap industry by distillation at reduced pressure, giving (B)-(III).
  2. Step 2 — Match Crude Oil (C) and Chloroform–Aniline (D): Different fractions of crude oil have closely spaced boiling points and are separated by fractional distillation, giving (C)-(II). Chloroform (b.p. $334\text{ K}$) and aniline (b.p. $457\text{ K}$) have a very large boiling point difference ($123\text{ K}$), so they are separated by simple distillation, giving (D)-(I).
  3. Step 3 — Final Verification: The complete matching is (A)-(IV), (B)-(III), (C)-(II), (D)-(I), confirming option (a).

Step 4: Chloroform (334 K) + Aniline (457 K) → Simple distillation =⇒ (D)–(I).

Q19.conceptHtml: Subtract aqueous tension from total pressure to get dry N<sub>2</sub> pressure, convert to STP, and apply %N = <sub>22</sub><sup>2</sup><sub>4</sub><sup>8</sup><sub>00</sub> × <sup>V</sup>S<sub>m</sub>TP × 100.
Q19.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Find the Pressure of Dry $\text{N}_2$ Gas: Subtract the aqueous tension from the total collected pressure: $P_1 = P_{\text{total}} - P_{\text{aq}} = 715 - 15 = 700\text{ mmHg}$.
  2. Step 2 — Convert Volume of $\text{N}_2$ to STP ($760\text{ mmHg}, 273\text{ K}$): Using $\frac{P_1 V_1}{T_1} = \frac{P_2 V_2}{T_2}$ with $V_1 = 60\text{ mL}$ and $T_1 = 300\text{ K}$: $V_{\text{STP}} = \frac{700 \times 60 \times 273}{760 \times 300} = \frac{700 \times 273}{760 \times 5} = \frac{1911}{38} \approx 50.29\text{ mL}$.
  3. Step 3 — Calculate the Percentage of Nitrogen: At STP, $22400\text{ mL}$ of $\text{N}_2$ weighs $28\text{ g}$. Therefore, for $m = 0.4\text{ g}$ of organic compound: $\%\text{N} = \frac{28 \times V_{\text{STP}}}{22400 \times m} \times 100 = \frac{28 \times 50.29}{22400 \times 0.4} \times 100 = \frac{50.29}{3.2} \approx 15.71\%$.
  4. Step 4 — Final Verification: The percentage of nitrogen in the compound is $15.71\%$, confirming option (a).

  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement II: Heating an organic compound with concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ to convert nitrogen into ammonium sulphate, $(\text{NH}_4)_2\text{SO}_4$, is the principle of Kjeldahl’s method, not Dumas’ method. Hence, Statement II is false.

Q23.subtopic: Lassaigne’s Test: N and S Together
Q23.conceptHtml: Sodium fusion converts covalent elements into ionic sodium salts; N + S together form NaSCN, giving a blood-red colour with Fe<sup>3+</sup>, not Prussian blue.
Q23.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement I: In Lassaigne’s test, fusing the organic compound with sodium metal converts covalently bonded elements (N, S, halogens) into water-soluble ionic sodium salts ($\text{NaCN}$, $\text{Na}_2\text{S}$, $\text{NaX}$). Hence, Statement I is true.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement II: When an organic compound contains both N and S, sodium fusion forms sodium thiocyanate ($\text{NaSCN}$), which reacts with $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ ions to give a blood-red colour due to $[\text{Fe(SCN)}]^{2+}$—not a Prussian blue colour (Prussian blue, $\text{Fe}_4[\text{Fe(CN)}_6]_3$, is obtained when N is present without S, or when excess Na decomposes $\text{NaSCN}$). Furthermore, $\text{Na}_4[\text{Fe(CN)}_6]$ is an intermediate formed with $\text{FeSO}_4$, not an added test reagent for N + S. Hence, Statement II is false.
  3. Step 3 — Final Verification: Statement I is true and Statement II is false, confirming option (d).

Q29.subtopic: Detection of Phosphorus: Yellow Precipitate Formula
Q29.conceptHtml: Phosphate reacts with ammonium molybdate in HNO<sub>3</sub> to form yellow ammonium phosphomolybdate.
Q29.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Oxidation of Phosphorus to Phosphate: The organic compound is heated with an oxidising agent (sodium peroxide, $\text{Na}_2\text{O}_2$), which oxidises phosphorus to sodium phosphate ($\text{Na}_3\text{PO}_4$).
  2. Step 2 — Reaction with Nitric Acid and Ammonium Molybdate: Boiling the aqueous extract with $\text{HNO}_3$ converts $\text{Na}_3\text{PO}_4$ into phosphoric acid ($\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4$). Treating this with ammonium molybdate, $(\text{NH}_4)_2\text{MoO}_4$, gives a canary-yellow precipitate of ammonium phosphomolybdate: $\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4 + 12(\text{NH}_4)_2\text{MoO}_4 + 21\text{HNO}_3 \to (\text{NH}_4)_3\text{PO}_4 \cdot 12\text{MoO}_3\downarrow + 21\text{NH}_4\text{NO}_3 + 12\text{H}_2\text{O}$.
  3. Step 3 — Final Verification: The yellow precipitate has the formula $(\text{NH}_4)_3\text{PO}_4 \cdot 12\text{MoO}_3$, confirming option (d).

Q30.conceptHtml: Fe<sup>2+</sup> ions undergo hydrolysis in neutral/alkaline water to form Fe(OH)<sub>2</sub>; dilute H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> suppresses this.
Q30.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Understand the Composition of Mohr’s Salt: Mohr’s salt is ferrous ammonium sulphate hexahydrate, $\text{FeSO}_4 \cdot (\text{NH}_4)_2\text{SO}_4 \cdot 6\text{H}_2\text{O}$, prepared by dissolving equimolar $\text{FeSO}_4 \cdot 7\text{H}_2\text{O}$ and $(\text{NH}_4)_2\text{SO}_4$ in water and crystallising.
  2. Step 2 — Role of Dilute $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$: In neutral water, $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ ions from ferrous sulphate undergo hydrolysis ($\text{Fe}^{2+} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{Fe(OH)}_2 + 2\text{H}^+$) and readily oxidise to brownish basic ferric salts, making the solution turbid. Adding a small amount of dilute $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ supplies $\text{H}^+$ ions, shifting the equilibrium backward and preventing the hydrolysis of ferrous sulphate.
  3. Step 3 — Final Verification: Dilute $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ is added specifically to prevent the hydrolysis of ferrous sulphate, confirming option (a).

Q31.conceptHtml: To form NaCN in Lassaigne’s test, the compound must contain BOTH carbon and nitrogen.
Q31.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the Principle of Lassaigne’s Test for Nitrogen: During sodium fusion, nitrogen is detected only when it combines with carbon from the compound and sodium metal to form sodium cyanide ($\text{NaCN}$): $\text{Na} + \text{C} + \text{N} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \text{NaCN}$, which then forms Prussian blue with $\text{FeSO}_4$ and $\text{FeCl}_3$.
  2. Step 2 — Inspect Carbon Content in Each Option: Glycine ($\text{H}_2\text{NCH}_2\text{COOH}$), phenyl hydrazine ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NHNH}_2$), and urea ($\text{NH}_2\text{CONH}_2$) all contain both carbon and nitrogen, so they form $\text{NaCN}$ and give a positive test. In contrast, hydrazine ($\text{NH}_2-\text{NH}_2$) contains no carbon atoms, so it cannot form $\text{NaCN}$.
  3. Step 3 — Final Verification: Therefore, hydrazine does not give Lassaigne’s test, confirming option (d).

fusion and fails Lassaigne’s test for N.

give positive tests.

  2. Step 2 — Eliminate Incomplete Options: Options (a), (b), and (d) each omit one or more of these four detectable elements, whereas option (c) lists all four.
  3. Step 3 — Final Verification: Lassaigne’s test is used for the detection of nitrogen, sulphur, phosphorus, and halogens, confirming option (c).

Q33.subtopic: Role of CuSO4 in Kjeldahl’s Method
Q33.conceptHtml: In Kjeldahl digestion, K<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> raises the boiling point of H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>, while CuSO<sub>4</sub> acts as a catalyst.
Q33.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the Digestion Step in Kjeldahl’s Method: The nitrogen-containing organic compound is heated with concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ (oxidising agent) along with $\text{K}_2\text{SO}_4$ (to raise the boiling point of $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$) and a small amount of $\text{CuSO}_4$.
  2. Step 2 — Identify the Specific Role of $\text{CuSO}_4$: Copper(II) sulphate ($\text{CuSO}_4$) acts as a catalyst (catalytic agent) that accelerates the oxidation/digestion of the organic matter into $\text{CO}_2$, $\text{H}_2\text{O}$, and $(\text{NH}_4)_2\text{SO}_4$.
  3. Step 3 — Final Verification: Hence, $\text{CuSO}_4$ acts as a catalytic agent, confirming option (a).

Q34.conceptHtml: Potassium hydrogen phthalate (KHP) is a stable, high-molar-mass weak acid primary standard; titrating it with strong base NaOH has equivalence pH > 7.
Q34.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement I (KHP as a Primary Standard): Potassium hydrogen phthalate ($\text{KHC}_8\text{H}_4\text{O}_4$, KHP) is non-hygroscopic, highly pure, air-stable, water-soluble, and has a high molar mass ($204.22\text{ g mol}^{-1}$). It is the classic primary standard used to standardise $\text{NaOH}$ solutions. Hence, Statement I is correct.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement II (Choice of Indicator): KHP is a weak monoprotic acid and $\text{NaOH}$ is a strong base. At the equivalence point, hydrolysis of the phthalate dianion makes the solution mildly basic ($\text{pH} \approx 8.5\text{–}9.0$), which falls squarely within the colour-change range of phenolphthalein ($\text{pH } 8.2\text{–}10.0$). Hence, Statement II is correct.
  3. Step 3 — Final Verification: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct, confirming option (a).

nolphthalein’s transition range (8.2–10.0).

Q35.conceptHtml: Steam-volatile, water-insoluble liquids are purified by steam distillation.

  2. Step 2 — Match to the Appropriate Extraction Technique: These are the exact defining conditions for steam distillation. Passing steam through the mixture causes the sum of the vapour pressures of water and the essential oil ($P_{\text{H}_2\text{O}} + P_{\text{oil}}$) to equal atmospheric pressure below $100^\circ\text{C}$, gently carrying the fragrance oil over with steam without thermal decomposition.
  3. Step 3 — Final Verification: The suitable extraction method is steam distillation, confirming option (b).

distillation.

Q36.subtopic: Halogen Test: Role of Boiling with HNO3
Q36.conceptHtml: Na<sub>2</sub>S and NaCN also form insoluble precipitates (Ag<sub>2</sub>S, AgCN) with AgNO<sub>3</sub>, interfering with the halogen test.
Q36.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify interfering ions in Lassaigne’s extract: During sodium fusion, if nitrogen and sulphur are also present in the organic compound, the extract contains $\text{NaCN}$ and $\text{Na}_2\text{S}$ along with sodium halides ($\text{NaX}$).
  2. Step 2 — Understand why they interfere with the halogen test: When $\text{AgNO}_3$ is added to test for halogens, $\text{CN}^-$ and $\text{S}^{2-}$ would also react to form precipitates of $\text{AgCN}$ (white) and $\text{Ag}_2\text{S}$ (black), masking the true silver halide precipitate.
  3. Step 3 — Action of boiling with dilute $\text{HNO}_3$: Boiling the extract with dilute $\text{HNO}_3$ decomposes $\text{NaCN}$ and $\text{Na}_2\text{S}$ into volatile gases $\text{HCN}$ and $\text{H}_2\text{S}$, which escape from the solution: $\text{NaCN} + \text{HNO}_3 \rightarrow \text{NaNO}_3 + \text{HCN}\uparrow$ and $\text{Na}_2\text{S} + 2\text{HNO}_3 \rightarrow 2\text{NaNO}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{S}\uparrow$.
  4. Step 4 — Match with the correct option: Therefore, Lassaigne’s extract is boiled with dilute $\text{HNO}_3$ because $\text{Na}_2\text{S}$ and $\text{NaCN}$ are decomposed by $\text{HNO}_3$, confirming option (c).

Q37.conceptHtml: Simultaneous presence of N and S forms sodium thiocyanate (NaSCN), which reacts with Fe<sup>3+</sup> to give blood-red [Fe(SCN)]<sup>2+</sup>.
Q37.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall sodium fusion when both N and S are present: When an organic compound containing both nitrogen and sulphur is fused with sodium metal, sodium thiocyanate ($\text{NaSCN}$) is formed: $\text{Na} + \text{C} + \text{N} + \text{S} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \text{NaSCN}$.
  2. Step 2 — Reaction with $\text{FeSO}_4$ and concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$: Acidifying the sodium fusion extract with concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ oxidises some $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ from $\text{FeSO}_4$ to $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ ions.
  3. Step 3 — Formation of the blood-red complex: The $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ ions react with thiocyanate ions ($\text{SCN}^-$) to produce the blood-red coloured ferric thiocyanate complex: $\text{Fe}^{3+} + \text{SCN}^- \rightarrow [\text{Fe(SCN)}]^{2+}$ (blood red).
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the elements detected: Appearance of a blood-red colour confirms the simultaneous presence of both nitrogen and sulphur ($\text{N}$ and $\text{S}$), which corresponds to option (c).

Q38.conceptHtml: Steam distillation purifies organic liquids that are steam-volatile and immiscible with water.
Q38.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the physical properties of the substance: The substance to be purified is steam-volatile (has a significant vapour pressure at steam temperatures) and immiscible with water.
  2. Step 2 — Apply the principle of steam distillation: In steam distillation, steam is passed through the heated mixture. Because the liquid and water are immiscible, their vapour pressures add independently: $P_{\text{total}} = p_{\text{water}} + p_{\text{organic}}$.
  3. Step 3 — Understand the boiling point advantage: The mixture boils as soon as $P_{\text{total}}$ equals atmospheric pressure, which occurs at a temperature lower than the normal boiling point of water ($100^\circ\text{C}$), allowing safe purification of heat-sensitive compounds like aniline.
  4. Step 4 — Select the correct technique: The technique specifically designed for steam-volatile, water-immiscible substances is steam distillation, confirming option (d).

Q39.conceptHtml: Phenols condense with phthalic anhydride in conc. H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> to form phenolphthalein, turning pink in NaOH (phthalein dye test).
Q39.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the phthalein dye test for phenols: Heating a phenol with phthalic anhydride in the presence of concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ produces a phthalein dye (such as phenolphthalein), which turns pink/red upon adding aqueous $\text{NaOH}$.
  2. Step 2 — Eliminate the other chemical tests: Tollens’ test identifies aldehydes (silver mirror), the carbylamine test identifies primary amines ($1^\circ$ amines give foul-smelling isocyanides), and the Lucas test distinguishes $1^\circ$, $2^\circ$, and $3^\circ$ aliphatic alcohols.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the correct option: Only the phthalein dye test specifically identifies the phenolic $-\text{OH}$ group, confirming option (b).

Q40.subtopic: Carius Estimation of Extra Element with BaCl2
Q40.conceptHtml: Heating a sulphur-containing compound with Na<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> / fuming HNO<sub>3</sub> forms H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (Y), which precipitates BaSO<sub>4</sub> (Z) with BaCl<sub>2</sub>.
Q40.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the Carius estimation reactions: In the Carius method for estimating sulphur, an organic compound ‘X’ containing sulphur is heated with sodium peroxide ($\text{Na}_2\text{O}_2$) or fuming $\text{HNO}_3$ to oxidise sulphur into sulphuric acid (‘Y’ $= \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$).
  2. Step 2 — Identify the precipitate ‘Z’: Adding $\text{BaCl}_2$ solution to $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ precipitates white barium sulphate (‘Z’ $= \text{BaSO}_4$), which is filtered, dried, and weighed to quantitatively estimate sulphur.
  3. Step 3 — Check which option contains sulphur: Cytosine ($\text{C}_4\text{H}_5\text{N}_3\text{O}$) has only $\text{C, H, N, O}$; chloroxylenol ($\text{C}_8\text{H}_9\text{ClO}$) contains $\text{Cl}$; a nucleotide contains $\text{C, H, O, N, P}$; whereas methionine is a sulphur-containing essential amino acid ($\text{CH}_3\text{-S-CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH(NH}_2)\text{COOH}$).
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the correct option: Since ‘X’ must contain sulphur, ‘X’ could be methionine, confirming option (b).
