ylenol (C,H,O,Cl), Nucleotide (C,H,N,O,P—wait: phosphate also precipitates with BaCl2 in neutral/basic medium,
but in acidic Carius mineral acid medium only BaSO4 is insoluble!).
Q40.trapHtml: Methionine and cysteine are the two classic sulphur-containing α-amino acids tested in JEE Main. Verified Answer: (B) Methionine

Q41.subtopic: Preparation of Mohr’s Salt: Avoiding Prolonged Heating
Q41.conceptHtml: Prolonged heating in air oxidises Fe<sup>2+</sup> to Fe<sup>3+</sup>, ruining the purity of Mohr’s salt.
Q41.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the composition of ferrous ammonium sulphate: Ferrous ammonium sulphate (Mohr’s salt, $\text{FeSO}_4\cdot(\text{NH}_4)_2\text{SO}_4\cdot 6\text{H}_2\text{O}$) contains iron in the $+2$ oxidation state ($\text{Fe}^{2+}$).
  2. Step 2 — Understand the effect of prolonged heating in air: In aqueous solution exposed to air, $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ ions are readily oxidised by atmospheric oxygen to $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ ions ($4\text{Fe}^{2+} + \text{O}_2 + 4\text{H}^+ \rightarrow 4\text{Fe}^{3+} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$), and prolonged heating accelerates this oxidation.
  3. Step 3 — Connect to the laboratory precaution: To keep iron strictly in the ferrous ($\text{Fe}^{2+}$) form and obtain pure pale-green crystals of Mohr’s salt, prolonged heating is avoided to prevent oxidation.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the correct option: Avoiding prolonged heating prevents oxidation of $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ to $\text{Fe}^{3+}$, confirming option (c).
Q41.stepsLatex:
Step 1: While concentrating the equimolar solution of FeSO4 and (NH4)2SO4 to the crystallisation point, prolonged
heating is avoided to prevent oxidation of Fe2+ to Fe3+.
Q41.trapHtml: Contrast with Q30: adding dil. H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> prevents hydrolysis; avoiding prolonged heating prevents oxidation. Verified Answer: (C) prevent oxidation

Q42.subtopic: K2Cr2O7 vs Na2Cr2O7 as Primary Standard
Q42.conceptHtml: Na<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> is deliquescent/hygroscopic and much more soluble in water than K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub>, so K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> is preferred as a primary standard.
Q42.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement I: A primary standard in volumetric analysis must be non-hygroscopic and easily weighed accurately. $\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$ is non-hygroscopic and stable, whereas $\text{Na}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$ is hygroscopic (absorbs moisture from air). Hence, aqueous $\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$ is preferred as a primary standard, making Statement I true.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement II: Sodium dichromate ($\text{Na}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$) is actually much more soluble in water than potassium dichromate ($\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$) — this difference in solubility is even used industrially to precipitate $\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$ by adding $\text{KCl}$ to $\text{Na}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$. Hence, Statement II is false.
  3. Step 3 — Match with the given options: Statement I is true and Statement II is false, confirming option (a).
Q42.stepsLatex:
Step 1: Statement I is true: K2Cr2O7 is non-hygroscopic and ideal as a primary standard over Na2Cr2O7.
Step 2: Statement II is false: Na2Cr2O7 has a higher solubility in water than K2Cr2O7 (this is why K2Cr2O7 is
prepared from Na2Cr2O7 + KCl and crystallised out!).
Q42.trapHtml: In d-block chemistry, K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> is less soluble than Na<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub>—the exact same fact appears here in volumetric analysis! Verified Answer: (A) Statement I is true but Statement II is false

Q43.conceptHtml: Phenol (historically called carbolic acid) reacts with phthalic anhydride in conc. H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> to form phenolph- thalein.
Q43.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the synthesis of phenolphthalein: When phenol (also known by its common name carbolic acid, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH}$) is heated with phthalic anhydride in the presence of concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ (a dehydrating agent), two moles of phenol condense with one mole of phthalic anhydride.
  2. Step 2 — Identify the product ‘Y’: The condensation product ‘Y’ is phenolphthalein, a classic acid–base indicator that is colourless in acidic medium and pink in basic medium.
  3. Step 3 — Match ‘X’ and ‘Y’ with the options: ‘X’ is carbolic acid (phenol) and ‘Y’ is phenolphthalein, confirming option (b).

Step 1: 2C6H5OH + C8H4O3 −c−o−nc−.−H−2−S−O→4 Phenolphthalein + H2O.
Step 2: Thus ‘X’ is Carbolic acid (phenol) and ‘Y’ is Phenolphthalein.
Q43.trapHtml: Carbolic acid = Phenol (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH), not benzoic acid or carbonic acid. Verified Answer: (B) Carbolic acid, Phenolphthalein

Q44.subtopic: Methyl Orange Indicator: Structure & Acid-Base Nature
Q44.conceptHtml: Methyl orange is a weak base (yellow benzenoid form in base → red quinonoid form in acid); the quinonoid form has extended conjugation and is more deeply coloured.
Q44.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement I: Methyl orange is an azo dye indicator that acts as a weak organic base (not a weak acid), accepting a proton in acidic medium to shift from its yellow basic form to its red protonated form. Thus, Statement I is incorrect.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement II: In acidic medium, protonation converts the yellow benzenoid form of methyl orange into the red quinonoid form. Because the quinonoid structure has more extensive conjugation and charge delocalisation, the quinonoid form is more deeply/intensely coloured than the benzenoid form. Thus, Statement II is also incorrect.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the correct option: Since both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect, the answer is option (a).
Q44.stepsLatex:
Step 1: Statement I is incorrect: Methyl orange acts as a weak base (protonated at the azo/dimethylamino
nitrogen in acidic medium; unlike phenolphthalein which is a weak acid).
Step 2: Statement II is incorrect: The quinonoid form (red, in acid) is more deeply/intensely coloured than the
benzenoid form (yellow, in base).
Q44.trapHtml: Phenolphthalein = weak acid; Methyl orange = weak base. Quinonoid form is always more deeply coloured than benzenoid. Verified Answer: (A) Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect

Q45.conceptHtml: Match each extra element to its diagnostic product/reagent in Lassaigne’s test.
Q45.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Match Nitrogen (A) and Sulphur (B): In Lassaigne’s test, nitrogen is detected as Prussian blue ferric ferrocyanide, $\text{Fe}_4[\text{Fe(CN)}_6]_3$ (A-III). Sulphur is detected using sodium nitroprusside, $\text{Na}_2[\text{Fe(CN)}_5\text{NO}]$, which gives a violet colour with $\text{S}^{2-}$ (B-I).
  2. Step 2 — Match Phosphorus (C) and Halogen (D): Phosphorus is oxidised to phosphate and tested with ammonium molybdate, $(\text{NH}_4)_2\text{MoO}_4$, giving a canary-yellow precipitate (C-IV). Halogens are detected by adding $\text{AgNO}_3$ to the acidified extract to precipitate $\text{AgX}$ (D-II).
  3. Step 3 — Combine all matches: The complete matching is A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II, confirming option (a).

Q46.subtopic: Sulphanilic Acid: Functional Group & Lassaigne’s Test
Q46.conceptHtml: Sulphanilic acid is p-H<sub>2</sub>N-C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>4</sub>-SO<sub>3</sub>H (contains −SO<sub>3</sub>H and −NH<sub>2</sub>, NO −COOH); it has both N and S.
Q46.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Examine the structure of sulphanilic acid: Sulphanilic acid is $p$-aminobenzenesulphonic acid ($\text{H}_2\text{N}-\text{C}_6\text{H}_4-\text{SO}_3\text{H}$), which exists primarily as a dipolar zwitterion ($\text{H}_3\text{N}^+-\text{C}_6\text{H}_4-\text{SO}_3^-$).
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement I: Sulphanilic acid contains a sulphonic acid group ($-\text{SO}_3\text{H}$), not a carboxyl group ($-\text{COOH}$), so it does not give the esterification test for a carboxyl group. Therefore, Statement I is incorrect.
  3. Step 3 — Evaluate Statement II: Because sulphanilic acid contains both nitrogen ($\text{N}$) and sulphur ($\text{S}$), sodium fusion forms $\text{NaSCN}$, which reacts with $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ to give a blood-red colour in Lassaigne’s test. Therefore, Statement II is correct.
  4. Step 4 — Match with the options: Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct, confirming option (d).
Q46.stepsLatex:
Step 1: Statement I is incorrect: Sulphanilic acid contains a sulphonic acid group (−SO3H), not a carboxyl group
(−COOH), so it does not give an esterification test for −COOH (and exists as a zwitterion).
Step 2: Statement II is correct: Because sulphanilic acid contains both N and S, sodium fusion forms NaSCN,
giving a blood-red colour with Fe3+ in Lassaigne’s test.
Q46.trapHtml: Do not confuse sulphanilic acid (p-aminobenzenesulphonic acid) with anthranilic acid (o-aminobenzoic acid). Verified Answer: (D) Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

Q47.conceptHtml: Strong bases (NaOH, KOH) absorb acidic CO<sub>2</sub> from air to form carbonates, lowering their effective hydroxide concentration.
Q47.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Reason (R): Potassium hydroxide ($\text{KOH}$) is a strong alkali that readily absorbs acidic atmospheric carbon dioxide ($\text{CO}_2$) on standing/aging to form potassium carbonate: $2\text{KOH} + \text{CO}_2 \rightarrow \text{K}_2\text{CO}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$. Thus, Reason (R) is correct.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Assertion (A) and its link to (R): Because absorption of $\text{CO}_2$ converts part of the $\text{KOH}$ into $\text{K}_2\text{CO}_3$, the effective concentration (molarity/normality) of the $\text{KOH}$ solution changes over time. Hence, its concentration must be standardised/checked against a primary standard before volumetric analysis.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the correct option: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are correct, and (R) is the exact explanation of (A), confirming option (d).
Q47.stepsLatex:
Step 1: Assertion (A) is correct: KOH is a secondary standard whose molarity changes over time and must be
checked before titration.
Step 2: Reason (R) is correct: 2KOH+CO2 → K2CO3+H2O, which directly explains why its concentration drifts.
Q47.trapHtml: Both NaOH and KOH absorb atmospheric CO<sub>2</sub> and moisture. Verified Answer: (D) Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)

Q48.conceptHtml: In Dumas’ method, nitrogen oxides formed during combustion with CuO are reduced back to N<sub>2</sub> by passing over hot reduced copper gauze.
Q48.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the combustion step in Dumas’ method: The nitrogen-containing organic compound is heated with excess copper(II) oxide ($\text{CuO}$) in an atmosphere of $\text{CO}_2$, producing $\text{CO}_2$, $\text{H}_2\text{O}$, free $\text{N}_2$, and small amounts of nitrogen oxides ($\text{NO}_x$).
  2. Step 2 — Identify the role of heated copper gauze: To ensure all nitrogen is measured accurately as $\text{N}_2$, the evolved gases are passed over a heated copper gauze, which reduces any oxides of nitrogen back to molecular nitrogen: $\text{NO}_x + x\text{Cu} \rightarrow \frac{1}{2}\text{N}_2 + x\text{CuO}$.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the correct option: The gas evolved is passed over heated copper gauze, confirming option (b).

2

Q49.conceptHtml: Starch forms an intense deep-blue inclusion complex with molecular iodine (I<sub>2</sub> / I<sup>−</sup><sub>3</sub> ).
Q49.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the reaction product ‘A’: In the clock-reaction kinetic study of iodide ion with hydrogen peroxide in acidic medium, $\text{H}_2\text{O}_2$ oxidises $\text{I}^-$ to molecular iodine ($\text{I}_2$): $\text{H}_2\text{O}_2 + 2\text{I}^- + 2\text{H}^+ \rightarrow 2\text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{I}_2$.
  2. Step 2 — Identify the indicator ‘X’: Freshly prepared starch solution is used as the indicator because it forms an intense deep-blue starch–iodine inclusion complex as soon as free iodine ($\text{I}_2$) appears in the solution.
  3. Step 3 — Match ‘X’ and ‘A’ with the options: Indicator ‘X’ is starch and compound ‘A’ is iodine, confirming option (d).

is consumed, free iodine (‘A’) forms a blue complex with starch.

Q50.conceptHtml: Only compounds containing carbon along with N and halogen can form NaCN and NaX in Lassaigne’s test.
Q50.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the carbon requirement for Lassaigne’s nitrogen test: To give a positive Lassaigne’s test for nitrogen (Prussian blue colour), sodium must form sodium cyanide ($\text{NaCN}$), which strictly requires carbon to be present in the compound along with nitrogen.
  2. Step 2 — Screen the given compounds for carbon: $\text{NH}_2\text{OH}\cdot\text{HCl}$, $\text{N}_2\text{H}_4\cdot\text{HCl}$, and $\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$ contain nitrogen and chlorine but no carbon, so they cannot form $\text{NaCN}$ and fail the Lassaigne’s test for nitrogen.
  3. Step 3 — Verify $\text{CH}_3\text{NH}_2\cdot\text{HCl}$: Methylammonium chloride ($\text{CH}_3\text{NH}_2\cdot\text{HCl}$) contains carbon, nitrogen, and chlorine, so sodium fusion produces both $\text{NaCN}$ (positive N test) and $\text{NaCl}$ (positive halogen test).
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the correct option: Only $\text{CH}_3\text{NH}_2\cdot\text{HCl}$ gives positive Lassaigne’s tests for both nitrogen and halogen, confirming option (c).
Q50.stepsLatex:
Step 1: NH2OH · HCl, N2H4 · HCl, and NH4Cl contain N and Cl, but zero carbon, so they cannot form NaCN
and fail Lassaigne’s test for nitrogen.
Step 2: Only methylammonium chloride (CH3NH2 · HCl) contains C, N, and Cl, giving positive tests for both N
and halogen.
Q50.trapHtml: Presence of N + Cl is not enough—carbon must be present to form CN<sup>−</sup>. Verified Answer: (C) CH<sub>3</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> · HCl

Q51.conceptHtml: %S = M<sub>S</sub> × <sup>m</sup>BaSO<sub>4</sub> × 100. MBaSO4 mcomp
Q51.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Write the Carius formula for percentage of sulphur: In the Carius method, all sulphur in the organic compound is converted quantitatively into $\text{BaSO}_4$, so $\%\text{S} = \frac{M(\text{S})}{M(\text{BaSO}_4)} \times \frac{\text{Mass of BaSO}_4}{\text{Mass of compound}} \times 100$.
  2. Step 2 — Substitute the given values: Mass of compound $= 0.2\text{ g}$, mass of $\text{BaSO}_4 = 0.6\text{ g}$, $M(\text{S}) = 32\text{ g mol}^{-1}$, and standard $M(\text{BaSO}_4) = 233\text{ g mol}^{-1}$ (note: the question prints $231$ as a typo for $233$).
  3. Step 3 — Compute the percentage: Using standard $233\text{ g mol}^{-1}$, $\%\text{S} = \frac{32}{233} \times \frac{0.6}{0.2} \times 100 = \frac{32 \times 300}{233} = \frac{9600}{233} = 41.20\%$ (using $231$ gives $41.56\%$).
  4. Step 4 — Round to the verified integer answer: Rounding $41.20\%$ to the nearest integer gives 41.

Q52.subtopic: Carius Method: Sulphur Estimation from Moles
Q52.conceptHtml: Convert given moles of organic compound (X) to mass via m = n × M.
Q52.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Find the mass of the organic compound (X): Given $n = 2.0 \times 10^{-3}\text{ mol}$ and molar mass $= 76\text{ g mol}^{-1}$, the mass of sample is $m = 2.0 \times 10^{-3} \times 76 = 0.152\text{ g}$.
  2. Step 2 — Calculate the mass of sulphur from $\text{BaSO}_4$: $1\text{ mol}$ of $\text{BaSO}_4$ ($233\text{ g}$) contains $1\text{ mol}$ of $\text{S}$ ($32\text{ g}$). Thus, mass of sulphur $= \frac{32}{233} \times 0.4813 = 0.06610\text{ g}$.
  3. Step 3 — Compute the percentage of sulphur: $\%\text{S} = \frac{0.06610}{0.152} \times 100 = 43.49\% \approx 43.5\%$.
  4. Step 4 — Express in the required $\times 10^{-1}\%$ format: Writing $43.5\%$ as $435 \times 10^{-1}\%$ gives the nearest integer answer 435.

Q53.conceptHtml: Determine %Br from AgBr, find %H by difference (100 − %C − %Br), and compute the simplest whole- number mole ratio.
Q53.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Calculate the percentage of bromine from Carius analysis: Molar mass of $\text{AgBr} = 108 + 80 = 188\text{ g mol}^{-1}$. Mass of $\text{Br} = \frac{80}{188} \times 3.36 = 1.43\text{ g}$, so $\%\text{Br} = \frac{1.43}{2.0} \times 100 = 71.49\%$.
  2. Step 2 — Find the percentage of hydrogen: Since (X) is a bromo hydrocarbon containing only $\text{C}$, $\text{H}$, and $\text{Br}$, $\%\text{H} = 100 - (26.7 + 71.49) = 1.81\%$.
  3. Step 3 — Determine the molar ratio of $\text{C}:\text{H}:\text{Br}$: Divide each percentage by its atomic mass: $\text{C} = \frac{26.7}{12} = 2.225$, $\text{H} = \frac{1.81}{1} = 1.81$, $\text{Br} = \frac{71.49}{80} = 0.894$.
  4. Step 4 — Convert to the simplest whole-number empirical formula: Dividing by the smallest value ($0.894$) gives $\text{C} : \text{H} : \text{Br} = 2.49 : 2.02 : 1 \approx 2.5 : 2 : 1$. Multiplying by $2$ gives the empirical formula $\text{C}_5\text{H}_4\text{Br}_2$.
  5. Step 5 — State the final count: The total number of carbon atoms in the empirical formula is 5.

Q54.conceptHtml: Trace the 4-step aromatic synthesis to identify (P), then apply Carius stoichiometry for 1.0 g of (P).
Q54.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Trace the reaction sequence to identify Major Product (P): Starting from $p$-nitrotoluene: (i) $\text{Sn}/\text{HCl}; \text{OH}^-$ reduces $-\text{NO}_2$ to $-\text{NH}_2$, giving $p$-toluidine; (ii) $(\text{CH}_3\text{CO})_2\text{O}$ protects the amine as $p$-methylacetanilide ($-\text{NHCOCH}_3$); (iii) $\text{Br}_2/\text{AlBr}_3$ monobrominates ortho to the stronger activating $-\text{NHCOCH}_3$ group; (iv) $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$ hydrolyses the amide back to $-\text{NH}_2$, yielding 2-bromo-4-methylaniline as (P).
  2. Step 2 — Calculate the molar masses of (P) and $\text{AgBr}$: The molecular formula of 2-bromo-4-methylaniline is $\text{C}_7\text{H}_8\text{NBr}$, so $M(\text{P}) = 7(12) + 8(1) + 14 + 80 = 186\text{ g mol}^{-1}$. For $\text{AgBr}$, $M(\text{AgBr}) = 108 + 80 = 188\text{ g mol}^{-1}$.
  3. Step 3 — Apply stoichiometry in Carius analysis: Each mole of (P) contains $1\text{ mol}$ of $\text{Br}$ and produces $1\text{ mol}$ of $\text{AgBr}$. Thus, $1.0\text{ g}$ of (P) yields $\frac{1.0}{186} \times 188 = 1.011\text{ g}$ of $\text{AgBr}$.
  4. Step 4 — Round to the nearest integer: Rounding $1.011\text{ g}$ to the nearest integer gives 1.

(ii) (CH3CO)2O protects −NH2 as p-methylacetanilide.
(iii) Br2/AlBr3 brominates ortho to the stronger activating −NHCOCH3 group.

Q60.subtopic: Dumas’ Method: Volume of N2 from Structure
Q60.conceptHtml: Identify the molecular formula of piperazine (C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub>N<sub>2</sub>); 1 mol of compound liberates 1 mol of N<sub>2</sub> (22400 mL at STP).

1. Step 1 — Identify compound X and its molar mass: The diagram shows piperazine, a 6-membered saturated ring with four $-\text{CH}_2-$ groups and two $-\text{NH}-$ groups, giving the formula $\text{C}_4\text{H}_{10}\text{N}_2$. Its molar mass is $M = 4(12) + 10(1) + 2(14) = 86\text{ g mol}^{-1}$.
  2. Step 2 — Find the moles of $\text{N}_2$ liberated: Moles of X $= \frac{0.42}{86}\text{ mol}$. Since each molecule of $\text{C}_4\text{H}_{10}\text{N}_2$ contains $2$ nitrogen atoms, $1\text{ mol}$ of X liberates $1\text{ mol}$ of $\text{N}_2$ gas, so $n(\text{N}_2) = \frac{0.42}{86}\text{ mol}$.
  3. Step 3 — Calculate the volume of $\text{N}_2$ at STP: Using $22400\text{ mL mol}^{-1}$ at STP, $V(\text{N}_2) = \frac{0.42}{86} \times 22400 = 109.4\text{ mL}$.

Q67.subtopic: Redox Titration: KMnO4 vs Mohr’s Salt
Q67.conceptHtml: Account for BOTH water formed from H<sup>+</sup> + O<sup>2−</sup> AND the 6 waters of crystallisation per Mohr’s salt molecule.
Q67.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Write the ionic redox equation: In acidic medium, $\text{MnO}_4^-$ oxidises $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ to $\text{Fe}^{3+}$: $2\text{MnO}_4^- + 10\text{Fe}^{2+} + 16\text{H}^+ \rightarrow 2\text{Mn}^{2+} + 10\text{Fe}^{3+} + 8\text{H}_2\text{O}$. This directly forms $8\text{ H}_2\text{O}$ molecules.
  2. Step 2 — Account for the water of crystallisation in Mohr’s salt: Ferrous ammonium sulphate hexahydrate has the formula $\text{FeSO}_4\cdot(\text{NH}_4)_2\text{SO}_4\cdot 6\text{H}_2\text{O}$. For $2$ molecules of $\text{KMnO}_4$, $10$ formula units of Mohr’s salt are consumed, releasing $10 \times 6 = 60$ molecules of $\text{H}_2\text{O}$.
  3. Step 3 — Write the complete balanced molecular equation: $2\text{KMnO}_4 + 10[\text{FeSO}_4\cdot(\text{NH}_4)_2\text{SO}_4\cdot 6\text{H}_2\text{O}] + 8\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \text{K}_2\text{SO}_4 + 2\text{MnSO}_4 + 5\text{Fe}_2(\text{SO}_4)_3 + 10(\text{NH}_4)_2\text{SO}_4 + 68\text{H}_2\text{O}$.
  4. Step 4 — Sum the total water molecules: Total water molecules produced $= 8 + 60 =$ 68.

Q67.trapHtml: Most students write 8 (forgetting the 60 H<sub>2</sub>O of crystallisation from 10 moles of Mohr’s salt hexahydrate)! Verified Answer: 68

Q68.conceptHtml: Both tests pass ONLY if the molecule has (i) an alcoholic −OH group (for red CAN colour) AND (ii) a CH<sub>3</sub>CH(OH)− unit (for yellow CHI<sub>3</sub>).
Q68.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — State the structural requirements for both tests: (i) Red colouration with ceric ammonium nitrate (CAN) requires an alcoholic $-\text{OH}$ group. (ii) A positive iodoform test in an alcohol requires the $\text{CH}_3\text{-CH(OH)-}$ structural unit (secondary methyl carbinol or ethanol).
  2. Step 2 — Check the first row of compounds: Acetophenone ($\text{PhCOCH}_3$) and acetaldehyde ($\text{CH}_3\text{CHO}$) give the iodoform test but are not alcohols, so they fail the CAN test. 1-phenylpropan-2-ol ($\text{PhCH}_2\text{CH(OH)CH}_3$) has the $\text{CH}_3\text{-CH(OH)-}$ unit, so it passes both tests (count $= 1$).
  3. Step 3 — Check the second row of compounds: Butan-2-ol ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CH}_2\text{CH}_3$) is an alcohol with the $\text{CH}_3\text{-CH(OH)-}$ unit, passing both tests (count $= 2$). Ethyl methyl ether fails both; 2-phenylethanol ($\text{PhCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$) passes CAN but lacks $\text{CH}_3\text{-CH(OH)-}$, so it fails the iodoform test.
  4. Step 4 — Check the third row of compounds: 1-cyclohexylpropan-2-ol ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_{11}\text{CH}_2\text{CH(OH)CH}_3$) contains $\text{CH}_3\text{-CH(OH)-}$ and passes both tests (count $= 3$). 2-cyclohexylpropan-2-ol is a tertiary alcohol (passes CAN, fails iodoform).
  5. Step 5 — Confirm the total count: Exactly 3 compounds give both a red colouration with CAN and a positive iodoform test.

trapCards.title: Trap 1: Distillation & Separation Mix-Ups
trapCards.html:
• Glycerol from spent-lye uses distillation under re- duced pressure (decomposes at normal b.p.), NOT sim- ple or steam distillation.
  • Aniline–water and essential oils use steam dis- tillation; chloroform–aniline (∆Tb = 123 K) uses simple distillation; o-/p-bromonitrobenzene and petrol/diesel use fractional distillation.
  • Azeotropes boil at constant composition and cannot be separated by fractional distillation.
  • On silica/alumina TLC, more polar = stronger ad- sorption = lower Rf.

trapCards.title: Trap 2: Lassaigne’s Test & Extra Elements
trapCards.html:
• Carbon is mandatory to form NaCN: N2H4, NH2OH · HCl, and NH4Cl fail Lassaigne’s test for N!
  • N + S together give blood-red [Fe(SCN)]2+, NOT Prussian blue (unless excess Na decomposes NaSCN).
  • Boil extract with conc. HNO3 before adding AgNO3 to decompose Na2S and NaCN into H2S ↑ and HCN ↑.
  • Phosphorus yellow ppt: (NH4)3PO4 · 12MoO3.
  • Fusion uses Sodium (Na), never Magnesium.

trapCards.title: Trap 3: Quantitative Estimation Pitfalls
trapCards.html:
• Dumas’ Method: Always subtract aqueous tension from total pressure before converting V to STP, and re- member copper gauze reduces NOx → N2.
  • Kjeldahl’s Method: Multiply H2SO4 molarity by 2 (N = 2M). Fails for −NO2, −N = N−, and ring-N (pyridine).
  • Carius / P: Use M(BaSO4) = 233 (or 231 if given), M(AgCl) = 143.5, M(AgBr) = 188, M(AgI) = 235, and 62 for Mg2P2O7 (two P atoms!). 222
  • Watch for ×10−1% or ×10−3 g multipliers in numerical blanks!

trapCards.title: Trap 4: Functional Group & Titrimetric Traps
trapCards.html:
• CAN test (red) detects alcoholic −OH; Neutral FeCl3 (violet) and Phthalein dye detect phenolic −OH.
  • Methyl orange is a weak base whose quinonoid form (red, in acid) is more deeply coloured than its benzenoid form (yellow).
  • Primary standards must be non-hygroscopic and have high molar mass (K2Cr2O7, KHP). KMnO4, NaOH/KOH, and Na2Cr2O7 are NOT primary standards.
  • Mohr’s salt: dil. H2SO4 prevents hydrolysis; avoid- ing prolonged heating prevents oxidation; remember its 6H2O in stoichiometry!

formulaCards.title: 1. Preparation of Alcohols (Alkene Hydration & Carbonyls)
formulaCards.html:
• Acid-Catalysed Hydration (H+/H2O): Markovnikov addition via carbocation intermediate =⇒ rearrange- ment possible (hydride/alkyl shift).
  • Oxymercuration–Demercuration (Hg(OAc)2, H2O/NaBH4): Markovnikov addition, anti stereochemistry, no carbocation rearrangement.
  • Hydroboration–Oxidation (B2H6/THF, H2O2/OH−): Anti-Markovnikov, syn addition of H and OH, no rearrangement.
  • Grignard (RMgX + H3O+): HCHO → 1◦ alcohol; R′CHO → 2◦ alcohol; R2′ C = O or ester (2 eq. RMgX) → 3◦ alcohol. Acidic H (−OH, −NH, −SH) consumes 1 eq. RMgX!
  • Reductions: LiAlH4 reduces aldehydes, ketones, acids, esters, amides; NaBH4 reduces only aldehydes, ketones, acyl halides (not acids/esters).
  • Industrial: CO + 2H −Z−n−O−−−C−r−2−O−3−,−57−3−K→ CH OH (water 2 3 gas + Co/ZnO catalyst).

formulaCards.title: 2. Identification (1<sup>◦</sup>/2<sup>◦</sup>/3<sup>◦</sup>) & Physical Trends
formulaCards.html:
• Lucas Test (conc. HCl + anhyd. ZnCl2): Rate follows carbocation stability: 3◦ (immediate turbidity) > 2◦ (∼ 5 min) > 1◦ (no turbidity at RT; only on heating). Al- lylic/benzylic 1◦ also give fast turbidity.
  • Victor Meyer Test (P/I2 → AgNO2 → HNO2 → NaOH): 1◦ → Nitrolic acid → Red; 2◦ → Pseudonitrol → Blue; 3◦ → Colourless.
  • Boiling Point Order: Alcohols > Ketones/Aldehydes > Ethers > Alkanes (comparable molar mass), due to inter- molecular H-bonding in alcohols. BP increases with C- chain length and decreases with branching.
  • Water Solubility: Lower alcohols (CH3OH, C2H5OH) and Me2O are soluble via H-bonding; higher ethers (Et2O) are sparingly soluble.
  • Drying Agent Trap: Na metal dries Et2O (unreactive), not EtOH (EtOH + Na → EtONa + 1H2). 2

formulaCards.title: 3. Dehydration of Alcohols & Pinacol Rearrange- ment
formulaCards.html:
• Acidic Dehydration (conc. H2SO4/∆ or H3PO4): Ini- tiation step is protonation of alcohol; RDS is for- mation of carbocation. Ease: 3◦ > 2◦ > 1◦ (and conjugated/aromatic-stabilised > simple).
  • Zaitsev Rule & Rearrangement: Carbocation under- goes 1, 2-hydride, 1, 2-methyl, or ring-expansion shift to form the most stable carbocation, then eliminates H+ to give the most substituted (Zaitsev) alkene.
  • Pinacol–Pinacolone Rearrangement (H+): Vicinal diol protonates at the −OH giving the more stable car- bocation → 1, 2-shift (migratory aptitude: H > Ar > R) → ketone.
  • Temperature Control (Ethanol + H2SO4): 443 K (170◦C) → CH2 = CH2 (E1/E2); 413 K (140◦C) → C2H5OC2H5 (SN2 ether).

formulaCards.title: 4. Oxidation & Dehydrogenation of Alcohols
formulaCards.html: • Reagent 1◦ Alcohol 2◦ Alcohol PCC/PDC/CrO3 · Py Aldehyde (RCHO) Ketone (R2CO) Cu/573 K Aldehyde Ketone CrO3/H2SO4 (Jones) Carboxylic acid Ketone KMnO4/H+ or OH− Carboxylic acid Ketone Critical 3◦ Alcohol Exception: Cu/573 K causes dehydra- tion of 3◦ alcohols to an alkene (NOT oxidation)! Iodoform (NaOI/I2 + NaOH): Positive (CHI3 yellow ppt) for CH3CH(OH) − R (incl. EtOH) and CH3CO − R.

formulaCards.title: 5. Phenols: Acidity, Named Reactions & EAS
formulaCards.html:
• Acidity (pKa Benchmarks): Picric acid (∼ 0.4) > p- Nitrophenol (7.1) > o-Nitrophenol (7.2) > m-Nitrophenol (8.3) > Phenol (10.0) > p-Cresol (10.2) > H2O (15.7) ≈ EtOH (15.9) > 3◦-BuOH (18).
  • Solubility Rule: Phenols dissolve in NaOH, not in NaHCO3 (except picric acid / dinitrophenols). Neutral FeCl3 gives violet/coloured complex with phenols.
  • Reimer–Tiemann (CHCl3 + aq. NaOH → H+): Forms salicylaldehyde (o-hydroxybenzaldehyde, major) via dichlorocarbene (: CCl2) and substituted benzal chloride (−CHCl2 phenoxide) intermediate. Separated from p- isomer by steam distillation (o-isomer has intramolec- ular H-bonding → steam volatile).
  • Kolbe’s Reaction (NaOH, CO2, 120◦C, P → H+): Forms salicylic acid (o-hydroxybenzoic acid).
  • EAS & Tests: Br2/H2O → 2, 4, 6-tribromophenol (white ppt); Br2/CS2 or CHCl3 (low polarity, NO Lewis acid needed!) → p-bromophenol (major); conc. HNO3 → pi- cric acid; Zn/∆ → benzene; Na2Cr2O7/H2SO4 → p- benzoquinone.

formulaCards.title: 6. Ethers: Williamson Synthesis & HX Cleavage
formulaCards.html:
• Williamson Ether Synthesis (R − O−Na+ + R′ − X → R − O − R′): Strictly SN2 on R′ − X! Use 1◦ alkyl halide (MeX, EtX, n-PrX) and 2◦/3◦ alkoxide or phenoxide. Using 3◦ (or 2◦) halide with strong alkoxide gives E2 elimination (alkene)! Aryl halides (Ph − Br) do NOT undergo SN2.
  • Cleavage with HI/HBr (R − O − R′ + HX): 1. Aryl–Alkyl Ether (Ph − O − R): Csp2 − O bond has partial double-bond character =⇒ NEVER cleaves! Always yields phenol (PhOH) + R − X. 2. Both 1◦/2◦ Alkyl: SN2 attack of I−/Br− on the less hindered (smaller) alkyl group =⇒ smaller R − I + larger R′ − OH. 3. 3◦/Benzylic/Allylic Group: SN1 cleavage gives the more stable carbocation =⇒ 3◦/benzylic halide (R − I) + other alcohol! (Excess hot HI con- verts aliphatic alcohol to R − I, NOT phenol).

Q01.subtopic: Cleavage of Benzyl Phenyl Ether with HI
Q01.conceptHtml: In aryl–alkyl ethers (Ph − O − R), the C<sub>sp2</sub> − O bond has partial double-bond character due to resonance and does not cleave; cleavage occurs at the O − R (O − CH<sub>2</sub>Ph) bond.
Q01.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the ether and reagent: The given substrate is benzyl phenyl ether ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5-\text{O}-\text{CH}_2-\text{C}_6\text{H}_5$), which is treated with $\text{HI}$.
  2. Step 2 — Determine which C–O bond cleaves: First, $\text{H}^+$ protonates the ether oxygen. The $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5-\text{O}$ bond has partial double-bond character due to resonance of the oxygen lone pair with the benzene ring and is very strong. In contrast, the $-\text{O}-\text{CH}_2-$ bond cleaves easily to form a resonance-stabilized benzyl carbocation ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2^+$).
  3. Step 3 — Identify the products formed: Nucleophilic attack of $\text{I}^-$ on the benzylic carbon yields benzyl iodide ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{I}$) and phenol ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH}$), not benzyl alcohol and iodobenzene.
  4. Step 4 — Evaluate both statements and conclude: Statement I is false (products are phenol and benzyl iodide) while Statement II is true (the $-\text{O}-\text{CH}_2-$ bond is cleaved). Hence, the correct option is (d).
Q01.stepsLatex:
+
1. Protonation of oxygen gives [Ph − O(H) − CH2Ph].
2. Cleavage occurs exclusively at the −O − CH2− bond (never the Ph − O bond) to give phenol (PhOH) and
benzyl iodide (PhCH2I).
3. Therefore, Statement I (claiming benzyl alcohol + iodobenzene) is false, while Statement II (cleavage of
−O − CH2−) is true.
Q01.trapHtml: Never form iodobenzene (PhI) from anisole or benzyl phenyl ether with HI; Ph − O bond is too strong to cleave.

Q02.subtopic: Dehydration of 3◦-Alcohol with Cu/573 K & Esterification
Q02.conceptHtml: Cu/573 K oxidises 1°/2° alcohols to carbonyls, but dehydrates 3° alcohols to alkenes; subsequent H+- catalysed addition of PhCOOH follows Markovnikov’s rule.
Q02.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Reaction with Cu at 573 K: The starting compound is tert-butyl alcohol, $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{COH}$ (a $3^\circ$ alcohol). Unlike $1^\circ$ and $2^\circ$ alcohols which undergo dehydrogenation over hot copper, $3^\circ$ alcohols undergo dehydration at $573\text{ K}$ to form an alkene: $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{COH} \xrightarrow{\text{Cu}/573\text{ K}} (\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C}=\text{CH}_2$ (2-methylpropene).
  2. Step 2 — Protonation of the alkene: In the second step ($\text{H}^+, \text{PhCOOH}$), protonation of 2-methylpropene follows Markovnikov's rule to generate the stable $3^\circ$ tert-butyl carbocation, $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}^+$.
  3. Step 3 — Nucleophilic addition of benzoic acid: Benzoic acid ($\text{PhCOOH}$) traps the tert-butyl carbocation via its oxygen atom (acid-catalyzed esterification of an alkene), followed by loss of $\text{H}^+$ to form tert-butyl benzoate, $\text{Ph}-\text{COO}-\text{C}(\text{CH}_3)_3$. Ring alkylation does not occur because $-\text{COOH}$ strongly deactivates the benzene ring.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The structure of tert-butyl benzoate corresponds to option (c).
Q02.stepsLatex:
1. Step (i): (CH3)3C − OH (3◦ alcohol) with Cu/573 K undergoes dehydration to form 2-methylpropene (isobutene),
(CH3)2C = CH2.
2. Step (ii): Protonation (H+) of isobutene forms the stable 3◦ carbocation (CH3)3C+, which is attacked by
PhCOOH to yield tert-butyl benzoate (PhCOOC(CH3)3, option C).
Q02.trapHtml: Remember the Cu/573 K 3°-alcohol rule: 1° → aldehyde, 2° → ketone, 3° → alkene (dehydration)!

Q03.conceptHtml: Conversion of an alcohol to an alkene requires an acid dehydrating agent (conc. H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> or H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>4</sub>), not an oxidising agent like PCC.
Q03.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the conversion from A to B: Compound $A$ is pentan-1-ol ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$) and compound $B$ is pent-1-ene ($\text{CH}_2=\text{CHCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$). Converting an alcohol into an alkene is a dehydration reaction (removal of $\text{H}_2\text{O}$).
  2. Step 2 — Choose the correct dehydrating reagent D: Acid-catalyzed dehydration requires a strong dehydrating acid such as $\text{Conc. H}_2\text{SO}_4$ or $\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4$ (with heat). PCC is a mild oxidizing agent that converts $1^\circ$ alcohols into aldehydes, so options (b) and (c) are ruled out.
  3. Step 3 — Predict product E from diol C: Compound $C$ is butane-1,3-diol ($\text{HO}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}(\text{OH})-\text{CH}_3$). With an excess of dehydrating reagent $D$, both $-\text{OH}$ groups eliminate as $2\text{ H}_2\text{O}$ to form the conjugated diene buta-1,3-diene: $E = \text{CH}_2=\text{CH}-\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Both reagent $D$ ($\text{Conc. H}_2\text{SO}_4$ or $\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4$) and product $E$ ($\text{CH}_2=\text{CH}-\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2$) match option (d).
Q03.stepsLatex:
1. A (pentan-1-ol) → B (pent-1-ene) is dehydration, requiring D = conc. H2SO4 or H3PO4.
2. Treating diol C (HO − CH2 − CH2 − CH(OH) − CH3) with excess D dehydrates both −OH groups to form the
conjugated diene E = CH2 = CH − CH = CH2 (1, 3-butadiene).
Q03.trapHtml: Excess dehydrating agent removes both −OH groups from the diol to give the conjugated 1, 3-diene.

Q04.subtopic: Phenolphthalein Indicator Equilibrium in Excess Alkali
Q04.conceptHtml: Phenolphthalein is colourless in acidic/neutral form, pink in its quinonoid dianion form (pH 8.2 − 10), and becomes colourless again in excess strong alkali due to loss of conjugation.
Q04.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the dye formed in step 1: Condensation of 2 equivalents of phenol with phthalic anhydride in the presence of $\text{conc. H}_2\text{SO}_4$ yields phenolphthalein in its closed lactone form, which is colourless.
  2. Step 2 — Effect of NaOH (pink form): Adding $\text{NaOH}$ opens the lactone ring and deprotonates the phenolic $-\text{OH}$ groups to produce a planar, extensively conjugated quinonoid dianion that absorbs visible light and appears pink.
  3. Step 3 — Effect of excess NaOH to form X: In strongly alkaline medium (excess $\text{NaOH}$), a hydroxide ion ($\text{OH}^-$) attacks the central $sp^2$-hybridized benzylic carbon, converting it into a tetrahedral $sp^3$ carbinol trianion (compound $X$).
  4. Step 4 — Determine the colour of X and conclude: Because the central carbon becomes $sp^3$, extended conjugation across the three aromatic rings is broken, so compound $X$ becomes colourless. Thus, the correct option is (d).
Q04.stepsLatex:
1. Phenol + phthalic anhydride / conc. H2SO4 gives phenolphthalein (lactone).
2. With NaOH, it opens to the pink quinonoid dianion.
3. With excess NaOH, OH− attacks the central sp2 carbon, converting it to an sp3 carbinol trianion ‘X’, breaking
extended conjugation =⇒ Colourless.
Q04.trapHtml: Don’t confuse the intermediate pink form with ‘X’ formed after adding excess NaOH—excess NaOH decolourises phenolphthalein!

Q05.subtopic: Controlled Oxidation of Alkanes to Alcohols
Q05.conceptHtml: NCERT Hydrocarbons/Alcohols: CH<sub>4</sub> + O<sub>2</sub> over Cu/523 K/100 atm gives CH<sub>3</sub>OH; 3°-alkane (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>CH with KMnO<sub>4</sub> oxidises to 3°-alcohol (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>COH.
Q05.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Check controlled oxidations of alkanes (A, B, D): In A, $\text{CH}_4 + \text{O}_2 \xrightarrow{\text{Mo}_2\text{O}_3, \Delta} \text{HCHO} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$ gives an aldehyde (methanal). In B, $2\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_3 + 3\text{O}_2 \xrightarrow{(\text{CH}_3\text{COO})_2\text{Mn}, \Delta} 2\text{CH}_3\text{COOH} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$ gives a carboxylic acid. In D, $2\text{CH}_4 + \text{O}_2 \xrightarrow{\text{Cu}/523\text{ K}/100\text{ atm}} 2\text{CH}_3\text{OH}$ produces methanol (an alcohol).
  2. Step 2 — Check oxidation of tertiary alkane (C): Alkanes normally resist $\text{KMnO}_4$, but alkanes with a tertiary hydrogen ($3^\circ\text{ C}-\text{H}$) are oxidized to tertiary alcohols: $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{CH} \xrightarrow{\text{KMnO}_4} (\text{CH}_3)_3\text{COH}$ (2-methylpropan-2-ol, an alcohol).
  3. Step 3 — Check oxidation of alkene (E): Acidic $\text{KMnO}_4$ ($\text{KMnO}_4/\text{H}^+$) oxidatively cleaves the double bond of but-2-ene to give ethanoic acid: $\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}=\text{CH}-\text{CH}_3 \xrightarrow{\text{KMnO}_4/\text{H}^+} 2\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$ (not an alcohol).
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Only reactions C and D produce alcohols, which matches option (d).
Q05.stepsLatex:
• A (Mo2O3, ∆): CH4 → HCHO (methanal).
• B ((CH3COO)2Mn, ∆): C2H6 → CH3COOH (ethanoic acid).
• C (KMnO4): (CH3)3CH → (CH3)3COH (alcohol!).
• D (Cu/523 K/100 atm): 2CH4 + O2 → 2CH3OH (alcohol!).
• E (KMnO4/H+): oxidative cleavage of 2-butene → 2CH3COOH.
Only C and D produce alcohols.
Q05.trapHtml: Keep Mo<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> (→ HCHO) and Cu/523 K/100 atm (→ CH<sub>3</sub>OH) distinct!

Q06.conceptHtml: Vapour density 47 =⇒ M = 94 g mol<sup>−1</sup> (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH, phenol); Kolbe’s reaction converts phenol into salicylic acid (2-hydroxybenzoic acid).
Q06.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Find the molecular formula of compound x: Molar mass of $x = 2 \times \text{Vapour Density} = 2 \times 47 = 94\text{ g mol}^{-1}$. Percentage of $\text{O} = 100 - (76.6 + 6.38) = 17.02\%$. Calculating atoms per molecule: $\text{C} = \frac{76.6 \times 94}{100 \times 12} \approx 6$, $\text{H} = \frac{6.38 \times 94}{100 \times 1} \approx 6$, and $\text{O} = \frac{17.02 \times 94}{100 \times 16} \approx 1$. Thus, $x$ is phenol ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH}$).
  2. Step 2 — Identify compound y from Kolbe's reaction: Treating phenol ($x$) with $\text{CO}_2, \text{NaOH}$ at $120^\circ\text{C}$ under high pressure followed by acidification ($\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$) is Kolbe's reaction, which yields salicylic acid (2-hydroxybenzoic acid) as the major product $y$. Its phenolic $-\text{OH}$ gives a characteristic violet colour with neutral $\text{FeCl}_3$.
  3. Step 3 — Test each statement against x and y: Statement (a) is true because salicylic acid ($-\text{COOH}$) dissolves in $\text{NaHCO}_3$ with $\text{CO}_2$ effervescence. Statement (c) is true since both phenol and salicylic acid react with $\text{NaOH}$. Statement (d) is true because both are aromatic compounds that burn with a sooty flame.
  4. Step 4 — Identify the incorrect statement and conclude: Salicylic acid ($y$, $\text{p}K_a \approx 3.0$) is much more acidic than phenol ($x$, $\text{p}K_a \approx 10.0$) due to its $-\text{COOH}$ group and intramolecular H-bonding in the salicylate ion. Therefore, stating that $x$ is more acidic than $y$ is INCORRECT, giving option (b).
Q06.stepsLatex:
1. For (x): M = 2 × 47 = 94 g mol−1; %O = 100 − 76.6 − 6.38 = 17.02% =⇒ C6H6O (phenol).
2. Kolbe’s reaction gives (y) = salicylic acid (gives violet colour with neutral FeCl3).
3. Checking options: (a) Salicylic acid has −COOH, so it evolves CO2 with NaHCO3 (true). (b) Phenol (x) is
less acidic than salicylic acid (y), so “x is more acidic than y” is incorrect. (c) Both dissolve in NaOH (true).
(d) Both are aromatic =⇒ sooty flame (true).
Q06.trapHtml: The question asks for the INCORRECT statement—always check pK<sub>a</sub>: salicylic acid (≈ 3.0) is far more acidic than phenol (10.0).

Q07.conceptHtml: A secondary (2°) alcohol has the −OH group attached to a carbon bonded to two other carbon atoms (−CH(OH)−).
Q07.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the definition of a secondary alcohol: A secondary ($2^\circ$) alcohol has its $-\text{OH}$ group attached to a carbon atom that is directly bonded to two other carbon atoms and one hydrogen atom ($-\text{CH}(\text{OH})-$).
  2. Step 2 — Classify compounds (I), (II), and (III): In (I), both alcohol $-\text{OH}$ groups are on $-\text{CH}_2-$ ($1^\circ$), and the third $-\text{OH}$ is a carboxylic acid. In (II) (butane-1,2-diol), C2 is $-\text{CH}(\text{OH})-$ ($2^\circ$ alcohol). In (III), both $-\text{OH}$ groups are on carbons bonded to three other carbons (both $3^\circ$).
  3. Step 3 — Classify compounds (IV), (V), and (VI): In (IV), both the side-chain $-\text{CH}(\text{OH})-$ and the ring $-\text{CH}(\text{OH})-$ are $2^\circ$ alcohols. In (V) (3-methylpentane-2,3-diol), C2 is $-\text{CH}(\text{OH})-$ ($2^\circ$ alcohol) while C3 is $3^\circ$. In (VI) (2,3-dimethylbutane-1,2,3-triol), C1 is $1^\circ$ while C2 and C3 are both $3^\circ$.
  4. Step 4 — Count qualifying compounds and conclude: Compounds (II), (IV), and (V) contain at least one secondary alcohol — a total of Three. Hence, the correct option is (a).
Q07.stepsLatex:
Inspecting structures (I)–(VI):
• (I): Top −OH is carboxylic acid (−COOH); bottom −OH is phenolic (Ar − OH). No 2◦ alcohol.
• (II): Contains C = O? No, −CH(OH)− on the ring (attached to two ring carbons, plus one H) =⇒ Yes (2◦
alcohol).
• (III): Both −OH groups are attached to 3◦ carbons (one is tertiary allylic/alkyl, one is 3◦ on ring). No 2◦
alcohol.
• (IV): Ring −OH is phenolic; side-chain has −CH(OH) − CH3 =⇒ Yes (2◦ alcohol).
• (V): −CH(OH)− on the 5-membered ring? Look closely: it is attached to 2 carbons (CH − OH), wait—in (V)
the −OH is at a 3◦ or 2◦ carbon? Let’s check: top −OH is on a tertiary carbon? No, in (V) there is a −CH3
and two ring carbons at the bottom, and top −OH is attached to a carbon with 2 ring bonds + H =⇒ Yes
(2◦ alcohol)!
• (VI): All three −OH groups are on tertiary carbons (−C(CH3)(OH)−). No 2◦ alcohol.
Total = Three ((II), (IV), (V)).
Q07.trapHtml: Do not count phenolic −OH or carboxylic −OH as alcohols!

Q08.subtopic: Stoichiometry of Acetylation of Polyhydric Alcohols
Q08.conceptHtml: Each −OH group acetylated (−OH → −OCOCH<sub>3</sub>) replaces H (1) with COCH<sub>3</sub> (43), increasing molar mass by ∆M = 42 g mol<sup>−1</sup>.
Q08.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Determine the mass change per hydroxyl group: During complete acetylation with acetic anhydride, $(\text{CH}_3\text{CO})_2\text{O}$, each $-\text{OH}$ group is converted into an acetate ester group ($-\text{OCOCH}_3$). This replaces one $\text{H}$ atom ($1\text{ g mol}^{-1}$) with an acetyl group, $-\text{COCH}_3$ ($43\text{ g mol}^{-1}$).
  2. Step 2 — Compute net increase per –OH group: The net molar mass increase for every $-\text{OH}$ group acetylated is: $\Delta M_{\text{per OH}} = 43 - 1 = 42\text{ g mol}^{-1}$.
  3. Step 3 — Calculate the number of –OH groups: Total molar mass increase $= 290 - 122 = 168\text{ g mol}^{-1}$. Dividing by $42\text{ g mol}^{-1}$ gives: $n = \frac{168}{42} = 4$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Compound $(X)$ contains 4 hydroxyl groups, which corresponds to option (b).
Q08.stepsLatex:
Mproduct − MX 290 − 122 168
nOH = = = = 4
42 42 42
Q08.trapHtml: Remember ∆M = 42 per −OH group (not 43 or 60!).

Q09.subtopic: Ether Cleavage with Excess HI + Iodoform Test
Q09.conceptHtml: Excess hot HI converts both alkyl groups of an aliphatic ether into R − I and R′ − I; aq. NaOH converts them to alcohols Q and R. Only alcohols with CH<sub>3</sub>CH(OH)− give a positive iodoform test (NaOI).
Q09.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Trace the reaction pathway: Heating a mixed ether $\text{R}-\text{O}-\text{R}'$ ($P$) with excess hot $\text{conc. HI}$ cleaves both $\text{C}-\text{O}$ bonds to give two alkyl iodides, $\text{R}-\text{I}$ and $\text{R}'-\text{I}$. Subsequent hydrolysis with $\text{aq. NaOH}$ converts them into two alcohols, $Q$ ($\text{R}-\text{OH}$) and $R$ ($\text{R}'-\text{OH}$).
  2. Step 2 — Apply the iodoform test condition: Both alcohols $Q$ and $R$ give a yellow precipitate ($\text{CHI}_3$) with $\text{NaOI}$. An alcohol gives a positive iodoform test only if it contains the $\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}(\text{OH})-$ group (i.e., ethanol or a methyl secondary alcohol).
  3. Step 3 — Check the alcohol pairs from each option: Option (b) is 2-ethoxybutane ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2-\text{O}-\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$). Cleavage and hydrolysis give ethanol ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$) and butan-2-ol ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}(\text{OH})\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$), both of which contain the $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}(\text{OH})-$ unit. In options (a), (c), and (d), at least one alcohol lacks this group (1-phenylpropan-1-ol, 2-phenylethanol/pentan-3-ol, or a $3^\circ$ alcohol).
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Only option (b) yields two iodoform-positive alcohols, so the correct answer is (b).
Q09.stepsLatex:
1. Both (Q) and (R) must contain CH3CH(OH)− (or be C2H5OH) to give a yellow CHI3 ppt with NaOI.
2. Option (B) is 2-ethoxypropane (CH3CH2 − O − CH(CH3)2). With excess HI, it gives CH3CH2I and (CH3)2CHI.
3. Hydrolysis with aq. NaOH gives CH3CH2OH (ethanol) and (CH3)2CHOH (propan-2-ol)—both give positive
iodoform!
4. Options (A), (C) contain Ph (phenol/iodobenzene don’t give iodoform), and (D) gives 1-propanol (negative
iodoform).
Q09.trapHtml: Ethanol (CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH) is the ONLY 1° alcohol that gives a positive iodoform test!

Q10.conceptHtml: Acid-catalysed hydration (H<sub>2</sub>O/H+) and oxymercuration/alkyne hydration follow Markovnikov’s rule; check carbocation rearrangements carefully!
Q10.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the target alcohol: The target molecule is 3,3-dimethylbutan-2-ol, $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}-\text{CH}(\text{OH})-\text{CH}_3$.
  2. Step 2 — Check reactions A, C, and D (which work): A: 2,2-Dimethylpropanal + $\text{MeMgBr}/\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$ directly yields $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}-\text{CH}(\text{OH})-\text{CH}_3$. C: Reductive ozonolysis ($\text{O}_3/\text{Zn}-\text{H}_2\text{O}$) of the symmetrical alkene gives pinacolone, $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}-\text{CO}-\text{CH}_3$, which $\text{NaBH}_4/\text{MeOH}$ reduces to the target alcohol. D: $\text{LiAlH}_4/\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$ directly reduces pinacolone to the target alcohol.
  3. Step 3 — Check reactions B and E (which fail): B: Acid-catalyzed hydration ($\text{H}_2\text{O}/\text{H}^+$) of 3,3-dimethylbut-1-ene forms a $2^\circ$ carbocation that undergoes a rapid 1,2-methyl shift to the more stable $3^\circ$ carbocation, yielding 2,3-dimethylbutan-2-ol instead. E: Hydration of 3,3-dimethylbut-1-yne with $\text{H}_2\text{O}, \text{Hg}^{2+}/\text{H}^+$ gives an enol that tautomerizes to a ketone (pinacolone), not an alcohol.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Thus, 3,3-dimethyl-2-butanol cannot be prepared by B and E Only, which is option (a).

Q11.conceptHtml: Reimer–Tiemann reaction (CHCl<sub>3</sub>/aq. KOH) yields salicylaldehyde (o-hydroxybenzaldehyde) as the major product, which is steam-volatile due to intramolecular H-bonding.
Q11.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement I (Reimer–Tiemann selectivity): When phenol is refluxed with $\text{CHCl}_3/\text{aq. KOH}$ followed by acidification (Reimer–Tiemann reaction), o-hydroxybenzaldehyde (salicylaldehyde) is formed as the major product and p-hydroxybenzaldehyde as the minor product. Because Statement I claims the reverse, Statement I is false.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement II (steam distillation): o-Hydroxybenzaldehyde forms intramolecular hydrogen bonds, making it volatile with steam. In contrast, p-hydroxybenzaldehyde forms intermolecular hydrogen bonds, causing molecular association and a much higher boiling point.
  3. Step 3 — Check separation feasibility: Because of this volatility difference, the mixture of o- and p-hydroxybenzaldehyde is easily separated by steam distillation. Hence, Statement II is true.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Statement I is false and Statement II is true, corresponding to option (d).
Q11.stepsLatex:
1. Statement I claims p-hydroxybenzaldehyde is major and o-isomer is minor =⇒ False (o-isomer is major).
2. Statement II states o- and p-hydroxybenzaldehyde are separated by steam distillation =⇒ True (o-isomer is
steam-volatile via intramolecular H-bonding; p-isomer has intermolecular H-bonding).
Q11.trapHtml: Don’t mix up Reimer–Tiemann (o-major) with Friedel–Crafts/nitration steric trends.

Q12.subtopic: Williamson Ether Synthesis: SN2 vs. E2 Elimination
Q12.conceptHtml: Williamson synthesis requires a primary (1°) alkyl halide; 2° or 3° alkyl halides with strong alkoxide bases undergo E2 elimination to form alkenes.
Q12.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the condition for Williamson ether synthesis: Williamson ether synthesis ($\text{R}-\text{O}^-\text{Na}^+ + \text{R}'-\text{X} \to \text{R}-\text{O}-\text{R}'$) proceeds via an $\text{S}_\text{N}2$ mechanism. For high ether yield, the alkyl halide ($\text{R}'-\text{X}$) must be primary ($1^\circ$) or methyl; secondary ($2^\circ$) or tertiary ($3^\circ$) halides undergo competing $\text{E}2$ elimination with strong alkoxide bases.
  2. Step 2 — Analyze the alkyl halides in options (a), (c), and (d): Option (a) uses $n\text{-PrBr}$ ($1^\circ$), option (c) uses $\text{CH}_3\text{Br}$ (methyl), and option (d) uses $\text{EtBr}$ ($1^\circ$). All three undergo smooth $\text{S}_\text{N}2$ substitution to yield the desired ether as the major product.
  3. Step 3 — Analyze option (b): Option (b) reacts a bulky strong base ($\text{iso-BuO}^-\text{Na}^+$) with a secondary alkyl halide ($\text{sec-BuBr}$). Due to steric hindrance at the $2^\circ$ carbon, $\text{E}2$ elimination predominates to give alkenes (but-2-ene/but-1-ene) instead of the desired ether.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Therefore, the reaction in option (b) will not lead to the desired ether in major proportion.
Q12.stepsLatex:
• (A) PhO−Na+ + n-PrBr (1◦ halide) → clean SN2 ether.
• (B) iso-BuO−Na+ + sec-BuBr (2◦ halide + bulky alkoxide) → major E2 elimination (butene), NOT desired
ether!
• (C) CyO−Na+ + CH3Br (1◦ methyl halide) → clean SN2.
• (D) tBuO−Na+ + EtBr (1◦ halide) → clean SN2.
Q12.trapHtml: Always check which partner is the halide: 3°-alkoxide +1°-halide works; 1°-alkoxide +2°/3°-halide fails via E2!

Q13.subtopic: Solubility of Ethers & Drying with Sodium Metal
Q13.conceptHtml: Dimethyl ether is completely miscible with water due to H-bonding, whereas diethyl ether has larger hydrophobic ethyl groups (sparingly soluble). Na dries Et<sub>2</sub>O without reacting, unlike EtOH.
Q13.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Analyze Statement I (water solubility of ethers): Ethers can accept hydrogen bonds from water via their oxygen lone pairs. Dimethyl ether ($\text{CH}_3\text{OCH}_3$) has very small alkyl groups, so it is completely soluble in water. In diethyl ether ($\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OC}_2\text{H}_5$), the larger hydrophobic ethyl groups outweigh H-bonding, making it only sparingly soluble in water. Thus, Statement I is true.
  2. Step 2 — Analyze Statement II (drying with sodium metal): Diethyl ether contains no acidic hydrogen and is inert toward $\text{Na}$ metal, so $\text{Na}$ selectively reacts with trace water ($2\text{Na} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} \to 2\text{NaOH} + \text{H}_2$) to dry it.
  3. Step 3 — Check why Na cannot dry ethanol: Ethyl alcohol ($\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}$) has an active acidic $-\text{OH}$ proton and reacts vigorously with sodium ($2\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH} + 2\text{Na} \to 2\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{ONa} + \text{H}_2$), so sodium metal cannot be used to dry it. Thus, Statement II is also true.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Both Statement I and Statement II are true, which matches option (c).
Q13.stepsLatex:
1. Statement I: Me2O is completely soluble in water; Et2O is soluble to a very small extent =⇒ True.
2. Statement II: Na metal reacts with trace water in Et2O (leaving Et2O dry) but reacts vigorously with EtOH
(EtOH + Na → EtONa + 1H2) =⇒ True.
2
Q13.trapHtml: Never use metallic Na to dry alcohols—it forms alkoxides!

Q14.conceptHtml: Connect NCERT everyday-chemistry clues: Methanol (toxic) → Acetic acid (vinegar/preservative) <sup>−B</sup>−2<sup>−H</sup>→6 Ethanol (petrol additive) <sup>−o</sup><sup>−le</sup><sup>−u</sup><sup>−m</sup><sup>−/H</sup>−2<sup>−S</sup><sup>−O</sup>−4<sup>−,</sup><sup>−14</sup><sup>−0</sup><sup>−°</sup>→<sup>C</sup> Diethyl ether (inhalable anesthetic).
Q14.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify A and B: Methanol ($\text{CH}_3\text{OH}$, compound $A$) is a well-known toxic alcohol. Conversion via cyanide in aqueous acidic medium (followed by hydrolysis of the nitrile) yields acetic acid ($\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$, compound $B$), the active component of vinegar used in cooking and food preservation.
  2. Step 2 — Identify C from diborane reduction: Diborane ($\text{B}_2\text{H}_6$) readily reduces carboxylic acids to primary alcohols: $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH} \xrightarrow{\text{B}_2\text{H}_6 / \text{H}_3\text{O}^+} \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ (ethanol, compound $C$), which is blended with petrol as a clean fuel additive to reduce emissions.
  3. Step 3 — Identify D from dehydration at 140 °C: Heating ethanol ($C$) with oleum / $\text{conc. H}_2\text{SO}_4$ at $140^\circ\text{C}$ ($413\text{ K}$) causes bimolecular dehydration to diethyl ether ($\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OC}_2\text{H}_5$, compound $D$), a classic inhalable anesthetic.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Matching $A, B, C, D$ gives Methanol; acetic acid; ethanol; diethyl ether, which is option (a).

1. ‘A’ = Methanol (toxic, causes blindness); ‘B’ = Acetic acid (edible vinegar, food preservative).
2. ‘B’ (CH3COOH) −B−2−H→6 ‘C’ = Ethanol (petrol additive to reduce emissions).
3. ‘C’ (C2H5OH) at 140◦C with H2SO4/oleum gives ‘D’ = Diethyl ether (anesthetic).
Q14.trapHtml: Note the temperature 140°C (413 K) gives diethyl ether, whereas 170°C gives ethene.

Q15.subtopic: Dow’s/Sulphonation Route to Phenol & Zn-Dust Reduction
Q15.conceptHtml: Benzene <sup>−o</sup><sup>−l</sup><sup>−eu</sup><sup>−m</sup>→ Benzenesulphonic acid <sup>−m</sup>−<sup>−ol</sup><sup>−te</sup><sup>−n</sup><sup>−N</sup><sup>−a</sup><sup>−O</sup><sup>−H</sup><sup>−,</sup><sup>−H</sup><sup>−+</sup>→ Phenol <sup>−Z</sup><sup>−n</sup><sup>−/∆</sup>→ Benzene.
Q15.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Sulphonation of benzene to X: Treating benzene ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_6$) with oleum ($\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 + \text{SO}_3$) produces benzenesulphonic acid ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{SO}_3\text{H}$, compound $X$).
  2. Step 2 — Alkali fusion to Y: Heating benzenesulphonic acid ($X$) with molten $\text{NaOH}$ converts it into sodium phenoxide ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{O}^-\text{Na}^+$), which upon acidification yields phenol ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH}$, compound $Y$).
  3. Step 3 — Reduction with zinc dust to Z: Heating phenol ($Y$) with zinc metal reduces it back to benzene: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH} + \text{Zn} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \text{C}_6\text{H}_6 + \text{ZnO}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Compound $(Z)$ is benzene, whose structure is shown in option (c).

1. Benzene + oleum → C6H5SO3H (X).
2. Fusion with molten NaOH followed by H+ → Phenol (Y).
3. Heating phenol with Zn dust reduces it back to Benzene (Z, option C) + ZnO.
Q15.trapHtml: Read carefully: it asks for ‘Z’ (after Zn treatment), not ‘Y’ (phenol)!

Q16.subtopic: Cleavage of Aryl Ethers with HBr
Q16.conceptHtml: Only ethers where oxygen is directly attached to the benzene ring (Ar − O − R) yield a phenol upon cleavage with HBr.
Q16.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the structural requirement to form a phenol: To obtain a phenol ($\text{Ar}-\text{OH}$) upon cleavage with $\text{HBr}$, the ether oxygen must be bonded directly to the benzene ring ($\text{Ar}-\text{O}-\text{R}$).
  2. Step 2 — Analyze the cleavage of anisole in option (a): Option (a) is anisole ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5-\text{O}-\text{CH}_3$). Because the $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5-\text{O}$ bond has partial double-bond character from resonance, $\text{HBr}$ cleaves the weaker $\text{O}-\text{CH}_3$ bond to give phenol ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH}$) and $\text{CH}_3\text{Br}$.
  3. Step 3 — Eliminate the other options: In options (b), (c), and (d), the oxygen atom is separated from the benzene ring by a $-\text{CH}_2-$ (benzylic) or $-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}-$ spacer, so cleavage with $\text{HBr}$ produces benzyl/aliphatic halides or alcohols rather than a phenol.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Only anisole gives phenol with $\text{HBr}$, corresponding to option (a).
