Q17.subtopic: Boiling Point Trends of Alcohols & Phenols
Q17.conceptHtml: Boiling points increase with molar mass (number of C atoms, stronger van der Waals forces) and are higher than ethers/haloalkanes due to intermolecular H-bonding.
Q17.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement I (effect of carbon chain length): As the number of carbon atoms in alcohols and phenols increases, both molecular mass and surface area increase. This strengthens intermolecular van der Waals (London dispersion) forces, causing the boiling points to increase. Thus, Statement I is true.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement II (comparison with ethers and haloalkanes): Alcohols and phenols contain polar $-\text{OH}$ groups that form strong intermolecular hydrogen bonds. Ethers and haloalkanes of comparable molar mass cannot form intermolecular H-bonds with themselves and only experience weaker dipole–dipole and van der Waals forces.
  3. Step 3 — Compare their boiling points: Consequently, alcohols and phenols have significantly higher boiling points than ethers and haloalkanes of similar molecular mass. Thus, Statement II is also true.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Both Statement I and Statement II are true, which matches option (b).
Q17.stepsLatex:
1. Statement (I): Increasing C-atoms increases molecular mass and van der Waals forces =⇒ higher BP (True).
2. Statement (II): Intermolecular H-bonding in alcohols/phenols gives much higher BPs than ethers/haloalkanes
of comparable mass (True).
Q17.trapHtml: Both statements are direct NCERT physical property facts.

Q18.subtopic: Dow’s Process Followed by Oxidation to p-Benzoquinone
Q18.conceptHtml: Chlorobenzene <sup>−N</sup><sup>−a</sup><sup>−O</sup><sup>−H</sup><sup>−,</sup><sup>−6</sup><sup>−23</sup><sup>−K</sup>−<sup>−,</sup> <sup>3</sup><sup>−0</sup><sup>−0</sup><sup>−a</sup><sup>−tm</sup><sup>−;</sup><sup>−H</sup><sup>−+</sup>→ Phenol ([A]) <sup>−N</sup><sup>−a</sup><sup>−2</sup><sup>−C</sup><sup>−r2</sup><sup>−O</sup><sup>−7</sup><sup>−/</sup><sup>−H</sup><sup>−2</sup><sup>−SO</sup>−→<sup>4</sup> p-Benzoquinone ([B]).
Q18.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify product [A] via Dow's process: Chlorobenzene ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{Cl}$) heated with $\text{NaOH}$ at $623\text{ K}$ and $300\text{ atm}$ forms sodium phenoxide, which on acidification ($\text{H}^+$) yields phenol ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH}$) as $[A]$.
  2. Step 2 — Identify product [B] via chromic acid oxidation: Treating phenol ($[A]$) with sodium dichromate in sulphuric acid ($\text{Na}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7/\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$) oxidizes it to a conjugated diketone, p-benzoquinone (cyclohexa-2,5-diene-1,4-dione) as $[B]$.
  3. Step 3 — Match structures to the options: Inspecting the given diagrams, $[A] =$ phenol and $[B] =$ p-benzoquinone are shown together in option (b).
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Hence, the correct option is (b).
Q18.stepsLatex:
1. Dow’s process converts chlorobenzene into phenol ([A]).
2. Oxidation of phenol with chromic acid (Na2Cr2O7/H2SO4) yields the conjugated diketone p-benzoquinone
([B], option B).
Q18.trapHtml: Phenol does NOT oxidise to a carboxylic acid with Na<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub>/H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>; it forms p-benzoquinone!

Q19.conceptHtml: 1 mol phenol (94 g) reacts with 3 mol Br<sub>2</sub> (3 × 160 = 480 g) to form 2, 4, 6-tribromophenol.
Q19.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Write the balanced chemical equation: Phenol reacts with bromine water to form 2,4,6-tribromophenol: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH} + 3\text{Br}_2 \to \text{C}_6\text{H}_2\text{Br}_3\text{OH} + 3\text{HBr}$. Thus, $1\text{ mol}$ of phenol requires $3\text{ mol}$ of $\text{Br}_2$.
  2. Step 2 — Calculate molar masses: Molar mass of phenol ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_6\text{O}$) $= 6(12) + 6(1) + 16 = 94\text{ g mol}^{-1}$. Molar mass of $\text{Br}_2 = 2 \times 80 = 160\text{ g mol}^{-1}$.
  3. Step 3 — Calculate the required mass of bromine: Moles of phenol $= \frac{2}{94}\text{ mol}$. Moles of $\text{Br}_2$ required $= 3 \times \frac{2}{94} = \frac{6}{94}\text{ mol}$. Therefore, mass of $\text{Br}_2 = \frac{6}{94} \times 160 = \frac{960}{94} \approx 10.213\text{ g} \approx 10.22\text{ g}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The amount of bromine required is $10.22\text{ g}$, matching option (b).
Q19.trapHtml: Remember bromine is Br<sub>2</sub> (160 g mol<sup>−1</sup>), not atomic Br (80), and 3 mol Br<sub>2</sub> are needed per mole of phenol.

Q20.conceptHtml: Diazonium hydrolysis → Phenol; Na<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub>/H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> → p-Benzoquinone; Reimer–Tiemann → Salicylalde- hyde; Kolbe’s → Salicylic acid.
Q20.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Match (A) and (B): (A) Aniline undergoes diazotization with $\text{NaNO}_2 + \text{HCl}$ followed by hydrolysis with warm $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ to give phenol (II). (B) Oxidation of phenol with $\text{Na}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7/\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ produces p-benzoquinone (IV).
  2. Step 2 — Match (C) and (D): (C) Phenol with $\text{CHCl}_3 + \text{aq. NaOH}$ followed by $\text{H}^+$ is the Reimer–Tiemann reaction, giving salicylaldehyde (I). (D) Phenol with $\text{NaOH}$, $\text{CO}_2$, and $\text{H}^+$ is Kolbe's reaction, yielding salicylic acid (III).
  3. Step 3 — Assemble the complete match: The verified pairings are: (A)–(II), (B)–(IV), (C)–(I), and (D)–(III).
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: This exact combination corresponds to option (a).
Q20.stepsLatex:
• (A) Aniline −N−a−N−O−2−+−H−C−l,−H−2−O−,∆→ Phenol =⇒ (II).
• (B) Phenol −N−a−2−C−r−2O−7−/−H−2−SO−→4 p-Benzoquinone =⇒ (IV).
• (C) Phenol −C−H−C−l−3+−−aq−.−N−aO−−H−,H−→+ Salicylaldehyde =⇒ (I).
• (D) Phenol −N−a−O−H−,−C−O−2−,H−→+ Salicylic acid =⇒ (III).
Q20.trapHtml: Distinguish Salicylaldehyde (−CHO, Reimer–Tiemann) from Salicylic acid (−COOH, Kolbe’s).

Q21.subtopic: Reaction of Phenol vs. Alcohols with Dilute NaOH
Q21.conceptHtml: Phenols (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 10) are acidic enough to react readily with aq. NaOH to form sodium phenoxide, whereas aliphatic/benzylic alcohols (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 16 − 18) do not.
Q21.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the condition for reacting with dilute NaOH: A compound reacts readily with dilute aqueous $\text{NaOH}$ only if it is significantly more acidic than water ($\text{p}K_a < 15.7$), so that acid–base equilibrium favors the salt.
  2. Step 2 — Compare acidity of phenol vs. alcohols: Phenol ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH}$, $\text{p}K_a \approx 10$) readily loses $\text{H}^+$ to $\text{NaOH}$ to form sodium phenoxide ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{O}^-\text{Na}^+$) because the phenoxide ion is strongly stabilized by resonance delocalization of its negative charge into the benzene ring.
  3. Step 3 — Eliminate the aliphatic and benzylic alcohols: Benzyl alcohol ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$), ethanol ($\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}$), and tert-butyl alcohol ($(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{COH}$) cannot delocalize the negative charge of their alkoxide ions into a ring; their $\text{p}K_a$ values ($\approx 15\text{--}18$) are too high to react readily with dilute $\text{NaOH}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Thus, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH}$ reacts readily with dilute $\text{NaOH}$, which is option (c).
Q21.stepsLatex:
Among benzyl alcohol, ethanol, phenol (C6H5OH), and tert-butanol, only phenol (C6H5OH)
has resonance-stabilised phenoxide ion and reacts readily with dilute NaOH.
Q21.trapHtml: Benzyl alcohol (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH) is an aliphatic-like alcohol (−OH not on the ring) and does NOT dissolve in dil. NaOH!

Q22.conceptHtml: Conc. H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>/∆ dehydrates 1-methylcyclohexanol to the endocyclic Zaitsev alkene (1-methylcyclohexene); CH<sub>3</sub>COCl/Pyridine esterifies the −OH group to the acetate.
Q22.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the starting alcohol: The starting compound is 1-methylcyclohexanol, a tertiary cyclic alcohol.
  2. Step 2 — Determine major product A (dehydration): Heating with $\text{Conc. H}_2\text{SO}_4, \Delta$ causes acid-catalyzed dehydration ($\text{E}1$). By Zaitsev's rule, the more substituted, more stable endocyclic alkene is formed as the major product: 1-methylcyclohexene (trisubstituted, $7\ \alpha\text{-H}$), rather than the less substituted exocyclic alkene.
  3. Step 3 — Determine major product B (acetylation): Treating the alcohol with acetyl chloride ($\text{CH}_3\text{COCl}$) in the presence of pyridine (a base that scavenges $\text{HCl}$) esterifies the $-\text{OH}$ group into an acetate group ($-\text{OCOCH}_3$), yielding 1-methylcyclohexyl acetate.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Both $A$ (1-methylcyclohexene) and $B$ (1-methylcyclohexyl acetate) are correctly shown in option (b).
Q22.stepsLatex:
1. Right arrow (conc. H2SO4/∆): Dehydration gives the more substituted endocyclic alkene 1-methylcyclohexene
as major product ‘A’ (Zaitsev).
2. Left arrow (CH3COCl/Pyridine): Nucleophilic acyl substitution at −OH gives the ester −OCOCH3 as ‘B’ (not
Friedel–Crafts, since the ring is saturated!).
Q22.trapHtml: Endocyclic 1-methylcyclohexene (trisubstituted) is more stable than exocyclic methylenecyclohexane (disubstituted).

Q23.conceptHtml: In nitration of anisole, 4-nitroanisole (p-isomer) is major; subsequent bromination (Br<sub>2</sub>/Fe) is directed by the strongly activating −OCH<sub>3</sub> group (ortho/para-directing) to the position ortho to −OCH<sub>3</sub>!
Q23.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Nitration of anisole to A: Anisole ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OCH}_3$) undergoes electrophilic nitration with $\text{HNO}_3/\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$. The $-\text{OCH}_3$ group is strongly activating and ortho/para-directing; because the para position has less steric hindrance, 4-nitroanisole (p-nitroanisole) is the major product $A$.
  2. Step 2 — Directing effects in 4-nitroanisole: In 4-nitroanisole, the $-\text{OCH}_3$ group directs incoming electrophiles to its ortho positions (C2 and C6), while the $-\text{NO}_2$ group directs to its meta positions (also C2 and C6). Both groups reinforce substitution at C2 and C6.
  3. Step 3 — Predict product B with excess Br2 / Fe: With excess $\text{Br}_2/\text{Fe}$, bromination takes place at both activated positions (C2 and C6) to yield 2,6-dibromo-4-nitroanisole as the major product $B$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The structures of $A$ (4-nitroanisole) and $B$ (2,6-dibromo-4-nitroanisole) match option (a).
Q23.stepsLatex:
1. Anisole + HNO3/H2SO4 → 4-nitroanisole (‘A’, major).
2. In 4-nitroanisole, −OCH3 (+M, o/p-directing) dominates over −NO2 (−M, m-directing). With excess Br2/Fe,
bromination occurs at both positions ortho to −OCH3 (giving 2, 6-dibromo-4-nitroanisole, option A).
Q23.trapHtml: Both −OCH<sub>3</sub> (o/p-directing) and −NO<sub>2</sub> (m-directing) reinforce substitution at the position ortho to −OCH<sub>3</sub>!

Q24.conceptHtml: In the Reimer–Tiemann reaction (CHCl<sub>3</sub> + aq. NaOH), the isolated/key substituted benzal chloride inter- mediate before hydrolysis is sodium 2-(dichloromethyl)phenoxide.
Q24.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Generate the active nucleophile and electrophile: In the Reimer–Tiemann reaction, aqueous $\text{NaOH}$ converts phenol into the strongly activated sodium phenoxide ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{O}^-\text{Na}^+$) and reacts with $\text{CHCl}_3$ to generate the neutral electrophile dichlorocarbene ($:\text{CCl}_2$).
  2. Step 2 — Form the substituted benzal chloride intermediate: Electrophilic attack of $:\text{CCl}_2$ at the ortho position of sodium phenoxide followed by rearomatization produces the ortho-dichloromethyl sodium phenoxide intermediate: $o\text{-}(\text{CHCl}_2)\text{C}_6\text{H}_4\text{O}^-\text{Na}^+$.
  3. Step 3 — Note how it converts to salicylaldehyde: Subsequent alkaline hydrolysis of the $-\text{CHCl}_2$ group with $\text{NaOH}$ forms sodium salicylaldehyde, which upon acidification yields salicylaldehyde.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: The intermediate $o\text{-}(\text{CHCl}_2)\text{C}_6\text{H}_4\text{O}^-\text{Na}^+$ is shown in option (b).
Q24.stepsLatex:
Phenol reacts with NaOH and : CCl2 (from CHCl3) to form the o-dichloromethyl phenoxide
intermediate (Ar(O−Na+)(CHCl2), option B), which upon further NaOH hydrolysis and acidification gives salicy-
laldehyde.
Q24.trapHtml: In basic medium, the phenolic group exists as −O−Na+, NOT −OH (distinguishes B from A)!

Q25.conceptHtml: Picric acid is 2, 4, 6-trinitrophenol (NOT trinitrotoluene!), and is prepared in high yield by treating phenol- 2, 4-disulphonic acid with conc. HNO<sub>3</sub>.
Q25.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement I (identity of picric acid): Picric acid is 2,4,6-trinitrophenol, not 2,4,6-trinitrotoluene (which is TNT). Therefore, Statement I is incorrect.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement II (preparation of picric acid): Direct nitration of phenol with $\text{conc. HNO}_3$ gives poor yields due to oxidative degradation. Industrially and in the lab, phenol is first treated with $\text{conc. H}_2\text{SO}_4$ to form phenol-2,4-disulphonic acid, which is then treated with $\text{conc. HNO}_3$ to replace the sulphonic acid groups and introduce nitro groups, giving picric acid in good yield.
  3. Step 3 — Judge both statements: Statement I is incorrect, whereas Statement II is correct.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: This matches option (a).
Q25.stepsLatex:
1. Statement I claims picric acid is 2, 4, 6-trinitrotoluene (TNT) =⇒ Incorrect (it is 2, 4, 6-trinitrophenol).
2. Statement II: Sulphonation of phenol followed by conc. HNO3 avoids oxidative ring destruction and gives picric
acid =⇒ Correct (direct NCERT).
Q25.trapHtml: TNT = 2, 4, 6-trinitrotoluene; Picric acid = 2, 4, 6-trinitrophenol.

Q26.conceptHtml: Jones reagent (CrO<sub>3</sub>/H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>) and KMnO<sub>4</sub> oxidise 1° alcohols to carboxylic acids; soda-lime (NaOH + CaO, ∆) decarboxylates RCOOH to R − H (1 C less).
Q26.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Oxidation of ethanol (Steps i and ii): Ethanol ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$) is a primary alcohol. Treatment with strong oxidizing agents like Jones reagent ($\text{CrO}_3/\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$) and $\text{KMnO}_4$ oxidizes it completely to ethanoic acid (acetic acid), $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$.
  2. Step 2 — Soda-lime decarboxylation (Step iii): Heating acetic acid with soda-lime ($\text{NaOH}, \text{CaO}, \Delta$) first neutralizes it to sodium acetate ($\text{CH}_3\text{COONa}$) and then removes $\text{CO}_2$ (as $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$): $\text{CH}_3\text{COONa} + \text{NaOH} \xrightarrow{\text{CaO}, \Delta} \text{CH}_4 + \text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$.
  3. Step 3 — Identify the major product P: The hydrocarbon formed has one carbon fewer than acetic acid, which is methane ($\text{CH}_4$).
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Methane corresponds to option (c).
Q26.stepsLatex: CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH <sup>−J</sup><sup>−o</sup><sup>−ne</sup><sup>−s</sup><sup>−/</sup><sup>−K</sup><sup>−M</sup>−<sup>−n</sup><sup>−O</sup>→4 CH<sub>3</sub>COOH <sup>−N</sup><sup>−a</sup><sup>−O</sup><sup>−H</sup><sup>−,</sup><sup>−C</sup><sup>−a</sup><sup>−O</sup><sup>−,</sup><sup>−∆</sup>→ CH<sub>4</sub> (Methane)
Q26.trapHtml: Soda-lime decarboxylation removes the −COOH carbon as Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>, so ethanoic acid gives methane (1 C), not ethane.

Q27.subtopic: Nucleophilic Aromatic Substitution vs. Phenol + HCl
Q27.conceptHtml: Phenol does NOT react with HCl to form chlorobenzene because the C<sub>sp2</sub> − O bond has partial double-bond character and OH− is a poor leaving group.
Q27.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Check feasibility of options (a), (b), and (d): (a) Chlorination of anisole with $\text{Cl}_2/\text{AlCl}_3$ readily gives p-chloroanisole via electrophilic aromatic substitution. (b) Chlorobenzene converts to phenol with $\text{NaOH}$ at high temperature followed by $\text{H}^+$ (Dow's process). (d) Anisole reacts with $\text{HBr}$ to cleave the $\text{O}-\text{CH}_3$ bond and yield phenol.
  2. Step 2 — Analyze option (c): Option (c) shows phenol reacting directly with $\text{HCl}$ to give chlorobenzene. In phenol, the lone pair on oxygen is delocalized into the benzene ring, giving the $\text{C}-\text{O}$ bond partial double-bond character.
  3. Step 3 — Explain why cleavage fails: Because the $\text{C}_{\text{aryl}}-\text{O}$ bond is unusually strong and the $sp^2$ ring carbon resists nucleophilic substitution, phenol cannot be converted to chlorobenzene by $\text{HCl}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Therefore, the reaction in option (c) is NOT possible.
Q27.stepsLatex:
• (A) Anisole + Cl2/AlCl3 → p-chloroanisole (possible).
• (B) Chlorobenzene + NaOH, high T, H+ → Phenol (Dow’s process, possible).
• (C) Phenol + HCl ̸→ Chlorobenzene (NOT possible).
• (D) Anisole + HBr → Phenol + MeBr (possible).
Q27.trapHtml: Unlike aliphatic alcohols, phenol cannot undergo S<sub>N</sub>1/S<sub>N</sub>2 substitution with HCl or HBr.

Q28.subtopic: Bromination of Phenol in Low-Polarity Solvents
Q28.conceptHtml: Because −OH is a very strong activating group (+M), bromination of phenol in CHCl<sub>3</sub> or CS<sub>2</sub> proceeds smoothly without any Lewis acid catalyst (unlike benzene).
Q28.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement I (bromination of phenol in low-polarity solvents): The $-\text{OH}$ group is a very strong ring-activating group. Therefore, bromination of phenol in low-polarity solvents like $\text{CHCl}_3$ or $\text{CS}_2$ at $273\text{ K}$ proceeds easily without any Lewis acid catalyst to yield monobromophenols (chiefly p-bromophenol). Hence, Statement I is false.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement II (role of a Lewis acid catalyst): In general aromatic bromination (such as with benzene), a Lewis acid catalyst (e.g., $\text{FeBr}_3$) coordinates to $\text{Br}_2$ and polarizes the $\text{Br}-\text{Br}$ bond to generate the electrophile $\text{Br}^+$ (or a strongly polarized $\text{Br}^{\delta+}-\text{Br}^{\delta-}\cdots\text{FeBr}_3$ complex). Hence, Statement II is true.
  3. Step 3 — Combine the results: Statement I is false while Statement II is true.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: This corresponds to option (c).
Q28.stepsLatex:
1. Statement I: Claims bromination of phenol in CHCl3/CS2 requires a Lewis acid catalyst =⇒ False (even at
273 K without FeBr3, phenol gives p-bromophenol).
2. Statement II: A Lewis acid catalyst polarises Br2 to generate Br+-like electrophile =⇒ True (general EAS
fact).
Q28.trapHtml: NCERT explicitly contrasts benzene (needs FeBr<sub>3</sub>) with phenol (needs NO Lewis acid even in CS<sub>2</sub>/CHCl<sub>3</sub>).

Q29.subtopic: Boiling Point Order Across Functional Groups
Q29.conceptHtml: For comparable molar masses: Alkane < Ether < Ketone/Aldehyde < Alcohol (due to increasing polarity and intermolecular H-bonding).
Q29.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the functional groups of all four compounds: All four compounds have 5 carbons and comparable molar masses ($72\text{--}88\text{ g mol}^{-1}$): (A) ethoxypropane (ether), (B) pentane (alkane), (C) pentan-3-one (ketone), and (D) pentan-2-ol (alcohol).
  2. Step 2 — Compare intermolecular forces: (B) Pentane is non-polar with only weak London dispersion forces (lowest boiling point). (A) Ethoxypropane has weak dipole–dipole forces. (C) Pentan-3-one has a strongly polar $\text{C}=\text{O}$ group, giving stronger dipole–dipole attractions than an ether. (D) Pentan-2-ol forms strong intermolecular hydrogen bonds (highest boiling point).
  3. Step 3 — Arrange in increasing order of boiling point: Ranking from weakest to strongest intermolecular forces gives: $(B) < (A) < (C) < (D)$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: This order matches option (b).
Q29.stepsLatex:
Comparing the 5-carbon / similar-mass compounds: (B) Pentane (non-polar, van der Waals)
< (A) Ethoxypropane (weak dipole) < (C) Pentan-3-one (strong C = O dipole) < (D) Pentan-2-ol (intermolecular
H-bonding).
Q29.trapHtml: Always check for H-bonding first (alcohol highest), then C = O dipole (ketone), then ether, then alkane.

Q30.conceptHtml: Benzenediols: 1, 2-diol = Catechol; 1, 3-diol = Resorcinol; 1, 4-diol = Quinol (Hydroquinone).
Q30.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the structure of benzene-1,2-diol: Benzene-1,2-diol is an aromatic diol with two $-\text{OH}$ groups at adjacent (ortho, 1,2) positions on the benzene ring.
  2. Step 2 — Recall common names of dihydroxybenzenes: The three isomeric benzenediols have standard common names: 1,2-diol is catechol, 1,3-diol is resorcinol, and 1,4-diol is quinol (hydroquinone). Meanwhile, o-cresol is 2-methylphenol.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the final answer: Therefore, the common name of benzene-1,2-diol is catechol, which is option (a).
Q30.stepsLatex:
Benzene-1, 2-diol has two −OH groups at adjacent (1, 2) positions, whose NCERT common
name is catechol.
Q30.trapHtml: Memorize the 1, 2/1, 3/1, 4 triplet: Catechol / Resorcinol / Quinol.

Q31.subtopic: Match List: Key Reactions of Phenol
Q31.conceptHtml: Direct NCERT phenol reactions: Zn/∆ → Benzene; CHCl<sub>3</sub>/NaOH → Salicylaldehyde; CO<sub>2</sub>/NaOH → Salicylic acid; Conc. HNO<sub>3</sub> → Picric acid.
Q31.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Match (A) and (B): (A) Phenol heated with $\text{Zn}$ dust is reduced to benzene (III). (B) Phenol treated with $\text{CHCl}_3, \text{NaOH}, \text{HCl}$ undergoes the Reimer–Tiemann reaction to form salicylaldehyde (I).
  2. Step 2 — Match (C) and (D): (C) Phenol treated with $\text{CO}_2, \text{NaOH}, \text{HCl}$ undergoes Kolbe's reaction to form salicylic acid (II). (D) Phenol treated with $\text{conc. HNO}_3$ undergoes nitration to yield picric acid (IV) (2,4,6-trinitrophenol).
  3. Step 3 — Combine all four matches: The correct matching is: (A)–(III), (B)–(I), (C)–(II), (D)–(IV).
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: This corresponds to option (b).
Q31.stepsLatex:
(A)-(III) Benzene; (B)-(I) Salicylaldehyde; (C)-(II) Salicylic acid; (D)-(IV) Picric acid =⇒
Option (b).
Q31.trapHtml: A single glance at (A)-(III) narrows down to (b) or (d), and (B)-(I) confirms (b).

Q32.conceptHtml: Alcohols act as nucleophiles (via O lone pair, cleaving O − H) and as electrophiles (when protonated R − O<sup>+</sup>H<sub>2</sub>, cleaving C − O). Reaction with active metals shows their acidic nature (O − H cleavage), not their dual behaviour.
Q32.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Assertion A: Alcohols are versatile reagents: they act as nucleophiles when the $\text{O}-\text{H}$ bond breaks (via the oxygen lone pair) and as electrophiles when protonated ($\text{R}-\text{OH}_2^+$) so the $\text{C}-\text{O}$ bond cleaves upon nucleophilic attack. Thus, Assertion A is true.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Reason R: Alcohols react with active metals such as $\text{Na}, \text{K},$ and $\text{Al}$ to form metal alkoxides and liberate hydrogen gas ($2\text{R}-\text{OH} + 2\text{Na} \to 2\text{R}-\text{ONa} + \text{H}_2$). Thus, Reason R is also true.
  3. Step 3 — Check whether R explains A: Reason R only demonstrates the acidic character of alcohols ($\text{O}-\text{H}$ cleavage with metals) and does not explain their dual nucleophilic and electrophilic behaviour.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A, which is option (b).
Q32.stepsLatex:
1. Assertion A is true (alcohols react both as nucleophiles and electrophiles).
2. Reason R is true (alcohols react with Na, K, Al to give alkoxides + H2).
3. However, R only demonstrates the acidic character of alcohols, NOT why they act as both nucleophiles and
electrophiles.
Q32.trapHtml: In Assertion–Reason, both statements being true from the same NCERT paragraph does NOT mean R explains A!

Q33.conceptHtml: Lower pK<sub>a</sub> means stronger acid: Phenol (pK<sub>a</sub> = 10.0) is ∼ 106 times more acidic than ethanol (pK<sub>a</sub> = 15.9).
Q33.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Assertion A: From standard NCERT data, the $\text{p}K_a$ of phenol is $10.0$ and the $\text{p}K_a$ of ethanol is $15.9$. Therefore, Assertion A is true.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Reason R using the pKa–acidity relationship: By definition, $\text{p}K_a = -\log K_a$, so a lower $\text{p}K_a$ means a larger $K_a$ and a stronger acid. Since $10.0 < 15.9$, phenol is a much stronger acid than ethanol (because the phenoxide ion is resonance-stabilized, whereas the ethoxide ion is destabilized by the $+I$ effect of the ethyl group).
  3. Step 3 — Judge Reason R: Saying that ethanol is a stronger acid than phenol is false.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Assertion A is true and Reason R is false, matching option (d).
Q33.stepsLatex:
1. Assertion A: pKa(phenol) = 10.0, pKa(ethanol) = 15.9 =⇒ True.
2. Reason R: Claims ethanol is a stronger acid than phenol =⇒ False (phenol is stronger due to resonance
stabilisation of phenoxide ion).
Q33.trapHtml: Never confuse pK<sub>a</sub> with K<sub>a</sub>: smaller pK<sub>a</sub> = stronger acid!

Q34.conceptHtml: Reimer–Tiemann reaction uses chloroform (HCCl<sub>3</sub>) and NaOH to convert phenol into salicylaldehyde.
Q34.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the name reaction: Converting phenol into salicylaldehyde (2-hydroxybenzaldehyde) is the classic Reimer–Tiemann reaction.
  2. Step 2 — Recall the required reagents: The Reimer–Tiemann reaction uses chloroform ($\text{HCCl}_3$) and aqueous $\text{NaOH}$ (followed by acidification) to introduce a $-\text{CHO}$ group at the ortho position of phenol via a dichlorocarbene ($:\text{CCl}_2$) intermediate.
  3. Step 3 — Eliminate the other options: $\text{CO}_2, \text{NaOH}$ (Kolbe's reaction) and $\text{CCl}_4, \text{NaOH}$ (Reimer–Tiemann carboxylation) both yield salicylic acid instead of salicylaldehyde.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the final answer: Hence, the required reagent pair is $\text{HCCl}_3, \text{NaOH}$, which is option (a).
Q34.stepsLatex:
Among the options: (A) HCCl3, NaOH gives salicylaldehyde; (B) CO2, NaOH gives salicylic
acid (Kolbe’s); (C) HCOCl, NaOH is not Reimer–Tiemann; (D) CCl4, NaOH gives salicylic acid.
Q34.trapHtml: Watch out for CCl<sub>4</sub>, NaOH (gives salicylic acid) vs. CHCl<sub>3</sub>, NaOH (gives salicylaldehyde).

Q35.conceptHtml: Reimer–Tiemann reaction of phenol with CHCl<sub>3</sub>/NaOH followed by acid hydrolysis introduces a −CHO group at the ortho position.
Q35.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the named reaction: Treating phenol ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH}$) with chloroform ($\text{CHCl}_3$) in aqueous sodium hydroxide ($\text{NaOH}$) followed by acidification is the classic Reimer–Tiemann reaction, which introduces an aldehyde ($-\text{CHO}$) group onto the aromatic ring.
  2. Step 2 — Generate the electrophile: In basic medium, $\text{NaOH}$ deprotonates $\text{CHCl}_3$ to form $\text{CCl}_3^-$, which loses $\text{Cl}^-$ to generate neutral dichlorocarbene ($:\text{CCl}_2$), a strong electrophile. Meanwhile, phenol is converted into the strongly activated phenoxide ion ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{O}^-$).
  3. Step 3 — Electrophilic attack and hydrolysis: The phenoxide ion attacks $:\text{CCl}_2$ predominantly at the ortho position to give a substituted benzal chloride intermediate ($o\text{-O}^-\text{C}_6\text{H}_4\text{CHCl}_2$). Base hydrolysis replaces the two $-\text{Cl}$ atoms with $-\text{OH}$ groups, which immediately lose $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ to form the $-\text{CHO}$ group.
  4. Step 4 — Acidification and final answer: Acid hydrolysis ($\text{H}^+/\text{H}_2\text{O}$) protonates the phenoxide oxygen to yield salicylaldehyde, whose IUPAC name is 2-hydroxybenzaldehyde. Hence, the correct option is (c).
Q35.stepsLatex: Phenol + CHCl<sub>3</sub> + NaOH → H+ yields salicylaldehyde, whose IUPAC name is 2-hydroxybenzaldehyde.
Q35.trapHtml: Don’t confuse 2-hydroxybenzaldehyde (Reimer–Tiemann) with salicylic acid (Kolbe’s).

Q36.subtopic: Match List: pKa Values of Ethanol & Nitrophenols
Q36.conceptHtml: Stronger acid =⇒ lower pK<sub>a</sub>. Order of acidity: p-nitrophenol (−M, −I) > m-nitrophenol (−I only) > phenol > ethanol.
Q36.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the relation between acidity and $\text{p}K_a$: A stronger acid has a more stable conjugate base and a lower $\text{p}K_a$ value; conversely, a weaker acid has a higher $\text{p}K_a$ value.
  2. Step 2 — Compare aliphatic alcohol vs. phenol: Ethanol ($\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}$) forms an ethoxide ion with no resonance stabilization and destabilizing $+I$ effect, so it is the weakest acid with the highest $\text{p}K_a = 15.9$ (A–II). Phenol forms a resonance-stabilized phenoxide ion, making it much more acidic with $\text{p}K_a = 10.0$ (B–I).
  3. Step 3 — Compare m-nitrophenol vs. p-nitrophenol: At the meta position, $-\text{NO}_2$ withdraws electrons only by the inductive ($-I$) effect, lowering $\text{p}K_a$ to $8.3$ (C–IV). At the para position, $-\text{NO}_2$ exerts both strong resonance ($-M$) and inductive ($-I$) effects, stabilizing the phenoxide ion most strongly and giving the lowest $\text{p}K_a = 7.1$ (D–III).
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the matching option: Combining the matches gives A–II, B–I, C–IV, D–III, which corresponds to option (c).
Q36.stepsLatex:
Matching from NCERT Table 11.3: (A) Ethanol → 15.9 (II); (B) Phenol → 10.0 (I); (C)
m-Nitrophenol → 8.3 (IV); (D) p-Nitrophenol → 7.1 (III).
Q36.trapHtml: In nitrophenols, p-nitrophenol (pK<sub>a</sub> = 7.1) is more acidic than m-nitrophenol (pK<sub>a</sub> = 8.3) due to the −M effect.

Q37.subtopic: Ether Cleavage + Alkene Addition with Excess Conc. HBr
Q37.conceptHtml: Excess conc. HBr/∆ cleaves the aryl–alkyl ether to phenol (since C<sub>sp2</sub> − O does not break) and adds HBr across the styrene double bond via the benzylic carbocation.
Q37.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the two reactive sites: The reactant, 3-ethoxystyrene, contains an aryl alkyl ether group ($-\text{OCH}_2\text{CH}_3$) and a vinyl double bond ($-\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2$) at the meta position, both of which react with excess concentrated $\text{HBr}$ on heating.
  2. Step 2 — Ether cleavage with conc. $\text{HBr}$: Protonation of the ether oxygen gives $\text{Ar}-\text{O}^+\text{H}-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$. Because the $\text{C}_{\text{aryl}}-\text{O}$ bond has partial double-bond character due to resonance, $\text{Br}^-$ attacks the ethyl carbon via $\text{S}_\text{N}2$, cleaving the $\text{O}-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ bond to give a phenolic $-\text{OH}$ group (plus $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$).
  3. Step 3 — Markovnikov addition to the alkene: Protonation of $-\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2$ by $\text{H}^+$ occurs at the terminal $=\text{CH}_2$ carbon to generate the resonance-stabilized secondary benzylic carbocation ($\text{Ar}-\text{CH}^+-\text{CH}_3$). Subsequent attack by $\text{Br}^-$ forms $-\text{CH(Br)CH}_3$.
  4. Step 4 — Identify the major product: Combining both transformations gives 3-(1-bromoethyl)phenol, which matches structure (C). Hence, the correct option is (c).
Q37.stepsLatex:
1. Ether cleavage: −OCH2CH3 with HBr/∆ gives −OH (phenol) + CH3CH2Br.
2. Alkene addition: −CH = CH2+HBr protonates at the terminal CH2 to form the resonance-stabilised 2◦ benzylic
+
carbocation −CH − CH3, giving −CH(Br) − CH3 (option C).
Q37.trapHtml: Phenol −OH is NEVER replaced by −Br with HBr; and −CH = CH<sub>2</sub> adds Markovnikov via the benzylic carbocation.

Q38.subtopic: SN1 Cleavage of tert-Butyl Phenyl Ether with HI
Q38.conceptHtml: In Ph − O − C(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub> + HI, protonation is followed by S<sub>N</sub>1 cleavage to form the stable 3° carbocation (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>C+ and phenol (PhOH).
Q38.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Protonate the ether oxygen: Cyclohexyl tert-butyl ether ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_{11}-\text{O}-\text{C(CH}_3)_3$) is first protonated by $\text{HI}$ to form the oxonium ion $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{11}-\text{O}^+\text{H}-\text{C(CH}_3)_3$.
  2. Step 2 — Determine the cleavage mechanism ($\text{S}_\text{N}1$ vs. $\text{S}_\text{N}2$): When an unsymmetrical ether contains a tertiary ($3^\circ$) alkyl group such as tert-butyl, cleavage proceeds via an $\text{S}_\text{N}1$ pathway because dissociation yields a highly stable $3^\circ$ carbocation.
  3. Step 3 — Form the alcohol and alkyl iodide: Breaking the $\text{O}-\text{C(CH}_3)_3$ bond releases cyclohexanol ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_{11}\text{OH}$) and the tert-butyl carbocation ($(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}^+$). The iodide ion ($\text{I}^-$) then captures $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}^+$ to form tert-butyl iodide ($(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}-\text{I}$).
  4. Step 4 — Match with the options: The resulting mixture of cyclohexanol and $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}-\text{I}$ is shown in option (d).
Q38.stepsLatex:
+
1. Ph − O(H) − C(CH3)3 cleaves via SN1 to release neutral PhOH (phenol) and (CH3)3C+.
2. I− traps (CH3)3C+ to give tert-butyl iodide, (CH3)3C − I (option D).
Q38.trapHtml: Remember: Ph − O NEVER cleaves; and for 3°-alkyl ethers, I− always goes to the 3° carbon (S<sub>N</sub>1)!

Q39.subtopic: Match List: Reactions & Reagents of Phenol
Q39.conceptHtml: Kolbe’s (NaOH, CO<sub>2</sub>, H+) → Salicylic acid; Reimer–Tiemann (NaOH, CHCl<sub>3</sub>, H+) → Salicylaldehyde; Na<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub>/H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> → p-Benzoquinone; Williamson (NaOH, CH<sub>3</sub>Cl) → Anisole.
Q39.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Match (A) and (B) using standard named reactions: Conversion of phenol to salicylic acid (2-hydroxybenzoic acid) is Kolbe’s reaction, which uses (i) $\text{NaOH}$, (ii) $\text{CO}_2$, (iii) $\text{HCl}$ (A–IV). Conversion of phenol to salicylaldehyde (2-hydroxybenzaldehyde) is the Reimer–Tiemann reaction, which uses (i) $\text{NaOH}, \text{CHCl}_3$, (ii) $\text{NaOH}$, (iii) $\text{HCl}$ (B–III).
  2. Step 2 — Match (C) oxidation of phenol: Oxidation of phenol with chromic acid ($\text{Na}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7, \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$) produces the conjugated diketone p-benzoquinone (C–I).
  3. Step 3 — Match (D) ether formation: Converting phenol to anisole ($\text{Ph}-\text{OCH}_3$) is a Williamson ether synthesis using (i) $\text{NaOH}$ to form sodium phenoxide followed by (ii) $\text{CH}_3\text{Cl}$ (D–II).
  4. Step 4 — Verify the complete match: The correct sequence is (A)–(IV), (B)–(III), (C)–(I), (D)–(II), which corresponds to option (c).
Q39.stepsLatex:
(A) Phenol → Salicylic acid =⇒ (IV); (B) Phenol → Salicylaldehyde =⇒ (III); (C) Phenol
→ p-Benzoquinone =⇒ (I); (D) Phenol → Anisole =⇒ (II).
Q39.trapHtml: Williamson synthesis on phenol works with NaOH + CH<sub>3</sub>Cl because phenoxide (PhO−) is easily formed in aq. NaOH.

Q40.conceptHtml: Hydroboration–oxidation gives anti-Markovnikov 1° alcohol; HBr converts it to 1° bromide; Grignard + HCHO extends the carbon chain by one −CH<sub>2</sub>OH unit.
Q40.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Hydroboration–oxidation (steps i & ii): Treating styrene ($\text{Ph}-\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2$) with $\text{BH}_3$ followed by $\text{H}_2\text{O}_2/\text{OH}^-$ adds $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ in an anti-Markovnikov fashion to yield the primary alcohol 2-phenylethanol, $\text{Ph}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{OH}$.
  2. Step 2 — Conversion to alkyl bromide (step iii): Reaction of the primary alcohol $\text{Ph}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{OH}$ with $\text{HBr}$ substitutes $-\text{OH}$ with $-\text{Br}$ (via $\text{S}_\text{N}2$, without rearrangement) to form $\text{Ph}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{Br}$.
  3. Step 3 — Grignard formation and homologation (step iv): Treating $\text{Ph}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{Br}$ with $\text{Mg}$ in dry ether generates the Grignard reagent $\text{Ph}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{MgBr}$. Nucleophilic addition to formaldehyde ($\text{HCHO}$) followed by acidic hydrolysis ($\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$) extends the carbon chain by one $-\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ unit.
  4. Step 4 — Identify final product A: The resulting primary alcohol is $\text{Ph}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{OH}$ (3-phenylpropan-1-ol), which corresponds to option (c).
Q40.stepsLatex:
1. Ph − CH = CH2 −(−i)−B−H−3−(−ii−)−H−2−O−2/−O−H−→− Ph − CH2 − CH2 − OH.
2. −(−iii−)−H−B→r Ph − CH2 − CH2 − Br.
3. −(−iv−)−M−g−,−e−th−e−r;−t−h−en−−H−C−H−O−/−H−3O−→+ Ph − CH2 − CH2 − CH2 − OH (option C).
Q40.trapHtml: Track the carbon count carefully: styrene (2-C side chain) + HCHO (1-C) gives a 3-carbon side chain!

Q41.subtopic: Acidity of Nitrophenols & Lucas Test of Ethanol
Q41.conceptHtml: p-Nitrophenol is more acidic than o-nitrophenol (intramolecular H-bonding in o-isomer hinders H+ release) and m-nitrophenol (−I only). Ethanol (1°) gives NO turbidity at RT with Lucas reagent.
Q41.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Evaluate Statement (I): In p-nitrophenol ($\text{p}K_a \approx 7.15$), the $-\text{NO}_2$ group strongly stabilizes the phenoxide ion through both $-M$ and $-I$ effects. In o-nitrophenol ($\text{p}K_a \approx 7.23$), intramolecular hydrogen bonding slightly hinders the release of $\text{H}^+$, while in m-nitrophenol ($\text{p}K_a \approx 8.35$), only the $-I$ effect operates. Hence, p-nitrophenol is more acidic than both, making Statement I true.
  2. Step 2 — Evaluate Statement (II): Lucas reagent (conc. $\text{HCl}$ + anhydrous $\text{ZnCl}_2$) distinguishes alcohols by their rate of carbocation formation: $3^\circ$ alcohols give immediate turbidity, $2^\circ$ alcohols take $5$–$10$ minutes, and $1^\circ$ alcohols like ethanol ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$) do not give turbidity at room temperature.
  3. Step 3 — Conclude on Statement (II) and match option: Since ethanol does not give immediate turbidity with Lucas reagent, Statement II is false. Therefore, Statement I is true and Statement II is false, matching option (a).
Q41.stepsLatex:
1. Statement (I): p-nitrophenol > o-nitrophenol > m-nitrophenol =⇒ True.
2. Statement (II): Ethanol is a 1◦ alcohol and does not give immediate turbidity with Lucas reagent at room
temperature =⇒ False.
Q41.trapHtml: Immediate turbidity in Lucas test is only for 3° (and allylic/benzylic) alcohols, never 1° ethanol!

Q42.subtopic: Ascending Order of Acidity of Alcohols & Phenols
Q42.conceptHtml: Aliphatic alcohols (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 16) are much weaker acids than phenols (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 7−10); within phenols, −M/−I groups (−NO<sub>2</sub>) increase acidity while +M groups (−OCH<sub>3</sub>) decrease it.
Q42.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Separate aliphatic alcohol from phenols: Butan-1-ol (A, $\text{Bu}-\text{OH}$) has no resonance stabilization of its conjugate base ($\text{BuO}^-$), so it is far less acidic ($\text{p}K_a \approx 16$) than any phenol. Thus, (A) is the least acidic.
  2. Step 2 — Compare electron-donating vs. unsubstituted phenol: In p-methoxyphenol (C), the $-\text{OMe}$ group exerts a strong electron-donating resonance ($+M$) effect that destabilizes the phenoxide ion, making (C) slightly less acidic ($\text{p}K_a \approx 10.2$) than unsubstituted phenol (D, $\text{p}K_a \approx 10.0$). Thus, $(\text{C}) < (\text{D})$.
  3. Step 3 — Compare electron-withdrawing nitro-substituted phenols: In p-nitrophenol (B), one $-\text{NO}_2$ group strongly stabilizes the phenoxide ion via $-M$ and $-I$ effects ($\text{p}K_a \approx 7.1$). In 2,4-dinitrophenol (E), two $-\text{NO}_2$ groups at ortho and para positions provide even greater stabilization ($\text{p}K_a \approx 4.0$), making (E) the most acidic.
  4. Step 4 — Assemble the ascending order: Arranging from weakest to strongest acid gives $(\text{A}) < (\text{C}) < (\text{D}) < (\text{B}) < (\text{E})$, which corresponds to option (d).
Q42.stepsLatex:
• (A) Bu − OH (aliphatic alcohol, least acidic).
• (C) p-Methoxyphenol (+M of −OMe destabilises phenoxide).
• (D) Phenol (reference).
• (B) p-Nitrophenol (one −NO2).
• (E) 2, 4-Dinitrophenol (two −NO2, most acidic).
Ascending order: (A) < (C) < (D) < (B) < (E).
Q42.trapHtml: Even p-methoxyphenol (C) is far more acidic than an aliphatic alcohol like Bu − OH (A) due to aromatic phenoxide resonance!

Q43.conceptHtml: Sulfur (−SH) is a softer, stronger nucleophile than oxygen (−OH), so it preferentially attacks the elec- trophilic carbon in nucleophilic substitution.
Q43.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the electrophile and reaction type: Acrylonitrile ($\text{CH}_2=\text{CH}-\text{CN}$) is an $\alpha,\beta$-unsaturated nitrile with an electron-deficient $\beta$-carbon due to conjugation with $-\text{CN}$. It readily undergoes nucleophilic conjugate addition (Michael / 1,4-addition) at the terminal $\beta$-carbon ($=\text{CH}_2$).
  2. Step 2 — Compare nucleophilicity of $-\text{SH}$ vs. $-\text{OH}$: The reagent 2-mercaptoethanol ($\text{HO}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{SH}$) has two nucleophilic sites. Sulfur is larger, less electronegative, and more polarizable than oxygen, making the thiol ($-\text{SH}$) group a much stronger and softer nucleophile than $-\text{OH}$.
  3. Step 3 — Perform conjugate addition: The $-\text{SH}$ group selectively attacks the $\beta$-carbon of $\text{CH}_2=\text{CH}-\text{CN}$, followed by proton transfer to the $\alpha$-carbon, leaving the $-\text{OH}$ and $-\text{CN}$ groups intact: $\text{HO}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{S}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{CN}$.
  4. Step 4 — Match with the options: The major product $\text{HOCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{SCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CN}$ matches structure (B). Hence, the correct option is (b).
Q43.stepsLatex:
In the reaction with HO − (CH2)2 − SH (or hydroxythiol), the −SH group is a much stronger
nucleophile than −OH. Thus, −SH preferentially forms the thioether (−S−) linkage while leaving the −OH group
free (option B).
Q43.trapHtml: Soft, larger sulfur (−SH) is a stronger nucleophile than oxygen (−OH).

Q44.conceptHtml: In p-halophenols, both −I and +M operate: F has stronger +M (2p − 2p overlap with benzene) than Cl (3p − 2p), making p-chlorophenol slightly more acidic than p-fluorophenol!
Q44.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the compounds and operative electronic effect: Compounds A (2-chlorocyclohexanol), B (4-fluorocyclohexanol), and C (3-methylcyclohexanol) are saturated cyclic alcohols, so their acidity is governed purely by the distance-dependent inductive ($I$) effect on the alkoxide conjugate base.
  2. Step 2 — Verify Assertion A: Although $-\text{F}$ has a stronger intrinsic $-I$ effect than $-\text{Cl}$, the inductive effect weakens sharply with distance. In A, $-\text{Cl}$ is at C−2 (adjacent to $-\text{OH}$), stabilizing the alkoxide more strongly than $-\text{F}$ at C−4 in B (two bonds farther away). In C, the $-\text{CH}_3$ group exerts a destabilizing $+I$ effect. Hence, acidity follows $\text{A} > \text{B} > \text{C}$, so Assertion A is correct.
  3. Step 3 — Verify Reason R and check causal link: Fluorine is indeed a stronger electron-withdrawing ($-I$) group than chlorine, so Reason R is also correct. However, R alone would predict $\text{B} > \text{A}$, not $\text{A} > \text{B}$; the actual reason for $\text{A} > \text{B}$ is the closer proximity of $-\text{Cl}$ to the $-\text{OH}$ group.
  4. Step 4 — Conclude the correct option: Both A and R are correct, but R is not the correct explanation of A. This matches option (a).
Q44.stepsLatex:
1. Assertion A: p-chlorophenol (A) > p-fluorophenol (B) > p-cresol (C) =⇒ True (pKa: 9.4 < 9.9 < 10.2).
2. Reason R: Fluoro is a stronger electron-withdrawing (−I) group than chloro =⇒ True.
3. However, R does NOT explain A (in fact, −I alone would predict B > A; A > B is due to F’s stronger +M
donation / d-orbital participation in Cl).
Q44.trapHtml: Classic NCERT/JEE exception: p-chlorophenol > p-fluorophenol in acidity, even though F has stronger −I!

Q45.conceptHtml: NaNO<sub>2</sub>/HCl performs electrophilic nitrosation/nitration ortho/para to −OH, and NH<sub>4</sub>SH/H<sub>2</sub>O selectively reduces the nitroso/nitro group to −NH<sub>2</sub>.
Q45.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the starting phenol: The starting compound is thymol (2-isopropyl-5-methylphenol), which has a strongly activating ortho/para-directing $-\text{OH}$ group.
  2. Step 2 — Nitrosation to form A: Treating phenol derivatives with $\text{NaNO}_2/\text{HCl}$ generates nitrous acid ($\text{HNO}_2$) and the nitrosonium ion ($\text{NO}^+$). Electrophilic aromatic nitrosation occurs selectively at the unhindered para position relative to $-\text{OH}$, giving 4-nitrosothymol as intermediate A.
  3. Step 3 — Reduction to form B: Ammonium hydrosulfide ($\text{NH}_4\text{SH}/\text{H}_2\text{O}$) acts as a mild reducing agent that reduces the nitroso group ($-\text{NO}$) cleanly to a primary amino group ($-\text{NH}_2$), leaving the phenolic $-\text{OH}$ group unchanged.
  4. Step 4 — Identify compound B: The major product B is 4-amino-2-isopropyl-5-methylphenol (4-aminothymol), which corresponds to option (a).
Q45.stepsLatex:
1. NaNO2/HCl introduces a nitroso/nitro group ortho to the −OH group (or para to −OH, directed by the
strongly activating −OH).
2. Subsequent treatment with NH4SH/H2O (selective reduction) reduces the nitro/nitroso group to −NH2, yield-
ing the aminophenol derivative ‘B‘ (option A).
Q45.trapHtml: NH<sub>4</sub>SH/H<sub>2</sub>O reduces nitro/nitroso groups to −NH<sub>2</sub> while leaving −OH untouched.

Q46.subtopic: Conversion of 2◦-Alcohol to Deuterated Alkane via Grignard
Q46.conceptHtml: R − OH <sup>−N</sup>−<sup>−aI</sup><sup>−/H</sup>−<sup>−3P</sup><sup>−O</sup><sup>−4</sup>→ R − I <sup>−M</sup>−<sup>−g,</sup><sup>−d</sup><sup>−r</sup><sup>−y</sup><sup>−e</sup><sup>−th</sup><sup>−e</sup>→<sup>r</sup> R − MgI <sup>−D</sup><sup>−2</sup><sup>−O</sup>→ R − D.
Q46.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Convert alcohol to alkyl iodide (step i): Heating $\text{NaI}$ with $\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4$ generates $\text{HI}$ in situ, which converts butan-2-ol ($\text{H}_3\text{C}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH(OH)}-\text{CH}_3$) into 2-iodobutane ($\text{H}_3\text{C}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH(I)}-\text{CH}_3$).
  2. Step 2 — Form the Grignard reagent (step ii): Treating 2-iodobutane with magnesium in dry ether inserts $\text{Mg}$ into the $\text{C}-\text{I}$ bond to yield sec-butylmagnesium iodide, $\text{H}_3\text{C}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH(MgI)}-\text{CH}_3$.
  3. Step 3 — Deuterolysis with $\text{D}_2\text{O}$ (step iii): The strongly basic carbanion-like carbon of the Grignard reagent abstracts a deuterium ion ($\text{D}^+$) from $\text{D}_2\text{O}$, replacing $-\text{MgI}$ with $-\text{D}$ to give $\text{H}_3\text{C}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH(D)}-\text{CH}_3$ (2-deuteriobutane).
  4. Step 4 — Match with the options: The product $\text{H}_3\text{C}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH(D)}-\text{CH}_3$ corresponds to option (b).
Q46.stepsLatex:
1. CH3CH2CH(OH)CH3 −N−a−I,−H−3−P−O→4 CH3CH2CH(I)CH3.
2. −M−−g,−d−r−y−e−th−e→r CH3CH2CH(MgI)CH3.
3. −D−2−O→ CH3CH2CH(D)CH3 (option B).
Q46.trapHtml: Grignard reagent + D<sub>2</sub>O replaces −MgX with −D (deuterium), NOT −OD!

Q47.conceptHtml: The rate of electrophilic aromatic substitution (EAS) increases with electron-donating (+M/ + I) groups and decreases with electron-withdrawing (−M/ − I) groups.
Q47.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the rule for EAS rate: The rate of aromatic electrophilic substitution (EAS) increases with the electron density of the benzene ring—electron-donating groups ($+M, +H, +I$) activate the ring, while electron-withdrawing groups ($-M, -I$) deactivate it.
  2. Step 2 — Analyze each ring’s direct substituents: In c ($\alpha$-tetralone), the $-\text{C}=\text{O}$ group is directly conjugated to the benzene ring and strongly deactivates it via $-M$. In a (1-tetralol), the ring is attached to two $\text{sp}^3$ carbons (mildly activating, slightly reduced by $-I$ of the benzylic $-\text{OH}$).
  3. Step 3 — Compare the strongly activated rings b and d: In b, the benzene ring has one strongly activating $+M$ group ($-\text{OH}$) directly attached along with an alkyl ring. In d, the benzene ring has two strong $+M$ electron-donating groups directly attached ($-\text{OH}$ and the ring ether oxygen $-\text{O}-$), making it the most electron-rich and fastest to react.
  4. Step 4 — Write the increasing order: Ordering from slowest to fastest gives $\text{c} < \text{a} < \text{b} < \text{d}$, which matches option (c).
Q47.stepsLatex:
Comparing the substituents on the aromatic rings (a)–(d): Ring ‘c‘ is deactivated (ketone/ester
C = O), ‘a‘ has −OH, ‘b‘ has −OH + alkyl/activating, and ‘d‘ has two strong +M groups (−OH and −O−) =⇒
increasing order: c < a < b < d (option C).
Q47.trapHtml: Strongly activating +M groups (−OH, −OR) accelerate EAS, while −M groups (−C = O, −NO<sub>2</sub>) deactivate the ring.

Q48.subtopic: Acidity Order of Alcohols & Substituted Phenols
Q48.conceptHtml: Phenols > Aliphatic alcohols (1° > 3°); within phenols, −M (−NO<sub>2</sub>) > H > +M (−OMe).
Q48.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Compare phenols vs. aliphatic alcohols: Phenols (C, D, E) are much more acidic than aliphatic alcohols (A, B) because phenoxide ions are stabilized by resonance delocalization of the negative charge into the aromatic ring.
  2. Step 2 — Rank the phenols (C, D, E): In p-nitrophenol (E), the $-\text{NO}_2$ group strongly stabilizes the phenoxide via $-M$ and $-I$ effects ($\text{p}K_a \approx 7.1$), making E the strongest acid. In p-methoxyphenol (D), the $-\text{OMe}$ group exerts a destabilizing $+M$ effect ($\text{p}K_a \approx 10.2$), making D slightly less acidic than unsubstituted phenol (C, $\text{p}K_a \approx 10.0$). Thus, $\text{E} > \text{C} > \text{D}$.
  3. Step 3 — Rank the aliphatic alcohols (A, B): Methanol (A, $\text{CH}_3\text{OH}$, $\text{p}K_a \approx 15.5$) is more acidic than tert-butanol (B, $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{COH}$, $\text{p}K_a \approx 18$) because the three methyl groups in B exert a strong $+I$ effect and sterically hinder solvation of the tert-butoxide ion. Thus, $\text{A} > \text{B}$.
  4. Step 4 — Combine the full order: Putting both groups together gives $\text{E} > \text{C} > \text{D} > \text{A} > \text{B}$, which corresponds to option (a).
Q48.stepsLatex:
• E (p-nitrophenol) > C (phenol) > D (p-methoxyphenol) > A (CH3OH) > B ((CH3)3COH).
Thus E > C > D > A > B (option A).
Q48.trapHtml: Methanol (CH<sub>3</sub>OH) is more acidic than tert-butanol due to +I effect and poorer solvation of t-BuO−.

Q49.conceptHtml: Ozonolysis of alkenes (O<sub>3</sub>, Zn/H<sub>2</sub>O) produces aldehydes and/or ketones, NOT alcohols!
Q49.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Check standard alcohol-forming methods: Hydroboration–oxidation of an alkene (option a) gives an anti-Markovnikov alcohol. Treating a ketone with a Grignard reagent ($\text{RMgBr}$) followed by hydrolysis (option b) yields a $3^\circ$ alcohol. Hydrolysis of an alkyl halide with aqueous $\text{NaOH}$ (option d) produces an alcohol via nucleophilic substitution.
  2. Step 2 — Check ozonolysis of alkenes (option c): Ozonolysis cleaves the $\text{C}=\text{C}$ double bond completely to yield aldehydes and/or ketones (under reductive workup like $\text{Zn}/\text{H}_2\text{O}$) or carboxylic acids/ketones (under oxidative workup)—it does not directly produce alcohols.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the answer: Therefore, ozonolysis of an alkene is the incorrect method for preparing alcohols, matching option (c).
Q49.stepsLatex:
Hydroboration–oxidation, ketone + RMgBr/H3O+, and alkyl halide + aq. NaOH all produce
alcohols, whereas reductive ozonolysis of alkenes yields carbonyl compounds.
Q49.trapHtml: Ozonolysis only gives alcohols if followed by a reducing agent like NaBH<sub>4</sub> or LiAlH<sub>4</sub> (not standard ozonolysis).

Q50.subtopic: Williamson Synthesis of Methyl Phenyl Ether (Anisole)
Q50.conceptHtml: Anisole (Ph − O − CH<sub>3</sub>) must be prepared from sodium phenoxide (PhO<sup>−</sup>Na<sup>+</sup>) and methyl bromide (MeBr), NOT from Ph − Br (aryl halides don’t undergo S<sub>N</sub>2).
Q50.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall Williamson ether synthesis requirements: Unsymmetrical ethers ($\text{R}-\text{O}-\text{R}'$) are prepared by an $\text{S}_\text{N}2$ attack of an alkoxide/phenoxide ion on an unhindered primary ($1^\circ$) alkyl halide.
  2. Step 2 — Compare the two retrosynthetic pairs for anisole ($\text{Ph}-\text{OCH}_3$): Using sodium phenoxide ($\text{PhO}^-\text{Na}^+$) with methyl bromide ($\text{MeBr}$) works smoothly because $\text{MeBr}$ is an unhindered methyl halide ideal for $\text{S}_\text{N}2$ attack.
  3. Step 3 — Rule out the other choices: Option (c) fails because bromobenzene ($\text{Ph}-\text{Br}$) does not undergo $\text{S}_\text{N}2$ due to the partial double-bond character of the $\text{C}_{\text{sp}^2}-\text{Br}$ bond. Option (a) gives Friedel–Crafts alkylation (not ether) only with a Lewis acid, and option (d) has no good leaving group ($-\text{OH}$).
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: The suitable condition is $\text{PhO}^-\text{Na}^+, \text{MeBr}$, which corresponds to option (b).
Q50.stepsLatex:
PhO−Na+ + MeBr −S−N→2 Ph − O − CH3 + NaBr (option B). Option (C) fails because Ph − Br
has partial double-bond character in Csp2 − Br.
Q50.trapHtml: Never choose aryl halide (Ph − Br) + alkoxide for Williamson synthesis!

Q51.conceptHtml: Butan-1-ol (118°C) has a much higher boiling point than isomeric ethoxyethane (35°C) due to extensive intermolecular H-bonding in the alcohol.
Q51.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Verify Assertion A: Butan-1-ol ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$, b.p. $\approx 118^\circ\text{C}$) and ethoxyethane ($\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OC}_2\text{H}_5$, b.p. $\approx 35^\circ\text{C}$) are functional isomers with the same molar mass ($74\text{ g mol}^{-1}$), yet butan-1-ol has a much higher boiling point. Thus, Assertion A is true.
  2. Step 2 — Verify Reason R: Alcohols contain polar $-\text{OH}$ bonds capable of forming extensive intermolecular hydrogen bonds, causing strong association between molecules, whereas ethers lack $-\text{OH}$ hydrogens and rely only on weak dipole–dipole forces. Thus, Reason R is true.
  3. Step 3 — Connect R to A and conclude: Because extra thermal energy is required to break these extensive intermolecular hydrogen bonds during vaporization, Reason R directly explains Assertion A. Hence, the correct option is (c).
Q51.stepsLatex:
Both Assertion A and Reason R are true, and extensive intermolecular H-bonding directly
explains why butan-1-ol boils much higher than ethoxyethane.
Q51.trapHtml: Isomeric alcohols and ethers have the same molar mass (C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O), so H-bonding is the sole decisive factor.

Q52.subtopic: Industrial Synthesis of Methanol from Water Gas
Q52.conceptHtml: Water gas (CO + H<sub>2</sub>) + H<sub>2</sub> in the presence of a ZnO − Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> (or cobalt) catalyst at 573 − 673 K and 200 − 300 atm forms methanol (CH<sub>3</sub>OH).
Q52.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the composition of water gas: Water gas (synthesis gas / syngas) is an equimolar mixture of carbon monoxide and dihydrogen ($\text{CO} + \text{H}_2$).
  2. Step 2 — Apply catalytic hydrogenation of $\text{CO}$: As given in NCERT (Hydrogen / Alcohols), heating water gas with additional $\text{H}_2$ in the presence of a cobalt catalyst (or $\text{ZnO}-\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_3$ at high temperature and pressure) produces methanol: $\text{CO}(g) + 2\text{H}_2(g) \xrightarrow{\text{Co catalyst}} \text{CH}_3\text{OH}(l)$.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the answer: The product formed is methanol, corresponding to option (b).
Q52.stepsLatex: CO(g) + 2H<sub>2</sub>(g) <sup>−C</sup><sup>−o</sup><sup>−c</sup><sup>−a</sup><sup>−ta</sup><sup>−ly</sup><sup>−s</sup>→<sup>t</sup> CH<sub>3</sub>OH(l) (Methanol, option B).
Q52.trapHtml: Direct NCERT Alcohols preparation fact: water gas → methanol (wood spirit).

Q53.conceptHtml: At the meta position, only the inductive (−I/ + I) effect operates; −NO<sub>2</sub> has the strongest −I effect, stabilising the phenoxide ion most.
Q53.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the four phenols: The options are (A) m-cresol ($m$-methylphenol), (B) m-nitrophenol, (C) unsubstituted phenol, and (D) m-chlorophenol.
  2. Step 2 — Apply the inductive effect at the meta position: Substituents at the meta position do not conjugate directly with the $-\text{O}^-$ charge of the phenoxide ion, so acidity is controlled primarily by the inductive ($I$) effect.
  3. Step 3 — Compare the substituent strengths: The $-\text{CH}_3$ group in (A) is electron-donating ($+I$), weakening acidity below phenol (C). Both $-\text{Cl}$ in (D) and $-\text{NO}_2$ in (B) are electron-withdrawing ($-I$), stabilizing the phenoxide ion; since $-\text{NO}_2$ has a much stronger $-I$ effect than $-\text{Cl}$, m-nitrophenol is the strongest acid.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: The strongest acid is m-nitrophenol, which corresponds to option (b).
Q53.stepsLatex:
Comparing m-cresol (+I), m-nitrophenol (strong −I), phenol, and m-chlorophenol (weaker
−I): m-nitrophenol (option B) is the strongest acid.
Q53.trapHtml: At the meta position, resonance (M) does not operate—rank purely by −I strength (−NO<sub>2</sub> > −Cl > −H > −CH<sub>3</sub>).

Q54.conceptHtml: Triphenylmethyl chloride ((C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>)<sub>3</sub>C − Cl) forms an exceptionally stable 3° benzylic carbocation, so it reacts via S<sub>N</sub>1: Rate = k[(C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>)<sub>3</sub>C − Cl]1.
Q54.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the substrate and mechanism: The reactant is triphenylmethyl chloride (trityl chloride, $(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5)_3\text{C}-\text{Cl}$). Upon ionization, it forms the triphenylmethyl carbocation $(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5)_3\text{C}^+$, which is exceptionally stabilized by resonance across three phenyl rings.
  2. Step 2 — Determine the rate law: Because the carbocation is highly stable and the carbon center is sterically bulky, substitution by $\text{OH}^-$ proceeds exclusively via the $\text{S}_\text{N}1$ mechanism. The slow, rate-determining step is unimolecular ionization of the substrate: $\text{Rate} = k[(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5)_3\text{C}-\text{Cl}]$.
  3. Step 3 — Match the rate law to the graphs: The rate is first-order (linearly proportional, straight line passing through the origin) with respect to $[(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5)_3\text{C}-\text{Cl}]$ and zero-order (independent) with respect to both $[\text{OH}^-]$ and $[\text{Pyridine}]$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: Graph (A) correctly shows a straight line through the origin for $\text{rate}$ vs. $[(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5)_3\text{C}-\text{Cl}]$. Hence, the correct option is (a).
Q54.stepsLatex:
In an SN1 reaction, the rate is directly proportional (linear graph passing through the origin)
to the substrate concentration [(C6H5)3C − Cl] and independent of [OH−] or [Pyridine]. This matches graph (A).
Q54.trapHtml: Read the x-axis labels carefully: (A) and (D) both have [(C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>)<sub>3</sub>C − Cl], but (A) is linear (order = 1) while (D) is zero-order!

Q55.subtopic: Ease of Acid-Catalysed Dehydration of Alcohols
Q55.conceptHtml: Rate of E1 dehydration parallels the stability of the resulting carbocation / conjugated alkene.
Q55.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Relate dehydration rate to carbocation & product stability: Acid-catalyzed dehydration of alcohols proceeds via carbocation formation; the faster the carbocation forms and the more stable the resulting product, the higher the rate of dehydration.
  2. Step 2 — Compare compounds b, d, and c: Compound b (cyclohexa-2,4-dien-1-ol) forms a doubly conjugated pentadienyl carbocation and immediately dehydrates to aromatic benzene, giving a huge thermodynamic driving force (fastest). Compound d (cyclohex-2-en-1-ol) forms a resonance-stabilized allylic carbocation and conjugated cyclohexa-1,3-diene (second fastest). Compound c (cyclohex-3-en-1-ol) forms an isolated, non-allylic $2^\circ$ carbocation (third).
  3. Step 3 — Place phenol (a): In phenol (a), the $\text{C}_{\text{sp}^2}-\text{OH}$ bond has partial double-bond character due to resonance, and breaking it would form an extremely unstable phenyl cation, so it resists dehydration (slowest).
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the decreasing order: The decreasing order of dehydration rate is $\text{b} > \text{d} > \text{c} > \text{a}$, which matches option (b).
Q55.stepsLatex:
Comparing the carbocation stability and conjugation of the resulting alkenes: ‘b‘ forms a
conjugated cyclohexadiene (allylic carbocation, fastest); ‘d‘ forms a conjugated/allylic or 3◦-like stabilised system;
‘c‘ is a 2◦ cyclohexanol with an electron-withdrawing/less stabilised double bond; ‘a‘ is unsubstituted cyclohexanol
(Wait: ‘b‘ > ‘d‘ > ‘c‘ > ‘a‘, option B).
Q55.trapHtml: Allylic/conjugated carbocations dehydrate far faster than simple 2° cyclic alcohols.

Q56.subtopic: Bromination of Phenol in Low-Polarity Solvent (CS2/CHCl3)
Q56.conceptHtml: C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>6</sub>O burning with a sooty flame is phenol; bromination in a low-polarity solvent (CS<sub>2</sub> or CHCl<sub>3</sub>) gives p-bromophenol as the major product in high yield.
Q56.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify compound A: The molecular formula $\text{C}_6\text{H}_6\text{O}$ combined with a sooty flame (characteristic of aromatic compounds with a high carbon-to-hydrogen ratio) identifies compound A as phenol ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH}$).
  2. Step 2 — Understand the solvent effect in bromination: In a polar solvent like water, phenol partially ionizes to the hyper-activated phenoxide ion, giving 2,4,6-tribromophenol. In a low-polarity solvent (such as $\text{CS}_2$ or $\text{CHCl}_3$ at $273\text{ K}$), ionization is suppressed, so phenol undergoes clean monobromination.
  3. Step 3 — Determine regioselectivity (ortho vs. para): Because the para position is much less sterically hindered than the ortho positions adjacent to $-\text{OH}$, 4-bromophenol (p-bromophenol) is obtained in high yield as the major product B.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: Structure (D) represents 4-bromophenol, so the correct option is (d).
Q56.stepsLatex:
In CS2/CHCl3, phenol does not ionise to phenoxide, so monobromination occurs preferentially
at the less sterically hindered para position to give 4-bromophenol (option D).
Q56.trapHtml: Br<sub>2</sub>/H<sub>2</sub>O gives 2, 4, 6-tribromophenol, whereas Br<sub>2</sub>/CS<sub>2</sub> or CHCl<sub>3</sub> gives p-bromophenol!

Q57.subtopic: pKa Order of Phenol, p-Nitrophenol, p-Aminophenol & p-Cresol
Q57.conceptHtml: Higher acidity =⇒ lower pK<sub>a</sub>. Electron-donating groups (−NH<sub>2</sub> > −CH<sub>3</sub>) increase pK<sub>a</sub>; −NO<sub>2</sub> decreases pK<sub>a</sub>.
Q57.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall that higher $\text{p}K_a$ means weaker acid: Electron-withdrawing groups increase acidity (lower $\text{p}K_a$), whereas electron-donating groups decrease acidity (higher $\text{p}K_a$).
  2. Step 2 — Identify the substituent effects at the para position: Compound c ($p$-nitrophenol) has a strong $-M, -I$ group ($-\text{NO}_2$), making it the strongest acid (lowest $\text{p}K_a$). Compound a (phenol) is the reference.
  3. Step 3 — Compare the electron-donating groups (d vs. b): Compound d ($p$-isopropylphenol) has a weak electron-donating alkyl group ($+I$/hyperconjugation), so it is slightly less acidic than phenol. Compound b ($p$-dimethylaminophenol) has $-\text{N(CH}_3)_2$, which exerts a very strong $+M$ electron-donating effect, strongly destabilizing the phenoxide ion and making it the weakest acid (highest $\text{p}K_a$).
  4. Step 4 — Write the $\text{p}K_a$ order: Acidity order is $\text{c} > \text{a} > \text{d} > \text{b}$, so the reverse order gives $\text{p}K_a$: $\text{b} > \text{d} > \text{a} > \text{c}$. This matches option (c).
Q57.stepsLatex:
Acidity order: ‘c‘ (p-nitrophenol, −M) > ‘a‘ (phenol) > ‘d‘ (p-cresol, +I/ + H) > ‘b‘ (p-
aminophenol, strong +M). Reversing for pKa: b > d > a > c (option C).
Q57.trapHtml: Check whether the question asks for K<sub>a</sub> (acidity) or pK<sub>a</sub> (pK<sub>a</sub> order is the reverse of acidity)!

Q58.conceptHtml: Protonation of −OH and loss of H<sub>2</sub>O forms a 2° carbocation, which undergoes 1, 2-methyl shift to a 3° carbocation, followed by Zaitsev elimination.
Q58.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Protonation and initial carbocation formation: The starting alcohol is 1-(1-methylcyclopentyl)ethan-1-ol. In acidic medium ($\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$), the $-\text{OH}$ group is protonated and leaves as $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ to generate a $2^\circ$ carbocation directly adjacent to the 5-membered cyclopentane ring.
  2. Step 2 — Ring expansion to relieve strain: A ring bond of the 5-membered ring migrates to the adjacent $2^\circ$ carbocation center, expanding the ring into a strain-free 6-membered cyclohexane ring and shifting the positive charge onto the $3^\circ$ carbon bearing the original methyl group (forming the 1,2-dimethylcyclohexyl carbocation).
  3. Step 3 — Zaitsev elimination: Loss of a $\beta$-proton from the adjacent methine ($-\text{CH(CH}_3)-$) carbon produces the most substituted, thermodynamically most stable tetrasubstituted alkene: 1,2-dimethylcyclohexene.
  4. Step 4 — Match with the options: 1,2-Dimethylcyclohexene is depicted in structure (C). Hence, the correct option is (c).
Q58.stepsLatex:
In 2, 2-dimethylcyclohexan-1-ol, protonation and loss of H2O with H3O+ gives a 2◦ carbocation
at C1. A 1, 2-methyl shift from C2 to C1 generates a stable 3◦ carbocation at C2, which eliminates H+ to give the
tetrasubstituted alkene 1, 2-dimethylcyclohexene (option C).
Q58.trapHtml: Never eliminate directly without checking for a 1, 2-methyl shift from an adjacent quaternary carbon!

Q59.subtopic: Increasing pKa Order of Substituted Phenols
Q59.conceptHtml: Increasing pK<sub>a</sub> means decreasing acidity: 2, 4-dinitrophenol < 4-nitrophenol < 3-chlorophenol < phenol < 2, 4, 5-trimethylphenol.
Q59.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Relate $\text{p}K_a$ to acidity: Increasing order of $\text{p}K_a$ means arranging the phenols from strongest acid (lowest $\text{p}K_a$) to weakest acid (highest $\text{p}K_a$).
  2. Step 2 — Rank the electron-withdrawing substituted phenols (A, B, E): (A) 2,4-Dinitrophenol has two $-\text{NO}_2$ groups at ortho and para positions (strongest acid, $\text{p}K_a \approx 4.0$). (B) 4-Nitrophenol has one para $-\text{NO}_2$ ($-M, -I$; $\text{p}K_a \approx 7.1$). (E) 3-Chlorophenol has a meta $-\text{Cl}$ exerting only a moderate $-I$ effect ($\text{p}K_a \approx 9.0$).
  3. Step 3 — Place phenol (D) and electron-donating trimethylphenol (C): (D) Unsubstituted phenol has $\text{p}K_a \approx 10.0$. (C) 2,4,5-Trimethylphenol has three electron-donating methyl groups ($+I$/hyperconjugation) that destabilize the phenoxide ion, making it the weakest acid (highest $\text{p}K_a > 10.5$).
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the increasing $\text{p}K_a$ order: The order from lowest to highest $\text{p}K_a$ is (A), (B), (E), (D), (C), which matches option (d).
Q59.stepsLatex:
Rank from most acidic (lowest pKa) to least acidic (highest pKa): (A) 2, 4-dinitrophenol
(−M ×2) < (B) 4-nitrophenol (−M) < (E) 3-chlorophenol (−I) < (D) Phenol < (C) 2, 4, 5-trimethylphenol (+I ×3).
Order: (A), (B), (E), (D), (C) (option D).
Q59.trapHtml: Double-check “increasing pK<sub>a</sub>” = strongest acid first!

Q60.conceptHtml: Protonation of −OH forms a 2° carbocation adjacent to a gem-dimethyl carbon; 1, 2-methyl shift yields a 3° carbocation and the tetrasubstituted Zaitsev alkene.
Q60.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Form the initial $2^\circ$ carbocation: Heating 2,2,6-trimethylcyclohexanol with concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ protonates the $-\text{OH}$ group and eliminates $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ to generate a $2^\circ$ carbocation at C−1.
  2. Step 2 — Carbocation rearrangement via 1,2-methyl shift: A 1,2-methyl shift from the quaternary C−2 carbon (which carries two methyl groups) to C−1 converts the $2^\circ$ carbocation into a more stable $3^\circ$ carbocation at C−2 (with methyl groups now at C−1, C−2, and C-6).
  3. Step 3 — Zaitsev deprotonation: Loss of a proton from C−1 yields the most substituted, thermodynamically favored tetrasubstituted alkene, 1,2,3-trimethylcyclohexene (whereas a hydride shift from C-6 would only yield a trisubstituted alkene).
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the answer: 1,2,3-Trimethylcyclohexene is shown in option (d).
Q60.stepsLatex:
Upon heating with conc. H2SO4, the 2◦ alcohol protonates and loses H2O to form a 2◦ carboca-
tion, which undergoes 1, 2-methyl shift to a 3◦ carbocation and eliminates H+ to give the most substituted endocyclic
alkene (option D).
Q60.trapHtml: Always check the position of the two methyl groups in the product: 1, 2-shift separates the gem-dimethyl into a 1, 2-dimethyl alkene!

Q61.conceptHtml: Industrial phenol synthesis: Cumene (isopropylbenzene) is air-oxidised to cumene hydroperoxide (Ph − C(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> − O − O − H), then cleaved with H+ to phenol + acetone.
Q61.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Recall the industrial cumene process: Phenol is manufactured commercially from cumene (isopropylbenzene, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5-\text{CH(CH}_3)_2$) in two stages: aerial oxidation followed by acid-catalyzed cleavage.
  2. Step 2 — Identify the aerial oxidation intermediate: Passing air ($\text{O}_2$) through cumene oxidizes the weak tertiary benzylic $\text{C}-\text{H}$ bond via a free-radical chain mechanism to form cumene hydroperoxide, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5-\text{C(CH}_3)_2-\text{O}-\text{O}-\text{H}$.
  3. Step 3 — Confirm the subsequent step and answer: Acid hydrolysis ($\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4/\text{H}_2\text{O}$) then cleaves cumene hydroperoxide into phenol and acetone. Structure (D) depicts cumene hydroperoxide, so the correct option is (d).
Q61.stepsLatex:
Aerial oxidation inserts O2 into the benzylic C − H bond of cumene to form cumene hydroper-
oxide (option D).
Q61.trapHtml: Look for the −O − O − H hydroperoxide linkage at the benzylic carbon!

Q62.subtopic: HBr/∆ Reactivity: Benzylic Alcohol vs. Phenolic Ether
Q62.conceptHtml: With HBr/∆: (1) Aliphatic/benzylic −CH<sub>2</sub>OH converts to −CH<sub>2</sub>Br while phenolic −OH stays intact; (2) Aryl–alkyl ether (−OCH<sub>3</sub>) cleaves to phenolic −OH!
Q62.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Analyze the first reaction (to form A): The substrate 3-(hydroxymethyl)phenol has a phenolic $-\text{OH}$ and a benzylic alcohol ($-\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$). With $\text{HBr}/\Delta$, the benzylic $-\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ readily undergoes nucleophilic substitution to form $-\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$, while the phenolic $\text{C}_{\text{sp}^2}-\text{O}$ bond cannot break due to partial double-bond character. Thus, A is 3-(bromomethyl)phenol.
  2. Step 2 — Analyze the second reaction (to form B): The substrate 3-methoxyphenol contains a phenolic $-\text{OH}$ and an aryl methyl ether ($-\text{OCH}_3$). Upon heating with $\text{HBr}$, protonation of the ether oxygen followed by $\text{S}_\text{N}2$ attack of $\text{Br}^-$ on the methyl carbon cleaves the $\text{O}-\text{CH}_3$ bond (never the $\text{C}_{\text{aryl}}-\text{O}$ bond), producing $-\text{OH}$ and $\text{CH}_3\text{Br}$.
  3. Step 3 — Identify B and match the option: Product B is benzene-1,3-diol (resorcinol). The pair A = 3-(bromomethyl)phenol and B = benzene-1,3-diol corresponds to option (c).
Q62.stepsLatex:
1. First reaction (4-hydroxybenzyl alcohol + HBr/∆): Benzylic −CH2OH undergoes nucleophilic substitution to
−CH2Br, while phenolic −OH does not react =⇒ ‘A’ = 4-(bromomethyl)phenol.
2. Second reaction (4-methoxyphenol + HBr/∆): −OCH3 cleaves to −OH + CH3Br =⇒ ‘B’ = hydroquinone
(benzene-1, 4-diol).
Matches option (C).
Q62.trapHtml: Phenolic −OH NEVER converts to −Br with HBr, whereas benzylic −CH<sub>2</sub>OH and −OCH<sub>3</sub> both react!

Q63.subtopic: Stoichiometry of Phenol + Zn Reduction with Yield
Q63.conceptHtml: C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH + Zn <sup>−∆</sup>→ C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>6</sub> + ZnO (1: 1 molar stoichiometry).
Q63.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Write the balanced reaction: Heating phenol with zinc dust reduces it to benzene (product X) in a $1:1$ molar ratio: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH} + \text{Zn} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \text{C}_6\text{H}_6\text{ (X)} + \text{ZnO}$.
  2. Step 2 — Calculate initial moles of phenol: Molar mass of phenol ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_6\text{O}$) $= 6(12) + 6(1) + 16 = 94\text{ g mol}^{-1}$. Therefore, moles of phenol $= \frac{4.7}{94} = 0.05\text{ mol}$.
  3. Step 3 — Apply the $60\%$ completion yield: Moles of benzene (X) formed $= 0.05 \times \frac{60}{100} = 0.03\text{ mol} = 3 \times 10^{-2}\text{ mol}$.
  4. Step 4 — Confirm the numerical answer: Expressing the answer in the form $\_\_ \times 10^{-2}$ gives 3.

Q64.subtopic: Nitration of Phenol & Oxygen Mass Percentage Change
Q64.conceptHtml: Phenol + dil. HNO<sub>3</sub> at 298 K gives o- and p-nitrophenol; the steam-volatile compound (X) is o-nitrophenol (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>NO<sub>3</sub>).
Q64.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the steam-volatile compound (X): Nitration of phenol with dilute $\text{HNO}_3$ at $298\text{ K}$ gives a mixture of o-nitrophenol and p-nitrophenol. Upon steam distillation, o-nitrophenol (X) distills over because it forms intramolecular hydrogen bonds (making it steam-volatile), whereas p-nitrophenol forms intermolecular H-bonds.
  2. Step 2 — Calculate mass percentage of oxygen in phenol: For phenol ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_6\text{O}$), molar mass $= 6(12) + 6(1) + 16 = 94\text{ g mol}^{-1}$. Thus, $\%\text{O in phenol} = \frac{16}{94} \times 100 \approx 17.021\%$.
  3. Step 3 — Calculate mass percentage of oxygen in o-nitrophenol (X): For o-nitrophenol ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NO}_3$), molar mass $= 6(12) + 5(1) + 14 + 3(16) = 139\text{ g mol}^{-1}$, and total mass of oxygen $= 48\text{ g}$. Thus, $\%\text{O in X} = \frac{48}{139} \times 100 \approx 34.532\%$.
  4. Step 4 — Find the increase in percentage of oxygen: Increase $= 34.532\% - 17.021\% = 17.511\% \approx 175 \times 10^{-1}\%$. Hence, the numerical answer is 175.
