Q65.subtopic: Multi-Step Synthesis: Protection with Ethylene Glycol &
Q65.conceptHtml: Excess CrO<sub>3</sub> oxidises 1° alcohol → −COOH and 2° alcohol → ketone. Ethylene glycol (H+) protects the ketone as a cyclic ketal; CH<sub>3</sub>MgI only deprotonates −COOH, and H<sub>3</sub>O+ deprotects the ketal back to ketone.
Q65.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Oxidation with excess $\text{CrO}_3$ (to form P): The starting diol, 2-(hydroxymethyl)cyclopentan-1-ol, has a $2^\circ$ ring alcohol and a $1^\circ$ $-\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ group. Anhydrous $\text{CrO}_3$ oxidizes the $2^\circ$ alcohol to a ketone ($=\text{O}$) and the $1^\circ$ alcohol to an aldehyde ($-\text{CHO}$), giving 2-oxocyclopentanecarbaldehyde (P).
  2. Step 2 — Chemoselective acetal protection (to form Q): With $1$ mole of ethylene glycol ($\text{HOCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$) and $\text{H}^+$, the more reactive aldehyde ($-\text{CHO}$) is selectively protected as a cyclic acetal, leaving the ring ketone unprotected (Q).
  3. Step 3 — Grignard addition, deprotection, and $\text{NaBH}_4$ reduction (Q $\to$ R $\to$ S): First, $\text{CH}_3\text{MgI}$ adds to the unprotected ring ketone to form a $3^\circ$ alcohol (adding one $-\text{CH}_3$ group), and subsequent $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$ workup hydrolyzes (deprotects) the cyclic acetal back to $-\text{CHO}$ to give R. Next, $\text{NaBH}_4/\text{H}_2\text{O}$ reduces $-\text{CHO}$ back to $-\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$, yielding S = 2-(hydroxymethyl)-1-methylcyclopentan-1-ol ($\text{C}_7\text{H}_{14}\text{O}_2$).
  4. Step 4 — Calculate the mass of $0.1\text{ mol}$ of S: Molar mass of $\text{C}_7\text{H}_{14}\text{O}_2 = 7(12) + 14(1) + 2(16) = 84 + 14 + 32 = 130\text{ g mol}^{-1}$. Therefore, $0.1\text{ mol}$ of S weighs $0.1 \times 130 = 13\text{ g}$. Hence, the numerical answer is 13.
Q65.stepsLatex:
1. P = 2-oxocyclopentanecarboxylic acid (C6H8O3).
2. Q = cyclic ketal of ketone + −COOH.
3. Q −(−1)−C−H−−3M−−gI−(−2−) −H−3O−→+ R (ketal is inert to Grignard; H3O+ deprotects ketal back to R = P).
4. R −N−a−B−H−4−, −H−2O→ S = 2-hydroxycyclopentanecarboxylic acid (C6H10O3, since NaBH4 reduces ketone but NOT
−COOH).
5. Molar mass of S = 6(12) + 10(1) + 3(16) = 130 g mol−1 =⇒ 0.1 mol weighs 0.1 × 130 = 13 g.
Q65.trapHtml: NaBH<sub>4</sub> does NOT reduce carboxylic acids, and cyclic ketals are completely stable to Grignard reagents!

Q66.subtopic: Sulphonation + Nitration of Phenol to Picric Acid
Q66.conceptHtml: Phenol + conc. H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> → Phenol-2, 4-disulphonic acid (Product A); further + conc. HNO<sub>3</sub> → 2, 4, 6- trinitrophenol (Picric acid, Product B).
Q66.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify Product A (sulfonation of phenol): In the standard NCERT preparation of picric acid, phenol is first treated with concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ to give phenol-2,4-disulfonic acid ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_3(\text{OH})(\text{SO}_3\text{H})_2$, Product A).
  2. Step 2 — Count oxygen atoms in Product A: Product A has $1$ oxygen atom in the $-\text{OH}$ group and $2 \times 3 = 6$ oxygen atoms in the two $-\text{SO}_3\text{H}$ groups, giving $1 + 6 = 7$ oxygen atoms.
  3. Step 3 — Identify Product B and count its oxygen atoms: Treating Product A with concentrated $\text{HNO}_3$ replaces the $-\text{SO}_3\text{H}$ groups and nitrates the remaining ortho position to form 2,4,6-trinitrophenol (picric acid), $\text{C}_6\text{H}_2(\text{OH})(\text{NO}_2)_3$. Product B has $1$ oxygen atom in $-\text{OH}$ and $3 \times 2 = 6$ oxygen atoms in the three $-\text{NO}_2$ groups, giving $1 + 6 = 7$ oxygen atoms.
  4. Step 4 — Sum the oxygen atoms: Total oxygen atoms in Product A and Product B $= 7 + 7 = 14$. Hence, the numerical answer is 14.
Q66.stepsLatex:
1. Product A (C6H3(OH)(SO3H)2): 1 + 2(3) = 7 oxygen atoms.
2. Product B (C6H2(OH)(NO2)3, picric acid): 1 + 3(2) = 7 oxygen atoms.
3. Total sum of oxygen atoms = 7 + 7 = 14.
Q66.trapHtml: Remember Product A is the 2,4-disulphonic acid (7 O atoms), not monosulphonic acid!

Q67.conceptHtml: Protonation of −OH and loss of H<sub>2</sub>O triggers ring-expansion / skeletal shift to a 3° carbocation; count the α-H atoms attached to carbons adjacent to C+.
Q67.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Form the initial $2^\circ$ carbocation: Protonation of the $-\text{OH}$ group by $\text{HBr}$ followed by loss of $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ generates a $2^\circ$ carbocation on the 5-membered ring (having only $2\ \alpha\text{-H}$), directly adjacent to the bridgehead carbon bearing the methyl group.
  2. Step 2 — First rearrangement (1,2-methyl shift): A 1,2-methyl shift from the bridgehead carbon to the positively charged carbon produces a more stable $3^\circ$ bridgehead carbocation with $4\ \alpha\text{-H}$ ($2$ from ring $-\text{CH}_2-$, $1$ from the other bridgehead $-\text{CH}-$, and $1$ from $-\text{CH(Me)}-$).
  3. Step 3 — Second rearrangement (1,2-hydride shift): A subsequent 1,2-hydride shift from the adjacent $-\text{CH(Me)}-$ carbon back to the bridgehead carbon produces an even more stable $3^\circ$ carbocation directly attached to the methyl group, which is stabilized by $3 + 2 + 1 = 6\ \alpha\text{-hydrogens}$.
  4. Step 4 — Count total hyperconjugation structures: Including the $6$ no-bond hyperconjugating structures (one for each $\alpha\text{ C}-\text{H}$ bond) plus the $1$ original canonical carbocation structure gives $6 + 1 = 7$ hyperconjugation structures. Hence, the numerical answer is 7.
Q67.stepsLatex:
1. Loss of H2O from the protonated bicyclic alcohol gives a 2◦ carbocation on the 5-membered ring.
2. Ring expansion of the 5-membered ring to a 6-membered ring places the positive charge on the 3◦ carbon
bearing the methyl group.
3. This 3◦ carbocation is adjacent to one −CH3 (3 α-H) and two −CH2− groups (2 + 2 = 4 α-H).
4. Total hyperconjugation structures = 3 + 2 + 2 = 7.
Q67.trapHtml: Include all α-H atoms from both the methyl group and the two adjacent ring CH<sub>2</sub> groups!

Q68.conceptHtml: Active/acidic hydrogen (−OH) consumes 1 eq. of MeMgBr via acid–base reaction, and the aldehyde (−CHO) consumes 1 eq. via nucleophilic addition.
Q68.stepsHtml:
1. Step 1 — Identify the reactive sites in the starting molecule: The reactant, 4-hydroxybutanal ($\text{HO}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{CHO}$), contains two groups that react with a Grignard reagent ($\text{MeMgBr}$): an acidic hydroxyl proton ($-\text{OH}$) and an electrophilic aldehyde carbonyl ($-\text{CHO}$).
  2. Step 2 — First equivalent of $\text{MeMgBr}$ (acid–base reaction): Grignard reagents act as very strong bases. The first $y\text{ mol}$ of $\text{MeMgBr}$ reacts rapidly with the acidic $-\text{OH}$ proton to form the magnesium alkoxide ($-\text{OMgBr}$) and evolve $\text{CH}_4$ gas.
  3. Step 3 — Second equivalent of $\text{MeMgBr}$ (nucleophilic addition): Once $-\text{OH}$ is deprotonated, a second $y\text{ mol}$ of $\text{MeMgBr}$ adds nucleophilically to the $-\text{CHO}$ group to yield $-\text{CH(OMgBr)Me}$. Acidic workup ($\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$) then protonates both alkoxides to produce pentane-1,4-diol.
  4. Step 4 — Calculate the ratio $x/y$: Complete conversion of $y\text{ mol}$ of substrate requires $x = 2y\text{ mol}$ of $\text{MeMgBr}$, so $\frac{x}{y} = 2$. Hence, the numerical answer is 2.
Q68.stepsLatex:
1. 1 mol of HO − CH2 − CH2 − CHO reacts with 1 mol MeMgBr at −OH (forming −OMgBr + CH4).
2. Another 1 mol MeMgBr adds to −CHO to give −CH(OMgBr)CH3, which upon H3O+ gives the diol.
3. Thus y mol substrate requires x = 2y mol of MeMgBr =⇒ x/y = 2.
Q68.trapHtml: Always count acidic −OH groups first—they consume 1 eq. RMgX before carbonyl addition!

trapCards.title: Trap 1: Ether Cleavage (HI/HBr) & Williamson Rules
trapCards.html:
• Aryl–Alkyl Ether Csp2 − O Never Breaks (Q01, Q16, Q37, Q38, Q62): Ph − O − R + HI/HBr ALWAYS gives phenol (PhOH) + R − X, never Ph − X!
  • SN1 vs. SN2 in Alkyl Ethers (Q38): 3◦/benzylic ethers cleave via SN1 (halide goes to the 3◦/benzylic carbon); 1◦/2◦ ethers cleave via SN2 (halide goes to the smaller group).
  • Williamson E2 Trap (Q12, Q50): Never use a 2◦/3◦ halide with an alkoxide (gives alkene via E2), and never use an aryl halide (Ph − Br). Always pair 1◦ halide + 2◦/3◦/aryl oxide.

trapCards.title: Trap 2: Alcohol Dehydration, Oxidation & Grig- nard
trapCards.html:
• Cu/573 K on 3◦ Alcohol (Q02): 1◦ → aldehyde, 2◦ → ketone, but 3◦ → alkene (dehydration)!
  • Carbocation Rearrangements (Q10, Q58, Q60, Q67): Acidic hydration (H+/H2O) and dehydration (H2SO4/∆) undergo 1, 2-hydride, 1, 2-methyl, or ring- expansion shifts to the most stable carbocation + Zaitsev alkene.
  • Grignard Active-H Tax (Q68): Every −OH, −NH, or −SH consumes 1 eq. RMgX before carbonyl addition!
  • Acetylation Mass Gain (Q08): Each −OH acetylated adds ∆M = 42 g mol−1 (not 43 or 60).

trapCards.title: Trap 3: Phenol Acidity (pK<sub>a</sub>) & Solubility Traps
trapCards.html:
• Lower pKa = Stronger Acid (Q33, Q36, Q57, Q59): Read carefully whether the prompt asks for acidity (Ka) or pKa order!
  • Nitrophenol & Halophenol Exceptions (Q41, Q44): p-nitrophenol > o-nitrophenol (intramolecular H-bonding in o-isomer); p-chlorophenol > p-fluorophenol (stronger +M of F).
  • NaOH vs. NaHCO3 (Q06, Q21): Phenols dissolve in NaOH but NOT NaHCO3 (only −COOH / picric acid evolve CO2). Benzyl alcohol does not dissolve in NaOH.

trapCards.title: Trap 4: Phenol Named Reactions & EAS Condi- tions
trapCards.html:
• Reimer–Tiemann vs. Kolbe’s (Q11, Q20, Q24, Q31, Q34, Q35): CHCl3/NaOH → salicylaldehyde (o-major, separated by steam distillation); CO2/NaOH, 120◦C → salicylic acid.
  • Bromination Medium (Q28, Q56): Br2/H2O → 2, 4, 6-tribromophenol (3 eq. Br2); Br2/CS2 or CHCl3 → p-bromophenol (NO Lewis acid catalyst needed!).
  • Phenolphthalein Excess NaOH (Q04): Pink in dil. NaOH, but turns colourless in excess NaOH!
  • Phenol + Zn vs. Na2Cr2O7 (Q15, Q18, Q63): Zn/∆ reduces phenol to benzene; Na2Cr2O7/H2SO4 oxidises it to p-benzoquinone.
